SA_GK22_ksdarppu.title: Darpadalana
SA_GK22_ksdarppu.author: Kṣemendra
SA_GK22_ksdarppu.summary: The Darpadalana ('Crushing of Pride') is a seven-chapter satirical and didactic poem (upadeśakāvya) composed by Kṣemendra. Each chapter (vicāra) targets one of seven traditional causes of conceit (madahetavaḥ)—noble birth (kula), wealth (vitta), erudition (śruta), physical beauty (rūpa), valor (śaurya), munificence (dāna), and asceticism (tapas)—demonstrating through general moral reflections and illustrative narratives (dṛṣṭānta) how excessive vanity leads to downfall and ridicule.
SA_GK22_ksdarppu.attribution: Authored by Kṣemendra. Kṣemendra explicitly names himself in the opening stanza (1.3).
SA_GK22_ksdarppu.edition: Durgāprasāda and Kāśīnātha Pāṇḍuraṅga Paraba (eds.), Darpadalana of Kṣemendra, in Kāvyamālā, Part VI, Bombay, 1890, pp. 66–118.
SA_GK22_ksdarppu.coverage: complete — Complete text in seven sections (vicāras), running from KDarp_1.1 to KDarp_7.73.

SA_GK19_bhattiku.title: Rāvaṇavadha
SA_GK19_bhattiku.author: Bhaṭṭi
SA_GK19_bhattiku.summary: The Rāvaṇavadha (widely known as Bhaṭṭikāvya) is a 22-canto classical mahākāvya composed by Bhaṭṭi at Valabhī under King Śrīdharasena. It narrates the story of the Rāmāyaṇa from Rāma's birth to his victory and coronation, serving to illustrate grammar and poetic usage.
SA_GK19_bhattiku.attribution: Attributed to the poet Bhaṭṭi. Verse 22.35 records that the poem was composed at Valabhī during the reign of King Śrīdharasena.
SA_GK19_bhattiku.coverage: complete — Complete: 22 sargas, ending with Bhaṭṭi's closing verses 22.33–35 (composed at Valabhī under Śrīdharasena). Root text only.

SA_GSP29_nyayasiddhanjana.title: Nyāyasiddhāñjana
SA_GSP29_nyayasiddhanjana.author: Vedānta Deśika
SA_GSP29_nyayasiddhanjana.summary: The Nyāyasiddhāñjana ('Collyrium of Nyāya Logic / Conclusions') is a foundational ontological prakaraṇa of the Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta tradition composed by Vedānta Deśika. Functioning as the ontological counterpart to his epistemological treatise Nyāyapariśuddhi, the work classifies and analyzes knowable reality (prameya) across six chapters (paricchedas): material substance (triguṇadravya/jaḍadravya), individual souls (jīva), God (īśvara), transcendental eternal realm (nityavibhūti), consciousness/cognition (buddhi/dharmabhūtajñāna), and non-substance/attributes (adravya). It adapts and reforms Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika dialectic within Rāmānuja's metaphysics and is historically indispensable for citing and preserving substantial fragments of lost early Viśiṣṭādvaita texts, particularly Nāthamuni's Nyāyatattva.
SA_GSP29_nyayasiddhanjana.attribution: Attributed to Vedānta Deśika (Veṅkaṭanātha) in scholarly literature.
SA_GSP29_nyayasiddhanjana.coverage: unclear — Empty placeholder stub; the catalog entry contains 0 segments and 0 characters.

SA_GE07_bhg.title: Bhagavadgītā
SA_GE07_bhg.summary: The Bhagavadgītā ('Song of the Lord') is an eighteen-chapter philosophical dialogue embedded within the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata (adhyāyas 23–40 in the critical edition). Set on the battlefield of Kurukṣetra on the brink of fratricidal war, the warrior Arjuna is overcome by moral despondency and is instructed by his charioteer Kṛṣṇa, revealed as the supreme deity. The text articulates a seminal synthesis of disciplined action without attachment to fruits (karma-yoga), metaphysical discernment (jñāna-yoga), and devotion (bhakti-yoga), culminating in the cosmic revelation of Kṛṣṇa's Viśvarūpa. As one of the three foundational authorities (prasthānatrayī) of Vedānta, it has generated continuous commentary across Indian philosophical schools and remains central to Hindu religious thought.

SA_GE07_hv_apppu.title: Harivaṃśa (Appendix I)
SA_GE07_hv_apppu.summary: Appendix I of the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute (BORI) Critical Edition of the Harivaṃśa, the supplementary epic (khila) to the Mahābhārata detailing the genealogy, incarnations, and deeds of Kṛṣṇa. During critical editing by P. L. Vaidya, 45 extended narrative and liturgical passages found only in specific regional recensions—including substantial episodes like the Pārijātaharaṇa, battle sequences, and devotional stotras—were excluded from the critically reconstructed archetype and collected in Appendix I. These materials are essential witnesses to the regional expansion and sectarian development of Kṛṣṇa-centered literature across the first and early second millennia CE.
SA_GE07_hv_apppu.attribution: Traditionally ascribed to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa as the khila ('supplement') to the Mahābhārata. Author field left empty in accordance with cataloguing conventions for epic and puranic literature.

SA_GE07_hv_conpu.title: Harivaṃśa
SA_GE07_hv_conpu.summary: The Harivaṃśa ('Genealogy of Hari') is the canonical supplement (khila) to the Mahābhārata, bridging late epic narrative with the early Purāṇas. Divided into three sections—Harivaṃśaparvan (cosmology and ancestral genealogies of the Solar and Lunar dynasties), Viṣṇuparvan (the earliest continuous biography of Kṛṣṇa, covering his pastoral youth in Vraja/Gokula and subsequent heroic feats), and Bhaviṣyaparvan (eschatology of the Kaliyuga, cosmogony, and devotional hymns)—it serves as the foundational narrative source for Kṛṣṇa's pastoral childhood (bālalīlā) across classical Vaiṣṇavism.
SA_GE07_hv_conpu.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa as the khila (supplement) to the Mahābhārata.
SA_GE07_hv_conpu.edition: The Harivaṁśa: Being the Khila or Supplement to the Mahābhārata (Critical Edition), edited by Parashuram Lakshman Vaidya. Poona: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, 1969.

SA_GE07_mbh_02_u.title: Mahābhārata: Sabhāparvan
SA_GE07_mbh_02_u.summary: The Sabhāparvan ('Book of the Assembly Hall') constitutes the second book of the Mahābhārata, comprising 72 adhyāyas in the Pune Critical Edition. It recounts the construction of the magnificent assembly hall at Indraprastha by the dānava Maya, King Yudhiṣṭhira's imperial Rājasūya sacrifice, and Kṛṣṇa's slaying of Śiśupāla. The narrative culminates in the fateful dice match rigged by Śakuni and Duryodhana, the public humiliation of Draupadī, and the subsequent banishment of the Pāṇḍavas to twelve years of exile and a thirteenth year incognito.
SA_GE07_mbh_02_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Sabhāparvan in 72 adhyāyas (adhyāyas 1–72, verses 02,001.001 through 02,072.036), including supplementary starred passages (*0001 through *0630).
translations: Kisari Mohan Ganguli (trans.), The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa Translated into English.. (English)

SA_GE07_mbh_03_u.title: Mahābhārata (book 3: Āraṇyakaparvan)
SA_GE07_mbh_03_u.summary: The Āraṇyakaparvan ('Book of the Forest', traditionally also known as the Vanaparvan) is the third and one of the longest books of the Mahābhārata. It chronicles the twelve years of forest exile endured by the five Pāṇḍava brothers and Draupadī following Yudhiṣṭhira's defeat in the game of dice. During this period, the narrative incorporates numerous celebrated inset episodes (upākhyānas) told to comfort and instruct the exiles, including the tales of Nala and Damayantī (Nalopākhyāna), Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, and Sāvitrī and Satyavān, as well as an abridged version of the Rāma story (Rāmopākhyāna). The book also details extensive pilgrimage circuits across sacred geography (Tīrthayātrā), divine encounters yielding celestial weapons for Arjuna, and the philosophical interrogation of Yudhiṣṭhira by the Yakṣa (Yakṣapraśna).
SA_GE07_mbh_03_u.edition: Vishnu S. Sukthankar (ed.), Mahābhārata: The Āraṇyakaparvan, Poona: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute.
SA_GE07_mbh_03_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of Book 3 (Āraṇyakaparvan) across all 299 adhyāyas (3.1.1 to 3.299.29) according to the BORI Critical Edition, including starred manuscript passages (*-lines) and curly-bracket insertions, but omitting Appendix 21A as noted in the source header.
translations: Kisari Mohan Ganguli (trans.), The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa Translated into English Prose, Pratap Chandra Roy (pub.)–. (English)

SA_GE07_mbh_04_u.title: Mahābhārata (book 4: Virāṭaparvan)
SA_GE07_mbh_04_u.summary: The Virāṭaparvan is the fourth book of the Mahābhārata, consisting of 67 chapters. It chronicles the thirteenth and final year of exile, which the five Pāṇḍava brothers and Draupadī are required to spend living in disguise (ajñātavāsa) without being recognized, seeking refuge at the court of King Virāṭa of Matsya. Assuming humble service personas—Yudhiṣṭhira as the courtier Kaṅka, Bhīma as the cook Ballava, Arjuna as the eunuch dance-instructor Bṛhannaḍā, Nakula and Sahadeva as stable masters, and Draupadī as the chambermaid Sairandhrī—they confront peril when the general Kīcaka attempts to violate Draupadī and is slain by Bhīma. The book reaches its climax during the dual cattle raids led by the Trigartas and the Kauravas, wherein Arjuna single-handedly routs the Kaurava forces, fulfilling their period of concealment and paving the way for diplomatic negotiations and the marriage of Abhimanyu to Princess Uttarā.
SA_GE07_mbh_04_u.edition: The Mahābhārata: For the first time critically edited: The Virāṭaparvan, Being the Fourth Book of the Mahābhārata, edited by Raghu Vira, Poona: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute.
SA_GE07_mbh_04_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the fourth book (Virāṭaparvan), comprising all 67 adhyāyas (chapters) of the Poona Critical Edition, including all starred apparatus passages (*) and Appendix I insertions (@) integrated by John D. Smith.

SA_GE07_mbh_07_u.title: Mahābhārata: Droṇaparvan
SA_GE07_mbh_07_u.summary: The Droṇaparvan is the seventh major book of the Mahābhārata, narrating days eleven through fifteen of the eighteen-day Kurukṣetra war when the Kaurava martial preceptor Droṇa commands the army after Bhīṣma's fall. Critical episodes include the deadly circular military formation (cakravyūha) in which Arjuna's teenage son Abhimanyu is trapped and killed, Arjuna's retaliatory vow culminating in the slaying of Jayadratha before sundown, an intense night engagement marked by Ghaṭotkaca's death at the hands of Karṇa, and the moral turning point wherein Yudhiṣṭhira utters the ambiguous half-truth concerning the death of Aśvatthāman, causing Droṇa to lay down his arms before being decapitated by Dhṛṣṭadyumna. The book captures the breakdown of traditional kṣatriya battlefield codes (dharmayuddha) under extreme existential stakes.
SA_GE07_mbh_07_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Droṇaparvan (Book 7 of the Mahābhārata) according to the Poona Critical Edition, comprising all 173 adhyāyas (adhyāyas 1–173; verses 07,001.001 to 07,173.107) along with the critical apparatus passages, including starred variant verses (*0001_01 through *1479_02) and Appendix I lines (marked with @).
translations: Mahabharata, Tr. by Pratapa Chandra Ray, Calcutta. (English)

SA_GE07_mbh_08_u.title: Mahābhārata (Karṇaparvan)
SA_GE07_mbh_08_u.summary: The Karṇaparvan is the eighth book of the Mahābhārata, chronicling the sixteenth and seventeenth days of the Kurukṣetra war after the death of Droṇa. It narrates Karṇa's appointment as commander-in-chief of the Kaurava army, the verbal dispute between Karṇa and his charioteer King Śalya of Madra, and Bhīmasena's slaying of Duḥśāsana to fulfill his vow. The parvan culminates in the climactic duel between Arjuna and Karṇa, ending with Karṇa's death when Arjuna shoots him while he is trying to free his sunken chariot wheel.

SA_GE07_mbh_08_u.edition: The Karṇaparvan: Being the Eighth Book of the Mahābhārata, the Great Epic of India, for the First Time Critically Edited, ed. Parashuram Lakshman Vaidya, Poona: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute (The Mahābhārata: Critical Edition).
SA_GE07_mbh_08_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Karṇaparvan (adhyāyas 1–69, concluding at verse 08,069.043 and apparatus addition *1228_02), including starred passages (*-passages) from the critical apparatus of the BORI Critical Edition; constitutes Book 8 of the eighteen parvans of the Mahābhārata.

SA_GE07_mbh_09_u.title: Mahābhārata: Śalyaparvan
SA_GE07_mbh_09_u.summary: The Śalyaparvan is the ninth book of the Mahābhārata, recounting the eighteenth and final day of the Kurukṣetra war. Following the death of Karṇa, Śalya, king of Madra, becomes the supreme commander of the surviving Kaurava forces but is slain at midday by Yudhiṣṭhira. The book contains major narrative digressions—notably Balarāma's pilgrimage along the sacred Sarasvatī river (Tīrthayātrāparvan)—and culminates in the Gadāparvan, where Bhīma mortally fells Duryodhana by smashing his thighs in a mace duel at Lake Dvaipāyana.

SA_GE07_mbh_u.title: Mahābhārata
SA_GE07_mbh_u.summary: The Mahābhārata is one of the two foundational Sanskrit epics (itihāsa) of ancient India, traditionally attributed to the sage Vyāsa. Comprising eighteen major books (parvans) and exceeding 75,000 stanzas in its Critical Edition, it centers on the bitter dynastic struggle and cataclysmic war between the Pāṇḍavas and Kauravas at Kurukṣetra. Beyond its narrative framework, the epic serves as an encyclopedic exposition of dharma, statecraft, cosmology, and soteriology, incorporating major philosophical texts such as the Bhagavadgītā, Sanatsujātīya, and the Mokṣadharmaparvan of the Śāntiparvan.

SA_GE09_ram_02_u.title: Rāmāyaṇa (books 2–3: Ayodhyākāṇḍa and Āraṇyakāṇḍa)
SA_GE09_ram_02_u.author: Vālmīki
SA_GE09_ram_02_u.summary: The Ayodhyākāṇḍa (Book 2) and Āraṇyakāṇḍa (Book 3) form the central narrative axis of the Rāmāyaṇa. In Book 2, Queen Kaikeyī's demands force King Daśaratha to abort Rāma's royal consecration and send him into fourteen-year exile with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa; Daśaratha dies of grief, and Bharata rejects the throne, governing from Nandigrāma with Rāma's wooden sandals on the seat of state. Book 3 recounts the trio's life in the Daṇḍaka forest, the mutilation of Śūrpaṇakhā and subsequent slaughter of the rākṣasa armies under Khara and Dūṣaṇa, the lure of the golden deer (Mārīca), the abduction of Sītā by Rāvaṇa, and Rāma's despairing trek toward Lake Pampā.

SA_GE09_ram_02su.title: Rāmāyaṇa (book 2: Ayodhyākāṇḍa)
SA_GE09_ram_02su.author: Vālmīki
SA_GE09_ram_02su.summary: The Ayodhyākāṇḍa forms the second book of Vālmīki's Rāmāyaṇa and depicts the succession crisis in Ayodhyā. Following Daśaratha's plan to crown Rāma as yuvarāja, Queen Kaikeyī, goaded by Mantharā, demands two boons: the exile of Rāma to the forest for fourteen years and the installation of Bharata as king. Rāma unhesitatingly departs with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, which precipitates Daśaratha's demise from grief; Bharata adamantly refuses the throne, follows Rāma to Citrakūṭa to plead for his return, and ultimately agrees to govern from Nandigrāma as regent for Rāma's wooden sandals (pādukā).
SA_GE09_ram_02su.attribution: Attributed by tradition to the poet-sage Vālmīki. The present e-text represents the textus receptus of the Southern recension as published in the Kumbhakonam edition edited by T. R. Krishnacarya.
SA_GE09_ram_02su.edition: T. R. Krishnacarya, ed., The Valmiki Ramayana: According to Southern Recension, 1905 (Repr. Delhi: Sri Satguru Publications, 1982).

It represents one of seven kāṇḍas of the complete epic.

SA_GK16_dkavy.title: Kāvyādarśa
SA_GK16_dkavy.author: Daṇḍin
SA_GK16_dkavy.summary: The Kāvyādarśa by Daṇḍin is a classical treatise on Sanskrit poetics. Comprising three chapters (paricchedas), it establishes a typology of poetic composition and outlines the poetic excellences (guṇas) (chapter 1), classifies figures of sense (arthālaṅkāra, chapter 2), and treats figures of sound (śabdālaṅkāra) and poetic flaws (doṣa, chapter 3).

SA_GK16_mamkprku.title: Kāvyaprakāśakārikāvalī
SA_GK16_mamkprku.author: Mammaṭa, Allaṭa
SA_GK16_mamkprku.summary: The Kāvyaprakāśa ('Light on Poetry') is a classical compendium of Sanskrit poetics (Alaṅkāraśāstra), composed in the late 11th century by Mammaṭa with the conclusion by Allaṭa. It treats the definition and purposes of poetry, semantic functions of words, poetic blemishes, qualities, and figures of speech. This e-text preserves the Kārikāvalī, the complete metrical core of 142 mnemonic stanzas formulating the work's doctrinal framework.
SA_GK16_mamkprku.attribution: The Kāvyaprakāśa was composed by Mammaṭa Bhaṭṭa in Kashmir; the last kārikās of the 10th ullāsa are traditionally attributed to Allaṭa/Alaka.

SA_GK19_agada.title: Āgamaḍambara
SA_GK19_agada.author: Jayanta Bhaṭṭa
SA_GK19_agada.summary: The Āgamaḍambara ('Much Ado About Religion') is a satirical and philosophical Sanskrit drama composed by the Kashmiri philosopher Jayanta Bhaṭṭa. Set during the reign of King Śaṅkaravarman of Kashmir, the drama depicts ideological debates and socio-religious friction among Vedic Mīmāṃsakas, Buddhists, Jains, Cārvākas, Kāpālikas, and antinomian Nīlāmbaras. The plot follows the zealous Vedic graduate Saṅkarṣaṇa as he campaigns to suppress heterodox movements, concluding with a state-mediated resolution that legitimizes multiple religious traditions conforming to common social morality.
SA_GK19_agada.attribution: Composed by the Kashmiri philosopher Jayanta Bhaṭṭa during the reign of King Śaṅkaravarman of Kashmir.

SA_GK19_asvbc_1u.title: Buddhacarita (cantos 1–14)
SA_GK19_asvbc_1u.author: Aśvaghoṣa
SA_GK19_asvbc_1u.summary: The Buddhacarita ('Acts of the Buddha') is a Buddhist kāvya composed by Aśvaghoṣa. It narrates the life of Gautama Buddha from his birth and early life through his departure and pursuit of awakening. In this e-text, the Sanskrit transmission ceases at canto 14.31, while Cowell's text continues with chapters 14 (to 14.91) and 15–17.

SA_GK19_asvsaunu.title: Saundarananda
SA_GK19_asvsaunu.author: Aśvaghoṣa
SA_GK19_asvsaunu.summary: The Saundarananda is an early Buddhist Sanskrit mahākāvya in 18 cantos by Aśvaghoṣa relating the conversion of Nanda, the Buddha's handsome half-brother. Deeply attached to his beautiful wife Sundarī, Nanda is drawn into the monastic saṅgha against his inclination; the Buddha then uses a pedagogical device (upāya), first showing him celestial nymphs in Indra's heaven before having him guided toward the realization that even heavenly realms are ephemeral and fraught with suffering. The second half of the epic serves as an exposition of Buddhist mental training, psychological analysis, and meditative praxis (śamatha and vipaśyanā), culminating in Nanda's attainment of arhatship. In the final verses (18.63–64), Aśvaghoṣa explicitly declares his poetic purpose: he employed the sweet ornamentation of kāvya to make the bitter medicine of liberation (mokṣa) palatable to worldly audiences.
SA_GK19_asvsaunu.attribution: Ascribed directly to Aśvaghoṣa in the concluding colophon (following verse 18.64: 'āryasuvarṇākṣīputrasya sāketakasya bhikṣor ācāryabhadantāśvaghoṣasya mahākaver mahāvādinaḥ kṛtir iyam').
SA_GK19_asvsaunu.edition: Seiren Matsunami (松濤誠廉), Memyō: Tanseinaru Nanda (馬鳴: 端正なる難陀), Tokyo: Sankibō Busshorin (山喜房佛書林), 1980.

SA_GK19_bahcar.title: Harṣacarita
SA_GK19_bahcar.author: Bāṇa
SA_GK19_bahcar.summary: The Harṣacarita ('The Deeds of Harṣa') is an ornate Sanskrit prose biography (ākhyāyikā) by court poet Bāṇabhaṭṭa celebrating King Harṣa. The work opens with an autobiographical account of Bāṇa's lineage and summons before recounting Harṣa's royal line, the demise of King Prabhākaravardhana, the death of Rājyavardhana, and Harṣa's recovery of his widowed sister Rājyaśrī from the Vindhya forest.

SA_GK19_bhall_pu.title: Bhallaṭaśataka
SA_GK19_bhall_pu.author: Bhallaṭa
SA_GK19_bhall_pu.summary: The Bhallaṭaśataka is a collection of allegorical epigrams in the anyokti mode composed by Bhallaṭa, using descriptions of natural phenomena, animals, and plants.

SA_GK19_dandkc_u.title: Daśakumāracarita
SA_GK19_dandkc_u.author: Daṇḍin
SA_GK19_dandkc_u.summary: The Daśakumāracarita ('Adventures of the Ten Princes') is a celebrated Sanskrit prose romance (gadyakāvya) by Daṇḍin, recounting the interwoven picaresque adventures of Prince Rājavāhana and his companions across India as they seek romantic conquests, wealth, and political power. Distinctive for its vivid portrayal of secular, sub-courtly, and underworld life—featuring thieves, gamblers, courtesans, corrupt ministers, ascetics, and charlatans—the work is also famous for rhetorical tours de force, notably the seventh chapter composed entirely without labial phonemes (aniroṣṭhya). The surviving text is framed by the introductory Pūrvapīṭhikā and concludes with the kathopasaṃhāra.
SA_GK19_dandkc_u.attribution: The work is attributed to Daṇḍin (attested in the headers and the final colophon: iti śrīdaṇḍinaḥ kṛtau daśakumāracarite kathopasaṃhāraḥ).
SA_GK19_dandkc_u.coverage: complete — Includes Pūrvapīṭhikā (prathamocchvāsaḥ ff.), central narrative sections, and Uttarapīṭhikā / kathopasaṃhāra ending with 'iti śrīmahāmahopādhyāyakavikulasārvabhaumanikhilavidyākumudinīśarvarīśvarasarasvatīniḥśvasitakaṣidaṇḍipaṇḍitaviracitaṃ daśakumāracaritaṃ saṃpūrṇam'.

SA_GK19_jaygit1u.title: Gītagovinda
SA_GK19_jaygit1u.author: Jayadeva
SA_GK19_jaygit1u.summary: The Gītagovinda by Jayadeva is a renowned lyric poem celebrating the love, painful estrangement, mutual longing in separation (viraha), and erotic-mystical reconciliation of Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā in Vṛndāvana, assisted by a confidante (sakhī). Divided into cantos comprising rhymed songs framed by classical Sanskrit metrical stanzas, the work blends classical court aesthetics with vernacular lyrical forms.
SA_GK19_jaygit1u.attribution: The poem explicitly identifies Jayadeva, son of Bhojadeva and Rāmādevī (GG 12.22).

SA_GK19_jaygit1u.coverage: complete — Complete root text spanning from GG 1.1 ('meghaiḥ meduram...') to GG 12.22 ('śrībhojadeva-prabhavasya...'). The e-text is formatted in sandhi-analyzed, word-divided form (in pausa) without commentary.

SA_GK19_kskala_u.title: Kalāvilāsa
SA_GK19_kskala_u.author: Kṣemendra
SA_GK19_kskala_u.summary: Kalāvilāsa is a satirical poem in ten cantos composed by Kṣemendra. Framed as instruction delivered by Mūladeva to his disciple Candragupta, the work catalogues and satirizes widespread forms of deceit, greed, and hypocrisy in society—exposing corrupt bureaucrats and scribes (kāyasthas), merchants, quack physicians, astrologers, courtesans, and false ascetics—before concluding with an exposition of genuine, auspicious arts.
SA_GK19_kskala_u.attribution: Kṣemendra's authorship is stated in the concluding stanza (10.43: 'kalāvilāsaḥ kṣemendrapratibhāmbhodhinirgataḥ') and in the closing colophon ('iti mahākaviśrīkṣemendraviracite kalāvilāse...').
SA_GK19_kskala_u.edition: Pandita Durgaprasada and Kasinatha Panduranga Paraba (eds.), Kavyamala (1st series), vol. 1, Bombay 1886, pp. 34–79.
SA_GK19_kskala_u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 10 sargas (cantos), concluding at 10.43 with the closing colophon of the tenth sarga.

SA_GK19_livasau.title: Līlāvatīsāra
SA_GK19_livasau.author: Jinaratna
SA_GK19_livasau.summary: The Līlāvatīsāra ('The Epitome of Līlāvatī') is a narrative kāvya by Jinaratna. Framed as a spiritual discourse delivered by the monk Samarasena to King Siṃha and Queen Līlāvatī of Rājagṛha, the narrative traces the transmigrations and karmic trajectories of a linked circle of souls through multiple rebirths, illustrating the destructive consequences of the passions (kaṣāya) and promoting core Jain ethics of nonviolence (ahiṃsā) and monastic renunciation.

SA_GK19_meghdk_u.title: Meghadūta
SA_GK19_meghdk_u.author: Kālidāsa
SA_GK19_meghdk_u.summary: The Meghadūta is a classical lyric poem composed by Kālidāsa. Banished for a year to the hermitage of Rāmagiri by his master for neglect of duty, a yakṣa beseeches a passing monsoon cloud to convey a message of longing to his wife in the city of Alakā. The first part charts a journey northward across rivers and cities; the second part describes Alakā, the condition of the yakṣa's beloved, and his message of fidelity and reunion.
SA_GK19_meghdk_u.attribution: Attributed to Kālidāsa. Although source headers mention Mallinātha's Sañjīvanī commentary, the digital text contains only the poetic stanzas.

SA_GK19_nkalivpu.title: Kaliviḍambana
SA_GK19_nkalivpu.author: Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita
SA_GK19_nkalivpu.summary: The Kaliviḍambana ('Mockery of the Kali Age') is an influential satirical poem of 102 anuṣṭubh verses composed by the 17th-century South Indian poet, polymath, and minister Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita. It offers sharp, epigrammatic lampoons of the corruption, hypocrisy, and professional charlatanism emblematic of the degenerate age. Its targets include quack physicians, greedy astrologers, fraudulent exorcists and tantric practitioners, unprincipled debaters, sycophantic courtiers, and venal relatives. Written in lucid, aphoristic Sanskrit, it is considered one of the masterpieces of post-classical Sanskrit satire.
SA_GK19_nkalivpu.attribution: Explicitly attributed to Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita in the final verse (verse 102: kavinā nīlakaṇṭhena kaler etad viḍambanam / racitaṃ ...) and the terminal colophon (iti Nīlakaṇṭhaviracitaṃ Kaliviḍambanaṃ saṃpūrṇam).

Kalyanasundara Sastri, Sastra Sanjeevinee Press Madras 1920; ed. Vaidika Vardhini Press Kumbakonam; L = lithograph Bod. 5.D.8, ed. by Keralavarma, Trivandrum 1886.

SA_GK19_ragh.title: Raghuvaṃśa (cantos 1–6)
SA_GK19_ragh.author: Kālidāsa
SA_GK19_ragh.summary: Kālidāsa's Raghuvaṃśa ('The Dynasty of Raghu') is a classic Sanskrit mahākāvya chronicling the legendary solar dynasty of Ayodhyā. Cantos 1–6 cover the reign and ascetic devotion of King Dilīpa and Queen Sudakṣiṇā to the sacred cow Nandinī, the birth and world-conquering digvijaya of King Raghu, Raghu's munificent gift-giving at the Viśvajit sacrifice, and the bridegroom-choice (svayaṃvara) assembly in which Princess Indumatī chooses Raghu's son Aja. This e-text transmits the root kāvya verses according to the Northern/Kashmirian textual transmission as preserved by the 10th-century Kashmirian commentator Vallabhadeva.
SA_GK19_ragh.attribution: Text of the Kashmirian recension of Kālidāsa's mahākāvya as reconstructed from the earliest surviving commentary, the Raghupañcikā of Vallabhadeva (10th c. CE).
SA_GK19_ragh.edition: Dominic Goodall and Harunaga Isaacson: The Raghupañcikā of Vallabhadeva, being the earliest commentary on the Raghuvaṃśa of Kālidāsa, Critical Edition with Introduction and Notes, Volume 1. Groningen: Egbert Forsten 2003.
SA_GK19_ragh.coverage: partial — Contains cantos 1–6 only (ending at 6.86, totaling 489 verses), out of the complete epic's 19 cantos.

SA_GK19_ruphamdu.title: Haṃsadūta
SA_GK19_ruphamdu.author: Rūpa Gosvāmin
SA_GK19_ruphamdu.summary: The Haṃsadūta ('The Swan Messenger') is a Sanskrit messenger poem (dūtakāvya) in 142 verses composed by Rūpa Gosvāmī. Modeled after Kālidāsa's Meghadūta, the poem describes Lalitā, a confidante of Rādhā, dispatching a swan from the banks of the Yamunā to Kṛṣṇa in Mathurā following his departure from Vraja. The bulk of the composition conveys Lalitā's message depicting Rādhā's distress in separation (vipralambha-śṛṅgāra) and reproaching Kṛṣṇa for abandoning the gopīs, synthesizing courtly lyric conventions with Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava devotional theology.
SA_GK19_ruphamdu.attribution: Authored by Rūpa Gosvāmī (16th cent.). Verse 141 refers to śākaratayā.
SA_GK19_ruphamdu.coverage: complete — Complete root text in 142 verses, beginning with verse 1 ('dukūlaṃ bibhrāṇo...') and concluding with verse 142 ('rasānām ādhārair...').

SA_GK19_utraca.title: Uttararāmacarita
SA_GK19_utraca.author: Bhavabhūti
SA_GK19_utraca.summary: The Uttararāmacarita ('The Later Deeds of Rāma') by Bhavabhūti is a classical Sanskrit drama in seven acts (nāṭaka) dramatizing the tragic events of the Uttarakāṇḍa of the Rāmāyaṇa. The plot centers on Rāma's agonizing abandonment of the pregnant Sītā in deference to public slander, his acute remorse and grief twelve years later upon revisiting the Daṇḍaka forest, and their psychological reconciliation culminating in a play-within-a-play (garbhāṅka). The work is celebrated across the Sanskrit dramaturgical tradition as the supreme artistic exemplar of karuṇarasa (the aesthetic sentiment of pathos and compassionate sorrow).

SA_GK20_ksakunpu.author: Kālidāsa
SA_GK20_ksakunpu.summary: The Abhijñānaśākuntala is a seven-act classical Sanskrit drama (nāṭaka) by Kālidāsa. It dramatizes the romantic encounter and marriage between King Duṣyanta and the hermitage-maiden Śakuntalā, Duṣyanta's repudiation of her, and their eventual reunion in the hermitage of Mārīca.

SA_GK20_mrtiu.title: Mṛcchakaṭikā
SA_GK20_mrtiu.author: Śūdraka

SA_GK20_urmc_u.title: Uttararāmacarita
SA_GK20_urmc_u.author: Bhavabhūti
SA_GK20_urmc_u.summary: The Uttararāmacarita ('The Later Deeds of Rāma') is a celebrated seven-act Sanskrit drama (nāṭaka) by Bhavabhūti, composed in the first half of the 8th century CE. It dramatizes the events following Rāma's coronation recounted in the Uttarakāṇḍa of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, focusing on the abandonment of Sītā due to popular reproach, Rāma's profound grief and remorse, and their eventual joyful reconciliation at Vālmīki's hermitage. Celebrated as Bhavabhūti's dramatic masterpiece, the play is famous in Sanskrit aesthetics for its poignant and sustained realization of the sentiment of pathos (karuṇa-rasa).

SA_GK21_hitop_u.title: Hitopadeśa
SA_GK21_hitop_u.author: Nārāyaṇa
SA_GK21_hitop_u.summary: The Hitopadeśa is a celebrated Sanskrit collection of animal fables and gnomic maxims composed in prosimetric campū form by Nārāyaṇa under the patronage of Prince Dhavalacandra [3882, 3887]. Drawing largely on the Pañcatantra as well as the Kāmandakīyanītisāra and the epics [19], the work is framed as practical instruction in statecraft and ethics given by the sage Viṣṇuśarman to the errant sons of King Sudarśana of Pāṭaliputra [21, 28]. It is divided into four thematic books: Mitralābha (Gaining Friends), Suhṛdbheda (Alienating Friends), Vigraha (War), and Sandhi (Peace) [18, 2076, 3889]. Renowned for its direct syntax and pragmatic political wisdom (nīti), it has served for centuries as an essential introductory reader for students of Sanskrit.
SA_GK21_hitop_u.attribution: The concluding verses (Hit_4.141 and 4.143) explicitly name Nārāyaṇa as the author/compiler and invoke blessings on his patron, Prince Dhavalacandra (māṇḍalika).

There is one small lacuna: the GRETIL header lists Hit_2.167–169 and 2.171–176 as missing, i.e. 9 verses of about 650. The text jumps from 2.167 to 2.170 and from 2.170 to 2.177; 2.167 has survived in part. Because only these verses are missing, the title is not marked as partial.

SA_GK21_sokss.title: Kathāsaritsāgara
SA_GK21_sokss.author: Somadeva
SA_GK21_sokss.summary: The Kathāsaritsāgara is an 18-book (lambaka) Sanskrit narrative work composed by Somadeva in Kashmir in the 11th century, based on the Bṛhatkathā, featuring the adventures of Naravāhanadatta along with embedded tales such as the Vetālapañcaviṃśatikā.

SA_GK21_suksaptu.title: Śukasaptati
SA_GK21_suksaptu.summary: The Śukasaptati ('Seventy Tales of the Parrot') is a popular Sanskrit frame-tale narrative (kathā). When the young merchant Madanavinoda embarks on a lengthy commercial journey abroad, his wife Prabhāvatī is tempted by dissolute companions to pursue illicit liaisons; her wise parrot keeps her at home each night by narrating an ingenious story of wit, trickery, or adulterous escape, cunningly breaking off the tale until dawn. Over the course of seventy consecutive nights, the parrot deters her from infidelity until the merchant returns. Renowned for its realistic depiction of rogue life and practical cleverness, the collection enjoyed immense popularity throughout Asia and formed the direct basis for the Persian Ṭūṭī-nāma.
SA_GK21_suksaptu.attribution: The core Śukasaptati collection is anonymous. The present e-text contains the simpler recension (textus simplicior).
SA_GK21_suksaptu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 70 tales within the framing narrative (textus simplicior). Contains the root Sanskrit prose and verse, including Prakrit verses with Sanskrit chāyā, concluding at tale 70 with 'iti śukasaptatau saptatitamī kathā / iti śukasaptatiḥ samāptā'. The modern Sanskrit and Hindi 'Vinodinī' commentary advertised in the opening line is omitted.
translations: Richard Schmidt (transl.), Die Çukasaptati (textus simplicior) aus dem Sanskrit übersetzt, Kiel: C. F. Haeseler, 1894. (German)

SA_GK22_vispancu_e.title: Pañcatantra
SA_GK22_vispancu_e.author: Viṣṇuśarman
SA_GK22_vispancu_e.summary: The Pañcatantra is India's most celebrated collection of frame narratives and animal fables designed to instruct princes in statecraft and practical wisdom (nītiśāstra). Framed by the introductory Kathāmukha, it comprises five books (tantras): Mitrabheda, Mitraprāpti, Kākolūkīya / Saṁdhivigraha, Labdhanāśa, and Aparīkṣitakāritva. Franklin Edgerton's 1924 edition represents a critical attempt to reconstruct the original Sanskrit text.
SA_GK22_vispancu_e.attribution: Attributed in tradition to Viṣṇuśarman, who figures in the framing Kathāmukha as tutor to the three sons of King Amaraśakti.
SA_GK22_vispancu_e.edition: Franklin Edgerton (ed.), The Panchatantra Reconstructed: An Attempt to Establish the Lost Original Sanskrit Text of the Most Celebrated of Indian Story-Collections on the Basis of the Principal Extant Versions: Text and Critical Apparatus, American Oriental Series, New Haven, Connecticut: American Oriental Society, 1924.
SA_GK22_vispancu_e.coverage: complete — Reconstructed Sanskrit text containing the introductory Kathāmukha and all five books (tantras): Mitrabheda, Mitraprāpti, Saṁdhivigraha / Kākolūkīya, Labdhanāśa, and Aparīkṣitakāritva.
translations: Franklin Edgerton (tr.), The Panchatantra Reconstructed: Introduction and Translation, American Oriental Series, New Haven: American Oriental Society, 1924. (English)
Patrick Olivelle (tr.), Pañcatantra: The Book of India's Folk Wisdom, Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1997. (English)

SA_GK22_vispancu_e_olivelle.title: Pañcatantra
SA_GK22_vispancu_e_olivelle.author: Viṣṇuśarman
SA_GK22_vispancu_e_olivelle.summary: The Pañcatantra is an ancient Indian collection of interwoven animal fables and frame tales in prose and gnomic verse, framed as the instruction of three princes by the sage Viṣṇuśarman in nīti (practical conduct and statecraft). The work is organized into five books (tantras): Mitrabheda (Separation of Friends), Mitrasamprāpti (Gaining of Friends), Kākolūkīya (War of Crows and Owls), Labdhapraṇāśa (Loss of Gains), and Aparīkṣitakāraka (Ill-considered Action).

SA_GP10_bhp.title: Bhāgavatapurāṇa
SA_GP10_bhp.summary: The Bhāgavatapurāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas and the canonical scripture of devotional Vaiṣṇavism, especially authoritative for the Gauḍīya, Vallabha, and Nimbārka traditions. Comprising twelve skandhas and approximately 14,000 to 18,000 verses, the work synthesizes Advaita metaphysics and Sāṅkhya cosmology with ecstatic bhakti directed to Kṛṣṇa as Svayaṃ Bhagavān. Framed as a dialogue between the sage Śuka and King Parīkṣit on the banks of the Gaṅgā, the narrative culminates in the tenth skandha depicting Kṛṣṇa's childhood, divine līlā, and the rāsalīlā in Vraja.

SA_GP11_brahmppu.title: Brahmapurāṇa
SA_GP11_brahmppu.summary: The Brahmapurāṇa is a purāṇic text set in Naimiṣāraṇya containing discourses by speakers such as Brahmā, Vyāsa, and Śiva.
SA_GP11_brahmppu.attribution: Attributed in textual excerpts to Vyāsa (e.g. {vyāsa uvāca}).
SA_GP11_brahmppu.coverage: complete — Contains the text in 246 chapters (adhyāyas 1–246, concluding at verse 246.40d: 'ājñāpayadhvaṃ munayo vrajāmi').
translations: Renate Söhnen and Peter Schreiner, Brahmapurāṇa: Summary of Contents, with Index of Names and Motifs, Purāṇa Research Publications 2, Wiesbaden: Otto Harrassowitz, 1989. (English)

SA_GP11_padmpp.title: Padmapurāṇa
SA_GP11_padmpp.summary: The Padmapurāṇa is one of the eighteen classical Mahāpurāṇas, traditionally ranking second in size with approximately 55,000 ślokas. Extant in distinct northern (five khaṇḍas) and western/southern (six or seven khaṇḍas) recensions, it comprises encyclopedic accounts of cosmogony, dynastic genealogies, pilgrimage guides (tīrthamāhātmya, notably for Puṣkara and the Gaṅgā), and substantial Vaiṣṇava narrative material including independent versions of the Rāma and Kṛṣṇa legends. While its oldest core dates to the Gupta period (c. 4th–8th centuries CE), extensive interpolations and sectarian expansions accrued well through the late medieval period.

SA_GP12_agp_bi_u.title: Agnipurāṇa
SA_GP12_agp_bi_u.summary: The Agnipurāṇa is one of the eighteen canonical Mahāpurāṇas, framed as a discourse imparted by the fire god Agni to the sage Vasiṣṭha. Renowned for its encyclopedic scope, it combines traditional Puranic cosmogony, genealogies, and avatāra narratives with extensive epitomes of classical and medieval technical disciplines. These include comprehensive manuals of temple architecture and iconography (vāstu- and śilpaśāstra), Vaiṣṇava and Śaiva tantric ritual and initiation (dīkṣā), statecraft and military science (rājanīti, dhanurveda), medicine (āyurveda), poetics (alaṅkāraśāstra), metrics (chandaḥ), and grammar. While preserving earlier epic-Puranic material, the compilation reached its extant encyclopedic form largely between the 9th and 11th centuries CE.
SA_GP12_agp_bi_u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa; framed as an instruction delivered by the god Agni to the sage Vasiṣṭha, who then narrates it to Vyāsa.
SA_GP12_agp_bi_u.edition: Agnipurāṇa: A Collection of Hindu Mythology and Traditions, edited by Rājendralāla Mitra, 3 vols., Calcutta: Asiatic Society of Bengal, 1870–1879 (Bibliotheca Indica, Work).
SA_GP12_agp_bi_u.coverage: complete — Contains the preliminary table of contents (anukramaṇikā), all 383 chapters of the core text, and the 6-chapter appendix (Agnipurāṇapariśiṣṭa, chapters *1–*6), breaking off at verse *6.40ab on p. 385 of volume 3 exactly where the printed text in Mitra's edition ends.

SA_GP12_garup.title: Garuḍapurāṇa
SA_GP12_garup.summary: The Garuḍapurāṇa is one of the eighteen major canonical Mahāpurāṇas of the Vaiṣṇava tradition, framed as a dialogue between Viṣṇu and his vahana Garuḍa, recounted by Sūta to the sages of the Naimiṣāraṇya. The text is encyclopedic: the Pūrvakhaṇḍa treats cosmology, temple ritual, pilgrimage sites (Gayamāhātmya), astronomy, gemmology (ratnaparīkṣā), medicine and diagnosis (nidāna/cikitsā), governance, and grammar; the Pretakhaṇḍa functions as a principal Hindu manual of eschatology and mortuary ritual, detailing death, posthumous suffering, funerary rites (antyeṣṭi), and śrāddha; and the Brahmakāṇḍa presents a theological exposition of Vaiṣṇava metaphysics displaying close ties to Dvaita Vedānta. The composite work ranges in date from c. the 8th–10th century CE for the early encyclopedic core to the 14th–16th century CE for the late medieval Brahmakāṇḍa.
SA_GP12_garup.attribution: Traditionally considered a Purāṇa narrated by Sūta in the Naimiṣa forest.
SA_GP12_garup.coverage: complete — Complete e-text encompassing all three divisions (khaṇḍas) of the Veṅkaṭeśvara recension: Pūrvakhaṇḍa (Ācārakāṇḍa/Karmakāṇḍa, 240 adhyāyas), Pretakhaṇḍa (Dharmakāṇḍa/Pretakalpa, 49 adhyāyas), and Uttarakhaṇḍa / Brahmakāṇḍa (29 adhyāyas), ending at Brahmakāṇḍa 29.17 with 'samāptamidaṃ garuḍamahāpurāṇam'.
translations: The Garuda Puranam, trans. M. N. Dutt, Calcutta, 1908. (English)

SA_GP12_sivap.title: Śivapurāṇa
SA_GP12_sivap.summary: The Śivapurāṇa is a canonical scripture of Śaivism organized into saṃhitās (including Vidyeśvarasaṃhitā and Rudrasaṃhitā), dealing with the mythology and worship of Śiva and the Goddess.

SA_GP12_skp01u.title: Skandapurāṇa (Māheśvarakhaṇḍa only)
SA_GP12_skp01u.summary: The Māheśvarakhaṇḍa is the opening book of the 81,000-verse recension of the Skandapurāṇa. It consists of three distinct sub-sections: the Kedārakhaṇḍa, recounting major Śaiva myths (such as Dakṣa's sacrifice, the churning of the ocean, and the marriage of Śiva and Pārvatī) alongside the sacred topography of Kedāranātha and Himalayan tīrthas; the Kaumārikākhaṇḍa, centering on Skanda's birth and the slaying of Tārakāsura, the pilgrimage site of Stambhatīrtha (Khambhāt, Gujarat), and the narrative of Barbarīka; and the Aruṇācalamāhātmya (Pūrvārdha and Uttarārdha), extolling the primordial linga of fire at Mount Aruṇācala (Tiruvannamalai, Tamil Nadu) and the merits of its circumambulation.
SA_GP12_skp01u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Vyāsa, as invoked in the opening chapter.
SA_GP12_skp01u.coverage: partial — Complete for the Māheśvarakhaṇḍa (including Kedārakhaṇḍa, Kaumārikākhaṇḍa, and Aruṇācalamāhātmya), but constitutes only the first book of the larger Skandapurāṇa corpus.

SA_GP12_skp02u.title: Skandapurāṇa (Vaiṣṇavakhaṇḍa only)
SA_GP12_skp02u.summary: The Vaiṣṇavakhaṇḍa is the second major book of the vulgate seven-part recension of the Skandapurāṇa, comprising nine distinct māhātmyas devoted to Vaiṣṇava sacred geography, liturgical calendars, and theology. It contains extensive sthala-māhātmyas sanctifying major pan-Indian pilgrimage destinations, including Veṅkaṭācala (Tirupati), Puruṣottamakṣetra (Puri Jagannātha), Badarikāśrama, and Ayodhyā, alongside liturgical manuals detailing the religious merit of vows and ablutions performed during the holy months of Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa, and Vaiśākha. It also includes the Bhāgavatamāhātmya and the Vāsudevamāhātmya, the latter integrating late Pāñcarātra theology with devotional cults of Kṛṣṇa-Vāsudeva.
SA_GP12_skp02u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the legendary sage Vyāsa (Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana) and framed as a dialogue between Sūta Ugraśravas and the ṛṣis of Naimiṣāraṇya.
SA_GP12_skp02u.coverage: partial — The complete Vaiṣṇavakhaṇḍa (khaṇḍa 2 of 7): Veṅkaṭācala-, Puruṣottamakṣetra-, Badarikāśrama-, Kārttikamāsa-, Mārgaśīrṣa-, Bhāgavata-, Vaiśākhamāsa-, Ayodhyā- and Vāsudevamāhātmya. It opens at Veṅkaṭācalamāhātmya 1.1 and ends 'iti śrīskānde mahāpurāṇe dvitīye vaiṣṇavakhaṇḍe vāsudevamāhātmyaṃ sampūrṇam || 9 || ... dvitīyaṃ vaiṣṇavakhaṇḍaṃ sampūrṇam || 2 ||'.

SA_GP12_skp03u.title: Skandapurāṇa (Brahmakhaṇḍa only, without Brahmottarakhaṇḍa chapter 22)
SA_GP12_skp03u.summary: The Brahmakhaṇḍa is the third major book (khaṇḍa) of the seven-khaṇḍa vulgate recension of the Skandapurāṇa. It brings together three independent medieval texts: the Setumāhātmya (52 chapters), which celebrates the pilgrimage to Rāmeśvaram, Mount Gandhamādana, Dhanuṣkoṭi, and the Rāmasetu; the Dharmāraṇyakhaṇḍa (40 chapters), a sthalapurāṇa focused on Dharmāraṇya (modern Modhera in northern Gujarat) chronicling Brahmā's sacrifice and the lineage traditions, gotras, and domestic rites of the Moḍha Brāhmaṇas and Moḍha Vāṇiyās; and the Brahmottarakhaṇḍa (chapters 1–21 in this text, 22 in full editions), an influential manual of Smārta-Śaiva devotional practice extolling the Pañcākṣaramantra, the Śivakavaca, holy ash (vibhūti/tripuṇḍra), rudrākṣa beads, and observances such as the Pradoṣa and Somavāravratas.
SA_GP12_skp03u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa; as with all Mahāpurāṇas, it is an anonymous and composite text.
SA_GP12_skp03u.coverage: partial — Setumāhātmya 1–52, Dharmāraṇyakhaṇḍa 1–40 and Brahmottarakhaṇḍa 1–21. The file ends with the colophon of Brahmottarakhaṇḍa 21 ('... rudrādhyāyamahimavarṇanaṃnāmaika viṃśo'dhyāyaḥ || 21 ||').

SA_GP12_skp04u.title: Skandapurāṇa (Kāśīkhaṇḍa only)
SA_GP12_skp04u.summary: The Kāśīkhaṇḍa constitutes Book 4 of the 7-khaṇḍa vulgate Skandapurāṇa and is the most extensive and authoritative premodern sthalamāhātmya on the sacred city of Vārāṇasī (Kāśī). Comprising 100 adhyāyas divided equally into Pūrvārdha and Uttarārdha, it establishes the city as the supreme cosmic center and abode of liberation (mokṣa) ruled by Śiva Viśveśvara. The work provides an exhaustive religious cartography detailing sacred pilgrimage circuits, hundreds of liṅgas, temples, tīrthas, ghāṭs, and guardian deities (including the 56 Vināyakas, Bhairavas, and yoginīs) within a narrative frame centered on the sage Agastya and Skanda.
SA_GP12_skp04u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Vyāsa as part of the 81,000-verse vulgate Skandapurāṇa (Ekāśītisāhasrī Saṃhitā).
SA_GP12_skp04u.coverage: complete — Contains the complete 100 adhyāyas of the Kāśīkhaṇḍa (divided into Pūrvārdha, adhyāyas 1–50, and Uttarārdha, adhyāyas 51–100, which are internally numbered 1–50). However, owing to a file-splitting error when partitioning the online digital dump of the Skandapurāṇa, the text is mistakenly preceded at the very beginning (segments 0 to approx. 85+) by the final chapter (adhyāya 22) of the Brahmottarakhaṇḍa (Book 3, Brahmakhaṇḍa).

SA_GP12_skp05u.title: Skandapurāṇa (Āvantyakhaṇḍa: Avantīkṣetramāhātmya and Caturaśītiliṅgamāhātmya chapters 1–80)
SA_GP12_skp05u.summary: The Āvantyakhaṇḍa forms a section of the Skandapurāṇa, opening with the Avantīkṣetramāhātmya praising Mahākālavana and sacred sites, and including dialogues between Umā and Maheśvara describing various liṅgas and tīrthas up to chapter 80 (Svapneśvaramāhātmyavarṇana).
SA_GP12_skp05u.attribution: Attributed to Vyāsa in the text (vyāsa uvāca).

SA_GP12_skp06u.title: Skandapurāṇa: Nāgarakhaṇḍa
SA_GP12_skp06u.summary: The Nāgarakhaṇḍa is the sixth book (khaṇḍa) of the vulgate seven-part recension of the Skandapurāṇa, comprising 279 chapters focused on the glorification of Hāṭakeśvarakṣetra (Camatkārapura, modern Vadnagar in northern Gujarat). Functioning as both a sthalamāhātmya and a jātipurāṇa, it records the sacred topography, shrines, gotras, rituals, and lineage histories of the Nāgara Brahmins. It also assimilates broad puranic narratives—including the stories of Triśaṅku, Hariścandra, and Viśvāmitra—re-situating them within this regional Śaiva sacred geography.
SA_GP12_skp06u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa.
SA_GP12_skp06u.coverage: complete — Complete for Nāgarakhaṇḍa proper (all 279 adhyāyas, terminating with the final book colophon). SA_GP12_skp07u.title: Skandapurāṇa (Prabhāsakhaṇḍa only)
SA_GP12_skp07u.summary: The Prabhāsakhaṇḍa constitutes the seventh and final major book of the vulgate 81,000-verse Skandapurāṇa. Arranged into four distinct sections—Prabhāsakṣetramāhātmya, Vastrāpathakṣetramāhātmya, Arbudakhaṇḍa, and Dvārakāmāhātmya—it forms a massive compendium of sacred geography and pilgrimage lore (tīrthamāhātmya) centered on western India, notably the Somanātha jyotirliṅga, Mount Girnar, Mount Abu, and Dwarka. Although primarily Śaiva in orientation, it integrates Vaiṣṇava, Śākta, and Saura sacred traditions, concluding with an epilogue (upasaṃhāra) that reviews the transmission and canonical extent of the entire Skandapurāṇa corpus.
SA_GP12_skp07u.attribution: Author field left empty per conventions for traditional/canonical Purāṇic literature.
SA_GP12_skp07u.coverage: partial — Complete Prabhāsakhaṇḍa (khaṇḍa 7 of 7): Prabhāsakṣetramāhātmya 1–365, Vastrāpathakṣetramāhātmya 1–19, Arbudakhaṇḍa 1–63, Dvārakāmāhātmya 1–44 (chapter runs confirmed from the colophons). It ends with the colophon closing the whole Skandapurāṇa ('... samastaskāndamahāpurāṇagranthasamāptyupasaṃhāra... catuścatvāriṃśattamo'dhyāyaḥ || 44 ||'). Partial only in that the other khaṇḍas are separate files.
translations: Tārākānta Kāvyatīrtha (trans.), edited by Pañcānana Tarkaratna, Skandapurāṇam, Calcutta: 1911. (Bengali)

SA_GP12_vipce.title: Viṣṇupurāṇa
SA_GP12_vipce.summary: The Viṣṇupurāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas and is widely regarded by Indologists as the most unified exemplar of the classical pañcalakṣaṇa ('five characteristics') genre. Structured as a six-book dialogue between the sage Parāśara and his disciple Maitreya, the text articulates a Vaiṣṇava cosmology and theology identifying Viṣṇu as the supreme, all-encompassing Brahman. Book 5 contains one of the earliest continuous accounts of the life and legends of Kṛṣṇa Gopāla, serving as a vital foundation for the later Bhāgavatapurāṇa, and the text's theological consistency made it an authoritative pramāṇa for Vedānta commentators, particularly Rāmānuja.

SA_GR14_garsa.title: Gargasaṃhitā
SA_GR14_garsa.summary: The Gargasaṃhitā is a Vaiṣṇava narrative text composed in classical Purāṇic style and structured into ten khaṇḍas (Goloka, Vṛndāvana, Girirāja, Mādhurya, Mathurā, Dvārakā, Viśvajit, Balabhadra, Vijaya, and Aśvamedha). While recounting the life and deeds of Kṛṣṇa in parallel to the Bhāgavata Purāṇa and Harivaṃśa, it distinctively elevates Rādhā to the position of supreme divine consort. The text includes narratives specific to northern devotional lore, such as the Gandharva marriage of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa solemnized by Brahmā in Bhāṇḍīravana, and serves as an important witness to the sacred topography and pilgrimage culture of Vraja.

SA_GR14_vedsy.title: Vedāntasyamantaka
SA_GR14_vedsy.author: Rādhādāmodara
SA_GR14_vedsy.summary: The Vedānta Symantaka (Vedāntasyamantaka) is an introductory compendium (prakaraṇa) of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava Vedānta divided into six chapters termed kiraṇas ('rays'). The work systematically expounds epistemology (pramāṇa-nirṇaya) and five core ontological categories: īśvara, jīva, prakṛti, kāla, and karma, integrating the concept of viśeṣa within acintya-bhedābheda theology.

SA_GS38_kautil.title: Arthaśāstra
SA_GS38_kautil.author: Kauṭilya
SA_GS38_kautil.summary: The Arthaśāstra is ancient India's foundational treatise on statecraft, political economy, judicial administration, and diplomatic strategy. Divided into fifteen books (adhikaraṇas), it systematically covers the education and discipline of the king, ministerial appointments, internal civil and revenue administration, civil and criminal law (dharmasthīya and kaṇṭakaśodhana), espionage, interstate relations (the mandala theory and the sixfold foreign policy, ṣāḍguṇya), military logistics and warfare, and the methodological hermeneutics of treatises (tantrayukti). Treating artha (material welfare and power) as the foundation of royal and societal flourishing, it provides an exceptionally detailed blueprint for state institutions in classical India.
SA_GS38_kautil.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Kauṭilya (also known as Viṣṇugupta or Cāṇakya).
SA_GS38_kautil.edition: R. P. Kangle (ed.), The Kauṭilīya Arthaśāstra, A critical Edition with a Glossary, Second edition, University of Bombay, 1969.

SA_GS39_kamasufu.title: Kāmasūtra
SA_GS39_kamasufu.author: Vātsyāyana
SA_GS39_kamasufu.summary: The Kāmasūtra of Vātsyāyana is a Sanskrit treatise on kāmaśāstra, systematically treating the pursuit of pleasure, courtship, love, and aesthetic refinement within the classical trivarga framework. Its seven books (adhikaraṇas) cover general principles of life, sexual technique, marriage, the duties of a wife, extramarital relations, courtesans, and erotic recipes. It provides a documentary view of urban culture (nāgaraka-vṛtta), gender relations, and material life in ancient India.
SA_GS39_kamasufu.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Vātsyāyana (often styled Mallanāga Vātsyāyana in later commentarial tradition).

SA_GS40_susruta.title: Suśrutasaṃhitā
SA_GS40_susruta.author: Suśruta
SA_GS40_susruta.summary: The Suśrutasaṃhitā is one of the three foundational classics of classical Āyurveda (the Bṛhat-trayī) and ancient India's premier authority on surgery (śalyatantra). Framed as instructions delivered by Divodāsa Dhanvantari, king of Kāśī, to his student Suśruta, it describes surgical instruments, practical anatomy through human cadaveric dissection, and operative procedures such as rhinoplasty, couching of cataracts, lithotomy, and abdominal suture. The treatise comprises 186 chapters divided across the five sthānas of the Pūrvatantra (Sūtra-, Nidāna-, Śārīra-, Cikitsā-, and Kalpasthāna) and the supplementary Uttaratantra, which treats ophthalmology and ENT (śālākya), pediatrics (kaumārabhṛtya), toxicology/psychiatry (bhūtavidyā), and general medicine (kāyacikitsā).
SA_GS40_susruta.attribution: Traditionally framed as teachings imparted by Divodāsa Dhanvantari, king of Kāśī, to Suśruta and other pupils.
SA_GS40_susruta.edition: Composite digital edition based on: (1) Sūtrasthāna and Śārīrasthāna: Suśrutasaṃhitā, ed. SA_GSD36_manu_o.title: Manusmṛti
SA_GSD36_manu_o.summary: The Manusmṛti (or Mānavadharmaśāstra), consisting of twelve chapters and roughly 2,694 ślokas, is the foundational and most influential treatise of the Brahmanical Dharmaśāstra tradition. It systematically codifies cosmogony, the sources of dharma, life-cycle rituals (saṃskāras), rules of the four social classes (varṇas) and life stages (āśramas), royal governance, civil and criminal jurisprudence across eighteen legal titles (vyavahārapada), as well as expiatory penances (prāyaścitta) and eschatological doctrine. It served as the preeminent authority on social ethics, ritual duties, and legal practice across South and Southeast Asia.

SA_GSD36_manu.title: Manusmṛti
SA_GSD36_manu.summary: The Manusmṛti (or Mānava-dharmaśāstra) is the foundational and most influential metrical treatise of the Hindu Dharmaśāstra tradition. Comprising twelve chapters and approximately 2,684 anuṣṭubh verses, it systematically delineates cosmogony, the sources of dharma, sacraments (saṃskāras), the duties of the four varṇas and āśramas, royal governance and statecraft (rājadharma), eighteen heads of civil and criminal litigation (vyavahārapada), rules of purification, penance (prāyaścitta), and karma doctrine. Generally dated between the 2nd century BCE and the 3rd century CE, the treatise established the benchmark for classical Indian jurisprudence and generated an extensive commentarial tradition.

SA_GSD36_manubhau.title: Manusmṛti with Manubhāṣya
SA_GSD36_manubhau.author: Manu, Medhātithi
SA_GSD36_manubhau.summary: The Manusmṛti (or Mānava-Dharmaśāstra) is ancient India's foundational and most influential metrical code of socio-religious duty (dharma), statecraft, jurisprudence, and penance. Medhātithi's Manubhāṣya (c. 9th–10th century CE) represents the earliest surviving and most comprehensive commentary on the text, celebrated for its rigorous application of Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā hermeneutical principles to reconcile textual tensions and develop sophisticated legal reasoning. Surviving incompletely in manuscript witnesses, the commentary was partially restored under King Madanapāla and remained a primary benchmark for subsequent Dharmaśāstra commentarial traditions and digests.
SA_GSD36_manubhau.attribution: The root treatise Manusmṛti (Mānavadharmaśāstra) is traditionally attributed to the sage Manu (revealed through Bhṛgu). The commentary Manubhāṣya was authored by Bhaṭṭa Medhātithi, son of Vīrasvāmin (c. 9th–10th century CE). As attested in the concluding colophon (12.126), parts of the commentary that had fallen into lacunae were restored under the patronage of King Madanapāla.
SA_GSD36_manubhau.edition: Manusmṛti with the Manubhāṣya of Medhātithi, ed. Gaṅgānātha Jhā, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 256, Calcutta: Asiatic Society of Bengal, 1932 (Vol. I publ. 1920, 1932–1939, in two volumes).
SA_GSD36_manubhau.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all 12 adhyāyas of the Manusmṛti along with Medhātithi's Manubhāṣya.

SA_GSD36_visnu.title: Viṣṇusmṛti
SA_GSD36_visnu.summary: The Viṣṇusmṛti is a major Sanskrit legal treatise combining prose dharmasūtra style with framing verse passages. Framed as a dialogue in which Viṣṇu as the cosmic boar (Varāha) instructs the rescued Earth goddess (Vasundharā), the work treats varṇāśramadharma, royal administration (rājadharma), civil and penal law (vyavahāra), inheritance, bodily purity, ancestor rites (śrāddha), penances (prāyaścitta), and devotional worship.
SA_GSD36_visnu.attribution: Traditionally presented as revelation expounded by the boar incarnation of Viṣṇu (Varāha) to the Earth goddess (Vasundharā).
SA_GSD36_visnu.edition: Viṣṇusmṛti, ed. V. Krishnamacharya, Adyar Library Series vol. 93 (2 parts), Madras: Adyar Library and Research Centre, 1964.
SA_GSD36_visnu.coverage: complete — Complete mūla text covering all 100 adhyāyas (chapters), from 1.1 through 100.4/5.
translations: Julius Jolly (tr.), The Institutes of Vishnu, Sacred Books of the East, 1880. (English)

SA_GSD37_apastd_u.title: Āpastambadharmasūtra
SA_GSD37_apastd_u.summary: The Āpastambadharmasūtra constitutes a section of the Kalpasūtra belonging to the Āpastamba school of the Black (Kṛṣṇa) Yajurveda, and is widely regarded as one of the oldest surviving Dharmasūtras. Written in an archaic aphoristic style, it treats the duties of the four varṇas, student initiation (upanayana) and codes of conduct, rules of dietary purity, householder duties, ancestor rites (śrāddha), legal procedure, inheritance, and royal duties (rājadharma). It also contains the Adhyātmapaṭala (1.8.22–23), an important early philosophical discourse on the Ātman, and is a vital witness for pre-classical grammar and early Vedic orthopraxy.
SA_GSD37_apastd_u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the Vedic sage Āpastamba, belonging to the school of the Black (Kṛṣṇa) Yajurveda.
SA_GSD37_apastd_u.edition: Georg Bühler (ed.), Āpastambīya Dharmasūtra, Bombay Sanskrit Series LIV & L, 3rd ed. rev. by M. G. Shastri, Bombay/Poona, 1932; with variant readings from A. Chinnaswami Sastri (ed.), Kashi Sanskrit Series No. 93, Benares, 1932.
SA_GSD37_apastd_u.coverage: complete — Contains the complete root text across two praśnas (Praśna 1: 11 paṭalas / 32 khaṇḍas; Praśna 2: 11 paṭalas / 29 khaṇḍas), concluding with sūtra 2.11.29.15 and the closing colophon '//samāptaṃ ca-idam āpastambīya.dharmasūtram//'. The e-text features morphological/grammatical tags and variant readings from Chinnaswami's edition.
translations: Georg Bühler (trans.), Sacred Books of the East, 1879. (English)
Patrick Olivelle (trans.), 1999. (English)

SA_GSD37_baudhasuu.title: Baudhāyanadharmasūtra
SA_GSD37_baudhasuu.summary: The Baudhāyanadharmasūtra is one of the four surviving Vedic Dharmasūtras, forming part of the larger Baudhāyana Kalpasūtra within the Taittirīya śākhā of the Kṛṣṇa (Black) Yajurveda. Divided into four praśnas (books), the treatise covers the sources of dharma, initiation and student life, duties of the householder and king, judicial procedure, civil and criminal law, inheritance, penances, and the āśramas. It is composite in composition: Praśnas 1 and 2 constitute the archaic core, whereas Praśnas 3 and 4 represent later accretions. The text is celebrated for its explicit recognition of regional customary law (ācāra), highlighting contrasting customs between northern and southern Brahmins.
SA_GSD37_baudhasuu.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the Vedic teacher/sage Baudhāyana (Bodhāyana).
SA_GSD37_baudhasuu.coverage: unclear — The e-text file is empty (0 segments, 0 characters).

SA_GSD37_gautdh_u.title: Gautamadharmasūtra
SA_GSD37_gautdh_u.author: Gautama
SA_GSD37_gautdh_u.summary: The Gautamadharmasūtra is one of the earliest extant aphoristic legal treatises of ancient India, traditionally affiliated with the Rāṇāyanīya and Kauthuma schools of the Sāmaveda. Composed in concise prose sūtras, it systematically expounds the sources of sacred law (dharma), rules for life stages (āśrama), student initiation (upanayana), householder duties, dietary and purification rules (śauca), occupations of the four social classes (varṇa), the duties and judicial functions of the king (rājadharma, vyavahāra), rules of inheritance and partition (dāyabhāga), and expiations for ritual and moral transgressions (prāyaścitta). Alongside the dharmasūtras of Āpastamba, Baudhāyana, and Vasiṣṭha, it forms an essential transitional bridge between late Vedic ritual manuals and the classical metrical dharma treatises such as the Manusmṛti.
SA_GSD37_gautdh_u.edition: Ganesa Sastrin Gokhale, Pune 1910, (Anandasrama Sanskrit Series, 61); with variants from: The Institutes of Gautama, ed.by A.F. Stenzler, London 1876.
SA_GSD37_gautdh_u.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all 28 adhyāyas (divided in the Ānandāśrama edition into 3 praśnas: 1.1–1.9, 2.1–2.9, 3.1–3.10; and in Stenzler's edition into 28 chapters), concluding at GautAA 3,10.51 / GautSt 28.52 with 'iti dharmo dharmaḥ'.

SA_GSD37_vasist_u.title: Vāsiṣṭhadharmasūtra
SA_GSD37_vasist_u.summary: The Vāsiṣṭhadharmasūtra is composed in a mixture of aphoristic prose sūtras and metrical stanzas. It covers the sources of dharma, duties of the four classes (varṇa) and life stages (āśrama), marriage and women's status, impurity and purification, dietary laws, civil and criminal law, inheritance, penances (prāyaścitta), and royal governance.
SA_GSD37_vasist_u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 30 adhyāyas (sūtras 1.1 to 30.11).

SA_GSP27_yogva.title: Yogavāsiṣṭha
SA_GSP27_yogva.author: Vālmīki
SA_GSP27_yogva.summary: The Yogavāsiṣṭha (also known as the Vāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa) is a philosophical work framed as a dialogue involving Vasiṣṭha and Rāma, representing an Advaita philosophical teaching. Modern scholarship connects the vulgate text to the core Kashmiri text Mokṣopāya.

SA_GSP28_tantrava.title: Tantravārttika
SA_GSP28_tantrava.author: Kumārila Bhaṭṭa
SA_GSP28_tantrava.summary: The Tantravārttika is the primary prose sub-commentary composed by the 7th-century philosopher Kumārila Bhaṭṭa on Śabarasvāmin's Śābarabhāṣya on Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra, covering Adhyāya 1, Pāda 2 through Adhyāya 3, Pāda 8. Serving as the central work in Kumārila's tripartite commentary on the Bhāṣya (flanked by the verse Ślokavārttika on 1.1 and the concise notes of the Ṭupṭīkā on Adhyāyas 4–12), it develops a comprehensive defense of Vedic ritualism, textual exegesis, and Brahmanical orthopraxy. The work is renowned for its seminal analyses of the semantic force of Vedic injunctions (vidhi), the epistemological and evidentiary authority of explanatory passages (arthavāda) and mantras, the validity of Smṛti and regional customs (ācāra), and the formal criteria governing ritual subordination (śeṣatva).
SA_GSP28_tantrava.attribution: The Tantravārttika is the work of Kumārila Bhaṭṭa, commenting on Śabarasvāmin's Śābarabhāṣya.
SA_GSP28_tantrava.coverage: complete — Complete; the Tantravārttika as an independent work covers Adhyāya 1, Pāda 2 through Adhyāya 3, Pāda 8 of Śabarasvāmin's Bhāṣya on Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra.
translations: Tantravārtika, 2 vols. [1903.] Delhi: MLBD, reprint 1983, translated by G. Jha. (English)

SA_GSP29_nyapra.title: Mīmāṃsānyāyaprakāśa
SA_GSP29_nyapra.author: Āpadeva
SA_GSP29_nyapra.summary: The Mīmāṃsānyāyaprakāśa (commonly called the Āpadevī) is a standard 17th-century introductory primer (prakaraṇa) of the Bhāṭṭa school of Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā composed by Āpadeva. Written in lucid prose, it provides an organized exposition of Vedic hermeneutics, defining dharma, explaining the two modes of productive efficiency (śābdī and ārthī bhāvanā), and classifying Vedic statements into injunctions (vidhi), mantras, appellations (nāmadheya), prohibitions (niṣedha), and explanatory eulogies (arthavāda). It further delineates the six textual criteria determining subsidiary status (aṅgatva: śruti, liṅga, vākya, prakaraṇa, sthāna, and samākhyā), concluding with a devotional synthesis attributing liberating value to ritual action dedicated to Govinda. The work served as the model for Laugākṣi Bhāskara's subsequent condensed textbook, the Arthasaṃgraha.
SA_GSP29_nyapra.attribution: Āpadeva was the son of Anantadeva; he flourished in the first half of the 17th century CE.
SA_GSP29_nyapra.edition: Āpadeva, Mīmāṃsānyāyaprakāśa (Āpadevī), ed. Vāsudeva Śāstrī Abhyankar, Government Oriental Series Class A No. 3, Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, Poona, 1937
SA_GSP29_nyapra.coverage: complete — Complete root text (mūla) without commentary, running from the opening maṅgala verses ('yatkṛpāleśamātreṇa...', 'anantaguṇasaṃpannam...') through the closing devotional verses ('kvāhaṃ mandamatiḥ...', 'grantharūpo madīyo 'yaṃ...') and final colophon.
translations: Franklin Edgerton, Mīmāṃsānyāyaprakāśa, New Haven, 1929. (English)

SA_GSP29_nyamanu.title: Nyāyamañjarī
SA_GSP29_nyamanu.author: Jayantabhaṭṭa
SA_GSP29_nyamanu.summary: The Nyāyamañjarī is an encyclopedic philosophical treatise composed in Kashmir by Jayantabhaṭṭa. Structured across twelve daily lessons (āhnikas), the work is an expansive, independent examination of the sixteen classical categories (padārthas) of the Nyāya school anchored around Gautama's Nyāyasūtra. Written in an engaging, satirical Sanskrit prose style, it provides robust defenses of the pramāṇas, Vedic and Āgamic revelation, and the existence of God (Īśvara), while articulating influential refutations of Buddhist epistemology (Dharmakīrti and Dharmottara), Mīmāṃsā, Cārvāka materialism, and the sphoṭa doctrine of the grammarians.
SA_GSP29_nyamanu.attribution: Authored by Jayantabhaṭṭa, son of Candra, an eminent Kashmiri philosopher. In the concluding verses, the author refers to himself as Jayanta, son of Candra, and notes that scholars refer to him as the 'Navavṛttikāra'.
SA_GSP29_nyamanu.coverage: complete — Contains all twelve āhnikas of the Nyāyamañjarī, opening with the maṅgalaślokas to Śiva, Sarasvatī, Gaṇapati, and Akṣapāda, and closing with the treatment of the sixteenth padārtha (nigrahasthāna) followed by Jayanta's final colophon verses.
translations: Janaki Vallabha Bhattacharyya (trans.), Nyāyamañjarī: The Compendium of Indian Speculative Logic, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1978. (English)

SA_GSP30_tantralu2.title: Tantrāloka
SA_GSP30_tantralu2.author: Abhinavagupta
SA_GSP30_tantralu2.summary: The Tantrāloka ('Light on the Tantras') is the magnum opus of Abhinavagupta and the foundational encyclopedic exposition of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism, synthesizing the Trika, Krama, and Pratyabhijñā traditions. Spanning 37 daily lectures (āhnikas) and nearly 5,800 metrical verses, the work organizes Śaiva ontology, theology, and ritual practice into four progressive means to realization (anupāya, śāmbhava, śākta, and āṇava) based primarily on the Mālinīvijayottaratantra. It integrates internal contemplative yogas with complex external ritual, mantra mechanics, and initiation procedures (dīkṣā) under an uncompromising philosophy of non-dual consciousness.

SA_GSP30_utipk.title: Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā with Īśvarapratyabhijñāvṛtti
SA_GSP30_utipk.author: Utpaladeva
SA_GSP30_utipk.summary: The Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā along with its autocommentary, the Īśvarapratyabhijñāvṛtti, constitutes the foundational doctrinal treatise of the Pratyabhijñā school within non-dual Kashmir Śaivism, composed by Utpaladeva. Through epistemological and metaphysical argumentation engaging Buddhist logicians, Grammarians, and Nyāya thinkers, Utpaladeva demonstrates that individual consciousness is essentially identical to the supreme Lord, possessed of intrinsic powers of knowledge and action.
SA_GSP30_utipk.attribution: Utpaladeva composed the Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā with his autocommentary (vṛtti).
