SA_GSP31_iskamatu.title: Sāṃkhyakārikā with Māṭharavṛtti
SA_GSP31_iskamatu.author: Īśvarakṛṣṇa, Māṭhara
SA_GSP31_iskamatu.summary: The Sāṃkhyakārikā of Īśvarakṛṣṇa is the classical foundational text of the Sāṅkhya philosophical tradition, formulating its dualist metaphysics of conscious self (puruṣa) and primordial nature (prakṛti), the evolution of the twenty-five cosmic principles (tattvas), the three guṇas, and liberation through discriminative insight (vivekakhyāti). The Māṭharavṛtti is an essential early-to-medieval Sanskrit prose commentary that preserves traditional mythological background—such as the transmission lineage of Kapila and Āsuri—as well as detailed illustrative parables. Because it shares extensive verbatim and doctrinal parallels with the Gauḍapādabhāṣya and Paramārtha's 6th-century Chinese Suvarṇasaptati, it is an indispensable witness for tracing the evolution of classical Sāṅkhya exegesis.
SA_GSP31_iskamatu.attribution: The root verses are composed by Īśvarakṛṣṇa. The prose commentary Māṭharavṛtti is attributed to Māṭhara (Māṭharācārya).
SA_GSP31_iskamatu.edition: Viṣṇu Prasāda Śarmā (ed.), Sāṃkhyakārikā: Māṭharācāryaviracita-"Māṭharavṛtti"-sahitā, Varanasi: The Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series Office, 1970 (Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series, no. 296 [Work no. 56]).
SA_GSP31_iskamatu.coverage: complete — Complete e-text of all 73 kārikās along with the Māṭharavṛtti commentary, including the introductory narrative upodghāta and concluding colophon (ity ācāryeśvarakṛṣṇaproktāyāḥ sāṅkhyasaptatyā vṛttir ācāryamāṭharakṛtiḥ samāptā).

SA_GSP31_jaymangu.title: Sāṃkhyakārikā with Jayamaṅgalā
SA_GSP31_jaymangu.author: Īśvarakṛṣṇa, Śaṅkarārya
SA_GSP31_jaymangu.summary: The Sāṃkhyakārikā of Īśvarakṛṣṇa is the classical foundational treatise of Sāṃkhya philosophy, articulating its dualist ontology of insentient nature (prakṛti) and pure consciousness (puruṣa), the evolution of the twenty-five tattvas, three epistemic pramāṇas, and liberation through discriminative insight. The Jayamaṅgalā is an important early medieval running commentary (ṭīkā) that provides lucid grammatical and philosophical expositions for all 72 verses. It constitutes an essential witness for the early textual and doctrinal transmission of classical Sāṃkhya alongside the Gauḍapādabhāṣya, the Māṭharavṛtti, and the Yuktidīpikā.
SA_GSP31_jaymangu.attribution: The root verses are composed by Īśvarakṛṣṇa. The commentary's manuscript colophon credits 'śrīmatparamahaṃsaparivrājakācāryaśrīgovindabhagavatpūjyapādaśiṣyeṇa śrīśaṅkarabhagavatā kṛtā sāṃkhyasaptatiṭīkā samāptā', while the tradition and headers also refer to the commentator as Śaṃkara / Śaṃkara ārya.
SA_GSP31_jaymangu.edition: H. Sarma: Jayamaṅgalā nāma Sāṃkhyasaptatiṭīkā, Calcutta 1926 (Calcutta Oriental Series, 19)
SA_GSP31_jaymangu.coverage: complete — Contains all 72 kārikās of the Sāṃkhyakārikā alongside the full Jayamaṅgalā commentary, beginning with its initial maṅgala verse ('adhigatatattvālokaṃ...') and concluding with the terminal colophon following kārikā 72.
translations: Gerald James Larson, and Ram Shankar Bhattacharya, eds. (1987) Sāṃkhya: A Dualist Tradition in Indian Philosophy. of The Encyclopedia of Indian Philosophies. Princeton: Princeton University Press. (English)

SA_GSP33_brasusau.title: Brahmasūtra with Brahmasūtrabhāṣya
SA_GSP33_brasusau.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Śaṅkara
SA_GSP33_brasusau.summary: The Brahmasūtrabhāṣya (or Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya) is Śaṅkara's magnum opus and the foundational commentary of Advaita Vedānta on the Brahmasūtra of Bādarāyaṇa. Preceded by the renowned Adhyāsabhāṣya on beginningless transcendental superimposition, the commentary demonstrates that empirical multiplicity is rooted in avidyā and establishes the absolute non-duality of Brahman and the identity of the individual self (ātman) with Brahman. Across four chapters (samanvaya, avirodha, sādhana, and phala), Śaṅkara harmonizes Upaniṣadic statements, refutes competing traditions (including Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, and Buddhism), and expounds knowledge of non-duality as the sole direct means to liberation.
SA_GSP33_brasusau.attribution: The root Brahmasūtras (Vedāntasūtras) are traditionally attributed to Bādarāyaṇa. The commentary is Śaṅkara's.
SA_GSP33_brasusau.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising all four adhyāyas (16 pādas) of the Brahmasūtra accompanied by Śaṅkara's commentary, prefaced by the traditional Vedic śāntipāṭhas and the introductory Adhyāsabhāṣya, and concluding with closing śāntipāṭhas and the sūtrānukramaṇikā.
translations: George Thibaut, The Vedânta-Sûtras with the Commentary by Saṅkarâkârya, Sacred Books of the East and 38, Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1890, 1896. (English)
Paul Deussen, Die Sûtra's des Vedânta oder die Çârīraka-Mîmâṅsâ des Bâdarāyana nebst dem vollständigen Kommentare des Çan̄kara, Leipzig: F. A. Brockhaus, 1887. (German)
Swami Gambhirananda, Brahma-Sutra Bhasya of Sri Sankaracarya, Calcutta: Advaita Ashrama, 1965. (English)
V. M. Apte, Brahma-Sutra Shankara-Bhashya, Bombay: Popular Book Depot, 1960. (English)

SA_GSP33_jimuvi.title: Jīvanmuktiviveka
SA_GSP33_jimuvi.author: Vidyāraṇya
SA_GSP33_jimuvi.summary: The Jīvanmuktiviveka ('Discrimination of Liberation while Living') is an influential 14th-century Advaita Vedānta treatise by Vidyāraṇya. Across five prakaraṇas, the text examines the nature of and scriptural authority for living liberation, the eradication of latent mental impressions (vāsanākṣaya), the dissolution of the mind (manonāśa), the five purposes served by liberation-in-life, and the renunciation of the enlightened knower (vidvatsaṃnyāsa). The work is celebrated for its synthesis of classical Advaita epistemology with the practical yogic disciplines of Patañjali's Yogasūtra and the Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha, maintaining that enduring experiential tranquility in life requires the coordinated practice of tattvajñāna, vāsanākṣaya, and manonāśa.
SA_GSP33_jimuvi.edition: Jīvan-Mukti-Viveka of Swami Vidyāraṇya, Kolkata: Advaita Ashrama, 1996 (3rd impression, August 2010).
SA_GSP33_jimuvi.coverage: complete — Complete Sanskrit text in five chapters (prakaraṇas), interspersed with an English translation and introductory/concluding editorial matter.
translations: S. Subrahmanya Sastri and T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (trs.), The Jīvanmuktiviveka of Vidyāraṇya, Adyar (rev. ed. 1978). (English)

SA_GSP33_vacbhamu.title: Bhāmatī
SA_GSP33_vacbhamu.author: Vācaspatimiśra
SA_GSP33_vacbhamu.summary: The Bhāmatī by Vācaspatimiśra is an authoritative Advaita Vedānta sub-commentary on Śaṅkara's Brahmasūtrabhāṣya.
SA_GSP33_vacbhamu.attribution: In the concluding signature verses at the end of Adhyāya 4, Vācaspati praises King Nṛga and mentions his earlier works: Nyāyakaṇikā, Tattvasamīkṣā, Tattvabindu, and his treatises on Nyāya, Sāṅkhya, Yoga, and Vedānta.
SA_GSP33_vacbhamu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Bhāmatī covering all four adhyāyas (1.1.1 through 4.4.22), beginning with the maṅgala verses and closing with the author's signature verses and the final colophon.

SA_GSP36_sadha.title: Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha
SA_GSP36_sadha.author: Mādhava
SA_GSP36_sadha.summary: The Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha is an encyclopedic Sanskrit doxographical survey of Indian philosophical systems composed by Mādhava (Sāyaṇa-Mādhava). It presents sixteen distinct schools in an ascending hierarchy of doctrinal adequacy, progressing from the materialist Cārvāka through Buddhism, Jainism, various Vaiṣṇava and Śaiva traditions, the classical orthodox systems (Vaiśeṣika, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, Pāṇinīya, Sāṅkhya, Yoga), and culminating in Advaita Vedānta (Śāṅkaradarśana) as the pinnacle of philosophical knowledge.
SA_GSP36_sadha.attribution: The introductory verses and colophons identify the author as Mādhava (Mādhavārya / Sāyaṇamādhava), whose preceptor was Sarvajñaviṣṇu.
SA_GSP36_sadha.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all 16 chapters (darśanas): Cārvāka, Bauddha, Ārhata (Jaina), Rāmānuja, Pūrṇaprajña (Madhva), Nakulīśapāśupata, Śaiva, Pratyabhijñā, Raseśvara, Vaiśeṣika (Aulūkya), Akṣapāda (Nyāya), Jaiminīya (Mīmāṃsā), Pāṇinīya, Sāṅkhya, Pātañjala (Yoga), and Śāṅkara (Advaita Vedānta).
translations: The Sarva-darśana-saṃgraha; or, Review of the Different Systems of Hindu Philosophy by Mádhava Áchárya, translated by E. B. Cowell and A. E. Gough, Trübner's Oriental Series, London: Trübner & Co. (English)

SA_GV00_avs.title: Atharvavedasaṃhitā
SA_GV00_avs.summary: The Atharvavedasaṃhitā (Śaunaka recension) is the canonical fourth Veda of ancient India, comprising 730 hymns arranged across 20 kāṇḍas. It encompasses healing charms, exorcisms, apotropaic formulas, domestic and royal rites, alongside sublime metaphysical and cosmogonic hymns such as the Pṛthivīsūkta (Hymn to the Earth, 12.1) and the Vrātya book (Book 15). Preserving both domestic ritual magic and esoteric sacerdotal speculation, the text provides critical evidence for early Vedic folk religion, archaic medicine, and everyday societal practices.
SA_GV00_avs.attribution: A traditional Vedic saṃhitā attributed to the ancestral ṛṣis Atharvan, Aṅgiras, and Bhṛgu (hence its ancient designations Ātharvāṅgirasaḥ and Bhṛgvaṅgirasaḥ); preserved here in the vulgate Śaunaka recension (Śaunakaśākhā).
SA_GV00_avs.edition: Gli inni dell' Atharvaveda (Saunaka), trasliterazione a cura di Chatia Orlandi, Pisa 1991, collated with the ed. R. Roth and W. D. Whitney: Atharva Veda Sanhita, Berlin 1856; with numbering of Books 11–20 following Vishva Bandhu: Atharvaveda (Saunaka), with the Pada-Patha and Sayanacarya's commentary, Hoshiarpur 1960-1964 (Vishveshvaranand indological series, 13-17).
SA_GV00_avs.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Śaunaka recension in 20 kāṇḍas, containing 730 hymns (sūktas) and 5,946 verses/segments (running from AVŚ 1.1.1 to 20.143.9), presented in unaccented transliteration with word segmentation based on the padapāṭha.
translations: William Dwight Whitney and Charles Rockwell Lanman (trans.), Atharva-Veda Samhitā, Harvard Oriental Series, Cambridge, Mass., 1905. (English)
Maurice Bloomfield (trans.), Atharva Veda, Sacred Books of the East 42, Oxford, 1897. (English)
Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), Hymns of the Atharvaveda, 1895–. (English)

SA_GV00_avs2.title: Atharvavedasaṃhitā
SA_GV00_avs2.summary: The Atharvavedasaṃhitā is the fourth collection of the Vedic scriptural canon, preserved principally in the Śaunaka and Paippalāda recensions. Unlike the sacrificial focus of the Ṛgveda, Sāmaveda, and Yajurveda, it encompasses a wide range of domestic, magical, and medical hymns, including incantations for healing, apotropaic charms against hostile powers, blessings for prosperity and harmony, and royal coronation rites. It also preserves notable speculative, cosmogonic, and philosophical hymns—such as the Bhūmisūkta (hymn to the Earth) and hymns to Skambha and Prāṇa—that mark an important conceptual transitional phase toward early Upaniṣadic thought.
translations: William Dwight Whitney (trans.), Atharva-Veda Samhitā, Cambridge: Harvard University, 1905 (Harvard Oriental Series). (English)
Maurice Bloomfield (trans.), Hymns of the Atharva-Veda, Together with Extracts from the Ritual Books and the Commentaries, 1897 (Sacred Books of the East). (English)
Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), Hymns of the Atharvaveda, 1895–. (English)

SA_GV00_samavedu.title: Sāmavedasaṃhitā
SA_GV00_samavedu.summary: The Sāmavedasaṃhitā is the liturgical verse collection (ārcika) providing the textual base (yoni) for the melodies (sāman) intoned by the Udgātṛ priest during Śrauta sacrificial rituals, particularly the Soma sacrifices. Preserved here in the standard Kauthuma recension, the collection comprises 1,875 mantras divided into the Pūrvārcika (single stanzas arranged by deity—principally Agni, Indra, and Soma Pavamāna—followed by the Āraṇyaka/Mahānāmnī section) and the Uttarārcika (strophes and triplets arranged according to ritual execution). With the exception of approximately 75 stanzas, all verses are drawn from the Ṛgvedasaṃhitā (predominantly Mandalas VIII and IX), frequently showing distinct dialectal and phonetic variations adapted to musical chant.
SA_GV00_samavedu.coverage: complete — Complete Kauthuma ārcika text, verses numbered continuously 1–1875: Pūrvārcika (Āgneya, Aindra and Pāvamāna kāṇḍas, vv. 1–585), Āraṇyaka kāṇḍa and Mahānāmnyārcika (vv. 586–650, ending with the five purīṣapadas), and Uttarārcika (vv. 651–1875). Ends with the colophon 'iti sāmavedasaṃhitā samāptā'. Unaccented; no gāna (song-book) texts.
translations: John Stevenson, Translation of the Sanhitá of the Sáma Veda, London: Oriental Translation Fund, 1842. (English)
Theodor Benfey, Die Hymnen des Sâma-Veda, herausgegeben, übersetzt und mit Glossar versehen, Leipzig: F. A. Brockhaus, 1848. (German)

SA_GV01_rvh.title: Ṛgveda
SA_GV01_rvh.summary: The Ṛgveda (or Ṛgvedasaṃhitā) is the oldest surviving work of Indo-Aryan literature and the foundational canonical text of the Vedic sacrificial tradition, composed in archaic Vedic Sanskrit in northwestern South Asia during the second millennium BCE. Arranged into ten books (maṇḍalas), its 1,028 hymns (sūktas) were primarily recited by the Hotṛ priest during Śrauta rituals to invoke deities such as Agni, Indra, Soma, and Varuṇa. In addition to liturgical praise, the collection contains dialogue hymns, riddles, and foundational cosmogonic and philosophical poetry, notably the Nāsadīyasūkta and Puruṣasūkta.
translations: Jamison, Stephanie W., and Joel P. Brereton, trs. The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India. An English Translation. 3 vols. New York: Oxford Univ. Press, 2014. (English)
Geldner, Karl Friedrich (trans.). Der Rig-Veda. Cambridge, MA: 1951–57. (German)
Renou, Louis (trans.). Études védiques et paninéennes. 17 vols. Paris: Publications de l’Institut de Civilisation Indienne, 1955–69. (French)
Griffith, R. T. H. (trans.). The Hymns of the Ṛgveda. London, 1889. (English)

SA_GV02_gopbra_u.title: Gopathabrāhmaṇa
SA_GV02_gopbra_u.summary: The Gopathabrāhmaṇa is the sole surviving Brāhmaṇa associated with the Atharvaveda and is universally recognized as the latest text in the Vedic Brāhmaṇa genre. It comprises two principal sections: the Pūrvabhāga (5 prapāṭhakas) and the Uttarabhāga (6 prapāṭhakas). The Pūrvabhāga presents cosmogony, esoteric expositions of the sacred syllable Oṃ and vyāhṛtis, the origins of the Atharvan and Aṅgiras traditions, and the supremacy of the Atharvan Brahman priest, while the Uttarabhāga deals with solemn sacrificial rituals (such as the Agniṣṭoma), heavily adapting and reinterpreting material borrowed from earlier Brāhmaṇas of the Ṛgveda and Yajurveda.
SA_GV02_gopbra_u.edition: Dieuke Gaastra (ed.), Das Gopatha Brāhmaṇa, Leiden: Brill, 1919.
SA_GV02_gopbra_u.coverage: complete — The e-text contains the entire text across both parts: Pūrvabhāga (5 prapāṭhakas) and Uttarabhāga (6 prapāṭhakas), concluding with section 2.6.16 and the final colophon 'ity atharvavedabrāhmaṇapūrvottaraṃ samāptam'.
translations: H.C. Patyal (unpublished translation) (English)

SA_GV03_sb.title: Śatapathabrāhmaṇa (kāṇḍas 1–11, 13–14)
SA_GV03_sb.summary: The Śatapathabrāhmaṇa is the prose ritual commentary attached to the White (Śukla) Yajurveda. It provides liturgical instructions, theological rationales, cosmological speculations, and mythological narratives for principal Vedic śrauta rituals, including the Darśapūrṇamāsa, Agnihotra, Cāturmāsya, Agnicayana, Aśvamedha, and Pravargya.
SA_GV03_sb.attribution: A Vedic prose brāhmaṇa belonging to the Śukla (White) Yajurveda (Mādhyandina recension). While Vedic texts are traditionally categorized as unauthored revelation (śruti/apauruṣeya), parts are associated with Yājñavalkya and Śāṇḍilya.
SA_GV03_sb.edition: Albrecht Weber (ed.), The Çatapatha-Brâhmaṇa in the Mâdhyandina-Çâkhâ, with extracts from the commentaries of Sâyaṇa, Harisvâmin and Dvivedaganga, Berlin/London, 1855 (repr. 1924; Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series, 1964).

SA_GV05_chup.title: Chāndogyopaniṣad
SA_GV05_chup.summary: The Chāndogyopaniṣad is one of the oldest, largest, and most authoritative of the principal (mukhya) Upaniṣads, belonging to the Sāmaveda tradition where it constitutes chapters 3–10 of the Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa. Its opening chapters interpret the udgītha liturgy and the sacred syllable Oṃ as objects of contemplative meditation (upāsanā), transforming ritual action into internalized inquiry. The subsequent prapāṭhakas develop foundational Vedāntic ontology, including the doctrine of the five fires (pañcāgnividyā), the Śāṇḍilyavidyā, Uddālaka Āruṇi's instruction of Śvetaketu culminating in the mahāvākya 'tat tvam asi', Sanatkumāra's teaching to Nārada on the Bhūman (the Infinite), and Prajāpati's progressive instruction to Indra on the true nature of the Ātman.
SA_GV05_chup.attribution: Vedic prose scripture preserved in the Kauthuma and Rāṇāyanīya śākhās of the Sāmaveda, constituting prapāṭhakas 3–10 of the Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa. Regarded as revealed śruti.
SA_GV05_chup.edition: V. P. Limaye and R. D. Vadekar (eds.), Eighteen Principal Upaniṣads, Vol. 1, Poona, 1958.
SA_GV05_chup.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 8 prapāṭhakas (chapters 1–8), beginning at 1.1.1 (om ity etad akṣaram udgītham upāsīta...) and concluding at 8.15.1 (...na ca punar āvartate na ca punar āvartate).
translations: Robert Ernest Hume, trans. 1921. The Thirteen Principal Upanishads. Oxford: Oxford. (English)
P. Deussen in Sechzig Upanishad's des Veda (Leipzig. (German)

SA_GV05_chupsau.title: Chāndogyopaniṣad with Chāndogyopaniṣadbhāṣya
SA_GV05_chupsau.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GV05_chupsau.summary: The Chāndogyopaniṣad, belonging to the Sāmaveda, is one of the Vedic Upaniṣads. Śaṅkara's running commentary provides an exposition across all eight chapters, interpreting ritual and upāsanā (such as the udgītha), Uddālaka Āruṇi's teaching including the mahāvākya 'tat tvam asi', and the nature of the Self.
SA_GV05_chupsau.attribution: The root Upaniṣad is an anonymous Vedic text of the Sāmaveda. The commentary is attributed to Śaṅkara.
SA_GV05_chupsau.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 8 adhyāyas of the Chāndogyopaniṣad alongside Śaṅkara's running bhāṣya, ending at the 15th khaṇḍa of the 8th adhyāya.

SA_GV05_kathop_u.title: Kaṭhopaniṣad
SA_GV05_kathop_u.summary: The Kaṭhopaniṣad is a classical mukhya Upaniṣad of the Kaṭha school of the Black (Kṛṣṇa) Yajurveda, framed as an initiatory dialogue between the boy Naciketas and Yama, the lord of death. When granted three boons, Naciketas bypasses earthly riches and longevity to demand knowledge of what transpires beyond death, prompting Yama to distinguish the path of spiritual good (śreyas) from the path of worldly pleasure (preyas) and reveal the immortal nature of the inner self (ātman). The text is renowned for its chariot allegory in Vallī 3—correlating the body with a chariot, the intellect with the charioteer, the mind with reins, and the senses with horses—and for providing one of the earliest textual formulations of proto-Sāṃkhya ontological gradations and the definition of yoga as steady sensorial restraint.
SA_GV05_kathop_u.edition: Patrick Olivelle (ed.), The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation, New York: Oxford University Press, 1998, pp. 374–402.
SA_GV05_kathop_u.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all six vallīs (structured as two adhyāyas of three vallīs each), running continuously from KaU 1.1 to KaU 6.18, concluding with '// iti ṣaṣṭhī vallī // // iti kaṭhopaniṣat //'.
translations: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation, New York: Oxford University Press, 1998, pp. 374–402. (English)
Robert Ernest Hume, The Thirteen Principal Upanishads, Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1921. (English)

Paul Deussen, Sechzig Upaniṣad's des Veda, Leipzig: F. A. Brockhaus, 1897. (German)

SA_GV06_apastgcu.title: Āpastambagṛhyasūtra with Haradatta's Anākulā and Sudarśana's Gṛhyatātparyadarśana
SA_GV06_apastgcu.author: Āpastamba, Haradatta, Sudarśanācārya
SA_GV06_apastgcu.summary: The Āpastambagṛhyasūtra is the domestic ritual manual of the Āpastamba school. Spanning 8 paṭalas (divided into 23 khaṇḍas), it sets forth domestic rites and sacraments. This e-text presents the sūtras accompanied by two commentaries: Haradatta's Anākulā and Sudarśanācārya's Gṛhyatātparyadarśana.
SA_GV06_apastgcu.attribution: The Āpastambagṛhyasūtra is traditionally attributed to Āpastamba. The Anākulā (Anākulāvṛtti) is by Haradatta, and the Gṛhyatātparyadarśana is by Sudarśanācārya (Sudarśanārya).
SA_GV06_apastgcu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 8 paṭalas (comprising 23 khaṇḍas) of the Āpastambagṛhyasūtra, along with Haradatta's Anākulā and Sudarśanācārya's Gṛhyatātparyadarśana, terminating with the final colophon of Sudarśanācārya at khaṇḍa 23 (paṭala 8).
translations: Hermann Oldenberg (tr.), The Grihya-Sūtras. Rules of Vedic domestic Ceremonies. Part II, 1892. (English)

SA_GV06_gogrsuu.title: Gobhilagṛhyasūtra
SA_GV06_gogrsuu.author: Gobhila
SA_GV06_gogrsuu.summary: The Gobhilagṛhyasūtra is a domestic ritual manual (gṛhyasūtra) laying down rules for domestic rites and life-cycle saṃskāras.
translations: Oldenberg, Hermann (trans.). The Grihya-Sūtras: Rules of Vedic Domestic Ceremonies. Part II. 1892. (English)
Knauer, Friedrich (trans.). Das Gobhilagṛhyasūtra, herausgegeben und übersetzt. Dorpat / Leipzig, 1884–. (German)

SA_GV06_sankhgsu.title: Śāṅkhāyanagṛhyasūtra
SA_GV06_sankhgsu.summary: The Śāṅkhāyanagṛhyasūtra is the domestic ritual manual (gṛhyasūtra) of the Śāṅkhāyana branch of the Ṛgveda. Across six adhyāyas, it sets out the rules for household sacraments (saṃskāra) such as upanayana and vivāha, daily morning and evening oblations, seasonal rites, ancestor worship (śrāddha), and expiations. The final two chapters contain supplementary rites and mantras. Closely related to the Kauṣītaki-Gṛhyasūtra, it forms one of the principal domestic authorities of the Ṛgvedic tradition.
SA_GV06_sankhgsu.edition: Hermann Oldenberg (ed.), Indische Studien; (Sehgal ed. upto 2.9, Delhi, 1960).
SA_GV06_sankhgsu.coverage: complete — Complete in 6 adhyāyas (adhyāyas 1–6), running from ŚGS 1.1.1 through ŚGS 6.6.16.
translations: Hermann Oldenberg (trans.), The Grihya-Sūtras: Rules of Vedic Domestic Ceremonies, Part 1, Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886. (English)

SA_GV_kyajurvedu.title: Kṛṣṇayajurveda
SA_GV_kyajurvedu.summary: The Kṛṣṇayajurveda ('Black Yajurveda') is one of the two primary branches of the Yajurveda, the Vedic liturgical corpus of mantras and formulas (yajus) used by the adhvaryu priest during solemn sacrificial rituals (śrauta). Unlike the Śuklayajurveda ('White Yajurveda'), which segregates mantras from their ritual explanations, the Kṛṣṇayajurveda characteristically interweaves liturgical mantras (saṃhitā) and brāhmaṇa-style prose ritual exegesis. Surviving recensions include the Taittirīya, Maitrāyaṇī, Kāṭhaka, and Kapiṣṭhala schools, of which the Taittirīya is the most complete and widely recited.
SA_GV_kyajurvedu.attribution: Vedic liturgical saṃhitā orally preserved across multiple śākhās (notably Taittirīya, Maitrāyaṇī, and Kaṭha/Kāṭhaka).
SA_GV_kyajurvedu.coverage: unclear — Empty file (0 segments, 0 characters). No Sanskrit text is present in the repository.
translations: Keith, Arthur Berriedale (trans.). The Veda of the Black Yajus School Entitled Taittiriya Sanhita. 2 vols. Harvard Oriental Series 18, 19. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1914. (English)

SA_GV_kyatp.title: Taittirīyaprātiśākhya
SA_GV_kyatp.summary: The Taittirīyaprātiśākhya is the foundational phonological and phonetic treatise of the Taittirīya school of the Kṛṣṇa (Black) Yajurveda. Arranged in 24 chapters (adhyāyas), the text specifies the sound inventory, articulation points, euphonic combination (sandhi), and accentuation patterns necessary to derive the continuous recitation (saṃhitāpāṭha) from the word-by-word text (padapāṭha). It is a central monument of ancient Indian phonetic science (śikṣā).
SA_GV_kyatp.attribution: Traditional phonetic treatise (prātiśākhya) of the Taittirīya śākhā of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, transmitted anonymously within the Vedic school.

SA_GV_syajurvedu2.title: Śuklayajurveda
SA_GV_syajurvedu2.summary: The Śuklayajurveda ('White Yajurveda') is the branch of the Yajurveda in which the sacrificial mantras (the Vājasaneyi-Saṃhitā) are preserved separately from their liturgical and exegetical prose explanations, which are collected in the Śatapatha-Brāhmaṇa. It serves as the ritual formulary for the adhvaryu priest during the solemn śrauta sacrifices, including the Darśapūrṇamāsa, Agnicayana, and Aśvamedha rites. The text survives in two major recensions, the Mādhyandina and the Kāṇva.
SA_GV_syajurvedu2.coverage: unclear — The entry contains 0 segment files, 0 segments, and 0 characters; it is an unpopulated placeholder or failed ingestion stub in the corpus.

SA_GV_syajurvedu.title: Vājasaneyisaṃhitā
SA_GV_syajurvedu.summary: The Vājasaneyisaṃhitā (Mādhyandina recension) is the foundational mantra collection of the White (Śukla) Yajurveda, preserving the formulas and verses recited by the adhvaryu priest during śrauta sacrificial rites. Unlike the Black (Kṛṣṇa) Yajurvedic saṃhitās, which intermingle liturgical formulas with brāhmaṇa prose exposition, the White Yajurveda separates the liturgical mantras into this collection, relegating exegesis to the Śatapatha-Brāhmaṇa. In 40 adhyāyas, it covers ceremonies including the New and Full Moon sacrifices (Darśapūrṇamāsa), the Soma ritual (Agniṣṭoma), the piling of the fire altar (Agnicayana), and major royal offerings (Vājapeya, Rājasūya, Aśvamedha, Puruṣamedha), concluding in its final chapter with the Īśāvāsyopaniṣad.
SA_GV_syajurvedu.attribution: Traditional revelation is associated with the sage Yājñavalkya.
SA_GV_syajurvedu.edition: Albrecht Weber (ed.), The Vājasaneyi-Sanhitā in the Mādhyandina and the Kāṇva Śākhā with the commentary of Mahīdhara, Berlin/London: Williams & Norgate, 1852 (The White Yajurveda, Part I).
SA_GV_syajurvedu.coverage: complete — Complete Mādhyandina Vājasaneyisaṃhitā, adhyāyas 1–40, one segment per verse (kaṇḍikā), from 1.1 'iṣe tvā' to 40.17 'o3m khaṃ brahma //'. Accents are removed and verses are unnumbered.

SA_K01_vinv06_u.title: Bhaiṣajyavastu (with lacunae)
SA_K01_vinv06_u.summary: The Bhaiṣajyavastu ('Chapter on Medicines') is the sixth section of the Vinayavastu in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya. While opening with monastic regulations concerning permissible medicines, dietary schedules, and the care of ill monks, the vast majority of the chapter is narrative, incorporating numerous avadānas, jātakas, legendary travels of the Buddha to northwest India, apotropaic formulas (including an early version of the Mahāmāyūrī spell), and prophecy accounts. The text survives in Sanskrit birch-bark manuscripts from Gilgit, alongside canonical translations into Tibetan and Chinese.
SA_K01_vinv06_u.attribution: Canonical Vinaya literature of the Mūlasarvāstivāda school, traditionally received as buddhavacana and transmitted anonymously within the monastic saṅgha.
SA_K01_vinv06_u.edition: Nalinaksha Dutt (ed.), Gilgit Manuscripts, vol. III: Mūlasarvāstivādavinayavastu, part 1: Bhaiṣajyavastu, Calcutta / Srinagar 1947 (input follows this 1st edition; 2nd ed. Delhi 1984). Portions re-edited in K. Wille, Die handschriftliche Überlieferung des Vinayavastu der Mūlasarvāstivādin (Stuttgart 1990) and in J. Chung & K. Wille, 'Fragmente aus dem Bhaiṣajyavastu der Sarvāstivādins' (SWTF Beiheft 9, 2002) replace Dutt's text. Some readings are corrected from the manuscript, and a gap is partly filled from Divyāvadāna (ed. E. B. Cowell and R. A. Neil, Cambridge 1886).
SA_K01_vinv06_u.coverage: partial — Begins with the piṇḍoddāna (fol. 91v3) and ends with 'bhaiṣajyavastu samāptam'. Contains lacunae including missing folios (partly supplemented from Divyāvadāna 453–461). The Tibetan translation of the vastu is complete by comparison.
translations: dul ba gzhi (Derge Kangyur D 1): translated by Vidyākaraprabha, Dharmakara, Sarvajñadeva, dpal gyi lhun po, ska ba dpal brtsegs (Tibetan)

SA_K06_bsu054_u.title: Prajñāpāramitāhṛdayasūtra (short recension)
SA_K06_bsu054_u.summary: The Prajñāpāramitāhṛdayasūtra ('Heart Sūtra') is one of the most widely recited and influential texts of Mahāyāna Buddhism, condensing the vast Prajñāpāramitā literature into an essential doctrinal summary. This e-text presents the short recension (saṃkṣiptamātṛkā), which omits the traditional introductory frame (nidāna) and concludes directly with the mantra. Avalokiteśvara explains to Śāriputra that the five aggregates and all constituent phenomena of Buddhist abhidharma are empty of inherent existence ('form is emptiness, emptiness is form'), culminating in the celebrated mantra 'gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā'.
SA_K06_bsu054_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna Buddhist scripture belonging to the Prajñāpāramitā corpus. Traditionally delivered by the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara to Śāriputra under the inspired sanction of the Buddha.
SA_K06_bsu054_u.edition: P. L. Vaidya, ed., Mahāyāna-sūtra-saṃgraha, Part 1, Buddhist Sanskrit Texts 17, Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute 1961.
SA_K06_bsu054_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the short recension (saṃkṣiptamātṛkā), including the opening salutation, the dialogue between Avalokiteśvara and Śāriputra, the mantra, and the closing colophon.
translations: Red Pine, 2004. (English)
Léon Feer, L'Essence de la science transcendante, 1866. (French)

SA_K08_bsu029_u.title: Rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchā
SA_K08_bsu029_u.summary: The Rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchā ('Questions of Rāṣṭrapāla') is an influential Mahāyāna sūtra included as assembly 18 in the Mahāratnakūṭa collection. Framed as a discourse at Gṛdhrakūṭa between the Buddha and the bodhisattva Rāṣṭrapāla, the text champions the ascetic ideal of forest dwelling (āraṇyaka) and dhūtaguṇa practice while mounting a severe critique against corrupt, comfortable urban monks of the decadent age (paścimakāla). The second half recounts fifty former-life tales (pūrvayoga) illustrating the Bodhisattva's extreme acts of self-sacrifice, culminating in the story of Prince Puṇyaraśmi.
SA_K08_bsu029_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra, traditionally transmitted as buddhavacana (the word of the Buddha).
SA_K08_bsu029_u.edition: P.L. Vaidya, ed., Mahāyāna-sūtra-saṃgraha, Part I (Sutra No. 12), Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute, 1961, pp. 120–160.
SA_K08_bsu029_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the sūtra in two parivartas (Nidānaparivarta and the Puṇyaraśmipūrvayoga section), corresponding to pp. 120–160 of Vaidya's edition; the appended verse index (ślokasūcī, pp. 161–164) is noted in segment 1282 but omitted.
translations: Jacob Ensink, The Question of Rāṣṭrapāla, 1952. (English)
Daniel Boucher, Bodhisattvas of the Forest and the Formation of the Early Mahāyāna, 2008. (English)

SA_K10_ayuhparu.title: Āyuḥparyantasūtra (incomplete)
SA_K10_ayuhparu.summary: The Āyuḥparyantasūtra ('Discourse on the Limits of Lifespan') is a canonical Buddhist discourse delivered by the Buddha at Jetavana in Śrāvastī. It provides a comprehensive catalogue of the life expectancies of beings across the cosmological realms, progressing from the hells (naraka) and hungry ghosts (preta), through the human realms to the heavens up to the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana. In addition to prose calculations correlating human and cosmological time spans, the sūtra incorporates verses explaining karmic results.
SA_K10_ayuhparu.attribution: Canonical discourse surviving in a Sanskrit manuscript from Gilgit, in Tibetan translation (D 307, translated by Viśuddhasimha and Dge ba'i dpal, revised by Vidyākarasimha and Dpal brtsegs), and in Chinese translation (Taishō 759, translated by Tianxizai).
SA_K10_ayuhparu.edition: Hisashi Matsumura, 'Āyuḥparyantasūtra: Das Sūtra von der Lebensdauer in den verschiedenen Welten. Text in Sanskrit und Tibetisch', in: Sanskrit-Texte aus dem buddhistischen Kanon: Neuentdeckungen und Neueditionen, Erste Folge (SWTF, Beiheft 2), Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 1989, pp. 69–100.
SA_K10_ayuhparu.coverage: partial — Āps 1–66: from the nidāna through the hells, animals, pretas, the four continents and the heavens, up to the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana (Āps 66). There is no closing formula, and the verse sections have lost akṣaras (marked X, +). The text uses GBM facsimile citations.
translations: Translated by Hisashi Matsumura, Review of the Shitennoji International Buddhist University, 1981. (Japanese)

SA_K10_arthaviniscaya.title: Arthaviniścayasūtra with Nibandhana
SA_K10_arthaviniscaya.author: Vīryaśrīdatta
SA_K10_arthaviniscaya.summary: The Arthaviniścayasūtra ('Discourse on the Ascertainment of Meaning') is an early Buddhist doctrinal compendium that systematically defines core doctrinal categories, serving as a sūtra-style Abhidharma mātṛkā. The Nibandhana is an extensive scholastic commentary on the discourse authored by Vīryaśrīdatta of Śrī-Nālandāvihāra during the reign of King Dharmapāla.
SA_K10_arthaviniscaya.attribution: The root sūtra is an anonymous canonical Buddhist discourse; the commentary Nibandhana was composed by Bhikṣu Vīryaśrīdatta of Śrī-Nālandāvihāra during the reign of King Dharmapāla.
SA_K10_arthaviniscaya.edition: N. H. Samtani (ed.), The Arthaviniścaya-sūtra and its Commentary (Nibandhana) (written by Bhikṣu Vīryaśrīdatta of Śrī-Nālandāvihāra), critically edited and annotated (Tibetan Sanskrit Works Series, vol. XIII), Patna: K. P. Jayaswal Research Institute, 1971.
SA_K10_arthaviniscaya.coverage: complete — Contains both the root text (Arthaviniścayasūtra) and the commentary (Nibandhana), concluding with verses referencing King Dharmapāla and the grantha count.

SA_K10_bsu005_u.title: Arthaviniścayasūtra
SA_K10_bsu005_u.summary: The Arthaviniścayasūtra ('Sūtra on the Ascertainment of Meanings') is an early Buddhist doctrinal compendium that enumerates and defines twenty-seven core technical categories (dharmaparyāyas), including the five aggregates, eighteen dhātus, twelve āyatanas, twelvefold dependent origination, four noble truths, spiritual faculties, limbs of awakening, and the marks of a Buddha. Preserved in Sanskrit, Tibetan (D 317), and Chinese (T 762, T 763), it is accompanied by the commentary Arthaviniścayasūtranibandhana.
SA_K10_bsu005_u.attribution: Canonical discourse attributed to the Buddha; doctrinally affiliated with mainstream Non-Mahāyāna Buddhist scholasticism (Sarvāstivāda/Sautrāntika) despite its preservation in Nepalese Mahāyāna manuscript collections.
SA_K10_bsu005_u.edition: P. L. Vaidya (ed.), Mahāyāna-sūtra-saṃgraha, Part 1, Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute, 1961 (Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, 17).
SA_K10_bsu005_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the sūtra across twenty-seven doctrinal categories, containing the opening thematic outline (uddeśa), detailed definitions (vibhaṅga), closing narrative, and colophon.
translations: Alfonsa Ferrari, Arthaviniścaya (Testo e versione), Roma: Reale Accademia d'Italia, 1944. (Italian)

SA_K10_bsu022_u.title: Lalitavistara
SA_K10_bsu022_u.summary: The Lalitavistara ('The Extensive Account of the [Buddha's] Play') is an elaborate Mahāyāna sūtra in 27 chapters composed in mixed Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit prose and verse. It narrates the sacred biography of Śākyamuni Buddha from his decision to descend from Tuṣita heaven, his miraculous conception and birth in Lumbinī, his luxurious princely youth, four encounters, and great renunciation, to his austerities, defeat of Māra, awakening beneath the Bodhi tree, and first turning of the wheel of Dharma in Ṛṣipatana. Blending early biographical accounts (primarily Sarvāstivādin) with a docetic Mahāyāna perspective, the sūtra depicts the Buddha's earthly career as the deliberate, compassionate sport (lalita) of an already fully enlightened being, and served as a major inspiration for classical Buddhist art and literature across Asia.
SA_K10_bsu022_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna sūtra traditionally regarded as buddhavacana; composed and elaborated in Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit prose and verse, incorporating older Sarvāstivāda biographical traditions.
SA_K10_bsu022_u.edition: P. L. Vaidya (ed.), Lalitavistara, Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute, 1958 (Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, 1).
SA_K10_bsu022_u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 27 chapters (parivartas), from the Nidānaparivarta (ch. 1) to the Nigamaparivarta (ch. 27).
translations: Philippe Édouard Foucaux, Le Lalita Vistara, Paris, 1884. (French)
Bijoya Goswami, 2001. (English)
Dharmachakra Translation Committee, 2013. (English)

SA_K10_bsu025_u.title: Nairātmyaparipṛcchā
SA_K10_bsu025_u.summary: The Nairātmyaparipṛcchā ('Questions on Selflessness') is a short Mahāyāna scripture consisting of a prose opening dialogue and 26 verses. Departing from standard sūtra narrative conventions, it depicts non-Buddhist wanderers (tīrthikas) approaching Mahāyāna practitioners to question how bodily actions and affective states (laughter, crying, anger, jealousy) can arise if the body is devoid of a supreme self (paramātman). The Buddhist respondents elucidate the non-duality of existence and non-existence, the distinction between conventional reality (saṃvṛti) and ultimate reality (paramārtha), and the nature of all phenomena as illusory, dream-like appearances empty of intrinsic self-nature.
SA_K10_bsu025_u.attribution: Transmitted anonymously as a sūtra in Sanskrit manuscripts and in the Tibetan Kangyur (Toh 173), as well as in the Chinese translation by Fatian (T846). A later Chinese translation by Richeng / Sūryakīrti (T1643) reinterprets the text as a śāstra and attributes it to Aśvaghoṣa, an attribution rejected by modern scholarship.
SA_K10_bsu025_u.edition: P. L. Vaidya, ed., Mahāyāna-sūtra-saṃgraha, Part 1, Buddhist Sanskrit Texts 17, Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute, 1961 (text no. 25).
SA_K10_bsu025_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the short sūtra, consisting of introductory prose dialogue followed by 26 verses and concluding prose, corresponding to P. L. Vaidya's edition, pp. 174–176.
translations: Léon Feer, trans., Fragments extraits du Kandjour, Paris 1883. (French)

SA_K10_bsu031.title: Śālistambasūtra
SA_K10_bsu031.summary: The Śālistambasūtra is a foundational Mahāyāna sūtra on the doctrine of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda). Prompted by the Buddha's concise statement that whoever sees dependent origination sees the Dharma and whoever sees the Dharma sees the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Maitreya expounds the teaching to Śāriputra using the analogy of a rice seedling sprouting and developing from a seed. The discourse distinguishes between external causality (the physical conditions governing plant growth) and internal causality (the twelvefold chain of psychic and karmic conditioning), demonstrating that all conditioned phenomena arise devoid of an independent agent, soul (ātman), or essence. Copiously cited by Madhyamaka authors such as Nāgārjuna, Candrakīrti, and Kamalaśīla, it served as one of the primary scriptural foundations for early Mahāyāna causal theory.
SA_K10_bsu031.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna sūtra set on Gṛdhrakūṭa in Rājagṛha, where the Bodhisattva Maitreya expounds the Buddha's brief utterance on dependent origination to the elder Śāriputra.
SA_K10_bsu031.edition: P.L. Vaidya in: Mahayana-sutra-samgrahah, Part 1. Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute 1961 (Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, 17)
SA_K10_bsu031.coverage: complete — Complete text of the sūtra as printed in Vaidya (1961).

SA_K10_bsu034_u.title: Samādhirājasūtra
SA_K10_bsu034_u.summary: The Samādhirājasūtra is an influential Mahāyāna scripture in 40 chapters expounding the meditative absorption (samādhi) that reveals the fundamental equality and emptiness of all phenomena (sarvadharmasvabhāvasamatā). Delivered by the Buddha on Vulture Peak to the youth Candraprabha, the text combines exposition of non-arising and ultimate reality with teachings on ethical discipline, ascetic practices (dhūtaguṇa), dhāraṇī formulas, and past-life narratives (jātakas).
SA_K10_bsu034_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna scripture presented as buddhavacana delivered by Gautama Buddha on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in Rājagṛha, addressed principally to the bodhisattva youth Candraprabha (Candraprabha Kumārabhūta).
SA_K10_bsu034_u.edition: P.L. Vaidya (ed.), Samādhirājasūtra, Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute, 1961 (Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, 2).
SA_K10_bsu034_u.coverage: complete — Complete text across all 40 chapters (parivartas), beginning with the Nidānaparivarta (Vaidya p. 1) and concluding with the colophon of the 40th chapter (Vaidya p. 304).
translations: Konstanty Régamey, Three Chapters from the Samādhirājasūtra, Warsaw, 1938. (English)
Chijun Tamura and Masamichi Ichigo (trs.), Daijō Butten. (Japanese)

SA_K10_bsu036_u.title: Saddharmapuṇḍarīkasūtra
SA_K10_bsu036_u.summary: The Saddharmapuṇḍarīkasūtra ('The White Lotus of the True Dharma') is one of the most celebrated and influential Mahāyāna scriptures. It propounds the doctrine of the One Vehicle (ekayāna), declaring that the apparent three vehicles (śrāvakayāna, pratyekabuddhayāna, and bodhisattvayāna) are provisional pedagogical devices (upāyakauśalya) and that all beings are destined for unexcelled awakening. Renowned for its rich parables—such as the burning house, the prodigal son, the medicinal herbs, and the gem concealed in the garment—the sūtra also reveals the Buddha's lifespan to be immeasurable and his parinirvāṇa an expedient display.
SA_K10_bsu036_u.edition: P. L. Vaidya, ed., Saddharmapuṇḍarīkasūtra, Buddhist Sanskrit Texts 6, Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute of Post-Graduate Studies and Research in Sanskrit Learning, 1960.
SA_K10_bsu036_u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 27 chapters (parivartas 1–27), matching the structure of the standard Nepalese Sanskrit recension and concluding with the Anuparīndanāparivarta (segment 7397).

SA_K10_bsu061_u.title: Vimalakīrtinirdeśasūtra
SA_K10_bsu061_u.summary: The Vimalakīrtinirdeśasūtra is a renowned Mahāyāna scripture set in Vaiśālī that centers on the enlightened householder bodhisattva Vimalakīrti, who feigns illness to create an occasion to teach visiting śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and celestial beings. Over twelve chapters, the text articulates core Mahāyāna themes including the purification of the Buddha realm (buddhakṣetrapariśuddhi), the exercise of skillful means (upāyakauśalya), the inconceivable liberation (acintyavimokṣa), and the realization of non-duality (advayadharmamukha), memorably epitomized by Vimalakīrti's eloquent silence. Notably, this particular e-text contains the modern Sanskrit reconstruction prepared from the Tibetan translation by L.M. Joshi and Bhikshu Pāsādika in 1981, prior to the 1999 recovery of the original Sanskrit palm-leaf manuscript in Lhasa.
SA_K10_bsu061_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna sūtra traditionally attributed to the Buddha and framed around the dialogues of the householder bodhisattva Vimalakīrti. This specific e-text represents a modern scholarly reconstruction into Sanskrit from the classical Tibetan translation.
SA_K10_bsu061_u.edition: L.M. Joshi and Bhiksu Pasadika: Vimalakīrtinirdeśa sūtram. Sarnath: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 1981. (Reconstructed Version)

SA_K10_jnalokau.title: Sarvabuddhaviṣayāvatārajñānālokālaṃkārasūtra
SA_K10_jnalokau.summary: The Sarvabuddhaviṣayāvatārajñānālokālaṃkārasūtra is a Mahāyāna sūtra presented through dialogues between the Buddha and Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta concerning the nature of awakening, the realm of the buddhas, and ultimate reality. The text emphasizes that all dharmas are unoriginated (anutpāda), non-dual, and that bodhi is calm and unattached.
SA_K10_jnalokau.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna sūtra presented as buddhavacana.

SA_K10_mkarmviu.title: Mahākarmavibhaṅga
SA_K10_mkarmviu.summary: The Mahākarmavibhaṅga (also referred to in manuscripts as Karmavibhaṅga or Karmavibhaṅgasūtra) is an early Buddhist discourse detailing the retributions of specific actions across cycles of rebirth. Expanding substantially upon the framework of the canonical Cūḷakammavibhaṅga-sutta (Majjhima-nikāya 135) and its Āgama parallels, the text presents 80 categories of wholesome and unwholesome deeds, frequently illustrating doctrinal points with narrative exempla and avadānas. The work was historically influential across Buddhist Asia and served as the direct textual source for the 160 relief panels carved on the hidden basement of Borobudur in Java.
SA_K10_mkarmviu.attribution: Canonical Buddhist discourse presented as the word of the Buddha (buddhavacana) delivered to the brahmin youth Śuka Taudeyaputra in Śrāvastī.
SA_K10_mkarmviu.edition: Sylvain Lévi, ed., Mahākarmavibhaṅga et Karmavibhaṅgopadeśa, Paris 1932, pp. 21–105.
SA_K10_mkarmviu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the sūtra in 80 sections (pp. 21–105 of Lévi's 1932 edition). The commentary edited in the second part of the volume (Karmavibhaṅgopadeśa) is not included.

SA_K10_n260u.title: Arthaviniścayasūtra
SA_K10_n260u.summary: The Arthaviniścayasūtra is a Buddhist doctrinal compendium that presents core categories of Buddhist doctrine and meditation practice. It opens with a thematic list (uddeśa) followed by analytical definitions (vibhaṅga) of the aggregates, elements, sense fields, dependent origination, four noble truths, faculties, absorptions (dhyānas), formless attainments, and the marks and secondary characteristics (anuvyañjana) of a Buddha.
SA_K10_n260u.attribution: Canonical discourse presented as spoken by the Buddha to the assembly of monks.
SA_K10_n260u.edition: N.H. Samtani (ed.), The Arthaviniścaya-sūtra & its Commentary (Nibandhana), Tibetan Sanskrit Works Series 13, K.P. Jayaswal Research Institute, Patna 1971
SA_K10_n260u.coverage: complete — Text of the sūtra, including the introductory uddeśa, analytical definitions (vibhaṅga), and the concluding exhortation to heedfulness with standard canonical closing formula.
translations: Yoshifumi Honjō (trans.), Japanese translation of the Arthaviniścayasūtra and its commentary, 1989. (Japanese)

SA_K10_n552u.title: Buddhabalādhānaprātihāryavikurvaṇanirdeśasūtra (fragment)
SA_K10_n552u.summary: A Mahāyāna sūtra set initially on the banks of the Nairañjanā and shifting to the Āmrapālī grove in Vārāṇasī, in which the Buddha performs miraculous displays (prātihārya) through samādhi with the aid of the bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Vajrapāṇi. The surviving Sanskrit portion teaches the docetic nature of the Tathāgata, explaining through metaphors such as a magician's illusions that the appearance and parinirvāṇa of buddhas are skillful means (upāya).
SA_K10_n552u.attribution: Traditional canonical sūtra attributed to the speech of the Buddha (buddhavacana).
SA_K10_n552u.coverage: fragment — Preserves a portion of the sūtra; D 186 preserves the full text in Tibetan translation.

SA_K10_vimkn_u.title: Vimalakīrtinirdeśa
SA_K10_vimkn_u.summary: The Vimalakīrtinirdeśa is an influential Mahāyāna sūtra set in Vaiśālī, centered on the lay bodhisattva Vimalakīrti, who feigns illness to receive visitors and instruct them. In a series of witty dialogues with major arhat disciples and bodhisattvas, Vimalakīrti dismantles dualistic attachments regarding renunciation, purity, and emptiness (śūnyatā), culminating in his famous silence to signify direct entry into non-duality (advayadharmamukha-praveśa). Long celebrated in East Asian Buddhism and Tibet via early translations, the complete Indic Sanskrit text was identified in 1999 in a 12th-century palm-leaf manuscript preserved at the Potala Palace in Lhasa.
SA_K10_vimkn_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna sūtra set at Vaiśālī, centering on the teaching and miraculous displays of the householder bodhisattva Vimalakīrti.
SA_K10_vimkn_u.edition: Study Group on Buddhist Sanskrit Literature: Vimalakīrtinirdeśa, A Sanskrit Edition Based upon the Manuscript Newly Found at the Potala Palace, Tokyo 2006 (The Institute for Comprehensive Studies of Buddhism, Taisho University)

SA_K12_bsu003_u.title: Aparimitāyuḥsūtra
SA_K12_bsu003_u.summary: The Aparimitāyuḥsūtra is a Mahāyāna dhāraṇī-sūtra in which the Buddha Śākyamuni instructs Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta at Śrāvastī concerning the tathāgata Aparimitāyurjñānasuviniścitatejorāja, who presides over the zenith Buddha-field Aparimitaguṇasaṃcaya. The sūtra extols the recitation, writing, and veneration of this scripture and its central longevity dhāraṇī, assuring that these acts extend human lifespan to a full hundred years, absolve grave karmic faults, avert untimely death, and secure rebirth in Sukhāvatī.
SA_K12_bsu003_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna scripture belonging to the dhāraṇī-sūtra genre, presented as the word of the Buddha (Śākyamuni) delivered to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta in the Jetavana hermitage at Śrāvastī.
SA_K12_bsu003_u.coverage: complete — Complete text divided into 40 numbered paragraphs, concluding with paragraph 40 (the canonical closing formula: idam vocadbhagavān...).

SA_K12_bsu007_u.title: Śrīmahādevīvyākaraṇa
SA_K12_bsu007_u.summary: The Śrīmahādevīvyākaraṇa (also known as the Dvādaśadaṇḍakanāmāṣṭaśatavimalīkaraṇā) is set in Sukhāvatī. The Buddha expounds to Avalokiteśvara the virtues and future enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) of the goddess Śrī Mahādevī, accompanied by a litany of Tathāgata names, her 108 names, and mantras/praises. Recitation of these names is prescribed to dispel sins, poverty, and obstacles, and confer prosperity.
SA_K12_bsu007_u.attribution: The title Śrīmahādevīvyākaraṇa is found in the Gilgit manuscript edition; the Chinese translation by Amoghavajra (T 1253) and Sanskrit text also identify it as Dvādaśadaṇḍakanāmāṣṭaśatavimalīkaraṇā.

SA_K12_mamuka.title: Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa
SA_K12_mamuka.summary: The Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa is a massive composite Buddhist scripture and ritual manual (kalparāja) focused on the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, representing a key transition between Mahāyāna sūtra literature and Mantrayāna/Kriyātantra ritual systems. Dating in its various historical strata from roughly the 6th to 8th centuries CE, the work provides exhaustive instructions for mudrās, maṇḍalas, cloth-painting (paṭa), fire oblations (homa), mantras, astrology, and practices for attaining mundane powers as well as awakening. It is particularly renowned for chapter 53 (Rājavyākaraṇaparivarta), which contains a verse prophecy detailing north Indian dynastic history up to the rise of the Pāla Empire.
SA_K12_mamuka.attribution: A vast composite canonical scripture presenting itself as a Mahāyāna vaipulyasūtra belonging to the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, traditionally classed in Tibetan doxography as a Kriyātantra.
SA_K12_mamuka.edition: T. Ganapati Sastri (ed.), The Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa, Trivandrum Sanskrit Series Nos. 70, 76, 84, 3 parts, Trivandrum, 1920-1925.
SA_K12_mamuka.coverage: complete — Complete text in 55 chapters (paṭalavisaras), ending with the 55th chapter (Hemasādhanapaṭala) and the scribal colophon of Paṇḍita Ravicandra of Śrīmūlaghoṣavihāra.
translations: Marcelle Lalou, Iconographie des étoffes peintes (paṭa) dans le Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, 1930. (French)

SA_K12_manjn1pu.title: Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti
SA_K12_manjn1pu.summary: The Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti ('Chanting the Names of Mañjuśrī') is one of the most revered and influential liturgical and doctrinal scriptures of late Indian Buddhism. Framed as an excerpt from the Māyājālatantra cycle delivered by Śākyamuni Buddha to Vajrapāṇi, the text presents Mañjuśrī as the embodiment of primordial non-dual gnosis (advayajñāna) and the ultimate source of all buddhas, systematically mapping his sacred epithets across mantric syllables and deity families. It played an essential role across Mahāyoga, Yoga, and Anuttarayoga tantric systems, including Kālacakra and rDzogs chen, and stimulated extensive commentarial traditions in India, Tibet, and East Asia.
SA_K12_manjn1pu.attribution: Canonical tantric scripture presented as the discourse of the Buddha Śākyamuni in response to the request of the Guhyaka lord Vajrapāṇi; colophons align it with the Samādhijālapaṭala of the 16,000-verse Māyājālamahāyogatantra.
SA_K12_manjn1pu.edition: Ronald M. Davidson, 'The Litany of Names of Mañjuśrī: Text and Translation of the Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti', in Tantric and Taoist Studies in Honour of R. A. Stein, ed. SA_K12_manjn1pu.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all 167 verses (Mns_1–Mns_167) along with the standard introductory lines, section rubrics, and final colophon.

SA_K12_mspram_u.title: Mahāsāhasrapramardanī
SA_K12_mspram_u.summary: The Mahāsāhasrapramardanī is a Buddhist sūtra and part of the Pañcarakṣā collection. Set at Gṛdhrakūṭa in Rājagṛha, the Buddha instructs on dhāraṇīs to protect beings and avert calamities. It was translated into Chinese (T 999) by 施護 (Dānapāla) in 980.
SA_K12_mspram_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna dhāraṇī sūtra, traditionally set at Gṛdhrakūṭa in Rājagṛha.
SA_K12_mspram_u.edition: Yutaka Iwamoto (ed.), Mahāsāhasrapramardanī, Pañcarakṣā I. (Beiträge zur Indologie, 1). Kyoto 1937.

SA_K12_n259u.title: Aparimitāyurnāmamahāyānasūtra
SA_K12_n259u.summary: The Aparimitāyurnāmamahāyānasūtra is a popular Mahāyāna dhāraṇī scripture wherein the Buddha instructs Mañjuśrī on the longevity dhāraṇī and boundless merits of the Buddha Aparimitāyurjñānasuviniścitatejorāja, who dwells in the pure land Aparimitaguṇasaṃcaya. The text explains that copying, reading, reciting, or honoring this sūtra neutralizes the danger of untimely death, extends lifespan to one hundred years, and guarantees favorable rebirth. Due to its association with longevity and merit accumulation, it became one of the most widely transcribed scriptures across Central Asia and Tibet, surviving in thousands of copies among the Dunhuang manuscript collections.
SA_K12_n259u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna Buddhist scripture presented as buddhavacana, spoken by the Buddha to Mañjuśrī in the Jetavana monastery at Śrāvastī.

SA_K12_n283u.title: Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabharājasūtra
SA_K12_n283u.summary: The Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabharājasūtra is a canonical Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra set in Vaiśālī, in which Śākyamuni Buddha expounds to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī the twelve past aspirations made by the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaiḍūryaprabha (the Medicine Buddha) during his bodhisattva career. The text describes his eastern pure realm, Vaiḍūryanirbhāsa, and prescribes ritual veneration—such as reciting his name and sūtra, erecting images, and offering banners and lamps—to heal diseases, prevent untimely death, and protect states from turmoil. The work concludes with protective pledges uttered by twelve yakṣa generals.
SA_K12_n283u.attribution: A canonical Mahāyāna Buddhist scripture presented as the teaching of Śākyamuni Buddha delivered in Vaiśālī in dialogue with the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.
SA_K12_n283u.edition: P. L. Vaidya (ed.), Mahāyāna-sūtra-saṃgrahaḥ, Part 1. Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute, 1961 (Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, 17).

SA_K12_n2967u.title: Śrīguhyasamājatantra
SA_K12_n2967u.summary: The Śrīguhyasamājatantra (also known as the Tathāgataguhyaka) is the foundational scripture of esoteric Mahāyāna Buddhism belonging to the Anuttarayoga / Mahāyoga class of tantras. In eighteen chapters (paṭalas 1–17 forming the root tantra and paṭala 18 serving as the Uttaratantra or explanatory continuation), it expounds the maṇḍala of the five Tathāgata families, deity yoga, consecration rituals, and subtle-body inner yogic practices. The scripture became the central root source for two major Indian commentarial lineages—the Ārya school associated with Nāgārjuna, Āryadeva, and Candrakīrti, and the Jñānapāda school—profoundly shaping the development of Indo-Tibetan Vajrayāna scholasticism and meditative praxis.
SA_K12_n2967u.attribution: Canonical Vajrayāna tantra (buddhavacana) revealed by the primordial Buddha / Sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittavajra (Vajradhara) residing in the source/womb of the cosmic Vajrayoṣit.
SA_K12_n2967u.edition: Sitansusekhar Bagchi (ed.), Guhyasamāja Tantra or Tathāgataguhyaka, Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute of Post-Graduate Studies and Research in Sanskrit Learning, 1965.
SA_K12_n2967u.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising all 18 chapters (paṭalas 1–17 of the root tantra and paṭala 18 functioning as the Uttaratantra), concluding with verse 18.217 and the final colophon.

SA_K14_mhvastuu.title: Mahāvastu
SA_K14_mhvastuu.summary: The Mahāvastu ('The Great Story') is an extensive Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit canonical text preserved by the Lokottaravāda sub-sect of the Mahāsāṃghika school, nominally forming the opening section of their Vinayapiṭaka. It presents an expansive biography of the Buddha Gautama, tracing his past lives, his bodhisattva path across the ten spiritual stages (daśabhūmi), his vow under previous Buddhas such as Dīpaṃkara, and his final awakening and initial teaching career. Rich in jātakas, avadānas, and early doctrinal discourses, the work was compiled and expanded over several centuries (c. 2nd century BCE to 4th century CE) and stands as a key witness for early Lokottaravāda supramundane buddhology and proto-Mahāyāna concepts.
SA_K14_mhvastuu.attribution: Canonical Vinaya scripture preserved in Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit belonging to the Lokottaravāda branch of the Mahāsāṃghika school.
SA_K14_mhvastuu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all three volumes of Émile Senart's edition, concluding with the scribal colophon (granthapramāṇaṃ śloka 25000, dated Saṃvat 842).

SA_T02_narsekou.title: Sekoddeśa
SA_T02_narsekou.summary: The Sekoddeśa consists of 174 verses traditionally considered an excerpt from the fifth chapter of the lost Kālacakra root tantra (Paramādibuddha). Presented as a dialogue between the Buddha and King Sucandra, it provides the exposition of the Kālacakra initiation system, including seven worldly initiations and higher empowerments. The text details subtle-body physiology, channels (nāḍī), and the realization of imperishable bliss (akṣarasukha).
SA_T02_narsekou.attribution: The Sekoddeśa is traditionally regarded as an excerpt from the fifth chapter of the lost Kālacakra root tantra (Paramādibuddha), delivered by the Buddha to Sucandra. Raniero Gnoli edited the Sanskrit text of the verses from a single manuscript folio, citations, and Sanskrit commentaries including that of Nāropa (Sekoddeśaṭīkā); this connection with Nāropa's commentary caused GRETIL to catalog the e-text under Nāropa.
SA_T02_narsekou.edition: Raniero Gnoli, appendix 'On the Sanskrit text', in Giacomella Orofino, Sekoddeśa: A Critical Edition of the Tibetan Translations, Serie Orientale Roma 72, Roma: Istituto Italiano per il Medio ed Estremo Oriente, 1994.
SA_T02_narsekou.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 174 verses of the Sekoddeśa (ending with 'iti śrīsekoddeśaḥ samāptaḥ').
translations: Raniero Gnoli and Giacomella Orofino, 1994. (Italian)

SA_T04_bsa047.title: Bhāvanākrama
SA_T04_bsa047.author: Kamalaśīla
SA_T04_bsa047.summary: The Bhāvanākrama ('Stages of Meditation') by Kamalaśīla (8th cent.) is an influential triad of treatises formulating the graduated Mahāyāna path. Across the works, Kamalaśīla systematizes the cultivation of compassion (mahākaruṇā), the awakening mind (bodhicitta), calm abiding (śamatha), and analytical discernment (vipaśyanā) leading to the non-conceptual realization of emptiness.
SA_T04_bsa047.attribution: Composed by the Indian Madhyamaka master Kamalaśīla (8th cent.). The Tibetan translation (D 3915) attributes the work to Jayasena (ka ma la shI la). The Tibetan translation (D 3916) attributes the work to Jayasena (A tsAr+ya ka ma la shI la). The Tibetan translation (D 3917) attributes the work to Jayasena (A tsaR+ya ka ma la shI la).

SA_T04_bsa047.coverage: complete — Complete corpus of all three Bhāvanākrama treatises: Bhāvanākrama I, Bhāvanākrama II, and Bhāvanākrama III.

SA_T04_sanssr.title: Śikṣāsamuccaya
SA_T04_sanssr.author: Śāntideva
SA_T04_sanssr.summary: The Śikṣāsamuccaya ('Compendium of Training') is a Mahāyāna manual composed by Śāntideva. Structured around mnemonic root verses (kārikā) and Śāntideva's own prose exposition, it organizes the bodhisattva training into the program of relinquishing, guarding, purifying, and increasing one's body, possessions, and religious merit. The work preserves extensive quotations from numerous sūtras.
SA_T04_sanssr.attribution: Traditional attribution to Śāntideva is supported by the colophon, secondary literature, and canonical records; preserved in the Tibetan Tengyur (Dbu ma, Toh 3940) translated by Jinamitra, Dānaśīla, and Ye-shes sde, and in the Chinese canon (Taishō 1636).
SA_T04_sanssr.edition: Cecil Bendall (ed.), Çikshāsamuccaya: A Compendium of Buddhistic Teaching compiled by Çāntideva, Bibliotheca Buddhica 1, St. Petersburg, 1897–1902.
SA_T04_sanssr.coverage: complete — Contains chapters from dānapāramitā to puṇyavṛddhi, including introductory verses and concluding colophon.

SA_T04_tat.title: Tattvasaṃgraha (kārikās 7–3646)
SA_T04_tat.author: Śāntarakṣita
SA_T04_tat.summary: The Tattvasaṃgraha ('Compendium of Reality') by the 8th-century Madhyamaka-Yogācāra master Śāntarakṣita is a monumental verse treatise providing an exhaustive critique of classical Indian philosophical systems. Grounded in the Buddhist epistemological framework (pramāṇa) of Dignāga and Dharmakīrti, it systematically refutes rival theories regarding primordial nature (prakṛti), God (īśvara), the eternal Self (ātman), the categories of Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, the eternity of sound and Vedic authority, and various non-Buddhist epistemologies, while establishing Buddhist tenets such as universal momentariness, nominal exclusion (apoha), dependent origination, and the omniscience of the Buddha. It serves as one of the most important doxographical sources for 8th-century Indian philosophy, preserving extensive fragments and doctrines of otherwise lost Brahmanical, Jaina, and materialist thinkers.
SA_T04_tat.attribution: Firmly attributed to Śāntarakṣita. The text consists of his verse kārikās; the accompanying prose commentary (Pañjikā) by Kamalaśīla is catalogued separately.
SA_T04_tat.edition: Embar Krishnamacharya (ed.), Tattvasaṅgraha of Śāntarakṣita with the commentary Pañjikā of Kamalaśīla, 2 vols., Gaekwad's Oriental Series 30-31, Baroda: Central Library/Oriental Institute, 1926.
SA_T04_tat.coverage: partial — Verse text only (no Pañjikā). Begins with kārikā 7 (aśeṣaśaktipracitāt pradhānād eva kevalāt, opening of the Prakṛtiparīkṣā) and ends with kārikā 3646 and the final colophon 'ity atīndriyadarśipuruṣaparīkṣā | śāntarakṣitaviracistatvasaṅgrahaḥ samāptaḥ' (sic). The six opening maṅgala/introductory kārikās (1–6) are absent.

SA_T04_tatpa.title: Tattvasaṃgraha with Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā (lacking verses 1–6)
SA_T04_tatpa.author: Śāntarakṣita, Kamalaśīla
SA_T04_tatpa.summary: The Tattvasaṃgraha by Śāntarakṣita and its Pañjikā by Kamalaśīla constitute an encyclopedic late 8th-century monument of Indian Buddhist philosophy. Integrating Yogācāra-Madhyamaka dialectics with Dignāga-Dharmakīrti epistemology, the work presents exhaustive critical examinations (parīkṣā) of all major rival Indian philosophical traditions—including Sāṅkhya, Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, Mīmāṃsā, Cārvāka, and Jainism—as well as competing Buddhist views across 26 topical chapters. Kamalaśīla's Pañjikā is indispensable for understanding Śāntarakṣita's condensed verses and serves as a vital historical repository preserving fragments of numerous otherwise lost classical Sanskrit texts.
SA_T04_tatpa.attribution: The root verses of the Tattvasaṃgraha are by Śāntarakṣita, and the commentary (pañjikā) is by Kamalaśīla. The colophon confirms Kamalaśīla's authorship ('kamalaśīlaviracitā pañjikā samāptā').
SA_T04_tatpa.edition: Kamalaśīla, Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā (commentary on Śāntarakṣita's Tattvasaṃgraha), ed. Embar Krishnamacharya, Gaekwad's Oriental Series nos. XXX-XXXI (2 vols.), Baroda: Central Library, 1926.
SA_T04_tatpa.coverage: partial — Contains chapters concluding with Atīndriyadarśipuruṣaparīkṣā, but lacks the opening introductory section.

SA_T06_asabhs_u.title: Abhidharmasamuccaya
SA_T06_asabhs_u.author: Asaṅga
SA_T06_asabhs_u.summary: The Abhidharmasamuccaya is Asaṅga's definitive synthesis of Abhidharma doctrine from a Mahāyāna and Yogācāra perspective. The treatise is structured into two main parts: the Lakṣaṇasamuccaya, which categorizes dharmas across the skandhas, dhātus, āyatanas, and fifty-one mental factors (caittas), and the Viniścayasamuccaya, which analyzes the noble truths, doctrinal exposition, attainment of liberation, and rules of philosophical dialectic. Providing the scholastic foundation of Yogācāra dogmatics, it served as the standard textbook for Abhidharma study in Tibetan and East Asian Buddhism.
SA_T06_asabhs_u.attribution: Attributed to Asaṅga (Thogs-med / 無著) in the Tibetan (D 4049) and Chinese (T 1605, tr. Xuanzang) canons.
SA_T06_asabhs_u.coverage: complete — Text comprising the Lakṣaṇasamuccaya and the Viniścayasamuccaya (concluding with sāṃkathyaviniścaya). Sanskrit restorations are marked in parentheses in the e-text.

Sara Boin-Webb (English tr. from Rahula's French), Abhidharmasamuccaya: The Compendium of the Higher Teaching (Philosophy) by Asaṅga, Fremont, CA: Asian Humanities Press, 2001. (English)

SA_T06_asmahsuu.title: Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkārakārikā with Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkārabhāṣya
SA_T06_asmahsuu.author: Maitreya, Vasubandhu
SA_T06_asmahsuu.summary: The Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra is a Yogācāra treatise in 21 chapters (adhikāras), transmitted together with its prose bhāṣya. It deals with Mahāyāna Buddhist doctrine and practice, culminating in caryāpratiṣṭhā and buddhahood. It is preserved in Sanskrit, Chinese (T 1604, translated by Prabhākaramitra), and Tibetan (D 4020, D 4026, translated by Śākyasiṃha and Dpal brtsegs).
SA_T06_asmahsuu.attribution: The verses are attributed in the Tibetan tradition to Maitreya (one of the 'five treatises of Maitreya', Tib. D 4020), in the Chinese tradition (T 1604) to Asaṅga; GRETIL edition title ascribes it to Asaṅga. The bhāṣya is generally attributed to Vasubandhu (D 4026; in the Sanskrit colophon: 'mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāreṣu vyavadātasamayamahābodhisattvabhāṣite').

SA_T06_bsa018.title: Triṃśikāvijñaptikārikā
SA_T06_bsa018.author: Vasubandhu
SA_T06_bsa018.summary: The Triṃśikāvijñaptikārikā (Thirty Verses on Representation-Only) by Vasubandhu is a foundational treatise of Yogācāra Buddhism. In thirty concise kārikās, it expounds the threefold transformation of consciousness (vijñānapariṇāma)—the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), the afflicted mentation (manas), and the six object-cognizing consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna)—alongside the doctrine of the three natures (trisvabhāva). The work outlines the path to realizing mere representation (vijñaptimātratā), culminating in the transformation of the psycho-physical base (āśrayaparāvṛtti) and liberation.
SA_T06_bsa018.attribution: Ascribed in the opening title line and concluding colophon to Ācārya Vasubandhu (kṛtir iyam ācāryavasubandhoḥ).
SA_T06_bsa018.coverage: complete — Complete: title line, ascription, all 30 kārikās (numbered Tvk_1–Tvk_30) and the closing colophon 'triṃśikāvijñaptikārikāḥ samāptāḥ / kṛtir iyam ācāryavasubandhoḥ'.
translations: Thomas A. Kochumuttom, A Buddhist Doctrine of Experience, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1982. (English)

SA_T06_bsa034.title: Bodhisattvabhūmi
SA_T06_bsa034.author: Asaṅga
SA_T06_bsa034.summary: The Bodhisattvabhūmi constitutes the fifteenth and most influential section of the encyclopedic Yogācārabhūmi, composed in approximately the 4th century CE. It serves as an exhaustive manual of the Mahāyāna bodhisattva path, systematically treating spiritual lineage (gotra), the generation of the aspiration for awakening (bodhicitta), the perfections (pāramitās), ethics (śīla), and the stages of spiritual maturation (vihāras and bhūmis). Its fourth chapter, the Tattvārthapaṭala, forms a cornerstone of early Yogācāra philosophy, presenting a foundational analysis of the inexpressible nature of reality (nirabhilāpyasvabhāva) underlying linguistic and conceptual designations (prajñapti).
SA_T06_bsa034.attribution: The Sanskrit manuscript tradition and the concluding colophon explicitly attribute the treatise to Ācārya Asaṅga ('kṛtir iyam ācāryāryāsaṅgapādānām'). In Tibetan and East Asian traditions, the Yogācārabhūmi corpus is revered either as transmitted to Asaṅga by the heavenly bodhisattva Maitreya or as compiled by Asaṅga himself.
SA_T06_bsa034.edition: Nalinaksha Dutt: Bodhisattvabhumi. Patna: K.P. Jayaswal Research Institute, 1966 (Tibetan Sanskrit Works Series, 7)
SA_T06_bsa034.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Bodhisattvabhūmi comprising all four yogasthānas (Ādhāra-, Ādhārānudharma-, Ādhārapratiniṣṭhā-, and Niṣṭhāgata-yogasthāna), running from the opening gotrapaṭala to the concluding pratiṣṭhāpaṭala and final colophon.
translations: Janice Dean Willis, trans. 1979. On Knowing Reality: The Tattvārtha Chapter of Asaṅga's Bodhisattvabhūmi. (English)

SA_T06_bsa065.title: Pañcaskandhaprakaraṇa
SA_T06_bsa065.author: Vasubandhu
SA_T06_bsa065.summary: The Pañcaskandhaprakaraṇa (or Pañcaskandhaka) is a treatise composed by Vasubandhu that presents a systematic categorization of mental and physical phenomena according to the five aggregates (skandhas), twelve sense fields (āyatanas), and eighteen elements (dhātus), discussing mind and mental factors as well as ālayavijñāna. This electronic text represents the Sanskrit retro-translation from Tibetan executed by Shanti Bhikshu Shastri.
SA_T06_bsa065.attribution: Root text authored by Vasubandhu. This electronic text represents a Sanskrit retro-translation/reconstruction from Tibetan made by Shanti Bhikshu Shastri. A Sanskrit edition of the text was published by Li Xuezhu and Ernst Steinkellner in 2008.
SA_T06_bsa065.edition: Shantibhiksu Shastri: Pañcaskandhaprakaraṇam. In: Journal of Sampurnanda Sanskrit University, 1955.
SA_T06_bsa065.coverage: complete — Complete Sanskrit retro-translation from Tibetan in three adhikāras, arranged into 167 numbered prose sections, concluding with Shastri's two-verse Sanskrit reconstruction colophon.

SA_T06_pskvbhu.title: Pañcaskandhakavibhāṣā
SA_T06_pskvbhu.author: Sthiramati
SA_T06_pskvbhu.summary: The Pañcaskandhakavibhāṣā is a Yogācāra Abhidharma commentary by Sthiramati on Vasubandhu's Pañcaskandhaka. It offers an analysis of the five aggregates (skandha), mental factors, consciousness including ālayavijñāna, and the sensory bases and elements.
SA_T06_pskvbhu.attribution: Attributed to Sthiramati, corroborated by the closing colophon: 'kṛtir ācāryasthiramateḥ'. The scribal colophon records the donation by the Śākyabhikṣu Vibhūtiśrīmitra during the reign of Govindapāla.

SA_T06_sthtvbh.title: Triṃśikāvijñaptikārikā with Triṃśikāvijñaptibhāṣya
SA_T06_sthtvbh.author: Vasubandhu, Sthiramati
SA_T06_sthtvbh.summary: Vasubandhu's Triṃśikāvijñaptikārikā is a foundational work of Yogācāra philosophy outlining the three transformations of consciousness (ālayavijñāna, kliṣṭamanas, and pravṛttivijñāna), the three intrinsic natures (trisvabhāva), and the realization of cognition-only (vijñaptimātratā). Sthiramati's Triṃśikāvijñaptibhāṣya is a commentary on the text, expounding the nature of mental factors (caitta), metaphorical designation (upacāra) in establishing consciousness-only without external objects, and the soteriological progression toward fundamental transformation (āśrayaparāvṛtti).
SA_T06_sthtvbh.attribution: Vasubandhu composed the root verses (Triṃśikāvijñaptikārikā). Sthiramati composed the prose commentary (bhāṣya), as confirmed by the closing colophon ('triṃśikāvijñaptibhāṣyaṃ samāptam // kṛtir ācāryastiramateḥ //').

SA_T06_sthtvbh.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all 30 kārikās embedded with Sthiramati's full bhāṣya, ending with the final work colophon.

SA_T06_bsa022_u.title: Viṃśatikāvijñaptimātratāsiddhi (kārikās only)
SA_T06_bsa022_u.author: Vasubandhu
SA_T06_bsa022_u.summary: The Viṃśatikāvijñaptimātratāsiddhi ('Proof of Mere Representation in Twenty Verses') is a foundational treatise of Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda philosophy composed by Vasubandhu. In twenty-two concise kārikās, Vasubandhu defends the thesis that external objects do not exist independently of cognition (vijñaptimātra), refuting realist objections regarding spatiotemporal determinacy, intersubjective consensus, and causal efficacy through comparisons with dreams and hell visions. The work also articulates a famous critique of atomism (paramāṇuvāda), arguing that indivisible partless atoms cannot coalesce into composite extended bodies without logical contradiction.
SA_T06_bsa022_u.attribution: Attributed to Vasubandhu in Sanskrit, Tibetan, and Chinese traditions.
SA_T06_bsa022_u.edition: Stefan Anacker (ed., tr.), Seven Works of Vasubandhu: The Buddhist Psychological Doctor, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1984.
SA_T06_bsa022_u.coverage: partial — Contains all 22 root verses (kārikās 1–22) and the final closing colophons, but the prose auto-commentary (svavṛtti) found in the printed source edition was completely omitted during digitization.
translations: Stefan Anacker, Seven Works of Vasubandhu, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1984. (English)
Sylvain Lévi, Matériaux pour l'étude du système Vijñaptimātra, Paris: 1932. (French)

SA_T06_vasvvmsu.title: Viṃśatikāvijñaptimātratāsiddhi with Viṃśatikāvṛtti
SA_T06_vasvvmsu.author: Vasubandhu
SA_T06_vasvvmsu.summary: The Viṃśatikāvijñaptimātratāsiddhi with its autocommentary (Viṃśatikāvṛtti) is Vasubandhu's foundational defense of the Yogācāra doctrine that reality is cognition-only (vijñaptimātra) and devoid of external, mind-independent physical objects. The text systematically counters realist objections regarding spatiotemporal coordination, collective experience, and causal efficacy through analogies to dreams, collective torment in hell, and shared karmic fruition. It is especially famous for stanzas 11–15, which formulate a decisive refutation of atomism by demonstrating that physical atoms can neither possess parts nor be partless without rendering composite macroscopic extension conceptually impossible.
SA_T06_vasvvmsu.attribution: Both the twenty-two stanzas (twenty doctrinal kārikās plus two concluding verses) and the prose autocommentary (vṛtti) are composed by Vasubandhu (c. 4th–5th century CE), attested by the concluding Sanskrit colophon ('kṛtir iyam ācāryavasubandhoḥ') and ancient Tibetan (D 4056, D 4057) and Chinese translations (T 1588, T 1589, T 1590).
SA_T06_vasvvmsu.edition: S. Lévi (ed.), Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi: Deux traités de Vasubandhu: Viṃśatikā (La Vingtaine) accompagnée d'une explication en prose et Triṃśikā (La trentaine) avec le commentaire de Sthiramati, Paris 1925, and the correction by Hakuju Ui: Shiyaku-taisyō Yuisiki nijū-ron Kenkyū (Daijō-bukkyō Kenkyū 4) [*Comparative Study of the Viṃśatikā vijñaptimātratāsiddhi with Four Translations (Studies of the Mahāyāna Buddhism, 4)], Tokyo 1953, pp. 20-21.
SA_T06_vasvvmsu.coverage: complete — Contains the complete work: introductory prose, all 22 stanzas, full autocommentary (vṛtti), and closing colophon.

SA_T06_vmvkbh_u.title: Madhyāntavibhāgakārikā with Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya
SA_T06_vmvkbh_u.author: Maitreya, Vasubandhu
SA_T06_vmvkbh_u.summary: The Madhyāntavibhāga is a Yogācāra verse treatise in five chapters, here transmitted with Vasubandhu's prose bhāṣya. It treats the characteristics of unreal imagination (abhūtaparikalpa) and emptiness, the obscurations (āvaraṇa), reality (tattva), the cultivation of the antidotes with its stages and results, and the supremacy of the Great Vehicle.
SA_T06_vmvkbh_u.attribution: The kārikās are attributed to Maitreya(nātha) (Tibetan tradition; GRETIL: 'Madhyantavibhagakarikas attributed to Maitreyanatha'); in the bhāṣya's opening verse Vasubandhu honours the treatise's author ('praṇetāram ... sugatātmajam') and its expounder ('vaktāraṃ'). The bhāṣya is ascribed to Vasubandhu in the colophon: 'madhyāntavibhāgakārikābhāṣyaṃ samāptam // kṛtir ācāryabhadantavasubandhoḥ'.
SA_T06_vmvkbh_u.coverage: complete — All five chapters (paricchedas: lakṣaṇa, āvaraṇa, tattva, pratipakṣabhāvanā/avasthā/phala, ānuttarya) with kārikās and bhāṣya, from the opening 'namo buddhāya' and maṅgala verse to the final colophon; Nagao page markers Mvbh 35, 77. Bracketed section headings (e.g. '[1. abhūtaparikalpa; a. sadasallakṣaṇa]') are editorial additions, not part of the work.

SA_T07_hvsatssu.title: Satyasiddhiśāstra
SA_T07_hvsatssu.author: Harivarman
SA_T07_hvsatssu.summary: The Satyasiddhiśāstra (also reconstructed as Tattvasiddhiśāstra; Chinese: Chengshi lun) is an extensive Buddhist scholastic treatise by Harivarman (c. 3rd–4th century CE), reflecting Bahuśrutīya and Dārṣṭāntika/Sautrāntika doctrines. Organized around an introductory section and doctrinal topics, it expounds Buddhist tenets including the Four Truths, emptiness, and prajñaptisat. While lost in India, Kumārajīva's Chinese translation formed the foundational text of the Chinese Chengshi (Japanese Jōjitsu) school.
SA_T07_hvsatssu.attribution: Authored in Sanskrit by Harivarman (c. 3rd–4th century CE). The original Sanskrit text was lost in India, surviving in Kumārajīva's Chinese translation (T 1646, 成實論 Chengshi lun, 406–412 CE). This Sanskrit e-text represents the modern retroversion/reconstruction from Chinese into Sanskrit by N. Aiyaswami Sastri.
SA_T07_hvsatssu.edition: N. Aiyaswami Sastri (ed. & reconstr.), Satyasiddhisastra of Harivarman, Vol. I, Baroda: Oriental Institute, 1975 (Gaekwad's Oriental Series, 159).
SA_T07_hvsatssu.coverage: complete — Complete Sanskrit reconstruction of all chapters across skandhas (including prasthānaskandha), corresponding to Vol. I of N. Aiyaswami Sastri's edition.

SA_T06_sthmavtyg.title: Madhyāntavibhāgaṭīkā
SA_T06_sthmavtyg.author: Sthiramati
SA_T06_sthmavtyg.summary: Sthiramati's Madhyāntavibhāgaṭīkā is a sub-commentary on Vasubandhu's bhāṣya to the Madhyāntavibhāga verses, explaining both kārikās and bhāṣya through pratīkas. Across five chapters it elaborates Yogācāra doctrine on unreal imagination (abhūtaparikalpa), emptiness, reality (tattva), and the Mahāyāna path. This e-text is an OCR of Yamaguchi's 1934 edition.
SA_T06_sthmavtyg.attribution: The ṭīkā itself names Maitreya as author (praṇetṛ) of the kārikās and Asaṅga as their expounder (vaktṛ), from whom Vasubandhu heard them and wrote the bhāṣya.
SA_T06_sthmavtyg.edition: Susumu Yamaguchi (ed.), Madhyāntavibhāgaṭīkā: Exposition systématique du Yogācāravijñaptivāda, Nagoya: Librairie Hajinkaku, 1934.
