SA_T06_sthmavt.title: Madhyāntavibhāgaṭīkā
SA_T06_sthmavt.author: Sthiramati
SA_T06_sthmavt.summary: The Madhyāntavibhāgaṭīkā (subtitled Āgamānusāriṇī) is Sthiramati's Sanskrit sub-commentary on Vasubandhu's Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya and the root verses attributed to Maitreya. Across five chapters, it expounds classical Yogācāra ontology and soteriology, giving extensive philosophical explanations of the constructive imagination of the unreal (abhūtaparikalpa), the three natures (trisvabhāva), emptiness (śūnyatā), obscurations to enlightenment and their antidotes, and the unexcelled Mahāyāna path. It constitutes one of the most comprehensive surviving Sanskrit expositions of early Vijñaptimātra thought.
SA_T06_sthmavt.attribution: Sthiramati is identified as the commentator, confirmed by the internal colophon: 'samāptā ceyam āgamānusāriṇī madhyāntavibhāgaṭīkā ācāryasthiramatyuparacitā'. The subtitle Āgamānusāriṇī is explicit in the Sanskrit colophons.
SA_T06_sthmavt.edition: Ramchandra Pandeya (ed.), Madhyānta-vibhāga-śāstra (containing the Kārikās of Maitreya, Bhāṣya of Vasubandhu and Ṭīkā of Sthiramati), Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1971.
SA_T06_sthmavt.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all five chapters (paricchedas): 1. Lakṣaṇapariccheda, 2. Āvaraṇapariccheda, 3. Tattvapariccheda, 4. Phalanirdeśapariccheda / Pratipakṣabhāvanāpariccheda, and 5. Yānānuttaryapariccheda.

SA_T06_sthmavt1.title: Madhyāntavibhāgaṭīkā (chapter 1: Lakṣaṇapariccheda)
SA_T06_sthmavt1.author: Sthiramati
SA_T06_sthmavt1.summary: The first chapter (Lakṣaṇapariccheda) of Sthiramati's sub-commentary (ṭīkā) on Vasubandhu's Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya. It provides a detailed Yogācāra analysis of the unreal mental construction (abhūtaparikalpa), the non-existence of subject-object duality (dvaya), and the reality of emptiness (śūnyatā).
SA_T06_sthmavt1.attribution: The root verses (kārikās) of the Madhyāntavibhāga are attributed to Maitreya and associated with Asaṅga. The bhāṣya is by Vasubandhu. The present sub-commentary (ṭīkā) is by Sthiramati.

SA_T06_sthmavt4.title: Madhyāntavibhāgaṭīkā (chapter 4, partial)
SA_T06_sthmavt4.author: Sthiramati
SA_T06_sthmavt4.summary: This text contains the opening portion of chapter 4 of Sthiramati's Madhyāntavibhāgaṭīkā, an exegesis on Vasubandhu's Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya. The chapter analyzes the cultivation of meditative antidotes (pratipakṣabhāvanā) formulated as the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣyadharma). The present e-text covers the exegesis through the four applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), and four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) to the five spiritual faculties (pañcendriya), explaining their functions in entering the four noble truths and progressing through the stages of preparation and penetration.
SA_T06_sthmavt4.attribution: The sub-commentary is authored by the 6th-century Yogācāra master Sthiramati (c. 510–570 CE) on Vasubandhu's Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya (which itself glosses the root kārikās attributed to Maitreya/Asaṅga).
SA_T06_sthmavt4.edition: Sebastian Nehrdich, The Fourth Chapter of the Madhyāntavibhāgaṭīkā: Critical Edition of the Sanskrit/Tibetan and Partial English Translation, M.A. thesis (Wissenschaftliche Hausarbeit zur Erlangung des akademischen Grades eines Master of Arts), University of Hamburg, Asia-Africa Institute, Department of Culture and History of India and Tibet, 2020.
SA_T06_sthmavt4.coverage: partial — Contains the opening portion of chapter 4 (traditionally Pratipakṣabhāvanāpariccheda), running from the introductory exposition of the thirty-seven bodhipakṣyadharmas through the commentary on kārikā IV.6 (on the five spiritual faculties, pañcendriya). It breaks off before the commentary on the five powers (pañca balāni), seven limbs of awakening (bodhyaṅga), eightfold noble path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga), and the subsequent exposition of the stages (avasthā) and fruits (phala).

SA_T07_vakobhau1.title: Abhidharmakośakārikā with Abhidharmakośabhāṣya (chapter 1: Dhātunirdeśa)
SA_T07_vakobhau1.author: Vasubandhu
SA_T07_vakobhau1.summary: Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośabhāṣya (c. 4th–5th century CE) is the foundational masterpiece of Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma taxonomy and philosophy, renowned for Vasubandhu's critical Sautrāntika assessments of Vaibhāṣika orthodoxy. Chapter 1 (Dhātunirdeśa, 'Exposition of the Elements') articulates the basic ontological building blocks of experience: conditioned (saṃskṛta) and unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas, the five aggregates (skandha), twelve sense-bases (āyatana), and eighteen elements (dhātu). Across 48 kārikās and accompanying prose analysis, Vasubandhu systematically elucidates their definitions, etymologies, taxonomic classifications, and mutual subsumption.
SA_T07_vakobhau1.attribution: Vasubandhu composed both the root verses (kārikā), setting out the Sarvāstivāda-Vaibhāṣika doctrinal taxonomy, and the auto-commentary (bhāṣya), in which he frequently evaluates and critiques Vaibhāṣika tenets from a Sautrāntika perspective.
SA_T07_vakobhau1.edition: Yasunori Ejima (ed.), Abhidharmakośabhāṣya of Vasubandhu, Chapter I: Dhātunirdeśa, Bibliotheca Indologica et Buddhologica 1, Tokyo: Sankibo Press, 1989.
SA_T07_vakobhau1.coverage: partial — Contains chapter 1 (Dhātunirdeśa) complete, comprising kārikās 1–48 along with their full prose bhāṣya, out of the nine chapters of the complete Abhidharmakośabhāṣya.

SA_T07_vakobhau.title: Abhidharmakośakārikā with Abhidharmakośabhāṣya
SA_T07_vakobhau.author: Vasubandhu
SA_T07_vakobhau.summary: The Abhidharmakośabhāṣya is Vasubandhu's prose auto-commentary on his metrical Abhidharmakośakārikā, standing as the foundational masterwork of Buddhist Abhidharma scholasticism. Across eight chapters, the work details the constituents of reality (dhātu), sensory and spiritual faculties (indriya), cosmology and rebirth (loka), action and its fruits (karma), latent defilements (anuśaya), the path and spiritual attainments (mārga and pudgala), direct knowledges (jñāna), and meditative absorptions (samāpatti). Vasubandhu articulates the Sarvāstivāda-Vaibhāṣika system while frequently subjecting it to trenchant Sautrāntika critiques, concluding with an appended ninth chapter that refutes both the Buddhist Pudgalavādin thesis of an inexpressible person and Brahmanical theories of a permanent self (ātman).
SA_T07_vakobhau.attribution: Both the root kārikās and the prose auto-commentary were composed by Vasubandhu (BDRC: P6119).
SA_T07_vakobhau.edition: P. Pradhan (ed.), Abhidharmakośabhāṣyam of Vasubandhu, rev. 2nd ed. by Aruna Haldar, Patna: K.P. Jayaswal Research Center, 1975; with Dwarikadas Shastri, Swami (ed.), Abhidharmakosa & Bhasya of Acarya Vasubandhu with Sphutartha Commentary of Acarya Yasomittra, 2 vols., Varanasi: Bauddha Bharati, 1998.
SA_T07_vakobhau.coverage: complete — Complete text encompassing all eight main chapters (kośasthānas 1–8: Dhātunirdeśa, Indriyanirdeśa, Lokanirdeśa, Karmanirdeśa, Anuśayanirdeśa, Mārgapudgalanirdeśa, Jñānanirdeśa, Samāpattinirdeśa) as well as the appended ninth chapter (Pudgalaviniścaya / Pudgalapratiṣedha / Pudgalakośa, ending at Pradhan p. 479).
translations: Louis de La Vallée Poussin (transl.), L'Abhidharmakośa de Vasubandhu, 6 vols., Paris, 1923–. (French)
Gelong Lodrö Sangpo (transl.), Abhidharmakośa-Bhāṣya of Vasubandhu: The Treasury of the Abhidharma and its (Auto) Commentary, 2012. (English)

SA_T07_vakobhau9.title: Abhidharmakośabhāṣya (chapter 9: Ātmavādapratiṣedha)
SA_T07_vakobhau9.author: Vasubandhu
SA_T07_vakobhau9.summary: The ninth chapter of the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, titled Ātmavādapratiṣedha ('Refutation of the Assertion of a Self') or Pudgalaviniścaya ('Investigation of the Person'), is an unversified prose treatise appended to Vasubandhu's masterwork. In this text, Vasubandhu defends the canonical Buddhist teaching of selflessness (anātman) against the personalist doctrines of the Buddhist Vātsīputrīya / Pudgalavādin tradition as well as non-Buddhist substantialist soul theories of the Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika schools. The treatise is a foundational locus classicus in Indian Buddhist philosophy for arguments addressing personal identity, reductionism, and causal continuity.
SA_T07_vakobhau9.attribution: Unlike chapters 1–8 of the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, which comment upon Vasubandhu's metrical Abhidharmakośakārikā, chapter 9 contains no root verses (kārikās) of its own; it is a standalone prose treatise appended by Vasubandhu to the Kośabhāṣya.
SA_T07_vakobhau9.edition: Jong Cheol Lee (ed.), Abhidharmakośabhāṣya of Vasubandhu, Chapter IX: Ātmavādapratiṣedha, Bibliotheca Indologica et Buddhologica 11, Tokyo: Sankibo Press, 2005.
SA_T07_vakobhau9.coverage: partial — Contains chapter 9 (Ātmavādapratiṣedha / Pudgalaviniścaya), the unversified polemical appendix on the refutation of the self, out of 9 total chapters of the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya.

SA_T07_vakobhk.title: Abhidharmakośakārikā
SA_T07_vakobhk.author: Vasubandhu
SA_T07_vakobhk.summary: The Abhidharmakośakārikā consists of verses in eight chapters composed by Vasubandhu, synthesizing the doctrinal system of the Sarvāstivāda-Vaibhāṣika school of Abhidharma. The text classifies conditioned and unconditioned phenomena across eight subjects: ultimate constituents (dhātu), sensory and psychological faculties (indriya), cosmological realms (loka), intentional action (karma), underlying afflictions (anuśaya), noble spiritual paths and attainers (mārgapudgala), transcendent cognitions (jñāna), and meditative absorptions (samāpatti). Designed for memorization, it served as the baseline verse manual upon which Vasubandhu constructed his famous auto-commentary (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya) offering critical Sautrāntika critiques of Vaibhāṣika tenets, and it remains the fundamental Abhidharma textbook throughout East Asian and Tibetan Buddhism.
SA_T07_vakobhk.attribution: Universally accepted as the work of the Buddhist master Vasubandhu, who also authored the auto-commentary (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya).
SA_T07_vakobhk.coverage: complete — Complete: all kārikās of chapters 1–8 (VAkK_1.1–8.43; chapter 9 has no kārikās), with chapter colophons. Numbering slip: kārikā 2.32 is labelled 'VAkK_2.33' (so 2.33 occurs twice and 2.32 seems missing), but the text is present.

SA_T17_bsa007_u.title: Dharmasaṃgraha
SA_T17_bsa007_u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T17_bsa007_u.summary: The Dharmasaṃgraha is a concise Sanskrit Buddhist glossary consisting of 140 numbered entries categorizing doctrinal concepts and numerical dharmas (mātṛkā). It enumerates foundational Buddhist frameworks common to early Buddhism and Mahāyāna, including the three jewels, three vehicles, five Buddhas, four immeasurables (brahmavihāra), perfections (pāramitā), aggregates (skandha), sense fields (āyatana), elements (dhātu), and conditioned mental factors (caitasika). The text served as an essential pedagogical and reference manual for monastic education, especially within the Nepalese Buddhist manuscript tradition.
SA_T17_bsa007_u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna in the closing colophon ('iti nāgārjunapādaviracito 'yaṃ dharmasaṃgrahaḥ samāptaḥ').
SA_T17_bsa007_u.edition: P.L. Vaidya (ed.), Dharmasangraha. Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute, 1961 (Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, 17).
SA_T17_bsa007_u.coverage: complete — Contains the complete text: the opening benedictory stanza, all 140 numbered sections of numerical categories, and the concluding colophon.

SA_XX_n2890u.title: Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra (chapters 1–8)

SA_GE07_bhg4c01u.title: Bhagavadgītā with the commentaries of Śrīdhara Svāmin, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (chapter 1)
SA_GE07_bhg4c01u.author: Vyāsa, Śrīdhara Svāmin, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa
SA_GE07_bhg4c01u.summary: Chapter 1 of the Bhagavadgītā provides the opening scene of the conflict on Kurukṣetra, followed by Arjuna's grief and dejection upon seeing his kinsmen. This digital file gives the 46 verses along with the commentaries of Śrīdhara, Viśvanātha, and Baladeva.

SA_GE07_bhg4c02u.title: Bhagavadgītā with the commentaries of Śrīdhara Svāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (chapter 2)
SA_GE07_bhg4c02u.author: Vyāsa, Śrīdhara Svāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa
SA_GE07_bhg4c02u.summary: Chapter 2 of the Bhagavadgītā (designated Sāṅkhyayoga, 72 verses) forms part of the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata and serves as a foundational synthesis of the poem's philosophical teaching. In it, Kṛṣṇa addresses Arjuna's despondency by distinguishing the eternal, indestructible self (ātman) from the perishable physical body, propounding action without attachment to results (karmayoga), and detailing the characteristics of the sage of steady wisdom (sthitaprajña). This e-text provides the Sanskrit root verses interwoven with four classic commentaries: the influential Subodhinī of Śrīdhara Svāmin, the dialectical Advaitic Gūḍhārthadīpikā of Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, and the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava expositions Sārārthavarṣiṇī of Viśvanātha Cakravartin and Gītābhūṣaṇa of Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa.
SA_GE07_bhg4c02u.attribution: The root Bhagavadgītā forms part of the Mahābhārata.
SA_GE07_bhg4c02u.coverage: partial — Contains chapter 2 (Sāṅkhyayoga, 72 verses) of the Bhagavadgītā complete with four continuous commentaries.

SA_GE07_bhg4c03u.title: Bhagavadgītā with the commentaries of Śrīdhara Svāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (chapter 3)
SA_GE07_bhg4c03u.author: Vyāsa, Śrīdhara Svāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa
SA_GE07_bhg4c03u.summary: Chapter 3 (Karma-yoga) of the Bhagavadgītā contains 43 verses wherein Kṛṣṇa resolves Arjuna's perplexity regarding the relative merits of renunciation/knowledge (jñāna) versus engagement in action (karma). Kṛṣṇa establishes that physical inaction is impossible and prescribes selfless performance of duty without desire for fruit (niṣkāma karma) as a sacred sacrifice (yajña), warning against desire (kāma) and anger (krodha) as the primary obstacles. This electronic file presents the chapter alongside four major Sanskrit commentaries: Śrīdhara Svāmin's Subodhinī, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Gūḍhārthadīpikā, Viśvanātha Cakravartin's Sārārthadarśinī, and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa's Gītābhūṣaṇa.
SA_GE07_bhg4c03u.attribution: The Bhagavadgītā is traditionally attributed to Vyāsa.
SA_GE07_bhg4c03u.coverage: partial — Chapter 3 (Karma-yoga) only, verses 3.1–3.43 complete with the four running commentaries.

SA_GE07_bhg4c04u.title: Bhagavadgītā with the commentaries of Śrīdhara, Madhusūdana, Viśvanātha, and Baladeva (chapter 4)
SA_GE07_bhg4c04u.author: Śrīdharasvāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa
SA_GE07_bhg4c04u.summary: Chapter 4 of the Bhagavadgītā (designated Brahmārpaṇayoga) spans 42 verses in which Kṛṣṇa outlines the ancient line of transmission (paramparā) of sacred wisdom, reveals the theological rationale for his divine descent (avatāra) in every age to preserve dharma, and expounds the nature of action (karma), improper action (vikarma), and inaction (akarma). He explains how work undertaken in the spirit of sacrifice and detached dedication to Brahman incurs no bondage, and exalts spiritual wisdom (jñāna) as the supreme sanctifier and fire that consumes all accumulated karma. In this e-text, each verse is presented with four distinct commentaries: the Subodhinī of Śrīdharasvāmin, the Gūḍhārthadīpikā of Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, the Sārārthadarśinī of Viśvanātha Cakravartin, and the Gītābhūṣaṇa of Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa.
SA_GE07_bhg4c04u.attribution: The root text of the Bhagavadgītā is an episode of the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata, traditionally ascribed to Vyāsa. The four commentaries are by Śrīdharasvāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa.
SA_GE07_bhg4c04u.coverage: partial — Complete chapter 4 (verses 1–42), including the root verses and four commentaries; part of an 18-file set covering the 18 chapters of the Bhagavadgītā.

SA_GE07_bhg4c05u.title: Bhagavadgītā with the commentaries of Śrīdharasvāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (chapter 5)
SA_GE07_bhg4c05u.author: Śrīdharasvāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa
SA_GE07_bhg4c05u.summary: Chapter 5 of the Bhagavadgītā, Karmasaṃnyāsayoga ('Yoga of Renunciation of Action'), addresses Arjuna's dilemma regarding the relative superiority of the renunciation of actions (saṃnyāsa) versus their disciplined performance (karmayoga). Kṛṣṇa demonstrates that while both paths lead to liberation, karmayoga is easier and safer for most practitioners, as true renunciation is an internal state of non-attachment rather than physical withdrawal. This e-text provides all 29 verses accompanied sequentially by four classical commentaries: Śrīdharasvāmin's Subodhinī, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Gūḍhārthadīpikā, Viśvanātha Cakravartin's Sārārthavarṣiṇī, and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa's Gītābhūṣaṇa.
SA_GE07_bhg4c05u.attribution: The four commentaries represent Advaita Vedānta / Bhakti synthesis (Śrīdharasvāmin), pure Advaita Vedānta (Madhusūdana Sarasvatī), and Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism (Viśvanātha Cakravartin and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa).
SA_GE07_bhg4c05u.coverage: partial — Complete text of chapter 5 (29 verses: BhG 5.1–5.29) with all four commentaries for each verse.
translations: Transl. van Buitenen 1981. (English)

SA_GE07_bhg4c06u.title: Bhagavadgītā with the commentaries of Śrīdhara, Madhusūdana, Viśvanātha and Baladeva (chapter 6)
SA_GE07_bhg4c06u.author: Śrīdhara Svāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa
SA_GE07_bhg4c06u.summary: Chapter 6 of the Bhagavadgītā, titled Dhyānayoga or Ātmasaṃyamayoga (47 verses), expounds the discipline of contemplative yoga, detailing proper posture, sensory restraint, and moderate conduct as prerequisites for stilling mental fluctuations. It introduces the celebrated simile of the disciplined mind resting steady like a lamp in a windless place, reassures Arjuna that an unsuccessful aspirant is preserved from destruction and reborn into propitious surroundings to resume spiritual pursuit, and concludes by designating the devotee absorbed in loving devotion to God as the foremost yogi. In this composite digital text, every verse is followed by four commentaries representing the Advaita tradition (Śrīdhara Svāmin's Subodhinī and Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Gūḍhārthadīpikā) and the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava tradition (Viśvanātha Cakravartin's Sārārthavarṣiṇī and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa's Gītābhūṣaṇa).
SA_GE07_bhg4c06u.attribution: Contains the sixth chapter of the Bhagavadgītā with commentaries by Śrīdhara, Madhusūdana, Viśvanātha, and Baladeva.
SA_GE07_bhg4c06u.coverage: partial — Contains chapter 6 (Dhyānayoga, 47 verses) of the Bhagavadgītā, with commentaries by Śrīdhara, Madhusūdana, Viśvanātha, and Baladeva.

SA_GE07_bhg4c07u.title: Bhagavadgītā with the commentaries of Śrīdharasvāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (chapter 7)
SA_GE07_bhg4c07u.author: Śrīdharasvāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa
SA_GE07_bhg4c07u.summary: Chapter 7 of the Bhagavadgītā (traditionally titled Jñānavijñānayoga, comprising 30 verses) opens the middle six chapters of the poem by distinguishing between the divine lower nature (aparā prakṛti: earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect, and ego) and higher nature (parā prakṛti: the living entities that sustain the world). Kṛṣṇa explains the bewildering power of divine māyā constituted of the three guṇas, classifies devotees who seek him into four types (the afflicted, the inquisitive, the seeker of wealth, and the person of knowledge), and declares devotion (bhakti) to be the supreme means of transcendence. The accompanying four classical commentaries illuminate the verses from differing theological viewpoints: Śrīdharasvāmin balances Advaita with deep devotion, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī provides rigorous Advaitic exegesis accommodating intense Kṛṣṇa-bhakti, while Viśvanātha Cakravartin and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa provide Acintyabhedābheda interpretations reflecting Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theology.
SA_GE07_bhg4c07u.attribution: The Bhagavadgītā is traditionally part of the Mahābhārata. The file includes commentaries by Śrīdharasvāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin (Sārārthavarṣiṇī), and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa.
SA_GE07_bhg4c07u.coverage: partial — Contains chapter 7 (all 30 verses) of the Bhagavadgītā, alongside full chapter 7 commentaries by Śrīdharasvāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa.

SA_GE07_bhg4c08u.title: Bhagavadgītā with the commentaries of Śrīdhara, Madhusūdana, Viśvanātha and Baladeva (chapter 8)
SA_GE07_bhg4c08u.author: Śrīdhara Svāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa
SA_GE07_bhg4c08u.summary: This e-text contains chapter 8 (Akṣarabrahmayoga, verses 8.1–8.28) of the Bhagavadgītā along with four verse-by-verse commentaries. The chapter treats the nature of the supreme, imperishable Brahman (akṣara brahma), the psychological and spiritual state at the time of death (antakālasmaraṇa), and the two post-mortem cosmic paths of departure (the luminous devayāna and the smoky pitṛyāna). The accompanying commentaries by Śrīdhara Svāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa articulate the distinct hermeneutical perspectives of early Advaitic devotion, classical Advaita Vedānta, and Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theology.
SA_GE07_bhg4c08u.attribution: The root work forms part of the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata. The e-text includes running commentaries by Śrīdhara Svāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa.
SA_GE07_bhg4c08u.coverage: partial — Contains chapter 8 complete (Akṣarabrahmayoga; verses 8.1–8.28) of the 18 chapters of the Bhagavadgītā, with four running commentaries.

SA_GE07_bhg4c09u.title: Bhagavadgītā with the commentaries of Śrīdhara Svāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (chapter 9)
SA_GE07_bhg4c09u.author: Śrīdhara Svāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa
SA_GE07_bhg4c09u.summary: Bhagavadgītā chapter 9 (Rājavidyārājaguhyayoga, 'The Yoga of Sovereign Knowledge and Sovereign Mystery') contains 34 verses expounding Kṛṣṇa's cosmic majesty, his simultaneous immanence and transcendence, and the paramount role of loving devotion (bhakti). It features the famous declarations that the Supreme accepts even the humblest offering of a leaf, flower, fruit, or water given with devotion (9.26), and that single-minded devotional refuge delivers even the most fallen from sin (9.30–31). This e-text pairs the root verses with four detailed commentaries: the Subodhinī of Śrīdhara Svāmin, the Gūḍhārthadīpikā of Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, the Sārārthavarṣiṇī of Viśvanātha Cakravartin, and the Gītābhūṣaṇa of Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa.
SA_GE07_bhg4c09u.attribution: The root work Bhagavadgītā is traditionally embedded in the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata.
SA_GE07_bhg4c09u.coverage: partial — Chapter 9 only (verses 9.1–9.34 complete, accompanied verse-by-verse with all four commentaries) out of the 18 chapters of the Bhagavadgītā.

SA_GE07_bhg4c10u.title: Bhagavadgītā with the commentaries of Śrīdhara Svāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (chapter 10)
SA_GE07_bhg4c10u.author: Śrīdhara Svāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa
SA_GE07_bhg4c10u.summary: Chapter 10 of the Bhagavadgītā, known as the Vibhūtiyoga ('Yoga of Divine Glories'), details Kṛṣṇa's cosmic manifestations and transcendent immanence at Arjuna's request. Declaring himself the origin of gods, great sages, and all cosmic faculties, Kṛṣṇa enumerates the foremost exemplars across diverse categories of existence as aspects of his supreme splendor, concluding that the entire universe is pervaded and sustained by a mere fraction of his power. In this digital text, each verse of chapter 10 is followed by four complete commentaries: the Advaitic yet bhakti-oriented expositions of Śrīdhara Svāmin (Subodhinī) and Madhusūdana Sarasvatī (Gūḍhārthadīpikā), followed by the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava hermeneutics of Viśvanātha Cakravartin (Sārārthavarṣiṇī) and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (Gītābhūṣaṇa).
SA_GE07_bhg4c10u.coverage: partial — Contains chapter 10 (Vibhūtiyoga) complete in 42 verses (10.1–10.42), each accompanied by four commentaries. Line 1342 contains an editorial citation of Mahābhārata 12.201.4–5.

SA_GE07_bhg4c11u.title: Bhagavadgītā with the commentaries of Śrīdharasvāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (chapter 11)
SA_GE07_bhg4c11u.author: Vyāsa, Śrīdharasvāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa
SA_GE07_bhg4c11u.summary: Chapter 11 of the Bhagavadgītā, titled Viśvarūpadarśanayoga ('The Yoga of the Vision of the Universal Form'), forms the dramatic and theophanic climax of the dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna. Arjuna asks to see the divine cosmic form of the Lord, whereupon Krishna grants him divine vision (divya-cakṣus) and reveals his all-encompassing body blazing with innumerable mouths, eyes, and weapons, into which all creatures and warring heroes are drawn to their demise as Kāla ('Time/Death'). Awestruck and terrified, Arjuna offers extensive stotras and begs Krishna to return to his gentle four-armed and two-armed human form. In this e-text, all 55 verses are accompanied verse-by-verse by four influential Sanskrit commentaries: Śrīdharasvāmin's Subodhinī, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Gūḍhārthadīpikā, Viśvanātha Cakravartin's Sārārthavarṣiṇī, and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa's Gītābhūṣaṇa.
SA_GE07_bhg4c11u.attribution: The mūla text forms chapter 11 of the Bhagavadgītā, accompanied by commentaries of Śrīdharasvāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa.
SA_GE07_bhg4c11u.coverage: partial — Complete text of chapter 11 (55 verses) of the Bhagavadgītā, with commentary on each verse by the commentators.

SA_GE07_bhg4c12u.title: Bhagavadgītā with the commentaries of Śrīdhara, Madhusūdana, Viśvanātha, and Baladeva (chapter 12)
SA_GE07_bhg4c12u.author: Vyāsa, Śrīdharasvāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa
SA_GE07_bhg4c12u.summary: Bhagavadgītā chapter 12 (Bhaktiyoga, 20 verses) evaluates the comparative spiritual efficacy of meditating upon the unmanifest, imperishable Absolute (nirguṇa / avyakta akṣara) versus worship of the personal Divine (saguṇa / vyakta). Kṛṣṇa explains that while both orientations lead to liberation, the contemplative path of the unmanifest is arduous for embodied beings, whereas single-minded devotion directed to the personal Lord brings swift liberation through divine grace. The chapter concludes with a delineation of the tranquil virtues—such as non-malice, friendliness, forbearance, detachment, and equanimity in pleasure and pain—that characterize the devotee dear to the Lord. The accompanying commentaries synthesize and contrast the Advaita-bhakti readings of Śrīdharasvāmin and Madhusūdana Sarasvatī with the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theological interpretations of Viśvanātha Cakravartin and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa.
SA_GE07_bhg4c12u.attribution: The root text of the Bhagavadgītā is embedded within the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata, traditionally ascribed to Vyāsa. The chapter includes commentaries by Śrīdharasvāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin (Sārārthavarṣiṇī), and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (titled in the colophon as Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītopaniṣad-bhāṣya).
SA_GE07_bhg4c12u.coverage: partial — Complete text of Chapter 12 (verses 12.1–12.20) together with all four commentaries for each verse, representing one chapter of the 18 chapters of the Bhagavadgītā.

SA_GE07_bhg4c15u.title: Bhagavadgītā with the commentaries of Śrīdhara Svāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (chapter 15)
SA_GE07_bhg4c15u.author: Śrīdhara Svāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa
SA_GE07_bhg4c15u.summary: Bhagavadgītā chapter 15 (Puruṣottamayoga, 20 verses) expounds the metaphysical hierarchy of reality through the metaphor of an inverted cosmic fig tree (aśvattha), whose branches must be severed by detachment. Kṛṣṇa explicates the nature of the transmigrating self, the divine power sustaining the cosmos, and the distinction between the perishable (kṣara), the imperishable (akṣara), and the transcendent Supreme Person (puruṣottama). The accompanying commentaries in this e-text offer both classical Advaitic exegesis (Śrīdhara Svāmin and Madhusūdana Sarasvatī) and Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theological exposition (Viśvanātha Cakravartin and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa).

SA_GE07_bhg4c16u.title: Bhagavadgītā with the commentaries of Śrīdhara Svāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (chapter 16)
SA_GE07_bhg4c16u.author: Vyāsa, Śrīdhara Svāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa
SA_GE07_bhg4c16u.summary: Chapter 16 of the Bhagavadgītā, titled Daivāsurasampadvibhāgayoga ('The Yoga of the Division between Divine and Demonic Endowments'), contrasts the twenty-six divine virtues (such as fearlessness, purity of mind, charity, non-violence, truthfulness, and humility) leading to spiritual liberation with demonic vices (including hypocrisy, arrogance, cruelty, lust, and greed) that bind souls to saṃsāra. Kṛṣṇa warns that materialistic and egoistic persons who reject transcendent moral orders descend into degraded births, concluding that scriptural ordinance (śāstra-pramāṇa) must serve as the authoritative standard for discerning duty from forbidden acts. In this e-text, the verses are accompanied by four influential commentaries by Śrīdhara Svāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa, each offering verse-by-verse philosophical analyses integrating Advaita Vedānta and Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava hermeneutics.
SA_GE07_bhg4c16u.attribution: The Bhagavadgītā root text is traditionally ascribed to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa within the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata.
SA_GE07_bhg4c16u.coverage: partial — Complete for chapter 16 (Daivāsurasampadvibhāgayoga, verses 1–24), including all 24 root verses and all four commentaries in full; chapter 16 of the eighteen chapters of the Bhagavadgītā.

SA_GE07_bhg4c17u.title: Bhagavadgītā with the commentaries of Śrīdhara Svāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (chapter 17)
SA_GE07_bhg4c17u.author: Vyāsa, Śrīdhara Svāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa
SA_GE07_bhg4c17u.summary: Chapter 17 of the Bhagavadgītā (Śraddhātrayavibhāgayoga, 'Yoga of the Threefold Division of Faith') comprises 28 verses in which Kṛṣṇa explains that faith (śraddhā), food (āhāra), sacrifice (yajña), austerity (tapas), and charitable gift (dāna) are differentiated into three modalities according to the three guṇas (sattva, rajas, and tamas). The chapter also defines the sacred formula 'oṃ tat sat' as a threefold designation of Brahman used to purify and dedicate sacrificial rites. This e-text features the mūla verses interspersed with four significant commentaries spanning Advaita Vedānta (Śrīdhara Svāmin's Subodhinī and Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Gūḍhārthadīpikā) and Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism (Viśvanātha Cakravartin's Sārārthavarṣiṇī and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa's Gītābhūṣaṇa).
SA_GE07_bhg4c17u.attribution: The root text is traditionally ascribed to Vyāsa.
SA_GE07_bhg4c17u.coverage: partial — Complete for chapter 17 (verses 1–28); one chapter out of 18 of the Bhagavadgītā.

SA_GE07_bhg4c18u.title: Bhagavadgītā with the commentaries of Śrīdhara Svāmin, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (chapter 18)
SA_GE07_bhg4c18u.author: Vyāsa, Śrīdhara Svāmin, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa
SA_GE07_bhg4c18u.summary: Chapter 18 of the Bhagavadgītā, Mokṣasaṃnyāsayoga ('The Yoga of Liberation through Renunciation'), provides a comprehensive summation of the epic dialogue. Kṛṣṇa clarifies the distinction between total renunciation (saṃnyāsa) and the relinquishment of the fruits of action (tyāga), classifies knowledge, action, actor, intellect, resolve, and pleasure according to the three guṇas, and affirms the necessity of svadharma. The philosophical discourse culminates in verse 18.66 (the caramaśloka), urging total surrender (śaraṇāgati/prapatti) to Kṛṣṇa alone. In this e-text, the root verses are paired with the commentaries of Śrīdhara Svāmin (Subodhinī), Viśvanātha Cakravartin (Sārārthavarṣiṇī), and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (Gītābhūṣaṇa).
SA_GE07_bhg4c18u.attribution: Vyāsa is the traditional composer of the Mahābhārata within which the Bhagavadgītā is set. Śrīdhara Svāmin authored the Subodhinī commentary. Viśvanātha Cakravartin authored the Sārārthavarṣiṇī commentary, and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa authored the Gītābhūṣaṇa.
SA_GE07_bhg4c18u.coverage: partial — Contains the entirety of chapter 18 (Mokṣasaṃnyāsayoga, 78 verses) along with all three commentaries.

SA_GE07_bhgce__u.title: Bhagavadgītā
SA_GE07_bhgce__u.summary: The Bhagavadgītā ('Song of the Lord') is an 18-chapter philosophical dialogue of 700 verses, set on the battlefield of Kurukṣetra within the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata. Addressing the existential and moral crisis of the warrior Arjuna before the fratricidal battle, Kṛṣṇa expounds the nature of the imperishable self (ātman) and synthesizes the disciplines of detached action (karmayoga), knowledge (jñānayoga), and devotional surrender (bhaktiyoga). Culminating in the theophany of Kṛṣṇa's cosmic form (viśvarūpa), the work became a foundational text of classical Vedānta as the smṛtiprasthāna of the prasthānatrayī and one of the most widely commented-upon works in Indian religious literature.
SA_GE07_bhgce__u.coverage: complete — Text of the Bhagavadgītā in 18 adhyāyas (700 verses, numbered Bhg_01.001 to Bhg_18.078).
translations: Charles Wilkins (trans.), 1785. (English)

SA_GE07_mbh_01_u.title: Mahābhārata: Ādiparvan
SA_GE07_mbh_01_u.summary: The Ādiparvan ('Book of the Beginning') is the first of the eighteen books of the Mahābhārata. It frames the entire epic through King Janamejaya's snake sacrifice (sarpasatra) and the narration by the bard Ugraśravas Sauti to the gathered sages in the Naimiṣa forest. The book recounts the genealogical descent of the Lunar Dynasty (Somavaṃśa), the birth and upbringing of the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas, their escalating rivalry in Hastināpura, the conspiracy of the burning lac house (Jatugṛhadāha), Arjuna winning Draupadī at her svayaṃvara, the establishment of Indraprastha, and the concluding burning of the Khāṇḍava forest.
SA_GE07_mbh_01_u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the sage Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa.
SA_GE07_mbh_01_u.edition: The Mahābhārata: For the first time critically edited: The Ādiparvan, edited by Vishnu S. Sukthankar, Poona: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, 1927–.
SA_GE07_mbh_01_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Ādiparvan (adhyāyas 1–225) as constituted in the BORI Critical Edition, including introductory stanzas (01,000), starred lines, and apparatus passages from Appendix I.

SA_GE07_mbh_05_u.title: Mahābhārata: Udyogaparvan
SA_GE07_mbh_05_u.summary: The Udyogaparvan ('Book of Preparation/Effort') is the fifth major book of the Mahābhārata. Following the conclusion of the Pāṇḍavas' thirteen-year period of exile, it narrates the failed diplomatic efforts to avert conflict, the recruitment of allies across the subcontinent, and Kṛṣṇa's embassy to Hastināpura, where Duryodhana refuses any compromise. The book contains celebrated philosophical and ethical digressions, notably Vidura's moral instruction to Dhṛtarāṣṭra (the Viduranīti) and the discourse on the nature of death and Brahman delivered by Sanatsujāta (the Sanatsujātīya), concluding with the mobilization of the opposing armies on the field of Kurukṣetra.
SA_GE07_mbh_05_u.coverage: complete — Text of the fifth parvan of the Mahābhārata, ending at adhyāya 05,197.021.
translations: Ganguli, Kisari Mohan (1886): The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa translated into English Prose. Virata and Udogya Parva. Calcutta: Bhārata Press. (English)

SA_GE07_mbh_06_u.title: Mahābhārata: Bhīṣmaparvan
SA_GE07_mbh_06_u.summary: The Bhīṣmaparvan is the sixth book of the Mahābhārata and marks the beginning of the battle narrative in the epic. It recounts the first ten days of the eighteen-day Kurukṣetra war under the supreme command of the Kuru patriarch Bhīṣma, culminating in Bhīṣma being fatally wounded by Arjuna and Śikhaṇḍin and placed upon a bed of arrows. The parvan is particularly celebrated for containing the Bhagavadgītā (adhyāyas 23–40), Kṛṣṇa's philosophical discourse to Arjuna delivered on the battlefield just prior to the outbreak of fighting.
SA_GE07_mbh_06_u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the legendary sage Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa; historically understood as a composite epic text.
SA_GE07_mbh_06_u.edition: The Mahābhārata: for the first time critically edited: The Bhīṣmaparvan, critically edited by Shripad Krishna Belvalkar, Poona: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute (BORI).
SA_GE07_mbh_06_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Bhīṣmaparvan in 117 adhyāyas (6.1–6.117), containing the Bhagavadgītā (adhyāyas 23–40), including star and appendix passage insertions keyed to the BORI Critical Edition.

SA_GE07_mbh_10_u.title: Mahābhārata (book 10: Sauptikaparvan)
SA_GE07_mbh_10_u.summary: The Sauptikaparvan ('Book of the Nocturnal Attack') is the tenth of the eighteen books of the Mahābhārata, comprising 18 adhyāyas. Following Duryodhana's mortal defeat at the close of the Kurukṣetra war, the surviving Kaurava warrior Aśvatthāman, driven by grief and vengeance and accompanied by Kṛpa and Kṛtavarman, conducts an unauthorized midnight raid on the sleeping Pāṇḍava encampment. Infused with the destructive power of Śiva, Aśvatthāman massacres Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the five sons of Draupadī (the Upapāṇḍavas), and the remaining allied army. When subsequently pursued by Arjuna and Krishna, Aśvatthāman discharges the apocalyptic brahmaśiras weapon; Krishna compels him to surrender his protective gem and curses him to wander the earth diseased and solitary for three thousand years, while ensuring the revival of Uttarā's unborn child Parīkṣit.
SA_GE07_mbh_10_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Sauptikaparvan (Book 10 of the Mahābhārata), containing all 18 adhyāyas (10.1.1 to 10.18.26 in the BORI Critical Edition numbering, comprising 806 stanzas and prose segments).

SA_GE07_mbh_11_u.title: Mahābhārata: Strīparvan
SA_GE07_mbh_11_u.author: Vyāsa
SA_GE07_mbh_11_u.summary: The Strīparvan ('Book of the Women') is the eleventh major book of the Mahābhārata. Set immediately after the devastating eighteen-day Kurukṣetra war and the nocturnal massacre in the Sauptikaparvan, it recounts the grief of the survivors, centered on Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Gāndhārī, and the bereaved women of both armies. Under the guidance of Vyāsa and Vidura, the royal women visit the corpse-strewn battlefield, where Queen Gāndhārī laments the fallen warriors (Strīvilāpa) and pronounces a catastrophic curse upon Kṛṣṇa, holding him accountable for the fratricidal destruction; the book concludes with the performance of collective cremation and water-offering rites (Jalapradānika), during which Kuntī reveals that Karṇa was her firstborn son.
SA_GE07_mbh_11_u.edition: Mahābhārata: Strīparvan. Electronic text, Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, Pune, 1999. On the basis of the text entered by Muneo Tokunaga et al., revised by John Smith, Cambridge, et al.
SA_GE07_mbh_11_u.coverage: complete — Text of adhyāyas 1–27 including starred passages (*-passages).

SA_GE07_mbh_12_u.title: Mahābhārata (book 12: Śāntiparvan)
SA_GE07_mbh_12_u.summary: The Śāntiparvan ('Book of Peace') is the twelfth and longest book of the Mahābhārata, comprising 353 chapters in the critical edition. Following the catastrophe of the Kurukṣetra war, a despondent King Yudhiṣṭhira approaches the dying grandsire Bhīṣma, who lies on a bed of arrows, seeking counsel on how to rule and attain peace of mind. The book is organized into three major sections: Rājadharmaparvan (duties, statecraft, and judicial ethics of monarchs), Āpaddharmaparvan (conduct and moral dispensations during dire crises), and Mokṣadharmaparvan (philosophical expositions on liberation, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, ethics, and early Vaiṣṇava theology, notably the Nārāyaṇīya).
SA_GE07_mbh_12_u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the sage Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa. In the epic's frame narration, it is recited by Vaiśaṃpāyana to King Janamejaya and consists primarily of the prolonged discourse given by the dying Bhīṣma to Yudhiṣṭhira.
SA_GE07_mbh_12_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of Book 12 (Śāntiparvan) in 353 adhyāyas according to the Pune Critical Edition, containing the Rājadharmaparvan (adhyāyas 1–128), Āpaddharmaparvan (adhyāyas 129–167), and Mokṣadharmaparvan (adhyāyas 168–353), together with starred verses (*) and Appendix I passages (@) from the critical apparatus.

SA_GE07_mbh_13_u.title: Mahābhārata: Anuśāsanaparvan
SA_GE07_mbh_13_u.summary: The Anuśāsanaparvan ('Book of Instructions') is the thirteenth book of the Mahābhārata, continuing and concluding Bhīṣma's post-war instructions to King Yudhiṣṭhira as the patriarch lies on his bed of arrows at Kurukṣetra. Diverging from the political and philosophical focus of the Śāntiparvan, it concentrates heavily on social, ritual, and religious duties, including exhaustive treatments of gift-giving (dānadharma), religious vows (vrata), funerary and ancestral rites (śrāddha), strict non-injury and vegetarianism (ahiṃsā), the conduct and status of women, and the veneration of brahmins. The parvan is particularly noted for preserving seminal Hindu devotional litanies, most famously the Viṣṇusahasranāmastotra (adhyāya 135) and the Śivasahasranāma, before culminating in the arrival of the auspicious winter solstice (uttarāyaṇa), Bhīṣma's ultimate yogic release, and his funerary rites.
SA_GE07_mbh_13_u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the legendary sage Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa.
SA_GE07_mbh_13_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Anuśāsanaparvan in 154 adhyāyas as constituted in the BORI Critical Edition (13.1.1–13.154.34), including all starred passages (* indicates lines relegated to the apparatus) and appendix passages (@ indicates long additions in the appendix) digitized in the Tokunaga–Smith edition.

SA_GE07_mbh_14_u.title: Mahābhārata: Aśvamedhikaparvan
SA_GE07_mbh_14_u.summary: The Aśvamedhikaparvan (Book 14 of the Mahābhārata) recounts the aftermath of the Kurukṣetra war and the death of Bhīṣma. Distressed by the catastrophic slaughter of his kin, King Yudhiṣṭhira is urged by Vyāsa and Kṛṣṇa to perform the royal horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) to expiate the sin of warfare and consolidate sovereign rule. Prior to the rite, Kṛṣṇa delivers the philosophical discourse known as the Anugītā to Arjuna, recapitulating and expanding upon the teachings on yoga, Sāṃkhya metaphysics, and liberation previously given in the Bhagavadgītā. The narrative then details Arjuna's military expeditions guarding the wandering sacrificial horse across the subcontinent, Kṛṣṇa's revival of Abhimanyu's stillborn son Parikṣit, the formal completion of the Vedic horse sacrifice, and the concluding fable of the golden-spotted mongoose (Nakulopākhyāna), which illustrates the spiritual superiority of humble, selfless charity over extravagant ritual pageantry.
SA_GE07_mbh_14_u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the legendary sage Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa.
SA_GE07_mbh_14_u.coverage: complete — Text of the 14th book of the Mahābhārata in 96 adhyāyas (adhyāyas 14.001–14.096), including invocatory stanzas, starred lines, and appendix passages (@004_3436–@004_3447).
translations: The Anugītā, translated by Kashinath Trimbak Telang, in Sacred Books of the East: The Bhagavadgîtâ with the Sanatsujâtîya and the Anugītā. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1882. (English)

SA_GE07_mbh_15_u.title: Mahābhārata (book 15: Āśramavāsikaparvan)
SA_GE07_mbh_15_u.author: Vyāsa
SA_GE07_mbh_15_u.summary: The Āśramavāsikaparvan ('Book of the Hermitage') is the fifteenth major book (parvan) of the Mahābhārata. Set fifteen years after the Kurukṣetra war and the coronation of Yudhiṣṭhira, it describes the departure of the elderly Kuru monarchs Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Gāndhārī, Kuntī, and Vidura to the forest to enter the vānaprastha (hermit) stage of life. In one of the epic's most celebrated narrative episodes, the sage Vyāsa temporarily resurrects the spirits of the slain warriors from the waters of the Ganges to comfort the surviving mourners, after which the royal ascetics perish peacefully in a forest fire on the banks of the Gaṅgā.
SA_GE07_mbh_15_u.edition: Mahābhārata, volume 19: Āśramavāsikaparvan, edited by Shripad Krishna Belvalkar. Poona: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute (BORI).
SA_GE07_mbh_15_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Āśramavāsikaparvan (Book 15 of the Mahābhārata) as constituted in the Critical Edition, comprising all 47 adhyāyas (15.1.1–15.47.27) together with marked starred lines from the critical apparatus.

SA_GE07_mbh_16_u.title: Mahābhārata (book 16: Mausalaparvan)
SA_GE07_mbh_16_u.author: Vyāsa
SA_GE07_mbh_16_u.summary: The Mausalaparvan ('Book of the Clubs') is the sixteenth of the eighteen major parvans of the Mahābhārata, consisting of 9 adhyāyas. Set thirty-six years after the Kurukṣetra war, it recounts the internal destruction and extinction of the Vṛṣṇi, Andhaka, and Bhoja clans at Prabhāsa through a drunken brawl fought with iron-hard erakā reeds, fulfilling the curses of visiting sages and Gāndhārī. The book relates the passing of Balarāma through yoga, Kṛṣṇa's mortal wounding by the hunter Jarā, the drowning of Dvārakā by the ocean, and Arjuna's sorrowful retreat with the surviving women and children to Indraprastha.
SA_GE07_mbh_16_u.coverage: partial — Book 16 of the 18 parvans of the Mahābhārata; contains the complete text of the Mausalaparvan across all 9 adhyāyas (16.1.1 to 16.9.38).

SA_GE07_mbh_17_u.title: Mahābhārata: Mahāprasthānikaparvan
SA_GE07_mbh_17_u.summary: The Mahāprasthānikaparvan ('The Book of the Great Departure') is the seventeenth book of the Mahābhārata, consisting of three adhyāyas. Following the mutual destruction of the Vṛṣṇis and the demise of Kṛṣṇa, King Yudhiṣṭhira coronates Parikṣit as ruler of Hastināpura and renounces the world along with his four brothers and Draupadī. Setting out on foot across the Himalayas toward Mount Meru and heaven accompanied by a faithful dog, Draupadī and the younger brothers collapse and perish one by one due to lingering flaws of attachment and hubris. Yudhiṣṭhira reaches the summit alone and refuses Indra's chariot without his loyal canine companion, who then reveals himself as the deity Dharma testing the king's supreme devotion to righteousness.
SA_GE07_mbh_17_u.coverage: complete — Text of the Mahāprasthānikaparvan in 3 adhyāyas (17.1.1–17.3.36).

SA_GE07_mbh_18_u.title: Mahābhārata: Svargārohaṇaparvan
SA_GE07_mbh_18_u.summary: The Svargārohaṇaparvan is the eighteenth and final book of the Mahābhārata, consisting of five adhyāyas. Arriving in svarga, Yudhiṣṭhira is appalled to discover Duryodhana seated in heavenly splendour while the other Pāṇḍavas and Draupadī are nowhere to be seen; upon demanding to join his kin, he is led through the foul tortures of naraka (hell) and elects to remain there sharing his brothers' torment rather than return to heaven alone. Indra and Dharma then disclose that the hellish vision was an illusory test (māyā) to burn away remaining demerit, after which Yudhiṣṭhira bathes in the celestial river Ākāśagaṅgā, casts off his mortal body, and is reunited with the Pāṇḍavas, Kauravas, Karṇa, and their allies in their transcendent celestial forms, closing with the divine origins of the heroes and the comprehensive phalaśruti (proclamation of merit) of the entire epic.
SA_GE07_mbh_18_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Svargārohaṇaparvan (Book 18), adhyāyas 1–5 (verses 18.1.1–18.5.54), including marked apparatus insertions (asterised * lines).

SA_GE07_naray__u.title: Nārāyaṇīya
SA_GE07_naray__u.summary: The Nārāyaṇīya (Mahābhārata 12.321–339) is a major theological tract of 19 chapters located near the end of the Mokṣadharmaparvan in the Śāntiparvan. It provides the earliest comprehensive textual witness to early Pāñcarātra and Bhāgavata doctrine within the epic literature, extolling Nārāyaṇa as the supreme transcendent deity and cosmic source of all manifestations. Key theological contributions include the systematic exposition of the fourfold emanation theory (caturvyūha: Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha), the practice of unswerving devotion (ekāntikabhakti), and the allegorical voyage of the celestial seer Nārada to Śvetadvīpa ('the White Island').
SA_GE07_naray__u.edition: Reinhold Grünendahl, Angelika Malinar, Thomas Oberlies, and Peter Schreiner: Narayaniya-Studien. Herausgegeben von Peter Schreiner. Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz, 1997 (Purana Research Publications Tuebingen, 5 / PRP, 6).
SA_GE07_naray__u.coverage: complete — Contains the complete 19-chapter Nārāyaṇīya (adhyāyas 12.321–339 of the Poona Critical Edition) together with associated star-passages and Critical Edition Appendix I (passage 32), marked in the Tübingen electronic encoding.

SA_GE09_ram_01_u.title: Rāmāyaṇa (book 1: Bālakāṇḍa)
SA_GE09_ram_01_u.author: Vālmīki
SA_GE09_ram_01_u.summary: The Bālakāṇḍa is the introductory book of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa. It recounts the origin of the kāvya form when Vālmīki utters the first śloka upon hearing Nārada's synopsis of Rāma's virtues, followed by King Daśaratha's putrakāmeṣṭi sacrifice and the subsequent birth of Rāma and his brothers. The narrative follows young Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa as they accompany the sage Viśvāmitra, protect sacrificial rituals from demons, and hear various mythological legends, culminating in Rāma stringing King Janaka's divine bow in Mithilā to marry Sītā, followed by the subduing of Paraśurāma.
SA_GE09_ram_01_u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the ādikavi Vālmīki.
SA_GE09_ram_01_u.coverage: partial — Contains the text of Book 1 (Bālakāṇḍa), sargas 1–76 (verses 1.001.001a–1.076.018c).

SA_GE09_ram_03_u.title: Rāmāyaṇa (book 3: Araṇyakāṇḍa)
SA_GE09_ram_03_u.author: Vālmīki
SA_GE09_ram_03_u.summary: The Araṇyakāṇḍa ('Book of the Forest') is the third book of Vālmīki's Sanskrit epic Rāmāyaṇa and forms part of its ancient narrative core. It chronicles Rāma, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa's forest exile in the Daṇḍaka and Pañcavaṭī regions, their encounters with woodland hermits, and the mutilation of the demoness Śūrpaṇakhā, which provokes the slaughter of Khara, Dūṣaṇa, and their demon legions. The narrative reaches its structural crisis with the abduction of Sītā by the demon king Rāvaṇa aided by Mārīca's golden-deer deception, followed by the mortal wounding of Jaṭāyus and Rāma's grief-stricken journey toward Mount Ṛśyamūka and Lake Pampā.
SA_GE09_ram_03_u.edition: The Valmiki-Ramayan: The Aranyakanda, edited by. Divanji, Baroda: Oriental Institute, 1963.
SA_GE09_ram_03_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of Book 3 (Araṇyakāṇḍa), comprising 71 sargas (verses 3.001.001a–3.071.026d).
translations: G. Gorresio, Ramayana: Poema indico di Valmici, 1843–1850. (Italian)

SA_GE09_ram_03pu.title: Rāmāyaṇa (Book 3: Araṇyakāṇḍa)
SA_GE09_ram_03pu.author: Vālmīki
SA_GE09_ram_03pu.summary: The Araṇyakāṇḍa ('Book of the Forest') is the third book of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa. It recounts the ten-year period of Rāma, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa's exile in the Daṇḍaka forest, including visits to holy hermitages of sages such as Śarabhaṅga, Sutīkṣṇa, and Agastya. The narrative turns tragic when the rākṣasī Śūrpaṇakhā attempts to seduce Rāma and attack Sītā, leading to Lakṣmaṇa disfiguring her, the annihilation of Khara and Dūṣaṇa's army, and Rāvaṇa's subsequent plot using Mārīca disguised as a golden deer to abduct Sītā; the book concludes with the mortal combat of the bird king Jaṭāyus and the brothers' grief-stricken quest leading toward Lake Pampā.
SA_GE09_ram_03pu.edition: P. C. Divanji (ed.), The Vālmīki-Rāmāyaṇa: Critical Edition.: The Āraṇyakāṇḍa, 1963.
SA_GE09_ram_03pu.coverage: partial — Text of Book 3 (Araṇyakāṇḍa), consisting of 71 sargas (sargas 1.1 through 71.26); partial coverage of the epic as a whole.

SA_GE09_ram_04_u.title: Rāmāyaṇa (book 4: Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa)
SA_GE09_ram_04_u.author: Vālmīki
SA_GE09_ram_04_u.summary: The Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa is the fourth book of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa. Following Sītā's abduction, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa reach Lake Pampā and form an alliance with the exiled vānara king Sugrīva through Hanumān's mediation. Rāma slays Sugrīva's elder brother Vālin—a focal point of classic ethical controversy—and restores Sugrīva to the throne of Kiṣkindhā. After the monsoon rains, Sugrīva dispatches search parties to all four quarters; the southern party led by Aṅgada and Hanumān receives confirmation of Sītā's imprisonment in Laṅkā from the vulture Sampāti, setting the stage for Hanumān's oceanic leap.
SA_GE09_ram_04_u.edition: Rāmāyaṇa, Critical Edition: Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa, ed. D. R. Mankad, 1965.
SA_GE09_ram_04_u.coverage: complete — Text of Book 4 (Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa), comprising 66 sargas (4.001.001a–4.066.044d).

SA_GE09_ram_05_u.title: Rāmāyaṇa (book 5: Sundarakāṇḍa)
SA_GE09_ram_05_u.author: Vālmīki
SA_GE09_ram_05_u.summary: The Sundarakāṇḍa is the fifth book of Vālmīki's Rāmāyaṇa and forms the dramatic turning point of the epic. It chronicles the exploits of Hanumān, who leaps across the ocean to the island citadel of Laṅkā, infiltrates Rāvaṇa's palace, and locates the captive Sītā in the Aśoka grove. After delivering Rāma's signet ring and receiving a token of recognition in return, Hanumān ravages the grove, slays several of Rāvaṇa's champions, allows himself to be captured, and sets Laṅkā ablaze before returning to Rāma with news of Sītā's survival.
SA_GE09_ram_05_u.edition: The Vālmīki-Rāmāyaṇa: Critically Edited for the First Time: The Sundarakāṇḍa, ed. G. C. Jhala, Baroda: Oriental Institute, 1966.
SA_GE09_ram_05_u.coverage: partial — Complete text of Book 5 (Sundarakāṇḍa, sargas 1–66; verses 5.001.001 to 5.066.029 in the Critical Edition), which forms the fifth of the seven kāṇḍas of the Rāmāyaṇa.

SA_GE09_ram_06_u.title: Rāmāyaṇa (book 6: Yuddhakāṇḍa)
SA_GE09_ram_06_u.author: Vālmīki
SA_GE09_ram_06_u.summary: The Yuddhakāṇḍa (Book of War, also known as Laṅkākāṇḍa) is the sixth book and narrative culmination of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa. It recounts the construction of the causeway across the ocean to Laṅkā by Nala and the monkey host, followed by prolonged and fierce warfare between Rāma's forces and Rāvaṇa's demons. After the falls of notable rākṣasa champions—including Kumbhakarṇa and Indrajit—and the final slaying of Rāvaṇa by Rāma, Sītā is liberated, undergoes the fire ordeal (agniparīkṣā) to vindicate her chastity, and the assembly returns triumphantly to Ayodhyā for Rāma's royal coronation (abhiṣeka).
SA_GE09_ram_06_u.attribution: Ascribed traditionally to the sage Vālmīki.
SA_GE09_ram_06_u.coverage: partial — Contains the text of Book 6 (Yuddhakāṇḍa), comprising 116 sargas, beginning at 6.001.001a and concluding at 6.116.090c.

SA_GE09_ram_07_u.title: Rāmāyaṇa (book 7: Uttarakāṇḍa)
SA_GE09_ram_07_u.author: Vālmīki
SA_GE09_ram_07_u.summary: The Uttarakāṇḍa is the seventh and concluding book of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, serving as an extensive narrative and mythological epilogue to the core epic. It begins with the sage Agastya narrating the origins, genealogy, and early exploits of Rāvaṇa and other rākṣasas, as well as the childhood deeds of Hanumān. The narrative then shifts to Rāma's reign in Ayodhyā, the public suspicion regarding Sītā's fidelity that compels Rāma to banish her to the forest, her sanctuary at Vālmīki's hermitage, and the birth of Lava and Kuśa. It culminates in the twins reciting the Rāmāyaṇa at the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha), Sītā's final vindication and descent into the earth, and the eventual departure of Rāma and the inhabitants of Ayodhyā to heaven.
SA_GE09_ram_07_u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the sage-poet Vālmīki.
SA_GE09_ram_07_u.edition: The Vālmīki-Rāmāyaṇa: Critically Edited for the First Time.: The Uttarakāṇḍa, critically edited by Umakant Premanand Shah. Baroda: Oriental Institute, 1975.
SA_GE09_ram_07_u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete text of the seventh and final book (Uttarakāṇḍa) of the Rāmāyaṇa across 100 sargas (7.001.001a–7.100.025a) according to the Baroda Critical Edition, excluding the critical apparatus, star passages, and appendices.

SA_GK16_andhvc1u.title: Dhvanyāloka with Locana and Bālapriyā (chapter 1)
SA_GK16_andhvc1u.author: Ānandavardhana, Abhinavagupta, Rāmaśāraka
SA_GK16_andhvc1u.summary: The first chapter (uddyota) of the Dhvanyāloka ('Light on Suggestion') by the 9th-century Kashmiri theorist Ānandavardhana, accompanied by Abhinavagupta's foundational commentary (Locana) and the sub-commentary Bālapriyā by Rāmaśāraka. In this opening chapter, Ānandavardhana establishes the central thesis of the dhvani school: that suggested meaning (vyaṅgyārtha / dhvani) constitutes the essential soul (ātman) of poetry, distinct from literal (abhidhā) and metaphorical (lakṣaṇā) semantics. The text methodically refutes the three primary anti-dhvani positions: those denying the existence of suggestion outright (abhāvavāda), those identifying it with figurative indication (bhāktavāda), and those deeming it undefinable or ineffable (anirvacanīyatāvāda).
SA_GK16_andhvc1u.attribution: A long-standing debate in Sanskrit poetics concerns whether the metrical kārikās and the prose vṛtti of the Dhvanyāloka are by distinct authors (an older 'Dhvanikāra' vs. Ānandavardhana) or whether Ānandavardhana authored both. Ānandavardhana flourished in Kashmir in the 9th century. Abhinavagupta composed the Locana. Rāmaśāraka composed the sub-commentary Bālapriyā (also styled Locanaṭippaṇī).
SA_GK16_andhvc1u.edition: Pattābhirāma Śāstrī (ed.), The Dhvanyāloka of Śrī Ānandavardhanāchārya with the Lochana & Bālapriyā Commentaries by Śrī Abhinavagupta & Panditarāja Sahṛdayatilaka Śrī Rāmaśāraka with the Divyāñjana Notes by Kavitārkika-Chakravarty Pandit Śrī Mahādeva Śāstri, Kashi Sanskrit Series, no. 135 (Alaṅkāra Section), Benares: Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series Office, 1940.

SA_GK16_andhvc2u.title: Dhvanyāloka with the commentaries Locana and Bālapriyā (chapter 2)
SA_GK16_andhvc2u.author: Ānandavardhana, Abhinavagupta, Rāmaśāraka
SA_GK16_andhvc2u.summary: The second chapter (uddyota) of the Dhvanyāloka outlines the fundamental divisions of poetic suggestion (dhvani), dividing it into suggestion where the literal meaning is unintended (avivakṣitavācya) and where it is intended but subordinated to another sense (vivakṣitānyaparavācya). Ānandavardhana demonstrates how aesthetic emotion (rasa) is conveyed through suggestive resonance (rasadhvani) rather than primary denotation, reinterpreting traditional poetic qualities (guṇas) and figures of speech (alaṃkāras) as secondary features that subserve rasa. This e-text presents the root kārikās and vṛtti intertwined with Abhinavagupta's seminal commentary Locana and Rāmaśāraka's sub-commentary Bālapriyā.
SA_GK16_andhvc2u.attribution: The core Dhvanyāloka comprises verse kārikās (associated with the Dhvanikāra) together with a vṛtti composed by Ānandavardhana in 9th-century Kashmir. The Locana commentary was authored by Abhinavagupta. The sub-commentary Bālapriyā was composed by Sahṛdayatilaka Paṇḍitarāja Rāmaśāraka.
SA_GK16_andhvc2u.edition: Dhvanyāloka of Ānandavardhana with the Locana of Abhinavagupta and the subcommentary of Rāmaṣāraka, ed. Pattabhirama Sastry. Kashi Sanskrit Series (KSS) 135. Benares / Varanasi: Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series Office, 1940.
SA_GK16_andhvc2u.coverage: partial — Chapter (uddyota) 2 only, complete from kārikā 2.1 through 2.33 with the accompanying vṛtti, Locana, and Bālapriyā sub-commentary.

SA_GK16_andhvc3u.title: Dhvanyāloka with Locana and Bālapriyā (chapter 3)
SA_GK16_andhvc3u.author: Ānandavardhana, Abhinavagupta, Rāmaśāraka
SA_GK16_andhvc3u.summary: The third and most extensive chapter (uddyota) of Ānandavardhana's 9th-century masterwork on Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra), which establishes suggestion (dhvani) and aesthetic experience (rasa) as central to poetic expression. Chapter 3 provides an exhaustive taxonomy of suggestive elements (vyañjaka), examining how dhvani functions at the level of phonemes, inflectional affixes, individual words, sentences, syntax, and entire compositions, while defining how poetic figures (alaṃkāra) and qualities (guṇa) serve the manifestation of rasa. The electronic text presents Ānandavardhana's root verses and vṛtti alongside Abhinavagupta's 10th/11th-century Locana commentary and the Bālapriyā sub-commentary of Rāmaśāraka.
SA_GK16_andhvc3u.attribution: Traditional commentators and modern scholars have debated whether the kārikās and the prose vṛtti were written by the same author (Ānandavardhana, c. 9th century CE) or if the kārikās are by an earlier 'dhvanikāra'; current consensus generally attributes both to Ānandavardhana. The Locana commentary was composed by Abhinavagupta (c. late 10th – early 11th century CE).
SA_GK16_andhvc3u.edition: The Dhvanyāloka of Śrī Ānandavardhanācārya with the Locana and Bālapriyā Commentaries by Śrī Abhinavagupta and Paṇḍitarāja Sahṛdayatilaka Śrī Rāmaśāraka, edited by Pandit Paṭṭābhirāma Śāstrī, Kashi Sanskrit Series, no. 135, Benares: Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series Office, 1940.

SA_GK16_andhvc4u.title: Dhvanyāloka with Locana and Bālapriyā (chapter 4)
SA_GK16_andhvc4u.author: Ānandavardhana, Abhinavagupta, Rāmaśāraka
SA_GK16_andhvc4u.summary: The fourth and final uddyota of Ānandavardhana's foundational treatise on poetics, the Dhvanyāloka, which argues that the domain of suggestion (dhvani) endows poetic genius (pratibhā) with boundless fertility, allowing even ancient themes to appear perpetually new. This e-text also includes the Locana commentary by Abhinavagupta, as well as the sub-commentary Bālapriyā by Rāmaśāraka.

SA_GK16_andhvy_u.title: Dhvanyāloka
SA_GK16_andhvy_u.author: Ānandavardhana
SA_GK16_andhvy_u.summary: The Dhvanyāloka composed by Ānandavardhana in 9th-century Kashmir (reign of Avantivarman) is a foundational text of the dhvani theory of poetics. Composed of mnemonic verses (kārikās) embedded within an extensive prose explanation (vṛtti) in four chapters (uddyotas), it argues that the essence or 'soul' of poetry is found in suggested meaning (vyaṅgyārtha/dhvani).

SA_GK16_bhakavpu.title: Kāvyālaṃkāra
SA_GK16_bhakavpu.author: Bhāmaha
SA_GK16_bhakavpu.summary: The Kāvyālaṃkāra of Bhāmaha (c. 7th century CE) is one of the earliest extant systematic treatises on classical Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra), establishing poetics as an autonomous discipline distinct from dramaturgy. In six chapters (paricchedas) comprising approximately 400 verses, the work treats poetic genres, thirty-nine figures of speech (alaṃkāra), poetic defects (doṣa), logical and epistemological argumentation (nyāya, including a famous refutation of the Buddhist apoha doctrine), and grammatical correctness (śabdaśuddhi). Bhāmaha famously defines kāvya as the unified harmony of word and meaning (śabdārthau sahitau kāvyam) and identifies vakrokti ('oblique/striking expression') as the indispensable hallmark of genuine poetic language.
SA_GK16_bhakavpu.attribution: The work is ascribed to the 7th-century rhetorician Bhāmaha.

SA_GK16_bhakavpu.coverage: complete — Complete in six paricchedas (chapters 1–6) comprising approximately 398–400 kārikās, concluding with verse 6.66 which summarizes the distribution of topics across the six chapters.

SA_GK16_jaycndpu.title: Candrāloka
SA_GK16_jaycndpu.author: Jayadeva
SA_GK16_jaycndpu.summary: The Candrāloka is an elementary verse treatise on Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra) composed by Jayadeva Pīyūṣavarṣa in ten chapters (mayūkhas) in straightforward anuṣṭubh meter. It methodically surveys poetic causes and definitions, word-powers (śaktivṛtti), poetic faults (doṣas), virtues (guṇas), figures of speech (alaṃkāras), and sentiment (rasa). The fifth mayūkha, treating figures of speech, is celebrated for its didactic technique wherein each definition serves simultaneously as an illustration of the figure defined; this chapter served as the direct basis for Appayya Dīkṣita's influential Kuvalayānanda.
SA_GK16_jaycndpu.attribution: Authored by Jayadeva, son of Mahādeva and Sumitrā, who bore the epithet Pīyūṣavarṣa ('rain of nectar'), dated to the 13th century CE. He is identical with the dramatist who composed the Prasannarāghava, but must not be confused with Jayadeva, son of Bhojadeva, the 12th-century author of the Gītagovinda.
SA_GK16_jaycndpu.coverage: complete — Complete text in 10 chapters (mayūkhas), comprising 350+ verses (594 segments / half-verses), concluding with verse JCand_10.7.

SA_GK16_kunvjivu.title: Vakroktijīvita
SA_GK16_kunvjivu.author: Kuntaka
SA_GK16_kunvjivu.summary: The Vakroktijīvita by Rājānaka Kuntaka is a landmark treatise in Sanskrit poetics that presents vakrokti ('oblique' or 'striking expression') as the essential life-principle (jīvita) of all literature. Composed in kārikā verses alongside Kuntaka's own prose commentary (svavṛtti) and hundreds of illustrative literary citations, the work systematizes creative poetic deviation (vakratā) across six hierarchical levels of linguistic organization: phoneme/letter arrangements (varṇavinyāsa), lexical stems (pada-pūrvārdha), inflectional morphology (pratyayāśraya), sentential composition (vākya), thematic episodes (prakaraṇa), and overall plot structure (prabandha). Responding to the dominant dhvani theory of Ānandavardhana, Kuntaka seeks to integrate alaṅkāra, guṇa, mārga, and rasa into an all-encompassing aesthetic framework centered on the imaginative faculty and creative activity of the poet (kavi-vyāpāra).
SA_GK16_kunvjivu.attribution: Rājānaka Kuntaka is the author of both the root kārikā verses (tagged Vjiv_) and the accompanying prose exposition with supplementary verses (svavṛtti and antaraślokas, tagged VjivC_).
SA_GK16_kunvjivu.coverage: complete — Contains the whole extant work: Unmeṣas 1–3 with final colophons and Unmeṣa 4 (prakaraṇa- and prabandha-vakratā) up to the point where the transmission breaks off; the e-text ends 'samāptaprāyo 'yaṃ granthaḥ' after antaraśloka VjivC_4.57.

SA_GK16_mamkavpu.title: Kāvyaprakāśa
SA_GK16_mamkavpu.author: Mammaṭa, Allaṭa
SA_GK16_mamkavpu.summary: The Kāvyaprakāśa is an 11th-century masterpiece of Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra) authored by the Kashmiri scholar Mammaṭa and completed in its tenth chapter by Allaṭa. Divided into ten chapters (ullāsas), it systematically synthesizes the dhvani (poetic suggestion) theory developed by Ānandavardhana and Abhinavagupta with the older traditions of poetic faults (doṣa), qualities (guṇa), and figurative ornaments (alaṃkāra). Combining terse theoretical kārikās with an auto-commentarial vṛtti and hundreds of illustrative verses drawn from classical literature, it served as the foremost textbook of literary theory across the subcontinent and inspired dozens of subcommentaries.
SA_GK16_mamkavpu.attribution: Mammaṭa (kārikā + most of the vṛtti); Allaṭa/Alaka (completion of the last portion).
