SA_GK16_mamkpb_u.title: Kāvyaprakāśa
SA_GK16_mamkpb_u.author: Mammaṭa, Allaṭa
SA_GK16_mamkpb_u.summary: The Kāvyaprakāśa is a foundational eleventh-century Sanskrit treatise on poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra) composed by the Kashmiri scholar Mammaṭa and completed by Allaṭa. Arranged into ten chapters (ullāsas) combining kārikā verses and an authoritative prose exposition (vṛtti), the work synthesizes the dhvani (suggestion) and rasa aesthetics of Ānandavardhana and Abhinavagupta with earlier taxonomic models of poetic figures and faults. It covers the definition and objectives of poetry, the three primary semantic functions of words (abhidhā, lakṣaṇā, and vyañjanā), stylistic blemishes (doṣas), excellences (guṇas), and phonological as well as semantic figures (śabdālaṃkāra and arthālaṃkāra), functioning as the preeminent textbook of classical Sanskrit literary theory.
SA_GK16_mamkpb_u.attribution: Although the GRETIL header records that the text was taken from an edition containing Vāmanācārya Rāmabhaṭṭa Jhalakīkar's commentary Bālabodhinī, Sansknet keyed only the kārikā and prose vṛtti.
SA_GK16_mamkpb_u.edition: Raghunath Damodar Karmarkar (ed.), Kāvyaprakāśa of Mammaṭa with the Sanskrit Commentary Bālabodhinī by Vamanacharya Ramabhatta Jhalakikar, 7th ed., Poona: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, 1965.
SA_GK16_mamkpb_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of all ten ullāsas of the Kāvyaprakāśa (kārikās and prose vṛtti), beginning with the mangala verse (niyatikṛtaniyamarahitāṃ...) and concluding with the terminal verse (ityeṣa mārgo viduṣāṃ...) and colophon: 'iti kāvyaprakāśe 'rthālaṃkāranirṇayo nāma daśama ullāsaḥ // samāptaśvāyaṃ kāvyaprakāśaḥ //'.
translations: The Kāvyaprakāśa of Mammaṭa, translated by Gaṅgānātha Jhā. (English)

SA_GK16_msabdvvu.title: Śabdavyāpāravicāra
SA_GK16_msabdvvu.author: Mammaṭa
SA_GK16_msabdvvu.summary: The Śabdavyāpāravicāra is a treatise on the operations of words by the aesthetician Mammaṭa (c. 1100 CE). Engaging directly with Mukula Bhaṭṭa's Abhidhāvṛttimātṛkā, Mammaṭa incorporates its analysis of literal and figurative usage consistent with the dhvani theory while defending the irreducible necessity of suggestion (dhvanana / vyañjanā) beyond denotation, purport, and indication against Mukula Bhaṭṭa's criticisms.
SA_GK16_msabdvvu.attribution: Attributed in the colophon and scholarly tradition to Rājānaka Mammaṭācārya (c. 1100 CE).
SA_GK16_msabdvvu.edition: Abhidhāvṛttimātṛkā of Mukula Bhaṭṭa and Śabdavyāpāravicāra of Rājānaka Mammaṭācārya, ed. Mangesh Ramkrishna Telang, Nirnaya Sagar Press, Bombay, 1916.
SA_GK16_msabdvvu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the treatise, opening with the introductory statement on epistemological means and closing with the concluding colophon (iti nikhilavipaściccakravartiśrīrājānakamammaṭācāryaviracitaḥ śabdavyāpāravicāraḥ).
translations: Śabdavyāpāravicāra of Mammaṭa, translated into Hindi by Rewaprasad Dwivedi, Vidyabhavana Samskrta granthamala 166, Varanasi: Caukhamba Vidyabhavana, 1974. (Hindi)

SA_GK16_rajkmimu.title: Kāvyamīmāṃsā
SA_GK16_rajkmimu.author: Rājaśekhara
SA_GK16_rajkmimu.summary: The Kāvyamīmāṃsā ('Inquiry into Poetry') by Rājaśekhara is a classic of Sanskrit literary theory focused on the practical training and culture of a poet (kaviśikṣā). Although planned on an encyclopedic scale of eighteen books, only the first book, the Kavirahasya ('The Poet's Secret') in eighteen chapters, is extant. The work offers valuable documentation of early medieval Indian literary life, describing the allegorical personification of poetry (Kāvyapuruṣa), the nature of innate poetic talent (pratibhā), royal assemblies and salons (kavisabhā), the classification of borrowing and plagiarism (haraṇa), poetic conventions (kavisamaya), and Pan-Indian cultural geography (deśavibhāga).
SA_GK16_rajkmimu.coverage: complete — Contains all 18 chapters (adhyāyas) of the first adhikaraṇa (titled Kavirahasya). Although Rājaśekhara projected an ambitious eighteen-adhikaraṇa treatise in chapter 1, only this first adhikaraṇa has survived in manuscript tradition (or was ever completed), making the e-text complete for the extant work.
translations: Nadine Stchoupak and Louis Renou, La Kāvyamīmāṃsā de Rājaśekhara, Paris, 1946. (French)
Sadhana Parashar, Kāvyamīmāṃsā of Rājaśekhara: Original Text in Sanskrit and Translation with Explanatory Notes, New Delhi: D.K. Printworld, 2000. (English)
Katsuhiko Kamimura, 'ラージャシェーカラ作Kāvyamīmāṃsā訳注', Tōyō Bunka Kenkyūjo Kiyō (Memoirs of the Institute of Oriental Culture), University of Tokyo, 1999 (chapters 1–3); 2000 (chapters 4–6). (Japanese)

SA_GK16_rnatc__u.title: Nāṭakacandrikā
SA_GK16_rnatc__u.author: Rūpa Gosvāmī
SA_GK16_rnatc__u.summary: The Nāṭakacandrikā ('Moonlight of Drama') is a 16th-century dramaturgical treatise by Rūpa Gosvāmī. Synthesizing Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra and especially the Rasapūrvasudhākara (Rasārṇavasudhākara)—while consciously rejecting the formulation of the Sāhitya-darpaṇa—the work systematizes plot structure (sandhi, sandhyaṅga), hero types, and emotional states for dramatic poetry. It serves as dramaturgical theory and draws dramatic examples from Lalitamādhava and other plays, establishing Kṛṣṇa as the ideal dramatic hero.
SA_GK16_rnatc__u.attribution: Authored by Rūpa Gosvāmī (active early 16th century), as confirmed by the closing colophon ('iti dhvani-prasthāpana-paramācārya-śrīmad-rūpa-gosvāmi-prabhupāda-praṇītā śrī-nāṭaka-candrikā samāptā').
SA_GK16_rnatc__u.coverage: complete — Complete text from the maṅgala verses (RNc_1) to the final verse RNc_269 and the closing colophon. The verse tags skip some numbers (e.g. RNc_12 is followed directly by RNc_17); the GRETIL header flags 14-16, 51, 53, 106, 261 as 'missing(?)', so small gaps in the text cannot be excluded.
translations: Rāsavihārin Saṃkhyātīrtha, Nāṭakacandrikā of Rūpagosvāmin (with Bengali translation), Kasimbazar: Satyaratna Press, 1907. (Bengali)

SA_GK16_ruvyavivya_pu.title: Vyaktivivekavyākhyā (chapter 2)
SA_GK16_ruvyavivya_pu.author: Ruyyaka
SA_GK16_ruvyavivya_pu.summary: The Vyaktivivekavyākhyā is a commentary by Ruyyaka on Mahimabhaṭṭa's Vyaktiviveka. This text contains the second chapter (dvitīya vimarśa), which analyzes poetic defects (doṣas) and syntactic improprieties (śabdānaucitya), examining five major faults: vidheyāvimarśa (faulty predication/emphasis), prakramabheda (lack of syntactic parallelism), kramabheda (misplaced word order), paunaruktya (redundancy), and vācyāvacana / avācyavacana (omission or unwarranted inclusion of expressions). Although Mahimabhaṭṭa composed the root work as a polemic against Ānandavardhana's dhvani doctrine by seeking to subsume suggestion into logical inference (anumāna), Ruyyaka's commentary provides indispensable grammatical and rhetorical elucidations while critically scrutinizing Mahimabhaṭṭa's positions.
SA_GK16_ruvyavivya_pu.attribution: The commentary on the Vyaktiviveka is attributed to Ruyyaka [Rājānaka].
SA_GK16_ruvyavivya_pu.coverage: partial — Contains the commentary on the second vimarśa (vimarśa 2), matching pp. 15–54 of the commentary in the 1909 TSS edition.
translations: Rewāprasāda Dwivedī, Vyaktiviveka of Mahimabhatta, with Hindi commentary and notes, Kashi Sanskrit Series 121, Varanasi: Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series, 1964. (Hindi)

SA_GK16_ruyalscu.title: Alaṅkārasarvasva with Sañjīvanī (sūtras only)
SA_GK16_ruyalscu.author: Ruyyaka, Vidyācakravartin
SA_GK16_ruyalscu.summary: The Alaṅkārasarvasva by Ruyyaka is a work on Sanskrit poetics analyzing about eighty poetic figures. Vidyācakravartin's Sañjīvanī is a commentary on the Alaṅkārasarvasva. In this digital text, Ruyyaka's sūtras are provided alongside Vidyācakravartin's Sañjīvanī commentary.
SA_GK16_ruyalscu.attribution: Ruyyaka (also called Rucaka) authored the Alaṅkārasarvasva, as corroborated in verse 2 ('rucakācāryopajñe... alaṅkārasarvasve'). Vidyācakravartin authored the Sañjīvanī commentary, as confirmed in the introductory verses and the concluding colophon.
SA_GK16_ruyalscu.edition: S. S. Janaki (ed.), Alamkara-sarvasva of Ruyyaka, with Sanjivani Commentary of Vidyacakravartin - Text and Study, Delhi: Meharchand Lachhmandas, 1965.
SA_GK16_ruyalscu.coverage: partial — Vidyācakravartin's Sañjīvanī commentary is preserved through the Arthālaṅkāraprakaraṇa. However, for Ruyyaka's root work, only the sūtras (prefixed in GRETIL markup with RuAss_) are provided.

SA_GK16_ruyalssu.title: Alaṅkārasarvasva (sūtras 1–34)
SA_GK16_ruyalssu.author: Ruyyaka
SA_GK16_ruyalssu.summary: The Alaṅkārasarvasva is an influential 12th-century Kashmiri treatise on Sanskrit poetics by Ruyyaka (c. 1135–1150 CE). Composed in concise sūtras accompanied by a prose vṛtti, the work provides an analytical and exhaustive classification of over eighty figures of sense and sound (alaṅkāra), integrating traditional rhetorical taxonomies with the dhvani framework established by earlier theorists. Its introductory Bhūmikā offers a critical historical review of earlier poetic theories (including Bhāmaha, Udbhaṭa, Vāmana, Rudraṭa, and Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka), demonstrating that ornamental figures are functionally related to suggested sense.
SA_GK16_ruyalssu.attribution: The Alaṅkārasarvasva consists of concise aphorisms (sūtras) accompanied by an explanatory prose commentary (vṛtti) and illustrative citations. While the South Indian commentator Samudrabandha and the later commentator Vidyācakravartin attribute both sūtras and vṛtti to Ruyyaka (also named Rājānaka Rucaka), Jayaratha in his commentary Vimarśinī attributes the prose vṛtti to Ruyyaka's pupil Maṅkha (Maṅkhuka). Modern critical scholarship generally treats Ruyyaka as the principal author of the treatise, or at least of the foundational sūtras.
SA_GK16_ruyalssu.edition: R. P. Dvivedi (ed.), Alamkara Sarvasva of Sri Rajanaka Ruyyaka & Mankha, with the Vimarsini of Jayaratha and with the translation and explanation of both in Hindi, Kashi Sanskrit Series, 206, Varanasi: Chowkhamba, 1971, pp. 1–352. (probable)
SA_GK16_ruyalssu.coverage: partial — Contains the introductory Bhūmikā and sūtras 1 through 34 (breaking off abruptly at p. 352 of Dvivedi's edition; remainder of 34 up to 87 not available).
translations: R. P. Dvivedi, Alamkara Sarvasva of Sri Rajanaka Ruyyaka & Mankha with the Vimarsini of Jayaratha and with the translation and explanation of both in Hindi, Kashi Sanskrit Series 206, Varanasi: Chowkhamba, 1971. (Hindi)

SA_GK16_ruyalsvu.title: Alaṅkārasarvasva with Vimarśinī (sūtras 1–34)
SA_GK16_ruyalsvu.author: Ruyyaka, Jayaratha
SA_GK16_ruyalsvu.summary: The Alaṅkārasarvasva of the Kashmiri theorist Rājānaka Ruyyaka is a classical treatise on Sanskrit poetics (alaṅkāraśāstra). Composed in sūtra style with an accompanying expository vṛtti, the work provides a taxonomy of poetic figures (alaṅkāras). This e-text contains the opening theoretical exposition and sūtras 1 through 34 along with the Vimarśinī commentary by Jayaratha.
SA_GK16_ruyalsvu.attribution: A traditional South Indian transmission (reflected in Samudrabandha's commentary) attributes the sūtras to Ruyyaka and the vṛtti to Maṅkha (Maṅkhuka / Maṅkhaka). In contrast, the commentary Vimarśinī refers to the granthakṛt.
SA_GK16_ruyalsvu.edition: Rewāprasāda Dvivedī (ed.), Alaṃkāra Sarvasva of Śrī Rājānaka Ruyyaka & Maṅkha, with the Vimarśinī of Jayaratha and with the translation and explanation of both in Hindi, Varanasi: Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series Office, 1971 (Kashi Sanskrit Series, 206).
SA_GK16_ruyalsvu.coverage: partial — Covers sūtras 1 through 34 only (out of 87 sūtras in total), terminating abruptly in the discussion of śleṣa at page 352 of the 1971 Chowkhamba edition.
translations: Rewāprasāda Dvivedī, Alaṃkāra Sarvasva of Śrī Rājānaka Ruyyaka & Maṅkha, with Hindi translation and explanation, Varanasi: Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series Office, 1971 (Kashi Sanskrit Series, 206). (Hindi)

SA_GK16_simhrs_u.title: Rasārṇavasudhākara
SA_GK16_simhrs_u.author: Siṃhabhūpāla
SA_GK16_simhrs_u.summary: The Rasārṇavasudhākara ('Nectar-Moon to the Ocean of Rasa') is an encyclopedic 14th-century Sanskrit treatise on dramaturgy and aesthetics composed by King Siṃhabhūpāla II of the Recherla dynasty. Arranged into three comprehensive 'rays' (vilāsas)—Rañjakollāsa (dealing with dramatic personae, the typology of hero and heroine, and their aesthetic embellishments), Rasollāsa (treating the primary sentiments, transient emotions, excitant/ensuant factors, and the nature of aesthetic delight), and Nāṭakollāsa (treating plot structure, junctures/sandhis, and dramatic genres)—it synthesizes the traditions of Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra, Dhanañjaya's Daśarūpaka, and Bhoja's Śṛṅgāraprakāśa. The work is especially prized by later commentators (notably Mallinātha and the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theorists such as Rūpa Gosvāmin) for its rigorous definitions and rich repertoire of illustrative quotations drawn from classical poetry and drama.
SA_GK16_simhrs_u.attribution: Attributed to Siṅgabhūpāla (1381), the Recarla King (also referenced as Siṃhabhūpāla / Śiṅgarāja).
SA_GK16_simhrs_u.edition: T. Venkatacharya, Madras: Adyar Library and Research Centre, 1979 (Adyar Library Series, 110).
SA_GK16_simhrs_u.coverage: complete — Complete work comprising all three vilāsas (1: Rañjakollāsa, 2: Rasollāsa, 3: Nāṭakollāsa), complete with kārikās, authorial vṛtti, and illustrative citations (udāharaṇas).

SA_GK16_simhrsku.title: Rasārṇavasudhākara (kārikās only)
SA_GK16_simhrsku.author: Siṃhabhūpāla
SA_GK16_simhrsku.summary: The Rasārṇavasudhākara of Siṃhabhūpāla is a manual of Sanskrit dramaturgy and aesthetic sentiment (rasa). Composed in three sections termed vilāsas (Rañjakollāsa, Rasikollāsa, and Bhāvakollāsa), the text provides classifications of heroes, heroines, bhāvas, rasas, and dramatic structures. This e-text preserves the metrical rules (kārikās) extracted from the treatise.
SA_GK16_simhrsku.attribution: Attributed to Siṃhabhūpāla (also referred to as Siṅgabhūpāla, Recarla king).
SA_GK16_simhrsku.edition: The Rasārṇavasudhākara of Siṃhabhūpāla, critically edited with introduction and notes by T. Venkatacharya, Madras: Adyar Library and Research Centre, 1979 (Adyar Library Series, 110).
SA_GK16_simhrsku.coverage: partial — Contains the kārikā verses of all three chapters (vilāsas: 1. Rañjakollāsa, 2. Rasikollāsa, 3. Bhāvakollāsa) in full, including introductory genealogical verses and concluding praśastis, but omits the prose vṛtti and illustrative verses.

SA_GK16_udkass_u.title: Kāvyālaṃkārasārasaṃgraha with Laghuvṛtti
SA_GK16_udkass_u.author: Udbhaṭa, Pratīhārendurāja
SA_GK16_udkass_u.summary: The Kāvyālaṃkārasārasaṃgraha ('Compendium of the Essence of Poetic Ornaments') by the Kashmiri rhetorician Udbhaṭa is a major foundational treatise of Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra). In six chapters (vargas), it defines, illustrates, and classifies poetic figures of sound and sense, modifying Bhāmaha's schema and introducing new categories such as punaruktavadābhāsa, kāvyahetu, and kāvyadṛṣṭānta. The accompanying Laghuvṛtti by Pratīhārendurāja is the earliest surviving commentary on the work, providing valuable syntactic analysis, philosophical contextualization (integrating Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya tenets), and critical discussion of the emerging dhvani doctrine.
SA_GK16_udkass_u.attribution: The root work is composed by Udbhaṭa (Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa, fl. c. 779–813 CE, sabhāpati of King Jayāpīḍa of Kashmir). The commentary Laghuvṛtti is by Pratīhārendurāja (also referred to as Kauṅkaṇa Śrīndurāja or Indurāja), a pupil of Mukula Bhaṭṭa who was from the Konkan region.
SA_GK16_udkass_u.edition: Missing passages added according to: The Kāvyālaṃkārasārasaṃgraha of Udbhaṭa, with the Laghuvṛtti of Pratīhārendurāja, edited by Narayana Daso Banhatti, Bombay Sanskrit and Prakrit Series, No. LXXIX, Poona: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, 1925; introductory prastāvanā dated Śake [ CE] by Maṅgeśaśarmā.
SA_GK16_udkass_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of all six vargas containing the kārikās, illustrative verses (many drawn from Udbhaṭa's lost Kumārasambhava), and Pratīhārendurāja's commentary; also includes the Sanskrit prastāvanā by the editor Maṅgeśaśarmā.

SA_GK16_udkassku.title: Kāvyālaṃkārasārasaṃgraha (kārikās only)
SA_GK16_udkassku.author: Udbhaṭa
SA_GK16_udkassku.summary: The Kāvyālaṃkārasārasaṃgraha by Udbhaṭa is an early work of Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra). Arranged in six vargas, it defines various poetic figures (alaṃkāras) such as punaruktavadābhāsa, anuprāsa, upamā, dīpaka, rūpaka, and others.
SA_GK16_udkassku.attribution: The kārikās are attributed to Udbhaṭa.
SA_GK16_udkassku.edition: Narayana Daso Banhatti (ed.), Kāvyālaṃkāra-sāra-saṃgraha of Udbhata: With the Commentary, the Laghuvṛtti of Indurāja. Bombay Sanskrit and Prakrit Series, No. LXXIX. Poona: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, 1925.
SA_GK16_udkassku.coverage: partial — Contains kārikās across the six vargas (UKss 1.1–6.8), excluding commentary.

SA_GK16_ujjvni_u.title: Ujjvalanīlamaṇi (prakaraṇas 1–6, 8–15)
SA_GK16_ujjvni_u.author: Rūpa Gosvāmin
SA_GK16_ujjvni_u.summary: The Ujjvalanīlamaṇi ('The Blazing Sapphire') is an influential treatise on devotional aesthetics and theology by Rūpa Gosvāmin. Written as a continuation of the madhura-rasa section of his Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu, the work presents an analysis of madhura-rasa (the erotic-devotional sentiment) in relation to Kṛṣṇa. Rūpa treats classifications of hero and heroine (nāyaka- and nāyikā-bheda), supporting characters, excitant factors (vibhāva), involuntary physical responses (anubhāva), and permanent emotions (sthāyibhāva) to explain loving relations between Kṛṣṇa and the gopīs of Vraja, culminating in the preeminence of Rādhā.
SA_GK16_ujjvni_u.coverage: partial — 15 prakaraṇas in the work; the e-text has prakaraṇas 1–6 and 8–15 (RUnm_6.26 is followed directly by RUnm_8.1, sakhī-prakaraṇa) and ends with the śṛṅgāra-bheda-prakaraṇa and the final colophon 'sampūrṇo 'yaṃ ... ujjvala-nīlamaṇir nāma granthaḥ'. Missing per GRETIL header and verified for ch. 7: 3.24–25, the whole of prakaraṇa 7 (Dūtībheda), 8.111–113, 8.115–121, 14.160. Only the mūla; the commentaries of Jīva Gosvāmin and Viśvanātha Cakravartin are not included.

SA_GK16_vamkalsu.title: Kāvyālaṅkārasūtra
SA_GK16_vamkalsu.author: Vāmana
SA_GK16_vamkalsu.summary: The Kāvyālaṅkārasūtra is a treatise on Sanskrit poetics by the Kashmiri author Vāmana. Divided into five adhikaraṇas (Śārīra, Doṣadarśana, Guṇavivecana, Ālaṅkārika, and Prāyogika), it deals with poetic styles, qualities (guṇas), defects (doṣas), and poetic figures. In this e-text, only the sūtras without the prose commentary are included.
SA_GK16_vamkalsu.attribution: Attributed to the Kashmiri writer Vāmana (c. 8th–9th century CE).
SA_GK16_vamkalsu.edition: śrīVāmanācāryaviracitāni Kāvyālaṅkārasūtrāni Svavṛttisamalaṅkṛtāni, ed. Nārāyaṇarāma Ācārya Kāvyatīrtha, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1983.
SA_GK16_vamkalsu.coverage: complete — Text of the aphorisms across 5 adhikaraṇas: Śārīra, Doṣadarśana, Guṇavivecana, Ālaṅkārika, and Prāyogika. The auto-commentary (vṛtti) printed in the source edition is omitted, except for the opening maṅgala verse.

SA_GK16_vamkalvu.title: Kāvyālaṅkārasūtra with Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti
SA_GK16_vamkalvu.author: Vāmana
SA_GK16_vamkalvu.summary: The Kāvyālaṅkārasūtra along with its auto-commentary (Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti or Kavipriyā) by Vāmana (fl. late 8th to early 9th century CE, Kashmir) constitutes the defining work of the Rīti school of classical Sanskrit poetics. Vāmana formulated the famous thesis that style (rīti) is the soul of poetry ('rītir ātmā kāvyasya', 1.2.6), distinguishing three primary styles (Vaidarbhī, Gauḍī, and Pāñcālī) based on the presence of specific poetic qualities (guṇas). Organised into five adhikaraṇas (Śārīra, Doṣadarśana, Guṇavivecana, Ālaṅkārika, and Prāyogika), the work presents a comprehensive taxonomy of poetic purpose, flaws (doṣas), aesthetic qualities (ten verbal and ten semantic guṇas), figures of speech (alaṅkāras), and rules for grammatical purity in poetry (śabdaśuddhi).
SA_GK16_vamkalvu.attribution: Vāmana composed both the root sūtras and the prose auto-commentary (vṛtti), which he designates as 'Kavipriyā' in the opening maṅgala stanza (1.1.3–4: 'praṇamya paramaṃ jyotir vāmanena kavipriyā / kāvyālaṅkārasūtrāṇāṃ teṣāṃ vṛttir vidhīyate'). Later tradition and manuscript colophons typically refer to the unitary work as the Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti.
SA_GK16_vamkalvu.edition: Masahiro Takano keyed the e-text based primarily on: Kāvyālaṅkāra sūtra of ācārya Vāmana, with the Kāvyālaṅkārakāmadhenu Sanskrit commentary of Śrī Gopendra Tripurahara Bhūpāla, edited with Hindi translation by Bechana Jhā, introduction by Rewāprasāda Dwivedī, 2nd ed., Varanasi: Caukhambha Sanskrit Sansthan, 1976 (Kashi Sanskrit Series, 209); collated with variant readings [marked 'k:...'] and alternate numbering [marked '*VKal_...'] from: ŚrīVāmanācāryaviracitāni Kāvyālaṅkārasūtrāṇi Svavṛttisamalaṅkṛtāni, edited by Śrīnārāyaṇarāma Ācārya Kāvyatīrtha, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1983 (reprint of the Nirnaya Sagar Press edition). Note: The e-text omits the Kāmadhenu commentary and Hindi translation found in the 1976 printed edition.
SA_GK16_vamkalvu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all five adhikaraṇas (comprising twelve adhyāyas): 1. Śārīra (3 adhyāyas), 2. Doṣadarśana (2 adhyāyas), 3. Guṇavivecana (2 adhyāyas), 4. Ālaṅkārika (3 adhyāyas), and 5. Prāyogika (2 adhyāyas, concluding at 5.2.91 with the author's final verses and colophon).
translations: Carl Cappeller (trans.), Vâmana's Stilregeln, Strassburg: Karl J. Trübner, 1880. (German)

SA_GK16_vcamkc_u.title: Camatkāracandrikā
SA_GK16_vcamkc_u.author: Viśveśvara Kavicandra
SA_GK16_vcamkc_u.summary: The Camatkāracandrikā is an eight-chapter (vilāsa) treatise on Sanskrit poetics by Viśveśvara Kavicandra dedicated to King Siṅgabhūpāla. It treats camatkāra as brought about by seven factors: guṇa, rīti, rasa, vṛtti, pāka, śayyā, and alaṅkāra.
SA_GK16_vcamkc_u.attribution: Viśveśvara Kavicandra was a poet and rhetorician, protégé of King Siṃhabhūpāla (Siṅgabhūpāla) of Rācakoṇḍa (c. 1400 CE).
SA_GK16_vcamkc_u.coverage: complete — Text in eight chapters (vilāsas 1–8), ending at 8.65 with 'samāpto 'yaṃ granthaḥ'.

SA_GK16_viprud_u.title: Pratāparudrīya
SA_GK16_viprud_u.author: Vidyānātha
SA_GK16_viprud_u.summary: The Pratāparudrīya (or Pratāparudrayaśobhūṣaṇa) by Vidyānātha is a manual of Sanskrit poetics and dramaturgy. Across nine chapters (prakaraṇas), it covers the hero (nāyaka), the nature of kāvya, dramaturgy (nāṭaka), rasa, poetic flaws (doṣa), poetic excellences (guṇa), and verbal and semantic ornaments (śabdālaṅkāra, arthālaṅkāra, miśrālaṅkāra). Its third chapter incorporates a play, the Pratāparudrakalyāṇa, designed as a model drama.
SA_GK16_viprud_u.attribution: Vidyānātha was a poet associated with Pratāparudra. Though the GRETIL header and opening caption announce the commentary Ratnāpaṇa by Kumārasvāmin, the digitizers omitted the commentary text.
SA_GK16_viprud_u.coverage: complete — Complete in all 9 prakaraṇas: (1) nāyaka, (2) kāvya, (3) nāṭaka (incorporating the full 5-act model play Pratāparudrakalyāṇa), (4) rasa, (5) doṣa, (6) guṇa, (7) śabdālaṅkāra, (8) arthālaṅkāra, and (9) miśrālaṅkāra. Kumārasvāmin's Ratnāpaṇa commentary was omitted by the digitizers.
translations: Pierre-Sylvain Filliozat, Le Pratāparudrīya de Vidyānātha avec le commentaire Ratnāpaṇa de Kumārasvāmin: ed. & tr. by Pierre Sylvain Filliozat, Publications de l'Institut Français d'Indologie. (French)

SA_GK16_visa01cu.title: Sāhityadarpaṇa with the commentaries Vijñapriyā and Locanā (chapter 1)
SA_GK16_visa01cu.author: Viśvanātha, Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra, Anantadāsa
SA_GK16_visa01cu.summary: This text comprises the first chapter (kāvyasvarūpanirūpaṇa) of Viśvanātha Kavirāja's Sāhityadarpaṇa. The opening chapter defends poetry and formulates Viśvanātha's definition of kāvya as 'vākyaṃ rasātmakaṃ kāvyam', critiquing previous definitions including that of the Kāvyaprakāśa. This e-text also incorporates two running commentaries: the Vijñapriyā of Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra Bhaṭṭācārya and the Locanā of Anantadāsa.
SA_GK16_visa01cu.attribution: Viśvanātha Kavirāja composed the root text and autocommentary. Anantadāsa and Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra Bhaṭṭācārya authored the commentaries Locanā and Vijñapriyā.
SA_GK16_visa01cu.edition: Śrīmadālaṃkārikacakravartitrikaliṅgagajapatisāmrājyasāndhivigrahakamahāpātra-Viśvanāthakavirāja-praṇītaḥ Sāhityadarpaṇaḥ granthakṛdātmabhuvā Sāhityadarpaṇavasudhākareṇa, Anantadāsena viracitayā Locanākhyayā, Bhaṭṭācārya-śrī-Maheśvara-Tarkālaṃkāra-praṇītayā Vijñapriyā-samākhyayā ca vyākhyayā samakaṃkṛtaḥ, Dillī: Bhāratīya Buk Kārporeśan 1998.

SA_GK16_visa02cu.title: Sāhityadarpaṇa with the commentaries Locanā and Vijñapriyā (chapter 2)
SA_GK16_visa02cu.author: Viśvanātha, Anantadāsa, Maheśvara Tarkālaṃkāra
SA_GK16_visa02cu.summary: The second chapter (pariccheda) of Viśvanātha Kavirāja's Sāhityadarpaṇa investigates the grammatical and semantic foundations of poetic discourse, focusing on the definitions of the sentence (vākya) and the word (pada). It elaborates the three classical conditions for syntactic and semantic coherence: semantic compatibility (yogyatā), mutual expectancy (ākāṅkṣā), and contiguity (āsatti). It systematically analyzes the primary linguistic powers (śabdavṛtti)—denotation (abhidhā), metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā), and poetic suggestion (vyañjanā)—as well as the sentence-purport function (tātparyavṛtti) of the Abhihitānvayavādins. This digital file presents Viśvanātha's kārikās and autocommentary interwoven with two important traditional commentaries: the Locanā of the author's son Anantadāsa and the Vijñapriyā of Maheśvara Tarkālaṃkāra.
SA_GK16_visa02cu.attribution: Viśvanātha Kavirāja composed both the metrical kārikās and the prose vṛtti of the Sāhityadarpaṇa. His son Anantadāsa composed the sub-commentary Locanā. Maheśvara Tarkālaṃkāra Bhaṭṭācārya composed the sub-commentary Vijñapriyā.
SA_GK16_visa02cu.edition: Śrīmadālaṃkārikacakravartitrikaliṅgagajapatisāmrājyasāndhivigrahakamahāpātra-Viśvanāthakavirāja-praṇītaḥ Sāhityadarpaṇaḥ granthakṛdātmabhuvā Sāhityadarpaṇavasudhākareṇa, Anantadāsena viracitayā Locanākhyayā, Bhaṭṭācārya-śrī-Maheśvara-Tarkālaṃkāra-praṇītayā Vijñapriyā-samākhyayā ca vyākhyayā samakaṃkṛtaḥ, Dillī: Bhāratīya Buk Kārporeśan, 1998.
SA_GK16_visa02cu.coverage: partial — Complete for pariccheda 2 (Vākyasvarūpanirūpaṇa) out of the ten paricchedas of the Sāhityadarpaṇa, including the kārikās, vṛtti, and the two commentaries Locanā and Vijñapriyā.

SA_GK16_visa03cu.title: Sāhityadarpaṇa with the commentaries Locanā and Vijñapriyā (chapter 3)
SA_GK16_visa03cu.author: Viśvanātha, Anantadāsa, Maheśvaratarkālaṅkāra
SA_GK16_visa03cu.summary: Pariccheda 3 (Rasādinirūpaṇa) of Viśvanātha Kavirāja's Sāhityadarpaṇa provides an in-depth exposition of rasa (aesthetic relish), analyzing how the sthāyibhāva is brought to relish via vibhāvas (determinants), anubhāvas (consequents), and vyabhicāribhāvas (transitory emotions). It also details the classification of the rasas (śṛṅgāra, hāsya, karuṇa, raudra, vīra, bhayānaka, bībhatsa, adbhuta, and śānta), dramatic character types, and the comprehensive taxonomy of heroes (nāyakas) and heroines (nāyikās). This digital edition integrates the root kārikās and autocommentary with two traditional commentaries: the Locanā by Viśvanātha's son Anantadāsa and the Vijñapriyā by Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra.
SA_GK16_visa03cu.attribution: Viśvanātha Kavirāja composed both the kārikās and the autocommentary of the Sāhityadarpaṇa. His son Anantadāsa composed the commentary Locanā. Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra composed the commentary Vijñapriyā.
SA_GK16_visa03cu.edition: Śrīmadālaṃkārikacakravartitrikaliṅgagajapatisāmrājyasāndhivigrahakamahāpātra-Viśvanāthakavirāja-praṇītaḥ Sāhityadarpaṇaḥ granthakṛdātmabhuvā Sāhityadarpaṇavasudhākareṇa, Anantadāsena viracitayā Locanākhyayā, Bhaṭṭācārya-śrī-Maheśvara-Tarkālaṃkāra-praṇītayā Vijñapriyā-samākhyayā ca vyākhyayā samakaṃkṛtaḥ. Dillī: Bhāratīya Buk Kārporeśan, 1998.
SA_GK16_visa03cu.coverage: partial — Complete text of chapter 3 (tṛtīyaḥ paricchedaḥ, titled Rasādinirūpaṇa) of the Sāhityadarpaṇa, comprising Viśvanātha's kārikās and vṛtti, along with the third-chapter sections of Anantadāsa's Locanā and Maheśvara's Vijñapriyā.

SA_GK16_visa04cu.title: Sāhityadarpaṇa with the commentaries Locana and Vijñapriyā (chapter 4)
SA_GK16_visa04cu.author: Viśvanātha, Anantadāsa, Maheśvara Tarkālaṃkāra
SA_GK16_visa04cu.summary: The fourth pariccheda of Viśvanātha's Sāhityadarpaṇa treats the classification of poetry based on the theory of aesthetic suggestion (dhvani), building upon the frameworks of Ānandavardhana and Mammaṭa. It defines first-rate poetry (dhvanikāvya or uttama kāvya) where implied meaning surpasses expressed meaning, detailing its major divisions (avivakṣitavācya and vivakṣitānyaparavācya) and their numerous varieties, and contrasts this with second-rate poetry of subordinate suggestion (guṇībhūtavyaṅgya or madhyama kāvya). This electronic text presents the root kārikās and Viśvanātha's autocommentary alongside two extensive Sanskrit commentaries: the Locana by the author's son Anantadāsa and the Vijñapriyā by Maheśvara Tarkālaṃkāra.
SA_GK16_visa04cu.attribution: Viśvanātha Kavirāja held the title of Sāndhivigrahika-mahāpātra. The Locana commentary was composed by his son Anantadāsa. The Vijñapriyā commentary was authored by Bhaṭṭācārya Maheśvara Tarkālaṃkāra.
SA_GK16_visa04cu.edition: Śrīmadālaṃkārikacakravartitrikaliṅgagajapatisāmrājyasāndhivigrahakamahāpātra-Viśvanāthakavirāja-praṇītaḥ Sāhityadarpaṇaḥ granthakṛdātmabhuvā Sāhityadarpaṇavasudhākareṇa, Anantadāsena viracitayā Locanākhyayā, Bhaṭṭācārya-śrī-Maheśvara-Tarkālaṃkāra-praṇītayā Vijñapriyā-samākhyayā ca vyākhyayā samakaṃkṛtaḥ. Dillī: Bhāratīya Buk Kārporeśan, 1998.

SA_GK16_visa05cu.title: Sāhityadarpaṇa with the commentaries Vijñapriyā and Locana (chapter 5)
SA_GK16_visa05cu.author: Viśvanātha, Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra, Anantadāsa
SA_GK16_visa05cu.summary: Chapter 5 of Viśvanātha Kavirāja's 14th-century treatise on poetics, the Sāhityadarpaṇa, presented alongside the Vijñapriyā commentary of Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra and the Locana commentary of the author's son Anantadāsa. This chapter is devoted to vindicating the dhvani school's doctrine of suggestion (vyañjanāvyāpāra) as an autonomous semantic function (vṛtti) indispensable for conveying aesthetic relish (rasa), vastudhvani, and alaṅkāradhvani. Viśvanātha and his commentators systematically refute competing theories advanced by Mīmāṃsā, Nyāya, and other schools that attempt to reduce suggestion to literal denotation (abhidhā), sentence purport (tātparya), or syllogistic inference (anumāna).
SA_GK16_visa05cu.attribution: Viśvanātha Kavirāja composed both the kārikās and the accompanying prose vṛtti of the Sāhityadarpaṇa. The commentary Locana is by his son Anantadāsa (referred to on title pages as 'granthakṛd-ātmabhū'). The commentary Vijñapriyā is by Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra Bhaṭṭācārya (also cited as Maheśvarabhaṭṭa or Maheśvaranyāyālaṅkāra). The phrase 'Sāhityadarpaṇavasudhākareṇa' on the title page was erroneously interpreted in the GRETIL header as an autocommentary named Vasudhākara.

Dillī: Bhāratīya Buk Kārporeśan, 1998.

SA_GK16_visa06cu.title: Sāhityadarpaṇa with the commentaries of Anantadāsa and Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra (chapter 6)
SA_GK16_visa06cu.author: Viśvanātha, Anantadāsa, Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra
SA_GK16_visa06cu.summary: Pariccheda 6 of Viśvanātha Kavirāja's Sāhityadarpaṇa provides an extensive treatment of Sanskrit dramaturgy (dṛśyakāvya). Viśvanātha systematically distinguishes dramatic art from audible literature (śravyakāvya) and classifies dramatic forms into major and minor types. In this digital text, the root text and autocommentary are accompanied by Anantadāsa's Locanā and Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra's Vijñapriyā.

Dillī: Bhāratīya Buk Kārporeśan, 1998.

SA_GK16_visa07cu.title: Sāhityadarpaṇa with the commentaries Vijñapriyā and Locana (chapter 7)
SA_GK16_visa07cu.author: Viśvanātha, Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra, Anantadāsa
SA_GK16_visa07cu.summary: Pariccheda 7 of Viśvanātha Kavirāja's Sāhityadarpaṇa treats poetic defects (doṣanirūpaṇa), classifying them and discussing conditions where defects cease to be faults or become poetic merits. In this e-text, the text is presented alongside two traditional commentaries: the Vijñapriyā of Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra and the Locana of Anantadāsa.

SA_GK16_visa08cu.title: Sāhityadarpaṇa with the commentaries Locanā and Vijñapriyā (chapter 8)
SA_GK16_visa08cu.author: Viśvanātha, Anantadāsa, Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra
SA_GK16_visa08cu.summary: Pariccheda 8 (Guṇavivecana) of Viśvanātha's fourteenth-century alaṅkāraśāstra treatise Sāhityadarpaṇa treats the poetic qualities (guṇa). Adopting the Kashmiri dhvani position elaborated by Mammaṭa, Viśvanātha argues that guṇas inhere essentially in the principal aesthetic emotion (rasa) rather than in mere sound or word configurations, reducing the traditional tenfold guṇa system of Daṇḍin and Vāmana to three primary qualities: mādhurya (sweetness/melting), ojas (vigor/expansion), and prasāda (perspicuity/clarity). This digital edition merges Viśvanātha's root kārikās (8.1–8.16) and svopajña vṛtti with two early commentaries: the Locanā by his son Anantadāsa and the Vijñapriyā by Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra Bhaṭṭācārya.
SA_GK16_visa08cu.attribution: Viśvanātha Kavirāja Mahāpātra authored the kārikās and the vṛtti. The Locanā was composed by his son Anantadāsa. The Vijñapriyā was authored by Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra Bhaṭṭācārya.
SA_GK16_visa08cu.edition: Sāhityadarpaṇa of Viśvanātha with the commentaries Locana of Anantadāsa and Vijñapriyā of Bhaṭṭācārya Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra, edited by Karuṇākara Kara, Lahore: Motilal Banarsidass, 1938 (reprinted Delhi: Bhāratīya Buk Kārporeśan, 1988 / 1998).

SA_GK16_visa09cu.title: Sāhityadarpaṇa with the commentaries Locana and Vijñapriyā (chapter 9)
SA_GK16_visa09cu.author: Viśvanātha, Anantadāsa, Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra
SA_GK16_visa09cu.summary: Pariccheda 9 of Viśvanātha Kavirāja's treatise Sāhityadarpaṇa is devoted to the analysis of poetic style and diction (rītiviveka). Viśvanātha defines rīti as the systematic configuration of words (padasaṃghaṭanā) that assists in the manifestation of rasa, drawing an analogy to the harmonious arrangement of bodily limbs. He presents four primary styles—Vaidarbhī, Gauḍī, Pāñcālī, and Lāṭikā—and elaborates their phonetic properties, compound lengths, and contextual decorum (aucitya). In this e-text, the root kārikās and prose explanations are accompanied by two traditional commentaries: the Locana by Anantadāsa and the Vijñapriyā by Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra.
SA_GK16_visa09cu.attribution: Viśvanātha Kavirāja composed the Sāhityadarpaṇa. The commentary Locana was composed by Anantadāsa (referred to as granthakṛdātmabhū). The commentary Vijñapriyā was authored by Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra.

SA_GK16_visa10cu.title: Sāhityadarpaṇa with the commentaries Locanā and Vijñapriyā (chapter 10)
SA_GK16_visa10cu.author: Viśvanātha Kavirāja, Anantadāsa, Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra
SA_GK16_visa10cu.summary: The tenth and longest pariccheda of Viśvanātha Kavirāja's Sāhityadarpaṇa provides an encyclopedic exposition of poetic ornaments (alaṅkāra), encompassing both figures of sound (śabdālaṅkāra, including anuprāsa, yamaka, and śleṣa) and figures of meaning (arthālaṅkāra, such as upamā, rūpaka, utprekṣā, and atiśayokti). Each ornament is defined and illustrated with extensive verse citations from Sanskrit classical literature. In this e-text, the root kārikās and Viśvanātha's prose auto-commentary are interwoven with the Locanā commentary by the author's son Anantadāsa and the Vijñapriyā commentary by Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra.
SA_GK16_visa10cu.attribution: Viśvanātha Kavirāja composed the Sāhityadarpaṇa. The Locanā commentary was composed by Anantadāsa (described as granthakṛdātmabhū). The Vijñapriyā commentary was authored by Bhaṭṭācārya Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra.

SA_GK16_visah1.title: Sāhityadarpaṇa
SA_GK16_visah1.author: Viśvanātha Kavirāja
SA_GK16_visah1.summary: The Sāhityadarpaṇa ('Mirror of Composition') is an encyclopedic treatise on Sanskrit literary theory and dramaturgy composed in ten chapters (paricchedas) in sūtra/kārikā and prose vṛtti by Viśvanātha Kavirāja. Its chapters systematically discuss the purpose and nature of poetry (1), word functions and semantics (abhidhā, lakṣaṇā, vyañjanā) (2), rasa theory and aesthetic emotion (3), types of suggestive poetry (dhvani and guṇībhūtavyaṅgya) (4–5), dramatic forms and stage conventions (rūpaka, uparūpaka) (6), poetic blemishes (doṣa) (7), poetic excellences (guṇa) (8), stylistic modes (rīti) (9), and figures of sound and sense (śabda- and arthālaṅkāras) (10).
SA_GK16_visah1.attribution: Viśvanātha Kavirāja, son of Candraśekhara (and titled Sāndhivigrahika Mahāpātra), is the author named in the colophon.
SA_GK16_visah1.coverage: complete — Complete text across 10 paricchedas, containing both kārikās and prose vṛtti, concluding with the author's final verses (10.99–10.100) and the tenth pariccheda colophon.

SA_GK16_visah.title: Sāhityadarpaṇa
SA_GK16_visah.author: Viśvanātha
SA_GK16_visah.summary: The Sāhityadarpaṇa ('Mirror of Composition') by Viśvanātha Kavirāja (14th century CE) is an encyclopedic manual of Sanskrit poetics (alaṅkāraśāstra) and dramaturgy (nāṭyaśāstra). Composed in ten chapters (paricchedas) combining verse kārikās and the author's own explanatory prose vṛtti, the work famously defines poetry as 'a sentence whose soul is rasa' (vākyaṃ rasātmakaṃ kāvyam). Across its ten chapters, it systematically covers the purpose and definition of kāvya, semantic functions of words (abhidhā, lakṣaṇā, vyañjanā), the nature of rasa and aesthetic experience, types of suggested meaning (dhvani), dramatic forms (rūpakas and uparūpakas), poetic faults (doṣas), poetic excellences (guṇas), stylistic rītis, and figures of sound and sense (śabdālaṅkāras and arthālaṅkāras).
SA_GK16_visah.coverage: complete — Paricchedas 1–10, ending 'iti sāhityadarpaṇe daśamaḥ paricchedaḥ samāptaḥ || samāptañcedaṃ sāhityadarpaṇaṃ ||' (seg. 8641–8642). Kārikās numbered continuously in parentheses ((1) ... (338) ... (668)) with Viśvanātha's vṛtti. Very poor OCR: line-end hyphenation, running heads ('sāhityadarpaye |', '• prathamaparichedaḥ |') and footnotes ('ṭī0', 'saṃ ṭī0' — Sanskrit chāyās/notes, mostly on Prakrit verses) are mixed into the text; frequent misreadings (va/ba, kṣa/ca: 'dharmārthakāmamotreṣu vaicacasyaṃ' for '...mokṣeṣu vaicakṣaṇyaṃ').
translations: Sāhitya-Darpaṇa or Mirror of Composition, transl. into English by James R. Ballantyne and Pramadā-Dāsa Mitra, Calcutta: Baptist Mission Press, 1851–1875. (English)

SA_GK16_visvsdpu.title: Sāhityadarpaṇa (kārikās only)
SA_GK16_visvsdpu.author: Viśvanātha
SA_GK16_visvsdpu.summary: The Sāhityadarpaṇa ('Mirror of Composition') by Viśvanātha Kavirāja is a comprehensive textbook of classical Sanskrit poetics (alaṅkāraśāstra) and dramaturgy (nāṭyaśāstra) structured into ten chapters (paricchedas). It is famous for its definitive formulation of poetry as 'a sentence whose soul is rasa' (vākyaṃ rasātmakaṃ kāvyam), integrating Dhvanyāloka's dhvani doctrine, dramatic theory, poetic qualities, blemishes, and figures of speech. This e-text provides only the metrical kārikās across all ten chapters, omitting the prose auto-commentary and illustrative quotations.
SA_GK16_visvsdpu.attribution: Viśvanātha (Viśvanātha Kavirāja), son of Candraśekhara Mahākavi, was an ālaṅkārika-cakravartin and sāndhivigrahika-mahāpātra.
SA_GK16_visvsdpu.edition: Satyavrata Simha, 9th edition. Varanasi: Chowkhamba Vidya Bhavan, 1992. (Vidya Bhavan Sanskrit Granthamala, 29)
SA_GK16_visvsdpu.coverage: partial — Contains the kārikā verses only (kārikā-mātra) for all ten paricchedas (chapters 1–10); the prose auto-commentary (vṛtti) and illustrative examples (udāharaṇas) are omitted.

SA_GK17_chandovu.title: Chandoviciti (fragment)
SA_GK17_chandovu.author: Mitradhara
SA_GK17_chandovu.summary: The Chandoviciti is a Sanskrit treatise on metrics preserved in fragments of a manuscript from the Turfan finds (SHT 654), edited by Dieter Schlingloff in 1958 with corrections by Ruixuan Chen (2013). The text treats Sanskrit metres and references the sūtras of Yāska and Piṅgala, naming Mitradhara as author.
SA_GK17_chandovu.attribution: Verse ChV_II_1_1 reads '... yāskapiṅgalasūtrebhyaḥ / mitradhareṇa ... kṛtiḥ cchandovicitiḥ'. The work is therefore presented as a composition by Mitradhara based on the sūtras of Yāska and Piṅgala. The attribution to Patañjali listed in legacy catalog records is not supported by the text.
SA_GK17_chandovu.edition: Dieter Schlingloff: Chandoviciti, Texte zur Sanskritmetrik, Berlin 1958 (Sanskrittexte aus den Turfanfunden, 5), incorporating corrections from Chen, Ruixuan: 'Beobachtungen zur Turfan-Chandoviciti', Indo-Iranian Journal, 56 (2013), pp. 41–60.
SA_GK17_chandovu.coverage: fragment — The e-text reproduces Schlingloff's arrangement of the surviving fragments of SHT 654: I. Regeln zur Metrik (Versgruppe A: A.1–15; B: B.1–31), II. Chandoviciti, III. Metrik-Lehrtext. It ends at ChV_III_2_5. Lost sections are explicitly marked (e.g. 'ChV_I_A_5 nicht erhalten').

SA_GK17_jvrtmspu.title: Vṛttamālāstuti
SA_GK17_jvrtmspu.author: Jñānaśrīmitra
SA_GK17_jvrtmspu.summary: The Vṛttamālāstuti is a Buddhist devotional hymn and versified manual of Sanskrit metrics (chandaśśāstra) by Jñānaśrīmitra. Comprising 154 stanzas praising the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī (Mañjughoṣa), the work illustrates approximately 150 classical metres by weaving the metrical name directly into each stanza while exemplifying its metrical structure. It was translated into Tibetan by Pang Lotsāwa Lodrö Tenpa (Dpal-ldan blo-gros brtan-pa) along with Śoṅ-ston Rdo-rje rgyal-mtshan.
SA_GK17_jvrtmspu.attribution: The concluding colophon identifies the author as Mahāpaṇḍitasthavira Jñānaśrīmitra. The attribution is corroborated by Tibetan tradition (Tōhoku 4305 / D4305) and modern scholarship.
SA_GK17_jvrtmspu.edition: M. Hahn: "The Sanskrit Text of Jñānaśrīmitra's Vṛttamālāstuti", in: Bauddhasāhityastabakāvalī: Essays and Studies on Buddhist Sanskrit Literature Dedicated to Claus Vogel by Colleagues, Students, and Friends, ed. by Dragomir Dimitrov, Michael Hahn and Roland Steiner. Marburg 2008 (Indica et Tibetica 36), pp. 93-170.
SA_GK17_jvrtmspu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 154 stanzas (JVms_1 through JVms_154), including the introductory prastāvanā and concluding viṣamavṛtta sections (sarvaviṣama, ardhaviṣama, and pādaviṣama), along with opening and closing colophons.
translations: Michael Hahn, Jñānaśrīmitras Vṛttamālāstuti: Eine Beispielsammlung zur altindischen Metrik, nach dem tibetischen Tanjur zusammen mit der mongolischen Version herausgegeben, übersetzt und erläutert, Wiesbaden: Otto Harrassowitz, 1971. (German)

SA_GK17_kedvratu.title: Vṛttaratnākara
SA_GK17_kedvratu.author: Kedārabhaṭṭa
SA_GK17_kedvratu.summary: The Vṛttaratnākara of Kedārabhaṭṭa is a widely known manual of classical Sanskrit prosody (chandaśśāstra). Structured in six concise chapters of 136 verses, it covers metrical definitions and the trika/gaṇa syllabic foot notation, mātrāvṛtta (moraic) metres, samavṛtta, ardhasamavṛtta, viṣamavṛtta, and the six metrical pratyayas (combinatorial algorithms such as prastāra, naṣṭa, and uddiṣṭa). Each metrical rule is composed in the very metre that it defines, serving simultaneously as definition and illustrative instance.
SA_GK17_kedvratu.attribution: Kedārabhaṭṭa, son of Pavyeka of the Kāśyapa gotra and a Śaiva, composed this handbook of metrics. The chapter-end colophons in the e-text are copied from the printed edition and mention Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa (son of Rāmeśvara Bhaṭṭa), but no commentary prose is included.
SA_GK17_kedvratu.edition: Śrī Kedāra Nātha Śarmā (ed.), Vṛttaratnākara: with a commentary of Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭ and notes etc. by Vaidya Nātha Śāstrī Varakale, edited with the Maṇimayī Hindī Commentary, 6th ed., Varanasi: Chaukhambha Sanskrit Sansthan, 1980 (The Kashi Sanskrit Series, 55).
SA_GK17_kedvratu.coverage: complete — Complete root text across all six chapters (adhyāyas 1–6, containing KedV_1.1 through KedV_6.10, covering terminology, mātrāvṛtta, samavṛtta, ardhasamavṛtta, viṣamavṛtta, and the six pratyayas).

SA_GK17_kvrtrsuu.title: Vṛttaratnākara with Sukavihṛdayānandinī
SA_GK17_kvrtrsuu.author: Kedārabhaṭṭa, Sulhaṇa
SA_GK17_kvrtrsuu.summary: The Vṛttaratnākara by Kedārabhaṭṭa is an influential classical Indian manual of metrics (chandaḥśāstra). It defines metrical gaṇas and scanning rules, illustrating classical syllabic and moraic meters via self-exemplifying verses. This text is accompanied by the Sukavihṛdayānandinī, a Sanskrit commentary by Sulhaṇa.
SA_GK17_kvrtrsuu.attribution: Sulhaṇa, son of Bhāskara and grandson of Velāditya of the Kṛṣṇātreya gotra, composed the commentary Sukavihṛdayānandinī on Kedārabhaṭṭa's Vṛttaratnākara.
SA_GK17_kvrtrsuu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all six chapters (adhyāyas 1–6: Saṃjñā, Mātrāvṛtta, Samavṛtta, Ardhasamavṛtta, Viṣamavṛtta, and Ṣaṭpratyaya) of Kedārabhaṭṭa's Vṛttaratnākara along with Sulhaṇa's commentary.

SA_GK18_abhidhau.title: Abhinayadarpaṇa
SA_GK18_abhidhau.author: Nandikeśvara
SA_GK18_abhidhau.summary: The Abhinayadarpaṇa ('Mirror of Gesture'), attributed to the legendary sage Nandikeśvara, is an indispensable Sanskrit manual on classical Indian performing arts, particularly central to the tradition of Bharatanatyam. It is primarily devoted to āṅgikābhinaya (bodily and gestural expression), systematically enumerating and defining gestures of the single and combined hands (asaṃyuta- and saṃyuta-hastas), movements of the head (śirobheda), eyes (dṛṣṭibheda), neck (grīvābheda), and eyebrows, as well as postures (sthāna), movements (cārī), and gaits (gati). The work functions as a practical handbook connecting theoretical dramaturgy with dance choreography.
SA_GK18_abhidhau.coverage: unclear — The catalog entry contains no e-text data.
translations: Coomaraswamy, Ananda K. 1917. New Delhi: Munishiram Manoharlal. (English)

SA_GK18_bharnatu.title: Nāṭyaśāstra (chapters 1–16, 18–30, 33, 35–37)
SA_GK18_bharnatu.author: Bharata
SA_GK18_bharnatu.summary: The Nāṭyaśāstra is the encyclopedic foundational treatise of classical Indian dramaturgy, performance, dance, and music, traditionally attributed to Bharata Muni. It provides detailed prescriptions on theatre architecture, preliminary rites (pūrvaraṅga), acting styles and bodily gestures (abhinaya), classifications of dramatic compositions (daśarūpaka), costuming, makeup, prosody, and musical scales and instruments. Its sixth and seventh chapters present the classical formulation of aesthetic relish (rasa) and emotional determinants and states (bhāva), establishing the bedrock of Indian aesthetic philosophy.
SA_GK18_bharnatu.attribution: Traditionally ascribed to the mythical sage Bharata Muni.
SA_GK18_bharnatu.coverage: partial — Contains 33 chapters out of 37 (chapters 1–16, 18–30, 33, 35–37). Chapters 17, 31, 32, and 34 are not included.
translations: Ghosh, M. (ed. and trans.), The Nāṭyaśāstra attributed to Bharata-Muni, Bibl. Ind. 272. (English)
Rangacharya, Adya (trans.), The Natyashastra, New Delhi: Munshiram Manoharlal, 1996. (English)

SA_GK18_dhandasu.title: Daśarūpaka
SA_GK18_dhandasu.author: Dhanañjaya
SA_GK18_dhandasu.summary: The Daśarūpaka ('Ten Forms of Dramatic Art') by Dhanañjaya is an influential treatise in four chapters (paricchedas) condensing and systematizing dramaturgical teachings. It offers an analytical framework for dramatic plot structure (vastu) and its stages of development (sandhis), classifications of dramatic heroes and heroines (netṛ), the ten major dramatic genres (rūpaka), and aesthetic emotional response (rasa and bhāva). Composed under the patronage of King Muñja at the Paramāra court, it served as a classic textbook of Sanskrit dramaturgy.
SA_GK18_dhandasu.attribution: Composed by Dhanañjaya, son of Viṣṇu, active at the Paramāra court of King Muñja of Dhārā, as attested in the concluding kārikā (4.80: muñjamahīśagoṣṭhīvaidagdhyabhājā).
SA_GK18_dhandasu.edition: Fitz-Edward Hall (ed.), The Daśa-rūpa, or Hindu canons of dramaturgy, by Dhanañjaya; with the exposition of Dhanika, the Avaloka. Calcutta: Baptist Mission Press 1865 (Bibliotheca Indica, 36).
SA_GK18_dhandasu.coverage: complete — Contains all four chapters (paricchedas) of the root kārikā text, from 1.1 to 4.80, without Dhanika's Avaloka commentary.
translations: George C. O. Haas, The Daśarūpa: A Treatise on Hindu Dramaturgy by Dhanañjaya, New York: Columbia University Press, 1912 (Columbia University Indo-Iranian Series, 7). (English)

SA_GK19_aghatkvu.title: Ghaṭakarparakāvya with Ghaṭakarparavivṛti
SA_GK19_aghatkvu.author: Ghaṭakarpara, Abhinavagupta
SA_GK19_aghatkvu.summary: The Ghaṭakarparakāvya is an early lyrical messenger poem (dūtakāvya) composed in virtuosic rhyming metres with elaborate paronomasia (yamaka). In it, a woman suffering separation (virahiṇī) at the onset of the monsoon season laments her solitude and appeals to rain clouds to convey a message to her absent husband. This e-text provides the text of the poem along with the Ghaṭakarparavivṛti (also styled Ghaṭakarparakulakavivṛti), a learned commentary by the Kashmiri aesthetician Abhinavagupta (fl. c. 1000 CE), who explicates its lexical and rhetorical intricacies and interprets the stanzas as an integrated poetic composition (kulaka).
SA_GK19_aghatkvu.attribution: Abhinavagupta explicitly cites an oral tradition attributing the poem to Kālidāsa ('atra kartā mahākaviḥ kālidāsa iti anuśrutam asmābhiḥ'). The commentary (Ghaṭakarparavivṛti) is by Abhinavagupta.
SA_GK19_aghatkvu.edition: Bernard Parlier (ed.), La Ghaṭakarparavivṛti d'Abhinavagupta, Paris: Institut de civilisation indienne, 1975 (Publications de l'Institut de civilisation indienne, fasc. 39).
SA_GK19_aghatkvu.coverage: complete — Text of the poem along with Abhinavagupta's commentary up to stanza 21, concluding verses, and colophon.
translations: B. Parlier, La Ghaṭakarparavivṛti d'Abhinavagupta, Paris: Institut de civilisation indienne, 1975. (French)

SA_GK19_akadambu.title: Kādambarīkathāsāra
SA_GK19_akadambu.author: Abhinanda
SA_GK19_akadambu.summary: The Kādambarīkathāsāra is an eight-canto metrical epitome of Bāṇabhaṭṭa's celebrated prose romance Kādambarī, composed in Kashmir by Abhinanda, son of the Nyāya logician Jayanta Bhaṭṭa. It compresses Bāṇa's intricate, multilayered narrative of reborn lovers (Candrāpīḍa, Puṇḍarīka, Kādambarī, and Mahāśvetā) into accessible verse, omitting the extensive descriptive prose digressions of the original. The autobiographical prologue in canto 1 preserves valuable historical evidence for the author's family genealogy, recording their migration from Gauḍa to Dārvābhisāra and Kashmir, and noting that his ancestor Śaktisvāmin served as a minister under the Kārkoṭa ruler Lalitāditya Muktāpīḍa.
SA_GK19_akadambu.attribution: Abhinanda explicitly identifies himself as the son of Jayanta Bhaṭṭa (the celebrated Kashmiri Nyāya philosopher, author of the Nyāyamañjarī) in the introductory verses (1.2) and in the canto colophons. He is distinct from his contemporary Gauḍa Abhinanda (son of Śatānanda), the author of the epic Rāmacarita.
SA_GK19_akadambu.edition: The Kādambarīkathāsāra of Abhinanda, edited by Pandit Durgāprasāda and Kāśīnātha Pāṇḍuraṅga Paraba, Kāvyamālā, Bombay: Nirṇaya Sāgara Press, 1888.
SA_GK19_akadambu.coverage: complete — Complete in 8 cantos (sargas 1–8), ending with verse 8.99 and the final work colophon.

SA_GK19_amaru_u.title: Amaruśataka
SA_GK19_amaru_u.author: Amaru
SA_GK19_amaru_u.summary: The Amaruśataka is an anthology of approximately one hundred independent single-stanza verses (muktaka) in classical meters devoted to erotic love (śṛṅgāra). Each stanza presents a self-contained vignette illustrating psychological and emotional dynamics between lovers—including youthful modesty, lovers' quarrels and wounded pride (māna), separation (vipralambha), and reconciliation.
SA_GK19_amaru_u.attribution: The anthology is traditionally attributed to the poet Amaru (or Amaruka).
SA_GK19_amaru_u.edition: Kāvya-saṅgraha, ed. Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara; compared with the Motilal Banarsidass edition (1983) containing the commentary of Arjunavarmadeva.
SA_GK19_amaru_u.coverage: complete — Contains 112 stanzas matching the recension in Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara's Kāvyasaṅgraha (with concordance numbers to the 102 stanzas of Arjunavarmadeva's recension).
translations: Bailey, Greg (trans.). Love Lyrics: Amaruśataka, Bhartṛhari's Śatakatraya, and Bilhaṇa's Caurapañcāśikā. Clay Sanskrit Library. New York: New York University Press / JJC Foundation, 2005. (English)

SA_GK19_anvallcu.title: Vallālacarita
SA_GK19_anvallcu.author: Ānandabhaṭṭa
SA_GK19_anvallcu.summary: The Vallālacarita is a Sanskrit work recounting the life, lineage, and reign of King Vallālasena of the Sena dynasty, dealing with the origin, divisions, and gotras of Brahmins and caste groups.
SA_GK19_anvallcu.edition: Haraprasāda Śāstrī (ed.), Vallāla Caritam, Calcutta: Asiatic Society, 1904 (Bibliotheca Indica, 164).
SA_GK19_anvallcu.coverage: complete — Complete text of Ānandabhaṭṭa's Vallālacarita matching Haraprasāda Śāstrī's 1904 Bibliotheca Indica edition.

SA_GK19_appvairu.title: Vairāgyaśataka
SA_GK19_appvairu.author: Appayadīkṣita
SA_GK19_appvairu.summary: The Vairāgyaśataka ('Century of Verses on Renunciation') by Appayadīkṣita is a didactic and devotional Sanskrit work consisting of 101 verses predominantly composed in the āryā metre. Following the classical gnomic tradition exemplified by Bhartṛhari, it reflects upon the vanity of worldly pursuits, the transient nature of wealth, youth, and bodily existence, and the pitfalls of sensual attachment. The poem culminates in praising the attainment of inner peace (śānti) and final spiritual liberation through devotion to Śiva at the holy sanctuary of Avimukta (Vārāṇasī).
SA_GK19_appvairu.attribution: Attributed to Appayadīkṣita in the text colophon and sources.
SA_GK19_appvairu.edition: Pdt. Durgaprasad and Kasinath Pandurang Parab, Kavyamala [old, cumulative series], vol. 1, 1886 (3rd ed., 1929), pp. 91-99.
SA_GK19_appvairu.coverage: complete — Complete text of 101 verses (numbered AppVs_1–AppVs_101) with closing colophon 'iti śrīmadappayadīkṣitaviracitaṃ vairāgyaśatakaṃ saṃpūrṇam'.

SA_GK19_asvbuc2u.author: Aśvaghoṣa
SA_GK19_asvbuc2u.summary: The Buddhacarita is a Sanskrit kāvya poem composed by Aśvaghoṣa narrating the life of the Buddha.

SA_GK19_asvsau2u.title: Saundarananda
SA_GK19_asvsau2u.author: Aśvaghoṣa
SA_GK19_asvsau2u.summary: The Saundarananda ('Handsome Nanda') by Aśvaghoṣa is one of the earliest extant Sanskrit mahākāvya court epics, preserved complete in eighteen cantos. It dramatizes the conversion of the Buddha's handsome half-brother Nanda, who is deeply attached to his sensual love for his consort Sundarī. Through skilful pedagogy, meditation instruction, and visions of heavenly nymphs juxtaposed with the perils of cyclic existence, the Buddha leads Nanda step by step to spiritual maturity and arhatship. In the closing stanzas (18.63–64), Aśvaghoṣa articulates a seminal defense of Buddhist kāvya, explaining that ornate poetry serves merely as a sweet coating to administer the bitter medicine of liberation (mokṣa).
SA_GK19_asvsau2u.attribution: Ascribed to the Buddhist poet and philosopher Aśvaghoṣa.
SA_GK19_asvsau2u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 18 cantos (sargas 1–18, verses 1.1 to 18.64).
translations: E. H. Johnston, The Saundarananda, or Nanda the Fair, London, 1932 (reprinted Delhi, 1975). (English)
Linda Covill, Handsome Nanda, Clay Sanskrit Library, 2007. (English)

SA_GK19_bahcar2u.title: Harṣacarita (chapter 2)
SA_GK19_bahcar2u.author: Bāṇa
SA_GK19_bahcar2u.summary: The second ucchvāsa of Bāṇabhaṭṭa's Harṣacarita, titled 'Rājadarśana', opens with a description of the poet's life among his scholarly kinsmen at his ancestral seat of Prītīkūṭa on the banks of the Śoṇa river. The arrival of the messenger Mekhalaka brings an invitation from Kṛṣṇa, brother of Emperor Harṣavardhana, urging the poet to seek an audience at the imperial court. The chapter details Bāṇa's journey to the royal camp (kaṭaka) near the Ajiravatī, the magnificent scene of the imperial court, and his tense first meeting with Harṣa, who initially receives him coldly as a youth of reckless ways before quickly taking him into deep affection and royal favor.
SA_GK19_bahcar2u.coverage: partial — Ucchvāsa 2 only, complete from the heading and opening verses (2.1–2.2) to the chapter colophon 'iti śrīmahākavibāṇabhaṭṭakṛte harṣañcarite rājadarśanaṃ nāma dvitīya ucchvāsaḥ'.

SA_GK19_bahcar3u.title: Harṣacarita (chapter 3)
SA_GK19_bahcar3u.author: Bāṇa
SA_GK19_bahcar3u.summary: The third ucchvāsa of Bāṇa's Harṣacarita bridges the autobiographical opening of the work with the imperial biography of Emperor Harṣa. Having returned from Harṣa's royal camp to his ancestral home of Prītikūṭa on the Śoṇa river, Bāṇa is requested by his kinsmen to recount the deeds of the emperor. In response, he initiates the dynastic history of the Vardhana rulers with a vivid depiction of the realm of Śrīkaṇṭha and its founding monarch Puṣyabhūti (Puṣpabhūti), narrating the king's Śaiva devotion and his partnership with the South Indian ascetic Bhairavācārya during a nocturnal tantric ritual that wins the favor of the goddess Lakṣmī.
SA_GK19_bahcar3u.coverage: partial — Ucchvāsa 3 only, from the heading and opening verses (3.1–3.2) to the chapter colophon 'iti mahākaviśrībāṇabhaṭṭakṛte harṣacarite rājadarśanaṃ nāma dṛtīya [sic] ucchvāsaḥ'.
translations: E. B. Cowell and F. W. Thomas (trans.), The Harṣacarita of Bāṇa, Oriental Translation Fund, New Series 2, London. (English)

SA_GK19_bahcar4u.title: Harṣacarita (chapter 4)
SA_GK19_bahcar4u.author: Bāṇa
SA_GK19_bahcar4u.summary: The fourth ucchvāsa (chapter), titled Cakravartijanmavarṇana ('Description of the Birth of the Sovereign'), of Bāṇabhaṭṭa's prose biography Harṣacarita. It recounts the royal lineage of Prabhākaravardhana of Sthāṇvīśvara and Queen Yaśomatī, the miraculous dreams announcing their offspring, the births of Rājyavardhana, Harṣavardhana, and princess Rājyaśrī, and concludes with Rājyaśrī's wedding to the Maukhari prince Grahavarman of Kanauj.
SA_GK19_bahcar4u.coverage: partial — Ucchvāsa 4 only, complete from the heading and opening verses (4.1–4.2) to the chapter colophon 'iti śrīmahākavibāṇamaṭṭakṛtau harṣacarite cakravartijanmavarṇanaṃ nāma caturtha ucchvāsaḥ'.

SA_GK19_bahcar5_pu.title: Harṣacarita (chapter 5)
SA_GK19_bahcar5_pu.author: Bāṇa
SA_GK19_bahcar5_pu.summary: Ucchvāsa 5 (Mahārājamaraṇavarṇana) of Bāṇabhaṭṭa's Harṣacarita. While crown prince Rājyavardhana is away on a military expedition against the Hūṇas in the north, Prince Harṣa receives sudden news from the courier Kuraṅgaka that King Prabhākaravardhana has fallen gravely ill. Harṣa rushes back to the capital Sthāṇvīśvara, finds the court plunged in despair, and witnesses Queen Yaśomatī commit self-immolation (satī) on the banks of the Sarasvatī before the king passes away. Following the king's death, the chapter concludes with Harṣa and the palace in profound mourning as they anxiously await Rājyavardhana's return.
SA_GK19_bahcar5_pu.edition: Bāṇabhaṭṭa's Harṣacarita with Śaṅkara's commentary Saṅketa, ed. A. A. Führer, Bombay Sanskrit and Prakrit Series LXVI, Bombay: Government Central Press, 1909.
SA_GK19_bahcar5_pu.coverage: partial — Contains chapter 5 (ucchvāsa 5, titled Mahārājamaraṇavarṇana) only, from the opening two verses (5.1–5.2) to the closing chapter colophon.
translations: Cowell, E. B. and F. W. Thomas, The Harṣacarita of Bāṇa, Oriental Translation Fund, New Series 2, London, 1897. (English)

SA_GK19_bahcar6u.title: Harṣacarita (chapter 6)
SA_GK19_bahcar6u.author: Bāṇa
SA_GK19_bahcar6u.summary: The sixth ucchvāsa of Bāṇabhaṭṭa's Harṣacarita depicts the critical turning point in the young Harṣa's life following the death of his father, Prabhākaravardhana. His elder brother Rājyavardhana returns wounded from the Hūṇa campaign, intending to renounce kingship, but is immediately confronted with news that their brother-in-law Grahavarman of Kanauj has been slain by the Mālava king and their sister Rājyaśrī imprisoned. After Rājyavardhana defeats Mālava, he is treacherously assassinated by the Gauḍa ruler (Śaśāṅka). Urged by his commander-in-chief Siṃhanāda, Harṣa takes a solemn vow (rājapratijñā) to destroy the treacherous enemies of his house and announces his campaign for the conquest of the earth.
SA_GK19_bahcar6u.coverage: partial — Ucchvāsa 6 only, from the heading and opening verses (6.1–6.2) to the chapter colophon 'iti śrībāṇamaṭṭakṛtau harṣacarite rājapratijñāvarṇanaṃ nāma ṣaṣṭha ucchvāsaḥ'.

SA_GK19_bahcar7u.title: Harṣacarita (chapter 7)
SA_GK19_bahcar7u.author: Bāṇa
SA_GK19_bahcar7u.summary: The seventh chapter (ucchvāsa), titled Chatralabdhi, of Bāṇabhaṭṭa's Harṣacarita. It depicts Emperor Harṣavardhana embarking upon his military expedition (daṇḍayātrā), the diplomatic alliance established when Haṃsavega arrives from King Bhāskaravarman bearing diplomatic gifts—notably the umbrella Abhoga—and Harṣa receiving word that his sister Rājyaśrī has escaped from imprisonment and taken refuge in the Vindhya forests.
SA_GK19_bahcar7u.coverage: partial — Ucchvāsa 7 only, from the heading and opening verses (7.1–7.2) to the chapter colophon 'iti śrīmahākavibāṇabhaṭṭakṛtau harṣacarite chatralabdhirnāma saptama ucchvāsa'.
translations: E. B. Cowell and F. W. Thomas (trans.), The Harṣacarita of Bāṇa, Oriental Translation Fund, New Series 2, London. (English)

SA_GK19_bahcar8u.title: Harṣacarita (chapter 8)
SA_GK19_bahcar8u.author: Bāṇa
SA_GK19_bahcar8u.summary: The eighth ucchvāsa (chapter) of Bāṇabhaṭṭa's prose work Harṣacarita. It recounts Harṣa's expedition into the Vindhya forest, his encounter with the Śabara youth Nirghāta, his visit to the woodland hermitage of the Buddhist ascetic Divākaramitra, and his dramatic rescue of his widowed sister Rājyaśrī as she prepares to immolate herself on a funeral pyre. The chapter concludes with Harṣa convincing her to abandon suicide and promising to adopt the ochre robes with her once his imperial vow is fulfilled, ending the biography at nightfall without a formal conclusion.
SA_GK19_bahcar8u.attribution: Attributed to Bāṇabhaṭṭa in the colophon (iti śrīmahākavibāṇabhaṭṭakṛtau harṣacarite 'ṣṭama ucchvāsaḥ).
SA_GK19_bahcar8u.coverage: partial — Ucchvāsa (chapter) 8 only; contains the text of the eighth chapter without commentary.

SA_GK19_bahcarpu.title: Bāṇapraśasti
SA_GK19_bahcarpu.summary: An appendix (pariśiṣṭa) of 18 Sanskrit stanzas in praise of Bāṇabhaṭṭa, appended to a printed Harṣacarita and keyed by the Sansknet project. The stanzas, partly labelled with their sources (e.g. Soḍḍhala's Udayasundarīkathā, Padmagupta's Navasāhasāṅkacarita, Trivikrama, Govardhana, Dhanapāla), praise Bāṇa's prose, his śleṣa, and his Kādambarī and Harṣacarita. It is a brief testimony to Bāṇa's reception in later Sanskrit literature.
SA_GK19_bahcarpu.attribution: Editorial appendix of 18 stanzas praising Bāṇa, gathered from later works. In the e-text the source labels follow the stanzas: (śrīcandradevasya) after v. 1, (ruyyakakṛtavyaktivivekavyākhyāne) after v. 2, (udayasundaryāṃ soḍhvalasya) after v. 3, (viśveśvarasya) after v. 4, (trivikramasya) after v. 6, (govardhanasya) after v. 7, (navasāhasāṅke) after v. 10, (vīranārāyaṇacarite) after v. 11, (raghunāthacarite) after v. 15, (dhanapālasya) after v. 17; several stanzas are unlabeled. The compiler of the appendix is not named.
SA_GK19_bahcarpu.coverage: complete — All 18 numbered stanzas under the heading "pariśiṣṭam / bāṇa-praśastayaḥ" (GRETIL bahcarpu.htm), presumably the appendix of the printed edition used by Sansknet.

SA_GK19_bankad1u.title: Kādambarī (Pūrvabhāga, varṇanas 84–122)
SA_GK19_bankad1u.author: Bāṇabhaṭṭa
SA_GK19_bankad1u.summary: The Kādambarī is a celebrated Sanskrit prose romance composed in the 7th century CE by Bāṇabhaṭṭa and finished by his son Bhūṣaṇabhaṭṭa. Renowned for its intricate sentence structure, ornate imagery, and complex nested frame stories spanning successive rebirths, it tells the intertwined tales of Prince Candrāpīḍa and Princess Kādambarī alongside Puṇḍarīka and Mahāśvetā. This e-text preserves the final section of Bāṇabhaṭṭa's Pūrvabhāga (varṇanas 84–122), describing Candrāpīḍa's journey to Mount Hemakūṭa with Mahāśvetā, his first meeting and deepening love with Kādambarī, and his eventual journey back to Ujjayinī.
SA_GK19_bankad1u.attribution: The Kādambarī was composed in the 7th century CE by Bāṇabhaṭṭa. His son Bhūṣaṇabhaṭṭa (referred to in some sources as Pulinda) wrote the second part. This e-text covers solely varṇanas 84–122 of Bāṇabhaṭṭa's Pūrvabhāga.
SA_GK19_bankad1u.edition: Kādambarī (Pūrvabhāga) of Bāṇa, ed. Srikrsnamohana Takkura, Varanasi: Caukhamba, 1960 (Kasi Sanskrit Series, 151), pp. 524–670.
SA_GK19_bankad1u.coverage: partial — Contains only the final portion of the Pūrvabhāga (varṇanas 84–122, spanning pp. 524–670 of Śrīkṛṣṇamohana Ṭhākura's edition). The initial 83 varṇanas and the entire Uttarabhāga are absent.
translations: Ridding, C. M. (tr.). The Kādambarī of Bāṇa. 1896. (English)
Layne, Gwendolyn (tr.). Kādambarī: A Classical Sanskrit Story of Magical Transformations. New York: Garland Publishing, 1991. (English)

SA_GK19_bhago.title: Stotrasaṅgraha with Rāmcaritmānas (excerpts)
SA_GK19_bhago.author: Śaṅkara, Caitanya, Tulsīdās
SA_GK19_bhago.summary: A mixed devotional file wrongly catalogued as Bhaj-Govindam. It opens with six short Sanskrit hymns: the Advaita stotras Nirvāṇaṣaṭka, Sādhanapañcaka, Dakṣiṇāmūrtistotra, Dhanyāṣṭaka and Hastāmalakastotra, and Caitanya's Śikṣāṣṭaka. Most of the file (about 1,900 of 2,161 segments) consists of Awadhi excerpts from Tulsīdās's Rāmcaritmānas in IAST.
SA_GK19_bhago.attribution: The five Advaita hymns are traditionally ascribed to Śaṅkara (the Hastāmalakastotra to his pupil Hastāmalaka); these ascriptions are traditional, not established. The Śikṣāṣṭaka is ascribed to Caitanya. The bulk of the file is Tulsīdās's Awadhi Rāmcaritmānas.
SA_GK19_bhago.coverage: excerpt — Six Sanskrit hymns (the first stanza of four of them reduced to its last pāda, an extraction artefact) followed by long Rāmcaritmānas excerpts (Araṇyakāṇḍa opening, then Bālakāṇḍa portions running back to the Bālakāṇḍa maṅgalācaraṇa and soraṭhās at the very end). No Bhajagovinda.

SA_GK19_bhakirpu.title: Kirātārjunīya
SA_GK19_bhakirpu.author: Bhāravi
SA_GK19_bhakirpu.summary: The Kirātārjunīya is an 18-canto mahākāvya composed by the poet Bhāravi, elaborating an episode from the Vanaparvan of the Mahābhārata. The epic narrates Arjuna's journey to Mount Indrakīla in the Himalayas to perform penance and procure divine weapons for the Pāṇḍavas, his duel and wrestling combat with Śiva disguised as a mountain hunter (kirāta) over a slain boar, and Śiva's revelation and bestowal of the Pāśupata weapon. Celebrated in classical Sanskrit literary theory for gravity of meaning (arthagaurava), political discourse (nīti), and virtuoso poetic ornamentation (especially the citrakāvya constraints of canto 15), it constitutes one of the traditional 'five great court epics' (pañcamahākāvya).
SA_GK19_bhakirpu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 18 cantos (BhKir_1.1–18.48; 2080 segments representing the full 1030+ verses of the poem).
translations: Carl Cappeller, Bhāravi's Poem Kirātārjunīya or Arjuna's Combat with the Kirāta: Translated from the original Sanskrit into German and explained. Harvard Oriental Series 15. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1912. (German)
Indira Viswanathan Peterson, Arjuna and the Hunter. Murty Classical Library of India 8. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 2016. (English)

SA_GK19_bhicau.title: Bhīṣmacarita
SA_GK19_bhicau.author: Harinārāyaṇa Dīkṣita
SA_GK19_bhicau.summary: A work titled Bhiṣma-Cāritra attributed to Dr. Hari Narayan Dikshit in the source headers. No e-text is present.
SA_GK19_bhicau.attribution: Attributed to Dr. Hari Narayan Dikshit in the source headers.

SA_GK19_bicauppu.title: Caurapañcāśikā
SA_GK19_bicauppu.author: Bilhaṇa
SA_GK19_bicauppu.summary: The Caurapañcāśikā is a famous classical Sanskrit lyrical sequence of fifty stanzas in the Vasantatilakā meter, each verse opening with the evocative anaphora 'adyāpi' ('even now'). Framed by tradition as the death-row lament of a clandestine lover awaiting execution after an illicit affair with a princess, each stanza presents a self-contained, vividly sensory recollection of the beloved's physical charms and their shared intimacy. Traditionally attributed to the 11th-century Kashmiri poet Bilhaṇa, the poem became one of the most celebrated works of classical Indian secular erotics (śṛṅgārakāvya), inspiring miniature painting cycles and vernacular adaptations throughout South Asia.
SA_GK19_bicauppu.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the 11th-century Kashmiri poet Bilhaṇa. The poem circulated in distinct recensions embedded in frame narratives such as the Vidyāsundara story.
SA_GK19_bicauppu.edition: S. N. Tadpatrikar (ed. & tr.), Caurapañcāśikā: An Indian Love Lament of Bilhaṇa Kavi, Poona: Oriental Book Agency, 1966 (Poona Oriental Series).
SA_GK19_bicauppu.coverage: complete — Complete 50 stanzas (numbered BiCaup_1 to BiCaup_50) corresponding to Tadpatrikar's edition.
translations: S. N. Tadpatrikar, Caurapañcāśikā: An Indian Love Lament of Bilhaṇa Kavi, POS 86. (English)

SA_GK19_damkuttu.title: Kuṭṭanīmata
SA_GK19_damkuttu.author: Dāmodaragupta
SA_GK19_damkuttu.summary: The Kuṭṭanīmata (also known as Śambhalīmata) is a satirical and didactic verse novel comprising 1,059 stanzas mostly in the āryā metre, composed by Dāmodaragupta, court poet to Jayāpīḍa of Kashmir. Framed as instruction imparted in Vārāṇasī by the experienced madam Vikarālā to the young courtesan Mālatī on extracting wealth from suitors, the text incorporates several embedded narrative tales, including an account of a dramatic staging of Harṣa's Ratnāvalī.
SA_GK19_damkuttu.attribution: Attributed to Dāmodaragupta internally in verse 2 (kuṭṭanyā matametaddāmodaraguptaviracitaṃ śṛṇuta).
SA_GK19_damkuttu.edition: Dāmodaraguptaviracitaṃ Kuṭṭanīmatam: The Bawd's Counsel, Being an eighth-century verse novel in Sanskrit by Dāmodaragupta, Newly edited and translated into English by Csaba Dezso & Dominic Goodall, Groningen: Egbert Forsten, 2012. ISBN 978 90 6980 158 2.
SA_GK19_damkuttu.coverage: complete — Complete text of 1,059 verses, including verses 1056–1059 preserved in two Nepalese manuscripts and in two editions.
translations: Csaba Dezső and Dominic Goodall, Dāmodaraguptaviracitaṃ Kuṭṭanīmatam: The Bawd's Counsel, Groningen Oriental Studies 23, Groningen: Egbert Forsten, 2012. (English)
Johann Jakob Meyer, Dāmodaragupta's Kuṭṭanīmata, Altindische Schelmenbücher 2, Leipzig: Lotus-Verlag, 1903. (German)

SA_GK19_danddk1u.title: Daśakumāracarita (ucchvāsas 3, 5, 6)
SA_GK19_danddk1u.author: Daṇḍin
SA_GK19_danddk1u.summary: The Daśakumāracarita is a celebrated Sanskrit prose romance (gadyakāvya) composed by Daṇḍin. Within a framing story of ten companion princes separated during an expedition and later reunited, each prince recounts his worldly adventures through the royal courts, forests, gambling dens, and underworlds of classical India. This e-text comprises three ucchvāsas: Ucchvāsa 3 (Upahāravarman's exploits regaining his ancestral realm of Mithilā through disguise, burglary, and court intrigue), Ucchvāsa 5 (Pramati's stratagems and winning of the princess Navamālikā in Ujjayinī), and Ucchvāsa 6 (Mitragupta's maritime adventures, capture by Yavanas, and four nested tales illustrating proper conduct).
SA_GK19_danddk1u.attribution: The three chapters preserved in this file (ucchvāsas 3, 5, and 6) are attributed to Daṇḍin.
SA_GK19_danddk1u.coverage: partial — Contains ucchvāsa 3 (Upahāravarma-carita), ucchvāsa 5 (Pramati-carita), and ucchvāsa 6 (Mitragupta-carita) of the Daśakumāracarita.
translations: Isabelle Onians (transl.), What Ten Young Men Did, Clay Sanskrit Library, New York: New York University Press / JJC Foundation, 2005. (English)

SA_GK19_dhoypavu.title: Pavanadūta
SA_GK19_dhoypavu.author: Dhoyī
SA_GK19_dhoypavu.summary: The Pavanadūta ('Wind Messenger') by Dhoyī is a 12th-century messenger poem composed in 104 verses. The poem describes Kuvalayavatī, a Gandharva maiden on Mount Malaya in South India, who falls in love with King Lakṣmaṇasena during his conquest (bhuvanavijaya) and sends the southern wind (malayapavana) to carry her message north to his capital (Vijayapura).
SA_GK19_dhoypavu.attribution: Composed by Dhoyī (also styled Dhoyī Kavirāja or Dhoyīka), court poet of Lakṣmaṇasena of Bengal (12th century).
SA_GK19_dhoypavu.edition: Chintaharan Chakravarti (ed.): Pavanadutam of Dhoyi. Edited with Critical and Historical Introduction, Sanskrit Notes, Variants etc. etc. Calcutta: Sanskrit Sahitya Parishat 1926. Sanskrit Sahitya Parishat Series No. 13.
SA_GK19_dhoypavu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 104 stanzas, concluding with the colophon: 'śrīdhoyīkavirājaviracitam+pavanadūtākhyam+kāvyam+samāptam/'.
translations: James Mallinson, Messenger Poems (Meghadūta, Pavanadūta & Haṃsadūta), Clay Sanskrit Library, 2006. (English)

SA_GK19_gakou.title: Gāhākosa
SA_GK19_gakou.author: Hāla
SA_GK19_gakou.summary: Catalog stub for the Gāhākosa (Sanskrit Gāthāsaptaśatī), the anthology of about 700 Māhārāṣṭrī Prakrit gāthās, mostly in the āryā metre, traditionally compiled by the Sātavāhana king Hāla. The single-stanza poems deal mostly with love and village life, often in a woman's voice, and the collection was the model for Govardhana's Sanskrit Āryāsaptaśatī. The e-text file is empty.
SA_GK19_gakou.coverage: unclear — No e-text present (0 segment files, 0 segments, 0 characters); nothing in git history for segments/SA_GK19_gakou*. Coverage cannot be assessed.

SA_GK19_ghatgu_u.title: Gūḍhārthadīpikā
SA_GK19_ghatgu_u.author: Kuśalamiśra
SA_GK19_ghatgu_u.summary: The Gūḍhārthadīpikā (entitled Gūḍhadīpikā by its author) is a Sanskrit commentary by Kuśalamiśra on the Ghaṭakharparakāvya (traditionally attributed to Kālidāsa). The text was composed in Saṃvat 1748. This e-text represents Walter Slaje's critical edition based on Ms. Cod. Sanskrit 23 in the Austrian National Library in Vienna.
SA_GK19_ghatgu_u.attribution: In verse 2, verse 5, and the concluding colophon, the commentary is designated as Gūḍhadīpikā. Kuśala identifies himself as the great-grandson of Kṣemaṅkara and son of Bālakṛṣṇa. Concluding verse 5 contains a chronogram: 'nāgavedācalābje [1748] tu cābde 'bhūd Gūḍhadīpikā'.
SA_GK19_ghatgu_u.edition: Walter Slaje, Śāradā: deskriptiv-synchrone Schriftkunde zur Bearbeitung kaschmirischer Sanskrit-Manuskripte, Reinbek: Verlag für Orientalistische Fachpublikationen, 1993.
SA_GK19_ghatgu_u.coverage: complete — Complete commentary on Ghaṭakharparakāvya, concluding verses by Kuśalamiśra, and scribal colophon of Rājānaka Ānandarāma dated Saṃvat 72.

SA_GK19_govass_u.title: Āryāsaptaśatī (lacking vv. 238–245, 480–489, 514–517, 531)
SA_GK19_govass_u.author: Govardhana
SA_GK19_govass_u.summary: The Āryāsaptaśatī of Govardhana is a collection of about 700 single stanzas in the āryā metre, mostly erotic and relying on suggestion. It is arranged in alphabetical sections (vrajyās) and imitates Hāla's Prakrit Sattasaī in Sanskrit. This e-text has the root verses only, lacking 23 verses.
SA_GK19_govass_u.attribution: Govardhana (c. 12th century; styled Govardhanācārya) composed the Āryāsaptaśatī. The e-text contains his root verses alone.
