SA_GK19_gp01-11u.title: Gopālacampū (Pūrvacampū, chapters 1–11)
SA_GK19_gp01-11u.author: Jīva Gosvāmin
SA_GK19_gp01-11u.summary: The Gopālacampū is an extensive Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava literary work in mixed prose and verse (campū) composed by Jīva Gosvāmin. Narrated through the discourses of two court poets, Snigdhakaṇṭha and Madhukaṇṭha, the Pūrvacampū recounts Kṛṣṇa's pastimes in Vraja. Chapters 1–11 cover the opening invocations, Kṛṣṇa's appearance and childhood exploits, concluding with the slaying of Aghāsura and the Brahmā episode.
SA_GK19_gp01-11u.coverage: partial — Contains the first 11 chapters (pūraṇas) of the Pūrvacampū.

SA_GK19_gp12-22u.title: Gopālacampū (Pūrvacampū, chapters 12–22)
SA_GK19_gp12-22u.author: Jīva Gosvāmin
SA_GK19_gp12-22u.summary: Chapters 12 through 22 of the Pūrvacampū of Jīva Gosvāmin's monumental campū work on the life and līlā of Kṛṣṇa in Vraja. Narrated within a frame story by two youth singers, Snigdhakaṇṭha and Madhukaṇṭha, this section chronicles Kṛṣṇa's transition into his youth (kaiśora), beginning with pasturing the calves and cows (gocāraṇa), the subduing of the serpent Kāliya, the slaying of Dhenukāsura and Pralambāsura, the lifting of Govardhana Hill, the extinguishing of the forest fire, and the granting of grace to the wives of the sacrificial brāhmaṇas (yajñapatnī-prasāda). The work elaborates on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa narrative through ornate classical kāvya conventions and Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava rasa theology.
SA_GK19_gp12-22u.coverage: partial — Contains chapters (pūraṇas) 12 through 22 of the Pūrvacampū. Verses 1.16.12, 1.21.27, 1.21.34, and 1.22.45 are omitted in this e-text.

SA_GK19_gp23-33u.title: Gopālacampū (Pūrvacampū, chapters 23–33)
SA_GK19_gp23-33u.author: Jīva Gosvāmin
SA_GK19_gp23-33u.summary: The Gopālacampū is an extensive campū composed by Jīva Gosvāmin. The work provides an elaborate poetic retelling of Kṛṣṇa's līlā based on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, framed as a narrative recited by the bards Madhukaṇṭha and Snigdhakaṇṭha before Kṛṣṇa and his courtiers. This concluding section of the Pūrvacampū (chapters 23–33) completes the narration of Kṛṣṇa's youth in Vraja (kaiśora-vilāsa), recounting the rāsa-līlā, the slaying of Ariṣṭa, Vyoma, and Keśin, the arrival of Akrūra, and the sorrowful departure of Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma for Mathurā.
SA_GK19_gp23-33u.attribution: Jīva Gosvāmin names himself in the closing verse of the Pūrvacampū (1.33.2: 'vilikhitā gopāla-campūr iyam / vṛndā-kānanam āśritena laghunā jīvena kenāpi...').
SA_GK19_gp23-33u.coverage: partial — Contains chapters (pūraṇas) 23 to 33 of the Pūrvacampū, concluding the first major part of the work (kaiśora-vilāsaḥ sampūrṇaḥ). GRETIL notes three missing verses in this file: 1.31.50, 1.33.45, and 1.33.96.

SA_GK19_gu01-03u.title: Gopālacampū (Uttaracampū, chapters 1–3)
SA_GK19_gu01-03u.author: Jīva Gosvāmin
SA_GK19_gu01-03u.summary: The Gopālacampū by Jīva Gosvāmin is an extensive campū kāvya (mixed prose and verse) presenting the narrative of Kṛṣṇa's pastimes framed through Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava rasa theology. The entire work is divided into the Pūrvacampū (33 pūraṇas) and the Uttaracampū (37 pūraṇas), portrayed as recitations by the bards Snigdhakaṇṭha and Madhukaṇṭha before Kṛṣṇa and his entourage in Goloka. This file comprises the first three pūraṇas of the Uttaracampū, covering the introductory narration, the prelude to Akrūra's visit to Vraja, and Kṛṣṇa's impending journey to Mathurā (Māthurapurasthānaprasthāna).
SA_GK19_gu01-03u.coverage: partial — Contains pūraṇas (chapters) 1–3 of the Uttaracampū.

SA_GK19_gu05-06u.title: Gopālacampū (Uttaracampū, chapters 5–6)
SA_GK19_gu05-06u.author: Jīva Gosvāmin
SA_GK19_gu05-06u.summary: The Gopālacampū of Jīva Gosvāmin is a campū work detailing pastimes of Kṛṣṇa. This file contains pūraṇas 5 and 6 of the Uttaracampū, recounting the slaying of Kaṃsa (Kaṃsavadhakathā) and Kṛṣṇa bidding farewell to Nanda Mahārāja and the Vraja cowherds (Vrajapativisarjanakaṣṭa).
SA_GK19_gu05-06u.coverage: partial — Contains pūraṇas (chapters) 5 and 6 of the Uttaracampū (the second part of Gopālacampū). Chapter 5 narrates the slaying of Kaṃsa (Kaṃsavadhakathā), and chapter 6 recounts Kṛṣṇa's sorrowful farewell to Nanda and the cowherds returning to Vraja (Vrajapativisarjanakaṣṭa).

SA_GK19_gu29___u.title: Gopālacampū (Uttaracampū, chapter 29)
SA_GK19_gu29___u.author: Jīva Gosvāmin
SA_GK19_gu29___u.summary: Chapter 29 of the Uttaracampū (entitled 'Bhāvikathāpramāṇaprathana') constitutes a theological narrative interlude within Jīva Gosvāmin's Gopālacampū. Set during Kṛṣṇa's absence from Vraja after departing for Mathurā and Dvārakā, the chapter depicts a dialogue between Vṛndā and Pūrṇimā (representing Kṛṣṇa's līlā-śakti and yogamāyā). Consulting an esoteric book given in a dream, they examine scriptural passages from the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, Padma Purāṇa (Uttarakhaṇḍa), Mahābhārata, and Harivaṃśa to harmonize apparent scriptural contradictions and establish the theological certainty of Kṛṣṇa's eternal presence in Goloka-Vṛndāvana and his eventual reunion with his Vraja devotees.
SA_GK19_gu29___u.coverage: partial — Contains chapter 29 (ekonatriṃśaṃ pūraṇam, titled 'Bhāvi-kathā-pramāṇa-prathanam') of the Uttaracampū only, complete for this single chapter (concluding with the colophon in section 127).

SA_GK19_jagpranu.title: Prāṇābharaṇa with Ṭippaṇī
SA_GK19_jagpranu.author: Jagannātha Paṇḍitarāja
SA_GK19_jagpranu.summary: A court panegyric (praśasti/kāvya) in 53 verses composed by Jagannātha Paṇḍitarāja in praise of the king of Kamatā/Kāmarūpa (Prāṇanārāyaṇa), accompanied by the author's own analytical prose gloss (ṭippaṇī). Each verse blends royal encomium with rhetorical patterning, and the commentary identifies and explains poetic figures (alaṃkāra) and suggestion (dhvani).
SA_GK19_jagpranu.attribution: Both the 53 verses of the panegyric and the accompanying analytical prose commentary identifying rhetorical figures (alaṃkāra) and suggestion (dhvani) are by Jagannātha Paṇḍitarāja.
SA_GK19_jagpranu.edition: Pdt. Durgaprasad and Kasinath Pandurang Parab, Kavyamala [old, cumulative series], vol. 1, 1886 (3rd ed., 1929), pp. 79-90.
SA_GK19_jagpranu.coverage: complete — Contains all 53 verses and the complete prose auto-commentary through to the terminal colophon.

SA_GK19_jagsudhu.title: Sudhālaharī
SA_GK19_jagsudhu.author: Jagannātha Paṇḍitarāja
SA_GK19_jagsudhu.summary: The Sudhālaharī ('Wave of Nectar') is a devotional hymn (stotra) of 30 verses composed by the poet-critic Jagannātha Paṇḍitarāja in praise of the Sun god (Sūrya). Part of Jagannātha's group of laharī poems, it vividly describes the rising sun, the dispersion of darkness, and the awakening of the cosmos, while praying for illumination and purification.
SA_GK19_jagsudhu.attribution: Colophons in the text confirm authorship by Paṇḍitarāja Jagannātha ('iti paṇḍitarājaśrījagannāthaviracitā sudhālaharī samāptā').
SA_GK19_jagsudhu.edition: Kāvyamālā [old, cumulative series], vol. 1, ed. Pdt. Durgaprasad and Kasinath Pandurang Parab, 1886 (3rd ed., 1929), pp. 16–22.
SA_GK19_jagsudhu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 30 verses with introductory heading and concluding colophon.

SA_GK19_jalmugpu.title: Mugdhopadeśa
SA_GK19_jalmugpu.author: Jalhaṇa
SA_GK19_jalmugpu.summary: The Mugdhopadeśa ('Instruction of the Naive') is a 12th-century didactic and satirical Sanskrit poem in 66 verses composed by the Kashmiri poet Jalhaṇa. Belonging to the Kashmiri satirical-cautionary tradition, it warns inexperienced young men against infatuation and the deceitful, mercenary arts of courtesans (veśyās). The poem concludes with autobiographical reflections on the stages of human life, travels to various courts, and the poet's resolve to spend his old age worshipping Śiva on the banks of the Ganges.
SA_GK19_jalmugpu.attribution: Attributed to the Kashmiri poet Jalhaṇa (c. first half of the 12th century, Kashmir), explicitly named in verse 65 ('so 'yaṃ saṃprati Jalhaṇena kavinā Mudghopadeśaḥ kṛtaḥ').
SA_GK19_jalmugpu.edition: Mugdhopadeśa of Jalhaṇa, in: The Kâvyamâlâ, Part VIII, edited by Paṇḍit Durgâprasâda and Kâśînâtha Pâṇḍuraṅga Paraba, Bombay: Nirṇaya Sāgara Press, 1891, pp. 125–135.
SA_GK19_jalmugpu.coverage: complete — Complete text in 66 stanzas (numbered JMu_1–JMu_66), composed predominantly in the śārdūlavikrīḍita metre, ending with the author's signature and concluding autobiographical verses.

SA_GK19_japa.title: Jānakīpariṇaya with Bālarañjanī
SA_GK19_japa.author: Rāmabhadra Dīkṣita, Śvetāraṇya Nārāyaṇa Śarman
SA_GK19_japa.summary: Jānakīpariṇaya ('The Marriage of Sītā') is a classical seven-act Sanskrit drama (nāṭaka) composed by Rāmabhadra Dīkṣita, dramatizing the Rāmāyaṇa narrative of Rāma winning and marrying Sītā. The dramatist introduces numerous plot innovations and comedic twists involving demonic illusions, deceptive disguises, and counterfeit figures staged by the rākṣasas Vidyujjihva and Mārīca to thwart the wedding. In this e-text, the drama is accompanied throughout by Śvetāraṇya Nārāyaṇa Śarman's commentary Bālarañjanī, which explains lexical meanings, dramaturgy, and poetic meters.
SA_GK19_japa.attribution: Rāmabhadra Dīkṣita composed the seven-act drama Jānakīpariṇaya. The commentary Bālarañjanī was composed by Śvetāraṇya Nārāyaṇa Śarman.
SA_GK19_japa.coverage: complete — Text of the drama interspersed with the commentary Bālarañjanī through the seventh act.

SA_GK19_jaravau.author: Goswami Hariraiji
SA_GK19_jaravau.summary: Poem on the slaying of Jarāsandha.

SA_GK19_jaygit2u.title: Gītagovinda
SA_GK19_jaygit2u.author: Jayadeva
SA_GK19_jaygit2u.summary: The Gītagovinda of Jayadeva (composed in late 12th-century Bengal) is a celebrated lyrical kāvya celebrating the passionate love, separation (viraha), and joyful reconciliation of Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā. Comprising 12 cantos structured around 24 rhymed aṣṭapadīs framed by narrative and descriptive stanzas in classical metres, the work innovatively bridges classical Sanskrit kāvya traditions with vernacular song performance. Its synthesis of theological bhakti and refined erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) deeply influenced Gauḍīya and pan-Indian Vaiṣṇavism.
SA_GK19_jaygit2u.attribution: Composed by Jayadeva, active during the reign of the Sena king Lakṣmaṇasena (late 12th century). Verse 1.4 mentions Jayadeva alongside poets Umāpatidhara, Govardhana, Śaraṇa, and Dhoyī.
SA_GK19_jaygit2u.edition: Based on the Kavyamala ed. (Calcutta 1878), checked against several other editions: Lee Siegel (Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1990 (1978), based on Nirnaya Sagara Edition, Bombay 1949 and Kulkarni edition, Ahmedabad 1965), Haridas Das (Nabadwip: Haribol Kutir, 470 Gaurābda [= 1955]), and Bhaktivedanta Narayana (Mathura: Gaudiya Vedanta Publications, 2005).
SA_GK19_jaygit2u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 12 sargas comprising prabandhas and connecting verses in classical metres, concluding at verse 12.32 with the colophon 'iti śrī-jayadeva kṛtau śrī-śrī-gīta-govinda-mahā-kāvye suprīta-pītāmbaro nāma dvādaśa sargaḥ' followed by 'samāptam idaṃ kāvyam'.
translations: Barbara Stoler Miller, Love Song of the Dark Lord: Jayadeva's Gītagovinda, New York: Columbia University Press, 1977. (English)
Lee Siegel, Sacred and Profane Dimensions of Love in Indian Traditions as Exemplified in the Gītagovinda of Jayadeva, Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1978/1990. (English)
Giuliano Boccali, Jayadeva: Gītagovinda, Piccola Biblioteca 138, Milano: Adelphi Edizioni, 1982. (Italian)
F. Rückert, Gita-Gowinda, aus dem Sanskrit übersetzt, Göttingen. (German)

SA_GK19_jivskd_u.title: Saṅkalpakalpadruma
SA_GK19_jivskd_u.author: Jīva Gosvāmin
SA_GK19_jivskd_u.summary: The Saṅkalpakalpadruma is a Sanskrit devotional-poetic work by Jīva Gosvāmin composed as an address to his own mind (manaḥ-śikṣā). The work employs the allegory of a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma) divided into four parts: root (janmādi-līlā, the manifest narrative pastimes of Kṛṣṇa), trunk (nitya-līlā, the eternal eightfold daily pastimes or aṣṭakālīya-līlā), branches (sarvartu-līlā, seasonal pastimes across the six seasons), and fruit (phala-niṣpatti, the ultimate attainment of loving service).
SA_GK19_jivskd_u.attribution: Firmly attributed to Jīva Gosvāmin; he names himself in the opening section (v. 4: 'vṛndāraṇye jaran jīvaḥ kaścit prāha manaḥ prati').
SA_GK19_jivskd_u.coverage: complete — Complete text structured in four parts corresponding to the parts of a wish-fulfilling tree: 1. mūla (janmādi-līlā, vv. 1–251), 2. skandha (nitya-līlā, vv. 1–257), 3. śākhā (sarvartu-līlā, vv. 1–126), and 4. phala (phala-niṣpatti, vv. 1–17), followed by an 8-verse epilogue and final colophon.

SA_GK19_kalrs_pu.title: Ṛtusaṃhāra
SA_GK19_kalrs_pu.author: Kālidāsa
SA_GK19_kalrs_pu.summary: The Ṛtusaṃhāra is a descriptive poem in six cantos, traditionally ascribed to Kālidāsa. In rich sensory imagery, the poem depicts the six classical Indian seasons—summer, rains, autumn, early winter, winter, and spring—intertwining panoramic nature scenes with the erotic moods and romantic longings of lovers.
SA_GK19_kalrs_pu.coverage: complete — Complete text in six cantos (sargas 1–6) describing each of the six Indian seasons (Grīṣma, Varṣā, Śarad, Hemanta, Śiśira, and Vasanta), comprising 154 verses across the cantos: 1.1–1.28, 2.1–2.28, 3.1–3.26, 4.1–4.18, 5.1–5.16, and 6.1–6.38.
translations: R. S. Pandit (trans.), Ṛtusaṃhāra or The Pageant of the Seasons, Bombay: The National Information & Publications Ltd., 1947. (English)

SA_GK19_kmeghdpu.title: Meghadūta
SA_GK19_kmeghdpu.author: Kālidāsa
SA_GK19_kmeghdpu.summary: The Meghadūta ('Cloud Messenger') is a poem composed in mandākrāntā stanzas by Kālidāsa. An exiled yakṣa, separated from his beloved wife and pining on Mount Rāmagiri, enlists a cloud to carry a message to Alakā. The poem includes descriptions of the cloud's route and of Alakā.
SA_GK19_kmeghdpu.attribution: Attributed to Kālidāsa; attested in Tibetan canonical translation records (D4302).
SA_GK19_kmeghdpu.edition: S. K. De: Megha-dūta of Kālidāsa, 2nd rev. ed. by V. Raghavan. New Delhi: Sahitya Akademi 1970
translations: Horace Hayman Wilson, The Meghadūta, or Cloud Messenger, A Poem in the Sanskrit Language by Cāladāsa, Calcutta: Hindoostanee Press, 1813. (English)
James Mallinson, Messenger Poems (Meghadūta, Pavanadūta & Haṃsadūta), Clay Sanskrit Library, New York: New York University Press & JJC Foundation, 2006. (English)

SA_GK19_kmeghvpu.title: Meghadūta
SA_GK19_kmeghvpu.author: Kālidāsa
SA_GK19_kmeghvpu.summary: The Meghadūta ('Cloud Messenger') of Kālidāsa is the foundational lyric poem of the sandeśakāvya genre in classical Sanskrit literature, composed entirely in the mandākrāntā meter. Exiled to Mount Rāmagiri for neglecting his duties, an attendant yakṣa begs a passing monsoon cloud to deliver a message of love and reassurance to his pining wife in the celestial city of Alakā. The poem comprises two sections: the Pūrvamegha, charting the cloud's scenic journey across the rivers, mountains, and cities of northern and central India, and the Uttaramegha, depicting the mythological splendors of Alakā and conveying the yakṣa's tender message. This e-text preserves the 111-stanza Kashmiri recension commented on by Vallabhadeva.
SA_GK19_kmeghvpu.attribution: Universally attributed to Kālidāsa (c. 4th–5th century CE). This digital text presents the poem according to the recension commented on by Vallabhadeva.
SA_GK19_kmeghvpu.edition: Eugen Hultzsch, ed., Kalidasa's Meghaduta, ed. from Manuscripts with the commentary of Vallabhadeva. London: Royal Asiatic Society, 1911 (Prize Publication Fund, 4).
SA_GK19_kmeghvpu.coverage: complete — Complete 111 stanzas of the Meghadūta according to Vallabhadeva's recension (tagged KMdV_1 through KMdV_111). The commentary text itself is omitted.
translations: Horace Hayman Wilson, The Meghadūta, or Cloud Messenger, A Poem in the Sanskrit Language by Cāladāsa. Calcutta, Hindoostanee Press, 1813. (English)
James Mallinson, in Messenger Poems (Meghadūta, Pavanadūta & Hamsadūta). Clay Sanskrit Library. New York: New York University Press & JJC Foundation, 2006. (English)

SA_GK19_kragh_pu.title: Raghuvaṃśa
SA_GK19_kragh_pu.author: Kālidāsa
SA_GK19_kragh_pu.summary: The Raghuvaṃśa is a nineteen-canto mahākāvya by Kālidāsa recounting the lineage of the solar kings (Sūryavaṃśa) of Ayodhyā. The narrative details the reign of Dilīpa, the world-conquest of Raghu, the tragic romance of Aja and Indumatī, Daśaratha, and the avatāra of Rāma (cantos 10–15), continuing through Kuśa down to the decline and death of the hedonistic Agnivarṇa and the accession of his pregnant queen. Renowned for its stylistic balance, evocative similes (upamā), and depiction of dharma, it is universally regarded as one of the twin pinnacles of classical Sanskrit epic poetry alongside the Kumārasambhava.
SA_GK19_kragh_pu.attribution: Work of Kālidāsa, referenced in the Aihole panegyric and commented on by early commentators including Vallabhadeva.
SA_GK19_kragh_pu.edition: A. Scharpé (ed.), Kalidasa Lexicon, Vol. 1, Brugge 1964 (Rijksuniversiteit te Gent, Werken uitgegeven door de Faculteit van de Letteren en Wijsbegeerte, 134).
SA_GK19_kragh_pu.coverage: complete — Complete text in 19 cantos (sargas 1–19), followed by interpolated verses marked with asterisks.
translations: Gopal Raghunath Nandargikar (trans.), The Raghuvamśa of Kālidāsa, Bombay 1891. (English)

SA_GK19_ksbhm06u.title: Bhāratamañjarī (chapter 6: Bhīṣmaparvan)
SA_GK19_ksbhm06u.author: Kṣemendra
SA_GK19_ksbhm06u.summary: The Bhāratamañjarī is a metrical condensation of the Mahābhārata by Kṣemendra. This file contains the sixth book (Bhīṣmaparvan), comprising 497 verses, which recounts the war up to Bhīṣma's fall and incorporates a condensation of the Bhagavadgītā.
SA_GK19_ksbhm06u.attribution: Attributed in the colophon to Kṣemendra (iti śrīkṣemendraviracitāyāṃ bhāratamañjaryā bhīṣmaparva).
SA_GK19_ksbhm06u.coverage: partial — Contains parvan 6 (Bhīṣmaparvan), consisting of 497 verses (labeled Bhmj_6.1 through Bhmj_6.497).

SA_GK19_ksbhm07u.title: Bhāratamañjarī (chapter 7: Droṇaparvan)
SA_GK19_ksbhm07u.author: Kṣemendra
SA_GK19_ksbhm07u.summary: The Droṇaparvan is the seventh book of Kṣemendra's Bhāratamañjarī, an 11th-century poetic condensation of the Mahābhārata in classical kāvya verse. In 804 stanzas, it recounts the five days of combat under the Kaurava supreme commander Droṇa, including the encirclement and death of Abhimanyu in the Cakravyūha, Arjuna's vengeance against Jayadratha, the midnight battle, and the fall of Droṇa following the report of Aśvatthāman's death.
SA_GK19_ksbhm07u.attribution: The Bhāratamañjarī is an abridgement of the Mahābhārata composed by Kṣemendra.
SA_GK19_ksbhm07u.coverage: partial — Droṇaparvan only (the 7th book of the 18 parvans of the Bhāratamañjarī, verses 7.1–7.804).

SA_GK19_ksbhm08u.title: Bhāratamañjarī (chapter 8: Karṇaparvan)
SA_GK19_ksbhm08u.author: Kṣemendra
SA_GK19_ksbhm08u.summary: The eighth book (Karṇaparvan) of Kṣemendra's Bhāratamañjarī. In 218 stanzas, it recounts the battle following the fall of Droṇa during which Karṇa commands the Kaurava forces, culminating in the duel between Karṇa and Arjuna and Karṇa's death.

SA_GK19_ksbhm08u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete Karṇaparvan (book 8, verses 1–218) of the Bhāratamañjarī; the remaining parvans are catalogued under separate files.

SA_GK19_ksbhm09u.title: Bhāratamañjarī (chapter 9: Śalyaparvan)
SA_GK19_ksbhm09u.author: Kṣemendra
SA_GK19_ksbhm09u.summary: The ninth parvan of Kṣemendra's Bhāratamañjarī. In 71 verses, it recounts the final day of the Kurukṣetra war under the generalship of Śalya, his subsequent death at the hands of Yudhiṣṭhira, the rout of the remaining Kaurava warriors, and Duryodhana taking refuge by solidifying the waters of the Dvaipāyana lake.
SA_GK19_ksbhm09u.attribution: Colophon explicitly reads: 'iti kṣemendraviracitāyāṃ bhāratamañjaryāṃ śalyaparva'.

SA_GK19_ksbhm10u.title: Bhāratamañjarī (parvan 10: Gadāparvan)
SA_GK19_ksbhm10u.author: Kṣemendra
SA_GK19_ksbhm10u.summary: The Gadāparvan is the tenth book in Kṣemendra's verse condensation of the Mahābhārata, the Bhāratamañjarī. In 111 classical verses, it recounts Duryodhana's emergence from Dvaipāyana lake, the arrival of Balarāma, the climactic mace duel between Bhīmasena and Duryodhana, the thigh-strike that mortally injures the Kaurava king, and the appointment of Aśvatthāman as commander.
SA_GK19_ksbhm10u.attribution: Attributed to Kṣemendra in the colophon.
SA_GK19_ksbhm10u.coverage: partial — Contains parvan 10 (Gadāparvan), verses 1–111, from Kṣemendra's Bhāratamañjarī.

SA_GK19_ksbhm11u.title: Bhāratamañjarī (chapter 11: Sauptikaparvan)
SA_GK19_ksbhm11u.author: Kṣemendra
SA_GK19_ksbhm11u.summary: The Sauptikaparvan forms the eleventh book of Kṣemendra's Bhāratamañjarī, an 11th-century Sanskrit poetic epitome of the Mahābhārata. In 101 verses, it condenses the events of the epic's night-raid: Aśvatthāman, accompanied by Kṛpa and Kṛtavarman, slips into the sleeping Pāñcāla encampment after receiving the blessing of Śiva, slaughters Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the sons of Draupadī, and other sleeping warriors, and reports back to the dying Duryodhana. The book concludes with the Pāṇḍavas' pursuit of Aśvatthāman, the discharge of the brahmaśiras weapon, and the curse condemning him to wander the earth.
SA_GK19_ksbhm11u.coverage: partial — Contains parvan 11 (Sauptikaparvan, vv. 1–101 with opening maṅgala and concluding colophon) of Kṣemendra's Bhāratamañjarī.

SA_GK19_ksbhm12u.title: Bhāratamañjarī (chapter 12: Strīparvan)
SA_GK19_ksbhm12u.author: Kṣemendra
SA_GK19_ksbhm12u.summary: The twelfth parvan (Strīparvan) of Kṣemendra's Mahābhārata epitome, condensing the epic narrative into 91 classical kāvya stanzas. The text portrays the grief of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Gāndhārī, the journey of the surviving Kuru women to the battlefield of Kurukṣetra, Gāndhārī's sorrowful lamentation upon beholding the corpses of her slain sons and allies, and the performance of funerary water libations (jalāñjali) on the banks of the Gaṅgā, where Kuntī reveals Karṇa's true parentage to Yudhiṣṭhira.
SA_GK19_ksbhm12u.attribution: A poetic abridgement of the Mahābhārata composed by Kṣemendra.
SA_GK19_ksbhm12u.coverage: partial — Contains parvan 12 (Strīparvan), verses 1–91, ending with the colophon 'iti kṣemendraviracitāyāṃ bhāratamañjaryāṃ strīparva'.

SA_GK19_ksbhm13u.title: Bhāratamañjarī (parvan 13: Śāntiparvan)
SA_GK19_ksbhm13u.author: Kṣemendra
SA_GK19_ksbhm13u.summary: The Bhāratamañjarī is a verse condensation of the Mahābhārata by Kṣemendra. This thirteenth book condenses the Śāntiparvan (incorporating Dānadharma) and includes instructions given to Yudhiṣṭhira after the war, ending with the demise of Bhīṣma.
SA_GK19_ksbhm13u.attribution: The Bhāratamañjarī is attributed to Kṣemendra.
SA_GK19_ksbhm13u.coverage: partial — Contains parvan 13 (Śāntiparvan, incorporating Dānadharmāḥ) comprising 1,800 verses (numbered Bhmj_13.1–Bhmj_13.1800).

SA_GK19_ksbhm14u.title: Bhāratamañjarī (parvan 14: Āśvamedhikaparvan)
SA_GK19_ksbhm14u.author: Kṣemendra
SA_GK19_ksbhm14u.summary: The fourteenth parvan (Āśvamedhikaparvan) of Kṣemendra's Bhāratamañjarī condenses the corresponding parvan of the Mahābhārata into 215 verses. It recounts King Yudhiṣṭhira's determination to perform the Vedic horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) to expiate the sins of the Kurukṣetra war, the recovery of King Marutta's buried Himalayan gold to finance the ritual, Arjuna's campaigns guarding the wandering sacrificial steed, and the concluding fable of the half-golden mongoose (nakulopākhyāna).
SA_GK19_ksbhm14u.attribution: The Bhāratamañjarī is an abridged verse condensation of the Mahābhārata by Kṣemendra.
SA_GK19_ksbhm14u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete fourteenth book (Āśvamedhikaparvan, 215 verses) of Kṣemendra's Bhāratamañjarī.

SA_GK19_ksbhm15u.title: Bhāratamañjarī (book 15: Āśramavāsikaparvan)
SA_GK19_ksbhm15u.author: Kṣemendra
SA_GK19_ksbhm15u.summary: The Āśramavāsikaparvan is the fifteenth book of Kṣemendra's Bhāratamañjarī, a Sanskrit verse epitome of the Mahābhārata. In 69 concise verses, it narrates the retirement of the aged king Dhṛtarāṣṭra to the forest along with Gāndhārī, Kuntī, and Vidura to lead a life of ascetic detachment. It describes Vidura's death, Vyāsa's granting of a temporary vision of the deceased warriors rising from the sacred waters to solace the bereaved survivors, the elders' eventual demise in a forest conflagration, and Yudhiṣṭhira's concluding funeral rites and philosophical meditations on impermanence.
SA_GK19_ksbhm15u.attribution: Attributed to Kṣemendra. The colophon explicitly confirms the authorship: 'iti śrīkṣemendraviracitāyāṃ bhāratamañjaryāmāśramavāsikaṃ parva'.
SA_GK19_ksbhm15u.coverage: partial — Contains the text of book 15 (Āśramavāsikaparvan, verses 1–69 plus closing colophon) of Kṣemendra's Bhāratamañjarī.

SA_GK19_ksbhm16u.title: Bhāratamañjarī (parvan 16: Mausalaparvan)
SA_GK19_ksbhm16u.author: Kṣemendra
SA_GK19_ksbhm16u.summary: The Mausalaparvan is the sixteenth book of Kṣemendra's Bhāratamañjarī, an 11th-century Sanskrit poetic condensation (saṃkṣepa) of the Mahābhārata. In 71 concise verses, Kṣemendra recounts the doom of the Yādava dynasty: the curse of the sages provoked by Sāmba, the creation and pulverization of the iron club (musala), the bloody drunken brawl at Prabhāsa, the passing of Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa, the submergence of Dvārakā, Arjuna's retreat with the surviving women, and Vyāsa's consolation of Arjuna on the inexorable power of time (kāla).
SA_GK19_ksbhm16u.coverage: partial — Contains parvan 16 (Mausalaparvan) complete in 71 verses (tagged Bhmj_16.1–Bhmj_16.71) with opening invocation and closing colophon, representing the sixteenth of the 18 parvans of the Bhāratamañjarī.

SA_GK19_ksbhm17u.title: Bhāratamañjarī (parvan 17: Mahāprasthānikaparvan)
SA_GK19_ksbhm17u.author: Kṣemendra
SA_GK19_ksbhm17u.summary: The Mahāprasthānikaparvan constitutes the seventeenth book of Kṣemendra's Bhāratamañjarī. In 33 verses, Kṣemendra summarizes the final departure of the Pāṇḍavas and Draupadī following the annihilation of the Vṛṣṇi clan: their abdication in favor of Parīkṣit, their pilgrimage across the Himalayas toward Mount Meru, the sequential collapse and death of Draupadī and the younger brothers, and Yudhiṣṭhira's steadfast refusal to enter heaven without the stray dog accompanying him, who is subsequently revealed as Dharma.
SA_GK19_ksbhm17u.attribution: Authentic work of Kṣemendra, explicitly attested in the closing colophon ('iti śrīkṣemendraviracitāyāṃ bhāratamañjaryāṃ mahāprasthānikaṃ parva').
SA_GK19_ksbhm17u.coverage: partial — Contains the 17th book (Mahāprasthānikaparvan) of Kṣemendra's Bhāratamañjarī, comprising 33 verses (numbered Bhmj_17.1–Bhmj_17.33), with an opening title and concluding colophon.

SA_GK19_ksbhm18u.title: Bhāratamañjarī (parvan 18: Svargaparvan)
SA_GK19_ksbhm18u.author: Kṣemendra
SA_GK19_ksbhm18u.summary: The Svargaparvan (or Svargārohaṇaparvan) is the eighteenth and concluding book of Kṣemendra's Bhāratamañjarī, an 11th-century Sanskrit kāvya epitomizing the Mahābhārata. In 34 concise stanzas, it describes Yudhiṣṭhira's arrival in svarga, his indignation at seeing Duryodhana enthroned while his brothers and Draupadī languish in an apparent hell, and Indra's revelation that this torment was merely a fleeting illusion designed to cleanse Yudhiṣṭhira of his single falsehood during Droṇa's death. Yudhiṣṭhira bathes in the celestial river, abandons his mortal form, and is reunited with the Pāṇḍavas, Karṇa, and the epic ancestors in divine bliss, concluding with the ritual culmination of Janamejaya's snake sacrifice and the rejoicing of the sages at Naimiṣāraṇya.
SA_GK19_ksbhm18u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete 18th book (Svargaparvan / Svargārohaṇaparvan), consisting of 34 verses (vv. 1–34) plus opening header and closing colophon, from Kṣemendra's 18-book condensation of the Mahābhārata.

SA_GK19_ksbhm19u.title: Bhāratamañjarī (book 19: Harivaṃśa)
SA_GK19_ksbhm19u.author: Kṣemendra
SA_GK19_ksbhm19u.summary: The Bhāratamañjarī is Kṣemendra's Sanskrit verse epitome of the epic tradition. This volume covers the nineteenth book, the Harivaṃśa, detailing the genealogy and accounts of Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa and the Yādavas, ending with reflections emphasizing śānti.
SA_GK19_ksbhm19u.attribution: Attributed to Kṣemendra in the final verses (v. 5: 'prāptaḥ sāmānyajalpo 'pi kṣemendro 'dya kavīndratām').
SA_GK19_ksbhm19u.coverage: partial — Contains book 19 (Harivaṃśa), concluding with 5 epilogue verses (vv. 1–5).

SA_GK19_ksyadndu.title: Śyāmalādaṇḍaka
SA_GK19_ksyadndu.author: Kālidāsa
SA_GK19_ksyadndu.summary: The Śyāmalādaṇḍaka is a devotional hymn (stotra) composed in daṇḍaka celebrating the goddess Śyāmalā (Mātaṅgī). The text praises the goddess, her vīṇā, attributes, and boons. It is attributed to Kālidāsa, though scholarship treats this attribution as doubtful.
SA_GK19_ksyadndu.attribution: Ascribed to Kālidāsa in text colophons; modern scholarship considers the work doubtful and not by the author of the Raghuvaṃśa.
SA_GK19_ksyadndu.edition: Kāvyamālā [old, cumulative series], vol. 1, edited by Pdt. Durgaprasad and Kasinath Pandurang Parab, 1886 (3rd ed., 1929), pp. 8–11.
SA_GK19_ksyadndu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the stotra, including the opening verse ('māṇikyavīṇām...'), 5 numbered sections, and the concluding verse ('mātā marakataśyāmā...').

SA_GK19_kulmukuu.title: Mukundamālā
SA_GK19_kulmukuu.author: Kulaśekhara
SA_GK19_kulmukuu.summary: The Mukundamālā is a Sanskrit devotional lyric (stotra) composed by King Kulaśekhara in praise of Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa. Using a variety of classical meters, the author expresses surrender, renunciation of mundane ambition, and the plea to remember Kṛṣṇa's lotus feet at the moment of death. This e-text contains the complete 34-verse recension printed in the Kāvyamālā.
SA_GK19_kulmukuu.attribution: The poem identifies its composer as King Kulaśekhara in the final verse (v. 34: rājñā kṛtā stutiriyaṃ kulaśekhareṇa). In traditional accounts, he is identified with Kulaśekhara Ālvār, a Tamil Vaiṣṇava saint. Mukundamālā is a stotra by Kulaśekhara.
SA_GK19_kulmukuu.edition: Pdt. Durgaprasad and Kasinath Pandurang Parab, Kavyamala [old, cumulative series], vol. 1, 1886 (3rd ed., 1929), pp. 11-16.
SA_GK19_kulmukuu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the 34-verse recension printed in Kāvyamālā (numbered KMuk_1 to KMuk_34), ending with the colophon 'iti śrīkulaśekharanṛpativiracitā mukundamālā samāptā'.

SA_GK19_lnksivsu.title: Śivastuti
SA_GK19_lnksivsu.author: Laṅkeśvara
SA_GK19_lnksivsu.summary: A 10-stanza Sanskrit devotional hymn (stuti) in praise of Śiva, attributed to Laṅkeśvara. The verses extol Śiva's ascetic iconography—the crescent moon, poison-darkened neck, skull ornament, and Gaṅgā flowing in his matted locks—while expressing detachment from worldly distraction and devotion to the deity.
SA_GK19_lnksivsu.attribution: The hymn is attributed in the colophon to Laṅkeśvara ('Lord of Laṅkā', i.e., Rāvaṇa).
SA_GK19_lnksivsu.edition: Pdt. Durgaprasad and Kasinath Pandurang Parab, Kavyamala [old, cumulative series], vol. 1, 1886 (3rd ed., 1929), pp. 6-8.
SA_GK19_lnksivsu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 10 verses as edited in Kāvyamālā, Part 1.

SA_GK19_maghspvu.title: Śiśupālavadha
SA_GK19_maghspvu.author: Māgha
SA_GK19_maghspvu.summary: The Śiśupālavadha ('The Slaying of Śiśupāla') is a canonical 20-canto court epic (mahākāvya) composed by the poet Māgha. Expanding an episode from the Sabhāparvan of the Mahābhārata, the narrative recounts the slaying of the insolent king Śiśupāla of Chedi by Kṛṣṇa during Yudhiṣṭhira's Rājasūya sacrifice. Celebrated in traditional Sanskrit literary criticism alongside Kālidāsa and Bhāravi, the work is renowned for its vigorous political debate (Canto 2), rich descriptive set pieces (Cantos 4–13), and intricate verbal pyrotechnics and visual poetry (citrakāvya, Canto 19).
SA_GK19_maghspvu.coverage: complete — Complete root text across 20 cantos (sargas), running from Canto 1, verse 1 (MSpv_1.01) through Canto 20, verse 79 (MSpv_20.79).
translations: Paul Dundas (trans.), The Killing of Shishupala, Murty Classical Library of India 11, Cambridge, Massachusetts: Harvard University Press, 2017. (English)

SA_GK19_mala.title: Mālatīmādhava with the commentary of Jagaddhara
SA_GK19_mala.author: Bhavabhūti, Jagaddhara
SA_GK19_mala.summary: The Mālatīmādhava is a ten-act drama of the prakaraṇa genre composed by the 8th-century poet Bhavabhūti. Set principally in the city of Padmāvatī, it depicts the fraught romance between Mādhava and Mālatī (alongside the subplot of Makaranda and Madayantikā), which faces obstacle from an imperial court betrothal and terror from Kāpālika sorcerers in cremation grounds before reaching resolution through the interventions of the Buddhist nun Kāmandakī and her disciple Saudāminī. This e-text contains the complete Sanskrit text of the play accompanied throughout by the detailed Sanskrit commentary (ṭīkā) of Jagaddhara.
SA_GK19_mala.attribution: The drama is by Bhavabhūti (Śrīkaṇṭha), associated with King Yaśovarman. The commentary is by Jagaddhara, son of Ratnadhara and grandson of Vidyādhara.
SA_GK19_mala.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 10 acts (aṅkas) of the prakaraṇa along with Jagaddhara's complete commentary, prefaced by an editorial Sanskrit introduction (upodghāta).
translations: Michael Coulson, Three Sanskrit Plays, London, 1981. (English)

SA_GK19_naicau.title: Naiṣadhīyacarita
SA_GK19_naicau.author: Śrīharṣa
SA_GK19_naicau.summary: The Naiṣadhīyacarita is a celebrated Sanskrit mahākāvya in 22 cantos composed by Śrīharṣa. Expanding the Nalopākhyāna from the Mahābhārata, it recounts the romance and svayaṃvara of King Nala of Niṣadha and Princess Damayantī of Vidarbha through their marriage and courtly union. It is famed for its extreme stylistic intricacy, mastery of śleṣa (puns), and wide-ranging philosophical erudition.
SA_GK19_naicau.coverage: unclear — Entry is empty (0 segments, 0 characters); the work has 22 cantos, but nothing can be said about what the intended e-text covers.

SA_GK19_padnscpu.title: Navasāhasāṅkacarita
SA_GK19_padnscpu.author: Padmagupta
SA_GK19_padnscpu.summary: The Navasāhasāṅkacarita is a poem composed by the court poet Padmagupta (Parimala) celebrating the Paramāra ruler Sindhurāja (Navasāhasāṅka).
SA_GK19_padnscpu.attribution: Padmagupta bore the alias Parimala. The epic was composed concerning king Sindhurāja (Navasāhasāṅka).
SA_GK19_padnscpu.edition: Vamanasastri Islampurakara, Bombay: Govt. Central Book Depot (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 53).

SA_GK19_padyavlu.title: Padyāvalī
SA_GK19_padyavlu.author: Rūpa Gosvāmī
SA_GK19_padyavlu.summary: The Padyāvalī is an anthology of devotional verses in Sanskrit compiled by Rūpa Gosvāmī (sixteenth century). It brings together stanzas from various poets arranged thematically.
SA_GK19_padyavlu.attribution: Compiled by Rūpa Gosvāmī. The anthology gathers verses by various poets (including Bilvamaṅgala, Kṣemendra, etc.).
SA_GK19_padyavlu.edition: The Padyāvalī of Rūpa Gosvāmin. Ed. by S. K. De. Dacca University Oriental Publication Series No. 3. Dacca 1934.
SA_GK19_padyavlu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the anthology, containing verses followed by extra verses and poet attributions.

SA_GK19_raggancu.title: Mahāgaṇapatistotra with Ṭippaṇī
SA_GK19_raggancu.author: Rāghavacaitanya
SA_GK19_raggancu.summary: The Mahāgaṇapatistotra is a 16-verse ornate stotra in praise of the tantric form of Mahāgaṇapati, composed in classical metres by the ascetic master Rāghavacaitanya. The verses systematically encode the Mahāgaṇapati mantra, yantra, dhyāna, and iconographic details—depicting the ten-armed red Ganapati embracing his consort upon a jewelled lotus throne in the ocean of sugarcane juice. The running prose ṭippaṇī, composed by the author's disciple, explicitly decodes the esoteric bījas and ritual symbols embedded within the verses.
SA_GK19_raggancu.attribution: The hymn is attributed in the opening title and final colophon to Paramahaṃsaparivrājakācāryavarya Rāghavacaitanya. The integrated prose commentary is explicitly ascribed to his unnamed disciple ('tacchiṣyakṛtā ṭippaṇī').
SA_GK19_raggancu.edition: Kāvyamālā [old, cumulative series], vol. 1, edited by Pdt. Durgaprasad and Kasinath Pandurang Parab, 1886 (3rd ed., 1929), pp. 1-6.
SA_GK19_raggancu.coverage: complete — Complete in 16 verses (RMgan_1–RMgan_16) interspersed with the disciple's prose gloss for each verse, including the closing colophon.

SA_GK19_ramodtpu.title: Rāmodanta
SA_GK19_ramodtpu.summary: The Rāmodanta is an anonymous pedagogical Sanskrit poem summarizing the complete narrative of the Rāmāyaṇa in simple anuṣṭubh verse. Widely used across South India—particularly Kerala—as an introductory reader, it traditionally served as a student's first narrative text following the memorization of basic grammatical declensions and conjugations (such as the Siddharūpa). The original recension comprises 156 verses, encoded by the kaṭapayādi chronogram 'cinmayaḥ' (156) in the final verse, while popular later print editions expanded the text to 199 verses organized into seven kāṇḍas.
SA_GK19_ramodtpu.attribution: The work is anonymous in the pedagogical tradition of South India (especially Kerala); no historical author is named or reliably identified.
SA_GK19_ramodtpu.edition: A synoptic digital edition compiled and entered by Christophe Vielle, based primarily on the 156-verse text in 'Siddharūpaṃ, Bālaprabodhaṃ, Samāsacakraṃ, vyākhyānavuṃ Śrīrāmodantavuṃ', ed. C. V. Ravisarma Raja (Si. Vi. Raviśarmma Rājāvu), Thrissur: Kerala Sahitya Akademi, 2010 (1st ed. 1948), collated with the expanded 199-verse 7-kāṇḍa recension in 'Śrīrāmodantam', ed. L. Anantarama Sastri, Kalpathi (Palghat): R. S. Vadhyar & Sons, 11th rev. ed. 1982 (repr. 2006), with reference to editions by Pūvattūr Rāmakṛṣṇa Piḷḷa (1990) and K. P. A. Menon (1996).
SA_GK19_ramodtpu.coverage: complete — Complete; the e-text presents a comparative synoptic version incorporating the verses of both the shorter 156-verse Kerala recension and the expanded 199-verse 7-kāṇḍa recension with dual verse numbering.
translations: K. P. A. Menon, Nine Gems of Sanskrit Literature, vol. 3, Delhi: Nag Publishers, 1996, pp. 150–210. (English)
Śrīrāmodantam / Story of Sri Rama: Sanskrit Text and English Translation, Chennai: Hindu e-Books, 2010. (English)

SA_GK19_setu.title: Setubandha
SA_GK19_setu.author: Pravarasena
SA_GK19_setu.summary: The Setubandha ('The Building of the Causeway'), also titled Rāvaṇavaha, is a celebrated mahākāvya in 15 cantos (āśvāsas) composed in Mahārāṣṭrī Prakrit. Based on the Yuddhakāṇḍa of the Rāmāyaṇa, it depicts Rāma's despair, the monkey army's arrival at the ocean, the heroic construction of the causeway to Laṅkā, and the ultimate destruction of Rāvaṇa. Praised by Daṇḍin and Bāṇabhaṭṭa, it is an important epic in Mahārāṣṭrī Prakrit.
SA_GK19_setu.attribution: Attributed to King Pravarasena. Indian tradition also associated Kālidāsa with its composition.
SA_GK19_setu.coverage: unclear — The entry in the DharmaNexus database contains 0 segment files and 0 characters (empty text / ingestion failure), so textual completeness cannot be verified.
translations: Siegfried Goldschmidt, Rāvaṇavaha oder Setubandha, 2. Lieferung: Übersetzung, Strassburg, 1884. (German)

SA_GK19_srngt_pu.title: Śṛṅgāratilaka
SA_GK19_srngt_pu.author: Rudrabhaṭṭa
SA_GK19_srngt_pu.summary: The Śṛṅgāratilaka of Rudrabhaṭṭa is an influential treatise on Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra) in three chapters (paricchedas). Focusing preeminently on the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) and the systematic typology of lovers and heroines (nāyaka- and nāyikā-bheda), Rudrabhaṭṭa illustrates theoretical definitions with original and anthologized kāvya stanzas.
SA_GK19_srngt_pu.coverage: complete — Complete in three chapters (paricchedas 1–3), ending at verse 3.57 and the closing colophon.

SA_GK19_suvasavu.title: Vāsavadattā
SA_GK19_suvasavu.author: Subandhu
SA_GK19_suvasavu.summary: The Vāsavadattā of Subandhu (dated to the sixth century) is a classical Sanskrit prose romance (kathā). The narrative recounts how Prince Kandarpaketu and Princess Vāsavadattā experience dreams of each other, seek each other out, elope, undergo separation after Vāsavadattā is petrified into stone by an ascetic's curse, and are reunited once the touch of Kandarpaketu restores her to life. The work is famed for its extreme rhetorical display, notably pervasive paronomasia (śleṣa) across almost every syllable and sentence, which served as a major stylistic predecessor to Bāṇabhaṭṭa's prose romances.
SA_GK19_suvasavu.attribution: Subandhu is identified in the final colophon (iti mahākavi-Subandhu-viracitā Vāsavadattā nāma kathā samāptā).
SA_GK19_suvasavu.edition: Jaydev Mohanlal Shukla: Vāsavadattā of Subandhu, Jodhpur 1966.
SA_GK19_suvasavu.coverage: complete — Text of the prose romance, concluding with section 60 and the colophon.
translations: L. H. Gray (ed. and trans.), Vāsavadattā of Subandhu, New York (Columbia University Indo-Iranian Series 8). (English)

SA_GK19_uddkokpu.title: Kokilasandeśa
SA_GK19_uddkokpu.author: Uddaṇḍa
SA_GK19_uddkokpu.summary: The Kokilasandeśa ('Message of the Cuckoo') is a Sanskrit messenger poem (sandeśakāvya) composed by Uddaṇḍa in two parts (Pūrvabhāga and Uttarabhāga) comprising 162 verses. Separated from his beloved and waking up in Kāñcī, a lover addresses a cuckoo (kokila) to bear a message across various regions and shrines to his beloved.
SA_GK19_uddkokpu.edition: Text prepared for the translation by Shankar Rajaraman and Venetia Kotamraju: The Message of the Koel: Uddaṇḍa Śāstrīs's Kokila Sandeśa, Bangalore: Rasāla 2012.
SA_GK19_uddkokpu.coverage: complete — Complete text in two parts comprising 162 verses (Pūrvabhāga: 93 verses, Kok_1.1–Kok_1.93; Uttarabhāga: 69 verses, Kok_2.1–Kok_2.69).
translations: Shankar Rajaraman and Venetia Kotamraju, The Message of the Koel: Uddaṇḍa Śāstrīs's Kokila Sandeśa, Bangalore: Rasāla, 2012. (English)

SA_GK20_bhasdutu.title: Dūtavākya
SA_GK20_bhasdutu.author: Bhāsa
SA_GK20_bhasdutu.summary: The Dūtavākya ('The Envoy's Message') is a one-act Sanskrit drama attributed to Bhāsa, based on Kṛṣṇa's peace embassy to the Kaurava court. In the drama, Duryodhana rejects Kṛṣṇa's proposal, gazes at a painted scroll (citrapaṭa) depicting Draupadī, and orders his attendants to bind the envoy. Kṛṣṇa summons his personified celestial weapons (āyudhapuruṣas: Sudarśana, Kaumodakī, Śārṅga, Nandaka, and Pāñcajanya) until Dhṛtarāṣṭra intercedes.
SA_GK20_bhasdutu.attribution: Ascribed to the classical playwright Bhāsa. T. Gaṇapati-Śāstrī discovered and published 13 plays including Dūtavākya, but controversy still exists as to the authorship and date.
SA_GK20_bhasdutu.edition: T. K. Ramachandra Iyer, Kalpathi: Palghat, S. India: R. S. Vadhyar and Sons, 1981; C. R. Devadhar, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1962 (reprinted in 1987).
SA_GK20_bhasdutu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the one-act play comprising all 56 verses and the final Bharatavākya; preceded by modern English dramatis personae.
translations: Ratna Basu (trans. into Bengali), in Saṃskṛta Sāhitya Sambhār, Calcutta, 1980–1986. (Bengali)

SA_GK20_bhassv_u.title: Svapnavāsavadatta
SA_GK20_bhassv_u.author: Bhāsa
SA_GK20_bhassv_u.summary: The Svapnavāsavadatta ('The Dream of Vāsavadattā') is a six-act classical Sanskrit drama (nāṭaka) dramatizing episodes from the Udayana legend cycle of the Bṛhatkathā. To facilitate King Udayana's political alliance with King Darśaka of Magadha and recapture his kingdom from the usurper Āruṇī, Minister Yaugandharāyaṇa arranges the staged death of Queen Vāsavadattā in a fire at Lāvāṇaka and conceals her under the identity of Lady Āvantikā in the care of Princess Padmāvatī. The dramatic and psychological climax occurs in Act 5 (the dream act / svapnāṅka), where the sleeping Udayana addresses Vāsavadattā in what he believes to be a dream while she secretly comforts him, leading to their eventual reunion and royal restoration in Act 6.
SA_GK20_bhassv_u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the playwright Bhāsa. Bhāsa's authorship of a Svapnavāsavadatta is recorded by Rājaśekhara (Sūktimuktāvalī 4.48) and mentioned by Kālidāsa (Mālavikāgnimitra). T. Gaṇapati Śāstrī discovered and published 13 plays including the Svapnavāsavadatta, which he believed to be works of Bhāsa, though whether they represent the genuine works remains debated.
SA_GK20_bhassv_u.coverage: complete — Complete drama in six acts (Acts 1–6), including opening stage directions, Prakrit dialogues accompanied inline by Sanskrit chāyā in square brackets, and concluding with the Bharatavākya (6.19) and colophon (iti svapnanāṭakam avasitam).

SA_GK20_bhveni_u.title: Veṇīsaṃhāra
SA_GK20_bhveni_u.author: Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa
SA_GK20_bhveni_u.summary: The Veṇīsaṃhāra ('The Binding of the Braid') is a six-act classical Sanskrit drama (nāṭaka) by Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa based on the Mahābhārata war. The plot centres on the vow taken by Bhīmasena to avenge the public humiliation of Draupadī by slaying Duḥśāsana and Duryodhana, refusing to let her braid her hair until it has been washed and bound with their blood.
SA_GK20_bhveni_u.attribution: The work is attributed to Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa. He is placed in the 7th or 8th century CE.
SA_GK20_bhveni_u.edition: Venisamhara: Die Ehrenrettung der Königin, Ein Drama in 6 Akten von Bhatta Narayana, ed. Julius Grill, Leipzig: Fues's Verlag (R. Reisland), 1871; and Venisamhara of Bhatta Narayana, ed. with the commentary of Jagaddhara by M. R. Kale, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1989.
SA_GK20_bhveni_u.coverage: complete — Complete six-act play (Acts 1–6), including stage directions, character speeches, editorial Prakrit chāyā, and the terminal verse following Act 6.
translations: Veṇīsaṃhāra: drame sanskrit, trans. Francine Bourgeois, Paris, 1971. (French)

SA_GK20_dramfrag_pu.title: Dramatic Fragments (Buddhist)
SA_GK20_dramfrag_pu.author: Aśvaghoṣa
SA_GK20_dramfrag_pu.summary: This e-text contains the oldest surviving specimens of Indian dramatic literature, discovered on palm-leaf fragments from Kizil near Turfan (Central Asia) and datable to the Kuṣāṇa period (c. 1st–2nd century CE). The principal identifiable play is Aśvaghoṣa's Śāriputraprakaraṇa (or Śāradvatīputraprakaraṇa), a nine-act play dramatizing the conversion of the Buddha's foremost disciples, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana. Preserved alongside it are fragments of two anonymous Buddhist plays: an allegorical drama featuring personifications (Buddhi, Dhṛti, Kīrti) and a prakaraṇa or social comedy involving a courtesan (gaṇikā), a rogue (duṣṭa), and a jester (vidūṣaka). These fragments are of foundational importance for the history of classical Sanskrit theatre and the early history of Middle Indo-Aryan dialects (archaic forms of Māgadhī, Ardhamāgadhī, and Śaurasenī).
SA_GK20_dramfrag_pu.attribution: The Śāriputraprakaraṇa (or Śāradvatīputraprakaraṇa) is explicitly attributed to Aśvaghoṣa (son of Suvarṇākṣī) in the surviving colophon of Act 9 (SHT 57). The two other plays preserved in the same manuscript find (SHT 16)—an allegorical play featuring personified qualities (Buddhi, Dhṛti, Kīrti) and a comedy featuring a courtesan (gaṇikā), a vidūṣaka (Komudagandha), and a rogue (duṣṭa)—are anonymous, though Lüders and subsequent scholarship suggest they stem from the same Kuṣāṇa-era Buddhist dramatic circle.
SA_GK20_dramfrag_pu.edition: Heinrich Lüders (ed.), Bruchstücke buddhistischer Dramen, Berlin 1911 (Kleinere Sanskrit-Texte 1); supplemented by Heinrich Lüders, 'Das Śāriputraprakaraṇa, ein Drama des Aśvaghoṣa', Sitzungsberichte der königlich Preussischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 17 (1911), pp. 388–411.
SA_GK20_dramfrag_pu.coverage: fragment — Extremely fragmentary remains of three early plays preserved on palm-leaf fragments from the Berlin Turfan collection (SHT 16 and SHT 57). For the Śāriputraprakaraṇa, only scattered portions of acts 8 and 9 (including the final colophon) are preserved; the allegorical drama and courtesan drama survive only as isolated speech and verse fragments.

SA_GK20_harnagau.title: Nāgānanda (verses only)
SA_GK20_harnagau.author: Harṣadeva
SA_GK20_harnagau.summary: The Nāgānanda ('Joy of the Serpents') is a five-act Sanskrit drama (nāṭaka) attributed to Harṣadeva (7th century CE), dramatizing the Buddhist legend of the Vidyādhara prince Jīmūtavāhana. The opening acts combine standard courtly kāvya romance with Jīmūtavāhana's courtship and marriage to Princess Malayavatī, while the fourth and fifth acts center on his Bodhisattva-like self-sacrifice: offering his own flesh on the slaughter stone to Garuḍa to rescue the young Nāga Śaṅkhacūḍa. Moved by Jīmūtavāhana's radical compassion and non-violence, Garuḍa renounces the slaughter of serpents and revives those previously consumed. Famous for invoking both the Buddha (munīndra / jina) and the Hindu goddess Gaurī, the work is an exceptional surviving exemplar of classical Buddhist dramatic literature.
SA_GK20_harnagau.attribution: Attributed to the 7th-century North Indian ruler Harṣadeva (Śrīharṣa).
SA_GK20_harnagau.coverage: partial — Contains only the metrical verses across all five acts (Nā_1.1 to Nā_5.41), omitting all intervening Sanskrit and Prakrit prose dialogue and stage directions.
translations: Palmer Boyd (trans.), Nâgânandam, London: Trübner & Co., 1872. (English)
Abel Bergaigne (trans.), Paris, 1879. (French)

SA_GK20_hdratn_u.title: Ratnāvalīnāṭikā (acts 1, 2, 4 and act 3 praveśaka)
SA_GK20_hdratn_u.author: Harṣadeva
SA_GK20_hdratn_u.summary: The Ratnāvalī is a four-act romantic court drama (nāṭikā) attributed to King Harṣadeva. Based on the Udayana legendary cycle, it depicts King Udayana falling in love with Sāgarikā, an attendant to Chief Queen Vāsavadattā.
SA_GK20_hdratn_u.attribution: Attributed in the header and tradition to King Harṣadeva.
SA_GK20_hdratn_u.edition: Carl Cappeller in: Otto Böhtlingk: Sanskrit-Chrestomathie, 3. verbesserte und vermehrte Auflage, herausgegeben von Richard Garbe, Leipzig 1909, pp. 326-382.
SA_GK20_hdratn_u.coverage: partial — Acts 1, 2, and 4 are complete; of Act 3, only the introductory interlude (praveśaka) is included.
translations: Wilson, Select Specimens of the Theatre of the Hindus (English)
L. Fritze, Schloss Chemnitz. (German)
M. Lehot, Ratnāvalī texte traduit par M. Lehot. Collection Émile Senart. Paris. (French)

SA_GK20_hpriydpu.title: Priyadarśikā
SA_GK20_hpriydpu.author: Harṣadeva
SA_GK20_hpriydpu.summary: The Priyadarśikā is a classical four-act court drama (nāṭikā) attributed to King Harṣadeva (Harṣavardhana of Kanauj, r. c. 606–647 CE). Drawing upon the popular romantic cycle of King Udayana of Vatsa, it depicts Udayana's romance with Princess Priyadarśikā of Aṅga, who lives incognito as the handmaiden Āraṇyakā in Queen Vāsavadattā's harem. The play is particularly noted for containing one of the earliest extant examples of a play-within-a-play (garbhanāṭaka) in Sanskrit dramatic literature (Act 3), which brings about the discovery of the lovers and the heroine's eventual royal marriage.
SA_GK20_hpriydpu.attribution: Attributed in the prologue and colophons to King Harṣadeva.
SA_GK20_hpriydpu.edition: M. R. Kale (ed.), Priyadarśikā of Śrī Harṣadeva, edited with an exhaustive introduction, a short Sanskrit commentary, various readings, a literal English translation, copious notes and useful appendices, Bombay: Gopal Narayana & Co., 1928 (reprinted Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1977).
SA_GK20_hpriydpu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all four acts (aṅkas 1–4, verses 1.1–4.12), including the opening benediction (nāndī), prologue (prastāvanā), stage directions, Prakrit dialogue accompanied by Sanskrit chāyā in brackets, and concluding bharatavākya.
translations: G. K. Nariman, A. V. Williams Jackson, and Charles J. Ogden, Priyadarśikā: A Sanskrit Drama by Harsha, New York: Columbia University Press, 1923. (English)
M. R. Kale, Priyadarśikā of Śrī Harṣadeva, Bombay: Gopal Narayana & Co., 1928. (English)

SA_GK20_mmatvipu.title: Mattavilāsaprahasana
SA_GK20_mmatvipu.author: Mahendravarman I
SA_GK20_mmatvipu.summary: The Mattavilāsaprahasana ('The Farce of Drunken Sport') is a 7th-century one-act Sanskrit satire (prahasana) by the Pallava monarch Mahendravarman I, set in Kāñcīpuram. The plot follows a drunken Kāpālika ascetic, Satyasoma, and his consort Devasomā, who misplace their skull begging bowl (kapāla) and wrongly accuse a Buddhist monk, Nāgasena, of having stolen it. A Pāśupata ascetic is called in to arbitrate the dispute until a madman arrives with the bowl, which he had recovered from a stray dog, clearing the monk of blame. The play satirizes contemporary sectarian friction and religious hypocrisy among Kāpālikas, Pāśupatas, Buddhists, and Jains, and survives as a staple piece in Kerala's classical Kūṭiyāṭṭam theater.
SA_GK20_mmatvipu.attribution: The drama names its author as Śrī Mahendravikramavarman. He is identified with the Pallava king Mahendravarman I.
SA_GK20_mmatvipu.edition: Collated edition by Christian Ferstl based on N.P. Unni (ed.), Mattavilāsa Prahasana of Mahendravikramavarman, Delhi: Nag Publishers, 1998, and T. Gaṇapati Śāstrī (ed.), The Mattavilāsaprahasana of Śrī Mahendravikramavarman, Trivandrum Sanskrit Series, 1917.
SA_GK20_mmatvipu.coverage: complete — One-act play with intervening prose dialogue and embedded Sanskrit chāyā in square brackets, followed by 18 editorial endnotes.
translations: N.P. Unni, Mattavilasaprahasana of Mahendravikramavarman, Trivandrum: College Book House, 1974. (English)

SA_GK20_murau.title: Mudrārākṣasa
SA_GK20_murau.author: Viśākhadatta
SA_GK20_murau.summary: The Mudrārākṣasa is a celebrated drama attributed to Viśākhadatta, dramatizing the statecraft of Cāṇakya following the overthrow of the Nanda dynasty. Uniquely devoid of romantic subplots or supernatural elements, the drama hinges on espionage, political psychology, and the minister Rākṣasa under emperor Candragupta.
SA_GK20_murau.attribution: A drama attributed to Viśākhadatta (or Vishākadatta).
SA_GK20_murau.coverage: unclear — The catalog entry contains no text payload.
translations: Michael Coulson (transl.), Rakshasa's Ring (Mudraraksasa) by Visakhadatta (Clay Sanskrit Library 15). (English)
J. A. B. van Buitenen (transl.), Delhi. (English)
H. H. Wilson (transl.), in Select Specimens of the Theatre of the Hindus. (English)
L. Fritze (transl.), Leipzig. (German)
V. Henry (transl.), Paris. (French)

SA_GK20_rmc1-3pu.title: Rāmacarita (cantos 1–3)
SA_GK20_rmc1-3pu.author: Abhinanda
SA_GK20_rmc1-3pu.summary: Cantos 1–3 of a Sanskrit court epic (mahākāvya) retelling the Rāmāyaṇa story. Unlike traditional epic narratives that start with Rāma's youth, the poem commences in medias res at Mount Mālyavat, where Rāma laments his separation from Sītā as the monsoon ends. Cantos 1–3 describe the onset of autumn, Lakṣmaṇa's words of consolation and resolve, nightfall and moonrise on the mountain, and morning rites followed by strategic deliberation before departing for Lake Pampā.
SA_GK20_rmc1-3pu.attribution: Composed by Abhinanda under the patronage of Prince Hāravarṣa (śrīhāravarṣayuvarāja).
SA_GK20_rmc1-3pu.edition: K. S. Ramaswami Sastri Siromani: Ramacarita of Abhinanda. Baroda: Oriental Institute, 1930. Gaekwad's Oriental Series No. XLVI.

SA_GK20_ruysahlu.title: Sahṛdayalīlā
SA_GK20_ruysahlu.author: Ruyyaka
SA_GK20_ruysahlu.summary: The Sahṛdayalīlā ('Play/Diversion of the Connoisseur') is a short aesthetic-erotic treatise in four chapters (ullekhas) by the Kashmirian literary theorist Rājānaka Ruyyaka. Transferring analytical categories from poetics (guṇa, alaṅkāra, jīvita, and parikara) to female physical charm, Ruyyaka provides a taxonomy of ten innate qualities of feminine beauty (such as lāvaṇya, chāyā, and saubhāgya), personal ornamentation (gems, gold, garments, cosmetics), vital expressions of youth, and accompanying settings and retinues from the perspective of an urban aesthete (nāgaraka / sahṛdaya).
SA_GK20_ruysahlu.attribution: Attributed to Rājānaka Ruyyaka (also known as Rucaka, son of Tilaka) in the chapter colophons ('iti śrīrājānakaruyyakaviracitāyāṃ sahṛdayalīlāyāṃ...').
SA_GK20_ruysahlu.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising four chapters (ullekhas), concluding with 'samāpteyaṃ sahṛdayalīlā'.

SA_GK20_sypadatu.title: Pādatāḍitaka
SA_GK20_sypadatu.author: Śyāmilaka
SA_GK20_sypadatu.summary: The Pādatāḍitaka ('The Kick') by the late Gupta-era poet Śyāmilaka is the longest and most celebrated of the four satirical monologue plays preserved in the Caturbhāṇī. Spoken entirely by a viṭa (cosmopolitan man-about-town), the play recounts his journey through the streets of Sārvabhaumanagara (Ujjayinī) to convene a council of rogues to prescribe a comedic expiation (prāyaścitta) for a high-caste gentleman kicked on the head by a courtesan during a lovers' quarrel. Rich in social satire, vivid urban character sketches, and linguistic wit, it provides unparalleled insight into late classical Indian courtly and demi-monde life.
SA_GK20_sypadatu.attribution: Attributed in the final colophon to the northern poet (udīcya) Śyāmilaka, son of Viśveśvaradatta.
SA_GK20_sypadatu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the one-act monologue play in 148 verses and intervening prose, from the opening stage directions and nāndī to the concluding bharatavākya (v. 148) and colophon.
translations: Csaba Dezső and Somadeva Vasudeva, The Quartet of Causeries: Caturbhāṇī, Clay Sanskrit Library, New York: New York University Press / JJC Foundation, 2009. (English)

SA_GK21_karaka.title: Kathāratnākara (German translation, taraṅgas 1–4)
SA_GK21_karaka.author: Hemavijaya
SA_GK21_karaka.summary: The Kathāratnākara ('Ocean of Story-Jewels') is a celebrated Sanskrit narrative compendium in prose and verse composed by the Śvetāmbara Jain monk Hemavijayagaṇi in 1600 CE. Divided into ten taraṅgas ('waves'), it compiles 258 didactic tales, moral fables, and humorous anecdotes. This digital file contains Volume 1 of Johannes Hertel's 1920 German translation comprising the first four taraṅgas.
SA_GK21_karaka.attribution: The original Sanskrit text was composed by the Śvetāmbara Jain monk Hemavijayagaṇi in 1600 CE. The German translation in this e-text was prepared by Johannes Hertel.
SA_GK21_karaka.edition: Johannes Hertel (trans.), Kathāratnākara: Das Märchenmeer. Eine Sammlung indischer Erzählungen von Hēmavijaya, Band I: Erste bis vierte Woge (Meisterwerke orientalischer Literaturen, Bd. 4), München: Georg Müller, 1920.
SA_GK21_karaka.coverage: partial — Contains only Volume 1 of Johannes Hertel's German translation (taraṅgas 1–4, stories 1–97 of the total 258 tales across 10 taraṅgas). No Sanskrit original text is present.
translations: Johannes Hertel, Kathāratnākara: Das Märchenmeer. Eine Sammlung indischer Erzählungen von Hēmavijaya, München: Georg Müller, 1920. (German)

SA_GK21_soksvppu.title: Kathāsaritsāgara (Vetālapañcaviṃśatikā)
SA_GK21_soksvppu.author: Somadeva
SA_GK21_soksvppu.summary: The Vetālapañcaviṃśatikā ('Twenty-Five Tales of the Vetāla') section of Somadeva's 11th-century Kashmirian epic Kathāsaritsāgara is embedded within Book 12 (Śaśāṅkavatīlambaka, taraṅgas 8.21–32.41). In this classic frame narrative, King Trivikramasena (the archetype of King Vikramāditya) undertakes to retrieve a corpse inhabited by a vetāla (ghoul) from a cremation ground for an ascetic named Kṣāntiśīla; during each transport, the vetāla tells an intricate riddle-tale that compels the king to break silence to render judgment, resetting the journey until the final tale exposes the mendicant's murderous deception. Somadeva's verse rendering is one of the two earliest surviving complete Sanskrit recensions of this world-famous cycle of wonder-tales.
SA_GK21_soksvppu.attribution: Composed in Kashmir in the 11th century (reign of Kalaśa, 1063–1081/2 CE) by Somadeva.
SA_GK21_soksvppu.edition: Based on the edition by Durgaprasad and Parab, Bombay: Nirnaya-Sagar Press 1915.
SA_GK21_soksvppu.coverage: partial — Contains only the Vetālapañcaviṃśatikā cycle embedded in Book 12, from taraṅga 8, verse 21 to taraṅga 32, verse 41 (verses SoKss_12,8.21–32.41 / Vet_0.1–25.41).
translations: C. H. Tawney (tr.), The Ocean of Story, edited with explanatory notes and terminal essay by N. M. Penzer, 10 volumes, London, 1924–1928 (reprinted Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass). (English)
Katsuhiko Kamimura (上村勝彥) (tr.), 『屍鬼二十五話 ― インド伝奇集』 (Sikinijugowa: Indodenkishu), Tokyo: Heibonsha, 1978. (Japanese)

SA_GK21_ttrkhy1u.title: Tantrākhyāyika (book 1: inserted stories)
SA_GK21_ttrkhy1u.summary: The Tantrākhyāyika preserves an early recension of the Pañcatantra. This e-text contains inserted apologues of Book 1, with the framing story stripped out.
SA_GK21_ttrkhy1u.attribution: The original recension of the Pañcatantra is anonymous.
SA_GK21_ttrkhy1u.coverage: excerpt — Contains inserted sub-stories/fables of Book 1, beginning with 1.1 ('Affe und Keil') and omitting the Kathāmukha and the overarching frame story.
translations: Johannes Hertel (trans.), Tantrākhyāyika: Die älteste Fassung des Pañcatantra, Leipzig and Berlin, 1909. (German)

SA_GK21_ttrkhy2u.title: Tantrākhyāyika (Book 2: embedded tales)
SA_GK21_ttrkhy2u.summary: Book 2 (Mitrasaṃprāpti) of the Tantrākhyāyika, representing the Kashmirian recension considered the oldest extant form of the Pañcatantra. This digital file contains only the embedded secondary fables of Book 2 (Tales II.1–II.5), completely omitting the overarching frame narrative of the alliance between the crow, mouse, turtle, and deer. The embedded fables illustrate practical wisdom (nīti), the perils of greed, and the inescapable nature of fate.
SA_GK21_ttrkhy2u.attribution: Modern scholarship treats the Tantrākhyāyika as the oldest recension of the Pañcatantra.
SA_GK21_ttrkhy2u.edition: Johannes Hertel (ed.), Tantrākhyāyika: Die älteste Fassung des Pañcatantra, Berlin 1910 (Abhandlungen der Königlichen Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften zu Göttingen, Philologisch-Historische Klasse, N.F., Bd. XII).
SA_GK21_ttrkhy2u.coverage: excerpt — Contains only the embedded tales of Book 2 (Tales II.1 through II.5), opening with Tale II.1 ('[II,1 Hiranyas Erlebnisse]') and ending with the close of Tale II.5 ('anubhūtabandhano 'py ahaṃ niyativaśāt punar baddha iti /').
translations: Johannes Hertel, Tantrākhyāyika: Die älteste Fassung des Pañcatantra. Aus dem Sanskrit übersetzt, 2 vols., Leipzig und Berlin 1909. (German)

SA_GK22_bharst_u.title: Śatakatraya
SA_GK22_bharst_u.author: Bhartṛhari
SA_GK22_bharst_u.summary: A collection of three 'centuries' (śataka) of gnomic and lyric epigrams traditionally attributed to Bhartṛhari: the Nītiśataka on worldly prudence, ethics, and civic conduct; the Śṛṅgāraśataka on the pleasures, moods, and pitfalls of erotic desire; and the Vairāgyaśataka on renunciation, transience, and ascetic withdrawal. The triad moves across the classic aims of life (dharma, artha, kāma) toward ultimate spiritual dispassion (vairāgya). Widely anthologized, memorized, and translated, it remains among the most influential works in the Sanskrit subhāṣita tradition.
SA_GK22_bharst_u.edition: Composite text input from three separate editions published by Chaukhamba Vidya Bhavan, Varanasi: (1) Nītiśataka, ed. Srhirkrishnanamani Tripathi, 1990; (2) Śṛṅgāraśataka, Vidyābhavana Saṃskṛta Granthamālā 61, Chowkhamba, 1988; (3) Vairāgyaśataka, Vidyābhavana Saṃskṛta Granthamālā 67, Chowkhamba, 1988.
SA_GK22_bharst_u.coverage: complete — Contains the complete texts of all three śatakas according to the printed editions used: Nītiśataka, Śṛṅgāraśataka, and Vairāgyaśataka.
translations: Roger, Abraham (tr.). De open-deure tot het verborgen heydendom. Leiden: Françoys Hackius, 1651. (Dutch)
Bohlen, Peter von (tr.). Die Sprüche des Bhartriharis. Aus dem Sanskrit metrisch übertragen. Hamburg: Perthes-Besser & Mauke. (German)

SA_GK22_subhashitasataka.title: Subhāṣitaśataka
SA_GK22_subhashitasataka.summary: A collection of subhāṣitas (gnomic and didactic Sanskrit verses). The e-text file contains no text.
SA_GK22_subhashitasataka.attribution: Unidentified. The e-text is empty and the title is generic.

SA_GK22_valsubhu.title: Subhāṣitāvalī (verses 1–1040)
SA_GK22_valsubhu.author: Vallabhadeva
SA_GK22_valsubhu.summary: The Subhāṣitāvalī ('A Garland of Eloquent Sayings') is a premier Sanskrit poetic anthology compiled by Vallabhadeva. The complete anthology comprises 3,527 verses according to Peterson's edition, citing various poets spanning classical Sanskrit literature. This digital file covers verses 1 to 1040, including invocations to deities (devatāstuti), gnomic and moral epigrams, and anyokti verses.
SA_GK22_valsubhu.attribution: Vallabhadeva is the compiler of this anthology, a compendium of Sanskrit verse.
SA_GK22_valsubhu.edition: The Subhāṣitāvali of Vallabhadeva, edited by Peter Peterson and Paṇḍit Durgāprasāda, Bombay: Education Society's Press, 1886 (Bombay Sanskrit Series).
SA_GK22_valsubhu.coverage: partial — Contains verses 1 to 1040 only (out of 3527 verses according to the edition by P. Peterson, Bombay 1886).

SA_GK22_vidsrgpu.title: Subhāṣitaratnakoṣa
SA_GK22_vidsrgpu.author: Vidyākara
SA_GK22_vidsrgpu.summary: The Subhāṣitaratnakoṣa ('Treasury of Well-Turned Verse') is an anthology of classical Sanskrit court poetry compiled by the Buddhist scholar Vidyākara around 1100 CE (with an expanded recension c. 1130 CE) in Bengal. Arranged into 50 thematic sections (vrajyās) encompassing 1,738 stanzas, it collects works from over two hundred poets, opening with Buddhist and Hindu devotional hymns and progressing through the seasons, love, social types, nature, gnomic sayings, and praise of poets. The work is a foundational witness to classical kāvya between 700 and 1050 CE, preserving extensive poetic material that would otherwise be entirely lost.
SA_GK22_vidsrgpu.attribution: Compiled by the Buddhist scholar-monk Vidyākara, associated with the Jagaddala Mahāvihāra in Bengal (fl. late 11th to early 12th century CE).
SA_GK22_vidsrgpu.edition: D. D. Kosambi and V. V. Gokhale (eds.), The Subhāṣitaratnakoṣa Compiled by Vidyākara, Harvard Oriental Series 42, Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1957.
SA_GK22_vidsrgpu.coverage: complete — Contains all 50 vrajyās (thematic sections) and 1,738 verses comprising the complete expanded recension of the anthology as edited in HOS 42.
translations: Daniel H. H. Ingalls, An Anthology of Sanskrit Court Poetry: Vidyākara's 'Subhāṣitaratnakoṣa', Harvard Oriental Series 44, Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1965. (English)

SA_GK22_vidsripu.title: Subhāṣitaratnakoṣa
SA_GK22_vidsripu.author: Vidyākara
SA_GK22_vidsripu.summary: The Subhāṣitaratnakoṣa is a major classical Sanskrit poetry anthology compiled in Bengal by the Buddhist monk Vidyākara (c. late 11th–early 12th century CE). Arranged into 50 thematic sections (vrajyās), it encompasses 1,738 verses opening with praises of the Buddha, Bodhisattvas, and Hindu deities before surveying seasons, eros, character types, and reflections on poetry. It remains an invaluable witness to classical kāvya, preserving otherwise lost compositions by numerous celebrated and minor poets.
SA_GK22_vidsripu.attribution: Compiled by Vidyākara, a Buddhist monk at Jagaddala Monastery in Bengal sometime during the end of the 11th or the beginning of the 12th century.
SA_GK22_vidsripu.edition: The Subhāṣitaratnakoṣa compiled by Vidyākara, edited by D. D. Kosambi and V. V. Gokhale. Cambridge, Massachusetts: Harvard University Press, 1957 (Harvard Oriental Series, 42).
SA_GK22_vidsripu.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all 50 vrajyās (thematic sections) and 1,738 numbered verses plus the maṅgala verse (VidSrk_0.1 to VidSrk_50.41 / *(1738)*), concluding with Vidyākara's epilogue and scribal colophons.
translations: Ingalls, Daniel H. H. An Anthology of Sanskrit Court Poetry: Vidyākara's "Subhāṣitaratnakoṣa". Cambridge, Massachusetts: Harvard University Press, 1965 (Harvard Oriental Series, 44). (English)

SA_GK23_jonart.title: Rājataraṅgiṇī
SA_GK23_jonart.author: Jonarāja
SA_GK23_jonart.summary: The Rājataraṅgiṇī of Jonarāja is a Sanskrit chronicle continuing Kalhaṇa's history of Kashmir.

SA_GK23_kaulpradsam_u.title: Pradeśasaṃgraha (entries 1–34)
SA_GK23_kaulpradsam_u.author: Govind Kaul
SA_GK23_kaulpradsam_u.summary: The Pradeśasaṃgraha is a topographical and geographical treatise compiled by Govind Kaul commenting on Kalhaṇa's Rājataraṅgiṇī. Arranged according to the verses of the Rājataraṅgiṇī, it examines settlements, rivers, shrines, and sacred sites, drawing on texts such as the Nīlamatapurāṇa and documenting local Kashmiri names and traditions.
SA_GK23_kaulpradsam_u.attribution: A work by Govind Kaul preserved in MS Stein or d 25 (listed as MS 128: Rājataraṅgiṇīpradeśavyākhyā in Clauson's catalogue of the Stein Collection, Bodleian Library).
SA_GK23_kaulpradsam_u.edition: Katrin Züfle: Govind Kaul: Pradeśasaṃgraha - Erstedition eines unikalen Manuskripts zur historischen Toponymie Kaśmīrs. Halle-Wittenberg 2014: Martin-Luther-Universität (unpublished Magister Thesis).
SA_GK23_kaulpradsam_u.coverage: partial — Partial text; covers approx. half the text of MS Stein or d 25 (MS 128), ending with 'anyathā kutrāpi vārttaitayor na labhyata iti bhadram //'.

SA_GP10_bhp_01u.title: Bhāgavatapurāṇa (skandha 1)
SA_GP10_bhp_01u.summary: The first skandha of the Bhāgavatapurāṇa establishes the narrative, theological, and devotional frame for the scripture. At an assembly in Naimiṣa forest, the sages headed by Śaunaka ask the bard Sūta to recount the essence of all sacred teachings, leading to the framing narrative of Vyāsa, who after composing the Mahābhārata finds inner peace only when Nārada instructs him to celebrate Kṛṣṇa's divine manifestations directly. The skandha recounts the previous birth of Nārada, the birth and reign of King Parīkṣit, the departure of the Pāṇḍavas, and the curse placed upon Parīkṣit to die in seven days, prompting the king's renunciation on the banks of the Ganges and his reception of Śuka's teaching.
SA_GP10_bhp_01u.attribution: Traditionally ascribed to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa, who within the narrative frame of the first skandha is guided by Nārada to compose the work to attain spiritual tranquility. Statistical dating models estimate a 95% credible interval of 888 CE – 1002 CE (posterior median 945 CE).
SA_GP10_bhp_01u.coverage: partial — Skandha 1 complete (adhyāyas 1–19, ending at 1.19.40); the full Bhāgavatapurāṇa has 12 skandhas (SA_GP10_bhp_01u–12u).
translations: Burnouf, Eugène, Le Bhāgavata Purâṇa ou histoire poétique de Krichna, Paris: Imprimerie Royale, 1840. (French)

SA_GP10_bhp_02u.title: Bhāgavatapurāṇa (skandha 2)
SA_GP10_bhp_02u.summary: The second book (Dvitīya Skandha) of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa contains 10 chapters in which the sage Śuka instructs King Parīkṣit on liberation, the practice of hearing the divine glories (śravaṇa), and meditation on Viṣṇu's cosmic form (virāṭ-rūpa). It details the stages of yogic departure, outlines cosmogony through the dialogue of Brahmā and Nārada, preserves the foundational four-verse summary (catuḥślokī-bhāgavata, 2.9.33–36), and defines the ten characteristic topics (lakṣaṇas) of a Mahāpurāṇa.
SA_GP10_bhp_02u.attribution: Modern historical-critical statistical dating models estimate the date of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa to approximately the 8th–11th centuries CE (median 897 CE).
SA_GP10_bhp_02u.coverage: partial — Skandha 2 complete (adhyāyas 1–10, ending at 2.10.51); the full Bhāgavatapurāṇa has 12 skandhas.
translations: Burnouf, Eugène (trans.), Le Bhāgavata Purâṇa ou histoire poétique de Krichna, Paris, 1840. (French)

SA_GP10_bhp_03u.title: Bhāgavatapurāṇa (skandha 3)
SA_GP10_bhp_03u.summary: The third skandha of the Bhāgavatapurāṇa comprises 33 chapters framed around the dialogue between Vidura and the sage Maitreya. It details the secondary cosmic creation (visarga) through Brahmā, cosmology, and the division of time from atomic units (paramāṇu) to kalpas. It relates the descent of the Varāha avatāra to lift the earth from the cosmic waters and slay the demon Hiraṇyākṣa, and concludes with the teachings of Kapila to his mother Devahūti, synthesizing Sāṅkhya metaphysics with the path of bhakti-yoga.
SA_GP10_bhp_03u.coverage: partial — Skandha 3 only: adhyāyas 1–33, ending at verse 3.33.37 (verse markers BhP_03.xx.yyy).

SA_GP10_bhp_04u.title: Bhāgavatapurāṇa (skandha 4)
SA_GP10_bhp_04u.summary: The fourth skandha (book) of the Bhāgavata-Purāṇa elaborates on secondary creation (visarga) through the lineages and histories of the daughters of Svāyambhuva Manu. It recounts the conflict between Śiva and Dakṣa leading to the destruction of Dakṣa's sacrifice and Satī's self-immolation, the ascetic devotion and cosmic elevation of child-bhakta Dhruva, and the reign and earth-leveling governance of King Pṛthu. The book culminates in the story of the Pracetasas and Nārada's philosophical allegory of King Purañjana, which illustrates the bondage and liberation of the embodied soul (jīva).
SA_GP10_bhp_04u.coverage: partial — Skandha 4 only, adhyāyas 1–31, ending at verse BhP_04.31.031/2.

SA_GP10_bhp_05u.title: Bhāgavatapurāṇa (skandha 5)
SA_GP10_bhp_05u.summary: The fifth book (skandha) of the Bhāgavata-Purāṇa opens with the genealogical history and spiritual narratives of King Priyavrata and his lineage, prominently detailing the biographies of the renunciant king Ṛṣabha (also honored in Jainism as the first tīrthaṅkara) and the avadhūta sage Jaḍa Bharata. The second half of the book (adhyāyas 16–26) constitutes the Purāṇa's comprehensive cosmography (bhuvana-kośa), detailing the geography of Jambūdvīpa, the surrounding concentric ring continents and oceans, the celestial movements of luminaries, the subterranean realms (pātāla), and the various hellish worlds (naraka).
SA_GP10_bhp_05u.coverage: partial — Skandha 5 only, apparently complete: adhyāyas 1–26, ending with verse 5.26.39 (verse markers BhP_05.xx.yyy).

SA_GP10_bhp_06u.title: Bhāgavatapurāṇa (skandha 6)
SA_GP10_bhp_06u.summary: The sixth skandha (book) of the Bhāgavatapurāṇa centers upon the themes of divine grace, the salvific efficacy of devotion (bhakti), and the repetition of the divine name (nāma-saṅkīrtana). Its central narratives begin with the deliverance of the wayward Brahmin Ajāmila through the utterance of 'Nārāyaṇa' at death, followed by the revelation of the protective Nārāyaṇa-kavaca, Dakṣa's genealogy, and his curse upon Nārada. The middle section narrates the war between the devas and the virtuous asura Vṛtra, who is slain by Indra using the vajra forged from the ascetic Dadhīci's bones, and recounts Vṛtra's previous life as King Citraketu. The book closes with Diti's performance of the Puṃsavana vrata and the miraculous emergence of the Maruts.
SA_GP10_bhp_06u.attribution: A statistical model estimates dating for the text with a 95% credible interval of 778 CE – 1007 CE (posterior median: 889 CE).
SA_GP10_bhp_06u.coverage: partial — Skandha 6 only, adhyāyas 1–19, ending with verse 6.19.28 (verse markers BhP_06.xx.yyy).

SA_GP10_bhp_07u.title: Bhāgavatapurāṇa (skandha 7)
SA_GP10_bhp_07u.summary: The seventh skandha of the Bhāgavatapurāṇa relates the narrative of Prahlāda and his devotion, the appearance of the man-lion form (narasiṃha / na mṛgaṃ na mānuṣam) from a pillar to protect his servant, and teachings on dharma, including duties of the stages of life (such as vānaprastha) and sacred places, delivered by Nārada.
SA_GP10_bhp_07u.coverage: partial — Skandha 7: adhyāyas 1–15, ending at 7.15.80 (BhP_07.01.001 to BhP_07.15.080).

SA_GP10_bhp_08u.title: Bhāgavatapurāṇa (skandha 8)
SA_GP10_bhp_08u.summary: The eighth skandha (book) of the Bhāgavatapurāṇa is structured around the cyclical epochs of the fourteen Manus (manvantaras) and the cosmic descents (avatāras) of Viṣṇu associated with them. It narrates several of the tradition's most renowned myths: the salvation of the elephant king Gajendra (Gajendramokṣa), the churning of the milk ocean (samudramanthana) accompanied by the emergence of amṛta and the manifestations of Kūrma, Dhanvantari, and the enchantress Mohinī, and Viṣṇu's descent as the dwarf Vāmana to reclaim the three worlds from the righteous demon king Bali. The book concludes with the story of the Matsya avatāra, who instructs King Satyavrata during the cosmic dissolution.
SA_GP10_bhp_08u.attribution: Modern statistical dating estimates the text to c. 777–1006 CE (median 893 CE).
SA_GP10_bhp_08u.coverage: partial — Skandha 8 only: adhyāyas 1–24, ending with verse 8.24.61 (verse markers BhP_08.xx.yyy).

SA_GP10_bhp_09u.title: Bhāgavatapurāṇa (skandha 9)
SA_GP10_bhp_09u.summary: The ninth book (skandha) of the Bhāgavatapurāṇa comprises 24 adhyāyas focused primarily on vaṃśānucarita (genealogies and historical accounts of legendary royal dynasties). It traces the lineages of the Solar (Sūryavaṃśa) and Lunar (Candravaṃśa) lines descending from Vaivasvata Manu, presenting narrative episodes such as the gender transformation of Sudyumna/Ilā, King Ambarīṣa's piety in the face of Durvāsas's wrath, Sagara, Hariścandra, and a summary of the Rāmakathā. The canto culminates in tracing the descendants of Puru and Yadu down to Śūra and Vasudeva, setting the genealogical and narrative stage for the advent of Kṛṣṇa in Skandha 10.
SA_GP10_bhp_09u.coverage: partial — Skandha 9 only, apparently complete: adhyāyas 1–24, ending with verse 9.24.67 (verse markers BhP_09.xx.yyy).

SA_GP10_bhp_10u.title: Bhāgavatapurāṇa (skandha 10)
SA_GP10_bhp_10u.summary: The tenth book (skandha) of the Bhāgavatapurāṇa comprises 90 chapters and forms the theological and devotional core of the Purāṇa, recounting the life of Kṛṣṇa. Divided traditionally into two halves (Pūrvārdha, chs. 1–49; Uttarārdha, chs. 50–90), it describes Kṛṣṇa's miraculous birth and childhood in Vraja/Gokula, the slaying of various demons, the lifting of Mount Govardhana, the autumnal love-dance (rāsalīlā) with the gopīs, the slaying of Kaṃsa in Mathurā, and his subsequent establishment in Dvārakā. It is the principal scriptural source for Kṛṣṇa devotion in later bhakti traditions.
SA_GP10_bhp_10u.coverage: partial — Skandha 10 only: adhyāyas 1–90, ending at verse 10.90.50 (verse markers BhP_10.xx.yyy).

SA_GP10_bhp_11u.title: Bhāgavatapurāṇa (skandha 11)
SA_GP10_bhp_11u.summary: The eleventh book (skandha) of the Bhāgavatapurāṇa narrates the events leading to the end of the Dvāpara Yuga, including the curse of the sages on the Yadu dynasty, their tragic fratricidal collapse at Prabhāsa, and Kṛṣṇa's ascension to his transcendent realm. The theological and philosophical core of the book (adhyāyas 6/7–29) is the Uddhavagītā, an extended exposition imparted by Kṛṣṇa to his companion Uddhava concerning jñāna, bhakti, renunciation, the nature of prakṛti and puruṣa, and the twenty-four spiritual teachers of the Avadhūta. It is among the most commented-upon parts of the Purāṇa in Vaiṣṇava traditions.
SA_GP10_bhp_11u.coverage: partial — Skandha 11 only, adhyāyas 1–31, ending with verse 11.31.28 (verse markers BhP_11.xx.yyy).

SA_GP10_bhp_12u.title: Bhāgavatapurāṇa (skandha 12)
SA_GP10_bhp_12u.summary: The twelfth and concluding skandha (book) of the Bhāgavatapurāṇa opens with a prophetic account of post-Mahābhārata royal dynasties up through the Kali Yuga (including the Nandas, Mauryas, and Śuṅgas), followed by a description of the moral, spiritual, and physical degeneration of humanity in the Kali age and the advent of the Kalki avatāra.
