It includes the Bhūmigītā (Song of the Earth) on the transient folly of kings, expounds the four kinds of cosmic dissolution (pralaya), and concludes King Parīkṣit's narrative with his death by Takṣaka after receiving final teachings on the immortal Ātman from Śuka. The book then covers the lineage and preservation of the Vedic śākhās and the Purāṇas, the spiritual vision of sage Mārkaṇḍeya, an overall thematic summary of the entire purāṇa, and final benedictory verses extolling devotion through nāmasaṅkīrtana.
SA_GP10_bhp_12u.attribution: Traditionally ascribed to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa (Bādarāyaṇa), who within the narrative imparts it to his son Śuka, who then recites it to King Parīkṣit on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
SA_GP10_bhp_12u.coverage: partial — Skandha 12 only, apparently complete: adhyāyas 1–13, ending with the standard final verse 12.13.23 (verse markers BhP_12.xx.yyy). The full Purāṇa has 12 skandhas; skandhas 1–12 are separate catalog entries (SA_GP10_bhp_01u–12u).

SA_GP10_bhpc101u.title: Bhāgavatapurāṇa with Bhāvārthadīpikā (skandha 10, chapters 29–33)
SA_GP10_bhpc101u.author: Śrīdharasvāmin
SA_GP10_bhpc101u.summary: Chapters 29–33 of the tenth skandha of the Bhāgavatapurāṇa, known as the Rāsa-pañcādhyāyī ('five chapters on the rāsa dance'), narrate Kṛṣṇa's autumn-night circle dance (rāsalīlā) with the cowherd maidens (gopīs) of Vraja, his temporary disappearance to dispel their pride, their anguished laments and song of longing (Gopīgīta), and his reunion with them in ecstatic devotional union. This section is universally regarded as the aesthetic and devotional climax of the Purāṇa. The included commentary, the Bhāvārthadīpikā by Śrīdharasvāmin (c. 14th century), interprets the erotic-devotional līlā within an Advaita-theistic framework as the triumph over desire (kāmavijaya) and served as the authoritative baseline for all subsequent Vaiṣṇava hermeneutics.
SA_GP10_bhpc101u.attribution: The commentary Bhāvārthadīpikā was authored by Śrīdharasvāmin, who is expressly named in the chapter colophon verse (v. 10.33.40 end: 'seyaṃ śrīparamānandaseviśrīdharanirmitā / śrībhāgavatabhāvārthadīpikā daśamāśrayā').
SA_GP10_bhpc101u.edition: Bombay: Nirnaya Sagar 1920 (repr. Caukhamba Surabharati Prakasan, Varanasi 1988).
SA_GP10_bhpc101u.coverage: excerpt — Contains skandha 10, chapters 29–33 (the five chapters comprising the Rāsa-pañcādhyāyī) of the Bhāgavatapurāṇa along with Śrīdharasvāmin's Bhāvārthadīpikā and select editorial footnotes.
translations: Burnouf, Eugène (tr.). Le Bhâgavata Purâṇa ou histoire poétique de Krichna. 1840. (French)

SA_GP11_nmtppu.title: Nīlamatapurāṇa
SA_GP11_nmtppu.summary: The Nīlamata-purāṇa is an extant work of the Māhātmya type from Kashmir concerning the worship of the Nāga Nīlamata, acknowledged by Kalhaṇa as a source.
SA_GP11_nmtppu.attribution: The Nīlamata-purāṇa is a work of the Māhātmya type from Kashmir associated with the worship of the Nāga Nīlamata.

SA_GP12_brndp1_u.title: Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa (Pūrvabhāga)
SA_GP12_brndp1_u.summary: The Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa is one of the eighteen major Mahāpurāṇas, closely affiliated with the Vāyupurāṇa, with which it shares substantial archaic text dating to the mid-first millennium CE. This e-text comprises the Pūrvabhāga (adhyāyas 1–38), containing the Prakriyāpāda (adhyāyas 1–5) and the Anuṣaṅgapāda (adhyāyas 6–38). It covers classic pañcalakṣaṇa subjects including the origin of the cosmos from the golden egg (brahmāṇḍa), the calculations of yugas and kalpas, geography, astronomy, and the genealogies of the manvantaras.
SA_GP12_brndp1_u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete Pūrvabhāga (adhyāyas 1–38), comprising the Prakriyāpāda (adhyāyas 1–5) and Anuṣaṅgapāda (adhyāyas 6–38). The subsequent sections (Madhyamabhāga/Upodghātapāda, Uttarabhāga/Upasaṃhārapāda, and Lalitāmāhātmya) are found in other files.

SA_GP12_brndp2_u.title: Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa (Madhyabhāga: Upodghātapāda)
SA_GP12_brndp2_u.summary: The Madhyabhāga of the Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa consists entirely of the third major pāda, the Upodghātapāda (chapters 1–74). It details the genealogies (vaṃśa and vaṃśānucarita) of Prajāpatis, Ṛṣis, and Pitṛs, as well as an extensive Śrāddhakalpa (chapters 9–20). It incorporates a substantial narrative cycle on the legends of Bhārgava Rāma (Paraśurāma) and Kārtavīryārjuna (chapters 21–58), before detailing the solar (Sūryavaṃśa) and lunar (Candravāṃśa) royal dynasties and concluding with a prophetic catalog of future Kaliyuga lineages (chapter 74).
SA_GP12_brndp2_u.attribution: Colophons designate the text as vāyuprokta.
SA_GP12_brndp2_u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete Madhyabhāga (Upodghātapāda, chapters 1–74) of the Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa, except for a known lacuna of verses 2.70.3–49 as noted in the GRETIL source header.

SA_GP12_brndp3_u.title: Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa (part 3: Uttarabhāga)
SA_GP12_brndp3_u.summary: The Uttarabhāga (Part 3) forms the concluding section of the Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa. It begins with the Upasaṃhārapāda (adhyāyas 1–4), describing manvantaras and cosmic destruction. The remainder (adhyāyas 5–44) consists of the Lalitopākhyāna, structured as a dialogue between Hayagrīva and Agastya describing the exploits of Lalitā, Śrīvidyā, and related narratives.
SA_GP12_brndp3_u.attribution: The overarching Purāṇic frame is narrated by the Sūta to the sages, whereas the Lalitopākhyāna is framed as a dialogue between Hayagrīva and the sage Agastya.
SA_GP12_brndp3_u.edition: Bombay: Venkatesvara Steam Press (or a reprint thereof, e.g. ed. J. L. Shastri, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1973). Revised by Raghunātha.
SA_GP12_brndp3_u.coverage: partial — Contains the Uttarabhāga (Part 3), running from adhyāya 1, verse 1 to adhyāya 44, verse 151. This comprises the Upasaṃhārapāda (adhyāyas 1–4) and the Lalitopākhyāna (adhyāyas 5–44).

SA_GP12_dbhp_dgu.title: Devīgītā
SA_GP12_dbhp_dgu.summary: The Devīgītā comprises chapters 31 through 40 of the seventh skandha of the Devībhāgavata-Purāṇa (507 verses). At the request of Himālaya, the Devī agrees to expound the secret meaning of Vedic revelation, teaching that she is brahma, creating the world through māyā, and explaining brahmajñāna, sacred places, and instructions for devotion.
SA_GP12_dbhp_dgu.attribution: Embedded in the Devībhāgavata-Purāṇa (Skandha 7, adhyāyas 31–40), which is traditionally attributed to Vyāsa.
SA_GP12_dbhp_dgu.coverage: complete — Complete: 10 adhyāyas, dual-numbered Dg_1.1 = DbhP_7,31.1 to Dg_10.45 = DbhP_7,40.45. Ends with 'iti devīgītāyāṃ daśamo 'dhyāyaḥ devīgītā samāptā' and the DBhP colophon 'iti śrīdevībhāgavate mahāpurāṇe saptamaskandhe devīgītāyāṃ catvāriṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ'.
translations: The Sri Mad Devi Bhagavatam -23), englische Übersetzung von Swami Vijnanananda, Allahabad. (English)

SA_GP12_garup2_u.title: Garuḍapurāṇa (part 2: Pretakhaṇḍa)
SA_GP12_garup2_u.summary: The Pretakhaṇḍa (variously styled Dharmakāṇḍa, Pretakalpa, or Uttarakhaṇḍa) forms the eschatological second division of the Garuḍapurāṇa, comprising 49 chapters in the Venkatesvara recension. Framed as a dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and his mount Garuḍa, the text expounds the post-mortem journey of the soul (jīva), the punishments in the realms and torments of Yama (yātanā), and liberation from the condition of a wandering ghost (pretatva). It provides comprehensive prescriptions for post-mortem rites (antyeṣṭi), ancestral offerings (śrāddha), and ritual gifting (dāna), serving as the standard scriptural authority recited in Hindu funerary rituals.
SA_GP12_garup2_u.attribution: The text is framed internally as an eschatological dialogue between Kṛṣṇa (Viṣṇu) and Garuḍa, narrated by Sūta to Śaunaka and the assembled ṛṣis at Naimiṣāraṇya.
SA_GP12_garup2_u.coverage: partial — Complete text of Part 2 (Pretakhaṇḍa / Dharmakāṇḍa / Uttarakhaṇḍa) in 49 adhyāyas (chapters 1–49), complete from the opening maṅgala to the final colophon, but representing only the second division of the Garuḍapurāṇa.
translations: M. N. Dutt (trans.), Garuḍa-purāṇam, in Wealth of India, Calcutta. (English)

SA_GP12_garup3_u.title: Garuḍapurāṇa (Brahmakāṇḍa)
SA_GP12_garup3_u.summary: The Brahmakāṇḍa (tṛtīyāṃśa of the Uttarakhaṇḍa) constitutes a division of the Garuḍapurāṇa, comprising 29 chapters. Framed as a discourse between Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa (kṛṣṇagaruḍasaṃvāda) narrated to Śaunaka and other ṛṣis at Naimiṣāraṇya, it expounds Vaiṣṇava theology, devotions to Nārāyaṇa/Viṣṇu and Śrīnivāsa, cosmology, and related religious themes.
SA_GP12_garup3_u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the mythical sage Vyāsa (Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana). Within the text, it is framed as a discourse between Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa narrated by Sūta to Śaunaka and other ṛṣis at Naimiṣāraṇya.
SA_GP12_garup3_u.coverage: partial — Contains the Brahmakāṇḍa (third book) of the Garuḍapurāṇa, comprising 29 chapters (GarP_3,1.1 through GarP_3,29.70).

SA_GP12_kurmp1_u.title: Kūrmapurāṇa (part 1: Pūrvavibhāga)
SA_GP12_kurmp1_u.summary: The first section (Pūrvavibhāga) of the Kūrmapurāṇa consists of 51 chapters recounting purāṇic cosmogony, creation myths, and the solar and lunar genealogies, framed through the dialogue between Viṣṇu in his tortoise (kūrma) avatāra and King Indradyumna. In addition to primary Purāṇapañcalakṣaṇa themes, it contains prominent tīrthamāhātmyas eulogizing sacred centers such as Prayāga and Vārāṇasī. The text represents an integration of Vaiṣṇava, Pāśupata Śaiva, and Śākta traditions, emphasizing devotion and advaitic metaphysics.
SA_GP12_kurmp1_u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Vyāsa (Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana); framed as Viṣṇu's revelation in his Kūrma incarnation to King Indradyumna, narrated by the Sūta Romaharṣaṇa to the ṛṣis gathered at Naimiṣāraṇya.
SA_GP12_kurmp1_u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete first major division (Pūrvavibhāga, chapters 1–51) of the Kūrmapurāṇa. The second division (Uttaravibhāga, chapters 1–44) is catalogued separately under SA_GP12_kurmp2_u.
translations: Kūrma-purāṇa (1972), herausgegeben von Anand Swarup Gupta und ins Englische übersetzt von Ahibhushan Bhattacharya u. a., Banaras: All-India Kashi Raj Trust. (English)

SA_GP12_kurmp2_u.title: Kūrmapurāṇa (part 2: Uttaravibhāga)
SA_GP12_kurmp2_u.summary: The second part (Uparivibhāga or Uttaravibhāga) of the Kūrmapurāṇa consists of 44 chapters. It opens with the Īśvaragītā (chapters 1–11), an influential philosophical text modeled after the Bhagavadgītā in which Śiva discourses on knowledge, yoga, and liberation, synthesizing Pāśupata-leaning Śaiva theology with Sāṃkhya-Yoga and Advaita Vedānta. This is followed by the Vyāsagītā (chapters 12–34), detailing varṇāśramadharma, ritual conduct, śrāddha rites, and expiations (prāyaścitta), while the final chapters (35–44) treat sacred geography (tīrthamāhātmya, especially Prayāga and Vārāṇasī) and the doctrines of dissolution (pralaya) and secondary creation (pratisarga).
SA_GP12_kurmp2_u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the sage Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa as part of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, with the tortoise avatar (Kūrma) of Viṣṇu and Śiva serving as inner narrators.
SA_GP12_kurmp2_u.edition: Anand Swarup Gupta (ed.), The Kūrma Purāṇa (Critically Edited), Varanasi: All-India Kashiraj Trust, 1971.
SA_GP12_kurmp2_u.coverage: partial — Contains the entire second part (Uparivibhāga / Uttaravibhāga, adhyāyas 1–44, verses 2.1.1–2.44.148) of the Kūrmapurāṇa. The first part (Pūrvavibhāga, adhyāyas 1–51) is catalogued separately as SA_GP12_kurmp1_u.
translations: Ganesh Vasudeo Tagare (trans.), Kūrma Purāņa, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1981. (English)
Ahibhushan Bhattacharya et al. (trans.), Kūrma-purāṇa, Banaras: All-India Kashi Raj Trust, 1972. (English)

SA_GP12_lip_1_pu.title: Liṅgapurāṇa (part 1: Pūrvabhāga)
SA_GP12_lip_1_pu.summary: The Liṅgapurāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas and a principal scripture of medieval Śaivism, distinguished by its strong Pāśupata orientation. This first section, the Pūrvabhāga (adhyāyas 1–108), presents the cosmogony and the primordial revelation of Śiva as an infinite pillar of cosmic fire (liṅgodbhava) confounding Brahmā and Viṣṇu. It treats the twenty-eight avatars of Śiva in the Kali yugas (concluding with Lakulīśa), ritual installation and worship of the liṅga, royal and householder gift rituals (ṣoḍaśamahādāna), sacred geography (Vārāṇasī), and Śaiva yoga disciplines alongside standard Purāṇic genealogies.
SA_GP12_lip_1_pu.attribution: Traditionally narrated by the Sūta paurāṇika in the Naimiṣa forest.
SA_GP12_lip_1_pu.edition: Bombay: Venkatesvara Steam Press, 1906; revised and corrected according to the ed. Calcutta, 1960 (Gurumandal Series No. XV).
SA_GP12_lip_1_pu.coverage: partial — Contains the complete first part (Pūrvabhāga), comprising 108 adhyāyas (LiP 1.1.1–1.108.19).
translations: The Linga-Purāṇa, trans. by a Board of Scholars, 2 vols., Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1973. (English)

SA_GP12_lip_2__u.title: Liṅgapurāṇa (part 2: Uttarabhāga)
SA_GP12_lip_2__u.summary: Chapters 1–55 comprise the entire second section (Uttarabhāga) of the Liṅgapurāṇa. While the initial chapters open with Vaiṣṇava devotional narratives and musical theory centered on the pious singer Kauśika, the bulk of the Uttarabhāga serves as an extensive Śaiva ritual manual detailing liṅga installation, daily pūjā rites, the sixteen great gift ceremonies (ṣoḍaśamahādāna), the significance of holy ashes (bhasma), and Pāśupata yoga practices.
SA_GP12_lip_2__u.coverage: partial — Complete for the Uttarabhāga (part 2), containing all 55 chapters (vv. 2.1.1–2.55.48); partial coverage of the whole Liṅgapurāṇa.
translations: The Linga-Purāṇa, übersetzt von einem Komitee von Forschern, 2 Teile, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1973. (English)

SA_GP12_mkp1-93u.title: Mārkaṇḍeyapurāṇa (chapters 1–93)
SA_GP12_mkp1-93u.summary: The Mārkaṇḍeyapurāṇa is considered one of the oldest and most narrative-driven of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, characterized by its general lack of sectarian bias. It opens with the sage Jaimini consulting four enlightened birds in the Vindhya mountains to resolve four perplexities left unresolved in the Mahābhārata, proceeding through discourses on cosmogony, dharma, eschatology, yoga, and the manvantara lineages. Adhyāyas 81–93 constitute the celebrated Devīmāhātmya (Durgāsaptaśatī), the seminal scripture of Hindu Śāktism celebrating the Supreme Goddess's subjugation of the demons Madhu, Kaiṭabha, Mahiṣāsura, and Śumbha-Niśumbha.
SA_GP12_mkp1-93u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the mythical sage Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa (indicated in the opening mangala verse 'śrīmanmaharṣivedavyāsapraṇītaṃ'). The narrative frame is presented as an exposition given by four wise, dharma-abiding birds (Droṇa's sons) to Jaimini on the instruction of the sage Mārkaṇḍeya.
SA_GP12_mkp1-93u.coverage: partial — Adhyāyas 1–93 only (MarkP_Mang.1–3, MarkP_1.1 ... 93.17). The text stops at the final colophon of the Devīmāhātmya ('... devīmāhātmye varapradānaṃ nāma trinavatitamo 'dhyāyaḥ'). GRETIL: 'Adhy. 94ff. not available at present'.
translations: F. Eden Pargiter (tr.), The Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: Translated with Notes, Calcutta: Asiatic Society of Bengal, 1904. (English)
Manmatha Nath Dutt (tr.), Markandeya Puranam: A Prose English Translation. (English)

SA_GP12_mtp176pu.title: Matsyapurāṇa (chapters 1–176)
SA_GP12_mtp176pu.summary: The Matsyapurāṇa is one of the eighteen classical Mahāpurāṇas, framed as an instruction delivered by Viṣṇu in his fish avatāra to King Manu during the cosmic deluge. This text segment contains adhyāyas 1–176, covering cosmogony, genealogies of the solar and lunar dynasties, rites and vratas, extensive descriptions of pilgrimage places (notably Prayāga and the Narmadā), and mythological cycles including the destruction of Tripura and the birth and penances of Pārvatī.
SA_GP12_mtp176pu.attribution: The text is framed as an exposition narrated by the bard Sūta to the sages gathered at Naimiṣāraṇya, recounting the instruction given by Viṣṇu in his Matsya (fish) avatāra.
SA_GP12_mtp176pu.coverage: partial — Contains adhyāyas 1–176 only (out of 291 chapters of the standard vulgate Matsyapurāṇa).
translations: Translated by Taluqdar of Oudh, Sacred Books of the Hindus (SBH) 17. (English)

SA_GP12_nardp1_u.title: Nāradapurāṇa (Pūrvabhāga, chapters 2–125)
SA_GP12_nardp1_u.summary: The Pūrvabhāga of the Nāradapurāṇa (or Nāradīyapurāṇa) is an encyclopedic Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa structured into pādas, framed as teachings given by the Sanakādi sages (including Sanatkumāra) to Nārada. It covers topics such as dharma, rituals, worship of Nārāyaṇa/Hari, and treatments of the Vedāṅgas (auxiliary sciences of the Veda).
SA_GP12_nardp1_u.attribution: Traditionally framed as a dialogue involving the Sanakādi sages and Nārada.
SA_GP12_nardp1_u.coverage: partial — Contains the Pūrvabhāga (First Part) of the Nāradapurāṇa, chapters 2–125 (NarP 1,2.1 to 1,125.50). Chapter 1 is omitted from the file.
translations: The Nārada-Purāṇa, trans. and annot. by G. V. Tagare, Part 1, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1980. (English)

SA_GP12_nardp2_u.title: Nāradapurāṇa (Uttarabhāga, chapters 1–43)
SA_GP12_nardp2_u.summary: The uttarabhāga of the Nāradapurāṇa is a late classical to medieval Vaiṣṇava Purāṇic text emphasizing bhakti, vow observance, and sacred geography. Its first half centers upon the narrative of King Rukmāṅgada and the apsaras Mohinī, demonstrating the supreme efficacy of fasting on Ekādaśī and Dvādaśī. This partial e-text encompasses chapters 1 through 43, terminating at the conclusion of the Gaṅgāmāhātmya section before the subsequent pilgrimage guides to Gayā, Kāśī, and Puruṣottamakṣetra.
SA_GP12_nardp2_u.attribution: Internal narrative frames feature dialogues between Vasiṣṭha and King Māndhātṛ, and Vasu and Mohinī.
SA_GP12_nardp2_u.coverage: partial — Contains only chapters 1 through 43 of the uttarabhāga, ending with the colophon of chapter 43 (iti śrībṛhannāradīyapurāṇottarabhāge mohinīvasusaṃvāde gaṅgāmāhātmye pūjādikathaṃ nāma tricatvāriṃśattamo 'dhyāyaḥ).
translations: The Nārada-Purāṇa, translated and annotated by G.V. Tagare, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1980. (English)

SA_GP12_narsippu.title: Narasiṃhapurāṇa
SA_GP12_narsippu.summary: The Narasiṃhapurāṇa is an early Vaiṣṇava Upapurāṇa consisting of 68 adhyāyas dedicated primarily to the worship of Viṣṇu in his man-lion (Narasiṃha) avatāra. Framed as a dialogue between Sūta and the sage Bharadvāja, it treats classical purāṇic themes including creation, geography, dynastic genealogies, varṇāśramadharma, and the avatāras of Viṣṇu (particularly Prahlāda's deliverance and an extensive Rāmacaritam).
SA_GP12_narsippu.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Vyāsa (indicated by the mangala verse to Vedavyāsa); framed as an interlocution between Sūta and Bharadvāja and other sages.
SA_GP12_narsippu.edition: Siddheswar Jena: The Narasiṃha Purāṇam. Delhi: Nag Publ. 1987.
SA_GP12_narsippu.coverage: complete — Complete text in 68 adhyāyas (chapters 1–68), ending with the māhātmya section in adhyāya 68.

SA_GP12_sivap7_u.title: Śivapurāṇa (Vāyavīyasaṃhitā only)
SA_GP12_sivap7_u.summary: The Vāyavīyasaṃhitā forms the seventh saṃhitā of the Śivapurāṇa. Structured in two divisions—Pūrvakhaṇḍa and Uttarakhaṇḍa—it includes teachings attributed to Upamanyu and Vyāsa, expounding devotion to Śiva, liṅga worship, and Śaiva doctrines.
SA_GP12_sivap7_u.coverage: partial — Contains the seventh saṃhitā (Vāyavīyasaṃhitā) of the Śivapurāṇa in two parts: Pūrvakhaṇḍa and Uttarakhaṇḍa (ending at adhyāya 41, concluding with the vyāsopadeśaśrīśivamahāpurāṇamāhātmyavarṇana).

SA_GP12_skprevku.title: Skandapurāṇa (Revākhaṇḍa only)
SA_GP12_skprevku.summary: The Revākhaṇḍa is a sacred geographical and pilgrimage text celebrating the holy sites along the course of the Narmadā (Revā) River in Central India. Structured largely around dialogues between the sage Mārkaṇḍeya and Yudhiṣṭhira, the work delineates pilgrimage and circumambulation along both the northern and southern banks, detailing origin legends, shrines, and devotional benefits. As noted by the contributor, Jürgen Neuss, this 116-chapter recension is the genuine Skandapurāṇa Revākhaṇḍa, distinct from the 232-chapter text of the Vāyupurāṇa tradition wrongly assigned to SkP 5.3 in the Veṅkaṭeśvara edition (Bombay: 1910).
SA_GP12_skprevku.attribution: Traditionally classified as a khaṇḍa of the Skandapurāṇa; framed primarily as a dialogue between the sage Mārkaṇḍeya and King Yudhiṣṭhira.
SA_GP12_skprevku.edition: Oṅkārānanda Giri (ed.), Atha Bṛhat-Śrīnarmadāpurāṇam Revākhaṇḍam (parivardhita tṛtīya saṃskaraṇa). Hośaṅgābāda: Jñānasatra Prakāśana Nyāsa, 1994.
SA_GP12_skprevku.coverage: partial — Contains the complete Revākhaṇḍa belonging to the Skandapurāṇa recension in 116 adhyāyas (1.1–116.22), which constitutes a single section of the vast Skandapurāṇa corpus.

SA_GP12_vamp__u.title: Vāmanapurāṇa
SA_GP12_vamp__u.summary: The Vāmanapurāṇa is one of the eighteen traditional Mahāpurāṇas, nominally named after Viṣṇu's dwarf avatāra who subdues Bali. Despite its formal classification as a Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa, the majority of its narrative content is eclectic, with substantial sections devoted to Śaiva and Śākta mythology, including the myths of Satī and Pārvatī, Śiva's penance, the birth of Kārttikeya, and the goddess's battles with Mahiṣāsura and Andhaka. It also contains detailed sacred geography and pilgrim itineraries (māhātmya), focusing heavily on Kurukṣetra, Sthāṇutīrtha, and Prayāga. Modern scholars assign the compilation of the surviving recension to between the 9th and 11th centuries CE.
SA_GP12_vamp__u.attribution: Within the internal narrative framework, the Purāṇa is narrated by the sage Pulastya in response to inquiries by Nārada.
SA_GP12_vamp__u.edition: The Vāmana Purāṇa: Critically Edited, ed. Anand Swarup Gupta, Varanasi: All-India Kashiraj Trust, 1967.
SA_GP12_vamp__u.coverage: complete — Contains all 69 adhyāyas of the critically constituted text of the Vāmanapurāṇa. The 28-adhyāya Saromāhātmya (dealing with Kurukṣetra tīrthas), which appears interpolated after adhyāya 23 in certain northern manuscripts and vulgate editions (yielding 95 chapters total), was edited as a separate section/appendix by Gupta and is provided separately in GRETIL as vamp_s_u.
translations: Vāmana-purāṇa, ed. Anand Swarup Gupta, trans. S. M. Mukhopadhyaya et al., Banaras: All-India Kashiraj Trust, 1968. (English)

SA_GP12_vampsm_u.title: Vāmanapurāṇa (Saromāhātmya)
SA_GP12_vampsm_u.summary: The Saromāhātmya is a 27-chapter pilgrimage manual (tīrthamāhātmya) preserved as an insertion or appendix to the Vāmanapurāṇa (placed between chapters 23 and 24 in the All-India Kashiraj Trust critical edition). Framed as a discourse delivered by the bard Lomaharṣaṇa to the ṛṣis assembled in Kurujāṅgala, it provides an elaborate eulogy of Kurukṣetra and its sacred lakes, notably Brahmasaras (identified with Rāmahrada and Samantapañcaka) and Sannihita-saras, alongside sacred sites along the Sarasvatī and Dṛṣadvatī rivers. The text blends pilgrimage itineraries with local mythology, celebrating Sthāṇutīrtha and recounting both Vaiṣṇava legends (the Vāmana avatāra) and Śaiva myths.
SA_GP12_vampsm_u.attribution: Framed as narrated by the Sūta Lomaharṣaṇa to the sages of Kurujāṅgala.
SA_GP12_vampsm_u.edition: Vāmana-Purāṇa, Saromāhātmya (inserted after Adhy. 23), edited by A. S. Gupta. Varanasi: All India Kashiraj Trust, 1967.
SA_GP12_vampsm_u.coverage: complete — Contains all 27 adhyāyas of the Saromāhātmya (verses VamPSm_1.1 to VamPSm_27.35), inserted after adhyāya 23 in the Kashiraj Trust critical edition.
translations: Vāmana-purāṇa, edited by Anand Swarup Gupta and translated into English by S. M. Mukhopadhyaya et al. Banaras: All-India Kashiraj Trust, 1968. (English)

SA_GP12_vd2127_u.title: Viṣṇudharmottarapurāṇa (khaṇḍa 2, chapter 127: Atharvavidhikathana)
SA_GP12_vd2127_u.summary: This text constitutes Chapter 127 of Khaṇḍa 2 of the Viṣṇudharmottarapurāṇa, framed as an exposition given by Puṣkara to Paraśurāma. It details the ritual application (vidhi) of Atharvavedic hymn groups (gaṇas) and specific mantras for appeasement (śānti), royal sovereignty, overcoming diseases, and warding off hostile forces. It is of particular Indological interest because its mantra citations preserve ritual formulas characteristic of the Paippalāda recension of the Atharvaveda.
SA_GP12_vd2127_u.attribution: Traditional Upapurāṇa framed as a dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and King Vajra, within which Puṣkara instructs Paraśurāma.
SA_GP12_vd2127_u.edition: Bombay 1912, adapted as "āgneya-viṣṇudharmottarapurāṇādibhya āhṛtya pratisaṃskritam [dūrgāmohanabhaṭṭācāryeṇa]" in D. Bhattacharyya, "Lights on the Paippalāda Recension of the Atharvaveda". In: Our Heritage, Vol. III, part I, 1955. pp. 1-14.
SA_GP12_vd2127_u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete text of Khaṇḍa 2, Adhyāya 127 (52 verses) of the Viṣṇudharmottarapurāṇa.

SA_GP12_vd3343pu.title: Viṣṇudharmottarapurāṇa (adhyāyas 3.343–353)
SA_GP12_vd3343pu.summary: The Viṣṇudharmottarapurāṇa is an encyclopedic Vaiṣṇava work framed as a dialogue between the sage Mārkaṇḍeya and King Vajra. This excerpt comprises adhyāyas 343 to 353 of the third khaṇḍa, focusing on narratives illustrating Viṣṇu's supreme power and boons of divine grace (prasāda). Notable narratives include the Sumukhopākhyāna (in which Garuḍa is humbled upon finding himself unable to lift even a single arm of Viṣṇu), the granting of boons to Nārada (Nāradaprasāda), and references to the manifestation of the cosmic form (viśvarūpa) to Arjuna and Uttaṅka.
SA_GP12_vd3343pu.attribution: The Viṣṇudharmottarapurāṇa is framed as a dialogue between the sage Mārkaṇḍeya and King Vajra.
SA_GP12_vd3343pu.coverage: partial — Contains adhyāyas 343 to 353 of Khaṇḍa 3. The excerpt begins with the dialogue of Vajra and Mārkaṇḍeya regarding Sumukha (3.343.1) and concludes with the colophon of adhyāya 353: 'iti śrīviṣṇudharmottare tṛtīyakhaṇḍe mārkaṇḍeyavajrasaṃvāde nāradaprasādo nāma tripañcāśaduttaratriśatatamo 'dhyāyaḥ // 353 //'.
translations: Kramrisch, Stella (trans.). The Viṣṇudharmottaram: a treatise on Indian painting. Calcutta, 1924. (English)

SA_GP12_visnup_u.title: Viṣṇupurāṇa
SA_GP12_visnup_u.summary: The Viṣṇupurāṇa is one of the eighteen canonical Mahāpurāṇas and the classical exemplar of the traditional pañcalakṣaṇa structure (primary cosmogony, secondary creation, genealogies of gods and patriarchs, manvantara cycles, and dynastic histories). Comprising six books (aṃśas) arranged as a dialogue between Parāśara and Maitreya, it treats cosmology, geography, varṇāśramadharma, and devotes book five to an extensive early biography of Kṛṣṇa. Frequently dated in its core to the Gupta period (c. 4th–5th century CE), it is a foundational scripture for classical Vaiṣṇava theology and Vedāntic exegesis.
SA_GP12_visnup_u.attribution: Internally framed as a dialogue narrated by Parāśara to Maitreya.
SA_GP12_visnup_u.coverage: complete — Text ending at ViP 6.8.64. The e-text transmits the mūla text; commentaries mentioned in the opening rubric (Viṣṇucittīya and Ātmaprakāśa / Śrīdharīya) are not included.
translations: Wilson, H. H. (trans.). London, 1840 (rev. ed. by F. Hall, London: Trübner & Co., 1864–. (English)
Dutt, M. N. (trans.). (English)

SA_GP12_vprevk_u.title: Revākhaṇḍa (Vāyupurāṇa; printed as Skandapurāṇa 5.3)
SA_GP12_vprevk_u.summary: The Revākhaṇḍa is a purāṇic text in 232 chapters glorifying the Narmadā (Revā) river, its sacred places (such as Amarakaṇṭaka and Bhṛgukaccha), and associated rites and legends.
SA_GP12_vprevk_u.attribution: Printed in the Veṅkaṭeśvara edition (1910) as part of the Skandapurāṇa (Āvantyakhaṇḍa 3) and retaining colophons naming the Skandapurāṇa ('iti śrīskānde mahāpurāṇa ekāśītisāhasryāṃ saṃhitāyāṃ pañcama āvantyakhaṇḍe revākhaṇḍe ...'); J. Neuss (GRETIL contributor note) states that all available manuscript evidence proves the text originally belonged to the Vāyupurāṇa. The final verse calls it 'pavanagaditam'. A separate, shorter Revākhaṇḍa of the Skandapurāṇa comprises 116 adhyāyas.
SA_GP12_vprevk_u.edition: Śrīkṛṣṇadās, Kṣemrāj (ed.): Śrīskandamahāpurāṇam. Veṅkateśvara Steam Press, Bombay: 1910. and its reprint: Siṃha, Nāgaśaraṇa (ed.): Śrīskandamahāpurāṇam. pañcama bhāga: śrī āvantyakhaṇḍam. Nag Publishers, Delhi: 1986.
SA_GP12_vprevk_u.coverage: complete — All 232 adhyāyas (RKV_1.1 – RKV_232.55), from the opening invocations ('śrīgaṇeśāya namaḥ', 'oṃ namaḥ śrīnarmadāyai') to the final colophon of adhyāya 232 ('revākhaṇḍasamāpti-revākhaṇḍapustakadānādimāhātmyavarṇanaṃ nāma dvātriṃśadadhikadviśatatamo 'dhyāyaḥ').

SA_GR12_hsasvrpu.title: Śāstravārtāsamuccaya
SA_GR12_hsasvrpu.author: Haribhadrasūri
SA_GR12_hsasvrpu.summary: The Śāstravārtāsamuccaya ('Compendium of Philosophical Discourses') is a major 8th-century doxographical and polemical treatise in 701 anuṣṭubh verses across 11 chapters (stabakas) by the Śvetāmbara master Haribhadrasūri. The work presents a systematic survey and critique of non-Jain philosophical traditions, including Cārvāka materialism, theism (Īśvaravāda), Sāṃkhya dualism, Buddhist theories of momentariness (kṣaṇikavāda) and idealism (vijñānavāda/śūnyavāda), Advaita monism, and Mīmāṃsā rejections of omniscience. Haribhadra examines each perspective critically while adhering to the Jain framework of non-one-sided ontology (anekāntavāda) and concludes with an exposition of the nature of omniscience and spiritual liberation.
SA_GR12_hsasvrpu.attribution: A secure composition of the Śvetāmbara philosopher-monk Haribhadrasūri (c. 8th century CE). Haribhadra identifies himself by name in verse 699 (ācāryaharibhadreṇa śāstravārtāsamuccayam) and incorporates his customary sobriquet bhavaviraha in verse 700.
SA_GR12_hsasvrpu.edition: K. K. Dixit, Ahmedabad: Lalbhai Dalpatbhai Bharatiya 1969 (L. D. Series, 22).
SA_GR12_hsasvrpu.coverage: complete — Complete mūla text in 701 anuṣṭubh verses arranged across 11 stabakas (chapters). The electronic text also prefixes K. K. Dixit's Hindi table of contents (Viṣayasūcī) and preserves his section headers.

SA_GR12_sasapa.title: Satyaśāsanaparīkṣā (incomplete; breaks off in the Mīmāṃsā section)
SA_GR12_sasapa.author: Vidyānanda
SA_GR12_sasapa.summary: The Satyaśāsanaparīkṣā ('Investigation into the True Teaching') is a philosophical treatise in prose and verse composed by Vidyānanda. The work examines rival Indian philosophical schools—including Advaita Vedānta (Parabrahmādvaita), Śabdādvaita, Buddhist Vijñānādvaita, Citrādvaita, Cārvāka, Sāṃkhya, Naiyāyika, Vaiśeṣika, and Mīmāṃsā—testing them against the criterion of dṛṣṭeṣṭāviruddhatva. The surviving text breaks off during the critique of Bhāṭṭa and Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā.
SA_GR12_sasapa.attribution: Authored by Vidyānanda. The opening maṅgala verse names him: 'vidyānandādhipaḥ svāmī vidvaddevo jineśvaraḥ' [0].
SA_GR12_sasapa.edition: Gokulchandra Jain (ed.), Satyaśāsanaparīkṣā of Vidyānandin, Jñānapīṭha Mūrtidevī Jaina Granthamālā, Saṃskṛta Grantha 30, Kashi/Delhi: Bharatiya Jnanpith, 1964. (probable)
SA_GR12_sasapa.coverage: partial — Contains the text as printed by G. C. Jain (1964): introduction, then Puruṣādvaita, Śabdādvaita, Vijñānādvaita, Citrādvaita, Cārvāka, Bauddha, Seśvara/Nirīśvara Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Nyāya, breaking off in the Mīmāṃsā section ('... bhāṭṭaprābhākarair iṣṭaṃ ...', followed by '<|| bhadraṃ bhūyāt>').

SA_GR13_bhnstcpu.title: Stavacintāmaṇi
SA_GR13_bhnstcpu.author: Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa
SA_GR13_bhnstcpu.summary: The Stavacintāmaṇi ('Wish-fulfilling Jewel of Praise') is a devotional hymn in 120 verses composed by Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa. Expressing the philosophy of non-dual Śaivism, it articulates intense devotion (bhakti) to Śiva as the experiential realization of identity between the individual consciousness and supreme reality. It was commented upon by Kṣemarāja.
SA_GR13_bhnstcpu.attribution: Composed by Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa. Although the base edition printed the root hymn along with Kṣemarāja's commentary (Vivṛti), only Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa's root kārikās were input into this e-text.
SA_GR13_bhnstcpu.edition: Mukunda Rama Shastri: The StavaChintamani of Bhatta Narayana with commentary by Kshemaraja. Srinagar 1918 (Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies; X)
SA_GR13_bhnstcpu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 120 verses (numbered BhStc_1 to BhStc_120), ending with the author's concluding signature stanza.
translations: Liliane Silburn, La Bhakti, Le Stavacintāmaṇi de Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa, texte traduit et commenté, Paris: E. De Boccard, 1964 (Publications de l'Institut de Civilisation Indienne, Fascicule 19). (French)

SA_GR13_bijnighu.title: Bījanighaṇṭu
SA_GR13_bijnighu.summary: The Bījanighaṇṭu (also termed Mantrakośa) is a tantric glossary in 87 verses containing cryptic names and esoteric designations for Sanskrit phonemes and mantric seed-syllables (bījas). Presented as a revelation spoken by Śiva and claiming derivation from the Bhūtaḍāmara and Yakṣaḍāmaratantra traditions, it supplies deity epithets and elemental associations for individual letters as well as composite syllables (such as śrīṃ, hrīṃ, krīṃ, and klīṃ). The work serves as a practical decoding key for reconstructing esoteric mantras (mantroddhāra) embedded in tantric ritual texts.
SA_GR13_bijnighu.attribution: Anonymous tantric glossary presented as a dialogue spoken by Śiva, internally styled as the Mantrakośa derived from the Bhūtaḍāmara and Yakṣaḍāmaratantra traditions.
SA_GR13_bijnighu.edition: Ram Kumar Rai, in: Dictionaries of Tantrashastra, Benares: Prachya Prakashan, 1984.
SA_GR13_bijnighu.coverage: complete — Complete text in 87 verses with introductory phoneme/bīja lists.

SA_GR13_cakbh_pu.title: Bhāvopahārastotra
SA_GR13_cakbh_pu.author: Cakrapāṇinātha
SA_GR13_cakbh_pu.summary: The Bhāvopahārastotra (or Bhāvopahāra, 'The Offering of Mental States') is a 47-verse non-dual devotional hymn to Śiva attributed to the Kashmirian master Cakrapāṇinātha (c. 11th–12th century), associated with the Krama and Trika traditions of Kashmir Śaivism. The stotra allegorically reinterprets the sequential ritual offerings of traditional pūjā—such as the bath, seat, arghya, incense, light, bell, and dakṣiṇā—into internal meditative processes, offering subjective cognitive states, perceptions, and vital breath as oblation to the supreme divine Consciousness. This digital text contains solely the 47 root verses extracted from KSTS 14.
SA_GR13_cakbh_pu.attribution: In the concluding stanza (v. 47), the author refers to himself only obliquely as an ascetic ('kaścid viśramya tāpasaḥ') offering praise to Śambhu as lord of the wheel of consciousness ('ciccakranāthasya śambhor bhāvanutiṃ parām').
SA_GR13_cakbh_pu.edition: Mukunda Ramashastri, Bombay: Tatva-vivechaka Press 1918 (Kashmir Series of Sanskrit Texts and Studies, 14).
SA_GR13_cakbh_pu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 47 stanzas (numbered CakBhst_1 through CakBhst_47) of the mūla stotra.
translations: Enrica Garzilli, The Bhāvopahāra of Cakrapāṇinātha: A Sanskrit Hymn to Śiva (11th-12th Century A.D.) (Napoli: Istituto Universitario Orientale, 1992). (English)

SA_GR13_cakbhavu.title: Bhāvopahārastotra with Vivaraṇa
SA_GR13_cakbhavu.author: Cakrapāṇinātha, Ramyadeva Bhaṭṭa
SA_GR13_cakbhavu.summary: The Bhāvopahārastotra is a 47-verse devotional hymn to Śiva composed by the Kashmirian master Cakrapāṇinātha, belonging to the non-dual Śaiva (Trika/Krama) tradition. The work interiorizes the liturgical implements and offerings of external ritual worship (pūjā), transforming each modality of perception and cognition into an oblation offered into supreme non-dual consciousness. The accompanying Vivaraṇa by Ramyadeva Bhaṭṭa provides a detailed philosophical commentary on the esoteric meaning of the hymn.
SA_GR13_cakbhavu.attribution: The root stotra of 47 verses is composed by Cakrapāṇinātha, who encodes his name in verse 47. The commentary (Vivaraṇa) was composed by Ramyadeva Bhaṭṭa, an initiate in the transmission of Yogānanda.
SA_GR13_cakbhavu.edition: Mukunda Ramashastri, Bombay: Tatva-vivechaka Press 1918 (Kashmir Series of Sanskrit Texts and Studies, 14)
SA_GR13_cakbhavu.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all 47 kārikās of the Bhāvopahārastotra along with the complete Vivaraṇa commentary by Ramyadeva Bhaṭṭa, including opening mangala verses and concluding colophon stanzas.

SA_GR13_devikapu.title: Devīkālottarāgama
SA_GR13_devikapu.summary: The Devīkālottarāgama (or Devīkālottara) is an 84-verse Śaiva scriptural text presented as a dialogue in which Śiva (Īśvara) reveals liberating knowledge (jñāna) and conduct (ācāra) to the Goddess. In contrast to external ritual worship, pilgrimage, and social duties, the work teaches the steadying of the mind and non-dual contemplation.
SA_GR13_devikapu.attribution: Revealed scriptural text of the Śaiva tradition, cast as an exposition given by Śiva (Īśvara) to the Goddess.
SA_GR13_devikapu.edition: Vrajavallabha Dwivedi (ed.), Devīkālottarāgamaḥ: Commentary in Sanskrit by Nirañjanasiddha, edited with Hindi Translation, Varanasi: Shaiva Bharati Shodha Pratishthanam, 2000 (Research Publication Series, 21).
SA_GR13_devikapu.coverage: complete — Complete root text in 84 verses (numbered Dka_1–Dka_84), matching the mula text edited by Vrajavallabha Dvivedī (2000). The Sanskrit commentary of Nirañjanasiddha is omitted from this e-text.
translations: Vrajavallabha Dwivedi (ed. & trans.), Devīkālottarāgamaḥ: Commentary in Sanskrit by Nirañjanasiddha, edited with Hindi Translation, Varanasi: Shaiva Bharati Shodha Pratishthanam, 2000 (Research Publication Series, 21). (Hindi)

SA_GR13_goramaru.title: Amaraughaśāsana
SA_GR13_goramaru.author: Gorakṣanātha
SA_GR13_goramaru.summary: The Amaraughaśāsana is a text attributed to Gorakṣanātha. Comprising 80 prose aphorisms interspersed with verses and commentary, it discusses subtle physiology (kanda, nāḍī, cakra), sāraṇā and pratisāraṇā techniques, prāṇa, kuṇḍalī/kuṇḍalinī, elements, and the nature of mokṣa and the paramātman.
SA_GR13_goramaru.attribution: Ascribed to Gorakṣanātha in the GRETIL header.
SA_GR13_goramaru.edition: Mukund Ram Shastri, Bombay: Nirnaya-Sagara Press, 1918.
SA_GR13_goramaru.coverage: complete — Text containing 80 numbered sections (prose and verses).

SA_GR13_gorst1pu.title: Gorakṣaśataka
SA_GR13_gorst1pu.author: Gorakṣanātha
SA_GR13_gorst1pu.summary: The Gorakṣaśataka ('Hundred Verses of Gorakṣa') is a manual of haṭhayoga traditionally attributed to Gorakṣanātha. The work expounds a six-limbed (ṣaḍaṅga) yoga system comprising posture (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), sense-withdrawal (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and absorption (samādhi). It describes esoteric anatomy—including cakras and nāḍīs—alongside mudrās and breath practices aimed at liberation.
SA_GR13_gorst1pu.edition: Swami Kuvalayananda and S. A. Shukla, eds., Gorakṣaśatakam, Lonavla: Kaivalyadhama, n.d.
SA_GR13_gorst1pu.coverage: complete — Text numbered GorS(1)_1 through GorS(1)_101, concluding with the colophon 'gorakṣa-śatakaṃ samāptam'.
translations: Svami Kuvalayananda and S. A. Shukla, Gorakṣaśatakam, Lonavla: Kaivalyadhama. (English)
Fausta Nowotny, Das Gorakṣaśataka, 1976. (German)

SA_GR13_gorst2pu.title: Gorakṣaśataka
SA_GR13_gorst2pu.author: Gorakṣanātha
SA_GR13_gorst2pu.summary: The Gorakṣaśataka is a foundational Sanskrit manual of Haṭhayoga attributed to Gorakṣanātha. This particular recension, recorded in Briggs (1938), consists of 101 verses describing postures (specifically siddhāsana and padmāsana), the subtle channels and energy centers (nāḍīs and cakras), kuṇḍalinī, and breath regulation (prāṇāyāma and nāḍīśodhana).
SA_GR13_gorst2pu.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the Nātha master Gorakṣanātha, who is named in the opening verses (vv. 3–4).
SA_GR13_gorst2pu.edition: George Weston Briggs, Gorakhnath and the Kanphata Yogis (1938), reprinted in 1989 by Motilal Banarsidass (pp. 284-304).
SA_GR13_gorst2pu.coverage: complete — Complete in 101 verses as edited in Briggs (1938), concluding with 'iti gorakṣa-śatakaṃ sampūrṇam'. Text covers āsana, subtle anatomy (cakras, nāḍīs), and prāṇāyāma.
translations: George Weston Briggs, Gorakhnath and the Kanphata Yogis, 1938, pp. 284–304. (English)
Swami Kuvalayananda and S. A. Shukla, Gorakṣaśatakam, Lonavla: Kaivalyadhama. (English)
Fausta Nowotny, Das Gorakṣaśataka, Köln: K.A. Nowotny, 1976. (German)

SA_GR13_jssivppu.title: Śivapūjāstava
SA_GR13_jssivppu.author: Jñānaśambhu
SA_GR13_jssivppu.summary: The Śivapūjāstava is a 47-verse liturgical hymn of the Śaiva Siddhānta tradition composed by Jñānaśambhu (c. 12th century). It systematically traces the sequential procedures of daily Śiva worship (śivapūjā)—from morning contemplation, purificatory baths, and sandhyā rites to āsana visualization, nyāsa, external worship, homa, and final dismissals (visarga)—while interpreting each ritual gesture in terms of internal yogic meditation, discernment, and complete self-dedication (svātmanivedana).
SA_GR13_jssivppu.attribution: The concluding verse (v. 47) explicitly names Jñānaśambhu, describing him as a learned scholar from the Cōḻa country (coladeśī sūriḥ) and master of the Siddhānta (siddhāntajñaḥ).
SA_GR13_jssivppu.edition: Śivapūjāstavaḥ savyākhyaḥ Jñānaśambhuśivācāryapraṇītaḥ, edited by K. M. Subrahmaṇyaśāstrī, Devakottai 1935.
SA_GR13_jssivppu.coverage: complete — Complete root text in 47 verses (JsSpst_1 to JsSpst_47). The commentary (savyākhya) mentioned in the title of the 1935 Devakottai edition was not keyed into this electronic text.

SA_GR13_kalhans_u.title: Ardhanārīśvarastotra
SA_GR13_kalhans_u.author: Kalhaṇa
SA_GR13_kalhans_u.summary: An 18-verse Kashmirian stotra praising Śiva in his composite androgynous form as Ardhanārīśvara, highlighting the aesthetic and paradoxical harmony between the divine male and female halves (Śiva and Pārvatī). Long catalogued as an independent work by Kalhaṇa, it brings together stanzas from Kalhaṇa's Rājataraṅgiṇī alongside verses from Jagaddhara Bhaṭṭa's Stutikusumāñjali and Śrīvara's Rājataraṅgiṇī.
SA_GR13_kalhans_u.attribution: Ascribed to Kalhaṇa. Verses include opening verses from Kalhaṇa's Rājataraṅgiṇī (RT), Jagaddhara's Stutikusumāñjali (SKA 15.37), and Śrīvara's Rājataraṅgiṇī (ŚRT 1.1.2).
SA_GR13_kalhans_u.edition: Walter Slaje, 'Kalhaṇas Ode an den androgynen Gott (Ardhanārīśvarastotra)', Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft (ZDMG), Bd. 165, H. 2 (2015), pp. 395–416.
SA_GR13_kalhans_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of 18 verses as edited by Walter Slaje.

SA_GR13_karatopu.title: Karatoyāmāhātmya
SA_GR13_karatopu.summary: The Karatoyāmāhātmya is an early medieval regional sthalamāhātmya in 85 verses extolling the sacred Karatoyā river and the holy precinct of Pauṇḍravardhana (modern Mahasthangarh, Bogra District, Bangladesh). Set as a dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī reported by Sūta to the sages, the text relates the mythic origin of the Karatoyā from the water poured onto Śiva's hands during his marriage to Pārvatī and surveys the holy bathing places, shrines, and lingas established by Paraśurāma in Pauṇḍrakṣetra. Verses from the text are cited in medieval dharmaśāstra and lexical commentaries as early as Sarvānanda's Ṭīkāsarvasva (1159 CE) and Devaṇabhaṭṭa's Smṛticandrikā, confirming its currency in the twelfth century.
SA_GR13_karatopu.attribution: A regional Purāṇic sthalamāhātmya purporting to belong to a larger lost work, the Uttara-Pauṇḍra-khaṇḍa. The closing colophon attributes composition to Paraśurāma (paraśurāmaviracitam), framed within a dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka recounting an interlocution between Śiva and Pārvatī. The historical author is anonymous.
SA_GR13_karatopu.edition: Prabhas Chandra Sen: Mahasthan and Its Environs, Rajshahi, Bengal: Varendra Research Society, 1929 (Varendra Research Society's Monographs, 2), Appendix I.
SA_GR13_karatopu.coverage: complete — Complete text in 85 anuṣṭubh stanzas (KtoM_01–85), comprising two thematic sections: Pauṇḍrakṣetramāhātmya (vv. 1–60) and Karatoyāmāhātmya proper (vv. 61–85), ending with the final colophon.
translations: Pandit Rajachandra Nyayapanchanan, Karatoyāmāhātmya, with Bengali translation, 1298 B.S. (1891 A.D.). (Bengali)

SA_GR13_kirtc_pu.title: Kiraṇatantra with Kiraṇavṛtti (chapters 1–6)
SA_GR13_kirtc_pu.author: Rāmakaṇṭha
SA_GR13_kirtc_pu.summary: The Kiraṇatantra is one of the foundational canonical scriptures of the dualist Śaiva Siddhānta, presented as an exposition revealed by Śiva to Garuḍa. This e-text contains the first six chapters of its doctrinal section (Vidyāpāda) along with the extensive philosophical commentary (Kiraṇavṛtti) of Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha II (c. late 10th century CE). The text articulates the core Saiddhāntika ontological categories of Lord (pati), individual soul (paśu), and bonds (pāśa—mala, karma, and māyā), establishing the necessity of ritual initiation (dīkṣā) and defending dualist theology against rival Buddhist, Advaita, and Sāṅkhya positions.
SA_GR13_kirtc_pu.attribution: The Kiraṇatantra is an early Śaiva Siddhānta scripture in the form of a dialogue between Śiva and Garuḍa. The commentary (Kiraṇavṛtti) is by Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha II.
SA_GR13_kirtc_pu.edition: Dominic Goodall (ed.), Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha's Commentary on the Kiraṇatantra, Vol. I: chapters 1–6, Critical Edition and Annotated Translation, Publications du département d'indologie 86.1, Pondicherry: Institut Français de Pondichéry / École française d'Extrême-Orient, 1998.
SA_GR13_kirtc_pu.coverage: partial — Contains chapters 1–6 of the doctrinal section (Vidyāpāda) along with Rāmakaṇṭha's commentary; the commentary abruptly breaks off at 6.26 due to a lacuna in the surviving manuscript tradition. The complete Kiraṇatantra consists of 64 chapters across four sections (vidyā, kriyā, yoga, and caryā).
translations: Dominic Goodall, Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha's Commentary on the Kiraṇatantra, Vol. I: chapters 1–6, Critical Edition and Annotated Translation, Pondicherry: Institut Français de Pondichéry / École française d'Extrême-Orient, 1998. (English)
Maria Pia Vivanti, Il «Kiraṇāgama»: Testo e traduzione del «Vidyāpāda», Napoli: Istituto Orientale di Napoli, 1975. (Italian)

SA_GR13_kirtm_pu.title: Kiraṇatantra (chapters 1–6)
SA_GR13_kirtm_pu.summary: The Kiraṇatantra (or Kiraṇāgama) is a foundational scripture of the dualistic Śaiva Siddhānta canon, structured as a dialogue between Bhagavān (Śiva) and Garuḍa. This electronic text contains chapters 1 to 6 (the vidyāpāda), which systematically expound classical Saiddhāntika metaphysics: the triple categories of Lord (pati), bound soul (paśu), and fetter (pāśa), the nature of beginningless innate impurity (mala), cosmic evolution through the tattvas, and initiation (dīkṣā) leading to liberation. Extracted from Dominic Goodall's critical edition of Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha's 10th-century Kashmirian commentary (Kiraṇavṛtti), these chapters represent the early northern recension preserved in Nepalese manuscripts.
SA_GR13_kirtm_pu.attribution: Canonical revelation of Śiva to Garuḍa. A single introductory maṅgala verse (KirT_0.1) by the Kashmirian commentator Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha II is preserved at the beginning, left over when Dominic Goodall extracted the root verses from his edition of Rāmakaṇṭha's commentary (Kiraṇavṛtti).
SA_GR13_kirtm_pu.edition: Dominic Goodall, Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha's Commentary on the Kiraṇatantra, Vol. I: Chapters 1–6, Critical Edition and Annotated Translation, Publications du département d'indologie 86.1, Pondichéry: Institut Français de Pondichéry / École française d'Extrême-Orient, 1998.
SA_GR13_kirtm_pu.coverage: partial — Chapters 1–6 only (KirT_1.1–6.26, preceded by Rāmakaṇṭha's maṅgala verse KirT_0.1). These six chapters constitute the philosophical/doctrinal portion (vidyāpāda) of the text, out of 64 chapters found in the full South Indian recension.
translations: Dominic Goodall, Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha's Commentary on the Kiraṇatantra, Vol. I: Chapters 1–6, Critical Edition and Annotated Translation, Pondichéry: Institut Français de Pondichéry / École française d'Extrême-Orient, 1998. (English)

SA_GR13_kubjt_pu.title: Kubjikāmatatantra
SA_GR13_kubjt_pu.summary: The Kubjikāmatatantra (also known as the Kulālikāmnāya or Śrīmata) is the foundational scripture of the Kubjikā cult within the Western Transmission (Paścimāmnāya) of Kaula Śākta-Śaivism, dating to approximately the 9th or 10th century CE. Preserved predominantly in early Nepalese manuscript witnesses, its 25 chapters articulate esoteric cosmology, initiation rituals, mantra systems (notably the Navātman and Aghorī mantras), and an early five-cakra model of the subtle body centered on the worship of the goddess Kubjikā ('the Crooked One') as kuṇḍalinī energy.
SA_GR13_kubjt_pu.attribution: Anonymous canonical revelation belonging to the Kaula Śākta-Śaiva tradition (Kulālikāmnāya / Paścimāmnāya), framed as an esoteric dialogue between Bhairava and the Goddess.
SA_GR13_kubjt_pu.edition: Teun Goudriaan and Jan A. Schoterman (eds.), The Kubjikāmatatantra: Kulālikāmnāya Version, Orientalia Rheno-traiectina 30, Leiden: E. J. Brill, 1988.
SA_GR13_kubjt_pu.coverage: complete — Complete text across all 25 chapters (paṭalas 1–25), running continuously from 1.1 through 25.232 and terminating with the final colophons.
translations: Dory H. Heilijgers-Seelen, The System of Five Cakras in Kubjikāmatatantra 14-16, Groningen Oriental Studies 9, Groningen: Egbert Forsten, 1994. (English (chapters 14–16 only))

SA_GR13_mabhedtu.title: Mātṛkābhedatantra
SA_GR13_mabhedtu.summary: The Mātṛkābhedatantra is a medieval Śākta-Śaiva Kaula scripture in 14 paṭalas, structured as a dialogue between Śaṅkara and Caṇḍikā on Mount Kailāsa [1.1]. While treating mantra-śāstra, phonological symbolism (mātṛkā), yantras, and ritual worship, it is notable for its alchemical (rasaśāstra) chapters (paṭalas 1, 5, and 8), which detail mercurial preparations, the transmutation of base metals into silver and gold, and the consecration of mercurial liṅgas (rasaliṅga). The work also addresses Kaula ritual practices, esoteric physiology, and the ritual purification of wine.
SA_GR13_mabhedtu.attribution: A revealed Śākta-Śaiva Kaula tantric scripture, framed as an esoteric dialogue between Śrīśaṅkara and Śrīcaṇḍikā on Mount Kailāsa.
SA_GR13_mabhedtu.coverage: complete — 14 paṭalas, MBhT_1.1 to MBhT_14.42 (559 numbered verses), ending with the last verse of paṭala 14 ('no yajed yadi mohena saiva pāpamayī bhavet').

SA_GR13_malinivu.title: Mālinīvijayottaratantra
SA_GR13_malinivu.summary: The Mālinīvijayottaratantra is the primary canonical scripture (mukhyaśāstra) of the Śaiva Trika tradition, datable to approximately the 8th to 9th century CE. It presents itself as a condensed successor to the wider Siddhayogeśvarīmata revelation, expounding the thirty-six principles (tattvas), esoteric phonology (the mātṛkā and mālinī orders of the Sanskrit alphabet), initiation rites (dīkṣā), mudrās, and an influential system of non-dual yoga and apperceptive levels (pramātṛs). The work served as the principal scriptural authority for Abhinavagupta's monumental synthesis in the Tantrāloka and was the subject of his Mālinīvijayavārttika.
SA_GR13_malinivu.attribution: A revealed scripture (tantra/āgama) of the non-dual Śaiva Trika school, framed as teachings transmitted by Śiva/Aghora to Devī and then to Kumāra (Kārttikeya) and the sages.
SA_GR13_malinivu.edition: Somadeva Vasudeva: Adhikāras 1–4, 7, and 11–17 from Somadeva Vasudeva's critical edition (Wolfson College, Oxford, July 2000, also publ. Pondichéry c2004, Collection indologie, 97; critical apparatus not included); Adhikāras 5, 6, 8–10, and 18–23 from the ed. by Madhusūdan Kaul Shāstrī, Bombay 1922 (Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies, 37).
SA_GR13_malinivu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 23 adhikāras (chapters 1–23).
translations: Somadeva Vasudeva, The Yoga of the Mālinīvijayottaratantra: Chapters 1–4, 7, 11–17, Collection Indologie 97, Pondichéry: Institut Français de Pondichéry / École française d'Extrême-Orient, 2004. (English)

Alexis Sanderson, 'The Doctrine of the Mālinīvijayottaratantra', in Teun Goudriaan (ed.), Ritual and Speculation in Early Tantrism: Studies in Honour of André Padoux, Albany: State University of New York Press, 1992, pp. 281–312. (English)

SA_GR13_mrgt1mpu.title: Mṛgendrāgama (Vidyāpāda)
SA_GR13_mrgt1mpu.summary: The Vidyāpāda (or Jñānapāda) of the Mṛgendrāgama constitutes the doctrinal division of one of the most prominent early Upāgamas of dualistic Śaiva Siddhānta. Spanning thirteen chapters, it elaborates the ontological foundation of the system: the Lord (pati), the bound souls (paśu), and the triple bonds (pāśa: mala, karman, and māyā), together with cosmology, the ontology of the levels of reality (tattvas), epistemology, and initiation leading to release. Widely cited across medieval Sanskrit philosophical literature, notably in Mādhavācārya's Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha, it represents a foundational synthesis of classical Saiddhāntika theology.
SA_GR13_mrgt1mpu.attribution: The text presents itself as revelation handed down from Śiva through Indra to the sage Bharadvāja.
SA_GR13_mrgt1mpu.edition: Madhusudan Kaul Shastri, Bombay (Srinagar): Nirnayasagara Press, 1930. (Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies, 50)
SA_GR13_mrgt1mpu.coverage: partial — Complete text of the Vidyāpāda (paṭalas 1–13, vv. 1.1–13.198, concluding with 'samāptaśca vidyāpādaḥ'), the first of four pādas comprising the Mṛgendrāgama (the other three being Yogapāda, Kriyāpāda, and Caryāpāda). Root verses only (mūla text), without commentary.
translations: Michel Hulin, Mṛgendrāgama: Sections de la doctrine et du yoga avec la vṛtti de Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇakaṇṭha et la Dīpikā d'Aghoraśivācārya, Pondichéry: Institut Français d'Indologie, 1980 (Publications de l'Institut Français d'Indologie, No. 63). (French)

Hélène Brunner-Lachaux, Mṛgendrāgama: Section des rites et section du comportement avec la vṛtti de Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇakaṇṭha, Pondichéry: Institut Français d'Indologie, 1985 (Publications de l'Institut Français d'Indologie, No. 69). (French)

SA_GR13_mrgt3mpu.title: Mṛgendrāgama (Caryāpāda)
SA_GR13_mrgt3mpu.summary: The Caryāpāda constitutes the conduct section of the Mṛgendrāgama, a classic dualistic Śaiva Siddhānta Upāgama. Comprising 130 verses, it details the codes of conduct, life-stages, daily observances, vows (vratas), and expiations (prāyaścittas) applicable to different classes of initiated practitioners (from samayin to deśika). It forms the fourth traditional division of the āgama alongside the Vidyā-, Kriyā-, and Yogapādas.
SA_GR13_mrgt3mpu.attribution: A revealed scripture (Upāgama) of the Śaiva Siddhānta tradition, traditionally regarded as a subordinate text (upatantra) to the Kāmikāgama.
SA_GR13_mrgt3mpu.edition: N.R. Bhatt (ed.), Mṛgendrāgama (Kriyāpāda et Caryāpāda), avec le commentaire de Bhaṭṭa-Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, Publications de l'Institut Français d'Indologie 23, Pondichéry: Institut Français d'Indologie, 1962, with corrections from the śuddhipattra (pp. 327–328) and Hélène Brunner-Lachaux (1985).
SA_GR13_mrgt3mpu.coverage: complete — Complete root text (mūla) of the Caryāpāda, comprising 130 verses plus 2 appendix verses (MrgT_3.App.1–2); verse 3.0 at the beginning is the commentator Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇakaṇṭha's introductory maṅgala verse.
translations: Hélène Brunner-Lachaux (trans., annot.), Mṛgendrāgama: Section des rites et section du comportement, avec la vṛtti de Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇakaṇṭha, Publications de l'Institut Français d'Indologie 69, Pondichéry: Institut Français d'Indologie, 1985. (French)

SA_GR13_mrgt4mpu.title: Mṛgendrāgama (Yogapāda)
SA_GR13_mrgt4mpu.summary: The Yogapāda is the fourth section of the Mṛgendrāgama (Mṛgendratantra), consisting of 65 verses expounding yoga. The chapter teaches an eight-limbed yoga comprising prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, dhyāna, vīkṣaṇa, japa, samādhi, and yoga itself as the eighth component. It details bodily purification, respiratory control (recaka, pūraka, kumbhaka), and meditative absorption.
SA_GR13_mrgt4mpu.attribution: The Mṛgendrāgama (or Mṛgendratantra) is an early Śaiva Siddhānta scripture commented upon by Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha and Aghoraśiva.
SA_GR13_mrgt4mpu.edition: Madhusudan Kaul Shastri, ed., Bombay (Srinagar): Nirnayasagara Press, 1930 (Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies, 50).
SA_GR13_mrgt4mpu.coverage: partial — Contains the complete mūla text of the Yogapāda (verses 1–65), without commentary.
translations: Michel Hulin, tr., Mṛgendrāgama. Sections de la doctrine et du yoga. Avec la vṛtti de Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇakaṇṭha et la Dīpikā d'Aghoraśivācārya, Institut Français d'Indologie (Pondicherry 1980). (French)

SA_GR13_parakspu.title: Paraśurāmakalpasūtra
SA_GR13_parakspu.summary: The Paraśurāmakalpasūtra is an aphoristic manual of the Śākta Śrīvidyā (Kaula) ritual tradition. Arranged in ten chapters (khaṇḍas), it sets forth instructions for initiation (dīkṣā), daily and occasional rites, fire offerings (homa), and the esoteric worship of Lalitā Tripurasundarī, the Śrīcakra, and associated deities including Mahāgaṇapati, Śyāmā (Mātaṅgī), Vārāhī, and Parā. Probably composed in South India around the 16th century CE, the work integrates classical Tantric metaphysics with ritual formats modeled after Vedic Kalpasūtras.
SA_GR13_parakspu.attribution: Colophons ascribe the compilation to the legendary sage Jāmadagnya Paraśurāma, depicted as disciple of Mahādeva (Śiva). Indological scholarship treats the work as a South Indian Śākta compilation, likely composed in the 16th century CE or slightly earlier.
SA_GR13_parakspu.edition: A. Mahadeva Sastri (ed.), Paraśurāmakalpasūtra with Rāmeśvara's Commentary, Baroda: Central Library, 1923 (Gaekwad's Oriental Series).
SA_GR13_parakspu.coverage: complete — Complete root text (mūlasūtra) in 10 khaṇḍas (sūtras Parks_1.1 to Parks_10.85); does not include Rāmeśvara's commentary.
translations: Claudia Weber, Das Paraśurāma-Kalpasūtra: Sanskrit-Edition mit deutscher Erstübersetzung, Kommentaren und weiteren Studien, Frankfurt et al: Peter Lang, 2010. (German)

SA_GR13_pasupbhu.title: Pāśupatasūtra with Pañcārthabhāṣya
SA_GR13_pasupbhu.author: Kauṇḍinya
SA_GR13_pasupbhu.summary: The Pāśupatasūtra is the foundational scriptural text of the Pāñcārthika Pāśupatas, the oldest documented initiatory Śaiva ascetic order (Atimārga). Organized around five cardinal doctrines (pañcārtha: kārya, kāraṇa, yoga, vidhi, and duḥkhānta), it outlines the ascetic path from initiatory vows to eccentric, antinomian behavior intended to solicit public disdain, culminating in total communion with Rudra-Śiva. Kauṇḍinya's Pañcārthabhāṣya provides a detailed theological, ritual, and philosophical commentary that systematizes Pāśupata metaphysics and spiritual practice.
SA_GR13_pasupbhu.attribution: The root aphorisms (Pāśupatasūtra or Pañcārtha) are scriptural and traditionally attributed to Lakulīśa. Kauṇḍinya names himself as the commentator in the opening maṅgala verse (1.1:1: 'pañcārthaṃ kriyate bhāṣyaṃ kauṇḍinyenānupūrvaśaḥ') and in the colophons.
SA_GR13_pasupbhu.edition: R. Anantakrishna Shastri (ed.), Pasupatasutra with Kaundinya's Pancarthabhasya, Trivandrum: The Oriental Manuscripts Library of the University of Travancore, 1940 (Trivandrum Sanskrit Series; 143).
SA_GR13_pasupbhu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 5 adhyāyas with Kauṇḍinya's Pañcārthabhāṣya, ending at 5.46:51.
translations: Haripada Chakraborti, Pāśupata Sūtram with the Pañcārtha-bhāṣya of Kauṇḍinya, Calcutta: Academic Publishers, 1970. (English)

SA_GR13_pasupspu.title: Pāśupatasūtra
SA_GR13_pasupspu.summary: The Pāśupatasūtra is the foundational aphoristic scripture of the Pāśupatas, the earliest documented sectarian Śaiva ascetic movement of the Atimārga. Arranged around the five doctrinal categories (pañcārtha: effect, cause, yoga, ritual observance, and cessation of suffering), the work outlines the discipline of the initiated ascetic. This regimen includes controversial practices such as acting crazed, trembling, limping, and courting social contempt to divest demerit onto onlookers, culminating in continuous contemplation of Rudra-Śiva to achieve the permanent end of suffering through divine grace (īśaprasāda).
SA_GR13_pasupspu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all five adhyāyas (PS 1.1–5.47) comprising the sūtrapāṭha only, without Kauṇḍinya's Pañcārthabhāṣya.
translations: Haripada Chakraborti (trans.), Pāśupata Sūtram with the Pañcārtha-bhāṣya of Kauṇḍinya, Calcutta: Academic Publishers, 1970. (English)

SA_GR13_pat.title: Parākhyatantra
SA_GR13_pat.summary: The Parākhyatantra (also called Saurabheyatantra) is a scripture of the Saiddhāntika Śaiva Siddhānta canon, quoted by early pan-Indian Śaiva Siddhānta authors up to Aghoraśiva. The surviving work includes teachings on epistemology, the evolution of language/phonemes from bindu, the soul, and yoga.
SA_GR13_pat.attribution: A revealed Śaiva scripture of the Saiddhāntika canon.
SA_GR13_pat.coverage: unclear — No e-text: there is no segments file for SA_GR13_pat (0 segments, 0 characters), and no other Parākhyatantra entry exists in the catalog.
translations: Dominic Goodall, trans., The Parākhyatantra: A Scripture of the Śaiva Siddhānta. Collection Indologie, 98. Pondicherry: Institut Français de Pondichéry / École française d'Extrême-Orient, 2004. (English)

SA_GR13_purekaku.title: Ekākṣarakośa (verses 1–27)
SA_GR13_purekaku.author: Puruṣottamadeva
SA_GR13_purekaku.summary: The Ekākṣarakośa is a short monosyllabic dictionary (ekākṣarakośa) attributed to Puruṣottamadeva, cataloguing individual vowels and consonant syllables together with various designations and meanings.
SA_GR13_purekaku.edition: Ram Kumar Rai (ed., trans.), Dictionaries of Tantra Sastra or The Tantrabhidhanam (Indological Reference Series No. 2), Varanasi: Prachya Prakashan, 1984.
SA_GR13_purekaku.coverage: partial — Contains 27 verses (numbered PEk_1–PEk_27), covering vowels through the consonant ma / mā.
translations: Ram Kumar Rai, Dictionaries of Tantra Sastra or The Tantrabhidhanam, Varanasi: Prachya Prakashan, 1984. (English)

SA_GR13_saulahpu.title: Saundaryalaharī
SA_GR13_saulahpu.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GR13_saulahpu.summary: The Saundaryalaharī ('Wave of Beauty') is a celebrated Tantric devotional hymn of 100 (or 103) stanzas composed in the śikhariṇī metre in praise of Tripurasundarī (the Great Goddess of the Śrīvidyā tradition). The hymn falls into two distinct divisions: the first 41 verses (frequently transmitted independently as the Ānandalaharī, or 'Wave of Bliss') articulate the esoteric doctrines of Śrīcakra worship, mantra, kuṇḍalinī-yoga, and the non-dual union of Śiva and Śakti; the second portion (verses 42–100/103) presents an elaborate head-to-toe (keśādipāda) poetic description of the Goddess's transcendent physical form.
SA_GR13_saulahpu.edition: W. Norman Brown (ed., tr.), The Saundaryalaharī or Flood of Beauty: Traditionally Ascribed to Śaṅkarācārya. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1958 (Harvard Oriental Series, vol. 43).
SA_GR13_saulahpu.coverage: complete — Complete text containing 103 stanzas in the śikhariṇī metre (numbered Saul_1 through Saul_103).
translations: W. Norman Brown, The Saundaryalaharī or Flood of Beauty, Traditionally Ascribed to Śaṅkarācārya. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1958 (Harvard Oriental Series, vol. 43). (English)

SA_GR13_sidr_1-3.title: Śivadṛṣṭi (chapters 1–3)
SA_GR13_sidr_1-3.author: Somānanda
SA_GR13_sidr_1-3.summary: The Śivadṛṣṭi of Somānanda is a Śaiva philosophical text accompanied by a commentary (Vṛtti) by Utpaladeva.
SA_GR13_sidr_1-3.attribution: Somānanda is the author of Śivadṛṣṭi with a Vṛtti by Utpaladeva.
SA_GR13_sidr_1-3.coverage: partial — Intended scope per catalog/filename: chapters 1–3 of the Śivadṛṣṭi.
translations: John Nemec, The Ubiquitous Śiva: Somānanda's Śivadrsti and His Tantric Interlocutors. New York: Oxford University Press, 2011. (English)

SA_GR13_sidr_4.title: Śivadṛṣṭi (chapter 4)
SA_GR13_sidr_4.author: Somānanda
SA_GR13_sidr_4.summary: The fourth chapter (āhnika) of the Śivadṛṣṭi debates rival classical Indian traditions—including Buddhist Epistemologists, Mīmāṃsakas, Nyāya-Vaiśeṣikas, and Sāṅkhya-Yoga—contending that their respective epistemological, semantic, and causal models cannot hold together unless integrated into an all-pervasive, conscious Śaiva monism.
SA_GR13_sidr_4.coverage: partial — Intended scope per catalog: Sivadrsti Chapter 4.

SA_GR13_sivmstpu.title: Śivamahimnastava
SA_GR13_sivmstpu.author: Puṣpadanta
SA_GR13_sivmstpu.summary: The Śivamahimnastava ('Mahimnastava') is a hymn in praise of Śiva. The text includes 31 core stanzas and 15 additional stanzas, with verses invoking Puṣpadanta as composer (Smst_Add_2, 8, 9). Brown's most important source is an inscription on the Amareśvara temple at Māndhātā on the northern bank of the Narmadā river, dated Samvat 1120 or 1220 (1063 or 1163 CE).
SA_GR13_sivmstpu.attribution: In the text, the stanzas Smst_Add_2, Smst_Add_8, and Smst_Add_9 attribute the work to Puṣpadanta. W. Norman Brown identified an inscription on the Amareśvara temple at Māndhātā (dated Samvat 1120 or 1220 / 1063 or 1163 CE) as a primary witness.
SA_GR13_sivmstpu.edition: The Mahimnastava or Praise of Shiva's Greatness. Edited, translated, and presented in illustrations by W. Norman Brown. Poona: American Institute of Indian Studies 1965.
SA_GR13_sivmstpu.coverage: complete — Contains 31 stanzas (tagged Smst_1–31) followed by 15 additional stanzas (tagged Smst_Add_1–15) based on W. Norman Brown's 1965 edition.
translations: W. Norman Brown, The Mahimnastava or Praise of Shiva's Greatness. Edited, translated, and presented in illustrations. Poona: American Institute of Indian Studies, 1965. (English)

SA_GR13_sivsutru.title: Śivasūtra with Śivasūtravārttika
SA_GR13_sivsutru.author: Vasugupta, Varadarāja
SA_GR13_sivsutru.summary: The Śivasūtra is the foundational revealed text of the non-dual Kashmiri Trika school, outlining the nature of supreme consciousness and the three successive means (upāyas)—śāmbhava, śākta, and āṇava—by which the bound soul realizes its inherent identity with Śiva. This e-text pairs the root sūtras with the Śivasūtravārttika of Varadarāja (alias Kṛṣṇadāsa), a verse exposition that versifies and condenses the classic prose interpretation provided in Kṣemarāja's Śivasūtravimarśinī. Through accessible anuṣṭubh verses, Varadarāja systematically elucidates the metaphysical definitions of bondage, the dynamics of divine energy (spanda/mātṛkā), and yogic integration.
SA_GR13_sivsutru.attribution: The Śivasūtra is the foundational text of Kashmirian non-dual Śaivism (Trika), traditionally revealed to Vasugupta (c. 9th cent.). The Śivasūtravārttika is a metrical commentary in anuṣṭubh verses composed by Varadarāja (who also refers to himself as Kṛṣṇadāsa). In the concluding verses (3.45:17), the author explicitly notes that his commentary follows the interpretative path established in Kṣemarāja.
SA_GR13_sivsutru.edition: Śivasūtra-Vārtikam by Varadarāja, ed. Madhusudan Kaul Shastri. Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies (KSTS). Srinagar: Kashmir Pratap Steam Press, 1925.
SA_GR13_sivsutru.coverage: complete — Contains the text of all three chapters (unmeṣas) following the recension of Kṣemarāja, each sūtra embedded within Varadarāja's versified vārttika commentary (concluding at SivSV 3.45:19).
translations: Lilian Silburn, Śivasūtra et Vimarśinī de Kṣemarāja (Publications de l'Institut de civilisation indienne, fasc. 47). Paris: De Boccard, 1980. (French)

SA_GR13_sivup_pu.title: Śivopaniṣad
SA_GR13_sivup_pu.summary: The Śivopaniṣad is an early medieval Śaiva treatise in seven chapters (adhyāyas) belonging to the eight-text Śivadharma corpus, preserved predominantly in Nepalese manuscripts. Framed as a dialogue between Mahākāla and the sage Ātreya, it outlines a path of liberation tailored for lay devotees, expounding the triadic ontology of paśu, pāśa, and pati/śiva, the recitation and power of the two-syllable name Śiva, external ritual and internal worship (mānasapūjā), yoga, and righteous conduct (śivācāra). Although mistakenly cataloged and published in 1933 among minor sectarian Upaniṣads due to its title, modern scholarship recognizes it as an integral text of the Śivadharma cycle.
SA_GR13_sivup_pu.attribution: Scriptural text framed as an instruction delivered by Mahākāla on Mount Kailāsa in response to questions from the sage Ātreya. It forms part of the eight-text Śivadharma corpus.
SA_GR13_sivup_pu.edition: Un-published Upanisads, edited by the Pandits of Adyar Library under the supervision of C. Kunhan Raja, Adyar, Madras: The Adyar Library, 1933 (The Adyar Library Series, 14).
SA_GR13_sivup_pu.coverage: complete — Complete in seven adhyāyas (1.1 to 7.140), concluding with the colophon 'iti śivopaniṣadi śivācārādhyāyaḥ saptamaḥ // iti śivopaniṣat samāptā //'.

SA_GR13_somsv_u.title: Śāktavijñāna
SA_GR13_somsv_u.author: Somānanda
SA_GR13_somsv_u.summary: The Śāktavijñāna is a brief 30-verse manual of esoteric Śaiva-Śākta yoga attributed to Somānanda. It expounds thirteen stages or modes (trayodaśavidha) of kuṇḍalinī practice taught across the Trika scriptures: locus (sthāna), penetration (praveśa), form (rūpa), contemplative focus (lakṣa), diagnostic signs (lakṣaṇa), elevation (utthāpana), awakening (bodhana), rest in the centers (cakraviśrāma), ascent through the levels (bhūmikāgamana), penultimate state (antāvasthā), supreme rest in Śiva (viśrāma), radical transformation (pariṇāma), and subsequent return (āgamana).
SA_GR13_somsv_u.attribution: Ascribed in the Kashmiri tradition to Somānanda (Somānandanātha).
SA_GR13_somsv_u.edition: J.D. Zaidoo (ed.), Srinagar: Research Department, 1947 [Parātriṃśikātātparyadīpikā and Śāktavijñānam of Somānanda, Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies (KSTS)].

SA_GR13_sratrppu.title: Ratnatrayaparīkṣā
SA_GR13_sratrppu.author: Śrīkaṇṭha
SA_GR13_sratrppu.summary: The Ratnatrayaparīkṣā ('Examination of the Three Jewels') is an influential 10th–11th-century Sanskrit doctrinal treatise in 322 verses by the Kashmirian Śaiva Siddhānta scholar Śrīkaṇṭhasūri. Instead of examining the school's general ontological triad (pati, paśu, and pāśa), the work focuses specifically on the 'three jewels' defined as bindu (the material cause of pure sound, language, and the pure universe), śakti (the conscious power of the Lord), and śiva (the supreme agent and consciousness). Drawing heavily on earlier Kashmirian exegesis (especially Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha), it provides a detailed metaphysical exposition of the pure path (śuddhādhvan), phonematic cosmogony, and soteriological initiation.
SA_GR13_sratrppu.attribution: The Kashmirian Śaiva Siddhānta scholar Śrīkaṇṭhasūri identifies himself in the concluding verse (v. 322: 'ratnatrayaparīkṣārthaḥ saṃkṣepeṇa prakāśitaḥ') and mentions his reliance on Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha (vv. 321–322: 'rāmakaṇṭhakṛtālokanirmalīkṛtacetasā ... śrīrāmakaṇṭhasadvṛttiṃ mayaivamanukurvatā'). He is generally dated to the late 10th or 11th century CE.
SA_GR13_sratrppu.edition: Aṣṭaprakaraṇam, edited with the commentaries of Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha and Aghoraśivācārya by Vrajavallabha Dvivedī, Varanasi: Sampurnanand Sanskrit University, 1988 (Yogatantragranthamālā), pp. 147–202.
SA_GR13_sratrppu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the root verses (kārikās 1–322) of the Ratnatrayaparīkṣā. The prose commentary by Aghoraśiva (the Ullekhinī), printed alongside the kārikās in the source edition, was not keyed.
translations: Francesco Sferra, 'Materials for the Study of the Levels of Sound in the Sanskrit Sources of the Śaivasiddhānta. Ratnatrayaparīkṣā 22, 70c–86b, 171c–173b and its Ullekhinī', in Mélanges tantriques à la mémoire d'Hélène Brunner, Pondichéry: IFP / EFEO, 2007. (English (partial))

SA_GR13_stkal_pu.title: Sārdhatriśatikālottarāgama (chapters 1–23)
SA_GR13_stkal_pu.summary: The Sārdhatriśatikālottarāgama is an early Śaiva scripture (of which chapters 1–23 are preserved in this e-text), derived from the Vātulāgama ('vātulāttantrād dadhno ghṛtamivoddhṛtam', Stk_1.4). It expounds sonic cosmogenesis (nāda: gross, subtle, and supreme), initiation (dīkṣā), abhiṣeka, and spiritual knowledge leading to liberation, accompanied by a commentary (vṛtti) by Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha.
SA_GR13_stkal_pu.attribution: A scripture associated with the Vātulāgama. Although the printed edition by N. R. Bhatt includes the commentary by Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha, only the mūla verses were transcribed in this electronic text.
SA_GR13_stkal_pu.edition: N. R. Bhatt (ed.), Sārdhatriśatikālottarāgama, avec le commentaire de Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha, Publications de l'Institut Français d'Indologie 61, Pondichéry: Institut Français d'Indologie, 1979.
SA_GR13_stkal_pu.coverage: partial — Contains paṭalas 1–23 only (Stk_1.1 to Stk_23.26), ending with 'iti trayoviṃśaḥ paṭalaḥ'. The commentary of Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha is not included.

SA_GR13_svact_pu.title: Svacchandatantra
SA_GR13_svact_pu.summary: The Svacchandatantra is an important Śaiva tantric scripture arranged in fifteen paṭalas, treating deity visualization, mantra installation, initiation (dīkṣā), cosmography and pathways (adhvan), subtle breath-yoga, and related rites centered on Bhairava. Kṣemarāja composed an extensive commentary (Uddyota / Svacchandatantroddyota) on the text.
SA_GR13_svact_pu.edition: Composite transcription from Dwivedi's edition (chapters 1, 3, 5, 6, 11, 13, 14, 15) and the KSTS edition (chapters 2, 4, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12).
SA_GR13_svact_pu.coverage: complete — Complete mūla text in 15 paṭalas (paṭalas 1–15, comprising 3,648.5 verses across 7,441 half-verse segments), without Kṣemarāja's commentary.

SA_GR13_todaltpu.title: Toḍalatantra
SA_GR13_todaltpu.summary: The Toḍalatantra is a concise Śākta scripture in ten chapters (paṭalas) preserved chiefly in eastern India. It expounds subtle yogic anatomy, microcosm-macrocosm homologies, and the pūjā, mantras, and iconography of Kālī, Tārā, and the Mahāvidyās along with their male Bhairava consorts. In its tenth chapter, it presents a well-known synthesis equating each of the ten Mahāvidyās with one of Viṣṇu's ten avatāras (such as Kālī with Kṛṣṇa and Tārā with the fish incarnation).
SA_GR13_todaltpu.attribution: A revealed Śākta tantra transmitted primarily in eastern Indian manuscripts, presented traditionally as an instruction delivered by Śiva to the Devī.
SA_GR13_todaltpu.edition: Gopinath Kaviraj (ed.), Tantrasaṃgraha, vol. 2, Varanasi: Vārāṇaseya Saṃskṛta Viśvavidyālaya, 1970 (Yogatantra-Granthamālā, 4).
SA_GR13_todaltpu.coverage: complete — Complete text in 10 paṭalas (ToT 1.1 to 10.12, approx. 400 verses).

SA_GR13_uddamt_u.title: Uḍḍāmareśvaratantra
SA_GR13_uddamt_u.summary: A Śaiva tantra dedicated to pragmatic magic and sorcery (ṣaṭkarman), structured as an interlocution between Śiva and Gaurī. Drawing from traditions associated with the Uḍḍīśatantra, it provides mantras, pharmaceutical preparations, and ritual procedures for pacification, subjugation (vaśīkaraṇa), eradication (uccāṭana), the siddhi of yakṣiṇīs and vetālas, discovering hidden treasures, and curing physical ailments.
SA_GR13_uddamt_u.attribution: A scriptural Tantric work presented as a revelation/dialogue between Śiva (Īśvara / Bhairava) and the goddess Gaurī.
SA_GR13_uddamt_u.edition: J.D. Zadoo, Srinagar: The Normal Press, 1947.
SA_GR13_uddamt_u.coverage: complete — Text ending at verse UT_15.13.

SA_GR13_utsivsau.title: Śivastotrāvalī
SA_GR13_utsivsau.author: Utpaladeva
SA_GR13_utsivsau.summary: The Śivastotrāvalī is a collection of devotional hymns composed by Utpaladeva.
SA_GR13_utsivsau.edition: Constantina Rhodes Bailly (repr. Delhi 1990, Garib Dass Oriental Series, 109)
SA_GR13_utsivsau.coverage: complete — Complete mūla text of all 20 stotras (verses 1.1 through 20.21).
translations: N.K. Kotru, Sivastotravali of Utpaladeva (Delhi). (English)

Constantina Rhodes Bailly, Shaiva Devotional Songs of Kashmir: A Translation and Study of Utpaladeva's Shivastotravali, State University of New York Press, 1987 (repr. Delhi 1990, Garib Dass Oriental Series, 109). (English)
