SA_GR13_vinst_pu.title: Vīṇāśikhatantra
SA_GR13_vinst_pu.summary: The Vīṇāśikhatantra is an early Śaiva tantra and primary scripture of the Vāmasrotas ('Left Current') branch of the Mantramārga. It centers on the esoteric cult of Tumburu (a form of Śiva) and his four surrounding sister goddesses (Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, and Aparājitā), detailing their maṇḍalas, mantra encodings, initiation rituals (dīkṣā), and sādhanā procedures. The work is historically connected with the Śiraścheda, Sammohana, and Nayottara.
SA_GR13_vinst_pu.attribution: Anonymous scriptural revelation; traditionally presented as an esoteric dialogue between Śiva (Īśvara) and the Goddess (Umā/Devī).
SA_GR13_vinst_pu.edition: Teun Goudriaan (ed., trans.), The Vīṇāśikhatantra: A Śaiva Tantra of the Left Current, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1985.
SA_GR13_vinst_pu.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising stanzas followed by prose/mantric appendix materials and concluding colophons.
translations: Teun Goudriaan, The Vīṇāśikhatantra: A Śaiva Tantra of the Left Current (with introduction, translation, and notes), Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1985. (English)

SA_GR14_astavgpu.title: Aṣṭāvakragītā
SA_GR14_astavgpu.summary: The Aṣṭāvakragītā is an influential Advaita Vedānta treatise composed in 298 anuṣṭubh verses across 20 chapters. Framed as a dialogue between the sage Aṣṭāvakra and King Janaka of Videha, the text expounds an uncompromising, radical non-dualism (kevalādvaita) close to ajātavāda: the Self is pure, unattached witnessing consciousness (sākṣin), and liberation consists in the immediate recognition of one's innate freedom rather than the fruit of ritual action, meditation, or moral striving.
SA_GR14_astavgpu.coverage: complete — All 20 chapters, 298 distinct verses Avg_1.1–Avg_20.14 (per chapter: 20, 25, 14, 6, 4, 4, 5, 4, 8, 8, 8, 8, 7, 4, 20, 11, 20, 100, 8, 14), the standard vulgate extent; ends with 20.14 'bahunātra kim uktena kiṃcin nottiṣṭhate mama'.

SA_GR14_bhrgus_u.title: Bhṛgusaṃhitā (Prakīrṇādhikāra)
SA_GR14_bhrgus_u.summary: The Prakīrṇādhikāra is a foundational canonical manual belonging to the Vaikhānasa Vaiṣṇava Āgama tradition, attributed to the sage Bhṛgu as part of the Bhṛgusaṃhitā. Arranged in 37 chapters (comprising roughly 6,000 verses), the work focuses on temple ritual praxis (kriyāpāda), expounding architectural and ground testing (bhūparīkṣā), iconography, image installation (pratiṣṭhā) of Viṣṇu and attendant deities, ceremonial processions and festivals (utsavas), and extensive expiatory procedures (prāyaścitta/niṣkṛti) for ritual deviations. It forms one of the indispensable textual authorities for traditional temple worship in South Indian Vaikhānasa sanctuaries, such as Tirumala.
SA_GR14_bhrgus_u.attribution: Traditionally ascribed to the Vedic sage Bhṛgu, revered as one of the four prime disciples of Sage Vikhanas (along with Atri, Marīci, and Kāśyapa) who formulated the canonical ritual scriptures of the Vaikhānasa Vaiṣṇava school.
SA_GR14_bhrgus_u.coverage: complete — Prakīrṇādhikāra of the Vaikhānasa Bhṛgusaṃhitā, adhyāyas 1–37 all present (5,629 numbered verses BhS_1.1–37.219), ending with the anukramaṇī of the 37 adhyāyas, the statement 'ṣaḍbhiḥ sahasraiḥ ślokais tu kriyāṅgam upavarṇitam', the colophon '... bhṛguproktāyāṃ caturviṃśatsāhasrikāyāṃ saṃhitāyāṃ prakīrṇādhikāre saptatriṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ / iti śrīmati prakīrṇādhikāre kriyāpādaḥ' and closing benedictions. GRETIL warns: not proof-read, sequence between 32.4 and 32.82 unclear.

SA_GR14_brhms5cu.title: Brahmasaṃhitā with Digdarśanī (chapter 5)
SA_GR14_brhms5cu.author: Jīva Gosvāmin
SA_GR14_brhms5cu.summary: The fifth chapter of the Brahmasaṃhitā is a foundational scripture in the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava tradition consisting of 62 verses spoken by Brahmā praising Kṛṣṇa (Govinda) as the Supreme Deity and primary cause of all causes. The text outlines the ontology and layout of Goloka Vṛndāvana, the mystery of the kāmagāyatrī mantra, cosmogenesis through the agency of Mahā-Viṣṇu, and the distinction between God, the jīvas, and material nature. Jīva Gosvāmin's commentary, the Digdarśanī, interprets the esoteric verses in accordance with Gauḍīya acintyabhedābheda theology, drawing extensively on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa.
SA_GR14_brhms5cu.attribution: The root text Brahmasaṃhitā is a Vaiṣṇava/Pāñcarātra scripture traditionally ascribed to the god Brahmā. The Digdarśanī commentary was authored by Jīva Gosvāmin, who mentions in his introductory verses that it summarises points established in his Kṛṣṇasandarbha.
SA_GR14_brhms5cu.coverage: partial — Contains the complete 5th chapter (62 verses) of the Brahmasaṃhitā along with Jīva Gosvāmin's complete Digdarśanī commentary on it. The Saṃhitā is traditionally believed to have comprised 100 chapters (as noted in Jīva's introduction), but only this chapter is extant in the Gauḍīya tradition.

SA_GR14_caitcanu.title: Caitanyacandrāmṛta
SA_GR14_caitcanu.author: Prabodhānanda Sarasvatī
SA_GR14_caitcanu.summary: Devotional Sanskrit text in verse praising Caitanya (Caitanyacandra) and celebrating divine devotional love and saṅkīrtana.
SA_GR14_caitcanu.edition: Stava-kalpa-druma, ed. Bhakti Sāraṅga Gosvāmī, Vrindavan, 1959; and Śrī-Śrī-Caitanya-candrāmṛta, ed. Bhakti Vilāsa Tīrtha, Mayapur: Caitanya Maṭha, 3rd ed., 1992.
SA_GR14_caitcanu.coverage: complete — Contains 144 stanzas (143 sequentially numbered verses plus 1 unnumbered verse marked '??' at the end), collating verses from both the 1959 and 1992 printed editions, with bracketed numerals indicating placement in a twelve-theme recension.

SA_GR14_dhyggs_u.title: Gauragovindārcanasmaraṇapaddhati
SA_GR14_dhyggs_u.author: Dhyānacandra Gosvāmī
SA_GR14_dhyggs_u.summary: The Gauragovindārcanasmaraṇapaddhati by Dhyānacandra Gosvāmī is a ritual and meditative guide (paddhati) in the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava tradition, providing systematic instructions for worship and contemplative remembrance (smaraṇa) of Caitanya and Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa through the periods of the day, concluding with meditation in the siddha-deha.
SA_GR14_dhyggs_u.coverage: complete — 362 numbered sections/verses GGS_1–GGS_362, from the morning nāma-smaraṇa ('sādhako brāhma-muhūrte cotthāya ...') to the concluding instruction on meditation in the siddha-deha ('smared evaṃ krameṇaiva siddha-dehena sādhakaḥ ...', GGS_362); no gaps in numbering.

SA_GR14_dhyrkk_u.title: Rādhākṛṣṇāṣṭakālīyalīlāsmaraṇakramapaddhati
SA_GR14_dhyrkk_u.author: Dhyānacandra Gosvāmī
SA_GR14_dhyrkk_u.summary: The Rādhākṛṣṇāṣṭakālīyalīlāsmaraṇakramapaddhati is a Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava manual for devotional meditation. It provides a framework for the continuous remembrance (smaraṇa) and mental service (sevā) of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa throughout eight daily temporal divisions (aṣṭakālīya-līlā), visualizing pastimes in an internalized spiritual identity (siddha-deha), accompanied by specific mantras and time allotments.
SA_GR14_dhyrkk_u.attribution: Attributed to Dhyānacandra Gosvāmī in the colophon (śrī-dhyāna-candra-gosvāmi-viracitā).
SA_GR14_dhyrkk_u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 171 verses (tagged RKK_1 through RKK_171), covering preliminary rites, the eight temporal periods of divine service, and meditation periods.

SA_GR14_harinc_u.title: Harināmacintāmaṇi (verses 11.2–25 missing)
SA_GR14_harinc_u.author: Kedāranātha Datta
SA_GR14_harinc_u.summary: Structured as an extended theological dialogue at Jagannātha Purī between Caitanya Mahāprabhu and Haridāsa Ṭhākura. Across fifteen chapters, it provides a comprehensive manual on the theology and contemplative practice of chanting the holy name of Kṛṣṇa (harināma). The treatise details offenses against the holy name (nāmāparādha), semblance chanting (nāmābhāsa), pure devotional chanting, and a meditative progression (bhajana-praṇālī).
SA_GR14_harinc_u.attribution: Composed by Kedāranātha Datta, also known as Bhaktivinoda (1838–1914).
SA_GR14_harinc_u.coverage: partial — Paricchedas 1–15 complete to the final colophon (iti śrī-hari-nāma-cintāmaṇau bhajana-praṇālī-pradarśanaṃ nāma pañcadaśaḥ paricchedaḥ, HNC_15.115), except a lacuna of verses in pariccheda 11 (HNC 11.2–11.25), as flagged in the GRETIL header.

SA_GR14_hbhvil_u.title: Haribhaktivilāsa (chapters 1–11)
SA_GR14_hbhvil_u.author: Gopālabhaṭṭa Gosvāmin, Sanātana Gosvāmin
SA_GR14_hbhvil_u.summary: The Haribhaktivilāsa is a Vaiṣṇava ritual and behavioural work. This portion (vilāsas 1–11) treats devotional duties, purification, and daily worship practices, citing various purāṇic and tantric scriptures.
SA_GR14_hbhvil_u.attribution: The Haribhaktivilāsa identifies Gopālabhaṭṭa (disciple of Prabodhānanda Sarasvatī) as compiler in its introductory verses (1.2) and colophon (iti śrī-gopāla-bhaṭṭa-vilikhite śrī-bhagavad-bhakti-vilāse).
SA_GR14_hbhvil_u.edition: Haribhaktivilāsa, edited by Haridāsa Śāstrī. 2 volumes. Vṛndāvana: Śrīgadādharagaurahari Press, 1986.
SA_GR14_hbhvil_u.coverage: partial — Contains vilāsas 1–11. Missing verses listed in the source header: 3.52, 3.223–224, 5.268, 10.294, and 11.244.

SA_GR14_jivrkadu.title: Rādhākṛṣṇārcanadīpikā
SA_GR14_jivrkadu.author: Jīva Gosvāmin
SA_GR14_jivrkadu.summary: The Rādhākṛṣṇārcanadīpikā ('Lamp Illuminating the Worship of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa') is a theological and ritual treatise in mixed prose and verse composed by Jīva Gosvāmin. It establishes the doctrinal justification for the paired worship of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa (specifically in the form of Rādhā-Dāmodara), drawing extensively on Purāṇic, Tantric, and Smṛti proof texts. Jīva argues that true worship of Bhagavān necessitates the worship of His devotees, establishes the gopīs as His foremost devotees, and demonstrates that Rādhā must be worshipped alongside Him.
SA_GR14_jivrkadu.attribution: Firmly attributed to Jīva Gosvāmin in the colophon ('iti śrī-vṛndāvana-vāsinaḥ kasyacij jīvasya śrī-rādhā-kṛṣṇārcana-dīpikā...') and opening verse with invocation of Sanātana and Rūpa Gosvāmin. Jīva also refers to this work under the variant title Kṛṣṇārcanadīpikā in his commentary on Brahma-saṃhitā (verse 4).
SA_GR14_jivrkadu.coverage: complete — Text in mixed prose and verse, concluding with the author's colophon followed by scribal/editorial cross-references.

SA_GR14_jnass01u.title: Jñānāmṛtasārasaṃhitā (rātra 1: chapters 1–15)
SA_GR14_jnass01u.summary: The Jñānāmṛtasārasaṃhitā (also called Nāradapañcarātra) is a Pāñcarātra Vaiṣṇava saṃhitā framed as a dialogue between Śiva and the celestial sage Nārada. The work emphasizes devotional mantras, Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa, and bhakti. This digital file covers only the first section (Prathamarātra, chapters 1–15).
SA_GR14_jnass01u.attribution: A Pāñcarātra revelatory saṃhitā framed as teachings expounded by Śiva to Nārada. In accordance with traditional classification for āgamas and saṃhitās, it has no individual human author.
SA_GR14_jnass01u.coverage: partial — Only the first rātra (prathamarātra), adhyāyas 1–15 (Jss_1,1.1 – Jss_1,15.31), ending 'samāptaś cedaṃ nārada-pañca-rātraika-rātram'.

SA_GR14_kbss_1-u.title: Bhāvanāsārasaṃgraha (chapters 1–2)
SA_GR14_kbss_1-u.author: Kṛṣṇadāsa Tātapāda
SA_GR14_kbss_1-u.summary: The Bhāvanāsārasaṃgraha is a Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava anthology compiled by Kṛṣṇadāsa Tātapāda. It gathers verses from texts such as Caitanya-candrāmṛta, Ānanda-vṛndāvana-campū, Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu, Govinda-līlāmṛta, Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta, and Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī, organized by daily pastimes (līlās). This electronic text preserves the first two divisions: Niśāntalīlā and Prātarlīlā.
SA_GR14_kbss_1-u.coverage: partial — Contains only the first two sections: Niśānta-līlā and Prātar-līlā. It terminates with the colophon: 'iti śrī-bhāvanā-sāra-saṅgrahe prātar-līlā-saṅgraho nāma dvitīya-saṅgrahaḥ'.

SA_GR14_krdipc_u.title: Kramadīpikā with Vivaraṇa
SA_GR14_krdipc_u.author: Keśava Kāśmīrī, Govindabhaṭṭācārya
SA_GR14_krdipc_u.summary: The Kramadīpikā is an eight-chapter Vaiṣṇava ritual and mantra manual (āgamanibandha) focused on the worship of Kṛṣṇa Gopāla, composed by Keśava Kāśmīrī. It expounds mantras (including the ten-syllable Gopāla mantra), daily worship, nyāsas, mudrās, and homa rites, accompanied in this e-text by Govindabhaṭṭācārya's commentary, the Vivaraṇa.
SA_GR14_krdipc_u.attribution: The root manual is authored by Keśava Kāśmīrī, designated in the colophons as Mahāmahopādhyāya Śrī-Keśava-Kāśmīri-Bhaṭṭa-Gosvāmin. The commentary Vivaraṇa is by Vidyāvinoda Govindabhaṭṭācārya.
SA_GR14_krdipc_u.edition: Sudhākara Mālavīya (ed.), Kramadīpikā with the commentary by Govindabhaṭṭācārya, Benares: Krishnadas Academy, 1989 (Krishnadas Sanskrit Series, 119).
SA_GR14_krdipc_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of all eight paṭalas of both the root Kramadīpikā and Govindabhaṭṭācārya's Vivaraṇa commentary.

SA_GR14_kumukumu.title: Mukundamālā
SA_GR14_kumukumu.author: Kulaśekhara
SA_GR14_kumukumu.summary: The Mukundamālā is a Sanskrit devotional hymn (stotra) attributed to Kulaśekhara. Addressed to Mukunda (Kṛṣṇa/Viṣṇu), the hymn focuses on devotional surrender, renunciation of mundane pursuits, and continuous remembrance of the deity's feet.
SA_GR14_kumukumu.attribution: Attributed to Kulaśekhara (identified as Kulaśekhara Āḻvār).
SA_GR14_kumukumu.edition: Stotramālā, ed. P. B. Aṇṇaṅgarācārya (P. B. Annangaracharya), Kanchipuram: Granthamala Office 1949, pp. 1–4.
SA_GR14_kumukumu.coverage: complete — Contains 40 verses plus an introductory verse ('ghuṣyate yasya nagare...').

SA_GR14_laghbh_u.title: Laghubhāgavatāmṛta
SA_GR14_laghbh_u.author: Rūpa Gosvāmī
SA_GR14_laghbh_u.summary: The Laghubhāgavatāmṛta is a theological treatise composed by Rūpa Gosvāmī summarizing and systematizing Vaiṣṇava ontology. The first part (Pūrvakhaṇḍa or Śrī-Kṛṣṇāmṛta) provides a scriptural classification of divine forms and avataric descents (svayaṃrūpa, tad-ekātma-rūpa, vilāsa, svāṃśa, āveśa, and prakāśa), demonstrating that Kṛṣṇa is the original supreme divinity (avatārī) rather than a subordinate incarnation of Viṣṇu. The shorter second part (Uttarakhaṇḍa or Śrī-Bhaktāmṛta) establishes a gradated hierarchy of devotees of Kṛṣṇa, culminating in the gopīs of Vraja and preeminently Śrī Rādhā.
SA_GR14_laghbh_u.coverage: complete — Pūrvakhaṇḍa (Kṛṣṇāmṛta, Lbh_1, 5 paricchedas) and Uttarakhaṇḍa (Bhaktāmṛta, Lbh_2,1.1–46), ending "iti śrī-laghu-bhāgavatāmṛtaṃ sampūrṇam"; five verses missing per GRETIL header (1,3.63; 1,5.478, 519–520, 535).

SA_GR14_mdhvkmou.title: Kṛṣṇāmṛtamahārṇava
SA_GR14_mdhvkmou.author: Madhva
SA_GR14_mdhvkmou.summary: The Kṛṣṇāmṛtamahārṇava ('The Great Ocean of the Nectar of Kṛṣṇa') is a devotional manual and anthology attributed to Madhva (Ānandatīrtha). The work highlights the supremacy of Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa and the salvific power of bhakti, detailing orthoprax Vaiṣṇava conduct (sadācāra), including the sanctity of the Ekādaśī fast, the veneration of Śālagrāma stones, and niṣkāma karma as the path to liberation.
SA_GR14_mdhvkmou.attribution: Authored by Madhva (also known as Ānandatīrtha).
SA_GR14_mdhvkmou.edition: Sri Anandatirtha Bhagavatpada, Sarvamulagranthah-Prasthanatrayi (ed. by Govindacarya), Vol. 5, Udupi: Akhila Bharata Madhva Maha Mandala, 1974, pp. 77-102 (cf. Thomas K. Gugler: Ozeanisches Gefühl der Unsterblichkeit: Der Krishnamritamaharnava des Madhva, Münster 2009, Leipziger Studien zu Kultur und Geschichte Süd- und Zentralasiens, 3).

SA_GR14_muktacau.title: Muktācarita
SA_GR14_muktacau.author: Raghunāthadāsa Gosvāmī
SA_GR14_muktacau.summary: The Muktācarita ('The Tale of the Pearl') is a campū-kāvya combining Sanskrit prose and verse, composed by Raghunāthadāsa Gosvāmī. Framed as a dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and his queen Satyabhāmā in Dvārakā, Kṛṣṇa recounts an incident from his youth in Vraja during the Dīpāvalī festival: when the gopīs refuse to give him pearls to ornament his beloved cows, Kṛṣṇa plants pearls in the earth and harvests bountiful pearl creepers, whereas the envious gopīs sow pearls with milk and butter but reap only thorny bushes. The work focuses on the witty banter, mock disputes, and commercial bargaining over the jewels between Kṛṣṇa, Subala, Madhumaṅgala, Rādhā, and Lalitā, illustrating the intimate erotic-devotional theology (mādhura-līlā) of the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava tradition.
SA_GR14_muktacau.attribution: Attributed to Raghunāthadāsa Gosvāmī. The work concludes with verses dedicating the poem to Rūpa Gosvāmī, mentioning Jīva Gosvāmī, and expressing affection for Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja ('kṛṣṇa-kavi-bhūpati').
SA_GR14_muktacau.coverage: complete — Prosimetric campū text, concluding with verses mentioning Rūpa, Jīva, and Kṛṣṇa-kavi-bhūpati.

SA_GR14_prakassu.title: Prakāśasaṃhitā (pariccheda 1 and pariccheda 2, chapters 1–6)
SA_GR14_prakassu.summary: The Prakāśasaṃhitā is a Vaiṣṇava Āgamic text belonging to the Pāñcarātra canon, framed as a dialogue between Śrīhaṃsa and an interlocutor addressing him as jagadguru. Its doctrines include the eightfold cosmic agency of Viṣṇu (sṛṣṭyādyaṣṭakartṛtva), cosmogony, and descriptions of the cosmic worlds and beings.
SA_GR14_prakassu.attribution: Scriptural saṃhitā framed as teachings delivered by Śrīhaṃsa (an incarnation of Viṣṇu) to Brahmā.
SA_GR14_prakassu.coverage: partial — Pariccheda 1, adhyāyas 1–15, and pariccheda 2, adhyāyas 1–6 (PS_1,1.1 – PS_2,6.60). The last line is the chapter colophon "iti śrī prakāśasaṃhitāyāṃ dvitīyaparicchede ṣaṣṭho 'dhyāyaḥ"; there is no end-of-work formula and the narrative (Yayāti → Yadu dynasty → Vasudeva, of whom Hari was born) breaks off, so the text is probably incomplete. The full extent of the work is not documented in the sources checked.

SA_GR14_ps27-43u.title: Pauṣkarasaṃhitā (chapters 27–43)
SA_GR14_ps27-43u.summary: The Pauṣkarasaṃhitā is a canonical text of Pāñcarātra Vaiṣṇavism, revered alongside the Sātvata- and Jayākhyasaṃhitās as one of the three gems. Framed as an exposition delivered by Bhagavān to Pauṣkara (Brahmā), it covers ritual procedure, ancestral rites (śrāddha), mandalas, and liturgies.
SA_GR14_ps27-43u.attribution: A canonical saṃhitā of the Pāñcarātra tradition, presented as a dialogue between Bhagavān and Pauṣkara (Abjaja). Together with the Sātvatasaṃhitā and Jayākhyasaṃhitā, it forms the 'ratnatraya' ('three gems') of the Pāñcarātra tradition.
SA_GR14_ps27-43u.edition: Prabhakar Pandurang Apte (ed.), Pauṣkarasaṃhitā: dvitīyo bhāgaḥ, Tirupati 2006 (Rashtriya Sanskrit Vidyapeetha Series, 120).
SA_GR14_ps27-43u.coverage: partial — Contains adhyāyas 27–43 of the text (verses 27.1 to 43.205).

SA_GR14_ruphbr_u.title: Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu
SA_GR14_ruphbr_u.author: Rūpa Gosvāmin
SA_GR14_ruphbr_u.summary: The Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu ('Ocean of the Nectar of Devotional Rasa'), composed by Rūpa Gosvāmin, is the foundational work of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava devotional theology and aesthetics. Adapting the classical rasa theory of Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra and medieval alaṃkāraśāstra, Rūpa establishes devotion (bhakti) directed toward Kṛṣṇa not merely as a bhāva (transient emotional state), but as the supreme aesthetic and ontological sentiment (bhakti-rasa). Organised in four quadrants (pūrva, dakṣiṇa, paścima, and uttara vibhāgas), the text comprehensively systematises the categories of devotional practice (sādhana, bhāva, prema), the constituent components of aesthetic emotion (vibhāva, anubhāva, sāttvikabhāva, vyabhicāribhāva), the primary rasas (śānta, dāsya, sakhya, vātsalya, madhura), and the secondary devotional sentiments along with discordant mixtures (rasābhāsa).
SA_GR14_ruphbr_u.attribution: Universally accepted as the work of Rūpa Gosvāmin.
SA_GR14_ruphbr_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the root work (kārikās, prose introductions, and illustrative verses) across all four divisions (vibhāgas: pūrva, dakṣiṇa, paścima, and uttara) and their component laharīs, concluding with the author's final stanzas and scribal/editorial colophon.

SA_GR14_sadhdipu.title: Sādhanādīpikā
SA_GR14_sadhdipu.author: Rādhākṛṣṇadāsa Gosvāmī
SA_GR14_sadhdipu.summary: The Sādhanādīpikā is a ritual and theological text focusing on devotional practice (sādhana), vigraha-sevā, deities, Gadādhara, and bhakti.
SA_GR14_sadhdipu.coverage: complete — Text concluding with 14 editorial endnotes.

SA_GR14_satvtanu.title: Sātvatatantra
SA_GR14_satvtanu.summary: The Sātvatatantra is a Vaiṣṇava scriptural text in nine paṭalas framed as a dialogue between Śiva and Nārada on Mount Kailāsa. Diverging from classical tantric ritual manuals, it centers on the philosophical cosmology of Viṣṇu-Kṛṣṇa, the emanation of cosmic puruṣa and avatāra forms, and the supreme efficacy of bhakti and the divine name.
SA_GR14_satvtanu.attribution: Presented within the narrative frame as revealed originally by Nārāyaṇa and communicated by Śiva to Nārada on Mount Kailāsa, related by the narrator Sūta. Although bearing the title 'tantra' and drawing upon Sātvata/Pāñcarātra terminology, it is an independent work distinct from the classical Pāñcarātra 'Sātvatasaṃhitā'.
SA_GR14_satvtanu.edition: Sātvatatantra, edited by A. Phadke (Ananta Śāstrī Phaḍke), Benares: Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series Office, 1934 (Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series No. 427).
SA_GR14_satvtanu.coverage: complete — Complete text across all 9 chapters (paṭalas 1–9), concluding at SatvT_9.57.

SA_GR14_sdahen_u.title: Daśavidhahetunirūpaṇa
SA_GR14_sdahen_u.author: Śrīnivāsamakhin
SA_GR14_sdahen_u.summary: The Daśavidhahetunirūpaṇa ('Demonstration of Ten Reasons') is a major polemical and theological treatise of the Vaikhānasa Vaiṣṇava tradition, composed by Śrīnivāsamakhin as the introductory treatise (upodghātabhāga) to his Vaikhānasasūtratātparyacintāmaṇi. The author sets out ten systematic arguments demonstrating the Vedic orthodoxy, ritual superiority, and primordial authority of the Vaikhānasa Kalpasūtra and temple image worship (arcāvatāra). Drawing heavily upon Vedic literature, Upaniṣads, Purāṇas, and Dharmasūtras, the treatise defends distinctive Vaikhānasa practices—such as prenatal branding (viṣṇubali) and exclusive hereditary priesthood—against rival traditions, particularly the Pāñcarātra and Smārta schools.
SA_GR14_sdahen_u.attribution: The colophon explicitly identifies the author as 'Śrīnivāsamakhivedāntadeśika' (also referred to in tradition as Śrīnivāsa Dīkṣita), associated with Veṅkaṭācala.
SA_GR14_sdahen_u.edition: Śrīvaikhānasagṛhyasūtra, ed. R. Parthasarathi Bhattacarya, 2 vols., Akulamannāḍu, 1967, pp. 1–122.
SA_GR14_sdahen_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of all ten sections/arguments (hetus 1–10) of the Daśavidhahetunirūpaṇa, corresponding to pages 1–122 of the 1967 edition. Preceded by an editorial abbreviation list compiled by Ute Hüsken.

SA_GR14_ss1_tatu.title: Tattvasandarbha with Tattvasandarbhaṭippaṇī
SA_GR14_ss1_tatu.author: Jīva Gosvāmī, Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa
SA_GR14_ss1_tatu.summary: Tattvasandarbha is the first treatise of Jīva Gosvāmī's Ṣaṭsandarbha (or Bhāgavatasandarbha). It establishes the epistemological foundation of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism, arguing that divine revelation (śabda-pramāṇa) is superior to perception and inference, and demonstrating that the Bhāgavata Purāṇa is the supreme pramāṇa. In this e-text, Jīva's text is accompanied by the Sanskrit gloss (Ṭippaṇī) of Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa.
SA_GR14_ss1_tatu.attribution: The commentary (prefixed with 'BD:') is by Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa.
SA_GR14_ss1_tatu.coverage: complete — Text of the Tattvasandarbha together with Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa's Ṭippaṇī commentary, concluding with Baladeva's concluding verses and colophon.

SA_GR14_ss2_bhgu.title: Ṣaṭsandarbha: 2. Bhagavatsandarbha
SA_GR14_ss2_bhgu.author: Jīva Gosvāmī
SA_GR14_ss2_bhgu.summary: The Bhagavatsandarbha is the second treatise of Jīva Gosvāmī's foundational 16th-century theological work, the Ṣaṭsandarbha (or Bhāgavatasandarbha). Centering its inquiry around the tripartite definition of Absolute Reality in Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.2.11 (brahmeti paramātmeti bhagavān iti śabdyate), the work establishes that Bhagavān—the supreme personal God possessed of all potencies—is the highest and most complete manifestation of Non-dual Consciousness (advaya-jñāna), whereas impersonal Brahman is an unmanifest, partial revelation. Across 118 anucchedas, Jīva details the intrinsic divine potency (svarūpa-śakti) with its threefold aspects of sandhinī (existence), saṃvit (knowledge), and hlādinī (bliss), expounds the trans-material nature of the divine realm (viśuddha-sattva), and defends the eternity of the Lord's transcendent anthropomorphic form (vigraha), abode (dhāman), and associates (parikara).
SA_GR14_ss2_bhgu.attribution: In the opening verses (vv. 2–3), Jīva Gosvāmī notes that he is re-organizing and completing an initial draft sketched by Gopāla Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī ('dākṣiṇātyena bhaṭṭena pnuar etad vivicyate / tasyādyaṃ granthanālekhaṃ krāntam utkrānta-khaṇḍitam / paryālocyātha paryāyaṃ kṛtvā likhati jīvakaḥ').
SA_GR14_ss2_bhgu.coverage: complete — Text of the Bhagavatsandarbha accompanied by editorial endnotes (up to endnote 62).

SA_GR14_ss3_paru.title: Paramātmasandarbha
SA_GR14_ss3_paru.author: Jīva Gosvāmī
SA_GR14_ss3_paru.summary: The Paramātmasandarbha is the third treatise of Jīva Gosvāmī's sixfold Bhāgavatasandarbha, expounding the sambandha-jñāna (metaphysical ontology) of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism on the basis of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa. It examines the nature of Paramātmā as the indwelling Lord, cosmic source, and regulator of material creation, and systematically defines the individual soul (jīva) as an atomic, conscious entity (aṃśa) and marginal potency (taṭasthā-śakti) distinct from both the material energy (māyā) and the Supreme Lord. Through detailed Purāṇic and Upaniṣadic exegesis, Jīva refutes Kevalādvaita monism and articulates the foundational tenets of the Gauḍīya acintyabhedābheda doctrine.
SA_GR14_ss3_paru.attribution: Third of the six Sandarbhas composing the Bhāgavatasandarbha (Ṣaṭsandarbha) authored by Jīva Gosvāmī, who in his opening verses acknowledges drawing upon the preparatory collation of Gopāla Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī.
SA_GR14_ss3_paru.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 105/106 anucchedas and concluding verses, followed by digitizer endnotes.

SA_GR14_ss4_krsu.title: Kṛṣṇasandarbha
SA_GR14_ss4_krsu.author: Jīva Gosvāmī
SA_GR14_ss4_krsu.summary: The Kṛṣṇasandarbha is the fourth treatise of Jīva Gosvāmī's masterwork, the Ṣaṭsandarbha (or Bhāgavatasandarbha), composed in 16th-century Vrindavan. Serving as the primary theological defense of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava ontology, the text systematically argues on the basis of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (particularly 1.3.28: 'kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam') that Kṛṣṇa is not merely an avatāra of Viṣṇu, but the ultimate and complete Godhead (Svayaṃ Bhagavān). It elaborates upon the ontological status of Kṛṣṇa's eternal abode (Goloka/Vraja), His transcendental entourage (parikara), the eternity of His manifest and unmanifest līlās, and the supreme status of the gopīs and Rādhārāṇī.
SA_GR14_ss4_krsu.attribution: In the opening verses (vv. 2–3), Jīva Gosvāmī acknowledges that he arranged, revised, and expanded upon notes and outlines originally gathered by Gopāla Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī (dākṣiṇātyena bhaṭṭena punar etad vivicyate / tasyādyaṃ granthanālekhaṃ krāntam utkrānta-khaṇḍitam / paryālocyātha paryāyaṃ kṛtvā likhati jīvakaḥ).
SA_GR14_ss4_krsu.coverage: complete — Introductory verses followed by the prose treatise and English endnotes.

SA_GR14_ss5_bhku.title: Bhaktisandarbha
SA_GR14_ss5_bhku.author: Jīva Gosvāmī
SA_GR14_ss5_bhku.summary: The Bhaktisandarbha is the fifth treatise in Jīva Gosvāmī's sixfold doctrinal compendium, the Ṣaṭsandarbha (or Bhāgavatasandarbha). While the preceding four sandarbhas establish ontology and theology (sambandha-tattva), the Bhaktisandarbha sets forth devotional service (bhakti) as the abhidheya-tattva.
SA_GR14_ss5_bhku.attribution: In the opening verses, Jīva acknowledges drawing upon and systematizing an initial draft or materials compiled by Gopāla Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī (referred to as 'dākṣiṇātya bhaṭṭa').
SA_GR14_ss5_bhku.coverage: complete — Text ending with the colophon 'bhakti-sandarbho nāma pañcamaḥ sandarbhaḥ // samāptaś cāyaṃ śrī-bhakti-sandarbhaḥ //'.

SA_GR14_ss6_priu.title: Prītisandarbha
SA_GR14_ss6_priu.author: Jīva Gosvāmī
SA_GR14_ss6_priu.summary: The Prītisandarbha ('Treatise on Divine Love') is the sixth and culminating treatise of Jīva Gosvāmī's Ṣaṭsandarbha (also designated as the Bhāgavatasandarbha). Following the discussions of sambandha (ontological knowledge of the Divine in Sandarbhas 1–4) and abhidheya (the practice of devotional service in the Bhaktisandarbha), this work examines prayojana, the ultimate goal of human life. Through extensive citations of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa and classical Indian poetics, Jīva defines prīti (pure devotional love, or prema) as transcending liberation (mokṣa), elucidates the ontology and psychology of devotional emotion (bhaktirasa), and details the varieties of loving relationships culminating in mahābhāva.
SA_GR14_ss6_priu.attribution: The work is an undisputed composition of Jīva Gosvāmī, who names himself in the opening verse ('likhati jīvakaḥ', v. 4).
SA_GR14_ss6_priu.coverage: complete — To the final colophons "prītyākhyaḥ ṣaṣṭhaḥ sandarbhaḥ samāptim iha saṅgataḥ || samāpto 'yaṃ ṣaṣṭhaḥ sandarbhaḥ | sampūrṇo 'yaṃ granthaḥ |".

SA_GR14_utajp_pu.title: Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi with Vṛtti
SA_GR14_utajp_pu.author: Utpaladeva, Harabhaṭṭa Śāstrī
SA_GR14_utajp_pu.summary: The Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi ('Proof of a Conscious Knower') is one of three short treatises comprising Utpaladeva's Siddhitrayī, written to establish the foundational tenets of non-dual Pratyabhijñā philosophy. In 27 kārikās, Utpaladeva argues against Buddhist momentariness and static Vedāntic consciousness, maintaining that both cognition and practical causal efficacy (arthakriyā) require an active, self-reflective subject (vimarśa, ahaṃbhāva) rather than an insentient (jaḍa) continuum. In this edition, the lost original auto-commentary is replaced by a concise Sanskrit Vṛtti composed in Śāka 1841 by Kashmiri scholar Harabhaṭṭa Śāstrī.
SA_GR14_utajp_pu.attribution: The root text consists of 27 kārikās by Utpaladeva, forming part of his Siddhitrayī. Utpaladeva's original auto-commentary being lost, the short Sanskrit Vṛtti accompanying the verses was composed in Śāka 1841 by the Kashmiri scholar Paṇḍit Harabhaṭṭa Śāstrī, as recorded in the concluding verse (candrābdhyaṣṭenduśākābde śāstrī vṛttiṃ haro vyadhāt).
SA_GR14_utajp_pu.edition: Siddhitrayī by Madhusudan Kaul Shastri Srinagar: Kashmir Pratap Steam Press 1921 (Kashmir Series of Sanskrit Texts and Studies, 34)
SA_GR14_utajp_pu.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all 27 kārikās of the Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi together with Harabhaṭṭa Śāstrī's Vṛtti, concluding with Harabhaṭṭa's verse, the colophon, and Madhusūdan Kaul Śāstrī's editorial verse.

SA_GR14_vaimp__u.title: Vaikhānasamantrapraśna (praśnas 5–8)
SA_GR14_vaimp__u.summary: The Vaikhānasamantrapraśna (also known as the Mantrasaṃhitā) is the fundamental liturgical mantra collection of the Vaikhānasa school of the Black Yajurveda, whose hereditary priests conduct worship in prominent South Indian Vaiṣṇava temples. The work comprises eight praśnas: Praśnas 1–4 accompany domestic life-cycle rituals (gṛhya), while Praśnas 5–8 (the Daivikacatuṣṭaya) provide the mantras for public temple worship, image installation, and ceremonies honoring Viṣṇu and attendant deities. This e-text contains Praśnas 5–8, preserving both accented Vedic formulas and distinctive early Vaiṣṇava theological invocations.
SA_GR14_vaimp__u.attribution: Scriptural mantra collection traditionally traced to the primordial seer Vikhanas; regarded in the Vaikhānasa school as its mantra-saṃhitā affiliated with the Taittirīya recension of the Black Yajurveda.
SA_GR14_vaimp__u.coverage: partial — Contains Praśnas 5 through 8 (the Daivikacatuṣṭaya) complete. Praśnas 1 through 4 (the smārta/gṛhya portion) are not included in this file.
translations: Resnick, Howard Jay, The 'Daivika-Catustayam' of the 'Vaikhanasa-mantra-prasna': A Translation, Thesis, Cambridge MA: Harvard Univ., 1996. (English)

SA_GR14_vdhapadu.title: Viṣṇudharma
SA_GR14_vdhapadu.summary: The Viṣṇudharma is an early Vaiṣṇava devotional and ritual handbook of approximately 4,200 verses in 105 chapters, generally dated to the 3rd–5th century CE. Framed as an exposition given by the sage Śaunaka to King Śatānīka, it instructs householders and lay devotees on the worship, liturgy, mental contemplation, vrata observances, and festivals dedicated to Viṣṇu. It represents one of the foundational texts of early non-sectarian Vaiṣṇavism, serving as a direct predecessor to the larger encyclopedic Viṣṇudharmottarapurāṇa and functioning alongside the roughly contemporary Śivadharmaśāstra as a crucial witness to early medieval devotional religion.
SA_GR14_vdhapadu.attribution: The Viṣṇudharma is an anonymous early Vaiṣṇava text belonging to the upapurāṇa / religious dharma genre, framed as an instruction delivered by the sage Śaunaka to the Pāṇḍava descendant King Śatānīka. Medieval digests cite it variously as a Purāṇa or as a Śāstra, but no historical author is attributed.
SA_GR14_vdhapadu.edition: R. Gruenendahl: Visnudharmah - Precepts for the worship of Visnu. Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz, 3 vols., 1983-1989
SA_GR14_vdhapadu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 105 chapters (adhyāyas 1–105) preceded by the opening maṅgala verses, formatted pāda by pāda in text sequence.

SA_GR14_visvaksu.title: Viṣvaksenasaṃhitā
SA_GR14_visvaksu.summary: The Viṣvaksenasaṃhitā is a canonical Pāñcarātra Vaiṣṇava Āgama comprising 39 chapters and around 2,800 verses, named after Viṣvaksena, the celestial marshal and gatekeeper of Viṣṇu. It treats temple site selection, prāsāda architecture, iconometry, the manufacture and consecration (pratiṣṭhā) of icons, temple worship rituals, festival observances, and atonement rites (prāyaścitta). The theological framework incorporates the classic Pāñcarātra doctrine of the vyūhas as well as cosmogonic and sociological accounts.
SA_GR14_visvaksu.attribution: A canonical Vaiṣṇava Āgama text belonging to the Pāñcarātra tradition, traditionally structured as a revelation delivered by Viṣvaksena, the commander and gate-guardian of Viṣṇu's host. It has no single historical author.
SA_GR14_visvaksu.edition: Viṣvaksenasaṃhitā, critically edited by Lakshmi Narasimha Bhatta, Tirupati: Kendriya Sanskrit Vidyapeetha, 1972 (Kendriya Sanskrit Vidyapeetha Series).
SA_GR14_visvaksu.coverage: complete — Complete text in 39 adhyāyas (approx. 2,800 verses), beginning with bhūparīkṣāvidhi (1.1) and ending with the colophon to chapter 39 on prāyaścittavidhi (39.351).

SA_GR14_yamcatpu.title: Catuḥślokī
SA_GR14_yamcatpu.author: Yāmuna
SA_GR14_yamcatpu.summary: The Catuḥślokī ('Four Stanzas') is a short Sanskrit devotional stotra composed by Yāmuna in praise of the goddess Śrī (Lakṣmī). It celebrates her supreme majesty as the consort of Puruṣottama (Viṣṇu) and describes her grace.
SA_GR14_yamcatpu.attribution: Attributed to Yāmuna. Commented upon by Vedānta Deśika in his Rahasyarakṣā.
SA_GR14_yamcatpu.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all 4 verses, numbered YCs_1 through YCs_4.

SA_GR14_yamsr_pu.title: Stotraratna (verses 1–64)
SA_GR14_yamsr_pu.author: Yāmuna
SA_GR14_yamsr_pu.summary: The Stotraratna is a devotional hymn composed by Yāmunācārya (c. 10th–early 11th century CE) in praise of Viṣṇu/Nārāyaṇa. The text opens with homage to ancestral figures such as Nāthamuni and Parāśara, and expresses complete surrender (śaraṇāgati/prapatti) and devotion. Verses 1–64 are preserved in this e-text.
SA_GR14_yamsr_pu.attribution: Attributed to Yāmuna (c. 10th–early 11th century CE), who extols his grandfather Nāthamuni.

SA_GS24_jvkasipu.title: Kāśikāvṛtti
SA_GS24_jvkasipu.author: Jayāditya, Vāmana
SA_GS24_jvkasipu.summary: The Kāśikāvṛtti is a running commentary (vṛtti) on the grammatical aphorisms of Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī, jointly authored by Jayāditya and Vāmana. It provides rule paraphrases, examples, and grammatical derivations.

SA_GS24_panini_u.title: Aṣṭādhyāyī

SA_GS24_paninipu.title: Aṣṭādhyāyī
SA_GS24_paninipu.author: Pāṇini

SA_GS24_paribhsu.title: Paribhāṣenduśekhara
SA_GS24_paribhsu.author: Nāgeśabhaṭṭa
SA_GS24_paribhsu.summary: The Paribhāṣenduśekhara by Nāgeśabhaṭṭa (Nāgojībhaṭṭa) is an authoritative grammatical treatise analyzing interpretive metarules (paribhāṣās) in the Pāṇinian system, drawing upon the Mahābhāṣya and Vārttikas.

SA_GS24_pmbhasuu.title: Vyākaraṇamahābhāṣya
SA_GS24_pmbhasuu.author: Patañjali
SA_GS24_pmbhasuu.summary: The Vyākaraṇamahābhāṣya ('Great Commentary on Grammar') by Patañjali is the foundational exegetical and theoretical masterwork of the Pāṇinian school of Sanskrit grammar (vyākaraṇa). Composed in the form of a lively, dialectical dialogue across 85 daily lessons (āhnikas), it comments on 1,228 sūtras of Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī, critically assessing the critical glosses (Vārttikas) of Kātyāyana. The text addresses fundamental questions of syntax, morphology, phonetics, semantics, ontology, and the philosophy of language, establishing the definitive doctrinal standard of the Pāṇinian 'trimuni' (three sages) tradition.
SA_GS24_pmbhasuu.attribution: The Vyākaraṇamahābhāṣya was composed by Patañjali (traditionally dated to c. 2nd century BCE) as an extensive discursive commentary on selected sūtras of Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī and primarily on Kātyāyana's Vārttikas. Kātyāyana's Vārttikas are embedded directly in Patañjali's discussion and are demarcated in the critical edition and digital dataset.
SA_GS24_pmbhasuu.edition: Franz Kielhorn (Bombay 1880-1885), revised by K.V. Abhyankar (Poona 1972-1996). With additional references of the edition Gurukuljhajjar, Rohatak (Rohtak): Hariyana sahitya samsthan, 1961-1963, 5 vols.
SA_GS24_pmbhasuu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 8 adhyāyas (all 85 āhnikas), beginning with the Paspaśāhnika ('atha śabdānuśāsanam') and concluding with the commentary on Pāṇini 8.4.68 ('a, a, a iti').

SA_GS24_samanv_u.title: Samanvayadiś with Samanvayapradīpa and Samanvayapradīpasaṅketa (fragments and extracts)
SA_GS24_samanv_u.author: Kuḍaka, Devaśarman
SA_GS24_samanv_u.summary: The Samanvayadiś by Kuḍaka is an Indian grammatical manual on syntax. Preserved in fragments in Vienna, this e-text reproduces Walter Slaje's 1992 edition of the Samanvayadiś fragments alongside parallel passages from Devaśarman's Samanvayapradīpa and extracts from his autocommentary, the Samanvayapradīpasaṅketa.
SA_GS24_samanv_u.attribution: Kuḍaka authored the prose manual Samanvayadiś. Devaśarman composed the versified text Samanvayapradīpa and its autocommentary Samanvayapradīpasaṅketa.
SA_GS24_samanv_u.edition: Walter Slaje, 'Materialien zu einer vergessenen lokalen Tradition der einheimischen indischen Grammatik: Kuḍakas Samanvayadiś und die Folgeliteratur', Wiener Zeitschrift für die Kunde Südasiens (WZKS), 36 (1992), pp. 105–126.
SA_GS24_samanv_u.coverage: fragment — Contains the surviving fragments of Kuḍaka's Samanvayadiś preserved in the Austrian National Library, Vienna, arranged synoptically with parallel verses of Devaśarman's Samanvayapradīpa and selected excerpts from Devaśarman's autocommentary Samanvayapradīpasaṅketa.
translations: Oliver Hahn, Kuḍakas Samanvayadiś nebst Kommentaren: Übersetzung der edierten Texte mit einer Studie der grammatisch-syntaktischen Lehren, M.A. thesis, Leipzig, 2000. (German)

SA_GS24_vakyp_pu.title: Vākyapadīya (kāṇḍas 1–2 and 3.1–7)
SA_GS24_vakyp_pu.author: Bhartṛhari
SA_GS24_vakyp_pu.summary: The Vākyapadīya by Bhartṛhari is the foundational treatise of the philosophy of grammar (Vaiyākaraṇadarśana) in ancient India. In verse form (kārikā), the text develops the metaphysics of the Word-Principle (Śabdabrahman) as ultimate reality, the sphoṭa doctrine of indivisible semantic units, and syntactic theory centered on sentence meaning (akhaṇḍavākyavāda). This digital file contains Kāṇḍas 1 and 2 in full, along with the first seven chapters (samuddeśas 1–7) of Kāṇḍa 3, concluding with the discussion of kāraka relations in the Sādhanasamuddeśa.
SA_GS24_vakyp_pu.coverage: partial — Contains Kāṇḍa 1 (Brahmakāṇḍa, vv. 1.1–1.156), Kāṇḍa 2 (Vākyakāṇḍa, vv. 2.1–2.485), and Kāṇḍa 3 (Prakīrṇakāṇḍa / Padakāṇḍa), samuddeśas 1–7 (Jāti-, Dravya-, Saṃbandha-, Bhūyodravya-, Guṇa-, Dik-, and Sādhanasamuddeśa, vv. 3.1.1–3.7.167). The remaining seven samuddeśas of the third kāṇḍa (8–14: Kriyā through Vṛtti) are not included.

SA_GS24_vakyp1pu.title: Vākyapadīya
SA_GS24_vakyp1pu.author: Bhartṛhari
SA_GS24_vakyp1pu.summary: The Vākyapadīya (also known as Trikāṇḍī) by Bhartṛhari is a foundational treatise of Classical Indian philosophy of grammar and language. Structured into three books—the Brahmakāṇḍa, Vākyakāṇḍa, and Padakāṇḍa—the text articulates the doctrine of Śabdabrahman and the theory of sentence meaning (sphoṭavāda).
SA_GS24_vakyp1pu.attribution: The kārikās of the Vākyapadīya are attributed to Bhartṛhari.
SA_GS24_vakyp1pu.edition: Bhartṛharis Vākyapadīya: Die Mūlakārikās nach den Handschriften herausgegeben und mit einem Pāda-Index versehen, ed. Wilhelm Rau, Wiesbaden: Deutsche Morgenländische Gesellschaft 1977 (Abhandlungen für die Kunde des Morgenlandes, Bd. 42, 4).
SA_GS24_vakyp1pu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all three books (kāṇḍas): Book 1 (Brahmakāṇḍa / Āgamakāṇḍa, vv. 1.1–1.156), Book 2 (Vākyakāṇḍa, vv. 2.1–2.485), and Book 3 (Padakāṇḍa / Prakīrṇakāṇḍa, comprising 14 samuddeśas, ending at 3.14.625).
translations: K. A. Subramaniya Iyer (tr.), The Vākyapadīya of Bhartṛhari with the Vṛtti. (English)

SA_GS24_varlghku.title: Laghusiddhāntakaumudī
SA_GS24_varlghku.author: Varadarāja
SA_GS24_varlghku.summary: The Laghusiddhāntakaumudī is an essential introductory primer of Pāṇinian Sanskrit grammar composed by Varadarāja in the seventeenth century. It condenses the comprehensive Siddhāntakaumudī of his teacher Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita into 1,279 select sūtras from Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī, reorganized according to a topical, derivation-focused order (prakriyā) rather than the sequential order of the eight adhyāyas. Accompanied by Varadarāja's concise explanatory commentary (vṛtti) and standard grammatical derivations, the work has served for centuries as the primary pedagogical manual in traditional pāṭhaśālās and modern academic institutions.
SA_GS24_varlghku.coverage: complete — Complete: from saṃjñāprakaraṇa (VLk_1 halantyam) to the end of the strīpratyaya section (VLk_1279 yūnas tiḥ, P 4.1.77), the standard end of the Laghusiddhāntakaumudī; running numbers 1–1279 with '374' skipped and '748' used twice. The opening maṅgala verse is not in the e-text.
translations: James R. Ballantyne (tr.), The Laghu Kaumudī: A Sanskrit Grammar by Varadarāja. (English)
Takasaki Jikidō 高崎直道, 『ラグ・シッダーンタ・カウムディ』訳註 (Laghu-Siddhānta-Kaumudī, annotated translation), Komazawa Daigaku Bukkyōgakubu Kenkyū Kiyō 駒澤大學佛敎學部硏究紀要, 1962. (Japanese)

SA_GS25_amark1pu.title: Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana (kāṇḍa 1)
SA_GS25_amark1pu.author: Amarasiṃha
SA_GS25_amark1pu.summary: The Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana (universally known as the Amarakoṣa) is classical India's most celebrated Sanskrit synonym dictionary and thesaurus, composed in śloka metre by the Buddhist lexicographer Amarasiṃha. This file contains the complete first division, which arranges nominal vocabulary conceptually into thematic sections (vargas): deities and heaven (svarga), sky and celestial bodies (vyoman), spatial directions (diś), time and seasons (kāla), intellect and mental states (dhī), speech and sound (śabda), theatre and musical performance (nāṭya), the subterranean realm and serpents (pātāla), hell (naraka), and water and aquatic flora (vāri). Alongside synonyms, the text systematically teaches grammatical gender (liṅgānuśāsana) through context, syntactic gender markers, and explicit exclusion rules.
SA_GS25_amark1pu.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the Buddhist lexicographer Amarasiṃha (c. 6th century CE).
SA_GS25_amark1pu.coverage: partial — Contains the complete first kāṇḍa, spanning introductory verses 1.0.1–1.0.10 (maṅgalācaraṇa, prastāvanā, paribhāṣā), all ten vargas (svarga, vyoma, diś, kāla, dhī, śabda, nāṭya, pātālabhogi, naraka, vāri), and concluding summary verses 1.11.605–1.11.608.

SA_GS25_amark2_u.title: Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana (kāṇḍa 2: Bhūmyādikāṇḍa)
SA_GS25_amark2_u.author: Amarasiṃha
SA_GS25_amark2_u.summary: The second book (kāṇḍa) of Amarasiṃha's Sanskrit lexicon, the Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana (commonly known as the Amarakoṣa). Designated the Bhūmyādikāṇḍa ('earthly division'), it arranges synonyms across ten sections (vargas) covering the terrestrial realm: the physical earth, settlements and architecture, mountains, flora and medicinal herbs, fauna, humanity, and the social classes and vocations (Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras). Composed in metrical verse with gender markers.
SA_GS25_amark2_u.attribution: Attributed to Amarasiṃha, a Buddhist lexicographer placed around the sixth century CE.
SA_GS25_amark2_u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete second kāṇḍa (Bhūmyādikāṇḍa) of the Amarakoṣa, comprising ten vargas (Bhūmivarga through Śūdravarga, numbered verses 2.0.1–2.8.1490 plus closing colophons and verse counts 2.8.1491–2.8.1494).

SA_GS25_amark3_u.title: Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana (kāṇḍa 3)
SA_GS25_amark3_u.author: Amarasiṃha
SA_GS25_amark3_u.summary: The Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana (commonly known as the Amarakoṣa) by Amarasiṃha is a Sanskrit metrical thesaurus. The third kāṇḍa, known as the Sāmānyakāṇḍa, classifies words by formal and grammatical criteria: adjectives and relative qualifiers (viśeṣyanighna), general miscellaneous terms (saṃkīrṇa), homonyms arranged by final consonant (nānārtha), indeclinables (avyaya), and rules for determining nominal gender (liṅgādisaṃgraha).
SA_GS25_amark3_u.attribution: Universal tradition attributes the work to Amarasiṃha, placed around the 6th century.
SA_GS25_amark3_u.coverage: partial — Contains the third book (Sāmānyakāṇḍa) of the Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana, comprising five sections: viśeṣyanighnavarga, saṃkīrṇavarga, nānārthavarga, avyayavarga, and liṅgādisaṃgrahavarga (480 root verses plus 25 interpolated verses, numbered through 3.5.1032 / 513 verses total). Kāṇḍas 1 and 2 are preserved in separate e-texts.

SA_GS26_jaytuppu.title: Tattvopaplavasiṃha (partial)
SA_GS26_jaytuppu.author: Jayarāśi
SA_GS26_jaytuppu.summary: The Tattvopaplavasiṃha ('The Lion that Devours all Principles/Categories') is a philosophical treatise of radical epistemological skepticism composed by Jayarāśi Bhaṭṭa in the 8th or 9th century CE. Affiliated with the tradition of Bṛhaspati / Cārvāka, Jayarāśi turns dialectical reasoning against accepted instruments of valid cognition (pramāṇas)—including perception and inference—arguing against established principles/categories (tattvas).
SA_GS26_jaytuppu.attribution: Authored by Jayarāśi (Jayarāśi Bhaṭṭa), active ca. late 8th to early 9th century CE. Although traditionally affiliated with the Bārhaspatya/Cārvāka tradition, Jayarāśi propounds radical epistemological skepticism, rejecting even the positive empirical/materialist assertions of classical Lokāyata.
SA_GS26_jaytuppu.edition: Sukhalalji Sanghavi and R.C. Parikh (eds.), Tattvopaplavasimha of Shri Jayarasi Bhatta, Baroda 1940 (Gaekwad's Oriental Series; 87); partly revised in: Eli Franco, Perception, Knowledge and Disbelief: A Study of Jayarāśi's Scepticism, Stuttgart 1987 (Alt- und Neu-Indische Studien; 35; 2nd ed. Delhi 1994).
SA_GS26_jaytuppu.coverage: partial — Covers pp. 1–83.7 of the 125 pages of Sanskrit text in the 1940 GOS editio princeps. It terminates abruptly at the close of the refutation of the Mīmāṃsā inference of the self (p. 83, line 7: 'na cākārāntarasāmānyam (perhaps: ākārāntaraṃ sāmānyasya) /'), breaking off before the critiques of Buddhist inference, the remaining pramāṇas (arthāpatti, upamāna, abhāva, sambhava, aitihya, śabda), and the final summary verses.
translations: Eli Franco, Perception, Knowledge and Disbelief: A Study of Jayarāśi's Scepticism, Stuttgart: Franz Steiner Verlag, 1987 (2nd ed. Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994). (English)

SA_GS26_sarvmtsu.title: Sarvamatasaṃgraha
SA_GS26_sarvmtsu.summary: The Sarvamatasaṃgraha is a concise Sanskrit doxography composed from an Advaita Vedānta perspective. It opens with an epistemological overview (pramāṇanirūpaṇa) detailing means of valid cognition, followed by an exposition of heterodox (Cārvāka/Lokāyata, Jaina, and Buddhist schools) and orthodox schools (including Nyāya, Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā, and Uttara-Mīmāṃsā). The systems conclude with non-dual Brahma-realization as the ultimate purport of philosophy.
SA_GS26_sarvmtsu.attribution: In Karl Potter's Encyclopedia of Indian Philosophies (DU554), the work is listed under (Mahopādhyāya) Rāghavānanda. Marek Mejor treats it as an anonymous 'Compendium of All Systems'. It is distinct from another compendium of the same title associated with Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭa.
SA_GS26_sarvmtsu.edition: T. Ganapati Sastri: The Sarvamatasangraha, Trivandrum 1918 (Trivandrum Sanskrit Series, 62).
SA_GS26_sarvmtsu.coverage: complete — Complete text corresponding to the Trivandrum Sanskrit Series edition (TSS 62).

SA_GS26_sbhami_u.title: Āptamīmāṃsā
SA_GS26_sbhami_u.author: Samantabhadra
SA_GS26_sbhami_u.summary: The Āptamīmāṃsā ('Critique of the Trustworthy Authority'), also known as the Devāgamastotra after its opening words, is a philosophical treatise by Samantabhadra. Beginning as a theological inquiry into what qualifies an individual as a truly omniscient, authoritative teacher (āpta), it establishes that miracles and external divine manifestations cannot establish authority; rather, true authority belongs only to one who has eradicated internal passions and whose teachings cannot be invalidated by reason or experience. Samantabhadra applies the sevenfold conditional predication (syādvāda / saptabhaṅgī) and many-sided ontology (anekāntavāda) to refute one-sided (ekānta) philosophical positions across rival Indian traditions, creating the dialectical framework that shaped subsequent Jain logic.
SA_GS26_sbhami_u.edition: Āptamīmāṃsā of Samantabhadra, edited by G. Jain [Gajādhara Lal Jain], Benares: Sanatana Jaina Granthamala [Jain Siddhant Prakashini Sanstha], 1914.
SA_GS26_sbhami_u.coverage: complete — Complete root text comprising 115 verses (numbered SAm_1–SAm_115).
translations: Samantabhadra's Āptamīmāṃsā: Critique of an Authority, translated by Nagin J. Shah, Ahmedabad, 1999. (English)

SA_GS39_jyopancu.title: Pañcasāyaka
SA_GS39_jyopancu.author: Jyotirīśvara Kaviśekhara
SA_GS39_jyopancu.summary: The Pañcasāyaka ('The Five Arrows') is a medieval Sanskrit handbook of erotology (kāmaśāstra) in five chapters composed by the Maithil poet Jyotirīśvara Kaviśekhara. It references earlier authorities including Vātsyāyana, Bābhravya, Nandīśvara, and Rantideva. The text covers topics of kāmaśāstra such as typologies of women (padminī, etc.) and men, marriages, copulatory postures (bandha), kissing, and various recipes.
SA_GS39_jyopancu.attribution: Composed by the Maithila poet Jyotirīśvara Kaviśekhara (also referred to as Jyotirīśa, author of Dhūrtasamāgama).
translations: Pañcaśāyaka of Śrī Kaviśekhara Jyotirīśvarācārya, translated into Hindi with 'Prakāśa' commentary by R. Sharma, Varanasi: Krishnadas Academy, 1995. (Hindi)

SA_GS39_kamasutu.title: Kāmasūtra
SA_GS39_kamasutu.author: Vātsyāyana
SA_GS39_kamasutu.summary: The Kāmasūtra of Vātsyāyana is the foundational Sanskrit treatise on kāma (erotic desire, pleasure, and aesthetic enjoyment), one of the traditional goals of human life (puruṣārtha). Divided into seven adhikaraṇas, the text surveys general principles of life, sexual union, courtship and marriage, the domestic conduct of wives, extramarital affairs, courtesans, and erotic/aphrodisiac recipes. Beyond physical intimacy, the work presents a detailed manual on urban sociology and the cultured lifestyle of the sophisticated citizen (nāgaraka), serving as the canonical source for all subsequent Indian erotic literature.
SA_GS39_kamasutu.attribution: Attributed to Vātsyāyana. Although the printed source edition includes Yaśodhara's Jayamaṅgalā commentary, only the root sūtras and concluding verses of Vātsyāyana were transcribed in this electronic text.
SA_GS39_kamasutu.edition: Kāmasūtram with commentary of Yaśodhara, 2nd ed. (dvitīyaṃ saṃskaraṇam), Nirṇayasāgarayantrālaya, 1900; with reference to Kāmasūtram edited by Śrī Devadatta Śāstrī, Chaukhambha Sanskrit Sansthan, Varanasi, saṃvat 2049.
SA_GS39_kamasutu.coverage: complete — Complete text covering all seven adhikaraṇas (Sādhāraṇam, Sāṃprayogikam, Kanyāsaṃprayuktakam, Bhāryādhikārikam, Pāradārikam, Vaiśikam, and Aupaniṣadikam) across 36 adhyāyas and 64 prakaraṇas, concluding at 7.2.59.

SA_GS39_minsmaru.title: Smaradīpikā
SA_GS39_minsmaru.author: Mīnanātha
SA_GS39_minsmaru.summary: The Smaradīpikā is a Sanskrit kāmaśāstra manual traditionally attributed to Mīnanātha. Composed in 230 stanzas, it categorizes men and women (padminī, citriṇī, śaṅkhinī, hastinī) by physical and psychological traits, describes erogenous points, outlines coital postures (bandha), and details amatory signals, messengers, and aphrodisiac recipes.
SA_GS39_minsmaru.attribution: Opening stanzas invoke Rudra (verse 3) and cite the sage Garga as the source of the teaching ('gargeṇābhāṣitāṃ samyag vakṣyāmi smaradīpikām', verse 5).
SA_GS39_minsmaru.edition: Smaradīpikā of Mīnanātha. In: Kāmakuñjalatā (A Collection of Old and Rare Works on Kāmaśāstra), edited by Paṇḍitrāj Dhuṇḍirāja Śāstri, Varanasi / Benares: Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series Office, 1967.
SA_GS39_minsmaru.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising 230 numbered units (225+ verses plus short section rubrics, tagged MinSd_1 to MinSd_230) matching the printed text in the Kāmakuñjalatā collection.

SA_GS39_purukadu.title: Kādambarasvīkaraṇasūtra with commentary
SA_GS39_purukadu.author: Purūravas
SA_GS39_purukadu.summary: The Kādambarasvīkaraṇasūtra with its accompanying prose commentary is preserved in the Kāmaśāstra tradition. In 34 aphorisms and prose commentary, it argues that the consumption of liquor (kādambara / vāruṇī) before and during lovemaking is an indispensable prerequisite for sexual fulfillment, concluding that observant practitioners will attain pleasure, offspring, and the celestial abode of Urvaśī.
SA_GS39_purukadu.attribution: Pseudepigraphically attributed to the legendary Purūravas, lover of Urvaśī (alluded to in the final verse 34.10: 'urvaśīlokam āpnoti antakāle tu saḥ pumān').
SA_GS39_purukadu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 34 sūtras with their prose commentary and concluding verses.

SA_GS40_anandk_u.title: Ānandakanda (lacking Amṛtīkaraṇaviśrānti chapter 18)
SA_GS40_anandk_u.summary: The Ānandakanda is an alchemical and tantric treatise (Rasaśāstra), structured in two major divisions: the Amṛtīkaraṇaviśrānti and the Kriyākaraṇaviśrānti. It deals with mercurial operations, rasāyana therapies, medicinal recipes, and botanical ingredients, presented in the frame of a dialogue between Bhairavī and Īśvara (Bhairava).
SA_GS40_anandk_u.attribution: Cast in the typical Śaiva Tantric form as an esoteric dialogue between Bhairava (Īśvara/Śiva) and Bhairavī (Pārvatī).
SA_GS40_anandk_u.edition: S. V. Rādhākṛṣṇa Śāstrī (ed.), Ānandakandaḥ Rasavādagranthaḥ, Tañjāpura: Tañjāpura Sarasvatīmahāla-granthālaya-nirvāhaka-samiti / Srirangam: Sri Vilasam Press, 1952.
SA_GS40_anandk_u.coverage: partial — Amṛtīkaraṇaviśrānti ullāsas 1–17 and 19–26 (1.18 omitted in the input, per GRETIL header) and Kriyākaraṇaviśrānti ullāsas 1–10, ending at Āk 2.10.59 (synonyms of bhṛṅgarāja).

SA_GS40_ashr.title: Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya
SA_GS40_ashr.author: Vāgbhaṭa
SA_GS40_ashr.summary: The Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya is a classical medical treatise attributed to Vāgbhaṭa (or Vāgbhaṭa the Younger). It covers sections such as Sūtrasthāna and Śārīrasthāna.
SA_GS40_ashr.attribution: Attributed to Vāgbhaṭa. Scholarly discussion mentions Vāgbhaṭa the Younger / Vāgbhaṭa and places related texts around the 6th to 8th century.

Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā: dt. von L. Hilgenberg u. W. Kirfel, Leiden 1941. (German)

SA_GS40_bhavpr_u.title: Bhāvaprakāśa (Vargaprakaraṇa: chapters 1–3, incomplete)
SA_GS40_bhavpr_u.author: Bhāvamiśra
SA_GS40_bhavpr_u.summary: The Bhāvaprakāśa is an Ayurvedic compendium composed by Bhāvamiśra. This e-text is an incomplete transcription containing three chapters from the Vargaprakaraṇa (Harītakyādivarga, Karpūrādivarga, and Guḍūcyādivarga up to verse 54).
SA_GS40_bhavpr_u.edition: Bhāvaprakāśa, Benares City: Jaya Krishna Das Hari Das Gupta, 1947.

SA_GS40_dhrasciu.title: Rasendracintāmaṇi
SA_GS40_dhrasciu.author: Ḍhuṇḍhukanātha
SA_GS40_dhrasciu.summary: The Rasendracintāmaṇi is a Sanskrit treatise on alchemy and medicine (Rasaśāstra) attributed to Ḍhuṇḍhukanātha, disciple of Kālanātha. The work treats the processing, purification, and calcination of mercury (sūta, pārada), metals, and minerals, as well as pharmaceutical preparations.
SA_GS40_dhrasciu.attribution: The introductory verses identify the author as Ḍhuṇḍhukanātha, disciple of Kālanātha. Scholarly literature also notes that the authorship of the Rasendracintāmaṇi is disputed.
SA_GS40_dhrasciu.coverage: partial — Contains chapters 1–8 (ending at 8.278); verses 3.93–95 are not included per GRETIL header note.

SA_GS40_grasht_u.title: Rasahṛdayatantra with Mugdhāvabodhinī
SA_GS40_grasht_u.author: Govindabhagavatpāda, Caturbhujamiśra
SA_GS40_grasht_u.summary: The Rasahṛdayatantra ('Heart of Mercury'), composed in 19 avabodhas (chapters) in āryā metre by Bhikṣu Govinda (Govindabhagavatpāda, c. 10th century CE), is the earliest surviving systematic treatise of the Sanskrit alchemical tradition (rasaśāstra). Written under the patronage of a Kirāta king, it details the operations on mercury, laboratory apparatuses (yantras), and formulas for transmuting base metals into gold (dhātuvedha) as well as creating elixirs for bodily immortality and rejuvenation (rasāyana). This e-text contains all 19 chapters of the root text accompanied by Caturbhujamiśra's Sanskrit commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī.
SA_GS40_grasht_u.attribution: The root work is attributed in the text to Bhikṣu Govinda (Govindabhagavatpāda; see closing verse 19.80), who composed it under the patronage of a Kirāta ruler. Modern scholarship dates the text to around the 10th or 11th century CE. The Mugdhāvabodhinī commentary was composed by Caturbhujamiśra, son of Maheśa and grandson of Hariharamiśra.
SA_GS40_grasht_u.edition: Rasahṛdayatantram, with the Commentary called Mugdhāvabodhinī of Caturbhuja Miśra, translated into Hindi by Daulatarāma Rasaśāstrī (Vidyavilas Ayurveda Series). Varanasi / Delhi: Chaukhambha Orientalia, 1989.
SA_GS40_grasht_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 19 avabodhas (chapters) with Caturbhujamiśra's Mugdhāvabodhinī commentary (ending at 19.80).
translations: Rasaśāstrī, Daulatarāma. Rasahṛdayatantram with Mugdhāvabodhinī and Hindi translation. Chaukhambha Orientalia, 1989. (Hindi)

SA_GS40_nitrrk_u.title: Rasaratnākara (Rasakhaṇḍa, Rasāyanakhaṇḍa and Vādakhaṇḍa)
SA_GS40_nitrrk_u.author: Nityanāthasiddha
SA_GS40_nitrrk_u.summary: The Rasaratnākara of Nityanātha is an alchemical treatise divided into five khaṇḍas. This e-text contains three: Rasakhaṇḍa, Rasāyanakhaṇḍa, and Vādakhaṇḍa.
SA_GS40_nitrrk_u.coverage: partial — Three of the five khaṇḍas named in the text (rasakhaṇḍe, rasendrake, vādakhaṇḍe, rasāyane, mantrakhaṇḍe): section RRĀ 1 (Rasakhaṇḍa), RRĀ 2 (Rasāyanakhaṇḍa), and RRĀ 3 (Vādakhaṇḍa). Rasendrakhaṇḍa and Mantrakhaṇḍa are absent.

SA_GS40_rajaniu.title: Rasajalanidhi
SA_GS40_rajaniu.author: Bhūdeva Mukhopādhyāya
SA_GS40_rajaniu.summary: The Rasajalanidhi ('Ocean of Indian Chemistry and Alchemy') is a compendium of Rasaśāstra (Indian alchemy and iatrochemistry) with English translation, compiled by B. Mookerji and published in Calcutta (1926).
SA_GS40_rajaniu.attribution: Compiled and translated into English by B. Mookerji.

SA_GS40_rajnighu.title: Rājanighaṇṭu
SA_GS40_rajnighu.author: Narahari
SA_GS40_rajnighu.summary: The Rājanighaṇṭu (also known as Nighaṇṭurāja or Abhidhānacūḍāmaṇi) by Narahari is a comprehensive Āyurvedic materia medica and medical lexicon. Arranged into 23 thematic chapters (vargas), it catalogs medical substances—including herbs, minerals, gemstones, animal products, and prepared foods—providing detailed lists of synonyms, pharmacological properties (guṇa), tastes (rasa), and post-digestive effects (vipāka). The lexicon synthesizes earlier nighaṇṭus and medical traditions.
SA_GS40_rajnighu.attribution: Authored by Narahari (also referred to as Narahari Paṇḍita or Nṛsiṃha). The text refers to itself as Rājanighaṇṭu, Nighaṇṭurāja, and Abhidhānacūḍāmaṇi.
SA_GS40_rajnighu.edition: Narahari, Rājanighaṇṭu, edited by Āśubodha Vidyābhūṣaṇa and Nityabodha Vidyāratna, Calcutta: Siddheshvara Press (Siddheśvarayantra), 1933 (first edition 1899).
SA_GS40_rajnighu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Rājanighaṇṭu, containing the Granthaprastāvanā and all 23 vargas, concluding with the Ekārthādivarga (explicitly identified as the 23rd varga in verse 23.5 / Rajni_33.5; tagged through 33 in the digital corpus because the 11 subsections of the 23rd varga are enumerated from Ekārtha through Ekādaśārtha).
translations: Richard Garbe, Die indischen Mineralien, ihre Namen und die ihnen zugeschriebenen Kräfte: Narahari's Râganighaṇṭu Varga XIII, Leipzig: S. Hirzel, 1882. (German)

SA_GS40_rasadh_u.title: Rasādhyāya with Kaṅkālādhyāyavārttika
SA_GS40_rasadh_u.author: Kaṅkālayayogiśiṣya, Merutuṅgasūri
SA_GS40_rasadh_u.summary: The Rasādhyāya is an alchemical treatise (Rasaśāstra) treating mercurial preparations, metallic transmutations (dhātuvāda), and related operations, accompanied by a commentary (Rasādhyāyaṭīkā / Kaṅkālādhyāyavārttika) authored by the Jain monk Merutuṅga.
SA_GS40_rasadh_u.attribution: Verse 1.1 of the commentary contains a Jina salutation and gives the title Kaṅkālādhyāyavārttika ('natvā tānarhataḥ kurve kaṅkālādhyāyavārttikam'). A. B. Keith and Mircea Eliade note that the 14th-century Jain monk Merutuṅga wrote a commentary on the Rasādhyāya. Verses 480–481 mention Rāvala Campaka, son of Bhādiga of the Yādava lineage.
SA_GS40_rasadh_u.edition: Ramakrsna Sarma (ed.), Rasadhyaya, with Rasadhyayatika (comm.), Adhyaya 1. Benares: Chaukhamba Sanskrit Series Office, 1930 (Haridasa Samskrtagranthamala, 79; Ayurvedasastravibhaga, 2).
SA_GS40_rasadh_u.coverage: partial — Verses 1–481 of adhyāya 1 with commentary (though a TEI header note indicates verses 303–481 were initially noted as not available, the full e-text contains stanzas up to 481).

SA_GS40_rasadhpu.title: Rasādhyāya with Kaṅkālādhyāyavārttika (verses 1–302)
SA_GS40_rasadhpu.author: Kaṅkālayayogiśiṣya, Merutuṅga
SA_GS40_rasadhpu.summary: An alchemical (Rasaśāstra) treatise dealing with the eighteen saṃskāras of mercury, digestion (jāraṇa), and the processing of metals and minerals, accompanied by a Sanskrit commentary (Kaṅkālādhyāyavārttika / Rasādhyāyaṭīkā) attributed to the Jain monk Merutuṅga.
SA_GS40_rasadhpu.attribution: The opening verses mention composing the Kaṅkālādhyāyavārttika after bowing to the Arhats (v. 1) and refer to Śrīkaṅkālayayogin (v. 7). Mircea Eliade notes that the 14th-century Jain monk Merutuṅga wrote a commentary on the alchemical treatise Rasādhyāya.
SA_GS40_rasadhpu.edition: Rasādhyāya (with Ṭīkā), verses 1–302, ed. Ramakrsna Sarma, Kashi Sanskrit Series, 79 (Haridas Sanskrit Granthamala, Ayurveda Section, 2), Benares: Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series, 1930.
SA_GS40_rasadhpu.coverage: partial — Verses 1–302 of the root text with commentary, ending with '... (to be continued)'. As noted in the GRETIL header, verses 303–481 of the printed edition were not available.

SA_GS40_rasarnpu.title: Rasārṇava (chapters 1–12)
SA_GS40_rasarnpu.summary: The Rasārṇava is a Śaiva Tantric treatise framed as a dialogue between Bhairava and Devī. It deals with alchemy and liberation-in-life (jīvanmukti), mercury, and related preparations. This e-text covers chapters 1–12.
SA_GS40_rasarnpu.attribution: Revealed Śaiva Tantric treatise cast as a dialogue between Bhairava and Devī (Pārvatī).
SA_GS40_rasarnpu.edition: Rasārṇava, Patalas 1-12, ed. Praphulla Chandra Ray. Calcutta: Asiatic Society, 1908–1910 (Bibliotheca Indica, 175).
SA_GS40_rasarnpu.coverage: partial — Contains chapters (paṭalas) 1–12 of the Rasārṇava, ending at verse 12.382.

SA_GS40_rascum_u.title: Rasendracūḍāmaṇi (chapters 3–5, 7–16)
SA_GS40_rascum_u.author: Somadeva
SA_GS40_rascum_u.summary: The Rasendracūḍāmaṇi ('Crest-Jewel of the Lord of Essences [Mercury]') is an alchemical and iatrochemical treatise composed by Somadeva. It systematically describes the layout and staffing of the alchemical laboratory (rasaśālā), technical apparatus (yantras), crucibles (mūṣās), furnaces (koṣṭhīs), pits (puṭas), as well as the pharmaceutical processing, purification, incineration, and digestion (jāraṇa) of mercury, metals, and minerals.
SA_GS40_rascum_u.edition: Rasendracūḍāmaṇi of Somadeva, edited by Siddhinandan Misra, Benares: Chaukhamba Orientalia, 1999.
SA_GS40_rascum_u.coverage: partial — Contains chapters 3–5 and 7–16 (verses Rcūm 3.1 through 16.98). Chapters 1–2 and 6 are absent from the e-text.

SA_GS40_rassanku.title: Rasasaṃketakalikā
SA_GS40_rassanku.author: Cāmuṇḍa
SA_GS40_rassanku.summary: The Rasasaṃketakalikā is a concise Rasaśāstra manual composed in Yoginīpura by Cāmuṇḍa of the Kāyastha lineage (dated around 1490 CE / 'bhvagnitithi' year in verse 5.40). Arranged across five chapters, the work details practical, streamlined methods for purifying (śodhana), binding (bandhana), and calcining (māraṇa) mercury and other metals, followed by diverse therapeutic formulations and treatments for mercury-induced toxicity.
SA_GS40_rassanku.attribution: The author identifies himself in the opening and concluding verses as Cāmuṇḍa of the Kāyastha lineage (Rsk 1.1: 'cāmuṇḍaḥ kāyasthavaṃśabhūḥ'; Rsk 5.40: 'cāmuṇḍo yoginīpure'). In manuscript colophons and secondary literature he is also cited as Cāmuṇḍa Kāyastha, Kāyasthacāmuṇḍa, or Caṇḍa.
SA_GS40_rassanku.edition: Jadavji Tricumji (ed.), Rasasaṃketakalikā, Benares: Caukhamba Amarabharati Prakashan, 1984 (Chaukhamba Ayurveda Granthamala, 10).
SA_GS40_rassanku.coverage: complete — Complete in five chapters, ending at verse 5.40 with the chronogram and place of composition.

SA_GS40_salrasmu.title: Rasamañjarī
SA_GS40_salrasmu.author: Śālinātha
SA_GS40_salrasmu.summary: The Rasamañjarī of Śālinātha (son of Vaidyanātha) is a Sanskrit treatise on rasaśāstra (Ayurvedic alchemy and iatrochemistry) organized into ten chapters (adhyāyas). The text details the classification, defect-removal (doṣaśodhana), and pharmaceutical processing of mercury (pārada), along with the preparation and therapeutic application of mineral, metallic, and herbo-mineral compounds. It also contains dedicated sections on rasāyana (rejuvenative therapy) and ariṣṭa (prognostic signs forecasting death).
SA_GS40_salrasmu.attribution: The author identifies himself as Śālinātha, son of Vaidyanātha, in verses 1.3 ('śrīvaidyanāthatanayaḥ sunayaḥ suśīlaḥ śrīśālinātha iti viśrutanāmadheyaḥ') and 10.58 ('vaidyanāthatanūjena śālināthena dhīmatā').
SA_GS40_salrasmu.edition: Rasamañjarī of Śālinātha, ed. Siddhinandan Mishra, Varanasi: Chaukhambha Orientalia, 1995.
SA_GS40_salrasmu.coverage: complete — Complete text in 10 chapters (adhyāyas), running from verse 1.1 through verse 10.58.

SA_GS40_samapviu.title: Āyurvedamahodadhi (Annapānavidhi)
SA_GS40_samapviu.author: Suṣeṇa
SA_GS40_samapviu.summary: The Āyurvedamahodadhi (Annapānavidhi section), attributed to Suṣeṇa, is a Sanskrit Ayurvedic treatise on dietetics and personal regimen. It treats beverages (pānīyavarga), fruits and vegetables (phalaśākavarga), fish (matsyaguṇāḥ), and concludes with garments (vastravarga).
SA_GS40_samapviu.attribution: The work is attributed in its colophons to Suṣeṇa (samāptāyaṃ suṣeṇakṛtagranthaḥ; ity āyurvedamahodadhau suṣeṇakṛte vastravargaḥ samāptaḥ).
SA_GS40_samapviu.edition: S. Venkatasubrahmanya Sastri: Sushena's Ayurveda Mahodadhi-annapanavidhi, Madras 1950 (Madras Government Oriental Series, 60).
SA_GS40_samapviu.coverage: partial — Extant text starts at verse 5, running through food and beverage sections to the concluding Vastravarga (v. 3) and colophon (samāptāyaṃ suṣeṇakṛtagranthaḥ).

SA_GS40_kalyanakaraka.title: Kalyāṇakāraka
SA_GS40_kalyanakaraka.author: Ugrāditya
SA_GS40_kalyanakaraka.summary: The Kalyāṇakāraka is a comprehensive 9th-century Sanskrit Ayurvedic treatise composed by the Digambara Jain monk Ugrāditya. Divided into 25 chapters across two main divisions—the Mūlatantra (chapters 1–20) and Uttaratantra (chapters 21–25)—along with a concluding section on the prognostication of fatal signs (Ariṣṭanirūpaṇa), it is among the earliest surviving Indian medical compendia to detail the chemical purification (śodhana) and incineration (māraṇa) of mercury and other minerals for therapeutic formulations. Consistently framed within Jain ethics of non-harm (ahiṃsā), the work prohibits meat, alcohol, and honey in pharmacological treatments, replacing them with herbal and mineral substitutes while harmonising classical Ayurvedic eight-fold medicine with Jain doctrinal philosophy.
SA_GS40_kalyanakaraka.attribution: Attributed to Ugrāditya. The work is placed around the 9th century CE (c. 825–875 CE in EDSHP; statistical model posterior median 811 CE).
SA_GS40_kalyanakaraka.edition: Kalyāṇakārakam of Ugrādityācārya, ed./tr. Vardhaman Parshwanath Shastri, Sholapur: Seth Govindji Raoji Doshi, 1940 (Sakhārāma Nemacaṃda Digambara Jaina Graṃthamālā / SNGM 129).
SA_GS40_kalyanakaraka.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 25 chapters (paricchedas), comprising the Mūlatantra / Cikitsādhikāra (chapters 1–20) and the Uttaratantra (chapters 21–25), followed by the concluding supplementary section on death prognostication (Ariṣṭanirūpaṇa) and the author's final colophon verses.
translations: Vardhaman Parshwanath Shastri, Hindi translation accompanying the Sanskrit text in the 1940 Sholapur edition (Sakhārāma Nemacaṃda Digambara Jaina Graṃthamālā 129). (Hindi)

SA_GS40_vagaah_u.title: Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā
SA_GS40_vagaah_u.author: Vāgbhaṭa
SA_GS40_vagaah_u.summary: The Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā is a foundational classical Ayurvedic treatise composed in metrical verse by Vāgbhaṭa, synthesizing core traditions including Caraka and Suśruta across divisions covering diagnosis, pathology, therapeutics, and specialized branches, terminating in the Uttarasthāna.
SA_GS40_vagaah_u.attribution: Attributed to Vāgbhaṭa. Statistical dating estimates posterior median 751 CE (95% credible interval: 690 CE – 810 CE).
SA_GS40_vagaah_u.coverage: complete — Complete text containing Sūtrasthāna, Śārīrasthāna, Nidānasthāna, Cikitsitasthāna, Kalpasiddhisthāna, and Uttarasthāna, terminating at Uttarasthāna 40.89.
translations: Murthy (1991). (English)

Vogel, C. Vāgbhaṭa's Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā. Wiesbaden, 1965. (English)

SA_GS40_vanighpu.title: Aṣṭāṅganighaṇṭu
SA_GS40_vanighpu.author: Vāhaṭa
SA_GS40_vanighpu.summary: The Aṣṭāṅganighaṇṭu is an Ayurvedic medical lexicon (nighaṇṭu) in 408 verses attributed to Vāhaṭa, glossing drugs and synonyms referenced in the Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha.
SA_GS40_vanighpu.edition: Priya Vat Sharma (ed.), Madras: The Kuppuswamy Sastri Research Institute, 1973.

SA_GS40_vrasrs_u.title: Rasaratnasamuccaya (chapters 1–12)
SA_GS40_vrasrs_u.author: Vāgbhaṭa
SA_GS40_vrasrs_u.summary: The Rasaratnasamuccaya is a Sanskrit work on alchemy and medicinal chemistry (rasaśāstra) attributed to Vāgbhaṭa. It deals with minerals, mercurial preparations, crucibles, apparatus (yantra), and medicinal formulations.
SA_GS40_vrasrs_u.attribution: The author calls himself son of Siṃhagupta, but scholarship considers this to be by a later Vāgbhaṭa dating around the 13th century.
SA_GS40_vrasrs_u.edition: Kṛṣṇarāvaśarman Vināyaka Bāpaṭa (ed.), Poona 1890 (Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series edition, vol. 19).
SA_GS40_vrasrs_u.coverage: partial — Contains adhyāyas 1 to 12 only (ending at 12.150 with formulations for navajvara).

SA_GS40_vrasrscu.title: Rasaratnasamuccaya with Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī and Rasaratnasamuccayaṭīkā (chapters 1–18.29ab)
SA_GS40_vrasrscu.author: Vāgbhaṭa, Āśubodhavidyābhūṣaṇa, Nityabodhavidyāratna
SA_GS40_vrasrscu.summary: The Rasaratnasamuccaya is a work on mercurial and mineral medicines, alchemy, and medicinal chemistry attributed to Vāgbhaṭa. It treats minerals having medicinal properties, categories such as rasa and uparasa, mercurial preparations, crucibles, apparatus (yantra), and compounding. This e-text covers chapters 1 through 18.29ab accompanied by the Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī and Rasaratnasamuccayaṭīkā commentaries.
SA_GS40_vrasrscu.attribution: The root work is attributed to Vāgbhaṭa, who identifies himself as the son of Siṃhagupta, and is dated by scholars (such as P. C. Ray) to around the 13th century. The commentary Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī is by Āśubodhavidyābhūṣaṇa and Nityabodhavidyāratna (Aśubodha and Nityabodha Senagupta, Calcutta-based editors and publishers).
SA_GS40_vrasrscu.coverage: partial — Covers adhyāyas 1 through 18.29ab, accompanied by commentaries; ends with the note '********(Other parts not available at present.)********'.

SA_GS40_yogasatu.title: Yogaśataka
SA_GS40_yogasatu.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_GS40_yogasatu.summary: The Yogaśataka ('Century of Formulations') is an influential early Āyurvedic formulary compiling approximately one hundred standard therapeutic recipes (yogas). Arranged largely according to the classical eight branches (aṣṭāṅga) of Indian medicine, it provides practical remedies for fevers, gastrointestinal and urinary disorders, respiratory complaints, poisoning, pediatrics, and eye conditions, concluding with general principles of humoral pathology and regimen. Its popularity across Buddhist Asia is attested by early translations into Tibetan and Tocharian B.
SA_GS40_yogasatu.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna (notably in the Tibetan Tengyur, D 4306) and alternately in certain South Asian traditions to Vararuci.
SA_GS40_yogasatu.edition: Heinz Helmuth Michael Schmidt: Das Yogaśata: Ein Zeugnis altindischer Medizin, Sanskrit und Tibetisch, Bonn 1978 (Diss.).
SA_GS40_yogasatu.coverage: complete — Contains stanzas Yś_1 to Yś_111, including opening invocations and the final dedication stanza.
translations: Jean Filliozat, Yogaśataka: Text médical attribué à Nāgārjuna, Pondichéry: Institut Français d'Indologie, 1979. (French)
Vaidya Bhagwan Dash, Tibetan Medicine, with Special Reference to Yoga Śataka, Dharamsala: Library of Tibetan Works and Archives, 1976. (English)

SA_GS40_yrasprpu.title: Rasaprakāśasudhākara
SA_GS40_yrasprpu.author: Yaśodhara
SA_GS40_yrasprpu.summary: The Rasaprakāśasudhākara is a major 13-chapter Sanskrit treatise on alchemy and iatrochemistry (rasaśāstra), composed by Yaśodhara Bhaṭṭa in Saurashtra (Gujarat). It describes the origins, grades, and eighteen purification and transmutational processes (aṣṭādaśa-saṃskāra) of mercury, followed by treatments of primary and secondary minerals (mahārasas and uparasas), metals, gemstones, and apparatus (yantras, crucibles). The text holds an important position in the history of Indian chemistry for offering one of the earliest explicit accounts of zinc (yaśada/rasaka-sattva) distillation extraction and for key iatrochemical formulations such as Somanāthī tāmrabhasma and calomel (karpūrarasa).
SA_GS40_yrasprpu.attribution: The concluding verses of the thirteenth chapter (13.15–17) state that the work was composed by Yaśodhara Bhaṭṭa (or Yaśodhara Kavi), son of Padmanābha of the Goḍa lineage, residing at Jīrṇadurga in Surarāṣṭra.
SA_GS40_yrasprpu.edition: Rasaprakāśasudhākara by Yaśodhara, ed. Jivram Kalidas Sastri, Gondal: Rasasala Ausadhasram, 1940.
SA_GS40_yrasprpu.coverage: complete — Complete text in 13 adhyāyas (verses 1.1 to 13.17), ending with the author's final strophes.
translations: Rasaprakāśasudhākara, Chaukhambhā Oriyanṭāliyā (Varanasi 2004). (Hindi)

SA_GS41_hayanaratna.title: Hāyanaratna
SA_GS41_hayanaratna.author: Balabhadra Daivajña
SA_GS41_hayanaratna.summary: The Hāyanaratna ('Jewel of the Year') is a Sanskrit treatise on annual horoscopy (varṣaphala) and Tājika astrology, dealing with planetary configurations, dignities, and lots.
SA_GS41_hayanaratna.coverage: unclear — No e-text data is present in the source headers or evidence.

SA_GS41_aryabh_u.title: Āryabhaṭīya
SA_GS41_aryabh_u.author: Āryabhaṭa
SA_GS41_aryabh_u.summary: The Āryabhaṭīya is a Sanskrit treatise on mathematics and astronomy composed by Āryabhaṭa in Kusumapura (dated to 499 CE). Across four sections (Gītikāpāda, Gaṇitapāda, Kālakriyāpāda, and Golapāda), it expounds mathematical and astronomical concepts, models, and calculations.
SA_GS41_aryabh_u.attribution: Composed by Āryabhaṭa (dated to 499 CE). The former catalog metadata listed commentators Bhāskara I and Someśvara.
SA_GS41_aryabh_u.edition: K. S. Shukla (ed.), New Delhi: INSA 1976.
SA_GS41_aryabh_u.coverage: complete — Text containing four pādas: Gītikāpāda, Gaṇitapāda, Kālakriyāpāda, and Golapāda, running through verse AB 4.50.

SA_GS41_aryabhcu.title: Āryabhaṭīya with the commentaries of Bhāskara I and Someśvara
SA_GS41_aryabhcu.author: Āryabhaṭa, Bhāskara I, Someśvara
SA_GS41_aryabhcu.summary: The Āryabhaṭīya of Āryabhaṭa (composed c. 499 CE) is an early Indian work on mathematics and astronomy, here presented with the commentary of Bhāskara I (629 CE) and the commentary of Someśvara.
SA_GS41_aryabhcu.attribution: The root work Āryabhaṭīya was composed by Āryabhaṭa (c. 499 CE). The commentary was written in 629 CE by Bhāskara I, with commentary by Someśvara summarizing Bhāskara's work.
SA_GS41_aryabhcu.edition: Āryabhaṭīya of Āryabhaṭa with the Commentary of Bhāskara I and Someśvara, critically edited with Introduction and Appendices by Kripa Shankar Shukla. New Delhi: Indian National Science Academy, 1976.
