SA_GS41_bijaganu.title: Bījagaṇita (incomplete)
SA_GS41_bijaganu.author: Bhāskara II
SA_GS41_bijaganu.summary: The Bījagaṇita of Bhāskara (fl. 1150 CE) expounds operations on negative and positive numbers, unknown quantities (avyakta, varṇa), indeterminate equations (kuṭṭaka), and equations involving vargaprakṛti.
SA_GS41_bijaganu.edition: Bījagaṇita, Bhāskarācārya, ASS 99, 1930 [V. G. Apate's edition], with the comm. Navāṅkura of Kṛṣṇa Daivajña.
SA_GS41_bijaganu.coverage: partial — The e-text is incomplete. It contains verses and short prose remarks numbered BG_1 to BG_149, breaking off mid-verse at BG_150c ('vistāritā') in the section on quadratic equations in multiple unknowns (aneka-varṇa-samī-karaṇa-antar-gatam madhyama-āharaṇam).

SA_GS41_brhajj_u.title: Bṛhajjātaka (fragment)
SA_GS41_brhajj_u.author: Varāhamihira
SA_GS41_brhajj_u.summary: The Bṛhajjātaka (or Horāśāstra), composed in the 6th century CE by Varāhamihira, is a classical Sanskrit manual of horoscopic astrology (jātaka / horā). It deals with the twelve houses (gṛha) and the effects of planetary constellations at birth, synthesizing Indian astral science with Greek horoscopy.
SA_GS41_brhajj_u.attribution: Composed by the 6th-century astronomer-astrologer Varāhamihira. Utpala (Bhaṭṭotpala) composed a commentary on the text.
SA_GS41_brhajj_u.edition: Oriental Books Reprint Corporation, Second Edition, 1979.
SA_GS41_brhajj_u.coverage: fragment — Our e-text contains only 152 lines, mostly metre labels like '(indravajrā)' plus scattered pādas (e.g. BJ_18.07b, BJ_27.20b) and the closing line 'End of Bṛhajjātaka'.
translations: Swami Vijnananda, tr., Varāhamihira, Bṛhajjātaka, 1912. (English)

SA_GS41_brhats_u.title: Bṛhatsaṃhitā
SA_GS41_brhats_u.author: Varāhamihira
SA_GS41_brhats_u.summary: The Bṛhatsaṃhitā ('Great Compendium') of Varāhamihira (ca. 6th century CE) is the fundamental classic of the saṃhitā (natural omen, divination, and mundane astrology) branch of Indian jyotiṣa. Arranged into 106 chapters and comprising nearly 4,000 stanzas, it serves as an encyclopaedia of classical Indian material and ritual life, treating topics such as planetary movements, eclipses, meteorology, ground water and rainfall, temple and residential architecture (vāstuvidyā), iconometry (pratimālakṣaṇa), gemmology (ratnaparīkṣā), perfumery (gandhayukti), agriculture, and physiognomy. It is an indispensable primary source for the history of science, material culture, and religious society in Gupta-era India.
SA_GS41_brhats_u.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising all 106 adhyāyas (1.01 through 106.14). Internal and external vowel sandhis are decomposed with carats (^) for searchability, and variant readings from Kern's edition (marked 'K.') and Bhaṭṭotpala's commentary (marked 'U.') are incorporated in square brackets.
translations: Kern, H., Bṛhat-saṃhitā, or Complete System of Natural Astrology of Varāhamihira, JRAS, 1870 (ch. I-VII); (ch. VIII-XV); (ch. XVI-XXV); (ch. XXVI-LII); (ch. LIII-LXIV);. (English)

SA_GS41_brhatparasarahorasastram.title: Bṛhatpārāśarahorāśāstra
SA_GS41_brhatparasarahorasastram.author: Parāśara
SA_GS41_brhatparasarahorasastram.summary: The Bṛhatpārāśarahorāśāstra is a classical compendium of Indian natal horoscopy (horāśāstra, a branch of jyotiṣa), framed as a pedagogical dialogue between Maharṣi Parāśara and his disciple Maitreya. The treatise covers planetary significations, zodiacal signs, divisional charts (vargas), auspicious and inauspicious planetary combinations (yogas), planetary strengths (ṣaḍbala), various daśā systems (most prominently Viṃśottarī), transits (gocara), and remedial measures (śānti).
SA_GS41_brhatparasarahorasastram.coverage: unclear — The catalog entry is an empty stub with 0 segments and 0 characters; no text data is present in the repository.

SA_GS41_phaladipika.title: Phaladīpikā
SA_GS41_phaladipika.author: Mantreśvara
SA_GS41_phaladipika.summary: The Phaladīpikā is an authoritative astrological handbook (jātaka / horā) by Mantreśvara, covering astrological principles including planetary periods, daśās, kālacakra, and aṣṭakavarga.
SA_GS41_phaladipika.attribution: In the concluding verses of Chapter 28 (vv. 5–6), the author names himself as Mantreśvara (śrīśālivāṭijātena mayā mantreśvareṇa vai), a Brahmin astrologer born in Śālivāṭi, who composed the text by the grace of goddess Sukuntalāmbā.
SA_GS41_phaladipika.coverage: complete — Complete: ending with the upasaṃhāra verses naming Mantreśvara of Śālivāṭi and Sukuntalāmbā (kṛtā yā phaladīpikā || 6||).

SA_GS41_brsphutu.title: Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta (chapters 12, 18–20, 21.17–23)
SA_GS41_brsphutu.author: Brahmagupta
SA_GS41_brsphutu.summary: The Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta is a treatise of Indian mathematical astronomy composed in 628 CE by Brahmagupta. This e-text comprises its mathematical sections: arithmetic and plane geometry (ch. 12), indeterminate equations and algebra (ch. 18), gnomon shadow analysis (ch. 19), combinatorics concerning Sanskrit prosody (ch. 20), and sine computations (ch. 21.17–23).
SA_GS41_brsphutu.attribution: Attributed to Brahmagupta (dated to 628 CE in the header).
SA_GS41_brsphutu.coverage: partial — Contains only the mathematical chapters of the 24-chapter work: chapter 12 (Gaṇita), chapter 18 (Kuṭṭaka), chapter 19 (Śaṅkuchāyāvijñāna), chapter 20 (Chandaścityuttara), and the Jyāprakaraṇa (vv. 17–23 on sine computation) of chapter 21 (Gola). Dvivedin's Sanskrit commentary is omitted, though Hayashi includes Dvivedin's variant suggestions and Colebrooke's stanza numbering concordances.

SA_GS41_lagrvvju.title: Ṛgvedavedāṅgajyotiṣa
SA_GS41_lagrvvju.author: Lagadha
SA_GS41_lagrvvju.summary: The Ṛgvedavedāṅgajyotiṣa (also known as Ārcajyotiṣa) is the Ṛgvedic recension of the Vedāṅgajyotiṣa, the earliest surviving Indian text on mathematical astronomy and calendrical calculation, traditionally attributed to Lagadha. In 35 concise anuṣṭubh verses, it lays out a lunisolar calendar designed to determine the precise times for Vedic sacrifices, based on a five-year yuga consisting of 62 synodic months (including two intercalary months) and 1,830 civil days. The text details the coordinate system of 27 nakṣatras with their presiding deities, the positions of the solstices and equinoxes, rules for calculating tithis and nakṣatra portions, and seasonal variations in daytime length measurable by a water-clock (clepsydra).
SA_GS41_lagrvvju.attribution: The treatise is traditionally attributed to the ancient sage Lagadha. Verses 2 and 29 explicitly invoke Lagadha ('kālajñānaṃ pravakṣyāmi lagadhasya mahātmanaḥ' and 'vyākhyānaṃ lagadho 'bravīt'), indicating that the text is framed as an exposition of Lagadha's teachings, possibly redacted by a disciple (identified by some scholars as Śuci, named in verse 1).
SA_GS41_lagrvvju.coverage: complete — Contains all 35 verses (numbered 1–35) comprising the complete text of the Ṛgveda recension.
translations: George Thibaut, 'Contributions to the Explanation of the Jyotisha-Vedānga', Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal 46, 1877. (English)

SA_GS41_lilavatu.title: Līlāvatī
SA_GS41_lilavatu.author: Bhāskara
SA_GS41_lilavatu.summary: The Līlāvatī is an arithmetic and geometry treatise composed around 1150 by Bhāskara as part of the Siddhāntaśiromaṇi. Composed in verse and framed as problems addressed to Līlāvatī, it treats arithmetic operations, fractions, suvarṇagaṇita, plane and solid mensuration, kuṭṭaka, and combinatorics (aṅkapāśa).
SA_GS41_lilavatu.edition: Composite digital text based on two editions: 1) Lilavati, ed with Ganesa's Buddhivilasini and Mahidhara's Lilavativivarana by V.G. Apate. Anandasrama Sanskrit Series 107. Poona 1937; 2) Lilavati, ed with Sankara's Kriyakramakari by K.V.Sarma. Hoshiarpur 1975.
SA_GS41_lilavatu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the treatise containing 272 numbered units of metrical rules along with prose examples (uddeśaka) and calculations (nyāsa), terminating with the final verse and colophon.
translations: Colebrooke, Henry Thomas (English translation referenced in GRETIL header notes as [Cb-]). (English)
Fayzī, Persian translation of the Lilavati. (Persian)

SA_GS41_surysidu.title: Sūryasiddhānta
SA_GS41_surysidu.summary: The Sūryasiddhānta is an astronomical classic framed as celestial instruction imparted by a solar deity (or solar emanation) to the asura Maya, structured in 14 adhyāyas treating astronomical calculations, planetary positions, eclipses, and cosmography.
SA_GS41_surysidu.attribution: The work is framed as a divine astronomical teaching delivered by an emanation of the Sun god (Sūrya / Vivasvat) to the asura Maya.
SA_GS41_surysidu.edition: Collated digital text prepared by Michio Yano (2002) based on three printed editions: B: The Surya-siddhanta with its commentary the Gudhartha-prakasaka, edited by Fits-Edward Hall, Bibliotheca Indica, Calcutta 1854 (reprinted as volume 25 of Bibliotheca Indica, Biblio Verlag, Osnabrück 1980); C: Kāśī saṃskṛta granthamālā 144, Caukhamba Sanskrit Samsthaana, Fourth edition, 1987; D: With the Commentary of Sudhakara Dvivedi, ed. by Dr. Sri Krsna Candra Dvivedii, Sampurnanand Sanskrit University, 1987.
SA_GS41_surysidu.coverage: complete — Complete text across all 14 adhyāyas (1.1 to 14.27).
translations: E. Burgess (trans.), Sūryasiddhānta. (English)
Bāpūdeva Śāstrī and L. Wilkinson (trans.), Translation of the Sūrya Siddhānta, Bibliotheca Indica, Calcutta. (English)

SA_GS41_tikaniku.title: Tikanikayātrā
SA_GS41_tikaniku.author: Varāhamihira
SA_GS41_tikaniku.summary: The Tikanikayātrā is a treatise on expedition and military astrology (yātrā) attributed to Varāhamihira. Across nine chapters totaling 103 verses, it sets forth rules for determining auspicious moments for military departures, astrological aspects of the planets and asterisms (nakṣatras), and auspicious and inauspicious omens.
SA_GS41_tikaniku.coverage: complete — Complete text in 9 adhyāyas comprising 103 verses (numbered TY 1.1 through TY 9.35).

SA_GS41_vivahapu.title: Vivāhapaṭala
SA_GS41_vivahapu.author: Varāhamihira
SA_GS41_vivahapu.summary: The Vivāhapaṭala is Varāhamihira's astrological treatise on marriage. It opens with a hymn to Manobhava (Kāma), followed by verses concerning the propitiation of Śacī (Indrāṇī) and rules concerning nakṣatras, lagna, and planetary combinations for marriage.
SA_GS41_vivahapu.attribution: Attributed to Varāhamihira, who is named in the concluding stanza (VP 91: 'cakre varāhamihiraḥ praṇipatya sādhūn samyak vivāhapaṭalaṃ pṛthutāṃ vihāya').
SA_GS41_vivahapu.edition: Deviprasada Lamsala, ed., Vivāhapaṭalam, Rastriya Abhilekhalayata, 2035 with reference to Utpala's commentary [marked by U.]
SA_GS41_vivahapu.coverage: complete — Complete text in 91 verses (VP 1–91), ending with the author's concluding signature stanza (VP 91).

SA_GS41_yogay1_u.title: Bṛhadyātrā
SA_GS41_yogay1_u.author: Varāhamihira
SA_GS41_yogay1_u.summary: The Bṛhadyātrā is a treatise on yātrā (journey/military astrology) attributed to Varāhamihira, distinct from the Yogayātrā. In 34 chapters, it covers topics such as fate and human effort (daivapuruṣakāra), auspicious lunar tithis, constellations (nakṣatra), planetary positions, and divination/omens for expedition.
SA_GS41_yogay1_u.edition: Pingree, David (ed.): Brhadyatra, Government of Tamil Nadu, 1972. Introduction by David Pingree Forward by R. N. Sampath.
SA_GS41_yogay1_u.coverage: complete — Text in 34 chapters concluding with 'End of Bṛhadyātrā' (verses tagged BY_1.1 to BY_34.6).

SA_GS41_yogay2_u.title: Yogayātrā
SA_GS41_yogay2_u.author: Varāhamihira
SA_GS41_yogay2_u.summary: The Yogayātrā by Varāhamihira is a Sanskrit treatise on military astrology (yātrā) and ritual preparations for warfare. The text expounds topics such as destiny and human effort, planetary combinations (yogas), offerings (bali), lustration (snāna), fire omens (agninimitta), elephants, horses, swords, and bird/animal omens (śakuna).
SA_GS41_yogay2_u.attribution: Ascribed to Varāhamihira; treats military omens and astrology alongside his other related works such as the Bṛhadyātrā.
SA_GS41_yogay2_u.edition: Ramacandra Jha, Darabhanga, KMSG 23, 1986 with reference to Kern, Hendrick, 'Die Yogayatra des Varahamihira, Adhyaya 1--9' Verspreide Geschriften, Vol. 1--168, Hague, 1913 and Bhattotpala's commentary in the Brhatsamhita.
SA_GS41_yogay2_u.coverage: complete — Text in 16 adhyāyas, concluding with an adhyāyasaṃgraha in verses 16.16–18.
translations: Hendrik Kern, 'Die Yogayâtrâ des Varâhamihira' (chapters 1–9), in Indischen Studien; repr. in Verspreide Geschriften, vol. 1, The Hague: Martinus Nijhoff, 1913. (German)

SA_GSD36_angirspu.title: Āṅgirasasmṛti
SA_GSD36_angirspu.summary: The Āṅgirasasmṛti is a dharmaśāstra manual traditionally ascribed to the sage Aṅgiras. Arranged in two sections—Pūrvāṅgiras and Uttarāṅgiras (the latter ending with the 12th adhyāya)—the work provides procedural guidance on domestic ritual ceremonies, śrāddha (ancestor offerings), and expiations/penances (prāyaścitta/kṛcchra).
SA_GSD36_angirspu.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the Vedic sage Aṅgiras.
SA_GSD36_angirspu.edition: A. N. Krishna Aiyangar (ed.), Āṅgirasasmṛti, Madras: Adyar Library, 1953 (Adyar Library Series).
SA_GSD36_angirspu.coverage: complete — Text divided into Pūrvāṅgiras and Uttarāṅgiras (the latter concluding in chapter 12).

SA_GSD36_brhasp_u.title: Bṛhaspatismṛti (Vyavahārakāṇḍa)
SA_GSD36_brhasp_u.summary: The Bṛhaspatismṛti is an ancient Hindu legal treatise of the classical Dharmaśāstra tradition, surviving only as quotations in medieval commentaries and legal digests. Closely linked to the Manusmṛti, it represents one of the most mature formulations of classical Hindu legal procedure and substantive law, defining the four 'feet' (catuṣpād) of judicial process, standards of evidence, and rules for the eighteen titles of law (vyavahārapada). This e-text covers the Vyavahārakāṇḍa (in 29 chapters) as reconstructed and edited by K. V. Rangaswami Aiyangar in 1941.
SA_GSD36_brhasp_u.edition: K. V. Rangaswami Aiyangar (ed.), Bṛhaspatismṛti (Reconstructed), Gaekwad's Oriental Series, No. 85, Baroda: Oriental Institute, 1941.
SA_GSD36_brhasp_u.coverage: partial — Contains the Vyavahārakāṇḍa only (chapters 1–29, tagged BP1.1.001a through BP1.29.016b plus concluding verses).

SA_GSD36_brhasppu.title: Bṛhaspatismṛti (Vyavahārakāṇḍa only)
SA_GSD36_brhasppu.author: Bṛhaspati
SA_GSD36_brhasppu.summary: The Vyavahārakāṇḍa of the Bṛhaspatismṛti is a legal treatise dealing with jurisprudence, administration of justice, court procedure, evidence, and titles of dispute (vyavahārapadas).
SA_GSD36_brhasppu.edition: K. V. Rangaswami Aiyangar (reconstr.), Bṛhaspatismṛti (reconstructed), Gaekwad's Oriental Series, No. 85, Baroda: Oriental Institute, 1941.
SA_GSD36_brhasppu.coverage: partial — Contains only the Vyavahārakāṇḍa (ending at verse Brh_1,29.16 followed by the concluding verse Brh_1,end: 'vedārthopanibaddhatvāt...').
translations: Julius Jolly (tr.), The Minor Law-Books, Part I: Nārada, Bṛhaspati, Sacred Books of the East, Oxford: Clarendon Press. (English)

SA_GSD36_katy2p_u.title: Kātyāyanasmṛti (vyavahāra fragments, reconstructed)
SA_GSD36_katy2p_u.summary: The Kātyāyanasmṛti is a lost legal smṛti, known only from verses quoted in later works and digests; it treats law and judicial procedure (vyavahāra). P. V. Kane collected and arranged 973 verses into a reconstructed text covering the qualities and duties of the king, the court and its procedure, evidence and ordeals, the titles of law such as debts, deposits, partition and women's property (strīdhana), and punishments. This e-text gives the Sanskrit verses of Kane's reconstruction.
SA_GSD36_katy2p_u.attribution: Ascribed traditionally to the sage Kātyāyana; the historical author is unknown. It is known only fragmentarily through quotations in later works/commentaries.
SA_GSD36_katy2p_u.edition: P. V. Kane (ed. and tr.), Kātyāyanasmṛtisāroddhāra or Kātyāyanasmṛti on Vyavahāra (Law and Procedure): Text (reconstructed), Translation, Notes and Introduction. Bombay, 1933 (reprint from the Hindu Law Quarterly).
SA_GSD36_katy2p_u.coverage: fragment — The original work is lost; the e-text reproduces P. V. Kane's full reconstruction of 973 verses (K_001–K_973) on rājadharma and vyavahāra (court procedure, the eighteen titles of law, ordeals, debts, deposits, partition, strīdhana, punishments), with Kane's bracketed topic headings (e.g. '[rājaguṇāḥ]', '[vyavahāralakṣaṇādi]'). Kane's translation, notes and introduction are not included. This is the GRETIL plain-text version (katy2p_u, header 'PLAIN TEXT VERSION').
translations: P. V. Kane, Kātyāyanasmṛti on Vyavahāra: Text (reconstructed), Translation, Notes and Introduction, Bombay 1933 (reprint from the Hindu Law Quarterly). (English)

SA_GSD36_mvir_sau.title: Vīramitrodaya: Samayaprakāśa
SA_GSD36_mvir_sau.author: Mitramiśra
SA_GSD36_mvir_sau.summary: The Samayaprakāśa ('Illumination of Ritual Times') is an extensive section of Mitramiśra's encyclopedic Dharmaśāstra digest, the Vīramitrodaya, composed under King Vīrasiṃhadeva. It systematically analyzes the calendrical and temporal rules (kāla/samaya) governing Hindu ritual obligations, discussing lunar days (tithi), intercalary months (malamāsa), solar ingresses (saṅkrānti), festivals, and vows (vrata). Drawing heavily upon smṛti and purāṇic sources as well as medieval authorities, it became a standard authority for ritual timing within the Banaras school of Dharmaśāstra.
SA_GSD36_mvir_sau.attribution: Composed by Mitramiśra, son of Paraśurāma Miśra and grandson of Haṃsa Paṇḍita, under the royal patronage of King Vīrasiṃhadeva.
SA_GSD36_mvir_sau.edition: Mitramisra: Viramitrodaya, Samayaprakasa, ed. Vishnu Prasada Bhandari, Benares 1935 (Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series; 30, XIII).
SA_GSD36_mvir_sau.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Samayaprakāśa section of the Vīramitrodaya, running from the opening maṅgala verses through the final somakāla section and closing colophon (iti somakālaḥ ... samayaprakāśanaparaḥ pūrttiṃ prakāśo 'gamat).

SA_GSD36_narads_u.title: Nāradasmṛti
SA_GSD36_narads_u.summary: The Nāradasmṛti is a classical Dharmaśāstra treatise uniquely devoted almost entirely to legal procedure and substantive law (vyavahāra), omitting the standard sections on customary conduct (ācāra) and expiation (prāyaścitta). It opens with an introductory section (mātṛkā) on the administration of justice, courts, plaint procedure, and evidence, followed by twenty chapters treating the eighteen traditional titles of law (vyavahārapadas) as well as theft and divine ordeals (divya). Dating to approximately the 5th–6th century CE, the work is notable for its sophisticated treatment of judicial evidence, contract law, and debt recovery, and for explicitly subordinating customary usage to royal edicts (rājaśāsana) in judicial disputes.
SA_GSD36_narads_u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Nārada as an abridgement of a legal code composed by Manu.
SA_GSD36_narads_u.edition: The Nāradasmṛti, Part One (critically edited text), edited by Richard W. Lariviere. Philadelphia: Department of South Asia Regional Studies, University of Pennsylvania, 1989 (University of Pennsylvania Studies on South Asia 4-5).
SA_GSD36_narads_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the recension edited by Richard W. Lariviere (1989), consisting of the judicial introduction (Mātṛkā 1–3) and title chapters (Vyavahāra 1–20), ending at N20.48.
translations: Richard W. Lariviere (trans.), The Naradasmrti, Pt. II, 1989. (English)
Julius Jolly (trans.), The minor law-books. Part I: Nârada, Brhaspati, Oxford, 1889 (The Sacred Books of the East, 33). (English)

SA_GSD36_nars2_pu.title: Nāradasmṛti
SA_GSD36_nars2_pu.summary: The Nāradasmṛti is a metrical Dharmaśāstra text dealing with civil and criminal jurisprudence (vyavahāra), including mātṛkā procedure and substantive titles of law (vyavahārapada).
SA_GSD36_nars2_pu.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the divine sage Nārada (often framed as an abridgement of the primeval legal code of Manu).
SA_GSD36_nars2_pu.edition: Richard W. Lariviere (ed.), The Nāradasmṛti. Critically edited with an introduction, annotated translation, and appendices. Part One: Text. Philadelphia: Dep. of South Asia Regional Studies, University of Pennsylvania (University of Pennsylvania studies on South Asia, 4-5), 1989.
SA_GSD36_nars2_pu.coverage: complete — Contains the critically edited metrical root text according to Lariviere's 1989 edition, consisting of 3 introductory chapters (Mātṛkā 1–3) and 20 substantive judicial chapters (Vyavahāra 1–20, ending at Nar_20.48 with 'nāradīyadharmaśāstraḥ samāptaḥ').
translations: Julius Jolly (trans.), The Minor Law-Books. Part I: Nārada, Bṛhaspati. Oxford: Clarendon Press (Sacred Books of the East), 1889. (English)

SA_GSD36_pars1__u.title: Parāśaradharmasaṃhitā (selected verses and collation notes)
SA_GSD36_pars1__u.summary: A short working file consisting of selected verses and collation notes from the Parāśaradharmasaṃhitā (Parāśarasmṛti), an influential dharmaśāstra of twelve adhyāyas traditionally regarded as the principal legal authority for the Kali age (kaliyuga). The text concentrates on ritual conduct (ācāra), the duties of the four varṇas, purification, and penance (prāyaścitta), omitting civil and criminal procedure (vyavahāra). This file is not the full smṛti, but an excerpt of a few verses from chapters 1 and 12 accompanied by collation notes comparing the Bombay Sanskrit Series and Bibliotheca Indica editions.
SA_GSD36_pars1__u.coverage: excerpt — Contains only 24 lines (approx. 990 characters) comprising a tiny excerpt: sample verses from adhyāya 1 (vv. 57–59) and adhyāya 12 (vv. 20, 24, 77), interspersed with editorial collation notes comparing the BSS and BI editions.

SA_GSD36_pars2_pu.title: Parāśaradharmasaṃhitā
SA_GSD36_pars2_pu.author: Parāśara
SA_GSD36_pars2_pu.summary: The Parāśaradharmasaṃhitā (or Parāśarasmṛti) is an influential classical Dharmaśāstra text canonical for its claim to define the yugadharma specifically designated for the Kali age (Kalau Pārāśarāḥ smṛtāḥ, 1.24). Comprising 592 anuṣṭubh verses organized into 12 chapters, it expounds rules of customary conduct and purity (ācāra, chs. 1–11) and rites of expiation (prāyaścitta, ch. 12). The treatise is notable for introducing pragmatic modifications to classical law tailored to the diminished moral capacity of the Kali age, such as permitting agriculture to twice-born householders and outlining conditions for the remarriage of women. It does not contain an internal section on jurisprudence (vyavahāra), a lacuna that was famously supplemented in the 14th century by Mādhavācārya in his comprehensive commentary, the Parāśaramādhavīya.
SA_GSD36_pars2_pu.edition: The Parâśara Dharma Saṃhitâ or Parâśara Smṛiti with the Commentary of Sâyaṇa Mâdhavâchârya, edited by Vāman Śāstri Islāmpurkar, Bombay: Government Central Book Depot, 1893–1919, Bombay Sanskrit Series nos. 47 (Vol. I, Part 1), 48 (Vol. I, Part 2), 59 (Vol. II, Part 1), and 64 (Vol. II, Part 2); partly compared with Candrakānta Tarkālaṅkāra's edition in Bibliotheca Indica (BI 94, 298).
SA_GSD36_pars2_pu.coverage: complete — Complete root text (mūla) in 12 adhyāyas comprising 592 verses (numbered up to 12.82 due to fractional/variant numbering). Adhyāyas 1–11 constitute the Ācārakāṇḍa and adhyāya 12 forms the Prāyaścittakāṇḍa. The Vyavahārakāṇḍa found in Mādhavācārya's commentary contains no mūla verses of Parāśara.

SA_GSD36_sa_vijJAnezvara-mitAkSarA.title: Yājñavalkyasmṛti with Mitākṣarā
SA_GSD36_sa_vijJAnezvara-mitAkSarA.author: Yājñavalkya, Vijñāneśvara
SA_GSD36_sa_vijJAnezvara-mitAkSarA.summary: The Mitākṣarā by the twelfth-century Sanskrit author Vijñāneśvara is a commentary on the Yājñavalkyasmṛti (Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra). Its subject is dharma, legal and religious duty, encompassing ācāra, vyavahāra, and prāyaścitta. Along with the Mānava-dharmaśāstra, it is one of the most influential works of classical Hindu law, forming the foundation of the Mitākṣarā legal school.
SA_GSD36_sa_vijJAnezvara-mitAkSarA.attribution: The root smṛti is traditionally attributed to Yājñavalkya. The commentary Mitākṣarā was composed by Vijñāneśvara, active during the reign of Vikramādityadeva.
SA_GSD36_sa_vijJAnezvara-mitAkSarA.edition: Narayan Ram Acharya (ed.), Yājñavalkyasmṛti of Yogīśvara Yājñavalkya with the commentary Mitākṣarā of Vijñāneśvara, notes, varient readings, etc., Bombay: Nirnaya Sagar Press; checked against Umesh Chandra Pandeya (ed.), Kāśī Saṃskṛta granthamālā 178, Vārāṇasī: Caukhambā Saṃskṛta Sīrīja Āphisa; and S. S. Setlur (ed.), Madras: Brahmavadin Press, 1912; electronic edition edited, formatted, and color-coded by Patrick Olivelle (2020).
SA_GSD36_sa_vijJAnezvara-mitAkSarA.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Yājñavalkyasmṛti accompanied by the Mitākṣarā commentary across all three adhyāyas (1.1 to 3.334).
translations: Samarao Narasimha Naraharayya and Rai Bahadur Srisa Chandra Vasu (trans.), The Sacred Laws of The Aryas as Taught in the School of Yajnavalkya and Explained by Vijnanesvara in his Well-known Commentary Named the Mitaksara. (English)

SA_GSD36_mitaksara.title: Yājñavalkyasmṛti with Mitākṣarā
SA_GSD36_mitaksara.author: Yājñavalkya, Vijñāneśvara
SA_GSD36_mitaksara.summary: The Mitākṣarā by Vijñāneśvara is an exhaustive running commentary on the Yājñavalkyasmṛti and stands among the most influential works of Hindu legal literature. Spanning all three divisions of the smṛti—customary conduct (ācāra), judicial procedure and substantive law (vyavāhara), and penance (prāyaścitta)—the work harmonizes conflicting smṛti authorities using sophisticated Mīmāṃsā hermeneutical principles. Vijñāneśvara's exposition, notably his formulation of coparcenary inheritance rights by birth (janmasvatvavāda) and women's property rights (strīdhana), formed the foundation of the Mitākṣarā school of Hindu law, which predominated across most regions of premodern and colonial India outside Bengal.
SA_GSD36_mitaksara.attribution: The root smṛti is traditionally attributed to the sage Yājñavalkya. The commentary Mitākṣarā was composed by Vijñāneśvara under King Vikramārka / Vikramāditya at Kalyāṇa.
SA_GSD36_mitaksara.edition: Yājñavalkyasmṛti of Yogīśvara Yājñavalkya with the commentary Mitākṣarā of Vijñāneśvara, ed. Narayan Ram Acharya, Nirnaya Sagar Press, Bombay, 1949.
SA_GSD36_mitaksara.coverage: complete — Complete text of all three chapters (adhyāyas) of the Yājñavalkyasmṛti with Vijñāneśvara's Mitākṣarā commentary: Ācārādhyāya, Vyavahārādhyāya, and Prāyaścittādhyāya, ending with the author's seven closing praśasti and benedictory verses.
translations: Colebrooke, H. T. (trans.), Two Treatises on the Hindu Law of Inheritance: Dāyabhāga and Mitākṣarā, Calcutta, 1810. (English)

SA_GSD36_yajn2_pu.title: Yājñavalkyasmṛti
SA_GSD36_yajn2_pu.author: Yājñavalkya
SA_GSD36_yajn2_pu.summary: The Yājñavalkyasmṛti is a metrical dharmaśāstra treatise attributed to Yājñavalkya, structured into three sections on customary conduct (ācāra), judicial procedure/law (vyavahāra), and expiation (prāyaścitta).
SA_GSD36_yajn2_pu.edition: Yajnavalkyasmrti of Yogisvara Yajnavalkya With the commentary Mitaksara of Vijñanesvara, Notes, Variant readings, etc. Ed. by Narayan Ram Acharya Nirnayasagara Press, Bombay, 1949.
SA_GSD36_yajn2_pu.coverage: complete — Complete verse text (mūla) of all three adhyāyas: Ācārādhyāya, Vyavahārādhyāya, and Prāyaścittādhyāya. The commentary Mitākṣarā printed in the source edition is omitted from this e-text.
translations: Adolf Friedrich Stenzler, Yâjñavalkya's Gesetzbuch: Sanskrit und Deutsch, 1849. (German)

SA_GSD36_ys-78_pu.title: Yamasmṛti
SA_GSD36_ys-78_pu.summary: A short metrical dharmaśāstra text in 78 verses containing rules on expiations (prāyaścitta) for various offences, ceremonial impurities, rules concerning women, and sandhyākāla prohibitions.
SA_GSD36_ys-78_pu.attribution: Traditionally ascribed to Yama (concluding with 'iti yamaproktaṃ dharmaśāstraṃ samāptam' at v. 78).
SA_GSD36_ys-78_pu.edition: Haridatta Sastri (ed.): The Smriti Sandarbha (6 Vols.), Calcutta: Gurumandal, 1952-1957, pp. 2083-90 (repr. Delhi: 1988), Gurumandal Series 9.
SA_GSD36_ys-78_pu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the 78-verse recension of the Yamasmṛti (verses 1–78, tagged YS78v_1 through YS78v_78), terminating with the colophon 'iti yamaproktaṃ dharmaśāstraṃ samāptam'.

SA_GSD36_ys-99_pu.title: Laghuyamasmṛti
SA_GSD36_ys-99_pu.summary: The Laghuyamasmṛti is a short metrical dharmaśāstra in 99 anuṣṭubh verses belonging to the textual cycle attributed to Yama. It focuses predominantly on prāyaścitta (penance and ritual expiation) for offences such as improper contact with outcastes or impure persons, forbidden food consumption, and failed suicide attempts, alongside rules for personal bodily purity (śauca) and ancestral offerings (śrāddha and tarpaṇa). In modern scholarly taxonomy, this 99-verse recension is distinguished from other recensions of the Yamasmṛti.
SA_GSD36_ys-99_pu.attribution: Ascribed in the text (verse 1 and colophon) to the mythical sage and deity of dharma Yama (Dharmarāja). The historical authorship of this metrical smṛti is anonymous.
SA_GSD36_ys-99_pu.edition: Vināyak Gaṇeś Āpṭe (ed.), Smṛtīnāṃ Samuccayaḥ, Poona: Ānandāśrama, 1929, pp. 112–116 (Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series 48).
SA_GSD36_ys-99_pu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the 99-verse recension (verses YS99v_1 through YS99v_99) including the opening invocation and closing colophons.

SA_GSD36_ys182_pu.title: Bṛhadyamasmṛti
SA_GSD36_ys182_pu.summary: The Bṛhadyamasmṛti is an expanded metrical Dharmaśāstra text in five adhyāyas comprising 182 ślokas, traditionally attributed to Yama. The first four adhyāyas focus heavily on prāyaścitta (penance and atonement) for ritual, moral, and inter-caste transgressions, rules of purification (śuddhi), and ancestral rites (śrāddha). The fifth chapter contains rules on civil and judicial procedure (vyavahāra), specifically addressing inheritance, partition of family property, and evidential hierarchy in judicial disputes.
SA_GSD36_ys182_pu.edition: Smṛtīnāṃ Samuccayaḥ, ed. Vināyaka Gaṇeśa Āpṭe (V. G. Apte), Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series 48, Pune: Ānandāśrama, 1905 (2nd ed. 1929), pp. 99–107.
SA_GSD36_ys182_pu.coverage: complete — Complete 182-verse text across five adhyāyas (YS182v_1.1–5.26), concluding with 'samāpteyaṃ bṛhadyamasmṛtiḥ'.

SA_GSD36_yssoutpu.title: Yamasmṛti (South Indian recension)
SA_GSD36_yssoutpu.summary: The Yamasmṛti is a metrical Dharmaśāstra code attributed to the sage and deity Yama. This South Indian recension consists of two adhyāyas: the first chapter deals with ritual purifications (śauca), bodily defilements, rules of diet, and expiations (prāyaścitta) for offenses such as suicide attempts and association with outcasts; the second chapter focuses on royal duties (rājadharma), judicial proceedings (vyavahāra), and the suppression of criminals (kaṇṭakaśodhana).
SA_GSD36_yssoutpu.attribution: Framed as a discourse spoken by the god/sage Yama in response to the questions of sages (v. 1.1–2).
SA_GSD36_yssoutpu.edition: Jürgen Neuss: Untersuchungen zur Textgeschichte der Yamasmṛti, Berlin 1999 (MA-thesis, Free University Berlin, unpublished); updated version available from the GRETIL e-library (http://resolver.sub.uni-goettingen.de/purl/?gr_elib-197).
SA_GSD36_yssoutpu.coverage: complete — South Indian recension: Adhyāya 1 (verses 1–38 in anuṣṭubh, verses 39–57 in indravajrā/upendravajrā) and Adhyāya 2 (77 verses in anuṣṭubh, ending at YSS_2.77).

SA_GSD37_gautdhcu.title: Gautamadharmasūtra with Maskaribhāṣya (chapters 1–3)
SA_GSD37_gautdhcu.author: Gautama, Maskarin
SA_GSD37_gautdhcu.summary: The Gautamadharmasūtra is one of the foundational and earliest extant prose treatises of the Hindu legal and ritual tradition, affiliated with the Rāṇāyanīya branch of the Sāmaveda. Chapters 1–3 treat the primary sources of dharma (Veda, smṛti, and ācāra), rules governing initiation (upanayana) and student life (brahmacarya), purification rituals (śauca and ācamana), and a debate on the four stages of life (āśrama), culminating in the assertion of the superiority of the householder stage (gārhasthya). Maskarin's commentary (Maskaribhāṣya) provides one of the two primary classical commentaries on the text alongside Haradatta's Mitākṣarā.
SA_GSD37_gautdhcu.attribution: The root Dharmasūtra is traditionally ascribed to the sage Gautama of the Sāmaveda school (Rāṇāyanīya recension). The commentary is composed by Maskarin, who identifies himself in the opening verses as the son of Vāmana (sūnunā vāmanasya).
SA_GSD37_gautdhcu.edition: Gautama-dharmasūtra with Maskarī Bhāṣya, ed. L. Śrīnivāsācārya, OLPSS 50.
SA_GSD37_gautdhcu.coverage: partial — Contains adhyāyas 1 through 3 only (ending at sūtra 3.36 and the adhyāya colophon), out of the complete work's 28 adhyāyas.
translations: The Sacred Laws of the Aryas, as taught in the Schools of Apastamba, Gautama, Vâsishtha, and Baudhâyana, Translated by G. Bühler, Sacred Books of the East and XIV, Oxford, 1879–82. (English)

SA_GSD37_vaikhd_u.title: Vaikhānasadharmasūtra
SA_GSD37_vaikhd_u.summary: The Vaikhānasadharmasūtra constitutes the dharmasūtra portion (Praśnas 8–10) of the Vaikhānasasmārtasūtra, belonging to the Taittirīya recension of the Black Yajurveda. Across three praśnas, the work details the duties and occupations of the four social classes (varṇas) and life-stages (āśramas), providing classical Sanskrit literature's most elaborate typology of hermits (vānaprasthas/vaikhānasas) and ascetics (bhikṣus). Combining late Vedic smārta jurisprudence with pronounced early Vaiṣṇava devotional features (such as the worship of Nārāyaṇa), the work is generally assigned to the 3rd or 4th century CE.
SA_GSD37_vaikhd_u.attribution: Traditionally ascribed to the seer Vikhanas (as reflected in the text's concluding words 'iti vikhanāḥ'). The work represents the dharmasūtra portion of the Vaikhānasa school affiliated with the Black Yajurveda.
SA_GSD37_vaikhd_u.edition: Willem Caland (ed.), Vaikhānasasmārtasūtram: The Domestic Rules of the Vaikhānasa School Belonging to the Black Yajurveda, Calcutta: Asiatic Society of Bengal, 1927, pp. 112–145.
SA_GSD37_vaikhd_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Vaikhānasadharmasūtra in 3 praśnas comprising 34 kāṇḍikās (Praśna 1: 11 kāṇḍikās; Praśna 2: 8 kāṇḍikās; Praśna 3: 15 kāṇḍikās). In the 10-praśna Vaikhānasasmārtasūtra, this corresponds to Praśnas 8–10 (Caland's edition, pp. 112–145, preserved as inline page/line markers in the e-text).
translations: Willem Caland (tr.), Vaikhānasasmārtasūtram: The Domestic Rules and Sacred Laws of the Vaikhānasa School Belonging to the Black Yajurveda, Calcutta: Asiatic Society of Bengal, 1929 (Bibliotheca Indica, Work). (English)
Wilhelm Eggers (tr.), Das Dharmasūtra der Vaikhānasas, Göttingen 1929. (German)

SA_GSP27_moksop_u.title: Mokṣopāya (prakaraṇas 1–5 and 6, part 1)
SA_GSP27_moksop_u.summary: The Mokṣopāya ('Means to Liberation') expounds a non-dual doctrine maintaining that the empirical cosmos is a mental projection created by cognitive construction (saṅkalpa / manas), and teaches liberation through detachment and inquiry. Framed as instructions delivered by the sage Vasiṣṭha to Prince Rāma (narrated by Vālmīki to Bharadvāja), its doctrine is communicated through philosophical teachings and narrative cycles. Philological research shows the Mokṣopāya to be the earlier recension of the Yogavāsiṣṭha.
SA_GSP27_moksop_u.attribution: Referred to by editors as 'Anonymus Casmiriensis'. In the text, the sage Vālmīki relates the dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Prince Rāma to Bharadvāja. Philological scholarship identifies the Mokṣopāya as the earlier Kashmirian recension underlying the Yogavāsiṣṭha.
SA_GSP27_moksop_u.edition: Anonymus Casmiriensis: Mokṣopāya. Historisch-kritische Gesamtausgabe. Herausgegeben unter der Leitung von Walter Slaje. Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz Verlag, 2011–2018. Vol. I: Prakaraṇas 1 & 2, ed. Krause-Stinner, 2011;: Prakaraṇa 3, ed. Hanneder, Stephan, and Jager, 2011;: Prakaraṇa 4, ed. Krause-Stinner and Stephan, 2012;: Prakaraṇa 5, ed. Krause-Stinner and Stephan, 2013; Vol. V: Prakaraṇa 6, Part 1, ed. Krause-Stinner and Stephan, 2018 (Akademie der Wissenschaften und der Literatur, Mainz. Veröffentlichungen der Indologischen Kommission [Vol. I–IV] / Veröffentlichungen der Fächergruppenkommission für Außereuropäische Sprachen und Kulturen. Studien zur Indologie [Vol. V]).
SA_GSP27_moksop_u.coverage: partial — Contains Prakaraṇa 1 (Vairāgya, 1.1–1.32), Prakaraṇa 2 (Mumukṣuvyavahāra, 2.1–2.20), Prakaraṇa 3 (Utpatti, 3.1–3.140), Prakaraṇa 4 (Sthiti, 4.1–4.44), Prakaraṇa 5 (Upaśānti, 5.1–5.94), and Prakaraṇa 6, Part 1 (Nirvāṇa, 6.1–6.119). Chapters 6.120–6.374 and khilas are not yet edited / omitted.

SA_GSP28_dhebta_u.title: Hetubinduṭīkāloka
SA_GSP28_dhebta_u.author: Durvekamiśra
SA_GSP28_dhebta_u.summary: The Hetubinduṭīkāloka (also known as Arcaṭāloka) is an extensive Sanskrit sub-commentary (anuṭīkā) by Durvekamiśra on Bhaṭṭa Arcaṭa's Hetubinduṭīkā, which comments on Dharmakīrti's Hetubindu. Durvekamiśra acknowledges his teacher Jitāri ('guror jitāreḥ sa khalu prasādaḥ') and offers detailed commentary on Arcaṭa's work.
SA_GSP28_dhebta_u.attribution: Durvekamiśra explicitly names himself as author in the opening title ('paṇḍitadurvekamiśrakṛto hetubinduṭīkālokaḥ'), in the concluding stanzas ('kṛto 'yam arcaṭāloko nibandho bālabāndhavaḥ'), and in the final colophon ('kṛtir iyaṃ paṇḍitadurvekamiśrasyeti'). In the concluding stanzas, he acknowledges his teacher Jitāri ('guror jitāreḥ sa khalu prasādaḥ').
SA_GSP28_dhebta_u.edition: Hetubinduṭīkā of Bhaṭṭa Arcaṭa with the Sub-Commentary entitled Āloka of Durveka Miśra, edited by Pandit Sukhlalji Sanghavi and Muni Shri Jinavijayaji, Gaekwad's Oriental Series, No. 113, Baroda: Oriental Institute, 1949, pp. 233–411.
SA_GSP28_dhebta_u.coverage: complete — The e-text contains the complete text of Durvekamiśra's sub-commentary as printed in the 1949 Baroda edition (pp. 233–411).

SA_GSP28_durdhpru.title: Nyāyabindu with Nyāyabinduṭīkā and Dharmottarapradīpa
SA_GSP28_durdhpru.author: Dharmakīrti, Dharmottara, Durveka Miśra
SA_GSP28_durdhpru.summary: The Dharmottarapradīpa, composed by Durveka Miśra, is an extensive Sanskrit sub-commentary on Dharmottara's Nyāyabinduṭīkā, which comments on Dharmakīrti's foundational logical manual, the Nyāyabindu. Spanning three chapters—direct perception (pratyakṣa), inference for oneself (svārthānumāna), and inference for others (parārthānumāna)—the work defends and refines Buddhist pramāṇavāda against rival interpretations and Brahmanical critiques.
SA_GSP28_durdhpru.attribution: Dharmakīrti authored the root Nyāyabindu, Dharmottara authored the commentary Nyāyabinduṭīkā, and Durveka Miśra authored the sub-commentary Dharmottarapradīpa.
SA_GSP28_durdhpru.edition: Dalsukhbhai Malvania (ed.), Paṇḍita Durveka Miśra's Dharmottarapradīpa: Being a Sub-commentary on Dharmottara's Nyāyabinduṭīkā, a Commentary on Dharmakīrti's Nyāyabindu. Tibetan Sanskrit Works Series, vol. 2. Patna: Kashi Prasad Jayaswal Research Institute, 1971.
SA_GSP28_durdhpru.coverage: complete — Complete text of all three chapters across all three texts, reflecting the printed text of Malvania's edition including apparatus notes.

SA_GSP28_jaimsutu.title: Mīmāṃsāsūtra
SA_GSP28_jaimsutu.author: Jaimini
SA_GSP28_jaimsutu.summary: The Mīmāṃsāsūtra (or Pūrvamīmāṃsāsūtra), traditionally attributed to Jaimini, is the foundational text of the Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā darśana. Arranged into twelve books (adhyāyas), hence known as the Dvādaśalakṣaṇī, the aphorisms formulate the rules of interpretation (nyāya) for the ritual injunctions (vidhi) of the Vedic corpus. The work provides systematic epistemological arguments for the intrinsicality of knowledge (svataḥprāmāṇya) and the eternality of language and the Veda, establishing hermeneutic canons that deeply influenced Dharmaśāstra, Vedānta, and Indian legal interpretation.
SA_GSP28_jaimsutu.edition: B.D. Basu (ed.), Allahabad 1923–1925 (Sacred Books of the Hindus, 27).
SA_GSP28_jaimsutu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 12 adhyāyas (spanning from 1.1.1 'athāto dharmajijñāsā' to 12.4.40 'anvāhārye ca darśanāt').

SA_GSP28_jsbh1-1u.title: Bhāṭṭadīpikā with Prabhāvalī (adhyāya 1, adhikaraṇa 1)
SA_GSP28_jsbh1-1u.author: Khaṇḍadeva, Śambhubhaṭṭa
SA_GSP28_jsbh1-1u.summary: This file contains the opening portion of Śambhubhaṭṭa's Prabhāvalī commentary on Khaṇḍadeva's Bhāṭṭadīpikā (a commentary on Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra), treating the first adhikaraṇa of Adhyāya 1.
SA_GSP28_jsbh1-1u.attribution: Khaṇḍadeva composed the root commentary Bhāṭṭadīpikā on Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra. His pupil Śambhubhaṭṭa authored the sub-commentary Prabhāvalī. Khaṇḍadeva's text provides the opening maṅgala verse; the discussion on Adhyāya 1, Adhikaraṇa 1 is accompanied by Śambhubhaṭṭa's Prabhāvalī.
SA_GSP28_jsbh1-1u.edition: N. S. Ananta Krishna Sastri, Bombay 1921–1922 (Reprint: Delhi 1987, Sri Garib Dass Oriental Series, 50-).
SA_GSP28_jsbh1-1u.coverage: partial — Adhyāya 1, Adhikaraṇa 1, containing Khaṇḍadeva's opening verse and Śambhubhaṭṭa's Prabhāvalī.

SA_GSP28_jsbh1-2u.title: Bhāṭṭadīpikā with Prabhāvalī (adhyāya 1, pāda 2)
SA_GSP28_jsbh1-2u.author: Khaṇḍadeva, Śambhubhaṭṭa
SA_GSP28_jsbh1-2u.summary: Khaṇḍadeva's Bhāṭṭadīpikā is a commentary on Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra. Accompanied by the Prabhāvalī sub-commentary of his student Śambhubhaṭṭa, this section comprises the Arthavādapāda (Adhyāya 1, Pāda 2). It establishes the authoritative epistemic status (prāmāṇya) and purposiveness of non-injunctive Vedic texts—namely commendatory and deprecatory passages (arthavāda) as well as ritual formulas (mantra)—by demonstrating that they form a unified semantic and syntactical unit (ekavākyatā) with ritual injunctions (vidhi).
SA_GSP28_jsbh1-2u.attribution: The Bhāṭṭadīpikā is by Khaṇḍadeva. The accompanying sub-commentary Prabhāvalī is by his student Śambhubhaṭṭa (son of Bālakṛṣṇa).
SA_GSP28_jsbh1-2u.edition: Ed. by N.S. Ananta Krishna Sastri, Bombay 1921-1922 (Reprint: Delhi 1987) (Sri Garib Dass Oriental Series, 50-).
SA_GSP28_jsbh1-2u.coverage: partial — Adhyāya 1, Pāda 2 in its entirety.

SA_GSP28_jsbh1-3u.title: Bhāṭṭadīpikā with Prabhāvalī (adhyāya 1, pāda 3)
SA_GSP28_jsbh1-3u.author: Khaṇḍadeva, Śambhubhaṭṭa
SA_GSP28_jsbh1-3u.summary: This e-text contains the third pāda (Smṛtipāda) of the first adhyāya of Khaṇḍadeva's Bhāṭṭadīpikā alongside the extensive sub-commentary Prabhāvalī by his pupil Śambhubhaṭṭa. It investigates the epistemological authority (prāmāṇya) of non-śruti normative sources, including smṛti texts, customary practice (ācāra), linguistic conventions (śabdaprayoga), and Vedic auxiliary texts, establishing that their authority derives indirectly from inferred Vedic injunctions (śrutikalpanā). The pāda encompasses nine adhikaraṇas and concludes with the famous Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa, which argues that words denote universal class character (jāti) rather than particular individuals (vyakti).
SA_GSP28_jsbh1-3u.attribution: The sub-commentary Prabhāvalī was composed by Khaṇḍadeva's disciple Śambhubhaṭṭa.
SA_GSP28_jsbh1-3u.edition: Based on the ed. by N.S. Ananta Krishna Sastri, Bombay 1921-1922 (Reprint: Delhi 1987) (Sri Garib Dass Oriental Series, 50-).
SA_GSP28_jsbh1-3u.coverage: partial — Contains the entirety of Adhyāya 1, Pāda 3 (Smṛtipāda, nine adhikaraṇas: sūtras 1.3.1–35, ending with the Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa) out of the twelve adhyāyas of the complete work.

SA_GSP28_jsbh1-4u.title: Bhāṭṭadīpikā with Prabhāvalī (Adhyāya 1, Pāda 4)
SA_GSP28_jsbh1-4u.author: Khaṇḍadeva, Śambhubhaṭṭa
SA_GSP28_jsbh1-4u.summary: This text comprises the fourth pāda of the first adhyāya of Khaṇḍadeva's Bhāṭṭadīpikā along with the Prabhāvalī subcommentary of his pupil Śambhubhaṭṭa. This section examines Vedic ritual designators—such as udbhid, citrā, agnihotra, śyena, and vājapeya—determining whether they function as proper names of rituals (nāmadheya) or as injunctions of subordinate ritual materials and accessories (guṇavidhi).
SA_GSP28_jsbh1-4u.attribution: The Bhāṭṭadīpikā was composed by Khaṇḍadeva. The Prabhāvalī subcommentary was composed by his pupil Śambhubhaṭṭa.
SA_GSP28_jsbh1-4u.edition: Based on the ed. by N.S. Ananta Krishna Sastri, Bombay 1921-1922 (Reprint: Delhi 1987) (Sri Garib Dass Oriental Series, 50-).

SA_GSP28_jsbh2-1u.title: Bhāṭṭadīpikā with Prabhāvalī (adhyāya 2, pāda 1)
SA_GSP28_jsbh2-1u.author: Khaṇḍadeva, Śambhubhaṭṭa
SA_GSP28_jsbh2-1u.summary: This section comprises the complete first pāda of Adhyāya 2 of Khaṇḍadeva's Bhāṭṭadīpikā alongside the Prabhāvalī sub-commentary by Śambhubhaṭṭa. In this pāda (covering 18 adhikaraṇas on Mīmāṃsāsūtra 2.1), Khaṇḍadeva analyzes the distinction (bheda) of ritual actions, establishing verbs (dhātvartha) as designating productive activity (bhāvanā) and distinguishing primary rites from auxiliary operations. The text also treats the criteria for sentence unity (ekavākyatā), syntactical split (vākyabheda), sentence continuation (anuṣaṅga), ellipsis (adhyāhāra), and the definitions of the liturgical classes of mantras, yajuṣ, sāman, and nigada.
SA_GSP28_jsbh2-1u.attribution: Khaṇḍadeva composed the Bhāṭṭadīpikā as an commentary on Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra, accompanied by Śambhubhaṭṭa's Prabhāvalī sub-commentary.
SA_GSP28_jsbh2-1u.coverage: partial — Text of Adhyāya 2, Pāda 1 (adhikaraṇas 1–18, concluding with Adhyāhārādhikaraṇa) of Khaṇḍadeva's Bhāṭṭadīpikā with Śambhubhaṭṭa's Prabhāvalī.

SA_GSP28_jsbh2-2u.title: Bhāṭṭadīpikā with Prabhāvalī (adhyāya 2, pāda 2)
SA_GSP28_jsbh2-2u.author: Khaṇḍadeva, Śambhubhaṭṭa
SA_GSP28_jsbh2-2u.summary: The Bhāṭṭadīpikā is Khaṇḍadeva's treatise on Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra. This section comprises the complete second pāda of Adhyāya 2 (adhikaraṇas 1–13), analyzing the primary criteria for distinguishing ritual actions (karmabheda), starting with difference in verbal root (śabdāntara) and continuing through repetition (abhyāsa) and number (saṃkhyā). Khaṇḍadeva's text is paired throughout with the Prabhāvalī commentary composed by his disciple Śambhubhaṭṭa.
SA_GSP28_jsbh2-2u.attribution: The Bhāṭṭadīpikā is composed by Khaṇḍadeva. The Prabhāvalī is a sub-commentary by his pupil Śambhubhaṭṭa.
SA_GSP28_jsbh2-2u.edition: N.S. Ananta Krishna Sastri, Bombay 1921-1922 (Reprint: Delhi 1987) (Sri Garib Dass Oriental Series, 50-).

SA_GSP28_jsbh2-3u.title: Bhāṭṭadīpikā with Prabhāvalī (adhyāya 2, pāda 3)
SA_GSP28_jsbh2-3u.author: Khaṇḍadeva, Śambhubhaṭṭa
SA_GSP28_jsbh2-3u.summary: This text comprises Adhyāya 2, Pāda 3 of Khaṇḍadeva's Bhāṭṭadīpikā together with Śambhubhaṭṭa's Prabhāvalī, expositing the Bhāṭṭa-Mīmāṃsā principles of karmabheda (differentiation of ritual acts). Across 14 adhikaraṇas commenting on Mīmāṃsāsūtra 2.3.1–30, it determines whether divergent Vedic formulations, subsidiary attributes (guṇa), or specific ritual contexts establish distinct rites (karmāntara) or merely modify already established sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and Agnicayana. The work exemplifies Khaṇḍadeva's Navya-Mīmāṃsā method, integrating technical Navya-Nyāya dialectic into classical sacrificial hermeneutics.
SA_GSP28_jsbh2-3u.attribution: The Bhāṭṭadīpikā is by Khaṇḍadeva, commenting on Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra, with the Prabhāvalī subcommentary by Śambhubhaṭṭa.
SA_GSP28_jsbh2-3u.edition: N.S. Ananta Krishna Sastri, Bombay 1921-1922 (Reprint: Delhi 1987) (Sri Garib Dass Oriental Series, 50-).
SA_GSP28_jsbh2-3u.coverage: partial — Contains Adhyāya 2, Pāda 3 in full (sūtras 2.3.1–30 across 14 adhikaraṇas), with both Khaṇḍadeva's Bhāṭṭadīpikā (prefixed '(B1)') and Śambhubhaṭṭa's Prabhāvalī (prefixed '(B2)').

SA_GSP28_jsbh2-4u.title: Bhāṭṭadīpikā with Prabhāvalī (adhyāya 2, pāda 4)
SA_GSP28_jsbh2-4u.author: Khaṇḍadeva, Śambhubhaṭṭa
SA_GSP28_jsbh2-4u.summary: This file comprises the entire fourth pāda of the second adhyāya of Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra alongside Khaṇḍadeva's Bhāṭṭadīpikā and Śambhubhaṭṭa's Prabhāvalī sub-commentary, concluding the book on the principles of ritual differentiation (bhedalakṣaṇa). The text addresses two major topics: the Yāvajjīvādhikaraṇa (establishing that lifelong ritual duties like Agnihotra and Darśapūrṇamāsa are occasional/naimittika rather than discrete, disjoint actions) and the celebrated Śākhāntarādhikaraṇa (demonstrating that Vedic rituals prescribed across multiple Vedic recensions constitute unified, identical sacrifices). Khaṇḍadeva's prose demonstrates the influence of Navya-Nyāya analytical precision on early modern Mīmāṃsā, while Śambhubhaṭṭa provides vital dialectical context and identifies contemporary interlocutors.
SA_GSP28_jsbh2-4u.attribution: The Bhāṭṭadīpikā is composed by Khaṇḍadeva. The Prabhāvalī is by his direct disciple Kavimaṇḍana Śambhubhaṭṭa. The embedded sūtras belong to Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra.
SA_GSP28_jsbh2-4u.edition: N.S. Ananta Krishna Sastri Bombay 1921-1922 (Reprint: Delhi 1987) (Sri Garib Dass Oriental Series, 50-)
SA_GSP28_jsbh2-4u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete fourth pāda of the second adhyāya (Adhyāya 2, Pāda 4) of Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra, Khaṇḍadeva's Bhāṭṭadīpikā, and Śambhubhaṭṭa's Prabhāvalī, encompassing both the Yāvajjīvādhikaraṇa (2.4.1–7) and the Śākhāntarādhikaraṇa (2.4.8–24).

SA_GSP28_jsbh3-1u.title: Bhāṭṭadīpikā with Prabhāvalī (adhyāya 3, pāda 1)
SA_GSP28_jsbh3-1u.author: Khaṇḍadeva, Śambhubhaṭṭa
SA_GSP28_jsbh3-1u.summary: This section comprises the complete first pāda of the third adhyāya of Khaṇḍadeva's Bhāṭṭadīpikā alongside Śambhubhaṭṭa's Prabhāvalī subcommentary, elucidating Mīmāṃsāsūtra 3.1. The text defines and analyzes subsidiariness (śeṣatva or aṅgatva) and the criteria governing ritual subservience across 15 adhikaraṇas.
SA_GSP28_jsbh3-1u.attribution: Khaṇḍadeva composed the Bhāṭṭadīpikā; his direct student Śambhubhaṭṭa composed the commentary Prabhāvalī thereon.

SA_GSP28_jsbh3-2u.title: Bhāṭṭadīpikā with Prabhāvalī (adhyāya 3, pāda 2)
SA_GSP28_jsbh3-2u.author: Khaṇḍadeva, Śambhubhaṭṭa
SA_GSP28_jsbh3-2u.summary: This portion of Khaṇḍadeva's Bhāṭṭadīpikā, together with Śambhubhaṭṭa's Prabhāvalī, covers the entirety of Adhyāya 3, Pāda 2 of Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra. It focuses on the second of the six Mīmāṃsā criteria for ritual subsidiariness (śeṣatva): liṅga (inherent expressive capacity or semantic force, covering vastusāmarthya and mantrasāmarthya). Across 20 adhikaraṇas, the text details the application (viniyoga) of mantras in Vedic performance, establishing that they must be applied according to their primary sense (mukhyārtha) rather than metaphorical or secondary meanings (gauṇārtha, lakṣaṇā), and addressing cases of textual modification (ūha) in derivative rites (vikṛti).
SA_GSP28_jsbh3-2u.attribution: The Bhāṭṭadīpikā is the work of Khaṇḍadeva. The subcommentary Prabhāvalī was composed by his disciple Śambhubhaṭṭa.
SA_GSP28_jsbh3-2u.edition: Based on the ed. by N.S. Ananta Krishna Sastri Bombay 1921-1922 (Reprint: Delhi 1987) (Sri Garib Dass Oriental Series, 50-).

SA_GSP28_jsbh3-3u.title: Bhāṭṭadīpikā with Prabhāvalī (adhyāya 3, pāda 3)
SA_GSP28_jsbh3-3u.author: Khaṇḍadeva, Śambhubhaṭṭa
SA_GSP28_jsbh3-3u.summary: This section of the Bhāṭṭadīpikā, along with Śambhubhaṭṭa's Prabhāvalī, covers the third pāda of Adhyāya 3 of the Mīmāṃsāsūtra, treating the relative hierarchy and conflicts among the six means of subsidiary application (viniyogapramāṇa): direct Vedic statement (śruti), indicative power (liṅga), syntactic unity (vākya), ritual context (prakaraṇa), serial position (sthāna), and ritual denomination (samākhyā). Khaṇḍadeva analyzes these exegetical principles using the refined conceptual toolkit of Navya-Nyāya, while Śambhubhaṭṭa's Prabhāvalī identifies implicit opponents and clarifies dense elliptical arguments.
SA_GSP28_jsbh3-3u.attribution: Śambhubhaṭṭa was a pupil of Khaṇḍadeva.
SA_GSP28_jsbh3-3u.edition: Based on the ed. by N.S. Ananta Krishna Sastri, Bombay 1921-1922 (Reprint: Delhi 1987) (Sri Garib Dass Oriental Series, 50-).

SA_GSP28_ktv_2-1u.title: Tantravārttika (2.1.1–4: Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa)
SA_GSP28_ktv_2-1u.author: Kumārilabhaṭṭa
SA_GSP28_ktv_2-1u.summary: This e-text contains Kumārilabhaṭṭa's Tantravārttika on Mīmāṃsāsūtra 2.1.1–4 (the Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa), expounding the opening section of Book 2 of Śabara's Śābarabhāṣya. In this foundational section, Kumārila articulates the core Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā doctrines of verbal efficiency (bhāvanā) and ritual action (karman), arguing against alternative grammatical and philosophical theories that verb roots and verbal terminations denote an efficient operation rather than a static substance. This analysis grounds the Mīmāṃsā doctrine that Vedic ritual injunctions directly motivate human agency and generate unseen transcendental potency (apūrva).
SA_GSP28_ktv_2-1u.attribution: Kumārila is acknowledged as the author of the Tantravārttika, a commentary on the Śābarabhāṣya.

ISBN 4-7963-0151-8.

SA_GSP28_mimslovu.title: Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika with Kāśikā (part 3)
SA_GSP28_mimslovu.author: Kumārila Bhaṭṭa, Sucaritamiśra
SA_GSP28_mimslovu.summary: This text comprises Part 3 of Kumārila Bhaṭṭa's verse work Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika accompanied by Sucaritamiśra's commentary Kāśikā. This portion expounds the Autpattikasūtra section, addressing key pramāṇa doctrines including inference (anumāna), verbal testimony (śabda), comparison (upamāna), presumption (arthāpatti), non-apprehension (abhāva), and the relationship between word and meaning (sambandhākṣepa / citrakṣepa).
SA_GSP28_mimslovu.attribution: Kumārila Bhaṭṭa authored the root verse treatise Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika (or Ślokavārttika). Sucaritamiśra composed the commentary titled Kāśikā.

SA_GSP28_mimsvtku.title: Mīmāṃsāślokavārttikakāśikā (Pratijñāsūtra to Sambandhākṣepa)
SA_GSP28_mimsvtku.author: Sucaritamiśra
SA_GSP28_mimsvtku.summary: The Kāśikā (or Ślokavārttikakāśikā) by Sucaritamiśra is an important classical commentary on Kumārila Bhaṭṭa's Ślokavārttika within the Bhāṭṭa school of Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā. Sucaritamiśra provides verse-by-verse exegesis defending Kumārila's epistemology of intrinsic validity (svataḥprāmāṇya), realism, and Vedic hermeneutics against Buddhist and rival philosophical schools. The present digital text covers only the portions edited across the three Trivandrum Sanskrit Series fascicles (nos. 90, 99, and 150), terminating at the end of the Sambandhākṣepa chapter.
SA_GSP28_mimsvtku.attribution: A running commentary (ṭīkā) by Sucaritamiśra on Kumārila Bhaṭṭa's Ślokavārttika. Kumārila's kārikās are embedded via pratīkas rather than transcribed in full as an independent work.
SA_GSP28_mimsvtku.edition: K. Sāmbaśiva Śāstrī (ed.), The Mimāṃsāślokavārt[t]ika with the Commentary Kāśikā of Sucaritamiśra, Trivandrum 1926, 1929, 1943 (Trivandrum Sanskrit Series, 90, 99, 150).
SA_GSP28_mimsvtku.coverage: partial — Covers only the portion published across the three Trivandrum Sanskrit Series fascicles (nos. 90, 99, 150), beginning at the Pratijñāsūtra and breaking off at the end of the Sambandhākṣepa chapter (v. 46). SA_GSP28_mjnya01u.title: Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara (chapter 1)
SA_GSP28_mjnya01u.author: Mādhava
SA_GSP28_mjnya01u.summary: The Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara is a Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā treatise composed by Mādhava under King Bukka. Modeling itself on Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra, the work provides a metrical exposition (nyāyamālā) and a prose commentary (vistara). This first chapter (Adhyāya 1) examines the foundational epistemology and authority of the Veda, establishing the authority of Smṛti and custom, and hermeneutical distinctions among injunctions (vidhi), explanatory eulogies (arthavāda), mantras, and ritual nomenclature (nāmadheya).
SA_GSP28_mjnya01u.attribution: Both the verse summary (kārikā) and the prose commentary (vistara) were composed by Mādhava, minister and teacher associated with King Bukka (Bukkaṇa).
SA_GSP28_mjnya01u.edition: Pandit Sivadatta, ed., Jaiminiyanyayamala, Poona 1892 (Anandasrama Sanskrit Series, 24).
SA_GSP28_mjnya01u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete first chapter (Adhyāya 1, across four pādas) of the treatise, closing with the colophon 'iti śrī mādhavīye jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistare prathamādhāyāyasya caturthaḥ pādaḥ samāptaśca prathamo 'dhyāyaḥ'.

SA_GSP28_mjnya02u.title: Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara (chapter 2)
SA_GSP28_mjnya02u.author: Mādhava
SA_GSP28_mjnya02u.summary: Adhyāya 2 of Mādhava's Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara, a metrical exposition and prose auto-commentary on Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra. This chapter treats the differentiation of ritual actions (karmabheda), examining injunctions and criteria for distinguishing rites across its four pādas.
SA_GSP28_mjnya02u.attribution: A metrical exposition of Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra with Mādhava's prose commentary.
SA_GSP28_mjnya02u.edition: Pandit Sivadatta, ed., Jaiminiyanyayamala, Poona 1892. (Anandasrama Sanskrit Series, 24) ADHYAYA 2
SA_GSP28_mjnya02u.coverage: partial — Complete text of Adhyāya 2 across all four pādas (2.1–2.4), containing Jaimini's sūtras, Mādhava's kārikās, and Mādhava's prose commentary.

SA_GSP28_mjnya03u.title: Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara (chapter 3)
SA_GSP28_mjnya03u.author: Mādhava
SA_GSP28_mjnya03u.summary: Adhyāya 3 of Mādhava's Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara, a metrical exposition and prose auto-commentary on the topical sections (adhikaraṇas) of Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra. Divided into eight pādas, this adhyāya is dedicated to the examination of subsidiary elements (śeṣatva / aṅgatva) in Vedic sacrificial ritual. It systematically analyzes the definition of a subsidiary act or substance (śeṣalakṣaṇa), the six hermeneutical criteria for determining subordination (direct Vedic assertion, indicative mark, syntactical connection, context, order/position, and appellation: śruti, liṅga, vākya, prakaraṇa, sthāna, and samākhyā), the rules of priority when these pramāṇas conflict, and ritual agency.
SA_GSP28_mjnya03u.attribution: Composed by Mādhava. Mādhava composed the metrical exposition (Jaiminīyanyāyamālā) and his prose commentary (Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara). The text also includes the respective sūtras of Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra.
SA_GSP28_mjnya03u.edition: Pandit Sivadatta: Jaiminiyanyayamala, Poona 1892. (Anandasrama Sanskrit Series, 24) ADHYAYA 3
SA_GSP28_mjnya03u.coverage: partial — Contains Adhyāya 3 only (concluding with tṛtīyādhyāyasyāṣṭamaḥ pādaḥ / samāptaścāyaṃ tṛtīyo 'dhyāyaḥ).

SA_GSP28_mjnya04u.title: Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara (chapter 4)
SA_GSP28_mjnya04u.author: Mādhava
SA_GSP28_mjnya04u.summary: Adhyāya 4 of the Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara provides Mādhava's versified summary and prose exposition for the fourth chapter of Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra. The chapter investigates prayukti (motivation or the teleological teleology of ritual performance), formulating the distinction between kratvartha (subsidiaries intended strictly to serve the structure of the sacrificial rite) and puruṣārtha (elements and rites aimed at fulfilling the desired end of the human agent).
SA_GSP28_mjnya04u.attribution: The e-text presents each adhikaraṇa of chapter 4 by citing the relevant sūtras of Jaimini, followed by Mādhava's metrical summary (kārikās, specifically the Jaiminīyanyāyamālā) and his prose auto-commentary (the Vistara).
SA_GSP28_mjnya04u.edition: Pandit Sivadatta (ed.), Jaiminiyanyayamala, Poona: Anandasrama Sanskrit Series, 24, 1892.
SA_GSP28_mjnya04u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete fourth chapter (adhyāya 4, across all four pādas, 4.1–4.4) of the 12-chapter work, concluding with the adhyāya colophon: 'iti śrīmādhavīye jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistare caturthādhyāyasya caturthapādaḥ caturtho 'dhyāyaśca samāptaḥ //'.

SA_GSP28_msbh1-7u.title: Mīmāṃsāsūtra with Śābarabhāṣya (chapters 1–7)
SA_GSP28_msbh1-7u.author: Jaimini, Śabarasvāmin
SA_GSP28_msbh1-7u.summary: The foundational aphorisms of the Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā school attributed to Jaimini, accompanied by its earliest surviving commentary, the Śābarabhāṣya of Śabarasvāmin. Together they establish the epistemological foundations of Vedic exegesis, arguing for the intrinsic validity of cognition (svataḥprāmāṇya), the eternal authorlessness of the Veda (apauruṣeyatva), the inherent relation between word and referent, and the concept of unseen ritual efficacy (apūrva). This partial e-text encompasses adhyāyas 1 through 7, treating the sources of dharma, ritual classifications, subsidiary relations (śeṣatva), and the opening rules governing the transfer of ritual details (atideśa).
