SA_GSP28_prakp01u.title: Prakaraṇapañcikā (chapter 1: Śāstramukha)
SA_GSP28_prakp01u.author: Śālikanāthamiśra
SA_GSP28_prakp01u.summary: The Prakaraṇapañcikā of Śālikanāthamiśra is a treatise of the Prābhākara school of Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā. In this first chapter, the Śāstramukha, the author establishes the necessity of commencing the inquiry into dharma and ritual exegesis (mīmāṃsārambha). Śālikanātha refutes the Bhāṭṭa pūrvapakṣa that Vedic study (svādhyāyādhyayana) yields its own fruit without requiring hermeneutical inquiry, establishing that the study injunction essentially aims at comprehension of Vedic meaning (arthāvabodha), which in turn mandates the exegetical rules codified in Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra.
SA_GSP28_prakp01u.coverage: partial — Contains the first chapter (Śāstramukha) of the Prakaraṇapañcikā.

SA_GSP28_prakp02u.title: Prakaraṇapañcikā (chapter 2: Nītipatha)
SA_GSP28_prakp02u.author: Śālikanāthamiśra
SA_GSP28_prakp02u.summary: The Nītipatha is the second chapter of Śālikanāthamiśra's foundational Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā manual, the Prakaraṇapañcikā. In fifty verses, Śālikanātha argues for the intrinsic capacity of verbal communication—specifically Vedic revelation—to yield true knowledge of external facts (arthasaṃsparśitā). While ordinary mundane speech requires inference about a fallible human speaker's reliability, authorless (apauruṣeya) Vedic statements provide immediate, non-inferential, and defect-free epistemic certainty.
SA_GSP28_prakp02u.attribution: Authored by Śālikanāthamiśra, exponent of the Prābhākara school of Mīmāṃsā. Although the source text mentions the Nyāyasiddhi commentary of Jayapurī Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭa, the digital file transcribes only Śālikanātha's kārikās.
SA_GSP28_prakp02u.edition: Prakaraṇa Pañcikā of Śālikanātha miśra, edited with Introduction and Notes by Mīmāṃsā Ratnam Pt. A. Subrahmanya Sastri, Banaras Hindu University Darśana Series, 1961.
SA_GSP28_prakp02u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete text of chapter 2 (prakaraṇa 2, Nītipatha, 50 verses plus topical headings) of the Prakaraṇapañcikā. The commentary text found in the printed edition is omitted.

SA_GSP28_prakp03u.title: Prakaraṇapañcikā (chapter 3: Nayavīthī)
SA_GSP28_prakp03u.author: Śālikanāthamiśra
SA_GSP28_prakp03u.summary: Nayavīthī ('The Path of Reasoning') is the third prakaraṇa of Śālikanāthamiśra's Prakaraṇapañcikā, a foundational 9th-century treatise of the Prābhākara school of Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā. Composed entirely in 77 kārikās, this chapter articulates and defends the distinctive Prābhākara thesis that all cognitions are intrinsically veridical (sarvavijñānayathārthatva). Śālikanātha expounds the Prābhākara non-apprehension theory of error (akhyāti), arguing that experiential illusions (such as mistaking mother-of-pearl for silver) do not constitute a single mistaken cognition (anyathākhyāti), but rather two distinct mental episodes—an incomplete perceptual apprehension and a memory stripped of its temporal reference (smṛtipramoṣa)—whose difference goes unnoticed due to non-discrimination (vivekāgraha).
SA_GSP28_prakp03u.attribution: Nayavīthī is the third chapter (prakaraṇa) of Śālikanāthamiśra's Prakaraṇapañcikā. Although the opening line copied from the 1961 print edition mentions Jayapuri Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭa's commentary Nyāyasiddhi, that commentary is completely omitted from the digital file.
SA_GSP28_prakp03u.edition: Prakaraṇa Pañcikā of Śrī Śālikanātha Miśra with Nyāya-siddhi, edited by A. Subrahmanya Sastri, Varanasi: Banaras Hindu University, 1961 (Banaras Hindu University Darśana Series).
SA_GSP28_prakp03u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete text of chapter 3 (Nayavīthī), consisting of 77 kārikās plus section headings, out of the 14 chapters comprising the Prakaraṇapañcikā. No commentary is included.
translations: Pandurangi, K. T. Prakaraṇapañjika of Šalikanātha with an Exposition in English. New Delhi: Indian Council of Philosophical Research, 2004. (English)

SA_GSP28_prakp04u.title: Prakaraṇapañcikā (chapter 4: Jātinirṇaya)
SA_GSP28_prakp04u.author: Śālikanāthamiśra
SA_GSP28_prakp04u.summary: Prakaraṇa 4 of Śālikanāthamiśra's Prakaraṇapañcikā, titled Jātinirṇaya ('Determination of Universals'), presents the Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā defense of realist ontology regarding universals (jāti / sāmānya). Śālikanātha systematically refutes Buddhist nominalism and the apoha doctrine, as well as the Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā and bhedābheda positions, establishing that a universal is real, ontologically distinct from its individual substrate (āśrayato bhinnā), and directly apprehended through recurrent perceptual cognition (anuvṛttākārāvabhāsinī buddhi).
SA_GSP28_prakp04u.attribution: Composed by Śālikanāthamiśra, associated with the Prābhākara branch of Mīmāṃsā. While GRETIL and the previous catalog entry listed Jayapurī Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa (author of the commentary Nyāyasiddhi), Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa's commentary text is absent from this digital file.

SA_GSP28_prakp05u.title: Prakaraṇapañcikā (chapter 5: Amṛtakalā)
SA_GSP28_prakp05u.author: Śālikanāthamiśra
SA_GSP28_prakp05u.summary: Amṛtakalā ('The Digit of Nectar') is the fifth chapter of Śālikanāthamiśra's Prakaraṇapañcikā, composed in 76 kārikās. It offers a concise metrical compendium of Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā epistemology, defining valid knowledge (pramāṇa) as apprehension distinct from memory (anubhūti) and defining the five pramāṇas admitted in the Prābhākara system: perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna), scripture/verbal testimony (śāstra), comparison (upamāna), and presumption/postulation (arthāpatti). The chapter concludes with a systematic refutation of non-apprehension (anupalabdhi/abhāva) as an independent sixth pramāṇa, defending the Prābhākara doctrine that absence is identical with the bare locus.
SA_GSP28_prakp05u.coverage: partial — Contains Chapter 5 (Amṛtakalā) complete in 76 kārikās with introductory topical headings, but without commentary; this is one chapter of the Prakaraṇapañcikā.

SA_GSP28_prakp06u.title: Prakaraṇapañcikā (prakaraṇa 6: Pramāṇapārāyaṇa, section 1: Pratyakṣapariccheda)
SA_GSP28_prakp06u.author: Śālikanāthamiśra
SA_GSP28_prakp06u.summary: The Pramāṇapārāyaṇa constitutes the epistemological core of Śālikanātha Miśra's Prakaraṇapañcikā, a primary textbook of the Prābhākara school of Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā. In this first section (Pratyakṣapariccheda), Śālikanātha establishes the definition of valid cognition (pramāṇa), rejecting Buddhist definitions of uncontradicted cognition (avisaṃvādijñāna), and details the Prābhākara theory of perception (pratyakṣa). The discussion famously expounds the hallmark Prābhākara theories of tripuṭīsaṃvit (the simultaneous revelation of knower, object, and knowledge in cognition) and akhyātivāda (error as non-apprehension).
SA_GSP28_prakp06u.attribution: Authored by Śālikanāthamiśra. Although the introductory lines transcribe the printed edition's title mentioning Jayapurī Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭa's commentary Nyāyasiddhi, the commentary text was omitted during transcription.
SA_GSP28_prakp06u.edition: Prakaraṇa Pañcikā of Śrī Śālikanātha Miśra with Nyāya-siddhi, edited with introduction and notes by A. Subrahmanya Sastri, Banaras Hindu University Darśana Series No. 4, Varanasi: Banaras Hindu University Press, 1961, pp. 107–281.
SA_GSP28_prakp06u.coverage: partial — Contains only section 1 (Pratyakṣapariccheda) of prakaraṇa 6 (Pramāṇapārāyaṇa), corresponding to pp. 107–281 of A. Subrahmanya Sastri's 1961 edition. The commentary Nyāyasiddhi printed alongside it was not entered.

SA_GSP28_prakp07u.title: Prakaraṇapañcikā (chapter 7: Vimalāñjana)
SA_GSP28_prakp07u.author: Śālikanāthamiśra
SA_GSP28_prakp07u.summary: The Vimalāñjana is the seventh chapter of Śālikanāthamiśra's Prakaraṇapañcikā. In this chapter, Śālikanātha defends the intrinsic, unoriginated relation (apauruṣeyatva) between word and meaning, which underpins the authoritative epistemic status of the Veda. He undertakes a critique of the view that language and creation originate with a supreme personal deity (Īśvara), demonstrating instead that language acquisition and semantic competence are rooted in a beginningless continuum of elder linguistic usage (anādi-vṛddhavyavahāra).
SA_GSP28_prakp07u.attribution: Authored by Śālikanāthamiśra. While the printed edition title block and GRETIL header mention the commentary Nyāyasiddhi by Jayapuri Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭa, the e-text transcribes solely Śālikanātha's root treatise.
SA_GSP28_prakp07u.edition: Prakaraṇa Pañcikā of Śrī Śālikanātha Miśra with Nyāya-siddhi, edited by A. Subrahmanya Sastri, Banaras Hindu University, 1961 (Banaras Hindu University Darśana Series, 4).
SA_GSP28_prakp07u.coverage: partial — Contains chapter 7 (Vimalāñjana) in full (opening kārikās 1–2, discursive prose, and final saṅgraha verse), which is one of the chapters forming the Prakaraṇapañcikā.

SA_GSP28_prakp08u.title: Prakaraṇapañcikā (chapter 8: Tattvāloka)
SA_GSP28_prakp08u.author: Śālikanāthamiśra
SA_GSP28_prakp08u.summary: Prakaraṇa 8 (Tattvāloka) of Śālikanāthamiśra's Prakaraṇapañcikā is a dedicated treatise on the nature of the self (ātman) according to the Prābhākara school of Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā. Śālikanātha establishes that the self is an omnipresent (vibhu), eternal (dhruva), and distinct individual substance that differs from the physical body, the senses, and stream of consciousness, refuting Cārvāka, Buddhist Vijñānavāda, and Advaita Vedānta monism. Central to the chapter is the Prābhākara epistemology of triple manifestation (tripuṭīsaṃvit), under which the self is never known as an object (viṣaya) but is immediately revealed as the knowing subject (grāhaka) in every valid cognition.
SA_GSP28_prakp08u.attribution: The text contains both metrical kārikās and prose exposition by Śālikanātha. The subcommentary Nyāyasiddhi of Jaipuri Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭa mentioned in the source edition's title is not included in the e-text.

SA_GSP28_prakp09u.title: Prakaraṇapañcikā (chapter 9: Nyāyaśuddhi)
SA_GSP28_prakp09u.author: Śālikanāthamiśra
SA_GSP28_prakp09u.summary: Chapter 9 (Nyāyaśuddhi) of Śālikanāthamiśra's Prakaraṇapañcikā provides the Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā defense of the eternal nature of sound and linguistic units (śabdanityatva). Refuting rival arguments from the Nyāya and Buddhist traditions that view sound as impermanent and caused, Śālikanātha argues that recognitive awareness (pratyabhijñā) proves phonemic permanence and identity across utterances, showing that human vocal effort merely manifests (abhivyañjaka) rather than creates pre-existing eternal phonemes. This defence is essential to the Mīmāṃsā establishment of authorless (apauruṣeya) Vedic authority.
SA_GSP28_prakp09u.attribution: Authored by Śālikanāthamiśra, principal authority of the Prābhākara school of Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā. Although the 1961 edition title page mentions Jayapurī Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa's commentary Nyāyasiddhi, only Śālikanātha's text and prose are transcribed.
SA_GSP28_prakp09u.edition: Prakaraṇa Pañcikā of Śālikanātha Miśra with the Nyāya-siddhi, edited with introduction and notes by A. Subrahmanya Sastri, Varanasi: Banaras Hindu University, 1961 (Banaras Hindu University Darśana Series, 4).
SA_GSP28_prakp09u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete text of chapter 9 (Nyāyaśuddhi) of the Prakaraṇapañcikā, consisting of 14 verses with Śālikanāthamiśra's connecting prose vṛtti.

SA_GSP28_prakp10u.title: Prakaraṇapañcikā (chapter 10: Mīmāṃsājīvarakṣā)
SA_GSP28_prakp10u.author: Śālikanāthamiśra
SA_GSP28_prakp10u.summary: The Mīmāṃsājīvarakṣā ('Preservation of the Vital Core of Mīmāṃsā') constitutes the tenth chapter of Śālikanāthamiśra's Prakaraṇapañcikā. In this section, Śālikanātha refutes the Buddhist doctrine of universal momentariness (kṣaṇikatvavāda/kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda) by critiquing both sequential and simultaneous causal efficiency (krama-yaugapadya) as the criterion of existence. Defending the permanence of substances and the veridicality of recognition (pratyabhijñā), he argues that refuting momentariness is indispensable for safeguarding the foundational Mīmāṃsā doctrines of ritual obligation, enduring agency, and the persistence of the self.
SA_GSP28_prakp10u.edition: Prakaraṇa Pañcikā of Śrī Śālikanātha Miśra with the Nyāya-siddhi, edited by A. Subrahmanya Sastri, Banaras: Banaras Hindu University, 1961 (Banaras Hindu University Darśana Series).
SA_GSP28_prakp10u.coverage: partial — Contains the 10th prakaraṇa (Mīmāṃsājīvarakṣā) of the Prakaraṇapañcikā. Although the GRETIL header mentions Jayapurī Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭa's commentary Nyāyasiddhi, only Śālikanātha's mūla text is keyed into this e-text.

SA_GSP28_prakp11u.title: Prakaraṇapañcikā (chapter 11: Vākyārthamātṛkā)
SA_GSP28_prakp11u.author: Śālikanāthamiśra
SA_GSP28_prakp11u.summary: The Vākyārthamātṛkā constitutes the eleventh chapter of Śālikanāthamiśra's Prakaraṇapañcikā, a treatise of the Prābhākara school of Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā. Comprising kārikās along with Śālikanātha's autocommentary (Vākyārthamātṛkāvṛtti), the chapter is divided into two sections (paricchedas). The first section (Upodghāta) formulates and defends the Prābhākara semantic theory of anvitābhidhānavāda (the direct verbal denotation of interrelated sentence meaning) against opposing doctrines, while the second section demonstrates how linguistic comprehension functions in scriptural injunctions, demonstrating that ritual obligation (kārya / niyoga / apūrva) is the primary meaning denoted by injunctive verb morphology.
SA_GSP28_prakp11u.attribution: Prakaraṇa 11 of the Prakaraṇapañcikā contains verses (kārikās) accompanied by Śālikanāthamiśra's own prose autocommentary (vṛtti), as confirmed by the author's concluding stanzas ('vākyārthamātṛkeyaṃ... śālikanāthena saṅgrathitā', 'vākyārthamātṛkāyā vṛttiriyaṃ śālikenaiva') and section colophons. Although the GRETIL header mentions Jayapuri Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭa's commentary Nyāyasiddhi, that sub-commentary was not transcribed into the electronic file.
SA_GSP28_prakp11u.edition: Prakaraṇapañcikā of Śrī Śālikanātha Miśra with the Nyāya-siddhi of Jaipuri Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa and Viṣamasthalaṭippaṇī, edited by A. Subrahmanya Sastri, Banaras Hindu University Darśana Series no. 4, Varanasi: Banaras Hindu University, 1961.
SA_GSP28_prakp11u.coverage: partial — Contains chapter 11 (prakaraṇa 11: Vākyārthamātṛkā, consisting of Paricchedas 1 and 2 with autocommentary) of Śālikanāthamiśra's Prakaraṇapañcikā.

SA_GSP28_prakp12u.title: Prakaraṇapañcikā (chapter 12: Viṣayakaraṇīya)
SA_GSP28_prakp12u.author: Śālikanāthamiśra
SA_GSP28_prakp12u.summary: Chapter 12 ('Viṣayakaraṇīya') of Śālikanāthamiśra's Prakaraṇapañcikā investigates the semantic and operational relationship between the verbal root action (dhātvartha) and the Vedic imperative obligation (niyoga/kārya) in the Prābhākara school of Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā. Śālikanātha explains how the sacrificial performance serves first as the cognitive object/scope (viṣaya) that delimits the transcendental injunction (apūrva) and then as the instrumental means (karaṇa) through which human effort (kṛti/prayatna) brings it into being. The chapter constitutes a concise yet pivotal exposition of Prābhākara hermeneutics concerning Vedic verbal efficacy and ritual duty.
SA_GSP28_prakp12u.attribution: Śālikanāthamiśra explicitly names himself as author in the concluding verse (v. 2: 'śālikanāthena kṛtaṃ kṛtināmupakārasiddhaye...') and in the chapter colophon.
SA_GSP28_prakp12u.coverage: partial — Contains chapter 12 (Viṣayakaraṇīya) of the Prakaraṇapañcikā complete (verses 1–2 with the author's intervening prose exposition).

SA_GSP28_prakp13u.title: Prakaraṇapañcikā (chapter 13: Aṅgapārāyaṇa)
SA_GSP28_prakp13u.author: Śālikanāthamiśra
SA_GSP28_prakp13u.summary: Prakaraṇa 13 of Śālikanāthamiśra's Prakaraṇapañcikā, titled Aṅgapārāyaṇa ('Investigation of Auxiliary Elements'), presents the Prābhākara school's comprehensive doctrine on the nature, function, and taxonomy of ritual accessories (aṅga). The chapter is divided into two paricchedas: the first investigates proximate or directly operating accessories (sannipattyopakāraka, such as thrashing or sprinkling), while the second examines unmediated or distantly operating auxiliaries (ārādupakāraka, such as the prayāja offerings). Śālikanātha refutes rival Bhāṭṭa views on accessory injunctions (aṅgavidhi) and establishes how both classes of subsidiaries contribute to the principal unseen efficacy (apūrva/niyoga).
SA_GSP28_prakp13u.attribution: Authored by Śālikanāthamiśra, an authority of the Prābhākara branch of Mīmāṃsā.
SA_GSP28_prakp13u.coverage: partial — Contains chapter 13, titled Aṅgapārāyaṇa, which is divided into two sections: Pariccheda 1 (Sannipattyopakārakāṅganirūpaṇa) and Pariccheda 2 (Ārādupakārakāṅganirūpaṇa).

SA_GSP28_prakp14u.title: Prakaraṇapañcikā (chapter 14: Atideśapārāyaṇa)
SA_GSP28_prakp14u.author: Śālikanāthamiśra
SA_GSP28_prakp14u.summary: The Atideśapārāyaṇa is the fourteenth and final chapter (prakaraṇa) of Śālikanāthamiśra's Prakaraṇapañcikā. Comprising 68 metrical verses (kārikās), this chapter analyzes the hermeneutical mechanism of atideśa (the extension or transfer of ritual accessories and modalities from a model archetype, prakṛti, to an adapted modification, vikṛti). Śālikanātha articulates how the injunctive command (vidhi) incorporates transferred accessories, defending the Prābhākara interpretation against potential contradictions concerning ritual annulment and modification (bādha).
SA_GSP28_prakp14u.attribution: Authored by Śālikanāthamiśra. Although the printed book title and GRETIL header reference the sub-commentary Nyāyasiddhi by Jayapurī Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭa, this e-text file contains only the root kārikā verses.
SA_GSP28_prakp14u.edition: Prakaraṇa Pañcikā of Sri Śālikanātha Miśra with Nyāya-siddhi, edited by A. Subrahmanya Sastri. Banaras: Banaras Hindu University, 1961 (BHUDS 4).
SA_GSP28_prakp14u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete text of the 14th and final chapter (Atideśapārāyaṇa, vv. 1–68) of the Prakaraṇapañcikā, along with section topical titles. The other 13 chapters of the treatise are omitted, and contrary to the GRETIL header, Jayapurī Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭa's commentary Nyāyasiddhi is not included.

SA_GSP28_sabbha1u.title: Mīmāṃsāsūtra with Mīmāṃsāsūtrabhāṣya (adhyāya 1, pāda 1, sūtras 1–5)
SA_GSP28_sabbha1u.author: Jaimini, Śabarasvāmin
SA_GSP28_sabbha1u.summary: This text comprises the opening epistemological section (Tarkapāda, sūtras 1.1.1–5) of Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra with the commentary of Śabarasvāmin (Śābarabhāṣya). It lays out the foundational epistemology of the Pūrva Mīmāṃsā school: the investigation of dharma (dharmajijñāsā), Vedic injunction (codanā) as the sole epistemic means for suprasensory dharma, the definition of perception (pratyakṣa), and the innate, beginningless relationship between linguistic expressions and their meanings (autpattikaḥ śabdārthasaṃbandhaḥ). Under sūtra 1.1.5, it includes discussion defending the permanent self (ātman) against Buddhist epistemological and idealist critiques.
SA_GSP28_sabbha1u.attribution: The root sūtras are attributed to Jaimini. The commentary is by Śabarasvāmin (Śabara).
SA_GSP28_sabbha1u.edition: Erich Frauwallner, Materialien zur ältesten Erkenntnislehre der Karmamīmāṃsā, Wien 1968, pp. 10–61 (Sitzungsberichte / Österreichische Akademie der Wissenschaften, Philosophisch-Historische Klasse; 259,2. Veröffentlichungen der Kommission für Sprachen und Kulturen Süd- und Ostasiens; 6).
SA_GSP28_sabbha1u.coverage: partial — Contains adhyāya 1, pāda 1, sūtras 1–5, ending with 'tasmād avirodhaḥ'.

SA_GSP28_sastrdiu.title: Śāstradīpikā (Tarkapāda, on Mīmāṃsāsūtra 1.1.1–23)
SA_GSP28_sastrdiu.author: Pārthasārathi Miśra
SA_GSP28_sastrdiu.summary: The Śāstradīpikā of Pārthasārathi Miśra (fl. c. late 11th century CE) is a major classical commentary on Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra adhering strictly to the Bhāṭṭa school of Kumārila Bhaṭṭa. Its introductory section, the Tarkapāda (Adhyāya 1, Pāda 1), constitutes one of the foundational works of Mīmāṃsā epistemology and metaphysics, defending the intrinsic validity of knowledge (svataḥprāmāṇya), perception, realism concerning universals, and the eternal, uncreated nature of sound and the Vedas against Buddhist, Nyāya, and Advaita opponents. This file contains the Sanskrit text of the Tarkapāda from sūtras 1.1.1 to 1.1.23, ending at the conclusion of the section on the eternality of language (śabdanityatā).
SA_GSP28_sastrdiu.attribution: Pārthasārathi Miśra's authorship is confirmed by the opening maṅgala verse ('kumārilamatenāhaṃ kariṣye śāstradīpikām') and universal tradition in the Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā school.
SA_GSP28_sastrdiu.coverage: partial — Contains only the Tarkapāda (Adhyāya 1, Pāda 1), sūtras 1.1.1 through 1.1.23, concluding with the defense of the eternality of language (śabdanityatā; 'tataścāsyāṃ diśi śabda iti viśiṣṭagrahaṇaṃ tāvatsiddham'). Sūtras 24–32 of the Tarkapāda and Adhyāyas 1.2–12 are omitted.

SA_GSP28_shabara.title: Mīmāṃsāsūtra with Śābarabhāṣya (adhyāyas 1–7)
SA_GSP28_shabara.author: Jaimini, Śabara
SA_GSP28_shabara.summary: The Mīmāṃsāsūtra of Jaimini is the foundational work of the Pūrva Mīmāṃsā school of Vedic hermeneutics, establishing guidelines for sacrificial ritual exegesis and inquiry into dharma. Śabarasvāmin's Śābarabhāṣya is the earliest extant comprehensive commentary on the sūtras, formulating foundational doctrines on epistemology, the uncreated and authorless nature of the Veda (apauruṣeyatva), injunctive syntax, and sentence meaning. The bhāṣya on the initial section (MS 1.1.5) notably preserves a substantial excerpt from an earlier commentary (the Vṛttikāragrantha). This e-text contains Adhyāyas 1 through 7.
SA_GSP28_shabara.attribution: The Mīmāṃsāsūtra is attributed to Jaimini, and the bhāṣya is by Śabara, incorporating an earlier Vṛttikāra layer (MS 1.1.1-5).
SA_GSP28_shabara.edition: Base ed.: Maheśacandra Nyāyaratna (ed.), Mīmāṃsāsūtra [with Śabarabhāṣya], Bibliotheca Indica 45, Calcutta: Asiatic Society, 1863-1889; collated with Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series 79, Poona, 1976-1984.
SA_GSP28_shabara.coverage: partial — Contains Adhyāyas 1–7 only (from MS 1.1.1 through MS 7.4.20 with bhāṣya), ending with 'evam āgatasyaitad darśanam iti', out of the complete 12 adhyāyas of the Mīmāṃsāsūtra.

SA_GSP29_antark.summary: The Tarkasaṃgraha of Annambhaṭṭa is an introductory primer of the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika school.
SA_GSP29_antark.attribution: Attributed to Annambhaṭṭa, author of the Tarkasaṃgrahadīpikā.

SA_GSP29_antsdi_u.title: Tarkasaṃgraha with Tarkasaṃgrahadīpikā, Dīpikāprakāśikā, and Bālapriyā (incomplete)
SA_GSP29_antsdi_u.author: Annambhaṭṭa, Nīlakaṇṭha, N.S. Rāmānuja Tātācārya
SA_GSP29_antsdi_u.summary: The Tarkasaṃgraha of Annambhaṭṭa is the introductory primer of the syncretic Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika system, outlining the seven ontological categories (padārtha) and four means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa). This composite e-text contains the root text embedded with Annambhaṭṭa's auto-commentary (Tarkasaṃgrahadīpikā), Nīlakaṇṭha's sub-commentary (Dīpikāprakāśikā or Nīlakaṇṭhī), and N.S. Rāmānuja Tātācārya's sub-commentary (Bālapriyā).
SA_GSP29_antsdi_u.attribution: Annambhaṭṭa composed both the root manual (Tarkasaṃgraha) and its auto-commentary (Dīpikā). Nīlakaṇṭha authored the sub-commentary Tarkasaṃgrahadīpikāprakāśikā (also known as Nīlakaṇṭhī). N.S. Rāmānuja Tātācārya composed the Bālapriyā.
SA_GSP29_antsdi_u.coverage: partial — Contains the text from the introductory Sanskrit Prastāvanā through the section on apavarga, breaking off incomplete at the end with 'jñānenaivetyevena tādṛ'.

SA_GSP29_gangtciu.title: Tattvacintāmaṇi (Śabdakhaṇḍa: Śabdaprāmāṇyavāda to Jātiśaktivāda)
SA_GSP29_gangtciu.author: Gaṅgeśa
SA_GSP29_gangtciu.summary: The Tattvacintāmaṇi by Gaṅgeśa Upādhyāya is the foundational text of the Navya-Nyāya school of Indian philosophy. Structured across four books corresponding to the four classical Nyāya pramāṇas (pratyakṣa, anumāna, upamāna, and śabda), this e-text contains the first portion of the Śabdakhaṇḍa, examining verbal testimony and semantics up to the Jātiśaktivāda.
SA_GSP29_gangtciu.attribution: Gaṅgeśa Upādhyāya is recognized as the author of the Tattvacintāmaṇi.
SA_GSP29_gangtciu.edition: Tattvacintāmaṇi, Śabdakhaṇḍa, part IV, vol. I to part IV, vol. II, p. 599, line 2. Bibliotheca Indica 98, edited by Kāmākhyānātha Tarkavāgīśa. Calcutta: Asiatic Society of Bengal.
SA_GSP29_gangtciu.coverage: partial — Contains the initial portion of the fourth book (Śabdakhaṇḍa) of the Tattvacintāmaṇi, from the opening of the Śabdaprāmāṇyavāda to the Jātiśaktivāda (where it breaks off). This corresponds to Part IV, Vol. 1, p. 1 through Part IV, Vol. 2, p. 599, l. 2 of the Bibliotheca Indica edition. The first three books (Pratyakṣa, Anumāna, Upamāna) and the latter half of the Śabdakhaṇḍa are omitted.

SA_GSP29_gaunys_u.title: Nyāyasūtra
SA_GSP29_gaunys_u.author: Gautama
SA_GSP29_gaunys_u.summary: The Nyāyasūtra, attributed to Akṣapāda Gautama, is the foundational treatise of the Nyāya school of classical Indian philosophy. In five books (adhyāyas), it expounds dialectical and epistemological categories (padārthas), beginning with pramāṇa, prameya, doubt, and points of defeat (nigrahasthāna), orienting rational inquiry toward liberation (apavarga).
SA_GSP29_gaunys_u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the sage Akṣapāda Gautama.
SA_GSP29_gaunys_u.coverage: complete — Root text comprising five adhyāyas (sūtras 1.1.1 to 5.2.25), accompanied by analytical prakaraṇa headings and topical sūtra labels in braces and brackets.
translations: Walter Ruben, Die Nyāyasūtra's: Text, Übersetzung, Erläuterung und Glossar, Leipzig: 1928. (German)

SA_GSP29_muva.title: Muktivāda
SA_GSP29_muva.author: Gadādhara Bhaṭṭācārya
SA_GSP29_muva.summary: The Muktivāda is an analytical Navya-Nyāya monograph composed by Gadādhara Bhaṭṭācārya investigating the soteriological concept of liberation (mukti / apavarga). Applying the school's precise formal definitions, Gadādhara demonstrates that liberation is fundamentally the absolute, permanent cessation of suffering (ātyantikaduḥkhanivṛtti) rather than experiential positive bliss. He critically refutes alternative doctrines from Advaita Vedānta and Mīmāṃsā, deliberates on whether the direct cause of release is self-knowledge (ātmatattvajñāna) or divine apprehension (paramātmasākṣātkāra), and assesses the causal role of ritual actions and auspicious death in holy places like Vārāṇasī.
SA_GSP29_muva.coverage: complete — Complete text of the monograph spanning pages 1 to 76 in the printed edition, beginning with 'prayojanam uddiśyaiva' and terminating with the final colophon 'iti śrīmahāmahopādhyāyagadādharabhaṭṭācāryakṛtamuktivādaḥ samāptaḥ'.

SA_GSP29_nvtp1_1u.title: Nyāyavārttikatātparyapariśuddhi (adhyāya 1, āhnika 1)
SA_GSP29_nvtp1_1u.author: Udayana
SA_GSP29_nvtp1_1u.summary: The Nyāyavārttikatātparyapariśuddhi (also known as Nyāyanibandha) is Udayana's sub-commentary on Vācaspati Miśra's Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā, constituting a commentary on Gautama's Nyāyasūtra. This opening section (Adhyāya 1, Āhnika 1) examines the definition and nature of the sixteen Nyāya categories (padārtha), beginning with the instruments of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), the knowables (prameya), and the prerequisites of philosophical debate through final ascertainment (nirṇaya). Udayana vigorously defends Nyāya realism, epistemology, and natural theology against contemporary Buddhist epistemological and anti-realist objections.
SA_GSP29_nvtp1_1u.attribution: Work of Udayana (Udayanācārya), written as a sub-commentary on Vācaspati Miśra's Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā.
SA_GSP29_nvtp1_1u.coverage: partial — Contains only Adhyāya 1, Āhnika 1 (ending with colophon: ityaudayana tātparyapariśuddhau prathamādhyāye prathamāhnikam).

SA_GSP29_nvtp1_2u.title: Nyāyavārttikatātparyapariśuddhi (adhyāya 1, āhnika 2)
SA_GSP29_nvtp1_2u.author: Udayana
SA_GSP29_nvtp1_2u.summary: The Nyāyavārttikatātparyapariśuddhi (commonly known as the Nyāyanibandha) by Udayana is an authoritative sub-commentary on Vācaspati Miśra's Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā, forming the culminating work in the classical Nyāyacaturgranthikā commentarial chain on Gautama's Nyāyasūtra. This section covers Nyāyasūtra Adhyāya 1, Āhnika 2, examining dialectical topics including the three types of debate (vāda, jalpa, vitaṇḍā), fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa), quibbling (chala), futile rejoinders (jāti), and grounds of defeat (nigrahasthāna). Udayana defends classical Nyāya realism and epistemic criteria against Buddhist critiques, refining the formal rules and categories of philosophical debate.
SA_GSP29_nvtp1_2u.attribution: Udayana composed the Pariśuddhi as a sub-commentary on Vācaspati Miśra's Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā.
SA_GSP29_nvtp1_2u.coverage: partial — Contains the text of Adhyāya 1, Āhnika 2 (from the kathālakṣaṇaprakaraṇa opening to the puruṣāśaktiliṅgadoṣasāmānyalakṣaṇaprakaraṇa colophon and verse 20).

SA_GSP29_nyabhu.title: Nyāyasāra with Nyāyabhūṣaṇa
SA_GSP29_nyabhu.author: Bhāsarvajña
SA_GSP29_nyabhu.summary: The Nyāyabhūṣaṇa ('Ornament of Nyāya') is Bhāsarvajña's extensive auto-commentary (saṅgrahavārttika) on his concise epistemological treatise, the Nyāyasāra. Structured across three chapters according to the three pramāṇas accepted by the author (perception, inference, and verbal testimony), the work introduces several heterodox positions within Nyāya, including the rejection of comparison (upamāna) as a distinct means of knowledge and the assertion that final liberation involves the positive experience of eternal bliss (nityasukhasaṃvedana). The treatise is a primary source for philosophical controversies, featuring extensive polemics against Buddhist epistemologists as well as Cārvāka skeptics and rival Brahmanical systems.
SA_GSP29_nyabhu.attribution: Both the root primer Nyāyasāra (introduced in its opening verse as the Nyāyasadarthasaṅgraha) and the expansive auto-commentary Nyāyabhūṣaṇa (subtitled Saṅgrahavārttika in the chapter colophons) are composed by Bhāsarvajña.
SA_GSP29_nyabhu.edition: Śrīmad-ācārya-Bhāsarvajña-praṇītasya Nyāyasārasya svopajñaṃ vyākhyānam Nyāyabhūṣaṇam, edited by Svāmī Yogīndrānanda, Ṣaḍdarśana Prakāśana Granthamālā 1, Vārāṇasī: Ṣaḍdarśanaprakāśana-pratiṣṭhānam, 1968.
SA_GSP29_nyabhu.coverage: complete — Complete text across all three chapters (Pratyakṣapariccheda, Anumānapariccheda, and Āgamapariccheda), concluding at segment [3246] with the final colophon: 'śrīmadācāryabhāsarvajñaviracite nyāyabhūṣaṇe saṅgrahavārttike tṛtīyaḥ paricchedaḥ samāptaḥ. sampūrṇo 'yaṃ granthaḥ.'
translations: Eli Franco, 'Bhāsarvajña and Jayarāśi: The Refutation of Skepticism in the Nyāyabhūṣaṇa', Berliner Indologische Studien 3 (1987). (English (partial: study and translation of selected skeptical passages))

SA_GSP29_nyaka.title: Padārthadharmasaṃgraha with Nyāyakandalī
SA_GSP29_nyaka.author: Praśastapāda, Śrīdhara
SA_GSP29_nyaka.summary: The Padārthadharmasaṃgraha by Praśastapāda is the classical prose reformulation of the Vaiśeṣika system, systematically classifying reality into six padārthas (substance, quality, action, universal, particularity, and inherence) and articulating classical Vaiśeṣika theories of perception, inference, atomic physics, and liberation. Śrīdhara's Nyāyakandalī is a commentary on Praśastapāda's work defending Vaiśeṣika ontology and epistemology against rival schools.
SA_GSP29_nyaka.attribution: Praśastapāda's Padārthadharmasaṃgraha (commonly known as Praśastapādabhāṣya) is the foundational comprehensive exposition of the classical Vaiśeṣika system. Śrīdhara names himself, his parents Baladeva and Acchokā, and his patron in the concluding praśasti verses.
SA_GSP29_nyaka.edition: The Bhāshya of Praśastapāda Together With the Nyāyakandalī of Śrīdhara, edited by Vindhyeśvarīprasāda Dvivedin (Vindhyeshwari Prasad Dvivedin), Vizianagram Sanskrit Series, Benares: 1895.
SA_GSP29_nyaka.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Padārthadharmasaṃgraha with the Nyāyakandalī, preceded by the Sanskrit editorial introduction (vijñāpana, lines 1–15) and concluding with Śrīdhara's praśasti and final colophons.

SA_GSP29_nybha.title: Nyāyasūtra with Nyāyabhāṣya
SA_GSP29_nybha.author: Gautama, Vātsyāyana
SA_GSP29_nybha.summary: The Nyāyasūtra of Akṣapāda Gautama is the foundational text of the Nyāya school of classical Indian philosophy, organizing epistemology, logic, dialectics, and soteriology around sixteen cognitive and debate topics (ṣoḍaśapadārtha). Vātsyāyana's Nyāyabhāṣya provides the earliest surviving and authoritative line-by-line exposition of the aphorisms, defending direct realism, pramāṇa validity, and the enduring self (ātman) against Buddhist and other non-realist positions. Together, the sūtras and bhāṣya established the bedrock conceptual vocabulary and logical apparatus that shaped subsequent Indian philosophical debate for well over a millennium.
SA_GSP29_nybha.attribution: The foundational Nyāyasūtras are traditionally attributed to Gautama. The Nyāyabhāṣya is composed by Vātsyāyana.
SA_GSP29_nybha.coverage: unclear — The catalog entry is currently an empty placeholder stub containing 0 segment files and 0 characters. Once populated, it is intended to encompass the five adhyāyas of the Nyāyasūtra along with Vātsyāyana's commentary.

SA_GSP29_nystik_u.title: Nyāyasūtra with Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā
SA_GSP29_nystik_u.author: Gautama, Vācaspatimiśra
SA_GSP29_nystik_u.summary: The Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā is Vācaspatimiśra's foundational sub-commentary written to elucidate and defend Uddyotakara's Nyāyavārttika against criticisms. The treatise provides an extensive exposition of Nyāya epistemology, realism, the pramāṇas, syllogistic inference, dialectical debate categories, and ontology.
SA_GSP29_nystik_u.attribution: The root aphorisms are traditionally ascribed to Akṣapāda Gautama. The commentary Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā is by Vācaspatimiśra, defending Uddyotakara's Nyāyavārttika.
SA_GSP29_nystik_u.coverage: complete — Complete: adhyāyas 1–5, ending with the author's closing verses, final colophon and the Nyāyasūcīnibandha count.

SA_GSP29_nysu51pu.title: Nyāyasūtra with Nyāyabhāṣya (adhyāya 5, āhnika 1)
SA_GSP29_nysu51pu.author: Akṣapāda Gautama, Vātsyāyana
SA_GSP29_nysu51pu.summary: This section covers the first daily lesson (āhnika) of Book 5 of the Nyāyasūtra together with Vātsyāyana's Nyāyabhāṣya, focusing entirely on futile rejoinders (jāti). Gautama enumerates and analyzes the twenty-four classes of jātis—illicit counter-arguments grounded in superficial similarity (sādharmya) or dissimilarity (vaidharmya) rather than valid universal concomitance. Vātsyāyana provides extensive exemplifications, diagnostic refutations (uttara), and demonstrates how such dialectical ploys collapse into mutual deadlock (e.g. in the six-step exchange known as the ṣaṭpakṣī).
SA_GSP29_nysu51pu.attribution: The root sūtras are traditionally attributed to Akṣapāda Gautama. The fundamental commentary (bhāṣya) is attributed to Vātsyāyana (also known as Pakṣilasvāmin).
SA_GSP29_nysu51pu.coverage: partial — Contains adhyāya 5, āhnika 1 only (NyS 5.1.1–5.1.43 along with Vātsyāyana's introductory, intermediate, and concluding bhāṣya on each sūtra, culminating in the discussion of the ṣaṭpakṣī debate format). Adhyāya 5.2 and adhyāyas 1–4 are absent.
translations: Ruben, Walter, Die Nyāyasūtra's: Text, Übersetzung, Erläuterung und Glossar, Leipzig: Deutsche Morgenländische Gesellschaft, 1928. (German)

SA_GSP29_nysvbh.title: Nyāyasūtra with Nyāyabhāṣya
SA_GSP29_nysvbh.author: Gautama, Vātsyāyana
SA_GSP29_nysvbh.summary: The Nyāyasūtra of Gautama (Akṣapāda) is the founding work of the classical Nyāya school, articulating an epistemology based on four means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa: perception, inference, analogy, and verbal testimony) and defining sixteen topics of philosophical inquiry and debate across five books. Vātsyāyana's Nyāyabhāṣya is the earliest surviving commentary on the aphorisms, articulating classical Nyāya realism, epistemology, and dialectic while responding to early Buddhist challenges. Together, these foundational treatises formed the core curriculum and point of departure for subsequent orthodox and Buddhist logical debates throughout classical Indian philosophy.
SA_GSP29_nysvbh.attribution: The Nyāyasūtra is traditionally attributed to Akṣapāda Gautama. The Nyāyabhāṣya is the commentary on the sūtras authored by Vātsyāyana.
SA_GSP29_nysvbh.coverage: unclear — Empty duplicate entry; the intended text (complete Nyāyasūtra with Nyāyabhāṣya, Sansknet) is SA_GSP29_nysvbh_u.
translations: Ganganatha Jha, Nyāyasūtras of Gautama: A System of Indian Logic with Vātsyāyana's Nyāyabhāṣya. (English)
Debiprasad Chattopadhyaya, Nyāya Philosophy, tr. with Vātsyāyana's Bhāṣya. (English)

SA_GSP29_nysvbh1u.title: Nyāyasūtra with Nyāyabhāṣya
SA_GSP29_nysvbh1u.author: Akṣapāda Gautama, Vātsyāyana
SA_GSP29_nysvbh1u.summary: The Nyāyasūtra, attributed to Akṣapāda Gautama, is the foundational treatise of the classical Nyāya school, defining sixteen epistemological and dialectical topics (ṣoḍaśa padārthāḥ), establishing four valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa: perception, inference, analogy, and testimony), and formulating the classical five-part inference schema alongside debate methodology. Vātsyāyana's Nyāyabhāṣya (c. 5th century CE) is the earliest extant commentary on the aphorisms, articulating a robust epistemological realism that defends the mind-independent reality of objects, the permanence of the self (ātman), and causal regularities against early Buddhist and skeptical challenges.
SA_GSP29_nysvbh1u.attribution: The root aphorisms (Nyāyasūtra) are traditionally attributed to Akṣapāda Gautama. The earliest extant commentary, the Nyāyabhāṣya, is attributed to Vātsyāyana.
SA_GSP29_nysvbh1u.edition: Nyāyadarśanam with Vātsyāyana's Bhāṣya, Uddyotakara's Vārttika, Vācaspati Miśra's Tātparyaṭīkā & Viśvanātha's Vṛtti. Edited by Taranatha Nyaya-Tarkatirtha and Amarendramohan Tarkatirtha. Calcutta: Metropolitan Printing & Publishing House, 1936–1944 (Calcutta Sanskrit Series, 18 & 19).
SA_GSP29_nysvbh1u.coverage: complete — Complete text of all five adhyāyas (each divided into two āhnikas) of the Nyāyasūtra accompanied by Vātsyāyana's complete Nyāyabhāṣya, concluding with the traditional final verse and colophon (iti śrīvātsyāyanīye nyāyabhāṣye pañcamo 'dhyāyaḥ).
translations: Gangopadhyaya, Mrinalkanti (trans.). Nyāya: Gautama's Nyāya-sūtra with Vātsyāyana's Commentary. Calcutta: Indian Studies, 1982. (English)
Ruben, Walter. Die Nyāyasūtra's: Text, Übersetzung, Erläuterung und Glossar. Leipzig: Deutsche Morgenländische Gesellschaft, 1928. (German)

SA_GSP29_snyayvpu.title: Nyāyāvatāra with Nyāyāvatāravivṛti
SA_GSP29_snyayvpu.author: Siddhasena Mahāmati, Siddharṣigaṇin
SA_GSP29_snyayvpu.summary: The Nyāyāvatāra is a concise 32-verse Jain treatise on epistemology and logic (pramāṇaśāstra) treating perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna), verbal testimony, internal pervasion (antarvyāpti), and the doctrine of perspectives (naya) in the context of anekāntavāda. Historically ascribed to Siddhasena Divākara, the text is also attributed to Siddhasena Mahāmati, who engaged systematically with Buddhist logic. Siddharṣigaṇin's commentary, the Nyāyāvatāravivṛti, provides an exposition of each verse, defending Jain epistemological positions against rival objections.
SA_GSP29_snyayvpu.attribution: The root work Nyāyāvatāra was traditionally ascribed to Siddhasena Divākara. Modern scholarship distinguishes a logician Siddhasena Mahāmati who composed the Nyāyāvatāra. The commentary Nyāyāvatāravivṛti was authored by Siddharṣigaṇin. Note that while the opening mentions Devabhadrasūri's Ṭippana, this e-text contains only the Vivṛti.
SA_GSP29_snyayvpu.edition: Piotr Balcerowicz, Jaina Epistemology in Historical and Comparative Perspective: Critical Edition and English Translation of Logical-Epistemological Treatises: Nyāyāvatāra, Nyāyāvatāra-vivṛti and Nyāyāvatāra-ṭippana with Introduction and Notes. 2 Volumes. Second revised edition, Motilal Banarsidass, New Delhi 2008.
SA_GSP29_snyayvpu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 32 kārikās of the Nyāyāvatāra along with Siddharṣigaṇin's complete Nyāyāvatāravivṛti (up to verse 32 and the commentator's concluding verses and colophon).
translations: Piotr Balcerowicz, Jaina Epistemology in Historical and Comparative Perspective: Critical Edition and English Translation of Logical-Epistemological Treatises: Nyāyāvatāra, Nyāyāvatāra-vivṛti and Nyāyāvatāra-ṭippana with Introduction and Notes. 2 vols. SA_GSP29_udnyku1u.title: Nyāyakusumāñjali (stavaka 1)
SA_GSP29_udnyku1u.author: Udayana
SA_GSP29_udnyku1u.summary: The Nyāyakusumāñjali by Udayana is a philosophical treatise defending theism. The work is composed in metrical verses (kārikās) accompanied by Udayana's extensive prose auto-commentary. In this first stavaka, Udayana addresses causal and ontological arguments relating to adṛṣṭa and the cosmic supervisor.
SA_GSP29_udnyku1u.attribution: Udayana authored both the metrical kārikās and the accompanying prose auto-commentary.
SA_GSP29_udnyku1u.coverage: partial — Stavaka 1 complete (kārikās 1–20 with Udayana's prose), ending 'iti śrīnyāyakusumāñjalau prathamaḥ stabakaḥ'.

SA_GSP29_udnyku2u.title: Nyāyakusumāñjali (stavaka 2)
SA_GSP29_udnyku2u.author: Udayana
SA_GSP29_udnyku2u.summary: The second chapter (stavaka) of Udayana's classic defense of Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika theism refutes the Mīmāṃsā contention that Vedic religious practice and moral order (dharma) can function without God through beginningless, unauthored revelation (apauruṣeyatva) and unbroken human succession. Udayana argues that cognitive validity is extraneous (parataḥprāmāṇya) and depends on the excellence of an agent-author, that the cosmos undergoes periodic total dissolution (pralaya) and cosmic recreation (sarga), and that God (Īśvara) is necessary as the trustworthy author and promulgator of Vedic revelation.
SA_GSP29_udnyku2u.attribution: Udayana is the author of the work.
SA_GSP29_udnyku2u.coverage: partial — Stavaka 2 only, complete (4 kārikās with prose commentary; keyed with section tags ku.2.202 to ku.2.288; embedded page numbers 70–153).

SA_GSP29_udnyku3u.title: Nyāyakusumāñjali (stavaka 3)
SA_GSP29_udnyku3u.author: Udayana
SA_GSP29_udnyku3u.summary: The third stabaka of Udayana's Nyāyakusumāñjali addresses the third major counter-position (vipratipatti), namely the contention of opponent schools (especially Mīmāṃsā and Buddhism) that there exist valid counter-proofs (bādhaka-pramāṇa) disproving God's existence. Udayana demonstrates that non-perception (anupalabdhi) only negates entities that are by nature perceptible (yogya), and cannot disprove an inherently supersensible (atīndriya) Lord. In the course of the chapter, Udayana defends the existence of an imperceptible self and mind, and systematically analyzes all recognized means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa)—perception, inference, analogy, testimony, presumption, and absence—to prove that none constitutes an obstacle to the establishment of Īśvara.
SA_GSP29_udnyku3u.attribution: Udayana composed both the metric verses (kārikā) and the accompanying prose exposition (gadya/svopajñavṛtti). The present e-text contains both parts for Stavaka 3.
SA_GSP29_udnyku3u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete third chapter (stavaka 3: 23 verses with prose auto-commentary) out of the five stavakas comprising the Nyāyakusumāñjali.

SA_GSP29_udnyku4u.title: Nyāyakusumāñjali (chapter 4)
SA_GSP29_udnyku4u.author: Udayana
SA_GSP29_udnyku4u.summary: The fourth chapter (Stavaka 4) of Udayana's Nyāyakusumāñjali refutes the Mīmāṃsaka challenge against divine omniscience. The opponent contends that God's cognition cannot be an instrument or instance of valid knowledge (pramā) because valid cognition requires apprehending what was not previously known (anadhigatārthagantṛ), an impossibility for an eternal, all-encompassing intellect. Udayana rejects both the anadhigatārthatva criterion and the Bhāṭṭa epistemological theory of cognizedness (jñātatā), defending the Nyāya definition of pramā as true experiential cognition (yathārthānubhava) independent of extraneous sources, and proving that continuous cognition (dhārāvāhikajñāna) and divine eternal awareness (nitya-sākṣātkāra) constitute genuine pramā.
SA_GSP29_udnyku4u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete fourth chapter (Stavaka 4) of the Nyāyakusumāñjali, comprising all 6 kārikās and the accompanying prose auto-commentary. The full treatise consists of five chapters.
translations: Chemparathy, George, An Indian Rational Theology: Introduction to Udayana's Nyāyakusumāñjali, Vienna, 1972. (English)

SA_GSP29_udnyku5u.title: Nyāyakusumāñjali (stavaka 5)
SA_GSP29_udnyku5u.author: Udayana
SA_GSP29_udnyku5u.summary: The fifth chapter (stavaka) of Udayana's Nyāyakusumāñjali presents arguments for the existence of God (Īśvara), formulated around the opening verse mentioning proofs from worldly effects (kāryāt), atomic combination (āyojanāt), support (dhṛteḥ), dissolution (saṃhārāt), word/convention (padāt), adṛṣṭa/experience (pratyayāt), Vedic authority (śruteḥ), sentences (vākyāt), and number (saṅkhyāviśeṣāt).
SA_GSP29_udnyku5u.attribution: The Nyāyakusumāñjali is attributed to Udayana.
translations: George Chemparathy, An Indian Rational Theology: Introduction to Udayana's Nyāyakusumāñjali, Vienna: De Nobili Research Library, 1972. (English)

SA_GSP29_vidhi.title: Tattvacintāmaṇi (Śabdakhaṇḍa: Vidhivāda)
SA_GSP29_vidhi.author: Gaṅgeśa
SA_GSP29_vidhi.summary: The Vidhivāda ('Discourse on Injunctions') is a section within the Śabdakhaṇḍa of Gaṅgeśa's Tattvacintāmaṇi investigating injunctive semantics (vidhi).
SA_GSP29_vidhi.coverage: unclear — No segment file exists for SA_GSP29_vidhi.

SA_GSP29_vnyps00u.title: Nyāyapariśuddhibhūmikā
SA_GSP29_vnyps00u.author: Lakṣmaṇācārya
SA_GSP29_vnyps00u.summary: The Nyāyapariśuddhibhūmikā is a modern Sanskrit scholarly introduction to Veṅkaṭanātha's Nyāyapariśuddhi. It outlines the epistemological methodology of Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta and Nyāya logic. It also provides a bio-bibliographical discussion of Veṅkaṭanātha (Vedāntadeśika), addressing his works such as the Tattvaṭīkā, Śatadūṣaṇī, Saṃkalpasūryodaya, and his interaction with Mādhavācārya.
SA_GSP29_vnyps00u.attribution: Erroneously catalogued under Veṅkaṭanātha because GRETIL bundled the introductory file (vnyps00u.htm) together with the text files of the Nyāyapariśuddhi. The text explicitly discusses Veṅkaṭanātha in the third person, discusses the history of the loss of parts of Veṅkaṭanātha's Tattvaṭīkā and Śatadūṣaṇī, and recounts legends regarding his encounters with Vidyāraṇya / Mādhavācārya.
SA_GSP29_vnyps00u.coverage: complete — Contains the Sanskrit editorial introduction (Bhūmikā) to the Nyāyapariśuddhi, concluding with traditional laudatory invocations (taniyans) to Veṅkaṭanātha.

SA_GSP29_vnyps11u.title: Nyāyapariśuddhi (adhyāya 1, āhnika 1)
SA_GSP29_vnyps11u.author: Veṅkaṭanātha
SA_GSP29_vnyps11u.summary: The Nyāyapariśuddhi is a treatise by Veṅkaṭanātha reviewing Nyāya categories and positions from the perspective of Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta. This initial section (adhyāya 1, āhnika 1 of the Pratyakṣādhyāya) discusses pramāṇas, Gautama's Nyāyasūtra, tarka, nirṇaya, vāda, jalpa, and perceptual error (khyāti).
SA_GSP29_vnyps11u.attribution: Veṅkaṭanātha is designated in the text colophon as Vedāntācārya and Kavitārkikasiṃha.
SA_GSP29_vnyps11u.coverage: partial — Contains the first āhnika of the first adhyāya (Pratyakṣādhyāya), concluding with the colophon: iti śrīkavitārkikasiṃhasya sarvatantrasvatantrasya śrīmadveṅkaṭanāthasya vedāntācāryasya kṛtiṣu nyāyapariśuddhau pratyakṣādhyāye prathamamāhnikam.

SA_GSP29_vnyps12u.title: Nyāyapariśuddhi (adhyāya 1, āhnika 2)
SA_GSP29_vnyps12u.author: Veṅkaṭanātha
SA_GSP29_vnyps12u.summary: The Nyāyapariśuddhi is Veṅkaṭanātha's major epistemological and dialectical treatise dedicated to reframing classical Nyāya concepts in accordance with Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta. This section (Adhyāya 1, Āhnika 2) completes the discussion of perception (Pratyakṣādhyāya), focusing on invalid cognition (saṃśaya and viparyaya), the enumeration of pramāṇas, indeterminate and determinate perception (nirvikalpaka and savikalpaka), and yogic direct realization. Throughout the discussion, Veṅkaṭanātha defends the Viśiṣṭādvaita realist theory of perception (yathārthakhyāti) against Buddhist, Advaita, and Mīmāṃsā opponents.
SA_GSP29_vnyps12u.attribution: Veṅkaṭanātha is also reverentially titled Vedāntadeśika, Vedāntācārya, and Kavitārkikasiṃha.
SA_GSP29_vnyps12u.coverage: partial — Contains Adhyāya 1 (Pratyakṣādhyāya), Āhnika 2 (prakaraṇas 9–25, covering viparyaya, saṃśaya, pramāṇasaṃkhyā, and the varieties of pratyakṣa down to the chapter colophon: 'samāptaśca pratyakṣādhyāyaḥ'). Āhnika 1 is preserved in SA_GSP29_vnyps11u, and subsequent adhyāyas are in companion files.

SA_GSP29_vnyps31u.title: Nyāyapariśuddhi (chapter 3: Śabdādhyāya, āhnika 1)
SA_GSP29_vnyps31u.author: Veṅkaṭanātha
SA_GSP29_vnyps31u.summary: The Nyāyapariśuddhi is Veṅkaṭanātha's major epistemological treatise intended to reconcile Nyāya logic with Rāmānuja's Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta. This portion (Adhyāya 3, Āhnika 1) treats verbal testimony (śabdapramāṇa), establishing it as an independent means of valid cognition against Vaiśeṣika and Buddhist attempts to subsume it under inference (anumāna). It further examines the nature of words and sentences, the eternity of Vedic language, semantic theories including anvitābhidhānavāda, and the doctrine of intrinsic validity (svataḥprāmāṇyavāda).
SA_GSP29_vnyps31u.attribution: Authored by Veṅkaṭanātha, also known as Vedāntadeśika. The closing colophon confirms his authorship: 'iti kavitārkikasiṃhasya sarvatantrasvatantrasya śrīmadveṅkaṭanāthasya vedāntācāryasya kṛtiṣu nyāyapariśuddhau śabdādhyāye prathamamāhnikam'.
SA_GSP29_vnyps31u.coverage: partial — Complete first āhnika of adhyāya 3 (Śabdādhyāya), sections 'nyā. pa. śa. 1–19', ending with the colophon 'iti kavitārkikasiṃhasya sarvatantrasvatantrasya śrīmadveṅkaṭanāthasya vedāntācāryasya kṛtiṣu nyāyapariśuddhau śabdādhyāye prathamamāhnikam'.

SA_GSP29_vnyps32u.title: Nyāyapariśuddhi (adhyāya 3: Śabdādhyāya, āhnika 2)
SA_GSP29_vnyps32u.author: Veṅkaṭanātha
SA_GSP29_vnyps32u.summary: The Nyāyapariśuddhi ('Purification of Logic') is an epistemological and logical treatise by the Viśiṣṭādvaita master Veṅkaṭanātha, designed to reformulate Nyāya epistemology to conform with Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta. This file contains the second diurnal section (dvitīyam āhnikam) of the third chapter (Śabdādhyāya), focusing on verbal testimony (śabda-pramāṇa). It provides an extensive defense of Vedic authorlessness (apauruṣeyatva) and intrinsic validity against both Naiyāyika divine authorship and non-Vedic rejections, analyzes verbal meaning and sentence comprehension (śābdabodha), refutes rival Prabhākara and Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā views on the primary import of injunctions (kārya vs. bhāvanā), vindicates the authority of Smṛti and Pāñcarātra, and concludes that all words ultimately culminate in designating Nārāyaṇa.
SA_GSP29_vnyps32u.attribution: Veṅkaṭanātha is explicitly identified in the chapter-closing colophon (iti śrīkavitārkikasiṃhasya sarvatantrasvatantrasya śrīmadveṅkaṭanāthasya vedāntānacāryasya kṛtiṣunyāyapariśuddhau śabdādhyāye dvitīyamāhnikam samāptaśca tṛtīyodhyāyaḥ).
SA_GSP29_vnyps32u.coverage: partial — Contains the second āhnika of Adhyāya 3 (Śabdādhyāya, numbered sections 20 to the end of the chapter) of the work.

SA_GSP29_vnyps41u.title: Nyāyapariśuddhi (chapter 4: Smṛtyadhyāya, āhnika 1)
SA_GSP29_vnyps41u.author: Veṅkaṭanātha
SA_GSP29_vnyps41u.summary: The Nyāyapariśuddhi is an epistemological treatise by the Viśiṣṭādvaita philosopher Veṅkaṭanātha (Vedāntadeśika). This section comprises the first āhnika of adhyāya 4 (Smṛtyadhyāya), which defines recollection/memory (smṛti) as cognitive awareness arising purely from latent mental impressions (saṃskāramātrajaṃ jñānaṃ smṛtiḥ) and discusses its validity as an epistemic means (pramāṇa) against rival views.
SA_GSP29_vnyps41u.attribution: Veṅkaṭanātha, traditionally known by the title Vedāntadeśika / Vedāntācārya, was a philosopher of Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta.
SA_GSP29_vnyps41u.coverage: partial — Complete first āhnika of adhyāya 4 (Smṛtyadhyāya), sections 'nyā. pa. śa. 49–50', from 'atha smṛtirnirūpyate' to the colophon '... nyāyapariśuddhau smṛtyadhyāye prathamamāhnikam'.

SA_GSP29_vnyps42u.title: Nyāyapariśuddhi (chapter 4: Smṛtyadhyāya, āhnika 2)
SA_GSP29_vnyps42u.author: Veṅkaṭanātha
SA_GSP29_vnyps42u.summary: The Nyāyapariśuddhi by Veṅkaṭanātha (Vedāntadeśika) is an epistemological treatise of Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta. This section represents the second āhnika of Adhyāya 4 (Smṛtyadhyāya). In this section, Veṅkaṭanātha surveys the number of pramāṇas admitted by various rival schools (from Cārvāka to Paurāṇika) and demonstrates that other putative pramāṇas—including pratyabhijñā (recognition), upamāna (analogy), arthāpatti (postulation), anupalabdhi (non-apprehension), aitihya (tradition), and sambhava (inclusion)—do not warrant independent status but are properly subsumed within perception, inference, or verbal testimony.
SA_GSP29_vnyps42u.attribution: Authored by Veṅkaṭanātha, also known as Vedāntadeśika. The chapter-ending colophon identifies the author as 'śrīkavitārkikasiṃhasya sarvatantrasvatantrasya śrīmadveṅkaṭanāthasya vedāntācāryasya'.
SA_GSP29_vnyps42u.coverage: partial — Complete second āhnika of adhyāya 4 (Smṛtyadhyāya), sections 'nyā. pa. śa. 51–55', ending with closing verses, the colophon and 'samāptaśca caturthodhyāyaḥ'. It reviews the number of pramāṇas admitted by other schools and their reduction.

SA_GSP29_vnyps51u.title: Nyāyapariśuddhi (chapter 5: Prameyādhyāya, āhnika 1)
SA_GSP29_vnyps51u.author: Veṅkaṭanātha
SA_GSP29_vnyps51u.summary: The Nyāyapariśuddhi is a treatise by Veṅkaṭanātha. This section contains the first lesson (prathamam āhnikam) of the fifth chapter (Prameyādhyāya), turning from the analysis of pramāṇas (epistemic instruments) to ontology and knowable entities (prameya). Veṅkaṭanātha critiques the classical Vaiśeṣika scheme of six or seven categories (padārthas), rejecting independent categories such as samavāya, viśeṣa, and separate abhāva, and develops an ontological taxonomy dividing reality into substance (dravya) and non-substance (adravya).
SA_GSP29_vnyps51u.attribution: Authorship is explicitly attested in the chapter colophon: 'iti śrīkavitārkikasiṃhasya sarvatantrasvatantrasya śrīmadveṅkaṭanāthasya vedāntācāryasya kṛtiṣu nyāyapariśuddhau prameyādhyāye prathamamāhnikam'.
SA_GSP29_vnyps51u.coverage: partial — Complete first āhnika of adhyāya 5 (Prameyādhyāya), ending with the colophon '... nyāyapariśuddhau prameyādhyāye prathamamāhnikam'.

SA_GSP29_vnyps52u.title: Nyāyapariśuddhi (chapter 5: Prameyādhyāya, āhnika 2)
SA_GSP29_vnyps52u.author: Veṅkaṭanātha
SA_GSP29_vnyps52u.summary: The Nyāyapariśuddhi ('Purification of Nyāya') by Veṅkaṭanātha (Vedānta Deśika) reframes classical Nyāya logic and dialectics within a Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedāntic epistemological and ontological framework. This final section contains the second āhnika of the fifth chapter (Prameyādhyāya), which evaluates knowable entities (prameya) following the Nyāyasūtra's twelvefold scheme (ātman, body, sense faculties, objects, intellect, mind, activity, faults, rebirth, result, suffering, and liberation). Veṅkaṭanātha critiques Vaiśeṣika atomism and categorical distinctions, proposes a twofold ontological classification into substance (dravya) and non-substance (adravya), and defines the ultimate goal of liberation (apavarga) as the soul's blissful experiential communion with Brahman.
SA_GSP29_vnyps52u.attribution: The Nyāyapariśuddhi is attributed to Veṅkaṭanātha, also called Vedānta Deśika or Nigamāntamahādeśika. The concluding colophon verses expressly identify him by name and title (veṅkaṭeśaviduṣā, kavitārkikasiṃhasya... śrīmadveṅkaṭanāthasya vedāntācāryasya).
SA_GSP29_vnyps52u.edition: Nyāyapariśuddhi, in: Vedāntadeśikagranthamālā [Vedāntavibhāge 2], ed. P. B. Aṇṇaṅgarācārya, Madras 1940.
SA_GSP29_vnyps52u.coverage: partial — Contains Adhyāya 5 (Prameyādhyāya), second āhnika (dvitīyam āhnikam), corresponding to pages 9–11 of the Prameyādhyāya section in P. B. Aṇṇaṅgarācārya's edition, concluding both chapter 5 and the entire treatise.

SA_GSP29_vyomavati.title: Vyomavatī
SA_GSP29_vyomavati.author: Vyomaśiva
SA_GSP29_vyomavati.summary: The Vyomavatī by the Śaiva-Vaiśeṣika master Vyomaśiva (10th century CE) is the earliest surviving commentary on Praśastapāda's Padārthadharmasaṅgraha, pre-dating the commentaries of Śrīdhara (Nyāyakandalī) and Udayana (Kiraṇāvalī). It provides an extensive defense and elaboration of the classical Vaiśeṣika categories (substance, quality, motion, universal, particularity, and inherence), addressing epistemology, ontology, and the Vaiśeṣika doctrine of liberation. The work is noted for its rigorous polemical engagements with Buddhist (especially Dharmakīrtian), Jaina, and Mīmāṃsaka positions, as well as its integration of Śaiva theological perspectives.
SA_GSP29_vyomavati.attribution: Vyomaśiva (c. 10th century CE), a Vaiśeṣika philosopher-ascetic affiliated with the Śaiva tradition, names himself in the concluding verses and final colophon ('iti viracitametad vyomanāmnā śivena... iti śrīvyomaśivācāryaviracitā padārthasaṃgrahaṭīkā vyomavatī samāptā').
SA_GSP29_vyomavati.edition: Vyomaśiva, Vyomavatī of Vyomaśivācārya, edited by Gaurinath Sastri, 2 vols., Varanasi: Sampurnanand Sanskrit University, 1983–1984 (M.M. Śivakumāraśāstri-Granthamālā). [Vol. 1: 1983;: 1984].
SA_GSP29_vyomavati.coverage: complete — Complete text of the commentary from the opening maṅgala through the concluding colophon, preserving manuscript lacunae and editorial reconstructions as printed in Gaurinath Sastri's two-volume edition.

SA_GSP29_vytrkt1u.title: Tarkatāṇḍava with Nyāyadīpa (chapter 1)
SA_GSP29_vytrkt1u.author: Vyāsatīrtha, Rāghavendratīrtha
SA_GSP29_vytrkt1u.summary: The Tarkatāṇḍava is a dialectical treatise by Vyāsatīrtha, forming one part of his triad of works (with Candrikā and Nyāyāmṛta). It presents a critique of Tarka/Nyāya positions, addressing topics such as the validity and origin of the Vedas, qualities of Īśvara, and liberation. This first chapter (prathamaḥ paricchedaḥ) covers 32 vādas, examining epistemological topics including prāmāṇyavāda, doṣābhāva, samavāya, and concluding with nirvikalpakavāda. The e-text is accompanied by the commentary Nyāyadīpa by Rāghavendratīrtha.
SA_GSP29_vytrkt1u.attribution: The root work Tarkatāṇḍava is by Vyāsatīrtha, forming part of the triad of works including Nyāyāmṛta and Tātparyacandrikā (Candrikā). The commentary Nyāyadīpa is by Rāghavendratīrtha (disciple of Sudhīndratīrtha).
SA_GSP29_vytrkt1u.coverage: partial — Contains the first chapter (prathamaḥ paricchedaḥ, covering 32 vādas, concluding with nirvikalpakavāda) along with the Sanskrit introduction (mukhopanyāsa).

SA_GSP29_vytrkt2u.title: Tarkatāṇḍava with Nyāyadīpa (pariccheda 2, prakaraṇas 1–35)
SA_GSP29_vytrkt2u.author: Vyāsatīrtha, Rāghavendratīrtha
SA_GSP29_vytrkt2u.summary: The Tarkatāṇḍava by Vyāsatīrtha, accompanied by Rāghavendratīrtha's commentary Nyāyadīpa, is an advanced dialectical classic of Dvaita Vedānta that critically examines Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika logic and epistemology (especially Gaṅgeśa's Tattvacintāmaṇi and Udayana) using Navya-Nyāya methods. This second section (Pariccheda 2) focuses on verbal testimony (śabdapramāṇa) and ontological categories, analyzing the prerequisites of sentential comprehension (ākāṅkṣā, āsatti, yogyatā), defending potency (śakti) as an autonomous category against Naiyāyika reductionism, examining universals (jāti), and dissecting the nature and motive force of Vedic injunctions (vidhivāda).
SA_GSP29_vytrkt2u.attribution: Vyāsatīrtha composed the root work Tarkatāṇḍava. Rāghavendratīrtha composed the commentary Nyāyadīpa.
SA_GSP29_vytrkt2u.coverage: partial — Covers Pariccheda 2 (Śabdapramāṇa and associated categories), prakaraṇas 1–35 (pp. 1–350 of the printed volume 2). The e-text stops at the end of prakaraṇa 35 (kṛtisādhyatvādiviśiṣṭeṣṭasādhanatvasya vidhitvabhaṅgaḥ).

SA_GSP29_vytrkt3u.title: Tarkatāṇḍava with Nyāyadīpa (chapter 3)
SA_GSP29_vytrkt3u.author: Vyāsatīrtha, Rāghavendratīrtha
SA_GSP29_vytrkt3u.summary: The Tarkatāṇḍava ('Dance of Logic') is one of the three principal treatises of Vyāsatīrtha (along with the Nyāyāmṛta and Tātparyacandrikā) that systematically challenge non-dualist and realist rivals using the analytical idiom of Navya-Nyāya. This third pariccheda, accompanied by Rāghavendratīrtha's commentary Nyāyadīpa, is devoted entirely to inferential cognition (anumāna), which Dvaita epistemologists place after verbal testimony (śabda) because inference serves as an auxiliary (anugrāhaka) to scriptural authority. Across forty disputations (vāda), Vyāsatīrtha offers a thorough critique of Gaṅgeśa Upādhyāya's Tattvacintāmaṇi and its commentaries, examining core topics such as invariable concomitance (vyāpti), conditioning factors (upādhi), inferential consideration (parāmarśa), hypothetical reasoning (tarka), and the typology of pseudo-reasons (hetvābhāsa).
SA_GSP29_vytrkt3u.attribution: The root treatise Tarkatāṇḍava was composed by Vyāsatīrtha. The commentary Nyāyadīpa is by Rāghavendratīrtha (disciple of Sudhīndratīrtha).
SA_GSP29_vytrkt3u.coverage: partial — Contains the third chapter (Tṛtīyapariccheda) with commentary, ending with the colophons 'iti śrīmatparamahaṃsaparivrājakācāryasudhīndratīrthagurupādaśiṣyarāghavendrayatikṛte tarkatāṇḍavavivṛttau nyāyadīpe tṛtīyaḥ paricchedaḥ' and 'saṃvyākhyaṃ tarkatāṇḍavaṃ samāptam'.

SA_GSP30_abhiprvu.title: Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā with Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī
SA_GSP30_abhiprvu.author: Utpaladeva, Abhinavagupta
SA_GSP30_abhiprvu.summary: The Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī (also known as the Laghuvimarśinī) is Abhinavagupta's running commentary on Utpaladeva's Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā, the foundational work of the Pratyabhijñā school of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism. Spanning four thematic sections (adhikāras)—addressing cognitive awareness (jñāna), sovereign action (kriyā), scriptural authority (āgama), and metaphysical synthesis (tattvasaṅgraha)—it argues that liberation consists in recognizing one's essential identity with the supreme Lord (Paramaśiva). Abhinavagupta articulates a philosophy of consciousness founded on self-manifestation (prakāśa), reflective awareness (vimarśa), and divine autonomy (svātantrya), engaging in detailed refutations of Buddhist epistemological, Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, and Sāṅkhya positions.
SA_GSP30_abhiprvu.attribution: The root verses (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā) are by Utpaladeva. The commentary (Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī, also referred to as Laghuvimarśinī) was composed by Abhinavagupta.
SA_GSP30_abhiprvu.edition: Īśvara-pratyabhijñā-Vimarśinī of Abhinavagupta: doctrine of devine recognition, Sanskrit Text with the commentary Bhāskarī. vol.1-2 / edited by K.A. Subramania Iyer and K.C.Pandey. Delhi, etc.: Motilal Banarsidass, 1986 (repr.) (First Edition: The Princess of Wales Saraswati Bahvana, 1938(text no. 70) and 1950(text no. 83).
SA_GSP30_abhiprvu.coverage: complete — Complete across all four adhikāras: Jñānādhikāra (8 āhnikas), Kriyādhikāra (4 āhnikas), Āgamādhikāra (2 āhnikas), and Tattvasaṅgrahādhikāra (18 verses; 190 kārikās in total), together with Abhinavagupta's commentary.
translations: Kanti Chandra Pandey, Bhāskarī: An English Translation of the Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī with An Outline of the History of Saiva Philosophy, Sarasvatibhavana Text, Lucknow / Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1986. (English)

Harvey Paul Alper, Abhinavagupta's Concept of Cognitive Power: A Translation of the Jnanasaktyahnika of the Isvarapratyabhijnavimarsini with Commentary and Introduction, Ph.D. dissertation, University of Pennsylvania, 1976. (English)

SA_GSP30_abhmal1u.title: Mālinīślokavārttika (kāṇḍa 1)
SA_GSP30_abhmal1u.author: Abhinavagupta
SA_GSP30_abhmal1u.summary: The Mālinīślokavārttika (or Mālinīvijayavārttika) is Abhinavagupta's extensive verse commentary on the Mālinīvijayottaratantra, the central scriptural authority of the nondual Trika Śaiva lineage. In Kāṇḍa 1, Abhinavagupta develops an expansive theological and philosophical exegesis primarily from the tantra's opening maṅgala, elaborating nondual metaphysics, epistemology, the ontology of Śakti, the theology of divine revelation (āgama), and the descent of divine grace (śaktipāta) while engaging rival Buddhist, Mīmāṃsā, and Nyāya perspectives.
SA_GSP30_abhmal1u.attribution: Work of Abhinavagupta. The opening verses invoke Śambhunātha and others.
SA_GSP30_abhmal1u.edition: Verses 1.1–399: Jürgen Hanneder (ed.), Abhinavagupta's Philosophy of Revelation: An Edition and Annotated Translation of Mālinīślokavārttika I, 1–399, Groningen Oriental Studies 14, Groningen: Egbert Forsten, 1998; verses 1.400–1135: Madhusūdan Kaul Shāstrī (ed.), Mālinīvijaya Vārttika / Mālinīvijayavārttikam, Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies (KSTS), Srinagar, 1921.
SA_GSP30_abhmal1u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete first kāṇḍa (prathamaḥ kāṇḍaḥ, verses 1.1–1.1135).
translations: Jürgen Hanneder, Abhinavagupta's Philosophy of Revelation: An Edition and Annotated Translation of Mālinīślokavārttika I, 1–399, Groningen Oriental Studies 14, Groningen: Egbert Forsten, 1998. (English)

SA_GSP30_abhmal2u.title: Mālinīślokavārttika (kāṇḍa 2)
SA_GSP30_abhmal2u.author: Abhinavagupta
SA_GSP30_abhmal2u.summary: The Mālinīślokavārttika (also known as Mālinīvijayavārttika) is Abhinavagupta's verse commentary on the opening verse of the Mālinīvijayottaratantra, the paramount scriptural authority of the Kashmirian non-dual Trika tradition. The work unfolds an extensive metaphysical, epistemological, and soteriological system across two books (kāṇḍas). This second kāṇḍa (verses 2.1–2.335) expounds the role of purified reasoning (tarka) as an indispensable aid to realization, the dynamic heart-vibration (hṛdayaspanda) of Śiva-Śakti, the ontology of bondage (mala, māyā), and non-dual initiation (dīkṣā).
SA_GSP30_abhmal2u.attribution: Uncontested work of the Kashmirian non-dual Śaiva master Abhinavagupta, who explicitly identifies himself in the final stanza (verse 2.335: kāśmīriko 'bhinavaguptaḥ / mālinyādimavākye vārttikam etad racayati sma).
SA_GSP30_abhmal2u.edition: Madhusudan Kaul Shastri (ed.), The Mālinīvijaya Vārttikam of Abhinava Gupta, Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies (KSTS), Srinagar: 1921.
SA_GSP30_abhmal2u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete second kāṇḍa (verses 2.1–2.335) of the Mālinīślokavārttika.
translations: Jürgen Hanneder, Abhinavagupta's Philosophy of Revelation: An Edition and Annotated Translation of Mālinīślokavārttika I, 1–399, Groningen Oriental Studies 14, Groningen: Egbert Forsten, 1998. (English (Kāṇḍa 1, verses 1–399 only))

SA_GSP30_abhtantu.title: Tantrasāra
SA_GSP30_abhtantu.author: Abhinavagupta
SA_GSP30_abhtantu.summary: The Tantrasāra ('Essence of Tantra') is Abhinavagupta's prose compendium summarizing the doctrinal and ritual core of his encyclopedic verse work, the Tantrāloka. Divided into twenty-two daily lessons (āhnikas), it expounds the non-dual metaphysics and soteriology of Trika Śaivism and Kaula ritual traditions, systematically covering the four means of liberation (anupāya, śāmbhava-, śākta-, and āṇavopāya) alongside detailed instructions for initiation (dīkṣā), mantras, and esoteric ritual practices.
SA_GSP30_abhtantu.attribution: A work composed by Abhinavagupta in Kashmir as a concise prose summary of his verse magnum opus, the Tantrāloka.
SA_GSP30_abhtantu.edition: Mukunda Rāma Śāstrī (ed.), The Tantrasāra of Abhinava Gupta, Bombay: Nirṇaya-Sāgara Press, 1918 (Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies, no. XVII [17]).
SA_GSP30_abhtantu.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising all 22 āhnikas, beginning with the opening maṅgala verses (AbhTs_1.1–1.3) and ending with chapter 22 verse 54 on the Kulayāga rite (AbhTs_22.54).

SA_GSP30_adyapppu.title: Anuttaraprakāśapañcāśikā
SA_GSP30_adyapppu.author: Ādyanātha
SA_GSP30_adyapppu.summary: A 50-verse nondual Śaiva philosophical poem expounding supreme consciousness (Śiva/anuttara) as pure awareness (prakāśa) intrinsically united with reflective dynamism (vimarśa). It explains the manifestation and withdrawal of cosmic manifestation across the thirty-six principles (tattvas), establishing that objective reality is non-different from the supreme light, and describes spiritual liberation as the reabsorption of differentiated perception into universal spanda.
SA_GSP30_adyapppu.attribution: Attributed in the colophon to Ādyanātha (iti śrīmadādyanāthaviracitā anuttaraprakāśapañcāśikā samāptā).
SA_GSP30_adyapppu.edition: Mukundarama Shastri, ed., Bombay: Tatva Vivechaka Press, 1918 (Kashmir Series of Sanskrit Texts and Studies, 13).
SA_GSP30_adyapppu.coverage: complete — Complete in 50 verses (Aprp_1–50) plus an editorial concluding śloka (Aprp_*1) by the editor Mukundarāma Śāstrī.

SA_GSP30_anuttaru.title: Anuttarāṣṭikā
SA_GSP30_anuttaru.author: Abhinavagupta
SA_GSP30_anuttaru.summary: The Anuttarāṣṭikā ('Eight Verses on the Supreme/Absolute') is a concise philosophical stotra in Śārdūlavikrīḍita metre composed by the Kashmir Śaiva master Abhinavagupta (fl. c. 975–1025 CE). It articulates the Trika doctrine of anupāya ('no-means'), demonstrating that because non-dual consciousness (cidadvaya) is already the intrinsic nature of all reality, outward spiritual transmission (saṃkrāma), formal meditation, and ascetic striving are superfluous. Rejection and acquisition are discarded in favor of resting peacefully in reality as it is (svastho yathāvasthitaḥ), recognizing the world as an effortless manifestation of one's own conscious nature.
SA_GSP30_anuttaru.attribution: A short philosophical hymn attributed to Abhinavagupta, corroborated by the closing colophon: iti śrīmadācāryābhinavaguptapādair viracitānuttarāṣṭikā samāptā.
SA_GSP30_anuttaru.coverage: complete — Complete: 8 verses and the closing colophon 'iti śrīmadācāryābhinavaguptapādair viracitānuttarāṣṭikā samāptā'; one variant noted in the file (v. 2 'vilasa' for 'vihara').
translations: Lilian Silburn, Hymnes de Abhinavagupta, traduits et commentés, Paris: De Boccard, 1970. (French)

SA_GSP30_aparmyou.title: Paramārthasāra with Paramārthasārasaṃgrahavivṛti
SA_GSP30_aparmyou.author: Abhinavagupta, Yogarāja
SA_GSP30_aparmyou.summary: The Paramārthasāra ('Essence of Ultimate Reality') is an introductory compendium of 105 āryā stanzas by the Kashmiri master Abhinavagupta, articulating the metaphysical and soteriological core of nondual Trika Śaivism. Adapted from an earlier Vaiṣṇava work attributed to Ādiśeṣa, the treatise outlines the emanation of the thirty-six principles (tattvas) through the playful self-expression (krīḍā) and sovereign freedom (svātantrya) of Śiva-consciousness, the contracted state of worldly bondage (saṃsāra), and liberation through self-recognition (pratyabhijñā). Yogarāja's vivṛti commentary expands Abhinavagupta's compressed verses into a systematic philosophical treatise, refuting Advaita Vedānta and Buddhist positions while clarifying the nondual Śaiva doctrine of divine grace (śaktipāta / anugrahaśakti).
SA_GSP30_aparmyou.attribution: The root work consists of 105 verses composed by Abhinavagupta. The commentary (vivṛti), explicitly titled Paramārthasārasaṃgrahavivṛti in the closing colophon, was composed by Rājānaka Yogarāja, who identifies himself in the concluding verses as a disciple of Kṣemarāja.
SA_GSP30_aparmyou.edition: Srinagar: Research Dept. Jammu and Kashmir State 1916 (The Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies edition, 7). The text of this edition has been revised after nine manuscripts [see L. Bansat-Boudon - K. D. Tripathi, An Introduction to Tantric Philosophy: The Paramārthasāra of Abhinavagupta with the Commentary of Yogarāja. Translated by Lyne Bansat-Boudon and Kamaleshadatta Tripathi. Introduction, notes, critically revised Sanskrit text, appendix, indices by Lyne Bansat-Boudon. London / New York: Routledge 2011 (Routledge Studies in Tantric Traditions, 3), pp. 347 ff.]
SA_GSP30_aparmyou.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 105 kārikās along with Yogarāja's complete commentary, opening maṅgala verses, and concluding colophon.
translations: Lyne Bansat-Boudon and Kamaleshadatta Tripathi, An Introduction to Tantric Philosophy: The Paramārthasāra of Abhinavagupta with the Commentary of Yogarāja, London / New York: Routledge, 2011. (English)
Lilian Silburn, Le Paramārthasāra: Texte sanskrit édité et traduit, Publications de l'Institut de Civilisation Indienne, Fasc. 5, Paris: E. de Boccard, 1957. (French)

SA_GSP30_bhairstu.title: Bhairavastava
SA_GSP30_bhairstu.author: Abhinavagupta
SA_GSP30_bhairstu.summary: The Bhairavastava (also titled Śivastuti or Abhinavākhyaṃ Padyanavakam) is a devotional hymn composed by Abhinavagupta. In the concluding stanza, the author states that he composed this praise on the tenth lunar day of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa ('vasurasapauṣe kṛṣṇadaśamyām abhinavaguptaḥ stavam imam akarot'). The hymn celebrates Bhairava and consciousness (saṃvid), addressing freedom from fear of death and saṃsāra.
SA_GSP30_bhairstu.attribution: Firmly attributed to Abhinavagupta; verse 10 explicitly gives the author's name: 'vasurasapauṣe kṛṣṇadaśamyām abhinavaguptaḥ stavam imam akarot'.
SA_GSP30_bhairstu.coverage: complete — Complete: 9 verses plus the concluding verse 'vasurasapauṣe kṛṣṇadaśamyām…' and the closing line 'samāptam stavam idam abhinavākhyam padyanavakam'; one variant noted for v. 7.
translations: Lilian Silburn, Hymnes de Abhinavagupta, PICI 1970. (French)

SA_GSP30_bhutisbs_u.title: Svabodhasiddhi
SA_GSP30_bhutisbs_u.author: Bhūtirāja
SA_GSP30_bhutisbs_u.summary: The Svabodhasiddhi is a Śaiva treatise in 33 verses attributed to Bhūti(rāja). The text teaches a path to liberation through absorption in self-awareness (svasaṃvedana, svabodha) and the overcoming of subject–object duality (grāhyagrāhakatā).
SA_GSP30_bhutisbs_u.edition: Hanneder, Jürgen: Bhūtis Svabodhasiddhi. IN: ZDMG 167 (2017), 153-166

SA_GSP30_bodhpanu.title: Bodhapañcadaśikā
SA_GSP30_bodhpanu.author: Abhinavagupta
SA_GSP30_bodhpanu.summary: The Bodhapañcadaśikā ('Fifteen Verses on Awakening') is a succinct didactic treatise composed by the Kashmiri polymath Abhinavagupta (fl. c. 975–1025 CE). As indicated in its concluding verse, it was written to introduce disciples of gentle intellect (sukumāramati) to the foundational non-dual metaphysics of Trika Śaivism. In fifteen kārikās, Abhinavagupta elucidates the single nature of consciousness (Bhairava/Parameśvara), the inseparability of the divine subject and creative power (śakti), the universe as an internal reflection (pratibimba) within the mirror of awareness, and the recognition that liberation (jīvanmukti) is the realization of unbroken wholeness.
SA_GSP30_bodhpanu.attribution: Explicitly attributed to Abhinavagupta in verse 16 ('ime 'bhinavaguptena ślokāḥ pañcadaśoditāḥ'). Abhinavagupta also refers to and cites verse 8 of this text under the variant title Prabodhapañcadaśikā.
SA_GSP30_bodhpanu.coverage: complete — Complete: 15 numbered verses plus the unnumbered closing verse 'sukumāramatīn śiṣyān … ime 'bhinavaguptena ślokāḥ pañcadaśoditāḥ'.
translations: Lilian Silburn, Hymnes de Abhinavagupta, Paris 1970. (French)

SA_GSP30_kramstou.title: Kramastotra
SA_GSP30_kramstou.author: Abhinavagupta
SA_GSP30_kramstou.summary: The Kramastotra is a 30-verse hymn composed by Abhinavagupta celebrating the esoteric doctrine of the Krama lineage within Kashmir Śaivism. It delineates the cyclic unfolding of dynamic consciousness across phases of creation (sṛṣṭi), preservation (sthiti), dissolution (saṃhāra), and praise of Lord Manthāna[bhairava] as the essence of the universe (jagadekasāra), closing with an authorial colophon dating the text.
SA_GSP30_kramstou.attribution: A work composed by Abhinavagupta, concluding with a verse dating it to the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, dark fortnight 9th tithi (ṣaṭṣaṣṭinām eke varṣe navamyām asite 'hani / mayā 'bhinavaguptena mārgaśīrṣe stutaḥ śivaḥ).
SA_GSP30_kramstou.coverage: complete — Complete text of 30 verses (verses 1–29 are numbered; the concluding verse naming Abhinavagupta is unnumbered before the colophon).
translations: Translated into French (referenced in Potter, Encyclopedia of Indian Philosophies, Vol. 1). (French)

SA_GSP30_ksembodhv_u.title: Bodhavilāsa
SA_GSP30_ksembodhv_u.author: Kṣemarāja
SA_GSP30_ksembodhv_u.summary: The Bodhavilāsa ('Play of Awakened Consciousness') is a concise Pratyabhijñā manual in 42 anuṣṭubh verses by the Kashmirian master Kṣemarāja (early 11th c. CE). Functioning as a versified epitome of the core doctrine set out in his Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya, the work expounds how autonomous universal consciousness (citi) contracts into individual minds (citta), continuously performs the five cosmic operations (pañcakṛtya), and recovers its innate liberation through steady contemplative discernment (vimarśa).
SA_GSP30_ksembodhv_u.attribution: The work is explicitly attributed in the final verse (v. 42: rājñaḥ kṣemābhidhānasya śāstram atyantanirmalam) and final colophon (iti śrīkṣemarājakṛtaṃ bodhavilāsākhyaṃ yogaśāstram) to Kṣemarāja (early 11th c. CE), the famous pupil of Abhinavagupta. It is distinct from another Kashmirian Śaiva text bearing the title Bodhavilāsa (also known as Dvayasaṃpatti) by Vāmanadatta.
SA_GSP30_ksembodhv_u.edition: Corrado Pensa, 'Il Bodhavilāsa di Kṣemarāja', Rivista di Studi Orientali 36 (1961), pp. 125–134.
SA_GSP30_ksembodhv_u.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising all 42 anuṣṭubh stanzas.

SA_GSP30_parmartu.title: Paramārthasāra
SA_GSP30_parmartu.author: Abhinavagupta
SA_GSP30_parmartu.summary: The Paramārthasāra ('Essence of the Supreme Truth') is a concise philosophical compendium consisting of 105 verses composed in the late 10th or early 11th century CE by the polymath Abhinavagupta. It serves as an introductory summary of nondual Kashmir Śaivism (Trika and Pratyabhijñā), setting forth the emanation of cosmic reality across thirty-six tattvas structured into four spheres (aṇḍas), the soul's contraction through the impurities (malas) and limiting veils (kañcukas), and liberation through spontaneous recognition (pratyabhijñā) of one's identity with Paramaśiva. Abhinavagupta explicitly adapted this work from an earlier Advaita/Vaiṣṇava treatise attributed to Ādiśeṣa, rearticulating its teachings in accordance with the monistic Śaiva view.
SA_GSP30_parmartu.attribution: The work is an adaptation and reinterpretation from a Śaiva perspective of an earlier work of the same title (also known as the Ādhārakārikā) attributed to Ādiśeṣa. Abhinavagupta explicitly mentions this source in verse 3 and concludes in verse 105.
SA_GSP30_parmartu.coverage: complete — Complete: all 105 āryā verses, ending with v. 105 'āryāśatena tad idaṃ…'; no commentary.
translations: Lilian Silburn, Le Paramārthasāra, Publications de l'Institut de Civilisation Indienne 5, Paris: E. de Boccard, 1957. (French)
Lyne Bansat-Boudon and Kamaleshadatta Tripathi, An Introduction to Tantric Philosophy: The Paramārthasāra of Abhinavagupta with the Commentary of Yogarāja, London/New York: Routledge, 2011. (English)

SA_GSP30_partr_pu.title: Parātriṃśikā (verses 1–33 and 35; verse 34 missing)
SA_GSP30_partr_pu.summary: The Parātriṃśikā (or Parātrīśikā) is an essential scripture of the Trika and Kaula traditions of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism, composed as an esoteric dialogue between the Goddess and Bhairava and traditionally held to be part of the Rudrayāmala.
