It articulates the absolute reality of unconditioned consciousness (anuttara), phonematic emanation, and esoteric mantra practice.
SA_GSP30_partr_pu.attribution: Scriptural work traditionally associated with the Rudrayāmala (as indicated in verse 35: ity etad rudrayāmalam).
SA_GSP30_partr_pu.coverage: partial — Verses ParTri_1–33 and ParTri_35 (verse 34 missing in this file).
translations: Raniero Gnoli (trans.), Il commento di Abhinavagupta alla Parātriṃśikā (Parātriṃśikātattvavivaraṇam). Traduzione e testo, Serie Orientale Roma 58, Roma: IsMEO, 1985. (Italian)
André Padoux (trans.), La Parātrīśikālaghuvṛtti de Abhinavagupta, Texte Traduit et Annoté, Publications de L'Institut de Civilisation Indienne 38, Paris, 1975. (French)

SA_GSP30_partrvpu.title: Parātriṃśikā with Parātriṃśikāvivaraṇa (without the Apabhraṃśa passages)
SA_GSP30_partrvpu.author: Abhinavagupta
SA_GSP30_partrvpu.summary: The Parātriṃśikāvivaraṇa (also entitled Parātriṃśikātattvavivaraṇa) is Abhinavagupta's philosophical commentary on the verses of the Parātriṃśikā. Building on Somānanda's earlier exegesis, Abhinavagupta articulates a metaphysics of absolute consciousness (saṃvid, anuttara) and the Goddess Parā, presenting a philosophy of the Word across its levels. The text provides theoretical grounding for phonematic cosmic emanation, the seed-syllable SAUḤ, and the Kaula contemplative path.
SA_GSP30_partrvpu.attribution: The Vivaraṇa is a work of Abhinavagupta.
SA_GSP30_partrvpu.edition: Ed. R. Gnoli, Roma 1985, with cross-references to J. Singh's ed. Delhi 1994.
SA_GSP30_partrvpu.coverage: partial — Root text and the Vivaraṇa; the GRETIL header states the e-text "lacks the Apabhramsa passages".
translations: Raniero Gnoli (trans.), Il Commento di Abhinavagupta alla Paratrimsika. (Italian)

SA_GSP30_parypanu.title: Paryantapañcāśikā
SA_GSP30_parypanu.author: Abhinavagupta
SA_GSP30_parypanu.summary: The Paryantapañcāśikā is a philosophical treatise in 52 anuṣṭubh verses attributed to Abhinavagupta, treating the nature of Bhairava, the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), and energies such as khecarī, gocarī, dikcarī, and bhūcarī issuing from Vyomeśvarī into unitary consciousness. The text is cited by Maheśvarānanda.
SA_GSP30_parypanu.attribution: Attributed to Abhinavagupta in the closing colophon (śrīmad-ābhinavaguptanāthasya). Verses from the text are also quoted by Maheśvarānanda.
SA_GSP30_parypanu.edition: V. Raghavan (ed.), The Paryanta Pañcāśikā of Abhinavagupta, Annals of Oriental Research 8, Madras, 1950–51; reprinted in Abhinavagupta and His Works, Varanasi.
SA_GSP30_parypanu.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising 52 anuṣṭubh verses, opening maṅgala, and closing colophons.

SA_GSP30_pratyabu.title: Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya
SA_GSP30_pratyabu.author: Kṣemarāja
SA_GSP30_pratyabu.summary: The Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya ('Heart of Recognition') is an influential introductory manual of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism composed in the first half of the 11th century CE by Kṣemarāja, the principal pupil of Abhinavagupta. Composed specifically for practitioners and novices lacking training in formal logic (tarka), the treatise distills the core metaphysics and soteriology of Utpaladeva's Īśvarapratyabhijñā into twenty concise aphorisms accompanied by Kṣemarāja's own explanatory commentary. It outlines the cosmic dynamics of Citi (supreme consciousness), which freely manifests the universe, contracts itself into limited individual experients (paśu), and achieves liberation through the intuitive recognition of its inherent oneness with Śiva.
SA_GSP30_pratyabu.attribution: Kṣemarāja composed both the twenty sūtras and the auto-commentary as a primer on the Pratyabhijñā doctrine for seekers not trained in dialectical philosophy.
SA_GSP30_pratyabu.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all 20 sūtras with Kṣemarāja's auto-commentary, introductory maṅgala verses, and concluding verses.
translations: Emil Baer, Das Geheimnis des Wiedererkennens (Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya), Zürich, 1926. (German)
Kurt F. Leidecker, Pratyabhijñāhṛdayam (The Secret of Recognition), Adyar, 1938. (English)
Jaideva Singh, Pratyabhijñāhṛdayam: The Secret of Self-Recognition, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1982. (English)

SA_GSP30_sa_avadhUtasiddha-bhagavadbhakt.title: Bhagavadbhaktistotra
SA_GSP30_sa_avadhUtasiddha-bhagavadbhakt.author: Avadhūtasiddha
SA_GSP30_sa_avadhUtasiddha-bhagavadbhakt.summary: The Bhagavadbhaktistotra (often called Bhaktistotra) is a 65-verse devotional hymn to Śiva composed by the early non-dual Kashmiri Śaiva master Avadhūtasiddha. Combining non-dual Trika and Pratyabhijñā theological themes (such as the Lord's infinite energies, divine autonomy, and the non-duality of worshipper and deity) with intense devotional surrender (bhakti), the hymn was influential in Kashmir and is cited by Abhinavagupta (in both the Laghu- and Bṛhadvimarśinī), Yogarāja, and Śrīkumāra.
SA_GSP30_sa_avadhUtasiddha-bhagavadbhakt.attribution: In the concluding stanza (v. 65), the poet refers to himself as 'avadhūtanāmnā' ('by one named Avadhūta'). Subsequent Kashmiri commentators (including Abhinavagupta, Yogarāja, and Śrīkumāra) cite him as Avadhūtasiddha.
SA_GSP30_sa_avadhUtasiddha-bhagavadbhakt.edition: Raniero Gnoli, "Miscellanea Indica: 1. The Bhagavadbhaktistotra by Avadhūtasiddha", East and West, New Series (1958), pp. 215–226.

SA_GSP30_sa_kSemarAja-bhairavAnukaraNast.title: Bhairavānukaraṇastotra
SA_GSP30_sa_kSemarAja-bhairavAnukaraNast.author: Kṣemarāja
SA_GSP30_sa_kSemarAja-bhairavAnukaraNast.summary: The Bhairavānukaraṇastotra ('Hymn on the Assimilation to Bhairava') is a 48-verse non-dual Śaiva hymn composed by Kṣemarāja in āryā metre. Rather than offering purely devotional praises, the hymn systematically decodes the terrifying Agamic iconography of Svacchandabhairava—his many weapons, ornaments of skulls and elephant skin, charnel-ground setting, and retinue—interpreting them as symbolic expressions of the dynamic powers of supreme, unconditioned consciousness (cidbhairava). The stotra illustrates the Trika and Krama synthesis of ritual visualization, aesthetic sentiment, and non-dual recognition (pratyabhijñā).
SA_GSP30_sa_kSemarAja-bhairavAnukaraNast.attribution: Attributed to Kṣemarāja, confirmed by the closing colophon (iti śrīmahāmāheśvarācāryaśrīkṣemarājaviracitaṃ bhairavānukaraṇastotraṃ samāptam) and scholarly consensus identifying him as the disciple of Abhinavagupta.
SA_GSP30_sa_kSemarAja-bhairavAnukaraNast.edition: Raniero Gnoli, 'Miscellanea Indica. 3. The Bhairavānukaraṇastotra by Kṣemarāja', East and West, New Series, no. 3 (September 1958), pp. 223–226.
SA_GSP30_sa_kSemarAja-bhairavAnukaraNast.coverage: complete — Complete text of 48 verses in āryā metre, preceded by an invocation (oṃ namaś cidbhairavāya) and concluding with the authorial colophon.

SA_GSP30_spandkau.title: Spandakārikā
SA_GSP30_spandkau.author: Vasugupta
SA_GSP30_spandkau.summary: The Spandakārikā is the primary doctrinal and meditative manual of the Spanda branch of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism, composed in the 9th century CE and attributed either to the sage Vasugupta or his disciple Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa. Across approximately 53 verses, the text expounds the principle of spanda—the dynamic, unceasing pulse and creative vibration of absolute Consciousness (Śiva-Śakti) that constitutes the true nature of both macrocosmic manifestation and microcosmic cognitive awareness. Rather than prescribing the complete suppression of mental and sensory operations, the text teaches that by sustained introspective mindfulness of the subtle throb underlying emotions, sense-perceptions, and transitions between mental states, the practitioner attains direct recognition of their essential divine autonomy (svātantrya) and mastery over the psychic energies (cakreśvaratva).
SA_GSP30_spandkau.attribution: Authorship has been disputed since the early medieval period. Kṣemarāja attributes the verses to Vasugupta, while others attribute them to Vasugupta's pupil Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa. Modern scholars (e.g. Alexis Sanderson) discuss Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa's authorship of the Spandakārikā.
SA_GSP30_spandkau.coverage: complete — All verses of the four-niḥṣyanda arrangement (25 + 7 + 19 + 2 = 53 numbered verses); the heading of the third niḥṣyanda is missing between 2.7 and 3.1. Verse counts of the work vary between recensions/commentators (51–53).
translations: Jaideva Singh, Spanda-Kārikās: The Divine Creative Pulsation, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1980. (English)

SA_GSP30_timudghu.title: Timirodghāṭana with Nirvāṇakārikā (incomplete manuscript transcription)
SA_GSP30_timudghu.summary: The Timirodghāṭana is an archaic Kaula Śaiva text preserved in a palm-leaf manuscript from Nepal (NGMPP A35/3). Framed as a dialogue with Bhairava, it teaches esoteric Śaiva doctrine, yoga, and rudraśakti, and is quoted by Abhinavagupta in the Parātriṃśikāvivaraṇa and Kṣemarāja in the Śivasūtravimarśinī. It is accompanied at the end of the transcription by the short Nirvāṇakārikā.
SA_GSP30_timudghu.attribution: Both works are scriptural/anonymous Śaiva esoteric compositions. The Timirodghāṭana is an archaic Kaula text framed as divine revelation of Bhairava, cited by Abhinavagupta in the Parātriṃśikāvivaraṇa and by Kṣemarāja (under the title Timirodghāṭa). The Nirvāṇakārikā is an anonymous short text found at the end of the codex.
SA_GSP30_timudghu.edition: Manuscript preserved in the National Archives, Kathmandu (NGMPP A35/3), Late Licchavi or early Kuṭila script on palmleaf, photocopy supplied by Diwakar Acharya; input by Somadeva Vasudeva for GRETIL.
SA_GSP30_timudghu.coverage: partial — Transcription of the palm-leaf MS NAK (NGMPP A35/3), starting at fol. 26r2. Timirodghāṭana with lacunae (the verse pīṭheśvaryo mahāghorā… quoted in PTV p. 201 and Śivasūtravimarśinī is noted in the GRETIL header as evidently on one of the missing folios), ending with the short Nirvāṇakārikā.

SA_GSP30_vamjanmu.title: Janmamaraṇavicāra
SA_GSP30_vamjanmu.author: Vāmadeva
SA_GSP30_vamjanmu.summary: The Janmamaraṇavicāra is a Kashmiri non-dual Śaiva philosophical treatise in mixed prose and verse by Bhaṭṭa Vāmadeva. Rooted in non-dual Śaiva philosophy, the work examines the cycle of transmigration, embryological development, and bodily death, interpreting empirical birth and dissolution in terms of supreme consciousness (Maheśvara). The treatise incorporates medical doctrine (referencing Suśruta) alongside Śaiva teachings.
SA_GSP30_vamjanmu.attribution: Attributed in the concluding colophon (segment 310: 'kṛtis tatrabhavanmahāmāheśvarācāryavaryaśrīmadbhaṭṭavāmadevasya') to Bhaṭṭa Vāmadeva.
SA_GSP30_vamjanmu.edition: Based on the edition by M.R. Shastri, Bombay: Nirnaya Sagar Press, 1918.
SA_GSP30_vamjanmu.coverage: complete — Complete work in prose and verse ending at segment 318, including concluding editorial praśasti stanzas mentioning Mukundarāma.

SA_GSP30_vamsbum_u.title: Svabodhodayamañjarī
SA_GSP30_vamsbum_u.author: Vāmanadatta
SA_GSP30_vamsbum_u.summary: The Svabodhodayamañjarī ('Inflorescence of the Arising of Innate Awareness') is a short Kashmiri Śaiva contemplative tract of 45 verses composed by Vāmanadatta, son of Harṣadatta. Cast in the style of the Vijñānabhairava, it presents methods for the effortless dissolution of conceptual thought (nirodha, vilaya) through ordinary perceptual and bodily experiences—such as eating, running, falling asleep, or attending to fading sounds and pleasant smells.
SA_GSP30_vamsbum_u.attribution: The final verse (v. 45) attributes the composition to Vāmanadatta, son of Harṣadatta (described as 'a lion in the forest of Mīmāṃsā', mīmāṃsāvanasiṃha). Modern scholars distinguish this author from other figures named Vāmanadatta.
SA_GSP30_vamsbum_u.edition: Torella, Raffaele: "The Svabodhodayamañjarī, or How to Suppress the Mind with No Effort". IN: R. Tsuchida and A. Wezler: Harānandalaharī. Studies in Honour of Prof. Minoru Hara on His Seventieth Birthday. Reinbeck: 2000, pp. 387-410.
SA_GSP30_vamsbum_u.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising all 45 verses (vv. 1–45), ending with the author's colophon verse.

SA_GSP30_vasspacu.title: Spandakārikā with Spandanirṇaya
SA_GSP30_vasspacu.author: Vasugupta, Kṣemarāja
SA_GSP30_vasspacu.summary: The Spandakārikā is a seminal verse treatise of the Spanda school of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism, expounding spanda—the dynamic, unceasing pulsation of supreme consciousness (Śiva/Śakti) that underlies all cosmic manifestation, maintenance, and dissolution. Composed across four sections (niḥṣyandas), the verses present a contemplative methodology for yogic practitioners to recognize this vibrating consciousness within all sensory, cognitive, and affective states, leading to liberation in this life (jīvanmukti). This e-text provides the complete text of the kārikās together with the Spandanirṇaya, the influential eleventh-century commentary by Abhinavagupta's disciple Kṣemarāja, which systematically interprets the work through the synthetic theological framework of Trika and Pratyabhijñā.
SA_GSP30_vasspacu.attribution: Authorship of the root verses (Spandakārikā) is traditionally debated between Vasugupta and Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa. The commentary Spandanirṇaya is by Kṣemarāja.
SA_GSP30_vasspacu.edition: The Spandakārikās of Vasugupta with the Nirṇaya by Kṣemarāja. Edited with preface, introduction and English translation by Madhusūdan Kaul Śāstrī. Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies (KSTS). Srinagar: Printed at the Kashmir Pratap Steam Press, 1925.
SA_GSP30_vasspacu.coverage: complete — Text of the Spandakārikā together with Kṣemarāja's Spandanirṇaya commentary.
translations: Kaul, Madhusūdan Śāstrī. The Spandakārikās of Vasugupta with the Nirṇaya by Kṣemarāja. Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies (KSTS). Srinagar: Kashmir Pratap Steam Press, 1925. (English)
Singh, Jaideva. Spanda-Kārikās: The Divine Creative Pulsation: The Kārikās and the Spanda-nirṇaya. Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1980. (English)
Dyczkowski, Mark S. G. The Stanzas on Vibration: The Spandakārikā with Four Commentaries. Albany: State University of New York Press, 1992. (English)

SA_GSP30_vatnsupu.title: Vātūlanāthasūtra with Vātūlanāthasūtravṛtti
SA_GSP30_vatnsupu.author: Vātūlanātha, Anantaśaktipāda
SA_GSP30_vatnsupu.summary: The Vātūlanāthasūtra consists of aphorisms framed as an oral revelation from the Yoginīs (Pīṭheśvarīs). It centers on unconditioned consciousness and the 'mahāsāhasavṛtti'. The accompanying classical Vṛtti by Anantaśaktipāda explains the text.
SA_GSP30_vatnsupu.attribution: The aphorisms are traditionally ascribed to Vātūlanātha as received from the Yoginīs (Pīṭheśvarīs). The Sanskrit commentary (Vṛtti) is composed by Anantaśaktipāda.
SA_GSP30_vatnsupu.edition: Madhusudana Kaul Sastri (ed.), Vatulanatha: Vatulanathasutra with the Vrtti of Anantasaktipada, Srinagar 1923 (Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies; 39).
SA_GSP30_vatnsupu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the sūtras along with the complete Vṛtti commentary of Anantaśaktipāda.
translations: Vātūlanāthasūtra avec le commentaire d'Anantaśaktipāda, French translation by Lilian Silburn. (French)

SA_GSP30_vijnbhau.title: Vijñānabhairava
SA_GSP30_vijnbhau.summary: The Vijñānabhairava is an influential scripture of the Trika and Kaula non-dual Śaiva traditions of Kashmir, presented as an esoteric dialogue between Bhairava and the goddess Bhairavī. Transcending external rituals and formal visualizations, Bhairava imparts 112 contemplative practices (dhāraṇās) intended to lead to direct experiential realization of non-dual consciousness. These techniques utilize breath movement, sensory and perceptual gateways, intervals between mental states, aesthetic absorption, and heightened affective experiences to induce spontaneous immersion (samāveśa) into the reality of Śiva.
SA_GSP30_vijnbhau.attribution: A revealed scripture traditionally regarded within Kashmir Śaivism as an essential extract or quintessence of the Rudrayāmala Tantra; it has no historical human author.
SA_GSP30_vijnbhau.coverage: complete — Complete root text consisting of 162 verses in this edition's numbering (spanning from the opening dialogue through verse 162: 'ity uktvānanditā devi ka.ṅthe lagnā śivasya tu').
translations: Singh, Jaideva, Vijñānabhairava or Divine Consciousness: A Treasury of 112 Types of Yoga, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1979. (English)
Silburn, Lilian, Le Vijñāna Bhairava: Texte traduit et commenté, 1961. (French)

SA_GSP31_bhgank_u.title: Gaṇakārikā with Ratnaṭīkā
SA_GSP31_bhgank_u.author: Haradatta, Bhāsarvajña
SA_GSP31_bhgank_u.summary: The Gaṇakārikā is a concise, eight-verse doctrinal manual of the Lākulīśa-Pāśupata Śaiva tradition, organizing its theology, ascetic practice, and soteriological path into nine sets or 'groups' (gaṇa) encompassing forty technical categories. Bhāsarvajña's commentary, the Ratnaṭīkā, provides an exposition of these terms, elucidating the duties of the religious preceptor (ācārya) and practitioner (sādhaka), yogic disciplines, and the ultimate attainment of duḥkhānta (the cessation of suffering).
SA_GSP31_bhgank_u.attribution: In the edition by C. D. Dalal, the work is edited as Gaṇakārikā of Ācārya Bhāsarvajña with the Ratnaṭīkā.
SA_GSP31_bhgank_u.edition: Chimanlal D. Dalal, ed., Gaṇakārikā of Ācārya Bhāsarvajña with the Ratnaṭīkā and four appendices, Gaekwad's Oriental Series, No. 15, Baroda: Oriental Institute, 1920 (reprinted 1966).
SA_GSP31_bhgank_u.coverage: complete — Text of the Gaṇakārikā and the Ratnaṭīkā commentary.

SA_GSP31_iskar_u.title: Sāṃkhyakārikā
SA_GSP31_iskar_u.author: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
SA_GSP31_iskar_u.summary: The Sāṃkhyakārikā (also known as Sāṃkhyasaptati), composed by Īśvarakṛṣṇa, is the foundational and earliest extant systematic treatise of the classical Sāṃkhya school of Indian philosophy. In 73 āryā verses, the text systematically expounds the dualistic metaphysics of pure conscious witness (puruṣa) and unmanifest primordial nature (prakṛti/pradhāna) along with its twenty-three evolutes. It details the three qualities (guṇas), the doctrine of pre-existent effect (satkāryavāda), epistemic means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), and the attainment of liberation (kaivalya) through discriminative knowledge (viveka).
SA_GSP31_iskar_u.attribution: The root verses are traditionally attributed to Īśvarakṛṣṇa. While the printed source edition includes the commentary Māṭharavṛtti by Māṭharācārya, the digital file extracts only the root kārikās.
SA_GSP31_iskar_u.edition: Viṣṇu Prasāda Śarmā (ed.), Sāṃkhyakārikā: Māṭharācāryaviracita-"Māṭharavṛtti"-sahitā, Varanasi: The Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series Office, 1970 (Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series, 296 [Work no. 56]).
SA_GSP31_iskar_u.coverage: complete — Root text concluding at verse 73 (72 āryā verses present: ISk_1–ISk_65, ISk_67–ISk_73; verse 66 is skipped/omitted in this digital file).

SA_GSP31_iskgaudu.title: Sāṃkhyakārikā with Gauḍapādabhāṣya
SA_GSP31_iskgaudu.author: Īśvarakṛṣṇa, Gauḍapāda
SA_GSP31_iskgaudu.summary: The Sāṃkhyakārikā of Īśvarakṛṣṇa is the foundational surviving treatise of classical dualist Sāṃkhya philosophy, outlining the twenty-five tattvas, the satkāryavāda theory of causation, and liberation through the discriminative insight separating conscious spirit (puruṣa) from primordial matter (prakṛti). The Gauḍapādabhāṣya is an early, accessible prose commentary providing word glosses, mythological illustrative stories, and cosmological expositions. The commentary covers verses 1 through 69, concluding with a colophon verse declaring the exposition of the seventy stanzas complete, followed by the concluding historical transmission kārikās (70–72).
SA_GSP31_iskgaudu.attribution: The root verses are attributed to Īśvarakṛṣṇa. The commentary is traditionally ascribed to Gauḍapāda.
SA_GSP31_iskgaudu.edition: The Sankhya Karika. By Iswara Krishna; Translated from the Sanscrit by Henry Thomas Colebrooke, also the Bhashya, or, Commentary of Gaudapada; Translated, and Illustrated by an Original Comment, by Horace Hayman Wilson. Bombay: Tookaram Tatya, 1887. [Karikas arranged according to the ed. by T. G. Mainkar: Samkhyakarika, with the commentary of Gaudapada, Poona: Oriental Book Agency, 1972.]
SA_GSP31_iskgaudu.coverage: complete — Contains the complete Sāṃkhyakārikā (72 kārikās) and Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya on kārikās 1–69, concluding with the commentator's colophon verse and the final three uncommented transmission kārikās (70–72), exactly matching the standard Gauḍapādabhāṣya manuscript tradition.
translations: Colebrooke, Henry Thomas & Horace Hayman Wilson, The Sankhya Karika. By Iswara Krishna; Translated from the Sanscrit by Henry Thomas Colebrooke, also the Bhashya, or, Commentary of Gaudapada; Translated, and Illustrated by an Original Comment, by Horace Hayman Wilson. Bombay: Tookaram Tatya, 1887. (English)
Mainkar, Trimbak Govind, The Sāṃkhyakārikā of Īśvarakṛṣṇa with the Commentary of Gauḍapāda. Poona: Oriental Book Agency, 1964; 2nd ed. 1972. (English)

SA_GSP31_isvskaru.title: Sāṃkhyakārikā
SA_GSP31_isvskaru.author: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
SA_GSP31_isvskaru.summary: The Sāṃkhyakārikā of Īśvarakṛṣṇa (c. 4th–5th century CE) is the foundational and most authoritative classical treatise of the Sāṃkhya darśana. In approximately 72–73 āryā stanzas, it systematically expounds the dualistic metaphysics of unmanifest and manifest primordial nature (avyakta- and vyakta-prakṛti) alongside the multiplicity of pure conscious subjects (puruṣa). The text establishes the satkāryavāda theory of causation, analyzes the triad of guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas), charts the 25 evolutionary principles (tattvas) and psychological schema (buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas, indriyas, tanmātras, mahābhūtas), and teaches that discriminative insight (vivekakhyāti) dissolves the misidentification of consciousness with nature to achieve final isolation and liberation (kaivalya).
SA_GSP31_isvskaru.attribution: Attributed to Īśvarakṛṣṇa; associated with Chinese translation Taishō 2137 (translated by Paramārtha).
SA_GSP31_isvskaru.edition: Īśvarakṛṣṇa: Sāṃkhyakārikā, input and collation by Ferenc Ruzsa (1998), utilizing editions: Solomon (1973: V1, V2), Takakusu (1904: T), Wilson (1837: G), Kumar & Bhargava (1990-92: Y), Sharma & Vangiya (1994: M & J), Bhattacarya (1967/1976: V), Lokesh Chandra (1982: K), Garbe (1943: B), Deussen (1922: D), Sinha (1915: S).
SA_GSP31_isvskaru.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Sāṃkhyakārikā with variant readings collated by Ferenc Ruzsa from published editions and manuscripts, followed by an alphabetical word index.
translations: Junjiro Takakusu, 'La Sāṃkhyakārikā étudiée à la lumière de sa version chinoise (II)', Bulletin de l'École française d'Extrême-Orient 4 (1904), pp. 978–1064. (French)
Richard Garbe, Der Mondschein der Sāṃkhya-Wahrheit, Vācaspatimiçra's Sāṃkhya-tattva-kaumudī, München, 1892. (German)

SA_GSP31_kavsttvu.title: Sāṃkhyatattvapradīpa
SA_GSP31_kavsttvu.author: Kavirājayati
SA_GSP31_kavsttvu.summary: A concise independent manual (prakaraṇa) of the Sāṃkhya system by Kavirājayati, composed for students who find the study of extensive classical texts too laborious. The treatise outlines the threefold suffering (duḥkhatraya) and the means of its absolute elimination via discriminating knowledge (vivekakhyāti), the twenty-five principles (tattvas), causality (satkāryavāda), and the mechanism of cosmic evolution and individual liberation. It quotes Vācaspatimiśra's Tattvakaumudī.
SA_GSP31_kavsttvu.attribution: The colophon attributes the work to Kavirājayati, disciple of Vaikuṇṭha: 'iti śrīmatparamahaṃsaparivrājakācāryapūjyapādaśrīvaikuṇṭhaśiṣyayatikavirājayatiprakāśitaḥ sāṃkhyatattvapradīpaḥ samāptaḥ'. GRETIL notes his alternate name as Kavirājagiri.
SA_GSP31_kavsttvu.edition: Vindhyesvari Prasada Dvivedin in: Sāṃkhyasaṃgrahaḥ (Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series, 50, pp. 151-178)
SA_GSP31_kavsttvu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the treatise from the opening maṅgala verse to the concluding colophon.

SA_GSP31_kestprau.title: Sāṃkhyatattvapradīpikā
SA_GSP31_kestprau.author: Keśava
SA_GSP31_kestprau.summary: The Sāṃkhyatattvapradīpikā (or Sāṃkhyārthatattvapradīpikā) is an introductory compendium of Sāṃkhya philosophy by Keśava, son of Sadānanda, following the system of Vijñānabhikṣu. It systematically defines prakṛti, puruṣa, and the evolutes before analyzing cognition and the eight states of the intellect (bhāvas). It concludes by demonstrating how knowledge alone frees the spirit from embodiment.
SA_GSP31_kestprau.attribution: In the second introductory stanza, the author specifies his lineage as the son of Sadānanda and grandson of Bhaṭṭa Keśava ('bhaṭṭakeśavasambhūtasadānandātmajaḥ sudhīḥ / yajurvit keśavaḥ prāha...').
SA_GSP31_kestprau.edition: Vindhyeśvarī Prasāda Dvivedin in: Sāṃkhyasaṅgrahaḥ (Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series, 50,2 [fasc. 286], pp. 141–149)
SA_GSP31_kestprau.coverage: complete — Complete short treatise comprising introductory verses, prose exposition, and concluding verse with the colophon 'iti sāṃkhyārthatattvapradīpikā samāptā'.

SA_GSP31_samkhsuu.title: Sāṃkhyasūtra with Tattvasamāsa
SA_GSP31_samkhsuu.author: Kapila
SA_GSP31_samkhsuu.summary: The Sāṃkhyasūtra (or Sāṃkhyapravacanasūtra) is an aphoristic treatise in six adhyāyas articulating Sāṃkhya metaphysics, traditionally attributed to Kapila. The first three books expound core ontological doctrines (puruṣa, prakṛti, the evolutes, and the mechanics of bondage and liberation), the fourth provides illustrative parables and allegories, and the final two refute rival philosophical schools and recapitulate the system. Appended to the root text in this file is the Tattvasamāsa, a concise mnemonic compendium detailing the twenty-five tattvas and auxiliary categories of Sāṃkhya, arranged here in two sections: Tattvapāda and Prakīrṇapāda.
SA_GSP31_samkhsuu.attribution: Both works are traditionally attributed to Kapila.
SA_GSP31_samkhsuu.coverage: complete — Complete. Sāṃkhyasūtra in six adhyāyas (KapSs 1.1–6.21+), each followed by topic headings and pū/si tags; then the Tattvasamāsa ending nāsau punaḥ trividhena duḥkhenābhibhūyate nābhibhīyate (Tats 2.18).
translations: Ballantyne, James R. (1885). (English)
Garbe, Richard. The Sāṃkhya-Pravacana-Bhāṣya. Abhandlungen für die Kunde des Morgenlandes 9.3. Leipzig: 1889. (German)

SA_GSP31_sparibhu.title: Sāṃkhyaparibhāṣā
SA_GSP31_sparibhu.summary: The Sāṃkhyaparibhāṣā is a late, syncretistic definitional manual composed in mixed prose and verse. Although titled as a Sāṃkhya work, it integrates Sāṃkhya cosmological categories (the twenty-five tattvas) with Advaita Vedānta concepts—explicitly citing the classical Advaita guru lineage from Gauḍapāda to Śaṅkara and the fourfold spiritual prerequisites (sādhanacatuṣṭaya)—as well as elements of Yoga and Haṭhayoga praxis. The work survives in a single fragmentary manuscript witness edited by Vindhyeśvarīprasāda Dvivedin.
SA_GSP31_sparibhu.attribution: The treatise is anonymous. In his concluding editorial footnote, Vindhyeśvarīprasāda Dvivedin states that the edition was prepared from a single manuscript.
SA_GSP31_sparibhu.edition: Vindhyesvari Prasada Dvivedin (ed.), Sāṃkhyasaṃgrahaḥ (Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series, 50), pp. 197–224.
SA_GSP31_sparibhu.coverage: complete — Complete text as published in Dvivedin's edition (pp. 197–224), including the editor's concluding footnote note. Dvivedin noted that the text in the unique exemplar appears damaged or broken off ('grantho 'pi khaṇḍita ivābhāti').

SA_GSP31_stk.title: Sāṃkhyakārikā with Sāṃkhyatattvakaumudī
SA_GSP31_stk.author: Īśvarakṛṣṇa, Vācaspatimiśra
SA_GSP31_stk.summary: The Sāṃkhyatattvakaumudī by Vācaspatimiśra is a commentary on Īśvarakṛṣṇa's Sāṃkhyakārikā. It expounds the classical Sāṃkhya philosophical system verse by verse, covering epistemology (the three pramāṇas: perception, inference, and verbal testimony), satkāryavāda, the twenty-five principles (tattvas), the operation of the three guṇas, and the dualism between insentient matter (prakṛti) and puruṣa.
SA_GSP31_stk.attribution: The root verses are attributed to Īśvarakṛṣṇa and the commentary to the Maithila Brāhmaṇa Vācaspatimiśra (placed c. 9th century CE). The English translation and introduction are by Babu Govinda-dasa and Ganganatha Jha.
SA_GSP31_stk.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Sāṃkhyakārikā with the Sāṃkhyatattvakaumudī commentary, accompanied by an English translation and introduction.
translations: Garbe, Richard (trans.), Der Mondschein der Sâmkhya-Wahrheit, München, 1891. (German)

SA_GSP31_tatsuvru.title: Tattvasamāsa with Tattvasamāsasūtravṛtti
SA_GSP31_tatsuvru.summary: The Tattvasamāsasūtravṛtti (or Kramadīpikā, cf. final verse) is an anonymous commentary on the Tattvasamāsa, an abstract of Sāṃkhya philosophy. Framed as a dialogue in which the sage Kapila instructs a brāhmaṇa overcome by threefold suffering, the text explains the Sāṃkhya principles and doctrines.
SA_GSP31_tatsuvru.attribution: The root sūtras of the Tattvasamāsa are traditionally attributed to the sage Kapila, as depicted in the frame dialogue. The prose commentary, titled internally as the Kramadīpikā in its penultimate verse, is anonymous.
SA_GSP31_tatsuvru.edition: Vindhyesvari Prasada Dvivedin in: Sāmkhyasaṅgrahaḥ (Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series, 50,1 [fasc. 286], pp. 117-140)
SA_GSP31_tatsuvru.coverage: complete — Text of the Tattvasamāsa along with the prose commentary Kramadīpikā, concluding with the verse specifying an extent of 300 anuṣṭubh verses (ślokaśatatrayam) and the final colophon.

SA_GSP31_tattvmiu.title: Tattvamīmāṃsā
SA_GSP31_tattvmiu.author: Kṛṣṇamitra
SA_GSP31_tattvmiu.summary: The Tattvamīmāṃsā is a late classical Sāṃkhya prose treatise composed around 1800 CE by Ācārya Kṛṣṇamitra. Structuring its inquiry around the classical framework of the Sāṃkhyakārikā, the work opens by establishing the necessity of philosophical inquiry due to the threefold misery (duḥkhatraya) and refuting both mundane and ritualistic Vedic remedies. It methodically expounds the twenty-five principles (tattvas) divided into primordial source (mūlaprakṛti), evolutes that produce further principles, mere modifications, and the transcendent conscious self (puruṣa), concluding with an exposition of the eight fundamental dispositions (bhāvas) and liberation through discriminative insight ('nāsmi na me nāham').
SA_GSP31_tattvmiu.attribution: The colophon attributes the work to Ācārya Kṛṣṇamitra, grandson of Devīdatta and son of Rāmasevaka (corrupted in print/e-text to 'gamasevakasūnu'). Kṛṣṇamitra (fl. ca. 1800) authored commentaries on Vyākaraṇa (such as the Kuñcikā on Nāgeśa's Mañjūṣā) and philosophical treatises (including Potter, text 18 under author Kṛṣṇamitra: Tattvamīmāṃsā).
SA_GSP31_tattvmiu.edition: Vindhyesvari Prasada Dvivedin in: Sāmkhyasaṅgrahaḥ Varanasi: The Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series Office 1920 (Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series, 50,1 [fasc. 286], pp. 179-196)
SA_GSP31_tattvmiu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the treatise across 264 segments, running from the introductory discussion of duḥkha to the closing author colophon.

SA_GSP31_tsc_bhau.title: Tattvasamāsa with Tattvayāthārthyadīpana
SA_GSP31_tsc_bhau.author: Bhāvāgaṇeśa
SA_GSP31_tsc_bhau.summary: The Tattvayāthārthyadīpana ('Illumination of the True Nature of the Principles') is a commentary by Bhāvāgaṇeśa Dīkṣita on the Tattvasamāsa, a concise 25-sūtra digest of Sāṃkhya philosophy. Following the theistic and Vedāntic harmonizing tendencies of his preceptor Vijñānabhikṣu, Bhāvāgaṇeśa synthesizes Sāṃkhya ontology with Vaiṣṇava theism and bhakti. The work systematically expounds the primary principles (tattva), cosmic evolution (saṃcara) and dissolution (pratisaṃcara), and the means of spiritual release.
SA_GSP31_tsc_bhau.attribution: The commentary Tattvayāthārthyadīpana was composed by Bhāvāgaṇeśa, son of Bhāvā Viśvanātha Dīkṣita and disciple of Vijñānabhikṣu.
SA_GSP31_tsc_bhau.edition: Vindhyeśvarīprasāda Dvivedin in: Sāṃkhyasaṅgrahaḥ (Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series, 50,1 [fasc. 246], pp. 51–92).
SA_GSP31_tsc_bhau.coverage: complete — Contains the full root text in 25 sūtras (Tats_1 to Tats_25) along with the complete commentary Tattvayāthārthyadīpana, from the opening maṅgala verses to the concluding verses and final colophon.

SA_GSP31_tsc_simu.title: Tattvasamāsa with Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
SA_GSP31_tsc_simu.author: Kṣemānanda
SA_GSP31_tsc_simu.summary: The Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana is a commentary on the Tattvasamāsa, an abstract of Sāṃkhya philosophy in 25 sūtras. Composed by Ṣimānanda (Kṣemānanda), son of Raghunandana and a Kānyakubja dvija resident in Iṣṭikāpura, the text expounds fundamental ontological categories including the eight prakṛtis, sixteen vikāras, puruṣa, the three guṇas, and liberation.
SA_GSP31_tsc_simu.attribution: The commentary explicitly names its author in verses 1 and 5 and the concluding colophon as Ṣimānanda (son of Raghunandana, a Kānyakubja Brahmin of Iṣṭikāpura), identified also as Kṣemānanda.
SA_GSP31_tsc_simu.edition: Vindhyesvari Prasada Dvivedin in: Sāmkhyasaṅgrahaḥ (Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series, 50,1 [fasc. 286], pp. 1-49)
SA_GSP31_tsc_simu.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all 25 sūtras of the Tattvasamāsa alongside Kṣemānanda's full commentary, starting with introductory verses 1–5 and ending with the complete work colophon.

SA_GSP31_tsc_vivu.title: Tattvasamāsa with Sāṃkhyasūtravivaraṇa
SA_GSP31_tsc_vivu.summary: The Sāṃkhyasūtravivaraṇa (also titled Kāpilasūtravṛtti in its closing colophon) is an anonymous post-classical commentary on the Tattvasamāsa, a concise 23-sūtra mnemonic compendium of orthodox Sāṃkhya topics traditionally ascribed to Kapila. The commentary glosses each sūtra in lucid prose, defining the eight creative causes (aṣṭau prakṛtayaḥ), sixteen modifications (ṣoḍaśa vikārāḥ), spirit (puruṣa), the three guṇas, cosmic emergence and dissolution (sañcara and pratisañcara), down to the three valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa). It represents a concise late scholastic handbook expounding the classical Sāṃkhya dualist ontology and epistemology.
SA_GSP31_tsc_vivu.attribution: The root work, Tattvasamāsa (preserved here in a 23-sūtra recension), is traditionally attributed to the sage Kapila (and hence termed Kāpilasūtra in the commentary's colophon). The commentary, Sāṃkhyasūtravivaraṇa (or Kāpilasūtravṛtti), is anonymous in the printed edition.
SA_GSP31_tsc_vivu.edition: Vindhyesvari Prasada Dvivedin in: Samkhyasangrahah (Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series, 50,2 [fasc. 286], pp. 105-116)
SA_GSP31_tsc_vivu.coverage: complete — Complete text of both works: all 23 sūtras of the Tattvasamāsa accompanied by the full Sāṃkhyasūtravivaraṇa, including the opening verse, introductory sentence, closing verse, and concluding colophon (iti sāṃkhyasūtravivaraṇākhyā kāpilasūtravṛttiḥ samāptā).

SA_GSP31_ttssarvu.title: Tattvasamāsa with Sarvopakāriṇī
SA_GSP31_ttssarvu.summary: The Sarvopakāriṇī ('The All-Benefiting Gloss') is a concise, anonymous Sanskrit commentary on the Tattvasamāsa (also called Samāsasūtra or Kāpilasūtra), an ancient mnemonic outline of classical Sāṃkhya philosophy. It comments systematically on the 22 sūtras of this recension, expounding the 25 principles (tattvas), the forward and reverse evolutions of the guṇas (sañcāra and pratisañcara), the three kinds of suffering, the sources of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and the nature of liberation (mokṣa). Its opening lines preserve a notable scholastic tradition asserting that this 22-sūtra work represents the original seed of the system taught by Kapila as an avatāra of Nārāyaṇa, in contrast to the six-chapter Sāṃkhyasūtra composed by Kapila as an avatāra of Vaiśvānara.
SA_GSP31_ttssarvu.attribution: The root work Tattvasamāsa is traditionally attributed to the legendary sage Kapila. The Sarvopakāriṇī's introductory passage distinguishes this 22-sūtra summary (revealed by Kapila as an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa) from the six-chapter Sāṃkhyasūtra (revealed by Kapila as an incarnation of Vaiśvānara). The commentator does not give their personal name, referring to themself in verse 2 merely as 'guṇavaśaṃvadaḥ'.
SA_GSP31_ttssarvu.edition: Vindhyesvari Prasada Dvivedin, in: Sāṃkhyasaṃgrahaḥ (Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series, 50,1 [fasc. 286], pp. 93-104)
SA_GSP31_ttssarvu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the 22-sūtra recension of the Tattvasamāsa together with the entire Sarvopakāriṇī commentary, including two mangala verses and the closing colophon ('iti sarvopakāriṇī saṃkṣiptakāpilasūtravṛttiḥ samāptā').

SA_GSP31_tttvsamu.title: Tattvasamāsa
SA_GSP31_tttvsamu.summary: The Tattvasamāsa ('Compendium of Principles') is a very brief mnemonic outline consisting of between 23 and 27 aphorisms (sūtras) that summarize the central ontological, cosmological, and psychological categories of classical Sāṃkhya philosophy. It lists the fundamental categories including the eight material causes (prakṛti), the sixteen evolutes (vikāra), the conscious subject (puruṣa), the three constituents (guṇa), cosmic evolution and dissolution, and the faculties and conditions governing bondage and release. Traditionally attributed to the mythic sage Kapila, the surviving text represents a medieval scholastic syllabus that served as the basis for several commentaries, such as those by Kṣemānanda, Bhāvāgaṇeśa, and the author of the Kramadīpikā.
SA_GSP31_tttvsamu.attribution: Traditionally ascribed to the sage Kapila.
SA_GSP31_tttvsamu.edition: Vindhyesvari Prasada Dvivedin (ed.), Sāmkhyasaṅgrahaḥ (Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series, 50,1 [fasc. 286], pp. 1-49); cf. also reprint/ed. Dvivedī 1969.
SA_GSP31_tttvsamu.coverage: complete — Complete sūtra text presented in four alternative textual recensions / sūtra divisions extracted from four commentaries in the source edition: (1) recension of 25 sūtras following Kṣemānanda's (Ṣimānanda's) Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana; (2) recension of 25 sūtras following Bhāvāgaṇeśa's Tattvayāthārthyadīpana; (3) recension of 23 sūtras following the anonymous Sāṃkhyasūtravivaraṇa; (4) recension of 27 sūtras arranged in two pādas (Tattvapāda, 9 sūtras; Prakīrṇapāda, 18 sūtras) following the Sarvopakāriṇī / Kramadīpikā commentary tradition.
translations: E. Roer, 'Review of a lecture on the Samkhya philosophy embracing the text of the Tattvasamasa by Dr. J. R. Ballantyne'. (English)
Nandalal Sinha (trans.), The Samkhya Philosophy: Containing the Tattvasamasa and Sāmkhyākārikā with other texts, Allahabad: Panini Office, 1915. (English)
Megumu Honda, 'タトヴァ・サマーサ(真理集成)解読' [Japanese translation of the Tattvasamāsa], Tōkai Bukkyō (東海仏教), 1959-06-01. (Japanese)

SA_GSP31_vijsamsu.title: Sāṅkhyasāra
SA_GSP31_vijsamsu.author: Vijñānabhikṣu
SA_GSP31_vijsamsu.summary: The Sāṅkhyasāra is an independent philosophical manual (prakaraṇa) of the Sāṅkhya system composed by the 16th-century synthesizer Vijñānabhikṣu. Structured into two parts—a Pūrvabhāga of four paricchedas and an Uttarabhāga of seven paricchedas—it sets out the nature of liberation (puruṣārtha), discriminative insight (vivekakhyāti), the material evolutes (prakṛti and tattvas), puruṣa, and the essential distinctions between self and non-self. The work encapsulates the core positions elaborated in his larger Sāṅkhyapravacanabhāṣya, harmonizing classic Sāṅkhya dualism with theistic elements and Pātañjala Yoga.
SA_GSP31_vijsamsu.attribution: Vijñānabhikṣu names himself in the opening verses (kārikā 2: 'sāṅkhyasāraviveko 'to vijñānena prapañcyate'; kārikā 4: 'sāṅkhyabhāṣye prakṛtyādeḥ svarūpaṃ vistarān mayā / proktaṃ tasmāt tadapyatra saṅkṣepādeva vakṣyate') and throughout the pariccheda colophons ('iti śrīvijñānabhikṣuviracite sāṅkhyasāre...').
SA_GSP31_vijsamsu.edition: Fitzedward Hall, ed., Sāṅkhyasāra, Bibliotheca Indica, Calcutta: Asiatic Society, 1862.
SA_GSP31_vijsamsu.coverage: complete — Complete text in two main divisions: Pūrvabhāga (4 paricchedas) and Uttarabhāga (7 paricchedas), concluding with the colophon 'iti sāṅkhyasārasyottarabhāgaḥ / sāṅkhyasārākhyaṃ prakaraṇaṃ samāptam'.

SA_GSP31_yuktdipu.title: Sāṃkhyakārikā with Yuktidīpikā
SA_GSP31_yuktdipu.author: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
SA_GSP31_yuktdipu.summary: The Yuktidīpikā is an extensive commentary on Īśvarakṛṣṇa's Sāṃkhyakārikā. Arranged into eleven daily lessons (āhnikas) grouped into four topical sections (prakaraṇas), it defends classical Sāṃkhya metaphysics, satkāryavāda, and epistemology against sharp critiques from opposing schools. The commentary preserves references to earlier Sāṃkhya masters (such as Vindhyavāsin and Pañcaśikha) and related traditions.
SA_GSP31_yuktdipu.attribution: The Yuktidīpikā is an anonymous commentary. A modern/scribal note appended to the final colophon in some manuscripts queries whether it is the work of Vācaspatimiśra ('kṛtiriyaṃ śrīvācaspatimiśrāṇām (?)'). The root verses (Sāṃkhyakārikā) are authored by Īśvarakṛṣṇa.
SA_GSP31_yuktdipu.edition: Shiv Kumar and D.N. Bhargava (eds.), Yuktidīpikā, 2 vols., Delhi, 1990–1992.
SA_GSP31_yuktdipu.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all 72 verses of the Sāṃkhyakārikā along with the full Yuktidīpikā commentary divided into 4 prakaraṇas and 11 āhnikas, including opening and concluding benedictory and summary verses.

SA_GSP32_paddhs_u.title: Padārthadharmasaṃgraha
SA_GSP32_paddhs_u.author: Praśastapāda
SA_GSP32_paddhs_u.summary: The Padārthadharmasaṃgraha (commonly known as the Praśastapādabhāṣya) is the definitive classical treatise of the Vaiśeṣika philosophical school, composed by Praśastapāda (c. 6th century CE). Rather than providing a sūtra-by-sūtra commentary on Kaṇāda's Vaiśeṣikasūtra, the work organizes Vaiśeṣika ontology topically into six categories (padārthas: dravya, guṇa, karma, sāmānya, viśeṣa, and samavāya), articulating their shared and distinctive attributes. It systematically incorporates advanced epistemology, natural philosophy, and atomistic theory, establishing the standard framework commented upon by Vyomaśiva, Śrīdhara, and Udayana.
SA_GSP32_paddhs_u.attribution: Praśastapāda (c. 6th century CE) composed the Padārthadharmasaṃgraha. Although traditionally termed a bhāṣya on Kaṇāda's Vaiśeṣikasūtra, it is an independent, foundational treatise of classical Vaiśeṣika ontology and epistemology rather than a line-by-line commentary.
SA_GSP32_paddhs_u.edition: V. P. Dvivedin (ed.), The Prasastapadabhasya with Commentary Nyayakandali of Sridhara, Sri Garbi Dass Oriental Ser., 13, Delhi: Sri Satguru Publications [Reprint of the edition Benares 1895, Vizianagram Sanskrit Series; 6].
SA_GSP32_paddhs_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Padārthadharmasaṃgraha from the initial maṅgalācaraṇa through to the concluding colophon and Kaṇāda-stuti (pp. 1–326 of the reference edition). Only Praśastapāda's bhāṣya is keyed; Śrīdhara's accompanying commentary Nyāyakandalī in the printed edition is omitted.
translations: Ganganatha Jha (tr.), The Padarthadharmasamgraha of Prasastapada with the Nyayakandali of Sridhara, Reprint from The Pandit, Banaras, 1916. (English)

SA_GSP32_vaisessu.title: Vaiśeṣikasūtra
SA_GSP32_vaisessu.author: Kaṇāda
SA_GSP32_vaisessu.summary: The Vaiśeṣikasūtra is the foundational treatise of the Vaiśeṣika school of classical Indian philosophy, traditionally attributed to Maharṣi Kaṇāda. Organised into ten adhyāyas of two āhnikas each, it elaborates an atomistic and pluralistic realist ontology structured around fundamental categories (padārtha): substance (dravya), quality (guṇa), motion/action (karman), generality (sāmānya), particularity (viśeṣa), and inherence (samavāya). The work investigates physical causation, the elementary constituents of matter, and perception and inference, maintaining that spiritual liberation (niḥśreyasa) arises from discriminative knowledge of reality induced by dharma.
SA_GSP32_vaisessu.attribution: The root aphorisms are traditionally ascribed to Kaṇāda.
SA_GSP32_vaisessu.coverage: complete — Complete sūtrapāṭha of the Upaskāra (vulgate) recension: 10 adhyāyas × 2 āhnikas, 369 numbered sūtras (KVs 1,1.1–10,2.9). Per-āhnika counts match the Upaskāra numbering (1.1: 31, 1.2: 17, 2.1: 31, 2.2: 37, … 10.2: 9) except 7.2, which has 27 sūtras where the usual Upaskāra count (total c. 370) has 28 — one sūtra appears to be missing or merged.

SA_GSP32_vaissu1u.title: Vaiśeṣikasūtra
SA_GSP32_vaissu1u.author: Kaṇāda
SA_GSP32_vaissu1u.summary: The Vaiśeṣikasūtra, attributed to Kaṇāda, is the foundational aphoristic treatise of the Vaiśeṣika school of Indian philosophy. The text develops an ontology dividing categories into substance (dravya), quality (guṇa), action (karman), universal (sāmānya), particularity (viśeṣa), and inherence (samavāya).
SA_GSP32_vaissu1u.coverage: complete — Complete text of all ten adhyāyas (ending with KVs_10.21), accompanied by variant readings collated from other recensions and commentaries.

SA_GSP32_vaissutika.title: Vaiśeṣikasūtra with Vaiśeṣikasūtravṛtti
SA_GSP32_vaissutika.author: Kaṇāda, Candrānanda
SA_GSP32_vaissutika.summary: The Vaiśeṣikasūtra is the foundational text of the Vaiśeṣika school of classical Indian philosophy. Candrānanda's running commentary (Vaiśeṣikasūtravṛtti) is an early commentary on the sūtras edited by Muni Jambūvijaya in 1961.
SA_GSP32_vaissutika.attribution: Kaṇāda is the traditional author of the Vaiśeṣikasūtras. Candrānanda is named as the commentator in the closing verse (10.21: 'ānandayati sa vṛttiṃ candrānando vyadhādetām').
SA_GSP32_vaissutika.edition: Muni Jambūvijaya (ed.), Vaiśeṣikasūtra of Kaṇāda with the Commentary of Candrānanda, Gaekwad's Oriental Series 136, Baroda: Oriental Institute, M.S. University of Baroda, 1961.
SA_GSP32_vaissutika.coverage: complete — Contains the text of the Vaiśeṣikasūtra alongside Candrānanda's commentary, from 1.1.1 to 10.21.

SA_GSP32_vvmanmhu.title: Mānamanohara
SA_GSP32_vvmanmhu.author: Vādivāgīśvara
SA_GSP32_vvmanmhu.summary: The Mānamanohara of Vādivāgīśvara is an independent treatise of the Vaiśeṣika school. Setting out to vanquish rival disputants, the work systematically presents and defends Vaiśeṣika ontology and epistemology, featuring proofs for the existence of God (īśvarasiddhi), indivisible atoms, and other categories, while defending category doctrines against rival schools such as Mīmāṃsā, Advaita Vedānta, and Buddhists. The work is cited by later authors such as Citsukha.
SA_GSP32_vvmanmhu.attribution: Authored by Vādivāgīśvara, explicitly identified in introductory verse 2 as the son of Vāgīśvarācārya (vāgīśvarācāryasutena vādivāgīśvareṇa).
SA_GSP32_vvmanmhu.edition: Swami Yogīndrānanda (ed.), Mānamanohara of Vādivāgīśvara, Varanasi: Ṣaḍdarśanaprakāśana Pratiṣṭhāna, 1973.
SA_GSP32_vvmanmhu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the treatise from the opening maṅgala stanzas to the concluding colophon.

SA_GSP33_vedanta-desika.title: Dramiḍopaniṣattātparyaratnāvalī with Dramiḍopaniṣatsāra (selected verses)
SA_GSP33_vedanta-desika.author: Vedānta Deśika
SA_GSP33_vedanta-desika.summary: The Dramiḍopaniṣattātparyaratnāvalī is a Sanskrit work by Vedānta Deśika setting out the purport of the Tiruvāymoḻi. Together with the companion work Dramiḍopaniṣatsāra, it expounds the teachings of the Tamil hymns in Sanskrit.
SA_GSP33_vedanta-desika.coverage: partial — Selected verses of Dramiḍopaniṣattātparyaratnāvalī and Dramiḍopaniṣatsāra.
translations: R. Rangachari (ed., tr.), Dramidopanishad Tatparya Ratnavali and Sara. Madras, 1974. (English)

SA_GSP33_bbdip11u.title: Brahmasūtra with Brahmasūtrabhāṣya and Brahmasūtrabhāṣyadīpikā (adhyāya 1, pāda 1)
SA_GSP33_bbdip11u.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Madhva, Jagannāthatīrtha
SA_GSP33_bbdip11u.summary: This text contains the opening quarter (adhyāya 1, pāda 1) of the Brahmasūtra according to the Dvaita (Mādhva) tradition of Vedānta, presenting Bādarāyaṇa's aphorisms together with Madhva's (Ānandatīrtha's) fundamental Brahmasūtrabhāṣya and Jagannāthatīrtha's sub-commentary (Brahmasūtrabhāṣyadīpikā). The section articulates the Dvaita hermeneutic foundation of the Samanvayādhyāya, establishing Lord Viṣṇu (Nārāyaṇa) as full of all perfections and devoid of all defects, and demonstrating that all Vedic revelation ultimately and primarily designates Him.
SA_GSP33_bbdip11u.attribution: The Dvaita Brahmasūtrabhāṣya is by Madhva (Ānandatīrtha). The sub-commentary Brahmasūtrabhāṣyadīpikā is by Jagannāthatīrtha, disciple of Raghunāthatīrtha.
SA_GSP33_bbdip11u.edition: Gopālakṛṣṇācārya: Śrīmad-Brahmasūtrāṇi, Śrīmaj-Jagannātha-yati-kṛta-ṭippaṇī-saṃvalita-Śrīman-Madhva-Bhāṣya-sametāni, Madras: The Grove Press 1900
SA_GSP33_bbdip11u.coverage: partial — Contains Adhyāya 1, Pāda 1 with the corresponding Bhāṣya of Madhva and Dīpikā of Jagannāthatīrtha.

SA_GSP33_bbdip12u.title: Brahmasūtra with Brahmasūtrabhāṣya and Brahmasūtrabhāṣyadīpikā (chapter 1, pāda 2)
SA_GSP33_bbdip12u.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Madhva, Jagannāthayati
SA_GSP33_bbdip12u.summary: This text contains the second quarter (pāda 2) of the first chapter (samanvayādhyāya) of the Brahmasūtra, accompanied by Madhva's Brahmasūtrabhāṣya and Jagannāthayati's Brahmasūtrabhāṣyadīpikā. It interprets ambiguous Upaniṣadic passages attributing traits such as being all-pervading (sarvagata), the consumer/destroyer (attṛ), the person within the eye and sun (antara), the inner controller (antaryāmin), and the cosmic fire (vaiśvānara), demonstrating in accordance with Dvaita Vedānta that they refer exclusively to Viṣṇu rather than the individual soul or insentient matter. Jagannāthayati's sub-commentary unpacks Madhva's concise argumentation and scriptural citations.
SA_GSP33_bbdip12u.attribution: The foundational aphorisms (Brahmasūtra) are traditionally attributed to Bādarāyaṇa (Vyāsa). The Dvaita commentary (Brahmasūtrabhāṣya) is by Madhvācārya (Ānandatīrtha). The sub-commentary (Brahmasūtrabhāṣyadīpikā / Ṭippaṇī) is by Jagannāthayati, identified in the colophon as a disciple of Raghunāthatīrtha.
SA_GSP33_bbdip12u.edition: Gopālakṛṣṇācārya (ed.), Śrīmad-Brahmasūtrāṇi, Śrīmaj-Jagannātha-yati-kṛta-ṭippaṇī-saṃvalita-Śrīman-Madhva-Bhāṣya-sametāni, Madras: The Grove Press 1900.
SA_GSP33_bbdip12u.coverage: partial — Contains Adhyāya 1, Pāda 2 only (adhikaraṇas 1–7: sarvagatatvādhikaraṇa through vaiśvānarādhikaraṇa), with integrated sūtra, bhāṣya, and dīpikā.

SA_GSP33_bbdip13u.title: Brahmasūtra with Brahmasūtrabhāṣya and Brahmasūtrabhāṣyadīpikā (adhyāya 1, pāda 3)
SA_GSP33_bbdip13u.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Madhva, Jagannāthatīrtha
SA_GSP33_bbdip13u.summary: This text comprises the third section (pāda) of the first chapter of Bādarāyaṇa's Brahmasūtra alongside Madhva's foundational Brahmasūtrabhāṣya and Jagannāthatīrtha's subcommentary (Brahmasūtrabhāṣyadīpikā). Within Dvaita Vedānta exegesis (samanvayādhyāya), this pāda demonstrates that scriptural designations that might prima facie suggest individual souls or other deities—such as the abode of heaven and earth (dyubhvādyāyatana), the akṣara, the dahara (subtle heart space), and vaiśvānara—exclusively and primarily denote Brahman/Viṣṇu. The section also contains the Devatādhikaraṇa and Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa concerning qualifications (adhikāra) for Vedic study and knowledge.
SA_GSP33_bbdip13u.attribution: The root aphorisms are traditionally ascribed to Bādarāyaṇa. The commentary is by Madhva (Ānandatīrtha). The subcommentary is by Jagannāthatīrtha (Jagannātha Yati), disciple of Raghunāthatīrtha.
SA_GSP33_bbdip13u.edition: Gopālakṛṣṇācārya: Śrīmad-Brahmasūtrāṇi, Śrīmaj-Jagannātha-yati-kṛta-ṭippaṇī-saṃvalita-Śrīman-Madhva-Bhāṣya-sametāni, Madras: The Grove Press 1900.
SA_GSP33_bbdip13u.coverage: partial — Contains Adhyāya 1, Pāda 3 complete (14 adhikaraṇas, from Dyubhvādyadhikaraṇa through Brāhmaṇādhikaraṇa, sūtras 1.3.1–1.3.43). Pādas 1.1 and 1.2 are catalogued under SA_GSP33_bbdip11u and SA_GSP33_bbdip12u.

SA_GSP33_brahms2u.title: Brahmasūtra
SA_GSP33_brahms2u.author: Bādarāyaṇa
SA_GSP33_brahms2u.summary: The Brahmasūtra (also known as the Vedāntasūtra or Śārīrakasūtra), traditionally attributed to Bādarāyaṇa, is the foundational systematizing text of the Vedānta school of Indian philosophy. Consisting of 555 terse aphorisms across four chapters (adhyāyas), it harmonizes Upaniṣadic statements regarding Brahman as the ultimate reality (samanvaya), defends Vedāntic doctrine against rival philosophical traditions such as Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Buddhism, and Jainism (avirodha), outlines spiritual discipline and contemplative methods (sādhana), and delineates the nature and fruits of liberation (phala). This e-text preserves the full root text as isolated from Śaṅkara's Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya.
SA_GSP33_brahms2u.attribution: In this e-text, the aphorisms are presented without commentary, having been extracted directly from Śaṅkara's Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya.
SA_GSP33_brahms2u.coverage: complete — Complete: 555 sūtras (BBs_1,1.1 to BBs_4,4.22) with the pāda distribution of Śaṅkara's sūtrapāṭha (31/32/43/28, 37/45/53/22, 27/41/66/52, 19/21/16/22). Sūtra text only, no commentary.
translations: George Thibaut (tr.), The Vedânta-Sûtras with the Commentary by Saṅkarâkârya, 2 vols., Sacred Books of the East & 38, Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1890, 1896. (English)
Swami Gambhirananda (tr.), Calcutta, 1965. (English)
Paul Deussen (tr.), Die Sūtras des Vedānta nebst dem vollständigen Commentare des Çankara, Leipzig: F. A. Brockhaus, 1887. (German)

SA_GSP33_brahmsuu.title: Brahmasūtra
SA_GSP33_brahmsuu.author: Bādarāyaṇa
SA_GSP33_brahmsuu.summary: The Brahmasūtra (also known as Vedāntasūtra), traditionally attributed to Bādarāyaṇa, is the foundational aphoristic treatise of Vedānta philosophy. In four chapters (adhyāyas)—devoted to samanvaya, avirodha, sādhana, and phala—it systematizes Upaniṣadic theology. This digital edition presents the complete root sūtra text in 545 sūtras.

SA_GSP33_brasi.title: Brahmasiddhi
SA_GSP33_brasi.author: Maṇḍanamiśra
SA_GSP33_brasi.summary: The Brahmasiddhi ('Establishment of Brahman') is a foundational treatise of early Advaita Vedānta composed by Maṇḍanamiśra in four chapters: Brahmakāṇḍa, Tarkakāṇḍa, Niyogakāṇḍa, and Siddhikāṇḍa. Written in kārikā form accompanied by an autocommentary in prose, it defends the non-dual reality of Brahman against the realistic epistemology of Mīmāṃsā, Buddhist nominalism and momentariness, and rivals in linguistics. Maṇḍana formulates key tenets that distinguish his philosophy from Śaṅkara's, such as locating ignorance (avidyā) in individual selves (jīva) rather than in Brahman, and arguing for repeated meditation (prasaṅkhyāna) to transform propositional śabda-cognition into immediate realization. The work served as a primary point of departure for Vācaspati Miśra's commentary (Tattvasamīkṣā) and the subsequent Bhāmatī tradition.
SA_GSP33_brasi.edition: Brahmasiddhi by Ācārya Maṇḍanamiśra, with Commentary by Śaṅkhapāṇi, ed. S. Kuppuswami Sastri, Madras Government Oriental Series 4, Madras: Government Press, 1937 (repr. Delhi: Sri Satguru Publications, 1984).
SA_GSP33_brasi.coverage: complete — Contains the complete text of all four chapters (Brahmakāṇḍa, Tarkakāṇḍa, Niyogakāṇḍa, and Siddhikāṇḍa) including both the metrical kārikās and Maṇḍana's prose autocommentary (svopajñavṛtti), concluding at verse 4.12 and the final colophon on page 159.
translations: Tilmann Vetter, Maṇḍanamiśra's Brahmasiddhiḥ, Brahmakāṇḍaḥ. Übersetzung, Einleitung und Anmerkungen, Wien: Hermann Böhlaus Nachfolger, 1969 (Österreichische Akademie der Wissenschaften, Phil.-Hist. Klasse, Sitzungsberichte 262, Abh. 2). (German)

SA_GSP33_brasurau.title: Brahmasūtra with Śrībhāṣya
SA_GSP33_brasurau.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Rāmānuja
SA_GSP33_brasurau.summary: The Śrībhāṣya is Rāmānuja's (ca. 11th–12th c. CE) fundamental commentary on Bādarāyaṇa's Brahmasūtra and the foundational systematic treatise of Viśiṣṭādvaita ('qualified non-dualism') Vedānta. Rāmānuja argues that Brahman is the supreme personal deity (Viṣṇu-Nārāyaṇa), possessor of infinite auspicious attributes, related to individual souls (cit) and material reality (acit) as the embodied soul to its physical body (śarīra-śarīrī-bhāva). The work offers an extensive, systematic refutation of Advaita Vedānta's doctrine of an unqualified (nirguṇa) Brahman and cosmic illusion (māyā/avidyā), particularly in the famous Mahāsiddhānta section of the opening adhyāya.

SA_GSP33_brsgor1u.title: Brahmasūtra with Ratnaprabhā (chapter 1)
SA_GSP33_brsgor1u.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Govindānanda
SA_GSP33_brsgor1u.summary: This e-text contains the first chapter (Samanvayādhyāya) of Bādarāyaṇa's Brahmasūtra alongside the Ratnaprabhā (Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā), an Advaita Vedānta sub-commentary on Śaṅkara's Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya. Adhyāya 1 establishes across four pādas (134 sūtras) the harmonious semantic concord (samanvaya) of all Vedic and Upaniṣadic revelation as signifying non-dual Brahman as both the material and efficient cause of the universe.
SA_GSP33_brsgor1u.attribution: The Brahmasūtra is traditionally attributed to Bādarāyaṇa (identified with Vyāsa). The sub-commentary Ratnaprabhā (Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā) on Śaṅkara's Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya is traditionally attributed to Govindānanda Sarasvatī. The opening heading of the e-text mentions 'śrīrāmānandayatipraṇītā'.
SA_GSP33_brsgor1u.coverage: partial — Adhyāya 1 (Samanvayādhyāya) complete: 134 sūtras (1.1.1–1.4.28) with the Ratnaprabhā. Ends with the colophon of pāda 1.4 and 'iti ... samanvayākhyaḥ prathamo 'dhyāyaḥ'.

SA_GSP33_brsgor2u.title: Brahmasūtra with Ratnaprabhā (chapter 2)
SA_GSP33_brsgor2u.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Govindānanda
SA_GSP33_brsgor2u.summary: Adhyāya 2 (Avirodhādhyāya) of the Brahmasūtra establishes the internal coherence and rational defensibility of Advaita Vedānta by systematically resolving objections. In the first pāda, attacks on Brahman as the sole material and efficient cause based on rival Smṛti doctrines (such as Sāṃkhya) and rational dialectic are rebutted. The second pāda offers a comprehensive philosophical critique of non-Vedāntic systems, including classical Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika atomism, Sarvāstivāda, Sautrāntika, Yogācāra, and Mādhyamika Buddhism, as well as Jainism, Pāśupata theism, and Bhāgavata/Pāñcarātra doctrine. The third and fourth pādas reconcile conflicting Upaniṣadic statements regarding the genesis of the physical elements, the unoriginated and eternal nature of the individual soul (jīva), and the vital faculties (prāṇas). Govindānanda's Ratnaprabhā provides a gloss on Śaṅkara's Bhāṣya.
SA_GSP33_brsgor2u.attribution: Bādarāyaṇa is the credited author of the Brahmasūtras. The Ratnaprabhā (also styled Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā) is by Govindānanda. Śaṅkara's Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya is the commentary being explicated, but only its lemma words (pratīkas) are cited.
SA_GSP33_brsgor2u.coverage: partial — Adhyāya 2 (Avirodhādhyāya; all 4 pādas, ending at 2.4.22 with Govindānanda's Ratnaprabhā thereon), covering chapter 2 of the Brahmasūtra.

SA_GSP33_brsgor3u.title: Brahmasūtra with Ratnaprabhā (chapter 3)
SA_GSP33_brsgor3u.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Govindānanda
SA_GSP33_brsgor3u.summary: This text comprises the third adhyāya (Sādhanādhyāya) of Bādarāyaṇa's Brahmasūtra accompanied by the Advaita sub-commentary Ratnaprabhā (Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā) of Govindānanda. The chapter investigates the spiritual means (sādhana) leading to Brahmavidyā and liberation: pāda 1 examines the transmigration and embodiment of the individual soul to foster renunciation (vairāgya); pāda 2 analyzes the nature of the self across waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and swoon alongside the nature of nirguṇa Brahman (clarifying the terms tat and tvam); pāda 3 harmonizes and synthesizes the various Upaniṣadic meditations (upāsanās and guṇopasaṃhāra); and pāda 4 establishes that direct knowledge of Brahman is an independent, sovereign means to mokṣa (puruṣārtha) distinct from and superior to ritual duties.
SA_GSP33_brsgor3u.attribution: The Brahmasūtra is traditionally attributed to Bādarāyaṇa. The sub-commentary Ratnaprabhā (or Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā) on Śaṅkara's Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya was authored by Govindānanda. Śaṅkara's bhāṣya text itself is not present as a continuous standalone text in this file, though lemmas are embedded in Govindānanda's ṭīkā.
SA_GSP33_brsgor3u.coverage: partial — Contains Adhyāya 3 in its entirety, spanning all four pādas, complete with Govindānanda's commentary on each sūtra.
translations: George Thibaut, The Vedānta-Sūtras with the Commentary by Śaṅkarācārya, 2 vols., Sacred Books of the East & 38, Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1890–1896. (English (translation of Śaṅkara's Bhāṣya))
Swami Gambhirananda, Brahma-Sūtra-Bhāṣya of Śrī Śaṅkarācārya, Calcutta: Advaita Ashrama, 1965. (English (translation of Śaṅkara's Bhāṣya))

SA_GSP33_brsgor4u.title: Brahmasūtra with Ratnaprabhā (chapter 4)
SA_GSP33_brsgor4u.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Govindānanda
SA_GSP33_brsgor4u.summary: The fourth adhyāya (Phalādhyāya) of Bādarāyaṇa's Brahmasūtra together with Govindānanda's Ratnaprabhā, a sub-commentary on Śaṅkara's Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya. This chapter deals with the fruit of Brahman-knowledge, examining the progressive destruction of sañcita and āgāmi karma, the persistence of prārabdha karma in jīvanmukti, the mechanics of the departure of the subtle body (utkrānti), the soul's journey via the path of the gods (devayāna / arcirādimārga), and the nature of final release (videhamukti) in both saguṇa and nirguṇa Brahman.
SA_GSP33_brsgor4u.attribution: The Brahmasūtra is traditionally attributed to Bādarāyaṇa. The sub-commentary Ratnaprabhā (gloss on Śaṅkara's Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya) is by Govindānanda Sarasvatī, disciple of Gopāla Sarasvatī.

SA_GSP33_brssbh1u.title: Brahmasūtra with Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya (chapter 1, without the Adhyāsabhāṣya)
SA_GSP33_brssbh1u.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Śaṅkara
SA_GSP33_brssbh1u.summary: Adhyāya 1 (the Samanvayādhyāya) of the Brahmasūtra together with Śaṅkara's Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya establishes the harmonious reconciliation (samanvaya) of all Upaniṣadic passages as teaching non-dual Brahman as the sole primary cause and ultimate reality of the universe. Across four pādas, Śaṅkara systematically interprets both explicit and obscure Vedic designations, refuting rival proto-Sāṃkhya (pradhāna) and Vaiśeṣika causal doctrines. In this particular e-text, the introductory Adhyāsabhāṣya on superimposition is omitted, and the file begins directly with the gloss on sūtra 1.1.1 (athāto brahmajijñāsā).

The introductory Adhyāsabhāṣya ('yuṣmadasmatpratyayagocarayor ...') is missing: the text opens with 'prathamādhyāye prathamaḥ pādaḥ' and the adhikaraṇa heading before sūtra 1.1.1. SA_GSP33_brssbh2u.title: Brahmasūtra with Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya (chapter 2)
SA_GSP33_brssbh2u.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Śaṅkara
SA_GSP33_brssbh2u.summary: The second adhyāya of the Brahmasūtra, traditionally designated as the Avirodhādhyāya ('chapter on non-contradiction'), accompanied by the foundational Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya of Śaṅkara, defends the Advaita Vedānta doctrine against internal scriptural and external philosophical challenges. Across four pādas, the text demonstrates that Vedānta does not conflict with orthodox Smṛti and shows the inadequacy of bare reasoning against Vedic revelation (pāda 1); presents extensive refutations of rival philosophical traditions, including Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Buddhist Sarvāstivāda and Vijñānavāda, Jainism, and theistic systems (pāda 2); harmonizes seemingly conflicting Upaniṣadic passages on the cosmogonic evolution of material elements and articulates the essential non-difference of the individual self (jīva) and Brahman (pāda 3); and reconciles Vedic teachings on the vital breaths (prāṇas) and sensory faculties (pāda 4).
SA_GSP33_brssbh2u.attribution: The root sūtras are attributed to Bādarāyaṇa. The commentary is by Śaṅkara.
SA_GSP33_brssbh2u.coverage: partial — Contains the second adhyāya (Avirodhādhyāya; all 4 pādas, sūtras 2.1.1–2.4.22) of the Brahmasūtra with Śaṅkara's commentary. The text ends with the pāda 2.4 colophon.
translations: Thibaut, George (trans.). The Vedânta-Sûtras with the Commentary by Saṅkarâcârya (Sacred Books of the East). Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1890. (English)

SA_GSP33_brssbh3u.title: Brahmasūtra with Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya (chapter 3)
SA_GSP33_brssbh3u.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Śaṅkara
SA_GSP33_brssbh3u.summary: Adhyāya 3 of the Brahmasūtra, traditionally termed the Sādhanādhyāya, investigates the practical means (sādhana) leading to the liberating knowledge of Brahman. Across four pādas, the text details the transmigration and rebirth of the embodied self (jīva) to foster detachment (vairāgya), analyzes dream and deep sleep states alongside the non-dual transcendence of Brahman, examines and harmonizes Upaniṣadic meditations (vidyās and upāsanās), and delineates the moral, renunciatory, and intellectual disciplines required for realization. Śaṅkara's commentary establishes the classical Advaita Vedānta doctrine that direct realization of nirguṇa Brahman alone, unmixed with ritual action, constitutes the immediate cause of release (mokṣa).
SA_GSP33_brssbh3u.attribution: The Brahmasūtra is traditionally attributed to Bādarāyaṇa. The Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya is the commentary of Śaṅkara.
SA_GSP33_brssbh3u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete third adhyāya (Sādhanādhyāya), comprising all four pādas: 3.1 (sūtras 1–27), 3.2 (sūtras 1–41), 3.3 (sūtras 1–66), and 3.4 (sūtras 1–52). The text ends with the pāda 3.4 colophon.
translations: Thibaut, G. Translation of Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Vedānta Sūtras, Oxford, 1896 (SBE 38). (English)
Gambhirananda. Calcutta, 1965. (English)
Deusseneipzig, 1887. (German)

SA_GSP33_brssbh4u.title: Brahmasūtra with Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya (chapter 4)
SA_GSP33_brssbh4u.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Śaṅkara
SA_GSP33_brssbh4u.summary: The fourth adhyāya of the Brahmasūtra, traditionally termed the Phalādhyāya, systematically examines the fruit (phala) of Brahman-realization across four pādas with Śaṅkara's commentary. Pāda 1 establishes the necessity of repeated contemplation (āvṛtti) of the Vedāntic mahāvākyas, the destruction and non-clinging of past sañcita and future āgāmi karma upon awakening, and the continued operation of prārabdha karma until bodily demise, establishing the validity of living liberation (jīvanmukti). Pādas 2 and 3 detail the process of dying, the non-departure of the vital faculties (prāṇas) in the case of the knower of the unqualified Brahman, and the ascent via the path of the gods (devayāna / arcirādimārga) for worshippers of saguṇa Brahman. Pāda 4 articulates the nature of liberation (mokṣa) as the manifestation (āvirbhāva) of the individual self's non-dual nature identical with Brahman, and the souls' eternal non-return to the cycle of rebirth.
SA_GSP33_brssbh4u.attribution: The Brahmasūtra (Vedāntasūtra) is traditionally attributed to Bādarāyaṇa. The commentary Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya is by Śaṅkara.
SA_GSP33_brssbh4u.coverage: partial — Complete fourth adhyāya (Phalādhyāya), pādas 1–4, sūtras 4.1.1–4.4.22 with Śaṅkara's bhāṣya, ending with the pāda colophon and 'samāptamidaṃ brahmasūtraśāṅkarabhāṣyam'.
translations: George Thibaut (tr.), The Vedānta-Sūtras with the Commentary of Śaṅkarācārya, 2 vols., Sacred Books of the East and 38, Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1890–1896. (English)

SA_GSP33_brssgo1u.title: Brahmasūtra with Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya and Ratnaprabhā (chapter 1, without the Adhyāsabhāṣya)
SA_GSP33_brssgo1u.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Śaṅkara, Govindānanda
SA_GSP33_brssgo1u.summary: Adhyāya 1 (Samanvayādhyāya) of the Brahmasūtra, which argues that all Upaniṣadic statements consistently refer to Brahman as the cause of the world, with Śaṅkara's Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya and the Ratnaprabhā sub-commentary. Śaṅkara's bhāṣya interprets the ambiguous Upaniṣadic passages pāda by pāda and refutes the Sāṅkhya pradhāna doctrine. The Ratnaprabhā, which opens with maṅgala verses and a gloss on the Adhyāsabhāṣya (whose bhāṣya text is absent from this e-text), explains Śaṅkara's argument phrase by phrase.
SA_GSP33_brssgo1u.attribution: Brahmasūtra traditionally attributed to Bādarāyaṇa; Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya by Śaṅkara; the sub-commentary Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā is attributed in its colophons to Govindānanda (colophons: 'śrīgovindānandabhagavatpādakṛtau … bhāṣyaratnaprabhāyām'), but the heading of the printed edition reproduced in the e-text reads 'bhāṣyaratnaprabhāvyākhyā śrīrāmānandayatipraṇītā', and maṅgala verse 4 has the author bow to 'śrīmadgovindavāṇī', so authorship is divided in the tradition between Govindānanda and Rāmānanda (Sarasvatī/Yati).
SA_GSP33_brssgo1u.coverage: partial — Adhyāya 1 (Samanvayādhyāya), pādas 1–4 (to BBs 1.4.28), with the Ratnaprabhā complete incl. its maṅgala and its gloss on the Adhyāsabhāṣya; but Śaṅkara's Adhyāsabhāṣya itself (the introduction 'yuṣmadasmatpratyayagocarayoḥ…') is missing — the bhāṣya starts at sūtra 1.1.1 'vedāntamīmāṃsāśāstrasya…', as in SA_GSP33_brssbh1u. Adhyāyas 2–4 are brssgo2u–4u.
translations: Thibaut, George, trans. The Vedânta-Sûtras with the Commentary by Saṅkarâcârya. 2 vols. Sacred Books of the East 34 & 38. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1890, 1896. (English)
Gambhirananda, Swami, trans. Calcutta: Advaita Ashrama, 1965. (English)

SA_GSP33_brssgo2u.title: Brahmasūtra with Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya and Ratnaprabhā (chapter 2)
SA_GSP33_brssgo2u.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Śaṅkara, Govindānanda
SA_GSP33_brssgo2u.summary: This e-text contains the complete second adhyāya (Avirodhādhyāya) of the Brahmasūtra with Śaṅkara's Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya and Govindānanda's sub-commentary Ratnaprabhā. In this chapter, the Vedāntic proposition that Brahman is the sole material and efficient cause of the universe is defended against competing philosophies and apparent contradictions in sacred tradition. Pāda 1 refutes objections founded on Sāṃkhya-Yoga smṛtis and rationalist arguments; Pāda 2 dismantles rival ontological systems, including classical Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika atomism, Buddhist Sarvāstivāda, Vijñānavāda, Madhyamaka, Jainism, Pāśupata theism, and Pāñcarātra theology; and Pādas 3 and 4 resolve conflicting śruti passages concerning the cosmic elements (ākāśa, vāyu, etc.), the nature and agency of the individual soul (jīva), and the vital faculties (prāṇas).
SA_GSP33_brssgo2u.attribution: Brahmasūtra traditionally attributed to Bādarāyaṇa; Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya by Śaṅkara; the sub-commentary Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā is attributed in its colophons to Govindānanda.
SA_GSP33_brssgo2u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete second adhyāya (Avirodhādhyāya, comprising 4 pādas, 157 sūtras: 2.1.1–2.4.22) along with Śaṅkara's bhāṣya and Govindānanda's Ratnaprabhā.
translations: George Thibaut (trans.), The Vedānta-Sūtras with the Commentary by Śaṅkarācārya, Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1890. (English)

SA_GSP33_brssgo3u.title: Brahmasūtra with Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya and Ratnaprabhā (chapter 3)
SA_GSP33_brssgo3u.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Śaṅkara, Govindānanda
SA_GSP33_brssgo3u.summary: Adhyāya 3 (Sādhanādhyāya) of the Brahmasūtra systematically examines the spiritual means leading to liberation (mokṣa). Pāda 1 examines the soul's transmigration via the five fires (pañcāgnividyā) to cultivate detachment (vairāgya); Pāda 2 analyzes the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and swoon to show that the true Self is transcendent and that Brahman is pure non-dual consciousness; Pāda 3 evaluates the Upaniṣadic meditations (vidyās) and establishes criteria for combining or separating divine attributes (guṇopasaṃhāra); and Pāda 4 establishes that knowledge of Brahman (brahmajñāna) directly accomplishes the ultimate puruṣārtha independent of ritual action, while specifying the role of ethical and contemplative disciplines. This e-text presents the sūtras with Śaṅkara's foundational bhāṣya and Govindānanda's Ratnaprabhā subcommentary.
SA_GSP33_brssgo3u.attribution: Brahmasūtra traditionally attributed to Bādarāyaṇa; Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya by Śaṅkara; the sub-commentary Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā is attributed in its colophon to Govindānanda (colophon: 'iti śrīmatparamahaṃsaparivrājakācāryaśrīgovindānandabhagavatkṛtau śārīrakavyākhyāyā bhāṣyaratnaprabhāṭīkāyāṃ tṛtīyasyādhyāyasya caturthaḥ pādaḥ').
SA_GSP33_brssgo3u.coverage: partial — Covers the entirety of Adhyāya 3 (Sādhanādhyāya), comprising all four pādas: 3.1 (sūtras 1–27), 3.2 (sūtras 1–41), 3.3 (sūtras 1–66), and 3.4 (sūtras 1–52).
translations: George Thibaut (trans.), The Vedānta-Sūtras with the Commentary by Śaṅkarācārya, Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1890–1896 (SBE 34, 38). (English)
Swami Gambhirananda (trans.), Calcutta, 1965. (English)
Paul Deussen (trans.), Die Sūtras des Vedānta nebst dem vollständigen Kommentare des Śaṅkara, Leipzig, 1887. (German)

SA_GSP33_brssgo4u.title: Brahmasūtra with Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya and Ratnaprabhā (chapter 4)
SA_GSP33_brssgo4u.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Śaṅkara, Govindānanda
SA_GSP33_brssgo4u.summary: Adhyāya 4 (Phalādhyāya) of Bādarāyaṇa's Brahmasūtra, accompanied by Śaṅkara's foundational Advaita commentary (Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya) and Govindānanda's subcommentary (Ratnaprabhā). Across four pādas, the chapter investigates the fruit (phala) of knowledge of Brahman: the necessity of repeated meditation (āvṛtti) until direct realization, the non-clinging and destruction of past karman, jīvanmukti, the soul's departure at death (utkrānti), the path of the gods (arcirādimārga) leading saguṇa meditators to Brahmaloka, and the definitive non-return and final liberation (mokṣa) of the knower of the Supreme Brahman.
SA_GSP33_brssgo4u.attribution: Brahmasūtra traditionally attributed to Bādarāyaṇa; Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya by Śaṅkara; the sub-commentary Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā is attributed in its colophon to Govindānanda (colophon: 'śrīmatparamahaṃsaparivrājakācāryaśrīmadgopālasarasvatīpūjyapādaśiṣyaśrīgovindānandabhagavatkṛtau … bhāṣyaratnaprabhāyām').
SA_GSP33_brssgo4u.coverage: partial — Contains Adhyāya 4 (Phalādhyāya) complete across all four pādas (sūtras 4.1.1 to 4.4.22) with Śaṅkara's bhāṣya and Govindānanda's Ratnaprabhā.
translations: Thibaut, George. The Vedānta-Sūtras with the Commentary by Śaṅkarācārya. Sacred Books of the East & 38. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1890, 1896. (English)

SA_GSP33_brsvbh1u.title: Brahmasūtra with Bhāmatī (adhyāya 1)
SA_GSP33_brsvbh1u.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Vācaspati Miśra
SA_GSP33_brsvbh1u.summary: Adhyāya 1 (Samanvayādhyāya) of Bādarāyaṇa's Brahmasūtra together with the Bhāmatī of Vācaspati Miśra, a sub-commentary on Śaṅkara's Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya. The first adhyāya harmonizes Upaniṣadic passages to establish Brahman as the ultimate material and efficient cause of the universe while systematically refuting rival interpretations.
SA_GSP33_brsvbh1u.attribution: The root aphorisms are traditionally ascribed to Bādarāyaṇa (identified with Vedavyāsa). The sub-commentary Bhāmatī was composed by Vācaspati Miśra on Śaṅkara's Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya. Śaṅkara's commentary is not included as an independent running text, though its words are cited as pratīkas throughout.
SA_GSP33_brsvbh1u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete first adhyāya (Samanvayādhyāya, pādas 1–4, sūtras 1.1.1–1.4.28) of the Brahmasūtra with the Bhāmatī.

SA_GSP33_brsvbh2u.title: Brahmasūtra with Bhāmatī (chapter 2)
SA_GSP33_brsvbh2u.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Vācaspati Miśra
SA_GSP33_brsvbh2u.summary: Adhyāya 2 of the Brahmasūtra, known as the Avirodhādhyāya ('chapter on non-contradiction'), reconciles Advaita Vedānta against external criticisms and internal scriptural inconsistencies across four pādas. Pāda 1 answers objections based on smṛti and reasoning; Pāda 2 (Tarkapāda) critiques rival philosophical schools including Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Sarvāstivāda, Vijñānavāda, Jainism, and theistic traditions; while Pādas 3 and 4 resolve apparent scriptural contradictions concerning the creation of the elements, the nature of the jīva, and the sense faculties (prāṇas). Vācaspati Miśra's Bhāmatī provides dialectical, logical, and grammatical analysis of Śaṅkara's bhāṣya, forming the foundational text of the Bhāmatī school of Advaita Vedānta.
SA_GSP33_brsvbh2u.attribution: The Brahmasūtra is traditionally attributed to Bādarāyaṇa. The Bhāmatī is a sub-commentary (ṭīkā / bhāṣyavibhāga) on Śaṅkara's Brahmasūtrabhāṣya composed by Vācaspati Miśra. In this e-text, Bādarāyaṇa's sūtras are embedded alongside Vācaspati's commentary, whereas Śaṅkara's bhāṣya appears only in pratīka citations.
SA_GSP33_brsvbh2u.coverage: partial — Complete text of Adhyāya 2 (Avirodhādhyāya: pādas 2.1 through 2.4, comprising sūtras 2.1.1 to 2.4.22) along with the Bhāmatī commentary.

SA_GSP33_brsvbh3u.title: Brahmasūtra with Bhāmatī (chapter 3)
SA_GSP33_brsvbh3u.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Vācaspati Miśra
SA_GSP33_brsvbh3u.summary: This text comprises the third adhyāya (Sādhanādhyāya) of Bādarāyaṇa's Brahmasūtra alongside Vācaspati Miśra's Advaita sub-commentary, the Bhāmatī. The chapter systematically examines the spiritual means (sādhana) to liberation across four pādas: the post-mortem transmigration of the soul and the cultivation of detachment (vairāgya; 3.1); the states of consciousness and the non-dual, relationless nature of Brahman (3.2); the collation and harmonization of Upaniṣadic meditations (upāsanā/vidyā; 3.3); and the primacy of direct metaphysical knowledge over ritual acts together with the necessary auxiliary virtues (3.4). Vācaspati Miśra clarifies and defends Śaṅkara's bhāṣya, providing influential formulations of the Bhāmatī school on ignorance (avidyā) and spiritual pedagogy.
SA_GSP33_brsvbh3u.attribution: The Brahmasūtra is traditionally attributed to Bādarāyaṇa. The Bhāmatī is Vācaspati Miśra's foundational sub-commentary on Śaṅkara's Brahmasūtrabhāṣya. Śaṅkara's bhāṣya is present only through cited pratīkas embedded in the Bhāmatī.
SA_GSP33_brsvbh3u.coverage: partial — Covers Adhyāya 3 complete across all four pādas (3.1.1 to 3.4.52).
translations: S. S. Suryanarayan Sastri and Kunhan Raja (trans.), The Bhāmati, first book, Adyar. (English)

SA_GSP33_brsvbh4u.title: Brahmasūtra with Bhāmatī (chapter 4)
SA_GSP33_brsvbh4u.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Vācaspati Miśra
SA_GSP33_brsvbh4u.summary: Adhyāya 4 (Phalādhyāya) of the Brahmasūtra forms the concluding chapter of Bādarāyaṇa's foundational Vedānta work, accompanied here by Vācaspati Miśra's sub-commentary Bhāmatī.
SA_GSP33_brsvbh4u.attribution: Bādarāyaṇa is the author of the Brahmasūtra. Vācaspati Miśra composed the sub-commentary Bhāmatī on Śaṅkara's Brahmasūtrabhāṣya.
SA_GSP33_brsvbh4u.coverage: partial — Complete adhyāya 4 with Vācaspati Miśra's Bhāmatī, opening with the Bhāmatī's introductory verses ('nābhyarthyā iha santaḥ…', 'śaṅke saṃprati…') and ending with the concluding colophon: 'iti śrīvācaspatimiśraviracite śaṅkarabhagavatpādabhāṣyavibhāge bhāmatyāṃ caturthasyādhyāyasya caturthaḥ pādaḥ samāptaḥ'.

SA_GSP33_gaukar.title: Āgamaśāstra
SA_GSP33_gaukar.author: Gauḍapāda
SA_GSP33_gaukar.summary: The Āgamaśāstra (commonly known as the Gauḍapādakārikā or Māṇḍūkyakārikā) is the earliest extant systematic treatise of Advaita Vedānta, consisting of 215 verses divided into four chapters (Āgamaprakaraṇa, Vaitathyaprakaraṇa, Advaitaprakaraṇa, and Alātaśāntiprakaraṇa). Elaborating on the states of consciousness outlined in the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, Gauḍapāda establishes the doctrine of absolute non-origination (ajātivāda), asserting that the unborn Self (ātman/brahman) alone is real while phenomenal multiplicity is an illusion akin to a dream or the circle traced by a whirling firebrand (alāta). The work is celebrated for its sophisticated dialectic, particularly in the fourth chapter, which draws heavily on Mahāyāna Buddhist concepts and terminology to articulate an orthodox Upaniṣadic non-dualism.
SA_GSP33_gaukar.edition: Vināyaka Gaṇeśa Āpaṭe, ed., Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series 10, Pune: 1921.
SA_GSP33_gaukar.coverage: complete — Complete text of Gauḍapāda's kārikās across all four chapters (Āgama-, Vaitathya-, Advaita-, and Alātaśāntiprakaraṇa; 215 verses total).
translations: Bhattacharya, Vidhushekhara, The Āgamaśāstra of Gauḍapāda, Calcutta: 1943. (English)
