SA_GSP33_m_mbhtnu.title: Mahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya with Yamakabhārata
SA_GSP33_m_mbhtnu.author: Madhva Ānandatīrtha
SA_GSP33_m_mbhtnu.summary: The Mahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya is Madhva Ānandatīrtha's major theological-exegetical treatise, interpreting the epics and Purāṇas according to Dvaita Vedānta. This e-text also includes at the end Madhva's Yamakabhārata.
SA_GSP33_m_mbhtnu.attribution: Both works are authentic canonical treatises of Madhva Ānandatīrtha.
SA_GSP33_m_mbhtnu.coverage: complete — Text of the Mahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya followed by the Yamakabhārata.

SA_GSP33_madhanuu.title: Anuvyākhyāna
SA_GSP33_madhanuu.author: Madhva
SA_GSP33_madhanuu.summary: The Anuvyākhyāna is Madhva's versified dialectical supplement to his own prose Brahmasūtrabhāṣya, expounding Dvaita (Tattvavāda) Vedānta across four adhyāyas. Composed in a concise and vigorously polemical style reminiscent of Kumārila Bhaṭṭa's Ślokavārttika, the work systematically refutes Advaita and rival schools while demonstrating the absolute supremacy of Viṣṇu and the reality of difference (bheda). It is regarded as Madhva's chief philosophical masterpiece and serves as the foundation for Jayatīrtha's celebrated sub-commentary, the Nyāyasudhā.
SA_GSP33_madhanuu.attribution: Authored by Madhva, who also uses his monastic name Ānandatīrtha in chapter colophons ('iti śrīmad-ānandatīrtha-bhagavatpādācārya-viracite...') and explicitly names himself as Madhva in the final signature verse (4.4.13: 'madhvo yattu tṛtīyam etadanumā granthaḥ kṛtaḥ keśave').
SA_GSP33_madhanuu.coverage: complete — Complete: adhyāyas 1–4 from the maṅgala 'nārāyaṇaṃ nikhilapūrṇaguṇaikadehaṃ' (MAnuv_1,1.1) to MAnuv_4,4.14 and the colophon 'iti śrīmadānandatīrthabhagavatpādācāryaviracite śrīmadbrahmasūtrānuvyākhyāne caturtho 'dhyāyaḥ'.
translations: Suzanne Siauve, La Voie vers la Connaissance de Dieu (Brahma-jijñāsā) selon l'Anuvyākhyāna de Madhva, Pondichéry: Institut Français d'Indologie, 1957. (French)

SA_GSP33_madhsiddhb_u.title: Siddhāntabindu
SA_GSP33_madhsiddhb_u.author: Madhusūdanasarasvatī
SA_GSP33_madhsiddhb_u.summary: The Siddhāntabindu is an Advaita Vedānta treatise composed by Madhusūdana Sarasvatī as a commentary on the Daśaślokī attributed to Śaṅkarācārya. Written at the behest of Balabhadra, the text provides an exposition of Advaita metaphysics and epistemology, discussing self-awareness, pramāṇa, and key debates including pratibimbavāda.
SA_GSP33_madhsiddhb_u.attribution: The Siddhāntabindu is an Advaita Vedānta commentary on the Daśaślokī attributed to Śaṅkarācārya, composed by Madhusūdana Sarasvatī (pupil of Viśveśvara Sarasvatī). In the fourth concluding stanza, Madhusūdana explicitly mentions that he composed this digest at the request of Balabhadra (bahuyācanayā mayāyam alpo balabhadrasya kṛte kṛto nibandhaḥ).
SA_GSP33_madhsiddhb_u.edition: P. C. Divanji (ed.), Siddhāntabindu of Madhusūdana with the Commentary of Purushottama, Gaekwad's Oriental Series no. 64, Baroda: Oriental Institute, 1933.
SA_GSP33_madhsiddhb_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Siddhāntabindu commenting on the Daśaślokī, including the introductory upodghāta, concluding verses by Madhusūdana, and closing colophon.
translations: Prahlad Chandrashekhar Divanji (trans.), Siddhāntabindu of Madhusūdana with the Commentary of Purushottama, Gaekwad's Oriental Series, Vol. 64, Baroda: Oriental Institute, 1933. (English)

SA_GSP33_mbrahsiu.title: Brahmasiddhi
SA_GSP33_mbrahsiu.author: Maṇḍanamiśra
SA_GSP33_mbrahsiu.summary: The Brahmasiddhi is a philosophical treatise of Advaita Vedānta by Maṇḍanamiśra, written in a mixture of kārikās and prose auto-commentary. Structured into four chapters—Brahmakāṇḍa, Tarkakāṇḍa, Niyogakāṇḍa, and Siddhikāṇḍa—the work establishes nondual Brahman as the sole ultimate reality, offers an epistemological critique of the perception of difference (bheda), and rejects the Mīmāṃsā theory that Vedic authority is tethered to action-oriented injunction (niyoga).
SA_GSP33_mbrahsiu.attribution: The Brahmasiddhi was composed in mixed kārikā verses and prose auto-commentary (vṛtti) by Maṇḍanamiśra.
SA_GSP33_mbrahsiu.edition: S. Kuppuswami Sastri. Madras: Government Press, 1937 (Madras Government Oriental Series, 4). [Reprint:Delhi: Sri Satguru, 1984] In a few places, older readings found in the Tattvasamīkṣā (ed. Acharya 2006) are adopted and Sastri's readings are given in brackets. Minor typos are silently corrected.
SA_GSP33_mbrahsiu.coverage: complete — Complete text of Maṇḍanamiśra's treatise across all four chapters (kāṇḍas): Brahmakāṇḍa, Tarkakāṇḍa, Niyogakāṇḍa, and Siddhikāṇḍa, ending with verse 4.12 and the final colophon.
translations: TILMANN VETTER: Maṇḍanamiśra's Brahmasiddhiḥ, Brahmakāṇḍaḥ. Übersetzung, Einleitung und Anmerkungen. Wien: Böhlau 1969. 126 S. (Österr. Ak. d. Wiss. Phil.-hist. Kl. Sitzungsberichte. Bd. 262, Abh. 2.) (German)

SA_GSP33_mndvivpu.title: Vibhramaviveka
SA_GSP33_mndvivpu.author: Maṇḍana Miśra
SA_GSP33_mndvivpu.summary: The Vibhramaviveka ('Discrimination of Error') is a verse treatise in 164 kārikās by Maṇḍana Miśra examining the epistemology of perceptual error (khyātivāda). It critically evaluates rival classical theories—specifically Yogācāra ātmakhyāti, Mādhyamika asatkhyāti, and Prābhākara akhyāti—before analyzing anyathākhyāti / viparītakhyāti and demonstrating how the ultimate nature of error points toward indeterminability (anirvacanīyatva). The treatise is a fundamental document for the synthesis between late Mīmāṃsā epistemology and early Advaita Vedānta.
SA_GSP33_mndvivpu.edition: Lambert Schmithausen (ed.), Maṇḍanamiśra's Vibhramavivekaḥ: mit einer Studie zur Entwicklung der indischen Irrtumslehre. Wien 1965 (Sitzungsberichte der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, Phil.-Hist. Klasse, 247,1; Veröffentlichungen der Kommission für Sprachen und Kulturen Südasiens, 2).
SA_GSP33_mndvivpu.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising all 164 kārikās (MVibhr_1 through MVibhr_164) including editorial lacuna markers corresponding to manuscript damages.

SA_GSP33_nabodhsu.title: Bodhasāra
SA_GSP33_nabodhsu.author: Narahari
SA_GSP33_nabodhsu.summary: Bodhasāra is an 18th-century Vedānta metrical treatise by Narahari. Arranged into 52 thematic sections concluding with prāmāṇyasiddhi verses, the work covers non-dual philosophy, guru devotion, and liberation, integrating Vedāntic thought with yogic and devotional elements. This electronic text contains the root text without Divākara's commentary.
SA_GSP33_nabodhsu.attribution: Composed by Narahari (18th century). His pupil Divākara composed the commentary (also referred to as Arthadīpa), which was printed with the root text in the 1905 Benares edition but was not transcribed in this electronic text.
SA_GSP33_nabodhsu.edition: Dayānanda Svāmī (ed.), Bodhasāraḥ: A Treatise on Vedānta by Narahari, With a Commentary by the Author's Pupil, Paṇḍit Divākar. Benares: Chowkhamba Sanskrit Book Depot, 1905 (Benares Sanskrit Series, 23).
SA_GSP33_nabodhsu.coverage: complete — Root text (mūla) in 52 sections (NBs_1.1 to NBs_52.9) followed by 3 concluding prāmāṇyasiddhi verses, corresponding to pp. 2–969 of the source printed edition. The commentary is omitted.
translations: Jennifer and Grahame Cover, Bodhasāra: The Surprise of Awareness, the Sanskrit and English Version. An 18th Century Sanskrit Treasure. North Charleston, S.C.: CreateSpace, 2014. (English)

SA_GSP33_nysu__1u.title: Brahmasūtra with Anuvyākhyāna and Nyāyasudhā (chapter 1, incomplete)
SA_GSP33_nysu__1u.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Madhva, Jayatīrtha
SA_GSP33_nysu__1u.summary: The Nyāyasudhā is Jayatīrtha's commentary expounding Madhva's Anuvyākhyāna on the Brahmasūtra of Bādarāyaṇa. Adhyāya 1 establishes that the ultimate purport (samanvaya) of all Vedic scripture is the supreme personal Brahman (Viṣṇu/Nārāyaṇa), endowed with limitless auspicious qualities and devoid of defect.
SA_GSP33_nysu__1u.attribution: Jayatīrtha authored the Nyāyasudhā as a sub-commentary on the Anuvyākhyāna of Madhva (Ānandatīrtha), which itself comments on the Brahmasūtra of Bādarāyaṇa.
SA_GSP33_nysu__1u.coverage: partial — Adhyāya 1 of the Nyāyasudhā, integrated by GRETIL with the Brahmasūtras and Madhva's Anuvyākhyāna. The Sansknet e-text lacks the Nyāyasudhā on Anuvyākhyāna 1.1.27–98 (incl. Brahmasūtra 1.1.2) = vol. 2, pp. 269–800 and vol. 3, pp. 1–38 of Pandurangi's edition (GRETIL header). Ends with Anuvyākhyāna 1.4.123 and the colophon of adhyāya 1, pāda 4.

SA_GSP33_nysu__2u.title: Brahmasūtra with Anuvyākhyāna and Nyāyasudhā (chapter 2)
SA_GSP33_nysu__2u.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Madhva, Jayatīrtha
SA_GSP33_nysu__2u.summary: The second adhyāya of Jayatīrtha's Nyāyasudhā, a sub-commentary on Madhva's metrical Anuvyākhyāna on the Brahmasūtra. The e-text incorporates the sūtras of Bādarāyaṇa and the verses of Madhva's Anuvyākhyāna along with Jayatīrtha's sub-commentary.
SA_GSP33_nysu__2u.attribution: Jayatīrtha authored the Nyāyasudhā (titled in colophons as Viṣamapadavākyārthavivṛti) as a sub-commentary on Madhva's (Pūrṇaprajña's) Anuvyākhyāna on Bādarāyaṇa's Brahmasūtra.
SA_GSP33_nysu__2u.coverage: partial — Adhyāya 2, pādas 1–4. It runs from the Smṛtyadhikaraṇa (*5,1*, MAnuv_2,1.1) to the closing colophons 'iti śrīmatpūrṇapramatibhagavatpādasukṛteranuvyākhyānasya praguṇajayatīrthākhyayatinā kṛtāyāṃ ṭīkāyāṃ viṣamapadavākyārthavivṛtau dvitīye 'dhyāye 'smiṃścaramacaraṇaḥ paryavasitaḥ' and 'iti śrīmannyāyasudhāyāṃ dvitīyādhyāyasya caturthaḥ pādaḥ'.

SA_GSP33_nysu__3u.title: Brahmasūtra with Anuvyākhyāna and Nyāyasudhā (chapter 3)
SA_GSP33_nysu__3u.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Madhva, Jayatīrtha
SA_GSP33_nysu__3u.summary: The third adhyāya (Sādhanādhyāya) of Jayatīrtha's Nyāyasudhā, the main sub-commentary on Madhva's metrical Anuvyākhyāna on the Brahmasūtra. GRETIL has worked the sūtras and Anuvyākhyāna verses into the text. It covers the means to liberation: detachment through reflection on transmigration (pāda 1), the nature of the Lord and devotion (pāda 2), the coordination of the upāsanās and the attributes of Brahman to be meditated on (pāda 3), and the role of knowledge, ritual and the āśramas (pāda 4).
SA_GSP33_nysu__3u.attribution: Madhva composed the metrical Anuvyākhyāna on Bādarāyaṇa's Brahmasūtra. Jayatīrtha authored the Nyāyasudhā (formally titled Viṣamapadavākyārthavivṛti) as a sub-commentary on Madhva's Anuvyākhyāna.
SA_GSP33_nysu__3u.coverage: partial — Adhyāya 3 (Sādhanādhyāya), pādas 1–4, complete. Pāda 1 begins at *9,1*, pāda 4 ends with the colophons '// iti śrīmatpūrṇapramatibhagavatpādasukṛteranuvyākhyānasya praguṇajayatīrthākhyayatinā / kṛtāyāṃ ṭīkāyāṃ viṣamapadavākyārthavivṛtau tṛtīyādhyāye 'smiṃścaramacaraṇaḥ paryavasitaḥ //' and '// iti śrīmannyāyasudhāyāṃ tṛtīyādhyāyasya caturthaḥ pādaḥ //'.

SA_GSP33_nysu__4u.title: Brahmasūtra with Anuvyākhyāna and Nyāyasudhā (chapter 4)
SA_GSP33_nysu__4u.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Madhva, Jayatīrtha
SA_GSP33_nysu__4u.summary: The fourth and last adhyāya (Phalādhyāya) of Jayatīrtha's Nyāyasudhā, the main sub-commentary on Madhva's metrical Anuvyākhyāna on the Brahmasūtra. GRETIL has worked the sūtras and Anuvyākhyāna verses into the text. It covers the fruits of knowledge: repeated meditation and the destruction of karma (pāda 1), the departure of the knower (pāda 2), the path of light to Brahman (pāda 3), and the state of the released soul (pāda 4), all argued from the Dvaita position.
SA_GSP33_nysu__4u.attribution: Madhva composed the metrical Anuvyākhyāna on Bādarāyaṇa's Brahmasūtra. Jayatīrtha authored the Nyāyasudhā (formally titled Viṣamapadavākyārthavivṛti) as an exhaustive philosophical sub-commentary.
SA_GSP33_nysu__4u.coverage: partial — Adhyāya 4 (Phalādhyāya), pādas 1–4, complete: from JNys_4,1.I (āvṛttyadhikaraṇa, *12,1*) to the closing verses and colophon of the Nyāyasudhā (*12,403*). GRETIL notes that BBs_ adhikaraṇa numbering is kept even where Madhva and Jayatīrtha do not comment on every adhikaraṇa.

SA_GSP33_pada.title: Pañcadaśī
SA_GSP33_pada.author: Vidyāraṇya
SA_GSP33_pada.summary: The Pañcadaśī is a verse prakaraṇa of Advaita Vedānta composed of fifteen chapters arranged into three pentads corresponding to the saccidānanda nature of Brahman: Viveka-pañcaka (discrimination of truth/reality, chs. 1–5), Dīpa-pañcaka (illumination of consciousness, chs. 6–10), and Ānanda-pañcaka (bliss of the Self, chs. 11–15). It serves as a comprehensive textbook explaining key Advaita concepts such as the mahāvākyas, cidābhāsa (reflected consciousness), māyā, and jīvanmukti.
SA_GSP33_pada.coverage: unclear — No e-text available in the record.

SA_GSP33_ramgbhpu.title: Bhagavadgītā with Bhagavadgītābhāṣya
SA_GSP33_ramgbhpu.author: Rāmānuja
SA_GSP33_ramgbhpu.summary: The Bhagavadgītābhāṣya is Rāmānuja's commentary on the Bhagavadgītā and one of the central scriptural pillars of the Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta tradition. Drawing on Yāmuna's Gītārthasaṅgraha, Rāmānuja expounds the dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna as teaching that Nārāyaṇa is the supreme personal Brahman, possessing innumerable auspicious attributes, whose body (śarīra) consists of both sentient souls and insentient matter. The commentary demonstrates how disinterested performance of duty (karma-yoga) and self-knowledge (jñāna-yoga) culminate in continuous loving meditation (bhakti-yoga) and self-surrender (śaraṇāgati) as the direct means of release from saṃsāra.
SA_GSP33_ramgbhpu.attribution: Commentary by Rāmānuja. In the introductory maṅgala verse, Rāmānuja acknowledges his debt to Yāmuna (yāmuneyaṃ namāmi tam).
SA_GSP33_ramgbhpu.coverage: complete — Complete text covering all 18 adhyāyas of the Bhagavadgītā alongside Rāmānuja's commentary, from the opening invocation and prose upodghāta to the final verse 18.78.

SA_GSP33_rams11pu.title: Śrībhāṣya (on Brahmasūtra 1.1.3)
SA_GSP33_rams11pu.author: Rāmānuja
SA_GSP33_rams11pu.summary: This text comprises Rāmānuja's commentary on Brahmasūtra 1.1.3 (śāstrayonitvāt) from the Śrībhāṣya. In this section, Rāmānuja presents a sustained critique of the inferential proof for the existence of God (īśvarānumāna), demonstrating that neither sensory perception nor cosmological inference can establish a transcendent creator. Consequently, he establishes that Brahman can be known only through scripture (śāstraikapramāṇakatva), which reveals the Supreme Person (puruṣottama) possessing infinite auspicious qualities and free from cosmic blemishes.
SA_GSP33_rams11pu.attribution: The Śrībhāṣya is the commentary on the Brahmasūtra attributed to Rāmānuja.
SA_GSP33_rams11pu.coverage: excerpt — Only the Śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇa, Rāmānuja's bhāṣya on Brahmasūtra 1.1.3, from 'jagajjanmādikāraṇaṃ brahma vedāntavedyam ity uktam' to the end of the adhikaraṇa.
translations: G. Thibaut (tr.), English translation of the Śrī Bhāṣya [The Vedānta-sūtras with the Commentary of Rāmānuja]. (English)

SA_GSP33_ramvaspu.title: Vedārthasaṃgraha
SA_GSP33_ramvaspu.author: Rāmānuja
SA_GSP33_ramvaspu.summary: The Vedārthasaṃgraha ('Compendium of the Meaning of the Veda') is an independent prose treatise by Rāmānuja (11th–12th century CE) expounding the central philosophical doctrines of Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta. It harmonizes diverse Upaniṣadic passages by demonstrating that sentient beings (cit) and insentient matter (acit) form the body (śarīra) of the supreme Brahman (śarīrin), who is identified with Bhagavān Nārāyaṇa. The work offers extensive polemics against Advaita Vedānta (the unconditioned monism of Śaṅkara), Bhāskara's conditioned identity-in-difference (aupādhika-bhedābheda), and Yādavaprakāśa's essential identity-in-difference (svābhāvika-bhedābheda), concluding that devotional meditation (bhakti / parabhakti) is the ultimate means to liberation.
SA_GSP33_ramvaspu.coverage: complete — Complete text across all 145 sections, from the opening maṅgalaślokas to the concluding verse (sārāsāravivekajñā ... kṛto vedārthasaṅgrahaḥ).
translations: J. A. B. van Buitenen, Rāmānuja's Vedārthasaṃgraha. (English)
S. S. Raghavachar, Vedārtha-Saṅgraha of Śrī Rāmānujācārya, Mysore: Sri Ramakrishna Ashrama, 1978. (English)

SA_GSP33_samkaubh_u.title: Kaṭhopaniṣad with Kaṭhopaniṣadbhāṣya
SA_GSP33_samkaubh_u.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GSP33_samkaubh_u.summary: The Kaṭhopaniṣad is a classical Vedic Upaniṣad framed as a dialogue between the young seeker Naciketas and Yama, the lord of death. Yama instructs Naciketas on the distinction between the pleasant (preyas) and the truly beneficial (śreyas), the famous chariot allegory illustrating the relationship between the self, intellect, mind, and senses, and the transcendent, immortal nature of the ātman. In his Kaṭhopaniṣadbhāṣya, Śaṅkara offers a rigorous Advaita Vedānta exposition, establishing that liberation (mokṣa) is achieved exclusively through the non-dual intuitive realization of the individual self's identity with Brahman rather than through ritual action or meditation.
SA_GSP33_samkaubh_u.attribution: The Kaṭhopaniṣad is a Vedic scriptural text. The commentary (bhāṣya) is attributed to Śaṅkara.
SA_GSP33_samkaubh_u.edition: Ten Principal Upaniṣads with Śaṅkarabhāṣya (Works of Śaṅkarācārya in Original Sanskrit, Vol. 1), Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1964 (reprinted 2007).
SA_GSP33_samkaubh_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of both adhyāyas (each comprising three vallīs, six vallīs in total) of the Kaṭhopaniṣad alongside Śaṅkara's Kaṭhopaniṣadbhāṣya, from the opening śāntipāṭha (1.1.1) to the final verse and concluding colophon at 2.3.19 (6.19).

SA_GSP33_samkupad_u.title: Upadeśasāhasrī
SA_GSP33_samkupad_u.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GSP33_samkupad_u.summary: The Upadeśasāhasrī ('Thousand Teachings') is a treatise (prakaraṇagrantha) attributed to Śaṅkara. Consisting of a metrical section (Padyabandha, 19 chapters) and a prose section (Gadyabandha, 3 chapters), it presents a concise exposition of Advaita Vedānta focusing on the identity of the individual self (ātman) with absolute reality (Brahman). The text emphasizes the complete renunciation of ritual action (karma) in favor of knowledge (jñāna), explicates Upaniṣadic mahāvākyas (especially 'tat tvam asi'), and demonstrates the pedagogical dialogue through which an enlightened teacher dismantles superimposition (adhyāsa) in a qualified pupil.
SA_GSP33_samkupad_u.attribution: Modern scholarship (notably Paul Hacker and Sengaku Mayeda) treats the Upadeśasāhasrī as an authentic work of Śaṅkara.
SA_GSP33_samkupad_u.edition: Sengaku Mayeda (ed.), Śaṅkara's Upadeśasāhasrī, Volume I: Introduction, Text & Indices. Tokyo: The Hokuseido Press, 1973; reprint: Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 2006.
SA_GSP33_samkupad_u.coverage: complete — Complete text containing both the metrical section (Padyabandha, 19 prakaraṇas, 675 kārikās) and the prose section (Gadyabandha, 3 prakaraṇas).
translations: Sengaku Mayeda, A Thousand Teachings: The Upadeśasāhasrī of Śaṅkara, Tokyo: University of Tokyo Press, 1979; reprint: Albany: State University of New York Press, 1992. (English)
Swami Jagadananda, Upadeśasāhasrī: A Thousand Teachings in Two Parts — Prose and Poetry of Sri Sankaracharya, Madras: Sri Ramakrishna Math, 1949. (English)
Paul Hacker, Śaṅkara: Upadeśasāhasrī, Bonn, 1949 (Religionsgeschichtliche Texte 2). (German)

SA_GSP33_vesa.title: Brahmasūtra with Vedāntasāra
SA_GSP33_vesa.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Rāmānuja
SA_GSP33_vesa.summary: The Vedāntasāra ('Essence of Vedānta') is a concise Viśiṣṭādvaita commentary by Rāmānuja on the Brahmasūtra of Bādarāyaṇa. Composed as an accessible companion to his detailed Śrībhāṣya and intermediate Vedāntadīpa, it summarizes the adhikaraṇa structure and logical determination of each sūtra. The work expounds Brahman as the supreme personal reality, Nārāyaṇa, characterized by innumerable auspicious attributes, to whom individual conscious souls (cit) and insentient matter (acit) stand in an inalienable body-soul relation (śarīra-śarīrī-bhāva).
SA_GSP33_vesa.attribution: Rāmānuja composed three commentaries on Bādarāyaṇa's Brahmasūtras: the extensive Śrībhāṣya, the intermediate Vedāntadīpa, and the concise Vedāntasāra.
SA_GSP33_vesa.edition: Vedāntasāra of Bhagavad Rāmānuja, ed. Pandit V. Krishnamacharya, with English translation by M. B. Narasimha Ayyangar, Adyar Library Series, Madras: The Adyar Library and Research Centre, 2nd ed., 1979 (1st ed. 1953).
SA_GSP33_vesa.coverage: complete — Complete text across all four adhyāyas with Rāmānuja's commentary, accompanied by an English translation and an index of scriptural citations.
translations: M. B. Narasimha Ayyangar (tr.), Vedāntasāra of Bhagavad Rāmānuja, Adyar Library Series, Madras: The Adyar Library and Research Centre, 1953 (2nd ed. 1979). (English)

SA_GSP33_vidhivi.title: Vidhiviveka
SA_GSP33_vidhivi.author: Maṇḍanamiśra
SA_GSP33_vidhivi.summary: The Vidhiviveka ('Discrimination of Injunction') is a seminal 8th-century treatise by Maṇḍanamiśra on Vedic hermeneutics and the philosophy of language. Composed in verse with an extensive prose autocommentary (svavṛtti), the work investigates the semantics of Vedic injunctions (vidhi) and the motive force that impels a person to act. Maṇḍanamiśra critically refutes rival theories—notably Kumārila Bhaṭṭa's concept of verbal efficient force (śabdabhāvanā) and the Prābhākara thesis of autonomous duty/obligation (niyoga/kārya)—establishing that prescriptive verbal forms convey that the enjoined act is an effective means to a desired end (iṣṭasādhanatā).
SA_GSP33_vidhivi.attribution: Authored by Maṇḍanamiśra (fl. c. 7th–8th century), who composed both the root verses (mūlakārikā) and the extensive prose autocommentary (svavṛtti).
SA_GSP33_vidhivi.edition: Mahāprabhu Lāla Gosvāmī (ed.), Vidhiviveka of Śrī Maṇḍana Miśra with the commentary Nyāyakaṇikā of Vācaspati Miśra, Varanasi: Tara Publications, 1978.
SA_GSP33_vidhivi.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Vidhiviveka (mūlakārikās and svavṛtti), spanning pp. 1–336 and ending with the final concluding colophon: <iti śrīmahāmahopādhyāyamaṇḍanamiśraviracito vidhivivekaḥ samāptaḥ>.

SA_GSP33_vivcud_u.title: Vivekacūḍāmaṇi
SA_GSP33_vivcud_u.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GSP33_vivcud_u.summary: The Vivekacūḍāmaṇi ('Crest-Jewel of Discrimination') is one of the most widely read verse manuals (prakaraṇa-grantha) of Advaita Vedānta, composed in 580 verses. Set as a pedagogical dialogue between a spiritual teacher and a qualified disciple, it outlines the fourfold qualifications of an aspirant (sādhana-catuṣṭaya), analyzes the three bodies and five sheaths (pañca-kośa), elucidates the nature of māyā and ignorance, and demonstrates the fundamental discrimination (viveka) between the eternal Self (ātman) and the non-Self (anātman). The work culminates in the direct realization of non-duality and the characteristics of the liberated sage (jīvanmukta).
SA_GSP33_vivcud_u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Śaṅkarācārya (the final colophon reads '//iti śaṃkarācāryaviracitaṃ vivekacuḍāmaṇi//'). The GRETIL file labels the attribution 'attrib.'.
SA_GSP33_vivcud_u.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising all 580 verses (vv. 1–580) of the standard vulgate recension, concluding with verse 580 (saṃsārādhvani tāpabhānu...) and the colophon '//iti śaṃkarācāryaviracitaṃ vivekacuḍāmaṇi//'.
translations: Swami Madhavananda, translation of Vivekacūḍāmaṇi. (English)
Christopher Isherwood and Prabhavananda, The Crest-Jewel of Discrimination, Hollywood, California, 1947. (English)

SA_GSP33_yaatsi_u.title: Siddhitraya with Siddhāñjana (part 1: Ātmasiddhi)
SA_GSP33_yaatsi_u.author: Yāmuna, Prativādibhayaṅkara Aṇṇaṅgarācārya
SA_GSP33_yaatsi_u.summary: The Ātmasiddhi is the first section of the Siddhitraya by Yāmunācārya. In this e-text, the surviving fragment of the root work is accompanied by the commentary Siddhāñjana by Prativādibhayaṅkara Aṇṇaṅgarācārya.
SA_GSP33_yaatsi_u.attribution: The root work Ātmasiddhi is part of the Siddhitraya by Yāmuna. The commentary Siddhāñjana was composed by Prativādibhayaṅkara Aṇṇaṅgarācārya.
SA_GSP33_yaatsi_u.coverage: partial — The e-text covers only the Ātmasiddhi, the first part of Yāmuna's three-part Siddhitraya, accompanied by the commentary Siddhāñjana. The text breaks off incomplete, as noted in the commentator's closing stanzas: 'granthabhāgo 'grimaḥ kvāpi netaḥ samupalabhyate / vyākhyānaṃ vihitaṃ yāvadupalabdhasya sārataḥ //'.
translations: The Siddhitraya by Yāmunācārya, edited and translated with notes by R. Ramanujachari and K. Srinivasacharya. Annamalai University Philosophy Series No. 4. Reprinted from Journal of Annamalai University 11, No. 1 (1943). (English)

SA_GSP33_yaissi_u.title: Īśvarasiddhi with Siddhāñjana (fragment)
SA_GSP33_yaissi_u.author: Yāmuna, Prativādibhayaṅkara Aṇṇaṅgarācārya
SA_GSP33_yaissi_u.summary: The Īśvarasiddhi is a treatise of Yāmuna's Siddhitraya. It examines the Mīmāṃsaka objection concerning an omniscient puruṣa and presents arguments concerning the Lord (Īśvara). This e-text gives the surviving text accompanied by the commentary Siddhāñjana by Prativādibhayaṅkara Aṇṇaṅgarācārya.
SA_GSP33_yaissi_u.attribution: Root text by Yāmunācārya. The commentary Siddhāñjana is by Prativādibhayaṅkara Aṇṇaṅgarācārya (pra.bha.aṇṇaṅgācārya), who names himself in the closing colophon.
SA_GSP33_yaissi_u.coverage: fragment — The surviving Īśvarasiddhi with the Siddhāñjana commentary. The mūla begins 'tatra kasyacidekasya vaśe viśvaṃ pravartate'. The commentator closes with 'granthabhāgo 'grimaḥ kvāpi netaḥ samupalabhyate / yāvallabdhasya vihitā vyākhyeyaṃ saralā mayā'.
translations: R. Ramanujachari and K. Srinivasacharya, The Siddhitraya by Yāmunācārya, Annamalai University Philosophy Series No. 4 (reprinted from Journal of Annamalai University 11, No. 1, 1943). (English)

SA_GSP33_yamgaspu.title: Gītārthasaṅgraha
SA_GSP33_yamgaspu.author: Yāmuna
SA_GSP33_yamgaspu.summary: The Gītārthasaṅgraha is a concise 32-verse treatise by Yāmuna synthesizing the teachings of the Bhagavadgītā. It structures the eighteen chapters into three distinct hexads (ṣaṭka), outlining how karma-yoga and jñāna-yoga culminate in bhakti-yoga and self-surrender to Nārāyaṇa as the Supreme Brahman.
SA_GSP33_yamgaspu.coverage: complete — Text of 32 kārikās (numbered YGas_1 to YGas_32).

SA_GSP33_yamis_pu.title: Īśvarasiddhi (fragment)
SA_GSP33_yamis_pu.author: Yāmuna
SA_GSP33_yamis_pu.summary: The Īśvarasiddhi ('Proof of the Lord') is part of Yāmuna's Siddhitraya (Siddhitrayī). Yāmuna first gives a long Mīmāṃsaka pūrvapakṣa arguing that no means of knowledge can establish an omniscient creator. He then answers it with a series of inferences that the world is directed by a single conscious agent, using the analogy of a realm under one king. The surviving text breaks off after the eighteenth kārikā.
SA_GSP33_yamis_pu.coverage: fragment — 18 kārikās (YIs_1–18) with Yāmuna's prose, from 'tatra kasyacid ekasya vaśe viśvaṃ pravartate' to 'ekapradhānapuruṣaṃ vivādādhyāsitaṃ jagat / cetanācetanātmatvād ekarājakadeśavat // 18 //'.
translations: The Siddhitraya by Yāmunācārya, ed. and tr. with notes by R. Ramanujachari and K. Srinivasacharya, Annamalai University Philosophy Series No. 4. Reprinted from Journal of Annamalai University 11, No. 1 (1943). (English)

SA_GSP33_yamss_pu.title: Saṃvitsiddhi (fragment)
SA_GSP33_yamss_pu.author: Yāmuna
SA_GSP33_yamss_pu.summary: The Saṃvitsiddhi, the third treatise of Yāmuna's Siddhitraya, is a verse polemic against Advaita Vedānta. It takes the Upaniṣadic 'ekam evādvitīyam' to deny any equal or superior to Brahman, not the reality of the world. It then criticises the doctrines of avidyā, of contentless consciousness, and of the non-difference of cognition and object. The surviving text breaks off during the refutation of the sahopalambhaniyama argument. Rāmānuja drew on it in the Śrībhāṣya's Mahāsiddhānta.
SA_GSP33_yamss_pu.attribution: A work of Yāmuna (also called Yāmunācārya, c. 950–1000 / 10th–early 11th c. CE), one of the ācāryas of Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta.
SA_GSP33_yamss_pu.coverage: fragment — 207 numbered verses with a few prose connectives (YSsi_1–207). They run from 'ekam evādvitīyaṃ tad brahmety upaniṣadvacaḥ' to 'ghaṭād ṛte 'pi nirbhātaḥ paṭād iva ghaṭaḥ svayam' (YSsi_207), in the middle of the refutation of the sahopalambhaniyama argument. The e-text therefore has all that survives, but the work is a fragment.
translations: Roque Mesquita, Yāmunācāryas Saṃvitsiddhi, Wien: ÖAW, 1988. (German)
R. Ramanujachari and K. Srinivasacharya, Siddhitraya of Yāmunācārya, Annamalainagar: Annamalai University, 1943. (English)

SA_GSP33_yamsvspu.title: Saṃvitsiddhi (fragment)
SA_GSP33_yamsvspu.author: Yāmuna
SA_GSP33_yamsvspu.summary: The Saṃvitsiddhi ('Proof of Consciousness') is the epistemological treatise of Yāmunācārya's Siddhitraya, presenting a systematic defense of Viśiṣṭādvaita realism against Advaita Vedānta and Buddhist Idealism. Yāmuna critiques Advaita interpretations of major Upaniṣadic statements (such as 'ekam evādvitīyam') and refutes the concept of anirvacanīyakhyāti, arguing that consciousness inherently reveals distinct, qualified objects. Surviving only as a fragment (439 half-verse lines in Mesquita's edition), it served as a direct conceptual and textual model for Rāmānuja's Mahāpūrvapakṣa and Mahāsiddhānta in the Śrībhāṣya.
SA_GSP33_yamsvspu.attribution: Composed by Yāmunācārya (c. 10th–11th c. CE), predecessor of Rāmānuja in the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition, as one of the three treatises comprising the Siddhitraya (alongside Ātmasiddhi and Īśvarasiddhi).
SA_GSP33_yamsvspu.edition: Roque Mesquita (ed.), Yāmunācāryas Saṃvitsiddhi: Kritische Edition, Übersetzung und Anmerkungen. Mit einem Rekonstruktionsversuch der verlorenen Abschnitte. Sitzungsberichte der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, Philosophisch-historische Klasse, Bd. 504 / Veröffentlichungen der Kommission für Sprachen und Kulturen Südasiens, Nr. 21. Wien: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, 1988.
SA_GSP33_yamsvspu.coverage: fragment — The extant text of the Saṃvitsiddhi, numbered YSvs_1–439 following Mesquita's lines (GRETIL: 'Line numbering follows ed.'). Each number is a half-verse line, not a kārikā. The text runs from 'ekam evādvitīyaṃ tad brahmety upaniṣadvacaḥ' to 'ghaṭād ṛte 'pi nirbhātaḥ paṭād iva ghaṭaḥ svayam'. The editor's short connective notes, lacuna markers and emendation notes (e.g. '(bādhanam)', '(...)') are kept. The Siddhitraya transmits the work incomplete, with lacunae, and Mesquita's attempted reconstruction of the lost portions is not part of the e-text.
translations: Roque Mesquita, Yāmunācāryas Saṃvitsiddhi: Kritische Edition, Übersetzung und Anmerkungen. Mit einem Rekonstruktionsversuch der verlorenen Abschnitte. (SBph 504), Wien: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, 1988. (German)

SA_GSP33_yasasi_u.title: Siddhitraya with Siddhāñjana (Saṃvitsiddhi only)
SA_GSP33_yasasi_u.author: Yāmuna, P. B. Aṇṇaṅgarācārya
SA_GSP33_yasasi_u.summary: The Saṃvitsiddhi is the third treatise of Yāmunācārya's celebrated Siddhitraya ('Triad of Demonstrations'), a foundational work of Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta. Written primarily in verse with argumentative prose transitions, the work offers an extensive critique of Advaita Vedānta epistemology and ontology, refuting the concept of contentless, undifferentiated consciousness (nirviśeṣa-cinmātra), the unreality of difference, and the doctrine of anirvacanīyatva. Instead, Yāmuna demonstrates that consciousness (saṃvit) is inherently qualified, intentional, and the attribute of an enduring knowing self (jñātṛ). This text directly influenced Rāmānuja's Mahāsiddhānta in the Śrībhāṣya. The digital file presents the surviving portions of the Saṃvitsiddhi accompanied by the Siddhāñjana commentary by P. B. Aṇṇaṅgarācārya.
SA_GSP33_yasasi_u.attribution: The root treatise Saṃvitsiddhi constitutes a section of the Siddhitraya by Yāmuna. The commentary Siddhāñjana was composed by P. B. Aṇṇaṅgarācārya.
SA_GSP33_yasasi_u.coverage: partial — Contains the surviving text of Saṃvitsiddhi accompanied by the Siddhāñjana commentary. The file contains only a section of the Siddhitraya. As noted by the commentator ('atra copakramamadhyāvasāneṣu bhūyān granthabhāgo luptaḥ'), the root text itself is preserved with major lacunae.

SA_GSP34_ghers_pu.title: Gheraṇḍasaṃhitā
SA_GSP34_ghers_pu.summary: The Gheraṇḍasaṃhitā is a classical manual of Haṭha Yoga structured as a dialogue between the sage Gheraṇḍa and his disciple Caṇḍakāpāli. Departing from the fourfold or eightfold structures of other yoga treatises, it teaches a sevenfold discipline (saptāṅga) termed ghaṭastha yoga ('yoga centered on the body-vessel'), consisting of purification (ṣaṭkarma), posture (āsana), mudrā, sensory withdrawal (pratyāhāra), breath regulation (prāṇāyāma), meditation (dhyāna), and samādhi. Alongside the Haṭhapradīpikā and the Śivasaṃhitā, it stands as one of the three principal texts of premodern Haṭha Yoga.
SA_GSP34_ghers_pu.attribution: The work is framed as an instruction delivered by the sage Gheraṇḍa to his student Caṇḍakāpāli.
SA_GSP34_ghers_pu.edition: Gherandasamhita: Sanskrit-deutsch, ed. and tr. Peter Thomi, Wichtrach: Institut für Indologie, 1993 (ISBN 3-7187-0013-1).
SA_GSP34_ghers_pu.coverage: complete — Complete text across all seven teaching lessons (upadeśas 1–7) in pausa (sandhi-split / analyzed) form, terminating at verse 7.23 and its concluding chapter colophon.
translations: Peter Thomi, Gherandasamhita: Sanskrit-deutsch, Wichtrach: Institut für Indologie, 1993. (German)
James Mallinson, Gherandasamhita, Yogavidya.com, 2004. (English)

SA_GSP34_hathyopu.title: Haṭhayogapradīpikā
SA_GSP34_hathyopu.author: Svātmārāma
SA_GSP34_hathyopu.summary: The Haṭhayogapradīpikā by Svātmārāma is a manual of haṭhayoga. In four upadeśas it treats āsana, then prāṇāyāma with the kumbhakas, then mudrās and bandhas for raising kuṇḍalinī, and finally samādhi. Throughout, haṭha is presented as an aid to rājayoga.
SA_GSP34_hathyopu.attribution: Explicitly named as Svātmārāma in verses 1.2–1.4. In secondary literature and commentaries he is often styled Svātmārāma Yogīndra.
SA_GSP34_hathyopu.coverage: complete — Complete four-upadeśa text ending with the colophon 'iti haṭha-yoga-pradīpikāyāṃ samādhi-lakṣaṇaṃ nāma caturthopadeśaḥ'.

SA_GSP34_patyog_u.title: Yogasūtra
SA_GSP34_patyog_u.author: Patañjali
SA_GSP34_patyog_u.summary: The foundational text of classical Pātañjala Yoga, comprising 195 aphorisms arranged into four chapters (pādas): Samādhipāda (on contemplation), Sādhanapāda (on spiritual practice), Vibhūtipāda (on extraordinary powers), and Kaivalyapāda (on liberation). The work defines yoga as the stilling of the fluctuations of consciousness (cittavṛttinirodha) and expounds the eight-limbed practice (aṣṭāṅgayoga) within a dualistic Sāṃkhya-oriented metaphysics of puruṣa and prakṛti.
SA_GSP34_patyog_u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Patañjali. This specific e-text contains solely the extracted sūtras without the bhāṣya.
SA_GSP34_patyog_u.edition: Kāśinātha Śāstrī Āgāśe (ed.), Vācaspatimiśraviracitaṭīkāsaṃvalitavyāsabhāṣyasametāni Pātañjalayogasūtrāṇi, tathā bhojadevaviracitarājamārtaṇḍābhidhavṛttisametāni pātañjalayogasūtrāṇi. sūtrapāṭhasūtravarṇānukramasūcībhyāṃ ca sanāthīkṛtāni..., Pune: Ānandāśrama Mudraṇālaya, 1904 (Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series, 47).
SA_GSP34_patyog_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the 195 sūtras across all four pādas: 1. Samādhipāda (1.1–1.51), 2. Sādhanapāda (2.1–2.55), 3. Vibhūtipāda (3.1–3.55), and 4. Kaivalyapāda (4.1–4.34).
translations: James Haughton Woods, The Yoga-System of Patañjali: Or the Ancient Hindu Doctrine of Concentration of Mind, 1914. (English)
Edwin F. Bryant, The Yoga Sutras of Patañjali: A New Edition, Translation, and Commentary, New York, 2009. (English)

SA_GSP34_patyogbu.title: Yogasūtra with Yogabhāṣya
SA_GSP34_patyogbu.author: Patañjali, Vyāsa
SA_GSP34_patyogbu.summary: The foundational text of classical Yoga philosophy (Pātañjala Yoga), comprising the root aphorisms and their earliest authoritative commentary across four chapters (Samādhipāda, Sādhanapāda, Vibhūtipāda, and Kaivalyapāda). Developing a dualist ontology closely allied with classical Sāṅkhya, the work provides a detailed analysis of mental modifications (cittavṛtti), afflictions (kleśa), meditative stages and extraordinary powers (vibhūti/siddhi), and the ultimate liberation of puruṣa in isolation (kaivalya).
SA_GSP34_patyogbu.attribution: The root aphorisms are traditionally attributed to Patañjali and the commentary to Vyāsa.
SA_GSP34_patyogbu.edition: Kāśinātha Śāstrī Āgāśe: Vācaspatimiśraviracitaṭīkāsaṃvalitavyāsabhāṣyasametāni Pātañjalayogasūtrāṇi, tathā bhojadevaviracitarājamārtaṇḍābhidhavṛttisametāni pātañjalayogasūtrāṇi. sūtrapāṭhasūtravarṇānukramasūcībhyāṃ ca sanāthīkṛtāni... Pune: Ānandāśramamudraṇālaye 1904 (Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series, 47).
SA_GSP34_patyogbu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all four pādas of the Yogasūtra and Yogabhāṣya: Samādhipāda (1.1–1.51), Sādhanapāda (2.1–2.55), Vibhūtipāda (3.1–3.55), and Kaivalyapāda (4.1–4.34), ending with the fourth pāda colophon: 'iti śrīpātañjale sāṃkhyapravacane yogaśāstre vyāsabhāṣye kaivalyapādaś caturthaḥ'.
translations: James Haughton Woods, The Yoga-System of Patañjali (translation of the Yogasūtra with Bhāṣya by Vyāsa and Tattvavaiśāradī by Vācaspatimiśra), Cambridge, Massachusetts 1914. (English)
Hariharānanda Āraṇya, Yoga Philosophy of Patañjali (1963). (English)

SA_GSP34_yogasubha.title: Yogasūtra with Yogasūtrabhāṣya
SA_GSP34_yogasubha.author: Patañjali, Vyāsa
SA_GSP34_yogasubha.summary: The Yogasūtra with Yogasūtrabhāṣya (together titled Pātañjalayogaśāstra) constitutes the foundational text of classical Yoga darśana, composed around 400 CE. Framed within a dualistic metaphysics closely aligned with classical Sāṃkhya, it provides a rigorous psychology and contemplative methodology covering mental fluctuations (cittavṛtti), the eightfold yogic practice (aṣṭāṅgayoga), forms of meditative absorption (samādhi), extraordinary powers (siddhis), and final spiritual isolation (kaivalya). It serves as the primary textual authority for all subsequent classical and post-classical Yoga commentary in India.
SA_GSP34_yogasubha.attribution: In classical Indian tradition, the aphorisms are ascribed to Patañjali and the commentary to Vyāsa (hence Vyāsabhāṣya).
SA_GSP34_yogasubha.edition: Kāśinātha Śāstrī Āgāśe (ed.), Vācaspatimiśraviracitaṭīkāsaṃvalitavyāsabhāṣyasametāni Pātañjalayogasūtrāṇi tathā Bhojadevaviracitarājamārtaṇḍābhidhavṛttisametāni Pātañjalayogasūtrāṇi, Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series 47, Pune: Ānandāśrama Press, 1904.
SA_GSP34_yogasubha.coverage: complete — Complete text of all four chapters (pādas): Samādhipāda (51 sūtras), Sādhanapāda (55 sūtras), Vibhūtipāda (55 sūtras), and Kaivalyapāda (34 sūtras), each with the full bhāṣya text.
translations: James Haughton Woods, The Yoga-System of Patañjali, or the Ancient Hindu Doctrine of Concentration of Mind, Harvard Oriental Series 17, Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1914. (English)
Hariharānanda Āraṇya, Yoga Philosophy of Patañjali, 1963. (English)

SA_GSP34_yogasutu.title: Yogasūtra
SA_GSP34_yogasutu.author: Patañjali
SA_GSP34_yogasutu.summary: The Yogasūtra of Patañjali is the foundational treatise of the classical Yoga school of Indian philosophy. Organized into four pādas (Samādhi-, Sādhana-, Vibhūti-, and Kaivalyapāda), the aphorisms define yoga as the cessation of mental fluctuations (cittavṛttinirodha) and expound psychological taxonomy, eightfold yogic practice (aṣṭāṅga), meditative absorptions, paranormal powers, and the metaphysical isolation of pure consciousness (kaivalya).
SA_GSP34_yogasutu.attribution: Ascribed to Patañjali in the text and tradition.

Krishnamurthi Sastri, Madras: Government Oriental Manuscripts Library, 1952.

SA_GSP34_yogsubhu.title: Yogasūtra with Yogasūtrabhāṣya
SA_GSP34_yogsubhu.author: Patañjali, Vyāsa
SA_GSP34_yogsubhu.summary: The Yogasūtra with the Yogasūtrabhāṣya constitutes the foundational text of the classical Yoga darśana. Divided into four chapters—Samādhipāda, Sādhanapāda, Vibhūtipāda, and Kaivalyapāda—it establishes the philosophical definition of yoga as the cessation of mental fluctuations (cittavṛttinirodha) and elaborates the eightfold path (aṣṭāṅgayoga). The work provides a systematic exposition of meditation, epistemic validity, karmic latent impressions (saṃskāra), contemplative attainments (siddhi), and the ultimate liberation (kaivalya) of conscious spirit (puruṣa) from primordial matter (prakṛti).
SA_GSP34_yogsubhu.attribution: Traditional Indian doxography attributes the aphorisms (sūtra) to Patañjali and the commentary to Vyāsa.
SA_GSP34_yogsubhu.edition: Pātañjalayogasūtrāṇi vācaspatimiśraviracitaṭīkāsaṃvalitavyāsabhāṣyasametāni … tathā bhojadevaviracitarājamārtaṇḍābhidhavṛttisametāni, edited by Kāśīnātha Śāstrī Āgāśe, Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series 47, Poona: Ānandāśrama Press, 1904 (reprinted 1978).

SA_GSP35_sa_mokSopAya.title: Mokṣopāya (prakaraṇas 1–5 and 6.1–252)
SA_GSP35_sa_mokSopAya.summary: The Mokṣopāya is a philosophical work framed in an epic setting (asmin rāmāyaṇe nāma) with Vālmīki narrating teaching to Bharadvāja. It combines discourse on liberation (mokṣopāya) with narratives across multiple prakaraṇas (Vairāgya, Mumukṣuvyavahāra, Utpatti, Sthiti, Upaśānti, and Nirvāṇa). Modern scholarship identifies it as the earlier Kashmiri recension closely related to the Yogavāsiṣṭha tradition.

SA_GV00_maitrs_pu.title: Maitrāyaṇīsaṃhitā
SA_GV00_maitrs_pu.summary: The Maitrāyaṇīsaṃhitā is one of the surviving saṃhitās of the Kṛṣṇa (Black) Yajurveda, representing the liturgical tradition of the Maitrāyaṇīya school. It intermixes sacrificial mantras with archaic explanatory prose (brāhmaṇa-type discussions) on the origin and performance of śrauta rituals. Spanning four kāṇḍas, the work details rites such as the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa), the Agnihotra, the Soma rituals, and the Agnicayana, serving as a principal source for early Vedic language and ritual theology.
SA_GV00_maitrs_pu.attribution: Canonical saṃhitā of the Maitrāyaṇīya school of the Black (Kṛṣṇa) Yajurveda; traditional Vedic revelation (śruti) without human authorship.

SA_GV00_sa_paippalAdasaMhitA.title: Paippalādasaṃhitā
SA_GV00_sa_paippalAdasaMhitA.summary: The Paippalādasaṃhitā is one of the two surviving recensions of the Atharvaveda (alongside the Śaunakasaṃhitā). Arranged into twenty kāṇḍas, it contains healing charms, protective spells, rituals for prosperity and defense, royal rites, and speculative cosmological hymns. Long known in modern scholarship only through a single, heavily corrupt birch-bark manuscript from Kashmir discovered in 1875, it was rediscovered in the late 1950s when Durgamohan Bhattacharyya located living communities and palm-leaf manuscripts in Odisha.
SA_GV00_sa_paippalAdasaMhitA.attribution: Traditional Vedic saṃhitā belonging to the Paippalāda school (śākhā) of the Atharvaveda, traditionally connected with the sage Pippalāda.

SA_GV01_aibra.title: Aitareyabrāhmaṇa
SA_GV01_aibra.summary: The Aitareyabrāhmaṇa is the main Brāhmaṇa of the Ṛgveda (Śākala school). It has 40 adhyāyas grouped into 8 pañcikās and sets out the duties of the hotṛ priest in the śrauta ritual. Most of it deals with the soma sacrifices. The later pañcikās cover the royal consecration rites, and pañcikā 7 tells the Śunaḥśepa story.

SA_GV01_rv_01_u.title: Ṛgveda (maṇḍala 1)
SA_GV01_rv_01_u.summary: Maṇḍala 1 is the opening book of the Ṛgvedasaṃhitā, consisting of 191 hymns addressed primarily to Agni, Indra, the Aśvins, the Maruts, Varuṇa, and Uṣas. It is composed of multiple smaller cycles attributed to distinct ṛṣi lineages (such as the Gotamas, Kutsas, and Agastyas), functioning alongside Maṇḍala 10 as an outer book framing the central 'family books' (Maṇḍalas 2–7). Among its most famous compositions are the riddle hymn of Dīrghatamas (1.164) and the early dialogue and riddle hymns.

SA_GV01_rv_02_u.title: Ṛgveda (maṇḍala 2)
SA_GV01_rv_02_u.summary: Maṇḍala 2 of the Ṛgveda is the first of the six 'family books' (Maṇḍalas 2–7), which represent the earliest core of the Saṃhitā. Traditionally attributed to the lineage of Gṛtsamada Śaunaka, it consists of 43 hymns (429 verses) organized according to the standard Vedic redaction scheme, principally addressed to Agni and Indra, as well as Bṛhaspati, the Maruts, and Rudra.
SA_GV01_rv_02_u.attribution: Traditional Vedic authorship assigns Maṇḍala 2 to the ṛṣi Gṛtsamada Śaunaka and his lineage (Gṛtsamadas / Bhārgavas). In orthodox Brahmanical tradition, Vedic saṃhitās are apauruṣeya ('unauthored' / eternal).

SA_GV01_rv_03_u.title: Ṛgveda (Maṇḍala 3)
SA_GV01_rv_03_u.summary: Maṇḍala 3 of the Ṛgveda is one of the core 'family books' (Maṇḍalas 2–7) of the Saṃhitā, traditionally attributed to the seer Viśvāmitra and his clan, the Kuśikas. It comprises 62 hymns addressed predominantly to Agni and Indra, alongside hymns to the Viśvedevāḥ, the Aśvins, and Savitṛ. Key passages include the famed Gāyatrī (Sāvitrī) mantra (RV 3.62.10) and the dialogue between Viśvāmitra and the rivers Vipāś and Śutudrī (RV 3.33).

SA_GV01_rv_05_u.title: Ṛgveda (maṇḍala 5)
SA_GV01_rv_05_u.summary: Maṇḍala 5 of the Ṛgveda is the Atri family book (Ātreya maṇḍala), comprising 87 hymns (sūktas 5.1–5.87) attributed to the seer Atri and his lineage. In standard Vedic liturgical ordering, it opens with hymns to Agni (5.1–28) and Indra (5.29–40), followed by collections for the Viśvedevas (5.41–51), the Maruts (5.52–61), Mitra-Varuṇa (5.62–72), and the Aśvins (5.73–78), concluding with hymns to diverse deities including the notable penitential hymn to Varuṇa (5.85) and the Evayāmarut hymn (5.87). As part of the archaic 'family books' (maṇḍalas 2–7), it represents one of the oldest literary strata of Vedic Sanskrit.

SA_GV01_rv_06_u.title: Ṛgveda (maṇḍala 6)
SA_GV01_rv_06_u.summary: Maṇḍala 6 of the Ṛgveda comprises 75 hymns (765 stanzas) and is traditionally grouped as one of the six 'family books' (maṇḍalas 2–7). Attributed to the Bharadvāja lineage of the Aṅgiras family, the hymns are arranged primarily by recipient deity: hymns 1–16 addressed to Agni, hymns 17–47 to Indra, followed by hymns to the Viśvedevāḥ, Pūṣan, the Aśvins, and other deities. Notable sections include hymn 6.75, an important hymn for warfare and chariot weaponry, and the collection of hymns devoted to the pastoral deity Pūṣan.
SA_GV01_rv_06_u.attribution: Maṇḍala 6 is one of the family books of the Ṛgveda, traditionally associated with the Bharadvāja lineage.

SA_GV01_rv_07_u.title: Ṛgveda (maṇḍala 7)
SA_GV01_rv_07_u.summary: Maṇḍala 7 of the Ṛgveda is one of the ancient family books (kula-maṇḍalas), traditionally attributed to the ṛṣi Vasiṣṭha and the Vasiṣṭha lineage. Comprising 104 hymns (841 verses), it contains cycles dedicated to Agni, Indra, Varuṇa, the Maruts, and the Viśvedevas. Among its most prominent compositions are the personal devotional hymns to Varuṇa seeking forgiveness from guilt and release from bonds (7.86–89), the historical narrative poetry concerning King Sudās and the Battle of the Ten Kings (Dāśarājña, 7.18 and 7.33), and the Frog Hymn (Maṇḍūka-sūkta, 7.103).

SA_GV01_rv_08_u.title: Ṛgveda (maṇḍala 8)
SA_GV01_rv_08_u.summary: Maṇḍala 8 of the Ṛgveda contains 103 sūktas (hymns 8.1–103), including the group of eleven supplementary Vālakhilya hymns (8.49–59). Situated alongside Book 1 outside the nuclear 'family books' (Maṇḍalas 2–7), it is primarily associated with the Kāṇva and Āṅgirasa poetic families and characterized by its distinctively frequent use of pragātha strophic meters (combining bṛhatī and satobṛhatī). The hymns are dedicated chiefly to Indra, the Aśvins, and Agni, and include numerous celebrated dānastutis (praise of donors) as well as substantial parallels in the liturgical chants of the Sāmaveda.

SA_GV01_rv_09_u.title: Ṛgveda (maṇḍala 9)
SA_GV01_rv_09_u.summary: Maṇḍala 9 of the Ṛgveda comprises 114 hymns addressed exclusively to Soma Pavamāna ('Soma undergoing purification'). Unlike the family books (Maṇḍalas 2–7), which group hymns by ancestral bardic lineage, Maṇḍala 9 is a thematic collection assembling Soma hymns of diverse origin, arranged primarily by metre. The hymns celebrate the extraction, pressing, straining through the sheep's wool filter (pavitra), and cosmic consecration of the deified soma draught.

SA_GV01_rv_10_u.title: Ṛgveda (maṇḍala 10)
SA_GV01_rv_10_u.summary: The tenth maṇḍala of the Ṛgveda contains 191 hymns and represents the latest chronological layer of the Saṃhitā (c. 1200–1000 BCE). Linguistically and thematically close to the Atharvaveda, it includes major philosophical and cosmogonic hymns such as the Nāsadīyasūkta (10.129), the Puruṣasūkta (10.90), and the Hiraṇyagarbhasūkta (10.121). It also preserves famous dialogue hymns (saṃvāda), funeral and wedding liturgies, and incantations for healing, offering invaluable insight into late Ṛgvedic religious and social thought.

SA_GV01_rv_hn01u.title: Ṛgveda (maṇḍala 1)
SA_GV01_rv_hn01u.summary: Maṇḍala 1 of the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā is a major introductory hymn collection consisting of 191 sūktas addressed to the Vedic pantheon, predominantly Agni, Indra, the Aśvins, Uṣas, and the Maruts. Unlike the core 'family books' (Maṇḍalas 2–7), each of which represents the poetry of an individual priestly clan, Maṇḍala 1 is composed of multiple smaller authorial cycles attributed to various rishi families (including the Kāṇvas, Gautamas, and Agastyas). In the relative chronology of the Vedic corpus, Maṇḍala 1 reflects a late stage of redaction contemporary with Maṇḍala 10, with which it shares an identical hymn count of 191.

SA_GV01_rv_hn02u.title: Ṛgveda (maṇḍala 2)
SA_GV01_rv_hn02u.summary: Maṇḍala 2 of the Ṛgveda is the first and shortest of the six 'family books' (kula-maṇḍalas, books 2–7) that constitute the earliest compositional core of the Saṃhitā. It comprises 43 hymns (429 verses), traditionally attributed to the seer Gṛtsamada Śaunaka and his clan. The hymns follow the standard Vedic structural arrangement by deity: opening with hymns to Agni (2.1–2.11), followed by Indra (2.12–2.22), other deities including Bṛhaspati/Brahmaṇaspati, the Maruts, and Rudra, and closing with two omen-bird hymns (2.42–2.43). The maṇḍala contains several celebrated compositions, including the famed Indra narrative hymn 2.12 ('He who as soon as born became the chief god') and the fervent prayer to Rudra in 2.33.

SA_GV01_rv_hn03u.title: Ṛgveda (Maṇḍala 3)
SA_GV01_rv_hn03u.summary: Maṇḍala 3 of the Ṛgveda is one of the six archaic 'family books' (Maṇḍalas 2–7), traditionally attributed to the seer Viśvāmitra and the Vaiśvāmitra poet family. Comprising 62 hymns, it begins with an extensive series dedicated to Agni (3.1–28) followed by hymns dedicated to Indra (3.30–53), as well as praises to the Viśvedevas, the Ṛbhus, and Mitra. Maṇḍala 3 is renowned for preserving the dialogue between Viśvāmitra and the rivers Vipāś and Śutudrī (RV 3.33) as well as the famous Gāyatrī or Sāvitrī mantra (RV 3.62.10).
SA_GV01_rv_hn03u.attribution: According to tradition, the hymns of Maṇḍala 3 are ascribed to Viśvāmitra and the Vaiśvāmitras.

The book concludes with the hymn to the Maruts (5.87) marked by the distinctive refrain evayāmarut.

SA_GV01_rv_hn06u.title: Ṛgveda (maṇḍala 6)
SA_GV01_rv_hn06u.summary: Maṇḍala 6 of the Ṛgveda is one of the ancient 'family books' (kula-maṇḍalas, books 2–7) of the Ṛgvedasaṃhitā, traditionally ascribed to Bharadvāja Bārhaspatya and the Bharadvāja lineage. Comprising 75 hymns (765 stanzas), the collection follows the characteristic deity ordering of the family books, opening with hymns to Agni (6.1–16) and Indra (6.17–47), followed by hymns to the Viśvedevas, the Aśvins, and a prominent group addressed to Pūṣan (6.53–58). The book concludes with the well-known martial hymn (6.75, saṅgrāma-sūkta), which provides valuable early Vedic evidence for chariot warfare, armor, and weaponry.
SA_GV01_rv_hn06u.edition: Th. Aufrecht: Die Hymnen des Rig Veda, 2nd ed., Bonn 1877.
SA_GV01_rv_hn06u.coverage: partial — Contains the text of Maṇḍala 6 (RV 6.1.1a–6.75.19c).
translations: Stephanie W. Jamison and Joel P. Brereton (transl.), The Rigveda. The Earliest Religious Poetry of India, Oxford, 2014. (English)

SA_GV01_rv_hn07u.title: Ṛgveda (Maṇḍala 7)
SA_GV01_rv_hn07u.summary: The seventh maṇḍala of the Ṛgveda is one of the core 'family books' (maṇḍalas 2–7), traditionally preserved and transmitted by the Vāsiṣṭha priestly lineage. It contains 104 hymns (841 stanzas) addressed primarily to Agni, Indra, Varuṇa, the Maruts, and other deities. Notable compositions include the deeply personal devotional hymns addressed to Varuṇa (RV 7.86–89), the historic account of King Sudās and the Battle of the Ten Kings (Dāśarājña, RV 7.18), and the celebrated Frog Hymn (RV 7.103).
SA_GV01_rv_hn07u.edition: Th. Aufrecht: Die Hymnen des Rig Veda, 2nd ed., Bonn 1877.
SA_GV01_rv_hn07u.coverage: partial — Contains the entirety of Maṇḍala 7 (hymns 7.1.1 to 7.104.25; 104 hymns, 841 stanzas, 1,642 pāda segments).
translations: JAMISON, Stephanie W., Joel P. BRERETON (transl.) (2014). The Rigveda. The Earliest Religious Poetry of India. Oxford. (English)

SA_GV01_rv_hn08u.title: Ṛgveda (maṇḍala 8)
SA_GV01_rv_hn08u.summary: Maṇḍala 8 of the Ṛgveda consists of 103 hymns predominantly addressed to Indra, Agni, and the Aśvins, largely attributed to poets of the Kāṇva and Āṅgirasa lineages. It contains the eleven Vālakhilya supplementary hymns (RV 8.49–8.59). Characterized prominently by pragmatic strophic meters (especially the pragātha meter), Maṇḍala 8 constitutes a distinctive structural grouping alongside the traditional family books (Maṇḍalas 2–7).
SA_GV01_rv_hn08u.edition: Th. Aufrecht: Die Hymnen des Rig Veda, 2nd ed., Bonn 1877.
SA_GV01_rv_hn08u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete eighth maṇḍala (hymns RV 8.1–103, comprising 1,716 stanzas, including the 11 Vālakhilya hymns 8.49–8.59) of the ten maṇḍalas of the Ṛgveda.
translations: Stephanie W. Jamison, Joel P. Brereton (transl.) (2014). The Rigveda. The Earliest Religious Poetry of India. Oxford. (English)

SA_GV01_rv_hn09u.title: Ṛgveda (Maṇḍala 9)
SA_GV01_rv_hn09u.summary: Maṇḍala 9 of the Ṛgveda comprises 114 hymns exclusively dedicated to Soma Pavamāna ('purifying Soma'). Unlike the family books (Maṇḍalas 2–7), which are organized by seer lineage, this collection is arranged thematically by meter and liturgical purpose, focusing on the preparation, pressing, and filtration of the sacred Soma juice through the wool strainer into wooden vats. Due to their ritual importance, the overwhelming majority of verses from this maṇḍala were incorporated into the Sāmaveda for musical recitation during the Soma sacrifice.
SA_GV01_rv_hn09u.attribution: The hymns of the ninth maṇḍala are attributed to diverse Vedic ṛṣis across multiple families (such as Kaśyapa, Asita, Devala), all addressing Soma Pavamāna. As a Vedic canonical saṃhitā, no author is assigned.
SA_GV01_rv_hn09u.edition: Th. Aufrecht: Die Hymnen des Rig Veda, 2nd ed., Bonn 1877.
SA_GV01_rv_hn09u.coverage: partial — Complete text of Maṇḍala 9 (all 114 sūktas, RV 9.1–9.114, comprising 1,108 verses/ṛcs) of the ten-book Ṛgveda-Saṃhitā.
translations: Stephanie W. Jamison and Joel P. Brereton (transl.), The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India, Oxford, 2014. (English)

SA_GV01_rv_hn10u.title: Ṛgveda (Maṇḍala 10)
SA_GV01_rv_hn10u.summary: Maṇḍala 10 is the final book of the Ṛgvedasaṃhitā, comprising 191 hymns that belong to the chronologically latest stratum of the text. It features celebrated cosmogonic and philosophical compositions such as the Nāsadīyasūkta (RV 10.129), Puruṣasūkta (RV 10.90), and Hiraṇyagarbhasūkta (RV 10.121), alongside domestic rituals, wedding (RV 10.85), funeral (RV 10.14–18), and dramatic dialogue hymns (saṃvāda). Linguistically and thematically, it bridges the older liturgical poetry of the family books with the Atharvavedic and Brāhmaṇa traditions.
SA_GV01_rv_hn10u.edition: Th. Aufrecht: Die Hymnen des Rig Veda, 2nd ed., Bonn 1877.
SA_GV01_rv_hn10u.coverage: partial — Complete text of Maṇḍala 10 (hymns RV 10.1.1 through RV 10.191.4); represents one of the ten books of the complete Ṛgvedasaṃhitā.
translations: Stephanie W. Jamison and Joel P. Brereton (trans.), The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India, Oxford, 2014. (English)
Wendy Doniger O'Flaherty (trans.), The Rig Veda: An Anthology, Middlesex, England / Harmondsworth: Penguin Books, 1981. (English)

SA_GV01_rvkhilau.title: Ṛgvedakhilāni
SA_GV01_rvkhilau.summary: The Ṛgvedakhilāni comprises supplementary or 'apocryphal' hymns (khila) preserved outside the canonical Śākala recension of the Ṛgveda-Saṃhitā, notably transmitted in the Bāṣkala tradition and in a famous sixteenth-century Śāradā birch-bark manuscript from Kashmir. Linguistically and historically belonging to the Mantra period of late Vedic Sanskrit, the corpus parallels the language of the Atharvaveda and the Yajurveda Saṃhitās. It preserves ritual and devotional hymns of major historical and liturgical significance, including the Śrīsūkta, the Medhāsūkta, the Śivasaṃkalpasūkta, and the Kuntāpa hymns recited during the Mahāvrata rite.
SA_GV01_rvkhilau.attribution: A collection of supplementary Vedic hymns. Individual hymns and verses are traditionally attributed to various Vedic seers (ṛṣis) in the accompanying Khilānukramaṇī.
SA_GV01_rvkhilau.edition: J. Scheftelowitz: Die Apokryphen des Rgveda (Khilani) Breslau 1906 (Indische Forschungen; 1)
SA_GV01_rvkhilau.coverage: complete — Complete relative to Scheftelowitz's 1906 edition. Contains the introductory Khilānukramaṇī (adhyāya 1 Introd.), all five adhyāyas of the Khilāni (RvKh 1.1–5.22, including the Śrīsūkta, Medhāsūkta, and Kuntāpa hymns), the scribal colophons of the Kashmirian birch-bark manuscript, and the Khilakhila appendix (KhKh 1–7).

SA_GV01_rvpp_01u.title: Ṛgvedapadapāṭha (maṇḍala 1)
SA_GV01_rvpp_01u.summary: The Padapāṭha ('word text') of Maṇḍala 1 of the Ṛgveda (hymns 1.1–1.191). It undoes sandhi, splits compounds and some suffixes with hyphens, and marks pragṛhya vowels with 'iti'.
translations: Stephanie W. Jamison and Joel P. Brereton, The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India, Oxford, 2014. (English)

SA_GV01_rvpp_02u.title: Ṛgvedapadapāṭha (maṇḍala 2)
SA_GV01_rvpp_02u.summary: The Padapāṭha ('word text') of Maṇḍala 2 of the Ṛgveda, the family book of the Gṛtsamadas (43 hymns, mainly to Agni and Indra). It undoes sandhi, splits compounds with hyphens, and marks pragṛhya vowels with 'iti'.
SA_GV01_rvpp_02u.coverage: partial — Maṇḍala 2 complete: 43 sūktas, 429 verses (RV 2.1.1–2.43.3). The refrain at 2.43.3 is abbreviated in the e-text ('vadema / v // RV_2,43.3 //').
translations: Stephanie W. Jamison and Joel P. Brereton (transl.), The Rigveda. The Earliest Religious Poetry of India, Oxford, 2014. (English)

SA_GV01_rvpp_03u.title: Ṛgvedapadapāṭha (maṇḍala 3)
SA_GV01_rvpp_03u.summary: Padapāṭha ("word text") of Maṇḍala 3 of the Ṛgveda, in which the continuous Saṃhitā text is resolved into pausal word forms: external sandhi is dissolved, compound members and some suffixes are separated by hyphens (e.g. "śam-āye", "su-putrā"). Maṇḍala 3 contains hymns up to RV 3.62.18.
translations: Stephanie W. Jamison, Joel P. Brereton (transl.) (2014). The Rigveda. The Earliest Religious Poetry of India. Oxford. (English)

SA_GV01_rvpp_04u.title: Ṛgvedapadapāṭha (maṇḍala 4)
SA_GV01_rvpp_04u.summary: Padapāṭha ("word text") of Maṇḍala 4 of the Ṛgveda, in which the continuous Saṃhitā text is resolved into pausal word forms: external sandhi is dissolved, compound members and some suffixes are separated by hyphens (e.g. "samit-bhiḥ"), and pragṛhya forms are marked with "iti". Maṇḍala 4 (58 hymns) is the family book of Vāmadeva Gautama. It includes the hymns on the bringing of Soma by the falcon (4.26–27) and the Ṛbhu hymns (4.33–37). The Padapāṭha, traditionally ascribed to Śākalya, is the basis of the Ṛkprātiśākhya and the earliest analytic treatment of the Vedic text.
translations: Stephanie W. Jamison and Joel P. Brereton (transl.), The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India, Oxford, 2014. (English)

SA_GV01_rvpp_05u.title: Ṛgvedapadapāṭha (maṇḍala 5)
SA_GV01_rvpp_05u.summary: Padapāṭha ("word text") of Maṇḍala 5 of the Ṛgveda, in which the continuous Saṃhitā text is resolved into pausal word forms: external sandhi is dissolved, compound members and some suffixes are separated by hyphens (e.g. "sam-idhā"). Maṇḍala 5 (87 hymns) contains hymns to Agni, Indra, and other deities.
translations: Stephanie W. Jamison, Joel P. Brereton (transl.), The Rigveda. The Earliest Religious Poetry of India, Oxford, 2014. (English)

SA_GV01_rvpp_06u.title: Ṛgvedapadapāṭha (maṇḍala 6)
SA_GV01_rvpp_06u.summary: Padapāṭha ("word text") of Maṇḍala 6 of the Ṛgveda, in which the continuous Saṃhitā text is resolved into pausal word forms: external sandhi is dissolved, compound members and some suffixes are separated by hyphens (e.g. "samit-bhiḥ"), and pragṛhya forms are marked with "iti". Maṇḍala 6 (75 hymns) is the family book of Bharadvāja Bārhaspatya and his lineage. It contains prominent hymns to Agni, Indra and Pūṣan, and ends with the weapon hymn 6.75. The Padapāṭha, traditionally ascribed to Śākalya, is the basis of the Ṛkprātiśākhya and the earliest analytic treatment of the Vedic text.

SA_GV01_rvpp_07u.title: Ṛgvedapadapāṭha (maṇḍala 7)
SA_GV01_rvpp_07u.summary: Padapāṭha ("word text") of Maṇḍala 7 of the Ṛgveda, in which the continuous Saṃhitā text is resolved into pausal word forms: external sandhi is dissolved, compound members and some suffixes are separated by hyphens (e.g. "samit-bhiḥ"), and pragṛhya forms are marked with "iti". Maṇḍala 7 (104 hymns) is the family book of Vasiṣṭha Maitrāvaruṇi and his descendants. It includes the hymns on the Battle of the Ten Kings (7.18, 7.33, 7.83) and the frog hymn (7.103). The Padapāṭha, traditionally ascribed to Śākalya, is the basis of the Ṛkprātiśākhya and the earliest analytic treatment of the Vedic text.

SA_GV01_rvpp_08u.title: Ṛgvedapadapāṭha (maṇḍala 8)
SA_GV01_rvpp_08u.summary: Padapāṭha ("word text") of Maṇḍala 8 of the Ṛgveda, in which the continuous Saṃhitā text is resolved into pausal word forms: external sandhi is dissolved, compound members and some suffixes are separated by hyphens (e.g. "samit-bhiḥ"), and pragṛhya forms are marked with "iti". Maṇḍala 8 (103 hymns) is a collection associated mainly with the Kaṇva and Āṅgirasa families, including the eleven Vālakhilya hymns (8.49–59). Its hymns are addressed mainly to Indra, Agni and the Aśvins. The Padapāṭha, traditionally ascribed to Śākalya, is the basis of the Ṛkprātiśākhya and the earliest analytic treatment of the Vedic text.

SA_GV01_rvpp_09u.title: Ṛgvedapadapāṭha (maṇḍala 9)
SA_GV01_rvpp_09u.summary: Padapāṭha ("word text") of Maṇḍala 9 of the Ṛgveda, in which the continuous Saṃhitā text is resolved into pausal word forms: external sandhi is dissolved, compound members and some suffixes are separated by hyphens (e.g. "samit-bhiḥ"), and pragṛhya forms are marked with "iti". Maṇḍala 9 (114 hymns) is the Pavamāna book, devoted entirely to Soma Pavamāna. Its hymns accompany the pressing and filtering of Soma.
SA_GV01_rvpp_09u.attribution: Maṇḍala 9 is the Pavamāna book, devoted entirely to Soma Pavamāna.

SA_GV01_rvpp_10u.summary: Padapāṭha ("word text") of Maṇḍala 10 of the Ṛgveda, in which the continuous Saṃhitā text is resolved into pausal word forms: external sandhi is dissolved, compound members and some suffixes are separated by hyphens (e.g. "su-aṅgaḥ", "jāta-vedaḥ"), and pragṛhya forms are marked with "iti". SA_GV02_gopthbru.title: Gopathabrāhmaṇa (Pūrvabhāga 1.1.1–1.3.6)
SA_GV02_gopthbru.summary: The Gopathabrāhmaṇa is a Brāhmaṇa text attached to the Atharvaveda tradition, concerned with the Brahman priest and sacrificial ceremonial.
SA_GV02_gopthbru.attribution: An anonymous Vedic prose text affiliated with the Atharvaveda tradition.
SA_GV02_gopthbru.edition: Rājendralāla Mitra and Harachandra Vidyābhūṣaṇa (eds.), Calcutta: Gaṇeśa Press, 1872 (Bibliotheca Indica; 69).
