SA_GV02_kausibru.title: Kauṣītakibrāhmaṇa
SA_GV02_kausibru.summary: The Kauṣītakibrāhmaṇa (also known as the Śāṅkhāyanabrāhmaṇa) is one of the two extant Brāhmaṇas belonging to the Ṛgveda, transmitted within the Kauṣītaki/Śāṅkhāyana śākhā. Across thirty adhyāyas, it systematically provides liturgical injunctions, mythological narratives, and theological interpretations primarily concerning the duties of the Hotṛ priest and his assistants. The work covers the fire installation (Agnyādhāna), daily fire offering (Agnihotra), New and Full Moon sacrifices (Darśapūrṇamāsa), seasonal rites (Cāturmāsya), animal sacrifice (Paśubandha), and the full range of Soma rituals including the Agniṣṭoma and multiday sessions (sattras).
SA_GV02_kausibru.attribution: Ascribed in Vedic tradition to the teacher Kauṣītaki (frequently cited as an authority throughout the text) and preserved within the Kauṣītaki/Śāṅkhāyana śākhā of the Ṛgveda.
SA_GV02_kausibru.edition: E. R. Sreekrishna Sarma (Wiesbaden 1968; VOHD, Suppl. 9,1)
SA_GV02_kausibru.coverage: complete — Complete text in 30 adhyāyas (running from KB 1.1.1 through KB 30.9.36).
translations: Arthur Berriedale Keith, Rigveda Brahmanas: The Aitareya and Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇas of the Rigveda, 1920. (English)

SA_GV02_pncvbr1u.title: Pañcaviṃśabrāhmaṇa
SA_GV02_pncvbr1u.summary: The Pañcaviṃśabrāhmaṇa (also known as the Tāṇḍyamahābrāhmaṇa) is a Brāhmaṇa text of the Sāmaveda. In 25 prapāṭhakas, it expounds ritual matters, sāman melodies, stomas, and sacrificial sessions culminating in the viśvasṛjām sattra (PB 25.18).
SA_GV02_pncvbr1u.coverage: complete — Text runs continuously from PB 1.1.1 to the concluding viśvasṛjām sattra section at PB 25.18.6.
translations: W. Caland (trans.), Pañcaviṃśabrāhmaṇa. (English)

SA_GV03_sb_01_u.title: Śatapathabrāhmaṇa (kāṇḍa 1)
SA_GV03_sb_01_u.summary: Kāṇḍa 1 of the Śatapathabrāhmaṇa systematically expounds the rites of the New- and Full-Moon sacrifices (Darśapūrṇamāsa) and related iṣṭis. Composed in late Vedic prose, it provides liturgical instruction for the rituals of the Śukla Yajurveda, interpreting each sacerdotal act through theological reasoning, etymological speculation, and foundational myths (such as the vow of truth, the creation and purification of offerings, and the conflict between devas and asuras). It serves as one of the central sources for Vedic sacrificial theology and early Indian cosmogony.
SA_GV03_sb_01_u.attribution: Belonging to the Śukla Yajurveda tradition. Associated with the sage Yājñavalkya.
SA_GV03_sb_01_u.coverage: partial — Contains the first kāṇḍa (from 1.1.1 through 1.9.3) of the Śatapathabrāhmaṇa.

SA_GV03_sb_02_u.title: Śatapathabrāhmaṇa (kāṇḍa 2)
SA_GV03_sb_02_u.summary: Kāṇḍa 2 of the Mādhyandina Śatapathabrāhmaṇa expounds foundational domestic and seasonal Śrauta rituals across six adhyāyas. It systematically presents the ritual procedures, theological rationale, and mythological aetiologies for setting up the sacred fires (Agnyādheya), the re-establishment of the fires (Punarādheya), the daily fire oblation (Agnihotra) and fire worship (Agnyupasthāna), ancestral offerings (Piṇḍapitṛyajña), the first-fruits sacrifice (Āgrayaṇeṣṭi), and the cyclical four-monthly sacrifices (Cāturmāsyas: Vaiśvadeva, Varuṇapraghāsa, Sākamedha, and Śunāsīrīya).
SA_GV03_sb_02_u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the sage Yājñavalkya as the chief authority of the Vājasaneyi school of the Śukla Yajurveda. Modern historical scholarship treats it as an anonymous composite prose text of the late Vedic period.
SA_GV03_sb_02_u.coverage: partial — Contains the text of Kāṇḍa 2 of the Mādhyandina recension of the Śatapathabrāhmaṇa.

SA_GV03_sb_04_u.title: Śatapathabrāhmaṇa (kāṇḍa 4)
SA_GV03_sb_04_u.summary: Kāṇḍa 4 of the Śatapathabrāhmaṇa (Mādhyandina recension) continues the ritual exposition of the Soma sacrifice (Agniṣṭoma) initiated in Kāṇḍa 3. It details the preparation and offering of various Soma cups and libations (grahas) during the morning, midday, and third pressings, as well as the recitation of śastras and singing of stotras. The kāṇḍa also expounds the distribution of sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇā), the concluding purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), the supplementary offering of an infertile cow (vaśā), and modifications required for extended and multi-day Soma rites (sattras and ahīnas).
SA_GV03_sb_04_u.attribution: A canonical Vedic ritual prose text belonging to the Mādhyandina school of the Śukla (White) Yajurveda.
SA_GV03_sb_04_u.coverage: partial — Contains Kāṇḍa 4 of the Śatapathabrāhmaṇa.

SA_GV03_sb_06_u.title: Śatapathabrāhmaṇa (kāṇḍa 6)
SA_GV03_sb_06_u.summary: Kāṇḍa 6 of the Śatapathabrāhmaṇa marks the opening of the Agnicayana ('piling of the fire altar') ritual and introduces the Śāṇḍilya portion of the text (kāṇḍas 6–10). It details the preliminary rites of altar construction, including the creation myth of Prajāpati, the preparation and firing of the clay fire pan (ukhā), and the consecration of the animal and earthen offerings. Throughout the kāṇḍa, the ritual procedures are systematized within a complex theological and cosmogonic framework that equates the falcon-shaped fire altar with Prajāpati, the year, and the cosmos.
SA_GV03_sb_06_u.coverage: partial — Complete text of Kāṇḍa 6 (adhyāyas 6.1 through 6.8, concluding at 6.8.2.12).

SA_GV03_sb_07_u.title: Śatapathabrāhmaṇa (kāṇḍa 7)
SA_GV03_sb_07_u.summary: Kāṇḍa 7 of the Śatapathabrāhmaṇa forms the second book of the five-kāṇḍa Agnicayana (fire-altar) cycle belonging to the Śāṇḍilya division of the Mādhyandina Śukla Yajurveda. It details the ritual operations for preparing the fire ground and constructing the first layer of bricks for the bird-shaped altar (mahāvedi), including the installation of the Gārhapatya hearth, the deposition of the svayamātṛṇṇā (naturally perforated) bricks, and the placing of the golden man (hiraṇmaya puruṣa). Throughout, ritual actions are systematically interpreted through cosmogonic and theological homologies linking the altar's architectural layers to the reconstitution of Prajāpati and the cosmos.
SA_GV03_sb_07_u.coverage: partial — Complete text of Kāṇḍa 7 (5 adhyāyas: 7.1–7.5, comprising 12 brāhmaṇas; numbered 7.1.1.1 to 7.5.2.63), representing one of the 14 kāṇḍas of the Mādhyandina recension.

SA_GV03_sb_08_u.title: Śatapathabrāhmaṇa (kāṇḍa 8)
SA_GV03_sb_08_u.summary: Kāṇḍa 8 of the Śatapathabrāhmaṇa forms part of the Śāṇḍilya Agnicayana section (Kāṇḍas 6–10) of the Mādhyandina recension. It details the ritual piling of the second, third, fourth, and fifth layers (citi) of the great bird-shaped fire altar, including the placement of specific brick arrangements such as the prāṇabhṛt ('breath-holding'), ṛtavyā ('seasonal'), and aśvinī bricks, accompanied by formulas from the Vājasaneyi-Saṃhitā. The prose systematically provides theological and esoteric identifications (bandhus), homologizing the bricks and spatial layers with the seasons, prāṇas, cosmic realms, Prajāpati, and the body of the sacrificer.
SA_GV03_sb_08_u.attribution: A core Brāhmaṇa of the Śukla Yajurveda (Mādhyandina recension). Kāṇḍas 6–10 form the Śāṇḍilya-kāṇḍa dealing with the Agnicayana (construction of the sacred fire altar), traditionally associated with the sage Śāṇḍilya.
SA_GV03_sb_08_u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete text of Kāṇḍa 8 (Adhyāyas 1–7, ending at 8.7.4.21) of the 14-kāṇḍa Mādhyandina recension.
translations: J. Eggeling (trans.), The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa Pt. IV (SBELIII). (English)

SA_GV03_sb_09_u.title: Śatapathabrāhmaṇa (kāṇḍa 9)
SA_GV03_sb_09_u.summary: Kāṇḍa 9 of the Śatapathabrāhmaṇa (Mādhyandina recension) constitutes the fourth book of the five-book Śāṇḍilya Agnicayana section (Kāṇḍas 6–10). It details the rites performed upon the completion of the fire altar, beginning with the Śatarudriya litany to pacify the wrathful aspects of Rudra incarnated in the altar. The text proceeds through the lustrations, the continuous libation of ghee known as the Vasordhārā, the physical mounting and vivification of the altar, and concludes with theological discussions and expiations attributed to Śāṇḍilya.
SA_GV03_sb_09_u.coverage: partial — Contains Kāṇḍa 9 complete (adhyāyas 9.1 through 9.5) of the 14 kāṇḍas of the Śatapathabrāhmaṇa in the Mādhyandina recension.
translations: J. Eggeling, The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa Pt. IV (SBELIII). (English)

SA_GV03_sb_10_u.title: Śatapathabrāhmaṇa (kāṇḍa 10: Agnirahasya)
SA_GV03_sb_10_u.summary: Kāṇḍa 10 of the Śatapathabrāhmaṇa (Mādhyandina recension), titled Agnirahasya ('The Mystery of the Fire Altar'), provides the esoteric and speculative interpretation of the Agnicayana ritual. It homologizes the five layers of the fire altar and the sacrificial bricks with Prajāpati, the cosmic year (saṃvatsara), death (mṛtyu), and the sacrificer's immortal inner self (ātman). By framing the physical construction of the altar as an interiorized regeneration of the cosmos and the self, it serves as a conceptual and philosophical bridge between ritual Brāhmaṇa prose and early Upaniṣadic thought.
SA_GV03_sb_10_u.attribution: According to Vedic tradition and the concluding teacher lineage (vaṃśa at 10.6.5.9), kāṇḍas 6–10 of the Mādhyandina recension constitute the Śāṇḍilya Agnicayana tradition, traced back via Tura Kāvaṣeya to Prajāpati.
SA_GV03_sb_10_u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete text of Kāṇḍa 10 (Agnirahasya) of the 14-kāṇḍa Mādhyandina recension, comprising adhyāyas 10.1 through 10.6 and concluding with the vaṃśa at 10.6.5.9.
translations: J. Eggeling (trans.), The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa Pt. IV (SBELIII). (English)

SA_GV03_sb_11_u.title: Śatapathabrāhmaṇa (kāṇḍa 11)
SA_GV03_sb_11_u.summary: Kāṇḍa 11 of the Śatapathabrāhmaṇa (Mādhyandina recension) provides ritual exegesis, expiatory rules (prāyaścitta), and theological explanations of supplementary and foundational rites, including the Full and New Moon sacrifices (Darśapūrṇamāsa), the Agnihotra, and the animal sacrifice (Paśubandha). It contains celebrated mythological and narrative episodes, notably the oldest prose version of the tale of Purūravas and Urvaśī (11.5.1), instruction on Vedic study as Brahmayajña (11.5.6), and philosophical dialogues involving King Janaka of Videha and the sage Yājñavalkya.
SA_GV03_sb_11_u.attribution: The Śatapathabrāhmaṇa is traditionally linked to the Vedic sage Yājñavalkya.
SA_GV03_sb_11_u.coverage: partial — Contains the eleventh kāṇḍa (ending at 11.8.4.6) of the Śatapathabrāhmaṇa.
translations: Eggeling, Julius (tr.) (1900): The Śatapatha-Brāhmaṇa, according to the text of the Mādhyandina School, SBE, Oxford, 1900. (English)

SA_GV03_sb_13_u.title: Śatapathabrāhmaṇa (kāṇḍa 13)
SA_GV03_sb_13_u.summary: The thirteenth kāṇḍa of the Śatapathabrāhmaṇa (Mādhyandina recension) constitutes one of the most important sources for the ideology and ritual of ancient Indian imperial kingship. Adhyāyas 1–5 give the full liturgical and symbolic exposition of the royal horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha), including the consecration of the stallion, celebratory royal eulogies (gāthās), and ritual riddling dialogues (brahmodya). Adhyāya 6 expounds the Puruṣamedha (cosmic/symbolic human sacrifice), Adhyāya 7 the Sarvamedha (all-sacrifice), and Adhyāya 8 the Pitṛmedha (ancestor and burial rites, including instructions for the construction of sepulchral mounds).
SA_GV03_sb_13_u.coverage: partial — Contains text of Kāṇḍa 13 (sections 13.1.1.2 through 13.8.4.12).

SA_GV03_sb_14_u.title: Śatapathabrāhmaṇa (kāṇḍa 14)
SA_GV03_sb_14_u.summary: Kāṇḍa 14 is the concluding book of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa of the White Yajurveda (Mādhyandina recension) and functions as the Āraṇyaka of this tradition. Adhyāyas 1–3 expound the Pravargya ceremony, detailing the mythic origin of Makha/Viṣṇu, the ritual fashioning and heating of the Mahāvīra clay pot, and the preparation and offering of the boiling milk oblation (Gharma). Adhyāyas 4–9 constitute the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, containing foundational Vedantic expositions on ātman and brahman through the debates and teachings of the sage Yājñavalkya with Janaka, Gārgī, Maitreyī, and other Vedic scholars.
SA_GV03_sb_14_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of Kāṇḍa 14 of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa in the Mādhyandina recension. It contains the Pravargya/Āraṇyaka ritual section followed by the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
translations: Julius Eggeling (trans.) (1900), The Śatapatha-Brāhmaṇa, according to the text of the Mâdhyandina School. (English)
Patrick Olivelle (trans.), Upaniṣads. Oxford World's Classics. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1996. (English)

SA_GV04_sankharu.title: Śāṅkhāyanāraṇyaka
SA_GV04_sankharu.summary: The Śāṅkhāyanāraṇyaka (also known as the Kauṣītakyāraṇyaka) is the forest treatise of the Śāṅkhāyana/Kauṣītaki recension of the Ṛgveda, organized into 15 adhyāyas. Adhyāyas 1–2 expound the ritual recitation and symbolism of the Mahāvrata ceremony. Adhyāyas 3–6 form the major Kauṣītaki-Upaniṣad, addressing eschatology, breath (prāṇa) doctrine, and King Pratardana's dialogue with Indra, followed by the Saṃhitopaniṣad (adhyāyas 7–8) on mystic phonetic analysis, internal sacrificial rites, and an authenticating teacher lineage (adhyāya 15).
SA_GV04_sankharu.attribution: A Vedic prose text belonging to the Śāṅkhāyana (Kauṣītaki) branch of the Ṛgveda. Adhyāya 15 preserves a vaṃśa (teacher lineage) tracing textual transmission through Guṇākhya Śāṅkhāyana, Kahola Kauṣītaki, Uddālaka Āruṇi, Viśvāmitra, Indra, and Prajāpati to Svayambhū Brahman.
SA_GV04_sankharu.edition: Bhim Dev (ed.), Śāṅkhāyanāraṇyakam, Vishveshvaranand Indological Series, Hoshiarpur: Vishveshvaranand Vedic Research Institute, 1980; collated with Arthur Berriedale Keith (ed.), 'Appendix containing the portion hitherto unpublished of the Sānkhāyana Āraṇyaka' (Adhyāyas 7–15), in The Aitareya Āraṇyaka, Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1909, pp. 305–328.
SA_GV04_sankharu.coverage: complete — Contains all 15 adhyāyas: adhyāyas 1–2 treat the Mahāvrata rite, 3–6 constitute the Kauṣītaki-Upaniṣad, 7–8 contain the Saṃhitopaniṣad, 9–13 discuss prāṇa speculations and esoteric rites, 14 discusses the self, and 15 gives the vaṃśa (teacher lineage). Ends with 'iti śāṅkhāyanāraṇyakaṃ samāptam'.
translations: Arthur Berriedale Keith (tr.), The Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka: With an Appendix on the Mahāvrata, London: Royal Asiatic Society, 1908. (English)

SA_GV05_agsas_1u.title: Āgamaśāstra with Āgamaśāstrabhāṣya (chapter 1: Āgamaprakaraṇa, with Māṇḍūkyopaniṣad)
SA_GV05_agsas_1u.author: Gauḍapāda, Śaṅkara
SA_GV05_agsas_1u.summary: This text comprises the first chapter (Āgamaprakaraṇa) of Gauḍapāda's Āgamaśāstra (also known as the Māṇḍūkyakārikā), containing 29 verses interwoven with the twelve prose mantras of the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad and the classic Advaita commentary (bhāṣya) ascribed to Śaṅkara. It expounds the nature of the non-dual Self (ātman/brahman) through an examination of the four states of consciousness—waking (viśva/vaiśvānara), dream (taijasa), deep dreamless sleep (prājña), and the transcendent fourth (turīya)—and correlates these states with the tripartite phonemes of the sacred syllable OM (A, U, M) and its partless silence (amātra). Gauḍapāda's treatise establishes the scriptural (āgama) foundation upon which the doctrine of non-origination (ajātivāda) is subsequently developed in the remaining three prakaraṇas.
SA_GV05_agsas_1u.attribution: The kārikās are attributed to Gauḍapāda. The commentary is ascribed to Śaṅkara.
SA_GV05_agsas_1u.coverage: partial — Complete text of chapter 1 (Āgamaprakaraṇa), containing all 12 mantras of the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad and all 29 kārikās of Gauḍapāda with Śaṅkara's commentary.

SA_GV05_agsas_2u.title: Āgamaśāstra with Āgamaśāstrabhāṣya (chapter 2: Vaitathyaprakaraṇa)
SA_GV05_agsas_2u.author: Gauḍapāda, Śaṅkara
SA_GV05_agsas_2u.summary: The second chapter (Vaitathyaprakaraṇa, 'Chapter on Unreality/Illusion', 38 kārikās) of Gauḍapāda's Āgamaśāstra along with the running commentary (bhāṣya) ascribed to Śaṅkara. Gauḍapāda employs dialectical reasoning (upapatti) and the analogy of dream phenomena to demonstrate that all objects perceived in the waking state are unreal (vitatha), because like dreams they are enclosed within temporal-spatial coordinates, dependent on cognition, and inherently evanescent. By refuting the reality of external duality, the chapter establishes that non-duality (advaita) alone is ultimate reality and that phenomenal distinctions are imagined through avidyā upon the invariant, self-luminous Ātman.
SA_GV05_agsas_2u.attribution: The kārikās are attributed to Gauḍapāda. The commentary is ascribed to Śaṃkara.
SA_GV05_agsas_2u.coverage: partial — Text and commentary for chapter 2 (Vaitathyaprakaraṇa, ending at verse 38).

SA_GV05_agsas_3u.title: Āgamaśāstra with Āgamaśāstrabhāṣya (chapter 3: Advaitaprakaraṇa)
SA_GV05_agsas_3u.author: Gauḍapāda, Śaṅkara
SA_GV05_agsas_3u.summary: The third chapter (Advaitaprakaraṇa, 48 kārikās) of Gauḍapāda's Māṇḍūkyopaniṣatkārikā, accompanied by the bhāṣya ascribed to Śaṅkara, establishes the absolute non-duality of Brahman through rational inquiry (tarka). Gauḍapāda expounds the doctrine of radical non-origination (ajātivāda), utilizing the classic analogy of ether enclosed in jars (ghaṭākāśa) to demonstrate that the apparent birth and manifold nature of individual souls (jīva) is illusory. The chapter also delineates the contemplative discipline known as asparśayoga ('yoga of non-contact') and the quietude of the mind (manonigraha) resulting in non-dual realization.
SA_GV05_agsas_3u.attribution: The kārikās are attributed to Gauḍapāda; the commentary is ascribed to Śaṅkara.
SA_GV05_agsas_3u.coverage: partial — Complete text of Chapter 3 (Advaitaprakaraṇa), comprising all 48 verses (kārikās 3.1–3.48) along with their complete bhāṣya. The full work spans four prakaraṇas.

SA_GV05_agsas_4u.title: Māṇḍūkyopaniṣatkārikā with Āgamaśāstrabhāṣya (chapter 4: Alātaśāntiprakaraṇa)
SA_GV05_agsas_4u.author: Gauḍapāda, Śaṅkara
SA_GV05_agsas_4u.summary: The Alātaśāntiprakaraṇa ('Quenching of the Firebrand') is the fourth and final chapter (100 kārikās) of the Māṇḍūkyopaniṣatkārikā, accompanied here by the prose bhāṣya traditionally ascribed to Śaṅkara. Using the metaphor of a whirled firebrand (alāta) that creates illusory luminous forms without producing real multiplicity, the chapter expounds absolute non-origination (ajātivāda) and non-relational meditation (asparśayoga). It is famous in Indian philosophical history for framing Advaitic non-dualism through the dialectical terminology of Madhyamaka and Yogācāra Buddhism.
SA_GV05_agsas_4u.attribution: The root kārikās are attributed to Gauḍapāda; the commentary (Āgamaśāstrabhāṣya) is ascribed to Śaṅkara.
SA_GV05_agsas_4u.edition: Gauḍapāda's Kārikās checked against ed. A.V. Kathavate, Poona 1890 (Anandasrama Sanskrit Series, 10).
SA_GV05_agsas_4u.coverage: partial — Contains chapter 4 (Alātaśāntiprakaraṇa), consisting of kārikās (4.1–4.100) and the accompanying bhāṣya, terminating with the colophon 'iti śaṅkarabhagavataḥ kṛtau gauḍapādīyāgamaśāstravivaraṇe 'lātaśāntyākhyaṃ caturthaṃ prakaraṇam'. Chapters 1–3 are absent from this file.
translations: Karmarkar (1953). (English)

SA_GV05_aitup__u.title: Aitareyopaniṣad
SA_GV05_aitup__u.summary: The Aitareyopaniṣad is one of the earliest classical prose Upaniṣads belonging to the Ṛgvedic school, embedded as chapters 4 through 6 in the second book of the Aitareya Āraṇyaka. It opens with a cosmogonic account in which the solitary ātman creates the cosmic realms, their divine guardians, and the cosmic person (puruṣa), into whom the cosmic deities subsequently enter as perceptual and physiological faculties. After reflecting on the threefold birth of the individual soul and liberation through the legendary Ṛgvedic seer Vāmadeva, the Upaniṣad concludes with an inquiry into the fundamental nature of the Self, identifying all phenomena and faculties with consciousness in the famous mahāvākya 'consciousness is brahman' (prajñānaṃ brahma).
SA_GV05_aitup__u.attribution: A principal (mukhya) Upaniṣad belonging to the Ṛgveda, embedded in the second book of the Aitareya Āraṇyaka (AitĀ 2.4–6).
SA_GV05_aitup__u.edition: V. P. Limaye and R. D. Vadekar (eds.), Eighteen Principal Upaniṣads, vol. 1: Upaniṣadic Texts with Parallels, Poona: Vaidika Saṃśodhana Maṇḍala, 1958.
SA_GV05_aitup__u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Aitareyopaniṣad in 3 adhyāyas (comprising 5 khaṇḍas: Adhyāya 1 with 3 khaṇḍas, Adhyāya 2 with 1 khaṇḍa, and Adhyāya 3 with 1 khaṇḍa; AitUp 1.1.1–3.4).
translations: Patrick Olivelle, Upaniṣads, Oxford World's Classics, Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1996. (English)

SA_GV05_aitupsbu.title: Aitareyopaniṣad with Aitareyopaniṣadbhāṣya
SA_GV05_aitupsbu.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GV05_aitupsbu.summary: The Aitareyopaniṣad, embedded in the Aitareya Āraṇyaka (II.4–6) of the Ṛgveda, is an early Vedic prose Upaniṣad that expounds the creation of the cosmos from the singular Ātman, the embodiment of cosmic faculties within man, the doctrine of the threefold births (trayo janmāḥ), and the foundational mahāvākya 'consciousness is Brahman' (prajñānaṃ brahma). This e-text contains the complete root text accompanied by Śaṅkara's classical Advaita Vedānta commentary (bhāṣya), which commences with an extensive Sambandhabhāṣya refuting the view that ritual works must be combined with knowledge (jñānakarmasamuccaya) to achieve liberation.
SA_GV05_aitupsbu.attribution: The root text constitutes chapters 4–6 of the second Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Āraṇyaka (Ṛgveda). The accompanying commentary is traditionally ascribed to Śaṃkara.
SA_GV05_aitupsbu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Aitareyopaniṣad across all 3 adhyāyas (5 khaṇḍas: Adhyāya 1 in 3 khaṇḍas, Adhyāya 2 in 1 khaṇḍa, and Adhyāya 3 in 1 khaṇḍa), accompanied by the introductory Sambandhabhāṣya and Śaṅkara's continuous commentary on all sections through the concluding mahāvākya and phala.
translations: Paul Deussen, Sechzig Upanishad's des Veda (German translation published 1897). (German)
Patrick Olivelle (tr.), Upaniṣads, Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1996. (English)

SA_GV05_brbiuppu.title: Brahmabindūpaniṣad
SA_GV05_brbiuppu.summary: The Brahmabindūpaniṣad (also known as Amṛtabindu) is a short 22-verse minor Upaniṣad belonging to the Yoga-Vedānta group. It famously opens by declaring the mind to be the root cause of both bondage and liberation (mana eva manuṣyāṇāṃ kāraṇaṃ bandhamokṣayoḥ). Combining yogic mental restraint with Advaitic metaphysics, it instructs the spiritual seeker to transcend scriptural verbalism and sound-based meditation on OM to realize the unconditioned, non-dual Brahman.
SA_GV05_brbiuppu.attribution: Anonymous Vedic scriptural text; transmitted in Atharvavedic collections and one of the 108 Upaniṣads.
SA_GV05_brbiuppu.edition: Ramamaya Tarkaratna (ed.), The Atharvana-Upanishads. Calcutta: Ganesha Press, 1872 (Bibliotheca Indica; 76).
SA_GV05_brbiuppu.coverage: complete — Complete text in 22 verses (numbered BrbUp_1–22).

SA_GV05_brup___u.title: Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad
SA_GV05_brup___u.summary: The Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad ('Great Forest Upaniṣad') is an early Upaniṣad belonging to the Vedic corpus. Preserved in the Kāṇva recension (among others), it features celebrated philosophical dialogues involving figures such as Yājñavalkya, King Janaka, and Gārgī.
SA_GV05_brup___u.attribution: Vedic Upaniṣadic text belonging to the Kāṇva recension.
SA_GV05_brup___u.edition: V.P. Limaye and R.D. Vadekar (eds.), Eighteen Principal Upanisads, vol. 1, Poona: 1958.
SA_GV05_brup___u.coverage: complete — Text of the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad in the Kāṇva recension running from BrhUp_1,1.1 through the final vaṃśa at BrhUp_6,5.4.
translations: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation, New York: Oxford University Press, 1998. (English)
Patrick Olivelle, Upaniṣads, Oxford World's Classics, Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1996. (English)
Paul Deussen, Sechzig Upanishad's des Veda, 1897. (German)

SA_GV05_brupsb.title: Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad with Śaṅkarabhāṣya
SA_GV05_brupsb.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GV05_brupsb.summary: The Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad, preserved as part of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, is an ancient Vedic Upaniṣad featuring discussions and debates involving the sage Yājñavalkya at King Janaka's court.
SA_GV05_brupsb.attribution: The root Upaniṣad belongs to the Vedic canon and is anonymous.
translations: Mādhavānanda, S. (trans.). The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad with the commentary of Śaṅkarācārya. 1934. (English)
Olivelle, Patrick (trans.). The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation. New York: Oxford University Press, 1998. (English)
Deussen, Paul (trans.). Sixty Upaniṣads of the Veda. German editions published 1897. (German)

SA_GV05_brupsb2u.title: Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad with Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣya (chapter 2)
SA_GV05_brupsb2u.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GV05_brupsb2u.summary: Adhyāya 2 of the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad (Kāṇva recension), accompanied by Śaṅkara's Advaita Vedānta commentary (Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣya), forming the concluding section of the Madhukāṇḍa. It opens with the dialogue between the proud sage Dṛpta Bālāki Gārgya and King Ajātaśatru of Kāśi on the progressive definitions and ultimate nature of Brahman beyond phenomenal forms (2.1), followed by the esoteric symbolism of the vital breath (2.2), and the renowned Mūrtāmūrta doctrine outlining the two forms of Brahman (gross/perishable and subtle/immortal) and culminating in the apophatic formula neti neti ('not this, not this') (2.3). The chapter concludes with the famous first dialogue between Yājñavalkya and his wife Maitreyī on universal love grounded in the Self (ātman) and the non-dual means to immortality (2.4), the 'honey doctrine' (madhuvidyā) presenting the mutual interconnectedness of all entities in the cosmic Self (2.5), and the traditional teacher lineage (vaṃśa) of the Madhukāṇḍa (2.6).
SA_GV05_brupsb2u.attribution: The root text belongs to the Kāṇva recension of the Śukla Yajurveda. The commentary is ascribed to Śaṅkara.
SA_GV05_brupsb2u.coverage: partial — Text and commentary for adhyāya 2 of the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad, comprising six brāhmaṇas: 2.1 (Gārgya-Ajātaśatru dialogue), 2.2, 2.3 (Mūrtāmūrta), 2.4 (first Maitreyī dialogue), 2.5 (Madhu), and 2.6 (Vaṃśa).
translations: Patrick Olivelle, ed. and trans., Upaniṣads, World's Classic Series, Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1996. (English)

SA_GV05_brupsb3u.title: Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad with Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣya (chapter 3)
SA_GV05_brupsb3u.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GV05_brupsb3u.summary: Adhyāya 3 of the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad (the first half of the Yājñavalkyakāṇḍa), accompanied paragraph by paragraph by Śaṅkara's Advaita commentary (Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣya). Set in the sacrificial assembly of King Janaka of Videha, the chapter depicts the celebrated philosophical tournament where sage Yājñavalkya debates challenging interlocutors—including Aśvala, Ārtabhāga, Bhujyu, Uṣasta, Kahola, Uddālaka Āruṇi, Vidagdha Śākalya, and the female philosopher Gārgī Vācaknavī. Śaṅkara's bhāṣya uses these dialogues to elucidate central Vedāntic doctrines, notably the nature of the inner controller (antaryāmin), the imperishable substrate (akṣara), and the apophatic character of the absolute Self (neti neti).
SA_GV05_brupsb3u.attribution: The mūla is the Kāṇva recension of the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad (Śukla Yajurveda; anonymous Vedic text). GRETIL describes the commentary as 'ascribed to Samkara'.
SA_GV05_brupsb3u.coverage: partial — Adhyāya 3 complete with Śaṅkara's bhāṣya, ending with the colophon 'iti bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣye tṛtīyo 'dhyāyaḥ'.

SA_GV05_brupsb4u.title: Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad with Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣya (chapter 4)
SA_GV05_brupsb4u.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GV05_brupsb4u.summary: Adhyāya 4 of the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad records sage Yājñavalkya's dialogues with King Janaka of Videha, covering topics such as waking, dream, and deep sleep, the nature of the Self, transmigration, and liberation. It also includes the dialogue with Maitreyī and the vaṃśa (lineage). Śaṅkara's bhāṣya interprets these discourses within Advaita Vedānta.

SA_GV05_brupsb5u.title: Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad with Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣya (chapter 5)
SA_GV05_brupsb5u.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GV05_brupsb5u.summary: Adhyāya 5 of the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad (Kāṇva recension) comprises fifteen brāhmaṇas setting forth a sequence of meditative disciplines and symbolic upāsanās, including the contemplation on the fullness of Brahman ('pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idam'), meditations on the syllable Om, and the instruction of Prajāpati ('da da da'). Accompanying commentary is ascribed to Śaṅkara.
SA_GV05_brupsb5u.attribution: The mūla is the Kāṇva recension of the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad. GRETIL describes the commentary as 'ascribed to Samkara'.

Paul Deussen (trans.), Sechzig Upanishad's des Veda, 1897. (German)

SA_GV05_brupsb6u.title: Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad with Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣya (chapter 6)
SA_GV05_brupsb6u.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GV05_brupsb6u.summary: Adhyāya 6 forms the concluding chapter of the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad (Kāṇva recension), accompanied by the commentary (bhāṣya) ascribed to Śaṅkara. It begins with the prāṇasaṃvāda illustrating the supremacy of the vital breath over bodily and cognitive faculties, presents the doctrine of the five fires (pañcāgnividyā) and the paths of the gods and ancestors, expounds rituals for prosperity (mantha) and procreation, and finishes with the traditional lineage of teachers (vaṃśa). Śaṅkara's bhāṣya explains the supplementary nature of this section (khilatva) and the relation of symbolic meditation (upāsanā) to the rest of the text.
SA_GV05_brupsb6u.attribution: The mūla is the Kāṇva recension of the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad (Śukla Yajurveda). GRETIL describes the commentary as 'ascribed to Samkara'.

translations: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation, New York: Oxford University Press, 1998. (English)
Paul Deussen, German translation of the Upaniṣads (published 1897). (German)

SA_GV05_chupmau.title: Chāndogyopaniṣadbhāṣya
SA_GV05_chupmau.author: Madhva
SA_GV05_chupmau.summary: The Chāndogyopaniṣadbhāṣya is Madhva's commentary on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad of the Sāmaveda. In it, Madhva interprets the Upaniṣadic narrative and teachings from an uncompromising Dvaita (dualist) theistic perspective, equating the supreme Brahman exclusively with Viṣṇu (Nārāyaṇa). He famously offers an alternative reading and explanation of the mahāvākya 'tat tvam asi' as 'atat tvam asi' ('thou art not that'), emphasizing the eternal and essential ontological distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the supreme Godhead.
SA_GV05_chupmau.coverage: unclear — No e-text provided in the corpus.

SA_GV05_garbhupu.title: Garbhopaniṣad
SA_GV05_garbhupu.summary: The Garbhopaniṣad is a minor Upaniṣad centered on embryology, human anatomy, and physiological contemplation integrated with Vedāntic and Sāṃkhya-Yoga soteriology. It details the month-by-month gestation of the embryo from conception to birth, the bodily components, humors, and tissues, and the fetus's awakening in the womb to memories of past lives and suffering, leading to a resolve to seek liberation through Maheśvara, Nārāyaṇa, or Yoga. The treatise concludes by homologizing the internal organs to the three Vedic fires and ritual instruments of the sacrificial arena and provides an enumeration of anatomical parts, identifying itself as a Paippalāda text on liberation.
SA_GV05_garbhupu.attribution: The concluding section at GarUp_12 identifies it as 'paippalādaṃ mokṣaśāstram', indicating historical affiliation with the Paippalāda tradition.
SA_GV05_garbhupu.edition: Ramamaya Tarkaratna in: The Atharvana-Upanishads, Calcutta: Ganesha Press, 1872 (Bibliotheca Indica; 76)
SA_GV05_garbhupu.coverage: complete — Complete root text in 12 numbered prose and metrical sections (GarUp_1 to GarUp_12), concluding with 'paippalādaṃ mokṣaśāstraṃ paippalādaṃ mokṣaśāstram iti'.
translations: Lakshmi Kapani, Garbhopaniṣad, Paris: A. Maisonneuve, 1976. (French)
Lakshmi Kapani, 'Upanisad of the Embryo and Notes on the Garbha-Upanisad', in Fragments for a History of the Human Body, ed. Michael Feher, Part 3, 1989, pp. 177–196. (English)

SA_GV05_gmandk_u.title: Māṇḍūkyopaniṣatkārikā
SA_GV05_gmandk_u.author: Gauḍapāda
SA_GV05_gmandk_u.summary: A seminal foundation text of early Advaita Vedānta comprising 215 verses across four prakaraṇas: Āgama, Vaitathya, Advaita, and Alātaśānti. Developing the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad's analysis of the four states of consciousness (waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth, turīya) correlated with the constituent morae of Oṃ, the text formulates the doctrine of ajātivāda (absolute non-origination) and asparśayoga. It represents the earliest extant systematic treatise of Advaita philosophy and is celebrated for its dialectical engagement with and creative absorption of Madhyamaka and Yogācāra terminology.
SA_GV05_gmandk_u.edition: Gauḍapāda's Kārikās, edited by A. V. Kathavate, Poona, 1890 (Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series, 10).
SA_GV05_gmandk_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 215 kārikās across four prakaraṇas (430 hemistich segments): 1. Āgamaprakaraṇa (29 kārikās), 2. Vaitathyaprakaraṇa (38 kārikās), 3. Advaitaprakaraṇa (48 kārikās), and 4. Alātaśāntiprakaraṇa (100 kārikās). Contains the verse text only, without the prose mantras of the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad or Śaṅkara's bhāṣya.
translations: Raghunath Damodar Karmarkar, Gauḍapāda-Kārikā, Poona: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, 1953 (Government Oriental Series, Class 13, No. 9). (English)

SA_GV05_isup___u.title: Īśopaniṣad
SA_GV05_isup___u.summary: The Īśopaniṣad (or Īśāvāsyopaniṣad) is one of the earliest and most influential mukhya (principal) Upaniṣads, consisting of 18 verses that constitute the 40th chapter of the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā of the Śukla (White) Yajurveda (here in the Kāṇva recension). Unlike most other classical Upaniṣads that belong to Brāhmaṇas or Āraṇyakas, it is uniquely positioned directly within the Saṃhitā proper. It reconciles active engagement in the world with radical spiritual renunciation under the overarching premise that everything is enveloped by the Lord (īśā vāsyam idaṃ sarvam), harmonizing ritual performance (avidyā) with higher meditative knowledge (vidyā), and concluding with invocations of the divine solar puruṣa and Agni.
SA_GV05_isup___u.attribution: A canonical Vedic Upaniṣad of the Yajurveda, presented here in the Kāṇva recension.
SA_GV05_isup___u.edition: Eighteen Principal Upanisads, vol. 1, edited by V. P. Limaye and R. D. Vadekar, Poona, 1958.
SA_GV05_isup___u.coverage: complete — Complete mūla text in 18 verses (IsUp_1–IsUp_18) of the Kāṇva recension. Although the GRETIL header reads 'with the commentary ascribed to Samkara', the e-text contains solely the root verses without commentary.
translations: Patrick Olivelle, Upaniṣads, Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1996. (English)

SA_GV05_isupsb_u.title: Īśāvāsyopaniṣad with Īśāvāsyopaniṣadbhāṣya
SA_GV05_isupsb_u.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GV05_isupsb_u.summary: The Īśāvāsyopaniṣad (or Īśopaniṣad) forms the 40th and final chapter of the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā of the Śukla Yajurveda, preserved here in its 18-mantra Kāṇva recension. It synthesizes the contemplation of the cosmos as pervaded by the Lord (īśa) with teachings on renunciation, the dual functions of action (avidyā/karman) and knowledge (vidyā), and final release. Śaṅkara's commentary (bhāṣya) interprets the work within classical Advaita Vedānta, arguing that ritual works pertain solely to worldly and heavenly ends while direct, non-dual knowledge of the self (ātman) alone eliminates ignorance and secures liberation.
SA_GV05_isupsb_u.attribution: GRETIL titles the text 'Kanva recension with the commentary ascribed to Samkara', and the text colophon names the author as Śrīśaṅkarabhagavat.

SA_GV05_isvupu.title: Īśāvāsyopaniṣad
SA_GV05_isvupu.summary: The Īśāvāsyopaniṣad (commonly called the Īśopaniṣad) is one of the shortest and earliest mukhya Upaniṣads, comprising 17 or 18 metrical verses forming chapter 40 of the Śukla Yajurveda Saṃhitā. Named after its opening phrase 'īśā vāsyam', it harmonizes worldly engagement (karman) with renunciation and spiritual knowledge (vidyā), asserting the omnipresence of the Lord and the ultimate non-duality of the Self.
SA_GV05_isvupu.coverage: unclear — Empty file (0 segments, 0 characters); no text to assess.

SA_GV05_kaivup_u.title: Kaivalyopaniṣad
SA_GV05_kaivup_u.summary: The Kaivalyopaniṣad is a celebrated text belonging to the Śaiva Upaniṣad corpus, preserved in recensions attached to both the Atharvaveda and the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. Framed as a dialogue in which Brahmā instructs the Vedic seer Āśvalāyana on Brahmavidyā, it expounds the attainment of kaivalya (isolation / supreme liberation) through renunciation, faith, and inward meditation. It harmonizes non-dual Advaitic metaphysics with theistic contemplation of Rudra-Śiva (Umāsahāya), identifying the cosmic Absolute with the innermost transcendent witness (sākṣin, cinmātra) abiding in the cave of the heart.
SA_GV05_kaivup_u.attribution: A traditional minor Upaniṣad classified among the Śaiva Upaniṣads; preserved in recensions affiliated with both the Atharvaveda and the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. It is framed as an instruction on Brahmavidyā given by Brahmā (Parameṣṭhin/Pitāmaha) to the sage Āśvalāyana.
SA_GV05_kaivup_u.edition: Ramamaya Tarkaratna (ed.), The Arthavana Upanisads, Calucutta 1872, pp. 456-464 (Bibliotheca Indica, 76); with additional material from the TITUS version.

SA_GV05_mand_upu.title: Māṇḍūkyopaniṣad with Māṇḍūkyakārikā (chapter 1: Āgamaprakaraṇa)
SA_GV05_mand_upu.author: Gauḍapāda
SA_GV05_mand_upu.summary: The text contains the Māṇḍūkyopaniṣad, an Atharvavedic prose work expounding the sacred syllable Oṃ and the four quarters (pādas) or states of the Self: waking (vaiśvānara), dreaming (taijasa), deep sleep (prājña), and the transcendent non-dual fourth (turīya). It is preserved in the traditional Advaita format where its 12 prose mantras are interleaved with the 29 verse kārikās of the first chapter (Āgamaprakaraṇa) of Gauḍapāda's Māṇḍūkyakārikā.
SA_GV05_mand_upu.attribution: The prose Māṇḍūkyopaniṣad is an anonymous Vedic text traditionally associated with the Atharvaveda. The accompanying 29 kārikās of the first chapter (Āgamaprakaraṇa) are authored by the Advaita teacher Gauḍapāda.
SA_GV05_mand_upu.coverage: partial — Complete for the Māṇḍūkyopaniṣad (all 12 prose mantras, preceded by Atharvavedic and Upaniṣadic śāntipāṭhas); partial for the Māṇḍūkyakārikā, containing only the 29 kārikās of chapter 1 (Āgamaprakaraṇa) interspersed between mantras. Chapters 2–4 of the Kārikā (Vaitathya-, Advaita-, and Alātaśāntiprakaraṇa) are not present.

SA_GV05_mandup_u.title: Māṇḍūkyopaniṣad
SA_GV05_mandup_u.summary: The Māṇḍūkyopaniṣad is a short prose Upaniṣad consisting of twelve mantras affiliated with the Atharvaveda. It equates the sacred syllable Oṃ with Brahman and the self (Ātman), correlating its constituent elements (A, U, M, and the phonetically unmanifest fourth aspect) with four states of consciousness: the waking state (vaiśvānara), the dream state (taijasa), deep dreamless sleep (prājña), and the transcendent non-dual state (turīya). Serving as the foundation for Gauḍapāda's Āgamaśāstra (Māṇḍūkyakārikā) and Śaṅkara's commentary, it is one of the central scriptural sources for Advaita Vedānta.
SA_GV05_mandup_u.attribution: A late-Vedic prose Upaniṣad traditionally affiliated with the Atharvaveda and preserved as revealed scripture (śruti).
SA_GV05_mandup_u.edition: Acharya V. P. Limaye and R. D. Vadekar (eds.), Eighteen Principal Upanisads, vol. 1, Poona, 1958.
SA_GV05_mandup_u.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising all 12 prose sections (khaṇḍas/mantras).
translations: Robert Ernest Hume (trans.), The Thirteen Principal Upanishads, 2nd ed., London: Oxford University Press, 1931. (English)
Paul Deussen, Sechzig Upanishad's des Veda, 1897. (German)

SA_GV05_ndbiuppu.title: Nādabindūpaniṣad
SA_GV05_ndbiuppu.summary: The Nādabindūpaniṣad is a minor Yoga Upaniṣad centered on meditation on the sacred syllable Oṃ (praṇava) through the symbolic visualization of the cosmic bird (haṃsa). It sets forth the twelve kalās (mātrās) of the praṇava, their associated deities and realms, and describes the spiritual rebirth or post-mortem destination attained by a practitioner who departs physical life during meditation on each respective measure. In this shorter 20-verse recension, the text concludes with dissolution of mental modifications into the transcendental, partless Brahman (paraṃ brahma) and the realization of supreme beatitude.
SA_GV05_ndbiuppu.edition: Ramamaya Tarkaratna (ed.), The Atharvana-Upanishads. Calcutta: Ganesha Press, 1872 (Bibliotheca Indica; 76).
SA_GV05_ndbiuppu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the 20 verses (vv. 1–20) as edited by Ramamaya Tarkaratna.

SA_GV05_prasup_u.title: Praśnopaniṣad
SA_GV05_prasup_u.summary: The Praśnopaniṣad is an Atharvavedic Upaniṣad. Arranged as six sequential inquiries (praśnas) addressed by six pupils to the sage Pippalāda, the text explores the dual cosmogonic principles of life-energy (prāṇa) and manifest matter (rayi), the supremacy and division of the vital breaths over sensory faculties, the physiology and metaphysics of dream, deep sleep, and waking states, meditation upon the syllable Om with its progressive cosmic stages, and the nature of the sixteen-fold Puruṣa in whom all parts dissolve.
SA_GV05_prasup_u.attribution: Belonging to the Atharvaveda tradition. Internally structured as a philosophical dialogue between the sage Pippalāda and six inquiring students.
SA_GV05_prasup_u.edition: V.P. Limaye and R.D. Vadekar (eds.), Eighteen Principal Upanisads, Vol. 1, Poona 1958; with section 6.4 rearranged and completed according to the Bibliotheca Indica edition.
SA_GV05_prasup_u.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising all six praśnas (PrUp 1.1–6.8).
translations: Patrick Olivelle, Upaniṣads, Oxford World's Classics, Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1996. (English)
Paul Deussen, Sechzig Upaniṣad's des Veda, 1897. (German)

SA_GV05_prasupbu.title: Praśnopaniṣad with Praśnopaniṣadbhāṣya
SA_GV05_prasupbu.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GV05_prasupbu.summary: The Praśnopaniṣad is a classical Upaniṣad associated with the Pippalāda śākhā of the Atharvaveda, composed in mixed prose and verse. It is organized around six philosophical questions addressed by the sage Pippalāda to six seekers concerning the cosmic generation of creatures, the primacy and functions of prāṇa (vital breath), deep sleep, the meditation on the sacred praṇava Oṃ, and the sixteen-part person (ṣoḍaśakala puruṣa). The accompanying Praśnopaniṣadbhāṣya attributed to Śaṅkara expounds these teachings from an Advaita Vedāntic perspective, distinguishing lower knowledge (aparam brahma) from higher realization of the non-dual Self (param brahma).
SA_GV05_prasupbu.attribution: The Praśnopaniṣad is an anonymous Vedic text belonging to the Atharvaveda. The accompanying bhāṣya is attributed to Śaṅkara.
SA_GV05_prasupbu.edition: Root text: V. P. Limaye and R. D. Vadekar (eds.), Eighteen Principal Upanisads, Vol. 1, Poona 1958, with PrUp 6.4 rearranged and completed from the Bibliotheca Indica edition.
SA_GV05_prasupbu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all six inquiries (praśnas, 1.1–6.8) of the Praśnopaniṣad alongside the complete bhāṣya attributed to Śaṅkara.
translations: Patrick Olivelle, Upaniṣads, World's Classics, Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1996. (English)
Paul Deussen, German translation of sixty Upaniṣads (published 1897). (German)

SA_GV05_sirup_u.title: Atharvaśiropaniṣad
SA_GV05_sirup_u.summary: The Atharvaśiropaniṣad ('Head of the Atharvaveda') is an early Śaiva and Pāśupata Upaniṣad traditionally attached to the Atharvaveda. It begins with the gods questioning Rudra about his identity, to which Rudra responds with a grandiose self-proclamation asserting that he is the sole eternal reality, transcendent and immanent in all deities, natural phenomena, and meters. The text expounds esoteric meditations on the sacred syllable Om (praṇava) and prescribes the observance of the Pāśupata vow (pāśupatavrata), including the application of sacred ashes (bhasmasnāna) for severance of worldly bondage (paśupāśa). Already cited in ancient Dharmasūtras (e.g. Gautama and Baudhāyana), it constitutes one of the foundational scriptural texts of early Śaivism.
SA_GV05_sirup_u.attribution: Canonical Upaniṣad belonging to the Atharvaveda tradition; traditionally considered apauruṣeya śruti and anonymous.
SA_GV05_sirup_u.edition: Ramamaya Tarkaratna (ed.), In: The Atharvana-Upanishads. Calcutta: Ganesha Press, 1872 (Bibliotheca Indica; 76).
SA_GV05_sirup_u.coverage: complete — Complete mūla text in 45 numbered prose and verse sections (SirUp_1–SirUp_45), concluding with the phalaśruti and colophon.

SA_GV05_svetu_pu.title: Śvetāśvataropaniṣad
SA_GV05_svetu_pu.summary: The Śvetāśvataropaniṣad is a verse Upaniṣad synthesizing Upaniṣadic thought with theistic devotion to Rudra/Śiva/Maheśvara and early meditative and philosophical concepts (including māyā, prakṛti, guṇas, and yoga). It contains teachings on Brahman, meditation, and liberation, concluding with an expression of devotion (bhakti) toward God and the teacher.
SA_GV05_svetu_pu.attribution: Internal attribution at ŚU 6.21 credits the revelation of this highest knowledge to the sage Śvetāśvatara through the power of his austerities and the grace of God (tapaḥprabhāvād devaprasādāt brahma ha śvetāśvataro 'tha vidvān / atyāśramibhyaḥ paramaṃ pavitraṃ provāca...).
