SA_GV05_svetugpu.title: Śvetāśvataropaniṣad
SA_GV05_svetugpu.summary: The Śvetāśvataropaniṣad is a classical metrical Upaniṣad belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda tradition, dating approximately to the late centuries BCE. Comprising six chapters, it synthesizes older Upaniṣadic non-dualism with an explicitly theistic framework, identifying the supreme transcendent Brahman with the personal deity Rudra-Śiva (also addressed as Hara, Īśa, and Maheśvara). The text incorporates concepts that later became central to classical Sāṃkhya and Yoga—such as pradhāna/prakṛti, puruṣa, the guṇas, and physical postures and breath control for meditation—and concludes with an influential early articulation of personal devotion (bhakti) toward God and the guru.
SA_GV05_svetugpu.attribution: Ascribed traditionally to the sage Śvetāśvatara (mentioned at 6.21: atyāśramibhyaḥ paramaṃ pavitraṃ provāca), belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda tradition.
SA_GV05_svetugpu.edition: Collated from two printed editions: (1) Īśādi nau upaniṣad, ed. Harikṛṣṇadāsa Goyandakā (Gorakhpur: Gitapress, Saṃvat 2038 [1981]); (2) Śrī Śrī Śruti-ratna-mālā, ed. Bhakti Sudhākara (Dhaka: Mañjuṣā Printing Works, n.d.).
SA_GV05_svetugpu.coverage: complete — Text in 6 adhyāyas with introductory and concluding śāntimantras ('saha nāv avatu...'). Includes editorial notes marking parallel Yajurveda and Rigveda mantras.
translations: Patrick Olivelle, trans., Upaniṣads, Oxford: Oxford University Press (World's Classics), 1996. (English)
Paul Deussen, Sechzig Upaniṣad's des Veda, Leipzig: F. A. Brockhaus, 1897. (German)

SA_GV06_.title: Pāraskaragṛhyasūtra
SA_GV06_.summary: The Pāraskaragṛhyasūtra is a manual of domestic ritual (gṛhyasūtra) setting out aphoristic rules for domestic rites and ceremonies such as the name-bestowing ceremony and alms-begging during upanayana.

SA_GV06_apsulb_u.title: Āpastambaśulbasūtra
SA_GV06_apsulb_u.summary: The Āpastambaśulbasūtra formulates practical geometric principles and rope-measuring procedures for surveying sacrificial grounds and laying out Vedic fire altars (citis) of varied forms. Landmark features include general formulations equivalent to the Pythagorean theorem, geometric methods for area-preserving shape transformations (such as squaring the circle and circling the square), and a famous rational approximation of the square root of 2.
translations: Bürk, Albert, 'Das Āpastamba-Śulba-sūtra', Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Bd. 55 (1901), pp. 543 ff. (German)

SA_GV06_asvgs_u.title: Āśvalāyanagṛhyasūtra
SA_GV06_asvgs_u.summary: The Āśvalāyanagṛhyasūtra is the domestic ritual manual (gṛhyasūtra) of the Āśvalāyana śākhā of the Ṛgveda, forming part of its Kalpasūtra corpus alongside the Āśvalāyana-Śrautasūtra. Arranged in four adhyāyas, it provides concise ritual directions for the domestic sacrifices (pākayajña), saṃskāras from conception and birth through initiation (upanayana) and marriage, daily observances, and funeral rites (antyeṣṭi). Mantras used in the domestic ceremonies are cited predominantly from the Ṛgveda.
SA_GV06_asvgs_u.attribution: The text concludes with a double salutation to Śaunaka (namaḥ śaunakāya namaḥ śaunakāya).
SA_GV06_asvgs_u.edition: A.F. Stenzler, Abhandlungen für die Kunde des Morgenlandes, 3,4 (1864)
SA_GV06_asvgs_u.coverage: complete — Contains all 4 adhyāyas (Adhyāya 1: 24 khaṇḍas; Adhyāya 2: 10 khaṇḍas; Adhyāya 3: 12 khaṇḍas; Adhyāya 4: 8 khaṇḍas), concluding at 4.8.44.

SA_GV06_asvss_u.title: Āśvalāyanaśrautasūtra
SA_GV06_asvss_u.summary: The Āśvalāyanaśrautasūtra is the primary ritual manual (kalpasūtra) of the Āśvalāyana recension of the Ṛgveda, codifying the sacrificial duties, recitations, and litanies of the hotṛ priest and his assistants. Structured into twelve adhyāyas (traditionally grouped into a pūrvārdha and an uttarārdha) and an appended Pravarādhyāya listing ancestral lineages, the text guides performances from the domestic Agnyādhāna, Agnihotra, and Darśapūrṇamāsa to complex Soma rituals, the Agnicayana, Sattras, and royal sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha. Closely affiliated with the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, it serves as an indispensable primary source for the liturgy and practical execution of classical Vedic śrauta ritualism.
SA_GV06_asvss_u.coverage: complete — Contains the complete text of all 12 adhyāyas (divided into Pūrvārdha 1–6 and Uttarārdha 7–12), concluding with the Pravarādhyāya / Pravarapariśiṣṭa.

SA_GV06_avpari_u.title: Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa
SA_GV06_avpari_u.summary: The Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa is a collection of supplementary tracts traditionally organized into 72 numbered sections. It addresses rituals, ceremonies, and lore, including manuals on purohita duties and śānti, divination and omen interpretation (adbhuta), and astral science (nakṣatrakalpa).
SA_GV06_avpari_u.edition: George Melville Bolling and Julius von Negelein (eds.), The Pariśiṣṭas of the Atharvaveda, Vol. 1, parts 1 and 2 (all published), Leipzig: Harrassowitz, 1909–1910.
SA_GV06_avpari_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 72 numbered pariśiṣṭas plus the initial invocatory formula (0.0), matching Bolling and von Negelein's edition.

SA_GV06_avpray_u.title: Atharvaprāyaścittāni
SA_GV06_avpray_u.summary: The Atharvaprāyaścittāni is an Atharvavedic ancillary ritual manual in six chapters (adhyāyas) prescribing expiations (prāyaścitta) for omissions, errors, ritual failures, and ominous occurrences during Vedic sacrificial rites. Associated with both the Śaunaka and Paippalāda traditions and closely related to the Vaitānasūtra and Kauśikasūtra, it presents penances and restorative mantras primarily formulated for the brahman priest supervising the sacrifice.
SA_GV06_avpray_u.attribution: An anonymous Vedic ancillary ritual manual belonging to the Atharvavedic tradition. In its internal chapter colophons it is designated as the prāyaścitta section of the Vaitānasūtra.
SA_GV06_avpray_u.edition: Julius von Negelein (ed.), 'Atharvaprāyaścittāni: Text mit Anmerkungen', Journal of the American Oriental Society 33 [1913] (text), 217–253 (indices and corrigenda); 34 [1914], pp. 229–277 (preface and introduction).
SA_GV06_avpray_u.coverage: complete — Complete text in six adhyāyas (adhyāyas 1–6).

SA_GV06_bhasrasuu.title: Bhāradvājaśrautasūtra
SA_GV06_bhasrasuu.summary: The Bhāradvājaśrautasūtra is an ancient Vedic ritual manual belonging to the Taittirīya branch of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, chronologically situated between the Baudhāyana and Āpastamba traditions. Surviving in 15 praśnas, it outlines the duties of the Adhvaryu priest for solemn rites including the agnyādheya, agnihotra, darśapūrṇamāsa, paśubandha, and soma sacrifices. Its language exhibits a transitional style of Vedic prose, retaining aspects of older brāhmaṇa formulation while developing concise sūtra syntax.
SA_GV06_bhasrasuu.coverage: unclear — Empty file stub (0 segments, 0 characters). The underlying text comprises 15 surviving praśnas, but no Sanskrit e-text data was ingested.

SA_GV06_dantyovu.title: Dantyoṣṭhavidhi
SA_GV06_dantyovu.summary: The Dantyoṣṭhavidhi is an Atharvavedic phonetic-orthographic treatise (lakṣaṇagrantha) comprising 23 ślokas in two adhyāyas. It addresses the practical doubt in recitation and manuscript copying regarding the distinction between the labial stop 'b' (oṣṭhya) and the labiodental semivowel 'v' (dantyoṣṭhya/dantya) in the Atharvavedasaṃhitā. Providing explicit lists of words and specific contextual exceptions where labial pronunciation is obligatory, it serves as a normative guide for accurate oral transmission and orthography.
SA_GV06_dantyovu.attribution: Traditional anonymous phonetic treatise (lakṣaṇagrantha / śikṣā) belonging to the Atharvavedic ancillary literature.
SA_GV06_dantyovu.edition: Pandita Ramagopala Sastri: The Dantosthavidhih or the Fourth Kahsna Treatise of the Atharvaveda edited with an introduction, translation and an index. Lahore, 1921.
SA_GV06_dantyovu.coverage: complete — Complete text in two adhyāyas (adhyāya 1 has 12 verses; adhyāya 2 has 11 verses; 23 verses total), concluding with the colophon 'dantyoṣṭhavidhiḥ samāptaḥ'.

SA_GV06_higrsuu.title: Hiraṇyakeśigṛhyasūtra
SA_GV06_higrsuu.summary: The Hiraṇyakeśigṛhyasūtra is a Vedic domestic ritual text (Gṛhyasūtra).
SA_GV06_higrsuu.coverage: unclear — The repository e-text file is completely empty (0 characters, 0 segments).

SA_GV06_jaimigsu.title: Jaiminigṛhyasūtra
SA_GV06_jaimigsu.summary: The Jaiminigṛhyasūtra is the domestic ritual manual of the Jaiminīya (or Talavakāra) śākhā of the Sāmaveda. Structured in two praśnas comprising 24 and 9 khaṇḍas respectively, it begins with the standard model of the pārvaṇasthālīpāka offering and details domestic life-cycle rites (saṃskāras) such as upanayana, godāna, vivāha, and śrāddha, concluding with a navagrahaśānti. It constitutes an indispensable source for the domestic ritual liturgy of the Sāmaveda preserved primarily in South India (Tamil Nadu and Kerala).
SA_GV06_jaimigsu.attribution: A domestic ritual manual (gṛhyasūtra) belonging to the Jaiminīya (Talavakāra) śākhā of the Sāmaveda. While traditionally ascribed to the Vedic sage Jaimini, the text is an anonymous school composition of the late Vedic period.
SA_GV06_jaimigsu.edition: Willem Caland (ed.), The Jaiminigṛhyasūtra belonging to the Sāmaveda, Lahore: Moti Lal Banarsi Dass (Punjab Sanskrit Series, 2).
SA_GV06_jaimigsu.coverage: complete — The complete sūtra text: part 1 in 24 khaṇḍas (JaimGS 1.1–1.24) and part 2 in 9 khaṇḍas (2.1–2.9). It ends with the grahaśānti verses ('grahā gāvo narendrāś ca ...') and the colophon '// iti jaiminisūtraṃ samāptam //'.

SA_GV06_kaussu_u.title: Kauśikasūtra
SA_GV06_kaussu_u.summary: The Kauśikasūtra is the principal ritual manual of the Atharvaveda (Śaunaka recension), arranged into 14 adhyāyas comprising 141 kaṇḍikās. Unlike standard Gṛhyasūtras of other Vedic śākhās, it encompasses both domestic life-cycle rituals (saṃskāras, marriage, ancestral rites) and an extensive repertoire of magical, medical, apotropaic, and omen-pacification rites (bhaiṣajyāni, abhicāra, śānti, adbhuta, and royal rites). It provides the indispensable ceremonial context and ritual application (viniyoga) for the hymns of the Atharvaveda-Saṃhitā.
SA_GV06_kaussu_u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the Vedic sage Kauśika. It is the principal ritual manual of the Śaunaka recension of the Atharvaveda.
SA_GV06_kaussu_u.edition: Bloomfield (1889/ (for adhyāyas 2–14 and collation of adhyāya 1); combined with S. S. Bahulkar, 'Kauśikasūtra' [Critical edition of chapter 1], in: Vedic Texts: A Revision: Prof. C.G. Kashikar Felicitation Volume, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1990 (for adhyāya 1).
SA_GV06_kaussu_u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 14 adhyāyas comprising 141 kaṇḍikās, concluding with the colophons: 'iti atharvavede kauśikasūtre caturdaśo 'dhyāyaḥ samāptaḥ / iti kauśikasūtraṃ samāptam'.
translations: Maurice Bloomfield (trans.), Atharva Veda, Oxford: Sacred Books of the East #42, 1897. (English)

SA_GV06_kauthgsu.title: Kauthumagṛhyasūtra
SA_GV06_kauthgsu.summary: The Kauthumagṛhyasūtra is a domestic-ritual text (gṛhyasūtra) in 21 brief khaṇḍas, treating domestic ritual procedures, expiatory offerings (prāyaścitta), and specific rites such as the marriage to a Calotropis procera plant (arkakanyādāna) before a third marriage.

SA_GV06_keskaupu.title: Kauśikapaddhati
SA_GV06_keskaupu.author: Keśava
SA_GV06_keskaupu.summary: The Kauśikapaddhati is a ritual manual (paddhati) by Keśava setting forth the procedural application of the Kauśikasūtra, the primary ritual handbook of the Śaunakīya Atharvaveda. Keśava arranges the aphoristic sūtras into a systematic, sequential ritual program for Atharvavedic priests, detailing domestic rites (saṃskāras), therapeutic rituals (bhaiṣajya), propitiatory ceremonies (śānti), and sorcery (abhicāra). Together with Dārila's earlier bhāṣya, Keśava's paddhati is the principal traditional authority for interpreting Atharvavedic ritual practice.
SA_GV06_keskaupu.attribution: Composed by Keśava, an Atharvavedic ritualist dated to the eleventh century (cf. Kauśikapaddhati, Introduction, pp. xxxv–xxxviii). The work glosses and arranges the rites of the Kauśikasūtra belonging to the Śaunaka recension of the Atharvaveda.
SA_GV06_keskaupu.edition: Keśava's Kauśikapaddhati on the Kauśikasūtra of the Atharvaveda, critically edited by V. P. Limaye, R. N. Dandekar, C. G. Kashikar, V. V. Bhide, and S. S. Bahulkar, Pune: Tilak Maharashtra Vidyapeeth, 1982.
SA_GV06_keskaupu.coverage: complete — Complete text of Keśava's paddhati, covering all 14 adhyāyas (141 kaṇḍikās) with the embedded sūtras of the Kauśikasūtra, concluding with the final colophon 'iti kauśikapaddhatiḥ samāptā'.

SA_GV06_khagrsuu.title: Khādiragṛhyasūtra
SA_GV06_khagrsuu.summary: The Khādiragṛhyasūtra is a manual of domestic ritual belonging to the Drāhyāyaṇa (or Rāṇāyanīya) branch of the Sāmaveda, arranged into four paṭalas. It provides concise aphoristic prescriptions for domestic rites (saṃskāras), including marriage, tonsure, initiation, and daily domestic sacrifices. The work represents a condensed and structurally regularised redaction of the Gobhilagṛhyasūtra.
SA_GV06_khagrsuu.coverage: unclear — Empty record: 0 segment files and 0 characters. Nothing can be said about coverage.

SA_GV06_manavgsu.title: Mānavagṛhyasūtra
SA_GV06_manavgsu.summary: The Mānavagṛhyasūtra is the domestic ritual manual belonging to the Mānava school of the Maitrāyaṇīya recension of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. Arranged into two divisions (puruṣas) containing 23 and 18 sections (khaṇḍas) respectively, it outlines the standard domestic sacraments (saṃskāras) from initiation and wedding rituals to ancestor worship (śrāddha) and domestic oblations. It is particularly renowned among Indologists for preserving ancient non-Śrauta folk cults, including an early rite for pacifying the four Vināyakas (2.14).
SA_GV06_manavgsu.attribution: The Mānavagṛhyasūtra belongs to the Mānava carana of the Maitrāyaṇīya śākhā of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. Although line [0] reproduces the edition title heading 'śrīmaitrāyaṇīyamānavagṛhyasūtrabhāṣyam', the e-text contains only the mūlasūtras.
SA_GV06_manavgsu.edition: Mānavagṛhyasūtra of the Maitrāyaṇīya Śākhā with the Commentary of Aṣṭāvakra, edited with an introduction, indexes, etc. by Ramakrishna Harshaji Sastri, Baroda: Central Library, 1926 (Gaekwad's Oriental Series).
SA_GV06_manavgsu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Mānavagṛhyasūtra in 2 puruṣas (Puruṣa 1 with 23 khaṇḍas, Puruṣa 2 with 18 khaṇḍas; sūtras 1.1.1 through 2.18.4).

SA_GV06_rgvidh_u.title: Ṛgvidhāna
SA_GV06_rgvidh_u.summary: The Ṛgvidhāna is a metrical ritual manual belonging to the ancillary literature (vidhāna / Vedāṅga) of the Ṛgveda, traditionally attributed to Śaunaka. Following the sequential order of hymns in the Ṛgveda-Saṃhitā, it details the apotropaic, curational, worldly, and expiatory applications (vidhi) of specific ṛcs and sūktas outside the solemn śrauta ritual context. It serves as a vital historical bridge connecting late Vedic domestic ritualism with early Tantric mantra application.
SA_GV06_rgvidh_u.attribution: Traditionally ascribed to the Vedic sage/teacher Śaunaka (e.g. 1.1.2: karmaṇāṃ ṛṣidṛṣṭānāṃ vidhiṃ provāca śaunakaḥ).
SA_GV06_rgvidh_u.edition: M.S. Bhat (ed., tr.), Vedic Tantrism: A Study of Ṛgvidhāna of Śaunaka with Text and Translation.
SA_GV06_rgvidh_u.coverage: complete — Complete text across all five adhyāyas (1.1.1 through 5.3.3), ending with traditional scribal post-colophon verses (yādṛśaṃ pustakaṃ dṛṣṭvā...).
translations: J. Gonda (tr.), English translation of Rgvidhana, Utrecht, 1951. (English)
M.S. Bhat (tr.), Vedic Tantrism: A Study of Ṛgvidhāna of Śaunaka with Text and Translation. (English)

SA_GV06_sankhssu.title: Śāṅkhāyanaśrautasūtra
SA_GV06_sankhssu.summary: The Śāṅkhāyanaśrautasūtra is the principal manual of solemn Vedic ritual (śrauta) belonging to the Śāṅkhāyana (Kauṣītaki) school of the Ṛgveda. It details the ritual roles, duties, and recitations of the hotṛ priest and his assistants (Maitrāvaruṇa, Acchāvāka, and Grāvastut) across the full spectrum of Vedic sacrifices, including the agnihotra, darśapūrṇamāsa, cāturmāsya, paśubandha, and extensive soma rituals (Agniṣṭoma, Ahīna, and Sattra). The text comprises 18 adhyāyas, of which chapters 1–16 form the primary sūtra core and chapters 17–18 constitute later supplementary sections (pariśiṣṭa).
SA_GV06_sankhssu.attribution: The Śrautasūtra belongs to the Śāṅkhāyana (Kauṣītaki) śākhā of the Ṛgveda.
SA_GV06_sankhssu.edition: Alfred Hillebrandt (ed.), The Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra together with the Commentary of Varadattasuta Ānartīya, Calcutta: Asiatic Society of Bengal, 1888 (Bibliotheca Indica, 99).
SA_GV06_sankhssu.coverage: complete — Contains the complete root sūtra text in 18 adhyāyas (1.1.1 through 18.24.34), without commentary.
translations: Willem Caland (trans.), edited with an introduction by Lokesh Chandra, Śaṅkhāyana-Śrautasūtra: Being a major yajñika text of the Ṛgveda, Nagpur: International Academy of Indian Culture, 1953 (Sarasvati-Vihara Series). (English)

SA_GV06_vaitss_u.title: Vaitānaśrautasūtra
SA_GV06_vaitss_u.summary: The Vaitānaśrautasūtra (commonly called Vaitānasūtra) is the sole surviving śrauta manual belonging to the Atharvavedic tradition. It sets out the solemn public Vedic sacrifices (vitāna) specifically from the standpoint of the Atharvan priesthood, focusing on the liturgical duties of the brahman priest and his assistant, the brāhmaṇācchaṃsin. Composed relatively late among the Vedic Śrautasūtras, the work borrows significantly from the domestic Kauśikasūtra as well as the Yajurvedic śrautasūtra tradition, and stands in close textual relation to the Gopatha-Brāhmaṇa.
SA_GV06_vaitss_u.attribution: The Vaitānaśrautasūtra is an anonymous ritual sūtra text of the Atharvaveda.
SA_GV06_vaitss_u.edition: Vishva Bandhu (et al.): Vaitāna-Śrauta-Sūtra, with the commentary called Ākṣepānuvidhi by Somāditya, Hoshiarpur: Vishveshvaranand Vedic Research Institute 1967 (Vishveshvaranand Institute publication, 430; Woolner Indological Series, 13)
SA_GV06_vaitss_u.coverage: complete — Complete sūtra text in 8 adhyāyas (corresponding to 43 kaṇḍikās; sūtras 1.1.1/1.1 to 8.5.47/43.47). The commentary Ākṣepānuvidhi by Somāditya printed in Vishva Bandhu's edition was not included in this e-text.
translations: R. Garbe, German translation of the Vaitāna-Śrautasūtra, Strassburg, 1878. (German)
W. Caland, German translation of Vaitāna-Śrautasūtra, Amsterdam, 1910. (German)

SA_GV06_vargs_u.title: Vārāhagṛhyasūtra
SA_GV06_vargs_u.summary: The Vārāhagṛhyasūtra is the domestic ritual manual (gṛhyasūtra) of the Vārāha school belonging to the Maitrāyaṇīya branch. Across 17 khaṇḍas, it prescribes the domestic ritual cycle, including pākayajñas, saṃskāras, and other domestic rites.
SA_GV06_vargs_u.attribution: A traditional domestic ritual manual belonging to the Vārāha branch of the Maitrāyaṇīya school.
SA_GV06_vargs_u.edition: Raghu Vira (ed.), Vārāhagṛhyasūtra. New Delhi: Meharchand Lachhmandas, 1982 (Panini Vaidika Granthamala, 2).
SA_GV06_vargs_u.coverage: complete — Complete root text in 17 khaṇḍas (VGrs 1.1–17.22).
translations: Pierre Rolland (tr.), Un rituel domestique védique: Le Vārāhagṛhyasūtra. Aix-en-Provence: Ophrys, 1971. (French)

SA_K01_abhisdhu.title: Abhisamācārikadharma
SA_K01_abhisdhu.summary: The Abhisamācārikadharma is a Vinaya treatise preserved by the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravāda school outlining everyday rules of proper conduct, deportment, and etiquette (abhisamācāra) for Buddhist monks, functioning as a vital complement to the formal offenses of the Prātimokṣasūtra. Preserved in a single 11th–12th century palm-leaf manuscript from Tibet, the text is arranged in seven sections (vargas) detailing duties regarding elders, lodging and furniture, the kaṭhina robe ceremony, wandering and resident monks, and daily bodily hygiene. Transmitted in an archaic layer of Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit, it provides uniquely detailed evidence for early to medieval Indian Buddhist monastic culture and daily praxis.
SA_K01_abhisdhu.attribution: Canonical Vinaya treatise belonging to the Ārya Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin school, specifically representing the Madhyuddeśika recension ('āryamahāsāṃghikānāṃ lokottaravādināṃ madhyuddeśa-pāṭhakānāṃ pāṭheneti').
SA_K01_abhisdhu.edition: Abhisamācārika-Dharma Study Group (ed.), A Digital edition of the Abhisamacarika-Dharma of the Mahasamghika-Lokottaravadins, Tokyo: The Institute for Comprehensive Studies of Buddhism, Taisho University.
SA_K01_abhisdhu.coverage: complete — Complete text covering all seven vargas (Saṃghasthavira, Śayyāsana, Kaṭhina, Āgantuka, Āraṇyaka, Nevāsika, Pradīpa), ending at folio 50b3.
translations: Singh, S. and K. Minowa, 'A Critical Edition and Translation of Abhisamācārikā Nāma Bhikṣu-Prakīrṇakaḥ: Chapter One'. (English)

SA_K01_bhikavau.title: Bhikṣuṇīkarmavācanā (incomplete)
SA_K01_bhikavau.summary: A Sanskrit Vinaya formulary (karmavācanā) for the going-forth (pravrajyā) and full ordination (upasaṃpadā) of Buddhist nuns. It opens with the story of Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī's request and the eight gurudharmas. It then gives the procedures and formulae for the candidate's preliminaries, the questioning about obstructive conditions (āntarāyikā dharmāḥ), and ordination before both saṅghas, and closes with admonitions to the newly ordained nun; the text breaks off in these admonitions. It survives in an incomplete manuscript in the Bodleian Library.
SA_K01_bhikavau.attribution: A Vinaya formulary for the ordination of nuns. The Chinese parallels linked in the catalogue are T1453 (Yijing's translation of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Ekottarakarmaśataka) and T1904 ('Phags-pa's manual).
SA_K01_bhikavau.edition: Michael Schmidt, 'Bhikṣuṇī-Karmavācanā: Die Handschrift Sansk. c. 25 (R) der Bodleian Library Oxford,' in Studien zur Indologie und Buddhismuskunde: Festgabe für Professor Dr. Heinz Bechert zum 60. Geburtstag am 26. Juni 1992, ed. Reinhold Grünendahl, Jens-Uwe Hartmann, and Petra Kieffer-Pülz, Indica et Tibetica 22 (Bonn: Indica et Tibetica Verlag, 1993), pp. 239–288.
SA_K01_bhikavau.coverage: partial — Edition of the single incomplete manuscript Bodleian MS Sansk. c. 25 (R). The text begins on the folio before 3a, in the Mahāprajāpatī narrative ('mahāprajāpatī gautamī bhagavantam idam avocat'). The text breaks off on fol. 31b in the admonitions after upasaṃpadā ('sabrahmacār.///').

SA_K01_bhivin_u.title: Bhikṣuṇīvinaya
SA_K01_bhivin_u.summary: The Bhikṣuṇīvinaya of the Ārya-Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin school is the monastic disciplinary code and case-law collection for Buddhist nuns (bhikṣuṇīs). Preserved in the madhy'udeśika recitation tradition, it comprises the monastic rules and case narratives for nuns (including Pācattika and Prātideśanika dharmas), followed by Prakīrṇaka sections.
SA_K01_bhivin_u.attribution: Canonical monastic code of the Ārya-Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin school (preserved in the madhy'udeśika recitation tradition).
SA_K01_bhivin_u.edition: Gustav Roth, Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya, Patna: K.P. Jayaswal Research Institute 1970 (Tibetan Sanskrit Works Series, 12; cf. 2nd ed. 2005, with 4 addenda).
SA_K01_bhivin_u.coverage: complete — Text of the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravāda Bhikṣuṇīvinaya as edited by Gustav Roth, containing the Bhikṣuṇīvinaya along with Bhikṣuṇīprakīrṇaka, and including Addenda 1 (text of folio 71 supplying the end of Pācattika 141 and Prātideśanika rules 1–8) appended from Roth's 2005 second edition.
translations: Édith Nolot, Règles de discipline des nonnes bouddhistes: Le Bhikṣuṇīvinaya de l'école Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin, Paris: Diffusion de Boccard, 1991 (Publications de l'Institut de civilisation indienne 8/60). (French)
Akira Hirakawa, Monastic Discipline for the Buddhist Nuns: An English Translation of the Chinese Text of the Mahāsāṃghika Bhikṣuṇī-Vinaya, 1982. (English)

SA_K01_bsa068_u.title: Bhikṣukarmavākya
SA_K01_bsa068_u.summary: The Bhikṣukarmavākya is a Buddhist monastic ritual formulary (karmavācanā). It sets forth the prescribed ecclesiastical formulas (jñapti and karmavācanā) and ceremonial procedures for admission into the order, covering going forth (pravrajyā), novice ordination (śrāmaṇera), and full higher ordination (upasaṃpadā). The text concludes with instructions regarding the basic training rules and the four root transgressions (pārājika) entailing defeat and expulsion.
SA_K01_bsa068_u.edition: A.C. Banerjee: Bhikṣukarmavākya. Indian Historical Quarterly 25 (1949), pp. 19-30; 2nd ed. in: Two Buddhist Vinaya Texts in Sanskrit, Prātimokṣa Sūtra and Bhikṣukarmavākya. Calcutta 1977.
SA_K01_bsa068_u.coverage: complete — Text of the Bhikṣukarmavākya containing the procedures for pravrajyā, śrāmaṇera ordination, and upasaṃpadā.

SA_K01_bsu011_u.title: Bodhisattvaprātimokṣasūtra (part 1: ritual for taking the bodhisattva vows)
SA_K01_bsu011_u.summary: This is a liturgical manual for conferring the threefold bodhisattva discipline: saṃvaraśīla, kuśaladharmasaṃgrāhakaśīla, and sattvārthakriyāśīla. It details the request to a qualified preceptor, confession of faults, taking refuge, the formal acceptance of vows, and instructions for taking the vows before an image of the Tathāgata when no qualified person is present.
SA_K01_bsu011_u.edition: Nalinaksa Dutt: Bodhisattva-prātimokṣa-sūtram. Calcutta: Calcutta Oriental Press, 1931, p 11-19.
SA_K01_bsu011_u.coverage: partial — Corresponds to pp. 11–19 of Nalinaksha Dutt's edition (Calcutta Oriental Press, 1931), covering the ritual for taking the bodhisattva vows from 'om namaḥ sarvvabuddhabodhisattvebhyaḥ' to '... māmitaḥ prabhṛti buddha bhagavanto bodhisattvāśca dhārayantviti vijñaptiḥ // 0 //'.

SA_K01_bsu046_u.title: Mahāsāṃghikaprātimokṣasūtra
SA_K01_bsu046_u.summary: The Mahāsāṃghikaprātimokṣasūtra is the liturgical rule code of monastic discipline for monks (bhikṣus) belonging to the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin lineage, recited fortnightly at the poṣadha (confession) assembly. It sets forth training rules systematically classified in descending order of severity: pārājika, saṃghātiśeṣa, aniyata, niḥsargika-pācattika, pācattika, pratideśanīya, śaikṣa, and adhikaraṇaśamatha.
SA_K01_bsu046_u.attribution: Canonical Vinaya scripture of the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin school of early Indian Buddhism.
SA_K01_bsu046_u.edition: W. Pachow and R. Mishra: The Prātimokṣa-Sūtra of the Mahāsāṅghikās. Allahabad 1956.
SA_K01_bsu046_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the monastic rule code for bhikṣus according to the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin tradition, containing the introductory verses and upodghāta liturgy, all eight classes of rules (4 pārājika, 13 saṃghātiśeṣa, 2 aniyata, 30 niḥsargika-pācattika, 92 pācattika, 4 pratideśanīya, 67 śaikṣa, 7 adhikaraṇaśamatha), the verses of the seven past Buddhas, and the scribal colophon.

SA_K01_bsu058_u.title: Vinayasūtra with Vinayasūtravṛtti (chapter 1: Pravrajyāvastu)
SA_K01_bsu058_u.author: Guṇaprabha
SA_K01_bsu058_u.summary: Guṇaprabha's Vinayasūtra is the definitive scholastic digest of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya, condensing canonical narrative and disciplinary legal codes into concise aphorisms. This first chapter, the Pravrajyāvastu, sets forth monastic regulations and formal legal acts (karmavācanā) regarding novice reception (śrāmaṇeratvopanayana) and full ordination (upasaṃpad). Accompanied here by Guṇaprabha's auto-commentary (Vinayasūtravṛtti or Svavyākhyāna), it served as an authoritative reference work for Buddhist monastic jurisprudence in late Indian and Tibetan Buddhism.
SA_K01_bsu058_u.attribution: Both the root sūtras and the auto-commentary (svavyākhyāna / vṛtti) are composed by Guṇaprabha (c. 6th–7th century CE), as declared in the opening verses (sūtrāṇi vinayasyeyaṃ vṛttis teṣāṃ nigadyate) and the chapter colophon (vinayavṛttau svavyākhyānataḥ pravrajyāvastu samāptam).
SA_K01_bsu058_u.edition: P.V. Bapat and V.V. Gokhale (eds.), Vinaya-sūtra and Auto-Commentary on the Same by Guṇaprabha. Chapter I: Pravrajyā-vastu, Compared with the Tibetan version. Tibetan Sanskrit Works Series, 22. Patna: K.P. Jayaswal Research Institute, 1982.
SA_K01_bsu058_u.coverage: partial — Contains chapter 1 (Pravrajyāvastu) only, covering sūtras 1–647 along with their complete auto-commentary. The full Vinayasūtra contains over 4,000 sūtras covering seventeen vastus and the prātimokṣa rules.
translations: Pravrajyāvastu of the Vinayasūtra and its Vṛtti (1)–(3). Sanskrit Text and Japanese Translation, Tokyo 2003–2005 (Annual of the Institute for Comprehensive Studies of Buddhism Taishō University 25–27). (Japanese)

SA_K01_n2853u.title: Śayanāsanavastu
SA_K01_n2853u.summary: The Śayanāsanavastu ('Chapter on Bedding and Seats') is the 15th section of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu. It lays down monastic rules regarding monastic lodgings, dwellings, beds, and seating, governing their proper allocation, maintenance, and seniority-based ranking within the saṅgha. The text incorporates major narrative accounts, including the conversion of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, the procurement and construction of the Jetavana monastery under the supervision of Śāriputra, and the Tittira Jātaka illustrating deference to elders.
SA_K01_n2853u.attribution: Canonical Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya scripture; traditionally regarded as Buddhavacana.
SA_K01_n2853u.edition: Raniero Gnoli (ed.), The Gilgit Manuscript of the Śayanāsanavastu and the Adhikaraṇavastu, Being the 15th and 16th Sections of the Vinaya of the Mūlasarvāstivādin, Serie Orientale Roma 50, Roma: IsMEO, 1978, pp. 1–56.
SA_K01_n2853u.coverage: complete — Text of the 15th section of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, concluding with the closing colophon 'śayanāsanavastu samāptam'.
translations: Gregory Schopen, 'Hierarchy and Housing in a Buddhist Monastic Code: A Translation of the Sanskrit Text of the Śayanāsanavastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya — Part One', Buddhist Literature 2. (English)

SA_K01_n2892u.title: Vajrasattvapārājikā
SA_K01_n2892u.summary: The Vajrasattvapārājikā is an anonymous Newar Buddhist manual on expiation (prāyaścitta) and ritual purity, framed by homage to Vajrasattva and to the ācārya as Vajradhara. Despite the Vinaya term pārājikā in its title, it is addressed to Vajrācārya and lay communities, not to celibate monastics. It adapts Dharmaśāstra-style rules on liability and penance for homicide and cow-killing (govadha), birth and death impurity (sūtaka), purification (śaucācāra, including pañcagavya) and ancestral rites (śrāddha). The Sanskrit is irregular.
SA_K01_n2892u.attribution: Anonymous Newar Buddhist work. It opens with homage to Vajrasattva and announces 'prāyaścittavidhiṃ vakṣye śaucācāraṃ ca' (v. 1).
SA_K01_n2892u.coverage: complete — It runs from the invocation of Vajrasattva through prāyaścitta for killing, govadha, sūtaka, śaucācāra and śrāddha, to the closing colophon 'iti prāyaścittavidhau śaucācāravidhe śrāddhaprakaraṇamiti'.

SA_K01_n2894u.title: Saddharmapārājikā
SA_K01_n2894u.summary: The Saddharmapārājikā is a late medieval Newar Buddhist ritual and expiation tract belonging to the distinctive Nepalese cluster of 'Pārājikā' texts (alongside the Vajrasattva-, Mañjuśrī-, Tārā-, and Lokeśvarapārājikā). Despite utilizing the monastic term pārājikā, the treatise does not govern monastic disciplinary codes, but rather adapts Dharmaśāstric notions of karmic ripening (karmavipāka) and atonement (prāyaścitta) to Newar Buddhist lay life. It specifies the penances and temporal periods required to purify grave sins (such as the slaughter of an arhat, a brahmin, or a cow), concluding with manual rites and mantras for purification with the five bovine products (pañcagavya) and kuśa water.

SA_K01_n2896u.title: Śrīlokeśvarabhāṣitaparājikā (incomplete)
SA_K01_n2896u.summary: A Buddhist ritual scripture presented as a dialogue between the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (Lokeśvara) and the goddess Tārā. Despite the word 'parājikā' in its title, the work expounds portents and ominous signs (utpātalakṣaṇa) and their ritual pacification (utpātaśāntikakrama) through the recitation of the Mahāpañcarakṣā, homa oblations, bali rites, and donations to priests.
SA_K01_n2896u.attribution: A scriptural dialogue set on Mount Potalaka (corrupted in the text as śrīmatyotarake ramye) between Avalokiteśvara and Tārā.
SA_K01_n2896u.coverage: partial — The text breaks off after the omen of an iron snake/horse entering the house without the corresponding pacification rite and without any colophon.

SA_K01_n2900u.title: Mañjuśrīpārājikā
SA_K01_n2900u.summary: The Mañjuśrīpārājikā (also known by its colophon title Pāpaparimocana) is a scripture framed as an exposition given by the Buddha to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī. Purporting to be extracted from a 12,000-verse Vinaya work (Sarvatathāgatadvādaśasāhasrapārājikāvinaya), it adapts traditional Indic life-cycle sacraments (saṃskāras / daśakarma from birth through tonsure and monastic ordination) into a Newar Vajrayāna framework, providing ritual and doctrinal legitimation for the hereditary Vajrācārya priesthood. The text also covers grave transgressions (pārājikā), funeral and post-mortuary rites, and expiatory purification procedures including the use of pañcagavya.
SA_K01_n2900u.attribution: Presented in traditional buddhavacana format as a discourse delivered by the Buddha to Mañjuśrī, claiming in the concluding colophon to be an excerpt from the Sarvatathāgatadvādaśasāhasrapārājikāvinaya.
SA_K01_n2900u.coverage: complete — Text terminates with the final colophon at folio marker ( 28 ).

SA_K01_n2904u.title: Lokeśvarapārājikā
SA_K01_n2904u.summary: A Newar Buddhist ritual manual belonging to the distinctive Nepalese 'Pārājikā' corpus. Cast as a revelation from Bodhisattva Lokeśvara (Avalokiteśvara) to Tārā on ominous portents (utpāta) and pacification procedures (śāntividhi), the text catalogues various domestic and environmental prodigies—such as eclipses, meteors, unnatural animal behavior, domestic intrusions by predators or serpents, and poisoned wells—and prescribes apotropaic rites (śānti) including homa fire offerings, recitation of the Pañcarakṣā, kalaśapūjā, and donations to the saṅgha. Despite adopting the classical Vinaya designation 'pārājikā', the work does not address monastic expulsion but rather lay and household expiatory and pacification rituals.
SA_K01_n2904u.attribution: Framed as a revelatory dialogue between Lokeśvara (Avalokiteśvara) and Tārā; anonymous ritual manual produced and preserved in the Newar Buddhist tradition of the Kathmandu Valley.
SA_K01_n2904u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the work in 63 numbered sections, terminating with the final colophon 'iti utpātalakṣaṇa-śāntividhisamāptiḥ'.

SA_K01_n2954u.title: Upasampadājñapti
SA_K01_n2954u.summary: The Upasampadājñapti is a Sanskrit ritual and legal manual (karmavācanā) for higher monastic ordination (upasampadā) according to the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya tradition, ending with the colophon 'upasampadā jñaptiḥ samāptaḥ'.
SA_K01_n2954u.attribution: A canonical monastic legal manual (karmavācanā) belonging to the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya tradition; no author is attributed.
SA_K01_n2954u.edition: Jin-il Chung (ed.), Handbuch für die buddhistische Mönchsordination bei den Mūlasarvāstivādins, Gimpo 2011. (Underlying ed.: B. Jinananda, Upasampadājñaptiḥ, Patna: K.P. Jayaswal Research Institute, 1961, Tibetan Sanskrit Works Series 6.)
SA_K01_n2954u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the manual ending with the colophon 'upasampadā jñaptiḥ samāptaḥ'.

SA_K01_n742u.title: Bhikṣuṇīvinaya
SA_K01_n742u.summary: The Bhikṣuṇīvinaya of the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin school is the sole Vinaya text governing Buddhist nuns preserved substantially in Sanskrit. It recounts the origin narrative of the nuns' order with Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and the formulation of the eight 'weighty rules' (gurudharma), followed by an extensive vibhaṅga (rule-by-rule casuistry and commentary) on the nuns' Prātimokṣa, miscellaneous disciplinary matters (Bhikṣuṇīprakīrṇaka), and a concluding uddāna summary of the monks' miscellaneous section (Bhikṣuprakīrṇaka). Preserved in an 11th–12th century palm-leaf manuscript, its Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit idioms make it a cornerstone witness for early Buddhist sectarian law and linguistics.
SA_K01_n742u.attribution: Canonical Vinaya scripture transmitted by the Ārya-Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin school; regarded in tradition as Buddhavacana.
SA_K01_n742u.edition: Gustav Roth (ed.), Bhikṣuṇī-Vinaya, including Bhikṣuṇī-Prakīrṇaka and a summary of the Bhikṣu-Prakīrṇaka of the Ārya-Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin. Patna: K.P. Jayaswal Research Institute, 1970 (Tibetan Sanskrit Works Series, 12).
SA_K01_n742u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the work as edited by Gustav Roth (1970). It encompasses the foundational narrative of Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and the eight gurudharmas (§§ 1–28), the full Bhikṣuṇīprātimokṣavibhaṅga (§§ 29–255; colophon at line 7849), the Bhikṣuṇīprakīrṇaka (§§ 256–289; colophon at line 8584), and the concluding Bhikṣuprakīrṇaka uddāna summary (§§ 290–294; colophon at line 8759).
translations: Édith Nolot, Règles de discipline des nonnes bouddhistes: le Bhikṣuṇīvinaya de l'école Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin: traduction annotée, commentaire, collation du manuscrit. Paris: Collège de France, Édition-diffusion de Boccard, 1991 (Publications de l'Institut de civilisation indienne, fascicule 60). (French)
Akira Hirakawa, Monastic Discipline for the Buddhist Nuns: An English Translation of the Chinese Text of the Mahāsāṃghika-Bhikṣuṇī-Vinaya. 1982. (English)

SA_K01_prmosu_u.title: Prātimokṣasūtra
SA_K01_prmosu_u.summary: The Prātimokṣasūtra of the Sarvāstivādins is the fundamental monastic disciplinary code for Buddhist monks (bhikṣus) according to the Sarvāstivāda school, designed for communal recitation at the bi-monthly poṣadha observance. The text comprises an introductory Nidāna and 263 disciplinary rules categorized into eight sections (4 pārājika, 13 saṃghāvaśeṣa, 2 aniyata, 30 naiḥsargika-prāyaścittika, 90 prāyaścittika, 4 pratideśanīya, 113 śaikṣa, and 7 adhikaraṇaśamatha dharmāḥ), followed by fifteen closing verses.
SA_K01_prmosu_u.attribution: Canonical Vinaya text belonging to the Sarvāstivāda school.
SA_K01_prmosu_u.edition: Georg von Simson: Pratimoksasutra der Sarvastivadins, Teil 1, Göttingen 1986 (Sanskrittexte aus den Turfanfunden, 11); Teil 2, Göttingen 2000.
SA_K01_prmosu_u.coverage: complete — Complete critically edited text of the Sarvāstivāda Bhikṣu-Prātimokṣasūtra, including the introductory Nidāna (sections I–V), all disciplinary rules (4 pārājika, 13 saṃghāvaśeṣa, 2 aniyata, 30 naiḥsargika-prāyaścittika, 90 prāyaścittika, 4 pratideśanīya, 113 śaikṣa, and 7 adhikaraṇaśamatha dharmāḥ), and the concluding 15 stanzas with closing poṣadha formula.
translations: Édouard Huber, in Louis Finot, 'Le Prātimokṣasūtra des Sarvāstivādins', Journal Asiatique, 1913. (French)

SA_K01_prmosubu.title: Prātimokṣasūtra
SA_K01_prmosubu.summary: The Prātimokṣasūtra of the Mūlasarvāstivāda tradition is the canonical legal code governing Buddhist monks (bhikṣus). It was recited fortnightly by the monastic community during the poṣadha observance. The text contains the disciplinary precepts grouped into categories such as pārājika, saṃghāvaśeṣa, aniyata, naiḥsargika-pāyattika, pāyattika, and śaikṣa, along with introductory and concluding verses. This digital text is based on the Gilgit manuscript facsimile in GBM 17–60.
SA_K01_prmosubu.attribution: Canonical Vinaya code of the Mūlasarvāstivāda school setting forth the disciplinary precepts for Buddhist monks (bhikṣus), traditionally attributed to Śākyamuni Buddha.
SA_K01_prmosubu.edition: Anukul Chandra Banerjee, ed., Prātimokṣa-sūtra (Mūlasarvāstivāda), Calcutta: Calcutta Oriental Press, 1954 [first published in IHQ 29 (1953), pp. 162-174]; reprinted with slight modifications (not indicated) as: Prātimokṣa Sūtra, in: Two Buddhist Vinaya Texts in Sanskrit, Prātimokṣa Sūtra and Bhikṣukarmavākya, ed. Anukul Chandra Banerjee, Calcutta 1977, pp. 1-56. Faks. in GBM 17-60.
SA_K01_prmosubu.coverage: complete — Text of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Bhikṣu-prātimokṣasūtra, including opening verses, precepts (such as saṃghāvaśeṣa, aniyata, naiḥsargika-pāyattika, pāyattika, śaikṣa), and concluding verses ending with '/// prātimokṣaḥ samāptaḥ ///'.
translations: so sor thar pa'i mdo (Derge Kangyur D 2): translated by Jinamitra, cog ro klu'i rgyal mtshan (Tibetan)

SA_K01_prmosufu.title: Prātimokṣasūtra (fragments)
SA_K01_prmosufu.summary: The Prātimokṣasūtra is the canonical monastic disciplinary code of Buddhism recited fortnightly by monks during the poṣadha observance, classifying monastic infractions in descending order of gravity from pārājika to śaikṣa. This e-text preserves surviving fragments from 16 Gilgit birchbark folios belonging to the Mūlasarvāstivāda recension.
SA_K01_prmosufu.attribution: Canonical Vinaya code recited by the monastic saṅgha. This text witness belongs to the Mūlasarvāstivāda tradition.
SA_K01_prmosufu.edition: Lokesh Chandra, "Unpublished Fragment of the Prātimokṣa-Sūtra", Wiener Zeitschrift für die Kunde des Morgenlandes 4 (1960), pp. 1-13. = GBM 1-16
SA_K01_prmosufu.coverage: fragment — Fragments from 16 folios of a Gilgit birchbark manuscript (GBM folios 1–16). Contains portions of Pārājika 2–4; Saṃghāvaśeṣa uddāna and SA 1–2; Pāyantikā 33–75 (with gaps); Pratideśanīya 1–4; and Śaikṣa 21–43 (with uddānas).

SA_K01_prmosulu.title: Prātimokṣasūtra
SA_K01_prmosulu.summary: The Prātimokṣasūtra of the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin school contains the fundamental disciplinary code of conduct recited bi-weekly by fully ordained monks (bhikṣus) during the poṣadha ceremony. The text opens with introductory stanzas praising the keeping of monastic vows (śīla) and the poṣadha liturgy, followed by training precepts organized into traditional offense categories (pārājika, saṃghātiśeṣa, aniyata, niḥsargika-pācattika, pācattika, pratideśanīya, śaikṣa, and adhikaraṇaśamatha). It concludes with verses attributed to the seven Buddhas of antiquity and a colophon identifying the recension as that of the Madhyoddeśika Lokottaravādin Mahāsāṃghikas.
SA_K01_prmosulu.attribution: Canonical Vinaya scripture containing the disciplinary code for monks (bhikṣu) according to the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin school, identified in the final colophon as representing the Madhyoddeśika recension ('āryamahāsāṃghikānāṃ lokottaravādināṃ madhyoddeśikānāṃ pāṭha iti') [1137].
SA_K01_prmosulu.edition: Nathmal Tatia (ed.), Prātimokṣasūtram of the Lokottaravādimahāsaṅghika School, Patna: Kashi Prasad Jayaswal Research Institute, 1976 (Tibetan Sanskrit Works Series, no. 16).
SA_K01_prmosulu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin Bhikṣu-Prātimokṣasūtra, including opening verses (upodghāta), poṣadha liturgical procedures, training rules across the traditional offense categories, stanzas of the seven Buddhas, and colophons.

SA_K01_upsmpjnu.title: Upasaṃpadājñapti
SA_K01_upsmpjnu.summary: The Upasaṃpadājñapti is a liturgical legal formulary (karmavācanā) of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya governing entry into the Buddhist monastic order. It sets out the motions (jñapti) and acts (karman) for the taking of lay vows (upāsakasaṃvara), the going forth from the household life (pravrajyā / novice ordination), and the higher monastic ordination (upasaṃpadā). The text details the formal examination of the candidate for disqualifying impediments (antarāyikā dharmāḥ), the request for preceptor and teachers, the unanimous declaration of the assembled saṅgha, and the subsequent instructions on fundamental monastic rules.
SA_K01_upsmpjnu.attribution: Traditional monastic ecclesiastic formulary (karmavācanā) of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya tradition; anonymous canonical ritual text.
SA_K01_upsmpjnu.edition: Jin-il Chung: Handbuch für die buddhistische Mönchsordination bei den Mūlasarvāstivādins. Gimpo 2011.
SA_K01_upsmpjnu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the higher ordination formulary according to the critical edition of Jin-il Chung (sections Uj II.i.1 through III.iv.7), concluding with the colophon '// upasaṃpādajñaptiḥ samāptaḥ // // //'.

SA_K01_vinsutru.title: Vinayasūtra
SA_K01_vinsutru.author: Guṇaprabha
SA_K01_vinsutru.summary: The Vinayasūtra is an aphoristic compendium of the Mūlasarvāstivāda monastic code compiled by Guṇaprabha. It condenses the chapters of the Vinayavastu as well as the Vibhaṅgas into terse sūtras. This e-text is a preliminary transliteration of the manuscript found in Tibet by Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana, copied by the scribe Dharmakīrti at Vikramaśīla.
SA_K01_vinsutru.attribution: Attributed to Guṇaprabha (c. 6th century). The attribution is corroborated both by the Sanskrit manuscript's opening rubrics and the Tibetan canonical tradition (Derge Tanjur Toh 4117).
SA_K01_vinsutru.edition: Preliminary transliteration of the ms. found in Tibet by Rahula Sankrityayana. Input by Yoshiyasu Yonezawa et al. (Institute for Comprehensive Studies of Buddhism, Taisho University).

SA_K01_vinv01_u.title: Pravrajyāvastu (fragments)
SA_K01_vinv01_u.summary: The Pravrajyāvastu ('Chapter on Going Forth') is the opening section of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, detailing the monastic protocols, criteria, and disqualifications for entering the Buddhist Order (pravrajyā) and receiving full ordination (upasaṃpadā). Interspersed with the legal guidelines are extensive narrative episodes, including accounts of King Bimbisāra, early converts to the saṃgha, and the avadāna tales of Saṃgharakṣita and Nāgakumāra. The surviving Sanskrit text is preserved in fragmentary manuscript leaves from Gilgit.
SA_K01_vinv01_u.attribution: Canonical Vinaya text of the Mūlasarvāstivāda school forming the first chapter of the Vinayavastu.
SA_K01_vinv01_u.edition: Vogel, Claus and Klaus Wille. 1. 'Some Hitherto Unidentified Fragments of the Pravrajyāvastu Portion of the Vinayavastu Manuscript Found Near Gilgit', Nachrichten der Akademie der Wissenschaften in Göttingen, Philologisch-Historische Klasse 1984, pp. 297–337 (foll. 7–12); 2. 'Some more Fragments of the Pravrajyāvastu Portion of the Vinayavastu Manuscript Found Near Gilgit', in Sanskrit-Texte aus dem buddhistischen Kanon: Neuentdeckungen und Neueditionen II, ed. H. Bechert, SWTF Beiheft 4, Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 1992 (foll. 2–6); 3. 'The Final Leaves of the Pravrajyāvastu Portion of the Vinayavastu Manuscript Found Near Gilgit, Part 1, Saṃgharakṣitāvadāna', in Sanskrit-Texte aus dem buddhistischen Kanon: Neuentdeckungen und Neueditionen III, ed. G. Bongard-Levin et al., SWTF Beiheft 6, Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 1996, pp. 241–296 (foll. 43–48v4); 4. Näther, Volkbert (ed.), Claus Vogel and Klaus Wille (rev. & trans.), 'The Final Leaves of the Pravrajyāvastu Portion of the Vinayavastu Manuscript Found Near Gilgit, Part 2, Nāgakumārāvadāna and Lévi Text...', in Sanskrit-Texte aus dem buddhistischen Kanon: Neuentdeckungen und Neueditionen IV, SWTF Beiheft 9, Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 2002, pp. 11–76 (foll. 48v4–53r10).
SA_K01_vinv01_u.coverage: fragment — Preserves the extant Sanskrit portions of the Gilgit manuscript: folios 2–12 (the beginning up to folio 12, folio 1 missing) and folios 43–53r10 (the conclusion, ending with 'Pravrajyāvastu samāptam'). Folios 13–42 are missing in Sanskrit, though the full text survives in Tibetan and Chinese (T. 1444).
translations: Vogel, Claus (ed. and trans.). The Teachings of the Six Heretics: According to the Pravrajyāvastu of the Tibetan Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya. Abhandlungen für die Kunde des Morgenlandes 39.4. Wiesbaden: Kommissionsverlag Franz Steiner, 1970. (English)
Vogel, Claus and Klaus Wille (trans.). English translations in their editions of folios 43–48v4 (1996) and folios 48v4–53r10 (2002). (English)

SA_K01_vinv02_u.title: Poṣadhavastu (incomplete)
SA_K01_vinv02_u.summary: The Poṣadhavastu is the second chapter of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, formulating legal and procedural regulations for the fortnightly monastic assembly (poṣadha / uposatha). It details the historical origin of the rite, the delimitation and consecration of monastic precincts (sīmā), the calculation of quorums, formal confession of infractions and declaration of communal purity (pariśuddhi), and the recitation of the Prātimokṣasūtra. It forms a primary source for the study of Indian Buddhist ecclesiastical law and monastic organization.
SA_K01_vinv02_u.attribution: Canonical monastic legal treatise of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayapiṭaka, presented as communal legislation and narrative teachings of Gautama Buddha.
SA_K01_vinv02_u.edition: Haiyan Hu-von Hinüber, Das Posadhavastu: Vorschriften für die buddhistische Beichtfeier im Vinaya der Mūlasarvāstivādins. Studien zur Indologie und Iranistik, Monographie 13. Reinbek: Dr. Inge Wezler, Verlag für Orientalistische Fachpublikationen, 1994.
SA_K01_vinv02_u.coverage: partial — Sanskrit text §§1–98.11 (Gilgit Vinayavastu MS fol. 53v–67r; Hu-von Hinüber pp. 256–494). The e-text ends with the editor's note 'folios 67 and 68 are lost', so the end of the Poṣadhavastu is not preserved in Sanskrit (it survives in the Tibetan and Chinese Vinaya translations).
translations: Haiyan Hu-von Hinüber, Das Posadhavastu: Vorschriften für die buddhistische Beichtfeier im Vinaya der Mūlasarvāstivādins, Studien zur Indologie und Iranistik, Monographie 13, Reinbek: Dr. Inge Wezler, Verlag für Orientalistische Fachpublikationen, 1994. (German)

SA_K01_vinv03_u.title: Pravāraṇāvastu (incomplete)
SA_K01_vinv03_u.summary: The Pravāraṇāvastu is the third chapter (vastu) of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, regulating the pravāraṇā ('invitation' / mutual admonition) rite held at the conclusion of the three-month rains-retreat (varṣā). In this ceremony, each monastic invites fellow members of the saṅgha to declare any transgression he may have committed—whether seen, heard, or suspected—enabling communal confession, amends, and reconciliation before the community departs. The text details the qualifications and appointment of the presiding pravāraka monk, the formal legal transactions (karmavācanā), provisions for sick monks participating by proxy, and regulations for postponing or staying the ceremony.
SA_K01_vinv03_u.attribution: Canonical Vinaya scripture of the Mūlasarvāstivāda tradition, surviving in Sanskrit manuscript witnesses from Gilgit and Turfan, as well as in Chinese canonical translation.
SA_K01_vinv03_u.edition: Jin-il Chung, Die Pravāraṇā in den kanonischen Vinaya-Texten der Mūlasarvāstivādin und der Sarvāstivādin, Göttingen 1998 (Sanskrit-Wörterbuch der buddhistischen Texte aus den Turfan-Funden, Beiheft 7).
SA_K01_vinv03_u.coverage: partial — Chung's §§2.3.2.1–13.4 (pp. 147–174). The e-text marks §§1.1.1–2.3.1 as 'Sanskrit text lost'. Survives in part from the Turfan fragment SHT 4473 and the Gilgit manuscript. The text ends at §13.4, with the note 'folio 74 is lost, therefore the Sanskrit text of Pravā-v 14.1 to 14.2.4 is not extant'.

SA_K01_vinv04_u.title: Varṣāvastu
SA_K01_vinv04_u.summary: The Varṣāvastu ('Chapter on the Rains Retreat') is the fourth chapter of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, regulating the mandatory three-month monastic retreat (varṣā or varṣāvāsa) observed during the monsoon. It sets out the formal legal procedures (saṃghakarman) for entering the retreat, the election and duties of the assigner of dwelling places (śayanāsanagrāhaka), the distribution of rooms and seats by casting voting markers or tallies (śalākā), communal regulations during the retreat, and the precise conditions under which a monk may temporarily cross the monastic boundary (sīmā) for up to seven days. Preserved in Sanskrit in the Gilgit manuscripts as well as in Tibetan (Toh 1) and Chinese (T 1445) translations, it closely corresponds to the Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka of the Theravāda Pali Vinaya.
SA_K01_vinv04_u.attribution: Canonical monastic code (Vinayavastu) of the Buddhist Mūlasarvāstivāda tradition.
SA_K01_vinv04_u.edition: Masanori Shono: Bukkyo ni okeru uki no toryuseikatsu ni kansuru kisoteki kenkyu - Varṣāvastu no sai-kotei, oyobi dokkai kenyu - (*A Fundamental Study on the Rain Retreat in Buddhism - A Re-edition of Varṣāvastu and Its Annotated Translation -). (Osaka) 2007. = Var-v
SA_K01_vinv04_u.coverage: complete — Text of the Varṣāvastu (Vastu 4 of the Vinayavastu), concluding with the colophon 'varṣāvastu samaptam* // //'.
translations: Masanori Shono, Bukkyo ni okeru uki no toryuseikatsu ni kansuru kisoteki kenkyu - Varṣāvastu no sai-kotei, oyobi dokkai kenyu - (*A Fundamental Study on the Rain Retreat in Buddhism - A Re-edition of Varṣāvastu and Its Annotated Translation -), (Osaka) 2007. (Japanese)

SA_K01_vinv05_u.title: Carmavastu
SA_K01_vinv05_u.summary: The Carmavastu is the fifth chapter of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, prescribing monastic rules governing the use of hides, leather mats, and footwear. It opens with the extensive narrative of the elder Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa, his perilous voyage, visit to the realm of pretas, and his subsequent ordination under Mahākātyāyana. Koṭīkarṇa's journey to visit the Buddha in Śrāvastī prompts the allowance of regional dispensations for monks residing in remote border territories (pratyantajanapada), such as wearing multiple-soled footwear, frequent bathing, and using leather sitting mats. The remainder of the vastu details monastic regulations regarding permissible and prohibited types of shoes and skins, as well as the authorized possession of leatherworking implements like awls, knives, and thongs.
SA_K01_vinv05_u.attribution: Canonical Vinaya chapter belonging to the Vinayavastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda school, preserved in Sanskrit in the Gilgit manuscripts.
SA_K01_vinv05_u.edition: N. Dutt (ed.), Gilgit Manuscript, vol. III: Mūlasarvāstivādavinayavastu, part IV, Calcutta, 1950, pp. 159–210: Carmavastu (second edition: Delhi 1984).
SA_K01_vinv05_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Carmavastu, beginning with the opening uddāna and running through to the final colophon 'carmavastu samāptam'.
translations: Taishō Tripiṭaka no. 1447 (vol. 23), Genbenshuoyiqieyoubu pinaiye pi'ge shi (根本說一切有部毘奈耶皮革事), translated into Chinese during the Tang dynasty by Yijing (700–711). (Chinese)

SA_K01_vinv07_u.title: Cīvaravastu
SA_K01_vinv07_u.summary: The Cīvaravastu ('Section on Robes') is the seventh section of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu. It prescribes the legal regulations governing monastic robes (cīvara), including permissible cloth materials, methods of cutting, sewing, and dyeing, distribution protocols, and the division and inheritance of the personal belongings of deceased monks (mṛtapariṣkāra). The legal rulings are embedded in extensive narrative material, notably the biography of the royal physician Jīvaka Kumārabhṛtya, accounts of King Bimbisāra and the courtesan Āmrapālī, and narratives concerning the care and nursing of sick monks.
SA_K01_vinv07_u.attribution: Canonical Vinaya scripture of the Mūlasarvāstivāda school, traditionally treated as the direct word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana).
SA_K01_vinv07_u.edition: Nalinaksha Dutt (ed.), Gilgit Manuscripts, vol. III: Mūlasarvāstivādavinayavastu, Part 2, Srinagar: Government of Jammu and Kashmir, 1942, pp. 1–148 (reprinted Delhi: Sri Satguru Publications, 1984), with corrections against the manuscript facsimile by Klaus Wille.
SA_K01_vinv07_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Cīvaravastu as preserved in the Sanskrit Gilgit manuscript, corresponding to pages 1–148 of Dutt's edition (part 2 of vol. III) and concluding with the colophon '// cīvaravastu samāptam* //'.
translations: Kosgoda Sobhita, 'Le Cīvaraskandhaka du Vinayapiṭaka des Mūlasarvāstivādin', Ph.D. dissertation, Université de Paris IV (Sorbonne). (French)

SA_K01_vinv08_u.title: Kaṭhinavastu
SA_K01_vinv08_u.summary: The Kaṭhinavastu is the eighth chapter of the Mūlasarvāstivāda-Vinayavastu, governing the ceremonial production, acceptance, and formal 'spreading' (kaṭhināstāra) of robes made from cloth offered by the laity after the annual rains-retreat (varṣā). It specifies the special monastic dispensations and privileges (anuśaṃsā) granted to participating monks during the kaṭhina season, the communal legal acts (karman) required for its validity, and the eight distinct circumstances that terminate those privileges (kaṭhinoddhāra). Preserved substantially in Sanskrit in the Gilgit manuscript collection, it corresponds to the Pali Kaṭhinakkhandhaka and canonical Tibetan and Chinese translations.
SA_K01_vinv08_u.attribution: Canonical Vinaya scripture representing the eighth chapter (vastu) of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu.
SA_K01_vinv08_u.edition: Hisashi Matsumura, 'The Kaṭhinavastu from the Vinayavastu of the Mūlasarvāstivādins', in: Sanskrit-Texte aus dem buddhistischen Kanon: Neuentdeckungen und Neueditionen III, Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 1996 (Sanskrit-Wörterbuch der buddhistischen Texte aus den Turfan-Funden, Beiheft 6), pp. 145–239.
SA_K01_vinv08_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Kaṭhinavastu (sections 1–67.ii, ending with the colophon 'kaṭhinavastu samāpta'), edited on pp. 186–239 of Matsumura (1996) based on folios 276r1–284v of the Gilgit manuscript (GBM 6.864–875).

SA_K01_vinv09_u.title: Kośāmbakavastu
SA_K01_vinv09_u.summary: The Kośāmbakavastu is the ninth section of the Vinayavastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya. It relates the famous schismatic dispute among the monks residing at Kauśāmbī, originating from an infraction over a communal water vessel in the privy and escalating into a bitter factional rift between scholars of the sūtras and masters of the vinaya. The text details the disciplinary procedures of suspension (utkṣepaṇīyakarma) for refusing to see or atone for an offense, the prescribed conduct of suspended monks, their subsequent rehabilitation (osāraṇā), and the performance of the concord ceremony (sāmagrīpoṣadha) restoring communal harmony.
SA_K01_vinv09_u.attribution: Canonical Vinaya work of the Mūlasarvāstivāda school, constituting the ninth chapter (vastu) of the seventeen-chapter Vinayavastu.
SA_K01_vinv09_u.edition: N. Dutt: Gilgit Manuscript, vol. III: Mūlasarvāstivādavinayavastu, part 2 (Srinagar 1942), pp. 173-196: Kośāmbakavastu (second edition: Delhi 1984), with readings corrected against the Gilgit manuscript facsimiles by Klaus Wille.
SA_K01_vinv09_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Kośāmbakavastu (chapter 9 of the Vinayavastu), beginning with the opening uddāna verses and concluding with 'kośāmbakavastu samāptam'.
translations: dul ba gzhi (Derge Kangyur D 1): translated by Vidyākaraprabha, Dharmakara, Sarvajñadeva, dpal gyi lhun po, ska ba dpal brtsegs (Tibetan)

SA_K01_vinv10_u.title: Karmavastu
SA_K01_vinv10_u.summary: The Karmavastu is the tenth chapter of the Vinayavastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda school, treating the validity and taxonomy of ecclesiastical legal acts (saṅghakarman). It categorizes monastic proceedings according to whether the monastic assembly is harmonious/complete (samagra) or fractured/incomplete (vyagra), and whether the execution adheres to the Dharma (dharmeṇa) or violates it (adharmeṇa). The chapter details procedures including motions (jñapti), single and fourfold proclamations (karmavācanā), and suspension (utkṣepaṇakarman) and rehabilitation (osāraṇakarman) of monks.
SA_K01_vinv10_u.attribution: Canonical Vinaya text belonging to the Vinayavastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda tradition; preserved in Sanskrit in the Gilgit manuscript collection, as well as in Tibetan (Kangyur, D 1).
SA_K01_vinv10_u.edition: N. Dutt: Gilgit Manuscript, vol. III: Mūlasarvāstivādavinayavastu, part 2 (Srinagar 1942), pp. 199-211: Karmavastu (second edition: Delhi 1984).
SA_K01_vinv10_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the tenth vastu (Karmavastu) of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, beginning with the uddāna at fol. 285v1 (GBM 6.883 / MSV II 199) and ending with the colophon 'karmavastu samāptam' at fol. 288v1 (GBM 6.889 / MSV II 211).
translations: Nobuyuki Yamagiwa (山極 伸之), '根本説一切有部律犍度部の研究(2)', 仏教史学研究, 1989. (Japanese)

SA_K01_vinv11_u.title: Pāṇḍulohitakavastu
SA_K01_vinv11_u.summary: The Pāṇḍulohitakavastu is the eleventh chapter (vastu) of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, governing disciplinary legal acts (karmans) carried out by the monastic saṅgha against contentious or recalcitrant monks. Named after the factions led by the monks Pāṇḍuka and Lohitaka, it details five disciplinary measures: censure (tarjanīyakarman), demotion to subordination (nigarhaṇīyakarman), temporary banishment (pravāsanīyakarman), formal reconciliation with aggrieved laity (pratisaṃharaṇīyakarman), and suspension (utkṣepaṇīyakarman) for refusing to see, atone for, or renounce an offense or false view. It also describes the saṅgha legal procedures for probation (parivāsa), retrospective resetting of seniority (mūlāpakarṣa), penance (mānāpya), and eventual reinstatement/rehabilitation (āvarhaṇa) for saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses.
SA_K01_vinv11_u.edition: Nobuyuki Yamagiwa: Das Pāṇḍulohitakavastu, Über die verschiedenen Verfahrensweisen der Bestrafung in der buddhistischen Gemeinde, Neuausgabe der Sanskrit-Handschrift aus Gilgit, tibetischer Text und deutsche Übersetzung, Marburg 2001 (Indica et Tibetica, 41).
SA_K01_vinv11_u.coverage: complete — Complete Sanskrit text of the Pāṇḍulohitakavastu preserved in the Gilgit manuscript, encompassing sections § 0.1 through § 7.5.12, concluding with the colophon '// pāṇḍulohitakavastu samāptaḥ //'.
translations: Nobuyuki Yamagiwa: Das Pāṇḍulohitakavastu, Über die verschiedenen Verfahrensweisen der Bestrafung in der buddhistischen Gemeinde, Neuausgabe der Sanskrit-Handschrift aus Gilgit, tibetischer Text und deutsche Übersetzung, Marburg 2001 (Indica et Tibetica, 41). (German)

SA_K01_vinv12_u.title: Pudgalavastu
SA_K01_vinv12_u.summary: The Pudgalavastu is the twelfth section (vastu) of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, setting forth ecclesiastical regulations for dealing with individuals (pudgala) guilty of saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses. Starting from the case of the monk Udāyī, the text classifies offending monks according to their degree of awareness, acknowledgment, and concealment of faults, prescribing corresponding sanctions such as probation (parivāsa), retroactive probation (mūlaparivāsa), demotion (mūlāpakarṣa), and the six-day penance (mānāpya). The Sanskrit text is preserved in the Gilgit manuscript discovery.
SA_K01_vinv12_u.attribution: Canonical Vinaya scripture belonging to the Mūlasarvāstivāda tradition, transmitted as part of the Vinayavastu.
SA_K01_vinv12_u.edition: Nalinaksha Dutt (ed.), Gilgit Manuscripts, Vol. III: Mūlasarvāstivādavinayavastu, Part 3, Srinagar: Government of Jammu and Kashmir, 1943, pp. 59–88 (2nd ed., Delhi: Sri Satguru Publications, 1984). With corrections against the manuscript facsimile by Klaus Wille.
SA_K01_vinv12_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Pudgalavastu (12th chapter of the Vinayavastu), beginning with the piṇḍoddāna and closing with the colophon 'pudgalavastu samāptam'.
translations: dul ba gzhi (Derge Kangyur D 1): translated by Vidyākaraprabha, Dharmakara, Sarvajñadeva, dpal gyi lhun po, ska ba dpal brtsegs (Tibetan)

SA_K01_vinv13_u.title: Pārivāsikavastu
SA_K01_vinv13_u.summary: The Pārivāsikavastu is the thirteenth section of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, setting forth the legal prescriptions and behavioral obligations for monks undergoing disciplinary penance for saṅghāvaśeṣa offenses. It details the sangha procedures for conferring probation (parivāsa), penance (mānāpya/mānatva), and setting back to the initial probation (mūlāpakarṣa) when an offense has been concealed. It also lays down the specific rules of conduct governing probationary monks (pārivāsika) in interactions with monks of regular standing (prakṛtisthaka), as well as the formal declarations required to suspend and resume probation.
SA_K01_vinv13_u.attribution: Canonical Buddhist Vinaya scripture of the Mūlasarvāstivāda tradition, forming the 13th vastu of the Vinayavastu section of the Vinayapiṭaka.
SA_K01_vinv13_u.edition: N. Dutt: Gilgit Manuscript, vol. III: Mūlasarvāstivādavinayavastu, part 3 (Srinagar 1943), pp. 89-103: Pārivāsikavastu (second edition: Delhi 1984).
SA_K01_vinv13_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Pārivāsikavastu (the 13th vastu of the Vinayavastu), beginning with the three-vastu summary verse (vastutrayasya piṇḍoddānam) and chapter uddāna, and concluding with 'pārivāsikavastu samāptam'.

SA_K01_vinv14_u.title: Poṣadhasthāpanavastu
SA_K01_vinv14_u.summary: The Poṣadhasthāpanavastu is the fourteenth chapter (vastu) of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, corresponding functionally to the Pātimokkhathapanakkhandhaka of the Pali Cullavagga. It sets forth the procedural and legal rules governing the suspension (sthāpana) of the fortnightly poṣadha (uposatha) Prātimokṣa recitation rite and the invitation rite (pravāraṇā) when a monk is deemed impure or charged with an ecclesiastical offense. The work systematically classifies valid (dhārmika) and invalid (adhārmika) suspensions, outlines appropriate dispute procedures, and defines four kinds of saṃghas.
SA_K01_vinv14_u.attribution: Canonical vinaya scripture of the Mūlasarvāstivāda school, traditionally preserved as the word of the Buddha (buddhavacana).
SA_K01_vinv14_u.edition: N. Dutt: Gilgit Manuscript, vol. III: Mūlasarvāstivādavinayavastu, part 3 (Srinagar 1943), pp. 105-117: Poṣadhasthāpanavastu (second edition: Delhi 1984).
SA_K01_vinv14_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the 14th section (Poṣadhasthāpanavastu) of the Vinayavastu as preserved in the Gilgit manuscript, extending from the introductory uddāna to the concluding colophon (poṣadhasthāpanavastu samāptam), corresponding to Dutt's edition pp. 105–117.
translations: dul ba gzhi (Derge Kangyur D 1): translated by Vidyākaraprabha, Dharmakara, Sarvajñadeva, dpal gyi lhun po, ska ba dpal brtsegs (Tibetan)

SA_K01_vinv15_u.title: Śayanāsanavastu
SA_K01_vinv15_u.summary: The Śayanāsanavastu ('Chapter on Dwellings and Bedding') is the fifteenth section of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, preserved in Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit in the 5th–6th-century Gilgit manuscripts. It lays down monastic regulations concerning monastic seniority, the architectural construction and distribution of lodging and furnishings (śayanāsana), and communal versus personal property. The vastu famously narrates the merchant Anāthapiṇḍada's purchase and construction of the Jetavana monastery in Śrāvastī under the supervision of Śāriputra, serving as an indispensable primary source for the study of ancient Indian monastic architecture, administration, and socio-economic institutions.
SA_K01_vinv15_u.attribution: Fifteenth of the seventeen vastus forming the Vinayavastu of the Mūlasarvāstivādin tradition, canonical Vinayapiṭaka literature preserved in Sanskrit in the Gilgit manuscripts.
SA_K01_vinv15_u.edition: Raniero Gnoli (ed.), The Gilgit Manuscript of the Śayanāsanavastu and the Adhikaraṇavastu, Being the 15th and 16th Sections of the Vinaya of the Mūlasarvāstivādin, Roma: Istituto Italiano per il Medio ed Estremo Oriente (IsMEO), 1978 (Serie Orientale Roma, vol. 50), pp. 1–56.
SA_K01_vinv15_u.coverage: complete — Complete Sanskrit text of the Śayanāsanavastu as preserved in the Gilgit manuscript, ending at segment 2017 with 'śayanāsanavastu samāptam'. Segments 2018–2057 represent a trailing apparatus index of Gnoli's English section headings.

SA_K01_vinv16_u.title: Adhikaraṇavastu
SA_K01_vinv16_u.summary: The Adhikaraṇavastu is the sixteenth chapter of the Vinayavastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda school. It systematically governs legal disputes within the monastic community, classifying conflicts into four types (vivādādhikaraṇa, anuvādādhikaraṇa, āpattādhikaraṇa, and kṛtyādhikaraṇa) and laying out procedures (adhikaraṇaśamatha) for resolving them.
SA_K01_vinv16_u.attribution: Part of the canonical monastic law (Vinayavastu) of the Mūlasarvāstivāda school, framed as Buddhavacana.
SA_K01_vinv16_u.edition: Raniero Gnoli (ed.), The Gilgit Manuscript of the Śayanāsanavastu and the Adhikaraṇavastu, Being the 15th and 16th Sections of the Vinaya of the Mūlasarvāstivādin, Roma: Istituto Italiano per il Medio ed Estremo Oriente (IsMEO), 1978 (Serie Orientale Roma, 50), pp. 57–110.
SA_K01_vinv16_u.coverage: complete — Contains the text of the Adhikaraṇavastu as edited from the Gilgit manuscript by Raniero Gnoli (pp. 57–110), followed by English section headings and notes.

SA_K01_vinv171u.title: Saṅghabhedavastu (part 1)
SA_K01_vinv171u.summary: The Saṅghabhedavastu ('Section on Schism in the Monastic Community') is the seventeenth and last section of the Mūlasarvāstivādin Vinaya. This first part relates the lineage of the Śākya clan, Prince Siddhārtha's conception, birth, renunciation, austerities, awakening, and his initial preaching circuit leading up to his arrival at Yaṣṭivana in Magadha.
SA_K01_vinv171u.attribution: Canonical monastic code (Vinaya) of the Mūlasarvāstivāda tradition, preserved and transmitted collectively by the monastic order.
SA_K01_vinv171u.edition: Raniero Gnoli with the assistance of T. Venkatacharya (eds.), The Gilgit Manuscript of the Saṅghabhedavastu, Being the 17th and Last Section of the Vinaya of the Mūlasarvāstivādin, Roma 1977-78 (Serie Orientale Roma, 49).
SA_K01_vinv171u.coverage: partial — Contains Part 1 of the Saṅghabhedavastu (pp. 1–234 of Gnoli's edition, corresponding to folios 350a–416b of Gilgit manuscript A). It covers the lineage of the Śākyas, the conception, birth, early life, renunciation, ascetic strivings, and awakening of Siddhārtha Gautama, through to his early teaching career ending with his arrival at Yaṣṭivana in Magadha. Part 2 is continued in SA_K01_vinv172u.

SA_K01_vinv172u.title: Saṅghabhedavastu (part 2)
SA_K01_vinv172u.summary: This text comprises the second part of the Saṅghabhedavastu ('Chapter on Schism in the Community'), the seventeenth and final chapter of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu. It contains substantial narrative cycles detailing the career of the Buddha, his encounters with figures such as King Ajātaśatru, the schismatic schemes instigated by Devadatta, and the formal legal classifications and karmic ramifications of dividing the monastic saṅgha.
SA_K01_vinv172u.attribution: Canonical monastic code (Vinaya) of the Mūlasarvāstivāda school.

SA_K02_bsu057_u.title: Advayaśatikā Prajñāpāramitāsūtra
SA_K02_bsu057_u.summary: Set at Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha, the Buddha instructs Subhūti that all spiritual paths and dharmas—including the six perfections, the eighteen kinds of emptiness, the bodhipakṣa dharmas, and the distinctive Buddha-qualities—are encompassed within the perfection of wisdom, which is ungraspable, intrinsically pure, and comparable to empty space.
SA_K02_bsu057_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna sūtra presented as a discourse between the Buddha and the elder Subhūti on Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa) in Rājagṛha.
SA_K02_bsu057_u.edition: M.B. Shakya: Buddhist Himalaya 1.2, Nepal: Nagarjuna Institute of Exact Methods, 1988, 82-84.

SA_K02_sspp2_1u.title: Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā (chapter 12)
SA_K02_sspp2_1u.summary: The Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in 100,000 Lines') is the most extensive extant text of the Large Prajñāpāramitā corpus. This file covers Chapter 12 (dvādaśaḥ parivartaḥ), the first chapter of the second division (Dvitīyakhaṇḍa), which takes the form of an exhaustive dialogue involving Śāradvatīputra and Subhūti. Through relentless formulaic negation, it demonstrates that all constituent factors of reality—including elements (dhātu), aggregates (skandha), sense fields (āyatana), and bodhisattva qualities—are empty of intrinsic existence (svabhāva) and non-dual (advaya).
SA_K02_sspp2_1u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna Buddhist scripture regarded as buddhavacana, framed as teachings delivered by the Buddha to disciples including Śāradvatīputra and Subhūti.
SA_K02_sspp2_1u.edition: Takayasu Kimura (ed.), Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā II-1, Tokyo: Sankibo Busshorin, 2009.

SA_K02_sspp2_2u.title: Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā (chapters 13–14)
SA_K02_sspp2_2u.summary: This text comprises chapters 13 and 14 of the Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā, completing the second major section (dvitīyakhaṇḍa) of the 100,000-line recension. It consists of an extensive dialogue between the venerable Subhūti and Śāriputra on the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, focusing on non-attachment and non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) of all dharmas across the skandhas, dhātus, and āyatanas. Subhūti clarifies that a bodhisattva practices without conceptually reifying dharmas, paths, or spiritual attainments.
SA_K02_sspp2_2u.attribution: Scriptural Mahāyāna sūtra traditionally regarded as buddhavacana; belongs to the Large Prajñāpāramitā corpus.

SA_K02_sspp2_3u.title: Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā (chapters 15–16)
SA_K02_sspp2_3u.summary: The Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in One Hundred Thousand Lines') represents the most voluminous Sanskrit recension of the Prajñāpāramitā corpus. This digital text corresponds to volume II-3 of Takayasu Kimura's critical edition and preserves chapters 15 and 16. It consists primarily of dialogues between the elder Subhūti and Śakra concerning how all dharmas, the expounding of the doctrine, and the hearers are like illusions (māyopama) and dreams (svapnopama), articulating the bodhisattva's non-apprehending practice and the supreme merit of venerating bodhisattvas over śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
SA_K02_sspp2_3u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna scripture presented as buddhavacana, framed as expositions and dialogues between Subhūti, Śakra Devendra, and the Buddha.
SA_K02_sspp2_3u.edition: Takayasu Kimura: Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā II-3. Tokyo: Sankibo Busshorin 2010.

SA_K02_sspp2_4u.title: Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā (chapters 17–23)
SA_K02_sspp2_4u.summary: The Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in One Hundred Thousand Lines') represents the most expansive recension of the Larger Prajñāpāramitā sūtras. This section encompasses chapters 17 through 23, concluding the second major division of the sūtra with the Śakraparivarta. Through dialogues involving the Buddha, Śakra Devānām Indra, and principal disciples, the text presents an exhaustive exposition of the emptiness of all dharmas (śūnyatā), the cultivation of the perfections and dhāraṇīs, the purification of buddhafields, and the progressive path of the bodhisattva toward unsurpassed complete awakening (anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi).

SA_K03_psp_1u.title: Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā (abhisamaya 1: Sarvākārajñatādhikāra)
SA_K03_psp_1u.summary: The Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in 25,000 Lines') is one of the principal recensions of the Large Prajñāpāramitā corpus, expounding universal emptiness (śūnyatā) and the bodhisattva path to full awakening. This first division (abhisamaya 1: Sarvākārajñatādhikāra) opens on Vulture Peak and details the qualities of 'all-knowledge of all aspects' (sarvākārajñatā), the generate-and-foster training of the bodhisattva, and the six perfections. As preserved in Nepalese manuscripts, the Sanskrit text has undergone an Indian structural revision mapping its discourses directly onto the topical categories of the Abhisamayālaṃkāra.
SA_K03_psp_1u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna scripture belonging to the Large Prajñāpāramitā group. In the Nepalese Sanskrit manuscript recension edited here, the text is structured according to the eight abhisamayas of the Abhisamayālaṃkāra.
SA_K03_psp_1u.edition: Takayasu Kimura (ed.): - Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā I-1, Tokyo: Sankibo Busshorin 2007. = PvsP1-1 - Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā I-2, Tokyo: Sankibo Busshorin 2009. = PvsP1-2.

SA_K03_psp_2-3u.title: Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā (chapters 2–3)
SA_K03_psp_2-3u.summary: The Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in 25,000 Lines') is one of the primary canonical Mahāyāna Prajñāpāramitā scriptures. This e-text contains chapters 2 and 3 of the Sanskrit recension redacted according to the scheme of the Abhisamayālaṃkāra. Chapter 2 expounds the Knowledge of the Paths (mārgajñatā) and the bodhisattva's practice free from extreme views, while Chapter 3 elucidates All-Knowledge / Knowledge of the Bases (sarvajñatā / vastujñatā), emphasizing universal non-apprehension (anupalambha) and the emptiness of all dharmas.
SA_K03_psp_2-3u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna Buddhist scripture traditionally regarded as buddhavacana. The Sanskrit text extant in Nepalese manuscripts represents the later recension systematically reorganized and divided into eight chapters (adhikāras/parivartas) corresponding to the eight realizations (aṣṭāv abhisamayāḥ) of the Abhisamayālaṃkāra.
SA_K03_psp_2-3u.edition: Takayasu Kimura (ed.), Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā II-III. Tokyo: Sankibo Busshorin, 1986.

SA_K03_psp_4u.title: Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā (abhisamaya 4: Sarvākārābhisaṃbodha)
SA_K03_psp_4u.summary: The Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in Twenty-Five Thousand Lines') is one of the foundational scriptures of the Larger Prajñāpāramitā literature. This file contains the text of the fourth division (Abhisamaya 4: Sarvākārābhisaṃbodha / Sarvākārābhisaṃbodhādhikāra), edited in Volume IV of Takayasu Kimura's critical edition. The Nepalese Sanskrit recension was systematically organized and annotated with topical headers to match the structural framework of the Abhisamayālaṃkāra, with this section detailing the bodhisattva's complete realization of all aspects of reality through emptiness, non-apprehension (anupalambha), and skill in means (upāyakauśala).
SA_K03_psp_4u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna scripture (Prajñāpāramitā literature), traditionally viewed as the word of the Buddha (buddhavacana). The surviving Sanskrit recension preserved in Nepalese manuscripts represents a medieval revision restructured to match the eight abhisamayas (realizations) of the Abhisamayālaṃkāra.
SA_K03_psp_4u.edition: Takayasu Kimura (ed.), Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā IV. Tokyo: Sankibo Busshorin, 1990.

SA_K03_psp_5u.title: Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā (Abhisamaya 5: Mūrdhābhisamaya)
SA_K03_psp_5u.summary: This text comprises the fifth section (Abhisamaya 5: Mūrdhābhisamayādhikāra, also known as the Śikṣāpariśuddhiparivarta) of the 25,000-line Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra (Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā) in its Abhisamayālaṃkāra-aligned Sanskrit recension. It details the 'culmination of clear realization' (mūrdhābhisamaya), commencing with the dream-signs and behavioral marks of an irreversible (avinivartanīya) bodhisattva. The dialogue between the Buddha and Subhūti progresses through the dismantling of conceptual proliferations (vikalpa) and erroneous views (vipratipatti), affirming that all dharmas and spiritual attainments are ultimately devoid of intrinsic nature (abhāvasvabhāva).
SA_K03_psp_5u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna Prajñāpāramitā sūtra preserved in the Nepalese Sanskrit recension that was systematically reorganized into eight chapters/sections according to the structural scheme of the Abhisamayālaṃkāra (abhisamayālaṃkārānusāreṇa saṃśodhitā).
