SA_K03_psp_6-8u.title: Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā (abhisamayas 6–8)
SA_K03_psp_6-8u.summary: The Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in Twenty-Five Thousand Lines') is one of the principal expansive scriptures of the Mahāyāna Prajñāpāramitā corpus. This portion comprises divisions VI through VIII of the Sanskrit recension that was systematically reorganized in medieval India to match the eight abhisamayas of the Abhisamayālaṃkāra. It expounds serial gradual training (anupūrvābhisamaya), instantaneous realization in a single thought-moment (ekakṣaṇābhisamaya), and the realization and activities of the Dharmakāya (dharmakāyābhisaṃbodha), concluding the entire sūtra.
SA_K03_psp_6-8u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna sūtra presented as dialogues between the Buddha and major disciples including Subhūti, Śāriputra, and Maitreya. The Sanskrit text in this edition represents the revised recension rearranged in India according to the eight topics (abhisamayas) of the Abhisamayālaṃkāra.
SA_K03_psp_6-8u.edition: Takayasu Kimura: Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā VI-VIII. Tokyo: Sankibo Busshorin 2006.

SA_K05_adsp55-u.title: Aṣṭādaśasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā (chapters 55–70)
SA_K05_adsp55-u.summary: The Aṣṭādaśasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in 18,000 Lines') is one of the principal recensions of the Large Prajñāpāramitā. This section covers chapters 55 to 70, correlating to the fifth realization in the exegetical system of the Abhisamayālaṃkāra. Transcribed from a birchbark manuscript discovered at Gilgit, the text discusses the signs and dreams of the irreversible (avaivartika) bodhisattva, the purification of buddhafields, and the ontological non-apprehension (anupalambha) of all phenomena.
SA_K05_adsp55-u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra traditionally attributed to the Buddha (buddhavacana) in dialogue with Subhūti and other disciples.

In the structural framework of the Abhisamayālaṃkāra, this section corresponds to the 6th, 7th, and 8th abhisamayas.

SA_K05_bsu049_u.title: Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā
SA_K05_bsu049_u.summary: The Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines') is the foundational and earliest extensive scripture in the Prajñāpāramitā corpus. Centered on dialogues between the Buddha and disciples including Subhūti, Śāriputra, and Ānanda at Vulture Peak, it expounds the core Mahāyāna doctrine of emptiness (śūnyatā), the non-apprehension (anupalambha) of independent dharmas, and the altruistic path of the bodhisattva aiming at omniscience (sarvākārajñatā). Across 32 chapters, it promotes the veneration, recitation, and copying of Prajñāpāramitā manuscripts, culminating in the pilgrimage and self-sacrifice of Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita under the teacher Dharmodgata.
SA_K05_bsu049_u.attribution: Traditional Mahāyāna scripture presented as the teaching of the Buddha, featuring interlocutors such as Subhūti, Śāriputra, Ānanda, and Śakra.
SA_K05_bsu049_u.edition: P. L. Vaidya (ed.), Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā with Haribhadra's Commentary called Ālokā, Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, no. 4, Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute of Post-Graduate Studies and Research in Sanskrit Learning, 1960 [root sūtra text only].

SA_K05_dsp1-2_u.title: Daśasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā (chapters 1–2)
SA_K05_dsp1-2_u.summary: The Daśasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in Ten Thousand Lines') is an intermediate recension belonging to the Large Prajñāpāramitā class of Mahāyāna sūtras, extant fully in Tibetan (Toh 11). This electronic text contains Chapters 1 and 2 (Nidānaparivarta and Sarvadharmaparivarta) as retroverted into Sanskrit from the Tibetan translation by Sten Konow in 1941. These opening chapters depict the setting on Vulture Peak and provide an extensive, systematic exposition of the non-substantiality and emptiness (śūnyatā) of all conditioned and unconditioned dharmas.

SA_K06_bsu030_u.title: Suvikrāntavikrāmiparipṛcchā
SA_K06_bsu030_u.summary: The Suvikrāntavikrāmiparipṛcchā (also known as the Sārdhadvisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā, or Perfection of Wisdom in 2,500 Lines) is a canonical Mahāyāna sūtra in seven chapters. Set at the Veṇuvana in Rājagṛha, it features an extensive dialogue between the Buddha and the Bodhisattva Suvikrāntavikrāmin detailing the nature and cultivation of prajñāpāramitā. The sūtra expounds the core doctrine of the non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) and lack of intrinsic existence (asvabhāvatva) of all dharmas, maintaining that true bodhisattva practice avoids attachment to conceptual markers or spiritual attainments.
SA_K06_bsu030_u.attribution: Mahāyāna sūtra traditionally attributed to the historical Buddha, delivered at the Veṇuvana in Rājagṛha in dialogue with the Bodhisattva Suvikrāntavikrāmin.

SA_K06_bsu051_u.title: Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā
SA_K06_bsu051_u.summary: The Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Diamond-Cutter Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra'), commonly known as the Diamond Sūtra or Triśatikā ('Three Hundred Lines'), is one of the most celebrated and influential scriptures in Mahāyāna Buddhism. Structured as a dialogue between the Buddha and the venerable Subhūti in the Jetavana grove at Śrāvastī, it systematically dismantles attachment to conceptual signs and ontological categories, teaching that bodhisattvas must practice generosity and cultivate supreme enlightenment without abiding in notions of self, living being, or dharma. The text is renowned for its characteristic dialectical formula asserting that a dharma is designated as such precisely because it is empty of intrinsic existence. First translated into Chinese by Kumārajīva in 401/402 CE, the sūtra became a cornerstone of East Asian Buddhist traditions—particularly Chan/Zen—and is celebrated for the 868 CE Dunhuang woodblock scroll, the world's earliest dated complete printed book.
SA_K06_bsu051_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna scripture presented as buddhavacana, framed as an interlocution between Śākyamuni Buddha and the elder Subhūti in the Jetavana hermitage at Śrāvastī.
SA_K06_bsu051_u.edition: P. L. Vaidya (ed.), Mahāyāna-sūtra-saṃgraha, Part 1, Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, 17, Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute, 1961.
SA_K06_bsu051_u.coverage: complete — Complete sūtra in 32 sections as numbered in modern editions (corresponding to pp. 75–89 of Vaidya's edition).

Set in Śrāvastī's Jeta Grove, it consists of dialogues between the Buddha, Śāriputra (Śāradvatīputra), and the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī emphasizing the unreality of dualistic categories, the unoriginated nature (anutpāda) of all dharmas, and the contemplation of the Tathāgata.

SA_K06_bsu053_u.title: Prajñāpāramitāhṛdayasūtra
SA_K06_bsu053_u.summary: The Prajñāpāramitāhṛdayasūtra ('Heart of the Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra') is one of the most widely recited and commented-upon texts in Mahāyāna Buddhism. This e-text preserves the complete longer recension (vistaramātṛkā), which includes the full narrative setting (nidāna) on Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha and concludes with the Buddha rising from samādhi to praise Avalokiteśvara's exposition. The bodhisattva expounds to Śāriputra the emptiness of intrinsic existence (svabhāvaśūnyatā) of all five aggregates, sense spheres, and Noble Truths, concluding with the famous mantra: gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā.
SA_K06_bsu053_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna scripture traditionally presented as buddhavacana, framed as a dialogue between the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and the elder Śāriputra under the inspired sanction of the Buddha.

SA_K06_vchedpgu.title: Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā (fragment)
SA_K06_vchedpgu.summary: The Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā is a Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra cast as a dialogue between the Buddha and the elder Subhūti in the Jetavana at Śrāvastī. The text deconstructs conceptual attachment and reification using iterative paradoxical formulas ('A is not A, therefore it is called A'), emphasizing that dharmas, bodhisattvas, and awakening itself lack svabhāva and must be practiced without fixed ideation (saṃjñā). This e-text provides Gregory Schopen's diplomatic edition of the Gilgit birchbark manuscript, preserving folios 5 and 7–12.

SA_K06_vchedppu.summary: The Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Diamond-Cutter Perfection of Wisdom') is a foundational Mahāyāna sūtra presented as a discourse between the Buddha and Subhūti in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī. It expounds the core doctrine of emptiness (śūnyatā) through radical deconstructive paradoxes, asserting that while bodhisattvas resolve to liberate all sentient beings, in ultimate reality no entities or self-subsisting dharmas exist. This e-text provides the critical transcription of an early Greater Gandhāran birchbark manuscript from Bamiyan (Schøyen Collection MS 2385/1/1, c. 5th–6th century CE), containing sections 1 through 16c before breaking off.

SA_K07_atrisatu.title: Triśatikāyāḥ prajñāpāramitāyāḥ kārikāsaptatiḥ
SA_K07_atrisatu.author: Asaṅga
SA_K07_atrisatu.summary: The Triśatikāyāḥ prajñāpāramitāyāḥ kārikāsaptatiḥ is a verse treatise on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā composed by Asaṅga. Consisting of 77 mnemonic kārikās (numbered TśPk_1 through TśPk_77), the work analyzes the sutra, elucidating the bodhisattva path, the elimination of conceptual attachments, and the non-apprehension of dharmas.
SA_K07_atrisatu.attribution: The colophon of the Sanskrit manuscript attributes the work to Asaṅga ('kṛtir iyam āryāsaṅgapādānām iti'). Yijing's 711 CE Chinese translation (Taishō 1514) likewise attributes the verses to Asaṅga (無著菩薩造).
SA_K07_atrisatu.edition: G. Tucci: Minor Buddhist Texts, part I. Roma 1956 (Serie Orientale Roma, 9), pp. 54-92.
SA_K07_atrisatu.coverage: complete — Contains all 77 kārikās (numbered TśPk_1 through TśPk_77) and the closing colophon.
translations: Giuseppe Tucci, Minor Buddhist Texts, Part I, Rome, 1956. (English)

Bodhiruci (tr.), Jin gang ban re bo luo mi jing lun 金剛般若波羅蜜經論, Taishō Tripiṭaka no. 1511, 509 CE. (Chinese)

SA_K07_bsu033_u.title: Sukhāvatīvyūha
SA_K07_bsu033_u.summary: The Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha is a foundational Mahāyāna sūtra and the principal scriptural authority for Pure Land Buddhism. Set on Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa) in Rājagṛha, the Buddha Śākyamuni narrates to Ānanda how the monk Dharmākara, in the presence of the Buddha Lokeśvararāja, generated the resolve for awakening and made forty-eight great vows to establish the western realm of Sukhāvatī and become the Buddha Amitābha (Amitāyus). The sūtra expounds the visual and spiritual splendors of this paradise, delineates the requirements for rebirth there through faith, recollection, and merits, and includes instructions addressed to the bodhisattva Ajita (Maitreya) on dispelling doubt.
SA_K07_bsu033_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna sūtra set at Gṛdhrakūṭaparvata in Rājagṛha, delivered by the Buddha Śākyamuni to Ānanda and Ajita (Maitreya).
SA_K07_bsu033_u.edition: P. L. Vaidya (ed.), Mahāyāna-sūtra-saṃgrahaḥ, Part 1, Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute, 1961, pp. 221–253 (Buddhist Sanskrit Texts).
SA_K07_bsu033_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha recension (vistaramātṛkā) across all 47 numbered sections (Sukhv 1–47), corresponding to P. L. Vaidya's 1961 edition, pp. 221–253, ending with the standard colophon and the ye dharmā hetuprabhavā stanza.
translations: Luis O. Gómez (trans.), The Land of Bliss: The Paradise of the Buddha of Measureless Light, Honolulu: University of Hawaiʻi Press, 1996. (English)
Hisao Inagaki (trans.), The Three Pure Land Sūtras, Berkeley: Numata Center for Buddhist Translation and Research, 1995. (English)

SA_K07_ppfrag_u.title: Fragments of Prajñāpāramitā texts
SA_K07_ppfrag_u.summary: A GRETIL compilation by Klaus Wille of Sanskrit manuscript fragments of Prajñāpāramitā literature from Central Asia, taken from sixteen published sources, including the Aṣṭādaśasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā, Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā, and unidentified texts.
SA_K07_ppfrag_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna scriptures regarded as the word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana).
SA_K07_ppfrag_u.edition: Compilation by Klaus Wille of 16 published fragment editions, including: Sten Konow, Central Asian Fragments of the Ashṭādaśasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā and of an Unidentified Text (MASI 69), Calcutta 1942; B. B. Bidyabinod, 'Fragment of a Prajnaparamita Manuscript from Central Asia', MASI 32 (1927), 1–11; H. Smith in G. Montell, Sven Hedin's Archaeological Collections from Khotan, Stockholm 1938; G. M. Bongard-Levin, 'A fragment of the Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā-Sūtra from Eastern Turkestan', JAOS 114 (1994), 383–385.
SA_K07_ppfrag_u.coverage: fragment — Collection of non-contiguous Central Asian manuscript fragments from 16 published sources. Preserved chapter colophons include the Aupamyaparivarta (11th).

SA_K07_pplg1__u.title: Larger Prajñāpāramitā (chapters 1–3)
SA_K07_pplg1__u.summary: An early Sanskrit witness of the Larger Prajñāpāramitā sūtra, comprising folios 1r1 to 27v1 of the Gilgit manuscript. This opening section includes the traditional nidāna on Vulture Peak, the catalogs of the arhat and bodhisattva assemblies, the Buddha's miraculous emanation of light illuminating countless world spheres, and initial dialogues with Śāriputra on practicing the perfection of wisdom through the radical non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) and emptiness of all dharmas.
SA_K07_pplg1__u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna sūtra traditionally attributed to the Buddha as buddhavacana.
SA_K07_pplg1__u.edition: Stefano Zacchetti, In Praise of the Light: A Critical Synoptic Edition with an Annotated Translation of Chapters 1-3 of Dharmarakṣa's Guang zan jing, Being the Earliest Chinese Translation of the Larger Prajñāpāramitā, Tokyo 2005 (Bibliotheca Philologica et Philosophica Buddhica, 8).
SA_K07_pplg1__u.coverage: partial — Contains folios 1r1 to 27v1 of the Gilgit manuscript (LPG), corresponding to chapters 1–3 in Zacchetti's edition of Dharmarakṣa's Guang zan jing.
translations: Stefano Zacchetti, In Praise of the Light: A Critical Synoptic Edition with an Annotated Translation of Chapters 1-3 of Dharmarakṣa's Guang zan jing, Being the Earliest Chinese Translation of the Larger Prajñāpāramitā, Tokyo 2005 (Bibliotheca Philologica et Philosophica Buddhica, 8). (English)

SA_K07_pplg202u.title: Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā (excerpt)
SA_K07_pplg202u.summary: This e-text contains an excerpt from the Gilgit manuscript of the Larger Prajñāpāramitā corresponding to folios 202r5–205r12 (GBM 571.5–577.12). In this dialogue between the Buddha and Subhūti, the text explains the distinct characteristics of an irreversible (avaivartika) bodhisattva, explores the profound nature (gambhīra) of the skandhas and all dharmas, and expounds how suchness (tathatā) is characterized by neither increase nor decrease (avṛddhyaparihāṇi).
SA_K07_pplg202u.edition: Yoke Meei Choong, Zum Problem der Leerheit (śūnyatā) in der Prajñāpāramitā, Frankfurt 2006 (Europäische Hochschulschriften, Reihe 27, Bd. 97), pp. 109-133.
SA_K07_pplg202u.coverage: excerpt — Contains a single short passage from the Gilgit manuscript of the Larger Prajñāpāramitā, specifically folios 202r5–205r12 (corresponding to facsimile pages GBM 571.5–577.12).
translations: Edward Conze (trans.), The Large Sutra on Perfect Wisdom with the Divisions of the Abhisamayālaṅkāra, 1975. (English)

SA_K07_sukhvylu.title: Sukhāvatīvyūha
SA_K07_sukhvylu.summary: The Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha is the primary canonical scripture of the Mahāyāna Pure Land tradition focusing on the Buddha Amitābha (Amitāyus) and his western realm, Sukhāvatī. Delivered by Śākyamuni Buddha on Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha, the sūtra relates the ancient past-life story of the monk Dharmākara, who took great bodhisattva vows to establish a supreme realm. The text depicts the wondrous topography, assemblies, and spiritual benefits of Sukhāvatī, while specifying the criteria for rebirth therein—chiefly generating the aspiration for awakening (bodhicittotpāda), sincere faith, ethical observance, and mindful recollection of Amitābha.
SA_K07_sukhvylu.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna scripture presented as the teaching of Śākyamuni Buddha delivered on Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa) in Rājagṛha to Ānanda, Maitreya, and an assembly of monks and bodhisattvas.
SA_K07_sukhvylu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha from the opening nidāna through to the final colophon (amitābhasya sukhāvatī-vyūha-parivartaḥ samāptaḥ), corresponding to pages 1–67 of Ashikaga's 1965 edition.
translations: Luis O. Gómez (trans.), The Land of Bliss: The Paradise of the Buddha of Measureless Light, Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press, 1996. (English)
Hisao Inagaki (trans.), The Three Pure Land Sutras: A Study and Translation, Kyoto: Nagata Bunshōdō, 1995 (also Berkeley: Numata Center). (English)

SA_K08_bsu020_u.title: Kāśyapaparivartasūtra (§§1–161, end lost)
SA_K08_bsu020_u.summary: The Kāśyapaparivartasūtra is an early Mahāyāna scripture cast as a dialogue between the Buddha and Mahākāśyapa on Vulture Peak at Rājagṛha. It expounds the bodhisattva path, emphasizing moral purity and warning against spiritual hypocrisy, attachment to monastic privileges, and intellectual pride. The text famously articulates the Middle Way between the extremes of eternalism and annihilationism and contains the influential simile comparing the dogmatic reification of emptiness to a medicine that itself becomes a deadly disease.
SA_K08_bsu020_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna scripture cited in literature as the Ratnakūṭasūtra, included in the Mahāratnakūṭa collection.
SA_K08_bsu020_u.edition: A. von Staël-Holstein (ed.), The Kāśyapaparivarta. A Mahāyānasūtra of the Ratnakūṭa Class, Shanghai: The Commercial Press, 1926.
SA_K08_bsu020_u.coverage: partial — The e-text covers sections up to KP.161, breaking off with '9 yathā niṣaṇ .................'.
translations: Bhikkhu Pāsādika, 2015. (English)
Bhikkhu Pāsādika, 1977–. (English)

SA_K08_bsu040_u.title: Vinayaviniścayopāliparipṛcchā (partial)
SA_K08_bsu040_u.summary: A Mahāyāna sūtra transmitted within the Ratnakūṭa collection that contrasts the monastic prātimokṣa rules of śrāvakas with the ethical conduct of bodhisattvas. The Buddha explains that while the śrāvaka discipline centers on strict detachment to avoid any rebirth in saṃsāra, bodhisattva discipline is guided by skillful means (upāyakauśalya) and intention, prioritizing the welfare and gathering of beings. Consequently, offenses rooted in aversion or hatred are considered severe for a bodhisattva because they cause abandonment of beings, whereas infractions rooted in desire can serve to gather beings and are deemed comparatively less obstructive. The sūtra concludes with an exposition by Mañjuśrī on the unconditioned, inherently pure nature of all dharmas.
SA_K08_bsu040_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna sūtra preserved as text 24 of the Ratnakūṭa collection (Toh 68; T 310[24]). Traditionally considered buddhavacana.
SA_K08_bsu040_u.edition: Nalinaksha Dutt, ed., Bodhisattva-prātimokṣa-sūtram, Calcutta: Calcutta Oriental Press, 1931, pp. 20–27 (also published in The Indian Historical Quarterly 7, 1931, text on).
SA_K08_bsu040_u.coverage: partial — Preserves only the second half of the sūtra (corresponding to §§ 1.61 to the end in Toh 68), commencing where Upāli arises from solitary meditation to inquire about the differences between śrāvaka and bodhisattva discipline, and ending with Mañjuśrī's discourse on the ultimate nature of vinaya ('iti bodhisattvaprātimokṣāḥ'). The earlier section (containing the setting, dialogue with Śāriputra, and the Thirty-Five Confession Buddhas liturgy / Triskandhaka) is absent.
translations: Pierre Python, Vinaya-viniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā: Enquête d'Upāli pour une exégèse de la discipline, Collection Jean Przyluski 5, Paris: Adrien-Maisonneuve, 1973. (French)

Garma C. C. Chang, ed., 'The Sutra on the Determination of the Vinaya (Upalipariprccha)', in A Treasury of Mahāyāna Sūtras: Selections from the Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra, University Park: Pennsylvania State University Press, 1983. (English)

SA_K08_bsu062_u.title: Guṇakāraṇḍavyūhasūtra
SA_K08_bsu062_u.summary: The Guṇakāraṇḍavyūhasūtra is a metrical Mahāyāna sūtra framed as a dialogue between Jinaśrīrāja and Jayaśrī. It glorifies Avalokiteśvara (Lokeśvara), promotes devotion to the Three Jewels, details stories including Siṃhala, and praises the recitation of the six-syllable mantra (ṣaḍakṣarī).
SA_K08_bsu062_u.attribution: Anonymous Mahāyāna sūtra. It is framed as an avadāna dialogue between Jinaśrīrāja and the arhat Jayaśrī.
SA_K08_bsu062_u.edition: Lokesh Chandra (ed.), Guṇakāraṇḍavyūhasūtram, New Delhi: International Academy of Indian Culture, 1999.
SA_K08_bsu062_u.coverage: complete — Complete e-text in verse, beginning with the opening verse of the śrītriratnabhajanānuśaṃsāvadāna and concluding with the sūtra colophon (iti jinaśrīrājaparipṛṣṭajayaśrīsaṃprabhāṣitaśrīmadāryāvalokiteśvaraguṇakāraṇḍavyūhasūtrarājaṃ samāptam).

SA_K08_kasyparu.title: Kāśyapaparivartasūtra (§§1–161, end lost)
SA_K08_kasyparu.summary: The Kāśyapaparivartasūtra (also known as the Kāśyapaparivarta or Ratnakūṭasūtra) is an archaic and foundational Mahāyāna scripture presented as a dialogue between Śākyamuni Buddha and Mahākāśyapa on Vulture Peak. It expounds core bodhisattva ethics, the Middle Way (madhyamā pratipad) avoiding eternalism and annihilationism, and the meditation on emptiness (śūnyatā), featuring the famous warning that reifying emptiness as a dogmatic view turns medicine into incurable poison. It also delivers severe critiques of counterfeit, self-serving monastics, providing essential scriptural authority frequently cited across Madhyamaka, Yogācāra, and Tibetan scholastic traditions.
SA_K08_kasyparu.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna scripture presented as a dialogue between Śākyamuni Buddha and the elder Mahākāśyapa on Vulture Peak (Gṛddhakūṭa) near Rājagṛha. It is one of the earliest historically attested Mahāyāna sūtras, first translated into Chinese by Lokakṣema in the late 2nd century CE (T 350).
SA_K08_kasyparu.edition: M. I. Vorobyova-Desyatovskaya (in collaboration with Seishi Karashima and Noriyuki Kudo), The Kāśyapaparivarta: Romanized Text and Facsimiles, Bibliotheca Philologica et Philosophica Buddhica V, Tokyo: The International Research Institute for Advanced Buddhology, Soka University, 2002.
SA_K08_kasyparu.coverage: partial — Line-by-line transcription of the Kashgar manuscript SI P/2, fol. 1v–81v, covering §§1–161 with lacunae and ending in §161 ('9 yathā niṣaṇā .āva .āy. + + +'). It is followed by the further fragments printed in the edition: SI P/85A (KP-VD pp. 58f.), Hoernle 143 S.B. 38+39 + Mannerheim 3 (pp. 60–62, ending in §136) and SHT I 374 (pp. 63f., §§151–153). The e-text therefore ends with SHT I 374 at §153, not where SI P/2 ends. §§162–166 are not extant in Sanskrit.
translations: Bhikkhu Pāsādika, The Kāśyapaparivarta: Romanized Sanskrit Text with the Tibetan and the Chinese Versions, Translated into English, Linh-Sơn - Publication d'études bouddhologiques, nos. 1–9, Joinville-le-Pont, 1977– (revised monograph: The Kāśyapaparivarta: English Translation and Commentary, 2015). (English)

Friedrich Weller, Zum Kāśyapaparivarta. Heft 2: Verdeutschung des sanskrit-tibetischen Textes, Abhandlungen der Sächsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Leipzig, Philologisch-historische Klasse 57.3, Berlin: Akademie-Verlag, 1965. (German)

SA_K09_bsu014_u.title: Daśabhūmikasūtra
SA_K09_bsu014_u.summary: The Daśabhūmikasūtra, also preserved as a major chapter of the Buddhāvataṃsakasūtra, is set in the realm of the Paranirmitavaśavartin deities, where the bodhisattva Vajragarbha details the progressive ten stages (bhūmis). Commented on in the Daśabhūmikavyākhyāna, it became the foundational source of the Chinese Dilun school.
SA_K09_bsu014_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna sūtra circulating both independently and as chapter 26 (in the 80-fascicle recension) or chapter 22 (in the 60-fascicle recension) of the Buddhāvataṃsakasūtra. The teaching is expounded by the bodhisattva Vajragarbha upon request by Vimukticandra in the palace of the king of the Paranirmitavaśavartin deities.
SA_K09_bsu014_u.edition: P. L. Vaidya (ed.), Daśabhūmikasūtram, Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute, 1967.
SA_K09_bsu014_u.coverage: complete — Corresponding to P.L. Vaidya's 1967 edition (Buddhist Sanskrit Texts 7): chapters 1–10 and chapter 11 (Parīndanāparivarta), concluding with editorial notes.
translations: Megumu Honda (trans.), 'An Annotated Translation of the Daśabhūmika', in: Denis Sinor (ed.), Studies in Southeast and Central Asia, Śata-Piṭaka Series 74, New Delhi: 1968, pp. 115–276. (English)
Thomas Cleary (trans.), The Flower Ornament Scripture: A Translation of the Avatamsaka Sutra, Boston: Shambhala, 1993. (English)
Ryūzan Tatsuyama (trans.), Bongo wayaku Jūjikyō (梵語和譯十地經), Nagoya: 1938. (Japanese)

SA_K09_bsu016_u.title: Gaṇḍavyūhasūtra
SA_K09_bsu016_u.summary: The Gaṇḍavyūhasūtra is a major Mahāyāna scripture that circulated both independently and as the climactic final section of the Buddhāvataṃsakasūtra. It recounts the spiritual pilgrimage of the youth Sudhana, who is instructed by Mañjuśrī to seek out fifty-three spiritual mentors (kalyāṇamitra)—representing varied genders, occupations, and stations—to learn the practice of a bodhisattva. The narrative culminates in visions of Maitreya's kūṭāgāra and Samantabhadra, depicting the cosmos (dharmadhātu) as an interconnected web of mutual interpenetration and closing with the famous Samantabhadracaryāpraṇidhāna aspiration.
SA_K09_bsu016_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna scripture traditionally received as the word of the Buddha (buddhavacana) and the bodhisattvas Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra. It circulated both independently and as the climactic concluding book of the Buddhāvataṃsakasūtra.
SA_K09_bsu016_u.edition: P. L. Vaidya, ed., Gaṇḍavyūhasūtram. Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, No. 5. Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute of Post-Graduate Studies and Research in Sanskrit Learning, 1960.
SA_K09_bsu016_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Gaṇḍavyūhasūtra according to the Nepalese Sanskrit manuscript transmission as edited by P. L. Vaidya (pp. 1–436), containing the introductory Nidānaparivarta, the encounters with the 53 kalyāṇamitras, and the concluding colophons.
translations: Thomas Cleary, trans., The Flower Ornament Scripture / Entry into the Realm of Reality, Boston: Shambhala, 1987. (English)

SA_K10_adbhutdu.title: Adbhutadharmaparyāya
SA_K10_adbhutdu.summary: A short Mahāyāna sūtra expounding the extraordinary karmic merit derived from erecting and venerating stūpas, images, and relics of a buddha. Prompted by Ānanda observing a magnificent eighty-gated multistoried hall (kūṭāgāra), the Buddha instructs that constructing even a miniature clay stūpa the size of an āmalaka fruit, with a parasol like a jujube leaf and a relic like a mustard seed, generates far greater merit than bestowing whole continents of jewels upon śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or the saṅgha, owing to the limitless nature of the Buddha's qualities. The sūtra survives in Sanskrit among the Gilgit manuscripts and the Potala collection, as well as in Tibetan (Toh 319) and Chinese versions (T 688, T 689, T 704).
SA_K10_adbhutdu.attribution: Preserved in three Sanskrit manuscript witnesses from Gilgit, in a Sanskrit palm-leaf manuscript from the Potala, and in Tibetan and Chinese translations.
SA_K10_adbhutdu.edition: Yael Bentor, 'The Redactions of the Adbhutadharmaparyāya from Gilgit', Journal of the International Association of Buddhist Studies, no. 2 (1988), pp. 21–52.
SA_K10_adbhutdu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the sūtra in 10 numbered sections following Yael Bentor's 1988 critical edition.
translations: Bhikṣuṇī Vinītā (Vinita Tseng), A Unique Collection of Twenty Sūtras in a Sanskrit Manuscript from the Potala: Editions and Translation, 2 vols., Beijing: China Tibetology Publishing House & Vienna: Austrian Academy of Sciences, 2010. (English)

SA_K10_ahovcs_u.title: Ahorātravratacaityasevānuśaṃsāvadāna
SA_K10_ahovcs_u.summary: The Ahorātravratacaityasevānuśaṃsāvadāna is a Buddhist narrative poem (avadāna) preserved in Nepalese Sanskrit manuscripts celebrating the spiritual merits and worldly rewards (anuśaṃsā) of the 'day-and-night vow' (ahorātravrata) performed during the worship and ritual service of caityas/stūpas. Framed as a dialogue between King Aśoka and the elder Upagupta, the text details the procedural rules of the vrata and illustrates its karmic efficacy through narratives of devotees whose stupa veneration purified negative karma and led to celestial rebirth and progress toward enlightenment. It constitutes a key textual witness for the devotional cult of the caitya and vow observances in Newar Buddhism.
SA_K10_ahovcs_u.attribution: Anonymous Buddhist didactic narrative poem (avadāna) in 356 metrical verses. Preserved in Nepalese Sanskrit manuscript codices both independently and within cyclical collections (e.g., Aśokāvadānamālā). The narrative is framed as an exposition given by Upagupta to Emperor Aśoka detailing teachings originally revealed by Śākyamuni Buddha.
SA_K10_ahovcs_u.edition: R. Handurukande, Three Sanskrit Texts on Caitya Worship ḥ In Relation to the Ahorātravrata, Tokyo 2000 (Studia Philologica Buddhica, Monograph Series, 16).
SA_K10_ahovcs_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Ahorātravratacaityasevānuśaṃsāvadāna in 356 verses (numbered Avc_1 through Avc_356), including critical apparatus notes recording manuscript variant readings (BCDE) and the scribal post-colophon.

SA_K10_anitysuu.title: Anityatāsūtra
SA_K10_anitysuu.summary: The Anityatāsūtra is a short discourse delivered by the Buddha at the Jetavana in Śrāvastī explaining that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskārāḥ) are impermanent, unstable, and subject to change. The Buddha illustrates universal mortality across all classes of society, heavenly beings across the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness, and even enlightened beings (arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and tathāgatas). The sūtra concludes with four gnomic verses on mortality and destruction parallel to stanzas found in the Anityavarga of the Udānavarga.
SA_K10_anitysuu.attribution: Canonical Buddhist discourse traditionally transmitted as buddhavacana.
SA_K10_anitysuu.edition: Isshi Yamada, 'Anityatāsūtra', Journal of Indian and Buddhist Studies (Indogaku Bukkyōgaku Kenkyū) 20 (1972), pp. 1001–996 [30–35].

SA_K10_avsata_u.title: Avadānaśataka
SA_K10_avsata_u.summary: The Avadānaśataka is an anthology of Buddhist narrative legends (avadāna), organized into ten thematic decades (vargas) containing ten stories each. Datable to roughly the 2nd–6th century CE, the work illustrates the inevitable workings of karma and retribution across rebirths, focusing on predictions of future buddhahood and pratyekabuddhahood, arhatship, past-life deeds of the Buddha (jātakas), the torments of pretas, and noble acts of charity (dāna). It survives in Sanskrit as well as canonical Tibetan (Toh 343) and Chinese (T 200) translations.
SA_K10_avsata_u.edition: P. L. Vaidya (ed.), Avadāna-śataka, Buddhist Sanskrit Texts 19, Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute, 1958, collated with J. S. Speyer (ed.), 2 vols., Bibliotheca Buddhica 3, St. Petersbourg, 1906–1909.
SA_K10_avsata_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of all one hundred stories arranged in ten vargas (AVŚ 1–100). The Kalpadrumāvadānamālā appended to Vaidya's edition is excluded here and maintained as a separate file in GRETIL.
translations: Léon Feer (trans.), 1891. (French)
Naomi Appleton (trans.), 2020. (English)
Naomi Appleton (trans.), 'The Second Decade of the Avadānaśataka'. (English)

SA_K10_bsu001_u.title: Āryānityatāsūtra
SA_K10_bsu001_u.summary: The Āryānityatāsūtra is a short canonical discourse delivered by the Buddha at Jetavana in Śrāvastī on the universal impermanence (anityatā) and inevitability of death for all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra). The Buddha surveys all beings and classes—wealthy householders, brahmins, kṣatriyas, universal rulers, forest ascetics, and the devas across the desire, form, and formless realms—noting that none can escape death. Even arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and tathāgatas must eventually cast off their physical bodies (kāyanikṣepaṇa). The sūtra concludes with similes of fragile earthen pots and ripe fruits liable to fall, followed by famous verses on the cessation of conditioned existence.
SA_K10_bsu001_u.attribution: Canonical Buddhist sūtra (Buddhavacana) set at the Jetavana monastery in Śrāvastī.
SA_K10_bsu001_u.edition: M.B. Shakya, Buddhist Himalaya Vol.1, No.1. Nepal: Nagarjuna Institute of Exact Methods, 1988, pp. 58-60.
SA_K10_bsu001_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the short sūtra, including the opening nidāna, prose discourse, four concluding gāthās, and concluding colophon (ity āryānityatā sūtraṃ samāptaṃ).
translations: Tibetan translation: Toh 310 (BO_K10_D0310). (Tibetan)

SA_K10_bsu006_u.title: Ajitasenavyākaraṇa
SA_K10_bsu006_u.summary: The Ajitasenavyākaraṇa (or Ajitasenavyākaraṇanirdeśa) is a Mahāyāna sūtra surviving in Sanskrit in the Gilgit cache and in Central Asian manuscript fragments, but absent from both the Tibetan and Chinese Buddhist canons. Structurally sharing traits with mainstream avadāna literature, it depicts the Buddha predicting future buddhahood (vyākaraṇa) for King Ajitasena. It embodies early Mahāyāna ideals while lacking the doctrine of emptiness (dharmaśūnyatā).
SA_K10_bsu006_u.attribution: Canonical Buddhist sūtra traditionally attributed to the speech of the Buddha (buddhavacana); no individual human author.
SA_K10_bsu006_u.edition: N. Dutt, Gilgit Manuscript, vol. I, Delhi: Sri Satguru Publ. 1984, pp. 101-136.
SA_K10_bsu006_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the sūtra according to the Gilgit manuscript as edited by Dutt (pp. 101–136).
translations: William Brian Rasmussen, 'An Annotated Transcription and Translation of the Gilgit Manuscript of the Ajitasenavyākaraṇanirdeśamahāyānasūtra', M.A. thesis, The University of Texas at Austin, 1995. (English)

SA_K10_bsu008_u.title: Buddhabalādhānaprātihāryavikurvāṇanirdeśasūtra (fragment)
SA_K10_bsu008_u.summary: The Buddhabalādhānaprātihāryavikurvāṇanirdeśasūtra is a Mahāyāna sūtra set on the banks of the Nairañjanā river and in the Āmrapālī grove at Vārāṇasī, centering on the miraculous transformations (vikurvaṇa) and superhuman displays (prātihārya) brought forth through the Buddha's samādhi. Prompted by the Buddha, the bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Vajrapāṇi project radiant light across the ten directions to convert stubborn, immoral, and unfaithful beings, purifying their karmic defilements and gathering them before the Tathāgata. Through dialogues primarily involving Mañjuśrī, the sūtra sets forth a docetic Mahāyāna Buddhology, teaching that all conditioned phenomena, as well as the Buddha's earthly life and physical parinirvāṇa, are mere illusory displays (upāyakauśalya) like reflections in a clear mirror.
SA_K10_bsu008_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna sūtra regarded as buddhavacana.
SA_K10_bsu008_u.edition: N. Dutt, ed., Gilgit Manuscripts, Delhi: Sri Satguru Publications, 1984, pp. 173–183.
SA_K10_bsu008_u.coverage: fragment — Extant Sanskrit text preserves an excerpt/fragment corresponding to pp. 173–183 in Dutt's edition.
translations: 'phags pa sangs rgyas kyi stobs bskyed pa'i cho 'phrul rnam par 'phrul ba bstan pa zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo (Derge Kangyur D 186) (Tibetan)

SA_K10_bsu009_u.title: Maitreyavyākaraṇa
SA_K10_bsu009_u.summary: The Maitreyavyākaraṇa ('Prophecy Concerning Maitreya') is a metrical Buddhist scripture in anuṣṭubh verse setting forth the future advent of the bodhisattva Maitreya as the next buddha of the current cosmic era. Framed as an exposition delivered by Śākyamuni Buddha to his disciple Śāriputra, the text describes the utopian state of Jambudvīpa and the capital Ketumatī ruled by the righteous universal monarch (cakravartin) Śaṅkha, Maitreya's birth into a brāhmaṇa family, his renunciation, enlightenment under the Nāga tree, and the three major preaching assemblies (saṃnipāta). It concludes by enjoining devotees to cultivate devotion toward the Three Jewels and practice Buddhist morality to ensure rebirth in Maitreya's presence.
SA_K10_bsu009_u.attribution: Canonical Buddhist prophecy (vyākaraṇa); framed as a discourse delivered by the Buddha Śākyamuni in response to the questions of his disciple Śāriputra regarding the future appearance of Maitreya.
SA_K10_bsu009_u.edition: N. Dutt (ed.): Gilgit Manuscripts, Vol IV. Delhi: Sri Satguru Publications, 1984, 185-214.
SA_K10_bsu009_u.coverage: complete — Complete in 108 verses (ślokas) and closing colophon (// maitreyavyākaraṇaṃ samāptaṃ //), representing the full metrical text as edited in Gilgit Manuscripts Vol. IV.
translations: Sylvain Lévi, 'Maitreya le consolateur', in Études d'orientalisme publiées par le Musée Guimet à la mémoire de Raymonde Linossier, Paris: Ernest Leroux, 1932. (French)

SA_K10_bsu010_u.title: Bhavasaṅkrāntisūtra
SA_K10_bsu010_u.summary: The Bhavasaṅkrāntisūtra is a short Mahāyāna sūtra set at the Veṇuvana near Rājagṛha, in which King Bimbisāra asks the Buddha how karmic actions that have long since ceased can reappear at the moment of death and produce rebirth if all conditioned entities (saṃskāra) are empty. The Buddha answers with the analogy of a man dreaming of a beautiful woman, demonstrating that although no permanent self or entity transmigrates from one world to another, rebirth occurs uninterruptedly through the causal stream of consciousness (cittasaṃtati). The text concludes with verses elucidating the relation between conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya) and ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).
SA_K10_bsu010_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna discourse traditionally attributed to the Buddha. The Sanskrit text was restored into Sanskrit from the Tibetan and Chinese versions by Pt. N. Aiyaswami Sastri.
SA_K10_bsu010_u.edition: N. Aiyaswami Shastri: Bhavasaṅkrānti Sūtra. Madras: Adyar Library, 1938, pp. 1-6.
SA_K10_bsu010_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of Sastri's 1938 Sanskrit reconstruction of the sūtra (15 sections, prose with concluding verses), terminating with the colophon 'āryabhavasaṅkrāntirnāma mahāyānasūtraṃ saṃpūrṇam' (pp. 1–6).
translations: phags pa srid pa 'pho ba zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo (Derge Kangyur D 226): translated by Jinamitra, Dānaśīla, sna nam btsun pa ye shes sde (Tibetan)

SA_K10_bsu013_u.title: Āryacaturdharmanirdeśasūtra
SA_K10_bsu013_u.summary: The Caturdharmanirdeśasūtra is a brief Mahāyāna scripture set in the Sudharmā council hall of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, in which the Buddha instructs the bodhisattva Maitreya on how to overcome and purify accumulated unwholesome actions. The discourse sets forth four factors, traditionally known as the four opponent powers (catuḥpratipakṣabala): remorse (vidūṣaṇāsamudācāra), antidotal virtuous deeds (pratipakṣasamudācāra), the resolve to refrain from repetition (pratyāpattibala), and reliance on refuge and bodhicitta (āśrayabala). Frequently cited by Indian masters, notably Śāntideva in the Śikṣāsamuccaya, it serves as the primary canonical foundation for Buddhist confession and purification rituals.
SA_K10_bsu013_u.attribution: A Mahāyāna sūtra set in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven where the Buddha instructs the bodhisattva Maitreya. The Sanskrit text in this edition is a modern Sanskrit reconstruction (punaruddhāra) prepared from the Tibetan translation by Ngawang Samten and Janardan Pandey.
SA_K10_bsu013_u.edition: Ngawang Samten and Janardan Pandey (eds.), 'Āryacaturdharmanirdeśasūtram' (saṃskṛte punaruddhāritam), Dhīḥ: Journal of Rare Buddhist Texts Research Unit, vol. 35, Sarnath, Varanasi: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 2003, pp. 45–52.
SA_K10_bsu013_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the short sūtra in 32 segments, including opening nidāna, central teaching on the four opponent factors, and the colophons.
translations: phags pa chos bzhi bstan pa zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo (Derge Kangyur D 249): translated by Surendrabodhi, sna nam btsun pa ye shes sde (Tibetan)

SA_K10_bsu018_u.title: Karuṇāpuṇḍarīkasūtra
SA_K10_bsu018_u.summary: The Karuṇāpuṇḍarīkasūtra contrasts the aspirations and vows of various buddhas and bodhisattvas: whereas buddhas such as Amitābha and Akṣobhya chose to preside over purified buddha-fields, Śākyamuni made vows to attain awakening and guide sentient beings in an impure world during the era of the five degenerations (pañcakaṣāya). The text celebrates Śākyamuni's supreme compassion, likening him to a white lotus (puṇḍarīka).
SA_K10_bsu018_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna sūtra, traditionally presented as the discourse of the Buddha Śākyamuni on Gṛdhrakūṭa mountain in Rājagṛha.
SA_K10_bsu018_u.edition: Isshi Yamada, Mahakarunapundarika Sutra. London: School of Oriental and African Studies, 1968, 1-420.
SA_K10_bsu018_u.coverage: complete — Complete Sanskrit text of the sūtra corresponding to pp. 1–420 of Isshi Yamada's 1968 SOAS critical edition.

SA_K10_bsu019.title: Kāraṇḍavyūhasūtra
SA_K10_bsu019.summary: A pivotal Mahāyāna sūtra dedicated to glorifying the salvific activities and cosmic compassion of Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara across various realms of saṃsāra, including Avīci hell and the preta realm. The text is historically famous as the earliest known source to teach the six-syllable mantra Oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ (the ṣaḍakṣarī mahāvidyā) and to detail its benefits and mandala ritual. Composed in northern India circa the 4th to 5th century CE, it demonstrates direct thematic engagements with contemporary Śaiva cosmologies—such as presenting Hindu deities like Maheśvara, Brahmā, and Nārāyaṇa as emanations from Avalokiteśvara's body—and provided the foundation for Avalokiteśvara worship and the Maṇi Kabum in Tibet.
SA_K10_bsu019.attribution: A canonical Mahāyāna sūtra delivered as the word of the Buddha (buddhavacana), set in the Jetavana monastery at Śrāvastī.
SA_K10_bsu019.edition: P.L. Vaidya (ed.), Mahāyāna-sūtra-saṃgrahaḥ, Part 1, Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute of Post-Graduate Studies and Research in Sanskrit Learning, 1961 (Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, 17), Text No. 12, pp. 258–308.
SA_K10_bsu019.coverage: complete — Complete text of the prose recension in two parts (nirvyūhas), corresponding to pp. 258–308 of P.L. Vaidya's edition.
translations: Alexander Studholme, The Origins of Oṃ Maṇipadme Hūṃ: A Study of the Kāraṇḍavyūha Sūtra, Albany: State University of New York Press, 2002. (English)

SA_K10_bsu021_u.title: Saddharmalaṅkāvatārasūtra
SA_K10_bsu021_u.summary: The Saddharmalaṅkāvatārasūtra is an influential Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra that synthesizes Yogācāra consciousness-only (vijñaptimātratā / cittamātra) doctrines with the tathāgatagarbha teaching. Framed as an exposition delivered by the Buddha on Mount Malaya in Laṅkā to the bodhisattva Mahāmati and king Rāvaṇa, it expounds the eight consciousnesses (especially ālayavijñāna), the five dharmas, the three intrinsic natures (trisvabhāva), the two kinds of selflessness (dharmanairātmya and pudgalanairātmya), and the doctrine of vegetarianism (māṃsabhakṣaṇaparivarta). The text exerted foundational influence across Mahāyāna philosophical schools, Tibetan scholasticism, and East Asian Chan/Zen traditions.
SA_K10_bsu021_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna scripture traditionally presented as the discourse of the Buddha delivered on Mount Malaya in Laṅkā to the rākṣasa king Rāvaṇa and Bodhisattva Mahāmati.
SA_K10_bsu021_u.edition: P. L. Vaidya (ed.), Saddharmalaṅkāvatārasūtra, Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute of Post-Graduate Studies and Research in Sanskrit Learning, 1963 (Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, 3).
SA_K10_bsu021_u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 10 chapters (parivartas 1–10), concluding with the Sagāthakam (verse 884) and the final colophon 'ity āryasaddharmalaṅkāvatāro nāma mahāyānasūtraṃ sagāthakaṃ samāptam iti'.

SA_K10_bsu023_u.title: Madhyamakaśālistambasūtra
SA_K10_bsu023_u.summary: The Madhyamakaśālistambasūtra is a Sanskrit work opening with the eight negations from the dedicatory verse of Nāgārjuna's Mūlamadhyamakakārikā and containing an exposition of internal and external dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda). The latter part incorporates a śāstric dialectic concerning the conditioned nature of entities (paratantrāś ca bhāvā vivādapadam) and cites the Candrapradīpasūtra.
SA_K10_bsu023_u.attribution: The work is an anonymous Buddhist work, whose latter part resembles a śāstric discussion by an unknown author.
SA_K10_bsu023_u.edition: P. L. Vaidya (ed.), Mahāyāna-sūtra-saṃgrahaḥ, Part 1, Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute, 1961 (Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, 17).

SA_K10_bsu024_u.title: Mahāsannipātaratnaketudhāraṇīsūtra (chapters 1–6, 10–11)
SA_K10_bsu024_u.summary: The Mahāsannipātaratnaketudhāraṇīsūtra (also known as the Ratnaketuparivarta) is an influential Mahāyāna scripture that circulated both independently and as a major component of the expansive Mahāsannipāta corpus. Set in Rājagṛha, the narrative depicts the conversion of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, the Buddha's subjugation of Māra and his host, discourses on karmic results and bodhisattva training, and potent protective dhāraṇī incantations. This digital text reproduces the incomplete Sanskrit text recovered from the Gilgit manuscript and edited by Nalinaksha Dutt, containing chapters 1–6 and 10–11.
SA_K10_bsu024_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra traditionally regarded as buddhavacana.

SA_K10_bsu026_u.title: Pratītyasamutpādamahāyānasūtra
SA_K10_bsu026_u.summary: The Pratītyasamutpādamahāyānasūtra is a brief Mahāyāna scripture set in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, where the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara petitions the Buddha to deliver a teaching yielding boundless merit for the assembly. In response, the Buddha recites the dependent arising verse (ye dharmā hetuprabhavā...) and teaches that fashioning even miniature caityas, bodhi trees, and umbrellas and reciting this verse yields vast Brahma merit (brāhmaṃ puṇyam) leading to rebirth in the Brahmaloka and the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
SA_K10_bsu026_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna sūtra set in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
SA_K10_bsu026_u.edition: P.L. Vaidya (ed.), Mahāyāna-sūtra-saṃgraha, Part 1, Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute, 1961 (Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, 17), p. 119.
SA_K10_bsu026_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the short sūtra (occupying p. 119 in Vaidya's edition), including opening nidāna and closing rejoinder.

SA_K10_bsu032_u.title: Sukhāvatīvyūhasūtra (saṃkṣiptamātṛkā)
SA_K10_bsu032_u.summary: The Smaller Sukhāvatīvyūhasūtra (saṃkṣiptamātṛkā), widely revered in East Asia as the Amitābha Sūtra, is a foundational scripture of Pure Land Buddhism. Set in Śrāvastī, Śākyamuni Buddha describes the western Buddha-field Sukhāvatī and its presiding Buddha Amitāyus (Amitābha) to his disciple Śāriputra, portraying in sensory detail its jeweled pavilions, radiant lotus ponds, music, and divine birds that ceaselessly proclaim the Dharma. The sūtra teaches that living beings who hear Amitāyus's name and hold it single-mindedly without distraction will be welcomed by Amitābha at the point of death and reborn in his realm, a promise affirmed by the Buddhas of the six directions.
SA_K10_bsu032_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna scripture presented as buddhavacana spoken by the Buddha Śākyamuni to the venerable Śāriputra at Śrāvastī; traditional Indian Mahāyāna scriptures carry no individual human author attribution.
SA_K10_bsu032_u.edition: P.L. Vaidya in: Mahayana-sutra-samgrahah, Part 1. Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute 1961 (Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, 17)
SA_K10_bsu032_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the shorter Sukhāvatīvyūhasūtra in 20 editorial sections (Sukhs_1 through Sukhs_20), corresponding to Vaidya's edition pp. 254–257.

SA_K10_bsu037_u.title: Sarvatathāgatādhiṣṭhānavyūhasūtra
SA_K10_bsu037_u.summary: The Sarvatathāgatādhiṣṭhānavyūhasūtra (also known by its longer title, Sarvatathāgatādhiṣṭhānasattvāvalokanabuddhakṣetrasaṃdarśanavyūha) is a Mahāyāna scripture set on Mount Potalaka, the abode of Avalokiteśvara. The Buddha is seated with an assembly of bhikṣus, bodhisattvas, lokapālas, and yakṣiṇīs. The scripture includes dhāraṇīs and ritual incantations along with instructions for use. Preserved in Sanskrit in the Gilgit manuscripts, it was translated into Chinese as 佛說莊嚴王陀羅尼呪經 (Taishō 1375) by Yijing in 701 CE, and into Tibetan (D 98).
SA_K10_bsu037_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna Buddhist scripture presented as the discourse of the Buddha; traditionally anonymous.
SA_K10_bsu037_u.edition: Nalinaksha Dutt, ed., Gilgit Manuscripts, vol. I. Delhi: Sri Satguru Publications, 1984 Second Edition, pp. 49-89.
SA_K10_bsu037_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the sūtra as edited by Nalinaksha Dutt (pp. 49–89), covering the entire work preserved in the Gilgit manuscript.

SA_K10_bsu038_u.title: Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchāsūtra
SA_K10_bsu038_u.summary: A brief Mahāyāna sūtra set in the dwelling of the nāga king Sāgara. The Buddha explains that teaching the four summaries or seals of the Dharma (caturdharmoddāna)—that all conditioned things are impermanent, all contaminated phenomena are suffering, all phenomena are without self, and nirvāṇa is peace—is equivalent to expounding all eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dharma (dharmaskandha).
SA_K10_bsu038_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna sūtra associated with Toh 155 in the Tibetan Kangyur. The text in this e-text is marked as a Sanskrit reconstruction (saṃskṛte punaruddhṛtam).
SA_K10_bsu038_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the short sūtra, containing the opening nidāna set in the dwelling of the nāga king Sāgara, the teaching equating the four seals of the Dharma (caturdharmoddāna) to the 84,000 aggregates of the Dharma, and the rejoicing of the retinue.
translations: Fo wei hai longwang shuo fayin jing (佛為海龍王說法印經, Taishō Tripiṭaka no. 599), trans. Yijing (義淨), 711. (Chinese)
phags pa klu'i rgyal po rgya mtshos zhus pa zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo (Derge Kangyur D 155): translated by Surendrabodhi, sna nam btsun pa ye shes sde (Tibetan)

SA_K10_bsu039_u.title: Triskandhasūtra
SA_K10_bsu039_u.summary: The Triskandhasūtra (or Āryatriskandhasūtra) is a Mahāyāna liturgical text focusing on confession of sins (pāpadeśanā), rejoicing at merit (anumodanā / puṇyānumodanā), and dedication (pariṇāmanā).
SA_K10_bsu039_u.edition: M.B. Shakya, Buddhist Himalaya X.1, Nepal: Nagarjuna Institute of Exact Methods, 2000, 1–6.
SA_K10_bsu039_u.coverage: complete — Text of the liturgical sūtra as edited by M.B. Shakya (containing refuge, homage to the Buddhas, confession, and concluding verses).
translations: Nancy J. Barnes, 'The Triskandha, Practice in Three Parts: Study of an Early Mahāyāna Buddhist Ritual', in N. K. Wagle and F. Watanabe (eds.), Studies on Buddhism in Honour of Professor A. K. Warder. (English)
Pierre Python (ed. & tr.), Vinaya-viniścaya-Upāli-paripṛcchā, Paris: Adrien-Maisonneuve, 1973. (French)

SA_K10_bsu045_u.title: Saṃghāṭasūtra
SA_K10_bsu045_u.summary: The Saṃghāṭasūtra is a canonical Mahāyāna scripture framed as a discourse delivered by the Buddha at Gṛddhrakūṭa to the bodhisattvas Sarvaśūra and Bhaiṣajyasena. The text is celebrated as a classic witness to the Mahāyāna 'cult of the book', repeatedly emphasizing the limitless karmic merit, protection, and purification accrued through hearing, reciting, copying, and worshiping the sūtra itself. Multiple birch-bark copies were recovered from the Gilgit cache; it also circulated in Central Asia, surviving in Khotanese fragments as well as early Chinese (T. 423 by 月婆首那 / Upaśūnya, 538 CE) and Tibetan translations.
SA_K10_bsu045_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra, traditionally presented as the words of the Buddha delivered at Gṛddhrakūṭa in Rājagṛha.
SA_K10_bsu045_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 260 numbered sections ([SaSū 1] to [SaSū 260]), concluding with colophons from Gilgit manuscripts B and D.
translations: Giotto Canevascini, The Khotanese Saṅghāṭasūtra: A Critical Edition, Wiesbaden: Dr. Ludwig Reichert Verlag, 1993 (Beiträge zur Iranistik 14). (English)
phags pa zung gi mdo'i chos kyi rnam grangs (Derge Kangyur D 102): translated by Jinamitra, Dānaśīla, sna nam btsun pa ye shes sde (Tibetan)

SA_K10_dbsu1-4u.title: Daśabalasūtra (1–4)
SA_K10_dbsu1-4u.summary: A compilation of four canonical Āgama discourses reconstructed from Sanskrit manuscript fragments found in Central Asia (Turfan collection) expounding the ten powers (daśabala) of a Tathāgata. These powers—including perfect knowledge of what is possible and impossible (sthānāsthāna), the ripening of karma (karmavipāka), the states of meditative attainment (dhyānavimokṣasamādhisamāpatti), the spiritual faculties of sentient beings (indriyaparāparatā), and the eradication of contaminants (āsravakṣaya)—form the foundation of the Buddha's authority to proclaim the wheel of Dharma and utter his lion's roar (siṃhanāda). Belonging to the (Mūla-)Sarvāstivāda transmission, these discourses parallel texts in the Chinese Saṃyuktāgama (T 99, no. 684) and Pāli Dasabala suttas in the Saṃyutta and Aṅguttara Nikāyas.
SA_K10_dbsu1-4u.attribution: Mainstream Āgama discourse preserved in Central Asian Sanskrit manuscript fragments (Turfan collection) belonging to the Sarvāstivāda / Mūlasarvāstivāda transmission.
SA_K10_dbsu1-4u.edition: Composite edition based on four scholarly publications: (1) Ernst Waldschmidt, Bruchstücke buddhistischer Sūtras aus dem zentralasiatischen Sanskritkanon I, Leipzig 1932 (Kleinere Sanskrit-Texte, 4; Nachdruck: Monographien zur indischen Archäologie, Kunst und Philologie, 2. Wiesbaden, Stuttgart 1979), pp. 207–225; and Ernst Waldschmidt, 'Ein zweites Daśabalasūtra', Mitteilungen des Instituts für Orientforschung 6 (1958), pp. 382–387, 397–403 [Nachdruck: Von Ceylon bis Turfan, Göttingen 1967, pp. 347–352, 362–368]; (2) Ernst Waldschmidt, 'Ein zweites Daśabalasūtra', Mitteilungen des Instituts für Orientforschung 6 (1958), pp. 388–392, 395f. [Nachdruck: Von Ceylon bis Turfan, Göttingen 1967, pp. 353–357, 360–361]; (3) Jin-il Chung, 'Ein drittes und ein viertes Daśabala-Sūtra', Sanko Bunka Kenkyūjo Nenpo 40 (2009), pp. 1–32 [4–16]; (4) Jin-il Chung, ibid., pp. 1–32 [17–29].
SA_K10_dbsu1-4u.coverage: partial — Contains four separate sūtras reconstructed from Central Asian manuscript fragments. Sūtras 1, 2, and 3 are preserved and reconstructed through to their respective colophons; Sūtra 4 is incomplete, breaking off at § 7.9–9 where the Sanskrit manuscript text is missing.
translations: Ernst Waldschmidt, 'Ein zweites Daśabalasūtra', Mitteilungen des Instituts für Orientforschung 6 (1958), pp. 382–405. (German)

SA_K10_disu.title: Dīpasūtra

SA_K10_divav29u.title: Aśokāvadāna
SA_K10_divav29u.summary: The Aśokāvadāna is a major Sanskrit Buddhist narrative recounting the legendary life, conversion, and reign of the Mauryan emperor Aśoka, together with legends of the elder Upagupta and Aśoka's son Kuṇāla. In Sanskrit the text is related to the Divyāvadāna anthology, while versions survive in Chinese translation (T 2042 and T 2043).
SA_K10_divav29u.edition: Sujitkumar Mukhopadhyaya, The Aśokāvadāna. New Delhi: Sahitya Akademi, 1963.
SA_K10_divav29u.coverage: complete — Text based on Sujitkumar Mukhopadhyaya's 1963 edition (pp. 1–135).
translations: John S. Strong, The Legend of King Aśoka: A Study and Translation of the Aśokāvadāna. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1983. (English)
Jean Przyluski, La légende de l'empereur Açoka (Açoka-Avadāna) dans les textes indiens et chinois. Paris: Paul Geuthner, 1923. (French)
Eugène Burnouf, Introduction à l'histoire du Buddhisme indien. Paris: Imprimerie Royale, 1844. (French)

SA_K10_divav33u.title: Śārdūlakarṇāvadāna
SA_K10_divav33u.summary: The Śārdūlakarṇāvadāna (Divyāvadāna Chapter 33) narrates how the low-caste Mātaṅga (Caṇḍāla) maiden Prakṛti falls in love with the Buddha's disciple Ānanda and attempts to entrap him with love sorcery, but is rescued by the Buddha, ordained as a bhikṣuṇī, and attains arhatship. In explaining this event, the Buddha recounts the past-life debate between Triśaṅku, the chieftain of the Caṇḍālas, and the learned Brahmin Puṣkarasārin, providing a vigorous critique of the Brahmanical hereditary caste hierarchy by arguing that the four varṇas are mere nominal conventions rather than innate biological categories. Within this dialogue, the text incorporates an encyclopedic treatise on pre-Hellenistic Indian divination, palmistry, and nakṣatra astronomy and astrology.
SA_K10_divav33u.attribution: Canonical Buddhist narrative traditionally transmitted both as Chapter 33 of the Divyāvadāna compilation and as an independent work in Sanskrit, Tibetan (Toh 358), and Chinese (Taishō 1300, 1301).
SA_K10_divav33u.edition: Mukhopadhyaya, Sujitkumar (ed.). The Śārdūlakarṇāvadāna. Santiniketan: The Visvabharati Publishing Department, 1954.
SA_K10_divav33u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the work as edited by Sujitkumar Mukhopadhyaya (pp. 1–210), containing both the framing narrative of Prakṛti and Ānanda and the extensive dialogue on caste and divination/astrology between Triśaṅku and Puṣkarasārin.
translations: stag rna'i rtogs pa brjod pa (Derge Kangyur D 358): translated by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna, 'bro seng dkar shAkya 'od (Tibetan)

SA_K10_divyav_u.title: Divyāvadāna
SA_K10_divyav_u.summary: The Divyāvadāna ('Divine Narratives') is an anthology of 38 Buddhist avadāna stories composed in Sanskrit, illustrating the workings of karma, past births, and moral causation through the lives of the Buddha, his disciples, householders, and monarchs. A major portion of the text draws directly from the Vinaya of the Mūlasarvāstivāda tradition. Famous narrative components include the Aśokāvadāna cycle, Kuṇālāvadāna, Pūrṇāvadāna, and Śārdūlakarṇāvadāna.
SA_K10_divyav_u.attribution: An anonymous anthology of Buddhist narrative literature. Narrative material corresponds directly to sections of the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, while other sections include well-known cycles such as the Aśokāvadāna and the Śārdūlakarṇāvadāna.
SA_K10_divyav_u.edition: P. L. Vaidya (ed.), Divyāvadāna, Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute of Post-Graduate Studies and Research in Sanskrit Learning, 1959.
SA_K10_divyav_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 38 avadānas as found in standard printed editions, opening with Avadāna 1 (Koṭikarṇāvadāna) and concluding with Avadāna 38 (Maitrakanyakāvadāna).
translations: Andy Rotman (transl.), Divine Stories: Divyāvadāna, Part 1, Classics of Indian Buddhism, Boston: Wisdom Publications, 2008; Part 2, Boston: Wisdom Publications, 2017. (English)
John S. Strong (transl.), The Legend of King Aśoka: A Study and Translation of the Aśokāvadāna, Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1983. (English)
Eugène Burnouf (transl.), Introduction à l'histoire du Buddhisme indien, Paris: Imprimerie Royale, 1844. (French)

SA_K10_dvavims_tu.title: Dvāviṃśatyavadānakathā
SA_K10_dvavims_tu.summary: The Dvāviṃśatyavadānakathā ('Narrative of Twenty-Two Avadānas') is a medieval Nepalese Buddhist narrative anthology organized around twenty-two core avadāna tales extolling the merits of donation (dāna), caitya and stūpa worship, and monastic veneration. Framed by an opening and closing dialogue between the Elder Upagupta and King Aśoka, it draws substantially on classical sources such as the Avadānaśataka and Divyāvadāna while also incorporating prose passages written in Newar Buddhist Sanskrit. The collection is arranged in 24 sections (kathās/sūtras), beginning with the exhortation to merit (puṇyaprotsāhana) and culminating in the Puṇyotsāhāvadānasūtra.
SA_K10_dvavims_tu.attribution: The work is an anonymous narrative compilation produced in Nepal, framed traditionally as a dialogue between the Elder Upagupta and King Aśoka.
SA_K10_dvavims_tu.edition: Mamiko Okada, ed., Dvāviṃśatyavadānakathā: Ein mittelalterlicher buddhistischer Text zur Spendenfrömmigkeit. Nach zweiundzwanzig nepalesischen Handschriften kritisch herausgegeben. Indica et Tibetica 24. Bonn: Indica et Tibetica Verlag, 1993.
SA_K10_dvavims_tu.coverage: complete — Contains the complete text in 24 chapters (sections I–XXIV) following the introductory verses (Dak_O.1–4 through Dak_24.14).

SA_K10_dvtasutu.title: Devatāsūtra with Alpadevatāsūtra (beginning only)
SA_K10_dvtasutu.summary: Two short canonical sūtras copied one after the other in Gilgit manuscript no. 13. In the Devatāsūtra, a radiant deity visits the Buddha at the Jetavana in Śrāvastī and asks a series of riddle-like questions in verse. The Buddha's verse answers name speech, passion, hatred and ignorance as the worst dangers, patience and wisdom as armour and weapon, merit as the one possession fire, water and thieves cannot take, and the Buddha as the only physician. The Alpadevatāsūtra has the same setting: a deity asks which people go to heaven. Only the Buddha's first answers survive, praising restraint and abstention from killing.
SA_K10_dvtasutu.attribution: Canonical discourses of the early Buddhist tradition, traditionally transmitted as the word of the Buddha (buddhavacana).
SA_K10_dvtasutu.edition: Adelheid Mette, 'Zwei kleine Fragmente aus Gilgit', Studien zur Indologie und Iranistik 7 (1981), pp. 133–151.
SA_K10_dvtasutu.coverage: partial — Devatāsūtra complete: prose frame, 23 verses and closing formula ('… bhagavato 'ntikāt prakrāntā', GBM 1545.3). Alpadevatāsūtra: only the introductory prose and verses 1–3 (GBM 1545.4–1545.8), where the Gilgit manuscript breaks off.
translations: Tian qingwen jing 天請問經, tr. Xuanzang (唐 玄奘譯, 648 CE), T 592 (T15n0592). (Chinese (parallel of the Devatāsūtra))
lha'i mdo (Derge Kangyur D 329) (Tibetan)

SA_K10_ekottaru.title: Ekottarāgama (fragments)
SA_K10_ekottaru.summary: The Ekottarāgama (or Ekottarikāgama, 'Increased by One Collection') is one of the four core Āgama collections in the early Buddhist canon, organizing discourses numerically according to groups of items (parallel to the Pāli Aṅguttara Nikāya). While the complete text survives only in an early Chinese translation (T 125), these Sanskrit fragments were identified among the Gilgit manuscripts in Jammu and Kashmir. The surviving portions include discourses on mental training, the senses, monastic offences (āpatti), and karmic retribution.
SA_K10_ekottaru.attribution: Canonical Buddhist āgama preserved through early monastic transmission and traditionally attributed to the Buddha. The Gilgit manuscript fragments represent a North Indian Sanskrit mainstream Buddhist tradition (often assigned to the Mūlasarvāstivāda or Sarvāstivāda school).
SA_K10_ekottaru.edition: Chandra Bhal Tripathi: Ekottarāgama-Fragmente der Gilgit-Handschrift, Reinbek 1995 (Studien zur Indologie und Iranistik, Monographie 2).
SA_K10_ekottaru.coverage: fragment — Manuscript fragments from the Gilgit find containing sections numbered EĀ.Trip 2.1 through 36.42, with substantial lacunae and missing leaves.
translations: Taishō Tripiṭaka, No. 125 (Zēngyī āhán jīng 增壹阿含經), translated by Gautama Saṃghadeva (瞿曇僧伽提婆) (397 CE). (Chinese)

SA_K10_kathinau.title: Kaṭhināvadāna
SA_K10_kathinau.summary: The Kaṭhināvadāna is a Buddhist narrative work belonging to the Sanskrit avadāna literature preserved in Nepalese manuscripts. It integrates Vinaya ritual prescriptions concerning the kaṭhina robe ceremony—detailing the cutting, sewing, ritual marking, and offering of monastic robes at the end of the rains retreat (varṣāvāsa)—with didactic avadāna stories illustrating the karmic merit of giving to the Saṅgha. The narrative episodes draw heavily upon and share motifs with canonical Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya sources such as the Bhaiṣajyavastu and the Anavataptagāthā.
SA_K10_kathinau.attribution: The Kaṭhināvadāna is an anonymous Buddhist narrative text belonging to the post-canonical avadāna literature of Nepal.
SA_K10_kathinau.edition: Almuth Degener, Das Kaṭhināvadāna: Eingeleitet, herausgegeben und übersetzt, Bonn: Indica et Tibetica Verlag, 1990 (Indica et Tibetica, 16).
SA_K10_kathinau.coverage: complete — Complete e-text of Almuth Degener's critical edition, containing the introductory vinaya/ritual section followed by narrative accounts, matching the printed text from opening homage to the concluding story of Sundarī.
translations: Almuth Degener, Das Kaṭhināvadāna: Eingeleitet, herausgegeben und übersetzt, Bonn: Indica et Tibetica Verlag, 1990 (Indica et Tibetica, 16). (German)

SA_K10_kbavk10u.title: Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā (chapter 10: Garbhāvakrāntyavadāna)
SA_K10_kbavk10u.author: Kṣemendra
SA_K10_kbavk10u.summary: The Garbhāvakrāntyavadāna (designated Garbhāvakrāntinirdeśa in its colophon) forms the 10th pallava of Kṣemendra's Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā. Set near Campā as a discourse given by the Buddha to Ānanda, the text expounds the physical and karmic mechanics of conception, intra-uterine gestation, childbirth, and life cycle sufferings. Modern printed editions by Das and Vaidya lacked the Sanskrit text; Michael Hahn edited the text from the Tibetan Tanjur in 1997.
SA_K10_kbavk10u.edition: Michael Hahn, 'Kṣemendras Garbhāvakrāntyavadāna (Sanskrittexte aus dem tibetischen Tanjur II)', Journal of the European Ayurvedic Society, vol. 5 (1997), pp. 82–112.
SA_K10_kbavk10u.coverage: partial — Complete for pallava (chapter) 10 (all 26 stanzas and the chapter colophon), which constitutes chapter 10 of the Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā.

SA_K10_kbavk75u.title: Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā (chapter 75: Pratītyasamutpādāvadāna)
SA_K10_kbavk75u.author: Kṣemendra
SA_K10_kbavk75u.summary: The Pratītyasamutpādāvadāna is the 75th pallava of Kṣemendra's Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā. In contrast to the narrative-heavy avadānas in the collection, this short piece of 11 verses presents the Buddha at Jetavana in Śrāvastī explaining the twelve links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) from ignorance (avidyā) through aging and death (jarāmaraṇa), concluding with instruction on their cessation through meditative reflection.
SA_K10_kbavk75u.attribution: Composed by Kṣemendra as the 75th chapter of his Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā.
SA_K10_kbavk75u.edition: Marek Mejor (ed.), Kṣemendra's Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā: Studies and Materials, Studia Philologica Buddhica, Monograph Series 8, Tokyo: The International Institute for Buddhist Studies, 1992, pp. 16–22.
SA_K10_kbavk75u.coverage: partial — Complete text of the 75th pallava (11 verses and concluding colophon) of the Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā.
translations: Marek Mejor, Kṣemendra's Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā: Studies and Materials, Studia Philologica Buddhica, Monograph Series 8, Tokyo: The International Institute for Buddhist Studies, 1992. (English)
Deborah Black (tr. as Padma-chos-'phel), Leaves of the Heaven Tree: The Great Compassion of the Buddha, Berkeley: Dharma Publishing, 1997. (English)

SA_K10_kbavk93u.title: Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā (pallava 93: Sumāgadhāvadāna)
SA_K10_kbavk93u.author: Kṣemendra
SA_K10_kbavk93u.summary: Pallava 93 of Kṣemendra's Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā comprises 111 classical Sanskrit verses retelling the legend of Sumāgadhā, daughter of the merchant Anāthapiṇḍada. Married into a non-Buddhist Jain (kṣapaṇaka) household in Puṇḍravardhana, Sumāgadhā is appalled by the behavior of the naked ascetics and miraculously invites the Buddha from Jetavana. The Buddha flies to Puṇḍravardhana with his retinue of arhats, converts her in-laws and the local populace through miracles and Dharma discourse, and reveals the karmic origins of her fortune from previous lifetimes.
SA_K10_kbavk93u.attribution: Composed by Kṣemendra in Kashmir. The pallava colophon explicitly confirms: 'iti kṣemendraviracitāyāṃ bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatāyāṃ sumāgadhāvadānaṃ trinavatitamaḥ pallavah.' The Tibetan translation (D 4155) attributes the work to Somendra.
SA_K10_kbavk93u.edition: P.L. Vaidya, Ksemendra's Avadanakalpalata, vol. II. Darbhanga: Mithila Institute 1959 (Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, 23), pp. 526-534 (Avadāna 93)
SA_K10_kbavk93u.coverage: partial — Contains pallava 93 (111 verses) of the Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā.
translations: byang chub sems dpa'i rtogs pa brjod pa dpag bsam gyi 'khri shing (Derge Tengyur D 4155): translated by Lakṣmīkara, shong lo tsA ba rdo rje rgyal mtshan/ shong ston rdo rje rgyal mtshan; revised by zhwa lu lo tsA ba chos skyong bzang po; at mang yul 'phags pa'i drung dge 'dun bzhi sde'i gtsug lag khang (Tibetan)

SA_K10_klpdrapu.title: Kalpadrumāvadānamālā (chapter 10: Subhūtyavadāna)
SA_K10_klpdrapu.summary: The Kalpadrumāvadānamālā is a Buddhist narrative collection in verse framed as a dialogue between the elder Upagupta and King Aśoka. This tenth chapter, the Subhūtyavadāna, relates the story and virtues of the elder Subhūti, extolling the practice of loving-kindness (maitrī) and rebirth in Sukhāvatī.
SA_K10_klpdrapu.attribution: The Kalpadrumāvadānamālā is an anonymous Buddhist avadānamālā collection in verse, framed as edifying discourses by the elder Upagupta to Emperor Aśoka.
SA_K10_klpdrapu.edition: text appended to P.L. Vaidya's edition of the Avadanasataka (Darbhanga 1958, Buddhist Sanskrit Texts; 19)
SA_K10_klpdrapu.coverage: partial — Contains solely chapter 10, the Subhūtyavadāna (486 verses, numbered KDA_1 to KDA_486 in the e-text).

SA_K10_mahama_u.title: Mahāmantrānusāriṇī
SA_K10_mahama_u.summary: The Mahāmantrānusāriṇī ('Follower of the Great Mantra') is a Buddhist apotropaic scripture belonging to the popular Pañcarakṣā ('Five Protections') collection and classified by Peter Skilling as an independent Mahāsūtra closely related to the Vaiśālīpraveśa-sūtra. Set in Rājagṛha and Vaiśālī, the Buddha instructs Ānanda to stand at the city threshold (indrakīla) of plague-ridden Vaiśālī and recite protective formulas and verses in the name of the Buddhas, Arhats, and gods to expel diseases and malevolent spirits. The text blends protective incantations (mantrapadas) with verses radiating universal loving-kindness (maitrī) to secure the well-being of all living beings.
SA_K10_mahama_u.attribution: Canonical Buddhist protective discourse (rakṣā/dhāraṇī) preserved in Nepalese Sanskrit manuscripts of the Pañcarakṣā pentad and edited by Peter Skilling in connection with the Vaiśālīpraveśa-mahāsūtra.
SA_K10_mahama_u.edition: Peter Skilling, Mahāsūtras: Great Discourses of the Buddha, Vol. I: Texts, Oxford 1994 (PTS), pp. 608-622.
SA_K10_mahama_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Sanskrit version covering sections C.0.1 through C.9.

SA_K10_maivy_pu.title: Maitreyavyākaraṇa
SA_K10_maivy_pu.summary: The Maitreyavyākaraṇa is an Indian Buddhist prophetic scripture (vyākaraṇa) in anuṣṭubh verse predicting the advent of the future Buddha Maitreya. Framed as a dialogue between the Buddha Śākyamuni and his disciple Śāriputra, the work describes the utopian prosperity of the city Ketumatī under the universal monarch (cakravartin) Śaṅkha, Maitreya's miraculous birth, renunciation, and attainment of bodhi beneath the Nāgavṛkṣa tree, concluding with an account of the three assemblies through which he leads countless beings to liberation.
SA_K10_maivy_pu.attribution: A Buddhist canonical / prophetic verse scripture (vyākaraṇa) framed as an exposition delivered by the Buddha Śākyamuni to Śāriputra, traditionally treated as buddhavacana.
SA_K10_maivy_pu.edition: 1. Gilgit Manuscript (incomplete), ed. Prabhas Chandra Majumder, Ārya Maitreya-vyākaraṇam, Calcutta 1959 (also published in Nalinaksha Dutt, Gilgit Manuscripts, vol. IV, Calcutta 1959, pp. xxix ff. and 185 ff., under P.C. Mazumder) = MvyG; 2. Calcutta Manuscript (incomplete), ed. Sylvain Lévi = MvyC; 3. Kathmandu Manuscript (complete), ed. Zennō Ishigami = MvyK.
SA_K10_maivy_pu.coverage: complete — The file contains three recensions/manuscript witnesses presented consecutively: (1) Gilgit manuscript (incomplete, vv. 31–108); (2) Calcutta manuscript; and (3) Kathmandu manuscript.
translations: Lévi, Sylvain. 1932. 'Maitreya le consolateur.' In Études d'orientalisme publiées par le Musée Guimet à la mémoire de Raymonde Linossier. (French)
Ishigami, Zennō. 1968. 'Maitreya-vyākaraṇa wayaku' [弥勒受記(Maitreya-vyākaraṇa)和訳]. Suzuki Gakujutsu Zaidan Kenkyū Nenpō 4. (Japanese)

SA_K10_n206u.title: Avikalpapraveśadhāraṇī
SA_K10_n206u.summary: The Avikalpapraveśadhāraṇī is a short Mahāyāna dhāraṇī-sūtra setting forth the doctrinal method for entering the nonconceptual realm. It outlines the sequential abandonment of four categories of conceptual signs—fundamental defiled phenomena (the five aggregates), remedies (the perfections), reality/suchness, and fruition/attainment—effected through non-mental engagement (amanasikāra). The sūtra was cited and commented upon by Indian authors including Kamalaśīla and Maitrīpa.
SA_K10_n206u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna Buddhist text delivered in sūtra format by the Buddha to the bodhisattva Avikalpaprabhāsa at Rājagṛha.
SA_K10_n206u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the dhāraṇī-sūtra, comprising the opening nidāna, the dialogue on entering nonconceptuality, the systematic abandonment of the four classes of conceptual signs via amanasikāra, similes, two concluding verses, and the rejoinder formula.
translations: Taishō Shinshū Daizōkyō No. 654 (Vol. 15), 'Foshuo ru wufenbie famen jing' (佛說入無分別法門經), trans. Shihu (施護), 980 CE. (Chinese)
phags pa rnam par mi rtog par 'jug pa zhes bya ba'i gzungs (Derge Kangyur D 142): translated by Jinamitra, Dānaśīla, ska ba dpal brtsegs (Tibetan)

SA_K10_n262u.title: Āryānityatāsūtra
SA_K10_n262u.summary: The Āryānityatāsūtra is a short canonical discourse set at Jetavana in Śrāvastī, where the Buddha expounds that all conditioned phenomena (sarvasaṃskāra) are impermanent, unstable, and destined to perish. The sūtra systematically demonstrates that death is inevitable for all beings, from wealthy householders and universal monarchs to ascetics, gods of the three realms, and even arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and tathāgatas. It concludes with famous gāthās comparing life to earthen vessels made by a potter and ripe fruit destined to fall, culminating in the stanza: sarve kṣayāntā nicayāḥ patanāntāḥ samucchrayāḥ / saṃyogāśca viyogāntā maraṇāntaṃ hi jīvitam.
SA_K10_n262u.attribution: A canonical discourse attributed to Śākyamuni Buddha.
SA_K10_n262u.edition: M.B. Shakya, 'Aryanityatasutra', Buddhist Himalaya 1, no. 1 (1988), pp. 58–60.
SA_K10_n262u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the short sūtra, including opening nidāna, prose exposition on all classes of beings, and the concluding four verses.

SA_K10_n266u.title: Āryasāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchānāmamahāyānasūtra
SA_K10_n266u.summary: The Āryasāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā (Toh 155 / T 599) is a concise Mahāyāna sūtra set in the underwater palace of the nāga king Sāgara. The Buddha explains that proclaiming and understanding the four aphorisms or summaries of the Dharma (caturdharmoddāna: all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, all contaminated phenomena are suffering, all phenomena are without self, and nirvāṇa is peace) is tantamount to expounding all eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dharma (caturaśītidharmaskandhasahasra). As no ancient Sanskrit manuscript witness of this short recension survives, the Sanskrit text preserved here is a modern scholarly reconstruction from the Tibetan Kangyur version.
SA_K10_n266u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna discourse traditionally considered buddhavacana. The Sanskrit e-text is a modern Sanskrit reconstruction (saṃskṛte punaruddhṛtam) from the Tibetan text.
SA_K10_n266u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the short sūtra on the four seals of the Dharma (caturdharmoddāna, Toh 155), including the opening nidāna, the discourse to Nāga King Sāgara, the conclusion, and the reconstructed Tibetan translation colophon naming Surendrabodhi and Bandé Yeshé Dé (Jñānasena).
translations: Yijing (義淨), trans., Fo wei hailongwang shuo fayin jing (佛為海龍王說法印經), Taishō Tripiṭaka, No. 599, 711 CE. (Chinese)
phags pa klu'i rgyal po rgya mtshos zhus pa zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo (Derge Kangyur D 155): translated by Surendrabodhi, sna nam btsun pa ye shes sde (Tibetan)

SA_K10_n267u.title: Saṃghāṭasūtra
SA_K10_n267u.summary: The Saṃghāṭasūtra is a prominent Mahāyāna scripture presented as a discourse delivered by the Buddha on Vulture Peak (Gṛddhrakūṭa) to the bodhisattva Sarvaśūra and a vast assembly. Operating as a devotional text and dharma-paryāya, it teaches the immense spiritual merit, purification of severe negative karma, and divine protection generated by hearing, copying, reciting, and revering the sūtra. Through extended parables, visionary accounts, and past-life narratives, the scripture underscores the inevitability of karmic consequences and the assurance of eventual awakening for all beings.
SA_K10_n267u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra, traditionally presented as the authentic discourse of Śākyamuni Buddha (buddhavacana); no individual historical author is attributed.
SA_K10_n267u.edition: Oskar von Hinüber & Noriyuki Kudo (eds.), Saṃghāṭasūtra (Gilgit Manuscripts in the National Archives of India), Tokyo: IRIAB/Soka University.
SA_K10_n267u.coverage: complete — Contains the Sanskrit text in numbered paragraphs, from the opening nidāna at Gṛddhrakūṭa through paragraph [260] and the final colophons of Gilgit manuscripts B and D.
translations: Giotto Canevascini, The Khotanese Saṅghāṭasūtra: A Critical Edition (Beiträge zur Iranistik 14), Wiesbaden: Dr. Ludwig Reichert Verlag, 1993. (English)
phags pa zung gi mdo'i chos kyi rnam grangs (Derge Kangyur D 102): translated by Jinamitra, Dānaśīla, sna nam btsun pa ye shes sde (Tibetan)

SA_K10_n269u.title: Āryatriratnānusmṛtisūtra
SA_K10_n269u.summary: A short Mahāyāna liturgical sūtra giving the formulas for recollecting (anusmṛti) the Buddha, the Dharma and the Saṅgha, each a list of epithets and qualities (the Buddha formula 'ityapi buddho bhagavān...' followed by an extended Mahāyāna praise, the Dharma and Saṅgha formulas largely as in the canonical stock passages). It is widely recited in the Tibetan tradition.
SA_K10_n269u.coverage: complete — Short liturgical text: Sanskrit/Tibetan title lines, then the three recollection formulas (buddhānusmṛti, dharmānusmṛti, saṃghānusmṛti), ending 'āryatriratnānusmṛtisūtraṃ samāptam'.
translations: 'phags pa sangs rgyas rjes su dran pa (Derge Kangyur D 279) (Tibetan)
chos rjes su dran pa (Derge Kangyur D 280) (Tibetan)

SA_K10_n2942u.title: Saddharmasmṛtyupasthānasūtra (chapter 2)
SA_K10_n2942u.summary: The Saddharmasmṛtyupasthānasūtra is an Indian Buddhist canonical sūtra. Chapter 2 focuses on internal mindfulness of phenomena (dharmānupaśyanā) undertaken by an ascetic practitioner (yogācāra), analyzing sensations and mental states.
SA_K10_n2942u.attribution: Scriptural canonical text of Indian Buddhism.
SA_K10_n2942u.edition: Daniel M. Stuart, A Less Traveled Path: Saddharmasmṛtyupasthānasūtra Chapter 2, Critically Edited with a Study on Its Structure and Significance..., 2 vols., Sanskrit Texts from the Tibetan Autonomous Region 18, Beijing/Vienna: Austrian Academy of Sciences Press / China Tibetology Publishing House, 2015.
SA_K10_n2942u.coverage: partial — Contains Chapter 2 of the scripture, spanning pages 1–111 of Stuart's 2015 edition.
