SA_K10_n443u.title: Mahāmeghasūtra (partial)
SA_K10_n443u.summary: The Mahāmeghasūtra (also known as the Meghasūtra) is an apotropaic Mahāyāna dhāraṇī scripture dedicated to rainmaking and drought alleviation. Set in the aquatic palace of the serpent kings Nanda and Upananda, the text relates the Buddha's instruction on loving-kindness (maitrī) as the supreme antidote to suffering, followed by protective dhāraṇīs and ritual manual procedures for bringing rain. While closely related to chapters 64–65 of the larger doctrinal Mahāmeghasūtra (T387 / Toh 232), this sūtra circulated independently throughout Asia as a specialized rain-ritual text (Tibetan Toh 235/657; Chinese T989, T991, T992, T993).
SA_K10_n443u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna Buddhist scripture presented traditionally as buddhavacana ('word of the Buddha'). It functions as an apotropaic rainmaking dhāraṇī-sūtra.
SA_K10_n443u.edition: Cecil Bendall (ed.), 'The Megha-sūtra', Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society of Great Britain and Ireland, New Series 12 (1880), pp. 286–311.
SA_K10_n443u.coverage: partial — The e-text covers only the initial section of Cecil Bendall's 1880 edition (pp. 287–297 out of 286–311). It includes the nidāna in the abode of the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda, the list of 177 nāgarājas, the discourse on loving-kindness (maitrī), and the Sarvasukhadā-dhāraṇī, breaking off abruptly at segment 241 ('sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhitāni sarva-sukha-pradānāni |') without the subsequent Buddha names, the second dhāraṇī, the Great Cloud mandala ritual, or the colophon.

SA_K10_n446u.title: Meghasūtra (abridged)
SA_K10_n446u.summary: The Meghasūtra is a Mahāyāna rain-making text set in the palace of the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda. A nāga king asks how nāgas may be freed from suffering and send rain; the Buddha teaches friendliness (maitrī), a dhāraṇī and the names of cloud-related Tathāgatas, and then prescribes a ritual with a 'great cloud circle' (mahāmeghamaṇḍala) for use in drought. The colophon identifies it as the 65th chapter (Vātamaṇḍalīparivarta) of the Mahāmeghasūtra.
SA_K10_n446u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna sūtra presented as the words of Śākyamuni Buddha delivered in the palace of the serpent kings Nanda and Upananda.
SA_K10_n446u.edition: Cecil Bendall, 'The Megha-Sūtra', Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society n.s. 12 (1880), pp. 286-311 (e-text via DSBC/Nagarjuna Institute).
SA_K10_n446u.coverage: partial — Runs from the opening nidāna to the colophon: iti śrīmahāmeghād mahāyānasūtrādvātamaṇḍalīparivartaḥ pañcaṣaṣṭitamaḥ samāptaḥ.

SA_K10_n526u.title: Sarvatathāgatādhiṣṭhānavyūhasūtra
SA_K10_n526u.summary: A Mahāyāna dhāraṇī scripture set on Mount Potalaka, the realm of Avalokiteśvara, where the Buddha Śākyamuni enters a samādhi called sarvasattvamahākaruṇājñānasthita, radiating light throughout the cosmos to illuminate the Buddha-fields and alleviate the sufferings of all beings. Bodhisattvas such as Avalokiteśvara, Mañjuśrī, and Vajrapāṇi, along with an assembly of directional kings (lokapālas), yakṣiṇīs, and deities, offer and endorse protective dhāraṇī mantras for the benefit and safeguard of dharma-reciters in future ages.
SA_K10_n526u.edition: Nalinaksha Dutt (ed.), Gilgit Manuscripts, vol. I, pp. 49-89, Delhi: Sri Satguru Publications, 1984 (2nd ed.).
SA_K10_n526u.coverage: complete — Text of the sūtra as edited by Nalinaksha Dutt in Gilgit Manuscripts, vol. I, pp. 49–89.
translations: Taishō Shinshū Daizōkyō, no. 1375 (佛說莊嚴王陀羅尼呪經), 1 fascicle, translated by Yijing (義淨) in 701 CE. (Chinese)

SA_K10_nagasu.title: Nagarasūtra
SA_K10_nagasu.summary: The Nagarasūtra ('City Sūtra') of the Sarvāstivāda Saṃyuktāgama (Nidānasaṃyukta, Sūtra 5 in Tripāṭhī's edition) describes the Bodhisattva's discovery of dependent origination and compares the noble eightfold path to an old road leading to an ancient city that a king then restores. It corresponds to the Pāli Nagarasutta (SN 12.65) and Chinese Saṃyuktāgama 287. An expanded version, the Nagaropamasūtra, was used as a protective text in Central Asia.
SA_K10_nagasu.attribution: Early Buddhist canonical discourse transmitted in the Sarvāstivāda Saṃyuktāgama / Nidānasaṃyukta.
SA_K10_nagasu.coverage: unclear — The catalog entry has no segment file (0 segments, 0 characters), so there is no e-text to check. The name 'nagarasūtra' matches the heading 'Sūtra 5: nagarasūtra' of Tripāṭhī's Nidānasaṃyukta in SA_K10_nidansyu, which suggests this entry was meant to be that sūtra split out.
translations: Bongard-Levin, Boucher, Fukita, Wille 1996 (SWTF Beiheft 6). (English)

SA_K10_nagsu_pu.title: Nagaropamasūtra
SA_K10_nagsu_pu.summary: The Nagaropamasūtra ('Discourse on the Simile of the City') is a canonical discourse of the Sarvāstivāda Saṃyuktāgama (Nidānasaṃyukta 14; paralleled in the Pāli Nagara Sutta, SN 12.65). In this discourse, the Buddha explains how prior to awakening he investigated the twelve links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), comparing his discovery of the ancient path to an explorer finding an overgrown trail leading to a majestic forgotten city. In Central Asian Sanskrit manuscript transmission, the discourse was preserved as an independent apotropaic text (rakṣā), enlarged with a narrative and ritual appendix extolling its recitation for protection against perils.
SA_K10_nagsu_pu.attribution: Early canonical Buddhist discourse transmitted within the Sarvāstivāda Saṃyuktāgama (Nidānasaṃyukta) and independently preserved as an apotropaic / protective (rakṣā) text across Central Asian Sanskrit manuscripts. The e-text includes both the canonical sermon (Part I) and its ritual narrative appendix (Part II).
SA_K10_nagsu_pu.edition: Gregory Bongard-Levin, Daniel Boucher, Takamichi Fukita, and Klaus Wille, 'The Nagaropamasūtra: An Apotropaic Text from the Saṃyuktāgama. A Transliteration, Reconstruction, and Translation of the Central Asian Sanskrit Manuscripts', in Sanskrit-Texte aus dem buddhistischen Kanon: Neuentdeckungen und Neueditionen III (Sanskrit-Wörterbuch der buddhistischen Texte aus den Turfan-Funden, Beiheft 6), Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 1996, pp. 7–131.
SA_K10_nagsu_pu.coverage: complete — Complete reconstructed composite Sanskrit text (NagSū I.1–II.32), comprising Part I (the canonical discourse, corresponding to Nidānasaṃyukta 14) and Part II (the apotropaic/narrative appendix), edited from the Pelliot, Stein, Petrovsky, and Hoernle manuscript fragments.
translations: Gregory Bongard-Levin, Daniel Boucher, Takamichi Fukita, and Klaus Wille, 'The Nagaropamasūtra: An Apotropaic Text from the Saṃyuktāgama', in Sanskrit-Texte aus dem buddhistischen Kanon: Neuentdeckungen und Neueditionen III, Göttingen 1996, pp. 7–131. (English)
Takamichi Fukita and Daniel Boucher, 'Kyōshu to shite no "Jōyukyō"' [The Nagaropamasūtra as the Deified Teacher], Bukkyō Daigaku Sōgō Kenkyūjo Kiyō. (Japanese)

SA_K10_nidansyu.title: Nidānasaṃyukta (25 sūtras)
SA_K10_nidansyu.summary: The Nidānasaṃyukta is the section of the Sarvāstivāda Saṃyuktāgama on dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda). This e-text has the 25 sūtras that Tripāṭhī edited from Turfan manuscripts, which explain causal doctrine with similes such as the tree, the lamp, the city, the bundle of reeds and the monkey. They correspond to sūtras of the Pāli Nidānasaṃyutta (SN 12) and the Chinese Saṃyuktāgama (T 99).
SA_K10_nidansyu.attribution: Canonical Sarvāstivāda Āgama collection, traditionally regarded as the word of the Buddha (buddhavacana).
SA_K10_nidansyu.edition: Chandrabhāl Tripāṭhī (ed.), Fünfundzwanzig Sūtras des Nidānasaṃyukta, Berlin: Akademie-Verlag, 1962 (Sanskrittexte aus den Turfanfunden, 8).
SA_K10_nidansyu.coverage: partial — Tripāṭhī's Sūtras 1–25 (3 and 4 printed together; Sūtra 5 = nagarasūtra), with lacunae marked '+' and '..'; ends with Sūtra 25.17 (abhavya). The Nidānasaṃyukta in the Sarvāstivāda Saṃyuktāgama has many more sūtras (cf. Chinese Saṃyuktāgama, T 99), so this is a selection of what survives in Sanskrit.

SA_K10_ratnakeu.title: Mahāsaṃnipātaratnaketudhāraṇīsūtra (chapters 1–6 and 10–13, with lacunae)
SA_K10_ratnakeu.summary: The Ratnaketuparivarta (Mahāsaṃnipātaratnaketudhāraṇīsūtra) is a Mahāyāna sūtra of the Mahāsaṃnipāta collection. It opens with the conversion of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana despite Māra's obstruction and goes on to the Buddha's subjugation of Māra and his hosts, the revelation of protective dhāraṇīs and the protection of the Dharma. The Sanskrit text survives in a Gilgit manuscript with a donor colophon of the Paṭola Ṣāhi king Vikramādityanandi.
SA_K10_ratnakeu.attribution: Anonymous Mahāyāna sūtra, part of the Mahāsaṃnipāta collection. Tibetan translation Toh 138; Chinese translation T 402 (catalog links ZH_T13_0402, BO_K10_D0138).
SA_K10_ratnakeu.edition: Yenshu Kurumiya (ed.), Ratnaketuparivarta, Sanskrit Text, Kyoto: Heirakuji-Shoten, 1978.
SA_K10_ratnakeu.coverage: partial — Extant Sanskrit text of the Gilgit manuscript as edited by Kurumiya (pp. 2–178): begins in ch. 1 ('folios 1-4 are missing'); notes in the e-text record the missing folios (including folio 99 and chapters 7 to 9); ends with ch. 13 (Niṣṭhāgamaparivarta) and the donor colophon of the Paṭola Ṣāhi king Vikramādityanandi. Survives in Tibetan (Toh 138) and Chinese.

SA_K10_samghscu.title: Saṃghāṭasūtra
SA_K10_samghscu.summary: The Saṃghāṭasūtra is a Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra set on Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha, consisting of dialogues between the Buddha and the bodhisattvas Sarvaśūra and Bhaiṣajyasena. It emphasizes the spiritual perils of cyclic existence, the visionary experiences of dying and intermediate states, karmic retribution and purification, and the boundless merit accrued from hearing, reciting, or copying the text. It was exceptionally widely copied in northwestern India and Central Asia, surviving in numerous Sanskrit manuscripts from Gilgit and Dunhuang, as well as Khotanese, Sogdian, Tibetan, and Chinese translations.
SA_K10_samghscu.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna sūtra presented as the word of the Buddha (buddhavacana); transmitted anonymously.
SA_K10_samghscu.edition: Giotto Canevascini: The Khotanese Saṅghāṭasūtra. Wiesbaden: Dr. Ludwig Reichert Verlag, 1993 (Beiträge zur Iranistik, 14).

SA_K10_samyu_wu.title: Saṃyuktāgama (Parivrājakasaṃyukta fragments)
SA_K10_samyu_wu.summary: This e-text contains Sanskrit fragments of seven sūtras belonging to the Parivrājakasaṃyukta of the canonical Saṃyuktāgama, recovered from Idykutšari in Chinese Turkestān. They correspond to sūtras 966–972 in the Chinese Za ahan jing (T 99) and record discussions between the Buddha or Ānanda and wandering non-Buddhist ascetics (including Pūrṇika, Kokanada, Dīrghanakha, and Śarabha) on metaphysical questions, views, and genuine 'Brahmin truths' (brāhmaṇasatya). The digital text reproduces the three-part critical edition published by Noriaki Hosoda between 1989 and 1991, which revised and completed Richard Pischel's editio princeps of 1904.
SA_K10_samyu_wu.attribution: Canonical discourse collection of early Buddhism.

SA_K10_sjdh_u.title: Sarvajñatākāradhāraṇī
SA_K10_sjdh_u.summary: The Sarvajñatākāradhāraṇī is a Mahāyāna Buddhist dhāraṇī scripture related to the Karuṇāpuṇḍarīkasūtra. It contains the dhāraṇī formula for entering into the mode of omniscience (sarvajñatākāradhāraṇīmukhapraveśa), granting bodhisattvas retention of the Dharma, and includes incantation phrases designated as Drāviḍamantrapada.
SA_K10_sjdh_u.attribution: Anonymous Mahāyāna Buddhist scripture presented as the word of the Buddha (buddhavacana).

SA_K10_srajsgiu.title: Samādhirājasūtra (chapters 1–11, 13, 15–22)
SA_K10_srajsgiu.summary: The Samādhirājasūtra (also known as the Candrapradīpasūtra) is a major Mahāyāna scripture centered on the meditative realization of the essential sameness of all phenomena (sarvadharmasvabhāvasamatā), through which all virtues of buddhahood and the bodhisattva path are perfected. It expounds the emptiness and non-substantiality of dharmas, the transcendent nature of the Tathāgata's dharmakāya, and the ideal ethical and ascetic conduct of bodhisattvas. The text is frequently cited by classical Indian Madhyamaka authors such as Candrakīrti and Śāntideva and plays a prominent role in Tibetan contemplative traditions.
SA_K10_srajsgiu.attribution: A canonical Mahāyāna sūtra traditionally received as buddhavacana, delivered by the Buddha Śākyamuni on Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭaparvata) to Candraprabha Kumārabhūta.
SA_K10_srajsgiu.coverage: partial — Diplomatic transcription of chapters 1–11, 13, and 15–22 (out of approximately 40 chapters of the complete text), corresponding to plates 2461–2613 of the Gilgit manuscript facsimile.
translations: Konstanty Régamey, Philosophy in the Samādhirājasūtra: Three Chapters from the Samādhirājasūtra (chapters 8, 19, 22), Warsaw, 1938. (English)
Chijun Tamura and Masamichi Ichigo, Daijō Butten, vols. 10 and 11. (Japanese)

SA_K10_sukhvysu.title: Sukhāvatīvyūhasūtra
SA_K10_sukhvysu.summary: The Sukhāvatīvyūhasūtra (commonly designated the Smaller or Shorter Sukhāvatīvyūha, and known in East Asian tradition as the Amitābhasūtra / Amituo jing) is a foundational Mahāyāna scripture of Pure Land Buddhism. Set in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī, Śākyamuni Buddha describes to Śāriputra the wondrous adornments and spiritual delights of Sukhāvatī, the western realm presided over by the Buddha Amitāyus. The sūtra proclaims that those who hear Amitāyus's name and maintain focused mindfulness on it will be reborn in Sukhāvatī, a message attested by the buddhas of all directions.
SA_K10_sukhvysu.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna sūtra traditionally delivered as buddhavacana by Śākyamuni Buddha to Śāriputra in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī.
SA_K10_sukhvysu.edition: F. Max Müller & Bunyiu Nanjio (eds.), Sukhāvatī-vyūha, Anecdota Oxoniensia, Aryan Series, Part 2, Oxford, 1883; with annotations by Unrai Wogihara, in Jōdoshū zensho, p. 194 (notes p. 212).
SA_K10_sukhvysu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Smaller Sukhāvatīvyūhasūtra in 20 numbered sections, including opening nidāna and closing rejoicing/colophon.
translations: F. Max Müller, 1894. (English)

SA_K10_tbimbk_u.title: Tathāgatabimbakārāpaṇasūtra (fragment)
SA_K10_tbimbk_u.summary: A Buddhist discourse extolling the karmic fruit and spiritual merit generated by fashioning, commissioning, and worshipping images of the Buddha (tathāgatabimba / buddhapratimā). The Buddha recounts the former life of Prince Suvarṇaprabha, who in the era of the past Buddha Vipaśyin was a destitute farmer who fashioned a Buddha image and as a consequence experienced countless rebirths as a universal emperor (cakravartin), Indra, and Brahmā before attaining arhatship. The sūtra systematically lists permissible image materials (clay, stone, ivory, wood, gold, bronze, brass/tin, silver, crystal, and gems) and provides rare early epigraphic/ritual textual evidence for enshrining either bodily relics (sadhātuka) or the Pratītyasamutpāda stanza (sapratītyasamutpāda) inside Buddha statues.
SA_K10_tbimbk_u.attribution: Canonical Buddhist sūtra traditionally attributed to the speech of the Buddha (buddhavacana).
SA_K10_tbimbk_u.edition: Adelheid Mette, "Zwei kleine Fragmente aus Gilgit", Studien zur Indologie und Iranistik 7 (1981), pp. 133-151.
SA_K10_tbimbk_u.coverage: fragment — Preserves folios 2r1–5v1 of Gilgit manuscript No. 18 (GBM 1684.1–1691.2). Folio 1 (containing the introductory setting/nidāna) is missing, but the text is preserved continuously through the conclusion and colophons on folio 5v.

SA_K10_vrksu.title: Vṛkṣasūtra
SA_K10_vrksu.summary: Empty catalog placeholder, presumably for the Vṛkṣasūtra(s) of the Sanskrit Nidānasaṃyukta (Turfan, Sarvāstivāda Saṃyuktāgama). In those two short sūtras a tree that is tended grows and flourishes, while one that is uprooted, dried and burnt cannot grow again; so craving grows in one who sees enjoyment in things that lead to clinging (upādānīya dharma) and drives the chain of dependent origination, while seeing them as impermanent, as passing away and with dispassion ends craving and the whole mass of suffering. Parallels are the Rukkha suttas of the Pali Nidānasaṃyutta (SN 12.55–57) and Chinese Saṃyuktāgama sūtras (T 99, nos. 283–284).
SA_K10_vrksu.coverage: unclear — Empty placeholder in the collection (no segments or text).

SA_K12_adhsatpu.title: Adhyardhaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā
SA_K12_adhsatpu.summary: The Adhyardhaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in 150 Lines') is an influential Buddhist scripture bridging late Mahāyāna Prajñāpāramitā thought and esoteric Mantrayāna doctrine. It expounds the essential purity of all dharmas, declaring that worldly desires, passions, and sensory engagements are fundamentally pure (viśuddhi) when realized through non-dual transcendent wisdom. Known in East Asia as the Rishukyō (理趣經), primarily via Amoghavajra's 8th-century Chinese translation (T 243), the sūtra became one of the central liturgical recitations of the Japanese Shingon and Tendai traditions.
SA_K12_adhsatpu.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna/esoteric scripture, framed as delivered by Mahāvairocana Tathāgata to Vajrapāṇi and the bodhisattva assembly.
SA_K12_adhsatpu.edition: Toru Tomabechi: Adhyardhaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā, Sanskrit and Tibetan Texts critically edited, Beijing/Vienna 2009 (Sanskrit Texts from the Tibetan Autonomous Region, 5).
SA_K12_adhsatpu.coverage: complete — Complete Sanskrit text in 43 numbered sections (AśP 1–43) matching Tomabechi's edition, concluding with the sūtra colophon: 'ity adhyardhaśatikā bhagavatī prajñāpāramitā samāptā //'.
translations: Edward Conze, 'The Adhyardhaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā' (English)

SA_K12_bsu004_u.title: Sarvatathāgatoṣṇīṣasitātapatrānāmāparājitāpratyaṅgirāmahāvidyārājñī
SA_K12_bsu004_u.summary: The Sarvatathāgatoṣṇīṣasitātapatrānāmāparājitāpratyaṅgirāmahāvidyārājñī is an influential Mahāyāna/Vajrayāna apotropaic dhāraṇī scripture centered on the goddess Sitātapatrā ('The White Parasol'). Set in the Sudharmā assembly hall of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the narrative recounts how Śākyamuni Buddha enters meditative absorption (samādhi), from whose crown protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) emanates this protective incantation. The text provides extensive salutations to buddhas, bodhisattvas, and brahmanical deities, followed by powerful averting and binding formulas (pratyaṅgirā) designed to protect practitioners against evil spirits, demonic afflictions, curses, diseases, and untimely death.
SA_K12_bsu004_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna/Vajrayāna Buddhist protective scripture, traditionally narrated as delivered by the Buddha Śākyamuni in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven by manifesting the goddess Sitātapatrā and her protective mantrapadas from his uṣṇīṣa.
SA_K12_bsu004_u.edition: Ngawang Samten and Janardan Pandey, in: Dhih Journal, vol. 33. Sarnath: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies 2002, pp. 145-154.
SA_K12_bsu004_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the scripture from the opening nidāna through homages, dhāraṇī invocations, averting formulas, and the closing colophon.
translations: Shārap (沙囉巴), trans. Foding da baisangai tuoluoni jing (佛頂大白傘蓋陀羅尼經), Taishō Tripiṭaka no. 976 (vol. 19), 1314 (Yuan dynasty). (Chinese)

SA_K12_bsu012_u.title: Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabharājasūtra
SA_K12_bsu012_u.summary: The Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabharājasūtra is an influential Mahāyāna scripture devoted to Bhaiṣajyaguru, the Medicine Buddha, who presides over the eastern realm of Vaidūryanirbhāsā. The text relates the twelve vows made by the Buddha during his bodhisattva career to heal physical and mental infirmities, alleviate poverty and distress, and lead beings onto the Mahāyāna path. It prescribes devotional and ritual practices—including reciting his name and dhāraṇī, setting up forty-nine lamps and banners, and calling upon the twelve great yakṣa generals—to avert premature death and protect nations from calamity.
SA_K12_bsu012_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna scripture presented as the teaching of Śākyamuni Buddha delivered at Vaiśālī upon the request of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
SA_K12_bsu012_u.edition: P. L. Vaidya (ed.), Mahāyāna-sūtra-saṃgrahaḥ, Part 1, Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute 1961 (Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, 17), text no. 12.
SA_K12_bsu012_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the single-Buddha Bhaiṣajyaguru sūtra as edited in P. L. Vaidya (pp. 165–173), from the opening nidāna at Vaiśālī through the twelve vows, the dhāraṇī, ritual instructions against untimely death, the invocation of the twelve yakṣa generals, to the final rejoinder and colophon.

SA_K12_bsu035_u.title: Suvarṇaprabhāsasūtra
SA_K12_bsu035_u.summary: The Suvarṇaprabhāsasūtra ('Sūtra of the Golden Light') is an influential Mahāyāna canonical scripture that synthesizes doctrinal expositions of emptiness (śūnyatā) and the boundless lifespan of the Tathāgata with rituals of repentance and state protection. A pivotal episode centers on the bodhisattva Ruciraketu's vision of a golden drum radiating stanzas on confession and purification (deśanā). Protective deities including the Four Heavenly Kings (Caturmahārāja), Sarasvatī, Śrī, and Dṛḍhā pledge to guard righteous sovereigns and realms that uphold the sūtra, while subsequent chapters recount past-life narratives of the Buddha, notably the Vyāghrīparivarta (Mahāsattva jātaka) where the bodhisattva sacrifices his life to feed a starving tigress and her cubs.
SA_K12_bsu035_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna sūtra traditionally transmitted as the word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana); anonymous.
SA_K12_bsu035_u.edition: S. Bagchi, ed., Suvarṇaprabhāsasūtram, Bauddha-Saṃskṛta-granthāvalī (Buddhist Sanskrit Texts), Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute, 1967.

SA_K12_bsu041_u.title: Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa
SA_K12_bsu041_u.summary: The Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa is an encyclopedic Buddhist ritual compendium in 55 chapters, classified as a Kriyā-tantra. It details ritual procedures centered on Mañjuśrī and the Tathāgata family, including mantras, maṇḍalas, cloth-painting rites (paṭavidhāna), mudrās, and homa rites. Chapter 53 (Rājavyākaraṇaparivarta) preserves an account of northern Indian dynasties through the early Pāla era (reign of Gopāla, composed around the middle of the 8th century CE).
SA_K12_bsu041_u.attribution: Scriptural Buddhist work; categorized in Tibetan canon taxonomies as a Kriyā-tantra.
SA_K12_bsu041_u.edition: M. M. T. Ganapati Sâstrî [T. SA_K12_bsu050_u.title: Svalpākṣarā prajñāpāramitā
SA_K12_bsu050_u.summary: The Svalpākṣarā prajñāpāramitā is a short scripture belonging to the late, tantric phase of the Prajñāpāramitā literature. Set on Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha, Avalokiteśvara asks Śākyamuni Buddha to teach a brief version of the Prajñāpāramitā accessible to beings of dull or lesser capacity (mandapudgala). The Buddha radiates light through all buddhafields and expounds essential ethical prerequisites together with a mantra/dhāraṇī formula.
SA_K12_bsu050_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna/esoteric scripture delivered as a discourse between Śākyamuni Buddha and Avalokiteśvara at Gṛdhrakūṭa in Rājagṛha.
SA_K12_bsu050_u.edition: P.L. Vaidya, in: Mahayana-sutra-samgrahah, Part 1. Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute 1961 (Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, 17)
SA_K12_bsu050_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the short sūtra matching P.L. Vaidya's edition (pp. 93–94), concluding with the standard colophon 'svalpākṣarā prajñāpāramitā samāptā'.

SA_K12_bsu055_u.title: Kauśikaprajñāpāramitāsūtra
SA_K12_bsu055_u.summary: A concise Mahāyāna Prajñāpāramitā sūtra spoken by the Buddha to Śakra (Kauśika) on Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha. The text expounds the nondual nature of the perfection of wisdom through negative dialectical statements, eighteen modes of emptiness (aṣṭādaśaśūnyatā), and verses found in the Vajracchedikā and the opening maṅgalācaraṇa of the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā. It concludes with a series of protective mantras and dhāraṇīs honoring Prajñāpāramitā, bridging exoteric Prajñāpāramitā philosophy with esoteric protective practice.
SA_K12_bsu055_u.attribution: Scriptural Mahāyāna work traditionally attributed to Gautama Buddha, delivered to Śakra Devānāmindra (addressed as Kauśika) on Gṛdhrakūṭa.
SA_K12_bsu055_u.edition: P. L. Vaidya (ed.), Mahāyāna-sūtra-saṃgrahaḥ, Part 1, Buddhist Sanskrit Texts 17, Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute, 1961 (Sutra section, text no. 55).
SA_K12_bsu055_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the short sūtra as edited in P. L. Vaidya (1961), pp. 95–96, terminating with the colophon 'kauśikanāma prajñāpāramitā samāptā'.

SA_K12_bsu056_u.title: Adhyardhaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā
SA_K12_bsu056_u.summary: The Adhyardhaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā, also known as Prajñāpāramitānaya or Rishukyō, is expounded by Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas including Mahāvairocana, Śākyamuni, and Vajrapāṇi. The text teaches viśuddhi-pada (purity of passion, sensory perception, etc.) and is preserved in Sanskrit, Chinese (e.g. T 240, T 241, T 242, T 243), and Tibetan canonical traditions (D 17, D 489).
SA_K12_bsu056_u.attribution: Canonical scripture traditionally expounded by the Buddha (Mahāvairocana / Śākyamuni) and various bodhisattvas; no human author is attributed.
SA_K12_bsu056_u.edition: P. L. Vaidya (ed.), 'Adhyardhaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā' (text no. 56), in: Mahāyāna-sūtra-saṃgraha, Part 1, Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute, 1961 (Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, 17).

SA_K12_dhvajkdu.title: Dhvajāgrakeyūrādhāraṇī with Dhvajāgrakeyūrāhṛdaya
SA_K12_dhvajkdu.summary: The Dhvajāgrakeyūrādhāraṇī is a protective Mahāyāna dhāraṇī set in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven. After being defeated in battle by the asura king Vemacitrin, Śakra devendra requests assistance from the Buddha, who reveals the invincible formula originally received during a past life from the Tathāgata Aparājitadhvaja. Affixing the formula to standard pennants (dhvajāgra) or wearing it around one's neck grants invulnerability and decisive victory in warfare and dispute. MS Tucci 3.2.16 contains an individualized amuletic version tailored for the practitioner Āvadhūta Śrī Ālakhavajra and concludes with the short Dhvajāgrakeyūrāhṛdaya mantra.
SA_K12_dhvajkdu.attribution: A Buddhist apotropaic dhāraṇī preserved across Sanskrit manuscripts from Nepal and Tibet, and canonical collections in Tibetan (Kanjur: Toh 612, Toh 923) and Chinese (Taishō 1363).
SA_K12_dhvajkdu.edition: Paolo Giunta, 'The Āryadhvajāgrakeyūrā nāma dhāriṇī: Diplomatic Edition of MS Tucci 3.2.16', in Sanskrit Texts from Giuseppe Tucci's Collection, Part I, ed. Francesco Sferra, Roma: Istituto Italiano per l'Africa e l'Oriente, 2008 (Manuscripta Buddhica, 1), pp. 187–194.
SA_K12_dhvajkdu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the dhāraṇī sūtra followed by the short Dhvajāgrakeyūrāhṛdaya mantra, edited diplomatically from MS Tucci 3.2.16.

SA_K12_dhvajkeu.title: Dhvajāgrakeyūrādhāraṇī (dhāraṇī only)
SA_K12_dhvajkeu.summary: The Dhvajāgrakeyūrādhāraṇī ('Armlet on the Crest of the Banner') is a Buddhist protective dhāraṇī in which the Buddha teaches Śakra a spell for victory after the gods' defeat by the asuras; attached to banners or worn on the body, it protects against enemies and fear. This e-text has only the spell itself with its closing svāhā formulas, in the form used in Newar liturgy, without the narrative frame.
SA_K12_dhvajkeu.attribution: Considered canonical buddhavacana in Mahāyāna and Tantric Buddhism. In the full sūtra narrative, the Buddha Śākyamuni preaches the protective spell to Śakra (Indra) on the Pāṇḍukambala rock in Trāyastriṃśa heaven after the gods have suffered defeat at the hands of Vemacitrin's asura host, stating he received it originally from Tathāgata Aparājitadhvaja.
SA_K12_dhvajkeu.coverage: excerpt — 22 lines (ca. 1,500 characters): homage to Dhvajāgrarāja tathāgata, the long dhāraṇī (jaya jaya vijaya ... jayantu dhvaje) and four closing svāhā formulas. The nidāna (Śakra's defeat by the asuras, the Buddha's teaching) and the concluding instructions of the full text (cf. MS Tucci 3.2.16 in SA_K12_dhvajkdu, Toh 612) are absent. Typical Newar liturgical form; no colophon.
translations: Chinese: 佛說無能勝幡王如來莊嚴陀羅尼經, Taishō 943, tr. Dānapāla (施護), 980 CE. (Chinese)

SA_K12_ekmuhr_u.title: Ekādaśamukhahṛdaya
SA_K12_ekmuhr_u.summary: The Ekādaśamukhahṛdaya is an early esoteric Buddhist dhāraṇī-sūtra set in Śrāvastī. Avalokiteśvara expounds the eleven-faced heart-mantra to Śākyamuni, explaining ten worldly protections (such as defense against disease, poison, weapons, fire, and untimely death) and four transcendental blessings experienced at the time of death. The work details specific ritual actions, including oblations, homa rites, and the consecration of water, which served as the primary scriptural basis for the widespread cult and iconography of the Eleven-Faced Avalokiteśvara across Asia.
SA_K12_ekmuhr_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna Buddhist dhāraṇī scripture spoken by Avalokiteśvara before Śākyamuni Buddha at Śrāvastī; traditional scriptural text without human author.
SA_K12_ekmuhr_u.edition: Nalinaksha Dutt (ed.), Giglit [sic] Manuscripts, Vol. 1, Srinagar 1939. (Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies, 71,1). Input by Somadeva Vasudeva.
SA_K12_ekmuhr_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Ekādaśamukhahṛdaya according to the Gilgit manuscript (MS 33a, fols. 1–14; Dutt 1939, pp. 35–40). Segments 173–177 transcribe an extra short mantra in a secondary scribal hand from the manuscript margin/end folios following the text.
translations: Amoghavajra (Bukong), trans., Shiyimian Guanzizai pusa xin miyan niansong yigui jing (十一面觀自在菩薩心密言念誦儀軌經), Taishō no. 1069 (Vol. 20), 746–774 CE. (Chinese)

SA_K12_ganphrdu.title: Gaṇapatihṛdayadhāraṇī
SA_K12_ganphrdu.summary: The Gaṇapatihṛdayadhāraṇī (also known as the Gaṇapatihṛdaya) is a concise esoteric Buddhist dhāraṇī scripture framed as a discourse delivered by the Buddha to Ānanda on Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa) near Rājagṛha. It teaches the heart-mantras of Gaṇapati (invoked under names such as Mahāgaṇapati, Gaṇapati, Gaṇādhipati, and Gaṇeśvara) alongside ritual procedures and worldly benefits such as prosperity, protection from adversity, and retentive memory.
SA_K12_ganphrdu.attribution: Canonical Buddhist dhāraṇī text presented as the word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana) taught to Ānanda on Vulture Peak.
SA_K12_ganphrdu.edition: Yutaka Iwamoto (ed.), Kleinere Dhāraṇī Texte (Beiträge zur Indologie, 2), Kyoto 1937, pp. 10–12.
SA_K12_ganphrdu.coverage: complete — Complete short dhāraṇī sūtra in 41 prose segments, containing the nidāna, the Gaṇapati mantras, ritual instructions and benefits (anuśaṃsā), and the closing colophon (āryamahāgaṇapatihṛdayaṃ samāptam).

SA_K12_grahmdhu.title: Grahamātṛkānāmadhāraṇī
SA_K12_grahmdhu.summary: The Grahamātṛkānāmadhāraṇī ('The Dhāraṇī of the Mother of Planets') is a short esoteric Buddhist astral-ritual text centered on Grahamātṛkā, the personified Buddhist Mother of Planets, and the propitiation of celestial bodies. Set in the city of Aḍakavatī where the Buddha instructs the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the text provides anthropomorphic iconographic descriptions, mandalas, offerings, and mantras for the nine planets (navagraha), the twenty-eight lunar asterisms (nakṣatra), and the twelve signs of the zodiac (rāśi) to avert astral and demonic afflictions. In Newar Buddhism, it forms the Saturday recitation within the widely recited Saptavāra ('Seven Days') dhāraṇī compendium.
SA_K12_grahmdhu.attribution: Esoteric Buddhist scriptural text presenting a dialogue between the Buddha and the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi; anonymous.
SA_K12_grahmdhu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the dhāraṇī as published in Dhīḥ 39 (2005), pp. 169–176.
translations: phags ma gza' rnams kyi yum zhes bya ba'i gzungs (Derge Kangyur D 660): revised by dge bsnyen grags pa rgyal (Tibetan)

SA_K12_madadh_u.title: Mahādaṇḍadhāraṇīśītavatī
SA_K12_madadh_u.summary: The Mahādaṇḍadhāraṇīśītavatī ('The Great Staff Dhāraṇī, the Cool One') is an apotropaic Mahāyāna Buddhist scripture that in later transmission became standardly included in the Pañcarakṣā ('Five Protections') collection under the title Mahāśītavatī. Set in the Śītavana charnel ground near Rājagṛha, the Buddha delivers the protective spell to his son Rāhula, who is afflicted by grahas, demons, and hostile creatures. The work presents the protective vidyā and ritual practices—including the knotting of enchanted protective cords—intended to shield the fourfold saṅgha from illnesses, poisons, weapons, wild animals, and malevolent supernatural beings.
SA_K12_madadh_u.attribution: Anonymous Mahāyāna apotropaic scripture traditionally framed as spoken by the Buddha to his son Rāhula at Śītavana.
SA_K12_madadh_u.edition: Hidas, Gergely (2017) Mahā-Daṇḍadhāraṇī-Śītavatī: A Buddhist Apotropaic Scripture. In: V. Vergiani, D. Cuneo, C.A. Formigatti (eds.) Indic Manuscript Cultures through the Ages. Material, Textual, and Historical Investigations. De Gruyter, Berlin: 449-486.
SA_K12_madadh_u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 10 numbered sections following Gergely Hidas's critical edition, concluding with 'āryamahādaṇḍadhāraṇīśītavatī samāptā'.

SA_K12_mahpratu.title: Mahāpratisarāmahāvidyārājñī
SA_K12_mahpratu.summary: The Mahāpratisarāmahāvidyārājñī ('Great Queen of Spells, the Great Amulet') is a widely influential Buddhist apotropaic scripture, forming the principal text in the Pañcarakṣā ('Five Protectors') pentad. Set atop Mount Vajrameru, it features the Buddha expounding potent dhāraṇīs, mantra syllables, and detailed ritual instructions for preparing and wearing protective amulets. The text integrates nine testimonial narratives illustrating the dhāraṇī's power to grant protection against poison, execution, disease, demonic affliction, and premature death.
SA_K12_mahpratu.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna Buddhist dhāraṇī scripture (classified under Kriyātantra in the Tibetan Kangyur, Toh 561); traditional buddhavacana presented as spoken by the Buddha.
SA_K12_mahpratu.edition: Gergely Hidas: Mahāpratisarā-Mahāvidyārājñī, The Great Amulet, Great Queen of Spells. Introduction, Critical Editions and Annotated Translation, New Delhi: International Academy of Indian Culture and Aditya Prakashan 2012 (Śata-Piṭaka Series: Indo-Asian Literatures, 636).
SA_K12_mahpratu.coverage: complete — Text of the edition in two kalpas matching Gergely Hidas (2012). Kalpa 2 concludes with: mahāpratisarāyā mahāvidyārājñyā rakṣāvidhānakalpo vidyādharasyāyaṃ samāptaḥ.

SA_K12_manivdhu.title: Mahāmaṇivipulavimānaviśvasupratiṣṭhitaguhyaparamarahasyakalparājadhāraṇī (fragment)
SA_K12_manivdhu.summary: A fragmentary Buddhist ritual text preserved in a Gilgit manuscript, containing maṇḍala ritual, abhiṣeka formulas, mudrās, mantras, and iconographic instructions including depictions of the Buddha, Vajrapāṇi, and Maṇivajra.
SA_K12_manivdhu.attribution: Buddhist dhāraṇī scripture preserved in a fragmentary Gilgit manuscript (dated ca. 488–726 CE by statistical dating model) and translated into Chinese and Tibetan.
SA_K12_manivdhu.edition: H. Matsumura, 'A Text on Esoteric Iconography from the Gilgit Manuscripts', in: The Mikkyo Zuzo (The Journal of Buddhist Iconography) 2 (1983), pp. 71-79.

SA_K12_manjnspu.title: Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti
SA_K12_manjnspu.summary: The Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti is an influential Buddhist tantric scripture presented as a discourse delivered by Śākyamuni Buddha at the request of Vajrapāṇi, praising Mañjuśrī as the non-dual primordial gnosis (jñānasattva). It has commentaries by figures such as Mañjuśrīkīrti and was widely transmitted and translated across Indian, Tibetan, and Chinese Buddhist traditions.
SA_K12_manjnspu.attribution: Canonical Buddhist scripture presented as an exposition by the Buddha Śākyamuni requested by Vajrapāṇi; identified in its colophon as extracted from the Samādhijālapaṭala of the sixteen-thousand-verse Māyājālatantra (Māyājālaṣoḍaśasāhasrika).

SA_K12_maricdhu.title: Mārīcīnāmadhāraṇī
SA_K12_maricdhu.summary: The Mārīcīnāmadhāraṇī is a short Buddhist apotropaic dhāraṇī sūtra focused on the solar goddess Mārīcī ('Ray of Light'). Set at the Jetavana grove in Śrāvastī, the Buddha describes Mārīcī as an invisible deity who moves before the sun and moon, and reveals that reciting her name and incantations protects the practitioner from capture, binding, burning, robbery, weapons, wild animals, and hostile foes. The text contains supplications for safety in traveling, followed by dhāraṇī mantras and binding spells designed to immobilize all adversaries.
SA_K12_maricdhu.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna/Vajrayāna dhāraṇīsūtra framed as a discourse delivered by the Buddha at Jetavana in Śrāvastī.
SA_K12_maricdhu.edition: Āryamārīcī-nāma-dhāraṇī, in: Dhīḥ: A Rare Buddhist Texts Research Journal, Sarnath, Varanasi: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 2006, pp. 157–158.

SA_K12_mekhdh_u.title: Mekhalādhāraṇī (Gilgit fragments)
SA_K12_mekhdh_u.summary: The Mekhalādhāraṇī ('Girdle spell') is a Buddhist protective dhāraṇī set in the Nyagrodhārāma at Kapilavastu: when the boy Rāhula is frightened at night by a rākṣasī, the Buddha teaches Ānanda the Mekhalā vidyā, which summons gods, yakṣa generals and four directional rākṣasīs to protect him. The text also gives ritual instructions (offerings, a protective thread, rubbing rites) and a list of hostile spells the vidyā cuts off. This e-text is Tripathi's 1981 edition of the incomplete Gilgit leaves.
SA_K12_mekhdh_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna dhāraṇī/rakṣā scripture presented as spoken by the Buddha to Ānanda.
SA_K12_mekhdh_u.edition: Chandrabhāl Tripathi, 'Gilgit-Blätter der Mekhalā-dhāraṇī', Studien zur Indologie und Iranistik 7 (1981), pp. 153–161.

SA_K12_mpratpru.title: Mahāpratisarāvidyārājñī
SA_K12_mpratpru.summary: The Mahāpratisarāvidyārājñī ('The Queen of Spells, the Great Amulet') is the primary and most widespread scripture in the Buddhist Pañcarakṣā ('Five Protections') collection. Preserved across two chapters—an initial narrative detailing the origins and efficacy of the spell (prathamakalpa) and an extensive ritual manual (rakṣāvidhānakalpa)—the sūtra teaches the dhāraṇī of Mahāpratisarā for averting physical and spiritual dangers such as poison, illness, untimely death, weapons, and lower rebirths. The work is particularly known for its instructions on manufacturing, consecrating, and wearing written dhāraṇī amulets on the body.
SA_K12_mpratpru.attribution: Canonical scripture preserved independently as well as in the popular Pañcarakṣā pentad; classified in the Tibetan Kangyur under D 561.
SA_K12_mpratpru.edition: Yutaka Iwamoto (ed.), Mahāpratisarā Pañcarakṣā II, Kyoto 1937 (Beiträge zur Indologie, 3).

SA_K12_mprsvdhu.title: Mahāpratisarāvidyādhāraṇī
SA_K12_mprsvdhu.summary: The Mahāpratisarāvidyādhāraṇī is an apotropaic Buddhist scripture centering on the goddess Mahāpratisarā. It contains extended protective dhāraṇīs, bīja mantras, and verses extolling the apotropaic efficacy of wearing and chanting the spell against illnesses, poisons, malignant spirits, and perils during pregnancy and childbirth.

SA_K12_n220u.title: Nārāyaṇaparipṛcchā āryamahāmāyāvijayavāhinī nāma dhāraṇī
SA_K12_n220u.summary: A Buddhist apotropaic dhāraṇī scripture focused on state protection and military victory. Set on Mount Svarṇaśṛṅga at the abode of Vaiśravaṇa, the Brahmanical deity Nārāyaṇa approaches the Buddha after suffering defeat at the hands of the asuras and requests a protective formula to ensure victory in combat. In response, the Buddha reveals the Mahāmāyāvijayavāhinī ('Victory-Bearing Great Illusion') dhāraṇī, recounts having received it in a previous age from Tathāgata Sarveśvara, and outlines the ritual application of the spell for monarchs facing battlefield conflict.
SA_K12_n220u.attribution: Canonical Buddhist dhāraṇī scripture regarded as Buddhavacana.
SA_K12_n220u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 9 numbered sections (1–9), including the opening nidāna and closing colophon.
translations: 'phags pa byams pas zhus pa zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo (Derge Kangyur D 149) (Tibetan)

SA_K12_n221u.title: Ṣaṇmukhīdhāraṇī
SA_K12_n221u.summary: The Ṣaṇmukhīdhāraṇī ('Dhāraṇī of the Six Gates') is a concise Mahāyāna dhāraṇī-sūtra set in the sky above the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, where the Buddha addresses an assembly of bodhisattvas. The text articulates six core aspirations (mukha) designed to transform samsaric experiences, confess negative deeds, comprehend Māra's actions, and dedicate all root virtues and liberation to all sentient beings, followed by the protective dhāraṇī formula. Recitation three times by day and three times by night is taught to purify karmic obscurations and rapidly yield unexcelled awakening.
SA_K12_n221u.attribution: Canonical dhāraṇī-sūtra attributed to Śākyamuni Buddha. Preserved in Sanskrit, Tibetan Kangyurs (D 141, D 526, D 916), and Chinese (T 1360, tr. Xuanzang, 645 CE).
SA_K12_n221u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the short dhāraṇī-sūtra, from the opening nidāna to the concluding recitation instructions and final colophon.
translations: Katsumi Mimaki, 'La Ṣaṇmukhī-dhāraṇī ou “Incantation des Six Portes”, texte attribue aux Sautran tika(II): Textes et Traduction', Nihon Chibetto Gakkai Kaihō (日本西蔵学会々報), 1977. (French)

SA_K12_n2920u.title: Amoghapāśakalparāja (chapter 27)
SA_K12_n2920u.summary: Chapter 27 of the Amoghapāśakalparāja, titled 'Amoghapāśavimokṣamaṇḍale lokottarasādhanavidhiḥ', details fire-offering (homa) and sādhana rites performed within the liberation maṇḍala (vimokṣamaṇḍala). It provides recipes and instructions for rituals involving aromatic substances, offerings, and mantras to destroy sins, cure ailments, avert perils, and attain spiritual accomplishments.
SA_K12_n2920u.attribution: A canonical tantra scripture without individual historical human author attribution.
SA_K12_n2920u.coverage: partial — Contains chapter 27 (paṭala 27), concluding with the colophon 'amoghapāśavimokṣamaṇḍale lokottarasādhanavidhiḥ samāptaḥ || (27)'.

SA_K12_n2922u.title: Amoghapāśakalparāja (chapter 21)
SA_K12_n2922u.summary: The Amoghapāśakalparāja is an extensive Buddhist Kriyātantra ritual manual focused on Amoghapāśa Avalokiteśvara. This portion (comprising Chapter 21, corresponding to Part VII of the modern diplomatic transcription, folios 91a1–97b4) opens with Vajrapāṇi questioning the Buddha Śākyamuni regarding the exhaustive ritual requirements, maṇḍala designs, and mudrās of the Amoghapāśahṛdaya cycle. The Buddha expounds the second sādhanavidhi for the Padmoṣṇīṣa maṇḍala, laying out fire rituals (homa), purification rites, visionary signs of siddhi, and the attainment of the status of a vidyādharacakravartin.
SA_K12_n2922u.attribution: A canonical Kriyātantra scripture framed as dialogues involving Śākyamuni Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, and Vajrapāṇi.

SA_K12_n2949u.title: Dhāraṇīsaṃgraha
SA_K12_n2949u.summary: The Dhāraṇīsaṃgraha is a comprehensive Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna liturgical anthology that collects numerous protective incantations (dhāraṇī), apotropaic sūtras, dhyāna/sādhana instructions, and stotras. Widely preserved and copied in Nepalese Buddhist manuscript culture, the compendium includes well-known scriptures such as the Pañcarakṣā texts, the Amoghapāśahṛdaya, the Vasudhārādhāraṇī, the Uṣṇīṣavijayādhāraṇī, and short Prajñāpāramitā texts. These texts were primarily copied and recited for ritual protection, longevity, healing, and the warding off of obstacles.
SA_K12_n2949u.attribution: A Newar Buddhist liturgical compendium comprising dozens of protective dhāraṇīs, sūtras, hṛdayas, dhāraṇī-kalpas, and stotras dedicated to various Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and tutelary deities.
SA_K12_n2949u.edition: Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha, ed. Atul Bhosekar (gen. ed. Venkataramana Reddy), New Delhi: National Mission for Manuscripts / New Bharatiya Book Corporation, 2017.
SA_K12_n2949u.coverage: complete — Complete transcription of the printed text in Atul Bhosekar's edition, corresponding to pp. 1–535 (page markers (1) through (535) embedded in the digital text).

SA_K12_n2990u.title: Grahamātṛkādhāraṇī
SA_K12_n2990u.summary: The Grahamātṛkādhāraṇī ('Mother of the planets') is a Buddhist dhāraṇī for pacifying the malign influence of the planets and lunar asterisms. Set in Aḍakavatī, it has the Buddha, at Vajrapāṇi's request, teach the worship, offerings and mantras of the grahas and asterisms, with rules for recitation and its benefits.
SA_K12_n2990u.attribution: Esoteric Buddhist canonical dhāraṇī scripture framed as the Buddha Śākyamuni's teaching in Aḍakavatī delivered upon the petition of Vajrapāṇi.
SA_K12_n2990u.coverage: complete — Complete: from the nidāna at Aḍakavatī with Vajrapāṇi, through the mantras and worship of the planets and asterisms, to the closing formula and colophon 'Āryyagrahamātṛkā nāma dhāraṇī samāptam'.
translations: Chinese: 諸星母陀羅尼經, Taishō 1302, tr. Facheng (法成), Tang dynasty, 856 CE; 佛說聖曜母陀羅尼經, Taishō 1303, tr. Fatian (法天), Song dynasty, 973 CE. (Chinese)

SA_K12_namekvsu.title: Namaskāraikaviṃśatistotra
SA_K12_namekvsu.summary: The Namaskāraikaviṃśatistotra is one of the most widely recited devotional hymns in Northern and Vajrayāna Buddhism, praising the goddess Tārā across twenty-one distinct manifestations. Each of the twenty-one core stanzas opens with the homage formula 'namas' and describes her specific iconographical features, protective attributes, and apotropaic qualities. The text concludes with a six-stanza phalaśruti detailing the apotropaic and spiritual benefits of reciting the hymn at dawn and dusk, concluding with an attribution to the Buddha Vairocana.
SA_K12_namekvsu.attribution: Traditionally regarded as canonical tantric revelation spoken by Buddha Vairocana, as formulated in the closing colophon: 'iti śrīsaṃyaksaṃbuddhavairocanabhāṣitaṃ bhagavatyāryatāradevyā namaskāraikaviṃśatistotraṃ saṃpūrṇaṃ samāptaṃ'. In the Tibetan Kangyur it is placed under D 438.
SA_K12_namekvsu.edition: Godefroy de Blonay, Matériaux pour servir à l'histoire de la déesse Tāra, Paris: 1895 (Bibliothèque de l'École des Hautes Études, 107), pp. 58-60.
SA_K12_namekvsu.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising the 21 homage verses praising the 21 aspects of Tārā (verses Nevs 1–21), followed by the 6-verse phalaśruti (verses 1–6) and the concluding colophon.

SA_K12_prajnhsu.title: Prajñāpāramitāhṛdayasūtra (short recension)
SA_K12_prajnhsu.summary: The Prajñāpāramitāhṛdayasūtra ('Heart of the Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra'), commonly known as the Heart Sūtra, is one of the most celebrated and widely recited scriptures in Mahāyāna Buddhism. In this short recension (saṃkṣiptamātṛkā), the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara explains to Śāriputra the insight of emptiness (śūnyatā), stating that form is emptiness and emptiness is form, and negating the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the aggregates, sense fields, and the twelve links of dependent origination. The text concludes with the famous dhāraṇī: 'gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā'.
SA_K12_prajnhsu.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna scripture. In the text, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara expounds the teaching of the emptiness (śūnyatā) of all dharmas to Śāriputra.
SA_K12_prajnhsu.coverage: complete — Text of the Prajñāpāramitāhṛdayasūtra opening with the namaskāra to Ārya-Prajñāpāramitā and concluding with the gate gate mantra and the colophon 'ity ārya-prajñāpāramitā-hṛdayaṃ samāptam'.
translations: Edward Conze, Buddhist Wisdom Books, London: Ruskin House, George Allen and Unwin, 1958. (English)

SA_K12_sarvttsu.title: Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṅgraha
SA_K12_sarvttsu.summary: The Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṅgraha is the foundational root tantra of the Yogatantra class in Indian esoteric Buddhism. Centered on Mahāvairocana and the five Buddha families (kulas) within the Vajradhātu maṇḍala, it expounds the enlightenment of Sarvārthasiddhi via the five progressive realizations (pañcākārābhisambodhi) along with extensive rituals for initiation (abhiṣeka), mudrās, and mantras. It forms the primary doctrinal and ritual bedrock for East Asian esoteric Buddhism (Zhenyan and Shingon) and directly influenced subsequent Indo-Tibetan tantric traditions.
SA_K12_sarvttsu.attribution: Canonical Buddhist Yogatantra scripture revealed by Bhagavān Mahāvairocana in the Akaniṣṭha heaven to Vajrapāṇi and the assembly of tathāgatas; anonymous scriptural revelation.
SA_K12_sarvttsu.edition: Lokesh Chandra (ed.), Sarva Tathāgata Tattva Saṅgraha. Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1987.
SA_K12_sarvttsu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all four primary sections (mahākalparājas: Sarvatathāgatamahāyānābhisamaya, Trilokavijaya, Sarvatathāgatadharmasamaya, and Sarvatathāgatakarmasamaya) and the concluding Uttarakalpa, ending with the canonical colophon: sarvatathāgatatatvasaṃgrahaṃ nāma mahāyānasūtraṃ samāptam.
translations: Giebel, Rolf W. (trans.), Two Esoteric Sutras: The Adamantine Pinnacle Sutra and The Susiddhikara Sutra, Berkeley: Numata Center for Buddhist Translation and Research, 2001. (English)

SA_K12_sdurst_u.title: Sarvadurgatipariśodhanatantra
SA_K12_sdurst_u.summary: The Sarvadurgatipariśodhanatantra ('Tantra of the Elimination of All Evil Destinies') is an influential Buddhist Yogatantra of the Vairocana cycle, dating roughly to the late 7th to 8th century CE. Set in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the tantra opens with Śakra pleading with Śākyamuni to deliver the god Vimalamaṇiprabha, who has fallen into the lower realms upon his death. Centering on Sarvavid Vairocana and his maṇḍalas, the text provides elaborate ritual instructions—including initiations, sādhanas, apotropaic rites, and especially mortuary and post-mortem ceremonies—designed to purify negative karmic imprints and ensure liberation from adverse transmigrations.
SA_K12_sdurst_u.attribution: Canonical Buddhist Yogatantra. The text was translated into Tibetan first toward the end of the eighth century (D 483, translated by Śāntagarbha and Jayarakṣita) and again in the thirteenth century by Chag Chos rje dpal with Devendradeva and Māṇikaśrījñāna (D 485).
SA_K12_sdurst_u.edition: Tadeusz Skorupski: The Sarvadurgatiparisodhana Tantra, Elimination of All Destinies, Sanskrit and Tibetan Texts with Introduction, English Translation and Notes. Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1983.
SA_K12_sdurst_u.coverage: complete — Text of the tantra corresponding to the edition by Tadeusz Skorupski (1983), beginning at p. 120 and concluding with the colophon: āryasarvadurgatipariśodhanatejorājasya tathāgatasyārhataḥ samyaksaṃbuddhasya kalpaikadeśaḥ samāptaḥ.
translations: Tadeusz Skorupski, The Sarvadurgatipariśodhana Tantra: Elimination of All Evil Destinies, Sanskrit and Tibetan Texts with Introduction, English Translation and Notes, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1983. (English)

SA_K12_tarb108u.title: Tārābhaṭṭārikānāmāṣṭottaraśatakastotra
SA_K12_tarb108u.summary: The Tārābhaṭṭārikānāmāṣṭottaraśatakastotra (Toh 727 / T 1106) is a canonical Vajrayāna/Mahāyāna litany praising the goddess Tārā by means of 108 sacred names and epithets. Set on Mount Potalaka, Avalokiteśvara reveals the names and associated mantras to the assembly in order to alleviate the sufferings of sentient beings. The hymn celebrates Tārā in both her benevolent and wrathful manifestations and concludes with a phalaśruti detailing the apotropaic, soteriological, and worldly benefits earned through its recitation.
SA_K12_tarb108u.attribution: Canonical scripture considered buddhavacana in Tibetan (Toh 727, Toh 745, Toh 1000) and Chinese (Taishō 1106) canons. The Sanskrit colophon explicitly designates it as buddhabhāṣita ('ity āryatārābhaṭṭārikāyā nāmāṣṭottaraśatakaṃ buddhabhāṣitaṃ samāptam').
SA_K12_tarb108u.edition: Godefroy de Blonay, Matériaux pour servir à l'histoire de la déesse buddhique Tārā, Paris: Émile Bouillon, 1895 (Bibliothèque de l'École des Hautes Études, 107), pp. 48–53.
SA_K12_tarb108u.coverage: complete — Complete text containing 57 verses along with introductory framing, prose/mantra invocations, and the concluding colophon, corresponding to pp. 48–53 of Godefroy de Blonay's 1895 edition.

SA_K12_vajvidhu.title: Vajravidāraṇīdhāraṇī
SA_K12_vajvidhu.summary: The Vajravidāraṇīdhāraṇī (also known as Vajravidāraṇādhāraṇī) is an apotropaic and purificatory dhāraṇī sūtra delivered by Vajrapāṇi through the spiritual power (anubhāva) of the Buddha. The scripture contains the root dhāraṇī along with heart (hṛdaya) and secondary heart (upahṛdaya) mantras intended to subdue harmful entities (grahas, bhūtas), neutralize sorcery, and clear karmic obscurations. It holds a major place in Indo-Tibetan Vajrayāna ritual as a primary text for ablution and purification (khrus chog).
SA_K12_vajvidhu.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna/Vajrayāna dhāraṇī scripture. The sūtra presents the dhāraṇī and mantras as proclaimed by Vajrapāṇi through the anubhāva and adhiṣṭhāna of the Buddha and all bodhisattvas.
SA_K12_vajvidhu.edition: Yutaka Iwamoto (ed.), Kleinere Dhāraṇī Texte, Kyoto 1937 (Beiträge zur Indologie, 2), pp. 7–9.
SA_K12_vajvidhu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the short dhāraṇī sūtra (pp. 7–9 in Iwamoto's edition), ending with the colophon 'iti śrī vajravidāraṇā nāma dhāraṇīhṛdayopahṛdayaṃ mūlasūtraṃ samāptam'.
translations: Shaluoba 沙囉巴 (tr.), Foshuo huaixiang jingang tuoluoni jing 佛說壞相金剛陀羅尼經 (Taishō Tripiṭaka no. 1417, 1314). (Chinese)

SA_K12_vjviddhu.title: Vajravidāraṇādhāraṇī
SA_K12_vjviddhu.summary: The Vajravidāraṇādhāraṇī is an apotropaic and purificatory dhāraṇī scripture classified under Kriyātantra. In its narrative framework, the Buddha enters an adamantine absorption and inspires the yakṣa lord Vajrapāṇi to proclaim an unbreakable vajra incantation designed to dispel malignant spirits, afflictions, and karmic impediments. The text concludes with instructional verses detailing an ablution (snāna) ritual using a consecrated vase to purify pollutants, pacify planetary obstacles, and promote longevity.
SA_K12_vjviddhu.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna/Vajrayāna dhāraṇī scripture (classified under Kriyātantra in Tibetan tradition). Spoken by Vajrapāṇi via the Buddha's empowerment.
SA_K12_vjviddhu.edition: "Āryavajravidāraṇā Nāma Dhāraṇī", in: Dhīḥ 40 (2005), eds. Ngawang Samten and Janardan Pandey, pp. 161–164.

SA_K12_bsu017_u.title: Hayagrīvavidyā
SA_K12_bsu017_u.summary: The Hayagrīvavidyā is a Buddhist dhāraṇī text preserved in the Gilgit manuscripts. Given without a frame story, it associates Hayagrīva with Avalokiteśvara and contains spells, ritual instructions, and mantras to counteract evil mantras, enemies, and misfortunes.
SA_K12_bsu017_u.attribution: Canonical text of early Buddhist dhāraṇī literature; opens with words of salutation eulogising Avalokiteśvara, though the reciter's name does not appear in the text.
SA_K12_bsu017_u.edition: Nalinaksha Dutt (ed.), Gilgit Manuscripts, Vol. I, Srinagar, 1939; reprinted Delhi: Sri Satguru Publications, 1984.

SA_K14_ahovk1_u.title: Ahorātravratakathā
SA_K14_ahovk1_u.summary: The Ahorātravratakathā details the ritual procedures and religious merits of observing the ahorātravrata centered on caitya worship. Framed as a discourse of the Buddha to Subhūti at Jetavana, it discusses the rules of the vow and praises caitya veneration.
SA_K14_ahovk1_u.edition: R. Handurukande, Three Sanskrit Texts on Caitya Worship: In Relation to the Ahorātravrata, Tokyo 2000 (Studia Philologica Buddhica, Monograph Series, 16).
SA_K14_ahovk1_u.coverage: complete — Text in 140 verses with prose passages, tagged Avk_1 through Avk_140.

SA_K14_ahovk2_u.title: Ahorātravratakathā (prose version)
SA_K14_ahovk2_u.summary: The prose recension of the Ahorātravratakathā is a Buddhist narrative explaining the ritual observance and benefits of the ahorātravrata in connection with caitya and Dharmadhātu worship. Set in Kapilavastu as an interchange involving the Buddha Śākyamuni, Subhūti, and Vajradhara, the narrative recounts the elder Śāriputra's visit to the city of Dharmapattana to instruct King Dharmadakṣa in the vow, ending with the king's attainment of liberation and seven maidens being reborn in Sukhāvatī.
SA_K14_ahovk2_u.attribution: Buddhist narrative text on the Ahorātravrata edited by Ratna Handurukande.
SA_K14_ahovk2_u.edition: R. Handurukande, Three Sanskrit Texts on Caitya Worship: In Relation to the Ahorātravrata, Tokyo 2000 (Studia Philologica Buddhica, Monograph Series, 16).
SA_K14_ahovk2_u.coverage: complete — Text of the prose recension in 27 editorial paragraphs (Avk_P_1 to Avk_P_27) concluding with 'iti ahorātravratakathā samāptā /'.

SA_K14_ajitsvyu.title: Ajitasenavyākaraṇa
SA_K14_ajitsvyu.summary: The Ajitasenavyākaraṇa (or Ajitasenavyākaraṇanirdeśa) is an early Mahāyāna scripture preserved in Sanskrit in the Gilgit find and Central Asian fragments, with no known Tibetan or Chinese translations. Framed in the manner of an avadāna, it relates how the Buddha instructs King Ajitasena through the śrāvaka disciple Nandimitra, emphasizing the merit of generous giving (dāna) and the salvific power of reciting Buddha names. Because it articulates universal buddhahood and Mahāyāna devotion within a mainstream narrative setting without the doctrine of dharmaśūnyatā, it is frequently cited in modern scholarship examining the transitional formation of the early Mahāyāna.
SA_K14_ajitsvyu.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna sūtra represented as the word of the Buddha (buddhavacana), preserved in a Gilgit manuscript and fragmentary Central Asian leaves.
SA_K14_ajitsvyu.edition: N. Dutt (ed.), Gilgit Manuscripts, vol. I, Srinagar 1939, pp. 103–136; 2nd ed. Delhi 1984.
SA_K14_ajitsvyu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the sūtra as edited by Nalinaksha Dutt from the Gilgit manuscript (pp. 103–136), concluding with the text colophon (ajitasenavyakaraṇanirdeśo nāma mahāyānasūtraṃ samāptam) and the scribal donative epilogue naming Bālosiṃha and Narendradatta.
translations: William Brian Rasmussen, 'An Annotated Transcription and Translation of the Gilgit Manuscript of the Ajitasenavyākaraṇanirdeśamahāyānasūtra', M.A. thesis, The University of Texas at Austin, 1995. (English)

SA_K14_amoghapu.title: Amoghapāśahṛdayasūtra
SA_K14_amoghapu.summary: The Amoghapāśahṛdayasūtra is a Mahāyāna dhāraṇī scripture centered on Amoghapāśa ('Infallible Noose'), an esoteric multi-armed manifestation of Avalokiteśvara. Set on Mount Potalaka, Avalokiteśvara discloses the heart-mantra bestowed upon him in an ancient kalpa by the Buddha Lokendrarāja. The sūtra outlines extensive apotropaic, curative, and karmic benefits accrued through hearing, reciting, or transcribing the dhāraṇī, and prescribes exact ritual procedures (vidhi) involving fasting, ritual bathing, image-veneration, and eye-ointment preparation to accomplish visions and spiritual siddhi.
SA_K14_amoghapu.attribution: Anonymous Mahāyāna dhāraṇī-sūtra (classified in the Tibetan Kangyur, Toh 682, translated by Amoghavajra and Rin chen grags); framed as Buddhavacana delivered on Mount Potalaka.
SA_K14_amoghapu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the sūtra as edited in Dhīḥ 38 (2004), pp. 157–169, from the opening nidāna through dhāraṇī recitation prescriptions and concluding colophon (// āryāmoghapāśanāmahṛdayaṃ mahāyānasūtraṃ samāptam* //).

SA_K14_bsa052_u.title: Dharmasamuccaya
SA_K14_bsa052_u.author: Avalokitasiṃha
SA_K14_bsa052_u.summary: The Dharmasamuccaya ('Compendium of Dharmas') is a Sanskrit Buddhist verse anthology compiled by Bhikṣu Avalokitasiṃha, organized into four thematic udānas. The verses are extracted from the canonical Saddharmasmṛtyupasthānasūtra to serve as a manual of Buddhist ethics, karma and the realms of rebirth, sense restraint, monastic conduct, and the cultivation of mindfulness. In the Song dynasty, the anthology was translated into Chinese by Richeng (日稱) and others under the title Zhufajiyaojing (諸法集要經, Taishō 728).
SA_K14_bsa052_u.attribution: Bhikṣu Avalokitasiṃha is explicitly named in the opening and closing rubrics/verses as having extracted and arranged these stanzas from the canonical Saddharmasmṛtyupasthānasūtra ('bhikṣuṇā avalokitasiṃhena samudbhāvitaḥ', 'vaipulyamahāgambhīrodadhisūtravarād bhikṣuṇā avalokitasiṃhenoddhṛtamiti').
SA_K14_bsa052_u.edition: Vijayaśaṅkara Caube, ed., Dharmasamuccaya, Varanasi: Sampurnanand Sanskrit University, 1993, pp. 1–278.
SA_K14_bsa052_u.coverage: complete — Anthology grouped into 4 udānas, including the maṅgala verses, introductory uddānas, and closing colophon.
translations: Lin Li-kouang, Dharma-Samuccaya: Compendium de la loi, 3 vols., Paris, 1946, 1969, 1973. (French)

SA_K14_bsu002_u.title: Amoghapāśahṛdayasūtra
SA_K14_bsu002_u.summary: The Amoghapāśahṛdayasūtra is a Mahāyāna dhāraṇī scripture focusing on Amoghapāśa Lokeśvara, an esoteric form of Avalokiteśvara. Set on Mount Potalaka, the text recounts how Avalokiteśvara received this root heart-mantra (hṛdaya) in an earlier aeon from the Buddha Lokendrarāja, and details the extensive soteriological and mundane benefits of hearing, reciting, or writing it. It provides the central dhāraṇī formula alongside ritual procedures (vidhi/kalpa) for healing ailments, protection against danger, and purifying severe karmic offenses.
SA_K14_bsu002_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna dhāraṇī-sūtra; presented as spoken by Avalokiteśvara in the presence of the Buddha on Mount Potalaka.
SA_K14_bsu002_u.edition: M.B. Shakya, Ārya Amoghpāsh hṛdaya nāma Mahāyāna Sūtra. Nepal: NIEM (Buddhist text translation Series, 2), 1988.
SA_K14_bsu002_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the shorter Amoghapāśahṛdayasūtra recension preserved in Nepalese manuscripts, opening with the nidāna at Mount Potalaka and concluding with the sūtra colophon (āryāmoghapāśahṛdayaṃ nāma mahāyāna sūtraṃ samāptas) followed by the ye dharmā stanza.
translations: Jñānagupta (tr.), Bukong juansuo zhou jing 不空羂索呪經, Taishō Tripitaka, no. 1093 (587). (Chinese)
Xuanzang (tr.), Bukong juansuo shenzhou xin jing 不空羂索神呪心經, Taishō Tripitaka, no. 1094 (659). (Chinese)
phags pa don yod zhags pa'i snying po zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo (Derge Kangyur D 682): translated by Amoghavajra II, ba ri lo tsA ba rin chen grags (Tibetan)

SA_K14_bsu015_u.title: Ekādaśamukha
SA_K14_bsu015_u.summary: The Ekādaśamukha (also known as Ekādaśamukhahṛdaya) is an early esoteric Buddhist dhāraṇī-sūtra in which the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara reveals his eleven-faced heart-spell (hṛdaya) before the Buddha in the Jetavana monastery at Śrāvastī. The text details ten mundane benefits (including freedom from illness, weapons, poison, fire, and untimely death) and four transcendental fruits (including beholding the Tathāgatas at death and rebirth in Sukhāvatī) promised to practitioners who recite the spell, followed by prescriptive ritual instructions for bali offerings, lustrations, and homa rites. Surviving in Sanskrit in a 5th- to 6th-century birch-bark manuscript unearthed at Gilgit, the scripture formed a foundational text for the cult of the Eleven-Faced Avalokiteśvara throughout Central and East Asia.
SA_K14_bsu015_u.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna dhāraṇī-sūtra in which the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara expounds the eleven-faced heart-spell (ekādaśamukhaṃ nāma hṛdayam) in the presence of the Buddha in Śrāvastī.
SA_K14_bsu015_u.edition: N. Dutt: Gilgit Manuscript, vol. I, Delhi: Sri Satguru Publication, 1984, 33-40.
SA_K14_bsu015_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the dhāraṇī-sūtra as preserved in the Gilgit manuscript, ending with the dismissal mantra āryāvalokiteśvara gaccha svabhavanam, corresponding to Dutt's edition, pp. 33–40.
translations: Yaśogupta (北周 耶舍崛多譯), Foshuo shiyimian Guanshiyin shenzhou jing 佛說十一面觀世音神呪經, Taishō no. 1070, translated 561–577 CE. (Chinese)
Xuanzang (唐 玄奘譯), Shiyimian shenzhou xinjing 十一面神呪心經, Taishō no. 1071, translated 656 CE. (Chinese)
Amoghavajra (唐 不空譯), Shiyimian Guanzizai Pusa xinmiyan niansong yigui jing 十一面觀自在菩薩心密言念誦儀軌經, Taishō no. 1069, translated 746–774 CE. (Chinese)
phags pa spyan ras gzigs dbang phyug zhal bcu gcig pa zhes bya ba'i gzungs (Derge Kangyur D 693): translated by Śīlendrabodhi, sna nam btsun pa ye shes sde (Tibetan)
phags pa zhal bcu gcig pa'i rig sngags kyi snying po zhes bya ba'i gzungs (Derge Kangyur D 694): translated by 'gos chos 'grub (Tibetan)

SA_K14_dhppat_u.title: Patna Dharmapada
SA_K14_dhppat_u.summary: The Patna Dharmapada is an early Buddhist collection of stanzas transmitted in a Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit / Middle Indo-Aryan idiom. It comprises 22 chapters with 414/415 stanzas, closely related to the Pāli Dhammapada, Gāndhārī Dharmapada, and Udānavarga.
SA_K14_dhppat_u.attribution: Canonical Buddhist verse collection. Edited by Gustav Roth, Margaret Cone, and others.
SA_K14_dhppat_u.edition: Margaret Cone: 'Patna Dharmapada, Part I: Text', JPTS 13 (1989), pp. 101-217.
SA_K14_dhppat_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Patna Dharmapada in 22 chapters (vargas) terminating at the scribal colophon ('samāptā dhammapadā amṛtapadāni gāthāśatāni pañca dve ca gāthe // yathā dṛṣṭaṃ tathā likhitam iti parihāroyam asmadīyaḥ // śubhaṃ astu sarvvasatvānānaṃ //'). The e-text alternates stanzas of the root text with parallel verses.

SA_K14_mavadsuu.title: Mahāvadānasūtra
SA_K14_mavadsuu.summary: The Mahāvadānasūtra ('The Great Legend Sūtra') is a canonical discourse of the Sarvāstivāda tradition belonging to the Dīrghāgama (part of the Ṣaṭsūtrakanipāta), corresponding to the Pali Mahāpadāna-sutta (DN 14) and the Chinese Dà běn jīng (T 1 / T 2). Spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha at Śrāvastī, it records the lineage, lifespan, tree of awakening, and chief disciples of the seven Buddhas of the past, and provides an extensive exemplary narrative of the conception, birth, renunciation, awakening, and first teaching of the previous Buddha Vipaśyin. This critical edition by Takamichi Fukita (2003) reedits and substantially supplements Ernst Waldschmidt's earlier pioneering edition using all available Northern Turkestan manuscript fragments.
SA_K14_mavadsuu.attribution: Canonical Buddhist sūtra of the Sarvāstivāda Dīrghāgama, preserved in Sanskrit manuscript fragments discovered in Northern Turkestan (Turfan collection).
SA_K14_mavadsuu.edition: Takamichi Fukita, The Mahāvadānasūtra: A New Edition Based on Manuscripts Discovered in Northern Turkestan, Sanskrit-Wörterbuch der buddhistischen Texte aus den Turfan-Funden, Beiheft 10, Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 2003.
SA_K14_mavadsuu.coverage: complete — Reconstructed continuous text of Takamichi Fukita's edition of the Mahāvadānasūtra based on Central Asian manuscript fragments with lacunae and metrical patterns indicated.
translations: Ernst Waldschmidt, Das Mahāvadānasūtra: ein kanonischer Text über die sieben letzten Buddhas..., Berlin: Akademie-Verlag, 1953, 1956. (German)

SA_K14_mpsu_w_u.title: Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra
SA_K14_mpsu_w_u.summary: The Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra is the canonical Mainstream Buddhist (Sarvāstivāda / Mūlasarvāstivāda) narrative depicting the final travels, teachings, parinirvāṇa, cremation, and relic division of Gautama Buddha. Parallel to the Pali Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (DN 16), it articulates key early Buddhist doctrinal lists such as the seven conditions of non-decline (saptāparihāṇīyā dharmāḥ) and incorporates the embedded Mahāsudarśanasūtra (episode 34). It is distinct from the later Mahāyāna sūtra of the same title.
SA_K14_mpsu_w_u.attribution: Canonical Buddhist scripture belonging to the Sarvāstivāda / Mūlasarvāstivāda tradition, closely parallel to the Pali Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (DN 16). In the Mūlasarvāstivāda tradition, it is preserved both as a distinct Dīrghāgama discourse and embedded in the Vinayavastu (Kṣudrakavastu). Distinct from the eponymous Mahāyāna scripture.
SA_K14_mpsu_w_u.edition: Ernst Waldschmidt (ed.), Das Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra: Text in Sanskrit und Tibetisch, verglichen mit dem Pāli nebst einer Übersetzung der chinesischen Entsprechung im Vinaya der Mūlasarvāstivādins, auf Grund von Turfan-Handschriften herausgegeben und bearbeitet. Teil I: Der Sanskrit-Text im handschriftlichen Befund (ADAW 1949.1); Teil II: Textbearbeitung: Vorgang 1–32 (ADAW 1950.2); Teil III: Textbearbeitung: Vorgang 33–51 (inbegriffen das Mahāsudarśanasūtra) (ADAW 1950.3). Berlin: Akademie-Verlag, 1950–1951.
SA_K14_mpsu_w_u.coverage: complete — Covers all 51 thematic episodes (Vorgang 1.1–51.27) reconstructed by Ernst Waldschmidt, including the embedded Mahāsudarśanasūtra (Vorgang 34). Reconstructed from Central Asian Sanskrit manuscripts, with physical lacunae reconstructed or supplemented from parallel witnesses.
translations: Ernst Waldschmidt, Das Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra, Teil II–III, Berlin: Akademie-Verlag, 1951 [German translation of the corresponding Chinese text from the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya and comparative apparatus]. (German)
Ernst Waldschmidt, Die Überlieferung vom Lebensende des Buddha: Eine vergleichende Analyse des Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra und seiner Textentsprechungen, Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht. (German)

SA_K14_msudarsu.title: Mahāsudarśanāvadāna
SA_K14_msudarsu.summary: The Mahāsudarśanāvadāna is a Buddhist narrative preserved in the Gilgit manuscripts recounting a former existence of the Buddha as the righteous universal monarch (cakravartin) Mahāsudarśana. Endowed with the seven royal jewels and four supernatural faculties, the king establishes boundless charity, erecting magnificent palaces and ponds for all beings in his city of Kuśāvatī. Moving beyond temporal sovereignty, he renounces sensuality, cultivates the four immeasurable minds (brahmavihāras), enters the meditative absorptions (dhyānas), and attains rebirth in the Brahmā realm, with the Buddha identifying the tale as an exposition of the accumulation of merit (saṃbhāra) necessary for supreme awakening.
SA_K14_msudarsu.attribution: Canonical Buddhist narrative (avadāna) belonging to the (Mūla-)Sarvāstivāda textual lineage, preserved in a manuscript from Gilgit.
SA_K14_msudarsu.edition: Hisashi Matsumura (ed.), The Mahāsudarśanāvadāna and the Mahāsudarśanasūtra, Bibliotheca Indo-Buddhica, Delhi: Sri Satguru Publications, 1988.
SA_K14_msudarsu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Mahāsudarśanāvadāna in 24 sections (MSuAv [1]–[24]), ending with the colophon 'mahāsudarśanāvadānaḥ samāpta.' It covers the entire Gilgit manuscript text (GBM 1451.8, 1550.1–1567.8).

SA_K14_n191u.title: Kaṭhināvadāna
SA_K14_n191u.summary: The Kaṭhināvadāna is an edifying Buddhist ritual and narrative text preserved in Nepalese manuscripts that extols the spiritual merit of offering the kaṭhina cloth to the monastic Saṃgha at the conclusion of the rains-retreat (varṣā). Opening with Mahākāśyapa questioning the Buddha on the proper time and ceremonial procedures for spreading the kaṭhina, the work outlines detailed Vinaya prescriptions for measuring, stitching, marking, and dedicating the robe before presenting past-life narratives that illustrate karmic retribution and the fruits of generosity. Several of its embedded story motifs have direct parallels in the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya Bhaiṣajyavastu.
SA_K14_n191u.attribution: Anonymous Buddhist narrative and ritual text preserved in Nepalese manuscripts. It incorporates Vinaya ritual rules concerning the offering and tailoring of the kaṭhina cloth as well as embedded avadāna narrative cycles closely connected with the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya.
SA_K14_n191u.edition: Almuth Degener (ed.), Das Kaṭhināvadāna: Eingeleitet, herausgegeben und übersetzt, Indica et Tibetica 16, Bonn: Indica et Tibetica Verlag, 1990 (vi, 103 pp.).
SA_K14_n191u.coverage: complete — Complete text corresponding to the edition by Almuth Degener.
translations: Almuth Degener (tr.), Das Kaṭhināvadāna: Eingeleitet, herausgegeben und übersetzt, Indica et Tibetica 16, Bonn: Indica et Tibetica Verlag, 1990. (German)

SA_K14_n192u.title: Mahāsattvamaṇicūḍamahārājabodhisattvāvadāna
SA_K14_n192u.summary: A Buddhist metrical avadāna in 1,077 verses forming chapter 49 of the late medieval Nepalese anthology Mahajjātakamālā. Framed as a dialogue between King Aśoka and the arhat Upagupta, the narrative recounts the past life of the Buddha as King Maṇicūḍa of Sāketa, who was born with a miraculous wish-granting jewel in his crest. To perfect the virtue of generosity (dāna-pāramitā), Maṇicūḍa gives away his magical elephant, his kingdom, and the merit of his sacrifice, undergoes voluntary exile in the forest, provides his own flesh and blood to satiate a demon, and ultimately allows his skull to be cleaved to extract and bestow his crest-jewel.
SA_K14_n192u.attribution: Anonymous; compiled in late medieval Nepal as part of the 50-chapter Mahajjātakamālā anthology.
SA_K14_n192u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 1,077 verses (ślokas), running from verse 1 to verse 1077, ending with the closing colophon.

SA_K14_n285u.title: Catuṣpariṣatsūtra (Vorgang E: The Enlightenment)
SA_K14_n285u.summary: The Catuṣpariṣatsūtra is a canonical text recounting events around the foundation of the Buddhist monastic community. This excerpt preserves sections 1–25, describing the Bodhisattva's meditation at Uruvilvā on the bank of the Nairañjanā river, attainment of supernormal knowledges (abhijñā) during the watches of the night, realization of the Four Noble Truths, destruction of the taints (āsrava), and entry into the fire element (tejodhātu).
SA_K14_n285u.attribution: A canonical scripture of the mainstream Buddhist tradition, preserved in Central Asian Sanskrit fragments. No human author is traditionally attributed.
SA_K14_n285u.coverage: excerpt — Preserves sections 1–25 recounting the Bodhisattva's meditation under the Bodhi tree at Uruvilvā across the watches of the night, leading to awakening and entering the fire element (tejodhātu).
translations: Ria Kloppenborg, The Sūtra on the Foundation of the Buddhist Order (Catuṣpariṣatsūtra), Leiden: E. J. Brill, 1973 (Religious Texts Translation Series, Nisaba 1). (English)
Víctor Giménez Morote, Barcelona, 1995. (Spanish)

SA_K14_n2947u.title: Vajrasattvaniṣpādanasūtra
SA_K14_n2947u.author: Candrakīrti
SA_K14_n2947u.summary: The Vajrasattvaniṣpādanasūtra (also known as the Vajrasattvasādhana) is a generation-stage (utpattikrama) meditation manual of the Guhyasamāja tantra, attributed to Candrakīrti. It delineates the generation of the deities of the Guhyasamāja maṇḍala centered on Vajrasattva in accordance with the process of human rebirth and embryonic development (bhavotpattikrameṇa). Structured across successive meditations including samādhirāja, maṇḍalarājāgrī, and karmarājāgrī, the practice systematically correlates ritual visualizations with canonical scriptural quotations cited across the chapters of the root Guhyasamājatantra.
SA_K14_n2947u.attribution: The colophon explicitly assigns authorship to Ācārya Candrakīrtipāda ('kṛtiriyamācāryacandrakīrtipādānām').
SA_K14_n2947u.edition: Luo Hong and Toru Tomabechi (eds.), Candrakīrti's Vajrasattvaniṣpādanasūtra (Vajrasattvasādhana): Sanskrit and Tibetan Texts. Sanskrit Texts from the Tibetan Autonomous Region (STTAR). Beijing: China Tibetology Publishing House / Vienna: Austrian Academy of Sciences Press, 2009.
SA_K14_n2947u.coverage: complete — The e-text preserves the entire work from opening namaskāra and introductory framing down through the concluding colophon, corresponding precisely to pages 3–32 of the critical edition by Luo Hong and Toru Tomabechi (2009).

SA_K14_n445u.title: Mahāvadānasūtra (Sanskrit back-translation from the Chinese Dīrghāgama; verses 20–43 missing)
SA_K14_n445u.summary: The Mahāvadānasūtra, the first discourse of the Dīrghāgama (Chinese 大本經, DĀ 1), tells the lives of the seven past Buddhas from Vipaśyin to Śākyamuni after a common pattern, with special detail on Vipaśyin. This e-text is an anonymous modern Sanskrit rendering of the Chinese version hosted by DSBC, not the Central Asian Sanskrit text edited by Waldschmidt and Fukita; verses 20–43 are missing.
SA_K14_n445u.attribution: Canonical discourse on the seven past Buddhas. This e-text is a modern Sanskrit rendering of the Chinese Dīrghāgama version (T 1, sūtra 1), not the Central Asian Sanskrit text; its translator is not named.
SA_K14_n445u.coverage: partial — Full narrative of DĀ 1 from 'evaṃ mayā śrutaṃ ... śrāvasthyāṃ ... puṣpavanaśālāyāṃ' to the end ('buddho 'vocad idaṃ mahāvadānasūtraṃ ...' and the colophon '(iti) buddhabhāṣite dīrghāgamasūtre prathamaḥ bhāgaḥ'), with 187 numbered verses, but verses 20–43 are missing.

SA_K14_pamsuavu.title: Pāṃśupradānāvadāna (fragment)
SA_K14_pamsuavu.summary: The Pāṃśupradānāvadāna constitutes chapter 26 of the Divyāvadāna and serves as the opening section of the Aśokāvadāna cycle. In the larger narrative, the boy Jaya offers a handful of dust to the Buddha and is prophesied to be reborn as the emperor Aśoka, framed by extended hagiographies of the Buddhist patriarchs Śāṇakavāsin and Upagupta. This e-text is an exact diplomatic transcription of surviving birchbark leaves from Gilgit preserving two episodes: the birth and trade of Upagupta, and Upagupta's subjugation of Māra, wherein Māra is persuaded to manifest the physical likeness of Śākyamuni Buddha.
SA_K14_pamsuavu.attribution: Mainstream Buddhist narrative traditionally preserved within the Gilgit birchbark collection and the Nepalese Divyāvadāna manuscript tradition.
SA_K14_pamsuavu.edition: Diplomatic transliteration by Klaus Wille (22.07.12) based on facsimiles in *Gilgit Buddhist Manuscripts (Facsimile Edition)*, ed. Raghu Vira and Lokesh Chandra (10 pts., New Delhi 1959-1974, Śata-Piṭaka Series 10; revised and enlarged compact edition, 3 vols., Delhi 1995, Bibliotheca Indo-Buddhica Series 150-152) and a microfilm in the possession of the Sanskrit-Wörterbuch der buddhistischen Texte aus den Turfan-Funden, Göttingen.
SA_K14_pamsuavu.coverage: fragment — Transcribes fragmentary birchbark leaves from the Gilgit manuscript find (GBM 1508–1517). The text preserves two discontinuous sections corresponding to Cowell & Neil's Divyāvadāna pp. 351.9–353.21 and pp. 359.28–362.29.
translations: Rotman, Andy, trans. *Divine Stories: Divyāvadāna*, Part 2. Somerville, MA: Wisdom Publications, 2017. (English)
Przyluski, Jean. *La légende de l'empereur Açoka (Açoka-avadāna) dans les textes indiens et chinois*. Paris: Paul Geuthner, 1923. (French)

SA_K14_ratnml_u.title: Ratnamālāvadāna
SA_K14_ratnml_u.summary: The Ratnamālāvadāna ('Garland of Jewels of Edifying Deeds') is a late Sanskrit Buddhist metrical collection of thirty-eight avadāna tales framed as instruction given by the arhat Upagupta to Emperor Aśoka. It versifies and expands narratives familiar from older collections such as the Avadānaśataka, illustrating the inexorable results of karma, devotion to the Three Jewels, and the cultivation of the Mahāyāna pāramitās. Preserved in Nepalese Sanskrit manuscripts, it was critically edited in full by Kanga Takahata in 1954.
SA_K14_ratnml_u.attribution: Anonymous late Buddhist metrical narrative compilation preserved in Nepalese Sanskrit manuscripts. The text belongs to the Aśoka-Upagupta narrative cycle.
SA_K14_ratnml_u.edition: Kanga Takahata (ed.), Ratnamālāvadāna: A Garland of Precious Gems or a Collection of Edifying Tales, Told in a Metrical Form, Belonging to the Mahāyāna, Tokyo: The Toyo Bunko, 1954 (Oriental Library Series D, 3).
SA_K14_ratnml_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 38 chapters (verses Rm_1.1 to Rm_38.1002), covering pp. 1–481 of Takahata's 1954 printed edition, concluding with the scribal colophon dated Saṃvat 1028.

SA_K14_sumagavu.title: Sumāgadhāvadāna
SA_K14_sumagavu.summary: The Sumāgadhāvadāna is an independent Buddhist narrative work (avadāna) in mixed prose and verse relating the story of Sumāgadhā, daughter of the prominent merchant and patron Anāthapiṇḍada of Śrāvastī.
