Married into the household of Vṛṣabhadatta in Puṇḍravardhana (Bengal), whose family reveres the Nirgranthas (Jains), she is repelled by the naked ascetics and miraculously summons the Buddha and his disciples from her roof. The aerial arrival and marvelous transformations of the Buddha and the arhats convert her husband's family and the entire city to Buddhism. The text concludes with karmic explanations by the Buddha, including Sumāgadhā's past lives and the ten prophetic dreams of King Kṛkin.
SA_K14_sumagavu.attribution: Anonymous canonical/edifying Buddhist avadāna. Transmitted as an independent text in Nepalese manuscripts (as well as in Tibetan and Chinese translations), distinct from Kṣemendra's versified rendition in the Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā (ch. 93).
SA_K14_sumagavu.edition: Yutaka Iwamoto (ed.), Sumāgadhāvadāna, Kyoto: Hōzōkan, 1968 (Studien zur buddhistischen Erzählungsliteratur, 2).
SA_K14_sumagavu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the independent Sumāgadhāvadāna across 270 numbered paragraphs (SumAv_1 through SumAv_270), concluding with the standard colophon 'sumāgadhāvadānaṃ samāptam'.
translations: Tsuru-Matsu Tokiwai, Studien zum Sumāgadhāvadāna, Darmstadt, 1898. (German)
ma ga d+hA bzang mo'i rtogs pa brjod pa (Derge Kangyur D 346): translated by Dharmaśrībhadra, tshul khrims yon tan; revised by lo chen rin chen bzang po (Tibetan)

SA_K14_svabhupu.title: Svayambhūpurāṇa
SA_K14_svabhupu.summary: The Svayambhūpurāṇa is the foundational mythic chronicle and pilgrimage guide (sthala-māhātmya) of Newar Buddhism in the Kathmandu Valley. It recounts the myth of the primordial lake (Nāgadaha) drained through the Chobhar gorge by the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, followed by the appearance of the primordial lotus and the self-existent flame (svayambhūjyotis) of the Dharmadhātu enshrined within the Svayambhū Mahācaitya (Swayambhunath). The work incorporates visits of the previous Buddhas of antiquity, legends of local tīrthas, deities, and nāgas, and the transformation of the valley into a Buddhist kingdom. This 10-chapter recension represents the intermediate (madhyama) version of the text.
SA_K14_svabhupu.attribution: Anonymous Buddhist purāṇa and sthala-māhātmya from the Kathmandu Valley, Nepal. The internal dialogue is framed as an exposition delivered by Jayaśrī to his disciple Jineśvara at the Bodhimaṇḍavihāra.
SA_K14_svabhupu.edition: Min Bahadu Shakyar & Shanta Harsa Bajracharya (trans.), Svayambhu Purāṇa, Nepal: Nagarjuna Institute of Exact Methods, 2001.
SA_K14_svabhupu.coverage: complete — Text with scribal colophon lines dated Nepāla Saṃvat 934 copied by Śrī Rāmānanda.
translations: Mana Bajra Bajracharya & Warren W. Smith Jr. (eds. & trs.), Mythological History of the Nepal Valley from Svayambhu Purana, Kathmandu: Avalok Publishers. (English)

SA_K14_visvantu.title: Viśvantarāvadāna (sections 35–39 lost)
SA_K14_visvantu.summary: An anonymous Sanskrit avadāna of Prince Viśvantara (Pali Vessantara), the Buddha's past life as the paragon of generosity, preserved in a single Gilgit birch-bark manuscript. Viśvantara is banished after giving away the state elephant, and in forest exile gives away his children and his wife Mādrī to the brahmin Jujjuka and to Śakra; the frame story identifies Jujjuka with Devadatta to illustrate ingratitude (akṛtajña). It is a Sanskrit parallel to the Pali Vessantarajātaka and to the tellings in the Saṅghabhedavastu and Āryaśūra's Jātakamālā.
SA_K14_visvantu.attribution: Anonymous avadāna preserved in a Gilgit manuscript (folios 5–14; fol. 14r also contains the colophon and the beginning of the Kapphiṇāvadāna).
SA_K14_visvantu.edition: Kabita Das Gupta, Viśvantarāvadāna: Eine buddhistische Legende, Edition eines Textes auf Sanskrit und auf Tibetisch eingeleitet und übersetzt (Inaugural-Dissertation, Freie Universität Berlin, 1978). Cf. GBM 157-174, 1332-1349, 3314-3315.
SA_K14_visvantu.coverage: partial — The text runs from Viśv 1 to Viśv 70 and ends with the colophon 'viśvantarāvadānaṃ samāptam', but folio 9 of the manuscript is lost; the e-text breaks off in Viśv 35 and resumes at Viśv 40. Otherwise complete as preserved.
translations: Kabita Das Gupta, Viśvantarāvadāna: Eine buddhistische Legende. Edition eines Textes auf Sanskrit und auf Tibetisch eingeleitet und übersetzt (Berlin 1978). (English)

SA_T01_busto1_u.title: Anaparāddhastotra, Praṇāmastava, Sattvārādhanastava and other Buddhist stotras (fragments)
SA_T01_busto1_u.summary: A GRETIL selection of Buddhist Sanskrit hymns recovered from Central Asian and Gilgit manuscripts, entered by Jens-Uwe Hartmann from the editions of Hartmann (1988, 1997), Lévi (1929) and Schlingloff (1955). It contains the surviving stanzas of Mātṛceṭa's Anaparāddhastotra, an unknown stotra, the Gilgit Praṇāmastava, the Sattvārādhanastava, and a selection of hymns and didactic verses from the Turfan finds edited by Schlingloff (including the Munayastava, Rāhulastava, and Saṅghastotrastava).
SA_T01_busto1_u.attribution: The opening work is attributed to Mātṛceṭa (Hartmann 1988; cf. 'anaparāddhastotram samāptam kṛtir ācāryasthaviramātṛceṭasya'). The remaining texts are anonymous hymns or stotra fragments preserved in Central Asian and Gilgit manuscripts.
SA_T01_busto1_u.edition: Composite digital collection based on four publications: (1) Jens-Uwe Hartmann, 'Neue Aśvaghośa- und Mātṛceṭa-Fragmente aus Ostturkistan', Nachrichten der Akademie der Wissenschaften in Göttingen, 1988 (Anaparāddhastotra of Mātṛceṭa and unknown Stotra); (2) Jens-Uwe Hartmann, 'Der Praṇāmastava. Ein Buddhastotra aus den Gilgit-Funden', in: Petra Kieffer-Pülz and Jens-Uwe Hartmann (eds.), Bauddhavidyāsudhākaraḥ. Studies in Honour of Heinz Bechert on the Occasion of His 65th Birthday, Swisttal-Odendorf (Indica et Tibetica, 30), 1997, pp. 285–296; (3) Sylvain Lévi, 'Autour d'Aśvaghoṣa', Journal Asiatique 1929, pp. 264–266 (Sattvārādhanastava); (4) Dieter Schlingloff, Buddhistische Stotras aus ostturkistanischen Sanskrittexten, Berlin 1955 (Sanskrittexte aus den Turfanfunden, 1) (Munayastava, Rāhulastava, Saṅghastotrastava, and other hymns).
SA_T01_busto1_u.coverage: fragment — A selection ('Selected:' in the GRETIL header) of fragmentary hymns from Central Asian and Gilgit manuscripts, with missing aksaras marked by 'x'. The Anaparāddhastotra begins at v. 10 and is incomplete (incorporating the fragment Hoernle 149/250 = British Library, Or. 15009/149); the Praṇāmastava and other stotras from Schlingloff 1955 are selections and fragments.

SA_T01_n2888u.title: Dvādaśakāranayastotra
SA_T01_n2888u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T01_n2888u.summary: The Dvādaśakāranayastotra is a Buddhist hymn praising the deeds of Śākyamuni Buddha, followed by verses praising the distribution of relics into eight portions and dedicating merit. It is preserved in the Tibetan Tengyur and traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna.
SA_T01_n2888u.attribution: Attributed to Nāgārjuna in Tibetan canonical collections (D 1135 / P 2026) and discussed among his hymnical works in modern scholarship.
SA_T01_n2888u.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising 1 initial unnumbered namaskāra stanza followed by 14 verses (verses 1–12 extolling the twelve deeds, verse 13 praising the relics, and verse 14 dedicating merit).
translations: mdzad pa bcu gnyis kyi tshul la bstod pa (Derge Tengyur D 1135) (Tibetan)

SA_T01_n2925u.title: Dharmadhātustava (verses 1–86)
SA_T01_n2925u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T01_n2925u.summary: The Dharmadhātustava ('In Praise of the Dharmadhātu') is a Mahāyāna devotional-philosophical hymn celebrating the dharmadhātu—the expanse of ultimate reality—as the inherently pure, radiant nature present in all sentient beings. Using classic similes such as butter concealed in milk, a lamp within a jar, and gold in ore, the poem illustrates how adventitious defilements veil this intrinsic purity, which is unveiled through spiritual cultivation and the realization of emptiness. The text serves as an influential bridge between Madhyamaka and buddha-nature (tathāgatagarbha) traditions, particularly within Tibetan exegesis.
SA_T01_n2925u.attribution: Ascribed to Nāgārjuna; this attribution has been questioned by Seyfort Ruegg (1971) and rejected by Lindtner (1982), noting the influence of the tathāgatagarbha tradition.
SA_T01_n2925u.edition: Zhen Liu (ed.), The Dharmadhātustava: A Critical Edition of the Sanskrit Text with the Tibetan and Chinese Translations, a Diplomatic Transliteration of the Manuscript and Notes, Sanskrit Texts from the Tibetan Autonomous Region (STTAR) 17, Beijing: China Tibetology Publishing House / Vienna: Austrian Academy of Sciences Press, 2015.
SA_T01_n2925u.coverage: partial — Preserves an unnumbered opening verse followed by numbered stanzas (1)–(84) and verse (85), breaking off at 'jātya ......... (19)'.
translations: Karl Brunnhölzl, In Praise of Dharmadhātu, by Rangjung Dorje, Nāgārjuna and the Third Karmapa, Ithaca: Snow Lion Publications, 2007. (English)
David Seyfort Ruegg, 'Le Dharmadhātustava de Nāgārjuna', in Études tibétaines dédiées à la mémoire de Marcelle Lalou, Paris, 1971. (French)
Osamu Hayashima, '『諸法界頌』考' [On the Dharmadhātustava], Nagasaki Daigaku Kyōikugakubu Shakaikagaku Ronsō 36, 1987. (Japanese)
chos kyi dbyings su bstod pa (Derge Tengyur D 1118): translated by Kṛṣṇapa, nag 'tsho lo tsA ba tshul khrims rgyal ba (Tibetan)

SA_T01_n2971u.title: Bhadracaryādeśanā (stanza 55 missing)
SA_T01_n2971u.summary: The Bhadracaryāpraṇidhāna (or Bhadracarīpraṇidhāna) consists of 62 verses formulating the bodhisattva Samantabhadra's supreme vows and aspiration prayer. It forms the climactic conclusion of the Gaṇḍavyūhasūtra (the final chapter of the Buddhāvataṃsakasūtra) and circulated widely throughout Mahāyāna Asia as an independent liturgical text and devotional hymn. It articulates the canonical sevenfold worship (saptavidhānapūjā: homage, offerings, confession of sins, rejoicing in merit, entreating buddhas to turn the Dharma wheel, requesting them to remain in the world, and dedication of merit) before concluding with aspirations for rebirth in Sukhāvatī.
SA_T01_n2971u.attribution: Spoken by the bodhisattva Samantabhadra at the culmination of the pilgrimage of Sudhana in the Gaṇḍavyūhasūtra; canonical scriptural text.
SA_T01_n2971u.edition: Jes Peter Asmussen (ed.), The Khotanese Bhadracaryādeśanā: Text, Translation, and Glossary, together with the Buddhist Sanskrit Original, Historisk-filosofiske Meddelelser udgivet af Det Kongelige Danske Videnskabernes Selskab 39.2, København: Ejnar Munksgaard, 1961.
SA_T01_n2971u.coverage: partial — 61 of the 62 stanzas of the Sanskrit Bhadracarīpraṇidhāna: numbering runs I-LIV, LVI-LX, LXII, LXI; stanza LV (the Mañjuśrī/Samantabhadra pariṇāmanā stanza) is missing and LXII precedes LXI. Stanza V is split over two lines only because of a page marker '(3)'. Whether the omission goes back to Asmussen's printed Sanskrit text or to DSBC keying was not verified (the Roman numbering, which skips LV, suggests the verse was dropped from a text that had it).
translations: Kaikioku Watanabe, Die Bhadracarī, eine Probe buddhistisch-religiöser Lyrik, Leipzig: Druck von G. Kreysing, 1912. (German)
Hōkei Idzumi, 'The Hymn of the Life and Vows of Samantabhadra', The Eastern Buddhist 5.2–3 (1930). (English)
Jes Peter Asmussen, The Khotanese Bhadracaryādeśanā: Text, Translation, and Glossary, together with the Buddhist Sanskrit Original, København: Ejnar Munksgaard, 1961. (English)

SA_T01_n802u.title: Ādibuddhadvādaśakastotra
SA_T01_n802u.summary: The Ādibuddhadvādaśakastotra is a short Sanskrit Buddhist devotional hymn of twelve anuṣṭubh verses, accompanied by a single phalaśruti verse, honoring the Primordial Buddha (Ādibuddha). The hymn identifies the Ādibuddha pantheistically and cosmically with the Three Jewels, the Five Buddhas, the cosmic elements, sensory powers, and the Brahmanical triad of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa. Attributed pseudepigraphically to Mañjuśrī, the text represents the late syncretic liturgical tradition of the Kathmandu Valley.
SA_T01_n802u.attribution: The colophon explicitly states 'śrīmañjuśrīkṛtamādibuddhadvādaśakastotraṃ samāptam' ('Thus ends the Ādibuddhadvādaśakastotra composed by Śrī Mañjuśrī').
SA_T01_n802u.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising 12 anuṣṭubh praise verses, 1 concluding phalaśruti verse, and the closing colophon.

SA_T01_n804u.title: Vikramāraccivaibhava
SA_T01_n804u.author: Śāntibhikṣu Śāstrī
SA_T01_n804u.summary: A modern Sanskrit panegyric (75 stanzas, BE 2510 = 1966/67) by Śāntibhikṣu Śāstrī, then Professor of Sanskrit at Vidyālaṅkāra University, Sri Lanka. It first praises Laṅkā (Rāma and Sītā, the Laṅkāvatāra teaching, Vijaya, Mahendra and his sister, Kālidāsa and Kumāradāsa, Buddhaghoṣa) and the village of Neduṅgamuva with its scenery and pious life, and then the Vikramārachchi family and the Ayurvedic physician of that family who founded a medical college at Gampaha (v. 71; i.e. Paṇḍit G. P. Wickramarachchi), wishing him a life of a hundred years.
SA_T01_n804u.attribution: The final stanza (75) and the prose colophon name the author as Śāntibhikṣu Śāstrī, pupil of Bhadanta Śrī Dharmānanda Nāyaka, native of Bībīpur near Lakhnau (Kosala), Leipzig doctorate, Professor (mahācārya) of Sanskrit at Vidyālaṅkāra University (Sri Lanka), residing abroad in Sri Lanka with wife and son (bhāryāsutābhyāṃ saha proṣitasya). Dated gatabuddhābdāḥ 2510 (= 1966/67 CE).
SA_T01_n804u.coverage: complete — 75 numbered stanzas (incl. a kulaka marked '(paṃcabhiḥ kulakam)'), prose colophon, date (BE 2510) and the ye dharmā verse.

SA_T01_n805u.title: Ākāśagarbhanāmāṣṭottaraśatastotra
SA_T01_n805u.summary: The Ākāśagarbhanāmāṣṭottaraśatastotra is a 16-verse Sanskrit Buddhist hymn enumerating epithets of Ākāśagarbha, praising his jewel-like nature, space-like purity, and boundless generosity, and concluding with a verse stating that whoever holds these names attains sarvabuddhābhiṣeka.
SA_T01_n805u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha. Varanasi/Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994. (Ākāśagarbhanāmāṣṭottaraśatastotra = stotra no. 3.)
SA_T01_n805u.coverage: complete — Independent devotional stotra of 16 verses ending with the colophon 'śrī ākāśagarbhanāmāṣṭaśatādhyeṣaṇāstotraṃ saṃpūrṇam'.
translations: Rolf W. Giebel (trans.), Two Esoteric Sutras: The Adamantine Pinnacle Sutra, The Susiddhikara Sutra, Berkeley: Numata Center for Buddhist Translation and Research, 2001. (English)

SA_T01_n806u.title: Āryatārānamaskāraikaviṃśatistotra
SA_T01_n806u.summary: The Āryatārānamaskāraikaviṃśatistotra praises twenty-one manifestations and aspects of the goddess Tārā. The stotra concludes with a six-verse phalaśruti (vv. 22–27) that expounds the benefits conferred by morning and evening recitation.
SA_T01_n806u.attribution: The concluding colophon attributes the hymn to the fully enlightened Buddha Vairocana (śrīsamyaksaṃbuddhavailocanabhāṣita / śrīsamyaksaṃbuddhavairocanabhāṣita).
SA_T01_n806u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha, Varanasi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994.
SA_T01_n806u.coverage: complete — Text in 27 verses, consisting of the 21 homage verses (vv. 1–21), followed by the 6-verse phalaśruti (vv. 22–27) and the concluding colophon.
translations: Martin Willson, In Praise of Tārā: Songs to the Saviouress, London: Wisdom Publications, 1986. (English)

SA_T01_n809u.title: Āryatārāstuti
SA_T01_n809u.author: Candradāsa
SA_T01_n809u.summary: A ten-stanza Buddhist hymn (stotra) composed in ornate 21-syllable Sragdharā metre praising the goddess Tārā by the author Candradāsa. Following an introductory verse (v. 1), stanzas 2 through 9 systematically invoke Tārā's protection from the eight great perils (aṣṭamahābhaya)—wild beasts/lions, elephants, fire, poisonous snakes, bandits, bondage/imprisonment, shipwreck/drowning, and demons/disease—concluding with a tenth stanza on the worldly and spiritual rewards of remembering her name.
SA_T01_n809u.attribution: Attributed in the colophon ('śrīcandradāsaviracitā''ryatārāstutiḥ samāptā') and opening heading to Candradāsa.
SA_T01_n809u.coverage: complete — Complete hymn of 10 stanzas in Sragdharā metre, consisting of an opening invocation (v. 1), eight stanzas invoking protection from the eight great perils (vv. 2–9), and a concluding stanza (v. 10).

SA_T01_n810u.title: Maṅgalāṣṭaka
SA_T01_n810u.summary: An eight-verse Sanskrit benedictory hymn (maṅgalāṣṭaka) composed in the classical Sragdharā metre. Every verse concludes with a refrain entreating the buddhas and bodhisattvas to grant success, auspiciousness, and realization ('tuṣṭāḥ sarvārthasiddhiṃ dadatu samarasā maṅgalaṃ bodhisattvāḥ'). The stanzas invoke the Three Jewels, wrathful protector figures, female wisdom deities and prajñās, sacred pilgrimage sites (such as Lumbinī, Śrāvastī, and Gṛdhrakūṭa), and auspicious emblems (aṣṭamaṅgala).
SA_T01_n810u.coverage: complete — Complete in 8 verses (in Sragdharā metre), with opening title and final colophon.

SA_T01_n811u.title: Aṣṭamātṛkāstotra
SA_T01_n811u.summary: The Aṣṭamātṛkāstotra is an 11-verse Sanskrit Buddhist hymn venerating the Eight Mothers (Aṣṭamātṛkā), preserved in Nepalese Newar Buddhist manuscript and ritual collections. Following an opening salutation to Vighneśvara (Gaṇeśa), each stanza addresses one of the eight protective mother goddesses assigned to a compass direction (Brahmāṇī in the East, Vārāhī in the South, Indrāṇī in the West, Māheśvarī in the North, Kaumārī in the Southeast, Vaiṣṇavī in the Southwest, Cāmuṇḍā in the Northwest, and Caṇḍikā/Mahālakṣmī in the Northeast), identifying her vehicle, complexion, and emblems. The final verses invoke the goddesses collectively in connection with the eight pilgrimage seats (aṣṭapīṭha), sacred trees, and the eight Bhairavas, concluding with reverence to the planetary deities (navagraha) and Yama.
SA_T01_n811u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 11 verses, including invocation to Vighneśvara (v. 1), praises to the eight individual Mother goddesses (vv. 2–9), veneration of the Eight Mothers with the eight pīṭhas, trees, and Bhairavas (v. 10), and closing homage to the Navagrahas and Yama (v. 11).

SA_T01_n812u.title: Avadhānastotra
SA_T01_n812u.summary: A 12-verse Sanskrit hymn of praise (stotra) dedicated to Avalokiteśvara (Lokanātha), preserved in the Nepalese Newar Buddhist tradition. Verses 1–10 describe the bodily marks, compassion, and salvific acts of the Bodhisattva, each closing with the refrain 'nityaṃ namāmi śirasā karuṇāmayāya'. Verse 11 provides a chronogram dating its composition to NS 587 (1467 CE), and verse 12 provides a phalaśruti promising rebirth in Sukhāvatī.
SA_T01_n812u.attribution: Anonymous Nepalese Buddhist stotra. Verse 11 provides an astrological chronogram giving the date of composition (saptāṣṭabhūtagate = NS 587 / 1467 CE, Vaiśākha śuklapakṣa, Friday), but does not record the author's name.
SA_T01_n812u.edition: Bauddha Stotra Saṃgraha, ed. Janardan Shastri Pandey, Motilal Banarsidass, Varanasi, 1994.
SA_T01_n812u.coverage: complete — Complete text of 12 verses, including opening salutation to Lokanātha and concluding colophon.

SA_T01_n813u.title: Avalokiteśvarahayagrīvadhāraṇī
SA_T01_n813u.summary: The Avalokiteśvarahayagrīvadhāraṇī is an esoteric Mahāyāna dhāraṇī text centering on Hayagrīva. Opening with homage to the Triratna and an epithet litany invoking Avalokiteśvara as the dispeller of fear and worldly suffering, the text proclaims the heart incantation of Hayagrīva (hayagrīvabrahma paramahṛdayam) to eliminate poisons, banish spirits, and destroy malevolent sorcery (kākhorda) and planetary afflictions (graha).
SA_T01_n813u.attribution: In the opening prose narrative, the vidyā is presented as issuing directly from the mouth of the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (idam āryāvalokiteśvaramukhodgīrṇam) to impart the heart mantra of Hayagrīva.
SA_T01_n813u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the short independent dhāraṇī concluding with the final svāhā mantra formulas.
translations: 'phags pa spyan ras gzigs dbang phyug ha ya garI ba'i gzungs (Derge Kangyur D 733) (Tibetan)
'phags pa spyan ras gzigs dbang phyug ha ya grI ba'i gzungs (Derge Kangyur D 906) (Tibetan)

SA_T01_n814u.title: Avalokiteśvarāṣṭakastotra
SA_T01_n814u.summary: The Avalokiteśvarāṣṭakastotra is an anonymous Sanskrit Buddhist hymn of praise addressed to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (Lokeśvara), consisting of eight descriptive stanzas followed by a benefit verse (phalaśruti). The hymn praises the bodhisattva's thirty-two physical marks, compassion toward suffering beings, retinue of deities and semi-divine beings, and role as supreme refuge from saṃsāra. The work forms part of the living liturgical stotra corpus transmitted among Newar Buddhists in the Kathmandu Valley.
SA_T01_n814u.attribution: Anonymous Mahāyāna devotional hymn preserved in the Nepalese Sanskrit stotra tradition.
SA_T01_n814u.edition: Avalokiteśvarāṣṭakastotra (BuSto 12), in: 108 Buddhist Stotras, based on Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha, Delhi/Varanasi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994.
SA_T01_n814u.coverage: complete — Complete text of 9 verses (8 praise stanzas plus 1 phalaśruti) concluding with 'śrī āryāvalokiteśvarasya ślokāṣṭakaṃ samāptam'.

SA_T01_n815u.title: Avalokiteśvarastava
SA_T01_n815u.author: Candrakāntā
SA_T01_n815u.summary: A devotional hymn (stava) of 9 verses composed in Toṭaka meter in praise of Avalokiteśvara, the bodhisattva of compassion. Proceeding in keśādipāda ('hair-to-foot') order, the hymn portrays the physical attributes, iconographic marks, and spiritual perfections of Avalokiteśvara, extolling his ten pāramitās, conquest over Māra, and residence on Mount Potalaka. Preserved in the Nepalese Sanskrit stotra corpus, it represents a rare surviving devotional work ascribed to an Indian Buddhist nun (bhikṣuṇī).
SA_T01_n815u.attribution: Ascribed to the Buddhist nun (bhikṣuṇī) Candrakāntā in the opening and closing rubrics ('candrakāntābhikṣuṇīkṛtaḥ', 'candrakāntābhikṣuṇīviracitaḥ stavaḥ').
SA_T01_n815u.coverage: complete — Complete in 9 verses in Toṭaka meter, followed by a concluding colophon rubric.

SA_T01_n816u.title: Avalokiteśvarastotra
SA_T01_n816u.summary: A short Mahāyāna devotional hymn in six verses addressed to Avalokiteśvara, legendary attributed to the Nāga king Vāsuki. Verses 1 to 5 celebrate the Bodhisattva's radiant beauty, compassionate eyes, cosmic multidimensional form (with a thousand arms, four or six arms), and nature born from wisdom and means, concluding with the refrain 'namāmi nāthaṃ maṇipadmasaṃbhavam' ('I revere the protector born from the jewel and lotus'). The final verse offers reverent praise to the lotus-bearing protector who bestows compassion upon all sentient beings.
SA_T01_n816u.attribution: Attributed in the title rubric ('vāsukināgarājakṛtam') and final colophon ('śrīvāsukināgarājakṛtamāryāvalokiteśvarastotraṃ samāptam') to the mythical serpent king Vāsuki (Vāsukināgarāja).
SA_T01_n816u.coverage: complete — Complete hymn of 6 verses with opening salutation and concluding colophon.

SA_T01_n817u.title: Avalokiteśvarastotra
SA_T01_n817u.author: Carpaṭipāda
SA_T01_n817u.summary: The Avalokiteśvarastotra (also known as Lokanāthastotra) is a 25-stanza hymn attributed to Carpaṭipāda (Carpaṭi) composed in the rhyming Mātrāsamaka metre. It petitions Avalokiteśvara for protection, confesses sins, and exists in three independent Tibetan translations.
SA_T01_n817u.attribution: Ascribed in the colophon to Carapatipāda (Carpaṭipāda). The text has three independent Tibetan translations.
SA_T01_n817u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994.
SA_T01_n817u.coverage: complete — 25 stanzas in Mātrāsamaka metre followed by colophon.
translations: phags pa spyan ras gzigs dbang phyug la tsar+p+pa Tis bstod pa (Derge Tengyur D 2726): translated by Vanaratna, 'gos lo tsA ba gzhon nu dpal (Tibetan)

SA_T01_n818u.title: Avalokiteśvarāṣṭottaraśatanāmastotra
SA_T01_n818u.summary: A Buddhist hymn of 108 names in praise of Avalokiteśvara consisting of 15 anuṣṭubh verses of epithets, each stanza concluding with the refrain 'namo 'stu te', followed by a concluding benedictory verse (phalaśruti) stating that recitation or meditation upon these names grants worldly sovereignty. The verses originate from the *Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha*, where Avalokiteśvara is formally entreated with 108 names.
SA_T01_n818u.attribution: Anonymous scriptural hymn. The verses originate from the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha, where the Tathāgatas entreat Avalokiteśvara with 108 names.
SA_T01_n818u.coverage: complete — Complete text of 16 anuṣṭubh verses (15 stanzas enumerating 108 epithets concluding with 'namo 'stu te', followed by 1 phalaśruti verse) with opening maṅgala and closing colophon.
translations: de bzhin gshegs pa thams cad kyi de kho na nyid bsdus pa zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo (Derge Kangyur D 479): translated by Śraddhākaravarman, lo chen rin chen bzang po (Tibetan)

SA_T01_n819u.title: Lokanāthastotra
SA_T01_n819u.summary: A short devotional hymn (stotra) of seven stanzas addressed to Lokanātha (Avalokiteśvara), each verse concluding with the refrain 'śrīlokanātha tava pādayugaṃ name 'ham' ('O holy Lokanātha, I bow to your pair of feet'). Reflecting the syncretic religious environment of late medieval Nepalese Buddhism, the hymn identifies Lokanātha simultaneously with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva (Gaṅgādhara), and the Buddhist Vajrasūrya. The hymn concludes with a modesty stanza asking forgiveness for any linguistic or metrical flaws, dedicating the verses as an offering of pure devotion.
SA_T01_n819u.attribution: Anonymous. No author is indicated in the text, colophon, or modern edition. It is distinct from the 25-stanza Lokanāthastotra / Avalokiteśvarastotra composed in the mātrāsamaka metre and attributed to the mahāsiddha Carpaṭi (or Candragomin).
SA_T01_n819u.coverage: complete — Complete in 7 verses followed by the concluding formula (śrīmadāryāvalokiteśvarabhaṭṭārakasya stotraṃ samāptam).

SA_T01_n820u.title: Lokeśvaraśataka
SA_T01_n820u.author: Vajradatta
SA_T01_n820u.summary: The Lokeśvaraśataka is a stotra of 100 Sragdharā stanzas composed during the reign of Devapāla by Vajradatta. Composed in an elaborate Gauḍīya style, the hymn describes Avalokiteśvara in devotion, extolling his attributes and virtues. It was also translated into Tibetan in the Tanjur.
SA_T01_n820u.attribution: Vajradatta composed the text during the reign of King Devapāla. Later traditions (including Tāranātha) record that he was cured of leprosy after composing stanzas in praise of Avalokiteśvara.
SA_T01_n820u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994 (Lokeśvaraśataka of Vajradatta; GRETIL/DSBC 'Buddhist stotras' corpus, n820).
SA_T01_n820u.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising 100 Sragdharā stanzas in devotion to Avalokiteśvara/Lokeśvara, followed by one concluding benedictory verse (v. 101) by the author, along with opening and final colophons.
translations: Suzanne Karpelès, 'Lokeśvaraśatakam ou Cent strophes en l'honneur du seigneur du monde, par Vajradatta', Journal Asiatique, 11e série, tome 14, 1919, pp. 357–465. (French)

SA_T01_n821u.title: Lokeśvarastotra
SA_T01_n821u.summary: An anonymous Buddhist devotional hymn in eleven verses praising the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara under the names Lokeśvara and Lokanātha. Verses 1–10 describe his iconography, compassionate intervention, and adoration by celestial and earthly beings, each concluding with the refrain 'śrīlokanāthavibudhaṃ śubhadaṃ bhajāmi'. Verse 6 alludes to his entry into an excellent chariot (rathavara). The final stanza (verse 11) serves as a phalaśruti promising the fulfillment of the reciter's desires.
SA_T01_n821u.attribution: Transmitted anonymously and published in Janardan Shastri Pandey's Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha.
SA_T01_n821u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha, Varanasi/Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994, p. 200.
SA_T01_n821u.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising all 11 verses (10 stanzas of praise sharing the refrain 'śrīlokanāthavibudhaṃ śubhadaṃ bhajāmi' plus 1 phalaśruti stanza) and the closing colophon.

SA_T01_n822u.title: Narakoddhārastotra
SA_T01_n822u.summary: The Narakoddhārastotra ('Hymn on Rescue from Hell') is a 15-verse Sanskrit Buddhist devotional prayer seeking salvation from the sufferings of saṃsāra and the tortures of the hell realms. The speaker confesses grievous misdeeds and repeatedly entreats the Buddha with the refrain 'trāhi māṃ hi tathāgata' ('rescue me, O Tathāgata!'). The concluding verse hails the Lord (Lokanātha) as the supreme king of physicians (vaidyarāja) capable of curing all diseases and delivering sentient beings across the three worlds.
SA_T01_n822u.attribution: Transmitted anonymously in Sanskrit manuscripts from Nepal as well as in Janardan Shastri Pandey's edition. In the Tibetan Tengyur (D 1137 / P 2028), it was translated by Tilakakalaśa and Pa tshab Nyi ma grags under the title Dmyal ba nas 'don pa and attributed to Nāgārjuna (Klu sgrub).
SA_T01_n822u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha, Varanasi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994.
SA_T01_n822u.coverage: complete — Complete text of 15 verses in anuṣṭubh (śloka) meter, ending with the closing formula narakoddhārastotraṃ samāptam.
translations: dmyal ba nas 'don pa zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 1137): translated by pa tshab lo tsA ba nyi ma grags pa (Tibetan)

SA_T01_n823u.title: Potalakāṣṭaka
SA_T01_n823u.summary: The Potalakāṣṭaka is an anonymous eight-verse Sanskrit Buddhist hymn (aṣṭaka) eulogizing Avalokiteśvara in association with his mythical mountain residence, Mount Potalaka. The verses praise his physical markers, his crown bearing Amitābha, and his salvific compassion in freeing sentient beings from disease and the cycles of samsara.
SA_T01_n823u.attribution: Anonymous Sanskrit Buddhist stotra praising the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
SA_T01_n823u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the eight verses (aṣṭaka) with opening title and concluding colophon.

SA_T01_n824u.title: Rakṣākālastava
SA_T01_n824u.summary: A 15-verse Sanskrit Buddhist hymn of praise (stotra) in anuṣṭubh metre addressed to Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (invoked as Lokanātha and Lokanāyaka). Verse 2 commemorates the Newar legend of the twelve-year drought in Nepal (dvādaśābdeṣu anāvṛṣṭiḥ) during the reign of Licchavi king Narendradeva (7th century CE), in which Avalokiteśvara (associated with Bungadyo / Karuṇāmaya) was established in Nepal to relieve famine and suffering. Most stanzas conclude with the prayerful refrain 'rakṣa māṃ lokanāyaka'.
SA_T01_n824u.attribution: Anonymous stotra preserved in Nepalese Buddhist manuscript collections and Newar Buddhist devotional practice.
SA_T01_n824u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha, Varanasi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994.
SA_T01_n824u.coverage: complete — Complete hymn comprising 15 verses in anuṣṭubh metre with opening maṅgala/namaskāra and concluding colophon.

SA_T01_n825u.title: Ratnamālāstotra
SA_T01_n825u.author: Vanaratna
SA_T01_n825u.summary: A 25-verse Sanskrit hymn of praise (stotra) dedicated to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (Lokeśvara), composed by the master Vanaratna. Drawing upon cosmological motifs, the hymn lauds Avalokiteśvara as the supreme protector from whose body divinities (including Maheśvara, Nārāyaṇa, Sarasvatī, and Varuṇa) emanate to guide diverse sentient beings.
SA_T01_n825u.attribution: A composition of the master Vanaratna. It is attested under his name in verse 25 as well as in the opening and closing rubrics. The work is also preserved in the Tibetan Tengyur (D 1174), translated by Nags kyi rin chen (Vanaratna) and Rgya mtsho sde.
SA_T01_n825u.edition: Ratnamālāstotra, in Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha (Bauddha Stotra Saṃgraha), ed. Janardan Shastri Pandey, Varanasi/Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994.
SA_T01_n825u.coverage: complete — Complete text of 25 verses, including opening attribution rubric and closing colophon.
translations: jig rten dbang phyug gi bstod pa rin po che'i phreng ba zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 1174): translated by Vanaratna, khrims khang lo tsA ba bsod nams rgya mtsho (Tibetan)

SA_T01_n826u.title: Rūpastava
SA_T01_n826u.summary: The Rūpastava is a 24-verse Sanskrit Buddhist hymn praising the divine bodily appearance and auspicious marks of an enlightened being. Preserved within the Newar Buddhist liturgical corpus of the Kathmandu Valley, it offers an anatomical sequence of veneration, praising in turn the hair, face, crown, eyes, voice, body, garments, arms, hands, navel, and wheel-marked feet. Although designated in its colophon as a hymn to Avalokiteśvara, the refrains consistently praise the 'Daśabala' and the phalaśruti terms it a Sugatastava.
SA_T01_n826u.attribution: Anonymous in the edition of Janārdan Śāstrī Pāṇḍeya and in general transmission. Some Nepalese manuscripts contain colophons attributing the hymn to King Narendradeva ('narendradeva-bhūpatikṛtaṃ rūpastavastotram'). While the final colophon dedicates the hymn to Āryāvalokiteśvara, the refrain addresses the deity with the epithet Daśabala ('ten-powered one'), which could apply to a Buddha, and verse 24 labels it a Sugatastava.
SA_T01_n826u.edition: Janārdan Śāstrī Pāṇḍeya (ed.), Bauddha Stotra Saṃgraha, Varanasi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994, text (BuSto_69).
SA_T01_n826u.coverage: complete — Complete text of 24 verses and the closing colophon.

SA_T01_n827u.title: Ṣaḍgatistotra
SA_T01_n827u.summary: The Ṣaḍgatistotra is a short six-verse Sanskrit Buddhist hymn dedicated to Avalokiteśvara. It venerates the Bodhisattva's physical iconography, auspicious ornaments, and boundless compassion in rescuing beings from cyclic existence across the six realms of rebirth (ṣaḍgati). The concluding verse offers a phalaśruti promising rebirth in the celestial realms of the gods for devoted recitation.
SA_T01_n827u.attribution: The hymn is anonymous. Verse 6 contains a phalaśruti referring to a composer or patron ('śaṃkhakarma puṇyārthato yacchatarājadhīmān'), but no identifiable author is known in standard Buddhist literature.
SA_T01_n827u.coverage: complete — Complete hymn of 6 verses with title header and concluding colophon.

SA_T01_n828u.title: Saptākṣarastotra
SA_T01_n828u.summary: The Saptākṣarastotra is an anonymous eight-verse Buddhist hymn (ślokāṣṭaka) addressed to Āryāvalokiteśvara, reflecting the syncretic Newar Buddhist milieu of the Kathmandu Valley. The text explicitly invokes Avalokiteśvara as Lokanātha, Matsyendra (Matsyendranātha / Karuṇāmaya), and Viṣṇu, praises him alongside the four Buddhist consorts (Locanā, Māmakī, Tārā, and Pāṇḍarā), and describes him wearing Amitābha on his crown while offering protection against yakṣas, rākṣasas, vetālas, and nāgas.
SA_T01_n828u.coverage: complete — Complete hymn in 8 verses (designated as a ślokāṣṭaka in verse 8b), ending with the colophon 'śrīmadāryāvalokiteśvarasya saptākṣarastotraṃ samāptam'.

SA_T01_n829u.title: Saptavidhānuttarastotra
SA_T01_n829u.summary: The Saptavidhānuttarastotra is an anonymous twelve-verse devotional hymn dedicated to Avalokiteśvara (invoked as Lokanātha). It adapts the classical Mahāyāna framework of the 'sevenfold supreme worship' (saptavidhā anuttarā pūjā)—salutation, veneration, refuge, confession, and merit-dedication—into a praise poem concluding with an aspiration for rebirth in Sukhāvatī. The hymn belongs to the liturgical corpus maintained in Nepalese Newar Buddhism.
SA_T01_n829u.attribution: Anonymous stotra addressed to Avalokiteśvara (Lokanātha), preserved in the Newar Buddhist liturgical manuscript tradition.
SA_T01_n829u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha, Varanasi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994.
SA_T01_n829u.coverage: complete — Complete 12-verse hymn, preceded by the opening salutation 'namaḥ śrīlokanāthāya' and concluding with the colophon 'śrīmadāryāvalokiteśvarasya saptavidhānuttararastotraṃ samāptam'.

SA_T01_n830u.title: Śāradāṣṭakastotra
SA_T01_n830u.summary: An eight-verse devotional hymn (aṣṭaka) praising Śāradā (Sarasvatī / Bhāratī) as the grantor of speech, wisdom, and freedom from mental dullness (jāḍyahantrī). Each stanza concludes with the refrain bowing before the blessed goddess (śrīśāradāṃ bhagavatīṃ satataṃ namāmi), describing her as swan-borne, radiantly white, and holding a vīṇā, crystal rosary, and manuscript.
SA_T01_n830u.coverage: complete — Complete text of 8 verses with opening title and closing colophon (śrīśāradāṣṭakastotraṃ samāptam).

SA_T01_n831u.title: Vāgvāṇīstotra
SA_T01_n831u.summary: The Vāgvāṇīstotra is a short devotional hymn of nine verses praising the goddess Sarasvatī under the designation Vāgvāṇī ('Speech/Voice'). Reflecting the syncretic devotional culture of the Kathmandu Valley, it invokes her simultaneously as 'jinapriyā' ('beloved of the Jina / Buddha') and 'keśavasya priyā' ('beloved of Viṣṇu'). In a brief narrative frame, the preceptor Bṛhaspati recites the hymn to obtain divine wisdom, and Sarasvatī promises eloquence, poetic inspiration (kavitva), and fame to all who recite it.
SA_T01_n831u.attribution: The concluding colophon attributes the hymn to Bṛhaspati ('bṛhaspatikṛtaṃ śrīvāgvāṇīstotraṃ samāptam'), who appears as the devotee and interlocutor in the framing dialogue (vv. 5–6). This is a traditional mythological attribution.
SA_T01_n831u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 9 verses with opening title, speaker indications, closing mantra, and colophon.

SA_T01_n832u.title: Daśabhūmīśvaro nāma mahāyānasūtraratnarājastotra
SA_T01_n832u.summary: A 54-verse Buddhist devotional and liturgical work with concluding prose summarizing the bodhisattva path across the ten spiritual stages (daśabhūmi) and their corresponding perfections (pāramitā). It is extracted from the concluding summary verses (upasaṃhāragāthāḥ) of the tenth chapter of the canonical Daśabhūmikasūtra. In Newar Buddhism, it circulated independently within ritual Dhāraṇīsaṃgraha compendia as an auspicious protective text and hymn.
SA_T01_n832u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgrahaḥ, Varanasi/Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994, text no. 26.
SA_T01_n832u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the stotra as edited by J. S. Pandey (1994, text no. 26), containing all 54 verses, concluding prose passage, and final colophon.
translations: Megumu Honda, 'An Annotated Translation of the Daśabhūmika', in: Denis Sinor (ed.), Studies in Southeast and Central Asia, Śata-piṭaka Series 74, New Delhi: International Academy of Indian Culture, 1968. (English)

SA_T01_n833u.title: Caityavandanāstotra
SA_T01_n833u.summary: A short anonymous hymn of five sragdharā verses venerating caityas (stūpas), relic shrines and Buddha images. It salutes the sites of the Buddha's life events (Lumbinī, Vaiśālī, Gṛdhrakūṭa, Śrāvastī, Kuśinagara, etc.), stūpas in mythical and cosmic realms, and those in lands such as Kashmir, China, Siṃhala, Nepal and Kāmarūpa. It belongs to the Nepalese Buddhist liturgical stotra corpus.
SA_T01_n833u.coverage: complete — Five sragdharā verses plus closing rubric 'śrī caityavandanā samāptā'.

SA_T01_n834u.title: Vidyākṣarastotra
SA_T01_n834u.summary: A short anonymous Newar Buddhist hymn (7 anuṣṭubh stanzas) to the Five Tathāgatas as arranged in a caitya: Vairocana in the centre and Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha and Amoghasiddhi in the four directions, each with his seed-syllable (oṃ, hūṃ, trāṃ, jhiṃ, khaṃ), colour, mudrā and animal throne. It then salutes the four goddesses (Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, Tārā) in the intermediate directions and Vajrasattva within the caitya; the colophon ascribes it to (the worship of) Buddhabhaṭṭāraka.
SA_T01_n834u.attribution: The concluding line 'śrī buddhabhaṭṭārakasya vidyākṣarastotraṃ samāptam' names the deity praised (Buddhabhaṭṭāraka / Caityabhaṭṭāraka) in the genitive case, not a human author.
SA_T01_n834u.coverage: complete — 7 anuṣṭubh stanzas and colophon 'śrī buddhabhaṭṭārakasya vidyākṣarastotraṃ samāptam'.

SA_T01_n835u.title: Cakrasaṃvarastuti
SA_T01_n835u.summary: An 18-verse Vajrayāna stotra celebrating the tutelary deity Cakrasaṃvara (Heruka) and his maṇḍala retinue. Following salutations to Heruka and Vajravārāhī, the hymn maps the twenty-four ḍākinīs to their traditional sacred pilgrimage sites (pīṭhas such as Pullīramalaya, Jālandhara, and Oḍḍiyāna) and the internal channels of the human body across the body, speech, and mind wheels (kāyavākcittacakra). The stotra concludes with praises to the four animal-faced peripheral goddesses (Kākāsyā, Ulūkāsyā, etc.) and four gatekeeping deities, ending with a dedication of merit wishing that all beings attain the status of Vajraḍāka.
SA_T01_n835u.attribution: An anonymous tantric stotra preserved in Nepalese Buddhist manuscript collections and liturgical anthologies.
SA_T01_n835u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha, Varanasi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994.
SA_T01_n835u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 18 verses with the opening salutation, alternate title header, and concluding colophon.

SA_T01_n836u.title: Catuḥṣaṣṭisaṃvarastotra
SA_T01_n836u.summary: The Catuḥṣaṣṭisaṃvarastotra is an anonymous Buddhist tantric hymn of the Cakrasaṃvara/Heruka cycle preserved in Nepalese manuscript collections. In 75 anuṣṭubh stanzas, it invokes Śrī Heruka Cakrasaṃvara and an elaborate retinue of sixty-four theriomorphic aspects or emanations (such as Meṣasaṃvara, Aśvasaṃvara, Vyāghrasaṃvara, and Kūrmasaṃvara) conjoined with their consorts. The final portion consists of an extensive phalaśruti detailing worldly protection, pacification of epidemics and famines, and the attainment of classical tantric accomplishments (siddhis).
SA_T01_n836u.attribution: Anonymous Buddhist tantric hymn preserved in Nepalese manuscripts. The closing colophonic line frames the stotra as deriving from a dialogue between Amitābha and Vairocana in the Saṃvarāgama (śrīsaṃvarāgame mahātantre amitābhavairocanasaṃvāde).
SA_T01_n836u.coverage: complete — Complete in 75 anuṣṭubh verses plus colophon, comprising 64 theriomorphic deity invocations (vv. 1–66), phalaśruti (vv. 67–75), and the concluding rubric.

SA_T01_n837u.title: Pīṭhastava
SA_T01_n837u.summary: A tantric Sanskrit hymn in 67 verses venerating Gaṇapati followed by the Eight Mothers (Aṣṭamātṛkā: Brahmāṇī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī/Śakreśvarī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Mahālakṣmī). Each goddess is invoked in conjunction with one of the directional sacred seats (pīṭhas/kṣetras, such as Prayāga, Vārāṇasī, Kolāpura, Aṭṭahāsa, and Jayantī) and corresponding sacred trees (udumbara, tāla, vaṭa, kadamba, nimba, karañja). Preserved in the Newar Buddhist tradition, the hymn concludes with a phalaśruti (vv. 61–67) promising protection from disease, conflicts, premature death, and hostile sorcery.
SA_T01_n837u.attribution: Anonymous stotra preserved in Newar Buddhist ritual collections and manuscripts.
SA_T01_n837u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha, Varanasi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994.
SA_T01_n837u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 67 verses with final colophon.

SA_T01_n838u.title: Ṣaṭtriṃśatsaṃvarastuti
SA_T01_n838u.summary: An anonymous tantric Buddhist stotra of 37 verses eulogizing the thirty-six deities of the Cakrasaṃvara maṇḍala. Following an opening homage to Cakrasaṃvara, Vajravārāhī, and the four inner yoginīs, the hymn praises the twenty-four hero-consort pairs stationed across the pīṭhas and internal body loci, followed by the eight directional and gate-guarding deities, concluding with an aspiration dedicating the merit toward reaching the state of Vajraḍāka.
SA_T01_n838u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha, Delhi/Varanasi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994.
SA_T01_n838u.coverage: complete — Complete text of 37 verses with closing colophon.

SA_T01_n839u.title: Vasantatilakāstuti
SA_T01_n839u.summary: A short four-verse Vajrayāna Buddhist hymn belonging to the Cakrasaṃvara/Heruka tradition. Verses 1 and 2 praise the male deity Heruka (addressed as Ubhayacittaheruka and Sahajātmaheruka) visualized within the internal centres (dhātumaṇḍala) and subtle channels (nāḍikā) of the body. Verses 3 and 4 praise the goddess Herukī (Vajravārāhī / Nairātmyā) emerging like lightning from the navel lotus to consume celestial ambrosia. The title refers to the esoteric 'spring drop' (vasantatilakā) central to subtle-body completion stage (niṣpannakrama) yoga.
SA_T01_n839u.coverage: complete — Complete 4-verse stotra with opening title and closing colophon (śrīvasantatilakāstutiḥ samāptā).

SA_T01_n840u.title: Dharmadhātunāmastava
SA_T01_n840u.summary: A brief seven-verse Buddhist tantric liturgical hymn. In each verse, an invocation and obeisance (namo 'stu te) are offered to one of the Five Tathāgatas (Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi), the Dharmadhātu, and Siddhivajra, associating each with an esoteric seed-syllable (bīja: vaṃ, a, ra, etc.) and elemental or cosmological attributes.
SA_T01_n840u.coverage: complete — Complete 7-verse hymn with closing colophon.

SA_T01_n841u.title: Pañcākṣarastotra
SA_T01_n841u.summary: A short Newar Buddhist devotional hymn in six anuṣṭubh verses explicating the five-syllable (pañcākṣara) phrase 'namo buddhāya'. The first five verses offer an acrostic doctrinal and symbolic interpretation for each constituent syllable (na, mo, bu, dha, ya), followed by a final verse (phalaśruti) describing the spiritual merit of day-and-night recitation.
SA_T01_n841u.coverage: complete — Complete hymn of six anuṣṭubh verses (five stanzas explicating the syllables na-mo-bu-dha-ya and a closing phalaśruti) ending with 'śrī pañcākṣarastotraṃ samāptam'.

SA_T01_n842u.title: Buddhagaṇḍīstava
SA_T01_n842u.author: Aśvaghoṣa
SA_T01_n842u.summary: The Buddhagaṇḍīstava (also known as Gaṇḍīstotragāthā or Buddhagaṇḍī) is a 32-stanza Sanskrit Buddhist hymn commemorating the Buddha's enlightenment and triumph over Māra through the rhythmic sounding of the gaṇḍī. The striking of the gaṇḍī is praised as awakening sentient beings and banishing impurities. The poem features rhythmic and onomatopoeic verses imitating percussive strikes (e.g., 'daṃ daṃ daṃ daṃ', 'tuṃ tuṃ tuṃ tuṃ', 'ṭuṃ ṭuṃ ṭuṃ ṭuṃ').
SA_T01_n842u.attribution: Attributed to Ācārya Aśvaghoṣa in the opening rubric and closing colophon, as well as in the Tibetan translation.
SA_T01_n842u.coverage: complete — Complete stotra in 32 verses with introductory rubric and closing colophon.
translations: Faxian (法賢 / Tianxizai / 天息災), 犍稚梵讚 (Jianzhi fanzan), Taishō Tripiṭaka no. 1683, 1001. (Chinese)
gaN+DI'i bstod pa tshigs su bcad pa (Derge Tengyur D 1149): translated by Jayasena III, sum pa lo tsA ba dar ma yon tan (Tibetan)

SA_T01_n843u.title: Gaṇḍīstava
SA_T01_n843u.author: Āryadeva
SA_T01_n843u.summary: A Buddhist devotional hymn (stotra) of 34 stanzas composed in elaborate classical kāvya style, primarily in the twenty-one-syllable sragdharā metre. It celebrates the sounding of the monastic wooden gong (gaṇḍī), framing its percussive rhythm as an acoustic manifestation of the Dharma that awakens living beings, summons the saṅgha, and dispels the hosts of Māra. Stanza 5 features acoustic mimicry of the gong strikes using onomatopoeic syllables ('ṛmpaṃ ṛmpaṃ... ṭama ṭama ṭaṭamaṃ...'). The colophon attributes the work to Āryadeva.
SA_T01_n843u.attribution: The e-text explicitly opens with 'ācārya-āryadevakṛtaḥ' and concludes with 'kṛtiriyam ācārya-āryadevapādānām'.
SA_T01_n843u.coverage: complete — Complete hymn of 34 stanzas, predominantly in sragdharā metre.

SA_T01_n844u.title: Gaṇeśastotra
SA_T01_n844u.summary: A 14-verse devotional hymn in praise of Gaṇeśa (invoked also as Heramba, Vināyaka, and Vighnarāja), preserved in the manuscript tradition of Newar Buddhism in Nepal. The hymn petitions the elephant-headed deity for success and the removal of obstacles, concluding with an enumeration of his sixteen well-known epithets (ṣoḍaśanāmāni) to be recited at the commencement of any enterprise. It illustrates the ritual incorporation of pan-Indian deities into the Newar Vajrayāna Buddhist devotional repertoire.
SA_T01_n844u.edition: Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha (A Collection of Buddhist Hymns), ed. Janardan Shastri Pandey, 1994.
SA_T01_n844u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 14 verses with final colophon formula.

SA_T01_n845u.title: Hāratīstotra
SA_T01_n845u.summary: The Hāratīstotra is a short nine-verse Buddhist devotional stotra addressed to Hārītī (spelled Hāratī in the text), revered as a protectress of children. The text describes her seated in lalitāsana upon an eight-petaled lotus on a jeweled throne, adorned with diadems and jewelry, embracing her child with her left arm while granting fearlessness with her right hand. The concluding verse promises health, wealth, and safety for children to anyone who recites the hymn in their household at daybreak.
SA_T01_n845u.attribution: The colophon reads: 'śrībhavaratnavinirgataṃ bālarakṣākaraṃ hāratīstotraṃ samāptam |'.
SA_T01_n845u.coverage: complete — Complete hymn of 9 verses with opening salutation ('śrī hāratīdevyaiḥ namaḥ') and concluding colophon.

SA_T01_n850u.title: Mahācakravartināmāṣṭottaraśatastotra
SA_T01_n850u.summary: The Mahācakravartināmāṣṭottaraśatastotra is a 20-verse Buddhist tantric litany and formal supplication (adhyeṣaṇā) addressed to Sarvatathāgatamahācakravartin, an esoteric manifestation of Vajrasattva associated with Trailokyavijaya. Verses 1–16 enumerate 108 devotional epithets and honorific invocations ending with 'namo 'stu te', followed by praise of the deity as the firm essence (vajradṛḍhaṃ cittam) and progenitor of all Tathāgatas (vv. 17–18), a benefit verse (phalaśruti, v. 19), and a formal prayer (adhyeṣaṇā, v. 20) entreating the lord to manifest his tantric family for the welfare of beings. Originally situated in Chapter 6 (Trilokavijayamahāmaṇḍalavidhivistara) of the Yoga Tantra scripture Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha, it also circulated as an independent liturgical hymn in the Newar Buddhist tradition.
SA_T01_n850u.attribution: Scriptural and anonymous. The text is a 20-verse excerpt from Chapter 6 (Trilokavijayamahāmaṇḍalavidhivistara) of the Yoga Tantra root scripture Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha (STTS), where the Tathāgatas entreat and praise the Bhagavan Sarvatathāgatamahācakravartin (Vajrasattva / Trailokyavijaya). In the Nepalese Newar Buddhist manuscript tradition, it was excerpted and circulated as an autonomous devotional and liturgical stotra.
SA_T01_n850u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha, Varanasi/Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994 (stotra no. 44 in the GRETIL 108-stotra collection).
SA_T01_n850u.coverage: complete — Complete 20 verses and closing colophon line of hymn no. 44 as published in Pandey's Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha.
translations: Giebel, Rolf W. (trans.), Two Esoteric Sutras: The Adamantine Pinnacle Sutra, The Susiddhikara Sutra, Berkeley: Numata Center for Buddhist Translation and Research, 2001. (English)

SA_T01_n851u.title: Mahākālastotra
SA_T01_n851u.summary: The Mahākālastotra is a short Buddhist devotional hymn in 13 anuṣṭubh stanzas addressed to the two-armed (dvibhuja) wrathful protector Mahākāla. It invokes the deity as the granter of all prosperity (sarvasampattidāyaka) and protector of practitioners (siddhasādhakarakṣaka), describing his fierce iconographic attributes including the crown of skulls, necklace of severed heads, adornment of eight serpents, tiger-skin garment, chopper (kartikā), and skull-cup (kapāla). The hymn concludes with a phalaśruti promising deliverance from fear and the realization of all spiritual accomplishments (sarvasiddhi).
SA_T01_n851u.coverage: complete — Complete hymn in 13 anuṣṭubh stanzas with final closing colophon (śrīmahākālastotraṃ sampūrṇam).

SA_T01_n852u.title: Vajramahākālastotra
SA_T01_n852u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T01_n852u.summary: The Vajramahākālastotra is a nine-stanza Vajrayāna hymn composed in the Sragdharā meter, traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna. Dedicated to the wrathful protector Mahākāla—invoked repeatedly throughout the text under his aspect or retinue identity of Kṣetrapāla ('field-protector')—each verse begins with alliterative chains of tantric seed-syllables (bījas) such as hāṃ, pheṃ, kṣaṃ, and klīṃ. The text details the deity's terrifying charnel-ground iconography and concludes with a phalaśruti promising health, renown, peace, and the removal of all obstacles.
SA_T01_n852u.attribution: Attributed in the opening rubric to Ācārya Nāgārjuna ('ācāryanāgārjunakṛtam').
SA_T01_n852u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha, Varanasi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994.
SA_T01_n852u.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising 9 Sragdharā stanzas (8 stanzas of praise followed by 1 phalaśruti stanza), ending with the colophon 'śrīvajramahākālastotraṃ samāptam'.

SA_T01_n853u.title: Mañjuśrīnāmāṣṭottaraśatakastotra
SA_T01_n853u.summary: A short Mahāyāna devotional litany consisting of 19 anuṣṭubh verses enumerating 108 names and epithets of Mañjuśrī, the bodhisattva of transcendent wisdom. Following an opening verse of obeisance, the hymn celebrates Mañjuśrī as embodiment of emptiness (śūnyatā), supreme guide, healer, Ādibuddha, and the cosmic source of deities across both Buddhist and classical Indic pantheons. It appears as hymn BuSto_4 in Pāṇḍeya's Bauddha Stotra Saṃgraha.
SA_T01_n853u.attribution: Anonymous Mahāyāna Buddhist litany transmitted in Sanskrit stotra collections.
SA_T01_n853u.edition: Janārdan Śāstrī Pāṇḍeya (ed.), Bauddha Stotra Saṃgraha, Varanasi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994, text no. BuSto_4.
SA_T01_n853u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 19 anuṣṭubh verses, matching stotra no. 4 (BuSto_4) in Janārdan Śāstrī Pāṇḍeya's Bauddha Stotra Saṃgraha.

SA_T01_n854u.title: Mañjuśrīstotra
SA_T01_n854u.summary: A short nine-verse Sanskrit devotional hymn (stotra) dedicated to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī (also addressed as Mañjunātha and Mañjughoṣa). The text extols his youthful appearance (sukumārarūpa, bālākṛti), ornaments, and iconographic emblems—specifically the sword cutting through ignorance, the sacred book, and the alms bowl. He is praised as the embodiment of discriminative insight (prajñānidhāna) who removes all affliction across the three worlds.
SA_T01_n854u.coverage: complete — Complete hymn of 9 verses with the concluding colophon formula: śrī mañjuśrīstavastotraṃ samāptam.

SA_T01_n855u.title: Guhyeśvarīstotra
SA_T01_n855u.summary: The Guhyeśvarīstotra is a seven-verse Newar Buddhist devotional hymn in Mālinī metre dedicated to the goddess Guhyeśvarī, venerated at her sacred shrine in the Kathmandu Valley as the root (mūla) of the lotus supporting the Svayambhū caitya and identified with Prajñāpāramitā or Nairātmyā. Extracted from the Svayambhūpurāṇa, the hymn is attributed in the narrative to the Bodhisattva Mañjunātha (Mañjuśrī), who praises the cosmic form (viśvarūpa) and transcendent nature of the goddess. The first six verses close with the uniform refrain praising her lotus feet ('caraṇakamalayugmaṃ naumi devi tvadīyam'), followed by a seventh verse detailing the spiritual accomplishments (siddhi) granted by devout recitation.
SA_T01_n855u.attribution: The colophon explicitly states that the hymn is an excerpt from the Svayambhūpurāṇa composed by Mañjunātha (śrī svayaṃbhūpurāṇoddhṛtaṃ mañjunāthakṛtaṃ guhyeśvarīstotram).
SA_T01_n855u.coverage: complete — Complete hymn of 7 verses in Mālinī metre (6 stanzas with the refrain 'caraṇakamalayugmaṃ naumi devi tvadīyam' and 1 phalaśruti stanza), followed by the closing colophon.

SA_T01_n856u.title: Nairātmāṣṭakastotra
SA_T01_n856u.summary: The Nairātmāṣṭakastotra is a short eight-verse hymn (aṣṭaka) in anuṣṭubh meter addressed to the tantric Buddhist goddess Nairātmyā (Nairātmā), consort of Hevajra and personification of selflessness (nairātmya). The hymn praises her absolute nature as free of conceptual construct (nirvikalpa) and without support (nirālamba), while describing her wrathful iconographic attributes (one-faced, three-eyed, dancing on a corpse, carrying a chopper and skull-cup) and her retinue of the eight maṇḍala yoginīs (Gaurī, Caurī, Vetālī, Ghasmarī, Pukkasī, Śabarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombī).
SA_T01_n856u.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 8 anuṣṭubh stanzas with opening title and closing colophon.

SA_T01_n857u.title: Pañcatathāgatastotra
SA_T01_n857u.summary: A short five-verse Sanskrit Buddhist devotional hymn (stotra) dedicated to the Five Tathāgatas presiding over the five Buddha families (kulas): Buddha/Vairocana, Vajra/Akṣobhya, Ratna/Ratnasambhava, Padma/Amitābha, and Viśva/Amoghasiddhi. Each stanza employs elaborate alliteration (yamaka) built upon the family name (buddha, vajra, ratna, padma, viśva) to celebrate the respective Tathāgata's enlightened qualities and salvific activity.
SA_T01_n857u.coverage: complete — Complete text in five verses, followed by the concluding formula 'śrīpañcatathāgatastotraṃ samāptam'.

SA_T01_n858u.title: Pañcatathāgatastutigāthā
SA_T01_n858u.summary: A short liturgical hymn praising the Five Tathāgatas with paradoxical epithets (buddharāga, buddhakāma, buddhahāsa, māyājāla, jñānakāya). The verses are identical, with minor variants, to the concluding praise verses 158–162 of the Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti and circulated independently in the Nepalese stotra tradition.
SA_T01_n858u.attribution: The five verses correspond to Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti vv. 158–162 (the 'pañcatathāgatastuti' at the end of the Nāmasaṃgīti), circulating separately as a liturgical stotra; preceded by an invocation 'om namaḥ śrīpañcabhūtāntāya'.
SA_T01_n858u.coverage: complete — Complete as transmitted (invocation + 5 verses + colophon). As part of the Nāmasaṃgīti it is an excerpt (vv. 158–162).

SA_T01_n859u.title: Sragdharāpañcakastotra
SA_T01_n859u.summary: The Sragdharāpañcakastotra is a short five-verse Sanskrit devotional hymn composed in the sragdharā metre. It praises the primordial Ādibuddha as the ultimate unmanifest, pristine mental caitya (cittacaitya) and primordial flame (jyotīrūpa), from which the Five Tathāgatas (Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amṛtaruc/Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi) and all beings proceed. The hymn is framed as an act of complete devotional surrender and dedication of merit uttered by Śākyamuni Buddha.
SA_T01_n859u.attribution: The concluding colophonic line reads: 'śrīśākyasiṃhabuddhakṛtaṃ sragdharāpañcakaṃ samāptam' ('The Sragdharāpañcaka composed by the glorious Śākyasiṃha Buddha is completed').
SA_T01_n859u.coverage: complete — Complete in 5 verses in the sragdharā metre plus the concluding colophon sentence.

SA_T01_n861u.title: Pañcarakṣādevīstotrāṇi
SA_T01_n861u.summary: Pañcarakṣādevīstotrāṇi is a cycle of five five-verse hymns (25 verses total) celebrating the five protective goddesses of the Pañcarakṣā pentad: Mahāpratisarā, Mahāmantrānusāriṇī, Mahāmāyūrī, Mahāśītavatī, and Mahāsāhasrapramardinī. Each hymn extols the apotropaic efficacy of the deity and her dhāraṇī in dispelling snakebites, illnesses, hostile planetary influences (graha), and calamities. The cycle forms a core component of traditional Newar Buddhist devotional and liturgical practice.
SA_T01_n861u.attribution: Anonymous; preserved in Nepalese Mahāyāna/Vajrayāna liturgical manuscripts.
SA_T01_n861u.coverage: complete — Complete cycle of 25 verses comprising five distinct 5-verse stotras dedicated individually to Mahāpratisarā, Mahāmantrānusāriṇī, Mahāmāyūrī, Mahāśītavatī, and Mahāsāhasrapramardinī.

SA_T01_n862u.title: Pratisarāstotra
SA_T01_n862u.summary: A 15-verse Buddhist devotional hymn addressed to the protective deity Mahāpratisarā, extracted from the Nepalese avadāna collection Bhadrakalpāvadāna. Narratively, the hymn is uttered by the unborn Rāhula from within the womb of Queen Yaśodharā when she faces an ordeal by fire after accusations of infidelity caused by her extended six-year pregnancy; invoking Mahāpratisarā causes the fire pit to miraculously transform into a cooling lotus pool.
SA_T01_n862u.attribution: The concluding colophon records the hymn as an extract from the Bhadrakalpāvadāna, composed dramatically by the child in Yaśodharā's womb ('śrībhadrakalpāvadānoddhṛtaṃ yaśodharāgarbhasthabālakṛtam'), representing Prince Rāhula during Yaśodharā's trial by fire.
SA_T01_n862u.coverage: complete — Complete text of 15 verses with closing prose colophon.

SA_T01_n867u.title: Bhaktiśataka
SA_T01_n867u.author: Rāmacandra Kavibhāratī
SA_T01_n867u.summary: The Bhaktiśataka ('Century of Devotion', also known as Bauddhaśataka) is a 15th-century Sanskrit stotra composed in 107 verses by the Bengali poet Rāmacandra Kavibhāratī, who went to Sri Lanka and converted to Buddhism. Extolling the Buddha as the supreme refuge free of passion and defilement, the poem contrasts him with deities such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. The text is accompanied in tradition by a commentary (vyākhyāna) by Sumaṅgala Muni.
SA_T01_n867u.attribution: Composed by the Bengali author Rāmacandra Kavibhāratī (Rāmacandra Bhāratin), who came from Bengal to Sri Lanka in the 15th century CE and converted to Buddhism. The text is followed by traditional closing verses mentioning the commentary (vyākhyāna) by Sumaṅgala Muni, pupil of Śrī Rāhula.
SA_T01_n867u.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising 107 stanzas of the root hymn followed by concluding verses.
translations: Haraprasād, Journal of the Buddhist Text Society, Calcutta, 1893. (English)

SA_T01_n868u.title: Buddhabhaṭṭārakastotra
SA_T01_n868u.summary: The Buddhabhaṭṭārakastotra is a Buddhist devotional hymn in anuṣṭubh meter eulogizing the Buddha under the honorific designation Bhaṭṭāraka. The first 15 stanzas weave together names and epithets celebrating the Buddha's wisdom, moral perfection, compassion, and victory over Māra, followed by 4 phalaśruti stanzas enumerating the spiritual and worldly benefits of daily morning recitation. The hymn concludes with a traditional colophonic attribution to Brahmā.
SA_T01_n868u.attribution: The closing colophon attributes the hymn to Brahmā ('buddhabhaṭṭārakasya brahmāviracitaṃ stotraṃ samāptam').
SA_T01_n868u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 19 verses (15 stanzas enumerating names/epithets of the Buddha, followed by 4 phalaśruti stanzas) with opening salutation and closing colophon.

SA_T01_n869u.title: Buddhagadya
SA_T01_n869u.summary: A Sanskrit eulogy of the Buddha transmitted in Sri Lanka (Sinhala Buddhagadyaya/Buddhagajjaya), in 41 numbered sections of rhymed, rhythmic strings of vocative epithets (jaya jaya dharmarāja ...), in the manner of a daṇḍaka-like 'gadya', closing with a mālinī stanza on the merit of copying, reciting or hearing this 'gadya of the Dharma-king'. It praises the Buddha's marks, virtues, victory over Māra, teaching and miracles.
SA_T01_n869u.attribution: No author is named in the text.
SA_T01_n869u.coverage: complete — 41 numbered stanzas, the last (v. 41, mālinī) a phalaśruti calling the work 'dharmmarājasya gadyam', followed by 'siddhir astu. śubham astu.' and the Sinhala closing 'buddhagadyaya nimi.' Nothing suggests missing text.

SA_T01_n870u.title: Buddhastotra
SA_T01_n870u.summary: An 11-verse Sanskrit devotional hymn praising the Buddha, featuring the colophon 'bodhisattvasamuccayānāma kuladevatāviracitaṃ buddhastotraṃ samāptam'. It praises the Buddha's rare appearance in the world like the udumbara flower, his entrance into the peaceful city (śāntapura), and the empty (śūnya) nature of dharmas and beings.
SA_T01_n870u.attribution: The colophon states: 'bodhisattvasamuccayānāma kuladevatāviracitaṃ buddhastotraṃ samāptam'.
SA_T01_n870u.coverage: complete — Complete 11-verse hymn ending with the colophon.

SA_T01_n871u.title: Nāmāṣṭaśataka
SA_T01_n871u.summary: A litany (nāmastotra) of epithets of the Buddha Śākyasiṃha in 15 anuṣṭubh stanzas, each ending 'namāmy aham', followed by three stanzas promising long life, health, prosperity and eloquence to those who recite it every morning. The e-text represents the version used in Sri Lanka (Sinhala Nāmāṣṭaśatakaya).
SA_T01_n871u.attribution: Anonymous litany of epithets of Śākyasiṃha. The present version carries Sinhala title and colophon forms.
SA_T01_n871u.coverage: complete — Opening 'namaḥ śākyasiṃhāya', 15 anuṣṭubh stanzas of epithets with refrain 'namāmy aham', 3 phalaśruti stanzas (16–18), closing 'nāmāṣṭaśatakaya nimi' (Sinhala 'ended').

SA_T01_n872u.title: Śākyasiṃhastotra (brahmaṇā kṛtam)
SA_T01_n872u.summary: The Śākyasiṃhastotra (brahmaṇā kṛtam) is a Sanskrit Buddhist hymn of praise comprising nine verses addressed to Buddha Śākyamuni. Framed as spoken by Brahmā, it lauds the Buddha's attainment of insight, his turning of the dharmacakra, his weaponless victory over Namuci (Māra), and his descent from Tuṣita heaven.
SA_T01_n872u.attribution: Attributed to Brahmā in the title, in verse 9 ('yaścāṣṭakaṃ brahmakṛtaṃ...'), and in the colophon ('brahmaṇā kṛtaṃ śrīśākyasiṃhastotraṃ samāptam').
SA_T01_n872u.coverage: complete — Complete text of 9 verses, including the opening maṅgala and final colophon.

SA_T01_n873u.title: Śākyasiṃhastotra
SA_T01_n873u.author: Amṛtānanda
SA_T01_n873u.summary: The Śākyasiṃhastotra (chando'mṛtoddhṛtam) is a short nine-verse Sanskrit Buddhist hymn praising Śākyasiṃha (the Buddha Śākyamuni).
SA_T01_n873u.coverage: complete — Complete 9-verse hymn concluding with 'chando'mṛtoddhṛtaṃ śrīśākyasiṃhastotraṃ samāptam'.

SA_T01_n875u.title: Śākyasiṃhastotra
SA_T01_n875u.summary: The Śākyasiṃhastotra (navagrahakṛtam) is a short Sanskrit Buddhist hymn of 10 stanzas composed in Toṭaka meter in praise of Śākyamuni Buddha (Śākyasiṃha). Verses 1–9 narrate key aspects of the Buddha's life and virtues: his golden appearance and destruction of Māra's army, his teaching of the ten pāramitās and four Noble Truths, his voluntary birth in the Śākya clan, his renunciation accompanied by Chandaka and Kaṇṭhaka, his forest austerities, his victory over Māra under the Bodhi tree, his reception of offerings from merchants, and his first turning of the wheel of the doctrine at the deer park in Vārāṇasī. The concluding phalaśruti stanza promises that whoever recites this hymn will be freed from disease and planetary afflictions (graharogabhaya) and will reach liberation.
SA_T01_n875u.attribution: Attributed in the opening rubric ('navagrahakṛtam') and concluding colophon ('ādityādinavagrahakṛtaṃ śrīśākyasiṃhastotraṃ samāptam') to the Navagrahas (the nine planetary deities).
SA_T01_n875u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha, Varanasi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994.
SA_T01_n875u.coverage: complete — Complete hymn comprising 10 stanzas in Toṭaka meter (9 verses of praise summarizing the life of the Buddha and 1 phalaśruti verse), preceded by title rubrics and followed by the closing colophon.

SA_T01_n876u.title: Śākyasiṃhastotra
SA_T01_n876u.summary: A short seven-verse Buddhist devotional hymn composed in the pañcacāmara metre praising Buddha Śākyamuni (Śākyasiṃha). The hymn is framed as having been uttered by Śaṅkara (Śiva / Hara), reflecting the well-attested Newar Buddhist trope of Brahmanical deities venerating the Buddha as the supreme teacher. The final verse functions as a phalaśruti, stating that those who recite this stotra before the Jina will obtain spiritual and worldly prosperity and attain rebirth in Sukhāvatī.
SA_T01_n876u.attribution: Attributed in the title rubric, v. 7 ('vinirmitaṃ hareṇa'), and colophon ('śaṅkarakṛtam') to the Hindu god Śaṅkara / Hara (Śiva). In Newar Buddhist devotional literature, attributing Buddhist hymns to major Brahmanical deities is a standard devotional framing device illustrating the subjugation and conversion of Hindu gods to the Buddha's dharma.
SA_T01_n876u.coverage: complete — Complete text of 7 verses (6 verses of praise in the pañcacāmara metre and 1 concluding phalaśruti verse) with opening heading and closing colophon.

SA_T01_n877u.title: Śākyasiṃhastotra (Surapatikṛta)
SA_T01_n877u.summary: A nine-verse Buddhist devotional hymn composed in the Sragdharā metre addressed to Buddha Śākyamuni (Śākyasiṃha), dramatically framed as spoken by Surapati (Indra). The hymn praises the Buddha's career: his descent from Tuṣita after commissioning Maitreya, birth from Queen Māyā, renunciation, the radiating lights of the ūrṇā delivering denizens of the hells, and the subjugation of Māra witnessed by the earth goddess Bhūmidevī. It concludes with the reflection that the Buddha's ocean of virtues cannot be exhausted even in an eon, and promises mundane protection by Indra and the Lokapālas as well as eventual rebirth in the realm of the Sugata's disciples for whoever recites it.
SA_T01_n877u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Surapati (Indra / Śakra, the king of the gods), who is depicted extolling the Buddha.
SA_T01_n877u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha, Varanasi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994.
SA_T01_n877u.coverage: complete — Complete text consisting of 9 verses in Sragdharā metre, including phalaśruti (v. 9) and the final colophon.

SA_T01_n878u.title: Śākyasiṃhastotra (Viṣṇukṛta)
SA_T01_n878u.summary: The Śākyasiṃhastotra (Viṣṇukṛta) is a short Sanskrit hymn of eleven verses in the Bhujaṅgaprayāta meter in praise of Gautama Buddha (Śākyasiṃha). Mythologically framed as a eulogy uttered by the Hindu deity Viṣṇu (addressed as Mādhava in verse 10), the stotra celebrates the Buddha's triumph over Māra, his teaching of the Four Noble Truths, his possession of the thirty-two major marks, and his vow to save sentient beings in the Kaliyuga. The text reflects the devotional and syncretic environment of medieval and early modern Newar Buddhism in the Kathmandu Valley.
SA_T01_n878u.attribution: The hymn is framed as having been composed by Viṣṇu under the name Mādhava in verse 10 ('bhujaṅgaprayātaṃ kṛtaṃ mādhavena') and in the colophon ('śrīśākyasiṃhasya viṣṇukṛtaṃ bhujaṅgaprayātastotraṃ samāptam').
SA_T01_n878u.edition: Bauddha Stotra Saṃgraha, ed. Janardan Shastri Pandey, Motilal Banarsidass, Varanasi, 1994.
SA_T01_n878u.coverage: complete — Complete in 11 stanzas composed in Bhujaṅgaprayāta meter, together with the opening maṅgala invocation and closing colophon.

SA_T01_n879u.title: Śākyasiṃhastotra
SA_T01_n879u.author: Yaśodharā
SA_T01_n879u.summary: A Sanskrit devotional hymn (stotra) of 18 verses. In verses 1–17, Yaśodharā speaks to her son Rāhula, recounting the Buddha's miraculous birth, renunciation, austerities by the Nairañjanā river, and enlightenment under the Bodhi tree, instructing the child to revere his father. The final verse narrates Rāhula's joyful response upon seeing the Buddha.
SA_T01_n879u.attribution: Attributed to Yaśodharā. Verses 1–17 are framed as Yaśodharā's speech instructing her son Rāhula to recognize and worship his father, while verse 18 describes Rāhula's joyful response.
SA_T01_n879u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha, Varanasi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994.
SA_T01_n879u.coverage: complete — Complete text of 18 verses, including introductory title and concluding colophon.

SA_T01_n880u.title: Sattvārādhanagāthā
SA_T01_n880u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T01_n880u.summary: A short Mahāyāna devotional hymn of eleven verses in which the Buddha proclaims that propitiating and compassionately serving living beings (sattvārādhana) constitutes the true and highest adoration of the Tathāgata. The Buddha explains that his spiritual career, bodily sacrifices, and attainment of awakening were carried out entirely for the welfare of beings; therefore, harming beings injures the Buddha, while benefiting them brings supreme delight to him.
SA_T01_n880u.attribution: Ascribed to Nāgārjuna in the introductory line ('ārya nāgārjunakṛtā') and in the Tibetan canonical records (such as Toh 1125 / Toh 4516). The colophon designates the text as spoken by the Buddha ('samyaksambuddhabhāṣitā').
SA_T01_n880u.coverage: complete — Complete in 11 verses with opening heading and concluding colophon.
translations: sems can mgu bar bya ba'i bstod pa (Derge Tengyur D 1125): translated by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna, nag 'tsho lo tsA ba tshul khrims rgyal ba (Tibetan)

SA_T01_n881u.title: Suprabhātastotra
SA_T01_n881u.author: Harṣadeva
SA_T01_n881u.summary: The Suprabhātastotra ('Auspicious Morning Hymn') is a 24-stanza devotional hymn in classical kāvya metres praising the Buddha (addressed throughout as Daśabala). Attributed to King Harṣadeva (Harṣavardhana), the composition contrasts the awakened state of the Buddha with celestial and Brahmanical gods (such as Śiva, Viṣṇu, Gaṇapati), as well as celebrated Vedic sages and worldly ascetics, depicting them as languishing in sleep, attachment, and ignorance. Verses 2 through 18 culminate in the recurring daily refrain 'daśabala tava nityaṃ suprabhātaṃ prabhātam' ('O Ten-Powered One, may you always have an auspicious dawn').
SA_T01_n881u.attribution: Attributed in colophons and manuscript tradition to King Harṣadeva (Harṣavardhana). The attribution is discussed in Indological scholarship (Thomas 1903; Ettinghausen 1906).
SA_T01_n881u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha, Varanasi/Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994 (BuSto_89).
SA_T01_n881u.coverage: complete — Complete stotra consisting of 24 verses (numbered 1–24), beginning with an invocation and ending with the author colophon.
translations: rab tu snga bar nam langs pa'i bstod pa (Derge Tengyur D 1167): translated by śrījñānamitra, khe'u brgad yon tan dpal (Tibetan)

SA_T01_n882u.title: Saptabuddhastotra
SA_T01_n882u.summary: The Saptabuddhastotra is an anonymous Sanskrit Buddhist hymn of praise (stotra) preserved in the Nepalese Newar manuscript tradition. Over nine verses in Sragdharā meter, it systematically enumerates each of the seven Buddhas of antiquity (Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Śākyamuni) and the future Buddha Maitreya, specifying the birthplace, clan/lineage, lifespan, and bodhi tree of each. The concluding verse dedicates the accumulated merit to the destruction of afflictions and the attainment of nirvāṇa.
SA_T01_n882u.attribution: No author is named in the manuscript tradition or in printed editions; the work is an anonymous Nepalese Buddhist hymn.
SA_T01_n882u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha, Varanasi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994.
SA_T01_n882u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 9 verses (vv. 1–7 eulogizing the seven past Buddhas Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Śākyamuni; v. 8 praising the future Buddha Maitreya; v. 9 dedication of merit).
translations: Horace Hayman Wilson, Works of the Late Horace Hayman Wilson, vol. II, London: Trübner & Co., 1862, p. 5. (English)

SA_T01_n883u.title: Saptajinastava
SA_T01_n883u.summary: The Saptajinastava ('Praise of the Seven Conquerors') is a short Buddhist hymn of praise composed in nine verses. The first seven stanzas venerate the lineage of the seven past Buddhas (Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Śākyamuni), followed by a stanza honoring the future Buddha Maitreya, and concluding with a dedication of merit. The hymn is known from Sanskrit as well as Chinese and Tibetan translations.
SA_T01_n883u.attribution: Anonymous Buddhist hymn of praise preserved in Tibetan (Degé Tengyur Toh 1165 / D 1165) and Chinese (Taishō 1682) translations.
SA_T01_n883u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 9 verses praising the seven Buddhas of the past (Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, Śākyamuni) and the future Buddha Maitreya, followed by a praṇidhāna verse and closing colophon.
translations: Taishō Shinshū Daizōkyō, no. 1682 (《七佛讚唄伽他》), translated by Fatian (法天), Song dynasty, 973. (Chinese)
de bzhin gshegs pa bdun gyi bstod pa (Derge Tengyur D 1165): translated by Padmākaravarman, Śraddhākaravarman, lo chen rin chen bzang po (Tibetan)

SA_T01_n885u.title: Kamalākarasarvatathāgatastotra
SA_T01_n885u.summary: The Kamalākarasarvatathāgatastotra is a 33-verse Buddhist devotional hymn from the Suvarṇabhāsottamasūtra. It praises the past, present, and future Buddhas across the ten directions and concludes with a praṇidhāna to clear karmic obscurations and attain awakening.
SA_T01_n885u.attribution: Colophon gives the attribution/source as 'śrīsuvarṇaprabhoktaṃ kamalākarasarvatathāgatastotraṃ samāptam'.
SA_T01_n885u.coverage: complete — Text of the stotra in 33 verses preceded by an introductory prose phrase and concluding with the colophon 'śrīsuvarṇaprabhoktaṃ kamalākarasarvatathāgatastotraṃ samāptam'.
translations: Johannes Nobel (trans.), Suvarṇabhāsottamasūtra: Das Goldglanz-Sūtra, Leiden: Brill, 1958. (German)

SA_T01_n886u.title: Ṣaḍabhijñastotra
SA_T01_n886u.summary: A brief Mahāyāna praise hymn consisting of seven anuṣṭubh verses addressed to the Buddha (Śrī Mahābuddhabhaṭṭāraka). Despite the title invoking the 'six higher cognitions' (ṣaḍabhijñā), the six central stanzas address the Buddha by correlating the six sensory fields (ṣaḍviṣaya: rūpa, śabda, gandha, rasa, sparśa, dharma) with the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā: dāna, śīla, kṣānti, vīrya, dhyāna, prajñā/buddhi). The final verse serves as a phalaśruti, stating that reciting the hymn thrice daily frees one from the bonds of saṃsāra.
SA_T01_n886u.attribution: Anonymous. The concluding line ('śrīmahābuddhabhaṭṭārakasya ṣaḍabhijñastotraṃ samāptam') designates the deity praised (Śrī Mahābuddha Bhaṭṭāraka) rather than an author.
SA_T01_n886u.coverage: complete — Complete hymn of 7 anuṣṭubh verses (6 stanzas of praise correlating sensory spheres with perfections, plus 1 phalaśruti stanza) and final colophon.

SA_T01_n888u.title: Maṅgalaṣoḍaśastuti
SA_T01_n888u.summary: The Maṅgalaṣoḍaśastuti ('Sixteen-Verse Auspicious Hymn of Praise') is a sixteen-verse Sanskrit Buddhist hymn dedicated to the Buddha Śākyamuni (Śākyasiṃha), extracted from the Bhadrakalpāvadāna, an avadānamālā collection preserved in Nepalese manuscripts. Each verse recalls a distinct narrative episode or previous life (jātaka/avadāna) of the Buddha—including Maitrakanyaka, Supriya, Sudhana, Kuśa, and Saudāsa, and concluding with his journey from Kapilavastu to venerate the Svayambhū caitya in the Kathmandu Valley—invoking his protective power with the refrain 'sa no rakṣatu'. The hymn exemplifies the ritual and liturgical repurposing of narrative avadāna literature within Newar Buddhism.
SA_T01_n888u.attribution: Anonymous. The concluding rubric explicitly identifies the stotra as an excerpt from the Bhadrakalpāvadāna ('bhadrakalpāvadānoddhṛtā śākyasiṃhasya maṅgalaṣoḍaśastutiḥ').
SA_T01_n888u.edition: Bauddha Stotra Saṃgraha, ed. Janardan Shastri Pandey, Varanasi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994.
SA_T01_n888u.coverage: complete — Complete hymn of 16 anuṣṭubh verses, preceded by an opening maṅgala ('om namaḥ samantabhadrāya') and followed by the colophon.

SA_T01_n889u.title: Mañjuvajrastotra
SA_T01_n889u.author: Mañjugarbha
SA_T01_n889u.summary: A devotional Buddhist hymn (stotra) of nine verses in the classical mālinī meter praising Mañjuśrī under the names Mañjuvajra and Mañjughoṣa. It depicts the youthful bodhisattva bearing his characteristic attributes—the sword of wisdom and the manuscript—accompanied by protective and attendant deities. The hymn evokes the founding legend of the Kathmandu Valley from the Svayambhūpurāṇa, in which Mañjuśrī cleaves the hills to drain the waters and reveal the primordial lotus light of the Svayambhū caitya, concluding with a verse on the spiritual and rhetorical fruits (phalaśruti) of reciting this prayer.
