SA_T01_n889u.attribution: The hymn opens with 'mañjugarbhakṛtam' and closes with 'svayambhūpurāṇoddhṛtaṃ mañjugarbhaviracittaṃ mañjuvajrastotraṃ samāptam'.
SA_T01_n889u.edition: Mañjuvajrastotra (from the Svayambhūpurāṇa); cf. Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha, ed. Janardan Shastri Pandey, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994.
SA_T01_n889u.coverage: complete — Complete hymn of 9 verses in mālinī meter, including opening invocations and concluding colophon.

SA_T01_n890u.title: Svayaṃbhūstava
SA_T01_n890u.summary: The Svayaṃbhūstava is a seven-verse Sanskrit Buddhist hymn of praise (stotra) addressed to Svayambhū, the primordial self-originated Buddha (Ādibuddha) manifest as flame or light (jyotīrūpa) at the Svayambhū Mahācaitya in Nepal. Reflecting medieval Nepalese syncretic devotion, the stotra identifies Svayambhū with the Three Jewels, the Bodhisattvas, the lokapālas, and major Hindu devas (Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa), as well as the source of cosmic creation via the five wisdoms (pañcajñāna). A concluding phalaśruti attributes the text to the Four Great Kings (Cāturmahārāja) and promises sovereignty and liberation to those who recite it.
SA_T01_n890u.attribution: Verse 7 (nutiṃ mahārājakṛtāṃ) and the colophon (śrīcāturmahārājakṛtaṃ svayaṃbhūstavaṃ samāptam) ascribe the hymn to the Four Heavenly Kings (Caturmahārājika / Caturmahārāja). In historical context, it is an anonymous medieval stotra transmitted in the Newar Buddhist tradition of the Kathmandu Valley.
SA_T01_n890u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha, Delhi/Varanasi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994.
SA_T01_n890u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 7 verses (vv. 1–6 hymn, v. 7 phalaśruti) with opening title and closing colophon.

SA_T01_n891u.title: Svayambhūstotra
SA_T01_n891u.summary: A short anonymous hymn of six stanzas to Svayambhū, each praise stanza ending 'svayaṃbhuvaṃ namāmy aham'. The colophon presents it as extracted from the Bṛhatsvayambhūpurāṇa and composed by Śikhin; the last stanza promises the three aims of life and liberation to those who recite it.
SA_T01_n891u.attribution: The colophon characterizes the hymn as extracted from the Bṛhatsvayambhūpurāṇa and composed/uttered by Śikhin ('śrībṛhatsvayaṃbhūpurāṇoddhṛtaṃ śikhinirmitaṃ').
SA_T01_n891u.coverage: complete — 6 stanzas with refrain 'svayaṃbhuvaṃ namāmy aham' and colophon 'śrībṛhatsvayaṃbhūpurāṇoddhṛtaṃ śikhinirmitaṃ svayambhūstotraṃ samāptam'.

SA_T01_n892u.title: Gururatnatrayastotra
SA_T01_n892u.summary: The Gururatnatrayastotra is a seven-verse Buddhist liturgical stotra praising the Three Jewels (Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha) and venerating the Guru. The text contains three distinct two-verse subsections praising the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. It concludes with a devotional verse equating the Guru directly with the Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha, and Vajradhara.
SA_T01_n892u.coverage: complete — Complete hymn of 7 verses structured into three two-verse sections dedicated respectively to the Buddha (vv. 1–2), Dharma (vv. 3–4), and Saṅgha (vv. 5–6), concluding with a final guru-homage verse (v. 7).

SA_T01_n893u.title: Caṇḍikādaṇḍakastotra
SA_T01_n893u.summary: A short rhythmic Sanskrit hymn of 9 verses in praise of the wrathful goddess Caṇḍikā (invoked as Siddhicaṇḍī and Ugracaṇḍī). The first eight stanzas feature repetitive, alliterative bījamantras and vivid descriptions of her terrifying aspects, weapons, and retinue, ending in a concluding devotional anuṣṭubh stanza.
SA_T01_n893u.coverage: complete — Complete in 9 verses (8 rhythmic stanzas in daṇḍaka-type meter with the refrain 'siddhicaṇḍī namaste', plus 1 concluding anuṣṭubh verse) with invocation and closing colophon.

SA_T01_n894u.title: Mahogratārāṣṭakastotra
SA_T01_n894u.summary: The Mahogratārāṣṭakastotra (widely transmitted in Śākta tantric literature as Tārāṣṭaka or Nīlasarasvatīstotra) is an anonymous tantric hymn of praise to the wrathful goddess Mahogratārā / Nīlasarasvatī. Composed of eight verses in ornate Sragdharā metre followed by a three-verse phalaśruti, it eulogizes her fierce iconography—standing in pratyālīḍha posture on a corpse (śava) and bearing a sword, kartrī (chopper), skull-cup (kapāla), and blue lotus—imploring her for literary brilliance, protection, and liberation. The hymn provides a clear example of shared ritual poetry spanning Newar Vajrayāna Buddhism and Śākta Tantra.
SA_T01_n894u.coverage: complete — Complete hymn of 11 verses: 8 praise verses in Sragdharā metre followed by a 3-verse phalaśruti in Anuṣṭubh.

SA_T01_n895u.title: Mahogratārāstuti
SA_T01_n895u.summary: The Mahogratārāstuti is a devotional hymn addressed to Mahogratārā ('Great Fierce Tārā'). Following an opening Sragdharā stanza celebrating her terrifying iconography—with protruding fangs, a garland of human heads, and a skull-cup—ten verses petition her for refuge using the refrain 'trāhi māṃ śaraṇāgatam'. The hymn identifies Tārā syncretically as śakti encompassing Gaurī, Lakṣmī, Mahāmāyā, Umā, and Sarasvatī, concluding with a five-verse phalaśruti that promises liberation, worldly boons, and victory in battle to reciters on auspicious lunar days.
SA_T01_n895u.edition: Janārdan Śāstrī Pāṇḍeya (ed.), Bauddha Stotra Saṃgraha, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994, text, p. 166.
SA_T01_n895u.coverage: complete — Complete text containing 1 unnumbered introductory verse in Sragdharā meter, 10 devotional petition verses with the refrain 'trāhi māṃ śaraṇāgatam', and 5 verses of phalaśruti (15 numbered verses in total), ending with the colophon 'śrīmahogratārāstutiḥ samāptā'.

SA_T01_n896u.title: Dharmadhātuvāgīśvaramaṇḍalastotra
SA_T01_n896u.summary: An anonymous Vajrayāna devotional hymn (stotra) of 45 anuṣṭubh stanzas praising the extensive assembly of the Dharmadhātuvāgīśvara-maṇḍala, centered on Mañjuśrī as Dharmadhātuvāgīśvara ('Lord of Speech of the Dharma-realm'). The stotra pays systematic homage to the central deity, the Tathāgatas and their families, consorts, gatekeepers, the ten bhūmis, the pāramitās, the vaśitās, dhāraṇī goddesses, pratisaṃvids, offering goddesses, bodhisattvas, wrathful deities, directional guardians, and astral bodies (nakṣatras). Preserved in the Newar Buddhist liturgical tradition of Nepal, it serves as a verse devotional accompaniment to the complex 219-deity maṇḍala described in the Niṣpannayogāvalī.
SA_T01_n896u.attribution: Anonymous; no author is attributed in the colophon or manuscript tradition.
SA_T01_n896u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 45 anuṣṭubh verses, ending with 'śrī dharmadhātuvāgīśvaramaṇḍalastotraṃ samāptam'.

SA_T01_n897u.title: Vāgīśvaravarṇanāstotra
SA_T01_n897u.summary: A six-verse Sanskrit Buddhist hymn (stotra) composed in adoration of Vāgīśvara ('Lord of Speech'). The hymn venerates him as master of scriptural wisdom, mantras, and learning, and describes his four-armed iconographic form holding an arrow, bow, book, and sword.
SA_T01_n897u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 6 verses (ślokas 1–6) followed by the closing rubric 'śrīvāgīśvaravarṇanāstotraṃ samāptam'.

SA_T01_n898u.title: Vajrapāṇināmāṣṭottaraśatastotra
SA_T01_n898u.summary: The Vajrapāṇināmāṣṭottaraśatastotra is a 21-verse Buddhist Sanskrit devotional hymn invoking the 108 epithets of the bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, identified here with Vajrasattva and primordial Bodhicitta. Verses 1–16 systematically invoke the deity under the attributes and virtues of the sixteen Vajrabodhisattvas of the Vajradhātu-maṇḍala (from Vajrasattva to Vajramuṣṭi), followed by verses 17–21 extolling his status as the origin of all Buddhas and declaring the spiritual fruit (phalaśruti) of reciting this litany. Derived from the culmination of the fundamental Yoga Tantra scripture Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha, the work long enjoyed independent circulation in the devotional liturgy of Newar Buddhism.
SA_T01_n898u.attribution: Anonymous canonical litany. The text originates in the concluding portion of the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgrahamahāyānasūtra (STTS), where the Tathāgatas praise Vajrapāṇi / Vajrasattva with these 108 names. In the Newar Buddhist manuscript tradition, it was excerpted and circulated independently as an aṣṭottaraśata devotional stotra.
SA_T01_n898u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha, Varanasi/Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994 (stotra no. 96 in the GRETIL 108-stotra collection).
SA_T01_n898u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the independent stotra in 21 anuṣṭubh stanzas (verses 1–16 enumerating 108 epithets keyed to the sixteen Vajrabodhisattvas, followed by verses 17–21 of praise and phalaśruti) with final colophon.

SA_T01_n899u.title: Mahābodhibhaṭṭārakastotra
SA_T01_n899u.summary: The Mahābodhibhaṭṭārakastotra is an eight-verse Sanskrit devotional hymn (aṣṭaka) celebrating Gautama Buddha under the epithet Mahābodhibhaṭṭāraka ('the Venerable Lord of the Great Awakening'). Every stanza concludes with the refraining hemistich 'śrīśākyasiṃhaṃ praṇamāmi nityam' ('I perpetually bow to the glorious Lion of the Śākyas'). The hymn extols the somatic perfection and auspicious major and minor marks (lakṣaṇa and anuvyañjana) of the Buddha—including his crown, ūrṇā, lotus-like eyes, golden hue, knee-reaching arms, and wheel-marked hands—while praising him as the supreme teacher who delivers beings from threefold suffering.
SA_T01_n899u.coverage: complete — Complete in 8 verses preceded by the maṅgala invocation 'oṃ namaḥ śākyasiṃhāya' and concluded with the colophon 'mahābodhibhaṭṭārakastotraṃ samāptam'.

SA_T01_n900u.title: Mahābodhivandanāṣṭaka
SA_T01_n900u.summary: The Mahābodhivandanāṣṭaka is an anonymous eight-verse Buddhist Sanskrit hymn of salutation (aṣṭaka) addressed to the Mahābodhi (the Great Enlightenment embodied in the Buddha and associated with the sacred site of Bodhgayā). The hymn extols the Buddha's physical marks, his golden complexion, the triumph over Māra, and his identity with the Three Jewels (Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha), concluding each verse with the refrain 'śrīmanmahābodhim ahaṃ namāmi' ('I bow to the glorious Mahābodhi').

SA_T01_n901u.title: Māravijayastotra
SA_T01_n901u.summary: A short Buddhist hymn in 12 verses, composed in the Toṭaka meter, celebrating Śākyamuni Buddha's victory over Māra (māravijaya) and attainment of awakening beneath the Bodhi tree. While lost in Indic manuscript transmissions, the Sanskrit text was preserved through Chinese phonetic transliteration in the esoteric section of the Chinese Buddhist Canon (Taishō 941), from which it was reconstructed into Sanskrit by Lokesh Chandra.
SA_T01_n901u.attribution: Anonymous Indian Buddhist stotra. The Indic original was preserved in Chinese phonetic transcription (Taishō Tripiṭaka no. 941) and was restored to Sanskrit by Lokesh Chandra.
SA_T01_n901u.edition: Lokesh Chandra, 'Māravijayastotra', in Cultural Horizons of India, vol. 2, p. 277, New Delhi: International Academy of Indian Culture / Aditya Prakashan, 1992.
SA_T01_n901u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 12 stanzas in Toṭaka meter (concluding with iti toṭakamantravarair atulaiḥ...) followed by the closing colophon title marker.

SA_T01_n902u.title: Vajrasattvastotra
SA_T01_n902u.summary: The Vajrasattvastotra is a short, eight-verse Newar Buddhist devotional hymn. While the opening two verses praise Vajrasattva as the supreme guide, embodiment of the Vajradhātu mandala, and dispeller of the darkness of delusion, subsequent verses invoke Lokanātha, Śākyamuni (Śākyasiṃha), Amoghapāśa, the Dharmadhātu caitya alongside four female consorts/prajñās (Māmakī, Locanā, Tārā, Padminī), and incorporate the widely cited Tārā praise formula ('namas tāre ture vīre...').
SA_T01_n902u.attribution: Anonymous praise poem preserved in Nepalese Buddhist manuscript collections and ritual repertoires.
SA_T01_n902u.edition: Janārdana Śāstrī Pāṇḍeya (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgrahaḥ, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994, p. 218.
SA_T01_n902u.coverage: complete — Complete 8-verse stotra with closing colophon 'śrīvajrasattvastotraṃ samāptam'.

SA_T01_n903u.title: Vajrasattvastuti
SA_T01_n903u.summary: A 5-verse tantric hymn of praise (stuti) addressing Mahāvajrasattva under his wrathful aspect as Yamāri (yamārir atibhīṣaṇaḥ). In each verse, Vajrasattva is invoked across various aspects (moha-, piśuna-, rāga-, īrṣyāvajrasvabhāva, kāyavajra, ratnavajra, vāgvajra, saṅgapāṇe), concluding with his glorification as sarvabuddhasvabhāva, sarvabuddhaikasaṃgraha, and maṇḍaleśa.
SA_T01_n903u.attribution: A Buddhist hymn where all the Tathāgatas (sarvatathāgatāḥ) praise Mahāvajrasattva.
SA_T01_n903u.coverage: complete — Complete 5-verse stuti with introductory prose narrative frame and closing colophon.
translations: de bzhin gshegs pa thams cad kyi sku gsung thugs gshin rje gshed nag po zhes bya ba'i rgyud (Derge Kangyur D 467): translated by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna, nag 'tsho lo tsA ba tshul khrims rgyal ba; revised by gnyan lo tsA ba dar ma grags, rwa lo tsA ba rdo rje grags (Tibetan)

SA_T01_n904u.title: Kalyāṇatriṃśatikāstotra
SA_T01_n904u.summary: The Kalyāṇatriṃśatikāstotra is an anonymous Buddhist tantric hymn of thirty verses in anuṣṭubh meter addressed to Vajradevī (identified in the colophon as Trikāyanivāsinī Vajradevī and in verse 17 as Vajrayoginī). Adopting the syntactic structure and famous refrain of the Hindu Devīmāhātmya (namas tasyai namas tasyai namas tasyai namo namaḥ), the stotra reframes the goddess within a Vajrayāna esoteric matrix, invoking the seed syllable evaṃ (v. 1), the vowels and consonants (ālikāli, v. 21), and the tantric sacred geography of internal and external pilgrimage centers (pīṭha, kṣetra, upapīlava, vv. 22–23). Preserved in the Newar Buddhist tradition of the Kathmandu Valley, it culminates in a phalaśruti promising the swift attainment of awakening (buddhatva).
SA_T01_n904u.attribution: Anonymous Buddhist tantric hymn preserved without authorial attribution.
SA_T01_n904u.coverage: complete — Complete text of 30 verses (triṃśatikā), opening with the title heading and concluding with verse 30 and the final colophon (śrī trikāyanivāsinīvajradevyāḥ kalyāṇatriṃśatikāstotraṃ samāptam).

SA_T01_n905u.title: Vajradevīstotra
SA_T01_n905u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T01_n905u.summary: The Vajradevīstotra is a 20-verse Vajrayāna hymn praising the goddess Vajradevī, specifically addressed as Vajravārāhī, Vajrayoginī, and Jñānaḍākinī. The opening verses present her fierce iconographic form: red-complexioned, three-eyed, nude, adorned with skull ornaments and the five bone mudrās, and carrying a khaṭvāṅga and kartikā while dancing. Subsequent verses praise her as the Mother of all Buddhas (sarvabuddhamātṛ), dispeller of Māra, and grantor of supreme bliss (mahāsukha) and spiritual accomplishments (ṛddhisiddhi).
SA_T01_n905u.attribution: The hymn is traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna (Nāgārjunapāda).
SA_T01_n905u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgrahaḥ, Varanasi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994, stotra no. 94.
SA_T01_n905u.coverage: complete — Complete text of 20 verses (verses 1–2 in Sragdharā metre, verses 3–20 in Anuṣṭubh) with opening rubric and concluding colophon.

SA_T01_n906u.title: Vajravilāsinīsādhanāstava
SA_T01_n906u.summary: The Vajravilāsinīsādhanāstava is a short seven-verse anonymous Tantric Buddhist hymn in praise of Vajravilāsinī, an aspect of Vajrayoginī/Vajravārāhī associated with Anuttarayogatantra cycles (notably Cakrasaṃvara). The verses depict esoteric internal yogic processes, the dissolution of duality symbolized by sun and moon, and the arising of innate bliss (sahaja). It concludes by emphasizing that definitive understanding of spiritual stages is obtained through direct oral instruction from a qualified master (gurumukha).
SA_T01_n906u.attribution: Anonymous Tantric Buddhist hymn connected with the sādhana ritual of Vajravilāsinī.
SA_T01_n906u.coverage: complete — Complete text of 7 verses with opening and closing colophons.

SA_T01_n907u.title: Vajravilāsinīstotra
SA_T01_n907u.author: Vibhūticandra
SA_T01_n907u.summary: The Vajravilāsinīstotra is a 22-verse Sanskrit hymn of praise composed by Mahāpaṇḍita Vibhūticandra. The hymn is dedicated to Vajravilāsinī, an amorous and playful form of the female buddha Vajrayoginī/Vajravārāhī in the Cakrasaṃvara cycle. Vibhūticandra weaves together vivid sensory descriptions of the goddess's physical beauty, ornaments, and union with Heruka with tantric esoteric physiology (nāḍīcakra) and realization of non-dual innate bliss (sahaja).
SA_T01_n907u.attribution: Attributed in both the incipit ('mahāpaṇḍitavibhūticandrapādakṛtam') and the explicit colophon ('kṛtiriyaṃ mahāpaṇḍitavibhūticandrapādānām') to Mahāpaṇḍita Vibhūticandra.
SA_T01_n907u.coverage: complete — Complete in 22 verses, followed by the concluding colophon identifying it from the Guhyasamayasādhana cycle ('guhyasamayasādhanatantre śrīvajravilāsinīstotraṃ samāptam').

SA_T01_n908u.title: Vajrayoginīpraṇāmaikaviṃśikā
SA_T01_n908u.summary: An anonymous Tantric Buddhist hymn of adoration (praṇāma) in twenty-one verses (ekaviṃśikā) praising the goddess Vajrayoginī. Each verse concludes with the refrain 'namaste vajrayogini', addressing her esoteric yogic aspects: seated on the evaṃkāra, embodying innate bliss (sahajānanda), bearing skull-cup (kapāla), khaṭvāṅga, and chopper (kartrī), and residing in the eight cremation grounds. The hymn notably expresses an ecumenical and syncretic perspective (vv. 13–14), describing Vajrayoginī as manifesting as Śakti in Śaivism, Caṇḍī in sacred pilgrimage sites, Veda in the Vedic stream, and Kubjikā in the Kula tradition.
SA_T01_n908u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgrahaḥ, Varanasi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994 (stotra no. 101).
SA_T01_n908u.coverage: complete — Complete stotra in 21 verses, with opening maṅgala and concluding colophon.

SA_T01_n909u.title: Vajrayoginyāḥ piṇḍārthastutiḥ
SA_T01_n909u.author: Virūpa
SA_T01_n909u.summary: A sixteen-verse Vajrayāna liturgical hymn (stuti) condensing the esoteric realization (piṇḍārtha) of Trikāyavajrayoginī, the triple-bodied, severed-headed form of the goddess precursor to Chinnamastā. The text equates the deity with non-dual supreme bliss (mahāsukha), transcendent wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), emptiness devoid of extremes, and the central yogic channel (avadhūtī). Preserved as part of the Guhyasamayasādhanamālā collection from Nepal, the hymn is traditionally attributed to the mahāsiddha Virūpa.
SA_T01_n909u.attribution: Attributed in the incipit ('siddhācārya-virūpādaviaracitā') and colophon ('kṛtiriyaṃ siddhācāryaśrīvirupādānāmiti') to Siddhācārya Virūpa.
SA_T01_n909u.coverage: complete — Complete in 16 verses, matching the colophon statement 'śrīguhyasamayatantre piṇḍārthāḥ ṣoḍaśaślokāstrikāyavajrayoginyāḥ samāptāḥ'.

SA_T01_n910u.title: Vajrayoginyāḥ stutipraṇidhānam
SA_T01_n910u.author: Virūpa
SA_T01_n910u.summary: The Vajrayoginyāḥ stutipraṇidhānam is an esoteric Vajrayāna hymn of praise and aspiration (stuti-praṇidhāna) dedicated to Trikāyavajrayoginī (the severed-headed form of Vajrayoginī, cognate with Chinnamuṇḍā / Chinnamastā). Attributed to the mahāsiddha Virūpa and associated with the Guhyasamayatantra cycle, the hymn details the visual and yogic iconography of the deity holding her severed head and drinking the nectar of blood along with her flanking yoginīs (Vajravarṇinī and Vajravairocanī), followed by a prayer for the purification of body, speech, and mind, destruction of obstacles, and the realization of mahāmudrā.
SA_T01_n910u.attribution: Attributed to Siddhācārya Virūpa (Virūpapāda). Colophon also associates the text with the Guhyasamayatantra cycle ('śrīguhyasamayatantre trikāyavajrayoginyāḥ stutipraṇidhānaṃ samāptam').
SA_T01_n910u.coverage: complete — Complete text containing 23 numbered units (opening prose invocation and mantra formula counted as unit 1, followed by 22 anuṣṭubh verses), complete with introductory formula and colophon.

SA_T01_n911u.title: Vasudhārānāmadhāraṇīstotra
SA_T01_n911u.summary: The Vasudhārānāmadhāraṇīstotra is an anonymous Buddhist devotional hymn praising the goddess Vasudhārā. Composed in 24 anuṣṭubh verses, the hymn lists 108 sacred names and epithets across the first 20 stanzas, invoking Vasudhārā simultaneously as a granter of worldly riches and as an embodiment of Mahāyāna perfections (Prajñāpāramitā, Dānapāramitā, Vīryapāramitā, Kṣāntipāramitā). The concluding stanzas (vv. 21–24) provide a phalaśruti describing the ritual efficacy of reciting the hymn thrice daily to eradicate grave karmic transgressions and attain rebirth in Sukhāvatī.
SA_T01_n911u.attribution: Traditionally attributed in the closing colophon to the Buddha (samyaksaṃbuddhabhāṣitam).
SA_T01_n911u.edition: Ngawang Samten & S. S. Bahulkar (eds.), Vasudhārādhāraṇīsūtra, Dhīḥ: Journal of Rare Buddhist Texts Research Project 44 (2007), pp. 129-147.
SA_T01_n911u.coverage: complete — Complete stotra in 24 anuṣṭubh verses (vv. 1–20 containing 108 names and epithets of Vasudhārā, followed by vv. 21–24 phalaśruti).

SA_T01_n912u.title: Vasudhārāstotra
SA_T01_n912u.summary: A concise four-verse Sanskrit devotional hymn (stotra) praising Vasudhārā, the Buddhist goddess of wealth and spiritual abundance. Extracted from the Śrīvasudhārākalpa ritual tradition, the hymn extols her as a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) who removes poverty, affliction, and misfortune, showering down jewels and treasures upon beings.
SA_T01_n912u.attribution: Anonymous. The text concludes with 'śrīvasudhārākalpoddhṛtaṃ vasudhārāstotraṃ samāptam', noting that it was extracted from the ritual work (kalpa) devoted to the goddess Vasudhārā.
SA_T01_n912u.coverage: complete — Complete 4-verse stotra with title and colophon.

SA_T01_nagast_u.title: Acintyastava
SA_T01_nagast_u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T01_nagast_u.summary: The Acintyastava ('Hymn to the Inconceivable [Buddha]') is a philosophical stotra of 59 anuṣṭubh verses attributed to Nāgārjuna, belonging to the Catuḥstava collection. Styled as praise of the Buddha, it articulates quintessential Madhyamaka philosophy by equating dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) with the non-substantiality (naiḥsvābhāvya) of all factors of existence. It examines the relativity of existence and non-existence, the four extremes of the tetralemma (catuṣkoṭi), the illusion-like character of conventional experience, the distinction between provisional (neyārtha) and definitive (nītārtha) teachings, and ultimate reality as transcending all discursive proliferation.
SA_T01_nagast_u.attribution: Traditionally ascribed to Nāgārjuna as part of his Catuḥstava hymn group. It is quoted under Nāgārjuna's name by Prajñākaramati (Bodhicaryāvatārapañjikā) and other Indian commentators, and modern scholars (such as Lindtner and Seyfort Ruegg) generally accept its authenticity as an early Madhyamaka work.
SA_T01_nagast_u.edition: Christian Lindtner, Nagarjuniana: Studies in the Writings and Philosophy of Nāgārjuna, Indiske Studier 4, Copenhagen: Akademisk Forlag, 1982.
SA_T01_nagast_u.coverage: complete — Contains all 59 anuṣṭubh stanzas of the text, concluding with the colophon 'ity acintyastavaḥ samāptaḥ'.
translations: Christian Lindtner, Nagarjuniana: Studies in the Writings and Philosophy of Nāgārjuna, Copenhagen: Akademisk Forlag, 1982. (English)
Fernando Tola and Carmen Dragonetti, 'Nāgārjuna's Catustava', Journal of Indian Philosophy 13, no. 1 (1985): 1–54. (English)
Christian Lindtner, Master of Wisdom: Writings of the Buddhist Master Nāgārjuna, Berkeley: Dharma Publishing, 1986. (English)
Hiroki Hachiriki, 'Japanese Translation of Nāgārjuna's Lokātītastava and Acintyastava' (『超世間讃』・『不可思議讃』試訳), Indo Tetsugaku Bukkyōgaku 1 (1986): 72–88. (Japanese)

SA_T01_naglok_u.title: Lokātītastava
SA_T01_naglok_u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T01_naglok_u.summary: The Lokātītastava ('Hymn to the World-Transcendent One') is a short hymn of 28 anuṣṭubh stanzas attributed to Nāgārjuna, traditionally ordered as the first text in the Catuḥstava collection. Framed as praise of the Buddha who has transcended worldly categories, it systematically presents foundational Madhyamaka philosophy: the five skandhas are revealed as dreamlike and illusory, subject and object lack intrinsic nature, and dependent arising (pratītyasamutpāda) is directly equated with emptiness (śūnyatā). Esteemed and cited by Candrakīrti and later commentators, it is considered one of the authentic works of Nāgārjuna.
SA_T01_naglok_u.attribution: Traditionally regarded as the opening hymn of Nāgārjuna's Catuḥstava ('Four Hymns'). Its authenticity is widely accepted by modern scholarship (e.g. Christian Lindtner, who includes it among the core authentic works of Nāgārjuna), supported by frequent citations in Indian Madhyamaka works such as Candrakīrti's Prasannapadā and Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya.
SA_T01_naglok_u.edition: Christian Lindtner (ed.), Nagarjuniana: Studies in the Writings and Philosophy of Nāgārjuna (Indiske Studier 4; Copenhagen: Akademisk Forlag, 1982).
SA_T01_naglok_u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 28 anuṣṭubh stanzas, ending with the closing colophon '// iti lokātītastavaḥ samāptaḥ //'.
translations: Christian Lindtner, Nagarjuniana: Studies in the Writings and Philosophy of Nāgārjuna (Copenhagen: Akademisk Forlag, 1982). (English)
Fernando Tola and Carmen Dragonetti, 'Nāgārjuna's Catustava', Journal of Indian Philosophy 13.1 (1985). (English)

SA_T01_rahppspu.title: Prajñāpāramitāstotra
SA_T01_rahppspu.author: Rāhulabhadra
SA_T01_rahppspu.summary: The Prajñāpāramitāstotra is an influential 21-verse hymn in praise of Prajñāpāramitā (the Perfection of Wisdom) personified as the mother and grandmother of all Buddhas and bodhisattvas. It blends devotional poetic sentiment with teachings on unconditioned, non-conceptual reality, declaring that seeing wisdom is seeing the Tathāgata. It is frequently prefixed to manuscripts of Prajñāpāramitā texts.
SA_T01_rahppspu.attribution: Attributed to Rāhulabhadra, teacher or disciple of Nāgārjuna; in the Tibetan Tengyur (Toh 1127) it is attributed to Nāgārjuna (Klu sgrub). Tibetan tradition also identifies Rāhulabhadra with Saraha. The Tibetan translation (D 1127) attributes the work to Nāgārjuna ('phags pa klu sgrub).
SA_T01_rahppspu.edition: Michael Hahn, 'Bemerkungen zu zwei Texten aus dem Phudrag-Kanjur', in: Helmut Eimer (ed.), Indology and Indo-Tibetology. Thirty Years of Indian and Indo-Tibetan Studies in Bonn, Bonn: Indica et Tibetica Verlag, 1988 (Indica et Tibetica 13), S. 53-80.
SA_T01_rahppspu.coverage: complete — Contains the complete text of all 21 verses (numbered RahPps_1 to RahPps_21).
translations: Edward Conze, Buddhist Scriptures, Harmondsworth: Penguin Books. (English)
shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin ma'i bstod pa (Derge Tengyur D 1127): translated by Tilakakalaśa, rngog blo ldan shes rab (Tibetan)

SA_T01_tarasdhu.title: Tārāsragdharāstotra
SA_T01_tarasdhu.author: Sarvajñamitra
SA_T01_tarasdhu.summary: The Tārāsragdharāstotra is a 37-verse Buddhist hymn composed in the sragdharā metre by the Kashmiri poet-monk Sarvajñamitra. The work invokes the goddess Āryatārā's compassionate protection against life-threatening perils and culminates in a prayer for rebirth in Sukhāvatī. The hymn was preserved with Jinarakṣita's Sanskrit commentary and multiple Tibetan translations.
SA_T01_tarasdhu.attribution: Consistently attributed to Sarvajñamitra of Kashmir (c. 8th century CE), who is also mentioned in Kalhaṇa's Rājataraṅgiṇī (4.210) as well as by Tāranātha and in Tanjur colophons (D 1690–1692).
SA_T01_tarasdhu.edition: Godefroy de Blonay: Matériaux pour servir à l'histoire de la déesse Tāra, Paris 1895 (Bibliothèque de l'École des Hautes Études, 107), pp. 34-40.
SA_T01_tarasdhu.coverage: complete — Complete stotra consisting of all 37 verses (Tss_1–37) in the sragdharā metre, preceded by an opening maṅgala / namaskāra.
translations: Martin Willson, In Praise of Tārā: Songs to the Saviouress, London: Wisdom Publications, 1986. (English)
phreng ba 'dzin pa'i bstod pa (Derge Tengyur D 1690) (Tibetan)

SA_T02_abhnispu.title: Niṣpannayogāvalī (chapter 1: Mañjuvajramaṇḍala)
SA_T02_abhnispu.author: Abhayākaragupta
SA_T02_abhnispu.summary: The Niṣpannayogāvalī of Abhayākaragupta (abbot of Vikramaśīla, late 11th–early 12th c.) is a compendium of iconographic descriptions of 26 tantric maṇḍalas, complementing his ritual manual Vajrāvalī. This e-text contains only its first chapter, the 19-deity Mañjuvajramaṇḍala of the Guhyasamāja cycle: after the introductory verses on the 'perfected' (niṣpanna) yoga, it describes the protective circle with the ten wrathful deities, the palace, the central Mañjuvajra and the surrounding deities with their colours, faces and attributes, and closes with a discussion of whether the protective circle (rakṣācakra) is to be drawn in painted maṇḍalas.
SA_T02_abhnispu.edition: R. O. Meisezahl, "Akṣobhya-Mañjuvajra, Ikonographie und Ikonologie des Ekonaviṃśadātmakamañjuvajramaṇḍala", Oriens 25–26 (1976), pp. 190–274.
SA_T02_abhnispu.coverage: partial — Only chapter 1 of 26 maṇḍala chapters: the 19-deity Mañjuvajramaṇḍala of the Guhyasamāja (Jñānapāda) cycle, from the opening maṅgala verses ('Oṃ namaḥ śrīvajrasattvāya') to the colophon 'iti mañjuvajramaṇḍalam'. Corresponds to Meisezahl's edition pp. 223–233 (page markers Am 223–233). Chapters 2–26 are not included.
translations: R. O. Meisezahl, Oriens 25–26 (1976), pp. 190–274 (chapter 1, with iconographic study) (German)

SA_T02_bsa005_u.title: Caryāsaṅgrahapradīpa
SA_T02_bsa005_u.author: Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna
SA_T02_bsa005_u.summary: The Caryāsaṅgrahapradīpa is a concise manual of daily Mahāyāna practice composed by Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna during his stay in Nepal. Written for an elder monk who sought instruction focused on the Pāramitā path, the treatise lays out the daily routine of a bodhisattva: moral restraint, sensory control, division of the night for meditation and sleep, the sevenfold worship (saptāṅgapūjā), making stupas and images, and sharing food offerings with deities and beings. While acknowledging that Secret Mantra also attains awakening, it deliberately restricts its exposition to the exoteric Pāramitānaya.
SA_T02_bsa005_u.attribution: By Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna, written in Nepal for an elder monk (sthavira) (v. 22 'nepālaviṣaye kṛtavān'). The work is transmitted in the Tibetan Tengyur (Spyod pa bsdus pa'i sgron ma, D 3960).
SA_T02_bsa005_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of 22 stanzas plus concluding half-verse (v. 23a) and colophon.
translations: Richard Sherburne, The Complete Works of Atiśa Śrī Dīpaṃkara Jñāna Jo-bo-rje, New Delhi: Aditya Prakashan, 2000. (English)
spyod pa bsdus pa'i sgron ma (Derge Tengyur D 3960): translated by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna, nag 'tsho lo tsA ba tshul khrims rgyal ba (Tibetan)

SA_T02_bsa006_u.title: Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa
SA_T02_bsa006_u.author: Āryadeva
SA_T02_bsa006_u.summary: The Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa is a verse treatise in 134 kārikās expounding that spiritual liberation depends on internal mental purity rather than external ritual ablutions. It argues that afflictions can be removed by passion itself or skilful means, just as poison or dirt is counteracted, emphasizing mental attitude (āśaya).
SA_T02_bsa006_u.edition: Prabhubhai Bhikhabhai Patel (ed.), Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa of Āryadeva: Sanskrit and Tibetan Texts, with a foreword by Vidhushekhara Bhattacharya, Santiniketan: Visva-Bharati, 1949.
SA_T02_bsa006_u.coverage: complete — Text of 134 verses with closing colophon.
translations: Christian K. Wedemeyer, 1999, pp. 357–382. (English)
Mathew Varghese, Principles of Buddhist Tantra: A Discourse on Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa of Āryadeva, New Delhi, 2008. (English)
David Snellgrove, in Edward Conze et al. (eds.), Buddhist Texts through the Ages, Oxford: Bruno Cassirer, 1954, p. 221. (English (selected verses))

SA_T02_garbhasamgraha.title: Garbhasaṃgraha
SA_T02_garbhasamgraha.author: Atiśa
SA_T02_garbhasamgraha.summary: The Garbhasaṃgraha ('Compendium of the Essence', Tib. Snying po bsdus pa) is a concise 14-verse doctrinal treatise composed by Atīśa Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna. It presents a summary of the Mahāyāna path, tracing the roots of cyclic suffering to dualistic grasping (dvaidhagrahaṇa) and prescribing meditation on space-like emptiness together with the cultivation of bodhicitta and universal compassion.
SA_T02_garbhasamgraha.attribution: Attributed to Atīśa Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna in the Tibetan Tengyur (Toh 3949 / Toh 4469), where it was translated by Mar-me-mdsad ye-shes (Atīśa) and Tshul-khrims 'byung-gnas.
SA_T02_garbhasamgraha.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 14 kārikās and the concluding colophon.
translations: snying po bsdus pa zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 3949): translated by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna, nag 'tsho lo tsA ba tshul khrims rgyal ba (Tibetan)

SA_T02_bsa043_u.title: Samādhisaṃbhāraparivarta
SA_T02_bsa043_u.author: Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna
SA_T02_bsa043_u.summary: A short verse treatise by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna detailing the prerequisites and auxiliary conditions (aṅga, saṃbhāra) necessary for cultivating meditative absorption (samādhi). In 11 anuṣṭubh stanzas and a closing hemistich, it sets forth requirements including firm bodhicitta, devotion to the guru, tantric empowerments (kumbha- and guhyābhiṣeka), maintenance of vows (samaya), moral purity, solitude, mindfulness of the Buddha, elimination of the five hindrances, and equanimity toward worldly phenomena.
SA_T02_bsa043_u.attribution: Attributed in the colophon to Mahāpaṇḍitācārya Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna (Atiśa). Preserved in the Tibetan Tengyur, translated by Atiśa (Mar me mdzad ye shes) and the Tibetan lo tsā ba Śākyamati (Shākya blo gros).
SA_T02_bsa043_u.coverage: complete — Complete short treatise of 11 anuṣṭubh verses, concluding hemistich (verse 12ab), and colophons.
translations: Kaie Mochizuki, '三種の『三昧資糧論』について' (On Three Tibetan Texts named the Samādhisaṃbhāraparivarta), 身延山大学仏教学部紀要 (2005). (Japanese)
ting nge 'dzin tshogs kyi le'u (Derge Tengyur D 2460): translated by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna, shAkya blo gros (Tibetan)

SA_T02_bsa045_u.title: Gurupañcāśikā
SA_T02_bsa045_u.author: Aśvaghoṣa
SA_T02_bsa045_u.summary: The Gurupañcāśikā ('Fifty Verses on the Guru') is a Vajrayāna manual prescribing the obligations, ritual protocols, and devotional posture of a disciple toward the spiritual master (vajrācārya). It details the criteria for examining a guru and disciple, behavioral etiquette, samaya vows, and the karmic consequences of guru disparagement.
SA_T02_bsa045_u.attribution: Ascribed in colophons and Indian/Tibetan/Chinese traditions to Aśvaghoṣa (or Āryadeva).
translations: Richeng et al. (日稱等) (tr.), 事師法五十頌, Taishō Shinshū Daizōkyō no. 1687 (Song Dynasty). (Chinese)
Geshe Ngawang Dhargyey et al. (trs.), The Fifty Verses of Guru Devotion (Bla ma lnga bcu pa), Dharamsala: Library of Tibetan Works and Archives, 1975. (English)
Gareth Sparham (tr.), The Fulfillment of All Hopes: Guru Devotion in Tibetan Buddhism, Boston: Wisdom Publications, 1999. (English)
bla ma lnga bcu pa (Derge Tengyur D 3721): translated by Padmākaravarman, lo chen rin chen bzang po (Tibetan)

SA_T02_bsa048_u.title: Caryāmelāpakapradīpa (verses only)
SA_T02_bsa048_u.author: Āryadeva
SA_T02_bsa048_u.summary: The Caryāmelāpakapradīpa ('Lamp that Integrates the Practices') by Āryadeva is a treatise associated with the Guhyasamāja literature. This e-text contains verses and chapter colophons across eleven chapters, concluding with samāpto 'yaṃ caryāmelāvaṇapradīpaḥ and kṛtirīyaṃ mahācārya-āryadevapādānām.
SA_T02_bsa048_u.attribution: Ascribed to the tantric Āryadeva in the Guhyasamāja tradition.
SA_T02_bsa048_u.coverage: excerpt — Verse portions only: the e-text gives for each of the eleven paricchedas the verses and the chapter colophons (ending with 'samāpto 'yaṃ caryāmelāvaṇapradīpaḥ' and 'kṛtirīyaṃ mahācārya-āryadevapādānām').
translations: spyod pa bsdus pa'i sgron ma (Derge Tengyur D 1803): translated by Śraddhākaravarman, lo chen rin chen bzang po (Tibetan)

SA_T02_dipguhsu.title: Guhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi (verses 1–416ab, end lost)
SA_T02_dipguhsu.author: Dīpaṃkarabhadra
SA_T02_dipguhsu.summary: A verse manual (c. 450 ślokas) by Dīpaṃkarabhadra, disciple of Buddhajñānapāda, on the maṇḍala rite of the Guhyasamāja in the Jñānapāda tradition. It covers the qualifications of the officiant, preliminary worship and visualisation, preparation of the site, construction of the maṇḍala, the consecrations (abhiṣeka) of the disciple, and ancillary rites. It was commented on by Ratnākaraśānti (Tōh. 1871).
SA_T02_dipguhsu.attribution: Attributed to Dīpaṃkarabhadra (Mar me mdzad bzang po), an immediate disciple of Buddhajñānapāda (Buddhaśrījñāna) in the Jñānapāda school of the Guhyasamājatantra. The Tibetan translation (D 1865) attributes the work to Dīpaṅkarabhadra (mar me mdzad bzang po).
SA_T02_dipguhsu.edition: MS Niedersächsische Staats- und Universitätsbibliothek Göttingen, Cod. ms. sanscr. 257, with additional references to Dhīḥ 42 (2006: 109–154). Input by S. Klein-Schwind, proofread and revised by H. Isaacson, released 18 February 2008 (rev. 1.0) by Centre for Tantric Studies, Hamburg.
SA_T02_dipguhsu.coverage: partial — Verses 1–415 and the beginning of 416 ('sākṣād asya virodhy evaṃ prajñopāyātma [...] 416'). The work has c. 450 ślokas according to Tibetan tradition and Ratnākaraśānti's commentary (Śrīguhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi-ṭīkā, Tōh. 1871), so roughly the last 35 verses are missing.
translations: dpal gsang ba 'dus pa'i dkyil 'khor gyi cho ga zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 1865): translated by Padmākaravarman, lo chen rin chen bzang po (Tibetan)

SA_T02_khasrpsu.title: Khasarpaṇasādhana
SA_T02_khasrpsu.author: Śubhaṅkara
SA_T02_khasrpsu.summary: A short Vajrayāna visualization manual (sādhana) for Khasarpaṇa. It begins with an account of the upāsaka Śubhaṅkara receiving instructions at Khasarpaṇa village and proceeds through visualization of the deity and retinue, offering mantras, and concluding verses.
SA_T02_khasrpsu.attribution: Attributed to Śubhaṅkara in the colophon ('śubhaṃkareṇa racitaṃ'). The opening narrative mentions the upāsaka Śubhaṅkara staying at Khasarpaṇa village in Khāḍīmaṇḍala and receiving instruction from Avalokiteśvara. The Tibetan translation (D 3411) attributes the work to dge byed (identified as *Kalyāṇakārin or *Śubhaṃkara).
SA_T02_khasrpsu.edition: Frederick William Thomas: "Deux collections sanscrites et tibétaines", in: Muséon 4.1 (1903), pp. 1-42.
SA_T02_khasrpsu.coverage: complete — Text of the sādhana edited by F. W. Thomas.
translations: dpal khar+sa pA Ni'i sgrub thabs (Derge Tengyur D 3411): translated by Kīrticandra, yar lung lo tsA ba grags pa rgyal mtshan (Tibetan)

SA_T02_mpvv_u.title: Mahāpratisarāvidyāvidhi
SA_T02_mpvv_u.summary: The Mahāpratisarāvidyāvidhi is a short Vajrayāna ritual manual describing the preparation and design of a protective amulet-diagram (rakṣācakra) centered on Mahāpratisarā, the preeminent deity of the Pañcarakṣā pentad. The text sets forth specific geometric concentric circles (puṭa) to be drawn on birch bark (bhūrjatvac) or cloth, inscribed with seed-syllables, dhāraṇī formulas, names of guardian deities, and ritual emblems. Once inscribed and worn by the practitioner, the cakra is held to provide complete protection against calamities, evil spirits, and illness while fostering pacification (śānti) and prosperity (puṣṭi).
SA_T02_mpvv_u.attribution: Anonymous Buddhist tantric manual. The Tibetan translation is preserved in the Tengyur as Āryā-mahāpratisarāvidyāvidhi ('Phags ma so sor 'brang ma chen mo'i rig pa'i cho ga, D3125 / P3946), translated by Paṇḍita Puruṣottama and Lotsāwa Nyi ma rgyal mtshan.
SA_T02_mpvv_u.edition: Gergely Hidas: "Mahāpratisarāvidyāvidhi. The spell-manual of the great amulet". IN: Acta Orientalia Academiae Scientiarum Hungaricae 63.4 (2010), pp. 473-484.
SA_T02_mpvv_u.coverage: complete — Complete text across 127 segments, from the introductory verse (natvā pratisarāṃ bhaktyā...) to the colophon (āryamahāpratisarāyā vidyāvidhiḥ samāptaḥ).
translations: phags ma so sor 'brang ma chen mo'i rig pa'i cho ga zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 3125): translated by Puruṣottama, thar pa lo tsA ba nyi ma rgyal mtshan; at gtsug lag khang chen po thar pa gling (Tibetan)

SA_T02_mrtvstsu.title: Mṛtyuvañcanasitatārāsādhana
SA_T02_mrtvstsu.summary: The Mṛtyuvañcanasitatārāsādhana ('Sādhana of White Tārā who Cheats Death') is a short 15-verse Vajrayāna ritual manual associated with the longevity cycle of Vāgīśvarakīrti. Preserved in the Sādhanamālā (no. 103) and re-edited as an appendix to Vāgīśvarakīrti's Mṛtyuvañcanopadeśa, the work describes the visualization of sixteen-year-old White Tārā with a white wheel at her heart, stating that six months of focused practice averts death, diseases, and fears while granting accomplishments.
SA_T02_mrtvstsu.attribution: Verse 2 notes that the practice is extracted from instructions compiled by Vāgīśvarakīrti (vāgīśvarakṛtādeśān mṛtyuvañcanasaṃgrahāt / uddhṛtā sitatārāyā bhāvanā), but the composition itself is anonymous; Tibetan colophons (D3496 / Toh 3496) attribute it to an unnamed senior disciple (slob dpon ngag gi dbang phyug grags pa'i slob ma thu bo) of Vāgīśvarakīrti.
SA_T02_mrtvstsu.edition: Johannes Schneider, Vāgīśvarakīrtis Mṛtyuvañcanopadeśa, eine buddhistische Lehrschrift zur Abwehr des Todes. Wien: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 2010. (Beiträge zur Kultur- und Geistesgeschichte Asiens; 66) (Denkschriften der philosophisch-historischen Klasse; 394) ISBN 978-3-7001-6722-8 p. 228
SA_T02_mrtvstsu.coverage: complete — Complete text in 15 anuṣṭubh verses (Mvsts 1–15) followed by the closing colophon.
translations: chi ba slu ba'i sgrol ma dkar mo'i sgrub thabs (Derge Tengyur D 3496): translated by Kīrticandra, yar lung lo tsA ba grags pa rgyal mtshan (Tibetan)

SA_T02_mrtvts_u.title: Mṛtyuvañcanatārāsādhana
SA_T02_mrtvts_u.author: Vāgīśvarakīrti
SA_T02_mrtvts_u.summary: The Mṛtyuvañcanatārāsādhana is a concise Vajrayāna visualization manual devoted to White Tārā (Sitatārā) for averting untimely death and extending lifespan. Across six verses framed by prose ritual instructions, it outlines the preliminary contemplation of emptiness, the visualization of the sixteen-year-old goddess seated in vajraparyaṅka, the contemplation of an eight-spoked white wheel inscribed with syllables in her heart, and the six-month recitation of her ten-syllable mantra (oṃ tāre tuttāre ture svāhā). Attributed to Vāgīśvarakīrti, the work constitutes a key liturgic summary of his 'cheating death' (mṛtyuvañcana) tradition, preserved independently in the Tengyur (Toh 3495) as well as within the Sādhanamālā anthology (no. 102).
SA_T02_mrtvts_u.edition: Johannes Schneider: Vāgīśvarakīrtis Mṛtyuvañcanopadeśa, eine buddhistische Lehrschrift zur Abwehr des Todes. Wien: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 2010. (Beiträge zur Kultur- und Geistesgeschichte Asiens; 66) (Denkschriften der philosophisch-historischen Klasse; 394) ISBN 978-3-7001-6722-8 p. 225
SA_T02_mrtvts_u.coverage: complete — Complete text consisting of opening salutation, introductory ritual prose, six metrical verses (Mvts 1–6), the ten-syllable mantra, and the closing colophon title; identified with Sādhanamālā no. 102.
translations: chi ba slu ba'i sgrol ma'i sgrub thabs (Derge Tengyur D 3495): translated by Kīrticandra, yar lung lo tsA ba grags pa rgyal mtshan (Tibetan)

SA_T02_mrtvutsu.title: Mṛtyuvañcanopadeśatārāsādhana
SA_T02_mrtvutsu.author: Vāgīśvarakīrti
SA_T02_mrtvutsu.summary: The Mṛtyuvañcanopadeśatārāsādhana is a 16-verse Sanskrit Tantric liturgy for prolonging life and averting premature death through the evocation of White Tārā, attributed to Vāgīśvarakīrti. Also associated with sādhana 112 in the Sādhanamālā, it instructs the practitioner to visualize two-armed White Tārā at dawn seated in vajraparyaṅka, perform preliminary offerings and refuge, and meditate upon a mantra wheel to conquer death.
SA_T02_mrtvutsu.attribution: The Sanskrit text concludes with the title colophon without an explicit author colophon line; traditional and catalog records attribute it to Vāgīśvarakīrti.
SA_T02_mrtvutsu.edition: Johannes Schneider: Vāgīśvarakīrtis Mṛtyuvañcanopadeśa, eine buddhistische Lehrschrift zur Abwehr des Todes. Wien: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 2010. (Beiträge zur Kultur- und Geistesgeschichte Asiens; 66) (Denkschriften der philosophisch-historischen Klasse; 394) ISBN 978-3-7001-6722-8, p. 235.
SA_T02_mrtvutsu.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all 16 verses (Mvupts_1–16) and the concluding title colophon.
translations: chi ba slu ba'i man ngag gi sgrol ma'i sgrub thabs (Derge Tengyur D 3504): translated by Kīrticandra, yar lung lo tsA ba grags pa rgyal mtshan (Tibetan)

SA_T02_msitvatu.title: Mahāśītavatīvidyārājñī
SA_T02_msitvatu.summary: The Mahāśītavatīvidyārājñī (also referred to in manuscripts as Mahā-daṇḍadhāraṇī-śītavatī) is a protective Buddhist dhāraṇī / vidyārājñī text. Set at the Śītavana charnel ground in Rājagṛha, the Buddha teaches this protective formula to Rāhula when he is tormented by grahas, animals, and other beings. The scripture provides mantric formulas and promises protection from dangers, diseases, and harm.
SA_T02_msitvatu.attribution: A canonical Buddhist protective dhāraṇī sūtra presented as the teaching of Śākyamuni Buddha to his son Rāhula; no human author is attributed.
SA_T02_msitvatu.edition: Yutaka Iwamoto: Kleinere Dhāraṇī Texte, Kyoto 1937 (Beiträge zur Indologie, 2), pp. 1-6.
SA_T02_msitvatu.coverage: complete — Text of the scripture corresponding to pp. 1–6 in Iwamoto's 1937 edition.
translations: Taishō Tripiṭaka, No. 1392 (《大寒林聖難拏陀羅尼經》), translated by 法天 (Fatian), 973. (Chinese)
bsil ba'i tshal chen po'i mdo (Derge Kangyur D 562): translated by Śīlendrabodhi, Jñānasiddhi, shAkya 'od, sna nam btsun pa ye shes sde; revised by 'gos lo tsA ba gzhon nu dpal (Tibetan)
phags pa be con chen po zhes bya ba'i gzungs (Derge Kangyur D 606): translated by Jinamitra, Dānaśīla, sna nam btsun pa ye shes sde (Tibetan)

SA_T02_n1397u.title: Guhyavajravilāsinīsādhana
SA_T02_n1397u.author: Śabarapāda
SA_T02_n1397u.summary: The Guhyavajravilāsinīsādhana (also entitled Yoginīsarvasva) is an extensive tantric evocation and ritual manual (sādhana) in 151 verses dedicated to Guhyavajravilāsinī ('Secret Vajra Playful One'), a form within the Vajrayoginī/Vajravārāhī tantric cycle. Attributed to the mahāsiddha Śabarapāda, it details the visualization of the deity, preparatory rites, mantras, offerings, and esoteric internal yogic practices (karmamudrā) undertaken in secluded mountain hermitage retreats. Preserved as text no. 10 (GSS 10) in the Nepalese codex of the Guhyasamayasādhanamālā, it is distinctive among works in that collection in that the practitioner visualizes himself as the male deity Padmanarteśvara while evoking the goddess.
SA_T02_n1397u.attribution: In the concluding colophon, the sādhana is framed as revealed or taught by Lokanātha in the Guhyasamayatantra / Mahāyoginījālatantra ('iti guhyasamayatantre mahāyoginījālatantre śrīmallokanāthapādena deśitaṃ...'), and its composition is attributed directly to the Mahāsiddha Śabarapāda ('kṛtiriyaṃ siddhācāryaśabarapādānām').
SA_T02_n1397u.edition: Guhyavajravilāsinīsādhana, ed. RBTRU, in: Dhīḥ: Durlabha Bauddha Grantha Śodha Patrikā, Vol. 17, pp. 6–17; later reprinted in: Bauddhalaghugranthasaṅgraha, CIHTS, Sarnath, 1997, pp. 55–72.
SA_T02_n1397u.coverage: complete — Complete text containing the introductory verses, all 151 numbered anuṣṭubh verses, and the final colophon.

SA_T02_n1398u.title: Guhyāvalī
SA_T02_n1398u.author: Dauḍīpāda
SA_T02_n1398u.summary: The Guhyāvalī is an esoteric Buddhist tantric treatise of 25 Sanskrit stanzas attributed to the siddhācārya Dauḍīpāda. Opening with an invocation to Vajrayoginī, it expounds Anuttarayoga tantric praxis, focusing on consort meditation (vajrābjayoga), immutable bliss (akṣarasukha), the four blisses, and the non-dual realization imparted directly through the spiritual guru's empowerment (adhiṣṭhāna). The text survives in manuscripts (such as Cambridge University Library MS Add. 1699-II), where it is preserved with a Sanskrit commentary (Guhyāvalīvivṛti) by Paṇḍitasthavira Śrīghanadeva.
SA_T02_n1398u.attribution: Attributed in the colophon to the tantric master Dauḍīpāda.
SA_T02_n1398u.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising all 25 stanzas, beginning with the maṅgala to Vajrayoginī and concluding with verse 25 and the author colophon.

SA_T02_n1399u.title: Kāṇhapādasya dohākoṣa with Dohākoṣamekhalāṭīkā
SA_T02_n1399u.author: Kāṇha
SA_T02_n1399u.summary: A collection of 32 rhymed couplets (dohās) in Apabhraṃśa composed by Kāṇha (Kṛṣṇavajra), embedded within a continuous Sanskrit commentary entitled Dohākoṣamekhalāṭīkā. The verses articulate tantric teachings, internal yogic realization through channels (lalanā, rasanā, avadhūtī), and innate bliss (mahāsuha/sahaja). The Sanskrit commentary provides word-by-word glosses and cites authorities such as the Śrīhevajra and Saraha.
SA_T02_n1399u.attribution: The 32 Apabhraṃśa couplets are attributed to Kāṇha (also known as Kṛṣṇavajra). The continuous Sanskrit commentary, the Dohākoṣamekhalāṭīkā, survives in the manuscript tradition, with its closing colophon attributing it to 'Ācāryapāda' (ity ācāryapādīya-dohākoṣamekhalāṭīkā samāptā).
SA_T02_n1399u.edition: Prabodh Chandra Bagchi (ed.), Dohākoṣa, Journal of the Department of Letters, University of Calcutta (1935).
SA_T02_n1399u.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all 32 Apabhraṃśa dohā verses of Kāṇha interspersed with the Sanskrit commentary Dohākoṣamekhalāṭīkā, ending at the closing colophon.
translations: Muhammad Shahidullah, Les chants mystiques de Kāṇha et de Saraha: les Dohā-koṣa, Paris: Adrien-Maisonneuve, 1928. (French)

SA_T02_n1401u.title: Mahāmāyāsādhanopāyikā
SA_T02_n1401u.author: Kukkuripa
SA_T02_n1401u.summary: A concise Vajrayāna liturgical manual (sādhana) for evoking the deity Mahāmāyā (Heruka) and his retinue, attributed to Kukkuripa. It details preliminary purification, generation of bodhicitta, and reflection on emptiness (śūnyatā). The yogin visualizes the central four-faced, four-armed Heruka (Karuṇācalavajra) amidst the cremation grounds, initiated through a vajragīti sung by four directional ḍākinīs, and concludes with mantra recitation.
SA_T02_n1401u.attribution: Attributed to Kukkuripa (Kukkurīpāda / Kukuraja) in both the opening line ('kukkurīpādānām') and the colophon ('kṛtiriyaṃ kukkuripādānāmiti').
SA_T02_n1401u.edition: Benoytosh Bhattacharyya (ed.), Sādhanamālā, Gaekwad's Oriental Series 26 & 41, Baroda: Oriental Institute, 1925-1928.
SA_T02_n1401u.coverage: complete — Text opens with 'mahāmāyāsādhanopāyikā / kukkurīpādānām / namo vajraḍākāya' and concludes with '|| mahāmāyāsādhanopāyikā samāptā || kṛtiriyaṃ kukkuripādānāmiti |'.

SA_T02_n1402u.title: Mahāmāyātantra with Guṇavatī
SA_T02_n1402u.author: Ratnākaraśānti, Kukkuripāda
SA_T02_n1402u.summary: The Mahāmāyātantra is an Anuttarayoga / Yoginī class Buddhist tantra in three chapters (nirdeśas) centered on the four-faced, four-armed deity Mahāmāyā and her retinue of ḍākinīs, renowned especially for teachings on dream yoga (svapnadarśana), subtle drop yoga (binduyoga), and transgressive yogic practices. The Guṇavatī commentary by the scholar-monk Ratnākaraśānti provides an exegesis grounded in a Yogācāra-Mādhyamika framework. The e-text concludes with two ancillary ritual practice texts: Ratnākaraśānti's Mahāmāyāsādhana and the mahāsiddha Kukkuripāda's Mahāmāyāsādhanopāyikā.
SA_T02_n1402u.attribution: The root Mahāmāyātantra is canonical scripture belonging to the Yoginī / Anuttarayogatantra class. The commentary Guṇavatī is by Ratnākaraśānti. The subsequent Mahāmāyāsādhana is likewise attributed to Ratnākaraśānti in the Tibetan Tanjur (D 1643). The concluding text, Mahāmāyāsādhanopāyikā, is explicitly attributed in the colophon to Kukkuripāda (kṛtiriyaṃ kukkuripādānām).
SA_T02_n1402u.edition: Mahāmāyātantram with the Guṇavatī commentary of Ratnākaraśānti, ed. Samdhong Rinpoche and Vrajavallabh Dwivedi, Rare Buddhist Texts Series 10, Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, Sarnath, Varanasi, 1992.
SA_T02_n1402u.coverage: complete — Text of the Mahāmāyātantra interspersed with Ratnākaraśānti's Guṇavatī, followed by two appended sādhanas: the Mahāmāyāsādhana and Kukkuripāda's Mahāmāyāsādhanopāyikā.
translations: dpal sgyu 'phrul chen po zhes bya ba'i rgyud kyi rgyal po (Derge Kangyur D 425): translated by Jinavara, 'gos lo tsA ba khug pa lhas btsas (Tibetan)
sgyu ma chen mo'i sgrub thabs (Derge Tengyur D 1643): translated by Śāntibhadra, 'gos lo tsA ba khug pa lhas btsas (Tibetan)

SA_T02_n1403u.title: Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhi with Marmakalikāpañjikā
SA_T02_n1403u.author: Śūnyasamādhipāda, Vīryaśrīmitra
SA_T02_n1403u.summary: The Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhi of Śūnyasamādhipāda is an Anuttarayogatantra treatise and sādhana centered on the cult of Vajravārāhī and Caṇḍālī yoga, expounding the realization of non-dual gnosis (tattvajñāna) through internal yogic control of prāṇa, bindu, and innate bliss (sahajānanda). The Marmakalikāpañjikā by the Vikramaśīla scholar-monk Vīryaśrīmitra provides an extensive commentary on the root verses, elucidating the esoteric vital points (marman) of practice and quoting extensively from early Siddha songs, Caryāpadas, and the lineage of Śabarapāda.
SA_T02_n1403u.attribution: The root work Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhi (Tōh. 1551) is attributed to Śūnyasamādhipāda (StoN-Nid tin-Ne-Hdsin). The Marmakalikāpañjikā (Tōh. 1585) was authored by Vīryaśrīmitra (Brtson-Hgrus dpal bSes-gNen), described in the concluding colophon as a mahāpaṇḍita and bhikṣu of the Vikramaśīla Mahāvihāra. The Tibetan translation (D 1551) attributes the work to Śūnyatāsamādhi (stong nyid ting nge 'dzin).
SA_T02_n1403u.edition: Janardana Shastri Pandey (ed.), Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhi with Marmakalikāpañjikā of Vīryaśrīmitra. Sarnath: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 2000.
SA_T02_n1403u.coverage: complete — Complete text of root text and commentary, ending with the author colophon (śrīmadvikramaśīladevamahāvihārīyamahāpaṇḍitabhikṣuvīryaśrīmitraviracitā marmakalikānāma tattvajñānasaṃsiddhipañjikā samāptā) and scribal colophon verses.
translations: dpal de kho na nyid ye shes grub pa (Derge Tengyur D 1551): translated by Varendraruci, rngog blo ldan shes rab (Tibetan)

de kho na nyid ye shes yang dag par grub pa'i rgya cher 'grel pa de kho na nyid bshad pa zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 1585): translated by Mañjuśrī, Jetakarṇa, thar pa lo tsA ba nyi ma rgyal mtshan; at gtsug lag khang chen po thar pa gling (Tibetan)

SA_T02_n1413u.title: Dohākoṣa with Dohākoṣapañjikā
SA_T02_n1413u.author: Saraha, Advayavajra
SA_T02_n1413u.summary: The Dohākoṣa of the siddha Saraha is a seminal collection of rhymed Apabhraṃśa couplets (dohās) teaching Sahajayāna and Mahāmudrā realisation. The poetry harshly critiques Vedic Brahmanism, Jain asceticism, and scholastic Buddhist classifications, pointing instead to the non-dual, spontaneously innate nature of the mind (sahaja). In this e-text, the dohās are preserved within the Sanskrit prose commentary (Dohākoṣapañjikā / Sahajāmnāyapañjikā) attributed to Advayavajra, which elucidates the tantric and philosophical meaning of each verse.
SA_T02_n1413u.attribution: The root couplets in Apabhraṃśa are traditionally attributed to the tantric mahāsiddha Saraha (Sarojavajra, Sarahapāda). The Sanskrit pañjikā commentary is attributed in its colophon to Advayavajra (śrī-Advayavajrapāda).
SA_T02_n1413u.edition: P. C. Bagchi (ed.), Dohākoṣa (Apabhraṃśa Texts of the Sahajayāna School), Calcutta Sanskrit Series 25c, Calcutta University Press, 1938.
SA_T02_n1413u.coverage: complete — Text of Saraha's Dohākoṣa and Advayavajra's Dohākoṣapañjikā (Sahajāmnāyapañjikā) as edited by P. C. Bagchi (1938), containing introductory verses, continuous prose commentary, and the author's concluding verse and colophon.
translations: Herbert V. Guenther, The Royal Song of Saraha, Seattle: University of Washington Press, 1969. (English)
Muhammad Shahidullah, Les chants mystiques de Kāṇha et de Saraha, Paris, 1928. (French)

SA_T02_n1414u.title: Śrīvajravārāhīsādhana
SA_T02_n1414u.author: Umāpatideva
SA_T02_n1414u.summary: The Śrīvajravārāhīsādhana is a tantric evocation manual composed by Umāpatideva addressed to Vikramasena. It details the visualization, mantras, ritual offerings, and charnel grounds associated with the deity Vajravārāhī / Vajrayoginī.
SA_T02_n1414u.attribution: Attributed in the Sanskrit colophon to Paṇḍitamahopādhyāya Śrī Umāpatideva; the Tibetan translation (D 1581) names the author Śrī-Umāpatidatta. The opening verse addresses Vikramasena ('vakṣyāmi yathopadeśaṃ tatsādhanaṃ vikramasena yatnāt').
SA_T02_n1414u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the sādhana, ending with verse 77 and colophon, with page references up to p. 312.
translations: rdo rje rnal 'byor ma'i sgrub thabs zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 1581): translated by Vāgīśvaragupta, rwa chos rab (Tibetan)

SA_T02_n1416u.title: Caryāgītikoṣa (Upodghāta)
SA_T02_n1416u.author: Śāntibhikṣu Śāstrī
SA_T02_n1416u.summary: The Upodghāta is a 57-verse Sanskrit metrical poem composed by Śāntibhikṣu Śāstrī as an introduction to the 1956 Visva-Bharati edition of the Caryāgīti-koṣa. The poem offers homages to the innate reality (sahaja), tantric twilight language (saṃdhyābhāṣā), the eighty-four Mahāsiddhas, the Nātha lineage, before closing with praise of the Tathāgata.
SA_T02_n1416u.attribution: Composed by Śāntibhikṣu Śāstrī as the Sanskrit metrical introduction (Upodghāta) to the edition of the Caryāgīti-koṣa published jointly with Prabodh Chandra Bagchi in 1956.
SA_T02_n1416u.edition: Prabodh Chandra Bagchi & Shanti Bhikshu Shastri (ed.), Caryāgīti-koṣa of Buddhist Siddhas, Visva-Bharati, Santiniketan, 1956.
translations: Per Kværne, An Anthology of Buddhist Tantric Songs: A Study of the Caryāgīti, Oslo: Universitetsforlaget, 1977. (English)

SA_T02_n1424u.title: Śrīguhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi
SA_T02_n1424u.author: Dīpaṃkarabhadra
SA_T02_n1424u.summary: The Śrīguhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi is a ritual manual composed by Dīpaṃkarabhadra belonging to the Jñānapāda lineage. Comprising 420 verses, it provides ritual instruction for maṇḍala rites, self-generation, and initiations.
SA_T02_n1424u.attribution: Attributed to Ācārya Dīpaṃkarabhadra, an advocate of the Jñānapāda lineage who established a liturgical system based on the teachings of Buddhaśrījñāna. The Tibetan translation (D 1865) attributes the work to Dīpaṅkarabhadra (mar me mdzad bzang po).
SA_T02_n1424u.edition: Dīpaṃkarabhadra, Guhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi, ed. from MS Göttingen Cod. ms. sanscr. 257 (S. Klein-Schwind; rev. H. Isaacson), with reference to the edition in Dhīḥ 42 (2006): 109-154.
SA_T02_n1424u.coverage: complete — Complete in 420 verses based on Göttingen MS Cod. ms. sanscr. 257; bracketed restorations in verse 420 and the closing colophon are editorially supplied.
translations: dpal gsang ba 'dus pa'i dkyil 'khor gyi cho ga zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 1865): translated by Padmākaravarman, lo chen rin chen bzang po (Tibetan)

SA_T02_n1426u.title: Tattvasiddhi
SA_T02_n1426u.author: Śāntarakṣita
SA_T02_n1426u.summary: The Tattvasiddhi is a Buddhist tantric treatise in prosimetrum (89 stanzas and extensive prose commentary) attributed to Śāntarakṣita. It provides a formal epistemological justification for esoteric Vajrayāna practices and transgressive sense enjoyment using Dharmakīrti's causal inference framework (kāryānumāna). Most remarkably, the concluding section argues that the ultimate cognition of the yogin retains a conceptual (savikalpaka) capacity that facilitates compassionate, altruistic manifestations in the world.
SA_T02_n1426u.attribution: The e-text's heading ([0]) ascribes the work to Ācārya Śāntarakṣita ('ācāryaśāntarakṣitaviracitā tattvasiddhiḥ'). It should not be confused with the Vyaktabhāvānugatatattvasiddhi or with Harivarman's *Tattvasiddhi (T 1646).
SA_T02_n1426u.coverage: complete — 89 numbered verses with interspersed prose, ending with v. 89 and the colophon '|| iti śrītattvasiddhināma-prakaraṇaṃ ... samāptam ||' at [588]. The colophon line is followed by stray text ('payet ||86||'), and segments [589]–[591] duplicate [580]–[582]. These are input artefacts of the DSBC file, not part of the work.

SA_T02_n2873u.title: Vāṅmaṇḍalanamaskāraślokāḥ
SA_T02_n2873u.summary: The Vāṅmaṇḍalanamaskāraślokāḥ is an anonymous 20-verse Vajrayāna liturgical hymn of homage and iconographical description dedicated to the deities of the Speech Maṇḍala (vāṅmaṇḍala) of the Kālacakratantra system. It praises the eight directional mother goddesses (Carcikā, Vārāhī, Raudrī, Aindrī, Brāhmī, Lakṣmī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī) together with their corresponding retinues of sixty-four yoginīs or nāyikās correlated with internal bodily channels (nāḍī) and seed syllables, concluding with the goddesses residing on the portals and verandas who embody the consonants of the Sanskrit alphabet.
SA_T02_n2873u.attribution: An anonymous tantric liturgical stotra praising the deity assemblies of the Speech Maṇḍala (vāṅmaṇḍala).
SA_T02_n2873u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha. Varanasi/Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994.
SA_T02_n2873u.coverage: complete — Complete in 20 verses (ślokas), terminating with the colophon 'iti vāṅmaṇḍalanamaskāraślokāḥ'.

SA_T02_n2877u.title: Bauddhapāribhāṣikaśabdāḥ
SA_T02_n2877u.summary: An alphabetical reference glossary of Buddhist technical terminology (pāribhāṣika-śabda) spanning from akṣaram to hūṃkāra. Entries define terms using citations excerpted from texts abbreviated in the e-text as 'se ṭī' and 'a va saṃ'.
SA_T02_n2877u.attribution: A glossary of Buddhist technical terms compiled with citations from texts abbreviated as 'se ṭī' and 'a va saṃ'.
SA_T02_n2877u.coverage: complete — Glossary arranged in alphabetical order from akṣaram to hūṃkāra.

SA_T02_n2884u.title: Samantabhadranāmasādhanaṭīkā (verses 50–141)
SA_T02_n2884u.author: Samantabhadra
SA_T02_n2884u.summary: A Sanskrit commentary on the Samantabhadranāmasādhana of Buddhajñānapāda, treating the four branches of ritual propitiation (sevā, upasādhana, sādhana, mahāsādhana) and elements associated with the Guhyasamājatantra and Mañjuvajra.
SA_T02_n2884u.attribution: A commentary on the Samantabhadranāmasādhana of Buddhajñānapāda, edited by Kimiaki Tanaka in 2017.
SA_T02_n2884u.edition: Kimiaki Tanaka (ed.), 梵文『普賢成就法註』研究 / The Sanskrit commentary on the Samantabhadra nāma sādhana of Buddhajñānapāda: Introduction, Romanized Sanskrit Text and Translation, Tokyo: Watanabe Publishing Co., Ltd., 2017.
SA_T02_n2884u.coverage: partial — The preserved text begins at verse 50 (sevā) and breaks off after verse 140.
translations: Kimiaki Tanaka, The Sanskrit commentary on the Samantabhadra nāma sādhana of Buddhajñānapāda: Introduction, Romanized Sanskrit Text and Translation, Tokyo: Watanabe Publishing Co., Ltd., 2017. (English)

SA_T02_n2886u.title: Samājasādhanavyavastholi
SA_T02_n2886u.author: Nāgabuddhi
SA_T02_n2886u.summary: The Samājasādhanavyavastholi is a foundational ritual treatise on the generation stage (utpattikrama) of the Guhyasamājatantra according to the Ārya (Nāgārjuna) school. It structures the Guhyasamāja sādhana by establishing correspondences between Buddhist cosmogony—the periodic dissolution and reappearance of the physical receptacle (bhājanaloka) and sentient beings (sattvaloka)—and the yogic generation of the maṇḍala and its thirty-two deities. The text served as an essential authority for later commentarial traditions, prominently utilized by Tsongkhapa in his exposition of the generation stage.
SA_T02_n2886u.attribution: Attributed in the final Sanskrit colophon to Ācārya Nāgabuddhi (kṛtir ācārya nāgabuddhipādānām). The author is known interchangeably as Nāgabuddhi or Nāgabodhi in Indo-Tibetan tantric literature (Tibetan: Klu'i blo).
SA_T02_n2886u.edition: Kimiaki Tanaka (ed.), Samājasādhana-Vyavastholi of Nāgabodhi/Nāgabuddhi: Introduction and Romanized Sanskrit and Tibetan Texts, Tokyo: Watanabe Publishing, 2016.
SA_T02_n2886u.coverage: complete — Complete text across five thematic sections (vyavasthā / pariccheda), running from the opening maṅgala through the final colophon at page 59.
translations: dus pa'i sgrub pa'i thabs rnam par gzhag pa'i rim pa zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 1809) (Tibetan)

SA_T02_n2906u.title: Mantroddhāra
SA_T02_n2906u.author: Candrakīrti
SA_T02_n2906u.summary: The Mantroddhāra (or Bhavotpattikramasādhanamantroddhāra) is a short Sanskrit liturgical text of the Guhyasamāja Ārya school attributed to Candrakīrti. Functioning as a mantra manual complementing the author's Vajrasattvaniṣpādanasūtra, it provides the mantras and seed syllables for the generation-stage (utpattikrama) practice across four phases: mantra retention/extraction (mantrāvadhāraṇa), deity placement (nyāsa), deity arrangement (vyavastholi), and realization of reality (tattvadarśana), concluding with verses of praise to the thirty-two mandala deities.
SA_T02_n2906u.attribution: Attributed in the colophon to Candrakīrti (Candrakīrtipāda).
SA_T02_n2906u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the short manual in eight numbered sections/pages, from the opening homage through to the concluding colophon.

SA_T02_n2908u.title: Balimālikā
SA_T02_n2908u.author: Sumatisiṃha
SA_T02_n2908u.summary: The Balimālikā ('Garland of Oblations') by Ācārya Sumatisiṃha is a tantric Buddhist ritual manual setting forth verses, mantras, and procedures for presenting bali offerings. Beginning with verses derived from the Subāhuparipṛcchātantra, the manual prescribes offerings addressed to diverse Vajrayāna deities and protectors, including Mahākāla, Kurukullā, Cakrasaṃvara, Vajrayoginī, Mahāpratyaṅgirā, Dhvajāgrakeyūra, and Pañcarakṣā deities. The text was preserved in Nepalese manuscript witnesses and translated into Tibetan by Chos skyong bzang po and Dharmadīpaṅkara.
SA_T02_n2908u.attribution: Identified within the text: in introductory verse 7 the author states 'mayā sumatisiṃhena granthitā balimālikā', and the colophon (line 331) reads 'kṛtir iyam ācāryasumatisiṃhapādānāṃ balimālikā samāptā'. Preserved in the Tibetan Tanjur under the title Gtor ma'i phreng ba (Tōh. 3771 / 4456), attributed to Ācārya Sumatisiṃha (Slob dpon Blo bzang seng ge).
SA_T02_n2908u.edition: Yūshō Miyasaka (宮坂宥勝), 'チベット所伝のBalimālikā梵本について' [On the Sanskrit Text of Balimālikā in the Tibetan Buddhist Canons], Mikkyōgaku (密教学) (1967).
SA_T02_n2908u.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising all 63 numbered ritual bali offering sections, beginning with invocations citing the Subāhuparipṛcchātantra and ending with the author colophon and protective dhāraṇī-mantra. Embedded pagination markers [1] through [17] track the 17 pages of the source edition.
translations: gtor ma'i phreng ba (Derge Tengyur D 4456): translated by Dharmadīpaṅkara, zhwa lu lo tsA ba chos skyong bzang po; at dpal e waM chos 'khor (Tibetan)

SA_T02_n2910u.title: Ādikarmapradīpa
SA_T02_n2910u.author: Anupamavajra
SA_T02_n2910u.summary: The Ādikarmapradīpa ('Lamp for the Initial Practices') by Anupamavajra is an influential ritual manual setting forth the daily liturgical, devotional, and meditative routine for novice Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna practitioners (ādikarmika). Starting with opening verses that outline the sequence of daily observances, followed by an extensive prose commentary, the manual details morning purification, recitation of the Mañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti and Praṇidhānas, water offerings to Jambhala and pretas, clay caitya molding (mṛccaitya), maṇḍala worship to the guru and tutelary deity, refuge and bodhisattva vows, and mealtime bali rituals. The work quotes extensively from canonical Mahāyāna sūtras and Vajrayāna tantras (notably preserving fragments of the lost Vidyādharapiṭaka) and remains a foundational prototype for Newar Buddhist daily rituals.
SA_T02_n2910u.attribution: Explicitly attributed to ācārya Anupamavajra in the authorial verse and colophon ('kṛtir ācāryānupamavajrasya').
SA_T02_n2910u.edition: Louis de La Vallée Poussin (ed.), Bouddhisme, études et matériaux: Ādikarmapradīpa, Bodhicaryāvatāraṭīkā, Mémoires couronnés et mémoires des savants étrangers tome LV, Bruxelles/London: Académie royale de Belgique / Luzac, 1898.
SA_T02_n2910u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the work, comprising the root kārikās and the running prose commentary (vivaraṇa/ṭīkā) by Anupamavajra, closing with the author colophon and scribal dating colophon (corresponding to pp. 186–204 of La Vallée Poussin 1898).

SA_T02_n2912u.title: Prajñopāyaviniścayasiddhi (chapters 1–4)
SA_T02_n2912u.author: Anaṅgavajra
SA_T02_n2912u.summary: The Prajñopāyaviniścayasiddhi ('The Attainment of the Realization of Wisdom and Means') by Anaṅgavajra is an exegetical tantric work. Its third chapter treats the bodhicittābhiṣeka (bodhicitta consecration), which is incorporated into the Saṃpuṭatantra / Saṃpuṭodbhavatantra, and chapter 4 treats tattvabhāvanā.
SA_T02_n2912u.attribution: Traditional attribution to Anaṅgavajra (Yan lag med pa'i rdo rje). Corresponds to Derge Tanjur D 2218 (translated by Śāntabhadra and 'Gos Lhas btsas).
SA_T02_n2912u.edition: Benoytosh Bhattacharyya (ed.), Two Vajrayāna Works (Prajñopāyaviniścayasiddhi of Anaṅgavajra and Jñānasiddhi of Indrabhūti), Gaekwad's Oriental Series No. 44, Baroda: Oriental Institute, 1929.
SA_T02_n2912u.coverage: partial — Contains chapters 1–4 only. The digital text ends at the colophon of chapter 4 (tattvabhāvanā nāma caturthaḥ paricchedaḥ).
translations: Takahashi, Shōfu (高橋尚夫), 'The Japanese translation -Prajñopāyaviniścayasiddhi-', Buzan Gakuhō (豊山学報), 1980; part 2 in Buzan Gakuhō, 1982. (Japanese)
Snellgrove, David, Indo-Tibetan Buddhism: Indian Buddhists and Their Tibetan Successors, 1987. (English)
