SA_T02_n2914u.title: Śrīsahajasiddhi
SA_T02_n2914u.author: Ḍombīheruka
SA_T02_n2914u.summary: The Śrīsahajasiddhi ('Accomplishment of the Innate') by the Mahāsiddha Ḍombīheruka is an early Vajrayāna treatise on completion-stage (utpannakrama) yoga in the Hevajra Tantra cycle. Across three concise chapters, it expounds the realization of sahaja through the four progressive blisses (caturānanda), internal subtle-body yoga (the arousal of the inner fire caṇḍālī at the navel cakra), the non-dual transformation of the passions (kleśa) into enlightened wisdom, and the observance of tantric commitments (samaya). Canonical Tibetan tradition classifies the work among the 'Seven Siddhi Texts' (Grub pa sde bdun).
SA_T02_n2914u.attribution: Composed by the Mahāsiddha Ḍombīheruka (Ḍombī Heruka / Dombīpāda), celebrated as a direct disciple of Virūpa. In Tibetan doxography, this treatise is counted among the canonical 'Seven Siddhi Texts' (Grub pa sde bdun) of early Vajrayāna.
SA_T02_n2914u.edition: Malati J. Shendge (ed.), Śrīsahajasiddhi, Indo-Iranian Journal 10, no. 2/3 (1967), pp. 126–149.
SA_T02_n2914u.coverage: complete — Complete in three chapters: 1. Sahajanirdeśa (15 verses), 2. [Samayatattva-]nirdeśa (numbered up to verse 12 in the e-text segments shown / 16 verses total in Shendge), and 3. Samayasiddhinirṇayanirdeśa (12 verses followed by a concluding prose section and colophon).
translations: Malati J. Shendge, 'Śrīsahajasiddhi', Indo-Iranian Journal 10, no. 2/3 (1967), pp. 126–149. (English)

SA_T02_n2918u.title: Tattvaratnāvalī
SA_T02_n2918u.author: Advayavajra
SA_T02_n2918u.summary: The Tattvaratnāvalī ('Jeweled Garland of Reality') is a doxographical treatise composed by the scholar-siddha Advayavajra (Maitrīpa). It classifies the Buddhist path into three vehicles (Śrāvakayāna, Pratyekabuddhayāna, and Mahāyāna) and four philosophical tenets (Vaibhāṣika, Sautrāntika, Yogācāra, and Madhyamaka), dividing the Mahāyāna into Pāramitānaya and Mantranaya. The treatise sets out bipartite divisions within Yogācāra (Sākāra and Nirākāra) and Madhyamaka (Māyopamādvayavāda and Sarvadharmāpratiṣṭhānavāda), making it a key primary source for late Indian Buddhist doxographical literature (siddhānta).
SA_T02_n2918u.attribution: The work is attributed in the Sanskrit colophon to the paṇḍita-avadhūta Advayavajra (paṇḍitāvadhūtādvayavajrapāda), who is traditionally identified with the Indian master Maitrīpa (Maitrīpāda).
SA_T02_n2918u.edition: Mahamahopadhyaya Haraprasad Shastri (ed.), Advayavajrasaṃgraha, Gaekwad's Oriental Series No. 40, Baroda: Oriental Institute, 1927.
SA_T02_n2918u.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all 47 kārikās with intervening prose, from the initial maṅgala and homage verse down to the concluding praśasti verse and authorial colophon.
translations: Hakuju Ui, 'The Tattvaratnāvalī' [真理の宝環], Nagoya Daigaku Bungakubu Kenkyū Ronshū: Tetsugaku, 1952. (Japanese)
Mark Tatz, 1987. (English)

SA_T02_n2932u.title: Adhyātmasāraśataka with Adhyātmasāraśatakaṭīkā (verses 1–17)
SA_T02_n2932u.author: Prabhākaragupta, Śiromaṇi
SA_T02_n2932u.summary: The Adhyātmasāraśataka, ascribed to the mahāpaṇḍita Prabhākaragupta, is a Buddhist Vajrayāna work in mandākrāntā and other long metres, given here with a word-by-word (anvaya) ṭīkā. The preserved verses argue that all things up to consciousness are without intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) and survey the doctrines of Buddhists, Sāṃkhyas, Jainas, Vaiṣṇavas, Śaivas and Cārvākas. They then turn to yogic practice with the winds, the central channel and the preservation of the bodily 'nectar' against ageing and death. The e-text stops after verse 17.
SA_T02_n2932u.attribution: The heading ([0]) ascribes the root verses to 'mahāpaṇḍita Śrīprabhākaragupta'; nothing further is known of this author here. The commentator's introductory verses invoke Ugratārā, the Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha and the guru, and verse 7 reads 'tathovāca yathāśaktyā tv ālāpo 'rthaṃ śiromaṇiḥ'. This is taken as the commentator's name (Śiromaṇi), but it could be an epithet.
SA_T02_n2932u.coverage: partial — The root verses 1–17 of a nominal 'śataka' of about 100 verses, each followed by an anvaya-style ṭīkā. The e-text ends after the commentary on v. 17 ('||17 ||17 ||') without a colophon.

SA_T02_n2934u.title: Abhayapaddhati (chapters 9–14)
SA_T02_n2934u.author: Abhayākaragupta
SA_T02_n2934u.summary: The Abhayapaddhati is an extensive commentary by the late Indian Buddhist master Abhayākaragupta on the Buddhakapālamahātantra, an important scripture of the Yoginītantra class. Written at Vikramaśīla monastery in the 25th regnal year of King Rāmapāla, it interprets esoteric ritual practices, internal alchemy, and completion-stage yoga aimed at realizing Mahāmudrā. This digital file comprises chapters 9 through 14, focusing on post-initiatory conduct (caryā), medicinal-alchemical lore (mahauṣadhi), and higher initiatory yogas.
SA_T02_n2934u.attribution: Composed by Abhayākaragupta at Vikramaśīla in the 25th regnal year of Pāla ruler Rāmapāla at the request of Prince Yakṣapāla of Magadha, as attested in the concluding praśasti verses (vv. 2–3) preserved at the end of chapter 14.
SA_T02_n2934u.coverage: partial — Contains chapters 9 through 14 (paṭala 9: Caryāpaṭala to paṭala 14), ending with the colophon (caturdaśaḥ paṭalaḥ samāptaḥ), the four concluding praśasti verses by Abhayākaragupta, and the grantha-extent statement (sapādaṣoḍaśaślokaśatī...), out of 14 chapters total.
translations: dpal sangs rgyas thod pa'i rgyud kyi rgyal po chen po'i rgya cher 'grel pa 'jigs pa med pa'i gzhung 'grel zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 1654): translated by chos grags; revised by dpang lo tsA ba blo gros brtan pa (Tibetan)

SA_T02_n2946u.title: Paribhāṣāvṛtti (paribhāṣās 1–102, adhyāyas 1–8)
SA_T02_n2946u.author: Sīradeva
SA_T02_n2946u.summary: The Paribhāṣāvṛtti, or Bṛhatparibhāṣāvṛtti, of Sīradeva is a commentary on grammatical paribhāṣās arranged by adhyāya and pāda.
SA_T02_n2946u.attribution: The work is also known as Bṛhatparibhāṣāvṛtti to distinguish it from Puruṣottamadeva's Laghuparibhāṣāvṛtti.
SA_T02_n2946u.edition: Harinātha Dube (ed.), Paribhāṣāvṛtti of Sīradeva, Benares, 1887 (Benares Sanskrit Series). E-text input by Milan Shakya and proofread by Miroj Shakya for DSBC (book 817).
SA_T02_n2946u.coverage: partial — The e-text runs from the opening maṅgala through the paribhāṣās arranged by adhyāyas and pādas. It ends with paribhāṣā 102 and the colophon 'iti paribhāṣāvṛttau rephapādaḥ || 3 || ityaṣṭamo'dhyāyaḥ || 8 || 8 ||'.

SA_T02_n2952u.title: Bauddhadharme tathā purāṇeṣu karuṇā
SA_T02_n2952u.author: Phra Suntharnadhammathada
SA_T02_n2952u.summary: A modern comparative scholarly treatise composed in Sanskrit examining the concept and practice of compassion (karuṇā) in Buddhism and the Hindu Purāṇas. The author analyzes the early Buddhist canonical understanding of compassion, the Bodhisattva ideal, and the cultivation of the brahmavihāras, comparing them with depictions of empathy, grace, and forgiveness in Purāṇic narratives (including the Matsya, Viṣṇu, and Kūrma Purāṇas). The work concludes by emphasizing the fundamental ethical affinity between Buddhist and Purāṇic philosophical thought, as exemplified by the Purāṇic assimilation of the Buddha into the daśāvatāra.
SA_T02_n2952u.attribution: Modern Sanskrit work edited or authored by Phra Suntharnadhammathada.
SA_T02_n2952u.coverage: complete — Monograph concluding with a comparison of Buddhist and Purāṇic compassion and the Purāṇic adoption of the Buddha among the daśāvatāra.

SA_T02_n2955u.title: Kriyāsaṃgrahapañjikā (selected sections)
SA_T02_n2955u.author: Kuladatta
SA_T02_n2955u.summary: The Kriyāsaṃgrahapañjikā by Kuladatta is an extensive manual of Tantric Buddhist ritual central to Newar Buddhism in the Kathmandu Valley, containing eight chapters. This digital text contains an excerpt (sections 1.4–3.5.8) from Ryūgen Tanemura's 2004 critical edition, dealing with site inspection (bhūmiparīkṣā), site testing, omens (nimittokti), and the ritual marking of foundation cords and lines (sūtrapātana).
SA_T02_n2955u.attribution: Authored by Kuladatta (mahāpaṇḍita niḥsaṅgācārya Kuladatta), whose ritual work is associated with Newar Buddhism in the Kathmandu Valley.
SA_T02_n2955u.edition: Ryugen Tanemura, Kuladatta's Kriyāsaṃgrahapañjikā: A Critical Edition and Annotated Translations of Selected Sections, Groningen Oriental Studies XIX, Egbert Forsten, Groningen, 2004.
SA_T02_n2955u.coverage: excerpt — Contains sections 1.4 to 3.5.8, opening with site examination (1-4 bhūmiparīkṣā) and ending with 3-5-8 (Drawing the lines).
translations: Ryugen Tanemura, Kuladatta's Kriyāsaṃgrahapañjikā: A Critical Edition and Annotated Translations of Selected Sections (2004). (English)
Tadeusz Skorupski (2002). (English)

SA_T02_n2961u.title: Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhi with Mahāsukhaprakāśikā
SA_T02_n2961u.author: Śūnyasamādhivajra, Dhyānacandra
SA_T02_n2961u.summary: The Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhi is a Tantric Buddhist treatise of the Cakrasaṃvara/Vajravārāhī cycle attributed to the master Śūnyasamādhivajra. It expounds the realization of the knowledge of ultimate reality (tattvajñāna) in terms of innate great bliss (mahāsukha) through ritual, somatic, and contemplative practices. The Mahāsukhaprakāśikā is a commentary by the monk Dhyānacandra that elucidates the text's rites and visualization.
SA_T02_n2961u.attribution: The root work is attributed in the opening passages to Ācārya Śūnyatāsamādhivajrapāda. The commentary is attributed in opening verses to Bhikṣu Dhyānacandra.
SA_T02_n2961u.coverage: complete — Commentary text with root verses.

SA_T02_n2963u.title: Āryamāyājālamahātantroddhṛtamaṇḍalagāthāṭippaṇī
SA_T02_n2963u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T02_n2963u.summary: The Āryamāyājālamahātantroddhṛtamaṇḍalagāthāṭippaṇī is an esoteric Buddhist annotation (ṭippaṇī) attributed to Nāgārjunapāda on two maṇḍala stanzas extracted from the Māyājālamahātantra. The work provides an internal, yogic, and perfection-oriented (ṣaṭpāramitā) reinterpretation of the materials and preparatory actions of maṇḍala ritual (such as smearing cow dung, sprinkling water, sweeping, and clearing insects) for practitioners of differing spiritual capacities (mṛdu, madhya, and adhimātra/nirālambana). Quoting repeatedly from the Hevajratantra, it interprets these ritual actions as internal cleansing of the mind, the rising of the inner caṇḍālī, and the cultivation of non-dual mahāmudrā.
SA_T02_n2963u.attribution: Traditionally attributed in the Sanskrit colophon to Ācārya Nāgārjuna (kṛtiriyaṁ ācāryaśrīnāgārjunapādānām).
SA_T02_n2963u.coverage: complete — Complete short gloss ending with the full colophon: iti āryamāyājālamahātantroddhṛtamaṇdalagāthāṭippaṇī samāptā / kṛtiriyaṁ ācāryaśrīnāgārjunapādānām.

SA_T02_n2965u.title: Kālacakrāvatāra
SA_T02_n2965u.author: Abhayākaragupta
SA_T02_n2965u.summary: The Kālacakrāvatāra is an introductory astronomical work on calendrical and astrological calculation by Abhayākaragupta. Its figure of 463 years is discussed in modern scholarship in relation to the Kālacakra epoch, and it is preserved in an Asiatic Society manuscript containing an appendix by Dānaśrīmitra dated Śaka 1047.
SA_T02_n2965u.attribution: Attributed to Abhayākaragupta (fl. late 11th c.) by the title rubric ('paṇḍita abhayākaraguptapādānām Kālacakrāvatāraḥ') and the closing verse ('...abhayasya...'); Newman also treats it as Abhayākaragupta's work.
SA_T02_n2965u.edition: Transcription from Asiatic Society MS G. 4732; DSBC romanized e-text, input Bibek Shakya, proofread Miroj Shakya, Nagarjuna Institute of Exact Methods / University of the West (book 838). (probable)
SA_T02_n2965u.coverage: complete — Complete text from the initial maṅgala and title rubric to the closing verses and colophon 'iti kālacakrāvatāraḥ samāptaḥ'. The appendix by Dānaśrīmitra found in the manuscript is not included.
translations: Tibetan translation: Dus-kyi-ḥkhor-lo-la ḥjug-pa shes-bya-ba (Kālacakrāvatāra-nāma), Tohoku 1383 / Otani 2098. Translated by Abhayākaragupta (Ḥjigs-med ḥbyuṅ-gnas sbas-pa) and Śrīdharmakīrti; revised by Rāhulaśrībhadra and Dpal-gyi mthaḥ-can. (Tibetan)

SA_T02_n2974u.title: Munimatālaṃkāra (chapter 1: saṃvṛtisatya section)
SA_T02_n2974u.author: Abhayākaragupta
SA_T02_n2974u.summary: The Munimatālaṅkāra by Abhayākaragupta is a Mahāyāna treatise. This excerpt from Chapter 1 investigates definitions of conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya).
SA_T02_n2974u.coverage: excerpt — Contains an excerpt from Chapter 1 discussing conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya).
translations: thub pa'i dgongs pa'i rgyan (Derge Tengyur D 3903): translated by spong zho gsal ba grags, dpang lo tsA ba blo gros brtan pa (Tibetan)

SA_T02_n2982u.title: Mañjuvajramukhyākhyāna
SA_T02_n2982u.summary: The Mañjuvajramukhyākhyāna is an anonymous ritual manual belonging to the mukhākhyāna genre, focusing on the generation and worship of the nineteen-deity maṇḍala of Mañjuvajra, affiliated with the Jñānapāda school (Jñānapādasaṃpradāya) of the Guhyasamājatantra.
SA_T02_n2982u.attribution: Anonymous Nepalese liturgical text of the mukhākhyāna genre. Extant in Nepalese Sanskrit manuscripts (such as IASWR); not preserved in the Tibetan or Chinese Buddhist canons.
SA_T02_n2982u.edition: Kimiaki Tanaka, Mañjuvajramukhyākhyāna: Introduction, Romanized Sanskrit Text and Related Articles, Tokyo: Watanabe Publishing, 2018 (ISBN 9784902119299).
SA_T02_n2982u.coverage: complete — Complete e-text of Tanaka's edition (pp. 1–20).

SA_T02_n2984u.title: Caryāsaṃgraha
SA_T02_n2984u.summary: The Caryāsaṃgraha is an anthology of tantric Buddhist caryā songs (caryāgīti / cacā). The songs, accompanied by melodic rāga and rhythmic tāla performance instructions, praise deities of the Anuttarayogatantras, including Cakrasaṃvara, Vajravārāhī, and Hevajra.
SA_T02_n2984u.attribution: A collection of esoteric Buddhist caryāgīti preserved in manuscript tradition.
SA_T02_n2984u.coverage: complete — Contains the text of caryā songs ending at page marker (128).

SA_T02_n2988u.title: Jñānasiddhi
SA_T02_n2988u.author: Indrabhūti
SA_T02_n2988u.summary: The Jñānasiddhi is a Vajrayāna treatise attributed to Indrabhūti. In multiple chapters, the work elucidates the nature of awakening, yogic discipline, and vajrasattva practices, quoting yogatantras.
SA_T02_n2988u.coverage: complete — Contains chapters concluding with the author colophon.
translations: Hisao Takahashi, 'Jñānasiddhi dai-15 shō' [The Fifteenth Chapter of the Jñānasiddhi, a Japanese Translation], Buzan Kyōgaku Taikai Kiyō 5, 1977. (Japanese)
ye shes grub pa zhes bya ba'i sgrub pa'i thabs (Derge Tengyur D 2219): translated by Śraddhākaravarman, lo chen rin chen bzang po; revised by nag 'tsho lo tsA ba tshul khrims rgyal ba (Tibetan)

SA_T02_n2998u.title: Laghutantraṭīkā
SA_T02_n2998u.author: Vajrapāṇi
SA_T02_n2998u.summary: The Laghutantraṭīkā is a commentary by Vajrapāṇi on the introductory portion (verses 1–10 1/2) of the Cakrasaṃvaratantra. Together with the Hevajratantrapiṇḍārthaṭīkā by Vajragarbha and Puṇḍarīka's Vimalaprabhā, it forms part of the early Kālacakra Bodhisattva corpus.
SA_T02_n2998u.edition: Claudio Cicuzza (ed.), The Laghutantraṭīkā by Vajrapāṇi: A Critical Edition of the Sanskrit Text, Serie Orientale Roma 86, Roma: Istituto Italiano per l'Africa e l'Oriente, 2001.
SA_T02_n2998u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the extant commentary concluding at the colophon of the first chapter ('iti lakṣābhidhānād uddhṛte laghvabhidhāne piṇḍārthavivaraṇaṁ nāma prathamaṭīkāparicchedaḥ') and its final verses, covering the introductory portion (first ten and a half verses) of the Cakrasaṃvaratantra.
translations: mngon par brjod pa 'bum pa las phyung ba nyung ngu'i rgyud kyi bsdus pa'i don rnam par bshad pa zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 1402): translated by ting 'dzin bzang po, shong lo tsA ba blo gros brtan pa/ shong blo gros brtan pa (Tibetan)

SA_T02_n3006u.title: Bauddhatantroktasiddhauṣadhisaṅgraha
SA_T02_n3006u.summary: An anonymous compilation of pharmacological and medical recipes (siddhauṣadhi) drawn from Buddhist tantric contexts, beginning with material headed by the Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra. It covers bodily purification, remedies, aphrodisiac and fertility preparations, rejuvenation, and medicated oils and unguents.
SA_T02_n3006u.attribution: Anonymous compilation of medical, aphrodisiac and rejuvenating recipes; the heading names the Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra as the source of the first section, and the opening recipes indeed parallel that tantra.
SA_T02_n3006u.coverage: unclear — Recipes opening with material heading 'Boudhatantrokta ṣiddhauadhi ṣagraha candamamahārośaṇa tantra' and concluding in a section on unguents ('kiṁ punarvākuci saha urddhatana vidhi') without a closing colophon.

SA_T02_n3011u.title: Laghusiddhāntakaumudī
SA_T02_n3011u.author: Varadarāja
SA_T02_n3011u.summary: The Laghusiddhāntakaumudī is a pedagogical abridgement of Pāṇinian Sanskrit grammar composed by Varadarāja. Reordering Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī topically, it arranges essential sūtras along with concise vṛtti glosses and illustrative derivations across core grammatical categories.
SA_T02_n3011u.edition: Varadarāja, The Laghu Kaumudí: A Sanskrit Grammar, with an English Version, Commentary, and References by James R. Ballantyne, Benares, 1867.
SA_T02_n3011u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the work from the initial invocation and Māheśvarasūtras through all major grammatical sections (Saṃjñā, Sandhi, Subanta, Tiṅanta, Kṛdanta, Samāsa, Taddhita, Strīpratyaya), terminating with the final signature verse and colophon.
translations: James R. Ballantyne, The Laghu Kaumudí: A Sanskrit Grammar, with an English Version, Commentary, and References, Benares, 1867. (English)

SA_T02_n691u.title: Cakrasaṃvaratantra with Cakrasaṃvaravivṛti (chapters 1–25)
SA_T02_n691u.author: Bhavabhaṭṭa
SA_T02_n691u.summary: The Cakrasaṃvaratantra is a scripture focused on the deity Heruka / Cakrasaṃvara. This digital text presents the first 25 chapters of the scripture accompanied by the commentary (Vivṛti) of Bhavabhaṭṭa.
SA_T02_n691u.attribution: The root scripture is an anonymous tantra. The commentary Cakrasaṃvaravivṛti is authored by Bhavabhaṭṭa.
SA_T02_n691u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey, ed., Śrīherukābhidhānam Cakrasamvaratantram with the Vivrti Commentary of Bhavabhatta, Sarnath: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies 2002.
SA_T02_n691u.coverage: partial — Contains chapters (paṭalas) 1 through 25 of the Cakrasaṃvaratantra embedded with Bhavabhaṭṭa's commentary (Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti).

SA_T02_n692u.title: Cakrasaṃvaratantra with Cakrasaṃvaravivṛti (chapters 26–51)
SA_T02_n692u.author: Bhavabhaṭṭa
SA_T02_n692u.summary: The Cakrasaṃvaratantra (also known as the Laghusaṃvara or Śrīherukābhidhāna) is an esoteric Buddhist scripture centered on Heruka and Vajravārāhī. This e-text contains chapters 26 through 51 of the root tantra together with the Sanskrit Vivṛti (Pañjikā) commentary composed by Bhavabhaṭṭa. The chapters discuss the examination of disciples, consecrations, sacred geography, yoginī retinues, mantra rites, and realization.
SA_T02_n692u.attribution: The root Cakrasaṃvaratantra is a canonical scripture and has no human author. The commentary (vivṛti / pañjikā) interwoven with the verses is explicitly attributed in the colophon to Paṇḍitācārya Bhavabhaṭṭa.
SA_T02_n692u.coverage: partial — Contains chapters (paṭalas) 26–51 of the root tantra together with Bhavabhaṭṭa's commentary, beginning at chapter 26 ('śiṣyaparīkṣāsaṃvaravidhipaṭalaḥ ṣaḍviṃśatimaḥ') and concluding with the colophon of chapter 51 ('iti śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛtāve kapañcāśattamaḥ paṭalaḥ samāptaḥ || 51 || paṇḍitācārya bhava bhaṭṭakṛtā śrīcakrasaṃvarapañjikā samāpteti'). Chapters 1–25 are found in Vol. 1.

SA_T02_n798u.title: Ḍākinījālasaṃvararahasya
SA_T02_n798u.author: Anaṅgayogin
SA_T02_n798u.summary: A Vajrayāna treatise belonging to the Yoginī/Ḍākinī tantra milieu associated with the Cakrasaṃvara and Abhidhānottara tantric cycles. It presents an exegesis of the four initiations (abhiṣeka), distinguishing transient physical pleasure (kṣarasukha) from the immutable bliss of gnosis (akṣarasukha / mahāsukha), and decodes the intentional twilight language (sandhyābhāṣā) of consort practices. The work quotes from texts including the Abhidhānottaratantra, the Vajrapañjara, and the Ratnacūḍāsūtra, concluding with verses emphasizing unwavering fidelity to the guru.
SA_T02_n798u.attribution: Attributed in the opening rubric ('anaṅgayogipraṇītam') and opening verse ('likhyate 'naṅgayoginā') to Anaṅgayogin. Although some modern scholars discuss potential links to the mahāsiddha Anaṅgavajra, the text itself names the author as Anaṅgayogin.
SA_T02_n798u.edition: Ḍākinījālasaṃvararahasya, edited by S. Rinpoche and V. V. Dwivedi [Vrajavallabha Dvivedī], Rare Buddhist Texts Series (RBTS) 8 / CIHTS, Sarnath, Varanasi, 1990.
SA_T02_n798u.coverage: complete — Ending with the colophon 'iti ḍākinījālasaṃvararahasyaṃ samāptam'.

SA_T02_n800u.title: Sekoddeśapañjikā (up to Sekoddeśa verse 146)
SA_T02_n800u.summary: The Sekoddeśapañjikā is an anonymous Sanskrit commentary on the Sekoddeśa of the Kālacakra (Paramādibuddha) tradition, discussing tantric consecration (seka), winds and channels (nāḍī, prāṇāyāma), and related yogic topics.
SA_T02_n800u.edition: Sekoddeśapañjikā, Annual of the Institute for Comprehensive Studies of Buddhism, Taishō University 16 (1994).
SA_T02_n800u.coverage: partial — Breaks off in the commentary on Sekoddeśa with 'śūnyād ākāśād udbhavaṃ bimbaṃ sarvākā....'.
translations: dbang mdor bstan pa'i dka' 'grel (Derge Tengyur D 1354): translated by bu ston rin chen grub (Tibetan)

SA_T02_nagbhc_u.title: Bodhicittavivaraṇa (fragments)
SA_T02_nagbhc_u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T02_nagbhc_u.summary: The Bodhicittavivaraṇa is a Buddhist verse treatise expounding bodhicitta under conventional and ultimate aspects, including refutation of other views and discussions of mind-only and emptiness.
SA_T02_nagbhc_u.attribution: Ascribed to Nāgārjuna. Regarded as authentic by Lindtner.
SA_T02_nagbhc_u.coverage: fragment — Contains 11 Sanskrit verses or half-verses (kārikās 12, 13ab, 20, 25, 27, 45, 46, 52ab, 57, 98, 99).
translations: Christian Lindtner, Nagarjuniana: Studies in the Writings and Philosophy of Nāgārjuna, Copenhagen: Akademisk Forlag, 1982. (English)
byang chub sems kyi 'grel pa zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 1800): translated by Guṇākaraśrībhadra, rab zhi bshes gnyen, Kanakavarman, pa tshab lo tsA ba nyi ma grags pa (Tibetan)

SA_T02_nagpancu.title: Pañcakrama
SA_T02_nagpancu.author: Nāgārjuna, Śākyamitra
SA_T02_nagpancu.summary: The Pañcakrama ('Five Stages') is a manual of the completion stage (sampannakrama / niṣpannakrama) of the Guhyasamāja Tantra tradition. It outlines five sequential yogic stages: speech isolation (vajrajāpa), mind purification, self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna), clear light / enlightenment (abhisaṃbodhi), and union (yuganaddha). Composed c. 8th–9th century CE, chapters 1 and 3–5 are attributed to Nāgārjuna, while chapter 2 is attributed to Śākyamitra.
SA_T02_nagpancu.attribution: Ascribed in the Ārya lineage of the Guhyasamāja tradition to the tantric master Nāgārjuna (chapters 1, 3, 4, and 5) and Śākyamitra (chapter 2).
SA_T02_nagpancu.edition: Ram Ram Shankar Tripathi: Piṇḍīkramaḥ Pañcakramaś ca, Varanasi/Sarnath 2001.
SA_T02_nagpancu.coverage: complete — Contains all five chapters (kramas) complete (vv. Pk_1.1–Pk_5.36), concluding with closing verses from Vidyākara's Subhāṣitaratnakośa, Raviśrī's Amṛtakaṇikā, and the Buddhist ye dharmā creed.
translations: rim pa lnga pa (Derge Tengyur D 1802): translated by Śraddhākaravarman, lo chen rin chen bzang po, Kamalagupta (Tibetan)

SA_T02_nagpindu.title: Piṇḍīkrama
SA_T02_nagpindu.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T02_nagpindu.summary: The Piṇḍīkrama (also known as Piṇḍīkramasādhana or Piṇḍīkṛtasādhana) is a generation-stage (utpattikrama) manual of the Ārya exegesis of the Guhyasamāja Tantra, traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna. Consisting of 226 verses and interspersed ritual mantras, it details the generation of the Akṣobhyaguhyasamāja maṇḍala and associated practices, and is transmitted alongside the Pañcakrama.
SA_T02_nagpindu.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna of the Ārya tradition of Guhyasamāja exegesis.
SA_T02_nagpindu.edition: Ram Ram Shankar Tripathi: Piṇḍīkramaḥ Pañcakramaś ca, Varanasi/Sarnath 2001.
SA_T02_nagpindu.coverage: complete — Complete text in 226 verses (numbered Pik_1 to Pik_226) with interspersed prose mantras and visualization instructions, concluding with the final dedication and author colophon (piṇḍīkramasādhanaṃ samāptam / kṛtirācāryaśrīnāgārjunapādānām).

SA_T02_nitkarpu.title: Nityakarmapūjāvidhi
SA_T02_nitkarpu.summary: The Nityakarmapūjāvidhi is a Sanskrit liturgical manual from the Newar Buddhist Vajrayāna tradition that details the sequence of rites for daily obligatory worship (nityakarma). It specifies preliminary purifications (ācamana, kāyaviśodhana), the consecration of offerings, worship of the guru and Vajrasattva, the construction and offering of the cosmic Meru maṇḍala, standard sensory offerings (pañcopacāra), and concluding prayers for forgiveness (kṣamāpaṇa) and dismissal of the invoked deities (visarjana).
SA_T02_nitkarpu.attribution: Anonymous liturgical manual preserved in Nepalese Buddhist Vajrayāna manuscripts.
SA_T02_nitkarpu.edition: Ngawang Samten and Janardan Pandey (eds.), 'Nityakarmapūjāvidhiḥ', in Dhīḥ: Journal of Rare Buddhist Texts Research Unit, vol. 33 (Sarnath, Varanasi: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 2002), pp. 155–166.
SA_T02_nitkarpu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the manual as edited, opening with 'atha nityakarmapūjāvidhiḥ prārabhyate' and concluding with the colophon 'iti nityakarmapūjāvidhiḥ samāptaḥ'.

SA_T02_psarkdhu.title: Pratisarākalpadhāraṇī
SA_T02_psarkdhu.summary: The Pratisarākalpadhāraṇī is a short Buddhist apotropaic text consisting of a protective dhāraṇī and kalpa formulas centered on Mahāpratisarā, the chief goddess of the Pañcarakṣā pentad. Opening with an announcement of the Vidyādharakalpa and salutations to the Triratna and Śākyamuni Buddha, the text prescribes incantations and svāhā-formulas intended to ward off diseases, hostile spirits, poisons, and obstacles, while providing universal safety and purifying karmic obscurations. It represents an extracted or parallel ritual witness closely corresponding to sections found in the broader Mahāpratisarā-mahāvidyārājñī corpus.
SA_T02_psarkdhu.attribution: A Buddhist apotropaic dhāraṇī and ritual kalpa text associated with Mahāpratisarā, traditionally regarded as buddhavacana.
SA_T02_psarkdhu.edition: “Pratisarākalpadhāraṇī”, edited by S. Rinpoche and Janardan Pandey, in Dhīḥ: Journal of Rare Buddhist Texts Research Project, vol. 28, Sarnath, Varanasi: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 1999, pp. 140–142.
SA_T02_psarkdhu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the dhāraṇī-kalpa as published in Dhīḥ 28 (1999), pp. 140–142.
translations: Hidas, Gergely. Mahāpratisarā-Mahāvidyārājñī: The Great Amulet, Great Queen of Spells. Introduction, Critical Editions and Annotated Translation. Śata-Piṭaka Series. New Delhi: International Academy of Indian Culture and Aditya Prakashan, 2012. (English)

SA_T02_rabhramu.title: Bhramaharanāma Hevajrasādhana
SA_T02_rabhramu.author: Ratnākaraśānti
SA_T02_rabhramu.summary: The Bhramaharanāma Hevajrasādhana is a sādhana of the sixteen-armed, eight-faced Heruka / Hevajra. It survives in Sanskrit and in a Tibetan translation (D 1245).
SA_T02_rabhramu.attribution: Authored by Ratnākaraśānti. The author is attested in the concluding verses of the work (guruguṇadhanadhāmnaḥ sādhanaṃ herukasya bhramaharam abhidhāya...) as well as the Tibetan canonical colophon (Derge Tengyur, D 1245).
SA_T02_rabhramu.edition: Harunaga Isaacson, 'Ratnākaraśānti's Bhramaharanāma Hevajrasādhana: Critical Edition (Studies in Ratnākaraśānti's tantric works III)', Journal of the International College for Advanced Buddhist Studies 5 (March 2002), Akira Hirakawa Memorial Volume, pp. 151–176.
SA_T02_rabhramu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the sādhana, matching the extent of the edition from the opening verses (p. 157) through the final dedication verse (p. 175).
translations: khrul pa spong ba zhes bya ba'i sgrub pa'i thabs (Derge Tengyur D 1245) (Tibetan)

SA_T02_sunytjsu.title: Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhi
SA_T02_sunytjsu.author: Śūnyasamādhipāda
SA_T02_sunytjsu.summary: A Buddhist tantric text focusing on Vajravārāhī and Vajrayoginī, treating ritual and visualization practices (including mantroddhāra and pūjāvidhi) for realizing gnosis.
SA_T02_sunytjsu.attribution: Ascribed to Śūnyasamādhipāda (Tibetan canon: sTong nyid ting nge 'dzin). The Tibetan translation (D 1551) attributes the work to Śūnyatāsamādhi (stong nyid ting nge 'dzin).
SA_T02_sunytjsu.edition: Janardan Pandey: Tattvajñanasamsiddhih, with Marmakalikapanjika of Viryasrimitra. Sarnath, Varanasi: Rare Buddhist Texts Research Unit, 2000 (Rare Buddhist Text Series, 23).
SA_T02_sunytjsu.coverage: complete — Root text; ends with the colophon 'samāptoyaṃ tatvajñānasaṃsiddhirnāma svādhiṣṭhānaśceti'.
translations: dpal de kho na nyid ye shes grub pa (Derge Tengyur D 1551): translated by Varendraruci, rngog blo ldan shes rab (Tibetan)

SA_T02_vadhdhdu.title: Vasudhārādhāraṇīsūtra
SA_T02_vadhdhdu.summary: The Vasudhārādhāraṇīsūtra is a canonical Mahāyāna dhāraṇī scripture set at Kauśāmbī, where the householder Sucandra asks Gautama Buddha how impoverished and ailing sentient beings may attain wealth, health, and relief from suffering. In response, the Buddha reveals the dhāraṇī and ritual procedures (kalpa).
SA_T02_vadhdhdu.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna Buddhist dhāraṇī sūtra delivered by Gautama Buddha; preserved in Tibetan Kangyur (D 662) and Chinese translations (T. 1162–1165).
SA_T02_vadhdhdu.edition: Ngawang Samten & S. S. Bahulkar (eds.), "Vasudhārādhāraṇīsūtra", Dhīḥ Journal 44 (2007), pp. 129–147.
SA_T02_vadhdhdu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the sūtra as edited in Dhīḥ 44 (2007), pp. 129–147, extending from the initial nidāna in Kauśāmbī through the dialogue with Sucandra and Ānanda to the final colophon and the ye dharmā stanza.

SA_T02_vadhdhgu.title: Vasudhārādhāraṇī (fragment)
SA_T02_vadhdhgu.summary: The Vasudhārādhāraṇī is a Mahāyāna dhāraṇī scripture framed by a narrative setting in Kauśāmbī. The impoverished householder Sucandra approaches the Buddha to ask how one may obtain abundant wealth, grain, and prosperity in order to provide for a large family and sustain extensive charitable offerings. In reply, the Buddha imparts the Vasudhārā dhāraṇī received from the past Tathāgata Vajradharasāgaranirghoṣa, detailing its ritual practice, protective benefits, and power to produce torrential rains of grain and precious treasures.
SA_T02_vadhdhgu.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna Buddhist scripture (buddhavacana) setting forth the dhāraṇī of Vasudhārā in response to the query of the householder Sucandra in Kauśāmbī. Identified in the Gilgit manuscript facsimiles as a recension of the Vasudhārādhāraṇī / Sucandrāvadāna by Paul Harrison.
SA_T02_vadhdhgu.edition: Facsimiles in: Gilgit Buddhist Manuscripts (Facsimile Edition), ed. by Raghu Vira and Lokesh Chandra, 10 pts., New Delhi 1959–1974 (Śata-Piṭaka Series 10). [revised and enlarged compact edition, 3 vols., Delhi 1995 (Bibliotheca Indo-Buddhica Series, 150-152)]. Transliterated from the manuscript by Klaus Wille (Göttingen).
SA_T02_vadhdhgu.coverage: fragment — Transcribes four birchbark folios from a single Gilgit manuscript: fol. 35r–v (GBM pp. 1426–1427), fol. 36r–v (GBM pp. 1286–1287, with margins broken and text lost on both sides), fol. 37r–v (GBM pp. 1428–1429), and fol. 38r–v (GBM pp. 1430–1431). The text opens with the standard nidāna ('evaṃ mayā śrutam...'), preserves Sucandra's inquiry, the dhāraṇī, ritual instructions, and Ānanda's udāna, but breaks off abruptly at segment 111 with '(End of manuscript missing/)' before the final formula and concluding colophon.

SA_T02_vadhdhju.title: Vasudhārādhāraṇī
SA_T02_vadhdhju.summary: The Vasudhārādhāraṇī is a widely recited Mahāyāna Buddhist dhāraṇī-sūtra centered on Vasudhārā, the goddess of wealth and grain. In the Kauśāmbī setting, the Buddha instructs the impoverished householder Sucandra on the protective incantation and ritual practices revealed by the ancient tathāgata Vajradharasāgaranirghoṣa to overcome poverty and dispel harm. This e-text preserves a unique recension copied in 1638 CE (Vikrama Saṃvat 1695) in Gujarat, documenting the cross-sectarian adoption and ritual use of the Buddhist prosperity spell by Jaina communities.
SA_T02_vadhdhju.attribution: A Buddhist Mahāyāna dhāraṇī scripture framed as a discourse of Śākyamuni Buddha. This specific e-text reproduces a manuscript transmitted and preserved in a Jaina milieu in Gujarat.
SA_T02_vadhdhju.edition: Padmanabh S. Jaini. Vasudhārā-dhāraṇī: A Buddhist work in use among the Jainas of Gujerat", Shri Mahavir Jaina Vidyalaya Golden Jubilee Volume, Part 1, Bombay 1968, pp. 30-45.
SA_T02_vadhdhju.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Jaina transmission of the Vasudhārādhāraṇī as edited by P. S. Jaini, beginning with the Jaina maṅgala verse ('oṃ namaḥ śrī jinaśāsanāya...') and ending with the canonical closing and scribal colophon dated Vikrama Saṃvat 1695 (1638 CE).

SA_T02_vamvuppu.title: Mṛtyuvañcanopadeśa
SA_T02_vamvuppu.author: Vāgīśvarakīrti
SA_T02_vamvuppu.summary: The Mṛtyuvañcanopadeśa ('Instruction on Cheating Death') by Vāgīśvarakīrti is a manual on diagnosing and averting untimely death. Across four chapters, the text details external and internal omens as well as physiological signs of impending death (ariṣṭa, maraṇalakṣaṇa) and outlines ritual, meditative, and yogic remedies (mṛtyuvañcana). The text was translated into Tibetan (D 1748) by Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna and Rin chen bzang po.
SA_T02_vamvuppu.attribution: Attributed in the colophon to śrī-paṇḍitācārya Vāgīśvarakīrti.
SA_T02_vamvuppu.edition: Johannes Schneider: Vāgīśvarakīrtis Mṛtyuvañcanopadeśa, eine buddhistische Lehrschrift zur Abwehr des Todes. Wien: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 2010. (Beiträge zur Kultur- und Geistesgeschichte Asiens; 66) (Denkschriften der philosophisch-historischen Klasse; 394)
SA_T02_vamvuppu.coverage: complete — Complete text in four chapters (paricchedas 1–4, ending at VMv_4.102 with the colophon iti śrīpaṇḍitācāryavāgīśvarakīrtiviracite mṛtyuvañcanopadeśe caturthaḥ paricchedaḥ samāptaḥ; verse 4.102 states granthapramāṇam ākhyātaṃ sāśītikaśatatrayam).

SA_T03_abhisamu.title: Abhisamayālaṅkāranāmaprajñāpāramitopadeśaśāstra
SA_T03_abhisamu.author: Maitreyanātha
SA_T03_abhisamu.summary: The Abhisamayālaṅkāranāmaprajñāpāramitopadeśaśāstra is a central Mahāyāna verse treatise of 273 kārikās in eight chapters outlining the hidden path-structure implicit in the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras (specifically the Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā). It classifies the spiritual path into eight clear realizations (aṣṭāv abhisamayāḥ) and seventy doctrinal topics (saptati padārthāḥ) leading from initial bodhicitta to complete omniscient buddhahood. Attributed to Maitreyanātha and transmitted to Asaṅga, it constitutes the foundational scholastic curriculum text for Prajñāpāramitā exegesis across Tibetan monastic institutions.
SA_T03_abhisamu.coverage: complete — Complete. The verses are numbered Abhs_1.1–8.40 (chapter counts 73/31/16/63/42/1/5/40 = 271), followed by the two concluding saṃgraha verses (total 273) and the colophon. Before verse 1.1 come the unnumbered homage verse "yā sarvajñatayā nayaty upaśamaṃ …", the usual maṅgala of the Abhisamayālaṅkāra (it also opens the Tibetan translation, D 3786), and a stray "kṛtir maitreyanāthasya // oṃ namo maitreyanāthāya //". The only internal chapter colophon kept is that of chapter 8.
translations: Conze, Edward. The Large Sutra on Perfect Wisdom, with the Divisions of the Abhisamayālaṅkāra. Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1975. (English)

SA_T03_bsa011_u.title: Prajñāpāramitāpiṇḍārtha
SA_T03_bsa011_u.author: Dignāga
SA_T03_bsa011_u.summary: The Prajñāpāramitāpiṇḍārtha (also known as the Prajñāpāramitāpiṇḍārthasaṃgraha or Prajñāpāramitāsaṃgrahakārikā) is a 58-verse synopsis of the Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā composed by the Buddhist philosopher-epistemologist Dignāga. Dignāga organizes the scripture into thirty-two core thematic topics (dvātriṃśad arthāḥ), interpreting its insight through a Yogācāra doctrinal lens. The synthesis notably correlates the sūtra's teachings with sixteen aspects of emptiness, the counteracting of ten types of mental distraction (cittavikṣepa), and the three natures (trisvabhāva).
SA_T03_bsa011_u.attribution: Ascribed to Dignāga in the closing colophon ('kṛtir ācāryadignāgapādānām'), the Tibetan translation (Derge Tanjur Toh 3809), and the Chinese translation (Taishō 1518) translated by Dānapāla (Shihu). Haribhadra cites it in the Abhisamayālaṃkārālokā.
SA_T03_bsa011_u.coverage: complete — Complete text consisting of all 58 verses and concluding colophon.
translations: Giuseppe Tucci, 'Minor Sanskrit Texts on the Prajñā-pāramitā: 1. The Prajñā-pāramitā-piṇḍārtha of Diṅnāga', Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society of Great Britain and Ireland (JRAS) 1947, pts. 1 and 2. (English)

SA_T03_bsa026_u.title: Abhisamayālaṅkāra
SA_T03_bsa026_u.author: Maitreya
SA_T03_bsa026_u.summary: The Abhisamayālaṅkāra ('Ornament for Clear Realization') is a foundational Mahāyāna verse treatise composed of kārikās arranged across eight chapters (adhikāras). Attributed to Maitreya/Asaṅga, it serves as a systematic hidden-meaning commentary on the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras, organizing the progressive path to enlightenment into eight clear realizations (aṣṭāv abhisamayāḥ) and seventy distinct topics (arthasaptati). Regarded as one of the Five Treatises of Maitreya, it remains the principal pedagogical framework for Prajñāpāramitā scholasticism in Tibetan Buddhist monastic curricula and inspired major Indian commentaries by Vimuktisena, Haribhadra, and Ratnākaraśānti.
SA_T03_bsa026_u.attribution: Traditionally regarded in the Indo-Tibetan tradition as having been revealed by the bodhisattva Maitreya to Asaṅga; modern scholars generally assign it either to a historical Maitreyanātha or to Asaṅga himself.
SA_T03_bsa026_u.edition: Ramsankar Tripathi: Abhisamayalankaravrttih Sphutartha. Sarnath: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies (CIHTS), 1977.
SA_T03_bsa026_u.coverage: complete — Contains all 8 chapters (adhikāras) and 273 kārikās of the root treatise (labeled Asa_1.1 to Asa_8.40).
translations: Edward Conze (tr.), Abhisamayālaṅkāra: Introduction and Translation from the Original Text, Serie Orientale Roma 6, Roma: IsMEO, 1954. (English)

shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa'i man ngag gi bstan bcos mngon par rtogs pa'i rgyan zhes bya ba'i tshig le'ur byas pa (Derge Tengyur D 3786): translated by Amaragomin, rngog blo ldan shes rab (Tibetan)

SA_T03_bsa031_u.title: Abhisamayālaṅkārakārikā with Abhisamayālaṅkāravṛtti Sphuṭārthā
SA_T03_bsa031_u.author: Maitreya, Haribhadra
SA_T03_bsa031_u.summary: Haribhadra's Sphuṭārthā (titled Abhisamayālaṅkārakārikāśāstravivṛti in the Sanskrit manuscript tradition) is a commentary (vṛtti) on the root kārikās of the Abhisamayālaṅkāra attributed to Maitreya. It systematically explicates the topics that align the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras across eight chapters (adhikāras).
SA_T03_bsa031_u.attribution: The root verses are traditionally attributed to Maitreya (revealed to Ārya Asaṅga). The commentary is by Ācārya Haribhadra. In the manuscript tradition edited by Hirofusa Amano, Haribhadra's commentary is designated as Abhisamayālaṅkārakārikāśāstravivṛti.
SA_T03_bsa031_u.edition: Ram Shankar Tripathi (ed.), Abhisamayalankaravrti sputartha. Sarnath: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 1977, pp. 3-44.
SA_T03_bsa031_u.coverage: complete — Complete text covering all eight chapters (adhikāras 1–8), encompassing both the root kārikās and Haribhadra's commentary, including the concluding verses and Sanskrit retro-translations of the Tibetan translation colophons.
translations: shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa'i man ngag gi bstan bcos mngon par rtogs pa'i rgyan zhes bya ba'i 'grel pa (Derge Tengyur D 3793): translated by Vidyākaraprabha, ska ba dpal brtsegs; revised by Amaragomin, rngog blo ldan shes rab (Tibetan)

SA_T03_bsa033_u.title: Abhisamayālaṅkārāntaḥpātināṃ padārthānāṃ saṃkṣepato vivaraṇam
SA_T03_bsa033_u.author: Rāmaśaṅkara Tripāṭhī
SA_T03_bsa033_u.summary: The Abhisamayālaṅkārāntaḥpātināṃ padārthānāṃ saṃkṣepato vivaraṇam is a modern Sanskrit scholastic manual written by Prof. Ram Shankar Tripathi as an appendix to his 1977 edition of Haribhadra's Abhisamayālaṅkāravṛtti Sphuṭārthā. Adopting the structure of traditional Tibetan monastic textbooks (don bdun cu), it delineates the eight general subjects (aṣṭau padārthāḥ) and seventy specific topics (saptatiḥ padārthāḥ) of the Abhisamayālaṅkāra. Each topic is systematically analyzed by its formal definition (lakṣaṇa), taxonomic divisions (bheda), and spiritual stage boundary (avadhi / sīmā).
SA_T03_bsa033_u.attribution: A 20th-century Sanskrit manual authored by modern scholar Prof. Ram Shankar Tripathi (CIHTS, Sarnath). It is based upon the traditional Tibetan scholastic curriculum (don bdun cu / yig cha) for analyzing the 8 subjects and 70 topics of the Abhisamayālaṅkāra.
SA_T03_bsa033_u.edition: Ram Shankar Tripathi: Abhisamayalankarantah patinam. Sarnath: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 1977, pp. 1-67.
SA_T03_bsa033_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of Appendix 1 (Pariśiṣṭam - 1, pp. 1–67 of the appendix section) from the 1977 Sarnath volume, from the opening maṅgala and thematic statement (lines 0–5) down to the closing dedication (pariṇāmanā) citing Haribhadra (lines 1596–1605).

SA_T03_bsa050_u.title: Pāramitāsamāsa
SA_T03_bsa050_u.author: Āryaśūra
SA_T03_bsa050_u.summary: The Pāramitāsamāsa ("Compendium of the Perfections") is a kāvya-style verse treatise in six chapters on the six perfections of the bodhisattva: generosity, morality, patience, vigour, meditation and wisdom. Each is presented as grounded in compassion and the bodhisattva's resolve, with the final chapter on prajñā. It is ascribed to (Ārya)Śūra and was translated into Tibetan by Vairocanarakṣita (D 3944).
SA_T03_bsa050_u.attribution: The closing stanza names the author as Śūra ("śurabhramareṇa"); tradition identifies him with Āryaśūra, author of the Jātakamālā. Meadows (1986) discusses the authorship and date; whether he is the Jātakamālā poet is debated.
SA_T03_bsa050_u.edition: Carol Meadows (ed. and tr.), Ārya-Śūra's Compendium of the Perfections: Text, Translation and Analysis of the Pāramitāsamāsa. Indica et Tibetica 8. Bonn: Indica et Tibetica Verlag, 1986.
SA_T03_bsa050_u.coverage: complete — Complete: six chapters (dāna, śīla, kṣānti, vīrya, dhyāna, prajñā) with 61/65/40/44/79/74 = 363 numbered stanzas (Ps_1.1–6.74), the final chapter colophon and the author's closing stanza.
translations: Alfonsa Ferrari 1946 (see other_editions). (Italian)
Carol Meadows 1986 (see edition_used). (English)
Seiji Satoh, "Ārya Śūra's Compendium of the Perfections (Pāramitāsamāsa) The 1st chapter. A Japanese translation", Ronshū (1991). (Japanese)

SA_T03_bsa051_u.title: Sāratamā
SA_T03_bsa051_u.author: Ratnākaraśānti
SA_T03_bsa051_u.summary: The Sāratamā is an extensive Sanskrit commentary (pañjikā) by Ratnākaraśānti on the Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā, connecting it to the Abhisamayālaṅkāra. It interprets the sūtra from a Yogācāra perspective, contrasting with Haribhadra's standard interpretation.
SA_T03_bsa051_u.attribution: Authored by Ratnākaraśānti (Śāntipa). The author names himself in introductory verse 2 ('mando 'pi ratnākaraḥ') and the colophon reads 'sāratamety abhisamaye sphuṭā ghanā pañjikeyaṃ me'.
SA_T03_bsa051_u.edition: Padmanabh S. Jaini (ed.), Sāratamā: A Pañjikā on the Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra by Ācārya Ratnākaraśānti, Tibetan Sanskrit Works Series, Patna: Kashi Prasad Jayaswal Research Institute, 1979.
SA_T03_bsa051_u.coverage: complete — Commentary on the Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā, from the opening maṅgala verses to the concluding verses, ye dharmā formula, and scribal colophon. Lacunae marked by dots reflect physical damages in the palm-leaf manuscript.
translations: Gregory Max Seton, 'Defining Wisdom: Ratnākaraśānti's Sāratamā', D.Phil. dissertation, University of Oxford, part II. (English)

SA_T03_kamvchtu.title: Prajñāpāramitāvajracchedikāṭīkā
SA_T03_kamvchtu.author: Kamalaśīla
SA_T03_kamvchtu.summary: The Prajñāpāramitāvajracchedikāṭīkā is an extensive commentary by the Indian master Kamalaśīla on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra. Following classical Indian scholastic structure—setting out the purpose (prayojana), concise overview (piṇḍārtha), word analysis (padārtha), internal connection (anusandhi), and answers to objections—Kamalaśīla expounds the sūtra from a Mādhyamika perspective. He details the path of the bodhisattva and refutes substantialist views while demonstrating two-fold selflessness. Because the ancient Sanskrit manuscript is lost, this e-text represents a modern Sanskrit reconstruction (punaruddhāra) made from the Tibetan canonical version by Pema Tenzin.
SA_T03_kamvchtu.attribution: The work is an extensive commentary (vistṛtaṭīkā) by Ācārya Kamalaśīla on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā. The original Sanskrit text is lost; this Sanskrit version is a modern restoration/reconstruction (punaruddhāra) made from the Tibetan canonical translation by Ācārya Pema Tenzin (Pemā Tenjin). The Tibetan translation (D 3817) attributes the work to Jayasena (ka ma la shI la).
SA_T03_kamvchtu.edition: Prajñāpāramitāvajracchedikāsūtram with Prajñāpāramitāvajracchedikāṭīkā of Ācārya Kamalaśīla, critically edited (Tibetan version) and restored into Sanskrit by Pema Tenzin, Sarnath, Varanasi: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 1994 (Bibliotheca Indo-Tibetica, 29).
SA_T03_kamvchtu.coverage: complete — Complete commentary as reconstructed into Sanskrit by Pema Tenzin, from the introductory maṅgalācaraṇa through the final closing verses and modern restoration colophon.

SA_T03_knavslou.title: Navaślokī
SA_T03_knavslou.author: Kambalapāda
SA_T03_knavslou.summary: The Navaślokī (also titled Āryāṣṭasāhasrikāyāḥ Prajñāpāramitāyāḥ Piṇḍārthaḥ) is a concise verse digest of the Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā attributed to Kambalapāda. The text consists of 14 ślokas: four introductory stanzas establishing that all perfections are unified in the Perfection of Wisdom, nine core stanzas that expound non-substantiality and emptiness using nine classical similes, and a concluding dedication to supreme gnosis.
SA_T03_knavslou.attribution: Attributed in the colophon to Śrī-Kambalāmbarapāda (Kambalapāda / La-ba-pa / 勝德赤衣).
SA_T03_knavslou.edition: G. Tucci, Minor Buddhist Texts, part I, Roma 1956 (Serie Orientale Roma, 9), pp. 216–217.
SA_T03_knavslou.coverage: complete — Contains the complete verse treatise: 14 ślokas in total, consisting of 4 introductory stanzas, the 9 core stanzas (numbered 5[1] to 13[9]) illustrating the 9 similes of emptiness, and 1 concluding stanza (verse 14), with opening and closing colophons. It contains the kārikās only and does not include the prose autocommentary (ṭīkā).
translations: Giuseppe Tucci, 'Navaślokī of Kambalapāda', in Minor Buddhist Texts, Part I, Rome: IsMEO, 1956, pp. 209–231. (English)
Taishō 1516 (聖佛母般若波羅蜜多九頌精義論), tr. 法護等 (Fahu et al.), Song dynasty (1004–1058). (Chinese)

SA_T03_n1146u.title: Abhisamayālaṅkārāloka
SA_T03_n1146u.author: Haribhadra
SA_T03_n1146u.summary: The Abhisamayālaṅkārāloka is Haribhadra's commentary composed under the reign of King Dharmapāla. It interprets the Prajñāpāramitā through the framework of Maitreya's Abhisamayālaṅkāra kārikās.
SA_T03_n1146u.attribution: Haribhadra was an Indian Buddhist scholar associated with the Yogācāra-Svātantrika-Madhyamaka tradition who flourished during the reign of King Dharmapāla, named in the concluding praśasti verse. BDRC ID: P7297; Tibetan Tanjur: D3791.
SA_T03_n1146u.edition: Unrai Wogihara (ed.), Abhisamayālaṃkārālokā Prajñāpāramitāvyākhyā: The Work of Haribhadra, Tokyo: Toyo Bunko, 1932-1935.
SA_T03_n1146u.coverage: complete — Opens with the five maṅgala stanzas ('yā sarvajñatayā nayatyupaśamaṃ...') and concludes with the praśasti of King Dharmapāla, concluding title verses ('yo'laṅkāro'bhisamaye tadālokaprakāśikā...'), author colophon ('kṛtiriyamācārya-haribhadrapādānām'), and ye dharmā pratītyasamutpāda verse.

SA_T03_n864u.title: Prajñāpāramitāstuti
SA_T03_n864u.summary: The Prajñāpāramitāstuti is a short five-verse devotional hymn (stotra) composed in anuṣṭubh metre extolling the Perfection of Wisdom. Prajñāpāramitā is addressed as the supreme goddess, free from conceptual construction and change, the mother of the Buddhas, the grandmother of the Bodhisattvas, and the embodiment of wisdom, mindfulness, and the ten perfections.
SA_T03_n864u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 5 anuṣṭubh verses with opening namaskāra ('om namaḥ śrīprajñāpāramitāyai') and closing rubric ('śrīprajñāpāramitāstutiḥ samāptā').

SA_T03_n865u.title: Ṣaṭpāramitāstotra
SA_T03_n865u.summary: A brief anonymous Buddhist devotional hymn (stotra) of six verses composed in Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit. Each stanza celebrates the Buddha ('narasiṃhe') as one who has attained awakening and supremacy through one of the six perfections (dāna, śīla, kṣānti, vīrya, dhyāna, and prajñā) entering the city.
SA_T03_n865u.attribution: The work is an anonymous Buddhist devotional hymn.
SA_T03_n865u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 6 verses celebrating each of the six perfections (dāna, śīla, kṣānti, vīrya, dhyāna, prajñā), concluded by the colophon 'śrīṣaṭpāramitāstotraṃ samāptam'.

SA_T04_acatstvu.title: Catuḥstavasamāsārtha (fragment)
SA_T04_acatstvu.author: Amṛtākara
SA_T04_acatstvu.summary: The Catuḥstavasamāsārtha by Paṇḍita Amṛtākara is a commentary clarifying the Catuḥstava attributed to Nāgārjuna. The extant text comments upon portions of the Niraupamyastava and the entirety of the Acintyastava and Paramārthastava.
SA_T04_acatstvu.attribution: Attributed in the final colophon to Paṇḍita Amṛtākara (catuḥstavasamāsārthaḥ paṇḍitāmṛtākarasyeti).
SA_T04_acatstvu.edition: Giuseppe Tucci, 'Catuḥstavasamāsārtha of Amṛtākara', in Minor Buddhist Texts, Part I, Serie Orientale Roma 9, Roma, 1956, pp. 238–246.
SA_T04_acatstvu.coverage: fragment — Surviving fragment of the treatise preserving the remaining portion of the Niraupamyastava commentary and complete commentaries on the Acintyastava and Paramārthastava (Tucci 1956, pp. 238–246).

SA_T04_bsa003_u.title: Bodhicaryāvatāra
SA_T04_bsa003_u.author: Śāntideva
SA_T04_bsa003_u.summary: The Bodhicaryāvatāra ('Entering the Way of Awakening') is an influential Mahāyāna verse manual and classic of Buddhist devotional-philosophical literature composed in ten chapters by Śāntideva. It outlines the spiritual cultivation of the bodhisattva, tracing the generation and stabilization of the awakening mind (bodhicitta), ritual confession, vigilance (apramāda), guard over awareness (saṃprajanya), and the perfections of patience (kṣānti), vigor (vīrya), meditative absorption (dhyāna), and dedication of merit (pariṇāmanā). The ninth chapter develops a Madhyamaka dialectical critique of intrinsic nature (svabhāva), refuting rival Buddhist and non-Buddhist philosophical systems.
SA_T04_bsa003_u.attribution: The Bodhicaryāvatāra is attributed to Śāntideva.
SA_T04_bsa003_u.edition: P. L. Vaidya: Bodhicaryavatara of Santideva. Darbhanga: Mithila Institute, 1960. (Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, 12)
SA_T04_bsa003_u.coverage: complete — Complete root text in 10 chapters, ending at verse 10.58 and the final colophon (kṛtir ācāryaśāntidevasya). The chapter colophons reflect those preserved in Prajñākaramati's Bodhicaryāvatārapañjikā as reproduced in P. L. Vaidya's edition.
translations: Kate Crosby and Andrew Skilton (trans.), 1996. (English)
Marion L. Matics (trans.), Entering the Path of Enlightenment: The Bodhicaryavatara of the Buddhist Poet Santideva, New York: Macmillan Co, 1970. (English)

SA_T04_bsa004_u.title: Bodhipathapradīpa
SA_T04_bsa004_u.author: Atiśa
SA_T04_bsa004_u.summary: The Bodhipathapradīpa ('Lamp for the Path to Enlightenment') is a treatise composed by Atiśa. In 69 verses, it outlines the spiritual development through the tripartite typology of spiritual capacities (adhama-, madhyama-, and uttamapuruṣa), presenting mahāyāna bodhisattva practices and discussing tantric vows. This digital file contains Losang Norbu Shastri's 1984 Sanskrit restoration from the Tibetan transmission.
SA_T04_bsa004_u.attribution: Composed in verse by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna. The original Sanskrit text is lost; this digital text is a modern Sanskrit restoration from the Tibetan version (Toh 3947 / D 3947) prepared by Losang Norbu Shastri.
SA_T04_bsa004_u.edition: Shastri, Losang Norbu: Bodhipathpradipa of Atisha. Sarnath: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 1984, 1-70. Restored Sanskrit text.
SA_T04_bsa004_u.coverage: complete — Restored text consisting of 69 verses (Bpp_1–69).

SA_T04_bsa008_u.title: Garbhasaṅgraha
SA_T04_bsa008_u.author: Atiśa
SA_T04_bsa008_u.summary: The Garbhasaṅgraha is a concise 14-verse Mahāyāna work attributed in the colophon to Mahācārya Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna (Atiśa). It sets forth the essential path of the Bodhisattva: recognizing suffering caused by dualistic grasping and afflictions, cultivating emptiness and compassion, and generating bodhicitta to attain liberation.
SA_T04_bsa008_u.attribution: The colophon reads: 'garbhasaṅgraho nāma mahācārya-dīpaṅkaraśrījñānaviracitaḥ samāptaḥ'. Mahācārya Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna is commonly known as Atiśa. In the Tibetan Tengyur (Toh 3949), the text is titled snying po bsdus pa zhes bya ba and attributed to Mar-me-mdsad ye-shes (Atiśa) and translated by Mar-me-mdsad ye-shes and Tshul-khrims 'byung-gnas.
SA_T04_bsa008_u.edition: Rameshchandra Negi: Atishaviracita ekadasha granthah. Varanasi: Central Institute of High Tibetan Studies (CIHTS) 1992, pp. 79-80.
SA_T04_bsa008_u.coverage: complete — Complete 14-verse text with opening maṅgala and closing colophon (pp. 79–80 in Negi 1992).
translations: snying po bsdus pa zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 3949): translated by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna, nag 'tsho lo tsA ba tshul khrims rgyal ba (Tibetan)

SA_T04_bsa009_u.title: Hastavālaprakaraṇa with Hastavālaprakaraṇavṛtti (incomplete)
SA_T04_bsa009_u.author: Dignāga
SA_T04_bsa009_u.summary: The Hastavālaprakaraṇa (comprising six root verses) and its autocommentary (vṛtti) analyze conventional reality using the classic Buddhist and Indian epistemological simile of a rope mistaken for a snake. It argues that composite entities and their constituent parts dissolve under analytical scrutiny into partless elements that lack substantial reality, demonstrating that empirical objects exist merely at the conventional level (saṃvṛti) and lack intrinsic nature (svabhāva). While the original Indic Sanskrit manuscript is lost and the published Sanskrit text is a retro-translation from Tibetan and Chinese recensions, this e-text contains the complete set of six root verses along with the opening mangala and single introductory sentence of the vṛtti, omitting the prose commentary on the verses.
SA_T04_bsa009_u.attribution: Ascribed in the Tibetan tradition to Āryadeva, but both Chinese translations (Paramārtha, T. 1620; Yijing, T. 1621) attribute it to Dignāga.
SA_T04_bsa009_u.edition: Bhagchandra Jain: Hastabalapranavrtti. Nagpur: Aloka Prakashan, 1971.
SA_T04_bsa009_u.coverage: partial — Complete for the root kārikās (all 6 verses are present), but incomplete for the prose vṛtti, preserving only the invocation and introductory sentence while omitting the prose commentary on verses 1–6.

SA_T04_bsa012_u.title: Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayakārikā
SA_T04_bsa012_u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T04_bsa012_u.summary: The Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayakārikā ('Verses on the Heart of Dependent Origination') is a concise seven-stanza Madhyamaka treatise that condenses the twelve links (nidāna) of dependent arising into three interrelated categories: defilements (kleśa), karma, and suffering (duḥkha). It demonstrates that empirical entities arise entirely through conditioned causal processes without any transmigrating soul or independent entity (sattva). Employing eight classical analogies (such as a lamp, an echo, a reflection in a mirror, and an imprint of a seal), the text establishes that cyclic rebirth takes place without substantial transmigration (asaṅkrama), culminating in the celebrated assertion that in ultimate reality nothing is to be subtracted and nothing added.
SA_T04_bsa012_u.attribution: Traditionally ascribed to Ācārya Nāgārjuna (c. 150–250 CE) and recognized as authentic in modern scholarship (e.g. by Chr. Lindtner). The kārikā text is accompanied in the tradition by an commentary (Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayavyākhyāna) whose authorship has sometimes been attributed to Nāgārjuna or Śuddhamati.
SA_T04_bsa012_u.edition: Gyaltsen Namdrol: Pratityasamutpadahrdaya and Aryadharmadhatugarbhavivarana. Sarnath: CIHTS 1997, p. 29.
SA_T04_bsa012_u.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all 7 stanzas, preceded by the opening title/attribution and concluded with the final colophon line.
translations: Jamieson, Robert Craig, A Study of Nāgārjuna's Twenty Verses on the Great Vehicle... and His Verses on the Heart of Dependent Origination, New York: Peter Lang, 2000. (English)
Lindtner, Christian, Master of Wisdom: Writings of the Buddhist Master Nāgārjuna, Dharma Publishing, 1986. (English)
La Vallée Poussin, Louis de, Théorie des douze causes, 1913. (French)
rten cing 'brel par 'byung ba'i snying po'i tshig le'ur byas pa (Derge Tengyur D 3836) (Tibetan)

SA_T04_bsa013_u.title: Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayakārikā with Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayavyākhyāna
SA_T04_bsa013_u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T04_bsa013_u.summary: The Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayakārikā with Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayavyākhyāna is an epitome of the doctrine of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) traditionally ascribed to Nāgārjuna. It reduces the twelve links of existence into three fundamental categories: afflictions (kleśa), karma, and suffering (duḥkha), explaining how they perpetuate cyclic existence like an endlessly turning wheel without any permanent agent or substantial soul transmigrating between lives. Emphasizing that purely empty factors arise from empty conditions, the text concludes with well-known verses declaring that in ultimate reality nothing is to be removed and nothing added.
SA_T04_bsa013_u.attribution: Both the root verses and the prose commentary are attributed to Nāgārjuna in the Tibetan canon (Toh 3836 and 3837) and in Chinese translation (T. 1654). However, an earlier Chinese translation (T. 1651 by Bodhiruci) attributes the work to Jingyi (*Śuddhamati). This discrepancy led Carmen Dragonetti to discuss authorship in favor of Śuddhamati, while Christian Lindtner has expressed doubt as to Nāgārjuna's authorship of the Vyākhyāna.
SA_T04_bsa013_u.edition: Gyaltsen Namdrol, ed. Pratityasamutpadahrdaya and Aryadharmadhatugarbhavivarana. Sarnath: CIHTS, 1997.
SA_T04_bsa013_u.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all seven root verses (kārikās 1–7) and the prose commentary (sections 1–5, with verses 6 and 7 quoted in conclusion without additional prose).
translations: R. C. Jamieson, A Study of Nāgārjuna's Twenty Verses on the Great Vehicle (Mahāyānaviṃśikā) and His Verses on the Heart of Dependent Origination (Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayakārikā), with the Interpretation of the Heart of Dependent Origination (Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayavyākhyāna), New York: Peter Lang, 2000. (English)

SA_T04_bsa014_u.title: Śikṣāsamuccayakārikā
SA_T04_bsa014_u.author: Śāntideva
SA_T04_bsa014_u.summary: The Śikṣāsamuccayakārikā comprises twenty-seven mnemonic stanzas composed by Śāntideva. Built upon a matrix introduced in kārikā 4, the work coordinates four bodhisattva practices—renunciation (utsarga), protection (rakṣā), purification (śuddhi), and enhancement (vardhana)—across three domains: one's person (ātmabhāva), material goods (bhoga), and merit (śubha/puṇya). In Tibetan canonical collections, these 27 verses are preserved under Toh 3939.
SA_T04_bsa014_u.attribution: The root stanzas are attributed to Śāntideva (Zhi-ba lha) in the Tibetan Tanjur (D 3939 / Toh 3939). In the Chinese canon record for T 1636 (大乘集菩薩學論), the author/contributor is given as Dharmakīrti (法稱).
SA_T04_bsa014_u.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising 27 root kārikās (Śsk 1–27).
translations: Amalia Pezzali, Śāntideva e il Bodhicaryāvatāra, Bologna, 1982. (Italian)

SA_T04_bsa015_u.title: Suhṛllekha
SA_T04_bsa015_u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T04_bsa015_u.summary: The Suhṛllekha ('Letter to a Friend') is a celebrated Buddhist didactic poem of 123 stanzas traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna and addressed to a king. Written in Āryāgīti metre, the text summarizes fundamental Mahāyāna and Buddhist lay ethics, including the six recollections, the ten virtuous actions, mindfulness, the hazards of sensory attachment, karma, the sufferings of cyclic existence (saṃsāra), and the bodhisattva path culminating in buddhahood. Because the original Sanskrit text has not survived in manuscript form and was preserved historically only in Tibetan and three Chinese translations, this electronic text reproduces a modern Sanskrit restoration (punaruddhāra) prepared by Padma Tendzin (CIHTS, 2002).
SA_T04_bsa015_u.attribution: The original Sanskrit text of Nāgārjuna's Suhṛllekha is non-extant. The Sanskrit verses in this e-text are a modern retroversion (punaruddhāra / reconstruction) from the Tibetan translation (Bstan 'gyur, D 4182) by Padma Tendzin (Pema Tenzin) and published by CIHTS in 2002. Historically, the didactic epistle is attributed to Nāgārjuna and addressed to a king (variously identified as Śātavāhana / Gautamīputra / Udayana).
SA_T04_bsa015_u.edition: Padma Tendzin: Suhridlekha [Suḥrllekha of Ācārya Nāgārjuna and Vyaktapadāṭīkā of Ācārya Mahāmati]. Varanasi: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies (CIHTS), 2002.
SA_T04_bsa015_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 123 verses of the Suhṛllekha in modern Sanskrit retroversion; does not include Mahāmati's commentary (Vyaktapadāṭīkā), which was edited alongside it in the 2002 CIHTS publication.
translations: Heinrich Wenzel, 'Friendly Epistle', Journal of the Pali Text Society (1886), pp. 1–32. (English)

SA_T04_bsa016_u.title: Śūnyatāsaptati
SA_T04_bsa016_u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T04_bsa016_u.summary: The Śūnyatāsaptati ('Seventy Verses on Emptiness') is one of the foundational works of the Yukti (reasoning) corpus attributed to Nāgārjuna. In 73 verses (predominantly in anuṣṭubh meter), the text argues that all conditioned and unconditioned dharmas—including the twelve links of dependent origination, time, the agent and object of action, and nirvāṇa itself—are empty of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) because they are dependently co-arisen (pratītyasamutpanna). Rather than promoting nihilism, Nāgārjuna explains that establishing ultimate emptiness (śūnyatā / paramārtha) enables the valid and unhindered operation of conventional transactional reality (laukikavyavahāra).
SA_T04_bsa016_u.attribution: The original Sanskrit text of Nāgārjuna's Śūnyatāsaptati survives completely only in Tibetan translation (Toh 3827 / D 3827, P 5227). The Sanskrit text in this e-text is an artificial modern reconstruction (punaruddhāra) made from the Tibetan by Ācārya Sempa Dorje (published 1985).
SA_T04_bsa016_u.edition: Acarya Sempa Dorje: Sunyata Saptati. Sarnath: Central Institute of High Tibetan Studies (CIHTS), 1985
SA_T04_bsa016_u.coverage: complete — Contains all 73 kārikās in modern Sanskrit reconstruction. Although the source volume includes both the kārikās and the autocommentary (Śūnyatāsaptativṛtti, Toh 3831) — and the e-text retains the heading fragment 'svopajñavṛttyā samanvitā' and the commentary colophon 'śūnyatāsaptatervṛttiḥ ācāryanāgārjunapādakṛtā samāptā' — only the 73 verse kārikās were input, omitting the prose vṛtti.

SA_T04_bsa021_u.title: Vigrahavyāvartanī (kārikās only)
SA_T04_bsa021_u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T04_bsa021_u.summary: The Vigrahavyāvartanī is a philosophical work by Nāgārjuna defending the doctrine of emptiness (śūnyatā). In the first portion (verses 1–20), objections are raised concerning the validity of refuting intrinsic reality (svabhāva), pramāṇas, and words if all things are empty. In the response, Nāgārjuna replies using examples such as an illusory person (nirmitaka / māyāpuruṣa), addresses pramāṇas, and famously clarifies his stance regarding having no thesis (pratijñā), concluding with verses of adoration to the Buddha who taught emptiness and dependent arising (pratītyasamutpāda).
SA_T04_bsa021_u.edition: P.L. Vaidya: Madhyamaka shastra. Darbhanga: Mithila Institute, 1960, pp. 277-295. (Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, 10).

SA_T04_bsa024_u.title: Satyadvayāvatāra
SA_T04_bsa024_u.author: Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna
SA_T04_bsa024_u.summary: The Satyadvayāvatāra ('Entry into the Two Truths') is a 30-verse treatise composed by Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna in Suvarṇadvīpa at the request of the monk Devamati on behalf of the King of Suvarṇadvīpa. It presents a perspective on the two truths, discussing conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya) and ultimate reality (paramārthasatya).
SA_T04_bsa024_u.attribution: Composed by Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna in Suvarṇadvīpa at the request of the bhikṣu Devamati on behalf of the King of Suvarṇadvīpa.
SA_T04_bsa024_u.edition: Sonam Rabten: Satyadvayavataradigrantha catustayam. Sarnath: Central Institute of High Tibetan Studies (CIHTS), 2000, pp. 91-94.

SA_T04_bsa027_u.title: Madhyamakaśāstra
SA_T04_bsa027_u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T04_bsa027_u.summary: The Madhyamakaśāstra (widely known as Mūlamadhyamakakārikā) is Nāgārjuna's foundational philosophical treatise and the central text of the Madhyamaka school of Mahāyāna Buddhism. Comprising twenty-seven chapters, it systematically analyzes causation, motion, sense faculties, the aggregates, selfhood, and nirvāṇa, demonstrating that no entity possesses independent intrinsic nature (svabhāva) and equating dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) directly with emptiness (śūnyatā).
SA_T04_bsa027_u.attribution: Attributed to the Buddhist author Nāgārjuna (posterior median 205 CE, credible interval 147–264 CE).
SA_T04_bsa027_u.edition: P. L. Vaidya (ed.), Madhyamakaśāstra of Nāgārjuna, Darbhanga: Mithila Institute, 1960 (Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, 10).

SA_T04_bsa028_u.title: Catuḥśatikā (selected verses)
SA_T04_bsa028_u.author: Āryadeva
SA_T04_bsa028_u.summary: The Catuḥśatikā ('Four Hundred Verses') is a Madhyamaka treatise by Āryadeva. This electronic text contains 21 verses from chapters 1–5 preserved in Sanskrit citations, corresponding to pp. 159–160 of Bhagchandra Jain's 1971 edition.

SA_T04_bsa035_u.title: Bodhisattvādikarmikamārgāvatāradeśanā
SA_T04_bsa035_u.author: Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna
SA_T04_bsa035_u.summary: The Bodhisattvādikarmikamārgāvatāradeśanā is a practical liturgical and behavioral handbook by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna outlining the progressive spiritual discipline required of a beginner bodhisattva (ādikarmika). It provides step-by-step guidance on relying on a qualified spiritual teacher (kalyāṇamitra), taking refuge, generating bodhicitta, and performing worship and confession. It instructs the practitioner on cultivating calm abiding (śamatha) and special insight (vipaśyanā) according to the nine limbs set forth in Bodhibhadra's Samādhisambhāraparivarta, maintaining mindfulness of all phenomena as illusion-like (māyopama) in post-meditation, and promptly purifying ethical infractions.
SA_T04_bsa035_u.attribution: Attributed to Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna (Mar-me-mdzad ye-shes) and translated into Tibetan by Atiśa together with Tshul-khrims rgyal-ba (Jayaśīla).
SA_T04_bsa035_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the work, consisting of the introductory homage, prose instructions interspersed with mnemonic/liturgical verses, concluding dedication stanzas, and translation colophon.
translations: Richard Sherburne, The Complete Works of Atīśa Śrī Dīpaṃkara, 2000. (English)

SA_T04_bsa036_u.title: Śaraṇagamanadeśanā
SA_T04_bsa036_u.author: Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna
SA_T04_bsa036_u.summary: The Śaraṇagamanadeśanā is a short instructional work on the practice and significance of going for refuge (śaraṇagamana) to the Three Jewels, composed by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna. The text structures the doctrine around fifteen headings: the foundation (adhiṣṭhāna), the twofold Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna states (sthiti), intentional disposition (āśaya), duration (avadhi), essence (svabhāva), standard measure (māna), method (naya), rules/precepts (śikṣā), etymological meaning (nirukti), functional role (kāritra), analogies (upamya), classification (bheda), faults of transgression (ādīnava), doctrinal meaning (artha), and twofold temporal benefits (anuśaṃsā).
SA_T04_bsa036_u.attribution: Attributed in the colophon to Guru Bodhisattva Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna.
SA_T04_bsa036_u.coverage: complete — Complete short treatise consisting of an introductory maṅgala verse, a summary verse setting out fifteen pedagogical topics (pañcadaśa vibhaktayaḥ) of refuge, interspersed prose explanations with illustrative verses (verses 3–9), and the author colophon.

SA_T04_bsa037_u.title: Mahāyānapathasādhanasaṅgraha
SA_T04_bsa037_u.author: Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna
SA_T04_bsa037_u.summary: The Mahāyānapathasādhanasaṅgraha (colophon title: Atisaṃkṣiptamahāyānapathasādhana) is a short 10-verse instructional manual outlining the bodhisattva path attributed to Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna. It condenses core Mahāyāna practice: taking refuge, abandoning non-virtue, adhering to pure ethical discipline (adhiśīla) as the vehicle of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta), mindfulness of death, adopting the bodhisattva vows and the six perfections, and the non-abiding nirvāṇa attained through the union of wisdom and means (prajñopāya).
SA_T04_bsa037_u.attribution: Attributed in the colophon to Mahācārya Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna (Atiśa). The colophon also records that it was translated by him together with the translator Bhikṣu Kalyāṇamati (dge ba'i blo gros).
SA_T04_bsa037_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of 10 verses (9 full anuṣṭubh verses and verse 10ab) with the closing colophon.

SA_T04_bsa038_u.title: Sūtrārthasamuccayopadeśa
SA_T04_bsa038_u.author: Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna
SA_T04_bsa038_u.summary: A short instructional digest listing fifty "jewel-like" qualities and practices of a bodhisattva, each introduced by a simile: bodhicitta like the life-breath, emptiness and compassion like mother and father, the perfections like kinsfolk. It ends with admonitions to avoid the deluded, seek a true teacher and study the sūtras. Because the original Sanskrit is lost, this e-text is modern Sanskrit restoration from the Tibetan.
SA_T04_bsa038_u.attribution: By Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna. The original Sanskrit does not survive; the work is extant in Tibetan translation (D 3957, D 4482), translated by Atiśa with Tshul khrims rgyal ba. The Sanskrit text here is modern restoration from the Tibetan; the closing segs. 153–154 are a Sanskritized rendering of the Tibetan translator colophon, keeping the Tibetan name "(chul khrimas rgyal va)".
SA_T04_bsa038_u.coverage: complete — Complete with respect to the Tibetan translation from which it was restored: opening verse, the fifty jewel-like dharmas of the bodhisattva, concluding admonitions, author colophon and the Sanskritized translator colophon.
translations: Richard Sherburne, The Complete Works of Atīśa Śrī Dīpaṃkara. 2000. (English)

SA_T04_bsa039_u.title: Daśākuśalakarmapathadeśanā
SA_T04_bsa039_u.author: Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna
SA_T04_bsa039_u.summary: The Daśākuśalakarmapathadeśanā is a concise ethical treatise setting forth the ten unwholesome paths of action (daśākuśalakarmapatha): three bodily, four verbal, and three mental. Each transgression is analyzed according to its constituent criteria and conditions, citing the Saddharmasmṛtyupasthānasūtra. Attributed to Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna and preserved in the Tibetan Tengyur (D 3958).
SA_T04_bsa039_u.attribution: Attributed in the colophon and Tibetan Tengyur (D 3958, D 4483) to Mahācārya Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna (Atiśa) and translated into Tibetan by Atiśa and Nag tsho Tshul khrims rgyal ba (Bhikṣu Jayaśīla). A related text is transmitted in the Tengyur under the name of Aśvaghoṣa (D 4178) and translated into Chinese in the Song dynasty as T 727.

SA_T04_bsa040_u.title: Cittotpādasaṃvaravidhikrama
SA_T04_bsa040_u.author: Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna
SA_T04_bsa040_u.summary: The Cittotpādasaṃvaravidhikrama is a liturgical manual composed by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna setting forth the rite and sequence for arousing bodhicitta and receiving the bodhisattva vows and discipline.
SA_T04_bsa040_u.attribution: Attributed to Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna. Preserved in Tibetan translation in the Tengyur (Toh 3969 / Toh 4490).
SA_T04_bsa040_u.coverage: complete — Text contains opening salutation, introductory verses, liturgical prose directions, and colophon.

SA_T04_bsa041_u.title: Āpattideśanāvidhi
SA_T04_bsa041_u.author: Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna
SA_T04_bsa041_u.summary: The Āpattideśanāvidhi is a concise liturgical manual attributed to Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna formulating the ritual confession and disclosure (deśanā) of downfalls and ethical lapses (āpatti). The officiant/practitioner declares and repudiates ten unwholesome deeds, the five immediate retributions (ānantarya) and their parallels, and violations of prātimokṣa vows, bodhisattva trainings, and tantric pledges (samaya) before the gurus, buddhas, bodhisattvas, and sangha.
SA_T04_bsa041_u.attribution: Ascribed in the Tibetan Tanjur to Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna and translated into Tibetan by Atiśa and Nag tsho Tshul khrims rgyal ba (Jayaśīla).

SA_T04_bsa042_u.title: Gurukriyākrama
SA_T04_bsa042_u.author: Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna
SA_T04_bsa042_u.summary: The Gurukriyākrama (also called Saṃkṣiptagurukriyākrama) is a brief manual detailing the liturgical and instructional sequence (krama) to be followed by a spiritual master (ācārya / guru) when guiding a disciple in the generation of bodhicitta and the Mahāyāna path. It covers inspiring faith and enthusiasm in the disciple, making offerings and performing the preliminary sevenfold worship (saptāṅgapūjā), arousing relative and ultimate bodhicitta, and conferring instruction on the perfections (pāramitā), means of gathering disciples (saṃgrahavastu), immeasurables (apramāṇa), and the threefold training.
SA_T04_bsa042_u.attribution: Attributed to Mahāpaṇḍitācārya Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna (Atiśa) in the concluding colophon and in Tibetan canonical collections (Tōh. 3977, 4489; Peking/Otani no. 5374, 5402), as well as cited under this title by Tsongkhapa in the Lam rim chen mo.
SA_T04_bsa042_u.coverage: complete — Short treatise including salutation and concluding colophon.

SA_T04_bsa053_u.title: Madhyamakāvatārakārikā with Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya (chapters 1–5)
SA_T04_bsa053_u.author: Candrakīrti
SA_T04_bsa053_u.summary: The Madhyamakāvatāra ('Introduction to the Middle Way') along with its autocommentary (Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya) is Candrakīrti's exposition of the Madhyamaka school. Structured around the bodhisattva stages (bhūmis) and their associated perfections (pāramitās), this e-text covers chapters 1 through 5, dealing respectively with the perfections of generosity (dāna), morality (śīla), patience (kṣānti), vigor (vīrya), and meditative absorption (dhyāna).
SA_T04_bsa053_u.attribution: Candrakīrti composed both the root verses (Madhyamakāvatārakārikā) and the autocommentary (Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya).

SA_T04_bsa054_u.title: Bodhicaryāvatāra with Bodhicaryāvatārapañjikā
SA_T04_bsa054_u.author: Śāntideva, Prajñākaramati
SA_T04_bsa054_u.summary: Śāntideva's Bodhicaryāvatāra is a Mahāyāna Buddhist treatise detailing the development and practice of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta). Prajñākaramati's Bodhicaryāvatārapañjikā is a Sanskrit commentary offering running glosses, citations, and Madhyamaka exegesis across chapters 1 through 9. Its commentary on chapter 9 (Prajñāpariccheda) treats key Madhyamaka philosophy.
SA_T04_bsa054_u.attribution: The root verses are composed by Śāntideva. The commentary (pañjikā) is composed by Prajñākaramati. Prajñākaramati's commentary covers chapters 1 through 9; chapter 10 (Pariṇāmanāpariccheda) contains only the root text of Śāntideva, as his commentary does not have the tenth chapter.
SA_T04_bsa054_u.edition: P.L. Vaidya: Bodhicaryāvatāra of Śāntideva with the Commentary Pañjika of Prajñākaramati. Darbhanga: Mithila Institute, 1960. (Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, 12).
SA_T04_bsa054_u.coverage: complete — Contains the complete ten chapters of Śāntideva's Bodhicaryāvatāra (concluding at verse 10.58) and the complete extant nine chapters of Prajñākaramati's Bodhicaryāvatārapañjikā (chapters 1–9).

SA_T04_bsa058_u.title: Bhavasaṅkrāntiṭīkā
SA_T04_bsa058_u.author: Maitreyanātha
SA_T04_bsa058_u.summary: The Bhavasaṅkrāntiṭīkā is an exegetical treatise attributed to Maitreyanātha that comments upon Nāgārjuna's Bhavasaṅkrāntiśāstra. It explains how rebirth and transmigration through existences occur across cyclic existence without an enduring self or substantial entity, reconciling karmic continuity with the Mahāyāna doctrine of emptiness and the two truths (saṃvṛti and paramārtha).
SA_T04_bsa058_u.attribution: The commentary is traditionally attributed in the Tibetan Tengyur (Toh 3841) to Paṇḍita Maitreyanātha (Tib. Byams-pa mgon-po), commenting on the Bhavasaṅkrāntiśāstra attributed to Nāgārjuna.

SA_T04_bsu060_u.title: Karmavibhaṅgopadeśa
SA_T04_bsu060_u.summary: The Karmavibhaṅgopadeśa is an anonymous Buddhist exegetical treatise (upadeśa) preserved in a single 15th-century Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript (dated Nepāla Saṃvat 531 / 1410 CE). Serving as an exposition and commentary to the Mahākarmavibhaṅga, it examines the mechanics of karma and karmic fruition (vipāka). The text defends and elucidates key doctrinal positions—such as why making offerings to a stūpa after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa remains profoundly meritorious despite the absence of an embodied recipient—by citing canonical Āgama/Nikāya, Abhidharma, and avadāna parallels.
SA_T04_bsu060_u.attribution: Anonymous Buddhist exegetical treatise (upadeśa) elaborating and commenting upon the Karmavibhaṅga / Mahākarmavibhaṅga tradition.

SA_T04_canprasu1.title: Prasannapadā (chapter 1: Pratyayaparīkṣā)
SA_T04_canprasu1.author: Candrakīrti
SA_T04_canprasu1.summary: Chapter 1 (pratyayaparīkṣā, "examination of conditions") of Candrakīrti's Prasannapadā, his commentary on Nāgārjuna's Mūlamadhyamakakārikā. Here Candrakīrti defends Buddhapālita's prasaṅga method against Bhāviveka's demand for independent inferences (svatantrānumāna), and criticizes Dignāga's epistemology. It refutes arising from self, other, both or neither and examines the four conditions. The chapter later became the locus classicus of the Prāsaṅgika–Svātantrika distinction.
SA_T04_canprasu1.attribution: Candrakīrti is the author of the Prasannapadā (Madhyamakaśāstravṛtti), a commentary on Nāgārjuna's Mūlamadhyamakakārikā.
