SA_T04_canprasu.title: Madhyamakaśāstra with Prasannapadā
SA_T04_canprasu.author: Nāgārjuna, Candrakīrti
SA_T04_canprasu.summary: Candrakīrti's Prasannapadā ('Clear Words'), also titled Madhyamakaśāstravṛtti, is a 7th-century CE Sanskrit prose commentary on the 27 chapters of Nāgārjuna's fundamental Madhyamakaśāstra (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā). It is the only fully surviving Indian commentary on Nāgārjuna's root verses preserved in Sanskrit. Candrakīrti defines the Prāsaṅgika-Madhyamaka approach by defending Buddhapālita's method of reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) against Bhāvaviveka's use of autonomous inference (svatantra), making the work an essential foundation for the study of Indian and Tibetan Madhyamaka philosophy.
SA_T04_canprasu.attribution: The root verses of the Madhyamakaśāstra (commonly known as Mūlamadhyamakakārikā) are composed by Nāgārjuna (c. 150–250 CE). The commentary Prasannapadā ('Clear Words', also known as Madhyamakavṛtti) is by Candrakīrti (c. 600–650 CE). The Tibetan translation (D 3860) attributes the work to Candrakīrti I (zla ba grags pa).
SA_T04_canprasu.edition: P. L. Vaidya (ed.), Madhyamakaśāstra of Nāgārjuna, with the Commentary: Prasannapadā by Candrakīrti. Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute of Post-Graduate Studies and Research in Sanskrit Learning, 1960 (Buddhist Sanskrit Texts, 10).
SA_T04_canprasu.coverage: complete — Complete in all 27 chapters (prakaraṇas), running from Chapter 1 (Pratyayaparīkṣā) to Chapter 27 (Dṛṣṭiparīkṣā), ending with the full final colophons.

SA_T04_ksmadhlu.title: Madhyamakāloka
SA_T04_ksmadhlu.author: Kamalaśīla
SA_T04_ksmadhlu.summary: The Madhyamakāloka ('Illumination of the Middle Way') is Kamalaśīla's independent treatise of Madhyamaka philosophy, defending the lack of intrinsic nature of all phenomena (sarvadharmaniḥsvabhāvatā) and expounding the doctrine of the two truths and the single vehicle (ekayāna).

SA_T04_n1002u.title: Hastavālaprakaraṇa with Hastavālaprakaraṇavṛtti
SA_T04_n1002u.author: Dignāga
SA_T04_n1002u.summary: The Hastavālaprakaraṇa ('Treatise of the Handful' or 'Hand-Grasp') with its autocommentary (vṛtti) consists of six anuṣṭubh verses and prose commentary demonstrating the lack of inherent existence (svabhāva) in both composite macro-objects and partless indivisible atoms (paramāṇu). Employing the classic analogy of the rope mistaken for a snake and mereological part-whole analysis, the treatise shows that external entities are conventional conceptual designations (vyavahāramātra) without ultimate reality. The Indic original having been lost, the text survives in Tibetan and Chinese recensions and is known in Sanskrit through modern reconstructions.
SA_T04_n1002u.attribution: Authorship is divided between the two Asian translation traditions. The Tibetan Tanjur and Dunhuang Tibetan manuscripts ascribe the work to Āryadeva, which was initially discussed by F. W. Thomas and H. Ui (1918). However, the Chinese translations (T 1620, T 1621) explicitly ascribe it to Dignāga (Chenna). The Tibetan translation (D 3844) attributes the work to Āryadeva ('phags pa lha). The Tibetan translation (D 3848) attributes the work to Āryadeva ('phags pa lha).
SA_T04_n1002u.coverage: complete — Contains all 6 kārikās and the full prose vṛtti in modern Sanskrit retroversion from the Tibetan and Chinese versions.
translations: F. W. Thomas and H. Ui, '"The Hand Treatise," a Work of Āryadeva', Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society, 1918, pp. 267 ff. (English)

SA_T04_n1003u.title: Madhyamakahṛdaya
SA_T04_n1003u.author: Bhāvaviveka
SA_T04_n1003u.summary: The Madhyamakahṛdaya ('Heart of the Middle Way') is an independent verse treatise by Bhāvaviveka (c. 500–570 CE). It systematizes the bodhisattva path and Madhyamaka philosophy, examining and refuting rival Śrāvaka, Yogācāra, Sāṃkhya, and Mīmāṃsā doctrines.
SA_T04_n1003u.attribution: Attributed to Bhāvaviveka (Bhavya / Bhāviveka, c. 500–570 CE).

SA_T04_n1047u.title: Madhyamārthasaṃgraha
SA_T04_n1047u.author: Bhāviveka
SA_T04_n1047u.summary: The Madhyamārthasaṃgraha is a concise Madhyamaka treatise in eleven stanzas setting forth the schema of the two truths (satyadvaya). It articulates a distinct hierarchical division of ultimate truth (paramārtha) into expressible/discursive (paryāyaparamārtha) and inexpressible/non-discursive (aparyāyaparamārtha), alongside conventional truth (saṃvṛti) classified into valid conventional reality (tathyasaṃvṛti) and false convention (mithyāsaṃvṛti). It is an influential pedagogical summary of Svātantrika epistemological taxonomy.
SA_T04_n1047u.attribution: Ascribed to Bhāviveka (Bhavya). However, modern scholarship views the authenticity of the attribution as doubtful.
SA_T04_n1047u.edition: N. Aiyaswami Sastri, 'Madhyamārthasaṃgraha of Bhāvaviveka (Restored from the Tibetan Version with an English Translation)', Journal of Oriental Research (Madras), 1931.

SA_T04_n2850u.title: Svabhāvavāda
SA_T04_n2850u.summary: A short anonymous Sanskrit prose tract defending svabhāvavāda (things arise from their own nature without causes) against Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika causal theory (including Īśvara as creator) and against Śaṅkara's explanation of creation as līlā. It closes by quoting verses introduced by 'ata evoktaṃ śāntarakṣitena'.
SA_T04_n2850u.attribution: Anonymous; no author is named in the e-text or in the DSBC catalogue. The work is a short Sanskrit prose tract (with quoted verses) arguing FOR svabhāvavāda/ahetuvāda against Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika causality and against Śaṅkara's līlā explanation of creation; the author speaks in the first person ('atra mayā ucyate') and cites the svabhāvavāda verses with 'ata evoktaṃ śāntarakṣitena'.
SA_T04_n2850u.coverage: complete — Short tract as given by DSBC book 721; ends with quoted svabhāvavāda verses and has no colophon.

SA_T04_n2980u.title: Madhyamakāvatārakārikā (chapter 6)
SA_T04_n2980u.author: Candrakīrti
SA_T04_n2980u.summary: Candrakīrti's Madhyamakāvatāra ('Introduction to the Middle Way'), composed in the 7th century CE, is a foundational Prāsaṅgika Madhyamaka treatise designed to introduce Nāgārjuna's Mūlamadhyamakakārikā along the structure of the Mahāyāna bodhisattva path. Structured around the ten bodhisattva stages (bhūmi), this sixth chapter corresponds to the abhimukhī-bhūmi ('Facing Ground') and the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Chapter 6 comprises the philosophical core and roughly two-thirds of the entire work, expounding the refutation of intrinsic production (the catuṣkoṭi), an extensive critique of Yogācāra positions (such as the reality of consciousness, reflexive awareness, and the ālayavijñāna), the two truths, and the sixteen forms of emptiness.
SA_T04_n2980u.attribution: Candrakīrti composed the Madhyamakāvatārakārikā alongside his autocommentary (Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya).
SA_T04_n2980u.coverage: partial — Chapter 6 only (kārikās 6.1–6.226). The complete work spans 330 metered verses.
translations: C. W. Huntington, The Emptiness of Emptiness: An Introduction to Early Indian Mādhyamika, Honolulu: University of Hawaii Press. (English)

SA_T04_n847u.title: Madhyamakaśāstrastuti
SA_T04_n847u.author: Candrakīrti
SA_T04_n847u.summary: The Madhyamakaśāstrastuti is a 14-verse hymnic eulogy composed by Candrakīrti (c. 7th century CE) in veneration of Nāgārjuna and his Mūlamadhyamakakārikā. Although transmitted independently in collections as a stotra, these verses originally formed the concluding stanzas of Candrakīrti's Prasannapadā. The text is of singular historiographical and doctrinal importance because stanza 10 enumerates eight core treatises authored by Nāgārjuna (including the Sūtrasamuccaya, Ratnāvalī, Yuktiṣaṣṭikā, Śūnyatāsaptati, and Vigrahavyāvartanī), and traces the lineage of Madhyamaka commentary through Buddhapālita down to Candrakīrti.
SA_T04_n847u.attribution: Firmly attributed to Candrakīrti (c. 7th century CE). These 14 verses constitute the concluding praise of his Prasannapadā (Mūlamadhyamakavṛtti), missing from Louis de La Vallée Poussin's edition, but preserved at the conclusion of the Tibetan translation and transmitted as an independent stotra in Sanskrit manuscripts from Nepal and Tibet.
SA_T04_n847u.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994, stotra no. 41.
SA_T04_n847u.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 14 verses with opening rubric and closing colophon.
translations: J. W. de Jong, 'La Madhyamakaśāstrastuti de Candrakīrti', Oriens Extremus 9 (1962), pp. 47–56. (French)
Jeffrey Hopkins, Meditation on Emptiness, London: Wisdom Publications, 1983. (English (partial: vv. 10–11))

SA_T04_n848u.title: Niraupamyastava
SA_T04_n848u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T04_n848u.summary: The Niraupamyastava ('Hymn to the Incomparable One') is a devotional philosophical poem of 25 stanzas in anuṣṭubh metre composed by Nāgārjuna, forming part of his famous Catuḥstava ('Four Hymns'). Composed as an encomium praising the Buddha, the work formulates foundational Madhyamaka themes in a devotional idiom: praising the Tathāgata as having neither originated nor extinguished any dharma, having spoken not a single syllable while yet teaching all disciples, and being empty of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) and conceptual proliferation (vikalpa). The hymn also contains prominent discussions of the two bodies of the Buddha (dharmakāya and janmakāya/rūpakāya) and affirms the ultimate unity of the vehicles (ekayāna) grounded in the non-differentiation of the dharmadhātu.
SA_T04_n848u.attribution: Traditionally regarded as one of the four hymns of Nāgārjuna's Catuḥstava, cited as such by Candrakīrti (Prasannapadā), Prajñākaramati (Bodhicaryāvatārapañjikā), and Amṛtākara (Catuḥstavasamāsārtha). While early modern scholarship debated which four stavas constituted the original quartet, the Niraupamyastava is universally included in the core four, and its authorship by Nāgārjuna is broadly accepted in critical scholarship.
SA_T04_n848u.edition: Chr. Lindtner (ed.), Niraupamyastava, in: Nagarjuniana: Studies in the Writings and Philosophy of Nāgārjuna. Copenhagen: Akademisk Forlag, 1982. (orig. ed. Tucci, JRAS 1932).
SA_T04_n848u.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 25 stanzas with closing colophon (niraupamyastavaḥ samāptaḥ).
translations: Giuseppe Tucci, Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society, 1932, pp. 309–325. (English)

SA_T04_n849u.title: Paramārthastava
SA_T04_n849u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T04_n849u.summary: The Paramārthastava ('Hymn to Ultimate Reality') is a short hymn of eleven verses attributed to Nāgārjuna and canonical as the fourth praise in the Catuḥstava quartet. It articulates Madhyamaka apophasis within devotional verse: because the Buddha is unarisen (anutpanna), unlocated (asthita), and beyond language (vākpathātīta), he cannot be praised in an ultimate sense (paramārtha). Consequently, praise can only take place conditionally via conventional designation (lokaprajñapti), culminating in the realization that in emptiness there is neither praised nor praiser.
SA_T04_n849u.attribution: Attributed to Nāgārjuna (c. 150–250 CE) in the Tibetan Tanjur (Toh 1122) and by Indian commentators such as Amṛtākara (Catuḥstavasamāsārtha). Modern scholarship (Tucci, Lindtner, Tola & Dragonetti) accepts it as a component of the Catuḥstava group.
SA_T04_n849u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 11 anuṣṭubh verses (verses 1–10 apophatic praise of the Buddha, verse 11 pariṇāmanā/dedication of merit), concluding with 'śrī paramārthastavaḥ samāptaḥ'.

SA_T04_nagmmk_u.title: Mūlamadhyamakakārikā
SA_T04_nagmmk_u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T04_nagmmk_u.summary: The Mūlamadhyamakakārikā ('Root Verses on the Middle Way'), comprising 448 verses in 27 chapters, is the foundational philosophical treatise of the Madhyamaka school of Mahāyāna Buddhism composed by Nāgārjuna. Through systematic dialectic, Nāgārjuna deconstructs essentialist claims regarding causality, motion, faculties, aggregates, the self, time, karma, and nirvāṇa, establishing that no entity possesses inherent existence (svabhāva). Identifying dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) with emptiness (śūnyatā) and conventional designation (prajñapti), the work articulates the Middle Way free from the extremes of eternalism and annihilationism.
SA_T04_nagmmk_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 27 chapters comprising 448 kārikās (MMK 1.1–27.30).
translations: Mark Siderits and Shoryu Katsura, Nāgārjuna's Middle Way: Mūlamadhyamakakārikā, Boston: Wisdom Publications, 2013. (English)

SA_T04_nagmyv_u.title: Mahāyānaviṃśikā
SA_T04_nagmyv_u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T04_nagmyv_u.summary: The Mahāyānaviṃśikā ('Twenty Verses on the Great Vehicle') is a brief Buddhist treatise traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna that synthesizes Madhyamaka and Yogācāra doctrines. It argues that external objects lack independent reality and that the world of saṃsāra is an illusory projection arising from conceptual fabrication (kalpanā) upon mind alone (cittamātra). The text concludes by urging practitioners to rely upon the Mahāyāna vehicle as the only means to cross the ocean of delusion.
SA_T04_nagmyv_u.attribution: The colophon attributes the text to Ārya Nāgārjuna ('mahāyānaviṃśikā kṛtirāryanāgārjunapādānāṃ'), as do the Tibetan (D 3833) and Chinese (T 1576, tr. Dānapāla / 施護) canonical records. However, modern scholarship lists Mahāyānaviṃśikā among the works attributed to Nāgārjuna whose authenticity is questioned.
SA_T04_nagmyv_u.edition: G. Tucci (ed.), Minor Buddhist Texts, part I, Roma 1956 (Serie Orientale Roma, 9), pp. 201-203.

SA_T04_nagvigvu.title: Vigrahavyāvartanīkārikā with Vigrahavyāvartanīvṛtti
SA_T04_nagvigvu.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T04_nagvigvu.summary: The Vigrahavyāvartanī is a dialectical treatise by Nāgārjuna consisting of verses accompanied by prose autocommentary (vṛtti), refuting objections against the emptiness of all things (śūnyatā), critiquing pramāṇas, and maintaining that the Madhyamaka asserts no independent proposition (pratijñā).

SA_T04_nagvvy_u.title: Vigrahavyāvartanīkārikā
SA_T04_nagvvy_u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T04_nagvvy_u.summary: The Vigrahavyāvartanīkārikā ('Verses on Turning Back Disputes') is a seminal epistemological treatise by Nāgārjuna defending the Madhyamaka doctrine of universal emptiness (sarvadharmaśūnyatā) against realist objections, notably from the Nyāya school. Verses 1–20 set forth the opponent's paradox: if all things lack intrinsic nature (svabhāva), Nāgārjuna's own statement lacks reality and cannot negate anything, or else valid means of knowing (pramāṇa) must be conceded. Verses 21–71 provide Nāgārjuna's counter-arguments, showing that negation and conceptual discourse function precisely because of dependently originated emptiness, and that pramāṇa and prameya are mutually established rather than inherently real.
SA_T04_nagvvy_u.attribution: Firmly attributed to Nāgārjuna; traditionally ranked among the works of Nāgārjuna's reasoning corpus (rigs tshogs) in Tibetan doxography.
SA_T04_nagvvy_u.coverage: complete — Contains the complete verse core of the text: 70 argumentative stanzas plus the closing mangala / homage stanza (NagVvy_01 to NagVvy_71). Does not include the prose autocommentary (vṛtti).

SA_T04_nagysk_u.title: Yuktiṣaṣṭikakārikā (fragments)
SA_T04_nagysk_u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T04_nagysk_u.summary: The Yuktiṣaṣṭikākārikā ('Sixty Stanzas on Reasoning') is a philosophical treatise by Nāgārjuna (ca. 150–250 CE) that articulates dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) and critiques clinging to existence and non-existence. Although preserved in Tibetan and Chinese translations alongside Candrakīrti's commentary, this e-text contains surviving Sanskrit stanzas preserved as citations, associated with Chr. Lindtner.

SA_T04_nagyuksu.title: Yuktiṣaṣṭikārikā
SA_T04_nagyuksu.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T04_nagyuksu.summary: The Yuktiṣaṣṭikārikā ('Sixty Stanzas on Reasoning') is a Madhyamaka treatise attributed to Nāgārjuna. In sixty verses following an opening homage, the work treats existence (bhāva) and non-existence (abhāva), dependent origination, and nirvāṇa. The continuous Sanskrit original having been lost, the e-text represents B. Kumar's modern Sanskrit reconstruction based on the Tibetan translation.

SA_T04_santbcpu.title: Bodhicaryāvatāra
SA_T04_santbcpu.author: Śāntideva
SA_T04_santbcpu.summary: The Bodhicaryāvatāra ('Entering the Bodhisattva Path') is an 8th-century Sanskrit didactic and philosophical poem by the Madhyamaka master Śāntideva. Arranged in ten chapters, it serves as a practical manual for generating and sustaining the awakening mind (bodhicitta) and cultivating the six bodhisattva perfections (pāramitās). The work is celebrated for its ethical power—notably the exchange of self and other (parātmaparivartana) in chapter 8—and its rigorous philosophical exposition in chapter 9 (Prajñāpariccheda), which defends Madhyamaka emptiness (śūnyatā) against rival Buddhist and non-Buddhist metaphysical positions.
SA_T04_santbcpu.coverage: complete — Complete root text in 10 chapters (paricchedas 1–10; ending with verse 10.58 and the final colophon 'bodhicaryāvatāre pariṇāmanā paricchedo daśamaḥ').

SA_T04_vasbocpu.title: Bodhicittotpādasūtraśāstra
SA_T04_vasbocpu.author: Vasubandhu
SA_T04_vasbocpu.summary: The Bodhicittotpādasūtraśāstra is a Mahāyāna treatise expounding the generation of the resolve for awakening (bodhicitta), the bodhisattva vow, and the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā). It corresponds to Chinese canon text T. 1659 attributed to Vasubandhu and translated by Kumārajīva.
SA_T04_vasbocpu.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Vasubandhu (天親菩薩造) and translated into Chinese by Kumārajīva (鳩摩羅什, dated 402–412 CE; Taishō no. 1659).
SA_T04_vasbocpu.coverage: complete — Runs from chapter 1 (adhyeṣaṇotpādaḥ) to chapter 12 (puṇyaparigrahaḥ), concluding with 'pariniṣṭhitaṃ bodhicittotpādasūtraśāstram'.

SA_T05_bsa062_u.title: Śālistambakakārikā
SA_T05_bsa062_u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T05_bsa062_u.summary: A 70-verse metrical treatise summarizing the teachings of the Śālistambasūtra. Using the botanical metaphor of a sprouting rice seed, it explains the Mahāyāna doctrine of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) by contrasting external and internal causal sequences, underscoring the absence of an agent (kartṛ) or enduring self (ātman). Represented in the e-text by Sonam Rabten's edition/restoration.
SA_T05_bsa062_u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna in the Tibetan Tengyur (Degé Toh 3985; Peking 5485) and the colophon.
SA_T05_bsa062_u.edition: Sonam Rabten (ed. & reconstructor), Ācāryanāgārjunapraṇītā saṭīkā Āryaśālistambakakārikā: Acarya Nagarjuna's Aryasalistambakakarika with the Autocommentary (Bibliotheca Indo-Tibetica Series), Sarnath, Varanasi: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies (CIHTS), 2004, pp. 255–261.
SA_T05_bsa062_u.coverage: complete — Complete 70 kārikās (vv. 1–70) along with opening maṅgala and translated colophons.
translations: Jeffrey D. Schoening, The Śālistamba Sūtra and its Indian Commentaries, 2 vols., Vienna, 1995. (English)
phags pa sA lu ljang pa'i tshig le'ur byas pa (Derge Tengyur D 3985) (Tibetan)

SA_T05_bsu027_u.title: Pratītyasamutpādādivibhaṅganirdeśasūtra
SA_T05_bsu027_u.summary: The Pratītyasamutpādādivibhaṅganirdeśasūtra is a canonical Buddhist discourse delivered by the Buddha at Jetavana in Śrāvastī. It is divided into two parts: the 'fundamental exposition' (ādi), which articulates the standard twelvefold formula of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) from ignorance (avidyā) to aging and death (jarāmaraṇa), and the 'detailed analysis' (vibhaṅga), which provides concise definitions of each link.
SA_T05_bsu027_u.attribution: Canonical Buddhist discourse traditionally attributed to Gautama Buddha preaching to monks at Jetavana in Śrāvastī. Vasubandhu composed a commentary on it, the Pratītyasamutpādavyākhyā.
SA_T05_bsu027_u.edition: P. L. Vaidya (ed.), Mahāyāna-sūtra-saṃgraha, Part 1, Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute of Post-Graduate Studies and Research in Sanskrit Learning, 1961 (Buddhist Sanskrit Texts).
SA_T05_bsu027_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the short sūtra (pp. 117–118 in Vaidya's edition), containing both the opening exposition of the twelve links (ādi) and their detailed analysis (vibhaṅga), concluding with the monks' rejoicing and the final colophon.
translations: Pratītyasamutpādādivibhaṅganirdeśasūtram: The Discourse giving the Explanation and Analysis of Conditional Origination from the Beginning, Ancient Buddhist Texts. (English)

SA_T05_n1110u.title: Bodhyāpattideśanāvṛtti
SA_T05_n1110u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T05_n1110u.summary: The Bodhyāpattideśanāvṛtti is a commentary on the Bodhyāpattideśanā (also referenced in relation to the Triskandhasūtra / Ratnakūṭa), traditionally ascribed to Nāgārjuna. It comments on the purification of bodhisattva transgressions and discusses the confession Buddhas and dedication of merit.
SA_T05_n1110u.attribution: Ascribed to Nāgārjuna in the Tibetan Tanjur colophon and translated into Tibetan by Śāntarakṣita and Rñe-ba Devaghoṣa (Rnyi Devaghoṣa).
SA_T05_n1110u.coverage: complete — Complete commentary, concluding with summary verses (numbered through 142), the author's colophon, and the translation colophon.
translations: byang chub kyi ltung ba bshags pa'i 'grel pa (Derge Tengyur D 4005): translated by Śāntirakṣita, rnyi ba de ba g+ho Sha (Tibetan)

SA_T05_nagsaliu.title: Śālistambakamahāyānasūtraṭīkā
SA_T05_nagsaliu.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T05_nagsaliu.summary: The Śālistambakamahāyānasūtraṭīkā (also known as Śālistambakavistarākhyāṭīkā) is an extensive commentary on the Śālistambasūtra, elucidating the core Buddhist doctrine of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) through outer and inner causal frameworks. Canonical Tibetan tradition ascribes the work to Nāgārjuna. The present e-text consists of a modern Sanskrit restoration (punaruddhāra) prepared by Dr. Sonam Rabten.
SA_T05_nagsaliu.attribution: Canonically attributed to Nāgārjuna in the Tibetan Tengyur (D 3986), where it is associated with the Śālistambakakārikā (D 3985). The Sanskrit text preserved in this e-text is a modern restoration made from the Tibetan by Dr. Sonam Rabten in 2004.
SA_T05_nagsaliu.edition: Sonam Rabten (restored, ed.), Ācārya Nāgārjuna's Āryaśālistambakakārikā with the Autocommentary, Bibliotheca Indo-Tibetica Series, Sarnath, Varanasi: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 2004.
SA_T05_nagsaliu.coverage: complete — Complete Sanskrit restoration of the commentary, ending with the concluding stanzas and colophon naming translators Dharmaśrībhadra, Sādhumati, Jñānakumāra, and reviser Śrīkuṭīra.
translations: phags pa sA lu ljang pa'i tshig le'ur byas pa (Derge Tengyur D 3985) (Tibetan)

phags pa sA lu ljang pa zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo'i rgya cher bshad pa (Derge Tengyur D 3986): translated by Dharmaśrīprabha, gnyags lo tsA ba ye shes gzhon nu, legs pa'i blo gros; revised by ska ba dpal brtsegs (Tibetan)

SA_T06_abhsubhu.title: Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya
SA_T06_abhsubhu.author: Jinaputra
SA_T06_abhsubhu.summary: The Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya is a Yogācāra prose commentary on Asaṅga's Abhidharmasamuccaya. It provides analytical glosses on aggregates (skandha) and other Abhidharma categories, concluding with the Sāṃkathyaviniścaya. It is traditionally attributed in the Tibetan tradition to Jinaputra.
SA_T06_abhsubhu.attribution: The Tibetan Tanjur (D 4053) attributes the Bhāṣya to Jinaputra (Rgyal-ba'i sras). The text ends with a scribal colophon noting paṇḍita-vaidya-śrī-Amaracandra.
SA_T06_abhsubhu.edition: N. Tatia (ed.), Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣyam, Tibetan Sanskrit Works Series, 17, Patna: K.P. Jayaswal Research Institute, 1976.
SA_T06_abhsubhu.coverage: complete — Text of the Bhāṣya as published in Tatia's 1976 edition, concluding with the fifth chapter (Sāṃkathyaviniścaya) and the colophon mentioning paṇḍita-vaidya-śrī-Amaracandra.
translations: chos mngon pa kun las btus pa'i bshad pa (Derge Tengyur D 4053): translated by Jinamitra, Śīlendrabodhi, sna nam btsun pa ye shes sde (Tibetan)

SA_T06_asmahsbu.title: Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra with Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkārabhāṣya
SA_T06_asmahsbu.author: Maitreya, Vasubandhu
SA_T06_asmahsbu.summary: The Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra ('Ornament of the Mahāyāna Sūtras') is a foundational treatise of the Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda tradition, consisting of approximately 800 verse kārikās across 21 chapters accompanied by Vasubandhu's prose commentary (bhāṣya). It establishes the scriptural validity of the Mahāyāna and provides an extensive exposition of the bodhisattva path, synthesizing emptiness with classical Yogācāra tenets including the three natures (trisvabhāva), consciousness-only (vijñaptimātratā), and the transformation of the basis (āśrayaparivṛtti). Topics range from lineage (gotra) and the generation of bodhicitta to the perfections (pāramitā), bodhisattva stages (bhūmi), and the resultant bodies of a Buddha (trikāya).
SA_T06_asmahsbu.attribution: In the Indo-Tibetan tradition, the root kārikās are attributed to Maitreya revealing the text to Asaṅga, counting as one of the 'Five Treatises of Maitreya' (byams chos sde lnga), with the prose bhāṣya attributed to Vasubandhu. In the East Asian tradition and among some modern scholars, the text is frequently attributed directly to Asaṅga.
SA_T06_asmahsbu.edition: Sylvain Lévi, ed., Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra: Exposé de la doctrine du Grand Véhicule, vol. I, Paris 1907.
SA_T06_asmahsbu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 21 adhikāras with continuous prose bhāṣya, ending at chapter 21 (Caryāpratiṣṭhādhikāra, segment 5836).
translations: Sylvain Lévi, trans., Mahāyānasūtrālamkāra, 2 vols. (Sanskrit text and French translation), Paris, 1907, 1911. (French)
mdo sde'i rgyan gyi bshad pa (Derge Tengyur D 4026): translated by Śākyasiṃha, ska ba dpal brtsegs (Tibetan)

SA_T06_asycsaru.title: Śarīrārthagāthā
SA_T06_asycsaru.author: Asaṅga
SA_T06_asycsaru.summary: The Śarīrārthagāthā is a collection of 41 canonical and paracanonical verse groups embedded in the Cintāmayībhūmi, part of the Yogācārabhūmi. The stanzas derive from Āgama texts and the Udānavarga, treating fundamental Buddhist themes such as mindfulness, vigilance, and liberation from craving. In the Yogācārabhūmi, these received early verses are systematically gathered to provide the basis for commentary.
SA_T06_asycsaru.attribution: The verses are canonical and paracanonical stanzas anthologized in the Cintāmayībhūmi of the Yogācārabhūmi. The overarching Yogācārabhūmi is catalogued under and traditionally attributed to Asaṅga (or Maitreya).
SA_T06_asycsaru.edition: Fumio Enomoto, 'Śarīrārthagāthā, A Collection of Canonical Verses in the Yogācārabhūmi, Part 1: Text', in Sanskrit-Texte aus dem buddhistischen Kanon: Neuentdeckungen und Neueditionen[, Erste Folge], ed. Heinz Bechert, Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 1989 (Sanskrit-Wörterbuch der buddhistischen Texte aus den Turfan-Funden, Beiheft 2), pp. 17–35.
SA_T06_asycsaru.coverage: complete — Complete for the verse text of the anthology (Śag 1.1–41.1) as critically edited by Fumio Enomoto; does not contain the prose commentary found in the Cintāmayībhūmi.

SA_T06_bsa010_u.title: Madhyāntavibhāgakārikā
SA_T06_bsa010_u.author: Maitreya
SA_T06_bsa010_u.summary: The Madhyāntavibhāgakārikā ('Verses Distinguishing the Middle from the Extremes') is a foundational doctrinal treatise of the Yogācāra school, traditionally counted as one of the 'Five Treatises of Maitreya'. In 111 verses across five chapters—on characteristics (lakṣaṇa), obscurations (āvaraṇa), reality (tattva), spiritual cultivation and results (pratipakṣabhāvanā-avasthā-phala), and the supreme vehicle (yānānuttarya)—it formulates the middle way (madhyamā pratipad) as avoiding both the extreme of reification and that of nihilistic denial. The treatise provides classical expositions of unreal mental construct (abhūtaparikalpa), the three natures (trisvabhāva), and emptiness (śūnyatā) understood as the absence of subject-object duality within that construct.
SA_T06_bsa010_u.attribution: In the Tibetan tradition, the root kārikās are attributed to Maitreya as one of the Five Treatises of Maitreya revealed to Asaṅga. In the Chinese canon (T 1601), the verses are attributed to Maitreya (彌勒菩薩說) and translated by Xuanzang.
SA_T06_bsa010_u.edition: Ramchandra Pandeya, ed., Madhyantavibhagashastram. Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1971.
SA_T06_bsa010_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the root verses across all five chapters: 1. Lakṣaṇapariccheda (vv. 1.1–1.23), 2. Āvaraṇapariccheda (vv. 2.1–2.17), 3. Tattvapariccheda (vv. 3.1–3.22), 4. Pratipakṣabhāvanāvasthāphalapariccheda (vv. 4.1–4.18), and 5. Yānānuttaryapariccheda (vv. 5.1–5.31), ending with the concluding verse and colophon (totaling 111 kārikās).
translations: Theodore Stcherbatsky, Madhyānta-Vibhaṅga: Discourse on Discrimination between Middle and Extremes, Ascribed to Bodhisattva Maitreya and Commented by Vasubandhu and Sthiramati. Bibliotheca Buddhica 30. Moscow / Leningrad: Academy of Sciences of the USSR, 1936. (English)
Stefan Anacker, Seven Works of Vasubandhu. Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1984. (English)
dbus dang mtha' rnam par 'byed pa'i tshig le'ur byas pa (Derge Tengyur D 4021): translated by Jinamitra, Śīlendrabodhi, sna nam btsun pa ye shes sde (Tibetan)

SA_T06_bsa017_u.title: Tattvaratnāvaloka
SA_T06_bsa017_u.author: Vāgīśvarakīrti
SA_T06_bsa017_u.summary: The Tattvaratnāvaloka is a concise 20-verse tantric philosophical treatise by Vāgīśvarakīrti. The work surveys and critiques diverse definitions of the spiritual goal (sādhya) and ultimate reality (tattva)—contrasting non-Buddhist views and standard Pāramitāyāna models with multiple Mantrayāna interpretations—and culminates in an exposition of the fourth initiation (caturthābhiṣeka / caturthaseka).
SA_T06_bsa017_u.attribution: Attributed in the colophon to paṇḍita Vāgīśvarakīrti (kṛtiriyaṃ paṇḍitavāgīśvarakīrtipādānām).
SA_T06_bsa017_u.edition: Janardan Pandey: Tattvaratnavaloka. Sarnath: Central Institute of High Tibetan Studies (CIHTS), 1997.
SA_T06_bsa017_u.coverage: complete — Complete root text consisting of 20 kārikās with opening maṅgala and final colophon. Does not include Vāgīśvarakīrti's prose autocommentary (Tattvaratnāvalokavivaraṇa).
translations: de kho na nyid rin po che snang ba (Derge Tengyur D 1889): translated by 'gos lo tsA ba khug pa lhas btsas (Tibetan)

SA_T06_trimsikatika.title: Triṃśikāṭīkā (fragment)
SA_T06_trimsikatika.author: Vinītadeva
SA_T06_trimsikatika.summary: The Triṃśikāṭīkā by Vinītadeva is an Indian Yogācāra sub-commentary that provides a detailed gloss on Sthiramati's Triṃśikāvijñaptibhāṣya, which comments upon Vasubandhu's Triṃśikāvijñaptikārikā. While preserved in Tibetan translation, the Sanskrit text is attested only in fragments covering kārikās 4cd through 30.
SA_T06_trimsikatika.attribution: A sub-commentary (ṭīkā) by Vinītadeva commenting on Sthiramati's Triṃśikāvijñaptibhāṣya, which expounds Vasubandhu's Triṃśikā. The Sanskrit survives in fragments.
SA_T06_trimsikatika.edition: P. S. Jaini, 'The Sanskrit Fragments of Vinītadeva's Triṃśikā-ṭīkā', Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies (BSOAS) (1985), pp. 470–492.
SA_T06_trimsikatika.coverage: fragment — Surviving Sanskrit portion covering the sub-commentary on Triṃśikā kārikās 4cd through 30, with internal lacunae. Kārikās 1–4 are reproduced at the beginning without commentary.

SA_T06_bsa019_u.title: Trisvabhāvanirdeśa
SA_T06_bsa019_u.author: Vasubandhu
SA_T06_bsa019_u.summary: The Trisvabhāvanirdeśa ('Exposition of the Three Natures') is a concise verse work of 38 kārikās by Vasubandhu presenting the classical Yogācāra doctrine of the three natures: the imagined (kalpita), dependent (paratantra), and consummate (pariniṣpanna). Using the simile of a magician conjuring an elephant from a piece of wood, Vasubandhu demonstrates how subject-object duality is an unreal mental construction upon causally dependent mental processes, and how liberation entails the cessation of this duality and the realization of non-dual reality (dharmadhātu).
SA_T06_bsa019_u.attribution: Attributed to Vasubandhu in the Sanskrit text and Tanjur D 4058. In Tibetan tradition, D 3843 is attributed to Nāgārjuna (Klu-sgrub). The Tibetan translation (D 3843) attributes the work to Nāgārjuna ('phags pa klu sgrub).
SA_T06_bsa019_u.edition: Stephen Anacker: Trisvabhavanirdesh. Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1986.
SA_T06_bsa019_u.coverage: complete — Contains the complete text of all 38 kārikās along with the opening maṅgala and closing colophon.
translations: Louis de La Vallée Poussin, translation into French of the Tibetan text of Trisvabhāvanirdeśa. (French)
Sujitkumar Mukhopadhyaya, The Trisvabhāvanirdeśa of Vasubandhu. Calcutta: Visva-Bharati, 1939. (English)
Stefan Anacker, Seven Works of Vasubandhu. Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1984. (English)

SA_T06_bsa030_u.title: Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkārakārikā
SA_T06_bsa030_u.author: Maitreya
SA_T06_bsa030_u.summary: The Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra is a foundational Yogācāra verse treatise in 21 chapters; this e-text gives the verses alone, without Vasubandhu's bhāṣya. It treats the word of the Buddha, bodhicitta, practice, and the bodhisattva's qualities. In Tibetan tradition it is attributed to Maitreya.
SA_T06_bsa030_u.attribution: Tibetan tradition: Maitreya (D 4020); Chinese tradition (T 1604) and Bagchi's edition title: Asaṅga. The chapter colophons call the work 'vyavadātasamayamahābodhisatvabhāṣite'. The kārikās were extracted from Bagchi's kārikā+bhāṣya edition.
SA_T06_bsa030_u.edition: S. Bagchi (ed.), Mahayana sutralankara of Asanga with its Svavrtti. Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute, 1970 (karika only).

SA_T06_bsa073_u.title: Ratnagotravibhāga with Ratnagotravibhāgavyākhyā
SA_T06_bsa073_u.author: Maitreya, Asaṅga
SA_T06_bsa073_u.summary: The Ratnagotravibhāga (also cited as the Mahāyānottaratantraśāstra or Uttaratantra) articulates the doctrine of buddha-nature (tathāgatagarbha). Structured around seven 'vajra points' (vajrapada)—Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha, dhātu, bodhi, guṇa, and karman—the text discusses the tathāgatagarbha and dharmakāya.
SA_T06_bsa073_u.attribution: Authorship is historically disputed across Buddhist traditions. The Tibetan tradition attributes the root verses to Maitreya and the prose commentary to Asaṅga. The Chinese tradition attributes the work (T 1611, translated by Ratnamati) to Sāramati.
SA_T06_bsa073_u.edition: E.H. Johnston, repr. in: H.S. Prasad. The Uttaratantra of Maitreya. Delhi 1991.
SA_T06_bsa073_u.coverage: complete — Text contains five chapters (paricchedas 1–5), including both root verses and prose commentary.
translations: Jikido Takasaki, A Study on the Ratnagotravibhāga (Uttaratantra): Being a Treatise on the Tathāgatagarbha Theory of Mahāyāna Buddhism, Rome: Istituto Italiano per il Medio ed Estremo Oriente (Serie Orientale Roma, 33), 1966. (English)
theg pa chen po rgyud bla ma'i bstan bcos rnam par bshad pa (Derge Tengyur D 4025): translated by Sajjana, rngog blo ldan shes rab; at grong khyer dpe med (Tibetan)

SA_T06_n1290u.title: Bāhyārthasiddhikārikā
SA_T06_n1290u.author: Śubhagupta
SA_T06_n1290u.summary: The Bāhyārthasiddhikārikā ('Verses Establishing External Objects') is a philosophical treatise in 188 kārikās by Śubhagupta defending external realism against Buddhist idealism.
SA_T06_n1290u.attribution: Authored by Śubhagupta. The continuous original Sanskrit text survives mainly in Tibetan translation (Toh 4244, translated by Jinamitra and dPal brtsegs rakṣita) and fragments/reconstructions.
translations: phyi rol gyi don grub pa zhes bya ba'i tshig le'ur byas pa (Derge Tengyur D 4244): translated by Jinamitra, ska ba dpal brtsegs (Tibetan)

SA_T06_n1333u.title: Cittatattvasaṅgraha
SA_T06_n1333u.author: Priyānanda
SA_T06_n1333u.summary: The Cittatattvasaṅgraha (also titled Vijñaptimātratāsiddhipañcāśikā in its colophon) is a Sanskrit verse composition in 50 kārikās by Bhikṣu Priyānanda. The work discusses skandha analysis, cognitive processing (vīthicitta), and early Buddhist psychology in connection with Yogācāra concepts of vijñaptimātratā.
SA_T06_n1333u.attribution: The closing colophon verses name the author as the Sri Lankan paṇḍitācārya and bhikṣu Priyānanda, styled āmerikādharmadūta ('Dharma missionary to America'), and give the title as Vijñaptimātratāsiddhipañcāśikā / Cittatatvasaṅgraha.
SA_T06_n1333u.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising a 5-line opening benediction, 50 numbered anuṣṭubh verses, and a 4-line closing author colophon.

SA_T06_n1394u.title: Yogācārabhūmi (chapters 1–5)
SA_T06_n1394u.author: Asaṅga
SA_T06_n1394u.summary: The Yogācārabhūmi is the fundamental encyclopedic compendium of the Yogācāra school of Indian Mahāyāna Buddhism. This digital text comprises the first five bhūmis of the seventeen stages in the basic section (Maulībhūmi): the stage connected with the five sensory consciousnesses (Pañcavijñānakāyasamprayuktā bhūmiḥ), the stage of mental consciousness (Manobhūmiḥ), and the three stages defined by the presence or absence of coarse discursive thinking and subtle investigation (Savitarkā savicārā, Avitarkā vicāramātrā, and Avitarkāvicārā bhūmayaḥ). These sections set out early Yogācāra psychology, sensory taxonomy, cognitive objects, caittas (mental concomitants), cosmology, the ālayavijñāna, karmic accumulation, and the degrees of spiritual realization (abhisamaya).
SA_T06_n1394u.attribution: Indo-Tibetan tradition attributes the text to Asaṅga, while East Asian tradition regards it as spoken by the bodhisattva Maitreya.

SA_T06_n2994u.summary: The Mahāyānasaṃgraha of Asaṅga is a Yogācāra treatise concerning doctrines such as ālayavijñāna and the three natures. It survives in Tibetan and Chinese translations, and this e-text contains a Sanskrit restoration.

SA_T06_ybh-laukikamarga.title: Śrāvakabhūmi (Laukikamārga section)
SA_T06_ybh-laukikamarga.author: Asaṅga
SA_T06_ybh-laukikamarga.summary: The Laukikamārga ('Mundane Path') section forms part of the Śrāvakabhūmi. It provides an extensive canonical description of worldly meditation practice, detailing how a meditator cultivates seven progressive mental orientations (manaskāra) to achieve detachment from the sensual realm (kāmavairāgya) and enter the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and formless realms. Unlike the supramundane path (lokottaramārga), the mundane path suppresses worldly passions through progressive mental refinement.
SA_T06_ybh-laukikamarga.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Asaṅga (or Maitreya in Chinese tradition T1579).

SA_T06_sambhu.title: Yogācārabhūmi (Samāhitābhūmi)
SA_T06_sambhu.author: Asaṅga
SA_T06_sambhu.summary: The Samāhitābhūmi ('Stage of Meditative Equipoise') constitutes the sixth chapter of the Maulī Bhūmi (Bahubhūmivastu) division of the Yogācārabhūmi. It offers an encyclopedic scholastic taxonomy of Buddhist concentration and meditation states, systematically treating the four dhyānas, eight liberations (vimokṣa), various samādhis, and meditative attainments (samāpatti), together with their accompanying mental factors (manaskāra) and meditative signs (nimitta).
SA_T06_sambhu.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Asaṅga in Tibetan tradition (Thogs-med), and to Maitreya Bodhisattva (彌勒菩薩) in Chinese tradition (translated by Xuanzang).
SA_T06_sambhu.edition: Martin Delhey (ed.), Samāhitā Bhūmiḥ: Das Kapitel über die meditative Versenkung im Grundteil der Yogācārabhūmi, Wiener Studien zur Tibetologie und Buddhismuskunde 73, Vienna: Arbeitskreis für Tibetische und Buddhistische Studien, 2009.

SA_T06_srabhu_u.title: Śrāvakabhūmi (chapters 1–2, with Asamāhitābhūmi, Śrutamayībhūmi, and Cintāmayībhūmi)
SA_T06_srabhu_u.summary: The Śrāvakabhūmi ('Stage of the Disciple') is the thirteenth and second-largest treatise within the Maulī Bhūmi (Basic Section) of the Yogācārabhūmi corpus, serving as an encyclopedic meditation manual structured across four yogasthānas. This e-text contains Yogasthānas 1 and 2, which systematically treat the spiritual requisites of practice, the classification of disciples, qualified spiritual masters, ālambana (meditative objects), and initial tranquilization and insight. In addition, the file incorporates three other independent bhūmis from the Yogācārabhūmi edited as appendices in the 2007 Taisho publication: the Asamāhitā bhūmi (unconcentrated state), the Śrutamayī bhūmi (stage arisen from hearing), and the Cintāmayī bhūmi (stage arisen from reflection, concluding with the Ābhiprāyikārthagāthānirdeśa).
SA_T06_srabhu_u.attribution: Traditionally attributed in the Tibetan canon (D 4036) to Thogs med (Asaṅga), translated by Jinamitra and Ye shes sde; and in the Chinese Buddhist tradition (T 1579) to Maitreya (彌勒菩薩), translated by Xuanzang (玄奘). Modern scholarship (such as Florin Deleanu) examines its independent textual layers.
SA_T06_srabhu_u.edition: Śrāvakabhūmi Study Group (The Institute for Comprehensive Studies of Buddhism, Taisho University), ed., (1) Srāvakabhūmi, The First Chapter, Revised Sanskrit Text and Japanese Translation, Tokyo 1998 (Taisho University Sogo Bukkyo Kenyujo, 4); and (2) Śrāvakabhūmi, The Second Chapter with Asamāhitā bhūmiḥ, Śrutamayī bhūmiḥ, Cintāmayī bhūmiḥ, Revised Sanskrit Text and Japanese Translation, Tokyo 2007 (Taisho Daigaku Sogobukkyo Kenyujo, 18).

SA_T06_srabhusu.title: Śrāvakabhūmi
SA_T06_srabhusu.author: Asaṅga
SA_T06_srabhusu.summary: The Śrāvakabhūmi ('Stage of the Disciple') is the thirteenth section of the Maulī Bhūmi (basic section) of the Yogācārabhūmi corpus, constituting an extensive and systematic manual of Buddhist meditation and spiritual development. Structured into four yogasthānas (stages of spiritual practice), it treats the prerequisites for monastic life, spiritual disposition (gotra), initial entry into practice (avatāra), and the dual cultivation of calm abiding (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā) culminating in liberation. Although preserved as part of the Yogācāra canon, it systematically articulates classical Mainstream (Śrāvakayāna) praxis and doctrine.
SA_T06_srabhusu.attribution: Attributed to Asaṅga in the Tibetan tradition and printed by Shukla under his name; East Asian tradition attributes the overarching Yogācārabhūmi to Maitreya Bodhisattva.

SA_T07_dhrmsk_u.title: Dharmaskandha (fragments)
SA_T07_dhrmsk_u.summary: The Dharmaskandha ('Aggregation of Dharmas') is one of the seven canonical treatises of the Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma Piṭaka (specifically counted among the 'six feet' or ṣaṭ-pādāḥ supporting the body of the Jñānaprasthāna) and is regarded alongside the Saṃgītiparyāya as representative of the earliest, sūtra-commentarial stratum of Abhidharma literature (c. 2nd–1st century BCE). The treatise compiles canonical doctrinal categories (mātṛkās)—such as the five precepts, stages of stream-entry, the limbs of awakening, dependent origination, and meditative absorptions—and glosses them with citations from early discourses. While preserved intact in Chinese translation (T 1537), the Indic text survives only in birch-bark manuscript leaves recovered from Gilgit and Central Asia.
SA_T07_dhrmsk_u.attribution: Traditional attributions diverge: the Sanskrit/Tibetan tradition attributes it to Śāriputra, whereas the Chinese tradition (T 1537) attributes it to Maudgalyāyana.
SA_T07_dhrmsk_u.edition: Composite critical edition drawn from: (1) Siglinde Dietz, Fragmente des Dharmaskandha: Ein Abhidharma-Text in Sanskrit aus Gilgit (Abhandlungen der Akademie der Wissenschaften in Göttingen, Philologisch-Historische Klasse, Dritte Folge, Nr. 142), Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 1984 (fols. 3–20, 26); and (2) Kazunobu Matsuda, 'Newly Identified Sanskrit Fragments of the Dharmaskandha in the Gilgit Manuscripts' (1), Sanskrit Fragments Transliterated, with an Appendix by Hajime Sakurabe, Kyoto: Bun'eidō, 1986, pp. 151–156 (fols. 21, 22, 27); with reference to K. Sankarnarayan, Kazunobu Matsuda, and Masaaki Yoritomi, Lokaprajñapti: A Critical Exposition of Buddhist Cosmology, Mumbai/New Delhi, 2002, pp. 15–24.
SA_T07_dhrmsk_u.coverage: fragment — Preserves birch-bark folios from Gilgit: fols. 3–20 and 26 (ed. Dietz 1984) and fols. 21, 22, and 27 (ed. Matsuda 1986).
translations: Xuanzang (玄奘), 阿毘達磨法蘊足論 (Apidamo fayunzu lun), Taishō Tripiṭaka no. 1537a–514b (12 fascicles, translated in 659 CE). (Chinese)

SA_T07_n772u.title: Abhidharmāmṛta
SA_T07_n772u.author: Ghoṣaka
SA_T07_n772u.summary: The Abhidharmāmṛta (or Abhidharmāmṛtarasaśāstra) is an early, systematic manual of Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma attributed to Bhadanta Ghoṣaka, one of the four great venerable masters of the Vaibhāṣika lineage associated with the western/Gandhāran tradition. Organized into sixteen chapters (bindus), it provides a clear exposition of Buddhist scholastic categories, including charity and moral discipline, realms of rebirth, the skandhas, dhātus, and āyatanas, causal conditions, latent defilements, the path of meditation, and unconditioned dharmas. No original Sanskrit manuscripts are extant; this digital text represents Shanti Bhikshu Sastri's 1953 retroversion into Sanskrit based on the Chinese translation preserved in the Taishō Canon (T 1553).
SA_T07_n772u.attribution: Attributed to the Sarvāstivādin master Bhadanta Ghoṣaka (traditionally identified as one of the four principal authorities of the Vaibhāṣika school or a prominent western/Gandhāran master). The original Indic text is lost; the present e-text is Shanti Bhikshu Sastri's 1953 modern reconstruction (retroversion) into Sanskrit from the surviving Chinese translation.
SA_T07_n772u.edition: Shanti Bhikshu Sastri (ed. & reconstr.), Abhidharmāmṛta of Ghoṣaka, Visva-Bharati Studies 17, Santiniketan: Visvabharati, 1953.
SA_T07_n772u.coverage: complete — Complete text of Shanti Bhikshu Sastri's 16-chapter (bindu) Sanskrit reconstruction, covering all 16 chapters of the Chinese translation (Taishō 1553).
translations: Apitan ganluwei lun (阿毘曇甘露味論), 2 fascicles, Taishō Tripiṭaka, no. 1553 (translator unknown; dated 220–265). (Chinese)

SA_T07_n797u.title: Subodhālaṅkāra
SA_T07_n797u.author: Saṅgharakkhita

SA_T07_nagdhdbu.title: Dharmadhātugarbhavivaraṇa
SA_T07_nagdhdbu.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T07_nagdhdbu.summary: The Dharmadhātugarbhavivaraṇa is a brief prose commentary attributed to Nāgārjuna that analyzes the famous Pratītyasamutpāda stanza ('ye dharmā hetuprabhavā hetuṃ teṣāṃ tathāgato hy avadat...'). The text provides an Abhidharmic classification of the twelve links into five causes (hetu: avidyā, saṃskāra, tṛṣṇā, upādāna, bhava) and seven results (phala: vijñāna, nāmarūpa, ṣaḍāyatana, sparśa, vedanā, jāti, jarāmaraṇa), concluding with an etymological gloss on the epithets 'Tathāgata' and 'Mahāśramaṇa' in terms of forward (anuloma) and reverse (pratiloma) dependent origination.
SA_T07_nagdhdbu.attribution: Attributed to Nāgārjuna in the Tibetan canonical colophon (Derge Tengyur Toh 4101 / D 4101, translated by Indian Upādhyāya Jñānagarbha and Ska ba Dpal brtsegs).

SA_T07_nagdhdbu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the short prose treatise corresponding to Toh 4101 / D 4101 (Derge Tengyur, mngon pa, vol. thu), including opening homage, full exposition of the 'ye dharmā hetuprabhavāḥ' stanza, and the retroverted Tibetan translation colophon.

SA_K10_udanav_u.title: Udānavarga
SA_K10_udanav_u.summary: The Udānavarga is a canonical northern Buddhist anthology of aphoristic stanzas (udāna) arranged topically across 33 chapters (vargas), primarily preserved in the Sarvāstivāda and Mūlasarvāstivāda traditions. Functioning as the Sanskrit counterpart to the Pāli Dhammapada, the Pāli Udāna, and the Gāndhārī Dharmapada, it shares an ancient core of stanzas while expanding the collection to over a thousand verses. Preserved in Sanskrit manuscripts from Central Asian oasis sites along the Northern and Southern Silk Roads as well as in Tibetan and Chinese translations, it is a crucial witness to early Buddhist verse anthologies and sectarian transmission.
SA_K10_udanav_u.attribution: Traditionally compiled or redacted by Dharmatrāta. Modern philology regards the work as an evolving canonical verse anthology sharing an archaic common verse corpus with the Pāli Dhammapada, Pāli Udāna, and the Gāndhārī Dharmapada.
SA_K10_udanav_u.edition: Franz Bernhard (ed.), Udānavarga, Band I: Einleitung, Beschreibung der Handschriften, Textausgabe, Bibliographie (Sanskrittexte aus den Turfanfunden X; Abhandlungen der Akademie der Wissenschaften in Göttingen, Philologisch-Historische Klasse, Dritte Folge), Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 1965.

SA_T07_vabhdicu.title: Abhidharmadīpa with Vibhāṣāprabhāvṛtti (incomplete)
SA_T07_vabhdicu.summary: The Abhidharmadīpa along with its prose auto-commentary (Vibhāṣāprabhāvṛtti) is an important post-Vasubandhu Sarvāstivāda-Vaibhāṣika treatise. Written by an anonymous author conventionally designated as the Dīpakāra, it parallels the structure of Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośabhāṣya across eight chapters while defending orthodox Kāśmīra Vaibhāṣika positions. The work is noted for its defense of Vaibhāṣika realism and its polemical critiques directed against Sautrāntika doctrines and Vasubandhu (called the 'Kośakāra').
SA_T07_vabhdicu.attribution: The root treatise and its prose auto-commentary are anonymous; in Indological scholarship the author is conventionally referred to as 'Dīpakāra'.
SA_T07_vabhdicu.edition: Padmanabh S. Jaini (ed.), Abhidharmadīpa with Vibhāṣāprabhāvṛtti, Patna: Kashi Prasad Jayaswal Research Institute, 1959 (Tibetan Sanskrit Works Series, 4).

SA_T07_sthtattva4.title: Tattvārthā Abhidharmakośaṭīkā (on Abhidharmakośabhāṣya 4.34–4.37)
SA_T07_sthtattva4.author: Sthiramati
SA_T07_sthtattva4.summary: This text preserves the surviving Sanskrit of Sthiramati's commentary (ṭīkā) entitled Tattvārthā on Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośabhāṣya 4.34–4.37, located in the fourth chapter on action (Karmanirdeśa). It treats the debate over whether drinking alcohol constitutes an offense by nature (prakṛtisāvadya) or solely by prohibition (pratikṣepaṇasāvadya), the attainment of the three types of moral discipline (saṃvara: prātimokṣa-, dhyāna-, and anāsrava-saṃvara), their relationship to karmic path stages, and the definition of non-restraint (asaṃvara). The work is historically vital for showing Sthiramati's engagement with the competing views of the Sautrāntika and Sarvāstivāda traditions (especially Saṃghabhadra).
SA_T07_sthtattva4.attribution: Composed by the Yogācāra master Sthiramati (c. 510–570 CE) as an extensive sub-commentary (ṭīkā) on Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośabhāṣya.
SA_T07_sthtattva4.edition: Aggregated from four published critical editions by Kazuo Kano and collaborators based on the Sanskrit manuscript from Tibet: (1) AK 4.34 in Kazuo Kano and Jowita Kramer, 'The Fourth Chapter of the Tattvārthā Abhidharmakośaṭīkā: On Forbidding Intoxicating Liquor', in Sanskrit Manuscripts from China III, Beijing: China Tibetology Publishing House, 2020; (2) AK 4.35 in Kazuo Kano et al., Taihō zasshi 2 (2021): 63–98; (3) AK 4.36ab in Kazuo Kano et al., Taihō zasshi 3 (2022): 43–95; (4) AK 4.36cd and 4.37 in Kazuo Kano and Jowita Kramer, China Tibetology 36, no. 1 (2021): 81–99.
SA_T07_sthtattva4.coverage: partial — Contains Sthiramati's commentary on Abhidharmakośabhāṣya 4.34–4.37 only (from chapter 4, Karmanirdeśa), covering folios 1r1–2r6 of the Sanskrit manuscript from Tibet.

SA_T08_jsphustu.title: Sphuṭārthā Śrīghanācārasaṃgrahaṭīkā
SA_T08_jsphustu.author: Jayarakṣita
SA_T08_jsphustu.summary: The Sphuṭārthā Śrīghanācārasaṃgrahaṭīkā is a Buddhist Vinaya commentary by Jayarakṣita on the Śrīghanācārasaṃgraha, detailing the disciplinary code and daily conduct of novices (śrāmaṇeras). It covers novice training precepts, infractions, ritual procedures, and monastic etiquette. The text is linked in modern scholarship to the Mahāsāṃghika lineage.
SA_T08_jsphustu.attribution: Authored by Jayarakṣita, named in the closing stanzas. The root text (Śrīghanācārasaṃgraha) is not included as an independent continuous text but is embedded via pratīkas cited and commented upon throughout the prose commentary.
SA_T08_jsphustu.edition: Sanghasena Singh (ed.), Sphuṭārthā Śrīghanācārasaṃgrahaṭīkā, 2nd ed., Patna: K.P. Jayaswal Research Institute, 1983 (Tibetan Sanskrit Works Series, 24).
SA_T08_jsphustu.coverage: complete — Complete commentary, spanning from the opening maṅgala verses to the final puṇyapariṇāmanā and author colophon verses.

SA_T08_sghancsu.title: Śrīghanācārasaṃgraha
SA_T08_sghancsu.summary: The Śrīghanācārasaṃgraha ('Compendium of Conduct according to the Buddha') is a Buddhist Vinaya manual in verse outlining monastic discipline and deportment for novices (śrāmaṇera). Affiliated with the Mahāsāṃghika (or Lokottaravādin) disciplinary lineage, the work is organized into four adhyāyas treating the three refuges, the ten novice precepts (śikṣāpada), and supplementary rules of conduct. Because no separate manuscript of the root verses survives, the e-text presents the modern philological reconstruction by Sanghasen Singh extracted from the lemmata and glosses of Jayarakṣita's Sphuṭārthā commentary.
SA_T08_sghancsu.attribution: The original author of the verse treatise is anonymous. The root verses were preserved embedded in Jayarakṣita's commentary (Sphuṭārthā Śrīghanācārasaṃgrahaṭīkā) and reconstructed by modern editor Sanghasen Singh, whose editorial reconstruction is acknowledged in each chapter colophon ('iti saṃghasenena saṃvihitoddhāre...').
SA_T08_sghancsu.edition: Sanghasena Singh: 'On the restauration of the Śrighanācārasaṃgraha', in: Philosophy, Grammar and Indology, Essays in Honour of Professor Gustav Roth, ed. H.S. Prasad, Delhi 1992, pp. 283-301.
SA_T08_sghancsu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the modern reconstruction across four chapters (adhyāyas 1–4, comprising ca. 200 kārikā verses), terminating with concluding verse 4.8 and colophon.

SA_T08_suvrnavu.title: Suvarṇavarṇāvadāna
SA_T08_suvrnavu.summary: The Suvarṇavarṇāvadāna is an avadāna narrative recounting the story of Suvarṇavarṇa, born as the son of the merchant Divākara of Rājagṛha after Śakra instructs the merchant to take refuge in the Three Jewels. After spurning the advances of the corrupt chief minister's wife, Suvarṇavarṇa is falsely accused and condemned to death, but is saved through the miraculous spiritual intervention of the Elder Ānanda and eventually renounces worldly life. The narrative illustrates karmic retribution, refuge in the Buddha and Saṅgha, and moral discipline.
SA_T08_suvrnavu.attribution: Anonymous Buddhist narrative work. The concluding dedication formula ('deyadharmo 'yaṃ pravaramahāyānayāyinaḥ śākyabhikṣubuddhākaraguptasya...') records the pious donation of the monk Buddhākaragupta.
SA_T08_suvrnavu.edition: Sitaram Roy: Suvarṇavarṇāvadāna [Decipherment and historical study of a palm-leaf Sanskrit manuscripts-an unknown Mahāyāna(avadāna) text from Tibet.], Patna: K.P. SA_T09_ajm_u.title: Jātakamālā (chapters 1–15)
SA_T09_ajm_u.author: Āryaśūra
SA_T09_ajm_u.summary: Āryaśūra's Jātakamālā is a classic Buddhist campū-kāvya composition in ornate alternating verse and prose recounting previous lives of the Buddha to illustrate the perfections (pāramitā), such as generosity (dāna), morality (śīla), and patience (kṣānti). This e-text provides the critically edited Sanskrit text of stories 1 through 15 prepared by Albrecht Hanisch (2005), including the Vyāghrī-, Śibi-, Śaśa-, and Viśvantara-jātakas. Celebrated for its literary craftsmanship and moral elevation, the text exerted widespread influence across Buddhist Asia.
SA_T09_ajm_u.edition: Albrecht Hanisch (ed.), Āryaśūras Jātakamālā: Philologische Untersuchungen zu den Legenden 1 bis 15. Teil 1: Einleitung, Textausgabe, Anhänge, Register. Indica et Tibetica, 43/1. Marburg: Indica et Tibetica Verlag, 2005.
SA_T09_ajm_u.coverage: partial — Contains chapters 1 through 15 only (from Vyāghrījātaka to Matsyajātaka, ending at verse 15.17 and colophon 'matsyajātakaṃ pañcadaśam //') out of the 34 jātakas comprising the complete text.
translations: Peter Khoroche (trans.), Once the Buddha Was a Monkey: Ārya Śūra's Jātakamālā. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1989. (English)
Justin Meiland (trans.), Garland of the Buddha's Past Lives. 2 vols. Clay Sanskrit Library. New York: New York University Press, 2009. (English)

SA_T09_bsa032.title: Jātakamālā
SA_T09_bsa032.author: Āryaśūra
SA_T09_bsa032.summary: The Jātakamālā ('Garland of Birth-Stories'), also entitled Bodhisattvāvadānamālā, is an ornate Buddhist campū composition (mixed verse and prose) by Āryaśūra. It retells thirty-four stories exemplifying the Bodhisattva's practice of the perfections (pāramitās), such as giving (dāna), moral discipline (śīla), and patience (kṣānti), in previous births as human, divine, or animal figures.
SA_T09_bsa032.attribution: Attributed to Āryaśūra in Sanskrit manuscript colophons ('kṛtir iyam āryaśūrapādānām'), the Tibetan Degé Tanjur (D 4150, skyes pa'i rabs kyi rgyud), and the Chinese canonical tradition (Taishō 160).
SA_T09_bsa032.edition: P. L. Vaidya (ed.), Jātaka-mālā by Āryaśūra. Buddhist Sanskrit Texts 21. Darbhanga: The Mithila Institute of Post-Graduate Studies and Research in Sanskrit Learning, 1959.
SA_T09_bsa032.coverage: complete — Contains all 34 jātakas in mixed ornate prose and verse (campū format), opening with 1. Vyāghrījātaka and concluding with 34. Śatapatrajātaka.

SA_T09_bsu078_u.title: Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā (pallavas 1–48)
SA_T09_bsu078_u.author: Kṣemendra
SA_T09_bsu078_u.summary: The Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā is an ornate Sanskrit kāvya collection composed by Kṣemendra, recounting 108 edifying Buddhist stories (jātakas and avadānas). This e-text preserves pallavas 1 through 48, from the Prabhāsāvadāna to the Hastakāvadāna.

SA_T09_gopjatmu.title: Jātakamālā (13 stories)
SA_T09_gopjatmu.author: Gopadatta
SA_T09_gopjatmu.summary: Gopadatta's Jātakamālā is an ornate Buddhist narrative work composed in campū style (alternating prose and verse). The collection brings together 13 legends available in the e-text, illustrating bodhisattva deeds and Buddhist ethical themes.

SA_T09_jatkstpu.title: Jātakastava
SA_T09_jatkstpu.author: Jñānayaśas
SA_T09_jatkstpu.summary: The Jātakastava ('Praise of the Buddha\'s Former Births') by Jñānayaśas is a 20-stanza Mahāyāna devotional hymn (stotra) composed in the classical Śārdūlavikrīḍita metre. Framed by an opening confession of inadequate poetic capacity (verses 1–3) and a concluding dedication of merit for universal enlightenment (verses 19–20), stanzas 4–18 succinctly celebrate the Bodhisattva's extreme self-sacrificing deeds in previous lives—including feeding the tigress, giving away his wife and children, jumping into fire as the hare, giving up his tusks as Ṣaḍdanta, and slicing off his flesh as King Śibi. The text is preserved in the Tengyur (Toh. 1178).
SA_T09_jatkstpu.attribution: Attributed in the colophon to Ācārya Jñānayaśas (jātakastava ācāryajñānayaśasaḥ; Tib. Ye shes grags pa).
SA_T09_jatkstpu.edition: D. R. Shackleton Bailey, 'The Jātakastava of Jñānayaśas', in Asiatica: Festschrift Friedrich Weller zum 65. Geburtstag gewidmet von seinen Freunden, Kollegen und Schülern, ed. Johannes Schubert and Ulrich Schneider, Leipzig: Otto Harrassowitz, 1954, pp. 22–29.
SA_T09_jatkstpu.coverage: complete — Complete work in 20 Śārdūlavikrīḍita stanzas (Js_1–Js_20) plus closing author colophon line.
translations: D. R. Shackleton Bailey, 'The Jātakastava of Jñānayaśas', in Asiatica: Festschrift Friedrich Weller, Leipzig: Harrassowitz, 1954, pp. 22–29. (English)

SA_T10_bsa025_u.title: Ratnāvalī (chapters 1, 2.1–46, 4)
SA_T10_bsa025_u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T10_bsa025_u.summary: The Ratnāvalī is an epistle/work composed by Nāgārjuna and addressed to a king. It expounds ethics, emptiness, and Buddhist teachings. The Sanskrit text of 2.47–95 and chapter 3 is lost in this recension.

SA_T10_bsa067_u.title: Bhavasaṅkrāntiparikathā
SA_T10_bsa067_u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T10_bsa067_u.summary: The Bhavasaṅkrāntiparikathā is a short Madhyamaka treatise of 16 stanzas traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna, explaining how transmigration across existences (bhavasaṃkrānti) occurs without an enduring self or transmigrating entity (ātman/pudgala). It reconciles karmic continuity and rebirth with emptiness (śūnyatā) and dependent origination through analogies of dreams, reflections, and city-of-gandharvas illusions. As the original Sanskrit text is lost, this e-text preserves the 1938 modern Sanskrit retroversion prepared by Pandit Aiswamy Shastri from Tibetan and Chinese sources.
SA_T10_bsa067_u.attribution: Ascribed in the Tibetan tradition (Dergé Tanjur Toh. 4162 and Toh. 3840) to Klu-sgrub (Nāgārjuna) and in the Chinese tradition (Taishō 1574, translated by Shihu) to Nāgārjuna. Furthermore, the original Sanskrit text of this work is reconstructed; the text in this file is a reconstructed Sanskrit edition by Pandit Aiswamy Shastri.
SA_T10_bsa067_u.edition: Pandit Aiswamy Shastri, Bhavasankrantiparikatha. Madras: Adyar Library, 1938, pp. 1-7.

SA_T10_cansisy2.title: Śiṣyalekha
SA_T10_cansisy2.author: Candragomin
SA_T10_cansisy2.summary: Candragomin's Śiṣyalekha is an ornate verse epistle (lekha) in 115 stanzas, traditionally addressed to a disciple to recall him from worldly attachment to religious life. After praise of the Buddha, it depicts the miseries of saṃsāra (gestation, birth, ageing, death, hot and cold hells, animal and preta births) and closes with exhortation to the bodhisattva path and a dedication of merit.

SA_T10_cansisyu.title: Śiṣyalekha
SA_T10_cansisyu.author: Candragomin
SA_T10_cansisyu.summary: The Śiṣyalekha ('Letter to a Disciple') is an ornate Buddhist didactic poem (dharmakāvya) in epistolary form (lekha) composed by Candragomin. It expounds the perils and sufferings of saṃsāra, the physical miseries of birth, aging, and death, the rarity of human life, and the compassionate ideal of the bodhisattva path dedicated to the liberation of all sentient beings.

SA_T10_n2902u.title: Daṇḍikathā
SA_T10_n2902u.summary: A short prose tale about the poor brahmin Daṇḍin, who, after losing a borrowed ox, is taken to the king's court and on the way causes a series of mishaps: he lames a runaway mare with a stone, falls from a wall and kills a weaver, and makes a carpenter drop the axe held in his mouth into a river. The king answers each plaintiff with a reciprocal penalty that makes the complaint absurd, so all withdraw and Daṇḍin is acquitted. The story corresponds to Xianyu jing (T 202).
SA_T10_n2902u.attribution: The tale of the poor brahmin Daṇḍin (Chin. 檀膩䩭) is associated with the Xianyu jing 賢愚經 (T 202).
SA_T10_n2902u.coverage: complete — Whole tale in 98 segments, from the opening 'kasmiṃścid deśe daṇḍītyabhihito brāhmaṇaḥ' to Daṇḍin's acquittal 'daṇḍī [ca] sarvāparādhebhyo mumuce iti ||'.
translations: Stanley Frye, The Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish (mdo bdzans blun) or the Ocean of Narratives (üliger-ün dalai), Dharamsala: Library of Tibetan Works and Archives, 1981 (translated from the Mongolian). (English)

SA_T10_n3009u.title: Vimalaratnalekha
SA_T10_n3009u.author: Atiśa
SA_T10_n3009u.summary: The Vimalaratnalekha is an epistolary work of 40 verses by Atiśa Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna addressed to King Nayapāla. SA_T10_nrat_1_u.title: Ratnāvalī (chapter 1, verses 1–77)
SA_T10_nrat_1_u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T10_nrat_1_u.summary: The Ratnāvalī (or Rājaparikathāratnāvalī) is addressed to a king, outlining dharma, abhyudaya ('higher status' / happiness) and naiḥśreyasa ('definite goodness' / liberation) through faith and wisdom, and refuting views of existence and non-existence.

SA_T10_nrat_2_u.title: Ratnāvalī (chapter 2, verses 1–46)
SA_T10_nrat_2_u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T10_nrat_2_u.summary: Chapter 2 of Nāgārjuna's Ratnāvalī expounds core teachings on selflessness and the illusion-like (māyopama) nature of entities, explaining why the Buddha left metaphysical extremes undeclared. It bridges emptiness with practical ethics, urging the king to maintain righteous conduct, pursue dharma, and avoid intoxicating drink.
SA_T10_nrat_2_u.attribution: Attributed to Nāgārjuna. Addressed to a king.
SA_T10_nrat_2_u.edition: Giuseppe Tucci: Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society of Great Britain and Ireland, 1934, pp. 307-325; 1936, pp. 237-252, 423-435.
translations: Giuseppe Tucci, 'Ratnāvalī of Nāgārjuna', Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society. (English)
Jeffrey Hopkins and Lati Rinpoche, The Precious Garland. (English)

SA_T10_nrat_4_u.title: Ratnāvalī (chapter 4)
SA_T10_nrat_4_u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T10_nrat_4_u.summary: The fourth chapter of Nāgārjuna's Ratnāvalī ('Precious Garland'), titled Rājavṛttopadeśa, provides ethical, administrative, and political counsel to a reigning monarch. Nāgārjuna enjoins the ruler to govern without malice or greed, select upright and competent ministers, maintain public welfare facilities for the sick and impoverished, and temper criminal justice with compassion. He seamlessly integrates practical statecraft with core Mahāyāna doctrine, emphasizing that legitimate kingship must be grounded in altruism (karuṇā) and insight into emptiness (śūnyatā).
SA_T10_nrat_4_u.attribution: Attributed to Nāgārjuna as a treatise addressed to a king.
SA_T10_nrat_4_u.edition: Giuseppe Tucci, 'The Ratnāvalī of Nāgārjuna', Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society of Great Britain and Ireland, 1934, pp. 307–325; 1936, pp. 237–252, 423–435.
SA_T10_nrat_4_u.coverage: partial — Contains the complete fourth chapter (verses 4.1–4.100, concluding with the colophon: 'ratnāvalyām rājavṛttopadeśe nāma caturthaḥ paricchedaḥ').
translations: Giuseppe Tucci, 'Ratnāvalī of Nāgārjuna', Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society. (English)
Jeffrey Hopkins and Lati Rinpoche, The Precious Garland and The Song of the Four Mindfulnesses. (English)

SA_T10_subhrk_u.title: Subhāṣitaratnakaraṇḍakathā
SA_T10_subhrk_u.author: Āryaśūra
SA_T10_subhrk_u.summary: The Subhāṣitaratnakaraṇḍakathā is a late Buddhist homiletic poem of 191 verses ending with a pāramitāparikathā. It offers didactic exhortations on the rarity of human rebirth, dharma hearing, merit-making (puṇya), and the practice of the perfections (pāramitās). Although traditionally attributed to Āryaśūra, the work is recognized by modern scholarship as a late Buddhist text on merit (spätbuddhistischer Text zur Verdienstlehre).
SA_T10_subhrk_u.attribution: The colophon names Ācārya Śūra (Āryaśūra), author of the Jātakamālā. However, philological studies by Heinz Zimmermann (1975) and Michael Hahn (1983) demonstrated that the attribution is pseudepigraphic.
SA_T10_subhrk_u.edition: M. Hahn: Die Subhāṣitaratnakaraṇḍakathā, Ein spätbuddhistischer Text zur Verdienstlehre. NAWG, phil.-hist. Kl. 1983, pp. 313-374.
SA_T10_subhrk_u.coverage: complete — Complete text containing 191 verses ending with '// iti pāramitāparikathā subhāṣitaratnakaraṇḍake samāptā // kṛtir ācāryaśūrasya //'.

SA_T11_arhebt_u.title: Hetubinduṭīkā
SA_T11_arhebt_u.author: Arcaṭa
SA_T11_arhebt_u.summary: The Hetubinduṭīkā is a major 8th-century commentary by Bhaṭṭa Arcaṭa on Dharmakīrti's Hetubindu ('Drop of Reason'), an independent tract dedicated to the logical reason (hetu) and Buddhist inferential theory. Arcaṭa offers comprehensive analyses of the three varieties of valid probans (svabhāva, kārya, and anupalabdhi), the formal criteria of the triple-character reason (trairūpya), perceptual judgments, and the inference of momentariness (kṣaṇikatvānumāna). It represents a crucial milestone in post-Dharmakīrti Pramāṇavāda and served as the primary basis for Durveka Miśra's sub-commentary Āloka.
SA_T11_arhebt_u.attribution: Authored by Bhaṭṭa Arcaṭa (fl. c. 8th century CE). Dharmakīrti's root text (Hetubindu) is commented upon through embedded lemmata and pratīkas, but is not included as an independent running text. The Tibetan translation (D 4235) attributes the work to Ācaṭa (a tsa Ta).
SA_T11_arhebt_u.edition: Pandit Sukhlalji Sanghavi and Muni Shri Jinavijayaji (eds.), Hetubinduṭīkā of Bhaṭṭa Arcaṭa with the Sub-Commentary entitled Āloka of Durveka Miśra, Baroda: Oriental Institute, 1949 (Gaekwad's Oriental Series, No. CXIII).
SA_T11_arhebt_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of Arcaṭa's commentary as edited from the single Patan manuscript, including editorial bracketed Sanskrit reconstructions from the Tibetan translation for folios missing in that manuscript.
translations: gtan tshigs thigs pa'i 'grel pa (Derge Tengyur D 4235): at dzam gling snying po kha che'i grong khyer (Tibetan)

SA_T11_arhebt2u.title: Hetubinduṭīkā
SA_T11_arhebt2u.author: Arcaṭa
SA_T11_arhebt2u.summary: The Hetubinduṭīkā by Bhaṭṭa Arcaṭa (c. 8th century CE) is an extensive commentary on Dharmakīrti's Hetubindu, an independent treatise examining the theory of logical reasons and inference. Arcaṭa discusses essential epistemological topics of Buddhist pramāṇavāda, including the preliminary statement of purpose (prayojana), the three conditions of a valid mark (trairūpya), the threefold classification of valid probantia, and the proof of momentariness (kṣaṇikatvānumāna). Preserved in Sanskrit and Tibetan, it served as a crucial intermediate authority between Dharmakīrti and later commentators such as Dharmottara and Durveka Miśra.
SA_T11_arhebt2u.attribution: Bhaṭṭa Arcaṭa (fl. c. 8th century CE), also referred to as Dharmākaradatta, was a Buddhist epistemologist whose commentary on Dharmakīrti's Hetubindu influenced Dharmottara and the Buddhist logical tradition. The Tibetan translation (D 4235) attributes the work to Ācaṭa (a tsa Ta).
SA_T11_arhebt2u.edition: Hetubinduṭīkā of Bhaṭṭa Arcaṭa, with the sub-commentary entitled Āloka of Durveka Miśra, edited by Pandit S. Sanghavi and Muni Shri Jinavijayaji, Gaekwad's Oriental Series, No. 113, Baroda: Oriental Institute, 1949.
SA_T11_arhebt2u.coverage: complete — Arcaṭa's Hetubinduṭīkā as printed in the 1949 edition, with missing pp. 176–177 supplied by Klaus Wille.
translations: gtan tshigs thigs pa'i 'grel pa (Derge Tengyur D 4235): at dzam gling snying po kha che'i grong khyer (Tibetan)

SA_T11_bsa001_u.title: Ālambanaparīkṣā
SA_T11_bsa001_u.author: Dignāga
SA_T11_bsa001_u.summary: The Ālambanaparīkṣā ('Investigation of the Percept') is a concise foundational treatise in eight verses by the Buddhist epistemologist Dignāga. Dignāga defines a perceptual cognitive object (ālambana) through two joint criteria: it must act as the causal condition producing the cognition, and the cognition must bear its subjective appearance or form. Arguing against externalist atomism, he demonstrates that neither individual atoms nor aggregated atomic composites meet both criteria, ultimately concluding that the object cognized is actually an internal mental aspect appearing as if external, establishing the Yogācāra idealist doctrine.
SA_T11_bsa001_u.attribution: Attributed to Dignāga across Sanskrit citations, Tibetan translation (D 4205), and Chinese translations (Taishō 1619 translated by Paramārtha, Taishō 1624 translated by Xuanzang). The text was restored into Sanskrit from Tibetan and Chinese versions by N. Aiyaswami Sastri.
SA_T11_bsa001_u.edition: N. Aiyaswami Shastri, Madras: The Adyar Library, 1942.
SA_T11_bsa001_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the eight root kārikās (verses 1–8) with introductory mangala and closing colophon. Dignāga's prose autocommentary (Ālambanaparīkṣāvṛtti) is omitted in this specific file.
translations: N. Aiyaswami Sastri, Alambanapariksa and Vrtti by Dinnaga with the Commentary of Dharmapala, Madras: The Adyar Library, 1942. (English)

SA_T11_bsa002_u.title: Ālambanaparīkṣā with Ālambanaparīkṣāvṛtti
SA_T11_bsa002_u.author: Dignāga
SA_T11_bsa002_u.summary: The Ālambanaparīkṣā ('Investigation of the Perceptual Object') with its auto-commentary (vṛtti) by Dignāga is a treatise in eight verses expounding Yogācāra-vijñānavāda epistemology. Dignāga argues that external matter cannot serve as an object of cognition (ālambana), because neither indivisible atoms nor aggregated gross bodies fulfill the necessary twin criteria: being the cause that produces the cognition and presenting their likeness (ākāra) to consciousness. He concludes that the cognitive object is an internal mental appearance projected outward by beginningless cognitive latencies (vāsanā / śakti), establishing an epistemological basis for mind-only idealism.
SA_T11_bsa002_u.attribution: Both the kārikās of the Ālambanaparīkṣā and the accompanying vṛtti are compositions of Dignāga.
SA_T11_bsa002_u.edition: Dignāga, Ālambanaparīkṣā and Vṛtti, with the Commentary of Dharmapāla, edited and reconstructed into Sanskrit with Tibetan and Chinese versions and an English translation by N. Aiyaswami Sastri, Madras: The Adyar Library, 1942.
SA_T11_bsa002_u.coverage: complete — Complete 8 verses with auto-commentary (vṛtti), in N. Aiyaswami Sastri's Sanskrit retroversion from Tibetan and Chinese.
translations: Aiyaswami Sastri, N. Ālambanaparīkṣā and Vṛtti by Diṅnāga with the Commentary of Dharmapāla. Madras: The Adyar Library, 1942. (English)
