SA_T11_bsa020_u.title: Vajrasūcī (verses only)
SA_T11_bsa020_u.author: Aśvaghoṣa
SA_T11_bsa020_u.summary: The Vajrasūcī is a Buddhist polemical text attacking the Brahmanical caste system, particularly the claim that brahminhood is determined by birth, arguing instead from Brahmanical scripture (Vedas, Manusmṛti, Mahābhārata) and conduct/character. The Chinese translation (T 1642) attributes it to Dharmakīrti.
SA_T11_bsa020_u.attribution: The GRETIL header lists the work as 'Asvaghosa (attrib.): Vajrasuci'. The Chinese translation (T 1642, tr. Fatian, 973 CE) ascribes it to Dharmakīrti (法稱菩薩造). A Brahmanical recension is classed among the Upanishads. Modern scholarship doubts the attribution to the classical Aśvaghoṣa.
SA_T11_bsa020_u.edition: Ramayana Prasad Dvivedi (ed.): Vajrasuchi. Varanasi: Chaukhamba Amarbharati Prakasan, 1985.
SA_T11_bsa020_u.coverage: excerpt — Only the verses: verse 1 (Vs_1) to concluding verse 53 (Vs_53) and the colophon 'kṛtiriyaṃ siddhācāryāśvaghoṣapādānāmiti vajrasūcī samāpteti śubham'.
translations: Albrecht Weber, 1860. (German)
B. H. Hodgson, 1831. (English)

SA_T11_bsa0551u.title: Apohasiddhi
SA_T11_bsa0551u.author: Ratnakīrti
SA_T11_bsa0551u.summary: The Apohasiddhi is a concise philosophical treatise on semantics and epistemology by the Buddhist logician Ratnakīrti. Ratnakīrti rejects both exclusive affirmationism (vidhivāda) and pure negative exclusion (pratiṣedhavāda), arguing that words convey a positive entity intrinsically qualified by the exclusion of dissimilar things (anyāpohaviśiṣṭo vidhiḥ śabdānāmarthaḥ).
SA_T11_bsa0551u.attribution: The colophon explicitly names Mahāpaṇḍita Ratnakīrti as author. The subsequent post-colophonic scribal stanza identifies the copyist as Trailokyadatta.
SA_T11_bsa0551u.edition: Haraprasad Shastri: Six Buddhist Nyaya tracts in Sanskrit. Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1989, pp. 1-114.
SA_T11_bsa0551u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the short treatise, from opening mangala and proposition through closing kārikās, author colophon, and scribal verses.
translations: D. Sharma, The Differentiation Theory of Meaning in Indian Logic (Being the Apohasiddhi of Ratnakīrti). (English)

SA_T11_bsa0552u.title: Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhir anvayātmikā
SA_T11_bsa0552u.author: Ratnakīrti
SA_T11_bsa0552u.summary: The Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhir anvayātmikā is a philosophical treatise by the eleventh-century Buddhist epistemologist Ratnakīrti of Vikramaśīla. It establishes the Buddhist doctrine of universal momentariness (kṣaṇabhaṅga) via positive pervasion (anvayavyāpti): whatever exists is causally efficient (arthakriyākārin), and causal efficiency can only occur instantaneously, not successively or simultaneously over time (kramākramābhyām). Defending the inference against Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika and Mīmāṃsā realists, Ratnakīrti deploys reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) and contraposition (prasaṅgaviparyaya) to show that permanent entities cannot possess causal efficacy.
SA_T11_bsa0552u.attribution: Firmly attributed to the 11th-century Vikramaśīla scholar Ratnakīrti based on the explicit end-colophon.
SA_T11_bsa0552u.edition: Haraprasad Shastri: Six Buddhist Nyaya tracts in Sanskrit. Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1989, 1-114.
SA_T11_bsa0552u.coverage: complete — Text of the treatise from the introductory verse (namaḥ samantabhadrāya / ākṣiptavyatirekā...) to the full work and author colophons (iti sādharmyadṛṣṭānte 'nvayarūpavyāptyā kṣaṇabhaṅgasidviḥ samāptā / kṛtiriyaṃ mahāpaṇḍitaratnakīrttipādānāmiti).

SA_T11_bsa0553u.title: Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi vyatirekātmikā
SA_T11_bsa0553u.author: Ratnakīrti
SA_T11_bsa0553u.summary: The Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi vyatirekātmikā is an epistemological treatise by the Buddhist master Ratnakīrti demonstrating the universal momentariness (kṣaṇikatva) of all existents by way of negative pervasion (vyatirekavyāpti) or contraposition. Developing the earlier insights of his teacher Jñānaśrīmitra, Ratnakīrti argues that whatever lacks causal efficiency through succession or simultaneity (kramākrama) cannot exist, thereby proving that eternal entities are impossible and that only momentary particulars are real. The treatise is particularly famous for its thorough refutation of the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika objection of an unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhi) when formulating inferences concerning uninstantiated or fictitious entities.
SA_T11_bsa0553u.attribution: Authentic work of the Buddhist logician Ratnakīrti, pupil of Jñānaśrīmitra. The work concludes with the author's colophon ('kṛtiriyaṃ mahāpaṇḍitaratnakīrttipādānām').
SA_T11_bsa0553u.edition: Haraprasad Shastri. Six Buddhist Nyaya tracts in Sanskrit. Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1989, 1-114.
SA_T11_bsa0553u.coverage: complete — Complete text of Ratnakīrti's Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi vyatirekātmikā, preserving the opening verse, full dialectical arguments, concluding summary verses, and the authorial colophon.
translations: A. C. Senape McDermott, An Eleventh-Century Buddhist Logic of 'Exists': Ratnakīrti's Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhiḥ Vyatirekātmikā, Foundations of Language Supplementary Series Vol. 11, Dordrecht: D. Reidel, 1969. (English)

SA_T11_bsa0554u.title: Avayavinirākaraṇa
SA_T11_bsa0554u.author: Aśoka
SA_T11_bsa0554u.summary: The Avayavinirākaraṇa is a short polemical treatise by the Buddhist logician Aśoka refuting the objective reality of the avayavin (composite whole). Applying the criterion of contradiction of properties (viruddhadharmādhyāsa), he demonstrates that gross objects cannot be established as single distinct composite wholes beyond parts.
SA_T11_bsa0554u.attribution: Ascribed in the introductory title line ('Paṇḍitāśokaracitam Avayavinirākaraṇam') and concluding colophon ('samāptañcedamavayavinirākaraṇamiti') to Paṇḍita Aśoka.
SA_T11_bsa0554u.edition: Haraprasad Shastri: Six Buddhist Nyaya tracts in Sanskrit. Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1989, 1-114.
SA_T11_bsa0554u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the short treatise, from the opening maṅgala verse ('namaḥ samantabhadrāya...') to the closing verse and colophon.
translations: Fernando Tola and Carmen Dragonetti, The Avayavinirākaraṇa of Paṇḍita Aśoka: Sanskrit Text Edited with an Annotated English Translation, Tokyo: The International Institute for Buddhist Studies, 1994 (Studia Philologica Buddhica, Monograph Series, 10). (English)
Yuichi Kajiyama, 'The Avayavinirākaraṇa of Paṇḍita Aśoka', Indogaku Bukkyōgaku Kenkyū (Journal of Indian and Buddhist Studies) 9/2 (1961). (Japanese)

SA_T11_bsa0555u.title: Sāmānyadūṣaṇa
SA_T11_bsa0555u.author: Aśoka
SA_T11_bsa0555u.summary: The Sāmānyadūṣaṇa by Aśoka is a short polemical treatise defending Buddhist nominalism against the realist ontology of universals (sāmānya). The text concludes with the celebrated five-fingers argument: one who claims to perceive a sixth common entity over and above the five distinct fingers might just as well perceive horns on their own head.
SA_T11_bsa0555u.attribution: Attributed in the opening rubric (Paṇḍitāśokaviracitā) and closing colophon (kṛtir iyaṃ paṇḍitāśokasya) to Paṇḍita Aśoka.
SA_T11_bsa0555u.edition: Haraprasad Shastri (ed.), Six Buddhist Nyāya Tracts in Sanskrit, Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1989 (reprint of 1910 ed., Bibliotheca Indica).
SA_T11_bsa0555u.coverage: complete — Preserves the complete short treatise, from the opening verse ('vyāpakannityamekañca sāmānyaṃ yaiḥ prakalpitaṃ...') to the closing verses ('etāsu pañcasvavabhāsanīṣu...'), ending with the colophon 'sāmānyasidvidūṣaṇadikprasāritā // 3 // kṛtiriyaṃ paṇḍitāśokasya'.

SA_T11_bsa0556u.title: Antarvyāptisamarthana
SA_T11_bsa0556u.author: Ratnākaraśānti
SA_T11_bsa0556u.summary: The Antarvyāptisamarthana by Ratnākaraśānti defends the doctrine of internal pervasion (antarvyāpti) in the proof of momentariness from existence (sattva / kṣaṇikatva), arguing that invariable concomitance is grasped directly without necessity of external corroborative examples (dṛṣṭānta / bahirvyāpti).
SA_T11_bsa0556u.attribution: Attributed to Ratnākaraśānti (11th century). The Sanskrit manuscript colophon names him as 'Ratnākaraśāntipāda', in agreement with the Tibetan canon (D 4260, 'Rin-chen HbyuN-gnas shi-ba').
SA_T11_bsa0556u.edition: Haraprasad Shastri (ed.), Six Buddhist Nyaya tracts in Sanskrit. Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1989, 1-114.
SA_T11_bsa0556u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the treatise, spanning from the opening formula ('om namo buddhāya / iha sattvam...') through to the final closing colophon ('antarvyāptisamarthanaṃ samāptamiti // 0 // kṛtiriyaṃ ratnākaraśāntipādānāmiti // 0 //').
translations: Alex Wayman, 'Antarvyaptisamarthana of Ratnākaraśānti', in Alex Wayman, A Millennium of Buddhist Logic. (English)

SA_T11_bsa057_u.title: Nyāyabindu
SA_T11_bsa057_u.author: Dharmakīrti
SA_T11_bsa057_u.summary: The Nyāyabindu is Dharmakīrti's concise primer on Buddhist epistemology and logic. Written in prose aphorisms (sūtras), the work is structured into three chapters: direct perception (pratyakṣa), inference for oneself (svārthānumāna), and inference for others (parārthānumāna). It defines perception as non-conceptual (kalpanāpoḍha) and non-erroneous (abhrānta), formulates the requirements of logical reasons, and classifies reasons into essential nature (svabhāva), effect (kārya), and non-cognition (anupalabdhi).
SA_T11_bsa057_u.edition: Svami Dwarikadas Shastri, Nyayabindu Prakaranam-karika. Bauddha bharati, 1994, pp. 42-50.
SA_T11_bsa057_u.coverage: complete — Complete root text comprising all three chapters (paricchedas): 1. Pratyakṣapariccheda (1/1–1/21), 2. Svārthānumānapariccheda (2/1–2/47), and 3. Parārthānumānapariccheda (3/1–3/140), concluding with 'nyāyabinduprakaraṇaṃ samāptam'.

SA_T11_bsa059_u.title: Santānāntarasiddhi
SA_T11_bsa059_u.author: Dharmakīrti
SA_T11_bsa059_u.summary: The Santānāntarasiddhi ('Proof of Other Mind-Streams') is a treatise by Dharmakīrti. Framed as a dialogue opening with a single verse and proceeding through 93 prose sections, it resolves the philosophical challenge of other minds from within the Vijñānavāda (Cittamātra) idealist system, directly rebutting the objection that idealism logically degenerates into solipsism. Dharmakīrti demonstrates that just as a realist infers intentional consciousness from observing physical movements and speech, an idealist can equally infer distinct intentional mental continua from coordinated sensory appearances without positing mind-independent external matter.
SA_T11_bsa059_u.attribution: Attributed to Dharmakīrti. This e-text presents a reconstructed Sanskrit edition based on J. S. Negi from the Tibetan translation (D 4219).
SA_T11_bsa059_u.edition: J. S. Negi, Santānāntarasiddhi kārikā ṭīkā. Sarnath: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 1997, pp. 1-30. (Reconstructed)
SA_T11_bsa059_u.coverage: complete — Complete reconstructed treatise comprising an initial anuṣṭubh verse followed by 93 prose dialogue units (bracketed [1-3] through [87-93]), ending with the author colophon.
translations: Th. Stcherbatsky, Russian translation and interpretation of Samtānāntarasiddhi and Samtānāntarasiddhiṭīkā, Petrograd, 1922. (Russian)

SA_T11_bsa061_u.title: Santānāntarasiddhi with Santānāntarasiddhiṭīkā
SA_T11_bsa061_u.author: Dharmakīrti, Vinītadeva
SA_T11_bsa061_u.summary: The Santānāntarasiddhi by Dharmakīrti is a treatise in 93 verses demonstrating from a Vijñānavāda standpoint that the rejection of external physical reality does not entail solipsism, establishing the existence of other mental continua. Vinītadeva's Santānāntarasiddhiṭīkā comments upon the text. This e-text comprises the reconstructed Sanskrit text edited by J. S. Negi.
SA_T11_bsa061_u.attribution: Dharmakīrti's root text and Vinītadeva's commentary survive in Tibetan canonical translation (D4219 and D4238). This e-text represents a modern Sanskrit reconstruction made from the Tibetan by J. S. Negi. The Tibetan translation (D 4219) attributes the work to Dharmakīrti I (d+harmA kI rti).
SA_T11_bsa061_u.edition: J.S. Negi: Santānāntarasiddhi kārikā ṭīkā. Sarnath: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 1997, 1-30.
SA_T11_bsa061_u.coverage: complete — Reconstructed text of Dharmakīrti's 93 verses embedded within Vinītadeva's commentary, from the initial maṅgala through verse 93 and Vinītadeva's concluding verses and colophon.

SA_T11_bsa063_u.title: Sambandhaparīkṣā with Sambandhaparīkṣāvyākhyā (kārikās 1–22)
SA_T11_bsa063_u.author: Dharmakīrti, Prabhācandra
SA_T11_bsa063_u.summary: The Sambandhaparīkṣā ('Investigation of Relation') is one of Dharmakīrti's pramāṇa works, dedicated to refuting real relations such as inherence (samavāya), contact (saṃyoga), and substantial causality. Dharmakīrti demonstrates that discrete entities exist in their own natures, and that relation is merely a conceptual construction (kalpanā). This digital text transmits kārikās 1–22 along with the Sanskrit commentary of Prabhācandra.
SA_T11_bsa063_u.attribution: The root verses are by Dharmakīrti. The commentary is by Prabhācandra. The Tibetan translation (D 4214) attributes the work to Dharmakīrti I (chos kyi grags pa).
SA_T11_bsa063_u.edition: Svami Dwarikadas Shastri: Sambandhapariksa of Dharmakirti. India: Bauddhabharati, 1972, pp. 139-163.
SA_T11_bsa063_u.coverage: partial — Contains kārikās 1–22 of the Sambandhaparīkṣā together with Prabhācandra's vyākhyā.

Shimizu, Yō. '“Dhramakīriti Sambandhaparīkṣā” no wayaku kaisetsu.' Bukkyōgaku kenkyū 37 (1981). (Japanese)

SA_T11_bsa064_u.title: Vādanyāya
SA_T11_bsa064_u.author: Dharmakīrti
SA_T11_bsa064_u.summary: The Vādanyāya ('The Logic of Debate') is the last of Dharmakīrti's seven core treatises on epistemology and logic (pramāṇa), expounding his reform of dialectical and debate theory. Dharmakīrti mounts an extensive critique of the classical Nyāya system of twenty-two points of defeat (nigrahasthāna), arguing that genuine defeat in truthful philosophical inquiry (vāda) occurs under only two fundamental circumstances: the proponent's failure to state an essential component of a valid proof (asādhanāṅgavacana), and the respondent's failure to point out an actual fallacy (adoṣodbhāvana). Preserved in Sanskrit and heavily commented upon by thinkers such as Śāntarakṣita (in the Vipañcitārthā) and Vinītadeva, the text served as a foundational model for Buddhist disputation.
SA_T11_bsa064_u.attribution: Universally accepted across Buddhist and non-Buddhist philosophical traditions as the final of Dharmakīrti's seven foundational pramāṇa treatises.
SA_T11_bsa064_u.edition: P.P. Gokhale (ed.), Vādanyāya of Dharmakīrti, Delhi: Srisatguru Publications, 1993 (Bibliotheca Indo-Buddhica Series, 126).
SA_T11_bsa064_u.coverage: complete — Complete text divided into 93 editorial sections, corresponding to pp. 3–149 of Gokhale's 1993 edition, concluding with the terminal verse (93: 'loke 'vidyātimirapaṭalollekhanas...') and the author colophon.
translations: Pradeep P. Gokhale, Vādanyāya of Dharmakīrti: The Logic of Debate, Delhi: Sri Satguru Publications, 1993 (Bibliotheca Indo-Buddhica Series, no. 126). (English)
Michael Torsten Much, Dharmakīrtis Vādanyāyaḥ, Teil II: Übersetzung und Anmerkungen, Wien: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, 1991. (German)

SA_T11_bsa066_u.title: Nyāyapraveśapravṛtti
SA_T11_bsa066_u.author: Haribhadrasūri
SA_T11_bsa066_u.summary: The Nyāyapraveśapravṛtti (also titled Śiṣyahitā or Nyāyapraveśakavyākhyā) is a commentary by Haribhadrasūri explaining definitions of valid proof (sādhana), refutation (dūṣaṇa), their fallacies (sābhāsa), direct perception (pratyakṣa), and inference (anumāna).
SA_T11_bsa066_u.attribution: The commentary is composed by Haribhadrasūri, who refers to it in the closing colophon as the 'Śiṣyahitā nāma Nyāyapraveśakaṭīkā'.
SA_T11_bsa066_u.edition: A.B. Dhruva (ed.), Nyāyapraveśapravṛtti, Delhi: Srisatguru Publications, 1987.
SA_T11_bsa066_u.coverage: complete — Text of Haribhadrasūri's commentary on the Nyāyapraveśa, from the opening maṅgala verse to the final colophon (corresponding to pp. 1–29 in Dhruva's edition).

SA_T11_bsa069_u.title: Tarkaśāstra
SA_T11_bsa069_u.author: Vasubandhu
SA_T11_bsa069_u.summary: The Tarkaśāstra (preserved in Chinese translation as the Rushi lun 如實論, Taishō 1633, translated by Paramārtha) is a Buddhist treatise on debate and logic representing pre-Diṅnāga Buddhist logic. It consists of three chapters treating wrong discussion/refutation, jāti, and nigrahasthāna. The Indic original is lost; the text survives in Sanskrit through Giuseppe Tucci's reconstructed text.
SA_T11_bsa069_u.attribution: The treatise is traditionally attributed to Vasubandhu in the Chinese tradition (Taishō no. 1633, translated by Paramārtha). The Sanskrit original is lost; the present text is Giuseppe Tucci's Sanskrit reconstruction from the Chinese.
SA_T11_bsa069_u.edition: G. Tucci, ed., Pre-Diṅnāga Buddhist texts on Logic from Chinese Sources, Baroda 1929 (Gaekwad's Oriental Series, 49). Reprint: Nepal: Pilgrims Book House, 1998, 1-40. (Reconstructed Text).
SA_T11_bsa069_u.coverage: complete — Complete reconstruction of the extant Chinese text in three prakaraṇas (chapter 1 on debate and refutation, chapter 2 on jāti, chapter 3 on nigrahasthāna), corresponding to pp. 1–40 of Giuseppe Tucci's 1929 edition.

SA_T11_bsa070_u.title: Upāyahṛdaya
SA_T11_bsa070_u.summary: The Upāyahṛdaya (preserved in the 472 CE Chinese translation Fangbian xin lun 方便心論, T 1632, and represented in Sanskrit by Giuseppe Tucci's retroversion) is an early Buddhist handbook of disputation. In four chapters (prakaraṇa), the text provides a justification of debate (beginning with vādo na kartavyaḥ) to defend the Saddharma, discussing pramāṇas, examples, occasions of defeat (nigrahasthāna), and false rejoinders (jāti). It constitutes an early witness to pre-Diṅnāga Indian logic and dialectic parallel to the Nyāyasūtra and Carakasaṃhitā.
SA_T11_bsa070_u.attribution: The original Sanskrit text is lost and survives only in a Chinese translation (Fangbian xin lun 方便心論, T 1632) dated to 472 CE by Jijiaye (吉迦夜). Later traditions and modern scholars (such as Kajiyama) have debated attribution to Nāgārjuna, though it is widely treated as an early debate treatise with uncertain or anonymous authorship (sometimes suggested as Bahuśrutīya).
SA_T11_bsa070_u.edition: Giuseppe Tucci (ed. & retroversion), Pre-Diṅnāga Buddhist texts on Logic from Chinese Sources, Gaekwad's Oriental Series 49, Baroda: Oriental Institute, 1929; reprint: Nepal: Pilgrims Book House, 1998, 1–40 (Reconstructed Text).
SA_T11_bsa070_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of Tucci's Sanskrit retroversion ending with iti caturthaṃ prakaraṇam / samāptaścāyaṃ granthaḥ, corresponding to the reconstructed text in Tucci (1929).

SA_T11_bsa071_u.title: Hetubindu
SA_T11_bsa071_u.author: Dharmakīrti
SA_T11_bsa071_u.summary: The Hetubindu ('Drop of Reason') is an epistemological and logical treatise by the Buddhist master Dharmakīrti, counted among his seven fundamental pramāṇa works. The text focuses specifically on the theory of the logical reason or probans (hetu), elucidating its threefold character (trairūpya) and classifying valid reasons into identity (svabhāva), effect (kārya), and non-cognition (anupalabdhi). It systematically investigates fallacies of reason (hetvābhāsa) and marks a pivotal development in Dharmakīrti's thought wherein explicit statement of the thesis (pakṣa) is treated as dispensable because it is already established by implication.
SA_T11_bsa071_u.attribution: The Hetubindu is one of the works composed by Dharmakīrti.
SA_T11_bsa071_u.edition: P.P. Gokhale: Hetubindu of Dharmakirti. Delhi: Sri Satguru Publications, 1997, 1-94.
SA_T11_bsa071_u.coverage: complete — Complete text divided into 5 sections/chapters with decimal subdivisions (from 1.1 at segment 2 to 5.15 at segment 669), concluding with the authentic colophon: 'hetubindurācāryadharmakīrtikṛtaḥ samāptaḥ'.
translations: Ernst Steinkellner, Dharmakīrti's Hetubinduḥ: Teil II. Übersetzung und Anmerkungen, Wien: Hermann Böhlaus Nachf., 1967. (German)

SA_T11_bsa072_u.title: Tarkabhāṣā
SA_T11_bsa072_u.author: Mokṣākaragupta
SA_T11_bsa072_u.summary: The Tarkabhāṣā ('Language of Logic') is a concise introductory manual of Buddhist epistemology and logic composed by Mokṣākaragupta, a monk-scholar of the Jagaddala Mahāvihāra. Structured in three chapters according to the Dignāga-Dharmakīrti epistemology—perception (pratyakṣa), inference for oneself (svārthānumāna), and inference for others (parārthānumāna)—it explains valid knowledge, definition and fallacies of the logical reason (hetu/liṅga), syllogistic debate, and core Mahāyāna philosophical doctrines.
SA_T11_bsa072_u.attribution: Mokṣākaragupta was a scholar-monk of the Jagaddala Mahāvihāra.
SA_T11_bsa072_u.edition: Losang Norbu Shastri: Tarkabhāṣā. Sarnath: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 2004, 1-76.
SA_T11_bsa072_u.coverage: complete — Complete text in three chapters (paricchedas): 1. Pratyakṣapariccheda, 2. Svārthānumānapariccheda, and 3. Parārthānumānapariccheda, followed by the granthāgra metric calculation (840 ślokas), authorial dedicatory verse, and scribal verses.
translations: Yuichi Kajiyama, An Introduction to Buddhist Philosophy: An Annotated Translation of the Tarkabhāṣā of Mokṣākaragupta, Kyoto, 1966 (reprint: Wiener Studien zur Tibetologie und Buddhismuskunde 42, Wien). (English)

SA_T11_bsa075_u.title: Ratnakīrtinibandhāvalī
SA_T11_bsa075_u.author: Ratnakīrti
SA_T11_bsa075_u.summary: The Ratnakīrtinibandhāvalī is a collection of ten philosophical monographs (nibandhas) composed by Ratnakīrti. The collection represents Buddhist Pramāṇavāda and philosophy in northern India, formulating responses to opponents. Major subjects addressed include the proof of the Buddha's omniscience (Sarvajñasiddhi), the refutation of God as creator (Īśvarasādhanadūṣaṇa), the apoha theory of word meaning (Apohasiddhi), proofs of universal momentariness (Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi), the refutation of enduring entities (Sthirasiddhidūṣaṇa), the logic of invariable concomitance and reduction of valid cognitions (Vyāptinirṇaya, Pramāṇāntarbhāvaprakaraṇa), and an ultimate idealist critique of external objects and other minds (Citrādvaitaprakāśavāda, Santānāntaradūṣaṇa).
SA_T11_bsa075_u.attribution: The ten philosophical treatises gathered here were composed by Ratnakīrti. The collective title Ratnakīrtinibandhāvalī is used in modern scholarship and editions.
SA_T11_bsa075_u.edition: Anantalal Thakur: Ratnakīrti Nibandhāvalī. Patna: Kashiprasad Jayaswal Research Institute, 1975, pp. 1-149.
SA_T11_bsa075_u.coverage: complete — Contains the complete text of the treatises edited by Anantalal Thakur (1975, pp. 1–149), opening with the Sarvajñasiddhi and concluding with the Santānāntaradūṣaṇa.
translations: Gudrun Bühnemann, Der allwissende Buddha: ein Beweis und seine Probleme: Ratnakīrtis Sarvajñasiddhi, Wien, 1980. (German)

SA_T11_dhkhetuu.title: Hetubindu
SA_T11_dhkhetuu.author: Dharmakīrti
SA_T11_dhkhetuu.summary: The Hetubindu is a core philosophical treatise by Dharmakīrti expounding the theory of the logical reason or probans (hetu). Dharmakīrti defines the triple characteristic of valid evidence (trairūpya), classifies inferential evidence into effect (kārya), essential nature (svabhāva), and non-cognition (anupalabdhi), and refutes rival non-Buddhist views such as the sixfold characterization of the reason (ṣaḍlakṣaṇa). This digital text presents Ernst Steinkellner's 1967 scholarly Sanskrit reconstruction from the Tibetan text and Arcaṭa's commentary.
SA_T11_dhkhetuu.attribution: Attributed to Dharmakīrti across Buddhist traditions as one of his works on logic/epistemology. Major Sanskrit commentaries include Arcaṭa's Hetubinduṭīkā (with Durveka Miśra's Āloka).
SA_T11_dhkhetuu.edition: Ernst Steinkellner, Dharmakīrti's Hetubinduḥ. Teil I: Tibetischer Text und rekonstruierter Sanskrit-Text. (VSKSO 4) Wien: Hermann Böhlaus Nachf., 1967.
SA_T11_dhkhetuu.coverage: complete — Reconstructed Sanskrit text ending with the colophon: 'hetubindur ācārya-dharmakīrti-kṛtaḥ samāptaḥ'.
translations: Ernst Steinkellner, Dharmakīrti's Hetubinduḥ. Teil II: Übersetzung und Anmerkungen. Wien: Hermann Böhlaus Nachf., 1967. (German)

SA_T11_dhknyayu.title: Nyāyabindu
SA_T11_dhknyayu.author: Dharmakīrti
SA_T11_dhknyayu.summary: The Nyāyabindu ('Drop of Logic') is Dharmakīrti's concise manual of Buddhist logic and epistemology. In three chapters, it presents perception (pratyakṣa) as non-conceptual and free from error, inference for oneself (svārthānumāna) grounded in the threefold mark and ontological relation, and inference for others (parārthānumāna) treating proof, examples, and logical fallacies.
SA_T11_dhknyayu.attribution: Ascribed to Dharmakīrti. The text in this file consists strictly of the sūtra root text and does not include the commentary of Dharmottara or the sub-commentary of Durvekamiśra.
SA_T11_dhknyayu.edition: Dalsukhbhai Malvania (ed.), Paṇḍita Durveka Miśra's Dharmottarapradīpa: [Being a sub-commentary on Dharmottara's Nyāyabinduṭīkā, a commentary on Dharmakīrti's Nyāyabindu], Patna: 2nd ed. 1971 (1st ed. 1955).
SA_T11_dhknyayu.coverage: complete — Root text across all three chapters (paricchedas): 1. Pratyakṣapariccheda (sūtras 1.1–1.20, numbered 01001–01020), 2. Svārthānumānapariccheda (sūtras 2.1–2.48, numbered 02001–02048), and 3. Parārthānumānapariccheda (sūtras 3.1–3.140, numbered 03001–03140).

SA_T11_dhkprviu.title: Pramāṇaviniścaya (fragment)
SA_T11_dhkprviu.author: Dharmakīrti
SA_T11_dhkprviu.summary: The Pramāṇaviniścaya ('Ascertainment of Valid Cognition') is Dharmakīrti's synthetic exposition of epistemology and logic across three chapters: perception (pratyakṣa), inference for oneself (svārthānumāna), and inference for others (parārthānumāna). This electronic file preserves only a single palm-leaf folio fragment from chapter 3, identified and published by Kazunobu Matsuda and Ernst Steinkellner in 1991 from the National Archives in Kathmandu before the discovery of complete Sanskrit manuscripts in Tibet. The passage comprises Dharmakīrti's prose autocommentary and a summarizing verse (saṃgrahaśloka v. 84) refuting the non-Buddhist proof of an enduring self (ātman) inferred from bodily activities such as breathing.
SA_T11_dhkprviu.attribution: The Pramāṇaviniścaya is undisputed as one of the seven primary epistemological treatises (tshad ma sde bdun) of Dharmakīrti (fl. c. 6th–7th c. CE), combining verses (kārikā) and prose autocommentary (vṛtti).
SA_T11_dhkprviu.edition: K. Matsuda und E. Steinkellner: "The Sanskrit Manuscripts of Dharmakīrti's Pramāṇaviniścaya: Report on a Single Folio Fragment from the National Archives Collection, Kathmandu", WZKS 35 (1991), pp. 139-149.
SA_T11_dhkprviu.coverage: fragment — A single palm-leaf folio fragment (recto lines 1–5, verso lines 1–5; 41 segments, 1,695 characters) from chapter 3 (Parārthānumāna), preserving Dharmakīrti's prose autocommentary around a saṃgrahaśloka (v. 84 in modern counting) refuting the non-Buddhist proof of an ātman deduced from vital functions (prāṇādi).
translations: Ernst Steinkellner, Dharmakīrti's Pramāṇaviniścayaḥ. Zweites Kapitel: Svārthānumānam, Wien, 1979. (German)

SA_T11_dhkprvku.title: Pramāṇavārttikakārikā (chapters 2–4)
SA_T11_dhkprvku.author: Dharmakīrti
SA_T11_dhkprvku.summary: The Pramāṇavārttika is Dharmakīrti's principal treatise on Buddhist epistemology, logic, and philosophy of language, composed as an extensive commentary in verse on Dignāga's Pramāṇasamuccaya. This e-text contains the kārikās of chapters 2–4: Pramāṇasiddhi (establishing the authority of the Buddha and the criteria for valid knowledge), Pratyakṣa (analyzing perception, svalakṣaṇa, and reflexive awareness), and Parārthānumāna (treating inference-for-others and fallacies of proof). Chapter 1 (Svārthānumāna), to which Dharmakīrti composed his own prose autocommentary (Svavṛtti), is omitted from this file.
SA_T11_dhkprvku.attribution: Attributed to Dharmakīrti as a verse work commenting upon Dignāga's Pramāṇasamuccaya.
SA_T11_dhkprvku.edition: Yūshō Miyasaka (ed.), 'Pramāṇavārttika-Kārikā (Sanskrit and Tibetan)', in Acta Indologica, 1971/1972.
SA_T11_dhkprvku.coverage: partial — Contains only the verses of chapters 2–4: ch. 2 (Pramāṇasiddhi, vv. 1–285), ch. 3 (Pratyakṣa, vv. 1–539), and ch. 4 (Parārthānumāna, vv. 1–286). Chapter 1 (Svārthānumāna) is not present in this file.

SA_T11_dhkpvsvu.title: Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛtti
SA_T11_dhkpvsvu.author: Dharmakīrti
SA_T11_dhkpvsvu.summary: The Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛtti is Dharmakīrti's extensive prose autocommentary on the first chapter (Svārthānumāna, 'inference-for-oneself') of the Pramāṇavārttika. Dharmakīrti composed an autocommentary only for this chapter, establishing core principles of Buddhist logic such as the threefold mark of the reason (trairūpya), the necessary ontological relation (svabhāvapratibandha) underlying vyāpti, and negative reasoning (anupalabdhi). It also contains his seminal exposition of the nominalist apoha ('exclusion') doctrine of semantics and conceptual differentiation, coupled with detailed refutations of rival Brahmanical theories of universals and Vedic scriptural infallibility.
SA_T11_dhkpvsvu.attribution: Dharmakīrti composed a prose autocommentary (svavṛtti) exclusively on the first chapter (Svārthānumānapariccheda) of his Pramāṇavārttika; the subsequent three chapters were commented upon by his direct pupil Devendrabuddhi and later commentators.
SA_T11_dhkpvsvu.edition: Raniero Gnoli (ed.), The Pramāṇavārttikam of Dharmakīrti: The First Chapter with the Autocommentary. Text and Critical Notes. Serie Orientale Roma. Roma: Istituto Italiano per il Medio ed Estremo Oriente (IsMEO), 1960.
SA_T11_dhkpvsvu.coverage: complete — Complete text of Dharmakīrti's autocommentary on chapter 1 (Svārthānumāna) of the Pramāṇavārttika (340 kārikās embedded in prose vṛtti, preceded by the introductory maṅgala verses), corresponding in full to pages 1–176 of Raniero Gnoli's 1960 edition.
translations: Satkari Mookerjee and Hojun Nagasaki, The Pramāṇavārttikam of Dharmakīrti: An English Translation of the First Chapter with the Autocommentary and with Elaborate Comments [Kārikās 1–51]. Nava Nālandā Mahāvihāra Research Publication. Patna: Nava Nālandā Mahāvihāra, 1964. (English)

SA_T11_dhksparu.title: Sambandhaparīkṣā
SA_T11_dhksparu.author: Dharmakīrti
SA_T11_dhksparu.summary: The Sambandhaparīkṣā is a treatise consisting of 25 verses by the Buddhist epistemologist Dharmakīrti. In this work, Dharmakīrti critiques the ontological reality of relations, discussing concepts such as inherence (samavāya), contact (saṃyoga), and cause and effect (kāryakāraṇa).
SA_T11_dhksparu.attribution: Attributed to Dharmakīrti as one of his treatises on pramāṇa. The present e-text contains the 25 root kārikās.

SA_T11_dhkvadnu.title: Vādanyāya
SA_T11_dhkvadnu.author: Dharmakīrti
SA_T11_dhkvadnu.summary: The Vādanyāya ('Logic of Debate') is Dharmakīrti's treatise dedicated to dialectical methodology and the formal rules of philosophical debate. Dharmakīrti mounts a critical examination of the Naiyāyika theory of debate, rejecting the classical Nyāyasūtra taxonomy of twenty-two points of defeat (nigrahasthāna). He replaces them with two overarching criteria: the proponent's failure to present an essential member of a valid proof (asādhanāṅgavacana), and the opponent's alleging of a defect where none exists (adoṣodbhāvana).
SA_T11_dhkvadnu.attribution: Authored by Dharmakīrti (c. 6th–7th century CE); traditionally viewed as one of his seven logical treatises.
SA_T11_dhkvadnu.edition: Michael Torsten Much (ed.), Dharmakīrtis Vādanyāyaḥ. Teil I: Sanskrit-Text. Veröffentlichungen der Kommission für Sprachen und Kulturen Südasiens. Wien: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, 1991.
SA_T11_dhkvadnu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Vādanyāya, corresponding to pp. 1–68 of Much's 1991 critical edition. Motoi Ono's text is prefixed with 5-digit locators indexing Much's pagination and line numbers. It concludes with the closing verse and colophon 'vādanyāyo nāma prakaraṇaṃ samāptam'.

SA_T11_dhnyabpu.title: Nyāyabinduprakaraṇa with the commentaries of Vinītadeva and Dharmottara, and the Nyāyabinduṭīkāṭippaṇī
SA_T11_dhnyabpu.author: Dharmakīrti, Vinītadeva, Dharmottara
SA_T11_dhnyabpu.summary: The Nyāyabinduprakaraṇa ('A Drop of Logic') is Dharmakīrti's foundational introductory manual of Buddhist epistemology and logic, divided into three chapters: direct perception (pratyakṣa), inference for oneself (svārthānumāna), and inference for others (parārthānumāna). It defines valid cognition (pramāṇa), establishes the threefold mark of a sound logical reason (trairūpya), classifies inferential reasons into essential identity (svabhāva), causality (kārya), and non-perception (anupalabdhi), and details valid arguments and pseudo-reasons. This composite e-text presents Dharmakīrti's complete root treatise interleaved with the commentaries of Vinītadeva (Nyāyabinduvistaraṭīkā / Śiṣyahitā) and Dharmottara (Nyāyabinduṭīkā), together with an anonymous subcommentary (Nyāyabinduṭīkāṭippaṇī) for the first chapter.
SA_T11_dhnyabpu.attribution: The root work Nyāyabindu is by Dharmakīrti. The commentary Nyāyabinduvistaraṭīkā (Śiṣyahitā) is attributed to Vinītadeva. The Nyāyabinduṭīkā is by Dharmottara. The anonymous Nyāyabinduṭīkāṭippaṇī comments on Dharmottara's text.
SA_T11_dhnyabpu.edition: Swami Dwarikadas Shastri, ed., Nyāyabindu Prakaraṇa of Ācārya Dharmakīrti, with Commentary of Ārya Vinītadeva and Dharmottara. Varanasi 1994 (Bauddha Bhārati Series, 18).
SA_T11_dhnyabpu.coverage: complete — Complete across all three chapters (pratyakṣa, svārthānumāna, parārthānumāna) for Dharmakīrti's Nyāyabindu, Vinītadeva's commentary, and Dharmottara's commentary. The anonymous Nyāyabinduṭīkāṭippaṇī covers only the first chapter (pratyakṣapariccheda), corresponding to the scope of that text in Shastri's edition.
translations: Stcherbatsky, Theodore (1930). Buddhist Logic. Leningrad. (English)
Gangopadhyaya, Mrinalkanti (1971). Vinītadeva's Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā. Calcutta: Indian Studies: Past and Present. (English)

SA_T11_jithettu.title: Hetutattvopadeśa
SA_T11_jithettu.author: Jitāri
SA_T11_jithettu.summary: The Hetutattvopadeśa is an introductory primer on Buddhist logic composed by Jitāri. Closely following the model of the Nyāyapraveśa, the work outlines the three characteristics of a valid logical mark (trairūpya), the varieties of correct inferential reasons, and provides an exhaustive taxonomy of fallacies including defective theses (pakṣābhāsa), fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa), and fallacious examples (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa).
SA_T11_jithettu.attribution: The Sanskrit colophon attributes the work to Jitāri: 'kṛtir iyaṃ paṇḍitarājajitāripādānām'. In Tibetan sources he is also known as Jetāri.
SA_T11_jithettu.edition: Giuseppe Tucci, 'Hetutattvopadeśa of Jitāri', in Minor Buddhist Texts, Part I, Serie Orientale Roma IX, Rome: Istituto Italiano per il Medio ed Estremo Oriente (Is.M.E.O.), 1956, pp. 261–274.
SA_T11_jithettu.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising all 110 numbered sections and the concluding colophon, corresponding to pp. 261–274 of Giuseppe Tucci's edition.
translations: Miyasaka Yūshō, 'The Translation into Japanese and notes of the Jitāri's Hetu-tattova-upadeśa', Mikkyō Bunka, 1955. (Japanese)

SA_T11_jithetuu.title: Hetutattvopadeśa
SA_T11_jithetuu.author: Jitāri
SA_T11_jithetuu.summary: The Hetutattvopadeśa is a treatise on Buddhist logic (hetuvidyā/pramāṇa) composed by Jitāri. It expounds proof (sādhana), refutation (dūṣaṇa), the threefold mark of the logical reason (trairūpya), and the various fallacies of the thesis, reason, and example. This e-text preserves Durgacharan Chattopadhyaya's 1939 Sanskrit reconstruction from the Tibetan translation.
SA_T11_jithetuu.edition: Durgacharan Chattopadhyaya: Hetutattvopadeśa by Jitāri: reconstructed Sanskrit text with the Tibetan version. Calcutta: University of Calcutta 1939.
SA_T11_jithetuu.coverage: complete — Reconstructed Sanskrit text in 111 numbered sections, including initial summary kārikās, prose treatise on inference and logical fallacies, author colophon, and translator colophon.

SA_T11_jnaniva.title: Nibandhāvalī (incomplete)
SA_T11_jnaniva.author: Jñānaśrīmitra
SA_T11_jnaniva.summary: The Nibandhāvalī is a corpus of philosophical monographs by Jñānaśrīmitra. This digital text corresponds to the 1959 edition by Anantalal Thakur, but it is incomplete, breaking off mid-way through the Sākārasiddhiśāstra.
SA_T11_jnaniva.attribution: A collection of philosophical monographs (nibandhas) by Jñānaśrīmitra. The first item in the e-text is an introductory Sanskrit preface by the modern editor Anantalal Thakur.
SA_T11_jnaniva.edition: Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali (Buddhist Philosophical Works of Jñānaśrīmitra), ed. Anantalal Thakur. Tibetan Sanskrit Works Series Vol. V. Patna: Kashi Prasad Jayaswal Research Institute, 1959.

SA_T11_kgpramv.title: Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛtti with Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā
SA_T11_kgpramv.author: Dharmakīrti, Karṇakagomin
SA_T11_kgpramv.summary: Karṇakagomin's Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā is an extensive Sanskrit sub-commentary (ṭīkā) on Dharmakīrti's autocommentary (Svavṛtti) to the first chapter (Svārthānumāna, 'Inference for Oneself') of the Pramāṇavārttika. Composed around the 8th to 9th century CE, it offers thorough expositions of Buddhist epistemology, the exclusion theory of meaning (apoha), the nature of logical grounds (hetu), and extensive polemics against rival traditions. Preserved in a manuscript brought to light by Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana, the text is a vital witness both for establishing the text of Dharmakīrti's Svavṛtti and for tracing post-Dharmakīrti epistemological debate.
SA_T11_kgpramv.attribution: Dharmakīrti authored the Pramāṇavārttika kārikās and the autocommentary (Svavṛtti) on the Svārthānumāna chapter. Karṇakagomin composed the sub-commentary (ṭīkā).
SA_T11_kgpramv.edition: Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana (ed.), Ācārya-Dharmakīrteḥ Pramāṇavārttikam (svārthānumānaparicchedaḥ) svopajñavṛttyā Karṇakagomi-viracitayā taṭṭīkayā ca sahitam, Ilahabad: Kitab Mahal, 1943.
SA_T11_kgpramv.coverage: complete — Complete text of chapter 1 (Svārthānumānapariccheda) as preserved and edited by Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana. Dharmakīrti's autocommentary and Karṇakagomin's sub-commentary exist only for this chapter.

SA_T11_n1226u.title: Vādanyāya with Vipañcitārthā
SA_T11_n1226u.author: Dharmakīrti, Śāntarakṣita
SA_T11_n1226u.summary: The Vādanyāya ('Logic of Debate') is Dharmakīrti's final treatise on debate theory and the grounds of defeat (nigrahasthāna). Critiquing the classic Naiyāyika scheme of twenty-two defeat situations, Dharmakīrti reduces all points of defeat to two fundamental categories: failure to state an essential component of proof (asādhanāṅgavacana) by the proponent, and falsely alleging a defect where none exists (adoṣodbhāvana) by the opponent. Śāntarakṣita's 8th-century Vipañcitārthā is the sole surviving Sanskrit commentary on the text, providing extensive lexical explanations, contextual arguments, and refutations of rival non-Buddhist schools.
SA_T11_n1226u.attribution: The root work is Dharmakīrti's Vādanyāya; the commentary is Śāntarakṣita's Vipañcitārthā, explicitly confirmed by the opening incipit ('ācāryaśāntarakṣitapraṇītayā vipañcitārthābhidhayā ṭīkayā saṃvalitaḥ') and concluding colophon ('vipañcitārthā nāma vādanyāyaṭīkā samāptā || || kṛtiriyaṃ śāntarakṣitapādanāmiti'). Vinītadeva composed a separate commentary on the Vādanyāya (Toh 4240); assigning his name here was a metadata error.
SA_T11_n1226u.edition: Swami Dwarikadas Shastri (ed.), Vādanyāyaprakaraṇa of Dharmakīrti with Śāntarakṣita's Vipañcitārthā ṭīkā, Varanasi: Bauddha Bharati, 1972.
SA_T11_n1226u.coverage: complete — Text of Dharmakīrti's Vādanyāya accompanied by Śāntarakṣita's commentary Vipañcitārthā, author colophon, and scribal colophon dated to the reign of King Ānandadeva.
translations: Michael Torsten Much, Dharmakīrtis Vādanyāyaḥ. Teil II: Übersetzung und Anmerkungen, Veröffentlichungen der Kommission für Sprachen und Kulturen Südasiens / Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, 1991. (German (root text))

SA_T11_n1238u.title: Jātinirākṛti
SA_T11_n1238u.author: Jitāri
SA_T11_n1238u.summary: The Jātinirākṛti is a short polemical treatise by Jitāri. It refutes the realist doctrine of universals (jāti / sāmānya) held by Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika and Mīmāṃsā thinkers, asserting the Buddhist view that sāmānya cannot be said to be either identical with or distinct from particular individuals, and refutes Kumārila.
SA_T11_n1238u.attribution: The final colophon names Jitāri ('jātinirākṛtir iyaṃ jitāripādānām'); Tucci pointed out that in the colophon of the Jātinirākṛti the name is spelt Jitāri. Jitāri is associated with Vikramaśīlā.
SA_T11_n1238u.coverage: complete — Whole tract from the Mañjuśrī benediction ('namo mañjuśriye', verse 'mugdhāṅgulīkisalaya…') to the author colophon, with lacunae marked by dots and '( )'.

SA_T11_n1242u.summary: An anonymous ṭippaṇī (glosses) on Dharmottara's Nyāyabinduṭīkā, commenting on the first chapter (pratyakṣa) and breaking off incomplete.
SA_T11_n1242u.edition: Th. Stcherbatsky (ed.), Nyāyabinduṭīkāṭippaṇī (толкованіе на сочиненіе Дармоттары Nyāyabinduṭīkā), Bibliotheca Buddhica XI, St. Petersburg, 1909.
SA_T11_n1242u.coverage: partial — Glosses on Dharmottara's Nyāyabinduṭīkā, chapter 1 only: from the maṅgala ('jayanti jātivyasana…') through discussions of samyagjñāna and perception, breaking off mid-word ('tataścādhyav') near the end of chapter 1.

SA_T11_n2848u.title: Bauddheṣu pramāṇamīmāṃsā
SA_T11_n2848u.author: Jagannātha Upādhyāya
SA_T11_n2848u.summary: A modern Sanskrit essay on Buddhist epistemology (pramāṇamīmāṃsā). It argues that Buddhist discussion of the means of knowledge cannot be shown to be later than the Nyāyasūtra, as Vidyabhusana and Dasgupta held, pointing to the Buddhist positions criticised in the Nyāyasūtra's pūrvapakṣas and to the canonical emphasis on refuting other doctrines (Udāna). It then discusses the doctrine of the twofold form (dvairūpya) of cognition, defended both on the externalist and on the Vijñānavāda view.
SA_T11_n2848u.attribution: Modern Sanskrit essay arguing against the view of S. C. Vidyabhusana and S. N. Dasgupta that Buddhist pramāṇa discussion is later than the Nyāyasūtra, and ending with a defence of the twofold form (dvairūpya) of cognition in Buddhist pramāṇa.
SA_T11_n2848u.coverage: complete — Essay from heading to the closing quotation of a verse on dvairūpya and sahasaṃvittiniyama ('astyeva viduṣāṃ vādo bāhyaṃ tvāśritya varṇyate …'); no sign of truncation.

SA_T11_n2859u.title: Anupalabdhirahasya
SA_T11_n2859u.author: Jñānaśrīmitra
SA_T11_n2859u.summary: The Anupalabdhirahasya is a treatise on Buddhist epistemology by Jñānaśrīmitra addressing the problem of negative cognition. Building on Dharmakīrti's framework, Jñānaśrīmitra defines non-perception (anupalabdhi) not as a mere absence of awareness (upalabdhivirahamātra), but as an implicative negation (paryudāsa) consisting in the apprehension of something incompatible or distinct. He defends the status of anupalabdhi as a valid inferential sign (liṅga) for proving absence (abhāva) against rival Buddhist formulations and non-Buddhist theories such as the Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā doctrine of an independent means of knowledge (abhāvapramāṇa).
SA_T11_n2859u.attribution: A philosophical work by Jñānaśrīmitra, preserved in the collection of his treatises (Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī).
SA_T11_n2859u.edition: Birgit Kellner, Jñānaśrīmitra's Anupalabdhirahasya and Sarvaśabdābhāvacarcā. A Critical Edition with a Survey of his Anupalabdhi-Theory. Wiener Studien zur Tibetologie und Buddhismuskunde, Heft 67. Wien: Arbeitskreis für Tibetische und Buddhistische Studien, 2007.
SA_T11_n2859u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the monograph in prose and verse, from the opening verse (siddhānte viprakīrṇasyānupalambhasya...) through the final colophon (anupalabdhirahasyaṃ samāptam).

SA_T11_n2992u.title: Viśālāmalavatī Pramāṇasamuccayaṭīkā (chapter 2)
SA_T11_n2992u.author: Jinendrabuddhi
SA_T11_n2992u.summary: The Viśālāmalavatī Pramāṇasamuccayaṭīkā by Jinendrabuddhi is a sub-commentary on Dignāga's Pramāṇasamuccaya. This e-text contains Chapter 2, treating inference (anumāna, svārtha, parārtha) and related doctrines.
SA_T11_n2992u.attribution: Jinendrabuddhi composed the Viśālāmalavatī as a commentary on Dignāga's Pramāṇasamuccaya.

SA_T11_n634u.title: Nyāyapraveśakasūtra
SA_T11_n634u.author: Śaṅkarasvāmin
SA_T11_n634u.summary: The Nyāyapraveśakasūtra (commonly known as the Nyāyapraveśa), authored by Dignāga's pupil Śaṅkarasvāmin (c. 6th century CE), is an influential introductory manual of Buddhist logic and epistemology (hetuvidyā). It systematically defines the members of formal proof (sādhana) and refutation (dūṣaṇa), the three characteristics of a valid logical reason (trairūpya), the varieties of logical fallacies (pakṣābhāsa, hetvābhāsa, dṛṣṭāntābhāsa), and valid cognition through perception and inference. Translated into Chinese as T1630, it became the standard foundational treatise for East Asian Buddhist logic, and was widely preserved and commented upon in medieval India, notably by Jaina scholars.
SA_T11_n634u.attribution: Tibetan tradition (Degé Tengyur D4208) attributes the work to Dignāga (Phyogs-kyi glang-po). However, Chinese tradition (T1630) and modern scholarship attribute the manual to Dignāga's disciple Śaṅkarasvāmin. The Tibetan translation (D 4208) attributes the work to Dignāga (phyogs kyi glang po).
SA_T11_n634u.edition: Anandshankar B. Dhruva (ed.), The Nyāyapraveśa, Part I: Sanskrit Text with Commentaries (Gaekwad's Oriental Series No. XXXVIII), Baroda: Oriental Institute, 1930.
SA_T11_n634u.coverage: complete — Complete root text (sūtra) across segments, without the commentaries of Haribhadrasūri and Pārśvadevagaṇi printed in Dhruva's volume.
translations: Tachikawa, Musashi, 'A Sixth-Century Manual of Indian Logic (A Translation of the Nyāyapraveśa)', 1971. (English)

SA_T11_pramanvu.title: Pramāṇavārttika
SA_T11_pramanvu.author: Dharmakīrti
SA_T11_pramanvu.summary: The Pramāṇavārttika is the foundational treatise of Dharmakīrti and a central text of Buddhist epistemology and logic. Composed in verse as an extensive development of Dignāga's Pramāṇasamuccaya, it establishes valid cognition and related doctrines. This e-text contains the metrical root verses (kārikās) across four chapters.
SA_T11_pramanvu.attribution: Composed by Dharmakīrti as an expansive verse treatise elaborating and defending Dignāga's Pramāṇasamuccaya. The e-text contains solely the root verses (kārikās) across all four chapters, without commentary.

SA_T11_prpva.title: Pramāṇavārttikakārikā with Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra (chapters 2–4)
SA_T11_prpva.author: Dharmakīrti, Prajñākaragupta
SA_T11_prpva.summary: The Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra (also known as the Pramāṇavārttikabhāṣya) is Prajñākaragupta's monumental commentary on Dharmakīrti's Pramāṇavārttika, covering the chapters on Pramāṇasiddhi, Pratyakṣa, and Parārthānumāna. Prajñākaragupta formulated an influential and distinct philosophical current in late Indian Buddhist epistemology, synthesising logico-epistemological rigor with Yogācāra-Mādhyamika non-dualism (advaitavāda) and religious soteriology. In Sanskrit, the work is preserved in a single palm-leaf manuscript brought to light by Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana, alongside an authoritative Tibetan translation in the Tanjur.
SA_T11_prpva.attribution: Dharmakīrti composed the root verses of the Pramāṇavārttika. Prajñākaragupta authored this commentary (referred to as Alaṅkāra or Mahābhāṣya), covering chapters 2–4.
SA_T11_prpva.edition: Pramāṇavārtikabhāṣyam or Vārtikālaṅkāraḥ of Prajñākaragupta (Being a Commentary on Dharmakīrti's Pramāṇavārtikam), edited by Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana, Tibetan Sanskrit Works Series, Patna: Kashi Prasad Jayaswal Research Institute, 1953.
SA_T11_prpva.coverage: partial — Contains Dharmakīrti's Pramāṇavārttikakārikā chapters 2–4 (Pramāṇasiddhi, Pratyakṣa, and Parārthānumāna; internal paricchedas 1–3 of the commentary). For Prajñākaragupta's commentary itself the text is complete, as he did not comment on chapter 1 (Svārthānumāna).
translations: Ono, Motoi. Prajñākaraguptas Erklärung der Definition gültiger Erkenntnis: Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra zu Pramāṇavārttika II 1–7. Teil II: Übersetzung und Anmerkungen. Vienna: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, 2000. (German)
tshad ma rnam 'grel gyi rgyan (Derge Tengyur D 4221): translated by Bhavyarāja, rngog blo ldan shes rab; revised by zangs dkar lo tsA ba 'phags pa shes rab, Kumāraśrī (Tibetan)

SA_T11_ratksanu.title: Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi Vyatirekātmikā
SA_T11_ratksanu.author: Ratnakīrti
SA_T11_ratksanu.summary: The Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi Vyatirekātmikā ('Proof of Universal Momentariness by Negative Concomitance') is a philosophical monograph by Ratnakīrti, defending the epistemological arguments of his master Jñānaśrīmitra. Complementing his Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi Anvayātmikā, this treatise argues from negative contraposition: non-momentary (enduring) entities cannot exercise causal efficiency (arthakriyāsāmarthya) either in succession (krama) or simultaneously (akrama), and therefore cannot exist. Ratnakīrti pays particular attention to defusing the Nyāya objection that an inference with a non-existent subject incurs the fallacy of lack of substratum (āśrayāsiddhi).
SA_T11_ratksanu.attribution: Authored by the Buddhist epistemologist Ratnakīrti (written about 1000–1050 CE), student of Jñānaśrīmitra. The text closes with the author colophon: iti kṛtir iyaṃ ratnakīrteḥ.
SA_T11_ratksanu.edition: A. Charlene Senape McDermott, An eleventh-century Buddhist logic of 'exists'. Dordrecht: Reidel, 1969 (Foundations of language; Supplementary series, 11).
SA_T11_ratksanu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi Vyatirekātmikā, corresponding to pp. 77–88 of Anantalal Thakur's 1957 edition of the Ratnakīrtinibandhāvalī.
translations: A. Charlene Senape McDermott, An Eleventh-Century Buddhist Logic of 'Exists': Ratnakīrti's Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhiḥ Vyatirekātmikā, Foundations of Language Supplementary Series, Vol. 11 (Dordrecht: Reidel, 1969). (English)
Tatsuhiko Shiraishi, 'A Study of Ratnakīrti's Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi Vyatirekātmikā (1)', Journal of Indian and Buddhist Studies (Indogaku Bukkyōgaku Kenkyū) 51 (2003). (Japanese)

SA_T11_rvadrahu.title: Vādarahasya
SA_T11_rvadrahu.summary: The Vādarahasya is a Buddhist philosophical treatise preserved in a manuscript photographed by Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana in Tibet (preserved on film and glass negatives at the Bihar Research Society, Patna). The work defends Buddhist philosophical positions against Udayana's Ātmatattvaviveka and references Jñānaśrīmitra.
SA_T11_rvadrahu.attribution: First edited by Raghunath Pandey in 1984 under the title 'Ācāryaratnakīrtiviracitam Udayananirākaraṇam', who conjecturally attributed it to Ratnakīrti. The manuscript does not name Ratnakīrti and the authorship is uncertain.
SA_T11_rvadrahu.coverage: complete — Text based on R. N. Pandey's 1984 edition.

SA_T11_samtasi.title: Saṃtānāntarasiddhi
SA_T11_samtasi.author: Dharmakīrti
SA_T11_samtasi.summary: The Saṃtānāntarasiddhi ('Proof of Other Mindstreams') is Dharmakīrti's short philosophical treatise on the problem of other minds and the refutation of solipsism. Beginning with a single introductory verse followed by concise prose dialectic, Dharmakīrti shows that inferring the presence of an external continuum of consciousness by observing bodily and vocal activity operates with equal logical validity in an idealist (cittamātra/vijñaptimātra) ontology as in a realist one. The treatise concludes by examining the status and scope of telepathic cognition (paracittajñāna) possessed by yogins and awakened buddhas within an anti-realist epistemological framework.
SA_T11_samtasi.attribution: The Saṃtānāntarasiddhi is traditionally listed as one of the seven treatises of Dharmakīrti, categorized as one of the four supplementary treatises ('branches'). The work survived completely in Tibetan translation (D 4219). This e-text is a modern reconstruction into Sanskrit by J. S. Negi.
SA_T11_samtasi.edition: J. S. Negi (ed.), Santānāntarasiddhi (kārikā & ṭīkā, reconstructed), Sarnath: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 1997, pp. 1-30.
SA_T11_samtasi.coverage: complete — Complete text of Dharmakīrti's prakaraṇa in Sanskrit reconstruction (opening with the introductory verse 'buddhipūrvāṃ kriyāṃ dṛṣṭvā svadehe...' and concluding with 'acintyo hi bhagavataḥ sarvārthādhigamaḥ...').
translations: Th. Stcherbatsky, Russian translation of Dharmakīrti's Saṃtānāntarasiddhi, Petrograd, 1922. (Russian)
H. C. Gupta (trans.), 'Papers of Th. Stcherbatsky', Calcutta, 1969, p. 73 sq. (English)
Hidenori Kitagawa, translation of Santanāntarasiddhi. (English)
Shōryū Katsura, 'Dharmakīrti's Saṃtānāntarasiddhi--Japanese translation and synopsis', 1983. (Japanese)
Thomas E. Wood, translation in Mind Only: A Philosophical and Doctrinal Analysis of the Vijñānavāda. (English)
rgyud gzhan grub pa zhes bya ba'i rab tu byed pa (Derge Tengyur D 4219): translated by Viśuddhasiṃha, ska ba dpal brtsegs (Tibetan)

SA_T11_sbpramvu.title: Pramāṇavārttikaṭīkā (fragments)
SA_T11_sbpramvu.author: Śākyabuddhi
SA_T11_sbpramvu.summary: The Pramāṇavārttikaṭīkā by Śākyabuddhi is a Buddhist epistemological sub-commentary on Dharmakīrti's Pramāṇavārttika and its autocommentary. The surviving Sanskrit fragments include discussions on nominal exclusion (apoha), universals (sāmānya), and non-perception (anupalabdhi). The complete text survives in Tibetan translation (D 4220).
SA_T11_sbpramvu.attribution: Śākyabuddhi is the author of this ṭīkā on Dharmakīrti's Pramāṇavārttika. The Tibetan translation (D 4220) attributes the work to Śākyamati (shAkya'i blo).
SA_T11_sbpramvu.edition: M. Inami, K. Matsuda und T. Tani: A study of the Pramāṇavārttikaṭīkā by Śākyabuddhi from the National Archives collection, Kathmandu, Tokyo 1992 (Studia Tibetica, 23)
SA_T11_sbpramvu.coverage: fragment — Surviving Sanskrit manuscript fragments from the National Archives collection, Kathmandu, commenting on Dharmakīrti's Pramāṇavārttika.
translations: tshad ma rnam 'grel gyi 'grel bshad (Derge Tengyur D 4220): translated by rma dge ba'i blo gros (Tibetan)

SA_T12_n2957u.title: Vṛttamālāstuti with Vṛttamālāvivṛti
SA_T12_n2957u.author: Jñānaśrīmitra, Śākyarakṣita
SA_T12_n2957u.summary: The Vṛttamālāstuti is a Buddhist devotional and prosodical work composed by Jñānaśrīmitra in praise of Mañjuśrī, illustrating meters. The e-text includes the root verses along with the commentary (vivṛti) by Śākyarakṣita.
SA_T12_n2957u.attribution: The root hymn was authored by Jñānaśrīmitra, identified in the colophon as mahāpaṇḍitasthavirajñānaśrīmitra. The commentary (Vṛttamālavivṛti) was identified by Michael Hahn as the work of Śākyarakṣita.
SA_T12_n2957u.coverage: complete — Text of the Vṛttamālāstuti along with commentary, ending at verse 154 and the author colophon.
translations: Michael Hahn, Jñānaśrīmitras Vṛttamālāstuti: Eine Beispielsammlung zur altindischen Metrik, Wiesbaden: Otto Harrassowitz, 1971. (German)
sdeb sbyor gyi phreng ba'i bstod pa (Derge Tengyur D 4305): translated by shong lo tsA ba rdo rje rgyal mtshan/ shong ston rdo rje rgyal mtshan, dpang lo tsA ba blo gros brtan pa (Tibetan)

SA_T12_n801u.title: Chandoratnākara with Chandoratnākaravṛtti
SA_T12_n801u.author: Ratnākaraśānti
SA_T12_n801u.summary: The Chandoratnākara along with its autocommentary (Chandoratnākaravṛtti) by Ratnākaraśānti is a Buddhist treatise on metrics (chandaḥśāstra), expounding syllabic metres (varṇavṛtta), moraic metres (jāti), and related topics.
SA_T12_n801u.attribution: Both the root verses and the accompanying svopajñavṛtti commentary are ascribed to Ratnākaraśānti.
SA_T12_n801u.edition: Chandoratnākaraḥ: Svopajñavṛttyā Samanvitaḥ [Chandoratnākara of Kalikālasarvajña Ratnākaraśāntipāda with Auto-commentary], Bhoṭa-Bhāratīya Granthamālā 18, Sarnath, Varanasi: Kendrīya Ucca Tibbatī Śikṣā Saṃsthāna, 1990.
SA_T12_n801u.coverage: complete — Contains the Chandoratnākara along with its autocommentary, followed by the colophons.
