SA_T13_bghsic_u.title: Padyacūḍāmaṇi
SA_T13_bghsic_u.author: Buddhaghoṣa
SA_T13_bghsic_u.summary: The Padyacūḍāmaṇi is a Sanskrit mahākāvya in ten cantos ascribed to Buddhaghoṣa, describing the life of prince Siddhārtha culminating in the defeat of Māra and awakening under the Bodhi tree.
SA_T13_bghsic_u.attribution: Ascribed in the text to Buddhaghoṣa (ācārya).
SA_T13_bghsic_u.coverage: complete — Ten sargas, from the maṅgala to the defeat of Māra and Awakening under the Bodhi tree (10.58), ending with the colophon 'iti buddhaghoṣaviracite padyacūḍāmaṇināmni mahākāvye siddhārthacarite daśamaḥ sargaḥ'.

SA_T13_davyasou.title: Yaśodharācarita (verses 1–55)
SA_T13_davyasou.author: Davuldeṇa Jñāneśvara
SA_T13_davyasou.summary: A modern Sanskrit narrative poem (kāvya) depicting the life and devotion of Princess Yaśodharā, the wife of Prince Siddhārtha Gautama. Drawing upon classical Buddhist narrative lore and the Sinhala Yasodharāvata tradition, this opening instalment (verses 1–55) portrays Yaśodharā's grief and confusion upon discovering Siddhārtha's secret departure, her frantic search throughout the royal palace, discarding her ornaments, supplicating the deities, and reminiscing about their early marriage.
SA_T13_davyasou.edition: Bhikkhu Pāsādika and Bhikkhu Tampalawela Dhammaratana, 'Contemporary Sri Lankan Sanskrit Poetry: The Yaśodharācaritam by Davuldeṇa Jñāneśvara Mahāsthavira', Bulletin d'etudes indienne 21.1 (2003), pp. 47-70.

SA_T13_n2940u.title: Triratnasaundaryagāthā
SA_T13_n2940u.author: Sundarānanda
SA_T13_n2940u.summary: The Triratnasaundaryagāthā is a Sanskrit historical work comprising 286 verses (concluding with 'iti śrītriratnasaundaryagāthāyāṁ prakṛtiratnaṁ samāptam'). It recounts events concerning Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha and the Shah dynasty, Prime Minister Bhīmasena Thāpā, and concludes with verses commemorating Queen Lalit Tripurasundarī.
SA_T13_n2940u.coverage: complete — Complete Sanskrit text (286 verses, designated 'prakṛtiratna' in the final colophon).

SA_T13_n2976u.title: Saṅgītamālikā
SA_T13_n2976u.author: Yatīndravimala Caturdhurīṇa
SA_T13_n2976u.summary: A modern Sanskrit cycle of four devotional songs on Yaśodharā (Gopā), wife of Prince Siddhārtha, by Yatīndravimala Caturdhurīṇa: a hymn of praise, her birth together with the Buddha's companions, her wedding day, and a final prayer that she bring peace to a world threatened by atomic weapons and Sputnik and spread the Five Precepts among the Buddhist countries of Asia and India.
SA_T13_n2976u.attribution: Modern Sanskrit composition by Yatīndravimala Caturdhurīṇa. The reference to the Soviet Sputnik ('rusa-sphuṭanika', 4.3) dates the songs to 1957 or later.
SA_T13_n2976u.coverage: complete — Four songs on Yaśodharā: (1) Śrīśrīyaśodharā-stuti (4 stanzas), (2) Yaśodharā-janma, (3) Vivāhavāsare Yaśodharā (6 stanzas), (4) 'Sukhado jananī-niyata-vikāśaḥ' (8 stanzas), ending with stanza 8 at printed page 137. Printed page numbers 116–137 in the e-text indicate a section of a larger book; the songs themselves are complete.

SA_T13_n3004u.title: Paścāttāpa
SA_T13_n3004u.author: Davuldena Jñāneśvara
SA_T13_n3004u.summary: A short modern Sanskrit poem of 15 anuṣṭubh stanzas addressed to Dharmaratna. The poet laments the infirmities of old age: trembling, failing sight that spectacles (upacakṣus) no longer help, loss of memory, and his books lying unread in the library to be gnawed by worms and mice. Recalling the Buddhist teaching that everything in saṃsāra ends in decay, except the imperishable liberation taught by the Muni, he voices regret (paścāttāpa) for his lost youth and his inability to compose further poetry.
SA_T13_n3004u.attribution: In the poem the author calls himself 87 years old ('ā janmano 'śitisaptavarṣiko', v. 15). Verse 1 addresses a Dharmaratna.

SA_T13_n929u.title: Saundarananda
SA_T13_n929u.author: Aśvaghoṣa
SA_T13_n929u.summary: The Saundarananda is an early classical Sanskrit mahākāvya in eighteen cantos composed by Aśvaghoṣa (c. 1st–2nd century CE). It recounts the conversion of the Buddha's handsome half-brother Nanda, depicting his infatuation with his wife Sundarī, his reluctant ordination, and his spiritual transformation guided by the Buddha. Employing ornate kāvya aesthetics, the work provides an elaborate exposition of Buddhist doctrine, sense-restraint, and meditation, culminating in Nanda's attainment of arhatship.
SA_T13_n929u.edition: E.H. Johnston (ed.), The Saundarananda of Aśvaghoṣa (Sanskrit text). London: Oxford University Press / Humphrey Milford, 1928 (Panjab University Oriental Publications)
SA_T13_n929u.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all 18 cantos (sargas), concluding at verse 18.64.
translations: E.H. Johnston (trans.), The Saundarananda, 1932. (English)
Linda Covill (trans.), 2007. (English)
Lobsang Jamspal (trans.), Saundarananda Mahākāvya of Ācārya Aśvaghoṣa, Sarnath: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies. (Tibetan)

SA_T14_bsa044_u.title: Kriyāsaṃgrahakārikā
SA_T14_bsa044_u.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T14_bsa044_u.summary: The Kriyāsaṃgrahakārikā is a concise ten-verse mnemonic summary (uddāna) attributed to Nāgārjuna, outlining the essential sequence of Vajrayāna temple construction, consecration, and monastic ritual procedures. It enumerates the preliminary examination of guru and disciple, site selection and purification, propitiation of the earth deity and site serpent (vāstunāgaparīkṣā), brick-laying and architectural measurements, maṇḍala layout and thread-casting, fire rites (homa), image installation and consecration (pratiṣṭhā), monastic ordination (pravrajyā), and the repair of dilapidated shrines (jīrṇoddhāra).
SA_T14_bsa044_u.attribution: Attributed in the colophon to Nāgārjunapāda ('kṛtiriyaṃ nāgārjunapādānām').
SA_T14_bsa044_u.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising all 10 anuṣṭubh verses and the closing colophons.

SA_T14_bsu059_u.title: Samyaksambuddhabhāṣitapratimālakṣaṇa
SA_T14_bsu059_u.summary: The Samyaksambuddhabhāṣitapratimālakṣaṇa is a manual of Buddhist iconometry. Framed as a discourse at Jetavana where the Buddha instructs Śāriputra on how devotees should fashion icons after the Teacher's departure or parinirvāṇa, the text establishes canonical proportions (pramāṇa) for images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Across 54 verses, it details precise measurements in bodily units (aṅgula, mātrā, vyāma) for the uṣṇīṣa, cranial contours, facial features, torso, and limbs, as well as distinct facial types for various classes of divine, human, and semi-divine beings.
SA_T14_bsu059_u.attribution: Framed in the standard form of a Buddhist sūtra (nidāna opening 'evaṃ mayā śrutamekasmin samaye...'): the Buddha, residing at Jetavana in Śrāvastī after returning from preaching to his mother in Tuṣita, explains the proportional rules (pramāṇa) of holy images to Śāriputra.
SA_T14_bsu059_u.edition: Ngawang Samten and Janardan Pandey (eds.), 'Samyaksambuddhabhāṣitaṃ pratimālakṣaṇam', in Dhīḥ: Journal of Rare Buddhist Texts Research Unit, Sarnath: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 2003, pp. 117–136.
SA_T14_bsu059_u.coverage: complete — Complete root text consisting of the opening prose nidāna and 54 verses, concluding with the colophon 'iti samyaksambuddhabhāṣitaṃ pratimālakṣaṇaṃ samāptam'.
translations: Charles Willemen, Defining the Image - Measurements in image-making, Sri Satguru Publications (Indian Books Centre), 2006. (English)

rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas kyis gsungs pa'i sku gzugs kyi mtshan nyid kyi rnam 'grel zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 4315): translated by Dharmadhara, yar lung lo tsA ba grags pa rgyal mtshan; at mang yul gung thang gi rgyal sa (Tibetan)

SA_T14_n1279u.title: Ātreyatilaka
SA_T14_n1279u.author: Ātreya
SA_T14_n1279u.summary: The Ātreyatilaka (also titled Pratibimbalakṣaṇa) is a Sanskrit Buddhist manual of iconometry (śilpaśāstra) traditionally attributed to the sage Ātreya. Comprising 144 anuṣṭubh verses, it defines the tālamāna proportional canons and precise dimensional units (aṅgula, yava, kalā, etc.) for constructing sacred Buddhist images from crown to pedestal. The final section (vv. 141–144) details jīrṇoddhāra, prescribing religious rites for repairing, re-installing, or ritually decommissioning damaged, broken, or weathered earthen and metal icons.
SA_T14_n1279u.attribution: The treatise is traditionally ascribed to the sage Ātreya (in Tibetan Tanjur D 4316 as Ātre). In the opening verses (1–2), the text describes itself as compiling image-proportion rules taught by former sages in Buddhist treatises (ātreyatilake bauddhaśāstre'nyatra purātanaiḥ | uktaṃ yatpūrvamunibhiḥ pratimāmānalakṣaṇam).
SA_T14_n1279u.edition: 'Ātreyaviracitam Ātreyatilakam (Pratibimbalakṣaṇam)', Dhīḥ: Rare Buddhist Texts Research Journal, pp. 137–154.
SA_T14_n1279u.coverage: complete — Contains the complete text of 144 verses, concluding with the jīrṇoddhāra (image restoration/disposal) chapter and final colophon.
translations: Phanindra Nath Bose, Pratimā-māna-lakṣaṇam, Lahore: Moti Lal Banarsi Das, 1929. (English)
sku gzugs kyi tshad kyi mtshan nyid ces bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 4316): translated by Dharmadhara, yar lung lo tsA ba grags pa rgyal mtshan (Tibetan)

SA_T14_n1282u.title: Pratimālakṣaṇavivaraṇa
SA_T14_n1282u.summary: The Pratimālakṣaṇavivaraṇa is a Buddhist Sanskrit commentary explaining the canonical iconometric treatise Pratimālakṣaṇa (or Samyaksambuddhabhāṣitapratimālakṣaṇa). It details the tālamāna and aṅgula measurement systems and proportions required to construct images of the Buddha (conforming to the nyagrodhaparimaṇḍala and ten-tāla canon), Bodhisattvas, goddesses (such as Locanā, nine tālas), wrathful figures (krodhas), and auxiliary deities.
SA_T14_n1282u.attribution: The commentary is traditionally titled Samyaksambuddhabhāṣitapratimālakṣaṇavivaraṇa. The specific historical author is unknown. The work was translated into Tibetan by the Indian paṇḍita Dharmadhara and the Tibetan translator Grags-pa rgyal-mtshan (D4315).
SA_T14_n1282u.edition: Ngawang Samten & Janardan Pandey (ed.), Samyaksaṃbuddhabhāṣitaṃ Pratimālakṣaṇam, in Dhīḥ: Journal of Rare Buddhist Texts Research 35 (2003), pp. 117-136, Sarnath: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies.
SA_T14_n1282u.coverage: complete — The commentary is complete up to the colophon at segment [194] ('iti samyaksambuddhabhāṣitaṃ pratimālakṣaṇavivaraṇaṃ samāptam'). Segments [195]–[201] are an accidental digital duplication of preceding lines (describing Rāhu, Ketu, Nāgas, and the five-tāla system) truncated mid-sentence.
translations: rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas kyis gsungs pa'i sku gzugs kyi mtshan nyid kyi rnam 'grel zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 4315): translated by Dharmadhara, yar lung lo tsA ba grags pa rgyal mtshan; at mang yul gung thang gi rgyal sa (Tibetan)

SA_T14_nagcitpu.title: Citralakṣaṇa
SA_T14_nagcitpu.author: Nagnajit
SA_T14_nagcitpu.summary: The Citralakṣaṇa is an Indian treatise on painting and image proportions (iconometry) attributed to Nagnajit. The text relates a narrative involving a king who disputes with Yama to retrieve a dead boy, where Brahmā intervenes, and details iconometric standards (parimāṇa) for universal monarchs (cakravartins) and figures. It is preserved in Tibetan in the Tanjur (Peking no. 5806).
SA_T14_nagcitpu.attribution: The original Sanskrit text survived in Tibetan translation in the Tanjur (Peking no. 5806). The Sanskrit text in this e-text is based on the edition by Asoke Chatterjee Sastri published in 1987.
SA_T14_nagcitpu.edition: Asoke Chatterjee Sastri, The Citralakṣaṇa: An Old Text of Indian Art, Sanskrit, Tibetan and English Version. Calcutta 1987 (Bibliotheca Indica Series, 315).
SA_T14_nagcitpu.coverage: complete — Preserved in three parivartas; chapter 1 relates the narrative of King Bhayajit/Nagnajit, Yama, and Brahmā, and chapter 3 covers iconometric proportions (parimāṇa), ending with 'iti citralakṣaṇe parimāṇo nāmstṛtīyaḥ parivartaḥ / yāvat brahmaṇaḥ parimāṇalekhayaḥ samāptaḥ'.
translations: Berthold Laufer, Das Citralakṣaṇa nach dem tibetischen Tanjur herausgegeben und übersetzt. Leipzig: Otto Harrassowitz, 1913 (Dokumente der indischen Kunst, Heft 1: Malerei). (German)
B. N. Goswamy and A. L. Dahmen-Dallapiccola, An Early Document of Indian Art: The Citralakṣaṇa of Nagnajit. New Delhi: Manohar, 1976. (English)
Asoke Chatterjee Sastri, The Citralakṣaṇa: An Old Text of Indian Art, Sanskrit, Tibetan and English Version. Calcutta, 1987 (Bibliotheca Indica Series, 315). (English)

SA_T14_stuplaku.title: Stūpalakṣaṇakārikā with Stūpalakṣaṇakārikāvivecana
SA_T14_stuplaku.author: Bhadravyūha
SA_T14_stuplaku.summary: The Stūpalakṣaṇakārikā is an architectural and ritual verse treatise composed by Bhadravyūha of the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin school, setting forth the canonical dimensions, proportions, and structural units of Buddhist stūpas alongside a systematic doctrinal mapping of its components onto Buddhist dharmas (such as the 37 bodhipakṣikadharmas, the four noble truths, and the elements). It is accompanied by the anonymous Stūpalakṣaṇakārikāvivecana, a detailed prose commentary that interprets each stanza with reference to the Lokottaravādin Prakīrṇakavinaya and related monastic traditions. Preserved in a single early Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript, the work constitutes one of the rare surviving Sanskrit treatises on non-Tantric Buddhist stūpa architecture and architectural symbolism.
SA_T14_stuplaku.attribution: The root kārikās and list of symbolic correspondences are explicitly attributed to Ācārya Bhadravyūha of the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin lineage in verse 2 ('sarvan tan setum iveha bhadravyūhena kathyate') and in the opening rubric ('ārya-lokottaravādino yat kṛtir ācārya-bhadravyūhasya'). The prose commentary (vivecana) is composed by an anonymous author who reveres Bhadravyūha.
SA_T14_stuplaku.edition: Gustav Roth, 'Edition of the Stūpa-lakṣaṇa-kārikā-vivecanaṃ, Including the prakīrṇaka-caitya-lakṣaṇaṃ', in: Dharmadūta: Mélanges offerts au Vénérable Thích Huyên-Vi à l'occasion de son soixante-dixième anniversaire, ed. Bhikkhu T. Dhammaratana, Bhikkhu Pāsādika, Paris 1997, pp. 205–231.
SA_T14_stuplaku.coverage: complete — Covers the entire text preserved in the manuscript. Folio 2 of the root text is missing, but fragmentary pieces of stanzas are quoted from the commentary. The commentary is followed by Newari notes.
translations: Gustav Roth, 'Symbolism of the Buddhist Stūpa According to the Tibetan Version of the Caitya-vibhāga-vinayodbhāva-sūtra, the Sanskrit Treatise Stūpa-lakṣaṇa-kārikā-vivecana, and the Corresponding Passage in Kuladatta's Kriyāsaṃgraha', in: The Stūpa: Its Religious, Historical and Architectural Significance, ed. Anna Libera Dallapiccola and Stephanie Zingel-Avé Lallemant, 1980. (English)

SA_T14_tarkrplu.title: Tarkarahasya (chapter 2: Pratyakṣalakṣaṇa)
SA_T14_tarkrplu.summary: This text constitutes the second chapter (Svaparapratyakṣalakṣaṇanyāyanirṇaya) of the Tarkarahasya. It defines sensory perception (pratyakṣa) as non-conceptual (kalpanāpoḍha) and non-erroneous (abhrānta). The chapter critiques alternative theories and definitions of perception formulated by other traditions—including the Bhāṭṭas, Śaivas, Vaiyākaraṇas, Naiyāyikas, Vaiśeṣikas, and Kāpilas/Mīmāṃsakas—as well as assessing Vasubandhu's definition.
SA_T14_tarkrplu.edition: YAITA, Hideomi: Tarkarahasya kenyū (I). Journal of Naritasan Institute for Buddhist Studies No. 12 (1988), 82-98.
SA_T14_tarkrplu.coverage: partial — Contains chapter 2 only (titled 'Svaparapratyakṣalakṣaṇanyāyanirṇaya', treating perception), corresponding to folios 16a–21b of the manuscript, pp. 33–44 of Paramanandan Shastri's 1979 edition, and pp. 82–98 of Hideomi Yaita's 1988 edition.

SA_T15_bsa060_u.title: Śatagāthā
SA_T15_bsa060_u.author: Vararuci
SA_T15_bsa060_u.summary: The Śatagāthā (also known as Gāthāśataka) is a Buddhist gnomic anthology (nītiśāstra) traditionally ascribed to Ācārya Vararuci. Preserved in the Tibetan Tanjur (D 4332), where it was translated by Vinayacandra and Dharmaprajña (Chos kyi shes rab), the work contains didactic verses on conduct, virtue, and ethics.
SA_T15_bsa060_u.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Ācārya Vararuci (Tib. Mchog sred) in the Tibetan Tanjur colophon (D 4332). Translated into Tibetan by Vinayacandra and Dharmaprajña (Chos kyi shes rab).
SA_T15_bsa060_u.edition: Losang Norbu Shastri: Śatagāthā. Sarnath: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 2001, pp. 59-158.
SA_T15_bsa060_u.coverage: complete — Complete text of 107 verses (vv. 1–107) along with the colophon.
translations: Losang Norbu Shastri, Śatagāthā of Ācārya Vararuci (Sanskrit Restoration, Tibetan Text, along with English and Hindi translations). (English)
Losang Norbu Shastri, Śatagāthā of Ācārya Vararuci (Sanskrit Restoration, Tibetan Text, along with English and Hindi translations). (Hindi)
tshigs su bcad pa brgya pa (Derge Tengyur D 4332): translated by Vinayacandra, shel dkar lo tsA ba chos kyi shes rab (Tibetan)

SA_T15_n1144u.title: Nītiśāstra
SA_T15_n1144u.author: Masūrākṣa
SA_T15_n1144u.summary: The Nītiśāstra of Masūrākṣa is a didactic collection of gnomic maxims in seven chapters. Preserved in the Tibetan Tanjur (D 4335) following its translation by the Indian paṇḍita Dharmaśrīvajra (Dharmaśrībhadra) and the Tibetan monk Śākyamati (Śākya blo-gros). The Sanskrit text in this digital collection constitutes the edition published by Sunitikumar Pathak.
SA_T15_n1144u.attribution: Ascribed to Masūrākṣa in the opening verse and the closing colophon. Preserved in the Tibetan Tanjur (D 4335), translated by the Indian paṇḍita Dharmaśrīvajra (Dharmaśrībhadra in Tanjur catalog) and the Tibetan monk Śākyamati (Śākya blo-gros). The Sanskrit text in this e-text represents Sunitikumar Pathak's edition/reconstruction from the Tibetan text.
SA_T15_n1144u.edition: Pathak, Sunitikumar (ed.). Nītiśāstra of Masūrākṣa (Tibetan and Sanskrit with an Introduction in English). Visva-Bharati Annals. Santiniketan: Visva-Bharati Research Publications, 1961.
SA_T15_n1144u.coverage: complete — Complete text in seven adhyāyas (chapters).
translations: lugs kyi bstan bcos (Derge Tengyur D 4335): translated by Dharmaśrībhadra, shAkya blo gros (Tibetan)

SA_T16_n1289u.title: Tarkabhāṣāṭīkā
SA_T16_n1289u.author: Embar Krishnamacharya
SA_T16_n1289u.summary: The Tarkabhāṣāṭīkā (or Tarkabhāṣāvyākhyā) is a Sanskrit commentary on the Tarkabhāṣā of Mokṣākaragupta (Jagaddhala Mahāvihāra). Composed by Embar Krishnamacharya for his 1942 edition in the Gaekwad's Oriental Series (No. 94), the commentary explicates the Buddhist logical manual.
SA_T16_n1289u.attribution: Embar Krishnamacharya composed this Sanskrit commentary for his 1942 edition. In the concluding verses, the author describes himself as living in Gujarat ('gurjareṣu vasan') and devoted to Padmanābha/Viṣṇu, yet composing a commentary on a Buddhist treatise ('viṣaye 'pi vasann eṣa tāthāgatakṛtiṃ vyadhāt').
SA_T16_n1289u.edition: Tarkabhāṣā of Mokṣākara Gupta, edited with a Sanskrit Commentary by Embar Krishnamacharya, Baroda: Oriental Institute, 1942 (Gaekwad's Oriental Series, No. XCIV [94]).
SA_T16_n1289u.coverage: complete — Commentary on Mokṣākaragupta's Tarkabhāṣā, ending with the verses and colophon 'iti tarkabhāṣāvyākhyā samāptā'.
translations: Yūichi Kajiyama, An Introduction to Buddhist Philosophy: An Annotated Translation of the Tarkabhāṣā of Mokṣākaragupta, Memoirs of the Faculty of Letters, Kyoto University 10 (1966). (English)

SA_T16_n2875u.title: Śvānastavakāvya
SA_T16_n2875u.author: Davuldeṇa Jñāneśvara
SA_T16_n2875u.summary: A Sanskrit kāvya in 55 classical metrical stanzas (plus a concluding signature verse) composed by Davuldeṇa Jñāneśvara Mahāsthavira. The poem depicts the steadfast loyalty, companionship, and grief of a dog attending an elderly and infirm ascetic master, contrasting the animal's noble devotion with human fickleness and drawing thematic parallels to the Bodhisattva's birth as a dog in Buddhist canonical lore.
SA_T16_n2875u.attribution: Composed by Davuldeṇa Jñāneśvara Mahāsthavira. The author identifies himself in the final signature strophe.
SA_T16_n2875u.edition: Bhikkhu Pāsādika, '‘Poem in Praise of a Dog’. Contemporary Sri Lankan Sanskrit Poetry: The Śvānastavakāvyam by Davuldeṇa Jñāneśvara Mahāsthavira', in: Dragomir Dimitrov, Ulrike Roesler and Roland Steiner (eds.), Śikhisamuccayaḥ: Indian and Tibetan Studies (Collectanea Marpurgensia Indologica et Tibetica 1), Wiener Studien zur Tibetologie und Buddhismuskunde, Heft 53, Wien: Arbeitskreis für Tibetische und Buddhistische Studien, Universität Wien, 2002.
SA_T16_n2875u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the 55 numbered stanzas plus 1 unnumbered concluding signature strophe identifying author and title (56 verses total).

SA_T16_n2916u.title: Svastyayanagāthā
SA_T16_n2916u.summary: The Svastyayanagāthā is a 17-verse benedictory hymn from the Chatravastu of the Mahāvastu representing a parallel to the Pāli Ratana Sutta (Sn / Khp). It praises the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha with the refrain 'etena satyena susvasti bhotu manuṣyato vā amanuṣyato vā'. It is preserved in the Tibetan canon under the title bDe legs su 'gyur ba'i tshigs su bcad pa (D818, D1102, D4401).
SA_T16_n2916u.attribution: Canonical verses extracted from the Chatravastu of the Mahāvastu, corresponding to the Pāli Ratana Sutta, also preserved as an independent text in the Tibetan canon (D818, D1102, D4401).
SA_T16_n2916u.edition: Svastyayanagāthā, input and proofread by Miroj Shakya, Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon (DSBC), Nagarjuna Institute of Exact Methods / University of the West, 2008 (book_788).
SA_T16_n2916u.coverage: complete — 17 stanzas extracted from the Chatravastu of the Mahāvastu.
translations: bde legs su 'gyur ba'i tshigs su bcad pa (Derge Kangyur D 818) (Tibetan)
bde legs su 'gyur ba'i tshigs su bcad pa (Derge Kangyur D 1102) (Tibetan)
bde legs su 'gyur ba'i tshigs su bcad pa (Derge Tengyur D 4401) (Tibetan)

SA_T16_n2959u.title: Vajrayānadarśanamīmāṃsā
SA_T16_n2959u.author: Wangchuk Dorjee Negi
SA_T16_n2959u.summary: The Vajrayānadarśanamīmāṃsā is a modern systematic treatise in Sanskrit composed by Bhikṣu Wangchuk Dorjee Negi examining the philosophy and hermeneutics of Vajrayāna Buddhism. Drawing upon major Tantras, classic Indian commentaries (including Candrakīrti's Pradīpodyotana and Ānandagarbha's works), and Tibetan scholastic sources, the author addresses the status of Tantra as buddhavacana, its relationship to the three turnings of the Dharma wheel, and the doctrine of the two stages (utpattikrama and niṣpannakrama). The treatise provides a thorough exposition of the integration of Madhyamaka emptiness, intrinsically luminous mind (prakṛtiprabhāsvara-citta), and tantric yogic praxis.
SA_T16_n2959u.attribution: A modern Sanskrit treatise composed by Bhikṣu Wangchuk Dorjee Negi and edited by Paṇḍita Dharmadatta Chaturvedi.
SA_T16_n2959u.coverage: complete — Complete text of the work from the initial pariccheda through the author's final dedicatory verses and concluding colophon (segments 0–6528).

SA_T16_tarkrsau.title: Tarkarahasya (chapters 1–4 and incomplete chapter 5)
SA_T16_tarkrsau.summary: The Tarkarahasya ('Secret of Logic/Reasoning') is an Indian Buddhist philosophical treatise and epistemological manual belonging to the pramāṇa tradition. In five topical chapters, the text presents the definitions and number of valid means of cognition (pramāṇa), perception (pratyakṣa) and its subdivisions, epistemic objects, and inference and relations (examining Dharmakīrti's Sambandhaparīkṣā), while refuting rival non-Buddhist views.
SA_T16_tarkrsau.attribution: In his editio princeps (Patna 1979), Paramanandan Shastri published the text. Gudrun Bühnemann discussed the text in 'Tarkarahasya and Vādarahasya'.
SA_T16_tarkrsau.edition: Acharya Paramanandan Shastri (ed.), Tarkarahasya, Tibetan Sanskrit Works Series 20, Patna: Kashi Prasad Jayaswal Research Institute, 1979.
SA_T16_tarkrsau.coverage: partial — Chapter colophons for chapter 1 (svaparapramāṇasaṃkhyānyāyanirṇaya), chapter 3 (pratyakṣaprabhedasvaparanyāyanirṇaya) and chapter 4 (viṣayādinyāyanirṇaya) are present. Chapter 5 begins 'anumānaṃ dvidhā — svārthaṃ, parārthaṃ ca' (Sh p. 75) and breaks off in the discussion of relation (sambandha, quoting Dharmakīrti's Sambandhaparīkṣā) with the editor's note '[itaḥ praṃ mūlapustakaṃ nopalabhyate /]'. The end of the work and its colophon are lost in the unique manuscript; the e-text reproduces everything that is preserved.

SA_T17_bsa046_u.title: Yogāvatāra
SA_T17_bsa046_u.author: Dignāga
SA_T17_bsa046_u.summary: A very short Yogācāra meditation manual in nine āryā stanzas, opening with homage to Tārā. After study and conviction, the yogin seated on a soft seat sees through the net of conceptualization, including the duality of grasped and grasper. He realizes the mind as without appearance and unarisen (anupalambha, tathatājñāna), and so reaches the path of the noble ones and works for the benefit of beings.
SA_T17_bsa046_u.attribution: The Tibetan translation (D 4074) attributes the Yogāvatāra to Dignāga. The e-text concludes with the colophon 'kṛtir iyam āryadignāgapādānām'. Studies include N. Yoshida (1967).
SA_T17_bsa046_u.coverage: complete — Complete 9-verse work including opening mangala (namas tārāyai) and closing colophon. Verse 8a contains the lacuna preserved in the manuscript tradition (............danaghavāyau...).
translations: rnal 'byor la 'jug pa (Derge Tengyur D 4074): translated by Dharmaśrībhadra, lo chen rin chen bzang po (Tibetan)

SA_T17_byogalbu.title: Buddhist Yoga Manual (fragments)
SA_T17_byogalbu.summary: The Buddhist Yoga Manual (conventionally known as Yogalehrbuch) is an untitled Sanskrit meditation handbook surviving in fragmentary manuscript leaves from the Kucha region along the northern Silk Road (dated palaeographically to c. 7th century CE). Rooted doctrinally in Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma while incorporating vivid internal visualizations and somatic manipulation of elements, it guides the practitioner (yogācāra) through stages of meditative contemplation such as ānāpānasmṛti, aśubhabhāvanā, and the four apramāṇas. The text constitutes a critical bridge between Indian meditation traditions and early medieval Chinese visualization texts (chanjing).
SA_T17_byogalbu.attribution: Anonymous Buddhist meditation manual. Composed by an unidentified meditation master associated with the Sarvāstivāda / Mūlasarvāstivāda scholastic and yogācāra meditation traditions of Central Asia or Northwest India.
SA_T17_byogalbu.edition: Dieter Schlingloff: Ein buddhistisches Yogalehrbuch. Berlin 1964 (Sanskrittexte aus den Turfanfunden, 7). - ders., Ein buddhistisches Yogalehrbuch. Tafelband. Berlin 1966 (Sanskrittexte aus den Turfanfunden, 7a). = YL [Cf. D. Schlingloff: Ein buddhistisches Yogalehrbuch. Unveränderter Nachdruck der Ausgabe von 1964 unter Beigabe aller seither bekannt gewordenen Fragmente, hg. J.-U. Hartmann und H.-J. Röllicke. München 2006 (Buddhismus-Studien, 5).] With a supplement of later additions.
SA_T17_byogalbu.coverage: fragment — Survives only in disjointed manuscript leaves and fragments discovered in the Kucha oasis (predominantly from the Ming-öi caves near Qizil), supplemented by fragments from the Pelliot collection in Paris (e.g. Pell.Skt. rouge 9.6).
translations: Dieter Schlingloff, Ein buddhistisches Yogalehrbuch, Berlin: Akademie-Verlag, 1964 (Sanskrittexte aus den Turfanfunden, 7). (German)

SA_T17_kukalpmu.title: Kalpanāmaṇḍitikā (fragments)
SA_T17_kukalpmu.author: Kumāralāta
SA_T17_kukalpmu.summary: The Kalpanāmaṇḍitikā (or Dṛṣṭāntapaṅkti) of Kumāralāta is an early Buddhist narrative collection composed in mixed ornate prose and verse (campū style). It presents illustrative moral tales (dṛṣṭānta/avadāna) teaching karma, devotion to the Buddha and Saṅgha, and early Dārṣṭāntika doctrinal stances. While preserved completely only in Kumārajīva's Chinese translation (T 201) under an erroneous attribution to Aśvaghoṣa, Central Asian manuscript discoveries confirmed Kumāralāta's authorship of the original Sanskrit text.
SA_T17_kukalpmu.attribution: Kumāralāta is named as the author in manuscript colophons. The work was historically confused with Aśvaghoṣa's Sūtrālaṃkāra due to Kumārajīva's Chinese translation (Da zhuangyan lun経, T 201).
SA_T17_kukalpmu.edition: Heinrich Lüders: Bruchstücke der Kalpanāmaṇḍitikā des Kumāralāta. Leipzig 1926 (Kleinere Sanskrit-Texte, 2) [= repr. in: Monographien zur indischen Archäologie, Kunst und Philologie, 1: Steiner Verlag Wiesbaden 1979, pp. 113-375], supplemented by Klaus Wille with further editions and transliterations of manuscript fragments: Lore Sander & Ernst Waldschmidt (SHT V, Stuttgart 1985), Shin'ichirō Hori (2011), Klaus Wille (2005), Seishi Karashima (2009), and unpublished transliterations of British Library fragments (IOL San 1242).
SA_T17_kukalpmu.coverage: fragment — Disjunct fragments from Central Asian manuscripts (Turfan SHT 21, SHT 638, SHT 1015; IOM St. Petersburg; British Library Stein and Hoernle collections).
translations: Édouard Huber, Sūtrālaṃkāra/Açvaghoṣa: Traduit en français sur la version chinoise de Kumārajīva, Paris: Leroux, 1908. (French (translated from Kumārajīva's Chinese translation, T 201))
Heinrich Lüders, Bruchstücke der Kalpanāmaṇḍitikā des Kumāralāta, Leipzig, 1926. (German)

SA_T17_matpra_u.title: Śatapañcāśatka
SA_T17_matpra_u.author: Mātṛceṭa
SA_T17_matpra_u.summary: The Śatapañcāśatka ('Hymn of 150 Verses', also known as Prasādapratibhodbhava, numbering 153 verses in total) is a foundational Buddhist hymn of praise (stotra) composed in classical Sanskrit by the 2nd-century poet Mātṛceṭa. Structured across thirteen thematic sections, the work extols the Buddha's peerless compassion, bodily marks, intellectual qualities, moral perfection, and liberating teachings in an elegant kāvya idiom. As testified by the 7th-century Chinese pilgrim Yijing, the work was committed to memory and chanted daily in Buddhist monastic communities throughout India and rapidly spread to Central Asia, Tibet, and China.
SA_T17_matpra_u.attribution: Attributed to the early Buddhist poet Mātṛceṭa. The Tibetan translation (D 1147) attributes the work to rta dbyangs (identified as Āryaśūra or Aśvaghoṣa).
SA_T17_matpra_u.edition: D. R. Shackleton Bailey, The Śatapañcāśatka of Mātṛceṭa, Cambridge 1951.
SA_T17_matpra_u.coverage: complete — Contains the complete hymn of 153 stanzas, from verse 1 ('sarvadā sarvathā sarve...') to verse 153 ('phalodayenāsya śubhasya karmaṇo muniprasādapratibhodbhavasya me...').
translations: Yijing 義淨 (tr.), Yibai wushi zanfo song 一百五十讚佛頌, Taishō Tripiṭaka no. 1680 (T 1680), 700–711. (Chinese)
brgya lnga bcu pa zhes bya ba'i bstod pa (Derge Tengyur D 1147): translated by Śraddhākaravarman, shAkya blo gros (Tibetan)

SA_T17_n2936u.title: Śabdabhedaprakāśa
SA_T17_n2936u.author: Maheśvara
SA_T17_n2936u.summary: The Śabdabhedaprakāśa ('Illumination of Distinctions among Words') is a Sanskrit orthographic lexicon composed by Maheśvara as a supplement to his Viśvaprakāśa. In four sections (nirdeśas), it catalogues allowable variations in Sanskrit phonology and spelling: general variants, the interchange of ba and va, alternations among sibilants, and differences of gender. It served as a reference for poets and scholars to verify legitimate variants and support verbal figures of speech like anuprāsa, yamaka, and śleṣa.
SA_T17_n2936u.attribution: By Maheśvara (Maheśvara Kavīndra), author of the Viśvaprakāśa, to which this work is appended, as the colophon shows ('viśvaprakāśe śabdabhedaprakāśaḥ'). The closing verses praise Maheśvara as a physician and poet. Jñānavimalagaṇi composed a commentary on the work.
SA_T17_n2936u.coverage: complete — Root text (mūla) consisting of 4 sections (nirdeśas): general orthographic variants, ba/va variants, sibilant variants, and gender variants, followed by closing verses and final colophon.

SA_T17_n2944u.title: Viśvaprakāśa
SA_T17_n2944u.author: Maheśvara
SA_T17_n2944u.summary: The Viśvaprakāśa is a twelfth-century Sanskrit lexicon (kośa) composed by Maheśvara, ending with a section on indeclinables (anekārthāvyayapariccheda).
SA_T17_n2944u.attribution: Maheśvara traces his medical lineage back to Haricandra (who commented on the Carakatantra) in opening verse 5. In the final stanzas (v. 5), the author gives the chronogram rāmānalavyomarūpaiḥ (Śaka 1033) for the composition of the work.
SA_T17_n2944u.edition: Viśvaprakāśa by Śrī Maheśvara, edited by Śilaskandha Sthavira and Gopāla Bhaṭṭa, The Chowkhambā Sanskrit Series, Nos. 160 & 168, Benares: Chowkhambā Sanskrit Book-Depot, 1911.
SA_T17_n2944u.coverage: complete — Complete text ending with the second pariccheda (anekārthāvyayaparicchedo dvitīyaḥ, samāpto'yaṁ viśvaprakāśaḥ).

SA_T17_n958u.title: Bauddhatantrakośa (part 1)
SA_T17_n958u.summary: A modern Sanskrit encyclopedic dictionary and sourcebook of Buddhist tantric terminology. It defines key Vajrayāna concepts by arranging technical terms alphabetically and citing extensive proof texts from canonical and commentarial Sanskrit tantric literature (including the Guhyasamāja and Hevajra cycles). Part 1 constitutes an alphabetical cycle from 'akaraṇasaṃvaraḥ' to 'homaḥ'.
SA_T17_n958u.attribution: A modern lexicographical compendium compiling definitions and citations from Vajrayāna tantric scriptures and commentaries.
SA_T17_n958u.coverage: complete — Text of Part 1, covering an alphabetical range of technical terms from 'akaraṇasaṃvaraḥ' through 'homaḥ'.

SA_T17_n996u.title: Mahāvyutpatti
SA_T17_n996u.summary: The Mahāvyutpatti is an early ninth-century bilingual Sanskrit–Tibetan glossary compiled in Tibet under imperial decree. It provided standardized vocabulary for Buddhist terminology and canonical translation into Tibetan.
SA_T17_n996u.attribution: Compiled under royal decree in Tibet (reign of Sad na legs / Ral pa can) by a commission of Tibetan and Indian scholars.
SA_T17_n996u.edition: Mahāvyutpatti (Honyaku myōgi taishū / Bon-zō-kan-wa shiyaku taikō), ed. Ryōzaburō Sakaki, Kyoto: Shingonshū Kyoto Daigaku, 1916.

SA_T17_sabhivpu.title: Sabhikasaugataśāsanapravrajyāvratacaraṇaparivarta
SA_T17_sabhivpu.summary: A Buddhist narrative poem constituting Chapter 14 of the Bhadrakalpāvadāna and Chapter 9 of the Saṃbhadrāvadānamālā. Framed as a discourse given by Upagupta to King Aśoka, it narrates the tale of Sabhika, opening in Mathurā with the birth of a girl, and her subsequent Buddhist monastic ordination (pravrajyā) and spiritual realization. Tilak Raj Chopra critically edited the text as a supplement to his article investigating the Buddhist and New Indo-Aryan folk belief surrounding triyantara/teṃtara.
SA_T17_sabhivpu.attribution: Framed as an instructional dialogue between Upagupta and King Aśoka.
SA_T17_sabhivpu.edition: Tilak Raj Chopra, 'BHS triyantara and Hindi teṃtara ḥ Notes on a Folk-belief in the Mahāvastu and Some Other Buddhist Sanskrit Texts (Supplement: Text of the Sabhika-Parivarta, edited for the First Time from Manuscripts)', in: Frank-Richard Hamm Memorial Volume, October 8, 1990, ed. H. Eimer, Bonn 1990 (Indica et Tibetica, 21), pp. 19–46.
SA_T17_sabhivpu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Sabhikasaugataśāsanapravrajyāvratacaraṇaparivarta (verses 1–219/222, plus opening/closing framing verses specific to the Saṃbhadrāvadānamālā recension), edited synoptically from manuscripts of the Bhadrakalpāvadāna and Saṃbhadrāvadānamālā.

SA_T17_vtrksopu.title: Tarkasopāna
SA_T17_vtrksopu.author: Vidyākaraśānti
SA_T17_vtrksopu.summary: The Tarkasopāna ('Staircase of Reasoning') is an introductory Sanskrit primer of Buddhist epistemological logic (pramāṇa) composed by Vidyākaraśānti. Structured into three chapters—perception (pratyakṣa), inference for oneself (svārthānumāna), and inference for others (parārthānumāna)—it provides a concise summary of Buddhist logic, utilizing the work of Dharmakīrti and Dharmottara.
SA_T17_vtrksopu.attribution: Attributed directly to Pandit Vidyākaraśānti in the concluding colophon: 'kṛtir iyaṃ paṇḍitavidyākaraśāntipādānām'.
SA_T17_vtrksopu.edition: Giuseppe Tucci, ed., Minor Buddhist Texts, Part I. Roma 1956 (Serie Orientale Roma, 9), pp. 275-310.
SA_T17_vtrksopu.coverage: complete — Complete text preserved in three chapters (pariccheda): 1. Pratyakṣapariccheda (direct perception), 2. Svārthānumānapariccheda (inference for oneself), and 3. Parārthānumānapariccheda (inference for others/debate), concluding with the dedication verse and author colophon.

SA_XX_bowermsu.title: Bower Manuscript
SA_XX_bowermsu.summary: The Bower Manuscript is an ancient birch-bark manuscript in Gupta script discovered in 1890 in a Buddhist stupa near Kucha/Kashgar and entrusted to the Bodleian Library. It contains medical texts, including the Navanītaka, as well as two dice-oracles.
SA_XX_bowermsu.attribution: The Bower Manuscript was discovered in 1890 near Kucha (Kashgar) by Lieutenant H. Bower in a Buddhist stupa. Written on birch-bark in Gupta characters.
SA_XX_bowermsu.edition: August Friedrich Rudolf Hoernle, 3 vols., Calcutta 1893-1912. (Archaeological Survey of India, New Imperial Series, 22)
SA_XX_bowermsu.coverage: complete — Transcription of the Bower Manuscript based on A. F. R. Hoernle's 1893–1912 edition.
translations: A. F. R. Hoernle (English)
Dominik Wujastyk, The Roots of Ayurveda: Selections from Sanskrit Medical Writings, Delhi: Penguin Books India, 1998. (English)

SA_XX_n1136u.title: Buddhamata
SA_XX_n1136u.summary: A short modern Sanskrit prose excerpt explaining the rise of Buddhism as a reaction to the rigidity of caste and Brahmanical sacrifice, listing Buddhist virtues, and recounting the life of the Buddha (birth at Kapilavastu, renunciation, awakening at Bodhgayā, teaching, nirvāṇa). It begins with the end of a preceding section on nāṭya.
SA_XX_n1136u.coverage: excerpt — The DSBC source file (ilx_skt dsbc/buddhamata_book_270.xml) contains the text for Buddhamata.

SA_XX_n1137u.title: Nāgānanda
SA_XX_n1137u.author: Harṣadeva
SA_XX_n1137u.summary: Nāgānanda is a drama attributed to Harṣadeva dramatizing the legend of Jīmūtavāhana who offered himself to Garuḍa in place of a Nāga.
translations: Palmer Boyd (trans.), London: Trübner, 1872. (English)
Abel Bergaigne (trans.), Paris, 1879. (French)

SA_XX_n1142u.title: Nālandādahana
SA_XX_n1142u.author: V. Subramaniam
SA_XX_n1142u.summary: A Sanskrit text entitled Nālandādahana preserved in the Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon.

SA_XX_n1143u.title: Nṛtyaprasūti
SA_XX_n1143u.author: V. Subramaniam
SA_XX_n1143u.summary: A Sanskrit work titled Nṛtyaprasūti cataloged in the Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon (DSBC book 273).

SA_XX_n2856u.title: Kalpoktamārīcīsādhana
SA_XX_n2856u.author: Ānandagarbha
SA_XX_n2856u.summary: A Vajrayāna meditation and ritual manual (sādhana) focused on the goddess Mārīcī, attributed in the Tibetan canon to Sñiṅ-po (Garbha).
SA_XX_n2856u.attribution: Attributed in the Tibetan Tanjur (Toh 3532) to Sñiṅ-po (Garbha) and in Sanskrit manuscript tradition to Paṇḍitācāryagarbha.
translations: rtog pa las gsungs pa'i cho gas 'od zer can dkar mo'i sgrub thabs (Derge Tengyur D 3342): translated by Amoghavajra II, ba ri lo tsA ba rin chen grags (Tibetan)

SA_XX_n2898u.title: Svapnādhyāya (fragment)
SA_XX_n2898u.author: Vibhūticandra
SA_XX_n2898u.summary: A Sanskrit work on dreams (svapnādhyāya). In the Tibetan canon (D 1749), a cognate work titled Svapnohana (rmi lam brtag pa) is preserved with Vibhūticandra listed as translator.
SA_XX_n2898u.attribution: In the Tibetan Tanjur (D 1749), the text is titled Svapnohana (rmi lam brtag pa) and records Vibhūticandra as translator ([Tr]).
translations: rmi lam brtag pa (Derge Tengyur D 1749): translated by Vibhūticandra (Tibetan)

SA_XX_n2927u.title: Buddhakapālatantra (chapters 9–14)
SA_XX_n2927u.summary: The Buddhakapālatantra is a Buddhist Yoginītantra centered on the wrathful deity Buddhakapāla ('Buddha-Skull') and his consort Citrasenā. Originating in the same esoteric milieu as the Cakrasaṃvara and Hevajra tantras, it features antinomian yogic discipline, cremation-ground rituals, and a prominent focus on Gāruḍa practices used for curing snakebite and counteracting poison. Chapters 9 through 14 cover post-initiatory caryā conduct, herbal and rasāyana lore, Gāruḍa-vidyādhara rites, sexual yoga, meditation on the subtle channels, and the ritual procedure of initiation (abhiṣeka).
SA_XX_n2927u.attribution: Canonical Vajrayāna scripture. The Tibetan translation was prepared by Gayādhara and Gyi jo Zla ba'i 'od zer (Toh 424 / Degé Kangyur rgyud nga 143a1–153a6).
translations: dpal sangs rgyas thod pa zhes bya ba rnal 'byor ma'i rgyud kyi rgyal po (Derge Kangyur D 424): translated by Gayādhara, gyi jo zla ba'i 'od zer (Tibetan)

SA_XX_n2938u.title: Ḍākārṇava
SA_XX_n2938u.summary: The Ḍākārṇava (Śrī-Ḍākārṇava-mahāyoginī-tantrarāja) is a Buddhist Yoginītantra work. Studies in its Apabhraṃśa texts were conducted by Nagendra Narayan Chaudhuri (1935).
SA_XX_n2938u.attribution: Preserved in canonical Tibetan translation (Kangyur, Toh. 372 / D 372).
SA_XX_n2938u.coverage: unclear — The digital file SA_XX_n2938u is completely unpopulated (0 segments, 0 characters). It represents an empty stub/placeholder record in DSBC (book 809) where TEI header metadata was registered but body text was never input.
translations: dpal mkha' 'gro rgya mtsho rnal 'byor ma'i rgyud kyi rgyal po chen po zhes bya ba (Derge Kangyur D 372): translated by Jayasena III, sum pa lo tsA ba dar ma yon tan; at dpal bal yul grub pa'i gnas mchog chen po yu tung lhun gyis grub pa'i gtsug lag khang chen po (Tibetan)

SA_XX_n690u.title: Nānāsiddhopadeśa
SA_XX_n690u.summary: The Nānāsiddhopadeśa ('Precepts of Various Siddhas') is a short anonymous Buddhist tantric compilation of instructions attributed to siddhas (Padmāṅkura, Prajñārakṣita, Nelīpāda, Ravigupta, Kṛṣṇācārya, Sarahapāda, Mahīdhara, Bhūripāda, Vīṇāpāda, Virūpācārya, Nāgabuddhi, Diṅnāga, Mātali, Matsyendra). Davidson notes a Sanskrit manuscript in the Nepal National Archives and observes that it contains meditative instructions and was not translated into Tibetan. Szántó notes it was published in 1994 with 14 siddhas.
SA_XX_n690u.attribution: Anonymous compilation. Precepts are attributed to 14 siddhas (Padmāṅkura, Prajñārakṣita, Nelīpāda, Ravigupta, Kṛṣṇācārya, Sarahapāda, Mahīdhara, Bhūripāda, Vīṇāpāda, Virūpācārya, Nāgabuddhi, Diṅnāga, Mātali, Matsyendra). Davidson counts thirteen, while Szántó counts fourteen.
SA_XX_n690u.edition: Nānāsiddhopadeśaḥ, published in Dhīḥ: Journal of Rare Buddhist Texts Research Unit (1994) ('Introduction to Rare Texts', text 6: 'The entire text has been reproduced here'). Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, Sarnath. (probable)
SA_XX_n690u.coverage: complete — Text runs through the precepts of the siddhas. Published in full in Dhīḥ 18 (Introduction to Rare Texts, pp. 5–18).

SA_XX_n693u.title: Advayavajrasaṃgraha
SA_XX_n693u.author: Advayavajra
SA_XX_n693u.summary: The Advayavajrasaṃgraha is a collection of short Sanskrit Buddhist treatises attributed to Advayavajra, treating topics such as tantric vows and transgressions (mūlāpattayaḥ, sthūlāpattayaḥ), philosophical tenets (Tattvaratnāvalī), consecration (Sekatātparyasaṃgraha), mudrās (Pañcatathāgatamudrāvivaraṇa), and amanasikāra.
SA_XX_n693u.attribution: A collection of short treatises edited by Haraprasad Shastri under the title Advayavajrasaṃgraha and attributed to Advayavajra.
SA_XX_n693u.edition: Haraprasad Shastri (ed.), Advayavajrasaṃgraha, Gaekwad's Oriental Series No. XL (40), Baroda: Oriental Institute, 1927.
SA_XX_n693u.coverage: complete — Complete digital text of DSBC book 82.
translations: Mikkyō-seiten Kenkyūkai, 'Advayavajrasaṃgraha – New Critical Edition with Japanese Translation', Annual of the Institute for Comprehensive Studies of Buddhism (Taisho University), Nos. 10–13, Tokyo, 1988–. (Japanese)

SA_XX_n740u.title: Advayasiddhi
SA_XX_n740u.author: Lakṣmīṅkarā
SA_XX_n740u.summary: The Advayasiddhi is a Vajrayāna treatise attributed to Lakṣmīṅkarā (c. 9th century CE), sister of King Indrabhūti of Oḍḍiyāna. Counted among the 'Seven Siddhi Texts' (Tib. grub pa sde bdun) in Indo-Tibetan traditions, it teaches Vajrayāna practices and the realization of non-duality.
SA_XX_n740u.attribution: Attributed to Lakṣmīṅkarā (c. 9th century CE), sister of King Indrabhūti of Oḍḍiyāna (Uḍḍiyāna).
SA_XX_n740u.coverage: complete — Corresponding to Tibetan Tengyur translations (Toh 2220; Peking Q 3064).
translations: gnyis su med par grub pa'i sgrub thabs zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 2220) (Tibetan)

SA_MB_saundaryalahariHK.title: Saundaryalaharī with Lakṣmīdharavyākhyā, Bhāvanopaniṣad with Bhāskararāyabhāṣya, and Devīpañcastavī
SA_MB_saundaryalahariHK.author: Śaṅkara, Lakṣmīdhara, Bhāskararāya
SA_MB_saundaryalahariHK.summary: The Saundaryalaharī is a celebrated Sanskrit devotional and tantric hymn in honor of the Goddess Tripurasundarī. This digital volume presents the edition featuring Lakṣmīdhara's commentary, accompanied by the Bhāvanopaniṣad with Bhāskararāya's commentary and the Devīpañcastavī.
SA_MB_saundaryalahariHK.attribution: The Saundaryalaharī is attributed to Śaṅkarācārya, with commentary by Lakṣmīdhara. The digital volume includes the Bhāvanopaniṣad with Bhāskararāya's commentary, and the Devīpañcastavī.
SA_MB_saundaryalahariHK.edition: Śrī Śaṅkarācāryaviracitā Saundaryalaharī Lakṣmīdharavyākhyāsamalaṅkṛtā karṇāṭakabhāṣānuvādena anubandhaiśca sahitā Bhāvanopaniṣat Śrībhāskararāyabhāṣyasahitā Devīpañcastavī ca, Prācyavidyāsaṃśodhanālayagranthamālā 114, 1959.
SA_MB_saundaryalahariHK.coverage: complete — Complete Sanskrit text of the Saundaryalaharī with Lakṣmīdhara's commentary, followed by the Bhāvanopaniṣad with Bhāskararāya's commentary and the Devīpañcastavī (ending with: 'iti pañcastavī ca samāptā sakalajananīstavaḥ pañcamaḥ').

SA_MB_kaalottaratantramHK.title: Bṛhatkālottara
SA_MB_kaalottaratantramHK.summary: The Bṛhatkālottara ('Great Kālottara', also known as the Kālottaramahātantra) is an extensive redaction of the Kālottara corpus of the Śaiva Siddhānta. Set as a dialogue between Īśvara and Kārtikeya, the text treats ritual, initiation, and related tantric subjects.
SA_MB_kaalottaratantramHK.attribution: Revealed Śaiva scripture presented as a dialogue between Īśvara (Śiva) and Kārtikeya.
SA_MB_kaalottaratantramHK.edition: Diplomatic transcript of National Archives, Kathmandu (NAK) palm-leaf manuscript MS pra-89 (filmed under NGMPP Reel No. B 29/59), input under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Muktabodha Indological Research Institute, 2013 (Catalog No. E00012).
SA_MB_kaalottaratantramHK.coverage: partial — Diplomatic transcript of NAK palm-leaf MS pra-89 (filmed as NGMPP Reel No. B 29/59; 288 folios). Although Muktabodha completed their transcription of this manuscript in two parts, the text itself is incomplete, breaking off on folio 288a with illegible portions ('not clear') and lacking a final colophon.

SA_MB_cinmantramaliniHK.title: Cinmantramālinī
SA_MB_cinmantramaliniHK.author: Prakāśānanda
SA_MB_cinmantramaliniHK.summary: The Cinmantramālinī (subtitled Nityopāsanākrama) is a brief Śākta liturgical ritual manual (paddhati) expounding the daily worship sequence of the fifteen Nityā devīs of the Śrīvidyā tradition according to the Kādimata. It sets forth initial preparatory acts (snāna, prāṇāyāma, bhūtaśuddhi, guru-dhyāna, mātṛkā-nyāsa, and ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa) followed by daily visualizations (dhyāna), bījamantras, mudrās, and recitation rules for each of the fifteen lunar days from Kāmeśvarī to Citrā.
SA_MB_cinmantramaliniHK.attribution: The work is attributed directly to Prakāśānanda in the end-colophon ('iti śrī prakāśānanda viracitāyāṃ cinmantramālinyāṃ nityopāsanākramaḥ samāptaḥ').
SA_MB_cinmantramaliniHK.edition: Unpublished manuscript transcription: Institut Français de Pondichéry transcript T. No. 578 (copied from MS R.No. 2572 belonging to the G.O.M.L., Madras).
SA_MB_cinmantramaliniHK.coverage: complete — Complete text of the manual as preserved in Institut Français de Pondichéry transcript T. No. 578 (pp. 40–50), covering the daily ritual procedure (upāsanākrama) for the fifteen Nityās and closing with the colophon.

SA_MB_dattatreyabodhaHK.title: Dattātreyabodha
SA_MB_dattatreyabodhaHK.summary: The Dattātreyabodha is a Sanskrit tract on Haṭha Yoga. The text discusses yogic practice (abhyāsa), diet, breath control (kumbhaka, pavanābhyāsa), retention of bindu, dhāraṇā, and attainment of yogic powers, concluding that yogābhyāsa is the true fruit of human birth.
SA_MB_dattatreyabodhaHK.edition: Manuscript transcript: Institut Français de Pondichéry (IFP) transcript T0638, copied from Government Oriental Manuscripts Library (GOML), Madras, MS No. D. 4346.
SA_MB_dattatreyabodhaHK.coverage: complete — Transcription of the text as found in IFP transcript T0638 (copied from Madras GOML MS D. 4346), ending with the colophon 'iti dattātreyabodhaḥ samāptaḥ'.

SA_MB_cinmayadiksavidhanamHK.title: Cinmayadīkṣāvidhāna
SA_MB_cinmayadiksavidhanamHK.summary: The Cinmayadīkṣāvidhāna is an anonymous Śaiva ritual manual (paddhati / vidhāna), closely aligned with the Vīraśaiva tradition, detailing the rite of consciousness-pervaded initiation (cinmayadīkṣā) and the accompanying worship and wearing of the liṅga (liṅgadhāraṇa). It lays down rules for constructing the ritual pavilion (maṇḍapa) and fire-altars (kuṇḍa), performing preliminary purifications and nyāsas, and administering the mantras aimed at effecting the identity of the soul with Śiva (śivajīvaikya).
SA_MB_cinmayadiksavidhanamHK.attribution: Anonymous ritual manual; no personal author is named in the text or transcript colophons.
SA_MB_cinmayadiksavidhanamHK.edition: Manuscript transcription: Institut Français de Pondichéry (IFP) transcript T0569 (copied from Adyar Library MS no. 67963, shelfmark 21-E-34)
SA_MB_cinmayadiksavidhanamHK.coverage: unclear — The text concludes with ritual prescriptions and a closing maṅgala ('|| sāmbaśivāya namaḥ ||'), but lacks a formal final colophon; whether the text is fully complete is therefore uncertain.

SA_MB_jnanadiksaHK.title: Jñānadīkṣā (incomplete)
SA_MB_jnanadiksaHK.summary: A brief anonymous Śaiva Siddhānta tract on jñānadīkṣā, initiation through knowledge. It sets out the categories of Pati, Paśu and Pāśa (mala, māyā, karma), citing Siddhāntāgamas such as the Mataṅgapārameśvara and Kiraṇa, and treats the awakening of the soul by Śiva's power, including the role of kuṇḍalinī-śakti (as noted in the Muktabodha description). It is not identical with the jñānadīkṣā chapters of the Acintyaviśvasādākhya or of Vedajñāna's Dīkṣādarśa, which open with a similar verse.
SA_MB_jnanadiksaHK.attribution: Anonymous Śaivasiddhānta tract. The IFP copyist Naṭarāja remarks that the Adyar palm-leaf manuscript seems to have been written by the copyist Mahāgaṇapati Śivācārya, but the author of the work is unknown.
SA_MB_jnanadiksaHK.edition: Unpublished manuscript transcript: Institut Français de Pondichéry (IFP) Transcript No. T0088, transcribed by Naṭarāja from Adyar Library palm-leaf manuscript No. 68462.
SA_MB_jnanadiksaHK.coverage: partial — Short tract (12 transcript pages) with many lacunae marked "* * *"; the final colophon is missing and the copyist Naṭarāja records that the concluding sentence of the work is lost ("samāptibodhakavākyaṃ tu naṣṭam"). The beginning (maṅgala "śivaṃ praṇamya paramaṃ ... jñānadīkṣāṃ pravakṣyā[mi]") is preserved.

SA_MB_jnanasiddhyagamaHK.title: Jñānasiddhyāgama (incomplete)
SA_MB_jnanasiddhyagamaHK.summary: A Śaiva text calling itself an āgama, which Muktabodha describes as reading more like a tract on miscellaneous topics of Śaiva yoga.
SA_MB_jnanasiddhyagamaHK.attribution: Anonymous scriptural text framed as an āgama.
SA_MB_jnanasiddhyagamaHK.edition: Unpublished manuscript transcript: IFP transcript T0178, copied from Government Oriental Manuscripts Library, Madras, MS R. 16810; e-text by Muktabodha (catalog no. E0006, 2013). No printed edition known.
SA_MB_jnanasiddhyagamaHK.coverage: partial — The text breaks off in the middle of a cosmogonic passage ("ṣaṭkoṭi viṣṇu madhyasthe śatakoṭi brahmaṇodbhavam ||") with no final colophon. The full extent of the work is not known.

SA_MB_dhyanaratnavaliHK.title: Dhyānaratnāvalī
SA_MB_dhyanaratnavaliHK.author: Trilocanaśivācārya
SA_MB_dhyanaratnavaliHK.summary: The Dhyānaratnāvalī is a compendium compiling iconographic visualization verses (dhyānaślokas) detailing the forms, attributes, weapons, postures, and retinues of Śiva, Devī, accompanying deities, cosmic principles (tattvas), kalās, and subtle somatic channels.
SA_MB_dhyanaratnavaliHK.edition: Unpublished manuscript transcription of Institut Français de Pondichéry (IFP) paper transcript T0232 (copied from a manuscript belonging to Rajamani Gurukkal, Perambar Kandikai, Madhurantakam).
SA_MB_dhyanaratnavaliHK.coverage: unclear — Transcribes the entirety of IFP transcript T0232; however, the transcript lacks a final colophon and terminates abruptly following a dhyāna verse on Cāmuṇḍī.

SA_MB_matatrayaikyaprakasikaHK.title: Matatrayaikyaprakāśikā
SA_MB_matatrayaikyaprakasikaHK.author: Aiyyaṇācārya
SA_MB_matatrayaikyaprakasikaHK.summary: The Matatrayaikyaprakāśikā (also titled Trimataikyaprakāśikā) is a Vedāntic treatise by Aiyyaṇācārya (disciple/follower of Vasudhendra Tīrtha, associated with the tradition of Ānandatīrtha / Madhvācārya). The work examines and harmonizes three views, with paricchedas addressing systems including Rāmānuja's view (Rāmānujamataikyaprakāśa).
SA_MB_matatrayaikyaprakasikaHK.attribution: In the colophon, the author is named as Aiyaṇa (Aiyyaṇācārya), son of Gopālācārya and grandson of Rāmācārya of Vāṇāturai, receiving the grace of Śrīmad Vasudhendra Tīrtha and devoted to the tradition of Ānandatīrtha.
SA_MB_matatrayaikyaprakasikaHK.edition: Manuscript transcription based on Institut Français de Pondichéry (IFP) transcript T0582, copied from manuscript TR 275 (shelfmark 38-A-21) belonging to the Adyar Library, Madras.
SA_MB_matatrayaikyaprakasikaHK.coverage: complete — Text concludes with the third pariccheda (Rāmānujamataikyaprakāśa) and 'samāptaścāpaṃ granthaḥ'.

SA_MB_vijayottaratantraHK.title: Vijayottaratantra
SA_MB_vijayottaratantraHK.summary: The Vijayottaratantra (also called Trisahasrasaṃhitā) is an Upāgama of the Śaivasiddhānta dealing with Śaiva ritual.
SA_MB_vijayottaratantraHK.attribution: Traditional Śaiva scripture; recognized in the Śaivasiddhānta canonical corpus as an Upāgama.
SA_MB_vijayottaratantraHK.edition: Manuscript transcript: Institut Français de Pondichéry (IFP) Transcript No. T0190, transcribed from Government Oriental Manuscripts Library (GOML), Madras, MS No. R 13659.
SA_MB_vijayottaratantraHK.coverage: complete — Concluding with the bhaktotsavapaṭala and the closing colophon 'iti vijayottaratantraṃ samāptam'.

SA_MB_kalottaratantraHK.title: Kālottaratantra
SA_MB_kalottaratantraHK.summary: The Kālottaratantra (or Kālottara) is one of the earliest and most influential scriptural authorities of the Śaiva Siddhānta Mantramārga. Transmitted in multiple recensions of differing lengths, its texts provided the foundational mantric, ritual, and yogic framework for medieval Saiddhāntika liturgies and paddhatis. This digital text is a diplomatic transcription of a composite Nepalese manuscript preserving seven recensions: the Jñānapañcāśikā, Śatikakālottara (Kālajñāna), Sārdhaśatikakālottara, Dviśatikakālottara, Adhyuṣṭaśatikakālottara (Sārdhatriśatika), Saptaśatikakālottara, and Trayodaśaśatikakālottara.
SA_MB_kalottaratantraHK.attribution: Canonical scriptural revelation of the Śaiva Siddhānta Mantramārga, transmitted across multiple recensions of varying verse length.
SA_MB_kalottaratantraHK.edition: Manuscript NGMPP Reel No. - B 118/7 manuscript no. 5-4632.
SA_MB_kalottaratantraHK.coverage: complete — Diplomatic transcription of manuscript NGMPP Reel No. B 118/7, manuscript no. 5-4632, containing seven recensions/versions: jñānapañcāsikā, śatikam (kālajñāna), kālottaram sārddhaśatikam, dviśatikam, adhyuṣṭaśatikam, saptaśatikam, and trayodaśaśatikam.

SA_MB_aagamapraamaanyamHK.title: Āgamaprāmāṇya
SA_MB_aagamapraamaanyamHK.author: Yāmunācārya
SA_MB_aagamapraamaanyamHK.summary: The Āgamaprāmāṇya is a foundational philosophical and polemical treatise by the Śrīvaiṣṇava master Yāmunācārya. The text defends the scriptural authority (prāmāṇya) and orthodox Vedic status of the Pāñcarātra Āgamas against charges of heterodoxy, invalidity, or non-Vedic origin raised primarily by Mīmāṃsakas and Advaitins. Yāmunācārya argues for the intrinsic validity and divine authorship of the Āgamas by Nārāyaṇa and defends the orthodox caste status and temple-worship rituals of the Bhāgavatas, laying the foundation for Rāmānuja's Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta.
SA_MB_aagamapraamaanyamHK.attribution: Authored by Yāmunācārya (also designated as śrī yāmunācāryaswāmin, the Paramaguru of Śrībhāṣyakāra / śrībhāśyācārya).
SA_MB_aagamapraamaanyamHK.coverage: complete — Complete text of the treatise ending with the colophon and verses eulogizing Nāthamuni.

SA_MB_ahirbudhnyasamhitaVol1HK.title: Ahirbudhnyasaṃhitā (chapters 1–36)
SA_MB_ahirbudhnyasamhitaVol1HK.summary: The Ahirbudhnyasaṃhitā is an important theological and ritual text of the Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra tradition, presented as a revelatory discourse taught by Ahirbudhnya (Śiva) to Nārada. This first volume (adhyāyas 1–36) details the cosmogony and metaphysics of the school, emphasizing the six divine attributes (ṣaḍguṇa), the emanations of Viṣṇu (vyūhas), and the cosmogenetic activity of his śakti embodied in the Sudarśana cakra. It also includes comprehensive treatises on mantravidyā, yoga, royal apotropaic rituals, and military/weapon sorcery (astramantra).
SA_MB_ahirbudhnyasamhitaVol1HK.attribution: Canonical Pāñcarātra scripture traditionally framed as a revelatory dialogue between Ahirbudhnya (Śiva/Rudra) and the sage Nārada, transmitted by Durvāsas to Bharadvāja.
SA_MB_ahirbudhnyasamhitaVol1HK.edition: Ahirbudhnya-Saṃhitā of the Pāñcarātrāgama, edited by Pandit M. D. Ramanujacarya under the supervision of F. Otto Schrader, Volume 1 (adhyāyas 1–36), Adyar, Madras: The Adyar Library and Research Centre, 1916.
SA_MB_ahirbudhnyasamhitaVol1HK.coverage: partial — Contains adhyāyas 1–36 (out of 60 total adhyāyas of the complete saṃhitā), corresponding precisely to Volume 1 of the 1916 Adyar editio princeps.

SA_MB_ahirbudhnyasamhitaa2HK.title: Ahirbudhnyasaṃhitā (chapters 37–60 and appendix)
SA_MB_ahirbudhnyasamhitaa2HK.summary: The Ahirbudhnyasaṃhitā is a foundational scripture of the Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra tradition, presented as an exposition given by Ahirbudhnya (Śiva as an enlightened devotee and manifestation of Saṃkarṣaṇa) to the sage Nārada. This second volume covers chapters 37 through 60, focusing on the esoteric iconography and worship of the sixteen-armed Sudarśana, mantra diagrams (yantras), royal protection rituals, the philosophy and six limbs of self-surrender (nyāsa/prapatti), and a significant survey of classical philosophical systems (including the Ṣaṣṭitantra tradition of Sāṃkhya and Yoga). The volume concludes with an appendix containing the Śrīsudarśanasahasranāmastotra.
SA_MB_ahirbudhnyasamhitaa2HK.attribution: Canonical scripture of the Pāñcarātra tradition, presented as a revelation by Ahirbudhnya (an aspect of Śiva identified with Saṃkarṣaṇa) to the sage Nārada.
SA_MB_ahirbudhnyasamhitaa2HK.edition: ahirbudhnya saṃhita of the pāñcarātrāgama volume 2, edited by Pandit M. D. Ramanujacarya under the supervision of F. Otto Schrader. The Adyar Library and Research Center, 1916.
SA_MB_ahirbudhnyasamhitaa2HK.coverage: partial — Contains chapters 37 through 60 (concluding the main Saṃhitā of 60 adhyāyas), followed by an appendix (Parisiṣṭa) comprising the Śrīsudarśanasahasranāmastotra.

SA_MB_akulaviiratantramHK.title: Akulavīratantra
SA_MB_akulaviiratantramHK.author: Matsyendranātha
SA_MB_akulaviiratantramHK.summary: The Akulavīratantra is an early Kaula / Yoginī Kaula scriptural text transmitted within the corpus ascribed to Matsyendranātha. It expounds an uncompromising non-dual realization of ultimate reality designated as the Akulavīra ('Hero of the Transcendent'), identified with innate bliss (sahajānanda) and the all-pervading divine nature within the practitioner's own body. Rejecting the doctrines of scholastic systems (Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Bauddha, Jaina, Somasiddhānta, Mīmāṃsā) as well as outward ritual and haṭhayogic technicalities, it teaches immediate liberation through effortless dwelling in the transcendent state.
SA_MB_akulaviiratantramHK.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Matsyendranātha (also named Macchagnapāda or Macchendra in catalog and colophon).
SA_MB_akulaviiratantramHK.edition: P. C. Bagchi (ed.), Kaulajñānanirṇaya and Some Minor Texts of the School of Matsyendranātha, Calcutta Sanskrit Series 3 (Calcutta: Metropolitan Printing and Pub. House, 1934).
SA_MB_akulaviiratantramHK.coverage: complete — Text ending with the colophon 'iti macchendrapādāvatārite kāmarūpisthāne yoginī prasādāllabdha(m) akulavīraṃ samāptam'.

SA_MB_anuttaraprakasapancasikaHK.title: Anuttaraprakāśapañcāśikā
SA_MB_anuttaraprakasapancasikaHK.author: Ādyanātha
SA_MB_anuttaraprakasapancasikaHK.summary: The Anuttaraprakāśapañcāśikā is a concise philosophical work in 51 anuṣṭubh verses belonging to the non-dual Śaiva (Trika/Spanda) tradition of Kashmir. It expounds the nature of ultimate reality (anuttara) as autonomous pure consciousness (cit, prakāśa) inherently endowed with dynamic self-awareness (vimarśa, svātantrya, spanda). The work systematically maps the manifestation and reabsorption of the thirty-six cosmic principles (ṣaṭtriṃśat-tattva) back into undivided supreme subjective awareness (aham).
SA_MB_anuttaraprakasapancasikaHK.attribution: Ascribed in the opening and concluding colophons to Ādyanātha (śrī-ādyanātha / śrīmad-ādyanātha).
SA_MB_anuttaraprakasapancasikaHK.edition: Mukunda Rāma Shāstrī (ed.), The Bhāvopahāra of Cakrapāṇinātha with Commentary by Ramyadeva Bhaṭṭa [includes Bodhapañcadaśikā and Anuttaraprakāśapañcāśikā], Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies, Bombay / Srinagar: Research Department, Jammu and Kashmir State, 1918.
SA_MB_anuttaraprakasapancasikaHK.coverage: complete — Complete text of 51 anuṣṭubh verses (vv. 1–50 and concluding verse 51, plus introductory mangala verse in brackets).

SA_MB_bhogakarikaHK.title: Bhogakārikā with Bhogakārikāvṛtti
SA_MB_bhogakarikaHK.author: Sadyojyoti, Aghoraśiva
SA_MB_bhogakarikaHK.summary: The Bhogakārikā ('Verses on Worldly Experience') by Sadyojyoti is a foundational philosophical treatise of the dualist Śaiva Siddhānta tradition and one of the eight canonical primers known collectively as the Aṣṭaprakaraṇa. In 146 verses, Sadyojyoti investigates the nature of bhoga (embodied experience of pleasure and pain), explaining how the bound individual soul (paśu)—whose innate powers of consciousness and action are obscured by beginningless primordial impurity (mala)—is endowed by Śiva with bodies, faculties, and worlds evolved out of māyā to experience karmic fruit and mature its impurity. Aghoraśiva's vṛtti elucidates Sadyojyoti's concise verses line by line, rigorously defending the realist ontology of pati (Lord), paśu (soul), and pāśa (bond) against rival arguments from Sāṅkhya, Nyāya, and Buddhist philosophy.
SA_MB_bhogakarikaHK.attribution: The root verses are composed by Sadyojyoti (also known as Kheṭakanandana). The vṛtti is by Aghoraśivācārya.
SA_MB_bhogakarikaHK.edition: Kṛṣṇa Śāstrī (ed.), Bhogakārikā [from Ratnatraya Bhogakārikā Nādakārikā Mokṣakārikā Paramokṣanirāsakārikāḥ], Devakottai: Śivāgamasiddhāntaparipālanasaṅgha, 1925.
SA_MB_bhogakarikaHK.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 146 kārikās of the Bhogakārikā accompanied by the full commentary (vṛtti) of Aghoraśiva, concluding with verse 146 and the final colophon.

SA_MB_moksakarikaHK.title: Mokṣakārikā with Mokṣakārikāvṛtti
SA_MB_moksakarikaHK.author: Sadyojyoti, Rāmakaṇṭha
SA_MB_moksakarikaHK.summary: The Mokṣakārikā is an authoritative doctrinal treatise of Śaiva Siddhānta composed by Sadyojyoti, traditionally included as one of the Aṣṭaprakaraṇa. Across 157 verses, it expounds the nature of liberation (mokṣa), rejecting non-dualist and nihilistic theories to argue that liberation consists in the eradication of innate impurity (mala) and karma, whereby the liberated soul realizes innate omniscience and omnipotence equal to Śiva (śivasāmya). It is accompanied by the commentary (vṛtti) of Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha, who elaborates the epistemological and ontological arguments against rival positions.
SA_MB_moksakarikaHK.attribution: The root verses (157 kārikās) are by Sadyojyoti, pupil of Ugrajyoti. The running commentary (vṛtti) is by Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha (son of Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha).
SA_MB_moksakarikaHK.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all 157 verses of Sadyojyoti's Mokṣakārikā along with Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha's complete Mokṣakārikāvṛtti.

SA_MB_nadakarikaHK.title: Nādakārikā with Nādakārikāvyākhyā
SA_MB_nadakarikaHK.author: Rāmakaṇṭha, Aghoraśiva
SA_MB_nadakarikaHK.summary: The Nādakārikā (also known as Nādasiddhi) is a 26-verse treatise by the Kashmirian master Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha establishing the dualist Śaiva Siddhānta metaphysics and epistemology of sound. Rāmakaṇṭha analyzes how momentary articulate speech sounds (dhvani, varṇa) convey meaning, critiquing both the Grammarians' sphoṭa doctrine and alternative models while positing nāda as a subtle, insentient material entity derived from bindu/kuṇḍalinī that serves as the substrate for speech manifestation. The text is accompanied by the vyākhyā of Aghoraśiva, which unpacks the polemical nuances and technical vocabulary.
SA_MB_nadakarikaHK.attribution: The root kārikās are by Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha (son of Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha), explicitly named in verse 27 ('iti nādasiddhimenāmakarot śrībhaṭṭarāmakaṇṭho 'tra | nārāyaṇakaṇṭhasutaḥ kāśmīre vṛttapañcaviṃśatyā'). The commentary is by Aghoraśivācārya, named in the closing colophon verse.
SA_MB_nadakarikaHK.edition: Kṛṣṇa Śāstrī, ed., Ratnatraya Bhogakārikā Nādakārikā Mokṣakārikā Paramokṣanirasakārikāḥ. Devakottai: Śivāgamasiddhāntaparipālanasaṅgha, 1925.
SA_MB_nadakarikaHK.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising all 26 doctrinal kārikās and the author's concluding verse 27 of the Nādakārikā, along with the full commentary by Aghoraśiva.

SA_MB_paramoksanirasakarikaHK.title: Paramokṣanirāsakārikā with Paramokṣanirāsakārikāvṛtti
SA_MB_paramoksanirasakarikaHK.author: Sadyojyoti, Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha
SA_MB_paramoksanirasakarikaHK.summary: The Paramokṣanirāsakārikā is an early Śaiva Siddhānta polemical and doxographical treatise by Sadyojyoti, accompanied here by the comprehensive commentary (vṛtti) of Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha. Across 59 kārikās expounding a passage of the Rauravasūtra, the work systematically refutes twenty non-Śaiva and heterodox soteriological viewpoints—including Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Vedānta, Pāñcarātra, Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Buddhist, Jaina, and non-Siddhānta Śaiva models—showing that liberation cannot consist in mere isolation, dissolution, cessation of consciousness, or acquisition of mundane qualities. In their place, Sadyojyoti and Rāmakaṇṭha defend the orthodox Siddhānta doctrine that liberation is the manifestation of the soul's innate, co-equal Śiva-nature (śivatvavyakti), consisting in unobstructed omniscience and omnipotence, actualized through initiation (dīkṣā).
SA_MB_paramoksanirasakarikaHK.attribution: The root kārikās are by Sadyojyoti. The commentary (vṛtti) is by Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha (son of Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha), explicitly identified in the final verses and the colophon (itiśrīmadbhaṭṭanārāyaṇakaṇṭhātmajaśrībhaṭṭarāmakaṇṭhaviracitā paramokṣanirāsakārikāvṛttiḥ samāptā).
SA_MB_paramoksanirasakarikaHK.edition: Kṛṣṇa Śāstrī (ed.), Aṣṭaprakaraṇam: Ratnatraya, Bhogakārikā, Nādakārikā, Mokṣakārikā, Paramokṣanirāsakārikāḥ. Devakottai: Śivāgamasiddhāntaparipālanasaṅgha, 1925.
SA_MB_paramoksanirasakarikaHK.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 59 kārikās along with Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha's vṛtti from the introductory Rauravasūtra citation through to the final verse and concluding colophons.

SA_MB_ratnatrayapariksaHK.title: Ratnatrayaparīkṣā with Ratnatrayollekhinī
SA_MB_ratnatrayapariksaHK.author: Śrīkaṇṭha, Aghoraśiva
SA_MB_ratnatrayapariksaHK.summary: The Ratnatrayaparīkṣā ('Examination of the Three Jewels') is one of the eight classical treatises (Aṣṭaprakaraṇa) of the dualist Sanskrit Śaiva Siddhānta tradition. Unlike the tripartite categorization of souls, bonds, and the Lord (paśu, pāśa, pati), the 'three jewels' investigated here are Śiva (the conscious efficient cause), Śakti (Śiva's innate conscious energy), and Bindu (the pure material cause / mahāmāyā). The accompanying commentary, the Ratnatrayollekhinī by Aghoraśivācārya, offers comprehensive ontological and exegetical analysis according to the dualist Śaiva Siddhānta school.
SA_MB_ratnatrayapariksaHK.attribution: The root kārikās (322 verses) are by Śrīkaṇṭhasūri, who in the closing verse notes following Rāmakaṇṭha's vṛtti. The commentary, Ratnatrayollekhinī, is composed by Aghoraśivācārya.
SA_MB_ratnatrayapariksaHK.edition: Kṛṣṇa Śāstrī, ed., Aṣṭaprakaraṇam: Ratnatraya, Bhogakārikā, Nādakārikā, Mokṣakārikā, Paramokṣanirāsakārikā. Devakottai: Śivāgama Siddhānta Paripālana Saṅgha, 1925.
SA_MB_ratnatrayapariksaHK.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 322 kārikās of the Ratnatrayaparīkṣā together with the complete Ratnatrayollekhinī commentary of Aghoraśiva.

SA_MB_tattvaprakasaHK.title: Tattvaprakāśa with the commentaries of Śrīkumāra and Aghoraśiva
SA_MB_tattvaprakasaHK.author: Bhojadeva, Śrīkumāra, Aghoraśiva
SA_MB_tattvaprakasaHK.summary: The Tattvaprakāśa ('Illumination of the Principles') is a canonical verse primer of Śaiva Siddhānta metaphysics traditionally attributed to King Bhojadeva of Dhārā (early 11th c.). The work systematically sets forth the dualist Siddhānta system structured by the three categories of Pati (Śiva), Paśu (individual souls), and Pāśa (bonds), mapping the unfolding of the 36 tattvas across the pure and impure realms. This digital text pairs the kārikās with two principal commentaries: Aghoraśivācārya's 12th-century Vṛtti, which rigorously defends classical dualist Siddhānta against monistic readings, and Śrīkumāra's Tātparyadīpikā, which seeks to harmonize Siddhānta philosophy with orthodox Vaidika and Mīmāṃsaka tenets.
SA_MB_tattvaprakasaHK.attribution: The root kārikās are attributed to Bhojadeva. The commentary Tattvaprakāśikāvṛtti is by Aghoraśivācārya. The commentary Tātparyadīpikā is by Śrīkumāra.
SA_MB_tattvaprakasaHK.edition: Kṛṣṇa Śāstrī (ed.), tatvaprakāśikā-tatvasaṃgraha-tatvatrayanirṇayāḥ savyākhyāḥ aghoraśivācarya of the devakottai series, Devakottai: Śivāgamasiddhāntaparipālanasaṅgham, 1923.
SA_MB_tattvaprakasaHK.coverage: complete — Complete text of Bhojadeva's Tattvaprakāśa along with both complete commentaries (Śrīkumāra's Tātparyadīpikā and Aghoraśiva's Vṛtti).

SA_MB_tattvasamgrahaHK.title: Tattvasaṃgraha with Tattvasaṃgrahaṭīkā
SA_MB_tattvasamgrahaHK.author: Sadyojyoti, Aghoraśiva
SA_MB_tattvasamgrahaHK.summary: The Tattvasaṃgraha ('Compendium of the Principles') by Sadyojyoti is an early classic of dualist Śaiva Siddhānta philosophy, consisting of 57 kārikās that systematically define and classify the thirty-six principles (tattvas) of reality. The text details their role as cosmic constituents and instruments of bondage and liberation for bound souls (paśu). In this e-text, the kārikās are accompanied by Aghoraśiva's Laghuṭīkā, which provides an authoritative gloss on each verse.
SA_MB_tattvasamgrahaHK.attribution: The 57 root kārikās are authored by Sadyojyoti (Kheṭakanandana). The commentary is the Laghuṭīkā (or Vivṛti) by Aghoraśivācārya.
SA_MB_tattvasamgrahaHK.edition: Aṣṭaprakaraṇam: Tattvaprakāśikā-Tattvasaṃgraha-Tattvatrayanirṇayāḥ Savyākhyāḥ Aghoraśivācārya, edited by Kṛṣṇa Śāstrī, Devakottai: Śivāgamasiddhāntaparipālanasaṅgha, 1925 (Devakottai Series).
SA_MB_tattvasamgrahaHK.coverage: complete — Complete text of Sadyojyoti's 57 kārikās together with Aghoraśiva's complete commentary, terminating at verse 57 and the author/commentator colophons.

SA_MB_tattvatrayanirnayaHK.title: Tattvatrayanirṇaya with Tattvatrayanirṇayavṛtti
SA_MB_tattvatrayanirnayaHK.author: Sadyojyoti, Aghoraśiva
SA_MB_tattvatrayanirnayaHK.summary: The Tattvatrayanirṇaya ('Determination of the Three Principles') by Sadyojyoti is a foundational philosophical treatise of dualist Śaiva Siddhānta, preserved as one of the Aṣṭaprakaraṇa. Across 32 kārikās condensing doctrines from the Svāyambhuvasūtrasaṅgraha, it establishes the three eternal realities: the Lord (Śiva / pati), bound souls (puruṣa / paśu), and the primordial material cause (māyā / pāśa), alongside the innate beginningless impurity (mala). Aghoraśiva's vṛtti provides an authoritative commentary on the treatise.
SA_MB_tattvatrayanirnayaHK.attribution: The root verses are by Sadyojyoti. The running commentary is by Aghoraśiva (Aghoraśivācārya).
SA_MB_tattvatrayanirnayaHK.coverage: complete — Contains all 32 kārikās of Sadyojyoti's Tattvatrayanirṇaya along with Aghoraśiva's complete running commentary (vṛtti), introductory and concluding verses, and final colophon.

SA_MB_brhattantrasaaraHK.title: Bṛhattantrasāra
SA_MB_brhattantrasaaraHK.author: Kṛṣṇānanda Āgamavāgīśa
SA_MB_brhattantrasaaraHK.summary: A large Tantric ritual compendium (nibandha) attributed to Kṛṣṇānanda Āgamavāgīśa, citing various tantric sources (e.g. Prapañcasāra, Yoginītantra). The text treats mantras, nyāsa, pūjā, and deities such as Mahākāla and Vaṭukabhairava, followed by a pariśiṣṭa.
SA_MB_brhattantrasaaraHK.attribution: Attributed to Kṛṣṇānanda Āgamavāgīśa in the headers and colophons.
SA_MB_brhattantrasaaraHK.coverage: complete — Includes colophon segments such as 'iti mahāmahopādhyāyaśrīkṛṣṇānandāgamavāgīśaviracite tantrasāre prathamaḥ paricchedaḥ' and ends with 'pariśiṣṭaṃ sampūrṇa'.

SA_MB_cidgaganacandrika-HK.title: Cidgaganacandrikā
SA_MB_cidgaganacandrika-HK.author: Śrīvatsa
SA_MB_cidgaganacandrika-HK.summary: The Cidgaganacandrikā is a philosophical and liturgical work of the Krama (Kālīkula) tradition of Śaivism attributed to Śrīvatsa alias Kālidāsa, focusing on Goddess Kālī.
SA_MB_cidgaganacandrika-HK.attribution: The colophon attributes the work to Kālīdāsa, while the metadata and verses record the author as Śrīvatsa alias Kālidāsa.
SA_MB_cidgaganacandrika-HK.edition: Trivikramatīrtha (ed.), Cidgaganacandrikā, Arthur Avalon series (Tantrik texts, 20), Calcutta: Sanskrit Book Depot / London: Luzac & Co., 1937.
SA_MB_cidgaganacandrika-HK.coverage: complete — Text ending with 8 concluding verses and the closing blessing 'śubhaṃ kulakramaṃ kuryāt'.

SA_MB_diiksaaprakaasaHK.title: Dīkṣāprakāśa
SA_MB_diiksaaprakaasaHK.author: Jīvanātha Śarman
SA_MB_diiksaaprakaasaHK.summary: A comprehensive late medieval or early modern tantric ritual handbook (paddhati) setting forth the procedures for initiation (dīkṣā), composed by the Maithila scholar Jīvanātha Śarman following Kṛṣṇānanda Āgamavāgīśa's Tantrasāra. The work explains the necessity of dīkṣā, the qualifications of the guru and disciple, astrological calculation of auspicious times and compatibility, the ten purifications of mantras (mantrasaṃskāra), preliminary rites and recitation (puraścaraṇa), sixteenfold worship (ṣoḍaśopacāra), and concluding offerings (śivābali).
SA_MB_diiksaaprakaasaHK.attribution: Authored by Maithila Paṇḍita Jīvanātha Śarman. Associated names in the metadata include Rāmateja Pāṇḍeya and Raghunandanaprasāda Śukla.
SA_MB_diiksaaprakaasaHK.edition: Dīkṣāprakāśa, by Maithila Paṇḍita Jīvanātha Śarman, Benares: Saṃskṛta Pustakālaya (Kacauṇīgalī), 1935.
SA_MB_diiksaaprakaasaHK.coverage: complete — Complete text ending with the colophon: 'iti śivamāhātmyavarṇanam | samāpto'yaṃ granthaḥ |'.

SA_MB_Isaanapaddhati-I-HK.title: Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati (part 1: Sāmānyapāda)
SA_MB_Isaanapaddhati-I-HK.author: Īśānaśivagurudeva
SA_MB_Isaanapaddhati-I-HK.summary: The Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati is an encyclopedic manual of ritual, temple consecration, and mantra-śāstra composed by the Kerala Śaiva authority Īśānaśivagurudeva (c. 11th–12th century CE). This opening division, the Sāmānyapāda (paṭalas 1–14), provides the common preliminary framework for ritual activity, including the classifications and recitation of mantras, the nature of letters (mātṛkā), the dimensions and preparation of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) and diagrams (maṇḍala), morning ablutions, and the rites of the sacred fire (agnikalpa). Synthesizing Śaivasiddhānta tenets with regional Kerala tantric traditions, it serves as a key witness to medieval South Indian ritual literature.
SA_MB_Isaanapaddhati-I-HK.attribution: Attributed in headers and colophons to Īśānaśivagurudeva (also named Īśānaśiva).
SA_MB_Isaanapaddhati-I-HK.edition: īśānaśivagurudevapaddhatiḥ Volume 1, edited by gaṇapati śāstrī, Delhi: bharatiya vidya prakāśan, 1921 (Volume 1 of 4 volume edition by University of Trivandrum, Gov. of Travancore, 1921).
SA_MB_Isaanapaddhati-I-HK.coverage: partial — Contains Sāmānyapāda (paṭalas 1–14), concluding with 'iti sāmānyapādaḥ prathamaḥ samāptaḥ'.

SA_MB_isaanagurudevapaddhati-II-HK.title: Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati (part 2: Mantrapāda, chapters 15–52)
SA_MB_isaanagurudevapaddhati-II-HK.author: Īśānaśivagurudeva
SA_MB_isaanagurudevapaddhati-II-HK.summary: The Mantrapāda forms the second division of Īśānaśivagurudeva's paddhati, completing its first half (Pūrvārdha). It provides an exhaustive treatment of mantravāda, including meditation verses (dhyāna), nyāsa, and japa for Gaṇapati, Sarasvatī, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Mṛtyuñjaya, and numerous forms of the Goddess. It also incorporates extensive sections on toxicology (viṣacikitsā), spirit exorcism (bhūtavidyā), magical protection (rakṣā), and martial sorcery (yuddhajaitrakarman).
SA_MB_isaanagurudevapaddhati-II-HK.attribution: The colophons credit the work to Īśānaśiva / Īśānaśivagurudeva. A statistical dating model estimates a posterior median of 1134 CE (95% credible interval: 1082 CE – 1185 CE).
SA_MB_isaanagurudevapaddhati-II-HK.edition: Gaṇapati Śāstrī (ed.), Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati Volume 2, University of Trivandrum, Gov. of Travancore, 1922 (reprinted Delhi: Bharatiya Vidya Prakashan).
SA_MB_isaanagurudevapaddhati-II-HK.coverage: partial — Contains the text of Part 2 (Mantrapāda, also termed Tantrasāra in the final colophon), concluding with paṭala 52 and the end of the Pūrvārdha.

SA_MB_iisaanagurudevapaddhati-III-HK.title: Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati (Kriyāpāda, paṭalas 1–30)
SA_MB_iisaanagurudevapaddhati-III-HK.author: Īśānaśivagurudeva
SA_MB_iisaanagurudevapaddhati-III-HK.summary: The Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati (also titled Siddhāntasāra) is an encyclopedic Śaivasiddhānta ritual compendium composed by Īśānaśivagurudeva. This volume preserves the first half of the Kriyāpāda (paṭalas 1–30), covering the theological foundations of Śaivism, daily liturgy (nityapūjā), the tiered structure of Śaiva initiation (dīkṣā), and extensive treatises on temple architecture, vāstu, and iconography (vimāna, upapīṭha, adhiṣṭhāna).
SA_MB_iisaanagurudevapaddhati-III-HK.attribution: Consistently attributed to Īśānaśivagurudeva (or Īśānaśiva) in the text headers and colophons.
SA_MB_iisaanagurudevapaddhati-III-HK.coverage: partial — Contains paṭalas 1–30 of the Kriyāpāda (the first section of the Uparibhāga), corresponding to Volume 3 of the 4-volume edition.

SA_MB_IPV_HK.title: Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā with Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī and Bhāskarī
SA_MB_IPV_HK.author: Utpaladeva, Abhinavagupta, Bhāskarakaṇṭha
