It extols Śiva and his Śakti as the pulsating supreme consciousness underlying the unfolding of speech (vāc) and the cosmos. Kṣemarāja's Vivṛti provides an extensive philosophical commentary elucidating the verses in terms of Trika and Spanda doctrines.
SA_MB_STAVACINTAAMANI_hk.attribution: Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa is the author of the Stavacintāmaṇi. Kṣemarāja is the author of the Vivṛti commentary.
SA_MB_STAVACINTAAMANI_hk.edition: The Stava-Cintāmaṇi of Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa with commentary by Kṣemarāja, ed. Mukunda Rāma Śāstrī. KSTS 10. Srinagar: Research Department, Jammu and Kashmir State, 1918.
SA_MB_STAVACINTAAMANI_hk.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 120 verses of the Stavacintāmaṇi together with Kṣemarāja's Vivṛti and Mukundarāma Śāstrī's verse-by-verse summary appendix (Dvitīyapariśiṣṭa).

SA_K10_sf277_sc.title: Agrajñasūtra (fragments)
SA_K10_sf277_sc.summary: The Agrajñasūtra describes the devolutionary cycle of cosmogony at the reconstitution of the world, detailing how radiant beings descending from the Ābhāsvara heaven ingest the savory crust of the earth (pṛthivīrasa), thereby developing physical density, losing their natural brilliance, and causing the emergence of celestial bodies (sun and moon).
SA_K10_sf277_sc.edition: Ernst Waldschmidt, Bruchstücke buddhistischer Sūtras aus dem zentralasiatischen Sanskritkanon, Kleine Sanskrit-Texte 4, Leipzig 1932 (Turfan editions); SuttaCentral 'Other Fragments' corpus.
SA_K10_sf277_sc.coverage: fragment — Preserves sections Wal_1 through Wal_7 covering the devolutionary cosmogonic cycle and the consumption of pṛthivīrasa, breaking off in section 7 ('etc. as in 4').

SA_GP12_vipce_pu.title: Viṣṇupurāṇa
SA_GP12_vipce_pu.summary: The Viṣṇupurāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas and a foundational scripture of classical Vaiṣṇavism, framed as a dialogue between the sage Parāśara and his pupil Maitreya. Arranged in six books (aṃśas), it exemplifies the traditional pañcalakṣaṇa schema encompassing cosmogony, cosmic dissolution and renewal, genealogies of sages and monarchs, manvantaras, and royal dynasties. Book 5 provides an early, influential narrative of Kṛṣṇa's life, while Book 6 treats the degeneration of the Kali age and liberation through devotion to Viṣṇu.
SA_GP12_vipce_pu.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the sage Parāśara narrating to his disciple Maitreya, and compiled in the tradition of Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa.
SA_GP12_vipce_pu.edition: The Critical Edition of the Viṣṇupurāṇam, critically edited by M. M. Pathak, Vadodara: Oriental Institute, 1997–1999.
SA_GP12_vipce_pu.coverage: complete — Complete in 6 aṃśas (adhyāyas 1.1 through 6.8), including star-passages recorded in the critical apparatus.
translations: Translated by H. H. Wilson, London: John Murray, 1840. (English)
Translated by M. N. Dutt. (English)

SA_T06_-ybh-klesa.title: Yogācārabhūmi (Kleśasaṃkleśa)
SA_T06_-ybh-klesa.author: Asaṅga
SA_T06_-ybh-klesa.summary: This excerpt from the Yogācārabhūmi presents the classical Yogācāra analysis of defilements (kleśasaṃkleśa). It defines the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of kleśa, details its division from 1-fold up to 128 varieties (mapped against the Four Noble Truths across the three realms of existence), and analyzes cognitive distortions (viparyāsa), latent dispositions (anuśaya), and karmic consequences (ādīnava).
SA_T06_-ybh-klesa.edition: Sung Doo Ahn (ed.), Die Lehre von den Kleśas in der Yogācārabhūmi, Alt- und Neu-Indische Studien 55, Stuttgart: Franz Steiner Verlag, 2003.
SA_T06_-ybh-klesa.coverage: excerpt — Excerpts the Kleśasaṃkleśa subsection from the Yogācārabhūmi, matching pp. 58–86 of Ahn's 2003 edition.

SA_T06_bsa023_u.title: Viṃśatikākārikā
SA_T06_bsa023_u.author: Vasubandhu
SA_T06_bsa023_u.summary: The Viṃśatikākārikā ('Twenty Verses on Representation-Only') is a foundational Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda polemical treatise composed by Vasubandhu. The text refutes the reality of mind-independent external physical objects (bāhyārtha) through a rigorous critique of atomism (paramāṇuvāda), demonstrating that atomic partlessness and spatial extension are mutually incompatible. Vasubandhu defends the thesis that all experiential phenomena are appearances only (vijñaptimātra), answering realist objections by showing that spatial-temporal determination, intersubjective consistency, and practical efficacy can function without external objects, as seen in dreams, collective karmic hallucinations, and demonic mental projections.
SA_T06_bsa023_u.edition: Ramshankar Tripathi (ed.), Vijnaptimatratasiddhi prakarana dvayam, Varanasi: Sampurnananda Sanskrit University, 1992.
SA_T06_bsa023_u.coverage: complete — Complete root text of 22 kārikās, ending with '// viṃśatikākārikāḥ samāptāḥ //'.
translations: Stefan Anacker, Seven Works of Vasubandhu, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1984.
Clarence H. Hamilton, Wei Shih Er Shih Lun, or The Treatise in Twenty Stanzas on Representation-Only, New Haven: American Oriental Society, 1938.
nyi shu pa'i tshig le'ur byas pa (Derge Tengyur D 4056): translated by Jinamitra, Śīlendrabodhi, Dānaśīla, sna nam btsun pa ye shes sde (Tibetan)

SA_K10_sf280_sc.title: Avasrutasūtra (fragment)
SA_K10_sf280_sc.summary: A fragmentary canonical discourse related to Chinese T 99. In the text, Mahāmaudgalyāyana delivers the discourse on the 'leaking and non-leaking' (avasruta-anavasruta) state, explaining that Māra finds no opening against a monk who masters sense-faculties and sense-objects; the Buddha subsequently praises the exposition and admonishes the saṅgha to uphold it.
SA_K10_sf280_sc.attribution: Canonical Buddhist sūtra preserved in Central Asian (Turfan) manuscript fragments.
SA_K10_sf280_sc.coverage: fragment — Six reconstructed text sections (tagged Wal_1 to Wal_6) from Turfan manuscript fragments.

SA_MB_kramasadbhava_images.title: Kramasadbhāva (manuscript header only, no text)
SA_MB_kramasadbhava_images.summary: The Kramasadbhāva is a scripture of the Kālī-centred Krama tradition of Kashmirian Śaivism, surviving in Nepalese manuscripts and cited by Krama authors. This catalog entry, however, contains only the manuscript description from Dyczkowski's edition file and none of the text.
SA_MB_kramasadbhava_images.attribution: A revealed tantric scripture of the Krama tradition of non-dual Śaivism/Śaktism preserved in Nepalese manuscripts.
SA_MB_kramasadbhava_images.edition: Header of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski's unpublished e-text/edition of the Kramasadbhāva based on National Archives Kathmandu MS 1-76 (Śaivatantra 144), NGMPP reel A 209/23; only the header survives in this file.
SA_MB_kramasadbhava_images.coverage: fragment — Empty stub: 8 lines (205 characters) of manuscript description (NAK 1-76 = Śaivatantra 144, NGMPP reel A 209/23, 15 paper leaves, 30 x 10 cm, Newari script) from Mark S. G. Dyczkowski's edition file; no Sanskrit text of the Kramasadbhāva is present.

SA_GV05_brupsb1u.title: Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad with Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣya (chapter 1)
SA_GV05_brupsb1u.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GV05_brupsb1u.summary: The first adhyāya of the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad (Kāṇva recension of the Śatapatha-Brāhmaṇa, Śukla Yajurveda) along with the Advaita Vedānta commentary (bhāṣya) attributed to Śaṅkara. The chapter opens with an allegorical meditation on the cosmic horse sacrifice (aśvamedha), describes cosmogenesis through death and hunger, and discusses the supremacy of the vital breath (prāṇa) over the sense faculties. It includes foundational Upaniṣadic teachings, notably the mahāvākya 'ahaṃ brahmāsmi' (1.4.10) and the division of the manifest world into name (nāma), form (rūpa), and action (karma). Śaṅkara's commentary elaborates the distinction between the ritual path (karmakāṇḍa) and knowledge of the non-dual self (jñānakāṇḍa), arguing that knowledge of Brahman alone destroys avidyā.
SA_GV05_brupsb1u.attribution: The Bṛhadāraṇyaka-Upaniṣad forms part of the Śatapatha-Brāhmaṇa (Kāṇva recension) of the Śukla Yajurveda. The commentary is ascribed to Śaṅkara.
SA_GV05_brupsb1u.coverage: partial — Contains Adhyāya 1 (brāhmaṇas 1–6) only, out of 6 adhyāyas. The remaining chapters are cataloged separately in files SA_GV05_brupsb2u through SA_GV05_brupsb6u.
translations: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation, New York, Oxford 1998. (English)

SA_GSP33_gaukarpu.title: Āgamaśāstra
SA_GSP33_gaukarpu.author: Gauḍapāda
SA_GSP33_gaukarpu.summary: The Āgamaśāstra (frequently called the Gauḍapādakārikā or Māṇḍūkyakārikā) is the earliest extant systematic verse treatise of Advaita Vedānta, traditionally attributed to Gauḍapāda (c. 6th century CE). Consisting of four prakaraṇas—Āgama, Vaitathya, Advaita, and Alātaśānti—the work expounds the doctrine of radical non-duality and absolute non-origination (ajātivāda). The first chapter interprets the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad's four states of consciousness culminating in turīya, while the subsequent chapters systematically deconstruct the ontological reality of external objects, change, and plurality, drawing extensively on the dialectic and terminology of contemporary Buddhist philosophy.
SA_GSP33_gaukarpu.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Gauḍapāda. Modern scholarship (notably Vidhushekhara Bhattacharya, Tilmann Vetter) has debated whether the four prakaraṇas were composed by a single author or represent distinct treatises assembled together, with the fourth prakaraṇa (Alātaśānti) displaying especially strong ties to Buddhist terminology and dialectic.
SA_GSP33_gaukarpu.edition: Māṇḍūkyopaniṣad Gauḍapādīyakārikāyutā Śaṅkarabhāṣyasahitā, ed. Vināyaka Gaṇeśa Āpaṭe, Pune: Ānandāśrama Press, 1921 (Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series). Variants in the text marked [S:], [B:], and [K:] are collated against: (1) Ishadi-dashopanishadah: Ten Principal Upanishads with Shankarabhashya, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1964; (2) The Āgamaśāstra of Gauḍapāda, ed. Vidhushekhara Bhattacharya, Calcutta: University of Calcutta, 1943; and (3) Gauḍapāda-Kārikā, ed. R. D. Karmarkar, Poona: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, 1963.
SA_GSP33_gaukarpu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all four prakaraṇas: 1. Āgamaprakaraṇa (29 kārikās), 2. Vaitathyaprakaraṇa (38 kārikās), 3. Advaitaprakaraṇa (48 kārikās), and 4. Alātaśāntiprakaraṇa (100 kārikās), totaling 215 verses.
translations: Bhattacharya, Vidhushekhara. The Āgamaśāstra of Gauḍapāda. Calcutta: University of Calcutta, 1943. (English)
Karmarkar, Raghunath Damodar. Gauḍapāda-Kārikā. Poona: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, 1963. (English)
Bouy, Christian. Gauḍapāda: L'Āgamaśāstra. Un traité védāntique en quatre chapitres. Paris: Collège de France / De Boccard, 2000. (French)

SA_GK19_bahcar1u.title: Harṣacarita (ucchvāsa 1)
SA_GK19_bahcar1u.author: Bāṇa
SA_GK19_bahcar1u.summary: The Harṣacarita is a biographical prose narrative (ākhyāyikā) by Bāṇabhaṭṭa recounting the life of Harṣavardhana. This first ucchvāsa opens with introductory verses paying homage to deities and celebrated earlier poets (including Vyāsa). It then narrates the celestial curse of Sarasvatī, her descent to earth, the mythical origins of the Vātsyāyana lineage, and Bāṇa's own youth and return to his ancestral home.
SA_GK19_bahcar1u.coverage: partial — Contains only ucchvāsa 1 (vātsyāyanavaṃśavarṇana), including the introductory verses (1.1–1.21) and the prose narrative down to the ucchvāsa colophon.

SA_GS40_caraka_u.title: Carakasaṃhitā with Āyurvedadīpikā (selected chapters)
SA_GS40_caraka_u.author: Caraka, Cakrapāṇidatta
SA_GS40_caraka_u.summary: The Carakasaṃhitā is one of the premier classical authorities of Āyurveda. Framed as instructions given by the sage Ātreya Punarvasu and compiled by his disciple Agniveśa, the compendium was redacted by Caraka and supplemented in several sections by Dṛḍhabala. This e-text preserves selected sections across several sthānas accompanied by Cakrapāṇidatta's commentary, the Āyurvedadīpikā.
SA_GS40_caraka_u.attribution: The root text is traditionally regarded as compiled by Agniveśa, revised by Caraka, and supplemented by Dṛḍhabala. The commentary Āyurvedadīpikā was composed by Cakrapāṇidatta.
SA_GS40_caraka_u.edition: Carakasaṃhitā (selected parts) with the Āyurvedadīpikā, based on the edition by J. Trikamji, Varanasi: Chaukhambha Sanskrit Sansthan, 1994 (Kashi Sanskrit Series, 228).
SA_GS40_caraka_u.coverage: partial — Selected portions only: Sūtrasthāna 1.1–43, 12.1–17, 26–28; Nidānasthāna 7.1–14; Vimānasthāna 1; Indriyasthāna 1.1–30; Cikitsāsthāna 1, 1.3–2.4, 22.

SA_GSP27_motik_2u.title: Mokṣopāya with Mokṣopāyaṭīkā (prakaraṇa 2: Mumukṣuvyavahāra)
SA_GSP27_motik_2u.author: Bhāskarakaṇṭha
SA_GSP27_motik_2u.summary: The Mumukṣuvyavahāraprakaraṇa is the second book of the Mokṣopāya, the Kashmirian philosophical ancestor of the widely known Yogavāsiṣṭha. It outlines the preliminary qualifications and conduct of a spiritual aspirant, placing central emphasis on personal exertion (pauruṣa) over fatalism (daiva) and detailing the four gatekeepers of liberation: tranquility (śama), inquiry (vicāra), contentment (saṃtoṣa), and association with virtuous teachers (sādhasaṅga). The embedded commentary by the Kashmirian scholar Bhāskarakaṇṭha provides a close gloss interpreting the text through the conceptual vocabulary of Kashmir Śaivism (Pratyabhijñā).
SA_GSP27_motik_2u.attribution: The root Mokṣopāya is an anonymous Kashmirian philosophical narrative. The commentary Mokṣopāyaṭīkā was composed by the Kashmirian scholar Bhāskarakaṇṭha, son of Avatārakaṇṭha and grandson of Vaiḍūryakaṇṭha, as explicitly confirmed in the closing colophon.
SA_GSP27_motik_2u.edition: Walter Slaje (ed.), Bhāskarakaṇṭhas Mokṣopāya-Ṭīkā. Ein Kommentar in der Tradition der kaschmirischen Yogavāsiṣṭha-Überlieferung. 2. Prakaraṇa (Mumukṣuvyavahāra). Graz, 1993.

SA_K10_sf253_sc.title: Saṅgītisūtra
SA_K10_sf253_sc.summary: An Āgama sūtra of the Sarvāstivāda Dīrghāgama, parallel to the Pāli Saṅgītisutta (DN 33). At Pāpā, in the new assembly hall of the Mallas, Śāriputra notes that the Jain community split after Nirgrantha Jñātiputra's death. To prevent such a split he recites the Buddha's teachings in numerical groups from one to ten, and the Buddha approves. It is the basis of the Abhidharma treatise Saṅgītiparyāya.
SA_K10_sf253_sc.attribution: Canonical discourse belonging to the Sanskrit Dīrghāgama of the Sarvāstivāda tradition, delivered primarily by Śāriputra and confirmed by the Buddha.
SA_K10_sf253_sc.coverage: complete — The whole sūtra as reconstructed: introduction (Wal_a–Wal_z: Pāpā, the new assembly hall of the Mallas, the schism of the Nirgranthas after Jñātiputra's death), groups of one to ten (Wal_1.1–Wal_10.2) and the Buddha's approval and closing (Wal_10.2.1–10.2.4). About 70 lacunae marked '…' and some missing items (e.g. 5.11–12, 8.5; 8.4 only the heading). The work is not truncated, so the title has no partial marker.
translations: Maurice Walshe, The Long Discourses of the Buddha, London: Wisdom Publications, 1987 (DN 33, Pāli parallel). (English)

SA_GV05_chup___u.title: Chāndogyopaniṣad
SA_GV05_chup___u.summary: The Chāndogyopaniṣad is one of the oldest and most extensive principal Upaniṣads, belonging to the Sāmaveda tradition. Across eight prapāṭhakas, it progresses from esoteric ritual reflections on the liturgical chant (udgītha) and the syllable Om to profound metaphysical inquiries into cosmology, the five fires (pañcāgnividyā), and the nature of Brahman. It contains celebrated pedagogical narratives such as Uddālaka Āruṇi's instruction of Śvetaketu featuring the mahāvākya 'tat tvam asi' and Sanatkumāra's discourse to Nārada on the infinite (bhūman).
SA_GV05_chup___u.attribution: A Vedic text of the Sāmaveda.
SA_GV05_chup___u.edition: V. P. Limaye and R. D. Vadekar (eds.), Eighteen Principal Upanisads, vol. 1, Poona: Vaidika Saṃśodhana Maṇḍala, 1958; collated with the TITUS e-text.
SA_GV05_chup___u.coverage: complete — Complete text in 8 prapāṭhakas (chapters 1.1.1 to 8.15.1), ending with the standard closing formula: 'brahmalokam abhisaṃpadyate / na ca punar āvartate na ca punar āvartate // ChUp_8,15.1 //'.
translations: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation, New York: Oxford University Press, 1998. (English)
Paul Deussen, German edition published 1897. (German)

SA_K10_sf276_sc.title: Candrasūtra
SA_K10_sf276_sc.summary: The Candrasūtra is a canonical Buddhist discourse relating the lunar eclipse myth corresponding to the Pāli Candima Sutta. When the moon deity is seized by the asura Rāhu, the deity seeks refuge in the Buddha, who instructs Rāhu to release the moon; frightened that his head might split into seven pieces, Rāhu promptly lets the moon go.
SA_K10_sf276_sc.attribution: Canonical Buddhist discourse preserved in Sanskrit manuscript fragments from Central Asia; corresponds to the Candima Sutta of the Pāli Saṃyutta Nikāya (SN 2.9) and the Chinese Saṃyuktāgama (T 99, T 100).
SA_K10_sf276_sc.edition: Waldschmidt, Ernst. 'Buddha frees the Disc of the Moon (Candrasūtra).' Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 33 (1970): 179–183.
SA_K10_sf276_sc.coverage: complete — Reconstructed text in 12 sections/paragraphs with verses, concluding with 'candrasūtraṁ samāptam //'.

SA_K12_Āgama_Vajrabhairavatantra_Wenta_2.title: Vajrabhairavatantra
SA_K12_Āgama_Vajrabhairavatantra_Wenta_2.summary: The Vajrabhairavatantra (also known as Vajramahābhairavatantra) is a central Anuttarayogatantra text centered on the wrathful deity Yamāntaka/Vajrabhairava, closely affiliated with the Mañjuśrī cycle. In seven kalpas, it details the construction of the wrathful maṇḍala in cremation grounds, ferocious magical and protective rites (ṣaṭkarmāṇi), visualisations of the buffalo-headed deity, and initiation protocols. First critically edited in Sanskrit by Aleksandra Wenta in 2020, it holds major historical significance for Tibetan Buddhist esoteric ritualism, particularly within the Sakya and Gelug traditions.
SA_K12_Āgama_Vajrabhairavatantra_Wenta_2.attribution: A Buddhist Anuttarayogatantra text revealed within the Yamāntaka / Vajrabhairava cycle; traditionally considered Buddhavacana.
SA_K12_Āgama_Vajrabhairavatantra_Wenta_2.edition: Aleksandra Wenta, The Vajramahābhairavatantra: Its Origins, Intertextuality, and Transmission, D.Phil. thesis, University of Oxford, 2020.
SA_K12_Āgama_Vajrabhairavatantra_Wenta_2.coverage: complete — Complete in 7 kalpas (chapters 1–7), concluding with the seventh chapter colophon (dhyānakarmasiddhiparīkṣākalpaḥ saptamaḥ).
translations: Bulcsu Siklos, The Vajrabhairava Tantras: Tibetan and Mongolian Versions, English Translation and Annotations, Tring, U.K.: The Institute of Buddhist Studies, 1996. (English (translated from Tibetan))

SA_K12_Āgama_Tantrasadbhāva_Bang_2018.title: Tantrasadbhāva (selected chapters: 1, 3, 9, 18, 24, 28)
SA_K12_Āgama_Tantrasadbhāva_Bang_2018.summary: The Tantrasadbhāva is a scripture of the Vidyāpīṭha of the Bhairavasrotas (colophons: 'bhairavasrotasi mahātantre vidyāpīṭhe saptakoṭipramāṇe'), cast as a dialogue between Bhairava and the Goddess and widely quoted by Kashmirian Śaiva authors. The chapters here cover the basic doctrine of Śakti, Kuṇḍalinī and the power of mantras (ch. 1), the nādiphānta mantra-encoding system (ch. 3), Śaiva initiation and the observances (samaya) of initiates (ch. 9), the code language of signs and words (chommaka) used to meet the yoginīs (ch. 18), a passage on knowing the time of death (ch. 24), and the inner yoga of the self's movement through the channels and lotuses of the body (ch. 28).
SA_K12_Āgama_Tantrasadbhāva_Bang_2018.attribution: Revealed Śaiva scripture of the Vidyāpīṭha / Bhairavasrotas, framed as an esoteric dialogue between Bhairava and the Devī.
SA_K12_Āgama_Tantrasadbhāva_Bang_2018.edition: Junglan Bang, 'Selected Chapters from the Tantrasadbhāva, Based on the Tradition of 11th-century Śaiva Sanskrit Manuscripts in Nepal', in Proceedings of the 17th World Sanskrit Conference, Vancouver 2018, Section 6: Tantra Studies, 2018.
SA_K12_Āgama_Tantrasadbhāva_Bang_2018.coverage: partial — Ch. 1 Praśnayogādhikāra (vv. 1–490, with colophon); ch. 3 Mantranirṇayādhikāra, only the nādiphāntakrama section (marked '[nādiphāntakramam]', vv. c. 96–131); ch. 9 Samayadīkṣādhikāra (vv. 1–577, with colophon); ch. 18 Chommakādhikāra (with colophon); ch. 24 Kālādhikāra, only the kālajñāna excerpt '[kālajñānam]' vv. 177–197; ch. 28 Ātmācārādhikāra (to v. 105 and colophon). The Tantrasadbhāva has 28 paṭalas in all; the other chapters are not included.

SA_T02_Ratnākaraśānti_Muktāvalī-Hevajrat.title: Hevajratantra with Muktāvalī
SA_T02_Ratnākaraśānti_Muktāvalī-Hevajrat.author: Ratnākaraśānti
SA_T02_Ratnākaraśānti_Muktāvalī-Hevajrat.summary: The Hevajratantra is a prominent Buddhist Anuttarayogatantra of the Heruka/Yoginī class, expounding internal yogic practices, maṇḍala rites, twilight language (sandhyābhāṣā), and the realization of mahāsukha and sahajakāya. The Muktāvalī is an extensive pañjikā commentary composed by Ratnākaraśānti, interpreting the tantra within a philosophical framework integrating Yogācāra and Madhyamaka. This e-text provides the complete text of both parts of the tantra along with Ratnākaraśānti's commentary.
SA_T02_Ratnākaraśānti_Muktāvalī-Hevajrat.attribution: The root tantra is an anonymous Anuttarayogatantra scripture. The commentary Muktāvalī is authored by the Mahāpaṇḍita Ratnākaraśānti.
SA_T02_Ratnākaraśānti_Muktāvalī-Hevajrat.edition: Hevajratantram with Muktāvalī Pañjikā of Mahāpaṇḍitācārya Ratnākaraśānti, ed. Ram Shankar Tripathi & Thakur Sain Negi, Bibliotheca Indo-Tibetica Series 48, Sarnath/Varanasi: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 2001.
SA_T02_Ratnākaraśānti_Muktāvalī-Hevajrat.coverage: complete — Complete text of both the root tantra and the commentary across both kalpas: Kalpa I and Kalpa II (12 paṭalas).
translations: dpal dgyes pa'i rdo rje'i dka' 'grel mu tig phreng ba zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 1189): translated by Śāntibhadra, 'gos lo tsA ba khug pa lhas btsas (Tibetan)

SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti_Minaev_.title: Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti
SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti_Minaev_.summary: The Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti is one of the most celebrated and authoritative tantric texts across Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna traditions, praising the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī as the ultimate personification of nondual gnosis (jñānakāya) and buddhahood. Formally situated within the Māyājālatantra cycle as a dialogue between Vajrapāṇi and Śākyamuni Buddha, the text catalogues the epithets and divine forms of gnosis distributed across six Buddha families (kula). Widely practiced liturgically across Northern India, Nepal, Tibet, and East Asia, it spawned an extensive commentary literature from the late 8th century onward.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti_Minaev_.attribution: Canonical Buddhist tantric scripture presented as spoken by the Buddha Śākyamuni in response to Vajrapāṇi; traditionally embedded in the Māyājālamahātantrarāja cycle.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti_Minaev_.edition: I.P. Minaev, edition of the Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti Sanskrit text in 'Buddizm: Issledovaniya i materialy', vol. I.2, St. Petersburg, 1887.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti_Minaev_.coverage: complete — Text of the Nāmasaṃgīti ending with the anuśaṃsāstuti.
translations: Davidson, Ronald M. (1981). 'The Litany of Names of Mañjuśrī', in Tantric and Taoist Studies in Honour of R. A. Stein. (English)
Wayman, Alex (1985). Chanting the Names of Manjushri. Boston: Shambhala Publications. (English)

SA_T02_Mañjuśrīyaśa_Laghukālacakratantra.title: Laghukālacakratantra with Vimalaprabhā (chapters 1–2)
SA_T02_Mañjuśrīyaśa_Laghukālacakratantra.author: Mañjuśrīyaśas, Puṇḍarīka
SA_T02_Mañjuśrīyaśa_Laghukālacakratantra.summary: The Laghukālacakratantra is the central canonical scripture of the Buddhist Kālacakra cycle, representing late Indian Anuttarayoga tantra. The Vimalaprabhā of Kalkin Puṇḍarīka is its primary authoritative commentary, detailing the external, internal, and alternative systems of the tantra. This first volume contains chapters 1 and 2, which cover the outer cosmos (cosmography, astronomy, and calendrical systems) and the inner individual (embryology, channels, prāṇas, and subtle anatomy).
SA_T02_Mañjuśrīyaśa_Laghukālacakratantra.attribution: Traditional Vajrayāna attribution assigns the abridgment of the root Laghukālacakratantra from the Paramādibuddha to Kalki King Mañjuśrīyaśas (Mañjuśrīkīrti), and the commentary Vimalaprabhā to his successor Kalkin Puṇḍarīka. Modern scholarship dates the compilation of the Kālacakratantra corpus to the early 11th century CE in India.
SA_T02_Mañjuśrīyaśa_Laghukālacakratantra.edition: Jagannatha Upadhyaya (ed.), Vimalaprabhāṭīkā of Kalkin Śrīpuṇḍarīka on Śrīlaghukālacakratantrarāja by Śrīmañjuśrīyaśas, Vol. 1, Bibliotheca Indo-Tibetica Series 11, Sarnath/Varanasi: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 1986.
SA_T02_Mañjuśrīyaśa_Laghukālacakratantra.coverage: partial — Chapters (paṭalas) 1 and 2 only (Lokadhātupaṭala and Adhyātmapaṭala), corresponding to Volume 1 of Upādhyāya's critical edition. The complete work comprises 5 chapters.

SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti_Mukherj.title: Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti
SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti_Mukherj.summary: The Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti ('Chanting the Names of Mañjuśrī') is an influential Vajrayāna liturgical and doctrinal scripture comprising 167 verses in 14 chapters. Framed as a dialogue between Śākyamuni Buddha and Vajrapāṇi within the Māyājālatantra cycle, it extols Mañjuśrī as the embodiment of nondual gnosis (jñānakāya) and enlightened awareness. It was extensively commented upon across all major Tibetan and late Indian Buddhist traditions, including important commentaries by Vilāsavajra.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti_Mukherj.edition: Durgadas Mukherji (ed.), Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti, Sanskrit and Tibetan texts. Santiniketan: Visva-Bharati, 1963.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti_Mukherj.coverage: complete — Complete Sanskrit text with interlinear/parallel Tibetan translation from Mukherji's bilingual edition.
translations: Davidson, Ronald M., 'The Litany of Names of Mañjuśrī', in Tantric and Taoist Studies in Honour of R. A. Stein, 1981. (English)
Wayman, Alex, Chanting the Names of Manjushri, Boston: Shambhala Publications, 1985. (English)

SA_T02_Jñānacandra_Mahāsukhaprakāśikā-Ta.title: Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhi with Mahāsukhaprakāśikā (incomplete: breaks off in the appended Mantroddhāra)
SA_T02_Jñānacandra_Mahāsukhaprakāśikā-Ta.author: Śūnyatāsamādhivajra, Jñānacandra
SA_T02_Jñānacandra_Mahāsukhaprakāśikā-Ta.summary: The Mahāsukhaprakāśikā on the Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhi is a Tantric text focusing on Vajravārāhī / Vajrayoginī practice, pūjāvidhi, layokrama, and mantroddhāra.
SA_T02_Jñānacandra_Mahāsukhaprakāśikā-Ta.attribution: The e-text names bhikṣu Jñānacandra in the opening verses (v. 3: 'bhikṣuṇā jñānandrēṇa').
SA_T02_Jñānacandra_Mahāsukhaprakāśikā-Ta.edition: Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhiḥ Mahāsukhaprakāśikā, Dharmodayagranthamālā (37), 2013 Vikrama Saṃvat [= 1956/57 CE].
SA_T02_Jñānacandra_Mahāsukhaprakāśikā-Ta.coverage: partial — The e-text breaks off mid-sentence in the mantroddhāra section ('akāramārabhya ṣoḍaśa').

SA_T02_Kṛṣṇācārya_Yogaratnamālā-Hevajrat.title: Hevajratantra with Yogaratnamālā
SA_T02_Kṛṣṇācārya_Yogaratnamālā-Hevajrat.author: Kṛṣṇācārya
SA_T02_Kṛṣṇācārya_Yogaratnamālā-Hevajrat.summary: The Hevajratantra is a pivotal Anuttarayogatantra of the Yoginī/Ḍākinī class comprising two kalpas of eleven and twelve chapters respectively, focusing on the deity Hevajra and his retinue, consecration rituals (abhiṣeka), sandhyābhāṣā (coded language), internal subtle body yoga, and the attainment of Sahaja (innate bliss). The Yogaratnamālā (Vajrapañjikā) by Kṛṣṇācārya (Kāṇhapāda) is the earliest surviving and most authoritative Sanskrit commentary on the tantra, explaining its complex ritual practices, yogic physiology, and non-dual Madhyamaka-Yogācāra philosophical synthesis.
SA_T02_Kṛṣṇācārya_Yogaratnamālā-Hevajrat.attribution: The commentary Yogaratnamālā (or Vajrapañjikā) is attributed to Mahāpaṇḍitācārya Śrī Kṛṣṇapāda / Kāṇhapāda (Kṛṣṇācārya).
SA_T02_Kṛṣṇācārya_Yogaratnamālā-Hevajrat.edition: Ram Shankar Tripathi & Thakur Sain Negi (eds.), Hevajratantram with Yogaratnamālā Pañjikā of Mahāpaṇḍitācārya Kṛṣṇācārya, Bibliotheca Indo-Tibetica Series 65, Sarnath: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 2006.
SA_T02_Kṛṣṇācārya_Yogaratnamālā-Hevajrat.coverage: complete — Text of the Hevajratantra interleaved with the Yogaratnamālā of Kṛṣṇācārya.
translations: David L. Snellgrove, The Hevajra Tantra: A Critical Study, Part 1: Introduction and Translation, London Oriental Series 6, London: Oxford University Press, 1959. (English)

SA_T02_Abhayākaragupta_Buddhakapālatantr.title: Abhayapaddhati
SA_T02_Abhayākaragupta_Buddhakapālatantr.author: Abhayākaragupta
SA_T02_Abhayākaragupta_Buddhakapālatantr.summary: The Abhayapaddhati is an extensive commentary on the Buddhakapālamahātantra composed by the late Indian tantric master Abhayākaragupta of Vikramaśīla monastery in the 25th regnal year of the Pāla king Rāmapāla (c. early 12th century). The work explains the rituals, maṇḍala layout, generation stage (utpattikrama), and completion stage (niṣpannakrama) of the Heruka-class Yoginītantra Buddhakapāla, integrating it into non-dual Mahāmudrā exegesis.
SA_T02_Abhayākaragupta_Buddhakapālatantr.attribution: Colophon explicitly verifies authorship: 'iti śrībuddhakapālamahātantraṭīkā abhayapaddhatiḥ samāptā | kṛti: paṇḍitasthavirābhayākaraguptapādānām' and dates composition to the 25th regnal year of King Rāmapāla ('rājyābde rāmapālasya pañcaviṃśe'karodimām').
SA_T02_Abhayākaragupta_Buddhakapālatantr.edition: Abhayapaddhati of Abhayākaragupta, Commentary on the Buddhakapālamahātantra, ed. Chog Dorje, Bibliotheca Indo-Tibetica Series 68, Sarnath/Varanasi: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 2009.
SA_T02_Abhayākaragupta_Buddhakapālatantr.coverage: complete — Complete commentary on all 14 paṭalas of the Buddhakapālamahātantra, including opening verses and concluding praśasti/colophon.
translations: Degé Tengyur Toh. 1654: Śrī-Buddhakapālamahātantrarājaṭīkā abhayapaddhati-nāma (ḥjigs-pa med-paḥi gśuṅ ḥgrel śes-bya-ba), translated by Diṅ-ri Chos-grags (?), revised by Blo-gros brtan-pa. (Tibetan)

SA_T02_Dauḍīpāda-Ghanadeva_Guhyāvalīvivṛ.title: Guhyāvalī with Guhyāvalīvivṛti
SA_T02_Dauḍīpāda-Ghanadeva_Guhyāvalīvivṛ.author: Dauḍīpāda, Ghanadeva
SA_T02_Dauḍīpāda-Ghanadeva_Guhyāvalīvivṛ.summary: The Guhyāvalī is a short 25-verse Vajrayāna treatise on the svādhiṣṭhānakrama ('stage of self-consecration') and the realization of mahāmudrā and sahajānanda, attributed to the master Dauḍīpāda. The accompanying Guhyāvalīvivṛti by Ghanadeva provides a word-by-word commentary elucidating its esoteric doctrines and Anuttarayogatantra terminology. The text survives in manuscript Add. 1699 copied in Eastern India during the reign of Govindapāla.
SA_T02_Dauḍīpāda-Ghanadeva_Guhyāvalīvivṛ.attribution: The root text is explicitly attributed in the commentary to Āryadauḍīpāda (segment 9: 'śrīmadāryadauḍīpādo... svādhiṣṭhānakramameva pañcaviṃśatyā ślokaiḥ kartumārabdhavān'). The commentary is attributed to Bhikṣu Paṇḍitasthavira Ghanadeva (segment 7: 'bhikṣuśrīghanadevena vivṛttiḥ kriyate sphuṭam'; segment 373: 'vivṛti: paṇḍitasthaviraśrīghanadevasya').
SA_T02_Dauḍīpāda-Ghanadeva_Guhyāvalīvivṛ.edition: Guhyāvalīvivṛti, ed. in Dhīḥ: Journal of Rare Buddhist Texts Research Unit, Sarnath, Varanasi: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies (CIHTS), 2008.
SA_T02_Dauḍīpāda-Ghanadeva_Guhyāvalīvivṛ.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all 25 verses of the Guhyāvalī along with Ghanadeva's Guhyāvalīvivṛti. Two lines from the succeeding text in the manuscript (Kāṇeripā's Śucikaraṇa) are erroneously appended at the very end.

SA_T02_Abhayākaragupta_Kālacakrāvatāra_U.title: Kālacakrāvatāra
SA_T02_Abhayākaragupta_Kālacakrāvatāra_U.author: Abhayākaragupta
SA_T02_Abhayākaragupta_Kālacakrāvatāra_U.summary: The Kālacakrāvatāra is a concise astronomical and calendrical manual (karaṇa) by the Mahāyāna master Abhayākaragupta. It outlines computational methods for determining solar and lunar calendar coordinates (varṣa-, māsa-, vāra-, and tithipiṇḍa), planetary positions, and astronomical events in accordance with the system of the Kālacakratantra.
SA_T02_Abhayākaragupta_Kālacakrāvatāra_U.attribution: A short astronomical and calendrical treatise (karaṇa/jyotiṣa) explaining Kālacakra calendar calculation, composed by Abhayākaragupta (fl. late 11th c.).
SA_T02_Abhayākaragupta_Kālacakrāvatāra_U.coverage: complete — Complete text preserved from the sole Sanskrit manuscript; extends from the opening salutation through verse 283, colophon line 284 ('iti kālacakrāvatāraḥ samāptaḥ'), and the appended zodiacal sign-table in segment 285.
translations: dpal dus kyi 'khor lo'i sdom tshig (Derge Tengyur D 1380): translated by Skt?? Tib??, khe'u gang 'khor lo grags (Tibetan)

SA_T02_Vajragarbha_Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-Hevajrat.title: Hevajrapiṇḍārthaṭīkā (chapter 10: Tattvapaṭala)
SA_T02_Vajragarbha_Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-Hevajrat.author: Vajragarbha
SA_T02_Vajragarbha_Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-Hevajrat.summary: The Hevajrapiṇḍārthaṭīkā (also known as the Ṣaṭsāhasrikā Hevajraṭīkā) is a commentary attributed to Vajragarbha that interprets the Hevajratantra in accordance with the Kālacakra system. In this tenth chapter, commenting upon the Tattvapaṭala (Hevajratantra I.5), Vajragarbha explicates the ultimate reality (tattva), the cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination and the eighteen sensory elements (dhātu), and internalizes the tantric mudrās into pure non-dual awareness and great bliss (mahāsukha).
SA_T02_Vajragarbha_Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-Hevajrat.attribution: Attributed to the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha; one of the three principal 'Bodhisattva commentaries' of the Kālacakra tradition (together with Puṇḍarīka's Vimalaprabhā and Vajrapāṇi's Lakṣābhidhānoddhṛtalaghutantrapiṇḍārthavivaraṇa).
SA_T02_Vajragarbha_Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-Hevajrat.edition: Francesco Sferra, 'The Elucidation of True Reality: The Kālacakra Commentary by Vajragarbha on the Tattvapaṭala of the Hevajratantra' (= ch. 10 of the Ṣaṭsāhasrikā Hevajrapiṇḍārthaṭīkā), in: As Long as Space Endures: Essays on the Kālacakra Tantra in Honor of H.H. the Dalai Lama, ed. E. A. Arnold, Ithaca: Snow Lion, 2009, pp. 93-126.
SA_T02_Vajragarbha_Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-Hevajrat.coverage: partial — Contains chapter 10 only (commenting on Hevajratantra I.5, Tattvapaṭala).
translations: Francesco Sferra, 'The Elucidation of True Reality: The Kālacakra Commentary by Vajragarbha on the Tattvapaṭala of the Hevajratantra', in: As Long as Space Endures, ed. Edward A. Arnold, Ithaca, NY: Snow Lion Publications, 2009, pp. 93–126. (English)

SA_T02_Anonymous_Kālacakrapūjāvidhi_RBTR.title: Kālacakrapūjāvidhi with Niṣpannayogāvalī (chapter 26: Kālacakramaṇḍala)
SA_T02_Anonymous_Kālacakrapūjāvidhi_RBTR.summary: The Kālacakrapūjāvidhi is a ritual manual detailing the worship (arcanakrama) of Kālacakra, citing the Paramādibuddhatantra. The text covers personal purification, mantra-snāna, body-mandala, and ritual offerings. It is accompanied by the Kālacakramaṇḍala section from Abhayākaragupta's Niṣpannayogāvalī.
SA_T02_Anonymous_Kālacakrapūjāvidhi_RBTR.attribution: The Kālacakrapūjāvidhi is an anonymous ritual manual. The appended Kālacakramaṇḍala is from the Niṣpannayogāvalī of Abhayākaragupta.
SA_T02_Anonymous_Kālacakrapūjāvidhi_RBTR.coverage: complete — Includes Kālacakrapūjāvidhi followed by chapter 26 (Kālacakramaṇḍala) of the Niṣpannayogāvalī, ending '|| iti kālacakramaṇḍalam || samāpteyaṃ niṣpannayogāvalī'.

SA_T02_Mañjuśrīyaśa_Laghukālacakratantra.title: Laghukālacakratantra with Vimalaprabhā (chapters 3–4)
SA_T02_Mañjuśrīyaśa_Laghukālacakratantra.author: Mañjuśrīyaśas, Puṇḍarīka
SA_T02_Mañjuśrīyaśa_Laghukālacakratantra.summary: The Laghukālacakratantra is the foundational condensed root scripture of the Kālacakra cycle, accompanied by the Vimalaprabhā commentary. This volume covers Chapter 3 (Abhiṣekapaṭala), treating tantric consecrations, and Chapter 4 (Sādhanapaṭala), presenting deity yoga, generation stage visualization, and the sixfold yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga) of the completion stage.
SA_T02_Mañjuśrīyaśa_Laghukālacakratantra.attribution: Traditional attribution credits the root tantra to Kalkin Mañjuśrīyaśas and the commentary Vimalaprabhā to Kalkin Puṇḍarīka.
SA_T02_Mañjuśrīyaśa_Laghukālacakratantra.edition: Vimalaprabhāṭīkā of Kalkin Śrīpuṇḍarīka on Śrī-Laghukālacakratantrarāja of Śrī-Mañjuśrīyaśas, Vol. 2, ed. Vrajavallabh Dwivedi & S. S. Bahulkar, Rare Buddhist Texts Series 13, Sarnath/Varanasi: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 1994.
SA_T02_Mañjuśrīyaśa_Laghukālacakratantra.coverage: partial — Contains chapters 3 (Abhiṣekapaṭala) and 4 (Sādhanapaṭala) of the 5-chapter tantra and commentary.

SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti_Vira-Ch.title: Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti
SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti_Vira-Ch.summary: The Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti ('Chanting the Names of Mañjuśrī') is one of the most revered and liturgically influential scriptural texts in esoteric Buddhism. Structured around an exchange between Vajrapāṇi and the Buddha Śākyamuni, it eulogizes Mañjuśrī as the ultimate wisdom-being (jñānasattva) and personification of non-dual gnosis (advayajñāna), mapping his epithets onto the five Buddha families and the path of transcendent awakening. Canonical tradition presents the text as an extract from the Māyājālatantra, and it was widely chanted and commented upon across northern India, Nepal, Tibet, and China.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti_Vira-Ch.attribution: Ascribed canonically to Śākyamuni Buddha teaching Vajrapāṇi; framed in its colophon as extracted from the Samādhijāla chapter of the 16,000-line Āryamāyājālamahāyogatantra.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti_Vira-Ch.edition: Raghu Vira & Lokesh Chandra (eds.), Sanskrit Texts from the Imperial Palace at Peking (incl. Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti / Kālacakra texts), Śata-Piṭaka Series 71 part 3, New Delhi: International Academy of Indian Culture, 1966.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti_Vira-Ch.coverage: complete — Complete text in 167 verses organized into canonical sections (adhyeṣaṇā, prativacana, etc.) ending with the upasaṃhāra-gāthāḥ and the standard closing colophon, though containing some OCR garbling.
translations: Davidson, Ronald M., 'The Litany of Names of Mañjuśrī: Text and Translation of the Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti', in Tantric and Taoist Studies in Honour of R.A. Stein, Bruxelles, 1981. (English)
Wayman, Alex, Chanting the Names of Mañjuśrī: The Mañjuśrī-nāma-saṃgīti, Sanskrit and Tibetan Texts, Boston: Shambhala, 1985. (English)

SA_T02_Vajragarbha_Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-Hevajrat.title: Hevajratantrapiṇḍārthaṭīkā (chapter 1: Iṣṭadevatāstava)
SA_T02_Vajragarbha_Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-Hevajrat.author: Vajragarbha
SA_T02_Vajragarbha_Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-Hevajrat.summary: The opening chapter (titled Iṣṭadevatāstava / Tantrāvatāra) of Vajragarbha's Ṣaṭsāhasrikā Hevajraṭīkā (Hevajratantrapiṇḍārthaṭīkā), composed within the Bodhisattva corpus exegetical movement closely related to the Kālacakratantra. It provides a stotra of the chosen deity Hevajra, addresses hermeneutical principles of the tantras, and critiques improper tantric teachers.
SA_T02_Vajragarbha_Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-Hevajrat.attribution: Attributed to Vajragarbha (referred to as daśabhūmīśvara in the text). The Bodhisattva corpus exegetical literature includes commentaries alongside Puṇḍarīka (Vimalaprabhā).
SA_T02_Vajragarbha_Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-Hevajrat.edition: Francesco Sferra, 'The Laud of the Chosen Deity, the First Chapter of the Hevajratantrapiṇḍārthaṭīkā by Vajragarbha', in Genesis and Development of Tantrism (ed. S. Einoo), Institute of Oriental Culture Special Series 23, Tokyo, 2009, pp. 435-468.
SA_T02_Vajragarbha_Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-Hevajrat.coverage: partial — Chapter 1 only (77 verses and colophon: 'iti ṣaṭsāhasrikāyām hevajraṭīkāyām iṣṭadevatāstavas tantrāvatāraḥ prathamaḥ paricchedaḥ').

SA_T02_Candrakīrti_Pradīpoddyotana-Guhya.title: Guhyasamājatantrapradīpoddyotana
SA_T02_Candrakīrti_Pradīpoddyotana-Guhya.author: Candrakīrti
SA_T02_Candrakīrti_Pradīpoddyotana-Guhya.summary: The Guhyasamājatantrapradīpoddyotana by Candrakīrti is the paramount Indian commentary on the Guhyasamājatantra belonging to the Ārya (Noble) tradition. It expounds a systematic hermeneutical method for unpacking the root tantra through the 'seven ornaments' (saptālaṅkāra) and the 'six alternatives' (ṣaṭkoṭi), integrating the stages of generation (utpattikrama) and completion (niṣpannakrama/pañcakrama). It has served as the definitive Indian commentary for later Guhyasamāja exegesis in India and Tibet.
SA_T02_Candrakīrti_Pradīpoddyotana-Guhya.attribution: Attributed to Candrakīrti, who is different from the Madhyamaka philosopher Candrakīrti.
SA_T02_Candrakīrti_Pradīpoddyotana-Guhya.edition: Chintaharan Chakravarti (ed.), Guhyasamājatantrapradīpodyotanaṭīkāṣaṭkoṭīvyākhyā, Tibetan Sanskrit Works Series vol. 25, Patna: Kashi Prasad Jayaswal Research Institute, 1984.
SA_T02_Candrakīrti_Pradīpoddyotana-Guhya.coverage: complete — Complete commentary on all 18 chapters of the Guhyasamājatantra, ending with the scribal colophon and donor formula (segments 6442–6451).

SA_K12_Āgama_Siddhayogeśvarīmatatantra_T.title: Siddhayogeśvarīmata (selected chapters)
SA_K12_Āgama_Siddhayogeśvarīmatatantra_T.summary: The Siddhayogeśvarīmata is an early and foundational scripture of the Trika lineage, datable roughly to the seventh century CE. It teaches the cult of the three goddesses (Parā and related deities) and yoginīs, presenting initiation (dīkṣā), mantras, mudrās, and related rites. The text served as an essential authority for later non-dual Śaiva masters of Kashmir, notably Abhinavagupta in his Tantrāloka.
SA_K12_Āgama_Siddhayogeśvarīmatatantra_T.attribution: Revealed Śaiva scripture of the Trika tradition.
SA_K12_Āgama_Siddhayogeśvarīmatatantra_T.edition: Judit Törzsök, 'The Doctrine of Magic Female Spirits: A Critical Edition of Selected Chapters of the Siddhayogeśvarīmata(tantra) with Annotated Translation and Analysis', D.Phil. thesis, University of Oxford, 1999.
SA_K12_Āgama_Siddhayogeśvarīmatatantra_T.coverage: partial — Contains selected chapters from Judit Törzsök's critical edition (Oxford, 1999). Due to OCR/extraction from the PDF, critical apparatus variants, notes, and parallel citations (e.g., to Mālinīvijayottara and Tantrāloka) are intermingled with root text verses.
translations: Judit Törzsök, 'The Doctrine of Magic Female Spirits: A Critical Edition of Selected Chapters of the Siddhayogeśvarīmata(tantra) with Annotated Translation and Analysis', D.Phil. thesis, University of Oxford, 1999 [includes English translation]. (English)

SA_T02_Anupamarakṣita_Ṣaḍaṇgayoga-with-G.title: Ṣaḍaṅgayoga with Guṇabharaṇī
SA_T02_Anupamarakṣita_Ṣaḍaṇgayoga-with-G.author: Anupamarakṣita, Raviśrījñāna
SA_T02_Anupamarakṣita_Ṣaḍaṇgayoga-with-G.summary: The Ṣaḍaṅgayoga of Anupamarakṣita and its commentary Guṇabharaṇī by Raviśrījñāna are key treatises of late Indian esoteric Buddhism associated with the Kālacakra and Guhyasamāja traditions. The text delineates the six limbs of yoga (pratyāhāra, dhyāna, prāṇāyāma, dhāraṇā, anusmṛti, and samādhi) as a systematic path for withdrawing the senses, mastering the subtle winds, and realizing Mahāmudrā.
SA_T02_Anupamarakṣita_Ṣaḍaṇgayoga-with-G.attribution: The root work is composed by Anupamarakṣita; the commentary (ṭippaṇī) Guṇabharaṇī is by Raviśrījñāna (also known as Raviśrī).
SA_T02_Anupamarakṣita_Ṣaḍaṇgayoga-with-G.edition: Francesco Sferra, The Ṣaḍaṅgayoga by Anupamarakṣita, with Raviśrījñāna's Guṇabharaṇīnāmaṣaḍaṅgayogaṭippaṇī. Text and Annotated Translation. Roma: Istituto Italiano per l'Africa e l'Oriente, 2000 (Serie Orientale Roma, LXXXV).
SA_T02_Anupamarakṣita_Ṣaḍaṇgayoga-with-G.coverage: complete — Text contains both root kārikās and commentary, along with sections of Tibetan text.
translations: Francesco Sferra, The Ṣaḍaṅgayoga by Anupamarakṣita, with Raviśrījñāna's Guṇabharaṇīnāmaṣaḍaṅgayogaṭippaṇī. Text and Annotated Translation. Roma: Istituto Italiano per l'Africa e l'Oriente, 2000 (Serie Orientale Roma, LXXXV). (English)

SA_T02_Abhayākaragupta_Kālacakrāvatāra_M.title: Kālacakrāvatāra
SA_T02_Abhayākaragupta_Kālacakrāvatāra_M.author: Abhayākaragupta
SA_T02_Abhayākaragupta_Kālacakrāvatāra_M.summary: The Kālacakrāvatāra is an introductory work on astronomical and calendrical calculation by Abhayākaragupta, based on the Kālacakra system. Its epoch calculation involves mleccha 463. The unique Sanskrit manuscript includes an appendix by Dānaśrīmitra giving Śaka 1047.
SA_T02_Abhayākaragupta_Kālacakrāvatāra_M.attribution: Attributed in the opening and closing colophons to paṇḍita Abhayākaragupta (fl. late 11th c.). The short calendrical appendix after the colophon is ascribed by Newman ('Epoch of the Kālacakra') to Dānaśrīmitra, who wrote it in the unique manuscript and records Śaka 1047.
SA_T02_Abhayākaragupta_Kālacakrāvatāra_M.coverage: complete — Complete text, closing 'iti kālacakrāvatāra: samāptaḥ || kṛtiriyaṃ paṇḍitā bhayākaraguptapādānāmiti', followed by Dānaśrīmitra's calendrical appendix with Śaka year 1047.
translations: dus kyi 'khor lo la 'jug pa zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 1383): translated by Abhayākaragupta, ba ri lo tsA ba rin chen grags; revised by Rāhulaśrībhadra, chag lo tsA ba chos rje dpal (Tibetan)

SA_T02_Rāghavabhaṭṭa_Śāradātilaka_Woodro.title: Śāradātilaka with Padārthādarśa (chapters 1–7, incomplete)
SA_T02_Rāghavabhaṭṭa_Śāradātilaka_Woodro.author: Lakṣmaṇadeśika, Rāghavabhaṭṭa
SA_T02_Rāghavabhaṭṭa_Śāradātilaka_Woodro.summary: The Śāradātilaka of Lakṣmaṇadeśika is an influential 25-chapter compendium of mantraśāstra and tantric ritual; this e-text gives its first seven chapters with Rāghavabhaṭṭa's commentary Padārthādarśa. The chapters covered treat cosmogony and the manifestation of sound (śabdabrahman), the qualifications of teacher and pupil, the construction of the ritual ground, maṇḍalas and fire altars, initiation (dīkṣā), and the mantras of Sarasvatī. Rāghavabhaṭṭa's commentary is valued for its many quotations from earlier tantric and other sources.
SA_T02_Rāghavabhaṭṭa_Śāradātilaka_Woodro.attribution: The root work is attributed to Lakṣmaṇadeśika. The commentary Padārthādarśa was composed by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
SA_T02_Rāghavabhaṭṭa_Śāradātilaka_Woodro.edition: Arthur Avalon (John Woodroffe) (ed.), Śāradā-Tilaka Tantra of Lakṣmaṇadeśikendra with Padārthādarśa commentary of Rāghavabhaṭṭa, Tantrik Texts vol. 16 (Part I, chapters 1–7), Calcutta: Āgamānusandhāna Samiti / London: Luzac & Co., 1933.
SA_T02_Rāghavabhaṭṭa_Śāradātilaka_Woodro.coverage: partial — Paṭalas 1–6 complete and paṭala 7 up to root verse 121, ending in Rāghavabhaṭṭa's comment on vv. 113–120 without a chapter colophon. The Śāradātilaka has 25 paṭalas; this corresponds to Part I (chapters 1–7) of the Tantrik Texts edition, and the end of paṭala 7 is missing.

SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti_Davidso.title: Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti
SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti_Davidso.summary: The Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti ('Chanting the Names of Mañjuśrī') is a central Buddhist tantric text celebrating Mañjuśrī as the personification of non-dual gnosis (jñānakāya) and of all enlightened qualities through a litany of sacred epithets. Formally situated within the framework of the Māyājālatantra, it is delivered by Śākyamuni Buddha in response to the request of Vajrapāṇi and his retinue. This e-text is an OCR transcription of Ronald M. Davidson's 1981 critical edition, which interleaves the Sanskrit text with Davidson's English translation and philological notes.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti_Davidso.attribution: Canonical Vajrayāna scripture framed as taught by the Buddha Śākyamuni to Vajrapāṇi / Vajradhara; traditionally preserved as an excerpt from the Māyājālatantra.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti_Davidso.edition: Ronald M. Davidson, 'The Litany of Names of Mañjuśrī: Text and Translation of the Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti', in Tantric and Taoist Studies in Honour of R.A. Stein, vol. 1 (ed. Michel Strickmann), Mélanges chinois et bouddhiques 20, Brussels: Institut Belge des Hautes Études Chinoises, 1981, pp. 1–69.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti_Davidso.coverage: complete — Contains the complete text of the Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti (introductory verses, names/mantras, prose sections, and concluding verses up to the final colophon), interleaved with OCR of Davidson's English translation and commentary apparatus.
translations: Davidson, Ronald M. 1981. 'The Litany of Names of Mañjuśrī: Text and Translation of the Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti', Mélanges chinois et bouddhiques 20: 1–69. (English)

SA_K12_Āgama-Jayasena_Ḍākārṇavatantra-15.title: Ḍākārṇavatantra (chapter 15) with Ratnapadmarāganidhi
SA_K12_Āgama-Jayasena_Ḍākārṇavatantra-15.author: Jayasena
SA_K12_Āgama-Jayasena_Ḍākārṇavatantra-15.summary: Chapter 15 of the Ḍākārṇavatantra presents the central Ḍākārṇavamahāmaṇḍala of this late Anuttarayoga Yoginītantra tradition (ca. 11th–12th century), describing thirteen concentric cakras centering on Heruka. Jayasena's Ratnapadmarāganidhi is a detailed sādhana manual explaining the generation stage (utpattikrama) and ritual practices based on Chapter 15.
SA_K12_Āgama-Jayasena_Ḍākārṇavatantra-15.attribution: The Ḍākārṇavatantra is an anonymous scriptural tantra. The accompanying sādhana manual Ratnapadmarāganidhi is attributed to Jayasena (mkhas pa Dza ya se na), translated into Tibetan by Dharma-yon-tan.
SA_K12_Āgama-Jayasena_Ḍākārṇavatantra-15.edition: Tsunehiko Sugiki, The Ocean of Heroes: A Critical Edition, Translation, and Analysis of the Ḍākārṇavatantra, Chapter 15, and Jayasena's Meditation Manual (Ratnapadmarāganidhi), MDPI, Basel 2022 (open access, OAPEN).
SA_K12_Āgama-Jayasena_Ḍākārṇavatantra-15.coverage: partial — Contains Chapter 15 of the Ḍākārṇavatantra in Sanskrit with critical apparatus, followed by the complete critical edition of Jayasena's Ratnapadmarāganidhi in Tibetan (its Sanskrit original is not extant).
translations: Tsunehiko Sugiki, The Ocean of Heroes: A Critical Edition, Translation, and Analysis of the Ḍākārṇavatantra, Chapter 15, and Jayasena's Meditation Manual (Ratnapadmarāganidhi), Basel: MDPI, 2022. (English)

SA_T02_Rāmapāla_Sekanirdeśapañjikā_Isaac.title: Sekanirdeśapañjikā
SA_T02_Rāmapāla_Sekanirdeśapañjikā_Isaac.author: Rāmapāla
SA_T02_Rāmapāla_Sekanirdeśapañjikā_Isaac.summary: The Sekanirdeśapañjikā is Rāmapāla's extensive commentary on the Sekanirdeśa of Maitreyanātha (Advayavajra), an important Late Vajrayāna treatise on tantric initiation (seka/abhiṣeka). It systematically analyzes the four consecrations, the four moments (kṣaṇa), and the four joys (ānanda), with particular emphasis on elucidating the fourth consecration (caturthābhiṣeka) and refuting flawed or violent initiation techniques (haṭhaseka, duḥseka).
SA_T02_Rāmapāla_Sekanirdeśapañjikā_Isaac.attribution: The root verses are attributed to Mahāpaṇḍitāvadhūta Maitreyanātha (Advayavajra), while the commentary is authored by Rāmapāla.
SA_T02_Rāmapāla_Sekanirdeśapañjikā_Isaac.edition: Harunaga Isaacson & Francesco Sferra (eds.), The Sekanirdeśa of Maitreyanātha (Advayavajra) with the Sekanirdeśapañjikā of Rāmapāla: Critical Edition of the Sanskrit and Tibetan Texts with English Translation, Manuscripta Buddhica 2 = Serie Orientale Roma CVII, Università degli Studi di Napoli "L'Orientale" / Universität Hamburg, Napoli 2014.
SA_T02_Rāmapāla_Sekanirdeśapañjikā_Isaac.coverage: complete — Complete commentary, spanning from the opening maṅgala and introduction to the final summary verses and authorial colophon.
translations: Harunaga Isaacson & Francesco Sferra, The Sekanirdeśa of Maitreyanātha (Advayavajra) with the Sekanirdeśapañjikā of Rāmapāla: Critical Edition of the Sanskrit and Tibetan Texts with English Translation, Manuscripta Buddhica 2 = Serie Orientale Roma CVII, Università degli Studi di Napoli "L'Orientale" / Universität Hamburg, Napoli 2014. (English)

SA_T02_Nāropā_Sekoddeśaṭīkā_Carelli_1941.title: Sekoddeśaṭīkā
SA_T02_Nāropā_Sekoddeśaṭīkā_Carelli_1941.author: Nāropā
SA_T02_Nāropā_Sekoddeśaṭīkā_Carelli_1941.summary: The Sekoddeśaṭīkā is an influential commentary by the mahāsiddha Nāropā (Nāḍapāda) on the Sekoddeśa, a foundational ritual section preserved from the Kālacakra root tantra (Paramādibuddhatantra). The work explains the ten esoteric initiations (abhiṣeka), the mechanics of the subtle body (nāḍī, prāṇa, bindu), the nature of unchanging supreme bliss (paramākṣara), and mahāmudrā realization. It remains one of the primary Sanskrit textual witnesses for the doctrinal and yogic foundations of the Anuttarayoga Kālacakra system.
SA_T02_Nāropā_Sekoddeśaṭīkā_Carelli_1941.attribution: Traditionally and textually attributed to Nāḍapāda (Nāropā). Colophon at segment [2214] explicitly states: 'kṛtiriyaṃ śrīnaḍa (nāro)pādānām'.
SA_T02_Nāropā_Sekoddeśaṭīkā_Carelli_1941.edition: Mario E. Carelli (ed.), Sekoddeśaṭīkā of Nāḍapāda (Nāropā), Being a Commentary of the Sekoddeśa Section of the Kālacakra Tantra, Gaekwad's Oriental Series no. 90, Baroda: Oriental Institute, 1941.
SA_T02_Nāropā_Sekoddeśaṭīkā_Carelli_1941.coverage: complete — Complete commentary, opening with 'śrīḥ sekoddeśaṭīkā namaḥ kālacakrāya' and concluding with the final verses and colophon at segments [2211]–[2214] ('iti sekoddeśaṭīkā samāptā || kṛtiriyaṃ śrīnaḍa (nāro)pādānām ||').
translations: Raniero Gnoli and Giacomella Orofino, 1994. (Italian)

SA_T02_Vajrapāṇi_Laghutantraṭīkā_Cicuzza.title: Laghutantraṭīkā (end missing)
SA_T02_Vajrapāṇi_Laghutantraṭīkā_Cicuzza.author: Vajrapāṇi
SA_T02_Vajrapāṇi_Laghutantraṭīkā_Cicuzza.summary: Vajrapāṇi's Laghutantraṭīkā is a commentary on the first chapter of the Cakrasaṃvara (Laghusaṃvara) tantra by one of the three Kālacakra-oriented "Bodhisattva" commentators. It sets out the purpose of the tantra and distinguishes neyārtha and nītārtha readings, with Kālacakra-style correlations of time, breath and the zodiac. It then gives detailed ritual instructions on samaya worship, the yoginīs' movement through the body, the pīṭhas, bali offerings and the recitation programmes for the mantras of the Cakrasaṃvara maṇḍala.
SA_T02_Vajrapāṇi_Laghutantraṭīkā_Cicuzza.attribution: The author is one of the three "Bodhisattva" commentators of the Kālacakra milieu (with Puṇḍarīka and Vajragarbha), and the commentary interprets the Cakrasaṃvara through Kālacakra doctrine.
SA_T02_Vajrapāṇi_Laghutantraṭīkā_Cicuzza.edition: Claudio Cicuzza (ed.), The Laghutantraṭīkā by Vajrapāṇi: A Critical Edition of the Sanskrit Text, Serie Orientale Roma 86, Roma: Istituto Italiano per l'Africa e l'Oriente, 2001
SA_T02_Vajrapāṇi_Laghutantraṭīkā_Cicuzza.coverage: partial — The work is a commentary on the first paṭala of the Cakrasaṃvaratantra only. The e-text has the root verses of chapter 1 (segs. 0–20), the opening verses of the ṭīkā and the commentary through the long ritual sections (samayapūjā, yoginīsaṃcāra, pīṭhabījanyāsa, bali, guṭikā, mantras). It breaks off in the section on the 24 pratyaṅga-padamantras: the fifth (Vīramatī) procedure ends at seg. 1570 without its mantra, and there is no colophon, so the rest of this section and the end of the work are missing.
translations: mngon par brjod pa 'bum pa las phyung ba nyung ngu'i rgyud kyi bsdus pa'i don rnam par bshad pa zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 1402): translated by ting 'dzin bzang po, shong lo tsA ba blo gros brtan pa/ shong blo gros brtan pa (Tibetan)

SA_T02_Saroruha_Hevajra_Gerloff_2017.title: Hevajrasādhanopāyikā
SA_T02_Saroruha_Hevajra_Gerloff_2017.author: Saroruha
SA_T02_Saroruha_Hevajra_Gerloff_2017.summary: The Hevajrasādhanopāyikā is an Anuttarayogatantra ritual practice manual (sādhana) for the visualization and realization of the deity Hevajra with his eight-goddess retinue. Composed by Saroruha, it details the visualization, seed syllables, maṇḍala palace, deity forms, and mantra recitation.
SA_T02_Saroruha_Hevajra_Gerloff_2017.attribution: Attributed to Ācārya Saroruha (also identified with Padmavajra).
SA_T02_Saroruha_Hevajra_Gerloff_2017.edition: Torsten Gerloff, Saroruhavajra's Hevajra-Lineage: A Close Study of the Surviving Sanskrit and Tibetan Works, 2 Parts (PhD diss. Univ. Hamburg 2017; publ. Indica et Tibetica), 2017.
SA_T02_Saroruha_Hevajra_Gerloff_2017.coverage: complete — Text of the sādhana followed by apparatus entries and notes.

SA_T02_Puṇḍarīka_Vimalaprabhā-Laghukālac.title: Laghukālacakratantra with Vimalaprabhā (chapters 1–2)
SA_T02_Puṇḍarīka_Vimalaprabhā-Laghukālac.author: Mañjuśrīyaśas, Puṇḍarīka
SA_T02_Puṇḍarīka_Vimalaprabhā-Laghukālac.summary: The Laghukālacakratantra is accompanied by the Vimalaprabhā commentary. This volume encompasses the first two paṭalas: the Lokadhātupaṭala, treating cosmology, astronomical cycles, and societal history; and the Adhyātmapaṭala, examining human embryology, anatomical structures, subtle winds, and physiological correspondences.
SA_T02_Puṇḍarīka_Vimalaprabhā-Laghukālac.attribution: In Buddhist tradition, the Laghukālacakratantra is attributed to Kalki Mañjuśrīyaśas and its commentary Vimalaprabhā to Kalki Puṇḍarīka.
SA_T02_Puṇḍarīka_Vimalaprabhā-Laghukālac.edition: Jagannatha Upadhyaya (ed.), Vimalaprabhāṭīkā of Kalki Śrī Puṇḍarīka on Śrī Laghukālacakratantrarāja by Śrī Mañjuśrīyaśas, Vol. I, Bibliotheca Indo-Tibetica Series XI, Sarnath/Varanasi: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 1986.
SA_T02_Puṇḍarīka_Vimalaprabhā-Laghukālac.coverage: partial — Contains chapters 1 (Lokadhātupaṭala) and 2 (Adhyātmapaṭala) of the Laghukālacakratantra and Vimalaprabhā, corresponding to Volume 1 of Upadhyaya's 1986 edition.
translations: Vesna A. Wallace, The Inner Kālacakratantra: A Buddhist Tantric View of the Individual, Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001. (English)

SA_T02_Candrakīrti_Pradīpoddyotana-Guhya.title: Pradīpoddyotana (chapters 1–2)
SA_T02_Candrakīrti_Pradīpoddyotana-Guhya.author: Candrakīrti
SA_T02_Candrakīrti_Pradīpoddyotana-Guhya.summary: The Pradīpoddyotana by Candrakīrti is the foundational commentary of the Ārya (Noble) tradition on the Guhyasamājatantra. It articulates the essential interpretive framework of the seven ornaments (saptālaṅkāra) and the six interpretive poles (ṣaṭkoṭi: sandhyā/nāsandhyā, neya/nītārtha, yathāruta/naruta). This portion covers the hermeneutical introduction and the commentary on chapters 1 and 2.
SA_T02_Candrakīrti_Pradīpoddyotana-Guhya.attribution: Attributed traditionally to Candrakīrti. Modern Indological scholarship distinguishes this tantric author (often designated Candrakīrti II or Ārya Candrakīrti, ca. late 8th to 9th century) from the 7th-century Madhyamaka philosopher of the same name.
SA_T02_Candrakīrti_Pradīpoddyotana-Guhya.edition: Candrakīrti, Guhyasamājatantrapradīpoddyotanaṭīkā-ṣaṭkoṭivyākhyā, ed. Shrikant Bahulkar, Dhīḥ: Journal of Rare Buddhist Texts Research Unit, vol. 48 (2009), pp. 119-156, CIHTS Sarnath.
SA_T02_Candrakīrti_Pradīpoddyotana-Guhya.coverage: partial — Contains the introductory hermeneutical section (upodghāta, saptālaṅkāra) and the sixfold commentary (ṣaṭkoṭivyākhyā) on chapters 1 and 2 of the Guhyasamājatantra, ending at the colophon of the dvitīyapaṭalaṣaṭkoṭivyākhyā.

SA_T02_Advayavajra_saṃgraha_Bhattacharyy.title: Advayavajrasaṃgraha
SA_T02_Advayavajra_saṃgraha_Bhattacharyy.author: Advayavajra
SA_T02_Advayavajra_saṃgraha_Bhattacharyy.summary: The Advayavajrasaṃgraha is a collection of short Buddhist doctrinal, tantric, and yogic treatises composed by Advayavajra, spanning topics such as consecration, view, and non-conceptual awareness.
SA_T02_Advayavajra_saṃgraha_Bhattacharyy.attribution: Advayavajra (c. 10th–11th c., also associated with Maitrīgupta / Maitrīpāda).
SA_T02_Advayavajra_saṃgraha_Bhattacharyy.edition: Advayavajrasaṃgraha, ed. Mahāmahopādhyāya Haraprasād Shāstri (gen. ed. B. Bhattacharyya), Gaekwad's Oriental Series No. 40, Baroda: Oriental Institute, 1927.
SA_T02_Advayavajra_saṃgraha_Bhattacharyy.coverage: complete — Collection of short treatises edited under the title Advayavajrasaṃgraha.

SA_K12_Āgama_Mahāmāyātantra_Damron_2014.title: Mahāmāyātantra with Guṇavatī
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahāmāyātantra_Damron_2014.author: Ratnākaraśānti
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahāmāyātantra_Damron_2014.summary: The Mahāmāyātantra is an esoteric Buddhist tantra centered on the deity Mahāmāyā and a retinue of ḍākinīs (Buddhaḍākinī, Vajraḍākinī, Ratnaḍākinī, and Padmaḍākinī). Ratnākaraśānti's Guṇavatī is a Sanskrit commentary on the tantra. The e-text contains Ryan Damron's 2014 critical edition of root verses and commentary.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahāmāyātantra_Damron_2014.attribution: The Mahāmāyātantra is an anonymous tantra scripture. The Guṇavatīṭīkā was composed by Ratnākaraśānti.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahāmāyātantra_Damron_2014.edition: Ryan Damron, 'The Mahāmāyā Tantra with the Commentary Guṇavatī by Ratnākaraśānti: A Critical Edition and Translation', MA thesis, 2014.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahāmāyātantra_Damron_2014.coverage: complete — Includes the concluding colophon of the Guṇavatī (guṇavatīnāma mahāmāyāṭīkā paṇḍitaratnākaraśāntipādānāṁ samāpteti) and critical apparatus notes.
translations: Ryan Damron / Dharmachakra Translation Committee, The Mahāmāyā Tantra (Toh 425), 84000: Translating the Words of the Buddha, 2013/2014. (English)

SA_T02_Prabhākaragupta-Śiromaṇi_Adhyātma.title: Adhyātmasāraśataka with Adhyātmasāraśatakaṭīkā (verses 1–68)
SA_T02_Prabhākaragupta-Śiromaṇi_Adhyātma.author: Prabhākaragupta, Śiromaṇi
SA_T02_Prabhākaragupta-Śiromaṇi_Adhyātma.summary: The Adhyātmasāraśataka is a Buddhist philosophical and tantric verse treatise on ultimate reality and internal meditation attributed to Prabhākaragupta. It is accompanied by a word-by-word gloss (khaṇḍānvaya) composed by the Nepalese scholar Śiromaṇi. The preserved text breaks off abruptly after verse 68 due to manuscript defect.
SA_T02_Prabhākaragupta-Śiromaṇi_Adhyātma.attribution: The root work is attributed in the text to Mahāpaṇḍita Prabhākaragupta ('mahāpaṇḍita śrīprabhākaraguptaviracitam adhyātmasāraśatakam'). The commentary is attributed to Ācārya Paṇḍita Śiromaṇi of the Nepal Mandala ('nāgaranepālamaṇḍalake ācārya paṇḍitaśiromaṇinā nipuṇena vyākhyānaṃ kṛtam', and intro verse 'tvālāpo'rthaṃ śiromaṇiḥ').
SA_T02_Prabhākaragupta-Śiromaṇi_Adhyātma.edition: Published in Dhīḥ: Journal of Rare Buddhist Texts Research Project, (1998), Sarnath: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies (Rare Buddhist Texts Project).
SA_T02_Prabhākaragupta-Śiromaṇi_Adhyātma.coverage: partial — Verses 1–68 with accompanying commentary out of an original 100 verses; editorial introduction confirms the commentary is missing the remainder.

SA_T02_Vanaratna_Rahasyadīpikā_Rinpoche-.title: Vasantatilakā with Rahasyadīpikā
SA_T02_Vanaratna_Rahasyadīpikā_Rinpoche-.author: Kṛṣṇācārya, Vanaratna
SA_T02_Vanaratna_Rahasyadīpikā_Rinpoche-.summary: The Vasantatilakā is a sādhanopāyikā associated with Heruka, attributed to Kṛṣṇapāda / Kṛṣṇācārya. It outlines subtle body yoga—including nāḍīs, cakras, and bindus—and the completion stage (niṣpannakrama) leading to Mahāmudrā realization. Vanaratna's commentary Rahasyadīpikā provides an exposition correlating yogic elements with bodhipakṣadharmas.
SA_T02_Vanaratna_Rahasyadīpikā_Rinpoche-.attribution: The root work Vasantatilakā is attributed to Caryāvratī Śrīkṛṣṇācārya (Kṛṣṇapāda). The commentary Rahasyadīpikā is by Vanaratna.
SA_T02_Vanaratna_Rahasyadīpikā_Rinpoche-.edition: Vasantatilakā of Caryāvratī Śrīkṛṣṇācārya with Rahasyadīpikā commentary by Vanaratna, ed. Samdhong Rinpoche & Vrajvallabh Dwivedi, Rare Buddhist Text Series 7, Sarnath/Varanasi: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 1990.
SA_T02_Vanaratna_Rahasyadīpikā_Rinpoche-.coverage: complete — Text of the Vasantatilakā with the Rahasyadīpikā commentary, including Tibetan parallel sections.

SA_T02_Vajragarbha_Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-Hevajrat.author: Vajragarbha
SA_T02_Vajragarbha_Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-Hevajrat.summary: Vajragarbha's Ṣaṭsāhasrikāhevajraṭīkā is an extensive commentary on the Hevajratantra.
SA_T02_Vajragarbha_Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-Hevajrat.attribution: The introductory verses name the author as "śrīmatā vajragarbheṇa … daśabhūmīśvareṇa" (verse 4).

SA_T02_Kuladatta_Kriyāsaṃgrahapañjikā-pa.title: Kriyāsaṃgrahapañjikā (Śalyoddhārapaṭala)
SA_T02_Kuladatta_Kriyāsaṃgrahapañjikā-pa.author: Kuladatta
SA_T02_Kuladatta_Kriyāsaṃgrahapañjikā-pa.summary: The Kriyāsaṃgrahapañjikā of Kuladatta is a Vajrayāna ritual handbook outlining procedures for temple construction, monastic ordination, mandalas, and consecration ceremonies. This excerpt contains the Śalyoddhārapaṭala, a section detailing the detection and extraction of subterranean faults and foreign bodies (śalya) from building sites through the interpretation of omens and physical gestures.
SA_T02_Kuladatta_Kriyāsaṃgrahapañjikā-pa.edition: Ryugen Tanemura, Kuladatta's Kriyāsaṃgrahapañjikā: A Critical Edition and Annotated Translation of Selected Sections (Groningen Oriental Studies 19), Groningen: Egbert Forsten, 2004.
SA_T02_Kuladatta_Kriyāsaṃgrahapañjikā-pa.coverage: partial — Contains the Śalyoddhārapaṭala (dealing with site examination and removal of subterranean impurities / śalya), with closing lines containing OCR debris from Tanemura's facing English translation and footnotes.

SA_T02_Munidatta_Caryāgītikoṣa_Bagchi_19.title: Caryāgīti with Munidatta's Caryāgītikoṣavṛtti
SA_T02_Munidatta_Caryāgītikoṣa_Bagchi_19.author: Munidatta
SA_T02_Munidatta_Caryāgītikoṣa_Bagchi_19.summary: The Caryāgītikoṣa is an anthology of 50 esoteric Buddhist Tantric songs (caryāgīti) composed in an early New Indo-Aryan vernacular (Old Bengali / Apabhraṃśa) by various Mahāsiddhas of the Sahajayāna tradition, accompanied by the Sanskrit commentary of Munidatta. The songs use 'twilight language' (sandhyābhāṣā) to depict esoteric yogic realization, channel and wind yoga, and innate bliss (sahajasukha), which Munidatta interprets in light of classical Buddhist tantras such as the Hevajratantra, Guhyasamājatantra, and Saṃpuṭatantra.
SA_T02_Munidatta_Caryāgītikoṣa_Bagchi_19.attribution: The root songs are attributed to around 23 Buddhist Sahajiyā/Tantric Mahāsiddhas (including Lūyīpāda, Kānha/Kṛṣṇācārya, Bhusukupāda, Sarahapāda, Tantrīpāda, Śabarapāda). The Sanskrit commentary (variously styled ṭīkā or vṛtti) is composed by Munidatta.
SA_T02_Munidatta_Caryāgītikoṣa_Bagchi_19.edition: Caryāgīti-koṣa of Buddhist Siddhas, ed. Prabodh Chandra Bagchi & Śānti Bhikṣu Śāstri, Santiniketan: Viśva-Bhāratī, 1956.
SA_T02_Munidatta_Caryāgītikoṣa_Bagchi_19.coverage: complete — Contains all 50 songs (including the surviving portions and editorial reconstructions/Sanskrit chāyā) together with Munidatta's commentary as published by Bagchi and Śāstrī.
translations: Kvaerne, P. An Anthology of Buddhist Tantric Songs-a Study of the Caryāgīti. Oslo: Universitetsforlaget, 1977. (English)
Mojumder, Atindra. The Caryāpadas. Calcutta: Naya Prokash, 1967. (English)

SA_T02_Vibhūticandra-Raviśrījñāna_Amṛtak.title: Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti with Amṛtakaṇikā and Amṛtakaṇikoddyotanibandha
SA_T02_Vibhūticandra-Raviśrījñāna_Amṛtak.author: Raviśrījñāna, Vibhūticandra
SA_T02_Vibhūticandra-Raviśrījñāna_Amṛtak.summary: The Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti is an influential Vajrayāna liturgical and doctrinal text celebrating Mañjuśrī as the primordial embodiment of all tathāgatas and nondual awareness (jñānakāya). Raviśrījñāna's Amṛtakaṇikā provides an extensive commentary interpreting the text through the framework of the Kālacakratantra and highest yoga tantric physiology. Vibhūticandra's sub-commentary, the Amṛtakaṇikoddyota, glosses linguistic nuances and esoteric points in the Amṛtakaṇikā, accompanied by a concluding liturgical practice (sādhana).
SA_T02_Vibhūticandra-Raviśrījñāna_Amṛtak.attribution: The root work Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti is traditionally classified under the Māyājālatantra / Advayaparamārtha cycles. The commentary Amṛtakaṇikā is by Raviśrījñāna. The sub-commentary Amṛtakaṇikoddyota and the closing Āryanāmasaṅgītisādhana are by Vibhūticandra.
SA_T02_Vibhūticandra-Raviśrījñāna_Amṛtak.edition: Banarsi Lal (ed.), Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti with Amṛtakaṇikā-ṭippaṇī by Bhikṣu Raviśrījñāna and Amṛtakaṇikoddyota-nibandha of Vibhūticandra (Sanskrit), Bhoṭa-Bhāratīya Granthamālā 30, Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, Sarnath/Varanasi 1994.
SA_T02_Vibhūticandra-Raviśrījñāna_Amṛtak.coverage: complete — Complete text of the 1994 CIHTS edition, containing the root text, commentary, sub-commentary, and the final Āryanāmasaṅgītisādhana.

SA_T02_Mañjuśrīyaśa_Laghukālacakratantra.title: Laghukālacakratantra with Vimalaprabhā (chapter 5)
SA_T02_Mañjuśrīyaśa_Laghukālacakratantra.author: Mañjuśrīyaśas, Puṇḍarīka
SA_T02_Mañjuśrīyaśa_Laghukālacakratantra.summary: The fifth and concluding chapter (Jñānapaṭala, 'Chapter on Gnosis') of the Laghukālacakratantra along with its authoritative commentary, the Vimalaprabhā by Kalkin Puṇḍarīka. It expounds advanced Vajrayāna yogic praxis and soteriology, detailing the six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga), the nature of the innate body (sahajakāya), the attainment of supreme unchanging bliss (paramākṣarasukha), and non-dual gnosis that synthesizes macrocosmic and microcosmic structures.
SA_T02_Mañjuśrīyaśa_Laghukālacakratantra.attribution: Traditional Vajrayāna attribution assigns the condensation of the Paramādibuddha/Mūlatantra into the Laghukālacakratantra to Mañjuśrīyaśas, and the commentary Vimalaprabhā to Puṇḍarīka.
SA_T02_Mañjuśrīyaśa_Laghukālacakratantra.edition: Vrajavallabha Dwivedi & S. S. Bahulkar (eds.), Vimalaprabhāṭīkā of Kalkin Śrīpuṇḍarīka on Śrīlaghukālacakratantrarāja by Śrīmañjuśrīyaśas, Vol. III, Rare Buddhist Texts Series 13, Sarnath, Varanasi: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 1994.
SA_T02_Mañjuśrīyaśa_Laghukālacakratantra.coverage: partial — Contains chapter 5 (Jñānapaṭala) complete, comprising all four mahoddeśas of the fifth chapter, with root kārikās and the full Vimalaprabhā commentary ending with the scribal colophon dated to Harivarmadeva regnal year 39.
translations: Vesna A. Wallace, The Inner Kālacakratantra: A Buddhist Tantric View of the Individual, Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001. (English)

SA_T02_Raviśrījñāna_Guṇabharaṇī-Ṣaḍaṅgay.title: Ṣaḍaṅgayoga with Guṇabharaṇī
SA_T02_Raviśrījñāna_Guṇabharaṇī-Ṣaḍaṅgay.author: Anupamarakṣita, Raviśrījñāna
SA_T02_Raviśrījñāna_Guṇabharaṇī-Ṣaḍaṅgay.summary: The Ṣaḍaṅgayoga of Anupamarakṣita is an important late Indian Buddhist manual on the six-phased yoga (pratyāhāra, dhyāna, prāṇāyāma, dhāraṇā, anusmṛti, and samādhi), synthesizing traditions from the Guhyasamājatantra and Kālacakratantra. Raviśrījñāna's commentary, the Guṇabharaṇī, offers an extensive explanation of completion stage (niṣpannakrama) practice and yogic physiology, citing extensively from the Vimalaprabhā, Sekoddeśa, and Laghukālacakratantra.
SA_T02_Raviśrījñāna_Guṇabharaṇī-Ṣaḍaṅgay.attribution: The root work is by Anupamarakṣita, who according to the narrative in the opening studied in Vikramapura; the commentary Guṇabharaṇī is by Raviśrījñāna, who outlines the guruparamparā (Anupamarakṣita → Śrīdhara → Bhāskaradeva → Dharmākaraśānti → Raviśrījñāna).
SA_T02_Raviśrījñāna_Guṇabharaṇī-Ṣaḍaṅgay.edition: Francesco Sferra (ed.), The Ṣaḍaṅgayoga by Anupamarakṣita with Raviśrījñāna's Guṇabharaṇīnāmaṣaḍaṅgayogaṭippaṇī: Text and Annotated Translation, Serie Orientale Roma 85, Roma: Istituto Italiano per l'Africa e l'Oriente (IsIAO), 2000.
SA_T02_Raviśrījñāna_Guṇabharaṇī-Ṣaḍaṅgay.coverage: complete — Complete Sanskrit critical text of the Ṣaḍaṅgayoga embedded in the Guṇabharaṇī commentary, corresponding to Francesco Sferra's 2000 critical edition.
translations: Francesco Sferra, The Ṣaḍaṅgayoga by Anupamarakṣita with Raviśrījñāna's Guṇabharaṇīnāmaṣaḍaṅgayogaṭippaṇī: Text and Annotated Translation, Serie Orientale Roma 85, Roma: IsIAO, 2000. (English)

SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa_Shastri_1.title: Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa (chapters 1–20)
SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa_Shastri_1.summary: The Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa is an encyclopedic Buddhist canonical scripture centered on Mañjuśrī, self-described as a Mahāyānavaipulyasūtra and retrospectively categorized in Tibetan doxography as a Kriyātantra. It provides extensive instructions on ritual drawing of cloths (paṭa) and mandalas, dharanis, mudrās, and divination. This e-text contains Part I (paṭalas 1–20), which covers the primary ritual procedures, visual iconography, altar preparations, recitation rituals, and divination through birds and omens (śakunajñāna).
SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa_Shastri_1.attribution: Scriptural Buddhist Mahāyānavaipulyasūtra / Kriyātantra traditionally presented as spoken by the Buddha Śākyamuni and Mañjuśrī.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa_Shastri_1.edition: T. Gaṇapati Śāstrī (ed.), The Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa, Part I, Trivandrum Sanskrit Series no. LXX, Trivandrum 1920.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa_Shastri_1.coverage: partial — Contains paṭalas 1–20 only (corresponding to Part I of Gaṇapati Śāstrī's Trivandrum edition; chapters 21–55 are absent).

SA_T02_Candrakīrti_Vajrasattvasādhana_Lu.title: Vajrasattvaniṣpādanasūtra
SA_T02_Candrakīrti_Vajrasattvasādhana_Lu.author: Candrakīrti
SA_T02_Candrakīrti_Vajrasattvasādhana_Lu.summary: The Vajrasattvaniṣpādanasūtra (also commonly called Vajrasattvasādhana) is an utpattikrama (generation stage) meditation manual on Vajrasattva within the Ārya lineage of the Guhyasamājatantra. The author extracts and structures passages from across the seventeen chapters of the tantra into a unified sādhana procedure. The e-text contains the complete critical edition of both the Sanskrit text and its canonical Tibetan translation prepared by Luo Hong and Toru Tomabechi in 2009.
SA_T02_Candrakīrti_Vajrasattvasādhana_Lu.edition: Luo Hong & Toru Tomabechi (eds.), Candrakīrti's Vajrasattvaniṣpādanasūtra (Vajrasattvasādhana): Sanskrit and Tibetan Texts (Sanskrit Texts from the Tibetan Autonomous Region, vol. 6), Beijing/Vienna: China Tibetology Publishing House / Austrian Academy of Sciences Press, 2009.
SA_T02_Candrakīrti_Vajrasattvasādhana_Lu.coverage: complete — Complete critical edition of the Sanskrit text followed by its Tibetan translation as edited in the 2009 editio princeps.
translations: Luo Hong & Toru Tomabechi (eds.), Candrakīrti's Vajrasattvaniṣpādanasūtra (Vajrasattvasādhana): Sanskrit and Tibetan Texts, Beijing/Vienna, 2009 (includes Tibetan translation edition and notes). (Tibetan)

SA_T02_Muniśrībhadra_Pañcakrama-Yogimano.title: Pañcakramaṭippaṇī Yogimanoharā
SA_T02_Muniśrībhadra_Pañcakrama-Yogimano.author: Muniśrībhadra
SA_T02_Muniśrībhadra_Pañcakrama-Yogimano.summary: The Pañcakramaṭippaṇī Yogimanoharā is a late Indian Sanskrit commentary composed by Muniśrībhadra of Jagaddala Mahāvihāra on the Pañcakrama, the foundational completion-stage (niṣpannakrama) treatise of the Guhyasamāja Tantra's Ārya lineage attributed to Nāgārjuna. It elucidates the technical yogic practices across the five stages—piṇḍīkrama, vajrajāpa, cittaviśuddhi, svādhiṣṭhāna, and yuganaddha—clarifying difficult words and esoteric hermeneutics.
SA_T02_Muniśrībhadra_Pañcakrama-Yogimano.attribution: Composed by Muniśrībhadra, a Buddhist scholar-monk from Magadha residing at Jagaddala Mahāvihāra, active around the late 11th to 12th century.
SA_T02_Muniśrībhadra_Pañcakrama-Yogimano.edition: Zhongxin Jiang & Tōru Tomabechi (eds.), The Pañcakramaṭippaṇī of Muniśrībhadra: Introduction and Romanized Sanskrit Text, Schweizer Asiatische Studien / Études asiatiques suisses, Monographie 23, Bern: Peter Lang, 1996.
SA_T02_Muniśrībhadra_Pañcakrama-Yogimano.coverage: complete — Complete commentary on the Pañcakrama, ending with the yuganaddhakrama section colophon ('iti yuganaddhakramasya yogimanoharā ṭippaṇī samāptā') and authorial praśasti verses.

SA_T02_Dharmākaraśānti_Kālacakrabhagavat.title: Kālacakrabhagavatsādhanavidhi
SA_T02_Dharmākaraśānti_Kālacakrabhagavat.author: Dharmākaraśānti
SA_T02_Dharmākaraśānti_Kālacakrabhagavat.summary: The Kālacakrabhagavatsādhanavidhi is an extensive Buddhist tantric meditation manual (sādhana) for Bhagavān Kālacakra and his maṇḍala retinue, compiled by Mahāpaṇḍita Dharmākaraśānti. Drawing directly from the Vimalaprabhā commentary on the Laghukālacakratantra, the text details the preliminary purifications, the generation of the protective sphere (rakṣācakra), nyāsa and seed syllables, the visualization of the three maṇḍalas (body, speech, and mind), mudrās, and dissolving rites.
SA_T02_Dharmākaraśānti_Kālacakrabhagavat.attribution: The colophon explicitly names Mahāpaṇḍita Dharmākaraśānti as the compiler/author and notes that the ritual was excerpted from the Vimalaprabhā commentary composed by Kalki Puṇḍarīka (śrīmallokeśvaranirmāṇapuṇḍarīkaviracitavimalaprabhoddhṛtaḥ). Yong-Hyun (2003) notes that although the text is ascribed to Dharmākaraśānti in the edition, some identify the author as Sādhuputra Śrīdharānanda.
SA_T02_Dharmākaraśānti_Kālacakrabhagavat.edition: Kālacakrabhagavatsādhanavidhi, Dhīḥ: Journal of Rare Buddhist Texts Research, Vol. 24 (1997), pp. 127–174, Sarnath: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies.
SA_T02_Dharmākaraśānti_Kālacakrabhagavat.coverage: complete — Complete ritual text extending from the initial maṅgala through the final verses and colophons.

SA_GV01_rvsb_01u.title: Ṛgvedasaṃhitā with Sāyaṇabhāṣya (Maṇḍala 1)
SA_GV01_rvsb_01u.author: Sāyaṇa
SA_GV01_rvsb_01u.summary: The first Maṇḍala of the Ṛgvedasaṃhitā accompanied by the introductory treatise (Upodghātaprakaraṇa) and running commentary (Vedārthaprakāśa) composed by Sāyaṇācārya. The commentary provides ritual applications (viniyoga) drawn from Śrautasūtras, detailed word-by-word Pāṇinian grammatical analysis (svara, accentuation, and morphology), and traditional mythological and Nirukta-based etymological explanations.
SA_GV01_rvsb_01u.attribution: The commentary is attributed to Sāyaṇācārya, associated with Mādhavācārya and patronized by king Bukka.
SA_GV01_rvsb_01u.coverage: complete — Complete text of Ṛgveda Maṇḍala 1 preceded by Sāyaṇa's Upodghātaprakaraṇa and followed by an errata list.

SA_GV01_rvsb_02u.title: Ṛgvedasaṃhitā with Vedārthaprakāśa (Maṇḍala 2)
SA_GV01_rvsb_02u.author: Sāyaṇa
SA_GV01_rvsb_02u.summary: This text contains the complete second Maṇḍala of the Ṛgvedasaṃhitā along with its Padapāṭha and the commentary (Vedārthaprakāśa) by Sāyaṇācārya. Maṇḍala 2 is traditionally regarded as the family book (kula-maṇḍala) of the Gṛtsamadas (Bhārgavas / Śaunakas) and comprises 43 sūktas primarily dedicated to Agni, Indra, Bṛhaspati/Brahmaṇaspati, and the Maruts. Sāyaṇa's commentary provides comprehensive grammatical derivations according to Pāṇinian vyākaraṇa, etymological explanations drawing upon Yāska's Nirukta, and liturgical applications (viniyoga) referencing Śrautasūtra and Brāhmaṇa literature.
SA_GV01_rvsb_02u.attribution: The Vedic hymns of Maṇḍala 2 are traditionally attributed to the ṛṣi Gṛtsamada Śaunaka. The commentary is titled Vedārthaprakāśa (styled Mādhavīye Vedārthaprakāśe in the colophon) by Sāyaṇācārya.
SA_GV01_rvsb_02u.coverage: complete — Complete text of Ṛgveda Maṇḍala 2 (all 43 sūktas across 4 anuvākas), including Saṃhitāpāṭha, Padapāṭha, and Sāyaṇa's commentary, concluding with 'samāptaṃ ca dvitīyaṃ maṇḍalam'.
translations: Jamison, Stephanie W., and Joel P. Brereton. The Rigveda. 2014. (English)
Geldner, Karl Friedrich. Der Rig-Veda aus dem Sanskrit ins Deutsche übersetzt. Harvard Oriental Series 33–36. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1951. (German)

SA_GV01_rvsb_03u.title: Ṛgvedasaṃhitā with Sāyaṇabhāṣya (maṇḍala 3)
SA_GV01_rvsb_03u.author: Sāyaṇa
SA_GV01_rvsb_03u.summary: This text contains the complete third Maṇḍala of the Ṛgveda-Saṃhitā along with its Padapāṭha and the Vedārthaprakāśa commentary by Sāyaṇācārya.
