SA_GV01_rvsb_03u.attribution: Traditional attribution of the third maṇḍala is to Viśvāmitra. The commentary is titled Mādhavīya Vedārthaprakāśa composed by Sāyaṇācārya.
SA_GV01_rvsb_03u.coverage: complete — Complete coverage of Maṇḍala 3 (including 5 anuvākas), including saṃhitāpāṭha, padapāṭha, and Sāyaṇa's bhāṣya.
translations: Jamison and Brereton (2014) (English)
K. F. Geldner, Der Rig-Veda aus dem Sanskrit ins Deutsche übersetzt, 4 Bde., Harvard Oriental Series 33–36, Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1951 bis. (German)

SA_GV01_rvsb_04u.title: Ṛgvedasaṃhitā with Sāyaṇabhāṣya (Maṇḍala 4)
SA_GV01_rvsb_04u.author: Sāyaṇa
SA_GV01_rvsb_04u.summary: Maṇḍala 4 of the Ṛgveda-Saṃhitā comprises 58 hymns (sūktas) traditionally attributed to the seer Vāmadeva Gautama, addressed principally to Agni, Indra, the Ṛbhus, and the Viśvedevāḥ. The e-text includes the Saṃhitā text, the Padapāṭha, and Sāyaṇācārya's commentary (Vedārthaprakāśa), which provides ritual application (viniyoga), extensive grammatical analysis based on Pāṇinian sūtras, and mythological exposition.
SA_GV01_rvsb_04u.coverage: partial — Complete text of Maṇḍala 4 of the Ṛgveda (58 sūktas, 589 ṛcs), containing Saṃhitāpāṭha, Padapāṭha, Sāyaṇa's bhāṣya, and editorial apparatus/variant readings. Maṇḍala 4 is one of the ten books of the Ṛgveda.

SA_GV01_rvsb_05u.title: Ṛgvedasaṃhitā with Sāyaṇabhāṣya (Maṇḍala 5)
SA_GV01_rvsb_05u.author: Sāyaṇa
SA_GV01_rvsb_05u.summary: The fifth Maṇḍala of the Ṛgvedasaṃhitā, traditionally known as the Ātreya family book, comprising 87 hymns primarily addressed to Agni, Indra, the Viśvedevas, and the Maruts. The text includes the Saṃhitāpāṭha, Padapāṭha, and Sāyaṇācārya's extensive scholastic commentary (Vedārthaprakāśa), which interprets the hymns within a ritualistic śrauta framework with grammatical analyses based on Pāṇini.
SA_GV01_rvsb_05u.attribution: The root hymns are traditionally revealed to the Ātreya seers.
SA_GV01_rvsb_05u.coverage: complete — Contains the complete fifth Maṇḍala of the Ṛgveda (87 sūktas) along with its Padapāṭha, Sāyaṇa's Vedārthaprakāśa commentary, critical footnotes, and errata lists from the VSM volume 2.

SA_GV01_rvsb_06u.title: Ṛgvedasaṃhitā with Sāyaṇabhāṣya (maṇḍala 6)
SA_GV01_rvsb_06u.author: Sāyaṇa
SA_GV01_rvsb_06u.summary: Maṇḍala 6 of the Ṛgvedasaṃhitā constitutes the Bhāradvāja family book, comprising 75 sūktas dedicated largely to Agni, Indra, and various Vedic deities, concluding with the martial hymn on battle gear and weapons (6.75). The e-text supplies the continuous Saṃhitā text, Śākalya's Padapāṭha word-breakdown, and Sāyaṇācārya's 14th-century CE commentary (Vedārthaprakāśa), which integrates liturgical directions from the Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra, Brāhmaṇa passages, and Nirukta etymologies.
SA_GV01_rvsb_06u.attribution: The root saṃhitā hymns of Maṇḍala 6 are traditionally attributed to the Bhāradvāja family of rishis; the padapāṭha is attributed to Śākalya; the commentary Vedārthaprakāśa was composed in the 14th century by Sāyaṇācārya at Vijayanagara.
SA_GV01_rvsb_06u.coverage: partial — Complete coverage of Maṇḍala 6 (75 sūktas, 765 verses: 6.1.1–6.75.19), representing a single maṇḍala (partial coverage) of the entire 10-maṇḍala Ṛgvedasaṃhitā. Contains Saṃhitāpāṭha, Padapāṭha, and Sāyaṇabhāṣya.
translations: Stephanie W. Jamison and Joel P. Brereton (trans.), The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India, Oxford, 2014. (English)

SA_GV01_rvsb_07u.title: Ṛgvedasaṃhitā with Sāyaṇabhāṣya (Maṇḍala 7)
SA_GV01_rvsb_07u.author: Sāyaṇa
SA_GV01_rvsb_07u.summary: Maṇḍala 7 of the Ṛgvedasaṃhitā is the family book (kula-grantha) of the Vasiṣṭha lineage, comprising 104 hymns dedicated predominantly to Agni, Indra, Varuṇa, the Maruts, and the Aśvins. Celebrated portions include the Vasiṣṭha-Varuṇa hymns (7.86–89), the Battle of the Ten Kings (Dāśarājña, 7.18, 7.33, 7.83), the Frog Hymn (Maṇḍūkasūkta, 7.103), and the Tryambakamantra (7.59.12). Sāyaṇācārya's 14th-century commentary (Vedārthaprakāśa) provides exhaustive ritual viniyoga from the Śrautasūtras, grammatical derivations according to Pāṇinian vyākaraṇa, and Nirukta etymologies.
SA_GV01_rvsb_07u.attribution: The root hymns of Maṇḍala 7 are traditionally attributed to Vasiṣṭha Maitrāvaruṇi and his descendants (Vasiṣṭhas). The commentary, Vedārthaprakāśa, was composed in the 14th century under the direction of Sāyaṇācārya.
SA_GV01_rvsb_07u.coverage: complete — Complete coverage of Maṇḍala 7 (hymns 7.1–7.104) with Saṃhitā, Padapāṭha, Sāyaṇabhāṣya, and critical apparatus. The file has a brief terminal overrun containing the opening five verses of Maṇḍala 8 (RV 8.1.1–5).
translations: Karl Friedrich Geldner, Der Rig-Veda aus dem Sanskrit ins Deutsche übersetzt und mit einem laufenden Kommentar versehen, Harvard Oriental Series, Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1951. (German)

SA_GV01_rvsb_08u.title: Ṛgvedasaṃhitā with Vedārthaprakāśa (Maṇḍala 8)
SA_GV01_rvsb_08u.author: Sāyaṇa
SA_GV01_rvsb_08u.summary: The eighth maṇḍala of the Ṛgveda contains 103 sūktas (including the 11 Vālakhilya hymns, 8.49–8.59), predominantly attributed to the Kaṇva and Āṅgirasa seer families. The hymns are primarily addressed to Indra, Agni, the Aśvins, and the Maruts, and feature distinctive strophic meters such as Pragātha. This volume presents the saṃhitā text along with its padapāṭha and Sāyaṇa's comprehensive 14th-century scholastic commentary (Vedārthaprakāśa), which explains grammatical forms according to Pāṇinian rules, supplies liturgical applications (viniyoga) according to Śrautasūtras, and elucidates Vedic ritual contexts.
SA_GV01_rvsb_08u.coverage: complete — Complete coverage of Maṇḍala 8 (all 103 sūktas across 10 anuvākas), including saṃhitāpāṭha, padapāṭha, commentary, apparatus footnotes, and concluding śuddhipatra (errata list).

SA_GV01_rvsb_09u.title: Ṛgvedasaṃhitā with Vedārthaprakāśa (Maṇḍala 9)
SA_GV01_rvsb_09u.author: Sāyaṇa
SA_GV01_rvsb_09u.summary: The ninth maṇḍala of the Ṛgvedasaṃhitā, known as the Pavamāna Maṇḍala, comprises 114 hymns exclusively addressed to Soma Pavamāna ('Soma clarifying himself'). The hymns describe the ritual extraction, filtration through sheep's wool, mixing, and offering of Soma during the Śrauta sacrifice. Sāyaṇa's commentary (Vedārthaprakāśa) provides detailed grammatical derivations following Pāṇini, ritual applications according to the Śrautasūtras (especially Āśvalāyana), and traditional mytho-theological explanations for each verse.
SA_GV01_rvsb_09u.attribution: The root saṃhitā verses are traditional Vedic hymns. The commentary, Vedārthaprakāśa (also known as Mādhavīya-vedārthaprakāśa), is attributed in the colophons to Sāyaṇācārya ('iti sāyaṇācāryaviracite mādhavīye vedārthaprakāśe').
SA_GV01_rvsb_09u.coverage: complete — Complete text of Maṇḍala 9 (all 7 anuvākas, 114 sūktas), containing saṃhitāpāṭha, padapāṭha, and the complete Sāyaṇabhāṣya, ending at anuvāka 7 with the colophon 'samāptaṃ ca navamaṃ maṇḍalam'.
translations: Jamison, Stephanie W., and Joel P. Brereton. The Rigveda. 2014. (English)
Geldner, Karl Friedrich. Der Rig-Veda aus dem Sanskrit ins Deutsche übersetzt. Harvard Oriental Series 33–36. Cambridge, Mass., 1951 bis 1957. (German)

SA_GV01_rvsb_10u.title: Ṛgvedasaṃhitā with Sāyaṇabhāṣya (maṇḍala 10)
SA_GV01_rvsb_10u.author: Sāyaṇa
SA_GV01_rvsb_10u.summary: Maṇḍala 10 is the final book of the Ṛgvedasaṃhitā, containing hymns accompanied by Padapāṭha and Sāyaṇa's commentary (Vedārthaprakāśa), which provides ritualistic, etymological, and grammatical interpretations rooted in Śrauta liturgy.
SA_GV01_rvsb_10u.attribution: The Ṛgvedasaṃhitā is canonical Vedic revelation; its Padapāṭha is traditionally attributed to Śākalya. Sāyaṇācārya authored the commentary.
SA_GV01_rvsb_10u.edition: R̥gveda-Saṃhitā with the Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya (commentary of Sāyaṇācārya) — Maṇḍala 10, Vaidika Saṃśodhana Maṇḍala (VSM) edition, Poona, 1933–1951.
SA_GV01_rvsb_10u.coverage: complete — Complete text of Ṛgveda Maṇḍala 10 with Saṃhitāpāṭha, Padapāṭha, and Sāyaṇabhāṣya, followed by a list of abbreviations and manuscript sigla.
translations: Stephanie W. Jamison and Joel P. Brereton (transl.), The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India, Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014. (English)

SA_GV01_rvsb_khilasu.title: Ṛgvedakhila
SA_GV01_rvsb_khilasu.summary: The Ṛgvedakhila is the collection of supplementary hymns (khilas) attached to the Ṛgveda-Saṃhitā, preserved across five adhyāyas. It contains prominent liturgical and devotional hymns not included in the main Śākala saṃhitā text, including the Śrīsūkta, Medhāsūkta, Śivasaṃkalpasūkta, and the Kuntāpa hymns. Philologically and ritually, it serves as an important bridge between late Ṛgvedic hymnody and Middle Vedic liturgy.
SA_GV01_rvsb_khilasu.attribution: The Khilas are supplementary Vedic hymns gathered across five adhyāyas. Sāyaṇācārya did not compose a commentary on the Khila hymns; the 'Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya' tag was erroneously inherited from the main title of the Vaidika Saṃśodhana Maṇḍala multi-volume Ṛgveda publication.
SA_GV01_rvsb_khilasu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Ṛgveda Khila collection in five adhyāyas (adhyāyas 1–5) as edited in VSM Vol. IV, along with editorial apparatus and the volume's concluding errata sheets (śuddhipatra).

SA_GSP28_mimkosa_01u.title: Mīmāṃsākośa (volume 1)
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_01u.author: Kevalānanda Sarasvatī
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_01u.summary: The Mīmāṃsākośa is a comprehensive encyclopedic dictionary and sourcebook of Pūrvamīmāṃsā terms, concepts, nyāyas, and ritual injunctions compiled by Svāmī Kevalānanda Sarasvatī. Sanskrit headwords are arranged alphabetically and illustrated with extensive excerpts and citations from foundational Mīmāṃsā works, including Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra, the Śābarabhāṣya, and commentaries. Volume 1 contains front matter followed by entries for the letter 'a'.
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_01u.attribution: Compiled by Svāmī Kevalānanda Sarasvatī at the Prājñapāṭhaśālā Maṇḍala in Wai.
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_01u.edition: Kevalānandasarasvatī (ed.), Mīmāṃsākoṣaḥ (Prathamo Bhāgaḥ). Prājñapāṭhaśālā Maṇḍala Granthamālā. Wai: Prājñapāṭhaśālā Maṇḍala, Śaka 1874 [1952].
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_01u.coverage: partial — Volume 1 (containing publisher's note, introductory front matter, and dictionary entries beginning with the letter 'a').

SA_GSP28_mimkosa_02u.title: Mīmāṃsākoṣa (vol. 2)
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_02u.author: Kevalānandasarasvatī
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_02u.summary: The Mīmāṃsākoṣa is a Sanskrit encyclopedia and concordance of Pūrvamīmāṃsā śāstra compiled by Kevalānandasarasvatī. Volume 2 covers terminology, nyāyas, and adhikaraṇas up to 'upāṃśuyāje...'. Entries synthesize definitions, context, and citations from classical Mīmāṃsā literature, including the Śābarabhāṣya and Maṇḍanamiśra.
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_02u.attribution: Compiled by Kevalānandasarasvatī under the auspices of the Prājñapāṭhaśālā Maṇḍala.
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_02u.edition: Kevalānandasarasvatī (ed.), Mīmāṃsākoṣaḥ, dvitīyo bhāgaḥ. Wai: Prājñapāṭhaśālā Maṇḍala, Śaka 1875 [], pp. 605–1200 (Prājñapāṭhaśālā Maṇḍala Granthamālā).
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_02u.coverage: partial — Complete for Volume 2 (pp. 605–1200) of the seven-volume work.

SA_GSP28_mimkosa_03u.title: Mīmāṃsākoṣa (vol. 3: u–ja)
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_03u.author: Kevalānanda Sarasvatī
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_03u.summary: The Mīmāṃsākoṣa is a Sanskrit encyclopedic dictionary and subject concordance of the Pūrvamīmāṃsā school compiled by Kevalānanda Sarasvatī and published in Wai. Volume 3 covers entries arranged alphabetically from 'u' to 'ja'. Each entry systematically collates adhikaraṇas, definitions, sūtras, and citations from primary Mīmāṃsā literature.
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_03u.attribution: Compiled by Kevalānanda Sarasvatī under the auspices of the Prājña Pāṭhaśālā Maṇḍala, Wai; preface by Lakṣmaṇaśāstrī Jośī.
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_03u.edition: Mīmāṃsākoṣaḥ, Tṛtīyo Bhāgaḥ (u–ja), ed. Kevalānandasarasvatī, Prājñapāṭhaśālā Maṇḍala Granthamālā, Wai: Prājña Pāṭhaśālā Maṇḍala, Śaka 1876 [].
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_03u.coverage: partial — Text of Volume 3 (entries from 'u' to 'ja') of the seven-volume work.

SA_GSP28_mimkosa_04u.title: Mīmāṃsākośa (vol. 4: ja–na)
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_04u.author: Kevalānandasarasvatī
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_04u.summary: The Mīmāṃsākośa is an encyclopedic dictionary and sourcebook of Mīmāṃsā terms, adhikaraṇas, and nyāyas compiled by Kevalānanda Sarasvatī. It systematically quotes and indexes passages from primary texts of both the Bhāṭṭa and Prābhākara traditions. Volume 4 contains entries spanning the consonants ja through na.
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_04u.attribution: Compiled by Kevalānanda Sarasvatī and published posthumously by his disciples at Prājña Pāṭhaśālā Maṇḍala.
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_04u.edition: Kevalānandasarasvatī (saṃp.), Mīmāṃsākoṣaḥ, caturtho bhāgaḥ (ja–na), Prājñapāṭhaśālāmaṇḍala Granthamālā, Wai: Prājña Pāṭhaśālā Maṇḍala, Śaka 1877.
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_04u.coverage: partial — Volume 4 (ja to na) out of 7 volumes.

SA_GSP28_mimkosa_05u.title: Mīmāṃsākoṣa (volume 5: pa–ba)
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_05u.author: Kevalānanda Sarasvatī
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_05u.summary: The Mīmāṃsākoṣa is an encyclopedic lexicon of Pūrvamīmāṃsā and Vedic hermeneutics compiled by Kevalānanda Sarasvatī. Volume 5 covers terms from pa through ba/va, providing citations, adhikaraṇa structures, and technical definitions compiled from Mīmāṃsā and Vedic texts.
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_05u.attribution: Compiled by Kevalānanda Sarasvatī; editorial revision work mentioned by Durgārāmaśāstrī Upādhye and Raṅganāthaśāstrī.
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_05u.edition: Mīmāṃsākoṣaḥ, pañcamo bhāgaḥ (pa-va), ed. Kevalānandasarasvatī, Prājñapāṭhaśālā Maṇḍala Granthamālā, Śaka 1882, pp. 2409–2995.
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_05u.coverage: partial — Volume 5 of the 7-volume encyclopedia, covering headwords from pa to ba/va, continuously paginated from pp. 2409 to 2995.

SA_GSP28_mimkosa_06u.title: Mīmāṃsākoṣa (vol. 6: bha–va)
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_06u.author: Kevalānandasarasvatī
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_06u.summary: The Mīmāṃsākoṣa is a seven-volume lexicon of the Pūrvamīmāṃsā philosophical system compiled by Kevalānandasarasvatī. This sixth volume encompasses headwords beginning with the Sanskrit consonants 'bha' through 'va', compiling technical terminology, adhikaraṇas, nyāyas, and textual extracts from primary sources.
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_06u.attribution: Compiled by Kevalānandasarasvatī. This volume was prepared by his pupil Dattātreyaśāstrī Tāmravedī and proofread/edited by Raṅganāthaśāstrī.
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_06u.edition: Kevalānandasarasvatī (comp.), Dattātreya Śāstrī Tāmravedī & Raṅganātha Śāstrī (eds.), Mīmāṃsākoṣaḥ, ṣaṣṭho bhāgaḥ (bha-va). Prājñapāṭhaśālāmaṇḍala-granthamālā. Śaka 1884.
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_06u.coverage: partial — Volume 6 of the 7-volume dictionary, containing headwords from 'bha' to 'va' (continuous pagination pp. 2997–3631).

SA_GSP28_mimkosa_07u.title: Mīmāṃsākośa (volume 7)
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_07u.author: Kevalānandasarasvatī
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_07u.summary: The Mīmāṃsākośa is a comprehensive seven-volume encyclopedic dictionary and sourcebook of Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā philosophy, terminology, and interpretative maxims (nyāyas), compiled by Kevalānandasarasvatī. Entries assemble extensive textual citations from fundamental Mīmāṃsā works, including the Śābarabhāṣya, Kumārila Bhaṭṭa's treatises, Prabhākara's Bṛhatī, and subsequent Bhāṭṭa and Prābhākara literature. Volume 7 brings the encyclopedia to completion, covering headwords through 'ha'.
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_07u.attribution: Compiled by Kevalānandasarasvatī; this concluding seventh volume was edited and prepared for publication by Dattātreyaśāstrī Tāmre and Raṅganāthaśāstrī Gadyāsa.
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_07u.edition: Kevalānandasarasvatī (ed.), Mīmāṃsākoṣaḥ, Saptamo Bhāgaḥ, edited and revised by Dattātreyaśāstrī Tāmre and Raṅganāthaśāstrī Gadyāsa. Wai: Prājñapāṭhaśālā Maṇḍala (Prājñapāṭhaśālā Maṇḍala Granthamālā), Śaka 1888 [ CE].
SA_GSP28_mimkosa_07u.coverage: partial — Volume 7 of 7, covering headwords terminating at the letter ha (pp. 3633–4542 of continuous pagination).

SA_T11_nairatmyasiu.title: Nairātmyasiddhi
SA_T11_nairatmyasiu.author: Jitāri
SA_T11_nairatmyasiu.summary: The Nairātmyasiddhi is an extremely succinct Buddhist epistemological treatise by Jitāri refuting the existence of an enduring self (sthirātman). Using the logical reason of the non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalabdhi), Jitāri demonstrates that no coherent ontological relation—neither essential identity (tādātmya), causal production (tadutpatti), contact (saṃyoga), nor inherence (samavāya)—can exist between an eternal self and an impermanent living body.
SA_T11_nairatmyasiu.attribution: Ascribed to the Buddhist epistemologist Jitāri based on the Bihar Research Society manuscript containing a collection of small texts by Jitāri.
SA_T11_nairatmyasiu.edition: Gudrun Bühnemann, Jitāri: Kleine Texte [Description of a manuscript from the Bihar Research Society with 10 small texts of Jitāri, and the edition of the following texts in Sanskrit: Vedāprāmāṇyasiddhi, Sarvajñasiddhi, Nairātmyasiddhi, Jātinirākṛti, *Īśvaravādimataparīkṣā], Wiener Studien zur Tibetologie und Buddhismuskunde 8, Wien: Arbeitskreis für tibetische und buddhistische Studien Universität Wien, 1982.
SA_T11_nairatmyasiu.coverage: complete — Complete short treatise (27 segments, ending with 'nairātmyasiddhiḥ samāpta [samāptā]').

SA_T11_sarvajnasidu.title: Sarvajñasiddhi
SA_T11_sarvajnasidu.author: Jitāri
SA_T11_sarvajnasidu.summary: The Sarvajñasiddhi is a concise epistemological tract by the late 10th-century Buddhist logician Jitāri establishing the omniscience of the Buddha. Operating within Dharmakīrti's pramāṇa framework, Jitāri argues that ascertainment of universal momentariness (sarvadharma-kṣaṇikatva) requires reliable instruction originating from an individual who directly perceives reality, thereby inferentially proving the Buddha's omniscience.
SA_T11_sarvajnasidu.attribution: The concluding colophon line explicitly names the author: 'paṇḍitajitāreḥ sarvajñasiddhiḥ'.
SA_T11_sarvajnasidu.edition: Gudrun Bühnemann, Sarvajñasiddhi, Wien: Arbeitskreis für tibetische und buddhisitsche Studien Universität Wien, 1982 (Wiener Studien zur Tibetologie und Buddhismskunde 8).
SA_T11_sarvajnasidu.coverage: complete — Complete text of Jitāri's short treatise. An initial manuscript folio missing in the manuscript was reconstructed by the editor from Ratnakīrti's Sarvajñasiddhi citation.

SA_T11_vedapramanyu.title: Vedāprāmāṇyasiddhi
SA_T11_vedapramanyu.author: Jitāri
SA_T11_vedapramanyu.summary: The Vedāprāmāṇyasiddhi ('Establishment of the Invalidity of the Veda') is a concise Buddhist epistemological tract by Jitāri. Applying Dharmakīrtian pramāṇa methodology (specifically vyāpakānupalabdhi), Jitāri refutes Mīmāṃsā claims of Vedic authoritativeness (apauruṣeyatva and svataḥprāmāṇya) by arguing that linguistic expressions possess neither essential identity (tādātmya) nor causal dependency (tadutpatti) in relation to external or imperceptible realities.
SA_T11_vedapramanyu.attribution: Ascribed to the Buddhist scholar-monk Jitāri in the closing colophon.
SA_T11_vedapramanyu.edition: Gudrun Bühnemann, Jitāri: Kleine Texte [Description of a manuscript from the Bihar Research Society with 10 small texts of Jitāri, and the edition of the following texts in Sanskrit: Vedāprāmāṇyasiddhi, Sarvajñasiddhi, Nairātmyasiddhi, Jātinirākṛti, Īśvaravādimataparīkṣā]. Wiener Studien zur Tibetologie und Buddhismuskunde, Heft 8. Wien: Arbeitskreis für tibetische und buddhistische Studien Universität Wien, 1982.
SA_T11_vedapramanyu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the short treatise, spanning from the opening thesis (yasya yatra pratibandho nāsti...) through to the author's colophon (vedāprāmāṇyasiddhiḥ kṛtiḥ paṇḍitajitāreḥ).

SA_T11_isvaravadimu.title: *Īśvaravādimataparīkṣā (fragment)
SA_T11_isvaravadimu.author: Jitāri
SA_T11_isvaravadimu.summary: The *Īśvaravādimataparīkṣā is a fragmentary Buddhist pramāṇa treatise by Jitāri refuting the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika teleological argument for God (Īśvara). Jitāri critically examines the inference that entities like trees and mountains must be produced by an intelligent creator because they are effects (kārya), pointing out that an invariable concomitance (vyāpti) between being an effect and being produced by a conscious agent cannot be established for natural phenomena.
SA_T11_isvaravadimu.attribution: The original title is not preserved due to the missing colophon. Editor Gudrun Bühnemann supplied the tentative title *Īśvaravādimataparīkṣā based on stylistic similarity to Jitāri's Digambaramataparīkṣā.
SA_T11_isvaravadimu.edition: Gudrun Bühnemann, *Īśvaravādimataparīkṣā, in: Jitāri: Kleine Texte, Wien: Arbeitskreis für tibetische und buddhistische Studien Universität Wien, 1982 (Wiener Studien zur Tibetologie und Buddhismuskunde 8).
SA_T11_isvaravadimu.coverage: fragment — Preserved on folios IIB 9–IIA 12 of a composite manuscript collection; the end of the text and colophon are missing.

SA_T11_vadasthananu.title: Vādasthānāni (Jātinirākṛti and Digambaramataparīkṣā)
SA_T11_vadasthananu.author: Jitāri
SA_T11_vadasthananu.summary: Jitāri's Vādasthānāni is a collection of polemical tracts. The e-text contains the first, the Jātinirākṛti (refuting universals/jāti), and the second, the Digambaramataparīkṣā (refuting the Jaina doctrine of anekāntavāda), breaking off after the opening half-verse of a section on pratyabhijñā.
SA_T11_vadasthananu.attribution: Colophons: 'jitāripādānāṃ kṛtir jātinirākṛtis samāptā' and 'digambaramataparikṣā samāptā kṛtir iyaṃ jitāripādānām'. The opening verse ('likhyante vādasthānāni kānicit') gives the collective title.
SA_T11_vadasthananu.edition: H. R. Rangaswami Iyengar, Tarkabhāṣa and Vādasthāna of Mokṣākaragupta and Jitāripāda, Mysore, The Hindusthan Press, 1952, pp. 72–85.
SA_T11_vadasthananu.coverage: partial — Sections 1 (Jātinirākṛti) and 2 (Digambaramataparīkṣā) complete; followed by the opening half-verse of a third section on pratyabhijñā ('pratyabhijñānasaṃjñātaṃ pramāṇaṃ kaiścidipyate ekatvaṃviṣayam...'). Iyengar's edition spans pp. 72–85 based on a palm-leaf manuscript in old Kannada script in Mysore.
translations: Kenjo Shirasaki, 'Jitāri no anekāntavāda hihan' [The Anekāntavādanirāsaḥ of Jitāri], Indogaku Bukkyōgaku Kenkyū (IBK) 1974. (Japanese (study of section 2))

SA_T11_dharmottarau.title: Dharmottaraṭippanaka
SA_T11_dharmottarau.author: Mallavādin
SA_T11_dharmottarau.summary: The Dharmottaraṭippanaka is an early gloss (ṭippanaka) by Mallavādin on Dharmottara's Nyāyabinduṭīkā (which comments on Dharmakīrti's Nyāyabindu), commenting on perception (pratyakṣa), inference for oneself (svārthānumāna), and inference for others (parārthānumāna).
SA_T11_dharmottarau.edition: Hideomi Yaita, Three Sanskrit Texts from the Buddhist Pramāṇa-Tradition: The Hetuvidyā Section in the Yogācārabhūmi, the Dharmottaraṭippanaka and the Tarkarahasya. Narita: Naritasan Shinshoji, 2005.
SA_T11_dharmottarau.coverage: complete — Text covering the chapters (Pratyakṣa, Svārthānumāna, Parārthānumāna) of Dharmottara's Nyāyabinduṭīkā, concluding with scribal verses and Patan manuscript references.

SA_T11_tattvasangru.title: Tattvasaṅgraha with Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā
SA_T11_tattvasangru.author: Śāntarakṣita, Kamalaśīla
SA_T11_tattvasangru.summary: The Tattvasaṅgraha ('Compendium of True Realities') is an encyclopedic philosophical and epistemological treatise by the Buddhist master Śāntarakṣita, consisting of 3,646 metrical verses divided into topical investigations (parīkṣā). From a late Madhyamaka-Yogācāra perspective informed by Dharmakīrtian pramāṇa methodology, it systematically examines and refutes rival non-Buddhist ontologies and epistemologies (including Sāṅkhya, Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, Mīmāṃsā, Jaina, and Cārvāka) as well as internal Buddhist positions on topics such as the soul (ātman), God (īśvara), substance, universals, causality, external reality, testimony, and omniscience. Kamalaśīla's companion commentary, the Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā, meticulously elucidates Śāntarakṣita's terse verses and preserves crucial quotations and arguments from otherwise lost classical Indian philosophical works.
SA_T11_tattvasangru.attribution: Attributed to Śāntarakṣita and Kamalaśīla, as confirmed by the opening and concluding colophons of both authors in the e-text.
SA_T11_tattvasangru.edition: Embar Krishnamacharya (ed.), Tattvasaṅgraha of Śāntarakṣita With the Commentary of Kamalaśīla, 2 vols., Gaekwad's Oriental Series, nos. 30 and 31, Baroda: Central Library / Oriental Institute, 1926.
SA_T11_tattvasangru.coverage: complete — Complete text containing up to verse 3,646 of the Tattvasaṅgraha along with Kamalaśīla's Pañjikā commentary down to the final verse and concluding colophon.
translations: Ganganatha Jha (trans.), The Tattvasaṅgraha of Śāntarakṣita with the Commentary of Kamalaśīla. (English)

SA_T11_pramanavartu.title: Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra
SA_T11_pramanavartu.author: Prajñākaragupta
SA_T11_pramanavartu.summary: The Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra (or Pramāṇavārttikabhāṣya) by Prajñākaragupta is a major Sanskrit commentary on chapters 2–4 of Dharmakīrti's Pramāṇavārttika. Blending kārikā verses with extensive prose, the text established the influential 'Alaṅkāra' sub-school of Buddhist epistemology. Prajñākaragupta interprets Dharmakīrtian logic from a sākāravāda and ultimate non-dual (advaita) standpoint, addressing foundational epistemological topics including the nature of valid cognition, perception, reflexivity (svasaṃvedana), and omniscience.
SA_T11_pramanavartu.attribution: Prajñākaragupta composed this extensive commentary combining verse (kārikā) and prose on chapters 2–4 of Dharmakīrti's Pramāṇavārttika. Dharmakīrti's chapter 1 (Svārthānumāna) was accompanied by Dharmakīrti's own Svavṛtti and was intentionally omitted by Prajñākaragupta.
SA_T11_pramanavartu.edition: Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana, Pramāṇavārtikabhāshyam or Vārtikālaṅkāraḥ of Prajñākaragupta (Being a Commentary on Dharmakīrti's Pramāṇavārtikam), Patna/Narita: Kashi Prasad Jayaswal Research Institute, 1953 (Tibetan Sanskrit Works Series 1).
SA_T11_pramanavartu.coverage: complete — Covers chapters 2 (Pramāṇasiddhi), 3 (Pratyakṣa), and 4 (Parārthānumāna), which constitutes the complete work as authored by Prajñākaragupta.

SA_T11_pramanavart2u.title: Pramāṇavārttikaṭippaṇī (Pariśiṣṭa 1)
SA_T11_pramanavart2u.author: Vibhūticandra
SA_T11_pramanavart2u.summary: Pramāṇavārttikaṭippaṇī (Pariśiṣṭa 1) consists of supplementary glosses on Dharmakīrti's Pramāṇavārttika and its relationship to Dignāga's Pramāṇasamuccaya, written by Vibhūticandra. Preserved on paper leaves bound at the end of the manuscript ('pustakānte kargadapatreṣu vibhūticandreṇaiva likhitam'), it discusses the motives of the treatise, the division of epistemological chapters, and technical discussions across perception (pratyakṣa) and inference (anumāna).
SA_T11_pramanavart2u.attribution: The paper leaves at the end bear Vibhūticandra's notes commenting on passages of the Pramāṇavārttika and Pramāṇasamuccaya.
SA_T11_pramanavart2u.edition: Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana, Appendix I, Patna, Bihar and Orissa Research Society, 1938-1940.
SA_T11_pramanavart2u.coverage: complete — Text of Appendix I (Pariśiṣṭa 1) as printed in Sāṅkṛtyāyana's 1938–1940 edition.

SA_T11_pramanavart3u.title: Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā
SA_T11_pramanavart3u.author: Karṇakagomin
SA_T11_pramanavart3u.summary: The Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā is Karṇakagomin's extensive Sanskrit sub-commentary on Dharmakīrti's auto-commentary (Svavṛtti) to the Svārthānumāna chapter of the Pramāṇavārttika. Relying on and engaging critically with Śākyabuddhi's earlier commentary, the work elaborates pivotal themes of Buddhist Pramāṇavāda, including the theory of apoha (conceptual exclusion), logical reasons (hetu), and polemics against Brahmanical darśanas.
SA_T11_pramanavart3u.attribution: Composed by Karṇakagomin. The original catalog entry misattributed the work to Dharmakīrti.
SA_T11_pramanavart3u.edition: Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana, Ācāryadharmakīrteḥ Pramāṇavārttikam (svārthānumānaparicchedaḥ) svopajñavṛttyā, Karṇakagomiviracitayā taṭṭīkayā ca sahitam, Ilāhābād, Kitāb Mahal, 1943
SA_T11_pramanavart3u.coverage: complete — Complete text of Karṇakagomin's ṭīkā on the Svārthānumānapariccheda (chapter 1) svavṛtti. Dharmakīrti's root kārikās and Svavṛtti were omitted during inputting.

SA_T11_pramanantaru.title: Pramāṇāntarbhāva
SA_T11_pramanantaru.summary: The Pramāṇāntarbhāva is a Buddhist epistemological (pramāṇa) treatise in verse and prose defending the Buddhist doctrine of exactly two pramāṇas (pratyakṣa and anumāna). It argues that additional epistemic instruments postulated by rival systems (such as śabda, upamāna, arthāpatti, and abhāva in Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya) are either subsumed under inference/perception or invalid.
SA_T11_pramanantaru.attribution: The surviving manuscript lacks an author colophon, and the work remains anonymous in modern scholarship. It is not to be confused with Ratnakīrti's Pramāṇāntarbhāvaprakaraṇa.
SA_T11_pramanantaru.edition: Satīndra Candra Nyāyācārya, Pramāṇātarbhāva, Calcutta, The Asiatic Society, 1969.
SA_T11_pramanantaru.coverage: complete — Complete text of the work as edited by Nyāyācārya, terminating at the colophon 'pramāṇāntarbhāvaḥ samāptaḥ'.

SA_T11_vadanyayatiu.title: Vādanyāyaṭīkā Vipañcitārthā
SA_T11_vadanyayatiu.author: Śāntarakṣita
SA_T11_vadanyayatiu.summary: The Vādanyāyaṭīkā Vipañcitārthā is an extensive 8th-century commentary by the Buddhist philosopher Śāntarakṣita on Dharmakīrti's debate treatise, the Vādanyāya. In the work, Dharmakīrti simplified the classical Indian debate theory by reducing the traditional twenty-two points of defeat (nigrahasthāna) to two fundamental categories: failure to state an essential part of the proof (asādhanāṅgavacana) and stating a non-existent defect in the opponent's argument (adoṣodbhāvana). Śāntarakṣita's commentary clarifies Dharmakīrti's dialectical definitions and engages extensively with opponent objections from Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and Sāṅkhya traditions.
SA_T11_vadanyayatiu.attribution: Attributed in the colophon to Śāntarakṣita (written in the manuscript as 'sāntarikṣapādānām').
SA_T11_vadanyayatiu.edition: Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana, Dharmakīrti's Vādanyāya, Patna, Bihar and Orissa Research Society, 1935-1936
SA_T11_vadanyayatiu.coverage: complete — Complete commentary, opening with the maṅgala verse to Mañjuśrī and concluding with verse 49, the commentary colophon, and the 1152 CE scribal postface.

SA_T11_tarkabhasau.title: Tarkabhāṣā
SA_T11_tarkabhasau.author: Mokṣākaragupta
SA_T11_tarkabhasau.summary: The Tarkabhāṣā of Mokṣākaragupta is a late Indian Buddhist primer of epistemology and pramāṇavāda composed at the Jagaddala Mahāvihāra. Structured in three paricchedas (perception, inference for oneself, and inference for others), it outlines the Pramāṇavārttika tradition, defending key doctrines such as universal momentariness (kṣaṇikavāda), conceptual exclusion (apoha), and reflexive awareness (svasaṃvedana) against Naiyāyika critics including Trilocana and Vācaspatimiśra.
SA_T11_tarkabhasau.attribution: Mokṣākaragupta was a Buddhist logician and bhikṣu associated with the Jagaddala Mahāvihāra, usually dated to the late 11th to 12th century CE.
SA_T11_tarkabhasau.edition: H. R. Rangaswami Iyengar, Tarkabhāṣa and Vādasthāna of Mokṣākaragupta and Jitāripāda, Mysore: The Hindusthan Press, 1952.
translations: Yuichi Kajiyama, An Introduction to Buddhist Philosophy: An Annotated Translation of the Tarkabhāṣā of Mokṣākaragupta, Memoirs of the Faculty of Letters, Kyoto University 10, Kyoto, 1966. (English)

SA_T11_avayavinirau.title: Avayavinirākaraṇa
SA_T11_avayavinirau.author: Aśoka
SA_T11_avayavinirau.summary: The Avayavinirākaraṇa is a short philosophical treatise by the late Buddhist logician Paṇḍita Aśoka (c. 10th–11th century CE) dedicated to refuting the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika doctrine of the 'whole' (avayavin) as an ontological real distinct from its parts (avayava). Operating in the tradition of Dharmakīrti, Aśoka utilizes the epistemological reason of vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi (perception of that which is incompatible with the pervader) to demonstrate that positing a single entity that simultaneously admits contradictory properties (such as moving and unmoving, covered and uncovered, or coloured and uncoloured) violates basic principles of non-contradiction.
SA_T11_avayavinirau.attribution: Ascribed to the Buddhist logician Paṇḍita Aśoka (c. 10th–11th century CE), distinct from the Mauryan emperor of the same name.
SA_T11_avayavinirau.edition: Anantalal Thakur, Aśokanibandhau Avayavinirākaraṇaṃ Samānyadūṣaṇaṃ ca, Patna, Kashi Prasad Jayaswal Research Institute, 1974
SA_T11_avayavinirau.coverage: complete — Complete text of the treatise, from the opening mangala (namo lokanāthāya) through the final closing verse and colophon (samāptaṃ cedamavayavinirākaraṇamiti).
translations: Fernando Tola and Carmen Dragonetti, The Avayavinirākaraṇa of Paṇḍita Aśoka, Sanskrit Text Edited with an Annotated English Translation, Studia Philologica Buddhica Monograph Series no. 10, Tokyo: The International Institute for Buddhist Studies, 1994. (English)
Yuichi Kajiyama, 'The Avayavinirākaraṇa of Pandita Aśoka', Journal of Indian and Buddhist Studies (Indogaku Bukkyōgaku Kenkyū) 9.2 (1961). (English)

SA_T11_samanyadusau.title: Sāmānyadūṣaṇa
SA_T11_samanyadusau.author: Aśoka
SA_T11_samanyadusau.summary: The Sāmānyadūṣaṇa is a Buddhist epistemological tract by Paṇḍita Aśoka refuting the realist doctrine of universals (sāmānya / jāti) maintained by Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika and Mīmāṃsā thinkers. Arguing from the standpoint of the Dignāga-Dharmakīrti school, Aśoka demonstrates through logic and prasanga arguments that unified conceptual cognition (anugatākārapratyaya) is a mentally constructed imputation (vikalpa) rooted in similarity and exclusion (apoha), rather than evidence for eternal, ubiquitous real universals.
SA_T11_samanyadusau.attribution: A Buddhist epistemologist (Paṇḍita Aśoka); author of two surviving tracts preserved together: Avayavinirākaraṇa and Sāmānyadūṣaṇa.
SA_T11_samanyadusau.edition: Anantalal Thakur, Aśokanibandhau Avayavinirākaraṇaṃ Samānyadūṣaṇaṃ ca, Patna, Kashi Prasad Jayaswal Research Institute, 1974
SA_T11_samanyadusau.coverage: complete — Text preserved up to the final verse and colophon.

SA_T02_caryamelapau.title: Caryāmelāpakapradīpa
SA_T02_caryamelapau.author: Āryadeva
SA_T02_caryamelapau.summary: The Caryāmelāpakapradīpa ('Lamp that Integrates the Practices') is an influential manual of tantric praxis and doctrine belonging to the Ārya (Noble) tradition of the Guhyasamājatantra, attributed to the tantric Āryadeva. Organized into eleven chapters, the treatise synthesizes the completion stage (niṣpannakrama) yogas from Nāgārjuna's Pañcakrama with transgressive yet nondual tantric conduct (caryā), systematically expounding body isolation, speech isolation, mind isolation, the three lights, and the integration of the illusory body with the clear light.
SA_T02_caryamelapau.attribution: Attributed traditionally to Āryadeva, a prominent master in the Ārya (Noble) lineage of Guhyasamājatantra exegesis; distinguished in modern scholarship from the 3rd-century Mādhyamika master Āryadeva.
SA_T02_caryamelapau.edition: Wedemeyer, Christian K., ed. Āryadeva's Lamp that Integrates the Practices (Caryāmelāpakapradīpa): The Gradual Path of Vajrayāna Buddhism According to the Esoteric Community Noble Tradition - Part Three: Critically Edited Sanskrit Text of Āryadeva's Caryāmelāpakapradīpa. Tengyur Translation Initiative, Treasury of the Buddhist Sciences series. New York: The American Institute of Buddhist Studies at Columbia University in New York with Columbia University's Center for Buddhist Studies and Tibet House US, 2007.
SA_T02_caryamelapau.coverage: complete — Contains all eleven chapters (paricchedas) with opening sigla, abbreviations, and front matter from Wedemeyer's critical edition.
translations: Wedemeyer, Christian K. Āryadeva's Lamp that Integrates the Practices (Caryāmelāpakapradīpa): The Gradual Path of Vajrayāna Buddhism According to the Esoteric Community Noble Tradition. New York: American Institute of Buddhist Studies, 2007. (English)

SA_GR12_dvadasaramnu.title: Dvādaśāraṃ Nayacakram with Nyāyāgamānusāriṇī
SA_GR12_dvadasaramnu.author: Mallavādin, Siṃhasūri
SA_GR12_dvadasaramnu.summary: The Dvādaśāranayacakra ('Twelve-Spoked Wheel of Standpoints') by the Śvetāmbara Jaina dialectician Mallavādin is an influential masterwork of classical Indian doxography and Jaina philosophical pluralism (anekāntavāda). Mallavādin arranges twelve non-Jaina philosophical standpoints into a self-contained dialectical wheel where each school systematically refutes the preceding one and is in turn overthrown by the next, demonstrating how partial viewpoints fall into internal contradiction unless synthesized within Jaina anekāntavāda. Because Mallavādin's original text survives only embedded as pratīkas within Siṃhasūri Gaṇin's commentary Nyāyāgamānusāriṇī, the commentary forms an integral part of the surviving tradition.
SA_GR12_dvadasaramnu.attribution: The original root work by Mallavādin Kṣamāśramaṇa does not survive in independent manuscripts; its text is reconstructed through pratīkas preserved in Siṃhasūri Gaṇin's commentary Nyāyāgamānusāriṇī (Nayacakravālavṛtti). The e-text also incorporates the editorial Sanskrit Ṭippaṇa by Muni Jambūvijaya.
SA_GR12_dvadasaramnu.edition: Muni Jambūvijayajī, Dvādaśāraṃ Nayacakraṃ of Ācārya Śrī Mallavādi Kṣamāśramaṇa With the Commentary Nyāyāgamānusāriṇī of Śrī Siṃhasūri Gaṇi Vādi Kṣamāśramaṇa, Bhavnagar, Śrī Jain Ātmānand Sabhā, 1966-1988 (Śrī Ātmānand Jain Granthamālā Serial 92, 94, 95)
SA_GR12_dvadasaramnu.coverage: complete — Dvādaśāranayacakra along with the Nyāyāgamānusāriṇī commentary and Jambūvijaya's Ṭippaṇa.

SA_GR12_laghiyastrau.title: Laghīyastraya with Laghīyastrayavivṛti and Nyāyakumudacandra
SA_GR12_laghiyastrau.author: Akalaṅka, Prabhācandra
SA_GR12_laghiyastrau.summary: The Laghīyastraya ('Three Shorter Treatises', comprising Pramāṇapraveśa, Nayapraveśa, and Nikṣepapraveśa) is a fundamental work of Digambara Jaina logic and epistemology by Akalaṅka (ca. 8th c.), accompanied by his auto-commentary (Vivṛti). In this file, the work is preserved within the Nyāyakumudacandra, a massive 11th-century commentary by Prabhācandra that systematically articulates Jaina epistemology, defensible realism, and non-one-sidedness (anekāntavāda), while examining and refuting rival doctrines of Buddhist, Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, Mīmāṃsā, and Advaita schools.
SA_GR12_laghiyastrau.attribution: Root kārikās and auto-commentary (Vivṛti) by Bhaṭṭākalaṅkadeva (ca. 8th century); the extensive sub-commentary Nyāyakumudacandra is by Prabhācandrācārya (ca. 11th century).
SA_GR12_laghiyastrau.edition: Nyāya-Kumuda-Candra of Śrīmat Prabhācandrācārya (A Commentary on Bhaṭṭākalaṅkadeva's Laghīyastraya), edited by Mahendra Kumar Nyāyācārya, 2 vols., Māṇikacandra Digambara Jaina Granthamālā Nos. 38 & 39, Bombay: Māṇikacandra Digambara Jaina Granthamālā Samiti, 1938–1941.
SA_GR12_laghiyastrau.coverage: complete — Complete text of Prabhācandra's Nyāyakumudacandra covering all three sections of the Laghīyastraya (Pramāṇapraveśa, Nayapraveśa, Nikṣepapraveśa), down to the concluding editorial verses of Mahendra Kumar Nyāyācārya.
translations: Clavel, Marion. 2008. Le Laghīyastraya d’Akalaṅka: traduction et étude. Doctoral dissertation, Université de Paris III – Sorbonne Nouvelle. (French)

SA_GR12_siddhivinisu.title: Siddhiviniścaya with Siddhiviniścayaṭīkā
SA_GR12_siddhivinisu.author: Akalaṅka, Anantavīrya
SA_GR12_siddhivinisu.summary: The Siddhiviniścaya is a major treatise on Jaina logic and epistemology by Bhaṭṭa Akalaṅka. Structured into twelve chapters (prastāvas) ranging from Pratyakṣasiddhi to Nikṣepasiddhi, the text establishes the validity of anekāntavāda and syādvāda while critiquing Buddhist epistemological views as well as Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, and Mīmāṃsā doctrines. This digital edition comprises Akalaṅka's kārikās and auto-commentary together with Anantavīrya's comprehensive ṭīkā and Mahendrakumar Jain's modern Āloka annotations.
SA_GR12_siddhivinisu.attribution: Bhaṭṭa Akalaṅka composed the root verses and svopajñavṛtti. Anantavīrya wrote the commentary. Modern Sanskrit annotations (Āloka-ṭippaṇa) were added by editor Mahendrakumar Jain.
SA_GR12_siddhivinisu.edition: Siddhivinishchayatika of Shri Anantaviryacharya, the Commentary on Siddhivinishchaya and its Vrtti of Bhatta Akalanka Deva, edited by Mahendrakumar Jain, 2 vols., Jñānapīṭha Mūrtidevī Jaina Granthamālā: Sanskrit Grantha Nos. 22 & 23, Varanasi: Bhāratīya Jñānapīṭha, 1959.
SA_GR12_siddhivinisu.coverage: complete — Complete in 12 prastāvas, concluding with nikṣepasiddhiḥ dvādaśamaḥ prastāvaḥ (lines 28022–28024).

SA_GR12_sarvarthasiu.title: Tattvārthasūtra with Sarvārthasiddhi
SA_GR12_sarvarthasiu.author: Umāsvāti, Pūjyapāda
SA_GR12_sarvarthasiu.summary: The Sarvārthasiddhi is a Digambara commentary on Umāsvāti's Tattvārthasūtra, authored by Ācārya Pūjyapāda (Devanandin). Across ten adhyāyas, it provides a comprehensive scholastic formulation of Jaina ontology (dravya), epistemology (pramāṇa, naya), cosmology, karmic mechanism, and the path to liberation (mokṣamārga). It stands as a cornerstone of Digambara doctrinal literature.
SA_GR12_sarvarthasiu.attribution: In the Digambara tradition, the author of the Tattvārthasūtra is identified as Ācārya Gṛddhapiccha (Umāsvāmin), while Śvetāmbaras refer to him as Umāsvāti. The commentary Sarvārthasiddhi is by Pūjyapāda (also known as Devanandin).
SA_GR12_sarvarthasiu.edition: Śrīmadācāryapūjyapādaviracitā Sarvārthasiddhiḥ, ed. with Hindi translation by Phūlcandra Śāstrī, Delhi: Bhāratīya Jñānapīṭha, 5th edition, 1991.
SA_GR12_sarvarthasiu.coverage: complete — Complete in all 10 adhyāyas, ending with 'iti tattvārthavṛttau sarvārthasiddhisaṃjñikāyāṃ daśamo ’dhyāyaḥ samāptaḥ'.
translations: S. A. Jain, Reality: English Translation of Shri Pujyapada's Sarvarthasiddhi, Calcutta: Vira Sasana Sangha, 1960. (English)

SA_GR12_pramanamimau.title: Pramāṇamīmāṃsā with Svopajñavṛtti
SA_GR12_pramanamimau.author: Hemacandra
SA_GR12_pramanamimau.summary: The Pramāṇamīmāṃsā is an influential manual of Jaina epistemology and logic composed in classical sūtra style by Hemacandra (flourished between 1145–1172 CE / 1088–1172 CE), accompanied by his own commentary (Svopajñavṛtti). Modeled formally after Akṣapāda Gautama's Nyāyasūtra and the Buddhist pramāṇa tradition, it defines pramāṇa, details direct and indirect perception (pratyakṣa, parokṣa), inference (anumāna), and dialectic from a syādvāda viewpoint while refuting Buddhist, Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, and Mīmāṃsā arguments. The surviving text breaks off midway through the second adhyāya.
SA_GR12_pramanamimau.attribution: Both the aphoristic sūtras and the prose vṛtti were composed by Hemacandra (Kalikāla Sarvajña).
SA_GR12_pramanamimau.edition: Sukhlalji Saṅghavi, Pramāṇa Mīmaṁsa of Kalikāla Sarvajña Śrī Hemacandrācārya, Ahmedabad, The Sañcālaka-Siṅghī Jaina Granthamālā, 1938.
SA_GR12_pramanamimau.coverage: complete — Complete for the extant text as preserved in the manuscript tradition (Adhyāya 1, Āhnikas 1–2, and Adhyāya 2, Āhnika 1). Although Hemacandra planned five adhyāyas (1.1 intro), the remainder is lost or was never finished.
translations: Hemacandra, Pramāṇamīmāṃsā: Text and Translation with Critical Notes, edited/translated by Satkari Mookerjee and Nathmal Tatia. (English)

SA_GSP32_padarthadhau.title: Padārthadharmasaṅgraha
SA_GSP32_padarthadhau.author: Praśastapāda
SA_GSP32_padarthadhau.summary: The Padārthadharmasaṅgraha (also known as the Praśastapādabhāṣya), composed by Praśastapāda around the 6th century CE, is the defining classical exposition of the Vaiśeṣika philosophical school. Rather than commenting sequentially on Kaṇāda's Vaiśeṣikasūtra, it presents an independent systematic categorization of reality into six fundamental ontological categories (padārthas: dravya, guṇa, karma, sāmānya, viśeṣa, and samavāya), establishing the conceptual foundation for all subsequent classical Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika philosophy.
SA_GSP32_padarthadhau.attribution: Composed by Praśastapāda (ca. 6th century CE); traditionally styled a bhāṣya on Kaṇāda's Vaiśeṣikasūtra, but in structure an independent compendium.
SA_GSP32_padarthadhau.edition: V. P. Dvivedin (ed.), The Praśastapādabhāṣya with Commentary Nyāyakandalī of Śrīdhara, Delhi: Sri Satguru Publications [Reprint of Benares 1895, Vizianagram Sanskrit Series, 6 / Sri Garbi Dass Oriental Ser., 13].
SA_GSP32_padarthadhau.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Padārthadharmasaṅgraha running from introductory mangala/uddeśa (sections 0–2) through the six padārthas to the samavāyapadārtha and final colophon (segments 0–427).
translations: Ganganatha Jha, Padārthadharmasaṅgraha of Praśastapāda with the Nyāyakandalī of Śrīdhara, Varanasi / Delhi: Chaukhambha Orientalia, 1982. (English)

SA_GSP34_patanjalayou.title: Pātañjalayogaśāstra
SA_GSP34_patanjalayou.author: Patañjali
SA_GSP34_patanjalayou.summary: The Pātañjalayogaśāstra is the foundational philosophical text of classical Yoga (Pātañjala Yoga). Organized into four chapters (Samādhipāda, Sādhanapāda, Vibhūtipāda, and Kaivalyapāda), it presents an eightfold discipline of practice (aṣṭāṅgayoga) and meditative absorption within a dualist Sāṅkhya metaphysical framework. The system directs the practitioner toward the cessation of mental operations (cittavṛttinirodha) and ultimate spiritual liberation (kaivalya), defined as the isolation of pure consciousness (puruṣa) from material nature (prakṛti).
SA_GSP34_patanjalayou.attribution: While later Indian tradition distinguishes the sūtras composed by Patañjali from an independent commentary (bhāṣya) composed by Vyāsa (hence 'Vyāsabhāṣya'), philological research demonstrates that the sūtras and bhāṣya form an integral textual whole (the Pātañjalayogaśāstra), composed or compiled by a single author named Patañjali.
SA_GSP34_patanjalayou.edition: Vācaspatimiśraviracitaṭīkāsaṃvalitavyāsabhāṣyasametāni Pātañjalayogasūtrāṇi, ed. Kāśinātha Śāstrī Āgāśe, Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series (ASS) 47, Poona: Ānandāśrama Press, 1904.
SA_GSP34_patanjalayou.coverage: complete — Complete text of all four pādas of the sūtras along with the bhāṣya: Samādhipāda (YS 1.1–1.51), Sādhanapāda (YS 2.1–2.55), Vibhūtipāda (YS 3.1–3.55), and Kaivalyapāda (YS 4.1–4.34), ending at segment 1795 with the final colophon.
translations: Woods, James Haughton, The Yoga-System of Patañjali; or, The Hindu Doctrine of Concentration of Mind, Harvard Oriental Series 17, Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1914. (English)
Hariharānanda Āraṇya, Swāmi, Yoga Philosophy of Patañjali: Containing His Yoga Aphorisms with the Commentary of Vyāsa, Calcutta: University of Calcutta, 1963 (rev. ed.. (English)

SA_GSP34_yogapradipau.title: Yogapradīpa
SA_GSP34_yogapradipau.summary: The Yogapradīpa is an anonymous Sanskrit yoga treatise in 141 anuṣṭubh verses emphasizing internal meditation and self-knowledge (ātmajñāna). It depreciates outward pilgrimages and rituals, identifying the body itself as the supreme tīrtha and celebrating the transcendent Self whether named Śaṅkara, Jineśa, or Brahman.
SA_GSP34_yogapradipau.attribution: No author is mentioned in the text. The scribal colophon notes manuscript ownership or copyist: 'pustakaṃ harilalyasya'.
SA_GSP34_yogapradipau.coverage: complete — Complete in 141 numbered verses plus a concluding verse and final colophon.

SA_GSP34_rajamartandu.title: Yogasūtra with Rājamārtaṇḍa
SA_GSP34_rajamartandu.author: Patañjali, Bhoja
SA_GSP34_rajamartandu.summary: The Rājamārtaṇḍa (Bhojavṛtti) is a commentary on Patañjali's Yogasūtra attributed to King Bhojadeva of Dhārā. In this e-text it is accompanied by an appended standalone sūtrapāṭha.
SA_GSP34_rajamartandu.attribution: The Rājamārtaṇḍa (Bhojavṛtti) is attributed to Bhojadeva of Dhārā. The root sūtras are attributed to Patañjali.
SA_GSP34_rajamartandu.coverage: complete — Four pādas of the Yogasūtra with Bhoja's vṛtti, followed by an appended sūtrapāṭha ending 'iti pātañjalayogasūtrāṇi'.

SA_GSP33_atmabodhapru.title: Ātmabodha with Ātmabodhaṭīkā
SA_GSP33_atmabodhapru.author: Śaṅkara, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī
SA_GSP33_atmabodhapru.summary: The Ātmabodha is an introductory Advaita Vedānta prakaraṇa in 68 verses traditionally attributed to Śaṅkara. It explains non-dual self-knowledge as the sole direct means to liberation, employing metaphors such as the snake and rope, the kataka nut purifying muddy water, and the sun obscured by clouds. The text is accompanied by an explanatory Sanskrit commentary (Ātmabodhaṭīkā) ascribed to Madhusūdana Sarasvatī.
SA_GSP33_atmabodhapru.attribution: The root prakaraṇa is traditionally attributed to Śaṅkarācārya (Ādi Śaṅkara). The commentary is ascribed to Madhusūdana Sarasvatī.
SA_GSP33_atmabodhapru.edition: Dinesh Chandra Bhaṭṭācārya, Ātmabodhaprakaraṇa of Śaṅkarācārya with a commentary ascribed to Mahusūdana Sarasvatī, Calcutta, Sanskrit College, 1961.
SA_GSP33_atmabodhapru.coverage: complete — Complete in 68 verses with commentary on each verse.
translations: Swami Nikhilananda, Self-Knowledge (Atmabodha): An English Translation of Sankaracharya's Atmabodha with Notes, Comments and Introduction, New York, 1946. (English)

SA_GSP33_aparoksanubu.title: Aparokṣānubhūti with Bhāṣāṭīkā
SA_GSP33_aparoksanubu.author: Śaṅkara, Jñānadāsa
SA_GSP33_aparoksanubu.summary: The Aparokṣānubhūti (also Aparokṣānubhava) is a short Advaita Vedānta prakaraṇa traditionally ascribed to Śaṅkara, treating inquiry into the self, the discrimination of self and body, and a Vedāntic fifteen-limbed yoga. In this e-text the Sanskrit verses are followed by a Braj Bhāṣā paraphrase in dohā and caupāī metres by Jñānadāsa.
SA_GSP33_aparoksanubu.attribution: The Sanskrit root text is traditionally ascribed to Śaṅkara (e-text: 'śaṃkara svāmī jo katyo aprokṣa anubhava joha'). The Braj Bhāṣā verse commentary is by Jñānadāsa, dated Kārtika kṛṣṇa caturdaśī at Rāmadvārā in Kaṭrā Nīl, Indraprastha.
SA_GSP33_aparoksanubu.coverage: complete — Complete Sanskrit text with interleaved Braj Bhāṣā commentary by Jñānadāsa, concluding with 'itiaparokṣānubhūtīkiaparokṣātubhavaṭīkāsamāptā'.

SA_GS24_siddhantakau.title: Siddhāntakaumudī
SA_GS24_siddhantakau.author: Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita
SA_GS24_siddhantakau.summary: The Siddhāntakaumudī (also called Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntakaumudī) is a grammatical treatise composed by Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita. It rearranges the rule inventory of Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī according to subject-matter categories appending concise explanatory prose glosses.
SA_GS24_siddhantakau.attribution: Universally attributed to Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita, who states in his introductory verse: 'vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntakaumudīyaṃ viracyate'. The text presents the sūtras of Pāṇini reorganized by grammatical topic accompanied by Bhaṭṭoji's commentary (vṛtti).
SA_GS24_siddhantakau.coverage: partial — The SARIT source TEI is complete, from the maṅgala and Śivasūtras to the end of the svaraprakaraṇa with the final verse 'itthaṃ vaidikaśabdānāṃ...'. In the DharmaNexus segmentation, however, the text of the sūtras (TEI <ab type="sūtra">, 4,816 elements) has been dropped. Only their labels ('SK n', 'AS a-p-s') and Bhaṭṭoji's vṛtti survive. For example, segments 15–17 have 'SK 00', 'AS 0-0-1', 'iti māheśvarāṇi sūtrāṇi...' without the Śivasūtras, and 'vṛddhirādaic' never occurs. The vārttikas, paribhāṣās and vṛtti prose are present.

SA_GS40_astangasangu.title: Aṣṭāṅgasaṅgraha
SA_GS40_astangasangu.author: Vāgbhaṭa
SA_GS40_astangasangu.summary: The Aṣṭāṅgasaṅgraha is one of the foundational comprehensive treatises of classical Āyurveda, composed by Vāgbhaṭa, son of Siṃhagupta. Combining metrical verse and prose, it covers the eight classical limbs of Indian medicine across six divisions (sthānas).
SA_GS40_astangasangu.attribution: Colophons designate the author as Vāgbhaṭa, son of Siṃhagupta (śrīsiṃhaguptasūnu).
SA_GS40_astangasangu.edition: Śrīmad Vṛddhavāgbhaṭaviracitaḥ Aṣṭāṅgasaṅgrahaḥ Induvyākhyāsahitaḥ, ed. Anaṃta Dāmodara Āṭhavale, Puṇyapattane, Śa. He. Gurjara at the Āyurvidyā Mudraṇālaya, 1980.
SA_GS40_astangasangu.coverage: complete — Complete mūla text in all six sthānas: Sūtrasthāna (40 chapters), Śārīrasthāna (12 chapters), Nidānasthāna (16 chapters), Cikitsitasthāna (24 chapters), Kalpasthāna (8 chapters), and Uttarasthāna (50 chapters, ending with Utt.50.211 and closing colophon).

SA_GS40_bhelasamhitu.title: Bhelasaṃhitā (incomplete: Sūtrasthāna 4 to Siddhisthāna 8)
SA_GS40_bhelasamhitu.author: Bhela
SA_GS40_bhelasamhitu.summary: The Bhelasaṃhitā is an Āyurvedic treatise expounding etiology, pathology, anatomy, embryology, and therapeutics across sthānas including Sūtrasthāna, Nidānasthāna, Śārīrasthāna, Cikitsāsthāna, and Siddhisthāna.
SA_GS40_bhelasamhitu.edition: V.S.Venkatasubramania Sastri, C.Raja Rajeswara Sarma, eds., Bhelasaṃhitā, New Delhi: Central Council for Research in Indian Medicine & Homoeopathy, 1977.
SA_GS40_bhelasamhitu.coverage: partial — The e-text starts with 'sūtrasthānam || caturtho ' dhyāyaḥ' (1.4.1) and breaks off at 8.8.88 followed by dots marking the loss.

SA_GS40_cakradattau.title: Cakradatta
SA_GS40_cakradattau.author: Cakrapāṇidatta
SA_GS40_cakradattau.summary: The Cakradatta (or Cikitsāsaṃgraha) is an 11th-century Sanskrit compendium of Ayurvedic therapeutics and clinical medicine composed by Cakrapāṇidatta, the celebrated commentator on the Carakasaṃhitā. Structured largely along the nosological classification established by Mādhava's Rugviniścaya (Mādhavanidāna), the treatise systematically details medicinal recipes, dietetics, and panchakarma treatment regimens. It is a landmark text in the history of Indian medicine for its early, widespread integration of metallic and mercurial preparations (rasaśāstra) into standard medical practice.
SA_GS40_cakradattau.attribution: Cakrapāṇidatta was the son of Nārāyaṇa (gauḍādhinātharasavatyadhikāripātra-nārāyaṇasya tanayaḥ) and flourished in the 11th century CE.
SA_GS40_cakradattau.edition: Hariprasāda Śarmā, Cakradattanāmamahāvaidyapraṇītaḥ Cakradattaḥ, Mumbai: Nirṇayasāgara Press, 1893.
SA_GS40_cakradattau.coverage: complete — Complete text covering all therapeutic sections from Jvarādhikāra through concluding authorial verses.
translations: Sharma. Cakradatta (Text with English Translation): A treatise on principles and practices of Ayurvedic medicine. Varanasi: Chaukhambha Orientalia, 1994. (English)

SA_GS40_carakasamhiu.title: Carakasaṃhitā with Āyurvedadīpikā
SA_GS40_carakasamhiu.author: Caraka, Cakrapāṇidatta
SA_GS40_carakasamhiu.summary: The Carakasaṃhitā is a foundational treatise of classical Indian medicine (Āyurveda). Cakrapāṇidatta's commentary is the Āyurvedadīpikā.
SA_GS40_carakasamhiu.attribution: The root text is attributed to Caraka and Dṛḍhabala. Cakrapāṇidatta composed the commentary Āyurvedadīpikā (also called Carakatātparyaṭīkā).
SA_GS40_carakasamhiu.edition: Carakasaṃhitā, śrīcakrapāṇidattaviracitayā āyurvedadīpikāvyākhyayā saṃvalitā = The Charakasaṃhitā of Agniveśa revised by Charaka and Dṛiḍhabala With the Āyurveda-dīpikā Commentary of Chakrapāṇidatta, Puṇyapattane: Śa. He. Gurjara at the Āyurvidyā Mudraṇālaya, 1981.
SA_GS40_carakasamhiu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 8 sthānas (120 adhyāyas: Sūtra 1–30, Nidāna 1–8, Vimāna 1–8, Śārīra 1–8, Indriya 1–12, Cikitsā 1–30, Kalpa 1–12, Siddhi 1–12) with Cakrapāṇidatta's commentary, concluding at Siddhisthāna 12.55.

SA_GS40_ayurvedasutu.title: Āyurvedasūtra (chapters 1–5)
SA_GS40_ayurvedasutu.summary: The Āyurvedasūtra is a Sanskrit medical-philosophical work that synthesizes classical Āyurveda with Haṭhayoga, Tantra, and Advaita Vedānta, emphasizing dietetics, digestive fire (agni), and breath control. This digital file contains only an empty skeleton of sūtra numbers and chapter markers for chapters 1–5.
SA_GS40_ayurvedasutu.attribution: The root sūtras are of anonymous authorship. The text is preserved with a commentary by Yogānandanātha, which is not included in this e-text.
SA_GS40_ayurvedasutu.edition: Rudrapatnam Shamasastry (1868–1944), Āyurvedasūtram Yogānandanāthakṛtabhāṣyasametam = The Ayurvedasutram; with the commentary of Yoganandanatha, Mysore, University of Mysore, 1922.
SA_GS40_ayurvedasutu.coverage: fragment — Covers chapters 1–5, but contains only section headings and numerical sūtra tags (1.1–5.116) without the actual Sanskrit text of the sūtras.

SA_GS40_rasarnavaetu.title: Rasārṇava
SA_GS40_rasarnavaetu.summary: The Rasārṇava is one of the principal classical treatises of Indian alchemy (Rasaśāstra), framed as a tantric dialogue between Bhairava and Devī. Across 18 chapters (paṭalas), it provides extensive descriptions of laboratory equipment (yantras), crucibles (mūṣās), furnaces, and mineralogical operations including the purification and fixation of mercury (rasabandha) and flame tests for metals. The physical transmutations are explicitly situated within a tantric soteriological framework aiming at bodily immortality (dehasiddhi) and living liberation (jīvanmukti).
SA_GS40_rasarnavaetu.attribution: A traditional Śaiva alchemical tantra framed as a dialogue between Bhairava and Devī. Praphulla Chandra Ray and Hariśchandra Kaviratna are modern editors.
SA_GS40_rasarnavaetu.edition: Praphulla Chandra Ray and Hariśchandra Kaviratna, The Rasārnavam or the Ocean of Mercury and Other Metals and Minerals, Calcutta, The Asiatic Society of Bengal, 1910.
SA_GS40_rasarnavaetu.coverage: partial — Contains all 18 paṭalas through the final verse (RA_1.1 to RA_18.230), but lacks the closing colophon/explicit.

SA_GS40_rasayanakhau.title: Rasaratnākara (Rasāyanakhaṇḍa)
SA_GS40_rasayanakhau.author: Nityanātha Siddha
SA_GS40_rasayanakhau.summary: The Rasāyanakhaṇḍa is the fourth book of the Rasaratnākara, a major Sanskrit alchemical and iatrochemical compendium composed by Nityanātha Siddha. Comprising eight chapters (upadeśas), it covers rejuvenation and longevity therapy (kāyakalpa, rasāyana), mercurial processing and calcination (pāradamāraṇa), rejuvenating medicinal pills (guṭikā), cosmetics and hair dyes, aphrodisiac formulations (vājīkaraṇa), and tantric alchemical practices associated with Mount Śrīśaila.
SA_GS40_rasayanakhau.attribution: The work is attributed in the colophons to Pārvatīputra Śrīnityanātha Siddha.
SA_GS40_rasayanakhau.edition: Yādavaśarmā Trivikrama Ācārya, Śrīnityanāthasiddhaviracitaḥ Rasaratnākarāntargataś caturthaḥ Rasāyanakhaṇḍaḥ = Rasâyanakhanda, Fourth Part of Rasaratnākara of Śrī Nitya Nātha Siddha edited by Vaidya Jâdavjî Tricumjî Âchârya, Banaras, Caukhambā Saṃskṛta Pustakālaya, 1939
SA_GS40_rasayanakhau.coverage: complete — Complete text of the fourth book (Rasāyanakhaṇḍa), containing all eight upadeśas (chapters 1–8).
translations: Rasaratnakara-Rasayanakhandah: Satippaņa 'Rasacandrikā' Hindivyākhopetah, Varanasi: Caukhamba Amarabharaei Prakasana, 1982. (Hindi)

SA_GS40_vrndamadhavu.title: Siddhayoga
SA_GS40_vrndamadhavu.author: Vṛnda
SA_GS40_vrndamadhavu.summary: The Siddhayoga (also known as Vṛndamādhava) by Vṛnda is a major Sanskrit medical treatise on therapeutics (cikitsā). It systematically arranges medicinal recipes and therapeutic treatments according to nosological order (gadaviniścayakrama).
SA_GS40_vrndamadhavu.attribution: Authored by Vṛnda. The printed source edition included the commentary Kusumāvalī by Śrīkaṇṭhadatta, but that commentary was not digitized in this file.
SA_GS40_vrndamadhavu.edition: Śrīmadvṛndapraṇīto Vṛndamādhavāparanāmā Siddhayogaḥ: Śrīkaṇṭhadattaviracitavyākhyākusumāvalyākhyaṭīkāsametaḥ, edited by Haṇamantaśāstrin Kṛṣṇaśāstrin Pādhye, Puṇe: Ānandāśrama, 1894 (Ānandāśramasaṃskṛtagranthāvaliḥ, 27).
SA_GS40_vrndamadhavu.coverage: complete — Complete root text across all chapters/adhikāras ending at verse 29 ('sapadi sa hi likhitvā siddhayogaḥ samāptaḥ'). The commentary Kusumāvalī present in the base printed edition was omitted during digitization, as explicitly noted in the e-text.

SA_GS40_kalyanakarau.title: Kalyāṇakāraka
SA_GS40_kalyanakarau.author: Ugrāditya
SA_GS40_kalyanakarau.summary: The Kalyāṇakāraka is an important early medieval Sanskrit medical compendium by the Digambara Jain monk Ugrāditya (c. 9th century CE). Conforming strictly to Jain ahimsā principles, the text famously replaces animal meats, fats, alcohol, and honey with vegetable and herbal substitutes throughout its therapeutic and pharmacological recipes. It covers the full scope of classical Āyurveda, including pathology, therapeutics, pediatrics, toxicology, and prognostication of fatal signs (ariṣṭa).
SA_GS40_kalyanakarau.attribution: Attributed to Ugrāditya, dated in scholarly sources to ca. 825–875 CE.
SA_GS40_kalyanakarau.edition: Vardhamāna Pārśvanātha Śāstrī (ed. & Hindi tr.), Ugrādityācāryakṛta Kalyāṇakāraka (rāṣṭrabhāṣānuvādasahita), Solāpura: Seṭha Goviṃdajī Rāvajī Dośī, 1940 (Sakhārāma Nemacaṃda Graṃthamālā, 129).
SA_GS40_kalyanakarau.coverage: complete — Complete Sanskrit verse text. The modern Hindi translation/commentary by Vardhamāna Pārśvanātha Śāstrī was systematically excluded during digitization, as explicitly flagged by SARIT with the note 'bhāvārthaḥ--The Hindi commentary was not digitized.'
translations: Vardhamāna Pārśvanātha Śāstrī, Ugrādityācāryakṛta Kalyāṇakāraka (rāṣṭrabhāṣānuvādasahita), Solāpura: Seṭha Goviṃdajī Rāvajī Dośī, 1940. (Hindi)

SA_GK19_ravanavahosu.title: Rāvaṇavaha
SA_GK19_ravanavahosu.author: Pravarasena
SA_GK19_ravanavahosu.summary: The Rāvaṇavaha ('The Slaying of Rāvaṇa', also known as Setubandha) is a celebrated Mahārāṣṭrī Prakrit mahākāvya attributed to Pravarasena. Composed chiefly in the skandhaka metre, the poem recounts the Rāmāyaṇa episode spanning the construction of the causeway across the ocean to Laṅkā up to the slaying of Rāvaṇa. Highly praised by classical Sanskrit literary theorists including Daṇḍin, Bāṇa, and Ānandavardhana, it stands as the preeminent masterwork of Prakrit court epic poetry.
SA_GK19_ravanavahosu.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Pravarasena. Tradition says that the Setubandha was actually composed by Kālidāsa.
SA_GK19_ravanavahosu.edition: Siegfried Goldschmidt (ed.), Râvaṇavaha oder Setubandha, Strassburg: Karl J. Trübner / London: Trübner & Co., 1880.
SA_GK19_ravanavahosu.coverage: complete — Complete text in 15 āśvāsas, concluding with the supplementary stanzas (ityadhikāni skandhakāni).
translations: Siegfried Goldschmidt, Rāvaṇavaha oder Setubandha (Übersetzung), Strassburg / London: Trübner & Co., 1884. (German)

SA_GK21_nalacampuu.title: Nalacampū
SA_GK21_nalacampuu.author: Trivikramabhaṭṭa
SA_GK21_nalacampuu.summary: The Nalacampū (also known as Damayantīkathā), composed by Trivikramabhaṭṭa circa 900 CE / 10th century, is the earliest extant representative of the campū genre in classical Sanskrit literature. Treating the Mahābhārata narrative of Nala and Damayantī, the text survives in seven ucchvāsas ending before Nala's downfall and separation. It is celebrated for its elaborate, highly ornate prose heavily laden with śleṣa (double entendre), yamaka, and alliteration.
SA_GK21_nalacampuu.attribution: Trivikramabhaṭṭa is also known as the composer of inscriptional panegyrics.
SA_GK21_nalacampuu.edition: Nanda Kishore Śarma, The Nalachampū or Damayantīkathā with the Viṣamapada Prakāśa Commentary by Chaṇḍapāla, Benares, The Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series Office, 1932 (Kashi Sanskrit Series No. 98)
SA_GK21_nalacampuu.coverage: complete — Extant in 7 ucchvāsas, concluding with 'saptama ucchvāsaḥ samāptaḥ granthō 'pi ca samāptaḥ'.

SA_GK22_saduktikarnu.title: Saduktikarṇāmṛta
SA_GK22_saduktikarnu.author: Śrīdharadāsa
SA_GK22_saduktikarnu.summary: The Saduktikarṇāmṛta is a Sanskrit anthology compiled by Śrīdharadāsa under King Lakṣmaṇasena of Bengal. It contains 476 vīcis and 2,380 verses with poet attributions.
SA_GK22_saduktikarnu.attribution: Compiled in Śaka 1127 (during the 27th regnal year of King Lakṣmaṇasena of Bengal) by the mahāmāṇḍalika Śrīdharadāsa, son of Baṭudāsa.
SA_GK22_saduktikarnu.edition: Sures Chandra Banerji (ed.), Sadukti-karṇāmṛta of Śrīdharadāsa, Calcutta: Firma K. L. Mukhopadhyaya, 1965.
SA_GK22_saduktikarnu.coverage: complete — Text containing 476 vīcis and 2,380 verses, along with introductory and concluding verses and individual poet attributions.

SA_GK16_sarasvatikau.title: Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa with the commentaries of Ratneśvara and Jagaddhara
SA_GK16_sarasvatikau.author: Bhoja, Ratneśvara, Jagaddhara
SA_GK16_sarasvatikau.summary: The Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa is an encyclopedic treatise on Sanskrit poetics and dramaturgy (Alaṃkāraśāstra) attributed to King Bhoja (11th century). In five exhaustive paricchedas, it systematically classifies poetic flaws (doṣa), excellences (guṇa), verbal figures (śabdālaṃkāra), semantic figures (arthālaṃkāra), and aesthetic experience (rasa), highlighting Bhoja's synthesis of poetic ornament with rasa theory. This digital text transmits the complete work alongside its primary classical commentaries: Ratneśvara's Ratnadarpaṇa on chapters 1–3 and Jagaddhara's gloss on chapters 4–5.
SA_GK16_sarasvatikau.attribution: The root work is attributed to King Bhoja. Ratneśvara composed the Ratnadarpaṇa on paricchedas 1–3 naming Rāmasiṃhadeva. The commentary on paricchedas 4–5 was supplied by Jagaddhara.
SA_GK16_sarasvatikau.edition: Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇam, edited by Paṇḍita Kedāranātha Śarmā, Bombay: Pāṇḍuraṅga Jāvajī, 1934 (Kāvyamālā 94).
SA_GK16_sarasvatikau.coverage: complete — Complete in five paricchedas (chapters 1–5), containing Bhoja's kārikās with prose exposition and illustrative stanzas, accompanied throughout chapters 1–3 by Ratneśvara's Ratnadarpaṇa and chapters 4–5 by Jagaddhara's commentary.

SA_K12_dakinivajrau.title: Ḍākinīvajrapañjaraṭippaṇī and Vasantatilakā with Rahasyadīpikā
SA_K12_dakinivajrau.author: Kṛṣṇācārya, Vanaratna
SA_K12_dakinivajrau.summary: This DSBC e-text combines two Buddhist tantric works: the anonymous Ḍākinīvajrapañjaraṭippaṇī, followed by the Vasantatilakā of Caryāvratin Kṛṣṇācārya embedded in the commentary Rahasyadīpikā by Vanaratna.
SA_K12_dakinivajrau.attribution: The opening Ḍākinīvajrapañjaraṭippaṇī contains no author attribution. The Vasantatilakā is explicitly attributed in the colophon to Caryāvratin Kṛṣṇa / Kṛṣṇācārya. Its commentary is the Rahasyadīpikā of Vanaratna.
SA_K12_dakinivajrau.edition: Vasantatilakā of Caryāvratī Śrīkṛṣṇācārya with Commentary: Rahasyadīpikā by Vanaratna, ed. Samdon Rinpoche and V. Dwivedi, Rare Buddhist Text Series 7, Sarnath: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 1990. Ḍākinīvajrapañjaraṭippaṇī: edited in Dhīḥ 55 (pp. 121–134). (probable)
SA_K12_dakinivajrau.coverage: complete — Ḍākinīvajrapañjaraṭippaṇī: begins with 'praṇamya ḍākinīvajrapañjaraṁ yasya likhyate'. Vasantatilakā with Rahasyadīpikā: includes 'iti vasantatilakā samāptā', 'iti vasantatilakāyāṁ niṣpannakramasādhanopāyikāyāṁ rahasyadīpikāyāṁ ṭīkāyāṁ daśamanirdeśe vistaravyākhyā ||10||', and 'iti vasantatilakaṭīkā samāptā'.

SA_K12_paramadyatau.title: Paramādya (fragments)
SA_K12_paramadyatau.summary: The Paramādya (Śrīparamādya) is a Yogatantra scripture closely related to the Adhyardhaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā (Nayasūtra) and the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha, centred on Vajrasattva and mahāsukha. No complete Sanskrit text has been published; the work survives in Tibetan and, in part, in Chinese. This e-text collects Sanskrit verses of the Paramādya quoted in later works such as the Sarvabuddhasamāyoga, the Trisamayarājatantraṭīkā, Abhayākaragupta's Āmnāyamañjarī and Vajrāvalī, and the Viṃśatividhi.
SA_K12_paramadyatau.attribution: Revealed tantric scripture of the Yogatantra class; traditionally considered the word of the Buddha (Vajrasattva / Tathāgatas).
SA_K12_paramadyatau.coverage: fragment — About 1,030 short lines (ca. 25,600 characters) of verses and some prose attributed to the Paramādya / Mahāsukhavajraguhya, each group followed by the name of the work quoting it: (sarvabuddhasamāyoga), (trisamayarājatantra-ṭīkā), (āmnāyamañjarī), (viṁśatividhi, vajrāvalī), (nayasūtra), etc. Many passages are repeated because they are quoted in several works; variants are given as '(=...)'. Not a continuous text of the tantra.
translations: Chinese: 佛說最上根本大樂金剛不空三昧大教王經, Taishō 244, tr. Faxian (法賢), 1001 CE. (Chinese)
dpal mchog dang po zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i rtog pa'i rgyal po (Derge Kangyur D 487): translated by Śraddhākaravarman, lo chen rin chen bzang po (Tibetan)
dpal mchog dang po'i sngags kyi rtog pa'i dum bu zhes bya ba (Derge Kangyur D 488): translated by Mantrakalaśa, lha zhi ba 'od (Tibetan)

SA_K10_mahapratihau.title: Mahāprātihāryasūtra (fragment)
SA_K10_mahapratihau.summary: A narrative recounting events surrounding the Buddha and rival teachers. Māra takes the form of rival teachers led by Pūraṇa to deceive them with displays of supernatural powers. The teachers resolve to challenge the Buddha to a contest of miracles, approaching King Bimbisāra and King Prasenajit of Kauśala. Preparations begin for the display of miracles, and Gaṇḍaka brings a tree from Mount Gandhamādana, at which point the text breaks off.
SA_K10_mahapratihau.coverage: fragment — Fragmentary text breaking off mid-sentence with '... anekapakṣigaṇ(a)|||'.

SA_T02_hevajrapraku.title: Hevajraprakāśa
SA_T02_hevajrapraku.author: Rāhulagupta
SA_T02_hevajrapraku.summary: A Hevajra sādhana by Rāhulagupta. It draws from Jālandharipāda's Vajrapradīpā on Saroruhapāda's Hevajrasādhana and Bhadrapāda's Dveṣavajrasādhana, combining utpattikrama and utpannakrama practice.
SA_T02_hevajrapraku.attribution: Colophon: 'kṛtir iyaṃ mahāmaṇḍalācāryaśrīrāhulaguptapādānām'. In the Tibetan canon the work is ascribed to Sgra gcan gsaṅ ba (Rāhulagupta; D 1238, tr. Śrīvanaratna and Gzhon nu dpal). In the introduction the author states that he draws together Jālandharipāda's Vajrapradīpā ṭippaṇī on Saroruhapāda's Hevajrasādhana and Bhadrapāda's Dveṣavajrasādhana.
SA_T02_hevajrapraku.coverage: complete — Complete text ending with the colophon 'pañcakramānuttarahevajraprakāśaḥ samāptaḥ', author attribution to Rāhulagupta, ye dharmā verse, and a scribal post-colophon. The e-text opens with an editorial placeholder '[namaskriyā, maṇgalācaraṇa, etc.]'.
translations: Torsten Gerloff, Saroruhavajra's Hevajra-Lineage: A Close Study of the Surviving Sanskrit and Tibetan Works. (English)

dpal kye rdo rje'i sgrub thabs rab tu gsal ba zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 1238): translated by Vanaratna, 'gos lo tsA ba gzhon nu dpal; at phyogs las rnam par rgyal pa'i pho brang chen po sne gdong rtse'i gtsug lag khang (Tibetan)

SA_T16_vajrapradipu.title: Vajrapradīpā
SA_T16_vajrapradipu.author: Suratavajra
SA_T16_vajrapradipu.summary: The Vajrapradīpā (also known as Vajrapradīpā nāma ṭippaṇī or Viśuddhikramaṭippaṇī) is a Vajrayāna commentary composed by Suratavajra (also known by his mahāsiddha epithet Jālandhari/Jālandharipāda) on Saroruhapāda's (Saroruhavajra's) Hevajrasādhana. Adhering to the utpattikrama (generation stage) of the Hevajra cycle, the work systematically explains thirty-two sadhana topics (dvātriṁśatsādhanasūtra), analyzing the purificatory symbolism (viśuddhi) of the mandala deities, the eight cremation grounds (śmaśāna), ritual implements, and seed syllables.
SA_T16_vajrapradipu.attribution: The author calls himself Suratavajra ('kṛtvā suratavajreṇa viśuddhikramaṭippaṇīm') and says he is known as Jālandharī ('mayā jālandharīti khyātena'); the colophon reads 'kṛtir iyaṁ paṇḍitācāryaśrīmatsuratapādānām'. Gerloff calls him Jālandharipāda. DSBC lists Saroruha as author, which is wrong: Saroruha wrote the root sādhana. The Tibetan translation is in the Tengyur (D 1237).
SA_T16_vajrapradipu.coverage: complete — Complete commentary explaining thirty-two sadhana limbs (dvātriṁśatsādhanasūtra), from the opening udghātaḥ to the concluding verses and colophon at segments 361–365.
translations: kye rdo rje'i sgrub thabs kyi mdor bshad pa dag pa rdo rje sgron ma zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 1237): translated by Mañjuśrī, thar pa lo tsA ba nyi ma rgyal mtshan (Tibetan)

SA_T01_srihevajrabu.title: Śrīhevajrabhaṭṭārakasya Cakraviṃśatikāstotra
SA_T01_srihevajrabu.author: Saroruhavajra
SA_T01_srihevajrabu.summary: The Śrīhevajrabhaṭṭārakasya Cakraviṃśatikāstotra is a 20-verse tantric hymn of praise (stotra) composed by the siddha Saroruhavajra honoring the Anuttarayogatantra deity Hevajra and his retinue. The verses systematically praise the eight-faced, sixteen-armed form of Hevajra embracing Nairātmyā (vv. 1–8), followed by individual invocations of the eight yoginīs of his maṇḍala (Gaurī, Caurī, Vetālī, Ghasmarī, Pukkasī, Śabarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombī; vv. 9–16), their collective qualities (vv. 17–19), and a concluding philosophical praise of the nondual deity (v. 20).
SA_T01_srihevajrabu.coverage: complete — Complete stotra consisting of 20 verses praising Hevajra and his mandala retinue, followed by a dedication verse and colophon.

SA_T16_saroruhavaju.title: Hevajrasādhanopāyikā
SA_T16_saroruhavaju.author: Saroruhavajra
SA_T16_saroruhavaju.summary: A sādhana for Hevajra, beginning with worship of Hevajra and Nairātmyā, confession of sins (pāpadeśanā), visualization of deities including Gaurī, Caurī, Nairātmyā, mantra recitation, and concluding dedicatory verses.
SA_T16_saroruhavaju.attribution: Attributed to Saroruhavajra in the DSBC header and to Padmavajra (Tib. dPal dgyes pa rdo rje'i sgrub thabs) in the Tibetan canon (D 1218). The e-text colophon reads: śrīhevajrasādhanopāyikā samāptā.
SA_T16_saroruhavaju.coverage: complete — Text concludes with dedicatory verses and the colophon: śrīhevajrasādhanopāyikā samāptā.

SA_T02_dvesavajrasu.title: Dveṣavajrasādhana
SA_T02_dvesavajrasu.author: Bhadrapāda
SA_T02_dvesavajrasu.summary: A Hevajra sādhana by Bhadrapāda, a later member of the lineage of Saroruhavajra. Following the Hevajratantra and Saroruha's instructions, it teaches the meditation on Hevajra/Heruka with Nairātmyā as 'Dveṣavajra' (the hatred-vajra form). It covers the preliminaries, worship by the eight goddesses (Gaurī, Caurī, etc.), the sevenfold worship and the brahmavihāras, the generation of the maṇḍala, consecration, mantra recitation, bali and subtle yoga, and closes with the assignment of the vajrīs to the senses. The concluding verses name Rāhulapāda among the author's gurus.
SA_T02_dvesavajrasu.attribution: The author calls himself Bhadra, a descendant in the lineage of Saroruhapāda ('saroruhapādanaptṛsutaputreṇa bhadranāmnā'), writing at the request of Kodāli, and names Rāhulapāda among his gurus. The colophon reads 'kṛtir iyaṁ siddhācāryaśrīmadbhadrapādānām'.
SA_T02_dvesavajrasu.coverage: complete — Complete sādhana from the opening homage (upodghāta) to the final colophon.

SA_T02_srihevajrasu.title: Śrīhevajrasādhanavajrapradīpanāmaṭippaṇīviśuddhi
SA_T02_srihevajrasu.author: Suratavajra
SA_T02_srihevajrasu.summary: The Śrīhevajrasādhanavajrapradīpanāmaṭippaṇīviśuddhi (also known as Vajrapradīpā) is a commentary by Suratavajra on the generation-stage (utpattikrama) Hevajrasādhana of Saroruhapāda. It elucidates thirty-two sequential limbs of the practice (dvātriṁśatsādhanasūtra), expounding the maṇḍala, visualization of deities, offerings, mantra recitation, and daily yogic conduct.
SA_T02_srihevajrasu.attribution: Commentary (ṭippaṇī) on Saroruhapāda's Hevajrasādhana. The author calls himself Suratavajra, known as Jālandhari; the colophon names Śrī Suratapāda; the Tibetan canon (D 1237) attributes it to Jalandha ri pa.
SA_T02_srihevajrasu.coverage: complete — Complete: benediction and statement of the 32 sādhanasūtra topics, commentary on all 32 (concluding with utthāna numbered 32), closing verses naming the author, colophon and ye dharmā verse.
translations: kye rdo rje'i sgrub thabs kyi mdor bshad pa dag pa rdo rje sgron ma zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 1237): translated by Mañjuśrī, thar pa lo tsA ba nyi ma rgyal mtshan (Tibetan)

SA_T01_jambhalastou.title: Jambhalastotra
SA_T01_jambhalastou.author: Candragomin
SA_T01_jambhalastou.summary: The Jambhalastotra is a concise nine-verse Sanskrit hymn in praise of Jambhala attributed to Candragomin. The devotee laments his distress and poverty before the compassionate deity and prays that living beings may become like Jambhala in granting desired fruits.
SA_T01_jambhalastou.attribution: Colophon: 'iti candragomiviracitaṁ jambhalastotraṁ samāptam'. Tibetan Tengyur (Tōh. 3748) attributes Ārya-Jambhalastotra to Zla ba (Candragomin).
SA_T01_jambhalastou.edition: Zhen Liu and Johannes Schneider (eds.), Buddhist Hymns: A New Collection, Sanskrit Texts from the Tibetan Autonomous Region (first publication of the Sanskrit text of Jambhalastotra).
SA_T01_jambhalastou.coverage: complete — Nine stanzas with opening 'oṁ namo jambhālāya' and colophon.
translations: Tibetan Tengyur translation (Tōh. 3748, 'Phags pa rmugs 'dzin la bstod pa) by Mutitaśrījñāna and Pa tshab Nyi ma grags. (Tibetan)

SA_T01_desanastavau.title: Deśanāstava
SA_T01_desanastavau.author: Candragomin
SA_T01_desanastavau.summary: The Deśanāstava ('Hymn in the form of a confession') is a 52-verse Mahāyāna hymn ascribed in its colophon to Candragomin. Hahn regards it as a genuine work of Candragomin, the author of the Lokānanda and Śiṣyalekha.
SA_T01_desanastavau.attribution: Colophon: 'kṛtir iyaṃ candragomipādānām'. Hahn counts the Deśanāstava, with the Lokānandanāṭaka and Śiṣyalekha, among the works safely attributable to Candragomin the poet and grammarian.
SA_T01_desanastavau.coverage: complete — Complete: 52 verses with 'namo buddhāya', the colophon 'deśanāstavaḥ samāptaḥ' and 'kṛtir iyaṃ candragomipādānām iti'.
translations: Mark Tatz, Difficult Beginnings: Three Works on the Bodhisattva Path by Candragomin, Boston: Shambhala, 1985 (from the Tibetan). (English)

SA_T01_devatisayasu.title: Devātiśayastotra
SA_T01_devatisayasu.author: Varāhasvāmin
SA_T01_devatisayasu.summary: A hymn of 21 stanzas arguing for the Buddha's superiority over Brahmanical gods such as Viṣṇu, Rudra/Śiva, and Skanda, contrasting their weapons, passions, and violent acts with the Buddha's peacefulness and compassion. It was translated into Tibetan together with Prajñāvarman's commentary.
SA_T01_devatisayasu.attribution: Colophon reads: 'kṛtir iyam ācāryabhaṭṭavarāhasvāminaḥ'. In the Tibetan Tanjur (Toh. 1112), the work is attributed to bDe byed bdag po (Śaṃkarasvāmin).
translations: Johannes Schneider, Eine buddhistische Kritik der indischen Götter: Śaṃkarasvāmins Devātiśayastotra mit Prajñāvarmans Kommentar. Nach dem tibetischen Tanjur herausgegeben und übersetzt. Wiener Studien zur Tibetologie und Buddhismuskunde 81, Wien: Arbeitskreis für Tibetische und Buddhistische Studien, 2014. (German)

SA_T16_prasadapratu.title: Prasādapratibhodbhava (verses 52–57, fragment)
SA_T16_prasadapratu.author: Mātṛceṭa
SA_T16_prasadapratu.summary: A short fragment of Mātṛceṭa's Śatapañcāśatka (Prasādapratibhodbhava), the Buddhist hymn in about 150 verses to the Buddha. The verses preserved here (52–57) praise the Buddha's bodily beauty and virtues.
SA_T16_prasadapratu.edition: D. R. Shackleton Bailey (ed.), The Śatapañcāśatka of Mātṛceṭa: Sanskrit text, Tibetan translation & commentary, and Chinese translation, Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1951 (vv. 52–57) (probable)
SA_T16_prasadapratu.coverage: fragment — Begins with heading 'prasādapratibhodbhava' followed by verse 52cd ('bhṛtaṁ corjitaṁ cedaṁ rūpaṁ kam iva nākṣipet||52||') and ends after pāda 57c with '...... ||57||'. This corresponds to vv. 52–57 of the hymn.
translations: D. R. Shackleton Bailey, The Śatapañcāśatka of Mātṛceṭa, Cambridge 1951 (English translation). (English)

SA_T01_visesastavau.title: Viśeṣastava
