SA_T01_visesastavau.author: Udbhaṭasiddhasvāmin
SA_T01_visesastavau.summary: The Viśeṣastava is a hymn praising the Buddha by contrasting his virtues and teachings with non-Buddhist figures and schools (such as Hari, Rudra, Kapila). In Tibet it was transmitted along with Prajñāvarman's commentary.
SA_T01_visesastavau.attribution: The colophon of the e-text reads 'bhaṭṭarādhasvāminaḥ'. Tibetan catalogues attribute the text to Mtho-btsun grub-rje (Udbhaṭasiddhasvāmin).
SA_T01_visesastavau.coverage: complete — Text preserved in 78 stanzas with verse numbering including double numbering in square brackets, ending with colophon 'viśeṣastavaḥ samāptaḥ || bhaṭṭarādhasvāminaḥ ||'.

SA_T01_suprabhatasu.title: Suprabhātastava
SA_T01_suprabhatasu.author: Harṣadeva
SA_T01_suprabhatasu.summary: The Suprabhātastava ('Praise of the Auspicious Dawn') is a Buddhist hymn, mostly in mālinī, in which the poet contrasts the ever-awake Buddha with Hindu gods and sages (Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Indra, Agni, Balarāma, Gaṇeśa, Kumāra, the ṛṣis), all shown as asleep in passion, under the refrain 'daśabala tava nityaṃ suprabhātaṃ prabhātam'. The colophon ascribes it to King Śrīharṣa. This e-text has 25 stanzas.
SA_T01_suprabhatasu.attribution: Colophon ascribes it to King Śrīharṣa ('kṛtir iyaṁ rājñaḥ śrīharṣasya').
SA_T01_suprabhatasu.edition: Zhen Liu and Johannes Schneider (eds.), Buddhist Hymns: A New Collection, section 3.6 Suprabhātastava.
SA_T01_suprabhatasu.coverage: complete — Complete in 25 stanzas, with title and author colophon. Bracketed numbers give the stanza numbers of an earlier edition.

SA_K12_srisarvabudu.title: Sarvabuddhasamāyogaḍākinījālaśaṃvara (chapters 1–9, incomplete)
SA_K12_srisarvabudu.summary: A Buddhist tantric text centred on Vajrasattva and the 'magic of women' (strīmāyā), treating mudrās, maṇḍalas, and yoga. This DSBC e-text breaks off after verse 161 following the mahāsamayamudrājñāna section.
SA_K12_srisarvabudu.attribution: Revealed Buddhist tantric scripture; translated into Tibetan in the Kangyur (Tōhoku 366).
SA_K12_srisarvabudu.coverage: partial — The e-text ends after mahāsamayamudrājñānam (verse 161) without colophon.
translations: dpal sangs rgyas thams cad dang mnyam par sbyor ba mkha' 'gro ma sgyu ma bde ba'i mchog ces bya ba'i rgyud bla ma (Derge Kangyur D 366): translated by Lha rin-po-che (Tibetan)

SA_T04_mulamadhyamu.title: Mūlamadhyamakakārikā
SA_T04_mulamadhyamu.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T04_mulamadhyamu.summary: The Mūlamadhyamakakārikā ('Root Verses on the Middle Way') is the foundational treatise composed by Nāgārjuna. Across 27 chapters, it examines and deconstructs core metaphysical categories and conceptual frameworks—including causation, motion, sense faculties, the skandhas, the self, time, suffering, defilements, the four noble truths, and nirvāṇa. Nāgārjuna demonstrates that all phenomena are empty (śūnya) of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) precisely because they are dependently originated (pratītyasamutpanna), establishing emptiness as the middle way between the ontological extremes of substantialism and nihilism.
SA_T04_mulamadhyamu.edition: J.W. de Jong (ed.), Nāgārjuna's Mūlamadhyamakakārikā Prajñā Nāma. Madras: Adyar Library and Research Centre, 1977.
SA_T04_mulamadhyamu.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 27 chapters (including the initial two mangala verses and final dedicatory verse to Gautama Buddha).
translations: Mark Siderits and Shōryū Katsura, Nāgārjuna's Middle Way: The Mūlamadhyamakakārikā, Boston: Wisdom Publications, 2013. (English)

SA_T16_adikarmavatu.title: Ādikarmāvatāra
SA_T16_adikarmavatu.author: Mañjukīrti
SA_T16_adikarmavatu.summary: The Ādikarmāvatāra is a Mahāyāna Buddhist ritual and daily practice manual intended for novice practitioners (ādikarmika). It delineates fundamental daily observances including taking refuge in the Three Jewels, moral confession (pāpadeśanā), generating bodhicitta, receiving the upāsaka precepts, cleaning and arranging the shrine, offering maṇḍalas and flowers, reciting dhāraṇīs, and honouring the spiritual teacher (guru). The work consists of instructional prose interspersed with 81 mnemonic verses and sūtra citations.
SA_T16_adikarmavatu.attribution: Ascribed to Paṇḍita Sthavira Mañjukīrti in the incipit and the colophon ('kṛtiriyaṁ paṇḍitasthaviramañjukīrtipādānām').
SA_T16_adikarmavatu.coverage: complete — Complete. Prose with 81 numbered verses, ending 'ādikarmāvatāraḥ samāptaḥ', followed by closing verses, the grantha count (śata 5) and the author colophon.

SA_T01_nairatmyayau.title: Nairātmyāśīḥstuti
SA_T01_nairatmyayau.summary: The Nairātmyāśīḥstuti is a seven-verse Buddhist tantric benedictory hymn celebrating the goddess Nairātmyā, the principal consort in the Hevajratantra cycle. The verses praise her terrifying dancing form adorned with bone ornaments, carrying the kartrī and kapāla, and invoke her blessing to eliminate mental afflictions and worldly evils. The concluding verse identifies her with the internal yogic subtle body, specifically the synthesis of the three channels lalanā, rasanā, and avadhūtikā.
SA_T01_nairatmyayau.coverage: complete — Complete in 7 verses, concluding with the closing colophon: samāpteyaṁ nairātmyāyā bhagavatyā āśī(śīḥ)stutiḥ.

SA_T01_srihevajrasu.title: Śrīhevajrasya Guṇasragdharānāmastuti
SA_T01_srihevajrasu.author: Śūnyasamādhivajra
SA_T01_srihevajrasu.summary: A hymn of 34 stanzas in sragdharā metre to Hevajra by the mahāpaṇḍita Śūnyasamādhivajra. It praises Hevajra's terrifying and compassionate aspects and identifies him with the five gnoses (e.g. ādarśajñāna as Vairocana, samatājñāna as Ratnarāja/Ratnasambhava, pratyavekṣaṇājñāna as Vāgīśa) and the buddha bodies, and ends with a dedication of merit.
SA_T01_srihevajrasu.coverage: complete — Complete in 34 sragdharā stanzas, with the author rubric at the start and the final colophon.

SA_T02_sahajadvibhu.title: Sahajadvibhujahevajrasādhana
SA_T02_sahajadvibhu.author: Alalavajra
SA_T02_sahajadvibhu.summary: The Sahajadvibhujahevajrasādhana is a Tantric liturgical ritual work (sādhana) dedicated to the two-armed (dvibhuja) innate (sahaja) form of Hevajra. Authored by Alalavajra on the instruction of Nandipāda, the 74-verse text articulates the non-dual philosophy of sahaja mind, standard preparatory elements including the generation of bodhicitta and refuge, emptiness meditation, and the sequential visualization of two-armed Hevajra and his retinue.
SA_T02_sahajadvibhu.attribution: The text names Ācārya Alalavajra (Alalavajrapāda) in both initial and final rubrics, and verse 72 states that the author composed it on the command of Nandipāda (nandipādājñayā svalpaṃ likhitaṃ siddhasādhanam).
SA_T02_sahajadvibhu.coverage: complete — Complete text of 74 numbered verses with title rubric, final colophon 'iti sahajadvibhujahevajrasādhanaṃ samāptam' and author colophon.
translations: kye rdo rje phyag gnyis pa'i sgrub thabs (Derge Tengyur D 1235) (Tibetan)

SA_T02_buddhadipuju.title: Buddhādipūjāvidhi (incomplete: Buddha worship and beginning of Khasarpaṇa worship)
SA_T02_buddhadipuju.summary: An anonymous Sanskrit manual (pūjākrama) for the daily worship of the Buddha and of the deities named in the opening verse: Lokeśa, Vāgīśa (Mañjuśrī) and Tāriṇī. The surviving part covers the morning observances and bath mantras, the preparation and consecration of the maṇḍalaka, and the visualisation of the Pañcatathāgatas with their consorts on Sumeru and the four continents, with mantras, offerings and praise. It then gives the arghya and pādya offerings with the iconography of the eight great Bodhisattvas, and breaks off at the beginning of the worship of Khasarpaṇa Avalokiteśvara.
SA_T02_buddhadipuju.coverage: partial — Opening verse 1: 'buddhaṃ praṇamya lokeśaṃ vāgīśaṃ tāriṇīm api / teṣāṃ pūjākramaṃ brūmo yathāmnāyaṃ samāsataḥ'. The e-text gives the daily preliminaries, the maṇḍalaka of the Pañcatathāgatas and their consorts, the pūjā and mantras (verses 1–35), 'buddhamaṇḍalaṃ samāptam', and the arghya/pādya offerings with the iconography of the eight Bodhisattvas. It then begins 'atha śrīmatkhasarpaṇabhaṭṭārakapūjā…' and breaks off mid-sentence ('pūrve pūrvavidehe vairocanam | dakṣiṇe'). The sections on Lokeśa/Khasarpaṇa (most of it), Vāgīśa (Mañjuśrī) and Tārā are missing.

SA_T16_adikarmavat2u.title: Ādikarmāvatārapratibaddha
SA_T16_adikarmavat2u.author: Mañjukīrti
SA_T16_adikarmavat2u.summary: A short supplement to the Ādikarmāvatāra, a manual for Buddhist beginners (ādikarmika). Opening with a salutation to Tārā, it explains how a spiritual friend should lead disciples of inferior, middling and superior capacity to refuge and bodhicitta. It cites instructions for the householder bodhisattva from the Ugraparipṛcchā and prescribes the refuge ritual, maṇḍala offerings and pūjā before an image of Śākyamuni. It closes with dedication verses, a prayer for the Teaching's long endurance and a meditation on benevolence (maitrīvihāra) with its dhāraṇī.
SA_T16_adikarmavat2u.attribution: The text itself names no author.
SA_T16_adikarmavat2u.coverage: complete — Prose with 50 numbered verses, from the opening 'bhagavati tāre namastubhyam' to the closing line 'maitrīvihāraḥ || etad apy ādikarmāvatārapratibaddham iti' and the grantha count.

SA_T11_sambandhapau.title: Sambandhaparīkṣā with Sambandhaparīkṣāvṛtti
SA_T11_sambandhapau.author: Dharmakīrti, Devendrabuddhi
SA_T11_sambandhapau.summary: Dharmakīrti's Sambandhaparīkṣā argues that relations are not real entities but conceptual constructions. This e-text gives the prose Vṛtti on the verses, ending with the colophon ascribing it to Devendrabuddhi ('kṛtir ācāryadevendrabuddheḥ').
SA_T11_sambandhapau.attribution: Root kārikās by Dharmakīrti. The Vṛtti was transmitted in Tibetan (Toh 4215 / D 4215) under Dharmakīrti, but the Sanskrit colophon names Devendrabuddhi ('kṛtir ācāryadevendrabuddheḥ'). The Tibetan translation (D 4215) attributes the work to Dharmakīrti I (smra ba'i seng ge slob dpon chen po chos kyi grags pa).
SA_T11_sambandhapau.coverage: complete — Prose Vṛtti with kārikās, ending with the colophon 'sambandhaparīkṣāvṛttiḥ samāptā| kṛtir ācāryadevendrabuddheḥ| krauddha-anvitasya pustakam|'.
translations: brel pa brtag pa'i 'grel pa (Derge Tengyur D 4215) (Tibetan)

SA_T16_yogasatakamu.title: Yogaśataka
SA_T16_yogasatakamu.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T16_yogasatakamu.summary: The Yogaśataka is a short medical work of 109 stanzas attributed to Nāgārjuna, opening with treatments for fevers and other ailments.
SA_T16_yogasatakamu.attribution: Ascribed to Nāgārjuna; the e-text's colophon reads 'kṛtir ācāryaśrīnāgārjunapādānām'. Manuscripts also witness ascription to Vararuci.
SA_T16_yogasatakamu.coverage: complete — Complete text in 109 verses with opening invocations and final colophon.
translations: Jean Filliozat, tr., Yogaśataka: texte médical attribué à Nāgārjuna, Publications de l'Institut Français d'Indologie 62, Pondichéry: Institut Français d'Indologie, 1979. (French)

SA_T02_nispannakrau.title: Vajrācāryanayottama (Niṣpannakrama)
SA_T02_nispannakrau.author: Rāhulagupta
SA_T02_nispannakrau.summary: The Vajrācāryanayottama is an Anuttarayoga Tantra manual composed by Rāhulagupta. This preserved section focuses on the completion stage (niṣpannakrama) in the Guhyasamāja lineage, expounding the three isolations (kāyaviveka, vāgviveka, cittaviveka), subtle breath yoga, the dissolution of psychophysical constituents into the voids, and the attainment of the clear light (prabhāsvara).
SA_T02_nispannakrau.coverage: partial — Contains the completion stage (niṣpannakrama) section of the work, concluding with the closing verse and colophon. The generation stage (utpattikrama) alluded to in line 1 ('pūrvvoktāni rakṣādīni') is not present in this transcript.

SA_T16_bhavanayogau.title: Catuṣpariṣatsūtra (fragment: §§ 0.1–0.11)
SA_T16_bhavanayogau.summary: The opening of the Catuṣpariṣatsūtra, in a fragmentary manuscript-line text with restorations. The Bodhisattva sits under the bodhi tree on the bank of the Nairañjanā at Uruvilvā, devoted to the cultivation of the factors of awakening. In the first watch of the night he experiences the supernormal powers (ṛddhiviṣaya) and recollects his former lives, and in the middle watch he attains the divine ear. The text breaks off there.
SA_T16_bhavanayogau.attribution: The same passage appears in the Saṅghabhedavastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya (Gnoli 1977, Part I).
SA_T16_bhavanayogau.coverage: fragment — Only §§ 0.1–0.11: the Bodhisattva at Uruvilvā in the first watch (ṛddhiviṣaya, pūrvanivāsānusmṛti) and the start of the middle watch (divyaśrotra). It breaks off before the divine eye, the knowledge of others' minds and the destruction of the āsravas. The layout keeps the manuscript lines with restorations in parentheses.
translations: Ria Kloppenborg, The Sūtra on the Foundation of the Buddhist Order (Catuṣpariṣatsūtra), Leiden: Brill, 1973.

SA_T04_alokamalanau.title: Ālokamālā
SA_T04_alokamalanau.author: Kambala
SA_T04_alokamalanau.summary: The Ālokamālā is a philosophical treatise in 281 verses composed by Kambala. It articulates Mahāyāna philosophy by harmonizing Yogācāra doctrine (the three natures and cittamātra) with Madhyamaka emptiness (śūnyatā), concluding that the ultimate nature of mind and all phenomena transcends conceptual duality.
SA_T04_alokamalanau.attribution: Attributed in the Tibetan Tengyur (D 3895) to Kampala (Kambala).
SA_T04_alokamalanau.edition: Christian Lindtner, 'Kambala’s Ālokamālā', in Miscellanea Buddhica, Indiske Studier 5, Copenhagen: Akademisk Forlag, 1985, pp. 109–220.
translations: snang ba'i phreng ba zhes bya ba'i rab tu byed pa (Derge Tengyur D 3895): translated by Kumārakalaśa, 'bro seng dkar shAkya 'od (Tibetan)

SA_T16_buddhodayaku.title: Buddhodayakāvya
SA_T16_buddhodayaku.author: Śāntibhikṣu Śāstrī
SA_T16_buddhodayaku.summary: Buddhodaya is a modern Sanskrit kāvya by Śāntibhikṣu Śāstrī, completed in Buddha era 2514 while he taught at Vidyālaṅkāra University. It celebrates the life of Śākyamuni, from the Bodhisattva's vow before Dīpaṃkara to his awakening and teaching. Classical metres alternate with song-like (geya) stanzas that have refrains.
SA_T16_buddhodayaku.attribution: Śāntibhikṣu Śāstrī came from Bībīpur near Lucknow (Kosala), held a Leipzig doctorate and was professor (mahācārya) of Sanskrit at Vidyālaṅkāra University. The colophon dates the work gata-buddhābdāḥ 2514.
SA_T16_buddhodayaku.coverage: complete — Cantos (prasaṅga) closed by 'iti śāntibhikṣuśāstriviracite śrībuddhodayakāvye' colophons. The text ends with the author's praśasti, the date (Buddha era 2514) and two copies of the ye dharmā verse.

SA_T01_prahanapurau.title: Prahāṇapūrakaśatavandanānāmamahāyānasūtra
SA_T01_prahanapurau.summary: The Prahāṇapūrakaśatavandanānāma Mahāyānasūtra (Tibetan: Dpang skong phyag brgya pa, D 267) is a Mahāyāna liturgical text consisting of homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions and various Buddha realms, followed by ritual verses on bodhicitta generation, confession of faults, rejoicing in merit (anumodanā), and praṇidhāna aspirations. In Tibetan tradition, it is celebrated as having appeared during the reign of King Lha Thothori Nyantsen.
SA_T01_prahanapurau.attribution: Corresponds to the Tibetan Kangyur text Dpang skong phyag brgya pa (D 267). No Indian Sanskrit original is known; the Sanskrit here is a modern back-translation from Tibetan.
SA_T01_prahanapurau.coverage: complete — Complete text ending with the colophon 'prahāṇapūrakaśatavandanānāma mahāyānasūtraṁ samāptam', followed by an explanatory note on the Tibetan legend that the text fell from the sky in the time of King Thothori Nyentsen.

SA_T16_prajnahrdayu.title: Prajñāhṛdayavyākhyā
SA_T16_prajnahrdayu.author: Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna
SA_T16_prajnahrdayu.summary: A short commentary on the Heart Sūtra (Prajñāpāramitāhṛdaya) attributed to Atīśa Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna, composed in Tibet at the request of a monk Sādhuprajña (per the closing verses). It frames the sūtra with Dignāga's account of the sūtra introduction (citing Prajñāpāramitāpiṇḍārtha 3–4) and Vimalamitra's eightfold exegesis, and reads the sūtra as teaching the five paths, the eight profound points and, for those of sharp faculties, the mantra. The Sanskrit text here is a modern restoration from the Tibetan translation.
SA_T16_prajnahrdayu.attribution: Attributed to Atīśa Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna; the work survives in Tibetan in the Tengyur (Śes-rab sñiṅ-poḥi rnam-par bśad-pa, Toh 3823), translated by Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna and Tshul khrims rgyal ba (rendered 'bhikṣu Śīlajina'). The Sanskrit e-text is a modern restoration from the Tibetan, not an original Sanskrit transmission.
SA_T16_prajnahrdayu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the commentary, ending with the author's final verses and the translators' colophon.

SA_T16_upasakasamvu.title: Upāsakasaṃvarāṣṭakavivaraṇa
SA_T16_upasakasamvu.author: Sunayaśrī
SA_T16_upasakasamvu.summary: The Upāsakasaṃvarāṣṭakavivaraṇa (also referenced as Upāsakasaṃvarāṣṭakapadavṛtti) by Sunayaśrī is an expository treatise commenting on the lay discipline (upāsakasaṃvara). It treats the three classes of individuals, the ritual formulas for taking the three refuges, the observance of the five lay precepts, conditions leading to transgression, and the method of confessing offenses.
SA_T16_upasakasamvu.attribution: The Sanskrit colophon reads 'ācāryasunayaśrīviracitopāsakasaṁvarāṣṭakavivaraṇaṁ samāptam', and the closing verse calls the work 'matprakāśitopāsakasaṁvarāṣṭakapadavṛtti'. This suggests that the author also wrote the eight-verse root text. Sunayaśrī is also credited as translator of the Tibetan version.
SA_T16_upasakasamvu.coverage: complete — Complete commentary running from opening salutation through concluding verse and colophon.
translations: dge bsnyen gyi sdom pa brgyad pa (Derge Tengyur D 4141): translated by Sunayaśrīmitra, gnyan lo tsA ba dar ma grags (Tibetan)
dge bsnyen gyi sdom pa brgyad pa'i bshad pa (Derge Tengyur D 4142): translated by Sunayaśrīmitra, gnyan lo tsA ba dar ma grags (Tibetan)

SA_T01_dharmadhatuu.title: Dharmadhātudarśanagīti
SA_T01_dharmadhatuu.author: Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna
SA_T01_dharmadhatuu.summary: A verse treatise (147 stanzas) attributed to Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna (Atiśa) on the vision of the dharmadhātu, preserved only in Tibetan and here given in a modern Sanskrit restoration. It explains the dharmadhātu with tathāgatagarbha-type similes (butter in milk, lamp in a pot, gem in rock, grain in husk) as obscured by defilements, presents the Madhyamaka two truths, and reviews Buddhist and non-Buddhist doctrinal positions (Sāṃkhya etc.), ending with a defence of the Mahāyāna.
SA_T01_dharmadhatuu.attribution: The colophon translates the Tibetan colophon: composed by Mahācārya Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna and translated by him with the bhikṣu Tshul khrims rgyal ba ('chulaṭhim gyala-vā (śīlavijeyana)'). The Sanskrit original is lost; the e-text is a modern Sanskrit restoration from the Tibetan. The Tibetan translation (D 2314) attributes the work to 'di paM ka ra (identified as Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna or Dīpaṃkararakṣita or *Adhīśa).
SA_T01_dharmadhatuu.coverage: complete — 147 numbered verses with the (restored) translators' colophon; corresponds to the whole Tibetan text.
translations: chos kyi dbyings lta ba'i glu (Derge Tengyur D 2314): translated by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna, nag 'tsho lo tsA ba tshul khrims rgyal ba (Tibetan)

SA_T16_kalacakragau.title: Kālacakragaṇitopadeśa
SA_T16_kalacakragau.summary: The Kālacakragaṇitopadeśa is an astronomical handbook affiliated with the Buddhist Kālacakratantra tradition. Beginning with calculations based on the epoch date Śakābda 1091 (1169 CE), it provides practical computational procedures for the sexagenary cycle (ṣaṣṭisaṁvatsara), intercalary months (adhikamāsa), lunar days, and planetary equations (manda- and śīghra-karma for Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, and Ketu).
SA_T16_kalacakragau.attribution: Anonymous manual of Kālacakra calendrical astronomy. The opening worked example uses the epoch Śaka 1091 (= 1169 CE; 'mlecchavarṣa [540]', 'śuddhavarṣa 364'), so the work probably dates from about that time, though the example year may just be the author's present.
SA_T16_kalacakragau.coverage: complete — Folio markers run from [1B] to [16A]. The text begins with the maṅgala and ends with the treatment of Ketu. The final colophon '[ iti kālacakragaṇitopadeśaḥ samāptaḥ | ]' is in square brackets, which this e-text uses for restored or damaged text, so the end of the manuscript is damaged. The content appears complete.

SA_K10_alavakasuttu.title: Ālavakasūtra
SA_K10_alavakasuttu.summary: A modern Sanskrit word-for-word rendering of the Pali Āḷavakasutta, signed Vidhuśekhara Śarmā. In it the yakṣa Āḷavaka repeatedly orders the Buddha out of and back into his dwelling. He then threatens him and asks in verse what is a man's best wealth and how one crosses the flood. The Buddha answers with faith, Dharma, truth, heedfulness, energy and wisdom, and Āḷavaka is converted. The e-text was taken from a Sanskrit periodical and includes parts of the neighbouring non-Buddhist articles.
SA_K10_alavakasuttu.attribution: A modern Sanskrit rendering 'mūlapālibhāṣātaḥ pratyakṣarānuvādarūpam' of the Pali Āḷavakasutta, signed 'vidhuśekharaśarmā'. Footnote numbers (1)–(4) from the printed source survive in the text.
SA_K10_alavakasuttu.coverage: complete — The sūtra itself is complete, ending 'iti ālavakasūtram | vidhuśekharaśarmā |'. The e-text also includes the end of a preceding periodical article ('Chatracaryā', signed Padmanābhaśāstrī, Trivandrum, praising Kerala Varma and Śrīmūlaka Mahārāja) and the beginning of a following article on the Sahara.

SA_T02_abhisekavidu.title: Abhiṣekavidhi
SA_T02_abhisekavidu.summary: An anonymous Vajrayāna ritual manual prescribing the procedure for conferring initiation (abhiṣeka) upon disciples entering the maṇḍala. It details preliminary rites—including refuge-taking, bodhicittotpāda, vow-taking (saṁvara), tooth-stick casting (dantakāṣṭhapātana), and protection rites—followed by sequential initiations including the flask, garland (mālā), crown (paṭṭa), vajra, bell (ghaṇṭā), mudrā, secret initiation (guhyābhiṣeka), and wisdom-knowledge initiation (prajñājñānābhiṣeka).
SA_T02_abhisekavidu.attribution: Anonymous Vajrayāna initiation manual (33 numbered sections). The extant text gives no author.
SA_T02_abhisekavidu.edition: Abhiṣeka-vidhiḥ, ed. Geshe Ngawang Samten, Kameshwar Nath Mishra, Rare Buddhist Texts Research Department, Central University of Tibetan Studies.
SA_T02_abhisekavidu.coverage: complete — Complete ritual text in 33 numbered sections, ending with '|| iti abhiṣekavidhiḥ samāptaḥ ||'.

SA_T16_madhyamakavu.title: Madhyamakāvatāra with Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya (chapters 1–5)
SA_T16_madhyamakavu.author: Candrakīrti
SA_T16_madhyamakavu.summary: The Madhyamakāvatāra ('Entrance to the Middle Way') along with its autocommentary (Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya) is Candrakīrti's systematic introduction to Nāgārjuna's Mūlamadhyamakakārikā. It integrates Madhyamaka philosophy into the Mahāyāna path structure of the ten bodhisattva stages (daśabhūmi) and perfections (pāramitā). This e-text preserves the Sanskrit text of chapters 1 through 5, covering the bodhisattva stages of joy (Pramuditā), purity (Vimalā), luminosity (Prabhākarī), radiance (Arciṣmatī), and invincibility (Sudurjayā).
SA_T16_madhyamakavu.attribution: Candrakīrti composed the Madhyamakāvatāra and its autocommentary as an introduction to Nāgārjuna's Treatise on the Middle Way.
SA_T16_madhyamakavu.edition: Lasic, Horst, Xuezhu Li, and Anne MacDonald, eds. Candrakīrti's Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya Chapters 1 to 5. Beijing and Vienna: China Tibetology Publishing House and Austrian Academy of Sciences Press, 2022.
SA_T16_madhyamakavu.coverage: partial — Contains chapters 1 to 5 (cittotpādas 1–5), breaking off at the end of chapter 5 ('madhyamakāvatāre sudurjayākhyaḥ pañcamaścittotpādaḥ').
translations: Helmut Tauscher, Candrakīrti: Madhyamakāvatāraḥ und Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣyam (Kapitel VI, Vers 166–226). Wien, 1981. (German)

dbu ma la 'jug pa'i bshad pa zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 3862): translated by Tilakakalaśa, pa tshab lo tsA ba nyi ma grags pa; revised by Kanakavarman; at kha che'i yul gyi grong khyer dpe med kyi dbus rin chen sbas pa'i gtsug lag khang (Tibetan)

SA_K14_mahavastuavu.title: Mahāvastvavadāna (volume 2)
SA_K14_mahavastuavu.summary: The Mahāvastu (or Mahāvastvavadāna) is an extensive canonical biography of the Buddha preserved in Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit, representing the Vinayapiṭaka tradition of the Lokottaravāda branch of the Mahāsāṅghika school. It frames the life of Śākyamuni Buddha within a cosmic perspective of past buddhas and numerous rebirth stories (jātakas and avadānas), reflecting early Lokottaravāda docetism. Volume 2 details the Bodhisattva's final rebirth from his descent from the Tuṣita heaven, conception, birth, princely life, and great renunciation through the attainment of awakening, interspersed with major narratives including the Śyāmajātaka and Kuśajātaka.
SA_K14_mahavastuavu.attribution: Traditional Vinaya text preserved by the Lokottaravādin school of the Mahāsāṅghika tradition.
SA_K14_mahavastuavu.edition: Par E. Senart, A L'imprimerie Nationale
SA_K14_mahavastuavu.coverage: partial — Contains volume 2 of the text, beginning with the Bodhisattva's descent from Tuṣita heaven ('atha bodhisattvo tuṣitabhavanāto cyavanakālasamaye...').
translations: J. J. Jones (trans.), The Mahāvastu: Translated from the Buddhist Sanskrit, London: Luzac & Co. / Sacred Books of the Buddhists. (English)

SA_T01_pratityasamu.title: Pratītyasamutpādastutisubhāṣitahṛdayam
SA_T01_pratityasamu.author: Tsongkhapa
SA_T01_pratityasamu.summary: The Pratītyasamutpādastutisubhāṣitahṛdaya (Tibetan: rTen 'brel bstod pa legs bshad snying po) is a 58-verse hymn of praise to the Buddha composed by the Tibetan master Tsongkhapa. It extols the Buddha for his profound realization and teaching of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) as the middle way between substantialism and nihilism. The present Sanskrit e-text is a 20th-century back-translation and restoration from the Tibetan produced at CIHTS, Sarnath.
SA_T01_pratityasamu.attribution: Originally composed in Tibetan by Tsongkhapa. The Sanskrit e-text represents a modern back-translation / reconstruction from the Tibetan text executed by Ācārya Gyaltsen Namdol and Ācārya Ngawang Samten.
SA_T01_pratityasamu.edition: Gyaltsen Namdol and Ngawang Samten (eds. and trans.), Pratītyasamutpādastutisubhāṣitahṛdayam of Ācārya Tsongkhapa, Sarnath, Varanasi: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies (CIHTS), 1982 (Dalai Lama's Tibeto-Indological Series, vol. 3).
SA_T01_pratityasamu.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all 58 verses and the colophon.
translations: Robert A. F. Thurman, Life and Teachings of Tsong Khapa, Dharamsala: Library of Tibetan Works and Archives, 1982. (English)

SA_GK22_chappannayau.title: Chappaṇṇayagāhāo
SA_GK22_chappannayau.author: Chappaṇṇaya
SA_GK22_chappannayau.summary: The Chappaṇṇayagāhāo is an anthology of 164 Prakrit didactic and gnomic stanzas (subhāṣita) composed in the gāhā (āryā) metre. Commencing with salutations to Jina Mahāvīra, the work imparts practical ethics, reflections on fate and karma, righteous conduct, the qualities of true friends and noble people (sujana), and worldly wisdom. It forms an integral part of the classical Jain tradition of sententious gnomic literature.
SA_GK22_chappannayau.edition: Hermann Jacobi, Chappaṇṇayagāhāō, Second revised edition by Muni Shri Punyavijayaji, Translated into Hindi by Shan[...], Prakrit Text Society, 2020.
SA_GK22_chappannayau.coverage: complete — Complete collection of 164 Prakrit gāhās (verses numbered Chapp.1 through Chapp.164).

SA_GS25_paiyalacchiu.title: Pāiyalacchīnāmamālā
SA_GS25_paiyalacchiu.author: Dhanapāla
SA_GS25_paiyalacchiu.summary: The Pāiyalacchīnāmamālā ('Garland of Names of the Prakrit Fortune') is a Prakrit synonym lexicon (koṣa) composed in 279 Āryā/Gāhā stanzas by the Jain poet Dhanapāla. As explicitly stated in verses 276–277, it was composed at Dhārā in Vikrama Samvat 1029 (972/973 CE) shortly after the sack of the Rāṣṭrakūṭa capital Mānyakheṭa by the Paramāra king Sīyaka II (Harṣa), as an instructional work for his sister Sundarī. It serves as one of the earliest extant Prakrit lexica, organizing synonyms (including deśī and tadbhava terms) to assist poets and readers of Prakrit kāvya.
SA_GS25_paiyalacchiu.attribution: Authored by the Jain poet Dhanapāla for his younger sister Sundarī. The author's name is confirmed by an acrostic/syllabic riddle in v. 278 (the final syllables of andha, jaṇa, kivā, kusala give dha-ṇa-pā-la).
SA_GS25_paiyalacchiu.edition: Georg Bühler, The Pâiyalachchhî Nâmamâlâ: A Prakrit Kosha by Dhanapâla, Göttingen: Robert Peppmüller, 1879.
SA_GS25_paiyalacchiu.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising all 279 gāthās, followed by the concluding formula.

SA_GR12_surasumdariu.title: Surasundarīcariya
SA_GR12_surasumdariu.author: Dhaneśvara
SA_GR12_surasumdariu.summary: The Surasundarīcariya (Surasundarīkahā) is an extensive Jaina Mahārāṣṭrī Prakrit narrative poem (kathā / caritra) in verse composed by Dhaneśvara Muni in 1038 CE (Vikrama Saṃvat 1095) in Candrāvatī. Extending across 16 chapters (paricchedas) and approximately 4,000 verses, the work recounts the romantic and karmic fortunes, separations, and eventual spiritual renunciation of Prince Amaradeva and Princess Surasundarī.
SA_GR12_surasumdariu.attribution: Composed by Dhaneśvara Muni in Caḍḍāvallī in Vikrama Saṃvat 1095, as explicitly stated in the concluding verses of the final chapter (16.249: 'bāṇaṅka-sunnōḍupē').
SA_GR12_surasumdariu.edition: Sādhvīśrī Mahāyaśāśrī, Surasuṁdarīcariyaṁ, Ā. Ōṁkārasūri JñānamaṀdira, 2020.
SA_GR12_surasumdariu.coverage: complete — Complete text in 16 paricchedas (chapters), concluding at chapter 16 verse 251: 'surasundarī kahāē sōlasamō iha paricchēō'.

SA_GR12_dhuttakkhanu.title: Dhuttakkhāṇa
SA_GR12_dhuttakkhanu.author: Haribhadrasūri
SA_GR12_dhuttakkhanu.summary: The Dhuttakkhāṇa is a Prakrit satirical narrative in verse composed by the Śvetāmbara master Haribhadrasūri at Citrakūṭa. Stranded during the monsoon season in Ujjayinī, five clever swindlers hold a contest where each narrates an absurd, impossible tall tale; every tale is vindicated by citing parallels from Brahmanical epics and Purāṇas, thereby satirizing Hindu mythic traditions while highlighting Jaina doctrine.
SA_GR12_dhuttakkhanu.attribution: Attributed in concluding verses 124–125 to Haribhadrasūri, composed at Citrakūṭa.

SA_GK19_sattasaiu.title: Sattasaī
SA_GK19_sattasaiu.author: Hāla
SA_GK19_sattasaiu.summary: The Sattasaī (Gāhāsattasaī, Sanskrit: Gāthāsaptaśatī) is an anthology of lyric stanzas (muktaka) in the āryā (gāhā) metre in Māhārāṣṭrī Prakrit, traditionally attributed to the Sātavāhana ruler Hāla. The poems evoke vignettes of pastoral and domestic life in the Deccan, focusing primarily on the nuances of erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), courtship, jealousy, and the distress of separation. It holds a pivotal place in Indian poetic tradition and was frequently cited by classical Sanskrit rhetoricians as the exemplar of dhvani (poetic suggestion).
SA_GK19_sattasaiu.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the Sātavāhana king Hāla (ca. 1st–2nd century CE) as collector/author. Modern scholarship treats the collection as an evolving anthology of Māhārāṣṭrī Prakrit muktaka stanzas compiled and augmented over several centuries (roughly 3rd to 8th centuries CE).
SA_GK19_sattasaiu.edition: Albrecht Weber, Das Saptaçatakam des Hâla, Brockhaus Leipzig 1881.
SA_GK19_sattasaiu.coverage: complete — Complete text of the 1,000 verses (numbered GāSa.1 to GāSa.1000) collected in Albrecht Weber's 1881 critical edition.

SA_GS25_desinamamalu.title: Deśīnāmamālā with Svopajñavṛtti (fragment)
SA_GS25_desinamamalu.author: Hemacandra
SA_GS25_desinamamalu.summary: The Deśīnāmamālā is Hemacandra's lexicographical treatise recording Prakrit deśī vocabulary. The Prakrit verses are accompanied by Hemacandra's Sanskrit auto-commentary (vṛtti). This e-text is an incomplete transcription fragment containing only the opening mangala and introductory verses 1–3.
SA_GS25_desinamamalu.attribution: Both the Prakrit kārikās and the Sanskrit prose commentary are by Hemacandra.
SA_GS25_desinamamalu.edition: Pischel Richard, The Deśînâmamâlâ of Hemachandra: Part I: Text and Critical Notes, Government Central Book Depôt, 2020.
SA_GS25_desinamamalu.coverage: fragment — Fragment containing verses 1–3 and the Sanskrit auto-commentary, breaking off mid-sentence in the introduction to verse 4 ('idānīṁ nānādēśaprasiddhabhāṣāsvativyāptiparihārārthaṁ dēśīlakṣaṇ').

SA_GK22_vajjalaggamu.title: Vajjālaggaṃ (incomplete)
SA_GK22_vajjalaggamu.author: Jayavallabha
SA_GK22_vajjalaggamu.summary: The Vajjālagga is a major anthology of Prakrit gāthās compiled by Jayavallabha, organized into thematic paddhatis (vajjās) treating topics across dharma and other subjects.
SA_GK22_vajjalaggamu.edition: M. V. Patwardhan (ed.), Jayavallabha’s Vajjālaggaṃ: A Prakrit Anthology, Ahmedabad: Prakrit Text Society (Prakrit Text Society Series, 14), 1969.
SA_GK22_vajjalaggamu.coverage: partial — Incomplete e-text breaking off at p. 267 (verse 652-1 in the pāusavajjā).
translations: M. V. Patwardhan, Jayavallabha's Vajjalaggam (with English translation), Prakrit Text Society Series, 14, Ahmedabad 1969. (English)

SA_GK22_gaharayanaku.title: Gāhārayaṇakosa
SA_GK22_gaharayanaku.author: Jineśvara
SA_GK22_gaharayanaku.summary: The Gāhārayaṇakosa (Sanskrit: Gāthāratnakośa) is a Prakrit poetic anthology compiled by the Śvetāmbara Jain monk Jineśvarasūri in VS 1251 (1194 CE). Arranged into 58 thematic sections (prakramas), the collection opens with invocations to Jinas, Hindu deities, and Sarasvatī, and covers topics of courtly conduct, gnomic wisdom, seasonal and nature descriptions, and erotics (śr̥ṅgāra). Following the tradition of the Gāhāsattasaī and the Vajjālagga, it preserves an extensive repertoire of classical and medieval Prakrit stanzas.
SA_GK22_gaharayanaku.attribution: Composed by the Śvetāmbara Jain teacher Jineśvarasūri, disciple of Candraprabhasūri, self-dated in verse 836 to Vikrama Samvat 1251 (1194 CE).
SA_GK22_gaharayanaku.edition: Jineśvarasūri’s Gāhārayaṇakosa, ed. Amritlal Mohanlal Bhojak and Nagin J. Shah, L.D. Series, Ahmedabad: L.D. Institute of Indology, 1975.
SA_GK22_gaharayanaku.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 58 thematic sections (prakramas) comprising 837 Prakrit gāthās, including the author's concluding praśasti and scribal colophon (pp. 1–66).

SA_GK22_subhasiyagau.title: Subhāsiyagāhāsaṅgaha (gāthās 1–128)
SA_GK22_subhasiyagau.summary: The Subhāsiyagāhāsaṅgahō is an anthology of Prakrit gāthās on gnomic and descriptive topics, including spring, bees, and the conduct of persons. The text breaks off at gāthā 128.
SA_GK22_subhasiyagau.attribution: Ascribed to Jinēśvara in the source header; printed in Amritlal Mohanlal Bhojak and Nagin P. Shah's edition of Jineśvarasūri's Gāhārayaṇakosa (1975).
SA_GK22_subhasiyagau.edition: Amritlal Mohanlal Bhojak and Nagin P. Shah (eds.), Jineśvarasūri’s Gāhārayaṇakosa, L.D. Institute of Indology, Ahmedabad 1975. The Subhāsiyagāhāsaṅgahō is printed beginning on p. 67.
SA_GK22_subhasiyagau.coverage: partial — Gāthās 1–128, printed edition pp. 67ff. The text breaks off at gāthā 128 after its first half-line ('maṇirayaṇāi vi gō… … …').

SA_GK22_subhasiyapau.title: Subhāsiyapajjasaṅgaho
SA_GK22_subhasiyapau.author: Jineśvara
SA_GK22_subhasiyapau.summary: The Subhāsiyapajjasaṅgaho is a Prakrit anthological collection of 91 gāthās attributed to Jineśvara. Following the classical Mahārāṣṭrī Prakrit muktaka lyric tradition of Hāla's Gāhāsattasaī, the stanzas portray themes of love, longing, separated lovers, and ethical conduct (nīti). The text is associated with Jineśvara's Gāhārayaṇakosa and edited by A. M. Bhojak.
SA_GK22_subhasiyapau.attribution: Attributed to Jineśvara (Jineśvarasūri), associated with the Gāhārayaṇakosa.
SA_GK22_subhasiyapau.edition: Amritlal Mohanlal Bhojak, Nagin P. Shah (eds.), Jineśvarasūri’s Gāhārayaṇakosa, Ahmedabad: L.D. Institute of Indology, 1975.
SA_GK22_subhasiyapau.coverage: complete — Collection of 91 Prakrit gāthās (verses 1–91), edited beginning on p. 76 of the printed edition.

SA_GK19_lilavaiu.title: Līlāvaī
SA_GK19_lilavaiu.author: Kautūhala
SA_GK19_lilavaiu.summary: The Līlāvaī is an 8th-century Mahārāṣṭrī Prakrit verse romance by the poet Koūhala (Kautūhala). It narrates the story involving King Sātavāhana and Princess Līlāvaī, with Nāgārjuna aiding Sātavāhana.
SA_GK19_lilavaiu.attribution: The poet is referred to as Koūhala / Kautūhala.
SA_GK19_lilavaiu.edition: Andrew Ollett, Kouhala: Lilavai, Harvard University Press Cambridge, Mass. 2021, Harvard University Press, 2020.
SA_GK19_lilavaiu.coverage: complete — Text of the romance ending at verse 1333A (with supplementary stanzas such as 5A, 1333A) and concluding formula 'ia līlāvaī ṇāma kahā samattā'.

SA_GK19_ravanavahou.title: Rāvaṇavaho
SA_GK19_ravanavahou.author: Pravarasena
SA_GK19_ravanavahou.summary: The Setubandha (also called Rāvaṇavaho or Rāvaṇavaha) is a Prakrit poem attributed to Pravarasena. Praised by writers such as Daṇḍin, Bāṇa, and Ānandavardhana, it retells events of the Rāmāyaṇa concerning Rāma, the monkey army, the building of the ocean causeway (setubandha), and Rāvaṇa.
SA_GK19_ravanavahou.attribution: Attributed to Pravarasena. Tradition also links the composition to Kālidāsa.
SA_GK19_ravanavahou.edition: Siegfried Goldschmidt (ed.), Râvaṇavaha oder Setubandha, Strassburg / London: Karl J. Trübner / Trübner & Co., 1880.
translations: Siegfried Goldschmidt, Râvaṇavaho oder Setubandha: Prākṛt und deutsch herausgegeben. 2. Lieferung: Übersetzung, Strassburg / London: Karl J. Trübner, 1884. (German)

SA_GK17_prakrtapainu.title: Prākṛtapaiṅgalam (chapter 1, verses 1–159)
SA_GK17_prakrtapainu.author: Piṅgala
SA_GK17_prakrtapainu.summary: The Prākṛtapaiṅgalam is a manual of Prakrit metrics associated with Piṅgala, containing rules and definitions for meters along with illustrative verses.
SA_GK17_prakrtapainu.attribution: Ascribed in the text to Piṅgala.
SA_GK17_prakrtapainu.edition: Bhōlāśaṅkara Vyāsa, Prākr̥tapaiṅgalam, Prākr̥ta Grantha Pariṣad, 2021.
SA_GK17_prakrtapainu.coverage: partial — The e-text covers pages 1 to 143 (ending at verse PrāPi.159).

SA_GS24_prakrtapraku.title: Prākṛtaprakāśa with Manoramā
SA_GS24_prakrtapraku.author: Vararuci, Bhāmaha
SA_GS24_prakrtapraku.summary: The Prākṛtaprakāśa of Vararuci is a treatise on Prakrit grammar. Consisting of twelve chapters, it derives Prakrit phonology and morphology from Sanskrit, concluding with chapter 12 on Śaurasenī. The accompanying commentary by Bhāmaha offers glosses and illustrative citations.
SA_GS24_prakrtapraku.attribution: The root aphorisms are traditionally ascribed to Vararuci. The introductory verse (VaraBhā.2) explicitly identifies the commentator as Bhāmaha ('vararuciracitaprākṛtalakṣaṇasūtrāṇi lakṣyamārgeṇa buddhvā cakāra vṛttiṃ saṃkṣiptāṃ bhāmahaḥ spaṣṭām').
SA_GS24_prakrtapraku.edition: P. L. Vaidya, Prākr̥taprakāśaḥ, The Oriental Book Agency, 2020.
SA_GS24_prakrtapraku.coverage: complete — Text of the work with Bhāmaha's commentary up through chapter 12, covering pp. 19–120 in P. L. Vaidya's edition.

SA_GS24_prakrtaprak2u.title: Prākṛtaprakāśa (chapters 1–8)
SA_GS24_prakrtaprak2u.author: Vararuci
SA_GS24_prakrtaprak2u.summary: The Prākṛtaprakāśa, attributed to Vararuci, is the earliest extant treatise on Prakrit grammar. Composed in Sanskrit sūtras, it systematically outlines the phonological and morphological transformations from Sanskrit to Prakrit, treating Mahārāṣṭrī Prakrit as the baseline language. This e-text preserves the sūtrapāṭha across eight paricchedas according to the recension associated with Vasantarāja's commentary Prākṛtasañjīvanī.
SA_GS24_prakrtaprak2u.attribution: The Prākṛtaprakāśa is traditionally attributed to Vararuci. The text here provides the sūtrapāṭha followed by colophons referencing Vasantarāja's Prākṛtasañjīvanī commentary, though the commentary prose itself is omitted.
SA_GS24_prakrtaprak2u.edition: Baladēva Upādhyāya, Vararuciviracitaḥ Prākr̥taprakāśaḥ, Sampūrṇānanda-Saṁskr̥ta-Viśvavidyālayaḥ Vārāṇasī 1996, Sampūrṇānanda-Saṁskr̥ta-Viśvavidyālayaḥ, 2020.
SA_GS24_prakrtaprak2u.coverage: partial — Contains the sūtras of paricchedas 1–8 (the core grammar of Mahārāṣṭrī Prakrit). Paricchedas 9–12 (treating Paiśācī, Māgadhī, and Śaurasenī), which belong to the twelve-chapter recension commented upon by Bhāmaha, are absent.

SA_GR12_paumacariyau.title: Paümacariya
SA_GR12_paumacariyau.author: Vimalasūri
SA_GR12_paumacariyau.summary: The Paümacariya (Padmacarita) of Vimalasūri is the earliest surviving Jaina retelling of the Rāma story (Rāmāyaṇa), composed in Jaina Māhārāṣṭrī Prakrit verse across 118 uddesas. The work explicitly rationalizes and corrects Vālmīki's epic in light of Jaina doctrine, presenting Rāvaṇa and the Rākṣasas as civilized Vidyādhara aerial beings rather than blood-drinking demons, and Sugrīva and the Vānaras as a dynasty bearing the monkey emblem rather than beasts. Emphasizing karma, ahiṃsā, and monastic renunciation, it culminates in Rāma's attainment of omniscience (kevalajñāna) and ultimate liberation (nirvāṇa), serving as the foundational prototype for subsequent Jaina Rāmakathā literature in Sanskrit, Prakrit, and Apabhraṃśa.
SA_GR12_paumacariyau.attribution: The concluding colophon of the text explicitly attributes authorship to Vimalasūri (sūrivimala), disciple of Vijayācārya and grand-disciple of Rāhusūri of the Nāilakula lineage.
SA_GR12_paumacariyau.edition: Ācārya Vimalasūri's Paumacariyaṁ with Hindi Translation, edited by Hermann Jacobi, second revised edition by Muni Shri Punyavijayaji, translated into Hindi by Shantilal M. Vora (Introduction by V. M. Kulkarni), 2 vols., Varanasi: Prakrit Text Society, 1962–, Prakrit Text Society Series Nos. 6, 12.
SA_GR12_paumacariyau.coverage: complete — Text across 118 uddesas (cantos), concluding with uddesa 118 (Padmanirvāṇagamana).
translations: Shantilal M. Vora (trans.), Hindi translation accompanying Hermann Jacobi's edition revised by Muni Shri Punyavijayaji, Paumacariyaṁ with Hindi Translation, 2 vols., Varanasi: Prakrit Text Society, 1962–. (Hindi)

SA_GK23_gaudavahamu.title: Gaüḍavaha
SA_GK23_gaudavahamu.author: Vākpatirāja
SA_GK23_gaudavahamu.summary: The Gaüḍavaha ('The Slaying of the Gauda [King]') is an 8th-century Maharashtri Prakrit mahākāvya composed in āryā meter by Vākpatirāja, court poet of King Yaśovarman of Kanauj (c. 725–753 CE). Although planned to celebrate Yaśovarman's digvijaya and victory over the Gauda monarch, the extant text preserves only the introductory portion (gāthāpīṭha, 1209 verses), concluding before the actual battle. The text contains elaborate invocations of Viṣṇu and Vindhyavāsinī (Durgā), reflections on the nature and sweetness of Prakrit poetry, descriptions of seasons and village life, and eulogies of King Yaśovarman.
SA_GK23_gaudavahamu.attribution: Vākpatirāja explicitly names himself in the text and colophon (kaïrāa-lañchaṇassa vappaïrāassa gauḍavahē gāhāvīḍhaṁ samattaṁ).
SA_GK23_gaudavahamu.edition: N. G. Suru, Gaüḍavahaṁ, Prakrit Text Society, 2020.
SA_GK23_gaudavahamu.coverage: complete — Complete as extant; contains all 1209 verses (gāthās) of the introductory section (gāthāpīṭha), which is all that survives of the poem in the manuscript tradition.

SA_GR12_ayarangasutu.title: Āyāraṅgasutta (Śrutaskandha 1)
SA_GR12_ayarangasutu.summary: The Āyāraṅgasutta (Sanskrit: Ācārāṅgasūtra) is the first of the eleven surviving Aṅgas of the Śvetāmbara Jaina canon. Composed in an archaic stratum of Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit, its first Śrutaskandha forms one of the earliest surviving witnesses to Jaina ascetic practice, laying down fundamental tenets of ahiṃsā (non-violence) toward all six classes of living beings, rigorous wandering discipline, and monastic detachment. Its ninth chapter, the Upadhānaśruta, preserves an ancient poetic account of the austerities, hardships, and enlightenment of Mahāvīra.
SA_GR12_ayarangasutu.coverage: partial — Contains only the first Śrutaskandha (Suyakkhandha 1), consisting of 9 adhyayanas (sections 1–552, marked // Āyār.1 to // Āyār.552). The second Śrutaskandha (Suyakkhandha 2) is omitted.
translations: Walther Schubring, Worte Mahāvīras, Göttingen, 1926. (German)

SA_GR12_suyagadangau.title: Sūyagaḍaṅga
SA_GR12_suyagadangau.summary: The Sūyagaḍaṅga (Sanskrit: Sūtrakṛtāṅga) is the second of the twelve Aṅgas of the Śvetāmbara Jaina canon. Composed in Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit, it comprises two books: the first in metrical verse and the second primarily in prose. It is historically significant for its doxographical refutations of rival religious and philosophical schools (including early Buddhist doctrines, materialists, and fatalist Niyativādins) and its detailed instructions on Jaina ascetic discipline, non-violence (ahiṃsā), and liberation from karma.
SA_GR12_suyagadangau.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Sūyagaḍaṅga across its two śrutaskandhas (Book 1 containing 16 adhyayanas in verse, Book 2 containing 7 adhyayanas in prose), ending with the conversion narrative of Udaka Pedhālaputta.
translations: Hermann Jacobi (trans.), 1895. (English)

SA_GR12_thanangasutu.title: Ṭhāṇaṅgasutta
SA_GR12_thanangasutu.summary: The Ṭhāṇaṅgasutta (Sanskrit: Sthānāṅgasūtra) is the third Aṅga of the Śvetāmbara Jaina canon. Organized numerically into ten sections (ṭhāṇas), it groups doctrinal, cosmological, and physical categories into numerical sets from one to ten, structurally resembling the Buddhist Aṅguttaranikāya. The text serves as an encyclopedic manual of early Jaina metaphysics, karma doctrine, ethics, and monastic life.
SA_GR12_thanangasutu.attribution: According to Śvetāmbara tradition, the text was compiled by Sudharman, the chief surviving disciple (gaṇadhara) of Mahāvīra.
SA_GR12_thanangasutu.coverage: complete — All ten ṭhāṇas; the e-text ends with the closing pudgala sūtras of ṭhāṇa 10 (last numbered marker Ṭhāṇa.1008, followed by the final unnumbered sūtras).

SA_GR12_nayadhammaku.title: Nāyadhammakahāō
SA_GR12_nayadhammaku.summary: The Nāyādhammakahāō (Skt. Jñātādharmakathāḥ) is the sixth Aṅga of the Śvetāmbara canon, in Ardhamāgadhī. Its first śrutaskandha contains nineteen exemplary narratives (nāya), among them the story of Mallī, the nineteenth Tīrthaṅkara, and that of Draupadī; the second contains ten vaggas of brief, formulaic stories of goddesses reborn as chief queens of the gods. It is a major source of early Jaina narrative literature.
SA_GR12_nayadhammaku.attribution: Traditional attribution to the teaching of Mahāvīra as transmitted by his disciple Sudharmasvāmin to Jambūsvāmin, codified in the Śvetāmbara canon.
SA_GR12_nayadhammaku.coverage: complete — Complete: suyakkhandha 1 (19 nāya-ajjhayaṇas) and suyakkhandha 2 (dhammakahā, 10 vaggas), ending 'dhammakahā-suyakkhandhō samattō dasahiṁ vaggēhiṁ nāyādhammakahāō samattāō'. Section numbers follow Deepratnasagar (last Nāyā.239).

SA_GR12_nisihasuttau.title: Nisīhasutta
SA_GR12_nisihasuttau.summary: The Nisīhasutta (Sanskrit: Niśīthasūtra) is the fifth Chedasūtra in standard lists (and one of the primary disciplinary treatises) of the Śvetāmbara Jaina canon. Written in Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit across twenty chapters (uddesas), it systematically enumerates monastic offenses (atīcāra) and specifies the required penances (prāyaścitta), serving as a central code of monastic discipline.
SA_GR12_nisihasuttau.attribution: Canonical Śvetāmbara scripture; traditionally preserved in the Chedasūtra division of the Siddhānta.
SA_GR12_nisihasuttau.coverage: complete — Complete mūla text of the Nisīhasutta, concluding at the end with the editorial colophon.

SA_GR12_baddakappou.title: Bṛhatkalpasūtra
SA_GR12_baddakappou.summary: The Bṛhatkalpasūtra is a Jaina canonical text (Cheyasutta / Chedasūtra). It regulates the conduct and rules of monks and nuns (nigganthas and nigganthīs), covering lodging, food, relations, and monastic rules, concluding with the six kinds of kappaṭṭhiti.
SA_GR12_baddakappou.coverage: complete — Complete mūla sūtras of the text, from the tālapalamba rules to the six kappaṭṭhitis and 'thēra kappaṭṭhitī, tti bēmi'. The e-text carries no uddēsa headings.

SA_GR12_pindanijjutu.title: Piṇḍanijjuttī
SA_GR12_pindanijjutu.author: Bhadrabāhu
SA_GR12_pindanijjutu.summary: The Piṇḍanijjuttī (Pindanijjutti) is a canonical Jaina verse treatise classified among the Mūlasūtras or Chedasūtras. It regulates the monastic reception of alms (food alms / piṇḍa) by wandering monks, detailing the faults (doṣas) connected with it.
SA_GR12_pindanijjutu.attribution: Counted in canonical lists variously as a Mūlasūtra or Chedasūtra (Cheyasutta).
SA_GR12_pindanijjutu.coverage: complete — Text in 713 Prakrit gāhās numbered PiṇḍNi.1 to PiṇḍNi.713.

SA_GR12_dasavaikaliu.title: Daśavaikālikasūtra
SA_GR12_dasavaikaliu.summary: The Daśavaikālikasūtra (Prakrit: Dasaveyāliyasutta) is one of the four Mūlasūtras of the Śvetāmbara Jain canonical tradition (Siddhānta). Composed in Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit in ten adhyayanas and two supplementary cūlikās, it is one of the foundational texts studied by newly ordained ascetics. It systematically sets forth the core vows, monastic rules of conduct (ācāra), the strict requirements for begging alms (piṇḍaiṣaṇā), and the cultivation of non-violence (ahiṃsā) and self-restraint.
SA_GR12_dasavaikaliu.coverage: complete — Complete root text (540 verses, numbered Dasavē.1 through Dasavē.540).
translations: Willem Schubring, Worte Mahaviras: Kritische Übersetzungen aus dem Kanon der Jaina, Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 1926. (German)

SA_GR12_uttarajjhayu.title: Uttarajjhayaṇasutta
SA_GR12_uttarajjhayu.summary: The Uttarajjhayaṇasutta (Sanskrit: Uttarādhyayanasūtra) is one of the four Mūlasūtras of the Śvetāmbara Jain canonical corpus, traditionally held to record the final discourses delivered by Vardhamāna Mahāvīra before his parinirvāṇa. Composed primarily in Ardhamāgadhī verse with some prose, its 36 chapters expound ascetic discipline, ethical vows, the nature of karma, cosmology, and spiritual liberation through dialogues, parables, and didactic homilies. It is among the most widely studied and revered instructional scriptures in the Jain tradition.
SA_GR12_uttarajjhayu.attribution: Traditional Śvetāmbara tradition regards this scripture as containing the final sermons and instructions of the 24th Tīrthaṅkara Mahāvīra shortly before his death at Pāvā.
SA_GR12_uttarajjhayu.coverage: complete — Complete text in all 36 chapters (ajjhayaṇas), totaling 1,731 numbered verses (Utt. 1–Utt. 1731).
translations: Hermann Jacobi (trans.), 1895. (English)

SA_GR12_nandisutramu.title: Nandīsūtra
SA_GR12_nandisutramu.summary: The Nandīsūtra is a canonical Śvetāmbara Jaina text composed in Prakrit, dealing with varieties of knowledge (jñāna) such as ābhinibodhika, śruta, avadhi, manaḥparyāya, and kevala, as well as canonical textual transmission.

SA_GR12_anuyogadvaru.title: Anuyogadvārasūtra
SA_GR12_anuyogadvaru.summary: The Anuyogadvārasūtra (Prakrit: Aṇuōgaddārāiṁ) is an important text of the Śvetāmbara Jaina canon. It incorporates treatments of doctrinal concepts, epistemology, the theory of partial viewpoints (naya), and discussions of arts, metrics, and rasas.
SA_GR12_anuyogadvaru.attribution: A text of the Śvetāmbara canon.
SA_GR12_anuyogadvaru.coverage: complete — Complete mūla text: from 'nāṇaṁ pañcavihaṁ pannattaṁ' to the final naya verses (AṇuŌg.349) and 'sē taṁ naē'.

SA_XX_ganapatitatu.title: Gaṇapatitattva
SA_XX_ganapatitatu.summary: An Old Javanese Śaiva doctrinal and philosophical dialogue (tutur/tattva) in which Śiva (Īśvara) instructs his son Gaṇapati. Consisting of 60 Sanskrit stanzas interspersed with Old Javanese prose commentary, it expounds Śaiva cosmogony, the emanation of the pañcadaivātmā and subtle elements, macrocosm-microcosm homologies, six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga), and mantra theology.
SA_XX_ganapatitatu.attribution: Anonymous Old Javanese tutelary text cast as an instruction given by Śiva (Īśvara) to Gaṇapati, combining Sanskrit verses (ślokas) and Old Javanese prose explanation.
SA_XX_ganapatitatu.edition: Gaṇapati-tattwa, an Old Javanese philosophic text, critically edited, annotated and translated by Mrs. Dr. Sudarshana Devi Singhal, New Delhi: International Academy of Indian Culture, 1958 (Śata-Piṭaka Series; Dvīpāntara-Piṭaka).
SA_XX_ganapatitatu.coverage: complete — Complete text of 60 Sanskrit śloka units and accompanying Old Javanese prose paraphrase, concluding with the colophon '[iti gaṇapatitattva samāpta]' at segment [260].
translations: Sudarshana Devi Singhal, Gaṇapati-tattwa, an Old Javanese philosophic text, critically edited, annotated and translated, New Delhi: International Academy of Indian Culture, 1958 (Śata-Piṭaka Series; Dvīpāntara-Piṭaka). (English)

SA_XX_kalpabuddhau.title: Kalpabuddha
SA_XX_kalpabuddhau.summary: The Kalpabuddha describes how the Buddha / Pañcatathāgata (including Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, Amoghasiddha) arise, detailing their directions, colors, consorts/deities, mantras, mudrās, and body correspondences.
SA_XX_kalpabuddhau.edition: F.D.K. Bosch: "Buddhist Data from Balinese Texts", Mededeelingen der Koninklijke Akademie van Wetenschappen, Afdeeling Letterkunde, Vol. 68, Ser. B, 1929, pp. 43-78 (reprinted in: Selected Studies in Indonesian Archaeology, pp. 108-133; 132-133)
SA_XX_kalpabuddhau.coverage: complete — Text opening with 'nihan haji nira bhaṭāra hyaṅ buddha' and containing the bracketed editorial addition '[bhaṭāra vajrayakṣa,]'.

SA_XX_kunjarakarnu.title: Kuñjarakarṇadharmakathana
SA_XX_kunjarakarnu.author: Mpu Ḍusun
SA_XX_kunjarakarnu.summary: An Old Javanese Buddhist narrative poem (kakawin) composed by Mpu Ḍusun. It relates the story of the yakṣa Kuñjarakarṇa, who receives instruction in Buddhist doctrine, tours the realms of hell, and witnesses karmic retribution, leading to purification and spiritual liberation.
SA_XX_kunjarakarnu.attribution: Mpu Ḍusun is named by the author in Canto 41.15.
SA_XX_kunjarakarnu.edition: Teeuw, A., S.O. Robson and A. J. Bernet Kempers, Kunjarakarna Dharmakathana, Liberation through the law of the Buddha: An Old Javanese poem by Mpu Ḍusun, The Hague, Martinus Nijhoff 1981; Koninklijk Instituut voor Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde, Bibliotheca Indonesica 21.
SA_XX_kunjarakarnu.coverage: complete — Text of the kakawin ending at Canto 41, including textual apparatus notes from Teeuw and Robson's edition.

SA_XX_sanhyanmahau.title: Saṅ Hyaṅ Mahājñāna
SA_XX_sanhyanmahau.summary: An Old Javanese Śaiva tutur (philosophical exposition) cast as a dialogue between Bhaṭāra Guru and Kumāra. It comprises 87 Sanskrit ślokas paired with Old Javanese prose commentary dealing with Śaiva-Siddhānta metaphysics, cosmic and microcosmic anatomy, the nature of pradhāna and the guṇas, and yoga leading to spiritual liberation (kalepasan).
SA_XX_sanhyanmahau.attribution: Traditional Old Javanese Śaiva tutur text; framed as a revelation by Bhaṭāra Guru to Kumāra.
SA_XX_sanhyanmahau.edition: Sudarshana Devi Singhal, ed., Tattwajnana and Mahajnana (two Kawi philosophical texts), Delhi: International Academy of Indian Culture, 1962. (Satapitaka Series, 23; Dvipantara-Pitaka, 6)
SA_XX_sanhyanmahau.coverage: complete — Complete text containing 87 Sanskrit ślokas alternating with Old Javanese prose commentary, ending at colophon: 'iti tattva saṅ hyaṅ mahājñāna / mulih ṅ antaviśeṣa'.

SA_XX_sanhyankamau.title: Saṅ Hyaṅ Kamahāyānikan
SA_XX_sanhyankamau.summary: The Saṅ Hyaṅ Kamahāyānikan is an Old Javanese Buddhist treatise. It presents Sanskrit verses alongside Old Javanese prose explanations, synthesising Mahāyāna philosophy (such as the daśapāramitā) with Mantrayāna/Vajrayāna ritual and esoteric doctrine (including the Five Tathāgatas, Caturdevī, and Vajrasattva).
SA_XX_sanhyankamau.edition: Saṅ Hyaṅ Kamahāyānikan, Oud-Javaansche tekst met Inleiding, Vertaling en Aanteekeningen door J. Kats, s'Gravenhage: Martinus Nijhoff, 1910.
SA_XX_sanhyankamau.coverage: complete — Complete text matching J. Kats' 1910 edition.

SA_XX_slokantarau.title: Ślokāntara
SA_XX_slokantarau.summary: The Ślokāntara is an Old Javanese didactic compendium combining 83 Sanskrit verses with Old Javanese prose commentary (kaliṅanya), followed by an ethical exposition of lists of virtues and vices (section 84). It draws upon Indian dharmaśāstra, nīti, and gnomic lore, emphasizing ethical conduct, the fruits of religious donations (dāna), social duties, the daśa paramārtha (ten supreme virtues), and the daśa mala (ten moral impurities).
SA_XX_slokantarau.attribution: Anonymous didactic text consisting of Sanskrit slokas with Old Javanese prose paraphrases (kaliṅanya) and concluding doctrinal lists.
SA_XX_slokantarau.edition: Sharada Rani: Ślokāntara, an Old Javanese Didactic Text, critically edited and annotated. New Delhi: International Academy of Indian Culture 1957.
SA_XX_slokantarau.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising 83 Sanskrit slokas with Old Javanese glosses, followed by section 84 detailing daśa paramārtha, daśa mala, and nava saṅa, concluding with '|| iti ślokāntara ||'.

SA_XX_sanhyantattu.title: Saṅ Hyaṅ Tattvajñāna
SA_XX_sanhyantattu.summary: The Saṅ Hyaṅ Tattvajñāna is an Old Javanese Śaiva doctrinal and yogic prose treatise (tutūr). It details a Śaivasiddhānta-based ontology centered on the distinction between consciousness (cetana / śivatattva, classified into Paramaśiva, Sadāśiva, and Ātman) and unconscious primordial nature (acetana / māyātattva), and expounds an internalized yogic practice (prayogasandhi, including ṣaḍaṅgayoga) aimed at overcoming the guṇas and attaining spiritual liberation and yogic perfections (aṣṭaiśvarya).
SA_XX_sanhyantattu.attribution: Traditional anonymous Old Javanese tutūr text of the Śaiva-Dharma tradition in pre-Islamic Java.
SA_XX_sanhyantattu.edition: Sudarshana Devi Singhal: Tattwajnana and Mahajnana (two Kawi philosophical texts). Delhi: International Academy of Indian Culture, 1962. (Satapitaka Series, 23; Dvipantara-Pitaka, 6)
SA_XX_sanhyantattu.coverage: complete — Complete text in 50 numbered sections, concluding with the explicit colophon 'iti saṅ hyaṅ tattvajñāna / saṅ hyaṅ prayogasandhi / parisamāpta'.

SA_XX_vratisasanau.title: Vratiśāsana
SA_XX_vratisasanau.summary: The Vratiśāsana is an Old Javanese Śaiva śāsana text establishing ethical precepts, ascetic disciplines, and monastic codes for Śaiva renunciants (viku). It pairs Sanskrit ślokas with an extensive Old Javanese prose exegesis, detailing the five yamas and five niyamas, ritual purifications, dietary regulations, social taboos, and procedural requirements for religious initiation and ordination.
SA_XX_vratisasanau.attribution: A traditional Old Javanese Śaiva śāsana work composed in Sanskrit ślokas accompanied by an Old Javanese (Kawi) prose paraphrase and commentary.
SA_XX_vratisasanau.edition: in Balinese and Devanagari scripts by Sharada Rani: Wratiśāsana: a Sanskrit text on ascetic discipline with Kawi exegesis. Śata-Piṭaka Series 20. New Delhi: International Academy of Indian Culture, 1961.
SA_XX_vratisasanau.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Vratiśāsana, including the Sanskrit verses, Old Javanese prose paraphrase/commentary, and the supplementary appendix section (up to VS_appendix-25ka).

SA_XX_vrhaspatitau.title: Vṛhaspatitattva
SA_XX_vrhaspatitau.summary: The Vṛhaspatitattva is an Old Javanese Śaiva philosophical text cast as a dialogue between Maheśvara (Śiva) and the sage Vṛhaspati on Mount Kailāsa. It consists of Sanskrit verses accompanied by an Old Javanese prose commentary that expounds Śaiva metaphysics, karmic transmigration, cosmology, the nature of the ātmā, yogic stages and siddhis (including the aṣṭaiśvarya powers), and meditational obstacles.
SA_XX_vrhaspatitau.attribution: A text framed as divine instruction imparted by Maheśvara to Vṛhaspati on Mount Kailāsa.
SA_XX_vrhaspatitau.edition: Sudarshana Devi, Vṛhaspati-tattva, an Old Javanese Philosophical Text, Nagpur: International Academy of Indian Culture, 1957.
SA_XX_vrhaspatitau.coverage: complete — Text ending with 'iti vṛhaspatitattva samāpta'.
translations: Alexander Zieseniss, Studien zur Geschichte des Śivaismus: Die Śaiva-Systematik des Vṛhaspatitattva, New Delhi: International Academy of Indian Culture, 1958. (German)

SA_K12_Āgama_Adhyardhaśatikā-Prajñāpāram.title: Adhyardhaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā (fragment)
SA_K12_Āgama_Adhyardhaśatikā-Prajñāpāram.summary: The Adhyardhaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā is an esoteric Buddhist sūtra organized around expositions of wisdom delivered by tathāgatas and bodhisattvas, each marked by a mystic syllable (bīja). This e-text preserves the Sanskrit portion of the bilingual Sanskrit-Khotanese manuscript.
SA_K12_Āgama_Adhyardhaśatikā-Prajñāpāram.attribution: Canonical scriptural Mahāyāna/esoteric Buddhist sūtra, anonymous.
SA_K12_Āgama_Adhyardhaśatikā-Prajñāpāram.edition: Shōun Toganoo & Hōkei Izumi (1917), based on Ernst Leumann (1912).
SA_K12_Āgama_Adhyardhaśatikā-Prajñāpāram.coverage: fragment — Fragmentary Sanskrit text of the bilingual Sanskrit-Khotanese manuscript, transcribed without the Khotanese interlinear translation.
translations: Astley-Kristensen, Ian (1991). The Rishukyō: The Sino-Japanese Tantric Prajñā-pāramitā in 150 Verses (Amoghavajra’s Version). Tring: The Institute of Buddhist Studies. (English)

SA_K12_Āgama_Amoghapāśahṛdaya.title: Amoghapāśahṛdaya
SA_K12_Āgama_Amoghapāśahṛdaya.summary: The Amoghapāśahṛdaya is an early Mahāyāna dhāraṇī-sūtra (classified in Tibetan doxography as a Kriyātantra) centered on the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara in his manifestation as Amoghapāśa ('Unfailing Noose'). On Mount Potalaka, Avalokiteśvara proclaims the 'heart' spell (hṛdaya) received from Lokendrarāja Tathāgata, outlining its power to purify karmic obscurations, avert afflictions, and secure mundane and supramundane blessings. The sūtra includes extensive ritual prescriptions (vidhi) and iconographic directives depicting Avalokiteśvara bearing ascetic Śaiva (Paśupati) attributes, serving as the foundational core around which the extensive Amoghapāśakalparāja expanded.
SA_K12_Āgama_Amoghapāśahṛdaya.attribution: Canonical scripture traditionally presented as a Mahāyāna sūtra spoken by Avalokiteśvara in the presence of the Buddha on Mount Potalaka.
SA_K12_Āgama_Amoghapāśahṛdaya.edition: Amoghapāśahṛdayasūtra, in Dhīḥ: Rare Buddhist Texts Research Journal 38 (2004), pp. 157–169.
SA_K12_Āgama_Amoghapāśahṛdaya.coverage: complete — Complete text of the short dhāraṇī-sūtra, from the opening nidāna ('evaṃ mayā śrutam...') through ritual prescriptions to the concluding colophon ('// āryāmoghapāśanāmahṛdayaṃ mahāyānasūtraṃ samāptam //').
translations: Meisezahl, R. O. 'The Amoghapāśahṛdaya-Dhāraṇī: The Early Sanskrit Manuscript of the Reiunji Critically Edited and Translated.' Monumenta Nipponica 17 (1962). (English)

SA_K12_Āgama_Amoghapāśakalparāja-ch1-7.title: Amoghapāśakalparāja (chapters 1–7)
SA_K12_Āgama_Amoghapāśakalparāja-ch1-7.summary: The Amoghapāśakalparāja is an extensive Buddhist Kriyātantra ritual compendium dedicated to Amoghapāśa Avalokiteśvara. Chapters 1–7 incorporate the foundational Amoghapāśahṛdayadhāraṇī and detail extensive ritual manuals (kalpa), homa and recitation procedures, iconographic descriptions, and maṇḍala configurations, including the Padmoṣṇīṣa- and Vimokṣamaṇḍala. The Sanskrit text is preserved in a single codex unicus discovered in Tibet/China.
SA_K12_Āgama_Amoghapāśakalparāja-ch1-7.attribution: A Buddhist Kriyātantra scripture traditionally framed as the revelation of Avalokiteśvara in the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha.
SA_K12_Āgama_Amoghapāśakalparāja-ch1-7.coverage: partial — Contains Part I of the text, ending at folio 97b.
translations: phags pa don yod pa'i zhags pa'i cho ga zhib mo'i rgyal po (Derge Kangyur D 686): translated by bu ston rin chen grub; revised by grub pa dpal bzang po (Tibetan)

SA_K12_Āgama_Amoghapāśakalparāja-edition.title: Amoghapāśakalparāja (post-chapter 7 sections)
SA_K12_Āgama_Amoghapāśakalparāja-edition.summary: The Amoghapāśakalparāja is an extensive Mahāyāna esoteric ritual compendium (kriyātantra / kalpa) dedicated to Amoghapāśa Lokeśvara, a prominent multi-armed form of Avalokiteśvara. The scripture prescribes rituals for protection, healing, maṇḍala construction, mantra recitations, and homa rites. This e-text preserves the four supplementary ritual sections that follow chapter 7 in the unique Sanskrit manuscript (designated 7+1 to 7+4 in scholarship), concluding with the homavidhisādhana rite.
SA_K12_Āgama_Amoghapāśakalparāja-edition.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna/esoteric Buddhist tantric scripture spoken by Avalokiteśvara and Vajrapāṇi.
SA_K12_Āgama_Amoghapāśakalparāja-edition.edition: Mikkyō Seiten Kenkyūkai (2015), 'Amoghapāśakalparāja. Preliminary Edition および和訳註 —サンスクリット語写本 Ff. 97v4‒99r2—', 大正大学綜合佛教研究所年報 (Taishō Daigaku Sōgō Bukkyō Kenkyūjo Nenpō) 37: 41–68.
SA_K12_Āgama_Amoghapāśakalparāja-edition.coverage: partial — Contains the four supplementary ritual sections preserved in the unique Sanskrit manuscript following chapter 7 (designated 7+1 to 7+4; MS folios approximately 90r–99r2), concluding at §23 with 'homavidhisādhanam'. Chapters 1–7 are not included in this file.
translations: phags pa don yod pa'i zhags pa'i cho ga zhib mo'i rgyal po (Derge Kangyur D 686): translated by bu ston rin chen grub; revised by grub pa dpal bzang po (Tibetan)

SA_K12_Āgama_Bhagavatyāsvedāmbujāyā-yath.title: Bhagavatyāḥ Svedāmbujāyāḥ Yathālabdhatantrarāja
SA_K12_Āgama_Bhagavatyāsvedāmbujāyā-yath.summary: A Buddhist esoteric ritual scripture (tantrarāja / kriyātantra) dedicated to the fierce rākṣasī Vidyujjvālākarālī Svedāmbujā ('Sweat-born Lotus Goddess'), who emerges from the perspiration of the Buddha Śākyamuni to protect a beleaguered merchant from King Caṇḍapradyota. Surviving in a unique dated palm-leaf manuscript from Nepal copied in 1024 CE, it details protective and destructive mantras, maṇḍala designs, yakṣiṇī-sādhanas, and aggressive sorcery (abhicāra), sharing significant ritual material with the Ekajaṭā and Vajrapāṇi cults.
SA_K12_Āgama_Bhagavatyāsvedāmbujāyā-yath.attribution: Esoteric Buddhist canonical scripture (tantrarāja) featuring Vidyujjvālākarālī Svedāmbujā.
SA_K12_Āgama_Bhagavatyāsvedāmbujāyā-yath.edition: Diplomatic edition by Péter-Dániel Szántó based on National Archives Kathmandu (NAK) MS 3-359 (NGMPP reel A 47/16), dated Nepāla Saṃvat 144 (10 July 1024 CE) during the reign of Lakṣmīkāmadeva.
SA_K12_Āgama_Bhagavatyāsvedāmbujāyā-yath.coverage: complete — Complete diplomatic transcription of manuscript NAK 3-359 / NGMPP reel A 47/16, folios 1r–56v, including opening invocations and scribal colophon.

SA_K12_Āgama_Bhūtaḍāmaratantra.title: Bhūtaḍāmaratantra
SA_K12_Āgama_Bhūtaḍāmaratantra.summary: The Bhūtaḍāmaratantra is a Buddhist esoteric scripture centered on the wrathful deity Bhūtaḍāmara, an emanation of Vajrapāṇi renowned as the subjugator of mundane spirits (bhūtas, yakṣas, nāgas, kiṃnaras, and yoginīs). The text provides detailed ritual instructions, mantras, mudrās, maṇḍalas, and sādhanas for subjugation, exorcism, and commanding supernatural female spirits (such as bhūtinīs and yakṣiṇīs) to grant wealth, longevity, and service. It shares significant ritual material and terminology with the Śaiva tantric tradition of the same name.
SA_K12_Āgama_Bhūtaḍāmaratantra.attribution: Canonical Buddhist tantra traditionally presented as revealed scripture spoken by Vajradhara/Vajrapāṇi.
SA_K12_Āgama_Bhūtaḍāmaratantra.edition: Bhūtaḍāmaratantra (digital appendix to Toh 747), 84000: Translating the Words of the Buddha, URL: https://84000.co/translation/toh747#UT22084-095-002-appendix.
SA_K12_Āgama_Bhūtaḍāmaratantra.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Buddhist tantra corresponding to Toh 747 in the Kangyur, ending with 'bhūtaḍāmaramahātantrarājaḥ samāptaḥ'.
translations: byung po 'dul ba zhes bya ba'i rgyud kyi rgyal po chen po (Derge Kangyur D 747): translated by Buddhākaravarman, shel dkar lo tsA ba chos kyi shes rab (Tibetan)

SA_K12_Āgama_Buddhakapālatantra-ch9-14.title: Buddhakapālatantra (chapters 9–14)
SA_K12_Āgama_Buddhakapālatantra-ch9-14.summary: The Buddhakapālatantra is a Buddhist Yoginītantra. Chapters 9–14 cover ascetical conduct (caryāpaṭala), internal alchemy and yoga (hemakapaṭala / rasāyana), the maṇḍala, recitation rituals, and conclude with the nidāna.
SA_K12_Āgama_Buddhakapālatantra-ch9-14.attribution: Canonical Buddhist Vajrayāna tantra belonging to the Yoginītantra / Niruttara class.
SA_K12_Āgama_Buddhakapālatantra-ch9-14.coverage: partial — Contains chapters 9 to 14 (verses 9.1–14.24 and closing prose colophon) of the 14-chapter tantra.

SA_K12_Āgama_Caturyoginīsampuṭa.title: Caturyoginīsaṃpuṭatantra
SA_K12_Āgama_Caturyoginīsampuṭa.summary: The Caturyoginīsaṃpuṭatantra (Tōhoku 376) is a short Yoginītantra affiliated with the Cakrasaṃvara (Heruka) corpus, consisting of around two hundred verses. It focuses on the conjunction (saṃpuṭa) of four yoginīs, elaborating internal esoteric physiology, maṇḍala structures, mantras, and yogic meditation. According to its colophon, the text was extracted by King Indrabhūti from a 12,000-verse Mahāyoginītantra originating in Oḍḍiyāna.
SA_K12_Āgama_Caturyoginīsampuṭa.attribution: A revealed Yoginītantra canonically preserved in the Kanjur (Tōhoku 376). The Sanskrit and Tibetan colophons state that the text was extracted from an extensive 12,000-verse Mahāyoginītantra of Oḍḍiyāna and publicized by Indrabhūti (śrī-oḍiyānavinirgatamahāyoginītantradvādaśasahasrād uddhṛtya ... śrī-indrabhūtipādāna kṛti prakāśitam).
SA_K12_Āgama_Caturyoginīsampuṭa.edition: Unpublished working edition and transcription by Péter-Dániel Szántó (Oxford, Summer 2012), based on the Tucci collection Sanskrit manuscript (folder 42) with parallel Tibetan text from the Degé Kanjur (Tōh. 376, rgyud, ga, 44v6–52v5).
SA_K12_Āgama_Caturyoginīsampuṭa.coverage: complete — Complete tantra in ca. 200 verses (noted as ślokaśatadvayam at line 574) with interlinear Tibetan translation, concluding with the final colophons.
translations: rnal 'byor ma bzhi'i kha sbyor gyi rgyud ces bya ba (Derge Kangyur D 376): translated by chings yon tan 'bar; revised by Agniveśa (Tibetan)

SA_K12_Āgama_Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra-ch26-.title: Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra (chapters 26–32)
SA_K12_Āgama_Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra-ch26-.summary: The Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra (also known as Ekallavīratantra) is an Anuttarayoga/Yoginītantra focused on the wrathful deity Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa (Acala) and his consort Dveṣaratī. While the standard canonical recension (witnessed in Nepalese Sanskrit manuscripts and the Tibetan bKa' 'gyur, Tōh. 431) has 25 chapters, this e-text contains chapters 26–32 found in NGMPP manuscript A 136/5. These supplementary chapters consist largely of borrowed material parallel to chapters 8–14 of the Kṛṣṇayamāritantra (and related texts), treating homa rites, vetālasādhana, and various samaya observances.
SA_K12_Āgama_Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra-ch26-.attribution: Canonical Buddhist Yoginītantra. Chapters 26–32 represent an extended recension attested uniquely in NGMPP manuscript A 136/5, whereas the standard recension translated into Tibetan (Tōh. 431) has 25 chapters.
SA_K12_Āgama_Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra-ch26-.edition: Unpublished manuscript transcription by Péter-Dániel Szántó based on NGMPP manuscript A 136/5.
SA_K12_Āgama_Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra-ch26-.coverage: partial — Chapters 26–32 from an extended recension preserved in NGMPP manuscript A 136/5.
translations: Christopher S. George, The Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa Tantra, Chapters I–VIII: A Critical Edition and English Translation, American Oriental Series 56, New Haven: American Oriental Society, 1974. (English)

dpal gtum po khro bo chen po'i rgyud kyi rgyal po dpa' bo gcig pa zhes bya ba (Derge Kangyur D 431): translated by Ratnaśrījñāna, yar lung lo tsA ba grags pa rgyal mtshan; at dpal ldan sa skya'i gtsug lag khang chen po (Tibetan)

SA_K12_Āgama_Dhvajāgrakeyūrādhāraṇī.title: Dhvajāgrakeyūrādhāraṇī
SA_K12_Āgama_Dhvajāgrakeyūrādhāraṇī.summary: The Dhvajāgrakeyūrādhāraṇī is an apotropaic Buddhist protective scripture set in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven. When Śakra and the thirty-three gods are defeated in battle by the asura king Vemacitrin, the Buddha teaches this aparājitā dhāraṇī—personified as the multi-armed, fierce goddess Dhvajāgrakeyūrā ('Armband on the Tip of the Banner')—which he had received from the Buddha Aparājitadhvaja in a past life. Tying the dhāraṇī to the crest of a battle standard or wearing it around the neck is stated to rout enemy armies and protect against all dangers.
SA_K12_Āgama_Dhvajāgrakeyūrādhāraṇī.attribution: Canonical Buddhist scripture (dhāraṇī / kriyātantra), traditionally presented as spoken by the Buddha to Śakra in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
SA_K12_Āgama_Dhvajāgrakeyūrādhāraṇī.edition: Paolo Giunta, “The Āryadhvajāgrakeyūrā nāma dhāriṇī. Diplomatic Edition of MS Tucci 3.2.16,” in: Sanskrit Texts from Giuseppe Tucci's Collection, edited by Francesco Sferra (Roma: Istituto Italiano per l’Africa e l’Oriente, 2008), pp. 187–194.
SA_K12_Āgama_Dhvajāgrakeyūrādhāraṇī.coverage: incomplete — Text of the dhāraṇī according to MS Tucci 3.2.16.
translations: phags pa rgyal mtshan gyi rtse mo'i dpung rgyan ces bya ba'i gzungs (Derge Kangyur D 612): translated by Jinamitra, Dānaśīla, sna nam btsun pa ye shes sde (Tibetan)
phags pa rgyal mtshan gyi rtse mo'i dpung rgyan ces bya ba'i gzungs (Derge Kangyur D 923): translated by Jinamitra, Dānaśīla, sna nam btsun pa ye shes sde (Tibetan)

SA_K12_Āgama_Ekajaṭākalpa.title: Ekajaṭākalpa (beginning missing)
SA_K12_Āgama_Ekajaṭākalpa.summary: A ritual manual (kalpa) of the fierce goddess Ekajaṭā ('she of the single matted lock'), here linked with Avalokiteśvara and Tārā. The surviving text gives instructions for drawing a maṇḍala with the Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, Tārā and Ekajaṭā and the mantras for summoning them, the painting of a cloth image (paṭa), rites of subjugation and harmful rites, followed by limb mantras and mantras for Ekajaṭā's attendants (ceṭī). It survives here in a single Nepalese paper manuscript copied in 1629 CE.
SA_K12_Āgama_Ekajaṭākalpa.edition: Unpublished diplomatic transcription and working edition prepared by Péter-Dániel Szántó (Budapest, February 2014) from Kathmandu, Kaiser Library MS 742 (NGMPP reel C 73/6; paper, Newari script, ff. 14, copied in NS 749 / 1629 CE by Vajrācārya Candradeva of Guṇadevavihāra).
SA_K12_Āgama_Ekajaṭākalpa.coverage: partial — Single manuscript, ff. 2r–14v; f. 1 is lost, so the opening is missing and the e-text begins '…tha pañcamyāṃ tathāṣṭamyāṃ caturdaśyāṃ'. Otherwise continuous up to the final colophon 'bhagavatyāryaikajaṭyāḥ kalpaḥ samāptam' and the scribal colophon (NS 749).

SA_K12_Āgama_Kurukullākalpa.title: Kurukullākalpa
SA_K12_Āgama_Kurukullākalpa.summary: The Kurukullākalpa is a tantric ritual manual in eight kalpas devoted to Kurukullā. It presents itself as taught by Avalokiteśvara on Mount Potalaka and as extracted from a Tārodbhava / Tārārṇava tantra. It covers the painting and consecration of her cloth image (paṭa), visualisation (abhisamaya), bodhicitta, and various rites. A Tibetan translation is in the Kangyur (D 437 / Toh 437, translated by Kṛṣṇa-paṇḍita and Tshul-khrims rgyal-ba).
SA_K12_Āgama_Kurukullākalpa.attribution: Canonical Buddhist tantra presented as an exposition by Avalokiteśvara on Mount Potalaka; the text's opening and closing verses state that it was extracted from the Tārodbhava section of the Tārārṇavamahāyogatantra.
SA_K12_Āgama_Kurukullākalpa.coverage: complete — Eight kalpas, from the opening 'oṃ namo bhagavatyai āryakurukullāyai / naṣṭe gate cāntarhite ca tantre…' to the final colophons 'iti śrībhagavatyāryatārāyāḥ kurukullākalpo ˈṣṭamaḥ samāptaḥ // āryakurukullākalpaḥ samāptaḥ // tārārṇavamahāyogatantrāntaḥpātitārodbhavād uddhṛta iti'.
translations: phags ma sgrol ma ku ru ku l+le'i rtog pa (Derge Kangyur D 437): translated by Kṛṣṇapa, nag 'tsho lo tsA ba tshul khrims rgyal ba (Tibetan)

SA_K12_Āgama_Kālacakrasekaprakriyā.title: Sekaprakriyā
SA_K12_Āgama_Kālacakrasekaprakriyā.summary: The Sekaprakriyā (Toh 365) is a short canonical text on Kālacakra initiation, made up mostly of stanzas also found in the Laghukālacakratantra. Szántó's e-text gives the Sanskrit stanzas with variants from tantra editions and from a Nepalese manuscript, together with the Tibetan translation. It ends with additional ritual material found in Kaiser Library manuscript 139.
SA_K12_Āgama_Kālacakrasekaprakriyā.attribution: A canonical Kālacakra initiation ritual work preserved in the Kanjur (Toh 365, translated by Samantaśrī and Chos rab). It incorporates verses from or shared with chapter 3 of the Laghukālacakratantra along with prose ritual prescriptions.
SA_K12_Āgama_Kālacakrasekaprakriyā.edition: Unpublished working edition by Péter-Dániel Szántó: Sanskrit stanzas collated from the editions of the Laghukālacakratantra (sigla S, B, L) and from Kathmandu, Kaiser Library MS 139, with the Tibetan translation of Toh 365 (Derge Kanjur, rgyud, ka, ff. 146r7–150r7; tr. Samantaśrī and Chos rab) in parallel.
SA_K12_Āgama_Kālacakrasekaprakriyā.coverage: complete — The Sekaprakriyā as translated in Toh 365 is complete: it runs from 'tyaktāveśasya …' (KCLT 3.92) to the Tibetan colophon. After that Szántó adds material found in Kaiser Library 139 (cf. LKCT 4.229 ff.). This appendix breaks off before the end ('% about two more lines missing', with the Tibetan of the missing lines cited).
translations: dbang gi rab tu byed pa (Derge Kangyur D 365): translated by Samantaśrī, rwa chos rab; revised by shong lo tsA ba blo gros brtan pa/ shong blo gros brtan pa (Tibetan)

SA_K12_Āgama_Laghuśamvaratantra.title: Laghuśaṃvaratantra (chapters 1–46)
SA_K12_Āgama_Laghuśamvaratantra.summary: The Laghuśaṃvaratantra (also known as Cakrasaṃvaratantra or Herukābhidhāna) is a root tantra of the Buddhist Yoginītantra class. A substantial portion of the text incorporates verses and parallels from earlier Śaiva scriptures, including the Brahmayāmala/Picumata and the Jayadrathayāmala (Yoginīsaṃcāraprakaraṇa).
SA_K12_Āgama_Laghuśamvaratantra.attribution: Traditional Vajrayāna canonical scripture (mūlatantra) regarded as an anonymous revelation.
SA_K12_Āgama_Laghuśamvaratantra.edition: Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Śrīherukābhidhānam Cakrasaṃvaratantram with the commentary of Bhavabhaṭṭa, Sarnath: CIHTS, 2002 (Rare Buddhist Texts Series 26); and Alexis Sanderson, The Śaiva sources of the Buddhist Tantras of Śaṃvara, Handout 2 and 3, Trinity Term, 1998 (edition based on Baroda MS no. 13290).
SA_K12_Āgama_Laghuśamvaratantra.coverage: partial — Contains chapters (paṭalas) 1 through 46, ending at 46.7 and colophon 'iti śrīherukābhidhāne pañcahakārakarmavidhipaṭalaḥ ṣaṭcālīśatimaḥ'.

SA_K12_Āgama_Mahādaṇḍadhāraṇīśītavatī_Hi.title: Mahādaṇḍadhāraṇīśītavatī
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahādaṇḍadhāraṇīśītavatī_Hi.summary: The Mahādaṇḍadhāraṇīśītavatī (commonly known in later transmission as Mahāśītavatī) is an apotropaic Mahāyāna dhāraṇī scripture, historically counted among the Pañcarakṣā ('Five Protections') group.
