Set at the Śītavana charnel ground in Rājagṛha, where the Buddha's son Rāhula is afflicted by malevolent spirits, grahas, and harmful beasts, the Buddha reveals this protective vidyā/dhāraṇī to ward off all dangers, poisons, illnesses, weapons, and demonic molestations for the fourfold Buddhist assembly.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahādaṇḍadhāraṇīśītavatī_Hi.attribution: A Buddhist apotropaic dhāraṇī-sūtra, traditionally classed among the Pañcarakṣā pentad and preserved as canonical Buddhavacana.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahādaṇḍadhāraṇīśītavatī_Hi.edition: Hidas, Gergely (2017) Mahā-Daṇḍadhāraṇī-Śītavatī: A Buddhist Apotropaic Scripture. In: V. Vergiani, D. Cuneo, C.A. Formigatti (eds.) Indic Manuscript Cultures through the Ages. Material, Textual, and Historical Investigations. De Gruyter, Berlin: 449-486.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahādaṇḍadhāraṇīśītavatī_Hi.coverage: complete — Text of the dhāraṇī scripture across paragraphs [0]–[5]+.
translations: phags pa be con chen po zhes bya ba'i gzungs (Derge Kangyur D 606): translated by Jinamitra, Dānaśīla, sna nam btsun pa ye shes sde (Tibetan)

SA_K12_Āgama_Mahādhāraṇī.title: Mahādhāraṇī
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahādhāraṇī.summary: The Mahādhāraṇī is an apotropaic Mahāyāna dhāraṇī sūtra set in the Jetavana grove at Śrāvasti. The Buddha instructs Ānanda in several sets of protective mantrapadas uttered by millions of past Buddhas, conferring protection from weapons, poison, fire, royal danger, malevolent spirits, and severe fevers, while granting memory of past births (jātismara) and preservation of bodhicitta.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahādhāraṇī.attribution: Anonymous canonical Mahāyāna dhāraṇī sūtra delivered by the Buddha to Ānanda at Śrāvasti.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahādhāraṇī.coverage: complete — Complete transcription of Cambridge University Library MS Add. 1680.8, from the opening nidāna through the mantrapadas and benefits to the concluding colophon.
translations: phags pa gzungs chen po (Derge Kangyur D 529): translated by Jinamitra, Dānaśīla, sna nam btsun pa ye shes sde (Tibetan)
phags pa gzungs chen po (Derge Kangyur D 888): translated by Jinamitra, Dānaśīla, sna nam btsun pa ye shes sde (Tibetan)

SA_K12_Āgama_Mahāmudrātilaka.title: Mahāmudrātilaka
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahāmudrātilaka.summary: The Mahāmudrātilaka ('Ornament of the Great Seal') is a 28-chapter Buddhist Yoginītantra associated with the Hevajra cycle, functioning as an explanatory or continuation scripture (uttaratantra). It covers esoteric yogic disciplines, the internal subtle body (nāḍī, prāṇa), female consorts, nondual realization of mahāmudrā, and various ritual and siddhi practices. The Sanskrit text survives in a unique manuscript preserved in Berlin (Hs. or. 8711).
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahāmudrātilaka.attribution: Revealed Buddhist scripture belonging to the Yoginītantra class, functioning as an explanatory or continuation tantra (uttaratantra) of the Hevajra cycle.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahāmudrātilaka.edition: Péter-Dániel Szántó, unpublished draft critical edition of the Mahāmudrātilaka based on Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin Hs. or. 8711 and the Tibetan translation (Tōh. 420).
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahāmudrātilaka.coverage: complete — Complete in 28 paṭalas, concluding with the colophon of chapter 28 and the scribal colophon of the Berlin manuscript.
translations: dpal phyag rgya chen po'i thig le zhes bya ba rnal 'byor ma chen mo'i rgyud kyi rgyal po'i mnga' bdag (Derge Kangyur D 420): translated by Prajñāśrīgupta, kam kam lo tsA ba chos kyi ye shes, phyug mtshams dgra bcom (Tibetan)

SA_K12_Āgama_Mahāsamājasūtra.title: Mahāsamājasūtra
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahāsamājasūtra.summary: The Mahāsamājasūtra ('Discourse of the Great Assembly') is a canonical discourse of the Sarvāstivāda Dīrghāgama, corresponding to the Pāli Mahāsamaya Sutta (DN 20). Set in the Mahāvana at Kapilavastu, it narrates the congregation of vast hosts of deities, yakṣas, gandharvas, nāgas, and asuras from throughout the cosmos to venerate the Buddha and his sangha of five hundred arhats. Because of its comprehensive catalogue of deities and the concluding defeat of Māra's hosts, the sūtra was traditionally employed as an apotropaic paritta/rakṣā text recited for protection and longevity.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahāsamājasūtra.attribution: Early canonical Buddhist discourse (Āgama) preserved in the Sarvāstivāda Dīrghāgama recension.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahāsamājasūtra.edition: Ernst Waldschmidt, 'Central Asian Sūtra Fragments and their Relations to the Chinese Āgamas', in Heinz Bechert (ed.), Die Sprache der ältesten buddhistischen Überlieferung / The Language of the Earliest Buddhist Tradition (Symposien zur Buddhismusforschung, II), Abhandlungen der Akademie der Wissenschaften in Göttingen, Phil.-Hist. Kl., 3. Folge, Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 1980 (text edition on).
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahāsamājasūtra.coverage: complete — Reconstructed text running from the opening nidāna through sections 1–33, ending with the antaroddāna and final colophon.

SA_K12_Āgama_Mahāvairocanābhisaṃbodhitan.title: Mahāvairocanābhisaṃbodhitantra (fragment)
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahāvairocanābhisaṃbodhitan.summary: A Sanskrit fragment (folio 23r–v) from the Uttaratantra portion of the Mahāvairocanābhisaṃbodhitantra, one of the foundational scriptures of esoteric Buddhism. The passage records teachings spoken by Mahāvairocana to Vajrapāṇi Guhyakādhipati on the mahāsamayāvatāra vow, the nature of bodhicitta as empty and non-dual like space, the five progressive realizations of awakening, and how the mantranaya allows one to achieve samyaksaṃbodhi in this very lifetime.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahāvairocanābhisaṃbodhitan.edition: Junqi Wang, 'A Preliminary Study of a Newly Discovered Sanskrit Manuscript of the Mahāvairocanābhisaṃbodhi', Journal of Indian and Buddhist Studies 70/3 (2022): (64) 1102–(70) 1108.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahāvairocanābhisaṃbodhitan.coverage: fragment — Folio 23 (recto and verso) of a Sanskrit manuscript, preserving a passage from the Uttaratantra section (corresponding to Tibetan D 494, D 255b6–257b2).
translations: Stephen Hodge, The Mahā-Vairocana-Abhisaṃbodhi Tantra: With Buddhaguhya's Commentary (London: RoutledgeCurzon, 2003). (English)

SA_K12_Āgama_Mahāśrīnāmadvādaśaka_Hidas.title: Mahāśrīnāmadvādaśaka
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahāśrīnāmadvādaśaka_Hidas.summary: A short Mahāyāna Buddhist dhāraṇī scripture centered on the twelve auspicious epithets (Lakṣmī, Śrī, Padmamālinī, Dhanādhipati, etc.) and spell formula of the goddess Mahāśrī. Set in Sukhāvatī, where the Buddha addresses Mañjuśrī and Avalokiteśvara, the text promises that knowing, memorizing, reciting, or copying these names will eliminate fear of poverty and bring wealth. Preserved in witnesses DS old1 and DS old2, corresponding to Degé Kangyur D 741 [=1006].
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahāśrīnāmadvādaśaka_Hidas.attribution: Canonical Buddhist dhāraṇī scripture, traditionally presented as spoken by the Buddha in Sukhāvatī to Avalokiteśvara and Mañjuśrī.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mahāśrīnāmadvādaśaka_Hidas.coverage: complete — Contains two witnesses/recensions: 'DS old1' (ending in the mantra: [Mahāśrī-nāma-dhāraṇī]) and 'DS old2' (with nidāna, twelve names, mantra, ritual instructions, phalaśruti).
translations: dpal gyi lha mo'i mtshan bcu gnyis pa (Derge Kangyur D 741): translated by Jinamitra, sna nam btsun pa ye shes sde (Tibetan)
dpal gyi lha mo'i mtshan bcu gnyis pa (Derge Kangyur D 1006): translated by Jinamitra, sna nam btsun pa ye shes sde (Tibetan)

SA_K12_Āgama_Manasvināgarājasūtra.title: Manasvināgarājasūtra (excerpts)
SA_K12_Āgama_Manasvināgarājasūtra.summary: Five excerpts from an early Buddhist protective (rakṣā) text written in Gāndhārī on birch-bark scroll 3 of the Bajaur Collection (datable to c. 1st–2nd century CE). The nāga king Manasvin approaches the Buddha and imparts a protective spell (vidyā/vidyārāja/mantra) guarding forest monks and the fourfold assembly against wild beasts, non-humans, fire, water, weapons, and great poisons (mahāviṣa). It represents the earliest surviving manuscript evidence for Buddhist rakṣā literature and shares close phraseological parallels with the Mahāmāyūrī.
SA_K12_Āgama_Manasvināgarājasūtra.attribution: Anonymous early Buddhist scripture. Reconstructed Sanskritized title *Manasvināgarājasūtra assigned by Ingo Strauch based on context and the role of the nāga king Manasvin.
SA_K12_Āgama_Manasvināgarājasūtra.coverage: excerpt — Contains five specific excerpts (Q1: lines 14–18, Q2: lines 39–42, Q3: lines 46–51, Q4: lines 34–38, Q5: lines 29–30) transcribed from birch-bark scroll 3 of the Bajaur Collection (BajC 3).

SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśriyamūlakalpa.title: Mañjuśriyamūlakalpa
SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśriyamūlakalpa.summary: The Mañjuśriyamūlakalpa is a massive Buddhist scripture traditionally classed as a Kriyātantra, though self-identifying as a Mahāyānavaipulyasūtra. It details rituals, maṇḍala construction, paṭa painting, mudrās, and mantras centered on Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśriyamūlakalpa.attribution: A composite Buddhist tantric scripture presenting itself internally as a Mahāyānavaipulyasūtra belonging to the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha.
SA_K12_Āgama_Mañjuśriyamūlakalpa.coverage: complete — Complete text in 54 chapters (paṭalavisaras), ending with the colophon of chapter 54 (Anuśaṃsāvigarhaṇaprabhāvapaṭalavisara).

SA_K12_Āgama_Māṇibhadradhāraṇī_Hidas.title: Māṇibhadradhāraṇī
SA_K12_Āgama_Māṇibhadradhāraṇī_Hidas.summary: The Māṇibhadradhāraṇī is a short canonical Buddhist protective spell text preserved in Nepalese Dhāraṇīsaṃgraha collections. In Jetavana, the yakṣa general Maṇibhadra approaches the Buddha and imparts his heart-dhāraṇī, promising to follow and provide food, clothes, gold, and wealth to any practitioner who recites it thrice daily. The text concludes with practical instructions (upacāra) for reciting the dhāraṇī 8,000 times while burning bdellium (guggulu) incense on the full moon to obtain a jar of gold.
SA_K12_Āgama_Māṇibhadradhāraṇī_Hidas.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna dhāraṇī spoken by the yakṣa general Maṇibhadra (Māṇibhadra) in the presence of the Buddha.
SA_K12_Āgama_Māṇibhadradhāraṇī_Hidas.edition: Gergely Hidas, 2021 edition (no. 73 in Cambridge University Library Ms. Add. 1326, p. 146).
SA_K12_Āgama_Māṇibhadradhāraṇī_Hidas.coverage: complete — Complete short dhāraṇī-sūtra, including nidāna, dhāraṇī spell, ritual prescription (upacāra), and concluding colophon.

SA_K12_Āgama_Nīlakaṇṭhadhāraṇī.title: Nīlakaṇṭhadhāraṇī (fragment)
SA_K12_Āgama_Nīlakaṇṭhadhāraṇī.summary: The Nīlakaṇṭhadhāraṇī is an incantation invoking Avalokiteśvara with epithets and iconographic attributes adopted from Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava deity imagery, notably Nīlakaṇṭha, Harihara, and Varāhamukha. Its Sanskrit witness was discovered by Stein at Dunhuang (Ch. 0092), written in Brāhmī script with an interlinear Sogdian phonetic transcription. This e-text contains the surviving concluding fragment of that manuscript as edited by Louis de La Vallée Poussin and Robert Gauthiot.
SA_K12_Āgama_Nīlakaṇṭhadhāraṇī.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna dhāraṇī invocation of Avalokiteśvara.
SA_K12_Āgama_Nīlakaṇṭhadhāraṇī.edition: Louis de La Vallée Poussin and Robert Gauthiot, 'XIX. Fragment final de la Nilakanthadharani en brahmi et en transcription sogdienne', Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society 44/3 (1912), pp. 629–645.
SA_K12_Āgama_Nīlakaṇṭhadhāraṇī.coverage: fragment — Final section of the dhāraṇī preserved in British Library manuscript (Stein Ch. 0092), beginning with 'siddhayogīśvara dhuru 2' and concluding with the colophon 'nīlakaṇṭhanāmadhāraṇī samāptā'.
translations: Louis de La Vallée Poussin and Robert Gauthiot, 'Fragment final de la Nilakanthadharani en brahmi et en transcription sogdienne', Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society (1912), pp. 629–645 (French translation). (French)

SA_K12_Āgama_Puṣpakūṭanāmadhāraṇī-testim.title: Puṣpakūṭanāmadhāraṇī (testimonia)
SA_K12_Āgama_Puṣpakūṭanāmadhāraṇī-testim.summary: The Puṣpakūṭanāmadhāraṇī is a canonical scripture (preserved in Tibetan translation as D 516) addressing Siṃhavikrīḍita regarding offerings to a Tathāgata, caitya, or stūpa. This e-text preserves Sanskrit testimonia.
SA_K12_Āgama_Puṣpakūṭanāmadhāraṇī-testim.coverage: fragment — Prose passages preserved as testimonia.

SA_K12_Āgama_Raktayamāritantra-diplomati.title: Raktayamāritantra
SA_K12_Āgama_Raktayamāritantra-diplomati.summary: The Raktayamāritantra is a Buddhist tantric text detailing deity yoga visualizations, maṇḍala construction, homa rituals for pacification and subjugation, protective circles, and esoteric yogic practices including transference and entering another's body (parapurapraveśa).
SA_K12_Āgama_Raktayamāritantra-diplomati.edition: Diplomatic transcription of a 37-folio manuscript of the Raktayamāritantra, prepared by Péter-Dániel Szántó.
SA_K12_Āgama_Raktayamāritantra-diplomati.coverage: complete — Complete transcription of the manuscript running from folio 1a1 to 37b5, ending with the final colophon: 'sarvvatathāgatakāyavākcittaraktayamāritantre parapurapraveśapaṭalaḥ samāptā || śubhaḥ'.

SA_K12_Āgama_Sahasrāvartādhāraṇī.title: Sahasrāvartādhāraṇī
SA_K12_Āgama_Sahasrāvartādhāraṇī.summary: The Sahasrāvartānāmadhāraṇī is a short Mahāyāna dhāraṇī scripture focused on the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, preserved in Sanskrit and Tibetan (D 710 / 930). It opens with salutations to the Three Jewels and Avalokiteśvara, followed by the core dhāraṇī formula and an explanation of its ritual application (upacāra) and spiritual benefits (anuśaṃsā). Recitation is said to eliminate karmic obscurations accumulated over a thousand kalpas, guarantee vision of a thousand Buddhas at death, and ensure rebirth in pure realms.
SA_K12_Āgama_Sahasrāvartādhāraṇī.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna Buddhist dhāraṇī scripture (Tibetan Kangyur, D 710 / D 930).
SA_K12_Āgama_Sahasrāvartādhāraṇī.edition: Gergely Hidas and Péter-Dániel Szántó, prepared for 84000 (D 710 [=930]).
SA_K12_Āgama_Sahasrāvartādhāraṇī.coverage: complete — Complete short dhāraṇī text including opening homage, mantra, ritual instructions (upacāra), and concluding colophon.

SA_K12_Āgama_Sampuṭatilaka.title: Sampuṭatilaka
SA_K12_Āgama_Sampuṭatilaka.summary: The Sampuṭatilaka is an explanatory tantra (vyākhyātantra) belonging to the late Yoginītantra literature (Hevajra-Cakrasaṃvara complex), serving as an exegetical continuation or eleventh chapter to the Sampuṭodbhavatantra. The work treats non-dual gnosis, ritual procedures, deity yoga, subtle body physiology, and hermeneutical principles while quoting and adapting extensively from earlier tantric and śāstric sources. In the Nepalese manuscript tradition, it is routinely transmitted alongside the root Sampuṭodbhava.
SA_K12_Āgama_Sampuṭatilaka.attribution: Revealed scripture (tantra/āgama) traditionally attributed to the Buddha (Vajradhara); Tibetan tradition associates its revelation or introduction into India with the Mahāsiddha Kṛṣṇācārya (Kāṇha).
SA_K12_Āgama_Sampuṭatilaka.edition: Péter-Dániel Szántó, unpublished working critical edition with parallel text from the Lhasa Kangyur, constituted from Wellcome Library ms. (ms. A/W, ff. 144v2–186r6) and Royal Asiatic Society London Hodgson ms. 37 (ms. H, ff. 99r–127v).
SA_K12_Āgama_Sampuṭatilaka.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Sampuṭatilaka accompanied by parallel Tibetan text from the Lhasa Kangyur, from the opening dialogue to the final colophon.
translations: rgyud kyi rgyal po chen po dpal yang dag par sbyor ba'i thig le zhes bya ba (Derge Kangyur D 382): translated by Gayādhara, 'brog mi lo tsA ba shAkya ye shes; revised by 'brog mi lo tsA ba shAkya ye shes (Tibetan)

SA_K12_Āgama_Sampuṭodbhava_84000.title: Sampuṭodbhava
SA_K12_Āgama_Sampuṭodbhava_84000.summary: The Sampuṭodbhava (or Sampuṭatantra) is a Buddhist Yoginītantra consisting of ten chapters (kalpa). Structured as an explanatory tantra (vyākhyātantra), it shares material with the Hevajra and related tantra cycles, presenting maṇḍala rites, consecrations, and subtle-body yoga (nāḍī). It was commented upon and cited by Abhayākaragupta.
SA_K12_Āgama_Sampuṭodbhava_84000.attribution: Anonymous Buddhist scripture (Yoginītantra / vyākhyātantra) framed as the word of the Buddha.
SA_K12_Āgama_Sampuṭodbhava_84000.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all 10 chapters (kalpa), ending with 10.4.21 and the final colophon iti śrīsaṃpuṭodbhavasarvatantranidānamahākalparājo daśamaḥ samāptaḥ.

SA_K12_Āgama_Sarvabuddhasamāyogaḍākinījā.title: Sarvabuddhasamāyogaḍākinījālaśaṃvara
SA_K12_Āgama_Sarvabuddhasamāyogaḍākinījā.summary: The Sarvabuddhasamāyogaḍākinījālaśaṃvara is an early Buddhist tantric scripture in verse, associated with the Yoginītantra tradition. It features teachings attributed to Vajrasattva / Bhagavat.
SA_K12_Āgama_Sarvabuddhasamāyogaḍākinījā.attribution: Canonical Vajrayāna scripture considered the word of the Buddha (specifically proclaimed by Vajrasattva / Bhagavat).
SA_K12_Āgama_Sarvabuddhasamāyogaḍākinījā.coverage: complete — Complete text through the concluding colophon.

SA_K12_Āgama_Sarvakarmāvaraṇaviśodhanīdh.title: Sarvakarmāvaraṇaviśodhanīdhāraṇī
SA_K12_Āgama_Sarvakarmāvaraṇaviśodhanīdh.summary: A brief Buddhist mantrayāna scripture transmitting the Akṣobhya dhāraṇī formula for the purification of karmic obscurations (sarvakarmāvaraṇaviśodhana). It states that merely seeing this incantation inscribed upon a wall purifies even the severe karmic consequences of the five heinous sins (pañcānantarya).
SA_K12_Āgama_Sarvakarmāvaraṇaviśodhanīdh.attribution: Canonical Buddhist scripture preserved in the Tibetan Kangyur (D 743 / D 1009).
SA_K12_Āgama_Sarvakarmāvaraṇaviśodhanīdh.edition: Unpublished diplomatic transcription by Péter-Dániel Szántó based on Cambridge University Library Ms. Add. 1680.8.3.
SA_K12_Āgama_Sarvakarmāvaraṇaviśodhanīdh.coverage: complete — Complete short dhāraṇī consisting of the homage to Akṣobhya, the mantra, and the phalaśruti ending with 'pañcānantaryāṇi parikṣayaṃ [explicit]'.

'phags pa las kyi sgrib pa thams cad rnam par sbyong ba zhes bya ba'i guz+ng+sa (Derge Kangyur D 1009) (Tibetan)

SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch11.title: Saṃvarodayatantra (chapter 11)
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch11.summary: Chapter 11 of the Saṃvarodayatantra, entitled Mantrajāpaniyamanirdeśapaṭala, outlines the rules and rites for mantra recitation (jāpa) and oblations (homa). It specifies the secluded settings (mountain caves, seashores, crossroads, cremation grounds), maṇḍala construction, and repetition counts for mantras dedicated to Heruka, the four Yoginīs (Ḍākinī, Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, Rūpiṇī), and related deities for achieving mundane and supramundane spiritual attainments (siddhi).
translations: Tsuda, S. (Trans.). The Saṃvarodaya Tantra. Selected Chapters. Tokyo: The Hokuseido Press, 1974. (English)

SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch12.title: Saṃvarodayatantra (chapter 12)
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch12.summary: The twelfth chapter of the Saṃvarodayatantra, titled Mantrajāpākṣamālānirdeśapaṭala ('Instruction on the Rosary for Mantra Recitation'). It details the bead materials, counts, and string fibers required for rosaries (akṣamālā) used in pacifying (śāntika), enriching (pauṣṭika), subjugating (vaśya), and destructive/sorcery (abhicāra) rituals, along with the fingers to be used and multiplier formulas across the four yugas.

SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch14.title: Saṃvarodayatantra (chapter 14)
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch14.summary: Chapter 14 of the Saṃvarodayatantra, titled Vajrayoginīpūjāvidhinirdeśapaṭala, sets forth the ritual worship of Vajrayoginī and the external yoginīs. It prescribes preliminary worship (pūrvasevā), offerings, and various signs indicating success (siddhi) or ritual fault.
translations: Tsuda, S. (Trans.). The Saṃvarodaya Tantra. Selected Chapters. Tokyo: The Hokuseido Press, 1974. (English)

SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch15.title: Saṃvarodayatantra (chapter 15)
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch15.summary: Chapter 15 of the Saṃvarodayatantra, titled Pātralakṣaṇanirdeśapaṭala ('Instruction on the Characteristics of the Vessel'). It systematically classifies ritual vessels (especially skull-cups / kapāla, as well as metallic, wooden, and earthen vessels), their marks, material components, subdivisions, and their esoteric efficacy in tantric sādhanas.
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch15.coverage: partial — Contains only Chapter 15 (Pātralakṣaṇanirdeśapaṭala, dealing with the characteristics of the ritual vessel/skull-cup), preserved here in a critical draft with variant readings from Sanskrit manuscripts, Ratnarakṣita's commentary, and Tibetan canonical verses.

SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch16.title: Saṃvarodayatantra (chapter 16)
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch16.summary: Chapter 16 of the Saṃvarodayatantra, titled Pañcāmṛtasādhanavidhinirdeśapaṭala, sets forth the esoteric compounding and ritual utilization of the five ambrosias (pañcāmṛta) and five lights/meats (pañcapradīpa). It instructs on procuring substances in connection with female consorts of the Buddha families, shaping them into medicinal rejuvenation pills (guṭikā) for rasāyana, and offering them within the gaṇacakra assembly to obtain the siddhi of Khecarī (khecarīpada).
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch16.attribution: Canonical Buddhist tantra, traditionally regarded as revealed scripture.
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch16.edition: Transcription by Péter-Dániel Szántó; based on Royal Asiatic Society, London, MS Hodgson 38, fols. 42r5–43r1, with editorial conjectures and reference to Ratnarakṣita's Padminī.

SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch1.title: Saṃvarodayatantra (chapter 1)
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch1.summary: Chapter 1 (Adhyeṣaṇāpaṭala) of the Saṃvarodayatantra serves as the solicitation wherein Vajrapāṇi requests the Bhagavān to expound the teaching.
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch1.edition: Transcription by Péter-Dániel Szántó; based ultimately on the published critical edition of Shinichi Tsuda (1974).
translations: Shinichi Tsuda, The Saṃvarodaya-Tantra: Selected Chapters, Tokyo: The Hokuseido Press, 1974. (English)

SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch20.title: Saṃvarodayatantra (chapter 20)
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch20.summary: Chapter 20 (Caturyuganirdeśapaṭala) of the Saṃvarodayatantra, an explanatory tantra (vyākhyātantra) belonging to the Cakrasaṃvara cycle. In ten verses, the chapter outlines the duration of the four cosmic ages (yugas: kṛta, tretā, dvāpara, and kali) and their transitional sandhis, followed by an enumeration of the four major continents (Pūrvavideha, Uttarakuru, Aparagodānīya, and Jambūdvīpa), designating Jambūdvīpa as the supreme realm for spiritual attainment and liberation (siddhibhūmi).

SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch22.title: Saṃvarodayatantra (chapter 22)
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch22.summary: Chapter 22 (Devatāpratiṣṭhāvidhipaṭala) of the Saṃvarodayatantra. It opens with figures for the size of scriptural corpora (yogatantras, yoginītantras, Mahāyāna sūtras, pāramitānaya, vinayapiṭaka) and sets out the rite for consecrating (pratiṣṭhā) images: purifying the ground, bathing, opening the eyes, and ritual offerings.
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch22.attribution: A Buddhist tantric text, traditionally regarded as canonical Buddhavacana / Āgama.
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch22.coverage: partial — Only chapter 22 (vv. 22.1–22.22 with colophon 'iti devatāpratiṣṭhāvidhipaṭalo dvāviṃśatimaḥ'). Title given in text header: 'tantrādipramāṇa/pratiṣṭhā'.

SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch24.title: Saṃvarodayatantra (chapter 24)
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch24.summary: Chapter 24 of the Saṃvarodayatantra, titled 'karmaprasara oṣadhiprayoganirdeśapaṭala', contains instructions and mantras for various ritual acts (karmaprasara) and medicinal/herbal applications (oṣadhiprayoga).
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch24.edition: Manuscript transcription of Tokyo University Library, Matsunami catalogue no. 404, fols. 66r3–72r1 by Péter-Dániel Szántó.
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch24.coverage: partial — Chapter 24 (verses 24.1–24.24, concluding with 'iti karmaprasara oṣadhiprayoganirdeśapaṭalaś caturviṃśatimaḥ').
translations: dpal bde mchog 'byung ba zhes bya ba'i rgyud kyi rgyal po chen po (Derge Kangyur D 373): translated by *Parahitānanta, rgyus smon lam grags; revised by 'gos lo tsA ba gzhon nu dpal (Tibetan)

SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch25_Yama.title: Saṃvarodayatantra (chapter 25)
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch25_Yama.summary: Chapter 25 of the Saṃvarodayatantra, entitled Rasāyanavidhipaṭala, expounds alchemical and rejuvenative practices (rasāyana). It describes ingredients such as musk, camphor, and herbal concoctions, instructions on solitary retreat and deity propitiation, and the physical benefits and siddhis achieved through prolonged practice.
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch25_Yama.edition: Chieko Yamano, The Chisan Gakuho/Journal of Chisan Studies, March 2006, pp. 73-86.
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch25_Yama.coverage: partial — Contains chapter 25 (iti rasāyanavidhipaṭalaḥ pañcaviṃśatitamaḥ, 28 verses).

SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch27.title: Saṃvarodayatantra (chapter 27)
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch27.summary: Chapter 27 (Mantroddhāravidhipaṭala) of the Saṃvarodayatantra expounds the systematic extraction and encryption/decryption of root and heart mantras using a 49-square matrix (ūnapañcāśatkoṣṭha), concluding with essential samaya precepts and guru devotion. This chapter was omitted from Shinichi Tsuda's 1974 edition of selected chapters.
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch27.attribution: Revealed scripture of the Cakrasaṃvara / Heruka cycle of the Yoginītantra class, traditionally regarded as an explanatory tantra (vyākhyātantra) of the Laghusaṃvara.
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch27.edition: Diplomatic manuscript transcription by Péter-Dániel Szántó from Tokyo University Library MS Matsunami no. 404, ff. 79r5ff.
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch27.coverage: partial — Contains chapter 27 (Mantroddhāravidhipaṭala) from fol. 79r5 to the chapter colophon.
translations: dpal bde mchog 'byung ba zhes bya ba'i rgyud kyi rgyal po chen po (Derge Kangyur D 373): translated by *Parahitānanta, rgyus smon lam grags; revised by 'gos lo tsA ba gzhon nu dpal (Tibetan)

SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch29_Tsud.title: Saṃvarodayatantra (chapter 29: Tattvanirdeśa)
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch29_Tsud.summary: Chapter 29 of the Saṃvarodayatantra (Tattvanirdeśapaṭala, 'Teaching on Reality') is a short contemplative chapter expounding the ultimate nature of reality in the Cakrasaṃvara/Heruka tradition. It teaches that true reality is innate bliss (sahajānanda), beyond dualistic conceptualization, and directly accessible through self-awareness (svasaṃvedana). The chapter internalizes the tantric mandala and ritual pantheon, equating all bodily channels (nāḍī) with ḍākinīs and all phenomenal appearances with the supreme Heruka form.
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch29_Tsud.edition: Shinichi Tsuda, '"Tattva-nirdeśa-paṭala" of the Saṃvarodaya-tantra: Sanskrit Text and a Japanese Translation', Bukkyo-Gaku (Journal of Buddhist Studies), Vol. 1, July 1976, pp. 27–45.
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch29_Tsud.coverage: partial — Complete text of Chapter 29 (Tattvanirdeśapaṭala), comprising 17 verses and 1 prose passage.
translations: Shinichi Tsuda, '"Tattva-nirdeśa-paṭala" of the Saṃvarodaya-tantra: Sanskrit Text and a Japanese Translation', Bukkyo-Gaku (Journal of Buddhist Studies), Vol. 1, July 1976, pp. 27–45. (Japanese)

SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch30_Cicu.title: Saṃvarodayatantra (chapter 30)
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch30_Cicu.summary: Chapter 30 of the Saṃvarodayatantra, titled Citrādirūpalakṣaṇanirdeśapaṭala ('Teaching on the characteristics of painted and sculpted divine forms'), details the iconometry (tālamāna), proportions, bodily stances, and major artistic defects (mahādoṣa) to be avoided when painting deities onto cloth (paṭa).
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch30_Cicu.edition: Claudio Cicuzza, 'Il capitolo XXX del Saṃvarodayatantra', in: Le parole e i marmi: Studi in onore di Raniero Gnoli nel suo 70° compleanno, ed. Raffaele Torella et al., Serie Orientale Roma 92 (Rome: Istituto Italiano per l'Africa e l'Oriente, 2001), pp. 213–228 (text on pp. 216–225).

SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch32.title: Saṃvarodayatantra (chapter 32)
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch32.summary: Chapter 32 (Balyupahāranirdeśapaṭala) of the Saṃvarodayatantra expounds the ritual procedures of bali offerings (balitattva), detailing preliminary visualization of the two-armed Saṃvara, the purification and transformation of the offering into the five ambrosias and lights within a vessel, the invocation and propitiation of directional protectors and ḍākinīs, recitation of bali mantras, and the final offering of leftovers (ucchiṣṭabali).
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch32.attribution: Canonical Buddhist tantra belonging to the Saṃvara cycle.
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch32.edition: Péter-Dániel Szántó, edition based on Tokyo University Library MS Matsunami no. 404, fols. 95v5–100r1.
SA_K12_Āgama_Saṃvarodayatantra-ch32.coverage: partial — Chapter 32 (Balyupahāranirdeśapaṭala, vv. 32.1–32.23 with interspersed ritual prose).

SA_K12_Āgama_Sumukhā.title: Sumukhadhāraṇī (fragments)
SA_K12_Āgama_Sumukhā.summary: The Sumukhadhāraṇī ('Dhāraṇī of the Auspicious Entrance', Toh 614/915) is a Buddhist protective text in which the Buddha and Vajrapāṇi, followed by protective figures, pronounce dhāraṇī-formulas to safeguard practitioners. Survives in Sanskrit manuscript fragments from Central Asia as well as Tibetan, Chinese, and Khotanese translations. This e-text provides a standardized composite transcription by Péter-Dániel Szántó of five published Sanskrit fragments.
SA_K12_Āgama_Sumukhā.attribution: Canonical Mahāyāna/proto-Vajrayāna dhāraṇī sūtra, traditionally presented as spoken by the Buddha and Vajrapāṇi.
SA_K12_Āgama_Sumukhā.edition: Péter-Dániel Szántó, composite electronic transcription and standardization of five Sanskrit fragments of the Sumukhadhāraṇī (Budapest, 2026, working e-text based on Bongard-Levin et al. and Emmerick).
SA_K12_Āgama_Sumukhā.coverage: fragment — Compilation of five Central Asian Sanskrit manuscript fragments representing disjointed sections of the text.
translations: Hù mìng fǎ mén shén zhòu jīng 護命法門神呪經 (Chinese)
Sumukhasūtra (Saka / Khotanese version). (Khotanese)

SA_K12_Āgama_Surūpādhāraṇī.title: Surūpādhāraṇī
SA_K12_Āgama_Surūpādhāraṇī.summary: The Surūpādhāraṇī (or Surūpānāmadhāraṇī) is a brief Mahāyāna dhāraṇī scripture centered on the Tathāgata Surūpa. It provides an incantation and ritual procedure for empowering food mixed with water and offering it to pretas (hungry ghosts) in a secluded spot, multiplying the offering so as to satiate all pretas across worlds. In return, the practitioner is promised strength, wealth, long life, and eventual rebirth in Sukhāvatī.
SA_K12_Āgama_Surūpādhāraṇī.attribution: Canonical Buddhist dhāraṇī; anonymous scriptural transmission preserved in the Tibetan Kangyur (D 540 / D 1078).
SA_K12_Āgama_Surūpādhāraṇī.coverage: complete — Complete text of the short dhāraṇī, comprising the homage to Tathāgata Surūpa, the mantra, the food-offering rite to pretas, and the phalaśruti colophon.

SA_K12_Āgama_Uṣṇīṣavijayādhāraṇī_Yuyama.title: Uṣṇīṣavijayādhāraṇī (dhāraṇī proper only)
SA_K12_Āgama_Uṣṇīṣavijayādhāraṇī_Yuyama.summary: The Uṣṇīṣavijayādhāraṇī is one of the most widely diffused Buddhist dhāraṇīs, recited to purify bad karma, avert rebirth in evil destinies and prolong life; it was translated into Chinese repeatedly and was inscribed on pillars and stūpas across East Asia. This e-text contains only the spell itself in two East Asian transmissions as reconstructed by Akira Yuyama (2006): Amoghavajra's Dunhuang transcription and a Siddhaṃ-script version attributed to Kūkai.
SA_K12_Āgama_Uṣṇīṣavijayādhāraṇī_Yuyama.attribution: Canonical Buddhist dhāraṇī. The e-text preserves two East Asian transmissions edited by Akira Yuyama: Amoghavajra's Chinese phonogram recension recovered from Dunhuang, and a Siddhaṃ-script recension traditionally attributed to Kūkai.
SA_K12_Āgama_Uṣṇīṣavijayādhāraṇī_Yuyama.edition: Akira Yuyama, 'Amoghavajra's Uṣṇīṣa-Vijayā Dhāraṇī from Tunhuang', Annual Report of the International Research Institute for Advanced Buddhology at Soka University, 2006, pp. 231–276; e-text = Text IB (p. 244) and Text IIIB (pp. 262–266).
SA_K12_Āgama_Uṣṇīṣavijayādhāraṇī_Yuyama.coverage: partial — Only the dhāraṇī formula (namo bhagavate trailokyaprativiśiṣṭāya ... svāhā), given twice: Yuyama's reconstructed text of Amoghavajra's Dunhuang transcription (Text IB, p. 244) and the Siddhaṃ-script version attributed to Kūkai (Text IIIB, pp. 262–266, with the inserted homages to the seven Buddhas and Avalokiteśvara). The narrative frame (nidāna) and ritual instructions (kalpa) of the full dhāraṇī-sūtra are absent, as are the other sections of Yuyama's article (Chinese phonograms, other text versions). About 2,600 characters.

SA_K12_Āgama_Vajravidāraṇādhāraṇī.title: Vajravidāraṇādhāraṇī
SA_K12_Āgama_Vajravidāraṇādhāraṇī.summary: The Vajravidāraṇādhāraṇī is an influential Buddhist apotropaic dhāraṇī associated with the Kriyātantra class. Spoken by the yakṣa commander Vajrapāṇi under the inspiration of all Buddhas, the text proclaims an adamantine spell (vajrasāra) intended to dispel hostile spirits (graha, bhūta), neutralize spells, pacify illnesses, and cleanse pollutions. It concludes with an apotropaic royal lustration liturgy (snāna) using a gold or silver pitcher infused with gems, mustard seeds, and sandalwood.
SA_K12_Āgama_Vajravidāraṇādhāraṇī.attribution: Canonical Buddhist dhāraṇī / Kriyātantra scripture spoken by Vajrapāṇi through the anubhāva of all Buddhas.
SA_K12_Āgama_Vajravidāraṇādhāraṇī.edition: Ngawang Samten and Janardan Pandey, eds., 'Āryavajravidāraṇā Nāma Dhāraṇī', Dhīḥ: Journal of Rare Buddhist Texts Research Unit 40 (2005), pp. 161–164.
SA_K12_Āgama_Vajravidāraṇādhāraṇī.coverage: complete — Complete text of the dhāraṇī from the nidāna (evaṃ mayā śrutam ...) to the closing royal bathing verses and colophon (āryavajravidāraṇā nāma dhāraṇī samāptā).

SA_K12_Āgama_Vajraḍākatantra-selected-ch.title: Vajraḍākatantra (selected chapters)
SA_K12_Āgama_Vajraḍākatantra-selected-ch.summary: The Vajraḍākatantra (Vajraḍākamahātantrarāja) is a major Yoginītantra of the Cakrasaṃvara/Ḍāka cycle, surviving in Sanskrit palm-leaf manuscripts and Tibetan translation. The text hypostatises Vajraḍāka as the supreme self-arisen Bhagavān embodying all ḍākinīs (sarvaḍākinīmaya), expounding maṇḍala construction, secret code language and sign language (chomā), ritual hand-gestures, cremation-ground practices, subtle yogic physiology, and extensive fire oblations (homa). This digital text collects critical editions of selected chapters edited by Tsunehiko Sugiki.
SA_K12_Āgama_Vajraḍākatantra-selected-ch.attribution: Canonical Buddhist Yoginītantra (revealed scripture / Āgama), traditionally framed as the teaching of Bhagavān Vajrasattva / Vajraḍāka.
SA_K12_Āgama_Vajraḍākatantra-selected-ch.edition: Composite of critical editions of selected chapters by Tsunehiko Sugiki, including: 'A Critical Study of The Vajraḍākamahātantrarāja (I) — Chapter. 1 and 42. —', The Chisan Gakuho / Journal of Chisan Studies 65 (2002); and 'Examples of the Subtle Yoga in the Vajraḍākatantra ― Critical Editions of the Vajraḍākatantra Chapters 11 and 15', WIAS Research Bulletin 8 (2016).
SA_K12_Āgama_Vajraḍākatantra-selected-ch.coverage: partial — Selected chapters from the tantra, including chapters 1, 8, 11, 13, 18, 19, 22, 44, and 48, with parallel Tibetan lines in chapters 19 and 48.

SA_K12_Āgama_Vajrāmṛtatantra.title: Vajrāmṛtatantra (fragment)
SA_K12_Āgama_Vajrāmṛtatantra.summary: The Vajrāmṛtamahātantra is an early Buddhist tantra surviving fragmentarily in Sanskrit (in a Cambridge University Library manuscript dated saṃvat 282), presented as an esoteric dialogue between Bhagavān Vajrin and the goddess Māmakī. It covers maṇḍala layout, homa rites, mantras, and practices centered on the deity Vajrāmṛta. This e-text reproduces Francesco Sferra's edition of the Cambridge manuscript, supplemented by lemmata and glosses from Śrībhānu's commentary.
SA_K12_Āgama_Vajrāmṛtatantra.attribution: Canonical Buddhist tantra framed as an esoteric discourse of Bhagavān Vajrin to the goddess Māmakī; commentary glosses marked '% Śrībhānu' are taken from Śrībhānu's commentary.
SA_K12_Āgama_Vajrāmṛtatantra.coverage: fragment — Preserves the text extant in CUL ms. (covering chapters 1–11 fragmentarily, chapter 4 partially restored from Sādhanamālā 180; concludes at chapter 11 with colophon dated saṃvat 282).
translations: rdo rje bdud rtsi'i rgyud (Derge Kangyur D 435): translated by gyi jo zla ba'i 'od zer (Tibetan)

SA_K12_Āgama_Vajrārallitantra-testimonia.title: Vajrāralimahātantra (testimonia)
SA_K12_Āgama_Vajrārallitantra-testimonia.summary: The Vajrāralimahātantra (also spelled Vajrārallī-) is an esoteric Buddhist Yoginītantra belonging to the Heruka/Saṃvara cycle, focusing on wrathful Heruka/Vajrārali practices and fierce yoginī rituals. The complete Sanskrit original is lost as an independent manuscript, surviving primarily in its Tibetan translation and as scattered citations in Sanskrit commentaries. This digital text presents the complete Tibetan Kanjur translation alongside Sanskrit testimonia gathered from surviving citations.
SA_K12_Āgama_Vajrārallitantra-testimonia.attribution: A scriptural Yoginītantra translated into Tibetan by the Indian paṇḍita Kāyasthapa Gayadhara and the Tibetan translator ['Brog mi] Shākya ye shes.
SA_K12_Āgama_Vajrārallitantra-testimonia.edition: Péter-Dániel Szántó, unpublished working transcription and testimonia collection (Budapest, summer 2008), based on the Tibetan Derge Kanjur (Tōh. 426, rgyud, nga, fols. 171r2–176r2), collated with the Peking Kanjur (Ōtani 65, rgyud, nga, fols. 157a–162a), with sub-chapter headings from Bu-ston's synopsis and Sanskrit testimonia added.
SA_K12_Āgama_Vajrārallitantra-testimonia.coverage: partial — Contains the complete Tibetan canonical text in 10 chapters (Derge fols. 171r2–176r2), but Sanskrit is represented only by partial/fragmentary testimonia recovered from citations.
translations: rdo rje A ra li zhes bya ba'i rgyud kyi rgyal po chen po (Derge Kangyur D 426): translated by Gayādhara, 'brog mi lo tsA ba shAkya ye shes (Tibetan)

SA_K12_Āgama_Vasudhārādhāraṇī-NAK-1-1076.title: Vasudhārādhāraṇī (fragment)
SA_K12_Āgama_Vasudhārādhāraṇī-NAK-1-1076.summary: The Vasudhārādhāraṇī is the dhāraṇī of Vasudhārā, used also by Jains. In the frame story the householder Sucandra asks the Buddha how the poor can become wealthy and the sick healthy, and is taught the dhāraṇī with its recitation rules and benefits. This e-text is Péter-Dániel Szántó's diplomatic transcription of nine disordered palm-leaf folios from Kathmandu (NAK 1-1076), which according to Szántó represent a recension differing from Jaini's edition and from the Tibetan Toh 662.
SA_K12_Āgama_Vasudhārādhāraṇī-NAK-1-1076.attribution: Traditional Mahāyāna Buddhist canonical scripture (dhāraṇī-sūtra) presenting teachings attributed to Śākyamuni Buddha.
SA_K12_Āgama_Vasudhārādhāraṇī-NAK-1-1076.edition: Unpublished diplomatic transcription of National Archives Kathmandu MS 1-1076 (NGMPP reel A 39/8; 9 fols., 33×4 cm, palm-leaf, catalogued as 'Bauddhagranthasya prakīrṇapattāni') by Péter-Dániel Szántó, Oxford, Michaelmas 2008.
SA_K12_Āgama_Vasudhārādhāraṇī-NAK-1-1076.coverage: fragment — Diplomatic transcription of 9 unnumbered, out-of-sequence palm-leaf folios (NAK 1-1076). The folios contain parts of the nidāna (Sucandra's question to the Buddha), the dhāraṇī and the mantrapadas with benefits; the beginning and the end are missing (the text breaks off mid-mantra, no colophon), and the order of the folios is not the order of the work.
translations: 'phags pa nor gyi rgyun ces bya ba'i gzungs (Derge Kangyur D 662) (Tibetan)
'phags pa nor gyi rgyun ces bya ba'i gzungs (Derge Kangyur D 1007) (Tibetan)

SA_K12_Āgama_Yoginījālamahātantra-fragme.title: Yoginījālamahātantra (chapter 26 fragment)
SA_K12_Āgama_Yoginījālamahātantra-fragme.summary: The Yoginījālamahātantra is an esoteric Buddhist Yoginītantra closely related to the Catuṣpīṭhatantra and the wider Saṃvara cycle. This Sanskrit manuscript fragment preserves verses from chapter 26 detailing the necessary qualifications of the vajrācārya, the qualities of an eligible disciple, and preliminary rites of the initiation (abhiṣeka) maṇḍala.
SA_K12_Āgama_Yoginījālamahātantra-fragme.attribution: A Buddhist tantra, canonical scripture (traditionally regarded as buddhavacana / Āgama).
SA_K12_Āgama_Yoginījālamahātantra-fragme.coverage: fragment — Fragment of chapter 26 on the ācārya (|| w/ CP) from manuscript Nep. prov. Takaoka DH 377.

SA_K12_Āgama_Yogāmbaratantra.title: Yogāmbaratantra (chapter 1)
SA_K12_Āgama_Yogāmbaratantra.summary: The Yogāmbaratantra (or Yogāmbaramahātantra) is an Anuttarayoga Buddhist tantra centered on the deity Yogāmbara and his consort Jñānaḍākinī, especially important in Nepalese Newar Buddhism and preserved also in Tibetan transmission. This transcribed first chapter (Vajrasattvasya saṃvegacittaparīkṣāsūtrapaṭala, 129 verses) expounds the non-conceptual realization of ultimate reality and identity with Vajrasattva, drawing on or sharing verses with canonical and scholastic works such as the Bodhicittavivaraṇa, Pañcakrama, and Abhidhānottaratantra.
SA_K12_Āgama_Yogāmbaratantra.attribution: A Buddhist Anuttarayoga tantra belonging to the Ḍākinī / Yoginītantra class, traditionally regarded as canonical revelation (Buddhavacana).
SA_K12_Āgama_Yogāmbaratantra.edition: Diplomatic transcription by Péter-Dániel Szántó (Oxford, late June–July 1, 2010), based on Nepalese manuscript MBB-II-120 (paper, ff. 56 [55]), with occasional variant readings from Nagoya University MS 09.4.
SA_K12_Āgama_Yogāmbaratantra.coverage: partial — Contains only chapter 1 (129 verses), concluding with the colophon 'iti yogāmbaramahātantre vajrasattva... gacittaparikṣāsūtrapaṭalaḥ prathamaḥ' (vv. 1–129). The following sādhana of Jagadānandajīvabhadra in the manuscript was not transcribed.

SA_T01_Candragomin_Deśanāstava.title: Deśanāstava
SA_T01_Candragomin_Deśanāstava.author: Candragomin
SA_T01_Candragomin_Deśanāstava.summary: The Deśanāstava ('Praise of Confession') is a 52-verse Mahāyāna Buddhist stotra composed in classical kāvya meters by Candragomin. Addressing the Buddha as the supreme physician (vaidyarāja), the poet confesses inner mental afflictions and psychological pitfalls encountered in the cultivation of the four immeasurables (apramāṇa) and Bodhisattva perfections. Known through its Tibetan canonical translation (D 1159) along with a commentary (D 1160), the Sanskrit original was published by Liu & Schneider (2022).
SA_T01_Candragomin_Deśanāstava.attribution: Colophon explicitly reads: 'kṛtir iyaṃ candragomipādānām iti'. The attribution is confirmed by the Tibetan Tanjur translation (D 1159) and the commentary (D 1160).
SA_T01_Candragomin_Deśanāstava.coverage: complete — Complete text in 52 verses including opening maṅgala and concluding colophon.
translations: Mark Tatz, Difficult Beginnings: Three Works on the Bodhisattva Path by Candragomin (1978 /. (English)
Michael Hahn, 'A Difficult Beginning: Comments on an English Translation of Candragomin's Deśanāstava' (1993). (English)
bshags pa'i bstod pa (Derge Tengyur D 1159): translated by Śraddhākaravarman, lo chen rin chen bzang po (Tibetan)

SA_T01_Harṣa_Aṣṭamahācaityavandanā.title: Aṣṭamahācaityavandanā
SA_T01_Harṣa_Aṣṭamahācaityavandanā.author: Harṣa
SA_T01_Harṣa_Aṣṭamahācaityavandanā.summary: The Aṣṭamahācaityavandanā (concluding with the colophon title aṣṭamahāsthānacaityavandanā) is a five-verse Sanskrit hymn paying homage to the reliquaries (caitya / dhātugarbha) of the Buddha across sacred pilgrimage places and cosmological realms. Attributed to King Harṣa, it is linked in the headers to Lévi (1894) reconstructing from a Chinese transcription by Fatian, and is preserved in Tibetan as D 1168.
SA_T01_Harṣa_Aṣṭamahācaityavandanā.attribution: Attributed in sources to King Harṣa (King Śrīharṣa / Harṣadeva / Harṣavardhana Śīlāditya of Kanauj).
translations: gnas chen po brgyad kyi mchod rten la phyag 'tshal ba'i bstod pa (Derge Tengyur D 1168): translated by śrījñānamitra, khe'u brgad yon tan dpal (Tibetan)

SA_T01_Harṣa_Mārajitstotra.title: Mārajitstotra
SA_T01_Harṣa_Mārajitstotra.author: Harṣa
SA_T01_Harṣa_Mārajitstotra.summary: The Mārajitstotra ('Praise of the Conqueror of Māra') is a short Buddhist hymn preserved in the Tibetan Tengyur (Toh 1117, Bdud btul ba la bstod pa) under the authorship of Harṣadeva (King Harṣa). The first two stanzas correspond directly to the benedictory opening (nāndī) of Harṣa's Buddhist drama Nāgānanda, while an additional third stanza is extant in Tibetan translation. In 1996, Michael Hahn demonstrated that the Tengyur text reflects an independent stotra transmission derived from the play's prologue.
SA_T01_Harṣa_Mārajitstotra.attribution: Ascribed to King Harṣadeva (Tibetan: Rab dga'i lha) in the Derge Tengyur colophon (Toh 1117). The first two stanzas correspond to the benedictory opening (nāndī) of Harṣa's drama Nāgānanda.
SA_T01_Harṣa_Mārajitstotra.edition: Michael Hahn, 'The *Mārajitstotra by Harṣadeva: A Third Version of the Nāndī of the Nāgānanda?', in: Festschrift für Dieter Schlingloff, ed. Friedrich Wilhelm, Reinbek: Dr. Inge Wezler Verlag für Orientalistische Fachpublikationen, 1996, pp. 109–126.
SA_T01_Harṣa_Mārajitstotra.coverage: complete — Complete text of the stotra as edited in Hahn (1996): 2 Sanskrit verses with Tibetan translation from D 1117, followed by a third stanza preserved only in Tibetan translation.
translations: bdud btul ba la bstod pa (Derge Tengyur D 1117) (Tibetan)

SA_T01_Harṣa_Suprabhātastava.title: Suprabhātastava
SA_T01_Harṣa_Suprabhātastava.author: Harṣa
SA_T01_Harṣa_Suprabhātastava.summary: The Suprabhātastava ('Praise of the Auspicious Dawn') is a 25-verse Buddhist morning hymn attributed to King Harṣa of Kanauj. Employing the recurring refrain 'daśabala tava nityaṃ suprabhātaṃ prabhātam', the poem depicts various Brahmanical gods, sages, and kings as still asleep in worldly slumber and attachment, whereas the Buddha alone is eternally awakened.
SA_T01_Harṣa_Suprabhātastava.attribution: Colophon states 'kṛtir iyaṃ rājñaḥ śrīharṣasya'. Traditionally ascribed to King Śrīharṣa (Harṣadeva / Harṣavardhana of Kanauj); preserved under this attribution in the Tibetan Tengyur (D 1167).
SA_T01_Harṣa_Suprabhātastava.coverage: complete — Complete hymn of 25 stanzas with closing colophon.
translations: Maurice L. Ettinghausen (1906). (French)
rab tu snga bar nam langs pa'i bstod pa (Derge Tengyur D 1167): translated by śrījñānamitra, khe'u brgad yon tan dpal (Tibetan)

SA_T01_Jñānayaśas_Jātakastava.title: Jātakastava
SA_T01_Jñānayaśas_Jātakastava.author: Jñānayaśas
SA_T01_Jñānayaśas_Jātakastava.summary: The Jātakastava ('Praise of the Birth Stories') is a short Sanskrit Buddhist stotra in 20 Sragdharā verses attributed to Ācārya Jñānayaśas. The hymn praises the Buddha through allusions to his heroic and compassionate deeds across previous lives (jātakas), such as the gifts of his head, eyes, tusks, and flesh, and throwing himself into a pit or to a starving tigress. The text is preserved in a Sanskrit manuscript transcribed in Tibetan script with Tibetan glosses, as well as in a canonical Tibetan translation in the Tengyur (Tōh. 1178).
SA_T01_Jñānayaśas_Jātakastava.attribution: Ascribed to Ācārya Jñānayaśas in the concluding colophon and Tibetan Tengyur (Tōh. 1178 / D 1178). Not to be confused with the Khotanese Jātakastava composed/translated by Vedyaśīla in the 10th century.
SA_T01_Jñānayaśas_Jātakastava.edition: D. R. Shackleton Bailey, 'The Jātakastava of Jñānayaśas', in Asiatica: Festschrift Friedrich Weller zum 65. Geburtstag, ed. Johannes Schubert and Ulrich Schneider, Leipzig: Otto Harrassowitz, 1954.
SA_T01_Jñānayaśas_Jātakastava.coverage: complete — Complete hymn of 20 stanzas (in Sragdharā metre) ending with colophon (Js_1 to Js_20).
translations: D. R. Shackleton Bailey, 'The Jātakastava of Jñānayaśas', in Asiatica: Festschrift Friedrich Weller, Leipzig: Otto Harrassowitz, 1954. (English)

SA_T01_Mātṛceṭa_Ekottarikastotra.title: Ekottarikastotra
SA_T01_Mātṛceṭa_Ekottarikastotra.author: Mātṛceṭa
SA_T01_Mātṛceṭa_Ekottarikastotra.summary: The Ekottarikastotra is an 11-verse Buddhist hymn of praise attributed to Mātṛceṭa. Following an ascending numerical framework (ekottarika), verses 1 through 10 honor the Buddha through sequential groupings of qualities, realizations, and abandonments from one to ten, ending with an 11th verse dedicating the resulting merit to the liberation of all sentient beings.
SA_T01_Mātṛceṭa_Ekottarikastotra.attribution: Attributed in the final Sanskrit colophon (kṛtir ācāryamātṛceṭasya) and in the Tibetan Tengyur (Toh 1141 / D 1141) to ācārya Mātṛceṭa (Maticitra).
SA_T01_Mātṛceṭa_Ekottarikastotra.coverage: complete — Complete text in 11 verses (verses 1–10 enumerating qualities from one to ten, verse 11 dedication/praṇidhāna) with final colophon.
translations: gcig las 'phros pa'i bstod pa (Derge Tengyur D 1141): translated by Dharmaśrībhadra, lo chen rin chen bzang po (Tibetan)

SA_T01_Mātṛceṭa_Varṇārhavarṇastotra.title: Varṇārhavarṇastotra
SA_T01_Mātṛceṭa_Varṇārhavarṇastotra.author: Mātṛceṭa
SA_T01_Mātṛceṭa_Varṇārhavarṇastotra.summary: The Varṇārhavarṇastotra is a Buddhist praise poem in thirteen chapters composed by Mātṛceṭa, praising the Buddha. It was edited and translated by Jens-Uwe Hartmann (1987).
SA_T01_Mātṛceṭa_Varṇārhavarṇastotra.edition: Jens-Uwe Hartmann, Das Varṇārhavarṇastotra des Mātṛceṭa (Sanskrittexte aus den Turfanfunden XII; Abhandlungen der Akademie der Wissenschaften in Göttingen, Philologisch-historische Klasse, Dritte Folge, Nr. 160). Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 1987.
SA_T01_Mātṛceṭa_Varṇārhavarṇastotra.coverage: complete — Complete text across 13 chapters as edited by Jens-Uwe Hartmann (1987), interleaved in the e-text with Tibetan and German translations.
translations: Jens-Uwe Hartmann, Das Varṇārhavarṇastotra des Mātṛceṭa, Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 1987. (German)

SA_T01_Mātṛceṭa_Śatapañcāśatka.title: Śatapañcāśatka
SA_T01_Mātṛceṭa_Śatapañcāśatka.author: Mātṛceṭa
SA_T01_Mātṛceṭa_Śatapañcāśatka.summary: The Śatapañcāśatka ('Hymn in One Hundred and Fifty Verses', also titled Prasādapratibhodbhava or Adhyardhaśataka) is a Buddhist devotional poem (stotra) composed by Mātṛceṭa. In 153 verses, the poet praises the extraordinary virtues, limitless compassion, and bodily self-sacrifices of the Buddha during his bodhisattva career. Extensively recited and memorized across ancient Indian monastic institutions as noted by the Chinese pilgrim Yijing, the work was preserved in Central Asian Sanskrit manuscript fragments and the Tibetan and Chinese Buddhist canons.
SA_T01_Mātṛceṭa_Śatapañcāśatka.attribution: Universal attribution across Sanskrit fragments, Tibetan Tanjur catalogs (D 1147), Chinese canon (Taishō 1680), and early external witnesses such as the pilgrim Yijing. The Tibetan translation (D 1147) attributes the work to rta dbyangs (identified as Āryaśūra or Aśvaghoṣa).
SA_T01_Mātṛceṭa_Śatapañcāśatka.edition: D. R. Shackleton Bailey (ed.), The Śatapañcāśatka of Mātṛceṭa: Sanskrit Text, Tibetan Translation and Commentary, and Chinese Translation, with an Introduction, English Translation and Notes. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1951.
SA_T01_Mātṛceṭa_Śatapañcāśatka.coverage: complete — Complete hymn in 153 verses (150 stanzas of praise plus 3 concluding verses).
translations: D. R. Shackleton Bailey, The Śatapañcāśatka of Mātṛceṭa: Sanskrit Text, Tibetan Translation and Commentary, and Chinese Translation, with an Introduction, English Translation and Notes. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1951. (English)
brgya lnga bcu pa zhes bya ba'i bstod pa (Derge Tengyur D 1147): translated by Śraddhākaravarman, shAkya blo gros (Tibetan)

SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Acintyastava.title: Acintyastava
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Acintyastava.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Acintyastava.summary: The Acintyastava ('Praise of the Inconceivable') is a Buddhist philosophical hymn in 59 verses attributed to Nāgārjuna and traditionally included in the Catuḥstava. It praises the Buddha not through conventional anthropomorphic attributes but via the ultimate realization of emptiness (śūnyatā) and dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), showing that conventional phenomena lack intrinsic nature (svabhāva) and are beyond conceptual proliferation. In this e-text, each Sanskrit kārikā is paired with its corresponding Tibetan canonical translation from the Tengyur (D1128).
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Acintyastava.attribution: Widely accepted as an authentic hymn by Nāgārjuna; traditionally included as one of the four hymns of the Catuḥstava.
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Acintyastava.coverage: complete — Complete in 59 verses, with matching Tibetan verses from the Derge Tengyur (D1128) intercalated.
translations: Christian Lindtner, Nagarjuniana: Studies in the Writings and Philosophy of Nāgārjuna (Copenhagen: Akademisk Forlag, 1982). (English)
Hiroki Hachiriki, 'Japanese Translation of Nāgārjuna's Lokātītastava and Acintyastava', 印度哲学仏教学 (1986). (Japanese)
bsam gyis mi khyab par bstod pa (Derge Tengyur D 1128): translated by nag 'tsho lo tsA ba tshul khrims rgyal ba (Tibetan)

SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Dharmadhātustava.title: Dharmadhātustava (verses 1–86)
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Dharmadhātustava.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Dharmadhātustava.summary: A Mahāyāna doctrinal hymn (stotra) traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna, celebrating the dharmadhātu as the fundamentally luminous and pure reality present within all sentient beings. It employs famous tathāgatagarbha similes—such as butter hidden within milk, a fire-purified garment, and a lamp inside an earthen jar—to illustrate how the pristine ground of awakening is obscured by adventitious afflictions (āgantukamala) and revealed on the spiritual path.
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Dharmadhātustava.attribution: Ascribed traditionally to Nāgārjuna. Modern scholars (e.g., Ruegg) discuss its relationship to tathāgatagarbha doctrine.
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Dharmadhātustava.edition: Liu Zhen, The Dharmadhātustava: A Critical Edition of the Sanskrit Text with the Tibetan and Chinese Translations, a Diplomatic Transliteration of the Manuscript and Notes, Beijing: China Tibetology Publishing House / Vienna: Austrian Academy of Sciences Press, 2015; implementing corrections in Kano 2015.
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Dharmadhātustava.coverage: partial — Verses 1–86, the last of them incomplete ('sattvānām alpapuṇyānāṃ bhagavān kiṃ kariṣyati| jātya x x . – – x [deest] || <86>').
translations: Karl Brunnhölzl, In Praise of Dharmadhātu, by Rangjung Dorje, Nāgārjuna and the Third Karmapa, Ithaca: Snow Lion Publications, 2007. (English)
chos kyi dbyings su bstod pa (Derge Tengyur D 1118): translated by Kṛṣṇapa, nag 'tsho lo tsA ba tshul khrims rgyal ba (Tibetan)

SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Lokātītastava.title: Lokātītastava
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Lokātītastava.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Lokātītastava.summary: The Lokātītastava ('Praise of the Supramundane One') is a short philosophical stotra of 28 anuṣṭubh verses attributed to Nāgārjuna, traditionally reckoned as the first member of the Catuḥstava. Rather than conventional mythological veneration, it praises the Buddha through Madhyamaka dialectic, demonstrating that entities such as the aggregates (skandhas), cause and effect, agents and actions, and samsara are dependent arisings (pratītyasamutpanna) and thus devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva).
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Lokātītastava.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna and recognized as one of the hymns constituting the Catuḥstava collection. Cited by Candrakīrti.
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Lokātītastava.coverage: complete — Complete hymn comprising all 28 verses (ślokas).
translations: Christian Lindtner, Nagarjuniana (1982). (English)

SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Narakoddharastava.title: Narakoddharastava
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Narakoddharastava.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Narakoddharastava.summary: A short Mahāyāna devotional hymn of 15 anuṣṭubh verses addressed to the Tathāgata (Lokanātha), supplicating deliverance from the horrors of hell and saṃsāra incurred through past misdeeds, including the pañcānantarya offenses. Preserved in Sanskrit manuscripts and the Tibetan Tanjur (D 1137), it belongs to the collection of devotional hymns traditionally ascribed to Nāgārjuna.
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Narakoddharastava.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna in the Tibetan Tanjur (bstod tshogs, D 1137), but regarded as apocryphal / not genuine by modern scholars (e.g. Christian Lindtner, Nagarjuniana, 1982, no. 35).
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Narakoddharastava.edition: Christian Lindtner, 'Narakoddharastava' (Acta Orientalia 40, 1979), collated with Tokyo University Library MS 205 (and comparing CUL MS Or.716.2) by Péter-Dániel Szántó.
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Narakoddharastava.coverage: complete — Complete text of 15 verses with scribal colophon and donor formula from Tokyo University Library MS 205.
translations: dmyal ba nas 'don pa zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 1137): translated by pa tshab lo tsA ba nyi ma grags pa (Tibetan)

SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Niraupamyastava.title: Niraupamyastava
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Niraupamyastava.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Niraupamyastava.summary: The Niraupamyastava ('Hymn to the Incomparable One') is a Buddhist philosophical hymn in 25 verses traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna and universally recognized as part of his Catuḥstava. It praises the Buddha from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārtha), expressing how the enlightened one acts with compassionate skill-in-means while knowing that no dharma is ultimately arisen, ceased, or possessed of intrinsic nature. Verse 21 famously argues for a single spiritual vehicle (ekayāna) based on the undifferentiated reality of the dharmadhātu.
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Niraupamyastava.attribution: Widely accepted as an authentic work of Nāgārjuna; one of the four constituent hymns of the Catuḥstava, commented upon by Amṛtākara (Catuḥstavasamāsārtha).
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Niraupamyastava.edition: Fernando Tola and Carmen Dragonetti, 'Nāgārjuna’s Catustava', Journal of Indian Philosophy 13 (1985) (Sanskrit text on pp. 12–14).
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Niraupamyastava.coverage: complete — Complete text of 25 verses, concluding with line 62: 'iti niraupamyastavaḥ samāptaḥ'.
translations: Giuseppe Tucci, 'Two Hymns of the Catuḥ-stava of Nāgārjuna', Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society 64, no. 2 (1932), pp. 309–325. (English)
dpe med par bstod pa (Derge Tengyur D 1119): translated by Kṛṣṇapa, nag 'tsho lo tsA ba tshul khrims rgyal ba (Tibetan)

SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Paramārthastava.title: Paramārthastava
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Paramārthastava.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Paramārthastava.summary: The Paramārthastava ('Hymn to the Ultimate') is a concise stotra of 11 verses in Anuṣṭubh metre traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna and reckoned as the concluding hymn of the Catuḥstava. It articulates the paradox of devotional praise from the vantage point of ultimate reality (paramārthasatya): while the Buddha is beyond arising, unlocatable, and transcendent of linguistic designation, he is nevertheless praised by taking recourse to conventional designation (lokaprajñaptim āgamya).
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Paramārthastava.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna and reckoned as one of the four hymns of the Catuḥstava (found in Amṛtākara's Catuḥstavasamāsārtha). Some modern scholars suspect a slightly later hand.
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Paramārthastava.edition: Fernando Tola and Carmen Dragonetti, 1985, pp. 19–20.
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Paramārthastava.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 11 verses, ending with the colophon 'paramārthastavaḥ samāptaḥ ||'.
translations: Giuseppe Tucci, 'Two Hymns of the Catuḥstava of Nāgārjuna', JRAS, 1932, pp. 309–325. (English)
Christian Lindtner, Nagarjuna: Juvelkaeden og andre skrifter, København, 1980. (Danish)

SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Sattvārādhanastava-Cheu.title: Sattvārādhanastava
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Sattvārādhanastava-Cheu.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Sattvārādhanastava-Cheu.summary: A short Mahāyāna stotra of 11 verses expounding the principle that the highest veneration (pūjā) of the Buddha consists in serving, aiding, and protecting sentient beings. The Buddha is portrayed as declaring that harming beings constitutes an offense against him, whereas compassion to beings is authentic worship.
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Sattvārādhanastava-Cheu.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna in the Tibetan canon (D 1125, D 4516). The manuscript colophon styles the work as a discourse spoken by the Buddha ('samyaksambuddhabhāṣitaṃ sattvārādhanaṃ nāma mahāyānasūtrāntaṃ').
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Sattvārādhanastava-Cheu.coverage: complete — Complete text in 11 verses with closing prose colophon.
translations: sems can mgu bar bya ba'i bstod pa (Derge Tengyur D 1125): translated by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna, nag 'tsho lo tsA ba tshul khrims rgyal ba (Tibetan)

SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Sattvārādhanastava-Lévi.title: Sattvārādhanastava
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Sattvārādhanastava-Lévi.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Sattvārādhanastava-Lévi.summary: The Sattvārādhanastava ('Hymn on Propitiating Sentient Beings') is a short Mahāyāna stotra of 11 verses traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna. It articulates the bodhisattva ethos that the highest worship (agrā pūjā) of the Buddha consists in serving and protecting sentient beings, declaring that the Buddha achieved awakening, mastered the perfections, and developed compassion solely on account of and for the sake of living beings.
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Sattvārādhanastava-Lévi.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna in the Tibetan bsTan 'gyur (D 1125, 4516).
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Sattvārādhanastava-Lévi.edition: Eclectic digital edition prepared by Péter-Dániel Szántó (Budapest, 2025), combining Sylvain Lévi's edition (1929, pp. 264–265; based on NAK 3-715 = NGMPP B 23/8) with readings from a manuscript fragment identified by Szántó (NAK 5-135 = NGMPP B 24/56), renumbered following Cheung.
translations: sems can mgu bar bya ba'i bstod pa (Derge Tengyur D 1125): translated by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna, nag 'tsho lo tsA ba tshul khrims rgyal ba (Tibetan)

SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Trikāyastava.title: Trikāyastava
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Trikāyastava.author: Nāgārjuna
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Trikāyastava.summary: The Trikāyastava is a short four-verse Mahāyāna hymn composed in the Sragdharā metre extolling the three bodies of the Buddha: dharmakāya, saṃbhogakāya, and nirmāṇakāya, concluding with a dedication verse (praṇidhāna). It is preserved in the Tibetan Tengyur under the name of Nāgārjuna (D 1123) and attested in an inscription at Mihintale in Sri Lanka as well as Chinese transliterations from Bodh Gayā.
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Trikāyastava.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna in the Tibetan Tengyur (D 1123). Modern scholarship notes that the trikāya doctrine is hardly compatible with the kāyadvaya of Nāgārjuna's genuine works (Yuktiṣaṣṭikā, Ratnāvalī).
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Trikāyastava.edition: John Newman, unpublished transcript with notes posted on academia.edu; prepared by Péter-Dániel Szántó
SA_T01_Nāgārjuna_Trikāyastava.coverage: complete — Complete text of 4 Sragdharā verses praising each of the three bodies respectively (vv. 1–3) followed by a praṇidhāna (v. 4).
translations: John S. Strong, translated from the Sanskrit Trikāyastava, ed. Sylvain Lévi in Edouard Chavannes, 'Les inscriptions chinoises de Bodh-Gayâ' (English)
George N. Roerich, The Blue Annals, Calcutta: 1949, pp. 1–2 (English)
sku gsum la bstod pa zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 1123): translated by Kṛṣṇapa, nag 'tsho lo tsA ba tshul khrims rgyal ba (Tibetan)

SA_T01_Rādhasvāmin_Viśeṣastava.title: Viśeṣastava
SA_T01_Rādhasvāmin_Viśeṣastava.author: Rādhasvāmin
SA_T01_Rādhasvāmin_Viśeṣastava.summary: The Viśeṣastava ('Hymn on the Distinction [of the Buddha]') is an influential Buddhist apologetic stotra of 76 verses that praises the Buddha by systematically contrasting his compassion, self-restraint, and faultlessness with the wrath, lust, and violence attributed to Hindu deities such as Śiva, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Indra. Long known primarily through its Tibetan translation at the head of the Tengyur stotra section and Prajñāvarman's commentary, its original Sanskrit text was rediscovered in a manuscript in Tibet and published by Johannes Schneider in 2023.
SA_T01_Rādhasvāmin_Viśeṣastava.attribution: Traditionally attributed in the Tibetan Tengyur (D 1109 / P 2001) to Udbhaṭasiddhasvāmin (mTho btsun grub rje). However, the colophon of the newly recovered Sanskrit manuscript names the author as Bhaṭṭarādhasvāmin (Rādhasvāmin). The Tibetan translation (D 1109) attributes the work to Udbhaṭasiddhasvāmin (mtho btsun grub rje).
SA_T01_Rādhasvāmin_Viśeṣastava.edition: Johannes Schneider, Viśeṣastava. Der Sanskrittext nach den Handschriften bearbeitet und übersetzt, Indica et Tibetica 61, Marburg: Indica et Tibetica Verlag, 2023, pp. 54–85.
SA_T01_Rādhasvāmin_Viśeṣastava.coverage: complete — Complete text of 76 verses plus one interpolated stanza (51*).
translations: Johannes Schneider, Viśeṣastava. Der Sanskrittext nach den Handschriften bearbeitet und übersetzt, Indica et Tibetica 61, Marburg: Indica et Tibetica Verlag, 2023. (German)

Johannes Schneider, Der Lobpreis der Vorzüglichkeit des Buddha: Udbhaṭasiddhasvāmins Viśeṣastava mit Prajñāvarmans Kommentar nach dem tibetischen Tanjur herausgegeben und übersetzt, Indica et Tibetica 23, Bonn: Indica et Tibetica Verlag, 1993. (German)
khyad par du 'phags pa'i bstod pa (Derge Tengyur D 1109): translated by Sarvajñadeva, rma thog rin chen/ rma rin chen mchog, ska ba dpal brtsegs (Tibetan)

SA_T01_Rāhulabhadra_Nirvikalpastuti.title: Nirvikalpastuti
SA_T01_Rāhulabhadra_Nirvikalpastuti.author: Rāhulabhadra
SA_T01_Rāhulabhadra_Nirvikalpastuti.summary: The Nirvikalpastuti (commonly known as the Prajñāpāramitāstotra) is a 21-verse devotional and philosophical hymn praising the perfection of wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā) in classical Madhyamaka terminology. Depicted as non-conceptual (nirvikalpa), beyond conceptual elaboration (niṣprapañca), and indistinguishable from the Buddha, Prajñāpāramitā is revered as the mother and grandmother of all Buddhas.
SA_T01_Rāhulabhadra_Nirvikalpastuti.attribution: Attributed to Rāhulabhadra in Sanskrit manuscripts and Tibetan sources; sometimes associated with or attributed to Nāgārjuna in Tibetan traditions. The Tibetan translation (D 1127) attributes the work to Nāgārjuna ('phags pa klu sgrub).
SA_T01_Rāhulabhadra_Nirvikalpastuti.edition: Diplomatic transcription and edition by Péter-Dániel Szántó (Kolozsvár, 2024), based on Kathmandu, Kaiser Library Ms 197 (NGMPP reel C 21/7), with variants noted from Michael Hahn (1988).
SA_T01_Rāhulabhadra_Nirvikalpastuti.coverage: complete — Complete hymn of 21 verses with opening mangala and closing colophon.
translations: shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin ma'i bstod pa (Derge Tengyur D 1127): translated by Tilakakalaśa, rngog blo ldan shes rab (Tibetan)

SA_T01_Sugataśrī_Kīrtidhvajapraśasti.title: Kīrtidhvajapraśasti
SA_T01_Sugataśrī_Kīrtidhvajapraśasti.author: Sugataśrī
SA_T01_Sugataśrī_Kīrtidhvajapraśasti.summary: A ten-verse Sanskrit Buddhist praise poem (praśasti) composed by Sugataśrī in honour of ācārya Kīrtidhvaja.
SA_T01_Sugataśrī_Kīrtidhvajapraśasti.attribution: Authored by Sugataśrī in praise of ācārya Kīrtidhvaja.
translations: Tibetan translation: D 1171. (Tibetan)

SA_T01_Vasudhārā_Buddhastotra.title: Buddhastotra (fragment)
SA_T01_Vasudhārā_Buddhastotra.author: Vasudhārā
SA_T01_Vasudhārā_Buddhastotra.summary: A Sanskrit fragment preserving approximately two and a half stanzas of an eight-verse hymn in praise of the Buddha (*Buddhastotra), matching Toh 1114 in the Tibetan Tengyur. The stanzas praise the Buddha's bodily self-sacrifice (duṣkarakārin) and mastery over passions and Māra.
SA_T01_Vasudhārā_Buddhastotra.attribution: Identified with Tibetan 1114 (Buddhastotra). E-text notes that it is 'possibly by a female poet.' Author reconstructed as *Vasudhārā.
SA_T01_Vasudhārā_Buddhastotra.edition: Manuscript transcription by Péter-Dániel Szántó (Budapest, 26 January 2025), based on Cambridge University Library MS Or.143.
SA_T01_Vasudhārā_Buddhastotra.coverage: fragment — Preserves approximately two and a half stanzas of an eight-stanza praise of the Buddha.
translations: sangs rgyas kyi bstod pa zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 1114): translated by *Jinabhadra, thar pa lo tsA ba nyi ma rgyal mtshan; at rab tu bsngags pa'i gnas chen po bal po yam bu'i grong khyer (Tibetan)

SA_T01_anon_Saptajinastava.title: Saptajinastava
SA_T01_anon_Saptajinastava.summary: The Saptajinastava is a concise Buddhist devotional hymn consisting of nine verses extolling the Seven Buddhas of antiquity (Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhuj, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Śākyamuni) and the future Buddha Maitreya, followed by a merit dedication verse. The Sanskrit original was restored by Alexander von Staël-Holstein from the Chinese phonetic transcription (Taishō 1682) alongside the Tibetan translation (D 1165).
SA_T01_anon_Saptajinastava.attribution: Anonymous Buddhist hymn; preserved in Tibetan translation in the Tanjur (D 1165, translated by Padmākaravarma and Rin chen bzang po) and translated/transcribed into Chinese during the Song dynasty by Fatian (Taishō 1682).
SA_T01_anon_Saptajinastava.edition: Alexander von Staël-Holstein, K'ien-ch'ui-fan-tsan (Gaṇḍīstotragāthā) sokhranivshijsia v kitajskoj transkriptsii sanskritskij gimn Açvaghoshi; Ts'i-fuh-tsan-pai-k'ie-t'o (Saptajinastava) i Fuh-shwoh-wan-shu-shi-li-yih-poh-pah-ming-fan-tsan (Āryamañjuśrīnāmāṣṭaka), izdal i pri pomoshchi tibetskago perevoda ob"jasnil. Bibliotheca Buddhica 15. St. Petersburg: Imprimerie de l'Académie Impériale des Sciences, 1913, pp. 82–84.
SA_T01_anon_Saptajinastava.coverage: complete — Complete text of 9 verses praising the Seven Buddhas of the past and Maitreya, ending with 'saptajinastavaḥ samāptaḥ'.
translations: de bzhin gshegs pa bdun gyi bstod pa (Derge Tengyur D 1165): translated by Padmākaravarman, Śraddhākaravarman, lo chen rin chen bzang po (Tibetan)

SA_T01_Āditya_Vanaratnastotra.title: Vanaratnastotra
SA_T01_Āditya_Vanaratnastotra.author: Āditya
SA_T01_Āditya_Vanaratnastotra.summary: The Vanaratnastotra (also known as the Vanaratnastotrasaptaka) is a seven-verse hymn composed in praise of Vanaratna by his Magadhan disciple Āditya. It was translated into Tibetan by Gzhon nu dpal (D 1177). The e-text contains the complete edited Sanskrit text alternating with the canonical Tibetan translation.
SA_T01_Āditya_Vanaratnastotra.attribution: The author is the Magadhan Buddhist lay disciple (dge bsnyen dam pa) Āditya. The Tibetan translation was made by Rtse thang Lo tsā ba Gzhon nu dpal at the request of Spyan snga Chos kyi rgyal po.
SA_T01_Āditya_Vanaratnastotra.edition: Hahn, Michael. 'Das Vanaratnastotra des Āditya.' In Suhṛllekhāḥ: Festgabe für Helmut Eimer, Indica et Tibetica, 1996.
SA_T01_Āditya_Vanaratnastotra.coverage: complete — Complete 7 verses of the saptaka in Sanskrit, interlinearly presented with the Tibetan translation (Degé Tanjur D1177) and both Sanskrit and Tibetan colophons.
translations: Hahn, Michael. 'Das Vanaratnastotra des Āditya.' 1996. (German)
dpal ldan bla ma nags kyi rin chen gyi bstod pa bdun pa (Derge Tengyur D 1177): translated by rtses thang lo tsA ba gzhon nu dpal (Tibetan)

SA_T01_Śaṃkarasvāmin_Devātiśayastotra.title: Devātiśayastotra
SA_T01_Śaṃkarasvāmin_Devātiśayastotra.author: Śaṅkarasvāmin
SA_T01_Śaṃkarasvāmin_Devātiśayastotra.summary: The Devātiśayastotra (also titled Devatāvimarśastuti in Sanskrit manuscripts) is a 21-verse Buddhist apologetic hymn attributed to Śaṅkarasvāmin. It contrasts the supreme peacefulness, freedom from passion, and universal benevolence of the Buddha with the warlike, passionate, and wrathful character of Brahmanical deities such as Viṣṇu, Śiva, Brahmā, Skanda, and Umā. Prajñāvarman's commentary made the hymn famous in Tibet, where it served as a foundational source for knowledge of Indian mythology and legendary history.
SA_T01_Śaṃkarasvāmin_Devātiśayastotra.attribution: Attributed to Śaṃkarasvāmin. The Sanskrit manuscript edition of Liu & Schneider (2023) records the variant attribution Varāhasvāmin.
SA_T01_Śaṃkarasvāmin_Devātiśayastotra.edition: Johannes Schneider, Eine buddhistische Kritik der indischen Götter: Śaṃkarasvāmins Devātiśayastotra mit Prajñāvarmans Kommentar, Nach dem tibetischen Tanjur herausgegeben und übersetzt, Wiener Studien zur Tibetologie und Buddhismuskunde, Heft 81 (Wien: Arbeitskreis für tibetische und buddhistische Studien Universität Wien, 2014), pp. 163–167.
SA_T01_Śaṃkarasvāmin_Devātiśayastotra.coverage: complete — Complete text of the stotra in 21 verses with concluding colophon.
translations: Johannes Schneider, Eine buddhistische Kritik der indischen Götter: Śaṃkarasvāmins Devātiśayastotra mit Prajñāvarmans Kommentar, Wien: Arbeitskreis für tibetische und buddhistische Studien, 2014. (German)

SA_GSD36_utaustin_apararka_yajnavalkya_b.title: Yājñavalkyasmṛti with Aparārka (chapter 1: Ācārādhyāya)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_apararka_yajnavalkya_b.author: Yājñavalkya, Aparārka
SA_GSD36_utaustin_apararka_yajnavalkya_b.summary: The Ācārādhyāya (first book) of the Yājñavalkyasmṛti together with the extensive commentary and digest (nibandha) Aparārka by the Śilāhāra ruler Aparāditya. This section treats religious conduct and personal status (ācāra), encompassing sacraments (saṃskāra), studenthood, marriage, food regulations, śrāddha ceremonies, worship of Vināyaka and the planets (grahaśānti), and statecraft (rājadharma). Aparārka's work is renowned in Dharmaśāstra literature as an encyclopedic nibandha that preserves numerous quotations from lost smṛti texts and Purāṇas.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_apararka_yajnavalkya_b.attribution: UT Austin South Asia Institute Sanskrit OER; editor/transcriber per source text.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_apararka_yajnavalkya_b.edition: Yājñavalkyasmṛtiḥ, edited by the Pandits of Ānandāśrama, Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series, Poona: Ānandāśrama, 1903–.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_apararka_yajnavalkya_b.coverage: partial — Complete text of Chapter 1 (Ācārādhyāya, verses 1.1–1.366) of the Yājñavalkyasmṛti along with Aparārka's commentary. The Vyavahāra and Prāyaścitta adhyāyas are held in separate files.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_apararka_yajnavalkya_b.title: Yājñavalkyasmṛti with Aparārka (chapter 2: Vyavahārādhyāya)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_apararka_yajnavalkya_b.author: Yājñavalkya, Aparārka
SA_GSD36_utaustin_apararka_yajnavalkya_b.summary: The Vyavahārādhyāya is the second chapter of the Yājñavalkyasmṛti, dealing comprehensively with civil and criminal law, court procedure, rules of evidence (documents, witnesses, and ordeals), and the standard eighteen titles of dispute (ṛṇādāna, nikṣepa, dāyavibhāga, sīmāvivāda, etc.). The commentary Aparārka, authored by King Aparāditya I of the Śilāhāra dynasty of North Konkan in the 12th century CE, is an encyclopedic digest (nibandha) renowned for preserving hundreds of valuable citations from otherwise lost smṛtis and purāṇas.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_apararka_yajnavalkya_b.attribution: UT Austin South Asia Institute Sanskrit OER; editor/transcriber per source text.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_apararka_yajnavalkya_b.coverage: partial — Contains the complete second book (Vyavahārādhyāya, verses 2.1–2.306) of the Yājñavalkyasmṛti with Aparārka's commentary; does not include Book 1 (Ācārādhyāya) or Book 3 (Prāyaścittādhyāya).

SA_GSD36_utaustin_apararka_yajnavalkya_b.title: Yājñavalkyasmṛti with Aparārka (Prāyaścittādhyāya)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_apararka_yajnavalkya_b.author: Yājñavalkya, Aparārka
SA_GSD36_utaustin_apararka_yajnavalkya_b.summary: The Prāyaścittādhyāya forms the third and final book of the Yājñavalkyasmṛti, treating ritual impurity and mourning periods (āśauca), the ascetic ashram stages (vānaprastha and parivrājaka), internal yoga and anatomy, and elaborate penances (prāyaścitta) for major and minor transgressions. Aparārka's commentary functions as an encyclopedic digest (nibandha), citing hundreds of otherwise lost or unpreserved Vedic, Smṛti, and Purāṇic verses.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_apararka_yajnavalkya_b.attribution: UT Austin South Asia Institute Sanskrit OER; editor/transcriber per source text.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_apararka_yajnavalkya_b.coverage: partial — Complete text of Book 3 (Prāyaścittādhyāya, vv. 3.1–3.334) with commentary; does not include Books 1 (Ācārādhyāya) and 2 (Vyavahārādhyāya).

SA_GSD36_utaustin_bharuci_manubhasya_der.author: Bhāruci

The text covers royal duties and statecraft (adhyāya 7), legal procedure and substantive law (adhyāyas 8–9), mixed castes (adhyāya 10), penances (adhyāya 11), and philosophical teachings and karma (adhyāya 12).

SA_GSD36_utaustin_devanabhatta_smrticand.title: Smṛticandrikā (Āhnikakāṇḍa)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_devanabhatta_smrticand.author: Devaṇabhaṭṭa
SA_GSD36_utaustin_devanabhatta_smrticand.summary: The Āhnikakāṇḍa is a major division of Devaṇabhaṭṭa's Smṛticandrikā, a Dharmaśāstra digest (nibandha). It systematically prescribes daily duties and rituals (āhnika) such as morning rising, bodily purification, bathing (snāna), twilight prayers (saṃdhyāvandana), devatārcana, baliharaṇa, and atithipūjā, quoting numerous smṛti and purāṇic sources.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_devanabhatta_smrticand.title: Smṛticandrikā (Āśaucakāṇḍa)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_devanabhatta_smrticand.author: Devaṇabhaṭṭa
SA_GSD36_utaustin_devanabhatta_smrticand.summary: The Āśaucakāṇḍa constitutes a section of the Smṛticandrikā by Devaṇabhaṭṭa. It systematizes legal and ritual traditions concerning ceremonial impurity (āśauca) caused by birth (sūtake) and death, specifying rules and periods for different varṇas, post-mortem rites, and eligibility for śrāddha (such as Gayāśrāddha).
