SA_GSD36_utaustin_devanabhatta_smrticand.title: Smṛticandrikā (Saṃskārakāṇḍa)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_devanabhatta_smrticand.author: Devaṇabhaṭṭa
SA_GSD36_utaustin_devanabhatta_smrticand.summary: The Saṃskārakāṇḍa is the first major section of Devaṇabhaṭṭa's dharma digest, the Smṛticandrikā. It opens with an examination of the sources of dharma (dharmapramāṇa, custom, and yugadharma), followed by detailed legal and ritual rules governing classical life-cycle rites (saṃskāras) from prenatal ceremonies through upanayana, studenthood (brahmacarya), and marriage (vivāha).
SA_GSD36_utaustin_devanabhatta_smrticand.attribution: UT Austin South Asia Institute Sanskrit OER; editor/transcriber per source text.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_devanabhatta_smrticand.edition: Smṛticandrikā by Devaṇṇabhaṭṭa: Saṃskārakāṇḍa, ed. L. Srinivasacharya. Bibliotheca Sanskrita. 1914.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_devanabhatta_smrticand.coverage: partial — Contains the whole Saṃskārakāṇḍa, the first of the five kāṇḍas. It begins with the table of contents (viṣayasūcikā), followed by the sources of dharma, deśa and yuga dharmas, the saṃskāras from garbhādhāna to upanayana, the student's duties, samāvartana and vivāha, and ends 'samāptaḥ saṃskarakāṇḍaḥ' (printed pp. 1–233). The other kāṇḍas are separate catalog entries.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_devanabhatta_smrticand.title: Smṛticandrikā (Śrāddhakāṇḍa)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_devanabhatta_smrticand.author: Devaṇabhaṭṭa
SA_GSD36_utaustin_devanabhatta_smrticand.summary: The Śrāddhakāṇḍa forms the fourth section of the Smṛticandrikā, a major late 12th- or early 13th-century nibandha composed by Devaṇabhaṭṭa in southern India. It constitutes an exhaustive digest on ancestral offerings (śrāddha), assembling and analyzing authoritative Vedic, smṛti, and purāṇic testimonia on ritual classifications (such as nitya, naimittika, kāmya, and sapiṇḍīkaraṇa), qualifications of performers and guests, lunar and seasonal timings, and rites performed at sacred pilgrimage places (tīrthaśrāddha).
SA_GSD36_utaustin_devanabhatta_smrticand.attribution: UT Austin South Asia Institute Sanskrit OER; editor/transcriber per source text.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_devanabhatta_smrticand.edition: Smṛticandrikā, Devaṇṇabhaṭṭa, ed. L. Śrīnivāsacharya: Śrāddhakāṇḍa, Bibliotheca Sanskrita, 1918.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_devanabhatta_smrticand.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Śrāddhakāṇḍa, covering introductory praise (śrāddhamahimā) through tīrthaśrāddha to the terminal colophon.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_devanabhatta_smrticand.title: Smṛticandrikā (Vyavahārakāṇḍa)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_devanabhatta_smrticand.author: Devaṇabhaṭṭa
SA_GSD36_utaustin_devanabhatta_smrticand.summary: The Smṛticandrikā is an influential South Indian Dharmaśāstra digest (nibandha) compiled by Devaṇabhaṭṭa. Its Vyavahārakāṇḍa treats civil and criminal jurisprudence in two parts: judicial court organization, plaint, reply, and proof (vyavahāramātṛkā, including documents, witnesses, and divine ordeals); and substantive adjudication over the eighteen classical titles of dispute (vyavahārapada, such as non-payment of debt, partition/inheritance, boundary disputes, and assault). It remains one of the foundational legal authorities of the Southern school of Hindu law.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_devanabhatta_smrticand.attribution: UT Austin South Asia Institute Sanskrit OER; editor/transcriber per source text.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_devanabhatta_smrticand.edition: Smṛticandrikā of Devaṇṇa Bhaṭṭa: Vyavahāra Kāṇḍa (Parts 1 & 2), edited by L. Śrīnivāsacharya. Mysore: Bibliotheca Sanskrita (Nos. 45 & 48), 1914–1916.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_devanabhatta_smrticand.coverage: partial — Contains the complete Vyavahārakāṇḍa (both Part 1 on legal procedure and Part 2 on the eighteen titles of law/vyavahārapada), which is the third and largest of the five major kāṇḍas of the Smṛticandrikā.

SA_GSD37_utaustin_haradatta_anakula_apas.title: Āpastambagṛhyasūtra with Anākulā
SA_GSD37_utaustin_haradatta_anakula_apas.author: Āpastamba, Haradatta
SA_GSD37_utaustin_haradatta_anakula_apas.summary: The Āpastambagṛhyasūtra is the domestic-ritual manual of the Āpastamba school of the Black Yajurveda (Taittirīya), in 8 paṭalas and 23 khaṇḍas. It covers marriage, the saṃskāras, upanayana, the snātaka, domestic offerings, śrāddha-related rites and expiations for portents. This e-text gives the sūtras with Haradatta's concise commentary Anākulā.

SA_GSD37_utaustin_haradatta_mitaksara_ga.title: Gautamadharmasūtra with Mitākṣarā
SA_GSD37_utaustin_haradatta_mitaksara_ga.author: Gautama, Haradatta
SA_GSD37_utaustin_haradatta_mitaksara_ga.summary: The Gautamadharmasūtra is among the earliest surviving prose Dharmasūtras, traditionally attached to the Sāmaveda. It delineates the foundational rules governing ritual life, studenthood, householder responsibilities, marriage, inheritance, kingship and legal procedure, as well as an extensive classification of penances (prāyaścitta). Haradatta's Mitākṣarā provides phrase-by-phrase exposition, syntactic glosses, and extensive reconciliations with other Smṛti texts.
SA_GSD37_utaustin_haradatta_mitaksara_ga.attribution: UT Austin South Asia Institute Sanskrit OER; editor/transcriber per source text.

SA_GSD37_utaustin_haradatta_ujjvala_apas.title: Āpastambadharmasūtra with Ujjvalā
SA_GSD37_utaustin_haradatta_ujjvala_apas.author: Āpastamba, Haradatta
SA_GSD37_utaustin_haradatta_ujjvala_apas.summary: The Āpastambadharmasūtra comprises the dharmākhyapraśnas of the Āpastamba school. It covers personal conduct (ācāra), studenthood and initiation (brahmacarya), domestic rituals, dietary rules, law and inheritance (vyavahāra), and expiatory penances (prāyaścitta). Haradatta's Ujjvalā is a commentary explaining the sūtras, elucidating grammatical points, and citing smṛti and Vedic parallels.

It provides an extensive compendium of śruti, smṛti, and purāṇic passages concerning religious gifting (dāna), detailing rules, mantras, eligible recipients, and various kinds of gifts.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_hemadri_caturvargacint.title: Caturvargacintāmaṇi (Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa: Kālanirṇaya)

It details the auspicious and inauspicious astronomical timings (tithi, vāra, nakṣatra, saṅkrānti, malamāsa, and ṛtu) for performing religious duties, vows, and ancestral rites (śrāddha), reconciling conflicting Smṛti passages using Mīmāṃsā hermeneutics.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_hemadri_caturvargacint.title: Caturvargacintāmaṇi (Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa: Śrāddhakalpa, part 2)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_hemadri_caturvargacint.author: Hemādri
SA_GSD36_utaustin_hemadri_caturvargacint.summary: The Śrāddhakalpa of the Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa is the encyclopaedic section on ancestral offerings in Hemādri's ritual digest, the Caturvargacintāmaṇi. This second half focuses on the practical performance of the śrāddha ritual, detailing purificatory baths (snāna), libations (tarpaṇa), brāhmaṇa invitations, preliminary preparations, homa offerings into the sacred fire, the presentation of funeral cakes (piṇḍadāna), and conclusion of the rites. Hemādri collates extensive textual authorities from the Vedas, Gṛhyasūtras, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas with exhaustive analytical commentary.

This first part opens with an index of Purāṇa citations and covers vrata principles along with observances up to the dvādaśī-vratas.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_jimutavahana_dayabhaga.author: Jīmūtavāhana
SA_GSD36_utaustin_jimutavahana_dayabhaga.summary: The Dāyabhāga ('Partition of Heritage') of Jīmūtavāhana is the foundational digest of the Bengal (Gauḍīya) school of traditional Hindu law, forming part of his compendium Dharmaratna. SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.author: Lakṣmīdhara
SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.summary: The Brahmacārikāṇḍa is a volume of the Kṛtyakalpataru, a Dharmaśāstra digest (nibandha) compiled by Bhaṭṭa Lakṣmīdhara. It gathers, organizes, and explains canonical Vedic, smṛti, and purāṇic texts concerning the student āśrama. Topics covered include the sacraments (saṃskāras) from conception to Vedic initiation (upanayana), student disciplines and study, and the concluding formal bath (snāna/samāvartana).

SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.title: Kṛtyakalpataru (Gṛhasthakāṇḍa)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.author: Lakṣmīdhara
SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.summary: The Gṛhasthakāṇḍa constitutes the second volume of Lakṣmīdhara's Dharmaśāstra digest Kṛtyakalpataru. It systematically collects, classifies, and annotates Vedic, Smṛti, and Purāṇic authorities governing the householder stage of life (gṛhasthāśrama). Major subjects include vivāha (marriage rules, rites, and forms), agnyādhāna and āvasthya (sacred domestic fires), varṇa occupations, āpaddharma (emergency livelihoods), and yamaniyamas.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.title: Kṛtyakalpataru (Mokṣakāṇḍa)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.author: Lakṣmīdhara
SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.summary: The Mokṣakāṇḍa is the fourteenth volume of Lakṣmīdhara's Kṛtyakalpataru. It collects, organizes, and annotates Vedic, Smṛti, and other passages concerning liberation (mokṣa), the duties and stages of renouncers (vānaprastha, saṃnyāsa, yati), the overcoming of passions, and the path to ultimate beatitude.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.title: Kṛtyakalpataru (Niyatakālakāṇḍa)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.author: Lakṣmīdhara
SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.summary: The Niyatakālakāṇḍa is the third kāṇḍa of the Kṛtyakalpataru, an influential Dharmaśāstra digest compiled by Bhaṭṭa Lakṣmīdhara for Govindacandra. It anthologizes and interprets smṛti and purāṇic passages governing scheduled daily and periodic duties (āhnika and niyatakāla), structured across topics including tooth-cleaning, morning bath, japa, tarpaṇa, five mahāyajñas, dining, night duties, and parvan observances.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.title: Kṛtyakalpataru (Pratiṣṭhākāṇḍa)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.author: Lakṣmīdhara
SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.summary: The Pratiṣṭhākāṇḍa is a section of Lakṣmīdhara's Kṛtyakalpataru. It compiles Dharmaśāstric and Purāṇic texts on the consecration and installation (pratiṣṭhā) of temples, deities, water reservoirs, sacred trees, and flags, along with procedures for the restoration of ruined shrines (jīrṇasaṃskāra).

SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.title: Kṛtyakalpataru (Rājadharmakāṇḍa)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.author: Lakṣmīdhara
SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.summary: The Rājadharmakāṇḍa is the eleventh book of the Kṛtyakalpataru, an influential 12th-century Dharmaśāstra digest compiled by Bhaṭṭa Lakṣmīdhara, royal minister under the Gāhaḍavāla ruler Govindacandra. It collects and arranges smṛti and purāṇic testimonia on statecraft and kingship (rājadharma), including the divine nature and duties of the ruler, royal consecration (abhiṣeka), the council of ministers (mantrin), fortresses (durga), vāstu layout, internal security, state treasury (kośa), army, espionage, foreign policy (ṣāḍguṇya), military campaigns (yātrā), and state festivals such as Kaumudīmahotsava and Mahānavamī.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.attribution: UT Austin South Asia Institute Sanskrit OER; editor/transcriber per source text.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.title: Kṛtyakalpataru (kāṇḍa 4: Śrāddhakāṇḍa)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.author: Lakṣmīdhara
SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.summary: The Śrāddhakāṇḍa constitutes the fourth book of Lakṣmīdhara's Dharmaśāstra digest, the Kṛtyakalpataru. It systematically synthesizes Vedic, Smṛti, and Purāṇic rulings governing ancestral offerings (śrāddha), encompassing proper times and places, qualification and exclusion of brāhmaṇas, ritual items, cooking, offering formulae, and individual rites such as sapiṇḍīkaraṇa, ekoddiṣṭa, āmaśrāddha, and jīvacchrāddha.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.title: Kṛtyakalpataru (Śuddhikāṇḍa)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.author: Lakṣmīdhara
SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.summary: The Śuddhikāṇḍa constitutes the tenth section of Bhaṭṭa Lakṣmīdhara's Dharmaśāstra digest Kṛtyakalpataru. It collects and systematizes Smṛti teachings on ritual pollution (āśauca) caused by birth and death, sapīṇḍa obligations, funerary and post-cremation duties, and purification procedures for the body, utensils, ground, and water.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.attribution: UT Austin South Asia Institute Sanskrit OER; editor/transcriber per source text.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.title: Kṛtyakalpataru (kāṇḍa 8: Tīrthavivecanakāṇḍa)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.author: Lakṣmīdhara
SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.summary: The Tīrthavivecanakāṇḍa is the eighth kāṇḍa of Bhaṭṭa Lakṣmīdhara's encyclopedic digest, the Kṛtyakalpataru. It forms a Dharmaśāstra treatise devoted specifically to pilgrimage (tīrthayātrā), systematizing scriptural excerpts from the Mahābhārata and Purāṇas on sacred geography, pilgrimage rituals, and the spiritual merits of prominent sacred centres across India, particularly Vārāṇasī, Prayāga, and Gayā.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.title: Kṛtyakalpataru (Vratakāṇḍa)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.author: Lakṣmīdhara
SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.summary: The Vratakāṇḍa forms the sixth volume of the Kṛtyakalpataru, an influential 12th-century Dharmaśāstra nibandha compiled by Bhaṭṭa Lakṣmīdhara at the Gāhaḍavāla court of King Govindacandra. It serves as an exhaustive ritual compendium on religious vows (vrata), arranging fasts and observances systematically according to lunar days (tithis), weekdays (vāra), months, and deities through extensive citations from Smṛtis and Purāṇas accompanied by brief glosses.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.title: Kṛtyakalpataru (Vyavahārakāṇḍa)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_laksmidhara_krtyakalpa.author: Lakṣmīdhara

It systematically covers civil and criminal procedure, judicial institutions, law of evidence (witnesses, written documents, ordeals), and substantive law structured under the traditional titles of law.

SA_GSD37_utaustin_lubin_dharmasutras_com.title: Dharmasūtras (compilation)
SA_GSD37_utaustin_lubin_dharmasutras_com.summary: A consolidated comparative dataset compiling the Sanskrit texts and critical variants of early prose Dharmasūtras—principally Gautama, Baudhāyana, Vasiṣṭha, and Vaikhānasa. The texts articulate the foundational norms of early Brahmanical orthopraxy, treating topics such as student initiation (upanayana), rites of the four varṇas and āśramas, purification, penances (prāyaścitta), and legal procedure (vyavahāra). The electronic collation was prepared for teaching and comparative research at the University of Texas at Austin.

It covers vyavahāra (legal procedure and titles of law) including debts (ṛṇādāna), evidence, ordeals, and other vyavahārapadas, citing various smṛti authorities such as Nārada, Bṛhaspati, Kātyāyana, Manu, and Yājñavalkya.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_madhava_parasaramadhav.title: Parāśarasmṛti with Pārāśaramādhavīya (Ācārakāṇḍa, adhyāya 1)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_madhava_parasaramadhav.author: Parāśara, Mādhava
SA_GSD36_utaustin_madhava_parasaramadhav.summary: The Pārāśaramādhavīya is a major Dharmaśāstra digest-commentary by Mādhava on the Parāśarasmṛti. This first adhyāya of the Ācārakāṇḍa begins with an introductory section establishing the authority (prāmāṇya) of Smṛti and Purāṇa on Mīmāṃsā principles. It then treats the concept of yugadharma (duties specific to the Kali age), followed by extensive exposition of daily obligatory rites (āhnika, snāna, sandhyāvandana, tarpaṇa, vaiśvadeva) and normative conduct (ācāra) across the four varṇas.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_madhava_parasaramadhav.title: Parāśarasmṛti with Pārāśaramādhavīya (Ācārakāṇḍa, adhyāyas 2–3)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_madhava_parasaramadhav.author: Parāśara, Mādhava
SA_GSD36_utaustin_madhava_parasaramadhav.summary: The Parāśaramādhavīya is the commentary by Mādhavācārya, minister of Bukka I, on the Parāśarasmṛti. This part covers adhyāyas 2 and 3: the means of livelihood permitted to householders in the Kali age (notably agriculture for Brahmins), and the rules of impurity after birth and death (āśauca) and of ancestral rites (śrāddha), with copious quotations from other smṛtis.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_madhava_parasaramadhav.title: Parāśarasmṛti with Mādhavīya (chapters 4–11)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_madhava_parasaramadhav.author: Parāśara, Mādhava
SA_GSD36_utaustin_madhava_parasaramadhav.summary: The Parāśarasmṛti is a major Dharmaśāstra work. The Mādhavīya (Parāśarasmṛtivyākhyā) by Mādhava is a commentary on it. This portion (Adhyāyas 4–11) forms part of the Prāyaścittakāṇḍa, analyzing sins, ritual impurities, expiations (prāyaścitta), penances such as kṛcchra and cāndrāyaṇa, and rules governing food and association.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_madhava_parasaramadhav.title: Parāśarasmṛti with Pārāśaramādhavīya (chapter 12)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_madhava_parasaramadhav.author: Parāśara, Mādhava
SA_GSD36_utaustin_madhava_parasaramadhav.summary: The twelfth and concluding chapter of the Parāśarasmṛti accompanied by the commentary of Mādhava. Positioned as a supplementary section (pariśiṣṭa) resolving remaining topics of both ritual conduct (ācāra) and penance (prāyaścitta), it addresses purificatory baths following bad dreams and defilements, re-initiation (punaḥsaṃskāra), secret expiations (rahasyaprāyaścitta), severe vows such as kṛcchra and cāndrāyaṇa, and the karmic retribution of sins in future lives (karmavipāka).
SA_GSD36_utaustin_madhava_parasaramadhav.attribution: UT Austin South Asia Institute Sanskrit OER; editor/transcriber per source text.

SA_GSD37_utaustin_maskarin_gautama_dharm.title: Gautamadharmasūtra with Maskaribhāṣya
SA_GSD37_utaustin_maskarin_gautama_dharm.author: Gautama, Maskarin
SA_GSD37_utaustin_maskarin_gautama_dharm.summary: The Gautamadharmasūtra is among the earliest extant prose aphoristic treatises of the Dharmaśāstra tradition. Maskarin's commentary (Maskaribhāṣya), composed by Maskarin son of Vāmana, is a comprehensive exposition providing detailed exegesis of the sūtras, integrating Vedic citations, Mīmāṃsā hermeneutics, and smṛti parallels on the duties of the four varṇas, life stages (āśramas), domestic rituals, legal proceedings, and penances.

SA_GSD37_utaustin_maskarin_haradatta_gau.title: Gautamadharmasūtra with the commentaries of Maskarin and Haradatta
SA_GSD37_utaustin_maskarin_haradatta_gau.author: Gautama, Maskarin, Haradatta
SA_GSD37_utaustin_maskarin_haradatta_gau.summary: The Gautamadharmasūtra is among the earliest extant legal codes in the Vedic tradition, traditionally tied to the Sāmaveda. It codifies rules concerning the four stages of life (āśrama), duties of the classes (varṇa), purity and pollution, civil and criminal law, governance, inheritance, and expiation (prāyaścitta). This composite e-text sets the root aphorisms side by side with their two chief traditional commentaries: the Maskaribhāṣya by Maskarin and the Mitākṣarā by Haradatta, covering the complete span of twenty-eight adhyāyas.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.author: Manu, Medhātithi
SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.summary: Chapter 1 of the Mānavadharmaśāstra narrates the frame story (the sages approaching Manu), the creation of the world, the cosmic ages (yugas, manvantaras), the origin of the four varṇas and the transmission of the śāstra through Bhṛgu, and ends with a table of contents of the work. Medhātithi's commentary opens with an extended Mīmāṃsā-based defence of the purpose and authority of the smṛti. The e-text adds an English/Sanskrit text-critical apparatus.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.author: Manu, Medhātithi
SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.summary: Chapter 2 of the Mānavadharmaśāstra defines dharma and its sources, with Medhātithi's Manubhāṣya providing commentary on the verses, accompanied by text-critical notes citing multiple editions/readings.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.title: Manusmṛti with Manubhāṣya (chapter 3)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.author: Medhātithi
SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.summary: Chapter 3 of the Manusmṛti and Medhātithi's Manubhāṣya addresses the rules governing the householder (gṛhastha). It begins with the student's return ceremony (samāvartana), qualifications for marriage, and a detailed discussion of the eight forms of marriage (brāhma, daiva, ārṣa, prājāpatya, āsura, gāndharva, rākṣasa, paiśāca). It further treats the daily duties of the householder, focusing on the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña), guest reception, and the ritual obligations of ancestral rites (śrāddha). Medhātithi utilizes classical Mīmāṃsā principles to interpret injunctions (vidhi) and eulogistic explanations (arthavāda).

SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.title: Mānavaśāstra with Manubhāṣya (adhyāya 4)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.author: Manu, Medhātithi
SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.summary: Chapter 4 of the Manusmṛti with Medhātithi's Manubhāṣya treats the duties, legitimate livelihoods, daily observances, and ritual obligations of the twice-born householder (gṛhastha / snātaka). Medhātithi discusses the various modes of subsistence (including ṛta, amṛta, mṛta, pramṛta, and the prohibition of śvavṛtti), the ethics of receiving gifts (pratigraha), rules for regular recitation (svādhyāya) and periods of cessation of study (anadhyāya), as well as general moral and purificatory disciplines.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.attribution: UT Austin South Asia Institute Sanskrit OER; editor/transcriber per source text.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.title: Mānavadharmaśāstra with Manubhāṣya (chapter 5)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.author: Manu, Medhātithi
SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.summary: Chapter 5 of the Mānavadharmaśāstra deals with permitted and forbidden food (including the extended discussion of meat-eating), impurity caused by death and birth (āśauca), the purification of persons and objects, and the duties of women. Medhātithi's Manubhāṣya treats these rules with Mīmāṃsā-based argument. The e-text adds an English/Sanskrit text-critical apparatus.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.title: Manusmṛti with Manubhāṣya (chapter 6)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.author: Medhātithi
SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.summary: Chapter 6 of the Manusmṛti and Medhātithi's Manubhāṣya detail the duties and lifestyles of the third and fourth stages of life (āśrama): the forest hermit (vānaprastha) and the wandering ascetic renouncer (yati / saṃnyāsin). Medhātithi analyzes the proper timing and conditions for entering the forest, ascetic dietary rules, the internal relocation of sacrificial fires, practices of breath control and meditation, and the theological controversy regarding whether renunciation is open to all dvija varṇas or restricted exclusively to Brahmins.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.title: Manusmṛti with Manubhāṣya (chapter 7)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.author: Manu, Medhātithi
SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.summary: Chapter 7 of the Manusmṛti constitutes the classic treatise on Rājadharma (royal duties, statecraft, administration, judicial governance, foreign policy, and war). Medhātithi's commentary is renowned for applying Mīmāṃsā principles to political thought, notably distinguishing between empirical/pragmatic statecraft (dṛṣṭārtha) drawn from Arthaśāstra traditions and transcendental moral duty (adṛṣṭārtha).

Medhātithi's commentary applies Mīmāṃsā principles of interpretation to Hindu jurisprudence.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.author: Manu, Medhātithi
SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.summary: This part of chapter 8 of the Mānavadharmaśāstra continues the rules of judicial procedure: the admonition of witnesses and the punishment of false testimony (with the cases where untruth is excused), the oath and ordeal, and then the title of law on non-payment of debts (interest, pledges, sureties), deposits (nikṣepa) and sale by a non-owner (asvāmivikraya). SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.author: Manu, Medhātithi
SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.summary: Chapter 9 of the Mānavadharmaśāstra deals with the law concerning husband and wife (guarding of women, levirate/niyoga, remarriage), inheritance and partition (classes of sons, shares of heirs), gambling and the suppression of criminals by the king, and closes with the duties of Vaiśyas and Śūdras. Medhātithi's Manubhāṣya, the oldest extant complete commentary on Manu, discusses these rules at length. The e-text adds an extensive text-critical apparatus.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.title: Manusmṛti with Manubhāṣya (chapter 10)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.author: Manu, Medhātithi
SA_GSD36_utaustin_medhatithi_manubhasya_.summary: Chapter 10 of the Manusmṛti with Medhātithi's Manubhāṣya covers the system of varṇas and jātis, treating the classification and origins of mixed castes (saṃkīrṇajāti), degraded communities (vrātya, caṇḍāla), and proper occupations for each group. The chapter also details āpaddharma—rules governing permissible livelihoods, ritual exemptions, and emergency conduct when normal varṇa duties cannot be sustained. Medhātithi applies Mīmāṃsā principles and legal reasoning to interpret these rules and reconcile conflicting smṛti traditions.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_narayanabhatta_tristha.author: Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa
SA_GSD36_utaustin_narayanabhatta_tristha.summary: The Tristhalīsetu is a Dharmaśāstra work on pilgrimage by Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa. This introductory section, the Sāmānyapraghaṭṭaka, establishes the general procedural, theological, and ritual principles of pilgrimage (tīrthayātrā), analyzing eligibility, travel regulations, vows, tonsure, and the performance of śrāddha and tarpaṇa at sacred sites before treating Prayāga, Kāśī, and Gayā individually.

SA_GSD37_utaustin_olivelle_apastamba_dha.title: Āpastambadharmasūtra
SA_GSD37_utaustin_olivelle_apastamba_dha.author: Āpastamba
SA_GSD37_utaustin_olivelle_apastamba_dha.summary: The Āpastambadharmasūtra is an early normative treatise on Dharma belonging to the Black Yajurveda. Arranged in two books (praśnas), it addresses social duty according to class (varṇa) and stage of life (āśrama), Vedic initiation (upanayana), student discipline (brahmacarya), household obligations, dietary rules, penances (prāyaścitta), civil and criminal law, and royal duties. It also contains the Adhyātmapaṭala on spiritual discipline and liberation.

SA_GSD37_utaustin_olivelle_baudhayana_dh.title: Baudhāyanadharmasūtra
SA_GSD37_utaustin_olivelle_baudhayana_dh.author: Baudhāyana

Arranged in four books (praśnas), it outlines sources of dharma, regional customs, student life, marriage, inheritance, penances (prāyaścitta), dietary rules, and ascetic codes.

SA_GSD37_utaustin_olivelle_gautama_dharm.title: Gautamadharmasūtra
SA_GSD37_utaustin_olivelle_gautama_dharm.author: Gautama
SA_GSD37_utaustin_olivelle_gautama_dharm.summary: The Gautamadharmasūtra is widely recognized as one of the oldest surviving prose manuals of Brahmanical law and ritual conduct (dharma), traditionally affiliated with the Sāmaveda and usually dated between the 5th and 3rd centuries BCE. Spanning 28 chapters in terse sūtra style, it details the obligations of the four varṇas and āśramas, rites of initiation (upanayana), study of the Veda, personal purification and dietary restrictions, domestic rites, royal administration and judicial procedure (rājadharma), inheritance laws (dāyabhāga), and a detailed catalog of penances and expiations (prāyaścitta).

SA_GSD36_utaustin_olivelle_manavadharmas.title: Mānavadharmaśāstra
SA_GSD36_utaustin_olivelle_manavadharmas.summary: The Mānavadharmaśāstra (or Manusmṛti) is the foremost and most influential classical Sanskrit treatise on dharma. Arranged in twelve adhyāyas, it covers cosmogony, the sources of dharma, sacraments (saṃskāra), studenthood, householder duties, dietary rules, ritual purity, death rites, kingship, civil and criminal law (the eighteen vyavahārapadas), the duties of women and castes, penances (prāyaścitta), and karma/transmigration leading to final liberation.

SA_GSD37_utaustin_olivelle_vasistha_dhar.title: Vāsiṣṭhadharmasūtra
SA_GSD37_utaustin_olivelle_vasistha_dhar.author: Vasiṣṭha
SA_GSD37_utaustin_olivelle_vasistha_dhar.summary: The Vāsiṣṭhadharmasūtra is one of the four surviving major prose-verse Dharmasūtras of ancient India, traditionally associated with the Ṛgveda. Across thirty adhyāyas, it treats the foundational topics of dharmaśāstra: the geographic boundaries of Āryāvarta, the valid sources of dharma, duties of the four varṇas and āśramas, marriage forms, adoption and inheritance, rules of purity and diet, the duties of the king, legal procedure, and extensive penances (prāyaścittas).

SA_GSD36_utaustin_olivelle_yajnavalkyadh.title: Yājñavalkyadharmaśāstra
SA_GSD36_utaustin_olivelle_yajnavalkyadh.author: Yājñavalkya
SA_GSD36_utaustin_olivelle_yajnavalkyadh.summary: The Yājñavalkyadharmaśāstra (commonly known as the Yājñavalkyasmṛti) is a metrical treatise of classical Hindu law and jurisprudence, divided into three sections: Ācāra, Vyavahāra, and Prāyaścitta.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_prataparudra_sarasvati.title: Sarasvatīvilāsa (Vyavahārakāṇḍa)
SA_GSD36_utaustin_prataparudra_sarasvati.author: Pratāparudra
SA_GSD36_utaustin_prataparudra_sarasvati.summary: The Sarasvatīvilāsa is a Dharmaśāstra nibandha work composed around the end of the 15th and the beginning of the 16th century, attributed to Śrī Pratāparudradeva. This Vyavahārakāṇḍa constitutes the legal branch of the nibandha, covering court procedure, evidence, and the eighteen titles of law (vivādapada). The work discusses earlier authorities, including Vijñāneśvara.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_prataparudra_sarasvati.attribution: UT Austin South Asia Institute Sanskrit OER; editor/transcriber per source text.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_prataparudra_sarasvati.edition: The Sarasvatīvilāsa, edited by R. Shama Sastry (OLPSS 71), Mysore.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_prataparudra_sarasvati.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Vyavahārakāṇḍa (five ullāsas treating legal procedure, evidence, and the eighteen vivādapadas through prakīrṇaka).

SA_GSD36_utaustin_raghunandana_divyatatt.title: Divyatattva
SA_GSD36_utaustin_raghunandana_divyatatt.author: Raghunandana
SA_GSD36_utaustin_raghunandana_divyatatt.summary: The Divyatattva is one of the twenty-eight treatises (tattvas) comprising the Smṛtitattva of the 16th-century Bengali jurist Raghunandana. It provides an exhaustive legal and ritual exposition of judicial ordeals (divya) in Hindu vyavahāra, detailing the nine classical ordeals (the balance, fire, water, poison, sacred libation/koṣa, grains of rice, heated coin, heated plowshare, and dharma/adharma tokens). The work examines their evidentiary validity, judicial qualifications, procedures of administration, and exemptions according to social status and severity of the accusation.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_raghunandana_divyatatt.attribution: UT Austin South Asia Institute Sanskrit OER; editor/transcriber per source text.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_raghunandana_divyatatt.edition: Richard W. Lariviere (ed. and tr.), The Divyatattva of Raghunandana Bhaṭṭācārya: Ordeals in Classical Hindu Law. [New Delhi: Manohar, 1981].
SA_GSD36_utaustin_raghunandana_divyatatt.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Divyatattva, spanning pages 80 to 158 of Lariviere's critical edition, concluding with the standard colophon: 'ity vadhyaghaṭīyaśrīhariharabhaṭṭācāryātmajaśrīraghunandanabhaṭṭācāryaviracite smṛtitattve divyatattvaṃ samāptam'.
translations: Richard W. Lariviere, The Divyatattva of Raghunandana Bhaṭṭācārya: Ordeals in Classical Hindu Law. Critically edited with English translation. (English)

SA_GSD36_utaustin_sridhara_smrtyarthasar.title: Smṛtyarthasāra
SA_GSD36_utaustin_sridhara_smrtyarthasar.author: Śrīdhara
SA_GSD36_utaustin_sridhara_smrtyarthasar.summary: The Smṛtyarthasāra of Śrīdhara (composed c. 1150–1200 CE) is a prominent medieval Dharmaśāstra digest (nibandha). It systematically summarizes canonical smṛti injunctions across two principal divisions: ācāraprakaraṇa (encompassing saṃskāras, daily rites, gotra/pravara rules, marriage, funeral rites, ritual purification, and āśauca) and prāyaścittaprakaraṇa (prescribing penances and expiations for transgressions and sins). The work is quoted by Hemādri.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_sridhara_smrtyarthasar.attribution: UT Austin South Asia Institute Sanskrit OER; editor/transcriber per source text.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_sridhara_smrtyarthasar.coverage: complete — Complete text covering both major prakaraṇas (ācāra/āhnika and prāyaścitta), preceded by a table of contents with page numbers.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_unknown_daksasmrti.title: Dakṣasmṛti
SA_GSD36_utaustin_unknown_daksasmrti.author: Dakṣa
SA_GSD36_utaustin_unknown_daksasmrti.summary: The Dakṣasmṛti (or Dakṣasaṃhitā) is a metrical Dharmaśāstra text in seven chapters traditionally attributed to the sage Dakṣa Prajāpati. It primarily outlines the daily duties (āhnika) and codes of conduct for the four life stages (āśrama), placing special emphasis on the virtues and responsibilities of the householder (gṛhastha). The work covers morning ablutions, ritual purity (śauca), gift-giving (dāna), domestic ethics, and concludes with a philosophical exposition of non-dualism (advaita) and self-knowledge.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_unknown_daksasmrti.attribution: UT Austin South Asia Institute Sanskrit OER; editor/transcriber per source text.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_unknown_daksasmrti.coverage: complete — Contains all 7 chapters (adhyāyas) ending with verse 7.54 and colophon 'iti dākṣe dharmaśāstre saptamo ‘dhyāyaḥ | samāptā ceyaṃ dakṣasaṃhitā ||'.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_unknown_vaisnavadharma.title: Vaiṣṇavadharmaśāstra
SA_GSD36_utaustin_unknown_vaisnavadharma.summary: The Vaiṣṇavadharmaśāstra (Viṣṇusmṛti) is a Dharmaśāstra in 100 chapters of mixed prose and verse, framed as Viṣṇu's teaching to the Earth after his rescue of her in the boar (Varāha) form. It covers the duties of the varṇas, kingship, law and punishment, inheritance, impurity, śrāddha, penance and other topics, with a distinctly Vaiṣṇava frame.
SA_GSD36_utaustin_unknown_vaisnavadharma.attribution: UT Austin South Asia Institute Sanskrit OER; editor/transcriber per source text.

SA_GSD36_utaustin_varadaraja_vyavaharani.title: Vyavahāranirṇaya
SA_GSD36_utaustin_varadaraja_vyavaharani.author: Varadarāja

SA_GSD36_utaustin_yadavaprakasa_yatidhar.title: Yatidharmasamuccaya
SA_GSD36_utaustin_yadavaprakasa_yatidhar.author: Yādavaprakāśa
SA_GSD36_utaustin_yadavaprakasa_yatidhar.summary: The Yatidharmasamuccaya is a digest (nibandha) on renunciation (saṃnyāsa) and ascetic discipline authored by Yādavaprakāśa. Arranged in eleven chapters (parvas), the work synthesizes injunctions from Vedic texts, Dharmaśāstras, and Purāṇas concerning the legitimacy and qualification for renunciation, the initiation ritual, ascetic emblems, daily observances, dietary restrictions, expiations, and post-mortem rites.

SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_aitareya_upani.title: Aitareya Upaniṣad
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_aitareya_upani.summary: The Aitareya Upaniṣad belongs to the Ṛgveda tradition. It begins with a cosmogonic account in which the Ātman creates the universe, cosmic deities, and human sensory faculties, describes the threefold birth of the individual self, and concludes with an inquiry into the nature of the self, culminating in the renowned mahāvākya 'prajñānaṃ brahma' (consciousness is brahman).
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_aitareya_upani.attribution: Patrick Olivelle; UT Austin South Asia Institute.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_aitareya_upani.edition: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation, Oxford University Press, 1998; electronic edition transcribed by Patrick Olivelle, UT Austin South Asia Institute OER (2025).
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_aitareya_upani.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 3 adhyāyas, closing with the final mantra 3.4 and the colophon 'iti aitareyopaniṣat'.

SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_brhadaranyaka_.title: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_brhadaranyaka_.summary: The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad forms the final portion of the Śukla Yajurveda's Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa. It centres on the philosophical debates and dialogues of the sage Yājñavalkya at the court of King Janaka of Videha, along with his exchanges with his wife Maitreyī. It provides foundational expositions of ātman, karma and rebirth.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_brhadaranyaka_.attribution: Patrick Olivelle; UT Austin South Asia Institute.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_brhadaranyaka_.edition: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation, Oxford University Press, 1998.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_brhadaranyaka_.coverage: complete — Complete text in six adhyāyas (1.1.1 through 6.5.4).

Patrick Olivelle, Upaniṣads, Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1996. (English)

SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_chandogya_upan.title: Chāndogyopaniṣad
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_chandogya_upan.summary: The Chāndogyopaniṣad is one of the earliest and most significant Vedic prose Upaniṣads, belonging to the Sāmaveda tradition. In eight chapters (adhyāyas), it begins with ritual and mystical expositions of the Sāman chant and the sacred syllable Om (udgītha), and develops into foundational Upaniṣadic philosophy. Key sections include the Pañcāgnividyā (five fires doctrine), Uddālaka Āruṇi's instruction to Śvetaketu culminating in the mahāvākya 'tat tvam asi', and teachings on the nature of the ātman in the heart and the city of brahman.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_chandogya_upan.attribution: Patrick Olivelle; UT Austin South Asia Institute.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_chandogya_upan.edition: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation (Oxford University Press, 1998).
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_chandogya_upan.coverage: complete — Complete text in 8 prapāṭhakas (adhyāyas), running from 1.1.1 to 8.15.1.
translations: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation, Oxford University Press, 1998. (English)

SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_isa_upanisad.title: Īśā Upaniṣad
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_isa_upanisad.summary: The Īśā Upaniṣad (or Īśopaniṣad) is a metrical Upaniṣad. Across eighteen verses, it addresses the tension between renunciation and worldly activity, proclaims the pervasive presence of the Self in all beings, reflects upon the dialectic between knowledge (vidyā) and ignorance (avidyā), and concludes with prayers addressed to Pūṣan and Agni.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_isa_upanisad.attribution: Patrick Olivelle; UT Austin South Asia Institute.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_isa_upanisad.edition: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation. Oxford University Press, 1998.

SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_katha_upanisad.title: Kaṭhopaniṣad
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_katha_upanisad.summary: The Kaṭhopaniṣad is a classical verse Upaniṣad belonging to the Kaṭha school of the Black Yajurveda (Kṛṣṇayajurveda). It is framed as a dialogue between the young seeker Naciketas and Yama, the god of death, who grants Naciketas three boons, the culmination of which is an inquiry into what happens to a person after death. The text provides foundational formulations of early Vedānta and Yoga philosophy, including the distinction between the pleasant (preyas) and the beneficial (śreyas), the chariot allegory for the psycho-physical faculties, and instructions on meditative absorption to realize the innermost self (ātman).
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_katha_upanisad.attribution: Patrick Olivelle; UT Austin South Asia Institute.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_katha_upanisad.edition: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation, New York: Oxford University Press, 1998.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_katha_upanisad.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising 6 vallīs (2 adhyāyas of 3 vallīs each), numbered consecutively 1.1 to 6.18, ending with 'iti ṣaṣṭhī vallī' and 'iti kaṭhopaniṣat'.
translations: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation, Oxford University Press, 1998. (English)

SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_kausitaki_upan.title: Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_kausitaki_upan.summary: The Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad is an ancient prose Upaniṣad of the Ṛgveda. Across four chapters, it expounds the post-mortem journey of the soul along the devayāna path (Chapter 1), sacrificial and domestic rituals focused on prāṇa as the central vital breath (Chapter 2), Indra's instruction to Pratardana identifying prāṇa with prajñātman (the conscious self) and Brahman (Chapter 3), and King Ajātaśatru's instruction of the proud Brahmin Gārgya Bālāki regarding the true nature of the self in deep sleep and waking consciousness (Chapter 4).
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_kausitaki_upan.attribution: Patrick Olivelle; UT Austin South Asia Institute.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_kausitaki_upan.edition: Patrick Olivelle (ed. & tr.), The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation, Oxford / New York: Oxford University Press, 1998.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_kausitaki_upan.coverage: complete — Complete text in 4 adhyāyas (1.1 to 4.20), ending with '|| iti caturtho 'dhyāyaḥ || || iti kauṣitaky upaniṣat ||'.

SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_kena_upanisad.title: Kena Upaniṣad
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_kena_upanisad.summary: The Kena Upaniṣad belongs to the Sāmaveda and is among the early Upaniṣads. Comprising verse sections followed by prose sections, it investigates the impelling ground behind speech, mind, breath, and sensation, concluding that Brahman is the transcendent cognizer that cannot be grasped as an objective phenomenon. The latter half relates the allegory of Vedic gods humbled by a mysterious spirit (yakṣa), whom the goddess Umā Haimavatī identifies as Brahman.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_kena_upanisad.attribution: Patrick Olivelle; UT Austin South Asia Institute.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_kena_upanisad.edition: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation, Oxford University Press, 1998.

translations: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation, Oxford University Press, 1998. (English)
Patrick Olivelle, Upaniṣads, Oxford: Oxford University Press (Oxford World's Classics), 1996. (English)

SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_mandukya_upani.title: Māṇḍūkyopaniṣad
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_mandukya_upani.summary: The Māṇḍūkyopaniṣad, canonically associated with the Atharvaveda, is the most concise of the principal classical Upaniṣads, comprising twelve prose mantras. It equates the Self (ātman) and Brahman with the sacred syllable Om, systematically analyzing consciousness into four quarters (pādas): waking (vaiśvānara/A), dreaming (taijasa/U), dreamless sleep (prājña/M), and the transcendent, unmanifest fourth state (turīya/amātra). Despite its brevity, it occupies a central place in Indian philosophy as the textual foundation for Gauḍapāda's Māṇḍūkyakārikā and the subsequent development of Advaita Vedānta.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_mandukya_upani.attribution: Patrick Olivelle; UT Austin South Asia Institute.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_mandukya_upani.edition: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation, Oxford University Press, 1998.

translations: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation, Oxford University Press, 1998. (English)
Patrick Olivelle, Upaniṣads, World's Classic Series, Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1996. (English)
