SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_mundaka_upanis.title: Muṇḍakopaniṣad
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_mundaka_upanis.summary: The Muṇḍakopaniṣad is a classical verse Upaniṣad affiliated with the Atharvaveda tradition. Divided into three muṇḍakas, each comprising two khaṇḍas, it structures its philosophical instruction as a dialogue between the sage Aṅgiras and the householder Śaunaka. The text is renowned for distinguishing lower ritual and empirical knowledge (aparā vidyā) from higher liberating knowledge of the imperishable Brahman (parā vidyā), and it contains foundational Upaniṣadic allegories including the two birds on the same tree, the bow and arrow aimed at Brahman, and the national motto of India ('satyam eva jayate').
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_mundaka_upanis.attribution: Patrick Olivelle; UT Austin South Asia Institute.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_mundaka_upanis.edition: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation, Oxford University Press, 1998.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_mundaka_upanis.coverage: complete — Complete text in three muṇḍakas, each divided into two khaṇḍas (1.1.1–3.2.11), ending with the colophon '|| iti tṛtīyaṃ muṇḍakam || iti muṇḍakopaniṣat ||'.
translations: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation, Oxford University Press, 1998. (English)
Patrick Olivelle (ed. and trans.), Upaniṣads, World's Classics Series, Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1996. (English)
Paul Deussen, German translation published 1897. (German)

SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_prasna_upanisa.title: Praśna Upaniṣad
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_prasna_upanisa.summary: The Praśna Upaniṣad is a classical Vedic text associated with the Pippalāda recension of the Atharvaveda, numbered among the principal (mukhya) Upaniṣads. Structured as an inquiry by six seekers of Brahman addressing the sage Pippalāda, the work unfolds in six sections (praśnas) addressing cosmogony through the polarity of rayi (matter) and prāṇa (breath/energy), the supremacy and functions of vital breath, physiological and psychic functions, the dream and deep sleep states, meditation on the syllable Om, and the nature of the sixteen-part Puruṣa.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_prasna_upanisa.attribution: Patrick Olivelle; UT Austin South Asia Institute.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_prasna_upanisa.edition: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation, Oxford University Press, 1998.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_prasna_upanisa.coverage: complete — Complete text in six praśnas, ending at 6.8 with 'iti praśnopaniṣatsamāptā'.
translations: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation, Oxford University Press, 1998. (English)
Patrick Olivelle, Upaniṣads, World's Classics Series, Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1996. (English)
S. Radhakrishnan, The Principal Upaniṣads, London: George Allen & Unwin. (English)

SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_svetasvatara_u.title: Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_svetasvatara_u.summary: The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad is a classical metrical Upaniṣad associated with the Black Yajurveda tradition, dating to approximately the late centuries BCE. It synthesizes Vedāntic non-dualism with early Sāṃkhya-Yoga categories, yogic contemplation and posture (adhyāya 2), and personal theism centered on Rudra-Śiva. The text outlines a threefold reality comprising the individual soul (bhoktṛ), the objective world (bhogya), and the supreme lord (preritṛ / īśa), and provides one of the earliest occurrences of the concept of bhakti in classical Sanskrit literature (6.23).
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_svetasvatara_u.attribution: Patrick Olivelle; UT Austin South Asia Institute.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_svetasvatara_u.edition: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation, New York / Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1998.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_svetasvatara_u.coverage: complete — Complete text in six adhyāyas (113 verses: 1.16, 2.17, 3.21, 4.22, 5.14, 6.23).
translations: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation, Oxford University Press, 1998. (English)
Paul Deussen, 1897. (German)
S. Radhakrishnan, The Principal Upaniṣads, London: George Allen & Unwin, 1953, p. 717. (English)

SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_taittiriya_upa.title: Taittirīya Upaniṣad
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_taittiriya_upa.summary: The Taittirīya Upaniṣad is one of the earliest and most influential mukhya (principal) Upaniṣads. It consists of three chapters: the Śīkṣāvallī, treating phonetics, cosmography, meditative correlation, and student duties; the Brahmavallī (or Ānandavallī), famous for defining Brahman (satyaṃ jñānam anantam) and articulating the five bodily sheaths/levels of self (pañcakośa); and the Bhṛguvallī, describing the sage Bhṛgu's progressive realization of Brahman through ascetic contemplation.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_taittiriya_upa.attribution: Patrick Olivelle; UT Austin South Asia Institute.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_taittiriya_upa.edition: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation, Oxford University Press, 1998.
SA_GV05_utaustin_olivelle_taittiriya_upa.coverage: complete — Complete text across all three vallīs: Śīkṣāvallī (1.1–12), Brahmavallī / Ānandavallī (2.1–9), and Bhṛguvallī (3.1–10).
translations: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation, Oxford University Press, 1998. (English)
Patrick Olivelle, Upaniṣads, World's Classics, Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1996. (English)

SA_T02_ilx_dsbc_advayasiddhi_book_85.title: Advayasiddhi
SA_T02_ilx_dsbc_advayasiddhi_book_85.author: Lakṣmīṅkarā
SA_T02_ilx_dsbc_advayasiddhi_book_85.summary: The Advayasiddhi is a foundational Sahajayāna/Vajrayāna treatise in 35 verses attributed to the female mahāsiddhā Lakṣmīṅkarā. It advocates non-dual realization (advaya) of innately luminous reality (prakṛti-prabhāsvara), critiquing external rituals, physical asceticism, and material deity worship while emphasizing internal somatic transformation, antinomian samaya practices, and devotion to the guru as the embodiment of Vajrasattva.
SA_T02_ilx_dsbc_advayasiddhi_book_85.attribution: Ascribed to the siddhā Lakṣmīṅkarā of Oḍḍiyāna, traditionally the sister of King Indrabhūti (Nakamura: 9th century). The text names only 'Śrī Lakṣmī' and Oḍḍiyāna in its colophon.
SA_T02_ilx_dsbc_advayasiddhi_book_85.coverage: complete — Complete: maṅgala, verses 1–35 and the prose colophon.

SA_T16_ilx_dsbc_buddhamata_book_270.title: Buddhamata (excerpts)
SA_T16_ilx_dsbc_buddhamata_book_270.summary: Short excerpts of modern Sanskrit prose. The first paragraph defines nāṭya as the triad of dance, song and instrumental music and names Bharata's Nāṭyaveda and Abhinavagupta's Abhinavabhāratī. The 'Buddhamata' section describes Buddhism as a reaction against rigid caste rules and animal sacrifice, lists its ethical values, cites the Sigālovāda and Mahārāhula suttas, and outlines its spread to China, Japan and Lanka. The 'Buddhamuni' section summarises the Buddha's life from his birth at Kapilavastu to his nirvāṇa, dating events in the Kali era and ending with the Purāṇic view of the Buddha as an avatāra of Viṣṇu.
SA_T16_ilx_dsbc_buddhamata_book_270.attribution: Anonymous modern Sanskrit prose. The three sections share one style and one chronology (Kali era: Abhinavagupta at Kali 4100, the Buddha born Kali 2544 and attaining nirvāṇa Kali 2624, Buddhism arising in the second half of the 26th Kali century). They therefore appear to be excerpts from a single modern Sanskrit work on Indian history and culture, not three separate works.

SA_K12_ilx_dsbc_candamaharosana_tantra_b.title: Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra (chapters 1–8)
SA_K12_ilx_dsbc_candamaharosana_tantra_b.summary: The Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra (also known as the Ekalavīratantra) is an Anuttarayoga / Yoginī tantra centered on the fierce deity Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa (a form of Acala) and his consort Dveṣavajrī. Chapters 1–8 cover the introduction to the tantra, maṇḍala construction, abhiṣeka rituals, iconographic forms of the deities, root and retinue mantras, and esoteric yogic and sexual practices.
SA_K12_ilx_dsbc_candamaharosana_tantra_b.attribution: A canonical Vajrayāna tantra belonging to the Anuttarayoga / Yoginītantra class, framed as a dialogue between the wrathful deity Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa (Acala) and Dveṣavajrī (Vajradhātvīśvarī). Considered buddhavacana.
SA_K12_ilx_dsbc_candamaharosana_tantra_b.edition: Christopher S. George (ed.), The Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa Tantra, Chapters I–VIII, American Oriental Series 56, New Haven: American Oriental Society, 1974.
SA_K12_ilx_dsbc_candamaharosana_tantra_b.coverage: partial — Contains chapters 1–8 (ending with the colophon of chapter 8, svarūpapaṭalaḥ). The full work consists of 25 chapters.
translations: Christopher S. George, The Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa Tantra, Chapters I–VIII, American Oriental Series 56, New Haven: American Oriental Society, 1974. (English)

SA_T01_ilx_dsbc_kalyanapancavimsatistotr.title: Kalyāṇapañcaviṃśatistotra
SA_T01_ilx_dsbc_kalyanapancavimsatistotr.summary: A 25-stanza benedictory hymn in sragdharā metre from the Newar Buddhist tradition, each stanza ending with the refrain 'kalyāṇaṃ vaḥ kriyāsuḥ ...' ('may they bring you well-being'). It invokes Svayambhū and the Five Buddhas with their Prajñās, the protective goddesses (Pañcarakṣā etc.), the past Buddhas, the great bodhisattvas, and the sacred sites (vītarāgas, Gokarṇeśvara, Mañjuśrī's caitya) of the Kathmandu Valley, following the legends of the Svayambhūpurāṇa, from which the colophon says it is extracted.
SA_T01_ilx_dsbc_kalyanapancavimsatistotr.attribution: Colophon explicitly identifies the text as extracted from the Svayambhūpurāṇa (śrī svayambhupurāṇoddhṛtā kalyāṇapañcaviṃśatistutiḥ samāptā).
SA_T01_ilx_dsbc_kalyanapancavimsatistotr.coverage: complete — 25 sragdharā stanzas with the refrain 'kalyāṇaṃ vaḥ kriyāsuḥ ...' and the colophon 'śrī svayambhupurāṇoddhṛtā kalyāṇapañcaviṃśatistutiḥ samāptā'.

SA_T16_ilx_dsbc_nalandadahana_book_272.title: Nālandādahana
SA_T16_ilx_dsbc_nalandadahana_book_272.author: V. Subramaniam
SA_T16_ilx_dsbc_nalandadahana_book_272.summary: Nālandādahana ('The Burning of Nālandā') is a Sanskrit dance-drama of the ḍima type. Composed with songs (pallavi, anupallavi, caraṇam) in various classical rāgas (such as Durgā, Pūrvakalyāṇī, Ābhogi, Siṃhendramadhyamam, Vihag) and ādi tāla. Students sing praise of Nālandā, the abbot and senior monks discuss the approaching Turkish army attack, followed by the assault and destruction. It concludes with the head librarian nun dancing and proclaiming the enduring fame of mother Nālandā.
SA_T16_ilx_dsbc_nalandadahana_book_272.attribution: A dance-drama attributed in the text to Subrahmaṇya (rubric: 'śrī subrahmaṇyaciracitaṃ [read: °viracitaṃ]'). The rubric designates it as a ḍima-style dance drama (ḍimargagarṇāyaṃ nṛtyanāṭakaṃ) emphasizing vīra, raudra, bhayānaka, and karuṇa sentiments, set to be performed at the main gate of the Nālandā University ruins.
SA_T16_ilx_dsbc_nalandadahana_book_272.coverage: complete — Nāndī, scenes at the gate of Nālandā, and closing hymn to mother Nālandā ('jaya jaya jananī nālandā').

SA_T02_ilx_dsbc_nanasiddhopadesa_book_79.title: Nānāsiddhopadeśa
SA_T02_ilx_dsbc_nanasiddhopadesa_book_79.summary: A short anonymous Sanskrit anthology of yogic instructions (upadeśa) ascribed to fourteen siddhas, among them Saraha, Kṛṣṇācārya, Virūpa, Vīṇāpāda, Diṅnāga and Matsyendra. The instructions deal with caṇḍālī, the 'swing' (dolā) of the breath, the drop (bindu) and seed-syllables in the cakras, and the kākatuṇḍī breathing technique. It has no Tibetan translation.
SA_T02_ilx_dsbc_nanasiddhopadesa_book_79.attribution: An anonymous compilation of short instructions ascribed to 14 siddhas: Padmāṅkura, Prajñārakṣita, Nelīpāda, Ravigupta, Kṛṣṇācārya, Sarahapāda, Mahīdhara, Bhūripāda, Vīṇāpāda, Virūpācārya, Nāgabuddhi, Diṅnāga, Mātali and Matsyendra. Davidson counts 13. There is no Tibetan translation.
SA_T02_ilx_dsbc_nanasiddhopadesa_book_79.edition: Nānāsiddhopadeśaḥ, published in Dhīḥ 18 (1994) ('Introduction to Rare Texts', where 'The entire text has been reproduced here'). (probable)
SA_T02_ilx_dsbc_nanasiddhopadesa_book_79.coverage: complete — Complete short text: the 14 siddhas' instructions and the closing 'iti nānāsiddhopadeśaḥ'.

SA_T14_ilx_dsbc_nrtyaprasuti_book_273.title: Nṛtyaprasūti
SA_T14_ilx_dsbc_nrtyaprasuti_book_273.author: V. Subramaniam
SA_T14_ilx_dsbc_nrtyaprasuti_book_273.summary: Nṛtyaprasūti ('The Birth of Dance') is a Sanskrit dance-drama written as songs set to Carnatic rāgas (Gauḷa, Haṃsadhvani, Darbār, Pantuvarāḷi, Nītimati, etc.) with pallavi/anupallavi/caraṇam divisions. The nāndī praises the Buddha as conqueror of Māra, tamer of the elephant and turner of the dharmacakra under the tree. The two scenes then show the gods oppressed by the Tripura demons and appealing to Śiva, the destruction of Tripura, and the celebration of Śiva's tāṇḍava and Pārvatī's lāsya at Kailāsa as the origin of dance.
SA_T14_ilx_dsbc_nrtyaprasuti_book_273.attribution: Dance-drama (nṛtyanāṭaka) composed by Subrahmaṇyadīkṣita (rubric: 'śrīsuvrahmaṇyadīkṣivena viracitaṃ nṛtyanāṭakama').
SA_T14_ilx_dsbc_nrtyaprasuti_book_273.coverage: complete — Nāndī and two scenes (prathamaṃ dṛśyam, dvitīyaṃ dṛśyam), ending with the closing song to Śiva and Pārvatī.

SA_T16_ilx_dsbc_svapnadhyaya_book_770.title: Svapnādhyāya (vv. 1–30, incomplete)
SA_T16_ilx_dsbc_svapnadhyaya_book_770.summary: A short Sanskrit verse manual of oneiromancy, which presents itself as composed by Bṛhaspati and opens with 'namo buddhāya'. It states when a dream bears fruit according to the watch of the night in which it is seen. It then lists auspicious and inauspicious dream images, such as mounting elephants and trees, eating human flesh, drinking milk, and things on fire.
SA_T16_ilx_dsbc_svapnadhyaya_book_770.attribution: Verse 1 presents the text as 'composed by Bṛhaspati' (bṛhaspativinirmitam), while the text opens 'namo buddhāya'. The Tibetan translation (D 1749) is translated by Vibhūticandra.
SA_T16_ilx_dsbc_svapnadhyaya_book_770.coverage: partial — Verses 1–30 and the first pāda of v. 31 ('sa vyādhimukto nirujo'). Angle brackets < > mark editorial additions and parentheses ( ) mark restorations of damaged akṣaras.
translations: rmi lam brtag pa (Derge Tengyur D 1749): translated by Vibhūticandra (Tibetan)

SA_T02_ilx_dsbc_sricakrasambarabhisamaya.title: Śrīcakrasambarābhisamayavyākhyā
SA_T02_ilx_dsbc_sricakrasambarabhisamaya.author: Śāśvatavajra
SA_T02_ilx_dsbc_sricakrasambarabhisamaya.summary: A Vajrayāna ritual and meditative commentary (abhisamayavyākhyā) associated with the Cakrasaṃvara (Heruka) tradition by Śāśvatavajra. It expounds the esoteric analysis of the syllables 'śrī-he-ru-ka', generation of the maṇḍala deities, symbolic transformation of the aggregates (skandha) into Tathāgatas, purification practices, and daily yoga during meals and twilight sessions (sandhyā).
SA_T02_ilx_dsbc_sricakrasambarabhisamaya.attribution: Attributed in the colophon directly to Śāśvatavajra (kṛtiriyaṃ śāśvatavajrasya).
SA_T02_ilx_dsbc_sricakrasambarabhisamaya.edition: Śrīcakrasambarābhisamayavyākhyā by Śāśvatavajra, published in Dhīḥ 53, pp. 135–137ff. E-text input and proofread by Rashmi Shakya for the Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon (DSBC), Nagarjuna Institute of Exact Methods / University of the West.
SA_T02_ilx_dsbc_sricakrasambarabhisamaya.coverage: complete — Complete short ritual exegesis treatise from opening salutation (namaḥ śrīcakrasambarāya) to the final authorial colophon (samāptā kṛtiriyaṃ śāśvatavajrasya).

SA_K12_ilx_dsbc_dakarnava_book_809.title: Ḍākārṇava (Apabhraṃśa songs I–XXVIII in Sanskrit rendering)
SA_K12_ilx_dsbc_dakarnava_book_809.summary: The Ḍākārṇava (Ḍākārṇavamahāyoginītantrarāja) is a tantra partly containing Apabhraṃśa verses. This e-text gives a Sanskrit rendering of 28 verse sections encoding bīja-mantras and treating sahaja and mahāsukha.
SA_K12_ilx_dsbc_dakarnava_book_809.attribution: Canonical Anuttarayoga tantra traditionally regarded as the word of the Buddha.
SA_K12_ilx_dsbc_dakarnava_book_809.coverage: excerpt — Sections I–XXVIII of Sanskritised verse: bīja-mantra codes and songs on sahaja and mahāsukha, with running markers (p1-2) ... (p 51-52) etc. The Sanskrit text of the full tantra is not included. The last section (XXVIII) ends without colophon.
translations: dpal mkha' 'gro rgya mtsho rnal 'byor ma'i rgyud kyi rgyal po chen po zhes bya ba (Derge Kangyur D 372): translated by Jayasena III, sum pa lo tsA ba dar ma yon tan; at dpal bal yul grub pa'i gnas mchog chen po yu tung lhun gyis grub pa'i gtsug lag khang chen po (Tibetan)

SA_GSP33_ilx_gr_AdizeSa_paramArthasAra.title: Paramārthasāra
SA_GSP33_ilx_gr_AdizeSa_paramArthasAra.author: Ādiśeṣa
SA_GSP33_ilx_gr_AdizeSa_paramArthasAra.summary: The Paramārthasāra ('Essence of Ultimate Truth'), traditionally attributed to Ādiśeṣa, is a concise philosophical poem of 85 āryā stanzas setting forth an early form of non-dualist Vedānta with strong Vaiṣṇava and Sāṅkhya-Yoga affinities. Identifying the ultimate reality (Brahman) with Viṣṇu, it elucidates the relationship between prakṛti and puruṣa, the nature of cosmic illusion (māyā/avidyā), and final release through knowledge. It is historically notable as the source text reworked by Abhinavagupta into his prominent treatise of the same title.
SA_GSP33_ilx_gr_AdizeSa_paramArthasAra.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Ādiśeṣa (Śeṣanāga / Bhagavadaśeṣa). The text represents an early Vaiṣṇava-oriented Vedāntic treatise that served as the base text for Abhinavagupta's adaptation of the same name.
SA_GSP33_ilx_gr_AdizeSa_paramArthasAra.edition: Henry Danielson, The Essence of Supreme Truth (Paramārthasāra). Sanskrit text with translation and notes, Leiden: Brill, 1980 (Nisaba, 10).
SA_GSP33_ilx_gr_AdizeSa_paramArthasAra.coverage: complete — Complete text of 85 āryā verses, ending with the author colophon verse (āryāpañcāśītyā babandha paramārthasāram idam) and closing colophon (iti paramārthasāraṃ samāptam).
translations: Henry Danielson, The Essence of Supreme Truth (Paramārthasāra). Sanskrit text with translation and notes, Leiden: Brill, 1980 (Nisaba, 10). (English)

SA_GV06_ilx_gr_ApastambazulbasUtra.title: Āpastambaśulbasūtra with the commentaries of Kapardisvāmin, Karavinda and Sundararāja
SA_GV06_ilx_gr_ApastambazulbasUtra.author: Āpastamba, Kapardisvāmin, Karavinda, Sundararāja
SA_GV06_ilx_gr_ApastambazulbasUtra.summary: A Śulbasūtra text belonging to the Āpastamba tradition with running commentaries (including Kapardibhāṣya and Sundararāja's Śulbapradīpa), treating altar construction, geometry, and layout of agnyāyatanas and vedis.
SA_GV06_ilx_gr_ApastambazulbasUtra.attribution: The colophon at the end of the text identifies the work as 'savyākhya āpastambīyaśulbapraśnaḥ'.
SA_GV06_ilx_gr_ApastambazulbasUtra.coverage: complete — Text of the Āpastambaśulbasūtra along with commentaries (Kapardibhāṣya, Karavinda, Sundararāja), concluding: 'iti sundararājīyaṃ saṃpūrṇaṃ samāptaḥ savyākhya āpastambīyaśulbapraśnaḥ'.

SA_GR14_ilx_gr_avadhUtasiddha_bhagavadbh.title: Bhagavadbhaktistotra
SA_GR14_ilx_gr_avadhUtasiddha_bhagavadbh.author: Avadhūtasiddha
SA_GR14_ilx_gr_avadhUtasiddha_bhagavadbh.summary: The Bhagavadbhaktistotra is a non-dual Śaiva devotional hymn composed in ca. 65 stanzas by Avadhūtasiddha. Extolling Śiva as the supreme reality encompassing and transcending the perspectives of diverse philosophical traditions (including Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Sāṃkhya, Buddhism, and Vedānta), it was highly regarded in Kashmirian Śaiva circles and is quoted by Abhinavagupta in the Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī and Yogarāja on the Paramārthasāra.
SA_GR14_ilx_gr_avadhUtasiddha_bhagavadbh.attribution: Explicitly attributed to Avadhūtasiddha in penultimate verse ('avadhūtanāmnā') and in the closing colophon ('iti śrīmadavadhūtasiddhaviracitaṃ bhagavadbhaktistotraṃ samāptam'). He was an early non-dual Śaiva author cited by Abhinavagupta, Yogarāja, and Śrīkumāra.
SA_GR14_ilx_gr_avadhUtasiddha_bhagavadbh.edition: Raniero Gnoli, 'Miscellanea Indica', East and West 9 (1958), pp. 215–226 [cited in TEI header as 451–455].
SA_GR14_ilx_gr_avadhUtasiddha_bhagavadbh.coverage: complete — Complete stotra of ca. 65 stanzas, with opening invocation to Netratantra/Śiva and final colophon.

SA_GS40_ilx_gr_bower_manuscript.title: Bower Manuscript
SA_GS40_ilx_gr_bower_manuscript.summary: The Bower Manuscript is a famous birch-bark codex discovered in 1890 in Kūcha, datable to ca. the 4th to 6th centuries CE. It contains Sanskrit texts including the Navanītaka (an early Ayurvedic compendium of medical recipes), two dice divination treatises (Pāśakakevalī), and portions of the Buddhist dhāraṇī scripture Mahāmāyūrīvidyārājñī.
SA_GS40_ilx_gr_bower_manuscript.attribution: A composite birch-bark manuscript written in Gupta script discovered in Kūcha (Central Asia) datable to ca. the 4th to 6th centuries CE. Mentions Yaśomitra.
SA_GS40_ilx_gr_bower_manuscript.edition: August Friedrich Rudolf Hoernle, 3 vols., Calcutta 1893-1912. (Archaeological Survey of India, New Imperial Series, 22)
SA_GS40_ilx_gr_bower_manuscript.coverage: complete — Complete transcription of the parts preserved in the Bower Manuscript as edited by Hoernle.
translations: August Friedrich Rudolf Hoernle [translation of the Bower Manuscript]. (English)

SA_T04_ilx_gr_candrakIrti_bodhisattvayog.title: Bodhisattvayogācāracatuḥśatakaṭīkā (fragments)
SA_T04_ilx_gr_candrakIrti_bodhisattvayog.author: Candrakīrti
SA_T04_ilx_gr_candrakIrti_bodhisattvayog.summary: The Bodhisattvayogācāracatuḥśatakaṭīkā by Candrakīrti is an authoritative commentary on Āryadeva's Catuḥśataka. The work expounds the bodhisattva path across sixteen chapters. Preserved fully in Tibetan translation (Toh 3865 / D 3865), this e-text contains the surviving Sanskrit palm-leaf fragments across all sixteen chapters, edited by Kōshin Suzuki.
SA_T04_ilx_gr_candrakIrti_bodhisattvayog.attribution: The root verses are by Āryadeva; the commentary is by Candrakīrti (seventh century).
SA_T04_ilx_gr_candrakIrti_bodhisattvayog.edition: Kōshin Suzuki, ed., Sanskrit Fragments and Tibetan Translation of Candrakīrti's Bodhisattvayogācāracatuḥśatakaṭīkā, Tokyo: The Sankibo Press, 1994.
SA_T04_ilx_gr_candrakIrti_bodhisattvayog.coverage: fragment — Fragmentary Sanskrit text of chapters 1–16 preserved in palm-leaf manuscripts. While chapter headings and portions of text from all 16 chapters are present, substantial portions of kārikās and commentary are missing with frequent lacunae.
translations: byang chub sems dpa'i rnal 'byor spyod pa bzhi brgya pa'i rgya cher 'grel pa (Derge Tengyur D 3865): translated by Sūkṣmajāna, pa tshab lo tsA ba nyi ma grags pa (Tibetan)

SA_K10_ilx_gr_candrasUtra.title: Candrasūtra
SA_K10_ilx_gr_candrasUtra.summary: The Candrasūtra is a short canonical Buddhist scripture belonging to the Saṃyuktāgama tradition (parallel to the Pāli Candimasutta, SN 2.9). It relates that when the moon deity is seized during an eclipse by the asura king Rāhu, the deity takes refuge in the Buddha. The Buddha then commands Rāhu to release the moon; terrified, Rāhu complies and explains to Bali Vairocana that disobedience to the Buddha's verse would cause his head to split into seven pieces.
SA_K10_ilx_gr_candrasUtra.attribution: Canonical discourse attributed to the Buddha; preserved in fragments belonging to the Sanskrit Saṃyuktāgama / Āgama tradition.
SA_K10_ilx_gr_candrasUtra.edition: Klaus Wille, 'Neue Fragmente des Candrasūtra', in: Bauddhasāhityastabakāvalī: Essays and Studies on Buddhist Sanskrit Literature Dedicated to Claus Vogel by Colleagues, Students, and Friends, ed. Dragomir Dimitrov, Michael Hahn, and Roland Steiner, Marburg: Indica et Tibetica Verlag, 2008 (Indica et Tibetica, 36), pp. 339–351.
SA_K10_ilx_gr_candrasUtra.coverage: complete — Complete 12-section critical reconstruction of the short sūtra from Central Asian manuscript fragments (Turfan and Pelliot Sanskrit bleu 449).

SA_GSP29_ilx_gr_hetvAbhAsadazaka.title: Hetvābhāsadaśaka
SA_GSP29_ilx_gr_hetvAbhAsadazaka.author: Yuvarāja of Koṭiliṅgapura
SA_GSP29_ilx_gr_hetvAbhAsadazaka.summary: The Hetvābhāsadaśaka is a short poem of eleven verses composed by a prince of Koṭiliṅgapura. It illustrates the classic logical fallacies (hetvābhāsas) through dramatic exchanges between figures from the epics, including Rāma and Sītā, Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā, and Lakṣmaṇa, Sugrīva, and Vibhīṣaṇa.
SA_GSP29_ilx_gr_hetvAbhAsadazaka.attribution: The concluding verse (v. 11) names the author as a yuvarāja residing in Koṭiliṅgapura.
SA_GSP29_ilx_gr_hetvAbhAsadazaka.edition: V. Varadachari, 'Hetvābhāsa-daśakam by a Prince of Koṭiliṅgapura', in: Rasiklal C. Parikh, Ratilal M. Trivedi, and Umashankar J. Joshi (eds.), Acharya Dhruva Smaraka Grantha, Part 3, Ahmedabad: Gujarat Vidya Sabha, pp. 213–221.
SA_GSP29_ilx_gr_hetvAbhAsadazaka.coverage: complete — Complete in 11 verses (10 illustrative stanzas and 1 concluding anustubh colophon verse).

SA_GK22_ilx_gr_kSemendra_caturvargasaMgr.title: Caturvargasaṃgraha
SA_GK22_ilx_gr_kSemendra_caturvargasaMgr.author: Kṣemendra
SA_GK22_ilx_gr_kSemendra_caturvargasaMgr.summary: The Caturvargasaṃgraha is a didactic kāvya composed by the poet Kṣemendra. Structured into four sections corresponding to the four ends of human life (puruṣārthas)—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—the work imparts ethical and practical instructions in gnomic verse.
SA_GK22_ilx_gr_kSemendra_caturvargasaMgr.attribution: Attributed internally in verses 1.2 ('kṣemendreṇa nijaślokaiḥ kriyate vargasaṃgrahaḥ') and 4.26 ('caturvargopadeśena kṣemendreṇa yad arjitam').
SA_GK22_ilx_gr_kSemendra_caturvargasaMgr.edition: Kāvyāmālā Part 5, edited by Paṇḍit Durgāprasād and Kāśīnāth Pāṇḍuraṅg Parab, Bombay: Nirnaya Sagar Press.
SA_GK22_ilx_gr_kSemendra_caturvargasaMgr.coverage: complete — Complete in four paricchedas dedicated to the four puruṣārthas (dharma, artha, kāma, mokṣa), concluding with 'samāpto 'yaṃ caturvargasaṃgrahaḥ'.

SA_GK19_ilx_gr_kSemendra_narmamAlA.title: Narmamālā
SA_GK19_ilx_gr_kSemendra_narmamAlA.author: Kṣemendra
SA_GK19_ilx_gr_kSemendra_narmamAlA.summary: The Narmamālā ('Garland of Mirth' or 'Garland of Satires') is a satirical poem in three chapters (parihāsas) composed in 11th-century Kashmir during the reign of King Ananta. It presents a caustic caricature and expose of corrupt scribe-officials (Kāyasthas and diviras), detailing their greed, oppression of the public, administrative malpractice, religious charlatanism, and domestic vices. Together with the Deśopadeśa, it is a key satirical source for socio-political life in medieval Kashmir.
SA_GK19_ilx_gr_kSemendra_narmamAlA.attribution: Explicitly attributed to Kṣemendra under his well-known epithet Vyāsadāsa in the colophon (KNarm_3.113ff.: kṛtir vyāsadāsāparanāmnaḥ kṣemendrasyeti śivam).
SA_GK19_ilx_gr_kSemendra_narmamAlA.edition: Fabrizia Baldissera (ed. and trans.), The Narmamālā of Kṣemendra. Critical Edition, Study and Translation, Beiträge zur Südasienforschung, Südasien-Institut Universität Heidelberg 197, Würzburg: Ergon Verlag, 2005.
SA_GK19_ilx_gr_kSemendra_narmamAlA.coverage: complete — Complete in three parihāsas (parihāsas 1–3), concluding at verse 3.113 and the author's final signature colophon.
translations: Fabrizia Baldissera, The Narmamālā of Kṣemendra: Critical Edition, Study and Translation, Beiträge zur Südasienforschung 197, Würzburg: Ergon Verlag, 2005. (English)

SA_GK22_ilx_gr_kSemendra_sevyasevakopade.title: Sevyasevakopadeśa
SA_GK22_ilx_gr_kSemendra_sevyasevakopade.author: Kṣemendra
SA_GK22_ilx_gr_kSemendra_sevyasevakopade.summary: The Sevyasevakopadeśa is a didactic and satirical poem (upadeśakāvya) composed by the Kashmiri writer Kṣemendra. It offers a critique of courtly dependence, describing the degradation, anxiety, and humiliation endured by servants and dependents (sevaka) at the hands of arrogant patrons and masters (sevya). The work ultimately praises self-reliance, moral autonomy, and inner contentment (saṃtoṣa).
SA_GK22_ilx_gr_kSemendra_sevyasevakopade.attribution: Attributed in the colophon to the Kashmiri poet Kṣemendra, who also bore the surname Vyāsadāsa.
SA_GK22_ilx_gr_kSemendra_sevyasevakopade.edition: Kṣemendrakṛtaḥ Sevyasevakopadeśaḥ, in: Kāvyamālā, Part 2, ed. Paṇḍit Durgāprasād, Kāśīnāth Pāṇḍuraṅg Parab, and Vāsudev Laxman Shāstrī Panshīkar, Bombay: Nirnaya Sagar Press.
SA_GK22_ilx_gr_kSemendra_sevyasevakopade.coverage: complete — Complete text concluding with the colophon.

SA_T09_ilx_gr_kSemendra_sudhanakinnaryav.title: Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā (chapter 64: Sudhanakinnaryavadāna)
SA_T09_ilx_gr_kSemendra_sudhanakinnaryav.author: Kṣemendra
SA_T09_ilx_gr_kSemendra_sudhanakinnaryav.summary: The Sudhanakinnaryavadāna constitutes the 64th chapter (pallava) of Kṣemendra's 11th-century kāvya work, the Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā. It narrates the romance of Prince Sudhana and the Kinnarī princess Manoharā, recounting their encounter, subsequent separation, Sudhana's perilous supernatural quest to find her in the Kinnara kingdom, and their eventual reunion. Framed in the context of the Buddha's past life, it explains karmic bonds relating to Yaśodharā.
SA_T09_ilx_gr_kSemendra_sudhanakinnaryav.attribution: Kṣemendra composed the work in the 11th century in Kashmir. Chapter 64 is authored by Kṣemendra.
SA_T09_ilx_gr_kSemendra_sudhanakinnaryav.edition: Martin Straube: Prinz Sudhana und die Kinnarī - Eine buddhistische Liebesgeschichte von Kṣemendra. Texte, Übersetzung, Studie. Marburg 2006 (Indica et Tibetica, 46)
SA_T09_ilx_gr_kSemendra_sudhanakinnaryav.coverage: partial — Contains the text of chapter (pallava) 64 (338 verses plus colophon) of the Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā.
translations: Martin Straube, Prinz Sudhana und die Kinnarī. Eine buddhistische Liebesgeschichte von Kṣemendra. Texte, Übersetzung, Studie, IeT 46, Marburg, 2006. (German)

SA_T02_ilx_gr_lakSmINkarA_advayasiddhi.title: Advayasiddhi
SA_T02_ilx_gr_lakSmINkarA_advayasiddhi.author: Lakṣmīṅkarā
SA_T02_ilx_gr_lakSmINkarA_advayasiddhi.summary: The Advayasiddhi ('Attainment of Non-Duality') is a concise Tantric treatise in 36 verses attributed to Lakṣmīṅkarā. It represents an early Sahajayāna orientation, teaching that enlightenment is directly attainable within the innate body without external asceticism, rituals, or conventional caste distinctions, while emphasizing guru devotion and the omnipresence of Vajrasattva. The work is counted as one of the Siddhi texts of Indian Vajrayāna.
SA_T02_ilx_gr_lakSmINkarA_advayasiddhi.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Lakṣmīṅkarā (c. 9th century, associated with Oḍḍiyāna and sister of Indrabhūti). The Tibetan Tengyur preserves a translation titled gNyis su med par grub pa'i sgrub thabs (D 2220 / TT 3064).
SA_T02_ilx_gr_lakSmINkarA_advayasiddhi.edition: Guhyādi-aṣṭasiddhisaṅgraha, ed. Samdhong Rinpoche and Vrajvallabh Dwivedi, Rare Buddhist Texts Series 1, Sarnath, Varanasi: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 1987, pp. 161–164.
SA_T02_ilx_gr_lakSmINkarA_advayasiddhi.coverage: complete — Complete text containing 36 verses and concluding prose colophon.

SA_GS40_ilx_gr_lolimbarAja_vaidyajIvana.title: Vaidyajīvana
SA_GS40_ilx_gr_lolimbarAja_vaidyajIvana.author: Lolimbarāja
SA_GS40_ilx_gr_lolimbarAja_vaidyajIvana.summary: The Vaidyajīvana ('Physician's Life') is an Āyurvedic treatise composed in ornate poetic verse (kāvya) by the poet-physician Lolimbarāja (17th cent.). In five vilāsas, it treats fevers, bowel and digestive disorders, women's diseases and aphrodisiacs, pulmonary consumption, and general ailments. Uniquely within Indian medical literature, the medical prescriptions and dietary rules are formulated as playful, erotic addresses to the author's beloved.
SA_GS40_ilx_gr_lolimbarAja_vaidyajIvana.attribution: The colophons throughout designate the author as Lolimbarāja, son of Divākara (divākarasūnu).
SA_GS40_ilx_gr_lolimbarAja_vaidyajIvana.edition: Jürgen Hanneder and Thomas Schäfer. Āyurveda und Poesie. Lolimbarājas Lehrgedicht »Leben des Arztes«. Marburg: Indica et Tibetica Verlag.
SA_GS40_ilx_gr_lolimbarAja_vaidyajIvana.coverage: complete — Complete work in 5 vilāsas, concluding with the final vilāsa colophon.

SA_K12_ilx_gr_mahAmAyUrIvidyArAjJI.title: Mahāmāyūrīvidyārājñī
SA_K12_ilx_gr_mahAmAyUrIvidyArAjJI.summary: The Mahāmāyūrīvidyārājñī ('Great Peacock Queen of Spells') is one of the earliest and most celebrated Buddhist rakṣā (protective) and dhāraṇī scriptures, subsequently included as one of the Five Protective Deities (Pañcarakṣā). Framed around the story of the novice monk Svāti being bitten by a poisonous snake while gathering wood for the bathhouse, the Buddha imparts the Mahāmāyūrī spell to Ānanda for protection against snakebites, poisons, malevolent spirits, and disasters. The scripture is also renowned for preserving an extensive geographical list of local tutelary yakṣas across the Indian subcontinent and adjacent regions.
SA_K12_ilx_gr_mahAmAyUrIvidyArAjJI.attribution: Canonical scripture traditionally delivered by the Buddha to Ānanda to heal the monk Svāti bitten by a black serpent.
SA_K12_ilx_gr_mahAmAyUrIvidyArAjJI.coverage: complete — Complete text of the Mahāmāyūrīvidyārājñī along with its ritual procedure (upacāra/maṇḍalavidhi) at the end, running through Takubo pp. 2–62.
translations: Bukong (Amoghavajra), Fomu da kongque mingwang jing (T 982, 746–774); Sanghabhara, Kongque wang zhou jing (T 984, 506–520); Yijing, Fo shuo da kongque zhou wang jing (T 985, 705). (Chinese)
rig sngags kyi rgyal mo rma bya chen mo (Derge Kangyur D 559): translated by Śīlendrabodhi, Jñānasiddhi, shAkya 'od, sna nam btsun pa ye shes sde (Tibetan)

SA_GR14_ilx_gr_nArAyaNabhaTTa_nArAyaNIya.title: Nārāyaṇīya
SA_GR14_ilx_gr_nArAyaNabhaTTa_nArAyaNIya.author: Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭa
SA_GR14_ilx_gr_nArAyaNabhaTTa_nArAyaNIya.summary: Devotional work (stotra/kāvya) addressed to the deity of Guruvāyūr (Gurupavanapura / Vātālayeśa / Kṛṣṇa), recounting divine manifestations and Purāṇic narratives.
SA_GR14_ilx_gr_nArAyaNabhaTTa_nArAyaNIya.attribution: According to tradition, Nārāyaṇa composed the work at Guruvāyūr while suffering from rheumatism, with the work's dating connected to a Kali chronogram in the work.
SA_GR14_ilx_gr_nArAyaNabhaTTa_nArAyaNIya.coverage: complete — Reference system in the e-text covers skandhas 1–12 and daśakas 1–100, ending with the verse containing 'ajñātvā te mahattvaṃ ... āyurārogyasaukhyam'.

SA_GR13_ilx_gr_pAzupatasUtra.title: Pāśupatasūtra
SA_GR13_ilx_gr_pAzupatasUtra.summary: The Pāśupatasūtra is the foundational textual authority of the Pāśupata order, the earliest attested sectarian Śaiva tradition. In five chapters, the work details the five primary ontological and practical principles (pañcārtha): cause (kāraṇa, Śiva/Paśupati), effect (kārya, the bound soul and created world), yoga (contemplative union with Rudra), vidhi (ascetic practices, including smearing ashes, ritual laughter and dance, simulated madness, and inducing public contempt), and duḥkhānta (the final cessation of suffering and attainment of divine powers/fellowship with Śiva).
SA_GR13_ilx_gr_pAzupatasUtra.coverage: complete — Complete across all five adhyāyas (ending with the closing Vedic Śatarudrīya/Īśāna formula at 5.47: śivaḥ). The e-text is an analytical version prepared by Reinhold Grünendahl, presenting each sūtra first in saṃhitāpāṭha form and then repeated in hyphenated padapāṭha analysis.
translations: Haripada Chakraborti, Pāśupata Sūtram with the Pañcārtha-bhāṣya of Kauṇḍinya, Calcutta: Academic Publishers, 1970. (English)

SA_GK22_ilx_gr_rAva_mithyAgrahaNa.title: Mithyāgrahaṇam
SA_GK22_ilx_gr_rAva_mithyAgrahaNa.author: Kṣamā Rāva
SA_GK22_ilx_gr_rAva_mithyAgrahaNa.summary: Mithyāgrahaṇam ('Misunderstanding') is a 20th-century Sanskrit short story set in Bombay (Mohamayī). It narrates the emotional ordeal and eventual reconciliation between two close friends, Amīnā and Saralā, dealing with the tensions of arranged marriage, jealousy, and socio-religious conventions.
SA_GK22_ilx_gr_rAva_mithyAgrahaNa.attribution: A modern Sanskrit short story by Kṣamā Rāva, included in her collection Kathāmuktāvalī.
SA_GK22_ilx_gr_rAva_mithyAgrahaNa.edition: Kṣamā Rāva, Kathāmuktāvalī: 15 laghukathānāṃ saṃgraḥaḥ, Mumbāpurī: Na. Mā. Tripāṭhī; re-edited with German translation by Beate Guttandin, '‚Missverständnis‘ – eine Novelle aus Indien von Kṣamā Rāva: Aus dem Sanskrit mit Vorbemerkungen und Sprachanalyse', Orientierungen: Zeitschrift zur Kultur Asiens 29.
translations: Beate Guttandin, '‚Missverständnis‘ – eine Novelle aus Indien von Kṣamā Rāva: Aus dem Sanskrit mit Vorbemerkungen und Sprachanalyse', Orientierungen. Zeitschrift zur Kultur Asiens 29. (German)

SA_GK19_ilx_gr_ravideva_rAkSasakAvyawith.title: Rākṣasakāvya with Sajjanānandadāyinī
SA_GK19_ilx_gr_ravideva_rAkSasakAvyawith.author: Ravideva
SA_GK19_ilx_gr_ravideva_rAkSasakAvyawith.summary: The Rākṣasakāvya is a brief 20-verse poem in the vasantatilakā meter describing the arrival of the monsoon season. Notable for its dense wordplay, alliteration (yamaka), and obscure periphrastic expressions, the poem depicts a youthful traveler admiring rain clouds, peacocks, and flowering trees before returning home in a bullock cart with his wife. It is accompanied by the Sajjanānandadāyinī commentary, traditionally attributed to Ravideva and expanded by Kṛṣṇadhara Vyāḍi.
SA_GK19_ilx_gr_ravideva_rAkSasakAvyawith.attribution: Colophons of the root text and commentary name Ravideva of the Malaya region as the author. The commentary colophon notes expansion/gloss by Kṛṣṇadhara Vyāḍi (kṛṣṇadhareṇa vyāḷinā prapañcitā).
SA_GK19_ilx_gr_ravideva_rAkSasakAvyawith.edition: Karl Gustav Hoefer (ed.), Kāvyarākṣasaṃ saṭīkam, in Sanskrit Lesebuch mit Benutzung handschriftlicher Quellen, Berlin: Besser, 1849, pp. 86–93; collated and critically constituted for the poem by Christophe Vielle against 19th-century editions (Häberlin 1861, Haridas Hirachand 1864, Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara 1872, K. P. Parab).
SA_GK19_ilx_gr_ravideva_rAkSasakAvyawith.coverage: complete — Complete work of 20 verses (viṃśatihṛdyapadyasameta) with corresponding commentary, word-division, and textual apparatus.
translations: Raja Pṛthvīpāla Siṃha (transl.), Allahabad: Indian Press, 1909. (English)

SA_GSP33_ilx_gr_taittirIyopaniSad_zaMkar.title: Taittirīyopaniṣad with Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣya
SA_GSP33_ilx_gr_taittirIyopaniSad_zaMkar.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GSP33_ilx_gr_taittirIyopaniSad_zaMkar.summary: The Taittirīyopaniṣad is a principal Upaniṣad of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, comprising three chapters: Śikṣāvallī, Brahmavallī (or Brahmānandavallī), and Bhṛguvallī. It covers traditional phonetic instruction, meditative upāsanās, the fivefold sheath analysis (pañcakośa), and the quintessential definition of absolute reality as satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma. Śaṅkara's commentary provides an authoritative Advaita Vedānta exposition, establishing that liberation is achieved not through ritual action (karman) but solely through direct knowledge (jñāna) of the non-dual Self.
SA_GSP33_ilx_gr_taittirIyopaniSad_zaMkar.attribution: The root text is a canonical Vedic Upaniṣad belonging to the Taittirīya śākhā of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. The commentary is universally accepted in both tradition and modern scholarship as an authentic work of Śaṅkarācārya.
SA_GSP33_ilx_gr_taittirIyopaniSad_zaMkar.edition: Ten Principal Upaniṣads with Śaṅkarabhāṣya, Works of Śaṅkarācārya in original Sanskrit, vol. 1, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass (first edition 1964, reprint 2007).
SA_GSP33_ilx_gr_taittirIyopaniSad_zaMkar.coverage: complete — Complete text of all three vallīs (Śikṣāvallī, Brahmavallī/Brahmānandavallī, and Bhṛguvallī) of the Taittirīyopaniṣad with Śaṅkara's commentary.
translations: Gambhirananda, Swami (tr.), Eight Upanisads, with the Commentary of Sankaracarya, Vol. 1, Calcutta: Advaita Ashrama, 1957. (English)

SA_GSP30_ilx_gr_vAmanadatta_dvayasaMpatt.title: Dvayasaṃpattivārttika
SA_GSP30_ilx_gr_vAmanadatta_dvayasaMpatt.author: Vāmanadatta
SA_GSP30_ilx_gr_vAmanadatta_dvayasaMpatt.summary: The Dvayasaṃpattivārttika is a short Kashmirian Śaiva work in 23 verses by Vāmanadatta (ca. 10th century CE). It comments on two scriptural verses outlining 'dvayasampatti' (the simultaneous realization/perfection of Śiva and Śakti), analyzing phonemic mysticism centering on 'a' (Śiva) and 'ha' / nādabindu (Śakti), and incorporates yogic techniques referenced from the Vijñānabhairava.
SA_GSP30_ilx_gr_vAmanadatta_dvayasaMpatt.attribution: The final verse identifies the author as the son of the scholar Harṣadatta from Jākadeśa. He is identified across literature as Vāmanadatta (ca. 10th century CE), who is also the author of the Saṃvitprakāśa.
SA_GSP30_ilx_gr_vAmanadatta_dvayasaMpatt.edition: Raniero Gnoli (ed.), 'Il Dvayasampattivārttikam di Vāmanadatta', in: Gururājamañjarikā: Studi in onore di Giuseppe Tucci, Napoli: Istituto Universitario Orientale, 1974, pp. 451–455.
SA_GSP30_ilx_gr_vAmanadatta_dvayasaMpatt.coverage: complete — Complete text consisting of 23 anuṣṭubh verses (46 metrical hemistichs) plus introductory maṅgala line.

SA_GS41_ilx_gr_varAhamihira_bRhajjAtaka.title: Bṛhajjātaka
SA_GS41_ilx_gr_varAhamihira_bRhajjAtaka.author: Varāhamihira
SA_GS41_ilx_gr_varAhamihira_bRhajjAtaka.summary: The Bṛhajjātaka (also known as Horāśāstra) by Varāhamihira is a Sanskrit treatise on natal astrology (horā / jātaka).
SA_GS41_ilx_gr_varAhamihira_bRhajjAtaka.attribution: Authored by Varāhamihira, son of Ādityadāsa, from Kāpitthaka (Avanti), as explicitly stated in the closing verses (āditya.dāsa.tanayas... kāpitthake... āvantiko... varāhamihiro... cakāra).
SA_GS41_ilx_gr_varAhamihira_bRhajjAtaka.edition: Oriental Books Reprint Corporation, Second Edition, 1979.
SA_GS41_ilx_gr_varAhamihira_bRhajjAtaka.coverage: complete — Ending with chapter 28 (segment marker E28) and 'End of Bṛhajjātaka'.

SA_K10_ilx_gr_vidyAsthAnopamasUtra.title: Vidyāsthānopamasūtra
SA_K10_ilx_gr_vidyAsthAnopamasUtra.summary: The Vidyāsthānopamasūtra is a short canonical Buddhist discourse contrasting mundane crafts and occult sciences (śilpa-, karmasthāna, incantations, herbal drugs, sorcery, medicine, clairvoyance, and supernatural powers) with the liberative doctrine of the Buddhas. While mundane branches of learning emerge during the evolution of the world, they cannot eliminate suffering; only the Buddhas disclose the supreme science—the Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path leading to nirvāṇa.
SA_K10_ilx_gr_vidyAsthAnopamasUtra.attribution: Canonical Buddhist sūtra preserved in Central Asian manuscript remains.
SA_K10_ilx_gr_vidyAsthAnopamasUtra.edition: Ernst Waldschmidt, 'Kleine Brāhmī-Schriftrolle', In: Nachrichten der Akademie der Wissenschaften in Göttingen 1959, pp. 3–7 (reprint in: E. Waldschmidt, Von Ceylon bis Turfan, Schriften zur Geschichte, Literatur, Religion und Kunst des indischen Kulturraumes (Festgabe zum 70. Geburtstag), Göttingen 1967, pp. 373–378).
SA_K10_ilx_gr_vidyAsthAnopamasUtra.coverage: complete — Complete text of the short sūtra as preserved on the Central Asian Brāhmī scroll, ending with the colophon 'vidyāsthānopamasūtraṃ samāptaḥ' and protective invocation; includes apparatus/comparative notes citing BL fragment Or. 15009/83v and Pelliot Sanskrit bleu 375.

SA_GV06_ilx_gr_yAska_nirukta.title: Nirukta
SA_GV06_ilx_gr_yAska_nirukta.author: Yāska
SA_GV06_ilx_gr_yAska_nirukta.summary: The Nirukta of Yāska is the foundational treatise of the Nirukta (Vedic etymology and semantic interpretation) Vedāṅga, composed c. 5th century BCE. Serving as an exegesis of the Vedic lexical list (Nighaṇṭu), it elaborates early linguistic theory regarding word classes (nāma, ākhyāta, upasarga, nipāta), root derivation, and Vedic theological-mythological hermeneutics across the Naighaṇṭuka, Naigama, and Daivata sections.
SA_GV06_ilx_gr_yAska_nirukta.attribution: Universally attributed in ancient Indic and modern Indological scholarship to Yāska (traditionally placed c. 5th century BCE).
SA_GV06_ilx_gr_yAska_nirukta.edition: Lakshman Sarup (ed.), The Nighaṇṭu and the Nirukta.
SA_GV06_ilx_gr_yAska_nirukta.coverage: complete — Complete text across 14 adhyāyas (adhyāyas 1–12 covering the Naighaṇṭuka-, Naigama-, and Daivata-kāṇḍas, concluding with the two supplementary pariśiṣṭa adhyāyas 13–14 ending at 14,37).
translations: Lakshman Sarup, The Nighaṇṭu and the Nirukta: English Translation and Notes, 1921. (English)

SA_T11_ilx_gr_zAntarakSita_tattvasaMgrah.title: Tattvasaṃgraha (word-by-word grammatical analysis)
SA_T11_ilx_gr_zAntarakSita_tattvasaMgrah.author: Śāntarakṣita
SA_T11_ilx_gr_zAntarakSita_tattvasaMgrah.summary: The Tattvasaṃgraha of Śāntarakṣita is a philosophical work. This e-text is not the running verse text but a word-by-word grammatical analysis of the text by Timothy C. Cahill and Elliot Stern, in which the words of each verse are listed in brackets with morphological tags.
SA_T11_ilx_gr_zAntarakSita_tattvasaMgrah.attribution: The e-text is a modern analytical derivative (grammatical analysis by Timothy C. Cahill and Elliot Stern), not a transcript of the Sanskrit verses.
SA_T11_ilx_gr_zAntarakSita_tattvasaMgrah.coverage: complete — Content is a word list per verse, not continuous text, so the Sanskrit word order and sandhi are lost.

SA_K02_ilx_gr_zatasAhasrikAprajJApAramit.title: Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā (chapters 1–12)
SA_K02_ilx_gr_zatasAhasrikAprajJApAramit.summary: The Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in One Hundred Thousand Lines') is the longest canonical recension of the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras. It expounds universal emptiness (śūnyatā), the non-arising and non-apprehendability (anupalambha) of all dharmas, and the comprehensive path of the bodhisattva through dialogues between the Buddha, Śāriputra, Subhūti, and other disciples. This volume covers chapters 1 through 12 (the first khanda), beginning with the opening assembly on Gṛdhrakūṭa and systematically examining the emptiness and ungraspability of the skandhas, dhātus, āyatanas, and pāramitās.
SA_K02_ilx_gr_zatasAhasrikAprajJApAramit.edition: Pratāpacandra Ghoṣa (ed.), Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā, Calcutta: Asiatic Society of Bengal, 1902–1913 (Bibliotheca Indica).
SA_K02_ilx_gr_zatasAhasrikAprajJApAramit.coverage: partial — Contains the first section (prathamakhaṇḍa), comprising chapters 1 to 12 (parivartas 1–12), closing with 'śatasāhasryāḥ prajñāpāramitāyāḥ dvādaśaḥ parivartaḥ // iti prathamakhaṇḍaḥ samāptaḥ //'.
translations: Edward Conze (tr.), The Large Sutra on Perfect Wisdom with the Divisions of the Abhisamayālaṁkāra, Delhi etc.: Motilal Banarsidass, 1975. (English)

SA_GR14_ilx_gr_ta_sa_periyavaccanpillai_.title: Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi with Vyākhyāna
SA_GR14_ilx_gr_ta_sa_periyavaccanpillai_.author: Kulacēkara Āḻvār, Periyavāccāṉ Piḷḷai
SA_GR14_ilx_gr_ta_sa_periyavaccanpillai_.summary: The Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi is an anthology of 105 Tamil devotional verses by Kulacēkara Āḻvār forming part of the canonical Nālāyira Divya Prabandham. The collection comprises ten decades dedicated to Viṣṇu in various manifestations and shrines (such as Śrīraṅgam, Veṅkaṭam, and Tillai Cittirakūṭam), exploring diverse devotional stances (bhāvas) including bridal devotion, maternal tenderness as Kauśalyā and Yaśodā, and devotion to Rāma. Periyavāccāṉ Piḷḷai's 13th-century Maṇipravāḷam commentary provides a line-by-line grammatical, theological, and devotional exposition reflecting classical Viśiṣṭādvaita doctrine.
SA_GR14_ilx_gr_ta_sa_periyavaccanpillai_.edition: Suganya Anandakichenin, My Sapphire-hued Lord, My Beloved. A Complete, Annotated Translation of Kulacēkara Āḻvār’s Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi and Periyavāccāṉ Piḷḷai’s Medieval Maṇipravāḷam Commentary, with an Introduction, Pondichéry: EFEO/IFP, Collection Indologie 136.
SA_GR14_ilx_gr_ta_sa_periyavaccanpillai_.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 10 decades (105 stanzas) of Kulacēkara Āḻvār's Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi alongside Periyavāccāṉ Piḷḷai's commentary, opening with the introductory avatārikai to decad 1 and concluding with the nigama verse of decad 10 (ellai il cīr tayarataṉ taṉ makaṉ āy...).
translations: Suganya Anandakichenin, My Sapphire-hued Lord, My Beloved. A Complete, Annotated Translation of Kulacēkara Āḻvār’s Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi and Periyavāccāṉ Piḷḷai’s Medieval Maṇipravāḷam Commentary, with an Introduction, Pondichéry: EFEO/IFP, Collection Indologie 136. (English)

SA_T02_ilx_hh_abhayakaragupta_vajravali.title: Vajrāvalī
SA_T02_ilx_hh_abhayakaragupta_vajravali.author: Abhayākaragupta
SA_T02_ilx_hh_abhayakaragupta_vajravali.summary: The Vajrāvalī (or Vajrāvalīnāmamaṇḍalopāyikā) by Abhayākaragupta is a comprehensive ritual compendium of late Indian tantric Buddhism. Structured around sequential rites (vidhi), it details the selection and purification of the ritual ground, maṇḍala construction and coloration, installation and consecration of images and monastic dwellings (pratiṣṭhā), the progression of tantric initiations (abhiṣeka), post-initiatory observances (vrata), fire rituals (homa), and maṇḍala dissolution. Providing the liturgical framework for maṇḍalas also described in Abhayākaragupta's Niṣpannayogāvalī, the work became a foundational ritual authority in Tibetan Buddhist traditions.
SA_T02_ilx_hh_abhayakaragupta_vajravali.attribution: Work of Abhayākaragupta; explicitly named in the opening verse (0.1: '... abhayasya mahasā vajrāvalī mīlatu') and closing colophon (p. 516: 'mahāpaṇḍita-abhayākaragupta-racitā vajrāvalī nāma maṇḍalopāyikā samāptā').
SA_T02_ilx_hh_abhayakaragupta_vajravali.coverage: complete — Text of ritual procedures (vidhis), beginning with opening verses at p. 47 and concluding with the final verses and colophon at p. 516.
translations: dkyil 'khor gyi cho ga rdo rje phreng ba zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 3140): translated by Abhayākaragupta, khe'u gang 'khor lo grags; revised by kre bo lo tsA ba shes rab dpal ba, Ratnarakṣita, Rāhulaśrībhadra, Maṇikaśrījñāna, chag lo tsA ba chos rje dpal, dpang lo tsA ba blo gros brtan pa (Tibetan)

SA_T02_ilx_hh_advayavajra_nairatmyapraka.title: Nairātmyāprakāśa
SA_T02_ilx_hh_advayavajra_nairatmyapraka.author: Advayavajra
SA_T02_ilx_hh_advayavajra_nairatmyapraka.summary: The Nairātmyāprakāśa is a Vajrayāna ritual and meditation treatise composed by Advayavajra (Maitrīpāda) associated with the Hevajratantra cycle. It provides an extensive exposition of the sādhana of the goddess Nairātmyā and her retinue of fifteen yoginīs, treating both the generation stage (utpattikrama) and completion stage (utpannakrama) culminating in non-dual great bliss (mahāsukha).
SA_T02_ilx_hh_advayavajra_nairatmyapraka.attribution: Advayavajra is traditionally identified with the mahāsiddha Maitrīpāda, disciple of Śabaranātha. The Tibetan translation (D 1308) attributes the work to Maitrīpa (dpal paN+Di ta gnyis su med pa'i rdo rje).
SA_T02_ilx_hh_advayavajra_nairatmyapraka.edition: Conlon, R. Advayavajra’s Nairātmyāprakāśa: A Critical Edition. J Indian Philos 53, 433–469 (2025). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10781-025-09611-0
SA_T02_ilx_hh_advayavajra_nairatmyapraka.coverage: complete — Complete text of the work from initial maṅgala through the concluding verses and final colophon (nairātmyāprakāśaḥ samāptaḥ).
translations: bdag med ma'i rab tu gsal ba (Derge Tengyur D 1308): translated by Vajrapāṇi, mtshur ston ye shes 'byung gnas (Tibetan)

SA_GS24_ilx_hh_anubhutisvarupacarya_sara.title: Sārasvatavyākaraṇa (incomplete)
SA_GS24_ilx_hh_anubhutisvarupacarya_sara.author: Anubhūtisvarūpācārya
SA_GS24_ilx_hh_anubhutisvarupacarya_sara.summary: The Sārasvataprakriyā (or Sārasvatavyākaraṇa) by Anubhūtisvarūpācārya is an introductory and procedural treatise of Sanskrit grammar arranged into topical prakaraṇas (including saṃjñā, saṃdhi, declension, compounding, and conjugation).
SA_GS24_ilx_hh_anubhutisvarupacarya_sara.attribution: Canonical recast and commentary of the Sārasvata school preserved in the Sārasvataprakriyā is the work of Anubhūtisvarūpācārya.
SA_GS24_ilx_hh_anubhutisvarupacarya_sara.edition: Sārasvata Vyākaraṇam of Anubhūti Svarūpāchārya Benares. 1935
SA_GS24_ilx_hh_anubhutisvarupacarya_sara.coverage: partial — Unfinished digital transcription. Covers the introductory sections (saṃjñā, saṃdhi), declension (subanta), strīpratyaya, samāsa, and verbal inflection up through the start of the svādigaṇa (stops at segment [790]: 'svādiṣu parasmaipadinaḥ. / SV_14 /').

SA_GK20_ilx_hh_bhavabhuti_malatimadhava_.title: Mālatīmādhava with Rasamañjarī
SA_GK20_ilx_hh_bhavabhuti_malatimadhava_.author: Bhavabhūti, Pūrṇasarasvatī
SA_GK20_ilx_hh_bhavabhuti_malatimadhava_.summary: Mālatīmādhava is a ten-act prakaraṇa (social drama) by Bhavabhūti portraying the intense love, hardships, and ultimate reunion of the youth Mādhava and the minister's daughter Mālatī in the city of Padmāvatī, incorporating scenes of tantric rites, charnel-ground sorcery, and courtly intrigue. This e-text provides the drama accompanied by the Rasamañjarī, an erudite commentary by Pūrṇasarasvatī detailing the aesthetic (rasa), dramaturgical, and linguistic aspects of the work.
SA_GK20_ilx_hh_bhavabhuti_malatimadhava_.attribution: The root drama Mālatīmādhava is by Bhavabhūti; the commentary Rasamañjarī is by Pūrṇasarasvatī.
SA_GK20_ilx_hh_bhavabhuti_malatimadhava_.edition: Mālatīmādhavaṃ śrīpūrṇasarasvatīviracitayā rasamañjaryākhyayā vyākhyayopetam, ed. K. S. Mahādeva Śāstrī, Trivandrum Sanskrit Series (Anantaśayanasaṃskṛtagranthāvaliḥ) No. 170, Trivandrum: Rajakiya Mudranayantralaya, 1953.
SA_GK20_ilx_hh_bhavabhuti_malatimadhava_.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 10 acts (daśamo 'ṅkaḥ) of Bhavabhūti's prakaraṇa along with Pūrṇasarasvatī's Rasamañjarī commentary.
translations: Coulson, Michael. Three Sanskrit Plays. London, 1981. (English)

SA_GP10_ilx_hh_bhagavata_03_four_comment.title: Bhāgavatapurāṇa with the commentaries of Madhva, Śrīdharasvāmin, Jīva Gosvāmin and Viśvanātha Cakravartin (skandha 3)
SA_GP10_ilx_hh_bhagavata_03_four_comment.author: Madhva, Śrīdharasvāmin, Jīva Gosvāmin, Viśvanātha Cakravartin
SA_GP10_ilx_hh_bhagavata_03_four_comment.summary: Skandha 3 (33 adhyāyas) is the Vidura–Maitreya dialogue. It covers Vidura's pilgrimage and meeting with Uddhava, the creation of the world (sarga and visarga), the Varāha avatāra and the killing of Hiraṇyākṣa, and the birth of Kapila and his teaching of Sāṃkhya and bhakti to his mother Devahūti (adhyāyas 25–33). In this e-text each verse is followed by the commentaries of Madhva (on selected verses), Śrīdharasvāmin (Bhāvārthadīpikā), Jīva Gosvāmin (Kramasandarbha) and Viśvanātha Cakravartin (Sārārthadarśinī).
SA_GP10_ilx_hh_bhagavata_03_four_comment.attribution: The Bhāgavatapurāṇa is traditionally ascribed to Vyāsa. The commentators are Madhva, Śrīdharasvāmin, Jīva Gosvāmin and Viśvanātha Cakravartin.
SA_GP10_ilx_hh_bhagavata_03_four_comment.coverage: partial — Complete text of skandha 3 (adhyāyas 1–33) of the Purāṇa, with commentaries under verses. The e-text ends with closing verses on the skandha ('tṛtīyaskandhaṭīkeyam apūri yamunātaṭe …') and the colophon of adhyāya 33.

SA_GP10_ilx_hh_bhagavata_06_four_comment.title: Bhāgavatapurāṇa with the commentaries of Madhva, Śrīdharasvāmin, Jīva Gosvāmin and Viśvanātha Cakravartin (skandha 6)
SA_GP10_ilx_hh_bhagavata_06_four_comment.author: Madhva, Śrīdharasvāmin, Jīva Gosvāmin, Viśvanātha Cakravartin
SA_GP10_ilx_hh_bhagavata_06_four_comment.summary: Skandha 6 deals with divine protection (poṣaṇa). Its stories include the deliverance of Ajāmila through the name of Nārāyaṇa, Citraketu, and Indra's conflict with Vṛtra. In this e-text verses are accompanied by commentaries including those of Madhva, Śrīdharasvāmin, Jīva Gosvāmin (Kramasandarbha) and Viśvanātha Cakravartin.
SA_GP10_ilx_hh_bhagavata_06_four_comment.attribution: The Bhāgavatapurāṇa is traditionally ascribed to Vyāsa. The commentaries are by Madhva, Śrīdharasvāmin, Jīva Gosvāmin (Kramasandarbha) and Viśvanātha Cakravartin (Sārārthadarśinī).
SA_GP10_ilx_hh_bhagavata_06_four_comment.coverage: partial — Complete text of skandha 6 of the Purāṇa, with commentaries under verses (including sections labelled madhvaḥ, śrīdharaḥ, kramasandarbhaḥ, and viśvanāthaḥ). The e-text ends with notes citing the Haribhaktivilāsa (e.g. 'haribhaktivilāsasthitapāṭhānusāreṇa').

SA_GP10_ilx_hh_bhagavata_07_four_comment.title: Bhāgavatapurāṇa with the commentaries of Madhva, Śrīdharasvāmin, Jīva Gosvāmin and Viśvanātha Cakravartin (skandha 7)
SA_GP10_ilx_hh_bhagavata_07_four_comment.author: Madhva, Śrīdharasvāmin, Jīva Gosvāmin, Viśvanātha Cakravartin
SA_GP10_ilx_hh_bhagavata_07_four_comment.summary: Skandha 7 (15 adhyāyas) is narrated by Nārada to Yudhiṣṭhira. It tells how enmity, too, can lead to Viṣṇu (Śiśupāla, Jaya and Vijaya), and gives the story of Hiraṇyakaśipu and his devotee son Prahlāda, Prahlāda's teaching, and the Nṛsiṃha avatāra (adhyāyas 1–10). It ends with Nārada's exposition of varṇāśramadharma and the conduct of renunciants (adhyāyas 11–15). In this e-text each verse is followed by the commentaries of Madhva (on selected verses), Śrīdharasvāmin (Bhāvārthadīpikā), Jīva Gosvāmin (Kramasandarbha) and Viśvanātha Cakravartin (Sārārthadarśinī).
SA_GP10_ilx_hh_bhagavata_07_four_comment.attribution: The Bhāgavatapurāṇa is traditionally ascribed to Vyāsa. Commentaries are by Madhva, Śrīdharasvāmin, Jīva Gosvāmin (Kramasandarbha), and Viśvanātha Cakravartin.
SA_GP10_ilx_hh_bhagavata_07_four_comment.coverage: partial — Complete text of skandha 7 (adhyāyas 1–15, last verse 7.15.80) of the 12-skandha Purāṇa, with commentaries under each verse. The e-text ends with the editors' notes and the Gaudiya Grantha Mandira closing notice ('This service is provided free of charge … The editors.').

SA_GP10_ilx_hh_bhagavata_10_rasapancadhy.title: Bhāgavatapurāṇa (skanda 10: Rāsapañcādhyāyī, with ten commentaries)
SA_GP10_ilx_hh_bhagavata_10_rasapancadhy.summary: This e-text contains the Rāsapañcādhyāyī (Bhāgavatapurāṇa 10.29–33), the celebrated five chapters depicting Kṛṣṇa's autumn circle dance (rāsalīlā) with the gopīs of Vraja. It is accompanied by a composite apparatus of up to ten prominent Vaiṣṇava commentaries, focusing particularly on Gauḍīya interpretations (Śrīdhara Svāmin, Sanātana Gosvāmin, Jīva Gosvāmin, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, and others). The Rāsapañcādhyāyī constitutes the theological and devotional core of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava aesthetics and rasa theory.
SA_GP10_ilx_hh_bhagavata_10_rasapancadhy.attribution: Traditional attribution of the root Purāṇa is to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa. The commentaries represent a lineage of commentators from the 13th to the 19th centuries, especially central to Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism.
SA_GP10_ilx_hh_bhagavata_10_rasapancadhy.edition: Composite e-text prepared primarily from: (1) Śrīmadbhāgavata-mahāpurāṇam with multiple commentaries, ed. Bhagavata Rishi and Krishna Shankar Shastri, Sola Karnavati: Bhagavata Vidya Pith, saṃvat 2052 / 1996, Vol. III; (2) Madhva's Bhāgavatatātparya, ed. Bhakti Ballabh Tirtha, Calcutta: Chaitanya Gaudiya Math, 1995; (3) Śrīdhara Svāmin's Bhāvārthadīpikā, ed. Ramateja Pandeya, Benares: Chowkhamba, 1996; (4) Haridas Das's edition for Caitanyamatamañjuṣā.
SA_GP10_ilx_hh_bhagavata_10_rasapancadhy.coverage: partial — Covers skanda 10, adhyāyas 29–33 (Rāsapañcādhyāyī) only; e-text version 0.77 (2006) was compiled as an ongoing project with varying coverage per chapter (10.29: 100%, 10.30: 100%, 10.31: 20%, 10.32: 85%, 10.33: 75%).

SA_T12_ilx_hh_candragomin_candravrtti.title: Candravṛtti with Candravyākaraṇasūtra and Varṇasūtra
SA_T12_ilx_hh_candragomin_candravrtti.author: Candragomin
SA_T12_ilx_hh_candragomin_candravrtti.summary: The Candravṛtti is the primary commentary on the Candravyākaraṇa, an influential non-sectarian Sanskrit grammar composed by the Buddhist scholar Candragomin (c. 5th–6th century CE). Reorganizing and simplifying the Pāṇinian grammatical system, it omits Vedic accents and rules irrelevant to classical usage. This e-text provides the complete six adhyāyas of the root sūtras with the vṛtti and concludes with Candragomin's Varṇasūtra on phonetics.
SA_T12_ilx_hh_candragomin_candravrtti.attribution: Bruno Liebich edited the Candra-vṛtti as Candragomin's autocommentary ('Der Originalkommentar Candragomin's zu seinem grammatischen Sūtra').
SA_T12_ilx_hh_candragomin_candravrtti.edition: Candragomin: Candra-vṛtti: Der Originalkommentar Candragomin's zu seinem grammatischen Sūtra, hrsg. von Bruno Liebich. Leipzig: Brockhaus 1918. [Abhandlungen für die Kunde des Morgenlandes, 14]
SA_T12_ilx_hh_candragomin_candravrtti.coverage: complete — Complete text of the 6 adhyāyas of the Candravyākaraṇasūtra with Candravṛtti, followed by the Varṇasūtra ('iti Candragomikṛtaṃ varṇasūtraṃ samāptam').

SA_K12_ilx_hh_candamaharosanatantra.title: Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra
SA_K12_ilx_hh_candamaharosanatantra.summary: The Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra (also known as the Ekallavīratantra) is an Anuttarayoga tantra centered on the wrathful deity Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa (Acala) and his consort Dveṣavajrī. Across 25 chapters, it covers maṇḍala construction, initiation rituals (abhiṣeka), the subtleties of the energetic channels and drops (nāḍī and bindu), the generation of the four joys (caturānanda) through yogic and erotic union, fierce magical and subjugation rites, and meditation upon non-duality.
SA_K12_ilx_hh_candamaharosanatantra.attribution: Canonical Anuttarayoga tantra set in dialogue between the Bhagavān Kṛṣṇācala / Vajrasattva / Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa and the Bhagavatī Dveṣavajrī / Vajradhātvīśvarī.
SA_K12_ilx_hh_candamaharosanatantra.edition: Edition by Wiesiek Mical in: 84000: Translating the Words of the Buddha. “The Glorious Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa Tantra ‘The Sole Hero’ (Ekallavīrākhyaśrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantram, dpal gtum po khro bo chen po’i rgyud kyi rgyal po dpa’ bo gcig pa zhes bya ba).” Translated by Dharmachakra Translation Committee. https://84000.co/translation/toh431, 2016.
SA_K12_ilx_hh_candamaharosanatantra.coverage: complete — Complete text in 25 chapters (paṭalas), ending with the devatāsādhanapaṭala (chapter 25) and concluding tantra colophon.
translations: Dharmachakra Translation Committee (trans.). The Glorious Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa Tantra 'The Sole Hero' (Ekallavīrākhyaśrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantram, Toh 431). 84000: Translating the Words of the Buddha, 2016. (English)

SA_T02_ilx_hh_darpanacarya_acaryakriyasa.title: Ācāryakriyāsamuccaya (Abhiṣeka section)
SA_T02_ilx_hh_darpanacarya_acaryakriyasa.author: Jagaddarpaṇa
SA_T02_ilx_hh_darpanacarya_acaryakriyasa.summary: The Ācāryakriyāsamuccaya (commonly known as the Kriyāsamuccaya), attributed to Jagaddarpaṇa (Darpaṇācārya), is a ritual work treating tantric rites. This excerpt preserves the initiation section, treating preliminary purifications, the gurumaṇḍala rite, taking vows, disciple admittance, and empowerment rites.
SA_T02_ilx_hh_darpanacarya_acaryakriyasa.attribution: Attributed to Jagaddarpaṇa or Darpaṇācārya. The Tibetan canonical tradition (D3305) attributes the work to 'Hgro-ba'i me-long.
SA_T02_ilx_hh_darpanacarya_acaryakriyasa.coverage: partial — Contains the Abhiṣeka section (empowerment and initiation rites), covering the gurumaṇḍala, poṣadha, disciple entry (śiṣyapraveśa), garland empowerment (mālābhiṣeka), and preliminary vase initiation rites, terminating incomplete at '(p.859-->)'.
translations: rdo rje slob dpon gyi bya ba kun las btus pa (Derge Tengyur D 3305): translated by Mañjuśrī, sa bzang ma ti paN chen blo gros rgyal mtshan; revised by badzra shrI (Tibetan)

SA_GK21_ilx_hh_dandin_avantisundarikatha.title: Avantisundarīkathā (incomplete)
SA_GK21_ilx_hh_dandin_avantisundarikatha.author: Daṇḍin
SA_GK21_ilx_hh_dandin_avantisundarikatha.summary: The Avantisundarīkathā is a prose romance ascribed to Daṇḍin. It opens with verses praising earlier poets (Subandhu, Sarvasena, and others). The surviving text is lacunose and breaks off incomplete.
SA_GK21_ilx_hh_dandin_avantisundarikatha.attribution: The opening rubric ('ācāryadaṇḍiviracitā avantisundarī') and the final colophon ('ityācāryadaṇḍinā kṛtā avantisundarī samāptā') ascribe the work to Daṇḍin, the author of the Kāvyādarśa, who is placed around the 7th century. The verse introduction praises earlier poets.
SA_GK21_ilx_hh_dandin_avantisundarikatha.edition: Avantisundarīkathā, ed. Sūranād Kunjan Pillai, Trivandrum Sanskrit Series 172, Trivandrum, 1954.
SA_GK21_ilx_hh_dandin_avantisundarikatha.coverage: partial — Covers everything the 1954 edition contains: the introductory verses, the prose frame, and narrative. Lacunae are frequent throughout. The text breaks off in mid-sentence in an embedded episode involving Mahāśvetā and Kādambarī, before the scribal colophon. The later portion of the work is lost; its contents are partly known from the verse summary Avantisundarīkathāsāra.

SA_GP12_ilx_hh_ganesapurana_1_upasanakha.title: Gaṇeśapurāṇa (Upāsanākhaṇḍa)
SA_GP12_ilx_hh_ganesapurana_1_upasanakha.summary: The Upāsanākhaṇḍa (or Pūrvakhaṇḍa) is the first part of the Gaṇeśapurāṇa, featuring a frame dialogue involving Vyāsa, Brahmā, the sage Bhṛgu, and King Somakānta.
SA_GP12_ilx_hh_ganesapurana_1_upasanakha.coverage: complete — Complete Upāsanākhaṇḍa (pūrvakhaṇḍa), ending with 92.58, the closing colophon 'iti śrīmadgaṇeśamahāpurāṇe pūrvakhaṇḍaṃ (upāsanākhaṇḍaṃ) samāptam', and verse count totals (4038 + 58 = 4096).

SA_GP12_ilx_hh_ganesapurana_2_kridakhand.title: Gaṇeśapurāṇa (Krīḍākhaṇḍa)
SA_GP12_ilx_hh_ganesapurana_2_kridakhand.summary: The Krīḍākhaṇḍa ('Book of Divine Play') is the second and concluding part of the Gaṇeśapurāṇa, an Upapurāṇa central to the Gāṇapatya tradition. In 155 chapters, it narrates the cosmic deeds and avataras of Gaṇeśa across the four yugas: Mahotkaṭa in the Kṛtayuga, Mayūreśvara in the Tretāyuga, Gajānana in the Dvāparayuga, and Dhūmraketu in the Kaliyuga. Chapters 138–148 form the celebrated Gaṇeśagītā, wherein Gaṇeśa expounds yoga and non-dualist devotion to King Vareṇya, modeling its philosophy and verse forms directly on the Bhagavadgītā.
SA_GP12_ilx_hh_ganesapurana_2_kridakhand.coverage: complete — Complete Krīḍākhaṇḍa (uttarakhaṇḍa), adhyāyas 1–155, with the Gaṇeśagītā (adhyāyas 138–148). Ends with the colophon of ch. 155, verse totals (7,021 for this khaṇḍa), and 'iti śrīgaṇeśapurāṇaṃ samāptam'.
translations: Yoroi, Kiyoshi. Gaṇeśagītā: A Study, Translation with Notes, and a Condensed Rendering of the Commentary of Nīlakaṇṭha. (English (Gaṇeśagītā only))

SA_T03_ilx_hh_haribhadra_ratnagunasancay.title: Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthāvyākhyā (chapters 3–32)
SA_T03_ilx_hh_haribhadra_ratnagunasancay.author: Haribhadra
SA_T03_ilx_hh_haribhadra_ratnagunasancay.summary: Commentary by Haribhadra on the Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā, connecting the text with the Abhisamayālaṅkāra. The present e-text covers chapters 3 to 32.
SA_T03_ilx_hh_haribhadra_ratnagunasancay.attribution: Attributed to Ācārya Haribhadra. The closing colophon states: 'kṛtir iyam ācāryaharibhadrapādānām'.
SA_T03_ilx_hh_haribhadra_ratnagunasancay.coverage: partial — Acephalous text covering chapters 3–32 (from aparimeyaguṇadhāraṇaparivarta to parīndanāparivarta), based on manuscript folios 39b–120a.
translations: bcom ldan 'das yon tan rin po che sdud pa'i tshigs su bcad pa'i dka' 'grel (Derge Tengyur D 3792): translated by Śāntibhadra, 'bro seng dkar shAkya 'od (Tibetan)

SA_GS24_ilx_hh_jinendrabuddhi_kasikaviva.title: Kāśikāvivaraṇapañjikā
SA_GS24_ilx_hh_jinendrabuddhi_kasikaviva.author: Jinendrabuddhi
SA_GS24_ilx_hh_jinendrabuddhi_kasikaviva.summary: The Kāśikāvivaraṇapañjikā, also known as the Nyāsa, is an extensive commentary composed by Jinendrabuddhi on the Kāśikāvṛtti. It elucidates the grammatical text and sūtras through verse 8.4.69.
SA_GS24_ilx_hh_jinendrabuddhi_kasikaviva.edition: Nyāsa = Kāśikāvivaraṇapañjikā, Jinendrabuddhi, 1913–, edited by Srish Chandra Chakravarti.
SA_GS24_ilx_hh_jinendrabuddhi_kasikaviva.coverage: complete — Commentary on the Kāśikāvṛtti, concluding at Pāṇini 8.4.69.

SA_GR12_ilx_hh_jvalamalinikalpa.title: Jvālāmālinīkalpa
SA_GR12_ilx_hh_jvalamalinikalpa.author: Indranandin
SA_GR12_ilx_hh_jvalamalinikalpa.summary: The Jvālāmālinīkalpa is a Digambara Jaina tantric manual in ten paricchedas attributed to Indranandin (ca. 10th century CE), dedicated to the propitiation of Jvālāmālinī (Vahnidevī), the yakṣī of the eighth Tīrthaṅkara, Candraprabha. According to the opening narrative, the rites trace back to Helācārya of the Draviḍa Saṅgha, who obtained them on the Nīlagiri hill to exorcise a brahmarākṣasa from his disciple Kamalaśrī. The text details mantra recitation, yantra diagram construction, homa rituals, mudrās, and various protective and pacifying rites.
SA_GR12_ilx_hh_jvalamalinikalpa.attribution: According to the introductory narrative (vv. 5–25), the vidyā was originally revealed by the goddess Jvālāmālinī (Vahnidevī) to Helācārya of the Draviḍa Saṅgha on the Nīlagiri hill to exorcise a demon possessing his disciple Kamalaśrī. It was subsequently passed down through a lineage of disciples to Guṇanandin, from whom Indranandin received it and composed this manual.
SA_GR12_ilx_hh_jvalamalinikalpa.edition: Śrījvālāmālinīkalpa: bhāṣā-ṭīkā aura mantra, tantra, yantra sahita, edited and translated by Candraśekhara Śāstrī, Sūrat: Digambara Jaina Pustakālaya, 1964.
SA_GR12_ilx_hh_jvalamalinikalpa.coverage: complete — Complete in 10 paricchedas (lines 0–1068). Contains the root Sanskrit kārikās and mantras with Hindi headings and colophons from the edition; the Hindi bhāṣāṭīkā was omitted by the transcriber.
translations: Candraśekhara Śāstrī (ed. & tr.), Śrījvālāmālinīkalpa: bhāṣā-ṭīkā aura mantra, tantra, yantra sahita, Sūrat: Digambara Jaina Pustakālaya, 1964. (Hindi)

SA_XX_ilx_hh_k_111_vat_sithor.title: Vat Sithor Inscription (K. 111)
SA_XX_ilx_hh_k_111_vat_sithor.summary: The Vat Sithor inscription (K. 111) is a 100-stanza Sanskrit Buddhist epigraph. The text opens with an invocation of the kāyas of the Buddha, Dharma, and Bodhisattvas, and contains verses on Buddhist practice, monastic conduct, and royal decrees/protection.
SA_XX_ilx_hh_k_111_vat_sithor.edition: George Cœdès, Inscriptions du Cambodge, Paris: EFEO, 1954, p. 195ff.; and Phillip Scott Ellis Green, 'The Vat Sithor Inscription: Translation, Commentary, and Reflections on Buddhist Traditions in tenth-century Cambodia', Ph.D. dissertation, University of Florida, 2014.
SA_XX_ilx_hh_k_111_vat_sithor.coverage: complete — Complete Sanskrit text of 100 verses (stanzas 1–100).
translations: Phillip Scott Ellis Green, 'The Vat Sithor Inscription: Translation, Commentary, and Reflections on Buddhist Traditions in tenth-century Cambodia', Ph.D. dissertation, University of Florida, 2014. (English)

SA_XX_ilx_hh_k_528_east_mebon.title: East Mebon Inscription (K. 528)
SA_XX_ilx_hh_k_528_east_mebon.summary: The East Mebon inscription (K. 528) is a monumental Sanskrit verse praśasti consisting of 218 stanzas inscribed on a stele at the East Mebon temple-mountain in Angkor, Cambodia. Commissioned by King Rājendravarman and dated Śāka 874 (952 CE), the text opens with invocations to Śiva, Gaurī, and Viṣṇu, traces the royal genealogy and mythological ancestry of the king, details his royal exploits, and records the consecration of the central liṅga Rājendreśvara alongside other deities.
SA_XX_ilx_hh_k_528_east_mebon.attribution: A Sanskrit praśasti composed for the Khmer monarch Rājendravarman on the occasion of the consecration of the temple of East Mebon (Rājendreśvara) in Śāka 874 (952 CE). The court poet is anonymous.
SA_XX_ilx_hh_k_528_east_mebon.edition: Goodall, Dominic. 2022. The East Mebon Stele Inscription from Angkor (K. 528): A Sanskrit Eulogy of the Tenth-Century Khmer Sovereign Rājendravarman. Vol. 154. Collection Indologie. Pondicherry: Institut Français de Pondichéry / École française d’Extrême-Orient.
SA_XX_ilx_hh_k_528_east_mebon.coverage: complete — Contains all 218 verses of the Sanskrit praśasti.

SA_XX_ilx_hh_k_806_pre_rup.title: Prè Rup Inscription (K. 806)
SA_XX_ilx_hh_k_806_pre_rup.summary: The Prè Rup inscription (K. 806) is a Sanskrit mahākāvya-style praśasti of 298 stanzas engraved on a four-sided stele at the temple-mountain of Prè Rup in Angkor, Cambodia, dated Śaka 883 (961 CE). Composed in elaborate classical metres, it commemorates the installation of Śiva-liṅgas (including Rājendrabhadreśvara) and various deities by King Rājendravarman II. The composition details royal genealogy, mythical lineages, religious foundations, and royal decrees with exceptional grammatical and literary sophistication.
SA_XX_ilx_hh_k_806_pre_rup.attribution: Monumental Sanskrit praśasti of the tenth-century Khmer emperor Rājendravarman.
SA_XX_ilx_hh_k_806_pre_rup.edition: Draft of forthcoming re-edition by Dominic Goodall, Harunaga Isaacson, and S.L.P. Anjaneya Sarma.
SA_XX_ilx_hh_k_806_pre_rup.coverage: complete — Complete inscription consisting of all 298 Sanskrit stanzas.

SA_GK23_ilx_hh_kalhana_rajatarangini.title: Rājataraṅgiṇī
SA_GK23_ilx_hh_kalhana_rajatarangini.author: Kalhaṇa
SA_GK23_ilx_hh_kalhana_rajatarangini.summary: The Rājataraṅgiṇī, composed by the poet Kalhaṇa, is a chronicle of Kashmir dealing with its history from the earliest times down to the period in which the author lived during the reign of King Jayasiṃha.
SA_GK23_ilx_hh_kalhana_rajatarangini.attribution: Kalhaṇa lived during the reign of King Jayasiṃha (A.D. 1128–55), beginning his work in 1148.
SA_GK23_ilx_hh_kalhana_rajatarangini.edition: Stein, M. A. 1960 (reprint). Kalhaṇa's Rājataraṅgiṇī or Chronicles of the Kings of Kashmir. Delhi: Munshi Ram and Manohar Lal.
SA_GK23_ilx_hh_kalhana_rajatarangini.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all eight taraṅgas, ending at 8.3449 (8.3449cb: viśrāntaye viśati rājataraṅgiṇīyam).
translations: Radjatarangini, histoire des rois du Kachmir, traduite du sanskrit par A. Troyer, 3 vol., Paris, 1840–1842. (French)
M. A. Stein, annotated translation of the Rajatarangini. (English)

SA_T02_ilx_hh_kuddalapada_acintyadvayakr.title: Acintyādvayakramopadeśa
SA_T02_ilx_hh_kuddalapada_acintyadvayakr.author: Kuddālapāda
SA_T02_ilx_hh_kuddalapada_acintyadvayakr.summary: The Acintyādvayakramopadeśa is an esoteric Buddhist tantric treatise of 124 verses attributed to the mahāsiddha Kuddālapāda, conveying an oral instruction lineage descending from Bhadrapāda. It presents the completion stage (utpannakrama) practice focused on realizing inconceivable nonduality (acintyādvaya), where insight (prajñā) and skillful means (upāya) are indivisibly experienced as Great Bliss (mahāsukha).
SA_T02_ilx_hh_kuddalapada_acintyadvayakr.attribution: Ascribed to Kuddālapāda (Kuddālanāma / Tog rtse zhabs) in verse 122 and the colophon; the text traces its lineage of oral instructions to Bhadrapāda.
SA_T02_ilx_hh_kuddalapada_acintyadvayakr.edition: Samdhong Rinpoche and Vrajvallabh Dwivedi (eds.), Guhyādi-aṣṭasiddhisaṅgraha, CIHTS, Sarnath, 1987, pp. 193–208.
SA_T02_ilx_hh_kuddalapada_acintyadvayakr.coverage: complete — Complete text containing all 124 verses along with the Sanskrit introductory verse and prose colophon (preceded by the Tibetan canonical title and salutation heading).
translations: bsam gyis mi khyab pa'i rim pa'i man ngag ces bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 2228): translated by Kṣemāṅchura, 'gos lo tsA ba khug pa lhas btsas (Tibetan)

SA_GK19_ilx_hh_kalidasa_meghaduta_w_four.title: Meghadūta with the commentaries of Vallabhadeva, Dakṣiṇāvartanātha, Mallinātha, and Sumativijaya (Pūrvamegha only for Sumativijaya)
SA_GK19_ilx_hh_kalidasa_meghaduta_w_four.author: Kālidāsa, Vallabhadeva, Dakṣiṇāvartanātha, Mallinātha, Sumativijaya
SA_GK19_ilx_hh_kalidasa_meghaduta_w_four.summary: The Meghadūta is a Sanskrit lyric poem attributed to Kālidāsa. This digital edition presents the text accompanied by commentaries of Vallabhadeva, Dakṣiṇāvartanātha, Mallinātha, and Sumativijaya (Sugamānvayā Vṛtti, covering the Pūrvamegha).
SA_GK19_ilx_hh_kalidasa_meghaduta_w_four.attribution: The root lyrical poem is attributed to Kālidāsa. The commentaries are by Vallabhadeva, Dakṣiṇāvartanātha, Mallinātha, and the Jain monk Sumativijaya.
SA_GK19_ilx_hh_kalidasa_meghaduta_w_four.edition: Composite text assembled from four printed editions: (1) Vallabhadeva: Kālidāsa's Meghadūta, ed. E. Hultzsch, Munshiram Manoharlal Publishers, New Delhi, 1998 (first published London: Royal Asiatic Society, 1911); (2) Dakṣiṇāvartanātha: The Meghasandeśa of Kālidāsa with the Commentary of Dakṣiṇāvartanātha, ed. T. Gaṇapati Śāstrī, Trivandrum: Government Press, 1919; (3) Mallinātha: The Meghadūta of Kālidāsa, ed. M. R. Kale, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass Publishers, 8th ed. 1974; (4) Sumativijaya: Sugamānvayā Vṛtti, ed. Walter Harding Maurer, Poona: Deccan College, 1965.
SA_GK19_ilx_hh_kalidasa_meghaduta_w_four.coverage: partial — Contains the Meghadūta with the commentaries of Vallabhadeva, Dakṣiṇāvartanātha, Mallinātha, and Sumativijaya (Pūrvamegha only for Sumativijaya).
translations: Beckh, Hermann, Die tibetische Übersetzung von Kālidāsas Meghadūta, Berlin: Abhandlungen der Preussischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, 1907. (German (study and Tibetan text))

SA_K12_ilx_hh_krsnayamaritantra.title: Kṛṣṇayamāritantra
SA_K12_ilx_hh_krsnayamaritantra.summary: The Kṛṣṇayamāritantra is an Indian Buddhist Anuttarayogatantra belonging to the Yamāntaka (Yamāri) cycle, classified in Indo-Tibetan traditions as a Father Tantra (upāyatantra). In eighteen chapters, it details the iconography, seed-syllables, maṇḍala layout, generation stage and completion practices, caturyoga, and wrathful subjugation rituals connected with Kṛṣṇayamāri.
SA_K12_ilx_hh_krsnayamaritantra.attribution: Canonical Buddhist tantra centered on the wrathful deity Kṛṣṇayamāri; traditional buddhavacana.
SA_K12_ilx_hh_krsnayamaritantra.edition: Samdhong Rinpoche and Vrajvallabh Dwivedi, eds., Kṛṣṇayamāritantram with Ratnāvalīpañjikā of Kumāracandra, Rare Buddhist Texts Series 9, Sarnath, Varanasi: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies (CIHTS), 1992.
SA_K12_ilx_hh_krsnayamaritantra.coverage: complete — Complete in 18 chapters (paṭalas 1–18), running from the opening nidāna to the colophon of chapter 18 (kāyavākcittakathāpaṭalo 'ṣṭādaśamaḥ) and final conclusion (śrīkṛṣṇayamāritantrarājaḥ samāptaḥ).

SA_T02_ilx_hh_ksitigarbha_dasatattvasamg.title: Daśatattvasaṃgraha
SA_T02_ilx_hh_ksitigarbha_dasatattvasamg.author: Kṣitigarbha
SA_T02_ilx_hh_ksitigarbha_dasatattvasamg.summary: The Daśatattvasaṃgraha is a manual of the Jñānapāda school of Guhyasamāja exegesis setting out ten ritual 'fundamentals' (tattva) of the tantric master: the protective circle, the maṇḍala visualisation centred on Vajrasattva/Samantabhadra, mantra recitation, the secret and wisdom-knowledge consecrations, forceful practice (haṭha), bali offerings, two kinds of counter-magic (pratyaṅgirā) and the 'opening of the casket' (puṭodghāta). It combines verse with prose explanation and quotes tantras.
SA_T02_ilx_hh_ksitigarbha_dasatattvasamg.attribution: Colophon: 'kṛtir iyaṃ daśatattvasaṃgrahaḥ paṇḍitakṣitiga⟨rbha⟩syeti' (supplement by the editor). Kṣitigarbha (paṇḍita) of the Jñānapāda school of Guhyasamāja exegesis.
SA_T02_ilx_hh_ksitigarbha_dasatattvasamg.edition: Klein-Schwind, Sabine Gudrun (Oktober 2012). The Compendium of the Ten Fundamentals: Daśatattvasaṃgraha of paṇḍita Kṣitigarbha. Critical Edition of the Sanskrit Text with Introduction and Annotated English Translation. Dissertation zur Erlangung der Würde eines Doktors der Philosophie der Universität Hamburg, Fakultät für Geisteswissenschaften.
