The text traces the successive insertions of standard technical delimitations (*avacchinnatva*, *pratiyogivyadhikaraṇatva*, etc.) required to avoid under-pervasion (*avyāpti*) and over-pervasion (*ativyāpti*).
SA_GSP29_ilx_ws_purvapaksiyavyaptih.attribution: The text is an anonymous pedagogical primer or kroḍapatra of the Navya-Nyāya pāṭhaśālā curriculum detailing the qualification of the first definition of vyāpti ('sādhyābhāvavadavṛttitvam') from the Vyāptipañcaka chapter of Gaṅgeśa's Tattvacintāmaṇi.
SA_GSP29_ilx_ws_purvapaksiyavyaptih.coverage: complete — Complete short tractate / explanatory note consisting of 18 prose segments.

SA_GS26_ilx_ws_sadacaranusandhanam.title: Sadācārānusandhāna
SA_GS26_ilx_ws_sadacaranusandhanam.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GS26_ilx_ws_sadacaranusandhanam.summary: The Sadācārānusandhāna is an Advaita Vedānta text in 55 anuṣṭubh verses attributed to Śaṅkara. It provides an allegorical interiorization of orthodox Hindu rites and duties—including ritual ablution (snāna), sandhyāvandana, agnihotra, and the four āśramas—interpreting true moral conduct (sadācāra) as persistent awareness of non-dual Brahman.
SA_GS26_ilx_ws_sadacaranusandhanam.attribution: Attributed to Śaṅkarācārya in the text colophon.
SA_GS26_ilx_ws_sadacaranusandhanam.coverage: complete — Complete in 55 verses plus final colophon.

SA_GSP29_ilx_ws_sarvalaksanapadarthalaks.title: Sarvatantrasiddhāntapadārthalakṣaṇasaṃgraha (fragment)
SA_GSP29_ilx_ws_sarvalaksanapadarthalaks.author: Gaurīśaṅkarabhikṣu
SA_GSP29_ilx_ws_sarvalaksanapadarthalaks.summary: The Sarvatantrasiddhāntapadārthalakṣaṇasaṃgraha by Gaurīśaṅkarabhikṣu is an alphabetical compendium defining philosophical terms and technical categories across Indian philosophical systems (principally Advaita Vedānta, Nyāya, and Mīmāṃsā). It begins with introductory verses establishing the necessity of definition (lakṣaṇa) in philosophical debate. The present e-text is an incomplete transcription fragment ending at the term 'anavasthā'.
SA_GSP29_ilx_ws_sarvalaksanapadarthalaks.attribution: Authored by Gaurīśaṅkarabhikṣu, who pays homage in verses 4–5 to his preceptors Cetanakiṅkara, Rāmapurī, and Dhīrālāla.
SA_GSP29_ilx_ws_sarvalaksanapadarthalaks.coverage: fragment — Extremely brief fragment breaking off abruptly within initial 'a-' entries at 'anavasthā' (segment 130).

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sarvavedantasiddhantasar.title: Sarvavedāntasiddhāntasārasaṃgraha
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sarvavedantasiddhantasar.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sarvavedantasiddhantasar.summary: The Sarvavedāntasiddhāntasārasaṃgraha is a comprehensive verse manual (prakaraṇa) of 1006 kārikās presenting an accessible overview of classical Advaita Vedānta philosophy. Structured largely as an instructional dialogue between guru and disciple, it systematically treats the four qualifications for study (anubandhacatuṣṭaya), discrimination of real and unreal (nityānityavastuviveka), renunciation, the nature of avidyā and superimposition (adhyāropa/apavāda), the interpretation of the Upaniṣadic mahāvākyas, and the attainment of jīvanmukti.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sarvavedantasiddhantasar.coverage: complete — Complete in 1006 verses (numbered 1–1006), ending with the final concluding verses and full colophon.

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_siddhantalesasangrahah.title: Siddhāntaleśasaṅgraha
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_siddhantalesasangrahah.author: Appayyadīkṣita
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_siddhantalesasangrahah.summary: The Siddhāntaleśasaṅgraha is an influential doxographical compendium of Advaita Vedānta by Appayyadīkṣita. Organized into four paricchedas, the work systematically presents and reconciles the divergent doctrines, sub-schools, and interpretations developed by post-Śaṅkara Advaitins (including the Bhāmatī and Vivaraṇa traditions). It analyzes key topics such as the nature and locus of avidyā, the ontological status of jīva and īśvara, the theory of error (adhyāsa), and the direct means of release.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_siddhantalesasangrahah.attribution: Authored by Appayyadīkṣita, son of Śrīraṅgarājamakhin, explicitly identified in the closing verses.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_siddhantalesasangrahah.coverage: complete — Complete in 4 paricchedas (chapters), ending with the fourth pariccheda colophon 'iti śāstrasiddhāntaleśasaṅgrahe caturthaḥ paricchedaḥ' and 'samāpto'yaṃ granthaḥ'.

SA_GS26_ilx_ws_smrtimuktavalih.title: Smṛtimuktāvalī (opening sections, up to the Ekabhuktanirṇaya)
SA_GS26_ilx_ws_smrtimuktavalih.author: Kṛṣṇācārya
SA_GS26_ilx_ws_smrtimuktavalih.summary: The Smṛtimuktāvalī of Kṛṣṇācārya, a pupil of Rāghavendra Tīrtha, is a dharmaśāstra digest (nibandha) written for the Mādhva (Dvaita) community. It argues that Mādhva practice rests on smṛti, that ritual duties are to be done without desire for results as worship of Hari, and that smṛti and purāṇa are authoritative. It then sets out calendrical rules (seasons, months, intercalary and 'empty' months, Cāturmāsya, fortnights). The e-text breaks off in the section on the time for the single daily meal (ekabhukta).
SA_GS26_ilx_ws_smrtimuktavalih.attribution: Compiled by Kṛṣṇācārya, who names himself in the opening verses ('kṛṣṇācāryasaṃgṛhītā', 'kṛṣṇācāryavipaścitā') and calls Rāghavendra Tīrtha his vidyāguru; a Mādhva (Dvaita) dharmaśāstra digest.
SA_GS26_ilx_ws_smrtimuktavalih.coverage: partial — The e-text contains the introductory verses and the sections karmaṇām anuṣṭheyatvanirūpaṇa, smṛtikartṛpurāṇanirṇaya, dharmalakṣaṇa, smṛtiprāmāṇyasamarthana, smṛtyadhyayanaphala, deśadharmanirūpaṇa, yuganirṇaya, and calendrical topics (ṛtu, māsa, adhimāsa/malamāsa, śūnyamāsa, cāturmāsya, pakṣa), ending with 'iti svatantraikabhuktanirṇayaḥ'. The last section announces three kinds of ekabhukta (svatantra, anyāṅga, upavāsapratinidhi) but only the first is treated, and there is no final colophon, so the text breaks off within the kāla section of the digest. The full extent of the work could not be checked against a printed edition.

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sumadhvavijayah.title: Sumadhvavijaya with Aṇumadhvavijaya and Prameyaphalamālikā
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sumadhvavijayah.author: Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya, Viṣṇutīrtha
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sumadhvavijayah.summary: The Sumadhvavijaya by Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya (c. 14th century) is a celebrated biographical epic (mahākāvya) in 16 sargas detailing the life, philosophy, travels, and deeds of Madhvācārya (Ānandatīrtha), the founder of Dvaita Vedānta. In addition to the primary kāvya, this e-text includes a 22-verse devotional fruit-exposition (Sumadhvavijayaprameyaphalamālikā) by Mādanūru Viṣṇutīrtha.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sumadhvavijayah.attribution: Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya (c. 14th century) composed the Sumadhvavijaya. Mādanūru Viṣṇutīrtha composed the concluding Phalamālikā.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sumadhvavijayah.coverage: complete — Complete in 16 sargas, followed by the complete Prameyaphalamālikā (22 verses).

SA_GSP31_ilx_ws_suvarnasaptatisastram.title: Suvarṇasaptatiśāstra (pūrvakhaṇḍa)
SA_GSP31_ilx_ws_suvarnasaptatisastram.author: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
SA_GSP31_ilx_ws_suvarnasaptatisastram.summary: The Suvarṇasaptatiśāstra is a commentary on Īśvarakṛṣṇa's Sāṃkhyakārikā preserved in Chinese translation (Jinqishi lun, T 2137 by Paramārtha). This e-text comprises the Pūrvakhaṇḍa, covering kārikās 1 through 55.
SA_GSP31_ilx_ws_suvarnasaptatisastram.attribution: The Suvarṇasaptati (Chinese 金七十論 Jinqishi lun, Taishō 2137) was translated into Chinese by Paramārtha during the Chen dynasty (548–569).
SA_GSP31_ilx_ws_suvarnasaptatisastram.coverage: partial — Contains only the Pūrvakhaṇḍa (kārikās 1–55 with commentary), ending at verse 55.

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_svarajyasiddhih.title: Svārājyasiddhi
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_svarajyasiddhih.author: Gaṅgādharendra Sarasvatī
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_svarajyasiddhih.summary: The Svārājyasiddhi is an Advaita Vedānta metrical treatise by Gaṅgādharendra Sarasvatī in three prakaraṇas (Adhyāropa, Apavāda, and Kaivalya). Written in classical metres, it systematically presents non-dualist ontology, refutes rival philosophical schools (Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, Sāṅkhya, and Buddhist views), and explicates liberation as self-sovereignty (svārājya) realized through Vedic mahāvākyas.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_svarajyasiddhih.attribution: Attributed to Gaṅgādhara / Gaṅgādharendra Sarasvatī along with its commentary Kaivalyakalpadruma.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_svarajyasiddhih.coverage: complete — Complete root verse text in three prakaraṇas: Adhyāropaprakaraṇa, Apavādaprakaraṇa, and Kaivalyaprakaraṇa (ending at verse 3.47 and 'kaivalyaprakaraṇaṃ sampūrṇam').

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_svarupanusandhanastakam.title: Svarūpānusandhānāṣṭaka
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_svarupanusandhanastakam.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_svarupanusandhanastakam.summary: The Svarūpānusandhānāṣṭaka is an eight-verse Advaita Vedānta hymn traditionally attributed to Śaṅkara, accompanied by a final phalaśruti verse. Each stanza contemplates the non-dual supreme reality (Brahman) beyond ignorance, mental modifications, and the three mundane states of consciousness, concluding with the refrain 'paraṃ brahma nityaṃ tadevāhamasmi' ('I am indeed that eternal Supreme Brahman').
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_svarupanusandhanastakam.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Śaṅkara in the closing colophon.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_svarupanusandhanastakam.coverage: complete — Complete text comprising 8 meditative verses with refrain, 1 concluding phalaśruti verse (verse 9), and closing colophon.

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_svatmanirupanam.title: Svātmanirūpaṇa
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_svatmanirupanam.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_svatmanirupanam.summary: The Svātmanirūpaṇa is an introductory Advaita Vedānta prakaraṇa text composed in 154 āryā verses, traditionally attributed to Śaṅkara. It guides the qualified spiritual seeker through the discernment of the five sheaths (pañcakośaviveka) to reveal the true Self (ātman) beyond body and mind, explains the mahāvākya 'tat tvam asi' via direct and implied meanings (vācyārtha and lakṣyārtha), and depicts the experiential state of kaivalya achieved upon liberation.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_svatmanirupanam.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Ādi Śaṅkarācārya as one of his prakaraṇagranthas.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_svatmanirupanam.coverage: complete — Contains 154 verses followed by the concluding colophon stating 'svātmanirūpaṇaṃ saṃpūrṇam'.
translations: S. Venkataramanan (ed. and tr.), Select Works of Sri Sankaracharya. (English)

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_svatmaprakasika.title: Svātmaprakāśikā
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_svatmaprakasika.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_svatmaprakasika.summary: An Advaita Vedānta verse tract (prakaraṇa) of 68 verses presented as a dialogue between master and disciple. The text asserts that empirical phenomena, agency, bondage, and bodily afflictions are superimposed upon the non-dual Self (ātman/brahman), which remains ever-pure, unattached consciousness (cinmātra).
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_svatmaprakasika.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Śaṅkarācārya, though widely treated in modern scholarship as a late apocryphal or pseudepigraphical Advaita Vedānta prakaraṇa.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_svatmaprakasika.coverage: complete — Complete in 68 verses with closing colophon.
translations: Burk, Michael Gainer. Svātmaprakāśikā: Light on One's Real Self. M.A. thesis, University of Texas at Austin, 1974. (English)

SA_GSP31_ilx_ws_samkhyadarsanam_srimadvi.title: Sāṃkhyasūtra with Sāṃkhyapravacanabhāṣya
SA_GSP31_ilx_ws_samkhyadarsanam_srimadvi.author: Kapila, Vijñānabhikṣu
SA_GSP31_ilx_ws_samkhyadarsanam_srimadvi.summary: The Sāṃkhyasūtra (also known as Sāṃkhyapravacanasūtra) is the aphoristic text of the Sāṃkhya tradition. Vijñānabhikṣu's commentary, the Sāṃkhyapravacanabhāṣya, provides an exposition of the sūtras across six chapters.
SA_GSP31_ilx_ws_samkhyadarsanam_srimadvi.attribution: Traditional Indian doxography attributes the Sāṃkhyasūtras to the sage Kapila. The commentary, Sāṃkhyapravacanabhāṣya, is attributed to Vijñānabhikṣu.
SA_GSP31_ilx_ws_samkhyadarsanam_srimadvi.coverage: complete — Concluding with the colophon of the Tantrādhyāya (chapter 6) and 'iti sāṅkhyapravacanabhāṣyaṃ sampūrṇam'.
translations: Richard Garbe, Sâṃkhya-pravacana-bhâshya: Vijñânabhikshu's Commentar zu den Sâmkhyasûtras, Abhandlungen für die Kunde des Morgenlandes 9.3, Leipzig: F. A. Brockhaus, 1889. (German)

SA_GSP31_ilx_ws_samkhyakosah.title: Sāṃkhyakośa
SA_GSP31_ilx_ws_samkhyakosah.author: Kedāranātha Tripāṭhī
SA_GSP31_ilx_ws_samkhyakosah.summary: The Sāṃkhyakośa is a 20th-century Sanskrit terminological lexicon of classical Sāṃkhya philosophy composed by Ācārya Kedāranātha Tripāṭhī in 1974 CE (VS 2030). Arranged in alphabetical order, it defines and explains core technical concepts, epistemological categories, ontological principles, and stock illustrations (dṛṣṭāntas) of the system, substantiating explanations with citations from the Sāṃkhyakārikā, Sāṃkhyasūtra, Gauḍapāda, and Vijñānabhikṣu.
SA_GSP31_ilx_ws_samkhyakosah.attribution: The concluding verses state that Kedāranātha Tripāṭhī was born in Viṣṇupura village in Sāraṇya maṇḍala, studied Nyāya and Vyākaraṇa under Sūryanārāyaṇa, and Vedānta under Harihara Kṛpālu. He completed this work in Vikrama Samvat 2030 (1974 CE; 'śūnyāgnyabhrakalocanaiḥ parimite saṃvatsare vaikrame').
SA_GSP31_ilx_ws_samkhyakosah.coverage: complete — Complete text of the glossary from the first entry 'akāmyam' to the final entry 'haṃsakṣīravat', followed by the concluding praśasti verses and closing colophon.

SA_GSP28_ilx_ws_sutradipika.title: Brahmasūtra with Sūtradīpikā
SA_GSP28_ilx_ws_sutradipika.author: Bādarāyaṇa, Jagannāthayati
SA_GSP28_ilx_ws_sutradipika.summary: The Sūtradīpikā (also known as Brahmasūtradīpikā) is a concise commentary on Bādarāyaṇa's Brahmasūtra from the perspective of Dvaita (Mādhva) Vedānta, composed by Jagannāthayati, a disciple of Raghunāthatīrtha. The work presents the sūtras organized by adhikaraṇa, glossing individual terms to demonstrate that Vedic revelation consistently proclaims Lord Viṣṇu as the supreme, unconditioned Brahman possessing infinite auspicious attributes.
SA_GSP28_ilx_ws_sutradipika.attribution: The opening verse (jagannāthākhyāyatinā kriyate sūtradīpikā) and the closing colophon (śrīmatparamahaṃsaparivrājakācāryāṇāṃ śrīmadraghunāthatīrthapujyapādānāṃ śiṣyeṇa jagannāthayatinā kṛtāyāṃ brahmasūtradīpikāyāṃ...) name the commentator as Jagannāthayati, disciple of Raghunāthatīrtha.
SA_GSP28_ilx_ws_sutradipika.coverage: complete — Complete text covering all four adhyāyas (16 pādas), opening with 1.1.1 (athāto brahmajijñāsā) and concluding with 4.4.22 (anāvṛttiḥ śabdādanāvṛttiḥ śabdāt).

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sutrartharatnavali.title: Brahmasūtra with Sūtrārtharatnāvalī
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sutrartharatnavali.author: Bādarāyaṇa
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sutrartharatnavali.summary: An anonymous Mādhva (Dvaita) commentary on the whole Brahmasūtra. For each adhikaraṇa it states the topic, gives the opponent's view (often an inference in navya-nyāya style), quotes the sūtra with a short word-gloss ('asyārthaḥ') and then argues the Dvaita conclusion. Throughout, Brahman is identified with Viṣṇu, and Viṣṇu, the souls and the world are held to be really different.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sutrartharatnavali.attribution: Commentator unidentified. The commentary is Mādhva (Dvaita). Brahman is glossed as 'guṇapūrṇasya brahmaṇo viṣṇoḥ', the anāvṛtti argument uses the Bhārata-war 'trayodaśī as pañcadaśī' example. Each adhikaraṇa follows the scheme saṅgati, pūrvapakṣa, sūtra with 'asyārthaḥ' gloss, siddhānta ('iti siddham').
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sutrartharatnavali.coverage: complete — All four adhyāyas, from the Jijñāsādhikaraṇa (BS 1.1.1) to the Anāvṛttyadhikaraṇa (BS 4.4), ending with '|| iti caturthādhyāyasya caturthaḥ pādaḥ samāptaḥ || iti caturthādhyāyaḥ samāptaḥ ||'. Pāda and adhikaraṇa colophons are given inconsistently.

SA_GSP28_ilx_ws_tantrarahasyam.title: Tantrarahasya (chapters 1–3)
SA_GSP28_ilx_ws_tantrarahasyam.author: Rāmānujācārya
SA_GSP28_ilx_ws_tantrarahasyam.summary: The Tantrarahasya of Rāmānujācārya is a manual of the Prābhākara school of Pūrvamīmāṃsā, opening with homage to Dharmapurī on the Godāvarī, Jaimini, Śabara, Prabhākara, and Śālikanātha. The chapters present in this e-text treat pramāṇa, prameya, and śāstra, concluding with the third pariccheda (śāstrapariccheda).
SA_GSP28_ilx_ws_tantrarahasyam.attribution: Rāmānujācārya was a Prābhākara Mīmāṃsaka scholar active at Dharmapurī on the Godāvarī.
SA_GSP28_ilx_ws_tantrarahasyam.coverage: partial — Contains paricchedas 1–3 only, ending with the colophon 'iti śrīmadrāmānujācāryaviracite tantrarahasye śāstraparicchedastṛtīyaḥ'.
translations: Elisa Freschi, Duty, Language and Exegesis in Prābhākara Mīmāmsā: Including an Edition and Translation of Rāmānujācārya's Tantrarahasya, Śāstraprameyapariccheda, Leiden: Brill, 2012. (English)

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_tantrasarasangrahah.title: Tantrasārasaṅgraha
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_tantrasarasangrahah.author: Madhva
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_tantrasarasangrahah.summary: The Tantrasārasaṅgraha is a practical liturgical and ritual treatise in four chapters by the Dvaita Vedānta teacher Madhva (13th century). Drawing upon Pāñcarātra and tantric ritual traditions, it outlines mantroddhāra (with particular focus on the Praṇava, Nārāyaṇāṣṭākṣara, and Dvādaśākṣara mantras), the construction of altars and sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa-maṇḍala), temple building, image installation (pratiṣṭhā), and daily icon worship grounded in Vedic hymns.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_tantrasarasangrahah.attribution: Attributed to Ānandatīrtha (Madhva) in the text header (śrīmadānandatīrthabhagavatpādapraṇītasarvamūsagranthāḥ).
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_tantrasarasangrahah.coverage: complete — Text preserved in the Wikisource transcription.

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_taptacakrankakavidhvamsa.title: Taptacakrāṅkanavidhvaṃsana
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_taptacakrankakavidhvamsa.author: Garuḍācalayajvan
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_taptacakrankakavidhvamsa.summary: The Taptacakrāṅkanavidhvaṃsana is an Advaita polemical treatise composed by Garuḍācalayajvan of the Veṅkaṭagiri court. It rejects the Pāñcarātra and Śrīvaiṣṇava practice of bodily branding with hot iron emblems of Viṣṇu's disc and conch (taptacakrāṅkana), demonstrating through Mīmāṃsā exegetical rules and Dharmaśāstra citations that Vedic passages like 'pavitraṃ te vitatam' pertain to Śrauta rituals (such as the droṇakalaśa filter in Somayāga) rather than corporal branding.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_taptacakrankakavidhvamsa.attribution: Garuḍācalayajvan identifies himself as court scholar (vidvacchiromaṇi) of the Veṅkaṭagiri royal estate (saṃsthāna) and a member of the Veluveṇṭi lineage.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_taptacakrankakavidhvamsa.coverage: complete — Complete work ending with the full concluding colophon.

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_tattvabodhah.title: Tattvabodha
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_tattvabodhah.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_tattvabodhah.summary: The Tattvabodha is a concise introductory catechism (prakaraṇa) of Advaita Vedānta traditionally attributed to Śaṅkara. Written primarily in simple didactic prose, it defines fundamental concepts and technical terms, including the fourfold preliminary qualifications (sādhanacatuṣṭaya), the three bodies (śarīratraya), the five sheaths (pañcakośa), the three states of experience (avasthātraya), and the manifestation of the twenty-four cosmic principles. It culminates in an exposition of the non-difference between the individual soul and the supreme reality (jīveśvaraikya) and describes the nature and state of the liberated being (jīvanmukta).
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_tattvabodhah.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Śaṅkara (the opening verse pays homage to Vāsudevendrayogīndra).
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_tattvabodhah.coverage: complete — Complete text of the prakaraṇa in 13 topical divisions, beginning with the maṅgala verse (vāsudevendrayogīndraṃ natvā...) and concluding with the standard colophon (iti tattvabodhaprakaraṇaṃ samāptam).

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_tattvasarah_ratnasariniv.title: Tattvasāra with Ratnasāriṇī
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_tattvasarah_ratnasariniv.author: Varadaguru, Vīrarāghavadāsa
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_tattvasarah_ratnasariniv.summary: The Tattvasāra is a metrical compendium in 104 verses by Varadaguru that systematically encapsulates the tenets of Rāmānuja's Śrībhāṣya on the Brahmasūtras according to Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta. It outlines the pramāṇas (epistemology), prameyas (ontology), the nature of Brahman as the antaryāmin and material/instrumental cause, the individual self (jīva), and liberation. This e-text includes the commentary Ratnasāriṇī composed by Vādhūla Vīrarāghavadāsa.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_tattvasarah_ratnasariniv.attribution: Varadaguru is the author of the 104 kārikās of the Tattvasāra. The commentary Ratnasāriṇī was composed by Vādhūla Vīrarāghavadāsa, son of Narasiṃhaguru.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_tattvasarah_ratnasariniv.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 104 kārikās of the Tattvasāra with the complete Ratnasāriṇī commentary down to verse 104 and the final colophon.

SA_GSP34_ilx_ws_tattvavaisaradi.title: Yogasūtra with Tattvavaiśāradī
SA_GSP34_ilx_ws_tattvavaisaradi.author: Patañjali, Vācaspatimiśra
SA_GSP34_ilx_ws_tattvavaisaradi.summary: The Tattvavaiśāradī (also known as Pātañjalabhāṣyavyākhyā) is the fundamental classical sub-commentary on the Pātañjalayogaśāstrabhāṣya (Vyāsabhāṣya), composed by the tenth-century polymath Vācaspatimiśra. This text presents the four pādas of the Yogasūtra together with Vācaspati's extensive explanation of the Bhāṣya, clarifying technical Yoga psychology and metaphysics while defending the dualist system against Buddhist and other philosophical interlocutors. It remains one of the primary authorities in the classical Yoga tradition.
SA_GSP34_ilx_ws_tattvavaisaradi.attribution: The root sūtras are traditionally attributed to Patañjali. The Tattvavaiśāradī is a sub-commentary on the Vyāsabhāṣya composed by Vācaspatimiśra (ca. 10th century CE).
SA_GSP34_ilx_ws_tattvavaisaradi.coverage: complete — Complete across all four pādas: Samādhipāda, Sādhanapāda, Vibhūtipāda, and Kaivalyapāda.
translations: James Haughton Woods (trans.), The Yoga-System of Patañjali: Or the Ancient Hindu Doctrine of Concentration of Mind, Embracing the Mnemonic Rules, Called Yoga-Sūtras, of Patañjali, and the Comment, Called Yoga-Bhāshya, Attributed to Veda-Vyāsa, and the Explanation, Called Tattva-Vaiçāradī, of Vācaspati-Miçra, Harvard Oriental Series 17, Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1914. (English)

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_tattvatika.title: Tattvaṭīkā (incomplete)
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_tattvatika.author: Veṅkaṭanātha
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_tattvatika.summary: The Tattvaṭīkā is an extensive sub-commentary by Veṅkaṭanātha (Vedāntadeśika) on Rāmānuja's Śrībhāṣya on the Brahmasūtra. Conceived as a line-by-line philosophical defense of Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta incorporating rigorous Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya hermeneutics, only the section on the first adhikaraṇa (Jijñāsādhikaraṇa, Brahmasūtra 1.1.1) survives. This digital text represents an incomplete transcription from Sanskrit Wikisource covering the introductory debates concerning the sūtra's opening word 'atha'.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_tattvatika.coverage: partial — Incomplete; transcribes only an opening portion of the commentary on the Jijñāsādhikaraṇa (Brahmasūtra 1.1.1), breaking off mid-argument on why inquiry into dharma must precede inquiry into Brahman, lacking any adhikaraṇa or chapter colophon.

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_tattvopadesah.title: Tattvopadeśa
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_tattvopadesah.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_tattvopadesah.summary: The Tattvopadeśa is an Advaita Vedānta prakaraṇa text of 87 verses traditionally attributed to Śaṅkara. Structured as pedagogical instructions from a preceptor to a disciple, the treatise analyzes the Upaniṣadic mahāvākya 'tat tvam asi' ('Thou art that'). It systematically isolates the conscious witness (ātman) from bodily, sensory, and mental superimpositions, elucidates the role of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) in understanding non-difference, and emphasizes steady devotion and non-duality toward the guru.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_tattvopadesah.attribution: Attributed in the colophon to Śaṅkara (disciple of Govindabhagavatpūjyapāda).
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_tattvopadesah.coverage: complete — Complete text in 87 anuṣṭubh verses ending with the concluding colophon.

SA_GS26_ilx_ws_tithinirnayah.title: Tithinirṇaya
SA_GS26_ilx_ws_tithinirnayah.author: Madhva
SA_GS26_ilx_ws_tithinirnayah.summary: The Tithinirṇaya is a short astronomical and calendrical treatise of 29 verses composed by Madhva (Ānandatīrtha) as part of his Sarvamūlagrantha corpus. It sets forth mathematical procedures, sine tables (jyāvākya), and correctional calculations (saṃskāra) for establishing the exact duration of lunar days (tithi). The text is intended to settle the proper timing for ritual fasts (upoṣaṇa), particularly Ekādaśī and Dvādaśī, in accordance with Dvaita tradition.
SA_GS26_ilx_ws_tithinirnayah.attribution: Attributed to Ānandatīrtha (Madhva) in the text.

SA_GSP32_ilx_ws_vaisesikasutropaskarah.title: Vaiśeṣikasūtra with Upaskāra
SA_GSP32_ilx_ws_vaisesikasutropaskarah.author: Kaṇāda, Śaṅkaramiśra
SA_GSP32_ilx_ws_vaisesikasutropaskarah.summary: The Vaiśeṣikasūtra attributed to Kaṇāda is the foundational text of the Vaiśeṣika school, establishing its realist ontological ontology around six ontological categories (padārthas): dravya, guṇa, karma, sāmānya, viśeṣa, and samavāya (with non-existence, abhāva, treated subsequently). The Upaskāra ('Supplement' / 'Exposition') by the philosopher Śaṅkaramiśra served historically as the primary transmitted commentary on the sūtras, elucidating the aphorisms through a lens influenced by classical and early Navya-Nyāya debate.
SA_GSP32_ilx_ws_vaisesikasutropaskarah.attribution: The foundational sūtras are traditionally attributed to Kaṇāda (also known as Ulūka). The commentary is identified in opening and concluding verses as composed by Śaṅkaramiśra, son of Bhavanātha and Bhavānī.
SA_GSP32_ilx_ws_vaisesikasutropaskarah.coverage: complete — Complete across all ten adhyāyas (each divided into two āhnikas), concluding with the 10.2 colophon and author's concluding verses.

SA_GSP29_ilx_ws_vedantakarikavali.title: Vedāntakārikāvalī
SA_GSP29_ilx_ws_vedantakarikavali.author: Bucci Veṅkaṭācārya
SA_GSP29_ilx_ws_vedantakarikavali.summary: The Vedāntakārikāvalī is an introductory verse compendium of Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta philosophy composed by Bucci Veṅkaṭācārya, summarizing Rāmānuja's system (referred to as Lakṣmaṇasiddhānta). In ten chapters, it systematically expounds epistemology (pramāṇa: direct perception, inference, and verbal testimony) and ontology (prameya: substance, divided into insentient and sentient, and ten non-substances).
SA_GSP29_ilx_ws_vedantakarikavali.attribution: Also referred to as Veṅkaṭācārya, Veṅkaṭārya, or Veṅkaṭadāsa; identified in verse 10.24 as the son of Aṇṇārya of the Śaṭhamarṣaṇa gotra.
SA_GSP29_ilx_ws_vedantakarikavali.coverage: complete — Complete in 10 prakaraṇas covering pramāṇa (chapters 1–3) and prameya (chapters 4–10).

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_vedantaparibhasa.title: Vedāntaparibhāṣā
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_vedantaparibhasa.author: Dharmarājādhvarīndra
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_vedantaparibhasa.summary: The Vedāntaparibhāṣā is a classic manual of Advaita Vedānta epistemology and ontology by Dharmarājādhvarīndra. Formulating Advaita concepts in technical philosophical style, the work defines and defends six pramāṇas (pratyakṣa, anumāna, upamāna, āgama, arthāpatti, and anupalabdhi). Its final chapters delineate the central subject matter (viṣaya) as the identity of jīva and Brahman, and the ultimate aim (prayojana) as liberation (mokṣa).
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_vedantaparibhasa.attribution: Authored by Dharmarājādhvarīndra, disciple of Nṛsiṃha and Veṅkaṭanātha, as stated in the opening verses and closing colophon.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_vedantaparibhasa.coverage: complete — Complete text in eight paricchedas: pratyakṣa, anumāna, upamāna, āgama, arthāpatti, anupalabdhi, viṣaya, and prayojana.
translations: Swami Madhavananda, Vedānta-Paribhāṣā of Dharmarāja Adhvarīndra, Belur Math: 1942. (English)
S. S. Suryanarayana Sastri, Vedāntaparibhāṣā by Dharmarāja Adhvarin, Madras: Adyar Library, 1942. (English)

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_vivaranaprameyasamgrahah.title: Vivaraṇaprameyasaṃgraha (partial)
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_vivaranaprameyasamgrahah.author: Vidyāraṇya
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_vivaranaprameyasamgrahah.summary: The Vivaraṇaprameyasaṃgraha is an influential 14th-century Advaita Vedānta compendium attributed to Vidyāraṇya (or Bhāratītīrtha), providing a systematic summary of Prakāśātman's Pañcapādikāvivaraṇa across nine varṇakas. It examines key tenets of the Vivaraṇa tradition including the locus and nature of avidyā, theories of error (khyātivāda), the nature of the witness consciousness (sākṣin), and the interpretation of the Mahāvākyas, while systematically refuting rival Mīmāṃsā, Nyāya, and Buddhist doctrines. This e-text is an incomplete transcription containing only the early sections of the first varṇaka.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_vivaranaprameyasamgrahah.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Vidyāraṇya (14th century); some scholars assign it to his senior contemporary Bhāratītīrtha. The opening verse bows to Śaṅkarānanda, characteristic of works associated with Vidyāraṇya.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_vivaranaprameyasamgrahah.coverage: partial — Incomplete; contains only introductory verses and portions of the first varṇaka on adhyāsa, breaking off mid-discussion during the refutation of ātmakhyāti and presentation of anirvacanīyakhyāti.
translations: The Vivaraṇaprameyasaṃgraha of Bhāratītīrtha, translated into English by S. S. Suryanarayana Sastri and Saileswar Sen, Andhra University Series, 1941. (English)
Vivaraṇaprameyasaṃgraha of Vidyaranya Muni, Bengali translation and exposition by Ashoke K. Gangopadhyaya, Calcutta: Navabharat Publishers, 1992. (Bengali)

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_vivekkacudamani_bhasyam.title: Vivekacūḍāmaṇi with Vivekacūḍāmaṇibhāṣya (verses 1–50)
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_vivekkacudamani_bhasyam.author: Śaṅkara, Candraśekhara Bhāratī
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_vivekkacudamani_bhasyam.summary: An Advaita Vedānta work consisting of the opening 50 verses of the Vivekacūḍāmaṇi accompanied by word-order reconstruction (anvaya) and a Sanskrit commentary (bhāṣya/vyākhyā).
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_vivekkacudamani_bhasyam.coverage: partial — Contains verses 1–50 with anvaya and commentary, breaking off after the commentary on verse 50.

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_visnutattvavinirnaya.title: Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_visnutattvavinirnaya.author: Madhva
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_visnutattvavinirnaya.summary: The Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya is the longest and doctrinally central treatise among the ten philosophical monographs (Daśaprakaraṇa) of Madhva (13th c. CE), the founder of Dvaita Vedānta. In three chapters (paricchedas), it establishes the intrinsic validity of knowledge (svataḥprāmāṇya), the authorlessness (apauruṣeyatva) and primary authority of the Vedas, and the ontological reality of difference (bheda) against Advaita non-dualism and the doctrine of māyā. The second and third chapters demonstrate that the supreme deity Viṣṇu (Nārāyaṇa) is entirely free from imperfections (nirdoṣa) and possessed of infinite auspicious attributes (aśeṣasadguṇapūrṇa).
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_visnutattvavinirnaya.attribution: Traditionally authored by Ānandatīrtha (Madhvācārya, c. 13th century CE), the founder of Dvaita Vedānta.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_visnutattvavinirnaya.coverage: complete — Complete text in three paricchedas (pariccheda 1 ends at line 508, pariccheda 2 at line 553, pariccheda 3 at line 606).
translations: Raghavachar, S. S., Viṣṇutattva-vinirṇaya of Śrī Madhvācārya: English Translation, Mangalore: Sri Ramakrishna Ashrama, 1959. (English)

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_vakyavrttih.title: Vākyavṛtti
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_vakyavrttih.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_vakyavrttih.summary: The Vākyavṛtti is an Advaita Vedānta prakaraṇa text in 53 verses framed as a dialogue between a preceptor and a spiritual aspirant. It offers an exposition of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad mahāvākya 'tat tvam asi' ('That thou art'). Through an analysis of the indirect meanings (lakṣaṇā) of 'tvam' (the inner conscious witness) and 'tat' (pure Brahman), it demonstrates the identity of the individual self and the absolute.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_vakyavrttih.coverage: complete — Complete in 53 verses with introductory mangala and closing colophon.
translations: S. Venkataramanan (trans.), Select Works of Sri Sankaracharya, Madras: G. A. Natesan & Co., 1911. (English)

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_yatindramatadipika.title: Yatīndramatadīpikā
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_yatindramatadipika.author: Śrīnivāsadāsa
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_yatindramatadipika.summary: The Yatīndramatadīpikā, also called the Śārīrakaparibhāṣā or Yatipatimatadīpikā, is an introductory manual of Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta by Śrīnivāsadāsa, disciple of Mahācārya (17th c.). Its ten chapters (avatāras) treat means of knowledge and categories of the knowable (including prakṛti, kāla, adravya).
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_yatindramatadipika.attribution: The author calls himself Śrīnivāsadāsa of the Vādhūla family, first disciple of Mahācārya. He is also referred to as Śrīnivāsa or Śrīnivāsācārya, and Otto's German translation names him Nivāsa. He is a 17th-century Viśiṣṭādvaitin.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_yatindramatadipika.coverage: complete — Text runs through to the final colophon of the 10th avatāra ('daśamo'vatāraḥ'). Includes Sanskrit topical subheadings (e.g. 'tattvaikyasya pratijñā', 'padārthasamuddeśaḥ').
translations: Swami Ādidevānanda, Yatīndramatadīpikā, Madras: Sri Ramakrishna Math. (English)
Rudolf Otto, Dīpikā des Nivāsa, Tübingen: Mohr. (German)

SA_GSP34_ilx_ws_yogadipika.title: Yogadīpikā
SA_GSP34_ilx_ws_yogadipika.author: Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya
SA_GSP34_ilx_ws_yogadipika.summary: The Yogadīpikā is a 10-chapter ritual and devotional treatise composed from the perspective of Dvaita Vedānta by Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya. Interpreting yoga as devotionally dedicated action and worship of Viṣṇu in accordance with the Gītā dictum 'yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam', it details daily religious observances, initiation (dīkṣā), kalaśasnāpana, meditation, and deity hierarchies (tāratamya).
SA_GSP34_ilx_ws_yogadipika.attribution: Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya was the son of Trivikrama Paṇḍitācārya.
SA_GSP34_ilx_ws_yogadipika.coverage: complete — Complete in 10 paṭalas, terminating with the final colophon 'iti yogadīpikāyāṃ daśamaḥ paṭalaḥ' and 'sampūrṇā'.

SA_GSP34_ilx_ws_yogasutrasarah.title: Yogasūtrasāra
SA_GSP34_ilx_ws_yogasutrasarah.author: Penna Madhusūdana
SA_GSP34_ilx_ws_yogasutrasarah.summary: The Yogasūtrasāra is a Sanskrit verse work with interspersed prose explanation on Pātañjala Yoga attributed to Pennāmadhusūdana. Across 220 verses, the work summarizes the core philosophy and practices of the Yogasūtra, drawing upon classical commentators such as the Vyāsabhāṣya and Vācaspatimiśra.
SA_GSP34_ilx_ws_yogasutrasarah.attribution: Attributed to Pennāmadhusūdana in the source headers and catalog records.
SA_GSP34_ilx_ws_yogasutrasarah.coverage: complete — Complete text in 220 numbered verses with interspersed prose explanations and concluding verses.

SA_GSP34_ilx_ws_yogataravali.title: Yogatārāvalī
SA_GSP34_ilx_ws_yogataravali.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GSP34_ilx_ws_yogataravali.summary: The Yogatārāvalī is a short Sanskrit treatise in 29 verses bridging Haṭhayoga physical practices with Rājayoga meditation. It describes the practice of the three bandhas (mūla, uḍḍīyana, jālandhara), kevalakumbhaka, and absorption in inner sound (nādānusandhāna) as the means to dissolve mental fluctuations into amanaska (the transcendent mindless state) and yoganidrā. While traditionally ascribed to Ādi Śaṅkara, it is characteristic of the late medieval syncretism between Haṭhayogic methods and non-dual Advaita metaphysics.
SA_GSP34_ilx_ws_yogataravali.attribution: Consistently attributed in the manuscript and printed tradition to Śaṅkarācārya (disciple of Govindabhagavatpūjyapāda). Bendall also notes that it is sometimes ascribed to Nandikeśvara.
SA_GSP34_ilx_ws_yogataravali.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 29 verses with the standard closing colophon.
translations: Mallinson, James and Mark Singleton, Roots of Yoga, London: Penguin Classics, 2017 (selected passages translated with Jason Birch). (English)

SA_GSP29_ilx_ws_sariravadah.title: Śarīravāda
SA_GSP29_ilx_ws_sariravadah.author: Anantārya
SA_GSP29_ilx_ws_sariravadah.summary: The Śarīravāda is a Viśiṣṭādvaita polemical treatise (vāda) by Anantārya of Yādavādri (Melkote) on the defining property (pravṛttinimitta) of the word 'body' (śarīra). It argues that 'bodyhood' is not a jāti and examines the Śrībhāṣya definition: a substance that a conscious being can wholly control and support for its own purposes, and that is entirely subsidiary (śeṣa) to it. It does so with reference to the Śrutaprakāśikā and the Nyāyasiddhāñjana, in Navya-Nyāya style. It also discusses related questions such as the inner self's entering (anupraveśa) and the soul's departure and movement.
SA_GSP29_ilx_ws_sariravadah.attribution: The opening verse names the author 'Anantasudhī', and the closing verse and colophon name him 'anantāryeṇa racito' and 'śrīśeṣāryavaṃśamuktāphalasya śrīyādavādrinivāsasikasya śrīmadanantāryavaryasya kṛtiṣu', i.e. Anantārya (Anantācārya) of the Śeṣārya lineage, resident at Yādavādri (Melkote).
SA_GSP29_ilx_ws_sariravadah.coverage: complete — Opens with the invocation (śrīḥ, title, maṅgala verse naming Anantasudhī) and ends with the author's verse, the colophon 'śarīravādaḥ samāptaḥ' and 'śrīḥ'.

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_satasloki.title: Śataślokī
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_satasloki.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_satasloki.summary: The Śataślokī is an Advaita Vedānta verse compendium composed in sragdharā metre and traditionally attributed to Śaṅkarācārya. Across 101 verses, it systematically expounds key Advaitic teachings, including the role of the guru, the illusion of the empirical world, self-realization through discrimination between ātman and anātman, the interpretation of Upaniṣadic Mahāvākyas, and the nature of jīvanmukti. While firmly integrated into the Advaita curriculum, modern philology regards the work as an unauthentic composition of the later Śaṅkara tradition.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_satasloki.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Ādi Śaṅkarācārya (disciple of Govinda Bhagavatpāda). Its authenticity has been questioned in modern scholarship (e.g. Watanabe, Ludwik Sternbach).
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_satasloki.coverage: complete — Complete in 101 sragdharā verses with closing colophon.
translations: Select Works of Sri Sankaracharya, Sanskrit text and English translation by S. Venkataramanan, Madras: G. A. Natesan & Co., 1911 (reprinted 1921). (English)

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sankarapadabhusanam.title: Śaṅkarapādabhūṣaṇa (end of Jyotiradhikaraṇa and Brahmasūtra 2.1 Smṛti- to Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa)
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sankarapadabhusanam.author: Raghunātha Parvate
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sankarapadabhusanam.summary: The Śaṅkarapādabhūṣaṇa is an Advaita work by Raghunātha Śāstrī Parvate. It defends Śaṅkara's interpretation of Brahmasūtra adhikaraṇas against the Mādhva criticism in the Tātparyacandrikā. This e-text contains the end of the Jyotiradhikaraṇa and BS 2.1 adhikaraṇas up to the Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sankarapadabhusanam.attribution: By Raghunātha Śāstrī Parvate, also known as Śrīraghunāthasūri. The closing verses mention completion under the patronage of the Pant Sacivs ('Nānāsāheb') residing near the Nīrā river, with support from the judge Viṣṇu Bhiḍe, son of Gopāla.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sankarapadabhusanam.coverage: partial — Partial. The e-text begins mid-way through the Jyotiradhikaraṇa; all earlier parts of BS 1.1 are missing. It continues with BS 2.1: Smṛti-, Vilakṣaṇa-, Śiṣṭāparigraha-, Bhoktrāpatti- and Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa, followed by the author's closing verses and 'samāpto 'yaṃ śāṃkarapādabhūṣaṇābhidho granthaḥ'.

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_srutapradipika.title: Śrutapradīpikā
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_srutapradipika.author: Sudarśanasūri
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_srutapradipika.summary: The Śrutapradīpikā is a commentary on Rāmānuja's Śrībhāṣya on the Brahmasūtras, composed by Sudarśanasūri.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_srutapradipika.attribution: Sudarśanasūri, also known as Sudarśanabhaṭṭāraka and Vedavyāsa Bhaṭṭāraka, was the son of Vāgvijayin of the Harita gotra and disciple of Varadarājārya.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_srutapradipika.coverage: complete — Complete text covering all four adhyāyas of the Brahmasūtras / Śrībhāṣya, ending at Brahmasūtra 4.4.22 with the closing colophon for adhyāya 4, pāda 4.

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_srutaprakasika.title: Śrutaprakāśikā
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_srutaprakasika.author: Sudarśanasūri
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_srutaprakasika.summary: The Śrutaprakāśikā is a sub-commentary on Rāmānuja's Śrībhāṣya on the Brahmasūtra by Sudarśanasūri.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_srutaprakasika.attribution: The final segments of the e-text contain the concluding verses and colophon of the Śārīrakādhikaraṇacintāmaṇi by Kumāra Vedāntācārya (Varadaguru / Varadārya).
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_srutaprakasika.coverage: complete — Sub-commentary on Rāmānuja's Śrībhāṣya, ending with colophon verses from Varadanātha's Śārīrakādhikaraṇacintāmaṇi (adhyāya 4, pāda 4).

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sribhasyam.title: Śrībhāṣya
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sribhasyam.author: Rāmānuja
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sribhasyam.summary: The Śrībhāṣya is Rāmānuja's commentary on the Brahmasūtra of Bādarāyaṇa, serving as a foundational philosophical text of Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta. In it, Rāmānuja systematically refutes Advaita non-dualism, establishing that the Supreme Brahman is identical with Nārāyaṇa, endowed with infinite auspicious qualities.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sribhasyam.coverage: complete — Covers the text of the Brahmasūtra with Rāmānuja's commentary, ending with the final colophon: iti śrībhagavadrāmānujaviracite śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣye caturthasyādhyāyasya caturthaḥ pādaḥ.
translations: The Vedanta-Sutras with Ramanuja's Sribhasya, G. Thibaut, Sacred Books of the East. (English)

SA_GS26_ilx_ws_santikamalakarah.title: Śāntikamalākara
SA_GS26_ilx_ws_santikamalakarah.author: Kamalākarabhaṭṭa
SA_GS26_ilx_ws_santikamalakarah.summary: The Śāntikamalākara is a ritual digest on pacification rites (śānti), portents, and averting liturgies, beginning with pūrvapīṭhikā svastivācana rituals.
SA_GS26_ilx_ws_santikamalakarah.coverage: complete — Runs from the preliminary svastivācana liturgies (pūrvapīṭhikā) to the closing colophon (śānti kamalākaranāma graṃtha samāpti).

SA_GSP29_ilx_ws_sarirakakarikavali.title: Śārīrakakārikāvalī
SA_GSP29_ilx_ws_sarirakakarikavali.summary: The Śārīrakakārikāvalī is a Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta metrical manual summarizing the adhikaraṇas (topical sections) of Rāmānuja's Śrībhāṣya on the Brahmasūtras. Written by a follower in the lineage of Vedānta Deśika and Śrīraṅgarāmānuja Muni, it concisely expounds the pūrvapakṣa (opponent's view) and siddhānta (established conclusion) of each topical section. The work serves as a mnemonic and pedagogical study guide to Rāmānuja's Brahmasūtrabhāṣya.
SA_GSP29_ilx_ws_sarirakakarikavali.attribution: The work was composed by a Viśiṣṭādvaita scholar in the lineage of Vedānta Deśika and Śrīraṅgarāmānuja Muni (mentioned in verse 5 as 'yatipatir mahān śrīraṅgarāmāvarajaḥ'), summarizing the Śrībhāṣya adhikaraṇa by adhikaraṇa, but the author's own name is omitted.
SA_GSP29_ilx_ws_sarirakakarikavali.coverage: incomplete — The provided text ends at the close of adhyāya 4, pāda 2 (iti caturthādhyāye dvitīyaḥ pādaḥ).

SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sarirakadhikaranaratnama.title: Śārīrakādhikaraṇaratnamālāprakāśa (Jijñāsādhikaraṇa only)
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sarirakadhikaranaratnama.author: Kauśikadeśika
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sarirakadhikaranaratnama.summary: The Prakāśa is Kauśikadeśika's own prose commentary on his Śārīrakādhikaraṇaratnamālā, a verse digest of the Brahmasūtra adhikaraṇas according to Rāmānuja's Śrībhāṣya. This fragment covers the maṅgala verse to Śrīnivāsa of the Śeṣaśaila and the Jijñāsādhikaraṇa (BS 1.1.1). It explains that inquiry into Brahman follows the inquiry into ritual (karmavicāra), argues against the pūrvapakṣa that all Veda is about injunctions, and identifies the Brahman to be known with Śrīnivāsa.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sarirakadhikaranaratnama.attribution: Both the verse summary (Śārīrakādhikaraṇaratnamālā) and its prose commentary Prakāśa are by Kauśikadeśika (Kauśikadeśikasūri), who wrote them 'at the command of Śrīnivāsa', i.e. the Lord of the Śeṣaśaila, who is invoked in the maṅgala verse. A Viśiṣṭādvaita author following Rāmānuja's Śrībhāṣya.
SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_sarirakadhikaranaratnama.coverage: fragment — Only the Prakāśa on the opening maṅgala verse and on the Jijñāsādhikaraṇa (BS 1.1.1), ending 'iti jijñāsādhikaraṇam || 1 ||'. The root verses are absent. The rest of the work (the remaining adhikaraṇas of the Brahmasūtra) is missing.

SA_GS26_ilx_ws_sad_darsanasamuccayah.title: Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya with Laghuvṛtti
SA_GS26_ilx_ws_sad_darsanasamuccayah.author: Haribhadrasūri, Maṇibhadra
SA_GS26_ilx_ws_sad_darsanasamuccayah.summary: The Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya of Haribhadrasūri is a doxographical treatise summarizing Indian philosophical traditions, followed by an examination of other systems. Composed in 87 stanzas, this e-text incorporates the root kārikās alongside the Laghuvṛtti commentary by Maṇibhadra.
SA_GS26_ilx_ws_sad_darsanasamuccayah.attribution: Root kārikās by Haribhadrasūri. The Laghuvṛtti is ascribed to Maṇibhadra in this text ('maṇibhadrakṛtā laghuvṛttiḥ samāptā').
SA_GS26_ilx_ws_sad_darsanasamuccayah.coverage: complete — Complete text of all 87 kārikās of Haribhadrasūri's Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya together with the complete Laghuvṛtti commentary by Maṇibhadra.

SA_GS25_ilx_ws_amarakosah_amaravivekavya.title: Amarakoṣa with Amaraviveka
SA_GS25_ilx_ws_amarakosah_amaravivekavya.author: Amarasiṃha, Maheśvara
SA_GS25_ilx_ws_amarakosah_amaravivekavya.summary: The Amarakoṣa (formally Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana) of Amarasiṃha is a lexicon of Classical Sanskrit structured into three kāṇḍas. The Amaraviveka of Maheśvara is a commentary elucidating word origins and grammatical readings.
SA_GS25_ilx_ws_amarakosah_amaravivekavya.attribution: The root lexicon is attributed to Amarasiṃha. The commentary Amaraviveka was composed by Maheśvara.
SA_GS25_ilx_ws_amarakosah_amaravivekavya.coverage: complete — Includes the editor's prastāvanā and all three kāṇḍas of the root text with Maheśvara's commentary.

SA_XX_ilx_ws_bismilasya_balidanakatha.title: Bismilasya Balidānakathā
SA_XX_ilx_ws_bismilasya_balidanakatha.summary: A modern narrative poem in vernacularized Sanskrit detailing the life and martyrdom of the Indian freedom fighter Ram Prasad Bismil (1897–1927). It recounts his early life in Shahjahanpur, participation in revolutionary movements including the Hindustan Republican Association and the Kakori action, his trial, and his hanging in December 1927 alongside Ashfaqullah Khan, Roshan Singh, and Rajendra Lahiri.
SA_XX_ilx_ws_bismilasya_balidanakatha.attribution: A contemporary vernacular/Hindi-influenced Sanskrit ballad eulogizing the Indian revolutionary Pandit Ram Prasad Bismil (1897–1927). No author is specified in the Wikisource source text.
SA_XX_ilx_ws_bismilasya_balidanakatha.coverage: complete — Complete text of the modern song/ballad in 74 lines with a recurring refrain.

SA_GS25_ilx_ws_ekarthanamamala.title: Ekārthanāmamālā
SA_GS25_ilx_ws_ekarthanamamala.author: Saubhari
SA_GS25_ilx_ws_ekarthanamamala.summary: The Ekārthanāmamālā (also called Ekākṣarīnāmamālā) is a short Sanskrit monosyllabic lexicon (ekākṣarakośa) attributed to Saubhari. Written in anuṣṭubh verse, it catalogs the diverse designations and conventional symbolic meanings assigned to individual vowels and consonants. Texts of this genre served as reference tools for poets (especially for citrakāvya), scribes, and practitioners interpreting tantric bījamantras.
SA_GS25_ilx_ws_ekarthanamamala.attribution: Attributed to the lexicographer Saubhari in the opening line (saubharikṛtā).
SA_GS25_ilx_ws_ekarthanamamala.coverage: complete — Complete text in ~121 anuṣṭubh verses (242 half-verse segments plus colophon), treating meanings of individual letters from 'a' through 'kṣa'.

SA_XX_ilx_ws_pakadarpanam.title: Pākadarpaṇa (excerpt)
SA_XX_ilx_ws_pakadarpanam.author: Nala
SA_XX_ilx_ws_pakadarpanam.summary: The Pākadarpaṇa ('Mirror of Culinary Art') is a traditional Sanskrit treatise on cooking and dietetics framed as the teachings of King Nala in his disguise as Bāhuka at the court of King Ṛtuparṇa. The full work covers the preparation of boiled rice, pulses, broths, meat dishes, vegetables, and sweets, as well as kitchen sanitation and the therapeutic effects of food. This fragmentary e-text contains only the first fifty verses, outlining Nala's divine boons, the qualities required of a royal cook, and defects arising from faulty cooking.
SA_XX_ilx_ws_pakadarpanam.attribution: The treatise is traditionally attributed to the legendary King Nala of the Mahābhārata, who obtained mastery over fire and cooking as a divine boon.
SA_XX_ilx_ws_pakadarpanam.coverage: excerpt — Verses 1–50 only of the introductory chapter (describing the narrative frame, the qualifications of a royal cook, and initial defects of cooked food), breaking off abruptly without colophon.

SA_GS38_ilx_ws_samaranganasutradhara.title: Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra
SA_GS38_ilx_ws_samaranganasutradhara.author: Bhoja
SA_GS38_ilx_ws_samaranganasutradhara.summary: The Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra is a Sanskrit treatise on architecture (vāstuśāstra), town planning, residential layout, temple styles, and painting, attributed to King Bhojadeva.
SA_GS38_ilx_ws_samaranganasutradhara.attribution: Attributed in colophons to Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Bhojadeva.
SA_GS38_ilx_ws_samaranganasutradhara.coverage: complete — Ending at verse 254 with 'śubhaṃ bhūyāt' and lacunae marked by dashes (e.g. at verse 253).

SA_GK18_ilx_ws_sangitaratnakarah.title: Saṅgītaratnākara
SA_GK18_ilx_ws_sangitaratnakarah.author: Śārṅgadeva
SA_GK18_ilx_ws_sangitaratnakarah.summary: The Saṅgītaratnākara is a foundational medieval treatise on Indian music and performing arts. Arranged into seven chapters (saptādhyāyī), it provides an exhaustive analysis of notes and intervals (svara), melodic modes (rāga), miscellaneous musicological concepts (prakīrṇa), song and meter forms (prabandha), rhythm and metrics (tāla), musical instruments (vādya), and dance (nartana). The treatise forms an essential transition between ancient dramatic musical theory (gāndharva/mārga) and regional performance traditions (deśī).
SA_GK18_ilx_ws_sangitaratnakarah.coverage: complete — Contains all seven adhyāyas (Svara, Rāgaviveka, Prakīrṇaka, Prabandha, Tāla, Vādya, and Nartana) of the root text without commentary, concluding with the standard end-matter rāga enumerations.
translations: Sangitaratnakara of Sarngadeva, translated by Dr. C. Kunhan Raja, Vol. II [Vol. I], Chap. I, Adyar Library Series no. 51, 1945. (English)

SA_GK18_ilx_ws_sangitasarasamgrahah.title: Saṅgītasārasaṃgraha (chapter 1, verses 1–110)
SA_GK18_ilx_ws_sangitasarasamgrahah.author: Narahari Cakravartin
SA_GK18_ilx_ws_sangitasarasamgrahah.summary: The Saṅgītasārasaṃgraha is a musicological treatise attributed to Ghanaśyāmadāsa. This partial e-text contains the first 110 verses of the opening chapter on vocal music (gītāprakaraṇam), discussing the origin of music, sound (nāda), notes (svara), microtones (śruti), and parent scales (jāti).
SA_GK18_ilx_ws_sangitasarasamgrahah.attribution: Mentioned in scholarly literature as Saṅgītasārasaṃgraha of Ghanaśyāmadāsa.
SA_GK18_ilx_ws_sangitasarasamgrahah.coverage: partial — Breaks off at verse 110 in the first adhyāya (gītāprakaraṇam).

SA_GP12_ilx_ws_bhavisyapurana.title: Bhaviṣyapurāṇa
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_bhavisyapurana.summary: The Bhaviṣyapurāṇa is one of the Purāṇas, containing mythological narratives, religious duties, vrata observances (such as the Anantavrata), and ritual instructions.
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_bhavisyapurana.coverage: complete — Text of the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa concluding with an Anantavrata section ('iti bhaviṣyapurāṇe anantavrataṃ samāptaṃ').

SA_GP12_ilx_ws_brahmavaivartapurana.title: Brahmavaivartapurāṇa
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_brahmavaivartapurana.summary: The Brahmavaivartapurāṇa is one of the eighteen major Purāṇas (Mahāpurāṇas), traditionally organized into four books: Brahmakhaṇḍa, Prakṛtikhaṇḍa, Gaṇeśakhaṇḍa, and Kṛṣṇajanmakhaṇḍa. It is notable for its theological synthesis celebrating Kṛṣṇa as the ultimate absolute reality (parabrahman) residing in Goloka, together with his eternal consort Rādhā, and provides detailed accounts of various goddesses considered manifestations of Prakṛti.
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_brahmavaivartapurana.coverage: complete — Contains all four major khaṇḍas: Brahmakhaṇḍa, Prakṛtikhaṇḍa, Gaṇeśakhaṇḍa, and Śrīkṛṣṇajanmakhaṇḍa (divided into pūrvārdha and uttarārdha), ending at chapter 133 of the uttarārdha of Śrīkṛṣṇajanmakhaṇḍa.

SA_GP12_ilx_ws_devibhagavatapurana.title: Devībhāgavatapurāṇa with Devībhāgavatamāhātmya
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_devibhagavatapurana.summary: The Devībhāgavatapurāṇa is a major purāṇa of the Śākta tradition celebrating the Goddess. In this e-text it is preceded by the Devībhāgavatamāhātmya.
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_devibhagavatapurana.coverage: complete — Devībhāgavatamāhātmya followed by the Devībhāgavatapurāṇa in 12 skandhas, ending with 12.14, 'dvādaśaḥ skandhaḥ samāptaḥ', and 'śrīmaddevībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa saṃpūrṇam'.

SA_GP12_ilx_ws_gargasamhita.title: Gargasaṃhitā
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_gargasamhita.summary: The Vaiṣṇava Gargasaṃhitā is a post-classical narrative and devotional text celebrating the life and divine pastimes (līlā) of Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā, divided into ten khaṇḍas. Framed primarily as dialogues between the sage Garga and Śaunaka, as well as King Bahulāśva of Mithilā and Nārada, it exalts Kṛṣṇa as the supreme paripūrṇatama avatāra and provides detailed descriptions of Goloka, Vraja, and Girirāja Govardhana.
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_gargasamhita.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the sage Garga (Gargamuni), family priest of the Yadus. This Vaiṣṇava narrative and devotional text is distinct from the ancient astrological/astronomical text also known as Gargasaṃhitā (or Vṛddhagargasaṃhitā).
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_gargasamhita.coverage: complete — Complete text across all ten khaṇḍas (Goloka-, Vṛndāvana-, Girirāja-, Mādhurya-, Mathurā-, Dvārakā-, Viśvajit-, Balabhadra-, Vijñāna-, and Aśvamedhakhaṇḍa), ending at Aśvamedhakhaṇḍa 62.53 and 'samāpto 'yaṃ granthaḥ'.

SA_GP12_ilx_ws_jaiminiyasvamedhaparva_in.title: Jaiminīyāśvamedhaparvan (chapters 1–10)
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_jaiminiyasvamedhaparva_in.summary: The Jaiminīyāśvamedhaparvan (or Jaiminibhārata) is an independent narrative of Yudhiṣṭhira's horse sacrifice (aśvamedha), framed as a dialogue between the sage Jaimini and King Janamejaya. Distinct in tone and episodes from Vyāsa's Mahābhārata, it strongly emphasizes Vaiṣṇava bhakti and legendary adventures during the wandering of the sacrificial horse. This partial e-text contains chapters 1–10, covering Yudhiṣṭhira's grief, Vyāsa's advice to perform the sacrifice, obtaining Marutta's wealth, and Kṛṣṇa's departure for Hastināpura.
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_jaiminiyasvamedhaparva_in.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the sage Jaimini, a disciple of Vedavyāsa, representing an alternative recension to Vyāsa's Mahābhārata.
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_jaiminiyasvamedhaparva_in.coverage: partial — Adhyāyas 1–10 only, ending with the colophon 'ityāśvamedhikeparvaṇi jaiminīye śrīkṛṣṇaprayāṇaṃ nāma daśamo'dhyāyaḥ ||10'.

SA_GP12_ilx_ws_kalkipurana_incomplete.title: Kalkipurāṇa
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_kalkipurana_incomplete.summary: The Kalkipurāṇa (also known as the Anubhāgavata) is an Upapurāṇa dedicated to Kalki, the tenth avatāra of Viṣṇu. Arranged in three sections (aṃśas), it narrates the descent of Kalki in the village of Śambhala to suppress the corruption of Kaliyuga, his campaigns against Buddhists, Jainas, and mlecchas, and the re-establishment of the dharma and the Kṛtayuga.
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_kalkipurana_incomplete.coverage: complete — Despite the repository filename suffix '_incomplete', the e-text covers all three aṃśas (prathama, dvitīya, and tṛtīya) and concludes with the colophon of chapter 21 of the third aṃśa (iti śrīkalkipurāṇe’nubhāgavate bhaviṣye tṛtīyāṃśe ekaviṃśo’dhyāyaḥ ||21).

SA_GP12_ilx_ws_kapilapurana.title: Kapilapurāṇa
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_kapilapurana.summary: The Kapilapurāṇa is a short Upapurāṇa in 21 chapters, in which the sage Kapila answers King Śalyajit about the holy places of Utkala (Odisha). It is essentially a tīrthamāhātmya: it covers the Mahānadī, Puruṣottama (Puri) with the Indradyumna legend, Ekāmra (Bhubaneswar) and its liṅgas at length, Virajā/Girijā and other sites, cāturmāsya vows, and a closing praise of the four kṣetras of Utkala (catuḥkṣetramāhātmya).
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_kapilapurana.attribution: An Upapurāṇa and māhātmya text on the tīrthas of Utkala (Odisha), in which the sage Kapila answers King Śalyajit.
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_kapilapurana.coverage: complete — Adhyāyas 1–21, each with a colophon ('iti śrīkapilapurāṇe ...'). Ends 'iti śrīkapilapurāṇe utkalakṣetropākhyāne catuḥkṣetramāhātmyaṃ nāmaikaviṃśatitamo'dhyāyaḥ / samāptamidaṃ kapilapurāṇam', followed by a four-line benediction by the modern editor.

SA_GP12_ilx_ws_laksminarayanasamhita_1.title: Lakṣmīnārāyaṇasaṃhitā (part 1 of 4: 1.1–1.362.51)
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_laksminarayanasamhita_1.summary: The Lakṣmīnārāyaṇasaṃhitā is a Vaiṣṇava saṃhitā framed as a dialogue/revelation involving Nārāyaṇa, Lakṣmī, Śvetavyāsa, and Lomaśa. It deals with cosmology, mythology, vratas, dāna, tīrthas, and devotion to Nārāyaṇa / Śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. This first part covers from the opening up to chapter 362 verse 51.
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_laksminarayanasamhita_1.attribution: Tradition attributes the work to Śvetavyāsa / Śvetāyana Vyāsa, with Lomaśa as narrator.
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_laksminarayanasamhita_1.coverage: partial — Begins at the opening of the text and runs to 1.362.51, breaking off mid-chapter at an arbitrary file split.

SA_GP12_ilx_ws_laksminarayanasamhita_2.title: Lakṣmīnārāyaṇasaṃhitā (part 2 of 4: 1.362.52–2.69.40)
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_laksminarayanasamhita_2.summary: The Lakṣmīnārāyaṇasaṃhitā is a Vaiṣṇava saṃhitā. This part covers verse portions spanning from 1.362.52 through the second khaṇḍa (Tretāsantāna) up to 2.69.40, containing narratives, vratas, dāna, and devotional teaching concerning Śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_laksminarayanasamhita_2.coverage: partial — From 1.362.52 to 2.69.40, breaking off mid-chapter at an arbitrary file split.

SA_GP12_ilx_ws_laksminarayanasamhita_3.title: Lakṣmīnārāyaṇasaṃhitā (part 3 of 4: 2.69.41–3.61.92)
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_laksminarayanasamhita_3.coverage: partial — Split into 4 parts for file-size reasons; this is part 3 (segments 127894–191840 of the original line sequence).

SA_GP12_ilx_ws_laksminarayanasamhita_4.title: Lakṣmīnārāyaṇasaṃhitā (part 4 of 4: 3.61.93–4.123)
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_laksminarayanasamhita_4.summary: The Lakṣmīnārāyaṇasaṃhitā is a very large Vaiṣṇava saṃhitā in four khaṇḍas named after the yugas. It is framed as a revelation of Nārāyaṇa to Lakṣmī. It deals with cosmology, mythology, vratas, dāna, tīrthas and devotion to Śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. This last part covers khaṇḍa 3 (Dvāparasantāna) from chapter 61 to its end and the whole of khaṇḍa 4 (Tiṣyasantāna), which closes with an account of how the Saṃhitā itself appeared and with benedictions.
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_laksminarayanasamhita_4.coverage: partial — From 3.61.93 to the end of the Dvāparasantāna (ch. 237), then the complete Tiṣyasantāna (4.1–4.123), ending 'iti śrītiṣyasantānakhaṇḍaḥ || sampūrṇeyaṃ catuḥkhaṇḍātmikā śrīlakṣmīnārāyaṇasaṃhitā vijayate'.

SA_GP12_ilx_ws_naradapurana_2_44_2_82.title: Nāradapurāṇa (Uttarabhāga, chapters 44–82)
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_naradapurana_2_44_2_82.summary: This portion of the Uttarabhāga of the Nāradapurāṇa (chapters 44–82) comprises an extensive collection of tīrthamāhātmyas detailing the sacred geography, legends, rituals, and pilgrimage fruits of Gayā, Prayāga, Kurukṣetra, Haridvāra, Badarikāśrama, Prabhāsa, Puṣkara, Gokarṇa, Mathurā, and other sites, concluding with the benefits of reciting and hearing the Purāṇa.
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_naradapurana_2_44_2_82.coverage: partial — Uttarabhāga chapters 44–82, containing various tīrthamāhātmyas (Gayā, Prayāga, Kurukṣetra, Haridvāra, Badarikāśrama, Prabhāsa, Puṣkara, Mathurā, etc.) and the closing chapter/phalaśruti (82).

SA_GP12_ilx_ws_padmapurana_1.title: Padmapurāṇa (Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa)
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_padmapurana_1.summary: The Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa ('Section on Creation') is the first major section of the Padmapurāṇa. Comprising 82 adhyāyas, it narrates cosmogony centered around Brahmā and Viṣṇu, extensive sacred geography and pilgrimage narratives focusing on Puṣkara (Pauṣkara-māhātmya), the legend of Pṛthu, genealogies of the solar and lunar dynasties, and ritual injunctions including planetary worship (grahārcana) and śrāddha rites.
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_padmapurana_1.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Vyāsa; narrated in the Purāṇic frame by Romaharṣaṇa/Ugraśravas.
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_padmapurana_1.coverage: partial — Contains the complete Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa (chapters 1–82) of the multi-khaṇḍa Padmapurāṇa.

SA_GP12_ilx_ws_padmapurana_2.title: Padmapurāṇa (khaṇḍas 2–5)
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_padmapurana_2.summary: This volume contains sections 2 through 5 of the Padmapurāṇa, one of the eighteen major Mahāpurāṇas. It comprises the Bhūmikhaṇḍa (featuring legends of King Vena, Sukalā, and Cyavana), the Svargakhaṇḍa (cosmology, tīrthamāhātmya, and the Prayāgamāhātmya), the Brahmakhaṇḍa (discourses on rituals, vrata observances, and Tulasī veneration), and the Pātālakhaṇḍa (containing the celebrated Rāmāśvamedha cycle, Kṛṣṇa-bhakti narratives, and the Vṛndāvanamāhātmya).
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_padmapurana_2.coverage: partial — Contains khaṇḍas 2 through 5 of the vulgate Padmapurāṇa: Bhūmikhaṇḍa, Svargakhaṇḍa, Brahmakhaṇḍa, and Pātālakhaṇḍa (adhyāyas 1–117, concluding at line 42894 with 'iti śrīpadmapurāṇe pañcamaṃ pātālakhaṇḍaṃ samāptam').

SA_GP12_ilx_ws_padmapurana_3.title: Padmapurāṇa (Kriyāyogasārakhaṇḍa, chapters 12–26)
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_padmapurana_3.summary: The Kriyāyogasārakhaṇḍa is a section of the Padmapurāṇa presented as a dialogue between Vyāsa and Jaimini. Chapters 12–26 treat monthly worship rituals, karmic retribution, righteous conduct, and the concluding purāṇamāhātmya.
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_padmapurana_3.attribution: Framed as a dialogue between Vyāsa and Jaimini.
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_padmapurana_3.coverage: partial — Contains chapters 12–26 of the Kriyāyogasārakhaṇḍa.

SA_GP12_ilx_ws_skandapurana_8.title: Skandapurāṇa (early recension)
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_skandapurana_8.summary: Framed as a dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Vyāsa, it narrates the birth and martial deeds of Skanda/Kārttikeya, major myths of Śiva and Devī, sacred geography, and related topics.

SA_GP12_ilx_ws_varahapurana.title: Varāhapurāṇa
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_varahapurana.summary: The Varāhapurāṇa is one of the Purāṇas. Structured primarily as an extensive dialogue between the boar incarnation of Viṣṇu (Varāha) and the Earth goddess (Dharaṇī), the text covers cosmogony, mythology, and genealogies, but places particular emphasis on ritual observance, vratas, dāna, Śaiva and Śākta legends, and tīrthamāhātmyas (most prominently the Mathurā-māhātmya).
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_varahapurana.attribution: Framed as a dialogue between the boar incarnation of Viṣṇu (Varāha) and the Earth goddess (Dharaṇī/Pṛthivī).
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_varahapurana.coverage: complete — Complete vulgate text in 218 adhyāyas, from the opening maṅgala to adhyāya 218 (Anukramaṇikā) and 'samāptaṃ vārāhaṃ mahāpurāṇaṃ śubham', followed by a scribal stanza ('yādṛśaṃ pustake dṛṣṭaṃ tādṛśaṃ likhitaṃ mayā ...').

SA_GP12_ilx_ws_visnudharmottarapurana_1.title: Viṣṇudharmottarapurāṇa (khaṇḍa 1)
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_visnudharmottarapurana_1.summary: The Viṣṇudharmottarapurāṇa presents itself as the second part of the Viṣṇupurāṇa and is framed as a dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and King Vajra. The first khaṇḍa (269 chapters) treats cosmogony and cosmography, astral lore, genealogies of gods, sages and kings, śrāddha, vratas and other rites, and includes narrative and devotional sections such as the Śaṅkaragītā and Rāma narratives ending with the meeting of Rāma and Bharata (ch. 269).
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_visnudharmottarapurana_1.attribution: Framed as an instructional dialogue between the sage Mārkaṇḍeya and King Vajra.
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_visnudharmottarapurana_1.coverage: partial — Complete first khaṇḍa (adhyāyas 1–269), ending 'samāptaścāyaṃ prathamakhaṇḍaḥ'.

SA_GP12_ilx_ws_visnudharmottarapurana_2.title: Viṣṇudharmottarapurāṇa (khaṇḍa 2)
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_visnudharmottarapurana_2.summary: The second khaṇḍa (183 chapters) of the Viṣṇudharmottarapurāṇa consists largely of Puṣkara's instruction to Rāma, narrated by Mārkaṇḍeya to Vajra. It includes rājadharma (royal duties, law, administration), rituals, and ends with dhanurveda (ch. 183).
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_visnudharmottarapurana_2.attribution: Framed as a dialogue between Puṣkara and Rāma narrated by Mārkaṇḍeya to Vajra.
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_visnudharmottarapurana_2.coverage: partial — Complete second khaṇḍa (adhyāyas 1–183), ending 'samāpto'yaṃ viṣṇudharmottaradvitīyakhaṇḍaḥ'.

SA_GP12_ilx_ws_visnudharmottarapurana_3.title: Viṣṇudharmottarapurāṇa (khaṇḍa 3)
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_visnudharmottarapurana_3.summary: The third khaṇḍa (355 chapters) of the Viṣṇudharmottarapurāṇa, framed as Mārkaṇḍeya's instruction to Vajra, treats religious and cultural topics, ending with a Narasiṃha hymn (ch. 355).
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_visnudharmottarapurana_3.attribution: Framed as a dialogue between the sage Mārkaṇḍeya and King Vajra.
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_visnudharmottarapurana_3.coverage: partial — Complete third khaṇḍa (adhyāyas 1–355), ending 'iti śrīviṣṇudharmottaraṃ samāptam'.

SA_GP12_ilx_ws_vayupurana.title: Vāyupurāṇa
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_vayupurana.summary: The Vāyupurāṇa is widely regarded by Indologists as one of the oldest surviving Mahāpurāṇas, closely related in content and wording to the Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa. Framed as a discourse recited by the wind god Vāyu to the sages in Naimiṣāraṇya, it preserves an archaic core adhering faithfully to the classical pañcalakṣaṇa topics: cosmogony, recreation, genealogies of gods and kings, manvantaras, and dynastic history. Its concluding section (chapters 2.43–50 / 105–112) comprises the well-known Gayāmāhātmya, a vital manual of pilgrimage rites, sacred geography, and ancestral offerings (śrāddha) at Gayā.
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_vayupurana.attribution: Traditionally attributed to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa and narrated by the Sūta Lomaharṣaṇa as recounted originally by the wind deity Vāyu.
SA_GP12_ilx_ws_vayupurana.coverage: complete — Complete: Pūrvārdha 61 adhyāyas (1.1–1.61) and Uttarārdha 50 adhyāyas (2.1–2.50), ending with the Gayāmāhātmya (2.43–2.50) and 'samāptamidaṃ vāyupurāṇam'. Every tenth verse of the Uttarārdha also carries the Ānandāśrama continuous numbering (e.g. '2.1.20|| 62.21', last '2.50.80|| 112.68').

SA_GSD36_ilx_ws_devalasmrti.title: Devalasmṛti
SA_GSD36_ilx_ws_devalasmrti.author: Devala
SA_GSD36_ilx_ws_devalasmrti.summary: The Devalasmṛti is a short metrical legal text of 90 verses framed as the teachings of the sage Devala to fellow sages on the banks of the Indus (Sindhu). It is uniquely significant in the Dharmaśāstra tradition for formulating lenient and detailed purificatory penances (śuddhi and prāyaścitta) allowing persons of all four varṇas, including women, who were abducted, forcibly converted, or otherwise compromised by foreigners (mlecchas) to be reintegrated into society.
SA_GSD36_ilx_ws_devalasmrti.attribution: Traditional attribution to the sage Devala.
SA_GSD36_ilx_ws_devalasmrti.coverage: complete — Complete in 90 verses, ending at verse 90 with 'samāpteyaṃ devalasmṛtiḥ'.

SA_GSD36_ilx_ws_kasyapasmrti.title: Kaśyapasmṛti
SA_GSD36_ilx_ws_kasyapasmrti.summary: The Kaśyapasmṛti is a brief Dharmaśāstra tract in mixed prose and verse attributed to the sage Kaśyapa. It sets forth gṛhastha duties, penances (prāyaścitta) for harming domestic and wild animals, purifications for ritual and food transgressions, rules regarding the five major sins (mahāpātaka), and strictures concerning the gifting and marriage of daughters (kanyādāna).
SA_GSD36_ilx_ws_kasyapasmrti.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the Vedic sage Kaśyapa (Kāśyapa).
SA_GSD36_ilx_ws_kasyapasmrti.coverage: complete — Complete short smṛti treatise in mixed prose and verse, concluding with 'iti kāśyapa praṇītaṃ dharmaśāstraṃ samāptam'.

SA_GSD36_ilx_ws_pulastyasmrti.title: Pulastyasmṛti
SA_GSD36_ilx_ws_pulastyasmrti.summary: The Pulastyasmṛti is a concise Dharmaśāstra text in 28 anuṣṭubh verses framed as instruction given by the sage Pulastya to ṛṣis gathered at Kurukṣetra. It defines five categories of dharma (varṇadharma, āśramadharma, varṇāśramadharma, guṇadharma, and naimittikadharma) and surveys the duties belonging to the four social classes and four life stages. The text concludes with summary principles on the sources and resolution of legal authority (śruti, smṛti, nyāya) and a concluding rule on purification.
SA_GSD36_ilx_ws_pulastyasmrti.attribution: Traditionally attributed to the legendary sage (ṛṣi) Pulastya, as stated in the opening framing dialogue (verse 1) and colophon (iti pulastyaproktaṃ dharmaśāstraṃ samāptam).
SA_GSD36_ilx_ws_pulastyasmrti.coverage: complete — Complete short recension of 28 anuṣṭubh verses, ending with the colophon 'iti pulastyaproktaṃ dharmaśāstraṃ samāptam'.

SA_GK19_ilx_ws_a_collection_of_six_drama.title: Rūpakaṣaṭka
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_a_collection_of_six_drama.author: Vatsarāja
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_a_collection_of_six_drama.summary: A collection of plays composed by Vatsarāja, minister to the Kālañjara king Paramardideva, illustrating distinct dramatic forms (rūpaka) including Kirātārjunīya (vyāyoga), Karpūracarita (bhāṇa), and Samudramathana (samavakāra).
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_a_collection_of_six_drama.attribution: Attributed in the text to the poet Vatsarāja, minister (amātya) to the Candella king Paramardideva of Kālañjara.
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_a_collection_of_six_drama.edition: Chimanlal D. Dalal (ed.), Rūpakaṣaṭkam, Baroda, 1918 (Gaekwad's Oriental Series 8).
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_a_collection_of_six_drama.coverage: complete — Text of the collection containing plays such as Kirātārjunīya (vyāyoga), Karpūracarita (bhāṇa), and Samudramathana (samavakāra).

SA_GK19_ilx_ws_abhangapadyam.title: Haripāṭha
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_abhangapadyam.author: Jñāneśvara
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_abhangapadyam.summary: A Sanskrit devotional work in verse attributed to Jñāneśvara (Jñānadeva) celebrating the practice of Haripāṭha and the recitation of the divine name (nāmasmaraṇa).
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_abhangapadyam.attribution: Attributed internally in the verse colophons to Jñāneśvara (Jñānadeva).
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_abhangapadyam.coverage: not determined — Devotional verse text attributed to Jñāneśvara / Jñānadeva on the recitation of Haripāṭha.

SA_GK19_ilx_ws_abhilasastakam.title: Abhilāṣāṣṭaka
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_abhilasastakam.author: Brahmānanda
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_abhilasastakam.summary: An eight-verse Vaiṣṇava devotional hymn (stotra) composed in the Śikhariṇī metre by Svāmī Brahmānanda. Each verse begins with the interrogative 'kadā' ('when?'), expressing longing for devotion to Viṣṇu/Hari, detachment from mundane existence, meditative focus, and ultimate liberation.
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_abhilasastakam.attribution: Attributed in the colophon to Paramahaṃsa Svāmī Brahmānanda.
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_abhilasastakam.coverage: complete — Complete in 8 verses (aṣṭaka) in Śikhariṇī metre, plus closing colophon.

SA_GK19_ilx_ws_abhisekanatakam.title: Abhiṣekanāṭaka
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_abhisekanatakam.author: Bhāsa
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_abhisekanatakam.summary: The Abhiṣekanāṭaka ('The Consecration Play') is a six-act Sanskrit drama dramatizing events from the Kiṣkindhā-, Sundara-, and Yuddha-kāṇḍas of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa. It depicts the alliance between Rāma and Sugrīva, the slaying of Vālin, the reconnaissance of Laṅkā, the final battle culminating in Rāvaṇa's defeat, Sītā's fire ordeal, and Rāma's consecration (abhiṣeka). Along with the Pratimānāṭaka, it forms Bhāsa's dramatic treatment of the Rāma narrative.
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_abhisekanatakam.coverage: complete — Complete text of all six acts (ending with act 6, Bharatavākya verse 6.35, and colophon 'ṣaṣṭho'ṅkaḥ | abhiṣekanāṭakaṃ samāptam').
translations: E. Beccarini-Crescenzi (trans.), 'L'Abhiṣekanāṭaka', Giornale della Società Asiatica Italiana. (Italian)

SA_GK19_ilx_ws_acyutastakam.title: Acyutāṣṭaka
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_acyutastakam.author: Śaṅkara
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_acyutastakam.summary: The Acyutāṣṭaka is an eight-verse Vaiṣṇava hymn (followed by a concluding phalaśruti) addressed to Viṣṇu in his forms as Kṛṣṇa and Rāma. Composed in rhythmic verse strung together by sacred epithets and allusions to mythological episodes, the hymn is traditionally attributed to Śaṅkarācārya and widely used in Smārta and Vaiṣṇava daily recitation.
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_acyutastakam.attribution: Attributed to Śaṅkarācārya in the colophon.
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_acyutastakam.coverage: complete — Complete text of 8 stanzas plus 1 phalaśruti stanza and concluding colophon.

SA_GK19_ilx_ws_acyutastakam_sridharavenk.title: Acyutāṣṭaka
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_acyutastakam_sridharavenk.author: Śrīdhara Veṅkaṭeśa
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_acyutastakam_sridharavenk.summary: The Acyutāṣṭaka of Śrīdhara Veṅkaṭeśa is an eight-verse Sanskrit devotional hymn extolling the holy name (nāman) of Acyuta/Kṛṣṇa, apostrophizing the divine name as a maternal, redemptive force (e.g., acyutākhye, śrīkṛṣṇākhye, govindākhye) capable of destroying sins and granting spiritual refuge.
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_acyutastakam_sridharavenk.attribution: Authored by Śrīdhara Veṅkaṭeśa as stated in the colophon ('iti śrīśrīdharaveṅkaṭeśāryakṛtau acyutāṣṭakaṃ sampūrṇam').
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_acyutastakam_sridharavenk.coverage: complete — Complete hymn of 8 verses with final colophon.

SA_GK19_ilx_ws_advaitasatakam.title: Advaitaśataka
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_advaitasatakam.summary: The Advaitaśataka ('Centuria on Non-Duality') is a 100-verse didactic Vedantic tract (prakaraṇa) summarizing fundamental teachings of Advaita ('sarvavedāntasaṃgraha'). It expounds the nature of the four bodies (sthūla, sūkṣma, kāraṇa, and the transcendent sāmānya/turīya deha), the jīva's bondage through ignorance (ajñāna) and identification with the bodily apparatus, the operation of prārabdha karma, and final emancipation through recognition of one's intrinsic identity with Śiva as unconditioned consciousness (jñaptimātra).
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_advaitasatakam.attribution: The opening verse describes the work as an 'advaitaśatakaṃ ... sarvavedāntasaṃgraham'. No specific author is named in the e-text or colophons.
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_advaitasatakam.coverage: complete — Complete text in 100 verses, concluding at verse 100.

SA_GK19_ilx_ws_aghorakastoddharanastotra.title: Ghorakaṣṭoddhāraṇastotra
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_aghorakastoddharanastotra.author: Vāsudevānandasarasvatī
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_aghorakastoddharanastotra.summary: The Ghorakaṣṭoddhāraṇastotra is a short Sanskrit devotional hymn composed by Vāsudevānanda Sarasvatī dedicated to Lord Dattātreya (saluted as Śrīpāda Śrīvallabha). Comprising five verses followed by a concluding phalaśruti, each stanza entreats the deity to deliver the devotee from acute worldly afflictions, sins, fear, and sorrow ('ghorāt kaṣṭād uddharāsmān namas te').
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_aghorakastoddharanastotra.attribution: Attributed in the colophon to Vāsudevānanda Sarasvatī ('śrīmatvāsudevānaṃdasarasvati').
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_aghorakastoddharanastotra.coverage: complete — Complete text consisting of the 5 core verses (ślokapañcaka), a phalaśruti verse, and the closing colophon.

SA_GK19_ilx_ws_ahalyakrtaramastotram.title: Ahalyākṛtarāmastotra
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_ahalyakrtaramastotram.summary: A 23-verse hymn in praise of Rāma recited by Ahalyā upon her liberation from Gautama's curse, taken from the Adhyātmarāmāyaṇa (Bālakāṇḍa, chapter 5). The stotra extols Rāma from an Advaita Vedāntic perspective as the supreme unmanifest Brahman (Para Puruṣa) who manifests through māyā in human form, concluding with narrative completion and a phalaśruti.
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_ahalyakrtaramastotram.attribution: Embedded stotra from the Adhyātmarāmāyaṇa, traditionally treated as part of the Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa.
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_ahalyakrtaramastotram.coverage: complete — Complete text of the stotra in 23 verses as preserved in the Sanskrit Wikisource text.

SA_GK19_ilx_ws_alankaramaniharah1.title: Alaṅkāramaṇihāra (part 1: saras 1–25)
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_alankaramaniharah1.author: Kṛṣṇabrahmatantraparakālasvāmin
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_alankaramaniharah1.summary: The Alaṅkāramaṇihāra is an alaṅkāra treatise consisting of definitions, illustrative verses, and prose commentary discussing earlier authorities including Appayya Dīkṣita and the Rasagaṅgādhara. This part covers the first 25 saras up through Samāsokti (verse 802), ending with 'pūrvabhāgassamāptaḥ'.
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_alankaramaniharah1.attribution: The root text, illustrative verses, and prose commentary are by Śrīkṛṣṇabrahmatantraparakālasaṃyamīndra (invoked in the opening verses).
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_alankaramaniharah1.coverage: partial — Covers saras 1–25 (verses 1–802), ending with the Samāsoktisara (pañcaviṃśaḥ saraḥ) and 'pūrvabhāgassamāptaḥ'.

SA_GK19_ilx_ws_alankaramaniharah2.title: Alaṅkāramaṇihāra (part 2: saras 26–50)
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_alankaramaniharah2.author: Kṛṣṇabrahmatantraparakālasvāmin
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_alankaramaniharah2.summary: The Alaṅkāramaṇihāra is a treatise on Sanskrit poetic figures (alaṅkāraśāstra) by Śrīkṛṣṇabrahmatantraparakālasaṃyamīndra. It is arranged in 'saras', each with definitions, illustrative verses, and prose commentary. This second part covers saras 26 to 50 (Parikarasara to Mālādīpakasara, verses 803–1406).
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_alankaramaniharah2.attribution: Root text, example verses and prose commentary are by Śrīkṛṣṇabrahmatantraparakālasaṃyamīndra.
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_alankaramaniharah2.coverage: partial — Part 2 (saras 26–50, verses 803–1406). Opens with 'alaṃkāramaṇihāre dvitīyabhāgaprārambhaḥ' (Parikarasara, verse 803) and ends with 'ityalaṃkāramāṇihāre mālādīpakasaraḥ pañcāśaḥ' (50th sara, verse 1406).

SA_GK19_ilx_ws_alankaramaniharah3.title: Alaṅkāramaṇihāra (part 3: saras 51–104)
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_alankaramaniharah3.author: Kṛṣṇabrahmatantraparakālasvāmin
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_alankaramaniharah3.summary: Part 3 of the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra, a treatise on Sanskrit poetic figures, covering sāra to hetu (saras 51–104, verses 1407–2000). Each section presents definitions, illustrative verses, and prose commentary.
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_alankaramaniharah3.attribution: Author name attested in source headers as Śrīkṛṣṇabrahmatantraparakālasaṃyamīndra.
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_alankaramaniharah3.coverage: partial — Part 3 (saras 51–104, verses 1407–2000). Opens with 'alaṅkāramaṇihāre tṛtīyabhāgaprārambhaḥ' (Sārasara, verse 1407) and ends with the Hetusara (104th sara, verse 2000).

SA_GK19_ilx_ws_alankaramaniharah4.title: Alaṅkāramaṇihāra (part 4: saras 105–126)
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_alankaramaniharah4.author: Kṛṣṇabrahmatantraparakālasvāmin
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_alankaramaniharah4.summary: Part 4 (caturthabhāgaḥ) of the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra, a treatise on Sanskrit poetics by Śrīkṛṣṇabrahmatantraparakālasaṃyamīndra. It opens with rasavadalaṅkāras (rasavat, preyas, ūrjasvin, samāhita, bhāvodaya, etc.) and discusses poetic figures with prose commentary and illustrative verses, concluding with an appended collection of definition verses (lakṣaṇaślokāḥ).
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_alankaramaniharah4.attribution: Attributed in the source headers to Śrīkṛṣṇabrahmatantraparakālasaṃyamīndra.
SA_GK19_ilx_ws_alankaramaniharah4.coverage: partial — Fourth part (caturthabhāgaḥ) of the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra, opening with the rasavadalaṅkāras and concluding with an appended collection of definition verses ending 'samāptā alaṃkāramaṇihāralakṣaṇaślokāḥ'.
